## Usage guidelines

Google is proud to partner with libraries to digitize these public domain materials and make them widely accessible. While these books belong to the collective public, Google acts as their temporary custodian. Because this digitization process is expensive, we have taken steps to prevent commercial misuse—including technical limits on automated searching—so that we can continue to provide this resource.

We also ask that you follow these guidelines:

+ **Use these files only for non-commercial purposes** We designed *Google Book Search* for use by individuals. We ask that you use these files for your own personal, non-commercial research and education.

+ **Refrain from automated searching** Do not send automated queries of any kind to Google’s system. If you are conducting research on machine translation, optical character recognition <note>often abbreviated as OCR; the technology that converts images of text into editable data</note>, or other fields where access to large amounts of text is necessary, please contact us. We encourage the use of public domain materials for these scholarly purposes and may be able to assist.

+ **Maintain attribution** The Google “watermark” you see on each file is essential for informing readers about this project and helping them find additional materials through *Google Book Search*. Please do not remove it.

+ **Keep it legal** You are responsible for ensuring that your use of this material is legal. Do not assume that because we believe a book is in the public domain for users in the United States, the work is also in the public domain in other countries. Copyright laws vary from country to country, and we cannot offer legal advice on whether a specific use is allowed. Please do not assume that a book’s appearance in *Google Book Search* means it can be used in any manner, anywhere in the world. The legal penalties for copyright infringement can be quite severe.

<margin>Papyrology Thin 1-9-25 11311</margin>

-> # FRIEDRICH CREUZER’S <-
-> ## ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS. <-

-> ### BOOK I. <-

**P. 1, 2. ENNEAD I]** *Dr. T. G. V. Engelhardt translated this first Ennead into German in the book entitled: The Enneads of Plotinus, translated and accompanied by continuous notes explaining the original text. First Part. Erlangen 1820. 8vo.* Pertaining to this first Ennead, which primarily contains Moral philosophy, is *J. F. Winzer’s Sketch of the decrees of Plotinus regarding matters belonging to moral doctrine. Wittenberg 1809.*
— **7. CONCERNING THE]** The source of this Plotinian book is in Plato’s *Timaeus* p. 42. a. <note>A foundational Platonic dialogue concerning the creation of the world and the nature of the soul.</note> on which compare Proclus p. 326. ff. Add Plato’s *Laws* I. p. 776. F. from which Porphyry also drew in *On Abstinence* I. 33. p. 54. Rhoer. Compare also Damascius *On Principles* p. 219. Wolf and Michael Psellus *On Universal Doctrine* chapter 44. p. 103. Fabricius. Plotinus had Aristotle no less before his eyes. For thus that author says in *On the Soul* book I. chapter I. p. 3. Sylburg:— <note>original: "Ἀπορίαν δὲ ἔχει..."</note> "The passions of the soul also present a difficulty: whether they are all common to the soul and that which possesses it, or whether there is something unique to the soul itself; for to grasp this is necessary, but not easy. It appears that in most cases the soul neither suffers nor acts without the body—for instance, being angry, feeling confident, desiring, or perceiving in general; but thinking seems most likely to be its own unique property," etc. Compare also page 4. The Stoics had also labored on this same argument. This is understood, to omit other things, from the fragment of Plutarch, *Whether sickness belongs to the Soul or the Body*, which, though mutilated by the injury of time, Wyttenbach remarkably restored in Vol. V. part 3. p. 700. A. of the minor edition and which J. Bake inserted in the *Fragments of Posidonius* p. 222. Olympiodorus, in his commentary on the *First Alcibiades* section 1. end, page 9 of the first edition, contends that Plotinus follows the same plan in this book as Plato did in the *First Alcibiades*. **For he has it thus:** <note>original: "καὶ αὖθις δ τῷ Πλωτίνῳ..."</note> "And again, the main point for Plotinus in the Enneads—what is the living being, and what is man—there he shows that the living being is the composite of both [soul and body], but man is the soul. This was also Plato’s aim in the Alcibiades."
— **9. PLEASURES AND]** Regarding the sentiment, see Plato’s *Phaedo* p. 69. A. p. 27. Bekker. Compare Plato’s *Philebus* p. 36. p. 185. Bekker, where Stallbaum §. 74. p. 106. also discusses the use of the plurals "pains," "fears," etc. From the *Laws* V. p. 732. E. p. 382. Bekker: "It is most especially in human nature to experience pleasures and pains and desires," etc. Cicero in *On Laws* I. 11. §. 32. p. 79. Moser edition and our own: "Troubles, joys, desires, and fears wander similarly through the minds of all." Macrobius in *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio* book II. chapter 12: "Plotinus, in the book *What is the animal, what is man*, asks to whom do our pleasures, sorrows, fears, desires, angers, or pains belong—and finally thoughts and intellect—whether to the soul alone, or to the soul using the body: and after many things which he discussed under a dense abundance of matter—he finally pronounces this: that the Animal is an animated body. But he did not leave neglected or uninvestigated by what benefit of the soul or by what path of fellowship it is animated. Therefore, he assigns all these passions we have mentioned to the animal, but he testifies that the true man is the soul itself." Macrobius therefore provides the same summary of this book as Olympiodorus in the passage cited above. Suidas, under the entry *Hedomēnos* (Vol. II. p. 46. Kuster) praises it thus: "Pleasures, pains; confidences; fears; aversions and the feeling of pain from both. In two ways—either [they belong to one] or it is something else resulting from the mixture." He does not have the rest.
— **11. or of some third thing]** This third member: "or of some third thing from both," was omitted by Macrobius, who treated several parts of this passage rather freely. The same author says in the same place regarding Our Author [Plotinus]: *Plotinus is more sparing of words than anyone.*
**p. 2, 1. some—others]** Ficinus translates as *some—others*. Engelhardt says that one *some* necessarily refers to the *passions*, and the other to *thought and opinion*, Ploti-
**VOL. II.**
**B**

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page continues the scholarly annotations on Plotinus, specifically focusing on the relationship between the soul and the body, and the nature of passions and desires.</meta>

# -> ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS <-

Whether he thought to write "the pleasures, the pains" <note>original: "αἱ... ἡδοναὶ, λῦπαι"</note>. But then he ought to have written "some—others" <note>original: "τὰ μὲν—τὰ δὲ"</note>, since "fears and boldness" <note>original: "φόβοι et θάῤῥη"</note> are added. Next, the same author prefers the correction: "of which of the two then are the passions" <note>original: "ποτέρας οὖν τὰ πάθη"</note>. Neither pleases me, nor do the Manuscripts support them. The simplest explanation is a use of *enallage* <term>enallage: a grammatical substitution of one form for another</term> regarding "some—others" <note>original: "αἱ μὲν—αἱ δὲ"</note>. The numbers refer to the nearest phrase, "thought and opinion" <note>original: "διάνοια καὶ δόξα"</note>, in this sense: it must be investigated whether thoughts and opinions arise from the same source as the passions (for example, from the soul joined with the body), while others arise from elsewhere (for example, from the soul alone).

**p. 3, 2. and itself [having] nothing from another]** <note>original: "αὐτὸ δὲ παρ' ἄλλου μηδὲν"</note> Understand "having" <note>original: "ἔχον"</note> from what follows. Regarding the meaning, anyone who consults Wyttenbach in his annotation on Plato’s *Phaedo* p. 281 ff. will lack nothing. See also Tiedemann’s book, titled: *The Spirit of Speculative Philosophy* (that is, on the causes of contemplative philosophy), Vol. III, p. 343 ff.

— **6. lest fearful things be present.]** <note>original: "τὰ φοβερὰ μὴ παρῇ."</note> Apply to this what Aristotle discusses concerning courage and cowardice, and likewise concerning "bold men," in the *Nicomachean Ethics* III. 7. p. 47 f. Sylburg edition; p. 137 f. Zell edition. Compare also the *Eudemian Ethics* p. 116 Sylburg. Add Andronicus of Rhodes *On the Passions* p. 753, Hoeschel edition, Leiden, 1617: "Boldness is the knowledge by which we know that we shall not fall into danger." <note>original: "Θαῤῥαλεότης ἐστὶν ἐπιστήμη, καθ' ἣν οἴδαμεν, ὅτι οὐ περιπεσόμεν."</note>

— **9. but how [it desires] a mixture]** <note>original: "πῶς δὲ μίξεως"</note> Namely, "it desires" <note>original: "ἐπιθυμοῖ"</note>, from the preceding "desires" <note>original: "ἐπιθυμίαι"</note>. This reasoning of Ficino is more convenient than that which pleases Engelhardt, who wishes to supply "it would be receptive" <note>original: "δεκτικὸν ἂν εἴη"</note> from the distant word "unreceptive" <note>original: "ἄδεκτον"</note>.

**p. 4, 1. the whole living being]** <note>original: "ζῶον τὸ σύμπαν"</note> Regarding the notion of the "living being" according to the mind of Plato, see the *Phaedrus* § 251 and Ast’s note there, p. 294. Compare also Hermias on that passage, p. 131. To this also belong several things which the so-called Hermes Trismegistus has in the *Poimandres* chapters X and XI, p. 26 ff., Flussas-Candalla edition, Cologne, 1630. Compare also Sallustius *On the Gods and the World* chapter VIII, and Holsten and Johann Conrad Orelli on him, p. 122 ff.

— **5. the passions from without]** <note>original: "τὰ ἔξωθεν παθήματα"</note> Compare below, Ennead III, Book VI. 3, 4. p. 305 ff. where at p. 307 I have placed a passage of Proclus *On Fate*, in which this opinion of Plotinus is considered. Michael Psellus also considers this in *On All-encompassing Doctrine* § 28, p. 90 ff. of Fabricius, where, after he had said that the soul is placed by Plato and Aristotle as using the body as an instrument, but by the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle's school</term> the same is mixed with the body, he brings forward these very words of Plotinus. Moreover, Aristotle had already employed the comparison in the *Eudemian Ethics* VII. 8. p. 201 Sylburg, thus: "since the soul stands to the body as a craftsman to his tool," etc. <note>original: "ἐπεὶ δ' ὁμοίως ἔχει ψυχὴ πρὸς σῶμα, καὶ τεχνίτης πρὸς ὄργανον κ. τ. λ."</note>

— **8. so that even desires]** <note>original: "ὥστε καὶ ἐπιθυμίαι"</note> These things are somewhat obscure in Ficino’s version. The meaning, however, is this: Even desires belong to the soul (or are not foreign to the soul), since it requires the service (or ministry) of its instrument, that is, the body. For it is understood from the preceding that the "instrument" <note>original: "ὄργανον"</note> is the body. Therefore, this very requirement for the service of the body, as its instrument, is desire. Or, the soul desires when it wishes to use the body as its instrument.

— **15. or a blending—as if interwoven]** <note>original: "ἢ κρᾶσις—ὡς διαπλακεῖσα"</note> That is, as they say today, either chemically or mechanically. The next words: "or one part of it in this way," etc. <note>original: "ἢ τὸ μὲν οὕτως αὐτοῦ κ. τ. λ."</note> contain a new question, namely this: **Whether the soul is partly separate, that is, using the body, but partly mixed with it in whatever way, and consequently taking on its turns [of experience] so that it may use it (that is, the turns of the body); whence this task of philosophy arises: to turn that very part which takes on the body's turns back toward that which uses it (the separate part), and to turn this very thing away from there (from the body) as far as possible (that is, insofar as the soul can do without the body).** See Ficino’s Commentary on this chapter. Perhaps there is a gap at the end, and several of our books have a comma after "always" <note>original: "ἀεὶ"</note>, so that you might fill it out and correct it thus: "so as not to be always separated nor always using," so that the soul is neither always severed from the body, nor always using it. — The next words, "or as an inseparable form" <note>original: "ἢ ὡς εἶδος ἀχώριστον"</note>, pertain to the opinion of Alexander of Aphrodisias, who, after he had contended that the soul is a form inseparable from the body, explodes that other opinion concerning a form touching the body, and says this very example of the pilot and the ship is worth nothing. See Alexander of Aphrodisias, *Exposition on the Soul*, from the translation of Hieronymus Donatus, Paris, 1528, folios 133–135.

**p. 5, 6. ...might receive perception as an addition]** <note>original: "π. ἀ. προσθήκην λάβοι τὸ αἰσθάνεσθαι"</note> Compare p. 609. A. above, "an addition of essence." However, the force of the word "addition" <note>original: "προσθήκη"</note> must be held, which Wyttenbach excellently declared in his notes to Plutarch’s *Moralia* p. 218 f., to be: an addendum, whatever is added in abundance to the proper parts, by which a thing is already completed as if by its own measures.

— **14. having wandered through]** <note>original: "διαπεφοιτηκυῖαν"</note> "To wander through" <note>original: "Διαφοιτᾷν"</note> is omitted...

The author cites various classical authorities, including Aristotle, Plato, and Alexander of Aphrodisias, to clarify the soul-body relationship as one of a craftsman to a tool or a pilot to a ship.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philological commentary on Plotinus's Enneads, specifically focusing on Book I, Ennead 1, pages 3 through 9. The translator is cross-referencing Plotinus's Greek terminology with classical authors and later Neoplatonic and Christian commentators.</meta>

-> BOOK I. ENNEAD ONE. pages 3—9. <-

In Stephanus’s *Thesaurus* <note>original: "Stephani Thes." — A famous Greek dictionary by Henri Estienne</note> (old edition), at this passage, it signifies the soul actively permeating the body, which was previously declared passively through the term "to be entwined" <note>original: "διαπλέκεσθαι" (diaplekesthai)</note>. This word is used regarding messengers and rumors of fame, and is then applied to various uses. See Herodotus I. 60; Plutarch, *On Garrulity* p. 505, where it is joined with "is diffused" <note>original: "διακέχυται" (diakechytai)</note>; Lucian, *The False Prophet* X. p. 217 (Amsterdam ed.). Add Sturz, *Xenophon Lexicon* under the word, and Irmisch, *Index to Herodian* p. 626 ff. — Closely related to this is "because of these things" <note>original: "παρὰ τοῦτο" (para touto)</note>, just as "for what reason" <note>original: "παρὰ τί" (para ti)</note> and "therefore" <note>original: "παρ' ὃ" (par' ho)</note>. See Stephanus’s *Thesaurus* p. 7200 ff. (London ed.); Fischer’s *Index to Aeschines' Axiochus* at III. 4; Viger, *On Idioms* IX. 6. 5. p. 645 with notes; cf. ibid. Hermann no. 412. p. 862. Add Proclus in *Elements of Theology* ch. 142. p. 210 (Frankfurt ed.).

**p. 6, 6. instrument]** <note>original: "ὀργάνῳ" (organō)</note> Regarding the body as the instrument of the soul, Wyttenbach supplies an abundance of examples from the philosophers in his notes on Plutarch’s *Dinner of the Seven Wise Men* p. 988. In the following: "for he says it is absurd to say the soul weaves," <note>original: "καὶ γὰρ ἀτοπόν φησι τὴν ψυχὴν ὑφαίνειν λέγειν"</note> he touches upon that passage of Cebes in Plato’s *Phaedo* p. 87d (p. 66 Bekker ed.): — "but the soul always re-weaves that which is worn away," <note>original: "ἀλλ' ἡ ψυχὴ ἀεὶ τὸ κατατριβόμενον ἀνυφαίνοι"</note> which Socrates discusses in the following sections. For it must be held that Plotinus is accustomed, when he especially refers to passages of Plato, to use his characteristic "he says" <note>original: "φησί" (phēsi)</note>. It is well known that the Greeks use their "he says" and the Latins *inquit* indefinitely, either for "they say" <note>original: "φασὶ" (phasi)</note> or when they imagine some adversary who might object. Hence they usually place it in parentheses. This observation, after Bentley on Horace’s *Satires* I. 4. 78, has been applied to Greek and Latin writers by: Davies on Cicero’s *Tusculan Disputations* I. 39; Toup on Longinus § 11. p. 275 (Oxford ed.); Heindorf on Plato’s *Gorgias* § 166. p. 262; Ruhkopf on Seneca’s *On Benefits* II. 11. p. 53; the interpreters of Marinus’s *Life of Proclus* p. 145 (Boissonade ed.); and himself on Cicero’s *On the Nature of the Gods* I. 36. p. 164. However, the Plotinian usage, by which Plato’s name is omitted through ellipsis <note>omission of a word</note>, has another cause and origin to be sought in the scholia <note>ancient marginal commentaries</note>; in these, since those disputing very often appealed to the authority of the supreme master, that "he says" became prevalent in almost the same way as that "he himself said" <note>original: "αὐτὸς ἔφα" (autos epha) — the famous Pythagorean appeal to authority</note> among the Pythagoreans. For no one was ignorant of which philosopher that "he says" referred to in the Platonic schools. Nor was the reasoning of the Stoics different, who designated either Zeno or Chrysippus with their "he says." From there the same usage was transferred into the recorded discussions of Arrian, who indeed wishes Epictetus to be understood by his "he says." For example, III. 2. 6: "this is beyond us, he says." Cf. I. 16. 8; II. 23. 16; I. 4. 28; and there Upton and Schweighäuser Vol. II. p. 62; cf. Vol. III. p. 472 ff.

**p. 7, 10. blood and bile must boil]** <note>original: "δεῖ αἷμα καὶ χολὴν ζέσαı" (dei haima kai cholēn zesai)</note> Anyte in the *Anthology* 15: "blood boiled through the skin." Cf. Jacobs VI. p. 432; IX. p. 203. Our author <note>Plotinus</note> p. 420. E: "boiling with blood and bile" <note>original: "ζέοντες αἵματι καὶ χολῇ"</note> (which passage should certainly be compared) and it is quite often joined with the dative "with anger" <note>original: "θυμῷ" (thymō)</note> and similar words. See Suidas under "boiling with anger." Zonaras p. 955 and there Tittmann. But nevertheless Himerius p. 62 (Stephanus ed.): "anger boils up more than is moderate." Cf. moreover Suicer, *Ecclesiastical Thesaurus* I. p. 1296; Matthaei on John Chrysostom’s *Four Homilies* I. p. 62; and Valckenaer’s *Scholia on the New Testament* II. p. 568. — Hence our author below p. 389: — "such blood is secreted by the boiling of anger."

**p. 8, 13. of psychic power]** <note>original: "ψυχικῆς δυνάμεως" (psychikēs dynameōs)</note> Regarding the word "psychic," hold these words of Aristotle, *On the Soul* II. 12. p. 47 (Sylburg ed.): "and why plants never perceive, though they have some psychic part and are affected by tangible things"; likewise Proclus in *On the Cratylus* § 99. p. 56, concerning Jupiter: "and as having received the whole of Saturn, he is the creator of the triple essence—indivisible, middle, and divisible; but according to the Rhea within himself, he pours forth a triple life: intellectual, psychic, and physical." Furthermore, Theophylactus on 1 Corinthians XV. p. 308: "a psychic body, that which is governed by psychic powers." To the Apostles and ecclesiastical writers, "psychic" <note>often translated as 'soulish' or 'natural' in Bibles</note> signifies generally one enslaved to the desires and pleasures of the body, and is the opposite of "spiritual" <note>original: "πνευματικῷ" (pneumatikō)</note>. See Suidas under "psychic man," Suicer’s *Thesaurus* under "psychic," and the interpreters on 1 Corinthians II. 14, especially L. C. Valckenaer’s *Scholia on the New Testament* Vol. II. p. 137 ff. It is therefore not infrequently the same as "fleshly" <note>original: "σαρκικός" (sarkikos)</note>. Cf. also *Theological Studies and Critiques* by *Ullmann* and *Umbreit* I. 2. page 436.

**p. 9, 8. For they are already Intelligibles]** <note>original: "Νοητὰ γὰρ ἤδη" (Noēta gar ēdē)</note> Consult Ficino’s *Commentary* on this passage and see Themistius’s *Paraphrase* of Book I of Aristotle’s *On the Soul* (ed. Hermolaus Barbarus, Basel 1533) p. 439 ff. and on Book II of *On the Soul* p. 460 ff.

— **12. where indeed we especially]** <note>original: "ἔνθα δὴ ἡμεῖς μάλιστα" (entha dē hēmeis malista)</note> Namely, "are." Not without reason in this passage has Engelhardt compared this Plotinian "we" <note>original: "ἡμεῖς" (hēmeis)</note> with that celebrated *Ego* of more recent Metaphysics, especially throughout Germany.

**B 2**

<summary>This page provides philological and philosophical commentary on Plotinus's Enneads, explaining his use of the term "he says" as a shorthand for Plato and comparing his psychological terminology with both Aristotelian and early Christian definitions.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, Plato, Aristotle, psychic vs spiritual, philology, Enneads, soul-body relationship, German metaphysics, Ego</keywords>

**### ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS ###**

**p. 9, 16. θηρίον (beast)]** [[abbrev: θηρίον → θηρίον]] Plato, *Republic* IX. 588. p. 458. ed. Bekker. Proclus touches upon the same in *Alcibiades I*, p. 160 of our edition, where I have cited more [references].

**ibid. Συνδρόμου—ὄντος—τῇ λογικῇ ψυχῇ (Being concurrent with the rational soul)]** Suidas III. p. 450. *σύνδρομος* (concurrent) = *σύμφωνος* (harmonious). Our passage ought to be added to the Lexicons for the sake of its construction. The word itself is quite suited to express the sense of this passage, and is clearly of a Plotinian character, which often approaches quite closely to Platonic elegance. Furthermore, Tiedemann judges in his book *Geist der speculativen Philosophie* (The Spirit of Speculative Philosophy), or *On the Causes of Contemplative Philosophy*, III. p. 347 sq., that this [point] is new and was first devised by Plotinus: namely, his undertaking to demonstrate that an active force resides in the senses, and that whatever the soul does is properly carried out by the thought of the mind. There, he also considers that these decrees of Plotinus provided the occasion for the decree of the so-called *pre-established harmony*.

**p. 10, 7. κεχωρισμένα (separated [things])]** Cf. our author V. 3. 6. p. 501. A. and our annotations there. Consult also Proclus, *Elements of Theology*, ch. 176. p. 262 sqq. Concerning the use of the verb *ἐποχεῖσθαι* (to be carried upon/mounted), notice was given in [the notes to] Plotinus *On Beauty*, p. 340 sqq. For the argument of this passage, compare Sallustius the philosopher, *On the Gods and the World*, ch. 8, where Holstenius, in his Annotations p. 120. ed. G. Conr. Orellius, praises a fragment of Theages the Pythagorean (in Gale’s *Opuscula Mythologica*, p. 688) and reminds [the reader] of the Plotinian passage. On the verb *ἀνελίττειν* (to unroll/unfold), consult Wyttenbach on Plutarch, p. 598.

**— 9. φησὶ (he says)]** Plato. He refers, however, to the doctrine set forth in the *Timaeus*, especially p. 87 sqq. Steph. [and] p. 132 sqq. Bekker. From both Plato and Plotinus, the so-called Hermes profited in Stobaeus, *Eclogues* I. 52. page 808 sqq. On the use of the Platonic and Plotinian verb *φαντάζεσθαι* (to imagine/appear), see our Annotations to Plotinus *On Beauty*, p. 135 sq.

**— 13. ἐλλάμπουσα εἰς αὐτὰ (shining into them)]** Note the construction, and regarding the use of the verb see Stephanus’ *Thesaurus*, p. 5598, new London edition. Add Olympiodorus in *Alcibiades I*, ch. 3. p. 13 below and p. 14 above, where *ἔλλαμψις* (illumination) is distinguished from *οὐσία* (essence); and Nicolaus of Methone’s *Refutation of Proclus’ Elements of Theology*, p. 88 [and] p. 92. Themistius, in Aristotle’s *On the Soul*, Book III, ch. 32, p. 562 sqq. ed. Basel, is relevant to the argument of our passage.

**p. 11, 10. ἡ δὲ τῶν ψευδῶν—φαντασία οὖσα (it being an imagination of false things)]** Add this passage to those which Stephanus and other learned men collected in the *Thesaurus*, p. 9915 sqq. London ed. Add further Proclus in *Alcibiades I*, p. 43: *φαντασία—καὶ αἴσθησις* (imagination and sensation), p. 162 where *φαντασία* and *αἴσθησις* are opposed to each other. Ibid.: *φαντασία καὶ αἴσθησις καὶ ἄλογα πάθη* (imagination, sensation, and irrational passions). Likewise Olympiodorus in the same Dialogue, p. 8, 51, 61, 101. Regarding the argument of this whole Plotinian passage, what Aristotle discusses in the third book of *On the Soul*, chapters 7 sqq., p. 60 sqq. ed. Sylburg, is especially pertinent.

**p. 12, 1. τύπων (of types/impressions)]** Gataker explained the various meanings of this word in *Adversaria*, ch. 4. Cf. furthermore Ast on Plato’s *Republic*, p. 473; Zell on Aristotle’s *Nicomachean Ethics* I. 2. p. 8; Stallbaum on *Philebus* § 144. p. 202; Boissonade on Eunapius, p. 409. Proclus in *Alcibiades I*, p. 298, joins *τύπους καθολικοὺς* (universal types) with *κοιναῖς ἐννοίαις* (common notions). In our author, at IV. 5. 3, it is properly *τύπος ἐν κηρῷ* (an impression in wax). He also uses *τύπωσις* (imprinting), as in III. 6. 1, and frequently the passive *τυποῦσθαι* (to be formed/impressed), V. 5. 1 and elsewhere. Closely related is that [phrase] *ἀτρεμήσει—ἡ ψυχὴ* (the soul shall be tranquil), to which *ὁ θόρυβος* (the tumult) is opposed; this is Platonic. Nor does our author use *ἀτρεμὴς* (unshaken/tranquil) otherwise regarding intelligible matters, as in I. 6. 5. p. 54. A.—"in a tranquil, waveless, and impassive state." Add a similar passage, p. 770. B. Furthermore, for understanding the argument of our passage, another passage, *Enneads* IV. 8. 3, is useful.

**— 10. κεχωρισμένων (of separated things)]** Engelhardt rightly compares the passage above in chapter 3: "but before the separating through philosophy."

**— 14. τὰς ἀρετὰς ἔχων (possessing the virtues)]** Plotinus treats the virtues more copiously in the following book. In the sentence *ὁ καθαρὸς τούτων* (the one pure of these), this last word refers to everything belonging to the body and thus to *τὰ πάθη* (the passions); however, the verb *ἱδρύεσθαι* (to be established/enshrined), most familiar to the Platonists and properly pertaining to temple statues, has been illustrated by me in the annotations to the book *On Beauty*, p. 177 and 332.

**— 16. ἐλλαμφθεῖσα (having been illuminated)]** This is the lower human soul, which is illuminated by the higher or intelligible soul. For that one (viz. the intelligible soul) is called *ἐλλάμπουσα* (illuminating) in chapter 8 above. Cf. also chapter 2 above. Furthermore, regarding what Ficinus mentions in his Commentary on our passage concerning Numenius: consult Stobaeus, *Eclogues* I. 52. p. 836, 866, 894, and 1066. Heeren, where the opinions of this philosopher on the soul are briefly set forth.

**p. 13, 2. τοῦ ἔνδον ἀνθρώπου (of the inner man)]** This can be compared with the "inner man" (*τῷ ἔσω... ἀνθρώπῳ*) of Paul's Epistle

--- Page 12 ---
to the Romans VII. 22; see there Hugo Grotius and Koppe, and cf. 2 Corinthians IV. 16, Ephesians III. 16. For Hesychius I. p. 1476. Alberti [says]: *ἔσω* (within) = *ἐντὸς, ἔνδον*; and Proclus in *Alcibiades I*, p. 132, uses the phrase *ἡ ἔνδον ζωή* (the inner life). Hence the substantive *ἐνδότης* (interiority) was fashioned by Dionysius the Areopagite, *Celestial Hierarchy* I. 2. Moreover, that which Plotinus uses above, *ὁ ἀληθὴς ἄνθρωπος* (the true man), corresponds most of all to similar formulas of Philo Judaeus; for example, *On the Planting of Noah*, p. 335 sq. Mangey: "that He placed the man who is truly within us, that is, the mind, in the most sacred sprouts and plants of nobility." Cf. the same author, p. 195, 267, 565.

**p. 13, 6. ἀντίληψιν (apprehension)]** A Platonic word, like *ἀντιλαμβάνεσθαι* (to apprehend/perceive; see Steph. *Thes.* p. 5563. London ed.) and also frequently used by Plotinus (see *Index Graecitatis Plotinianae*). For the meaning of the whole passage, consult Ficinus’ Commentary. Furthermore, not a few things concerning the souls of infants and children are read in the monuments of the Platonic philosophers. See, for example, Proclus in *Alcibiades I*, p. 195 sq., and the *Key* of Hermes, page 11. ed. Francesco Patrizi (in *Nova de Universis Philosophia*).

**— 13. εἰ δὲ μὴ ἀνθρώπου ψυχὴ εἰσέδυ (but if the soul of a man has not entered)]** Viz. into the beasts. See above. A memorable passage and one to be noted all the more because Wyttenbach did not notice it on Plato’s *Phaedo*, p. 210 sqq. He indeed says that the older Platonists and Plotinus himself retained the opinion of Plato, who posited that souls migrate into the bodies of brutes. But in this passage, we see Plotinus positing this same opinion quite hesitantly, or rather leaving it as an open question. This is evidence that he, who had previously pronounced more confidently on this matter, withheld his assent near the end of his life, at which time this book was written by him.

**p. 14, 1. ἀσυμφωνεῖ (is discordant)]** See *Index Graecitatis Plotinianae*. Presently, on the verb *μετενσωματοῦσθαι* (to be reincarnated/transmigrated), see annotation on II. 9. 6. below, p. 203. G. On the word *ἀναμάρτητος* (sinless/unerring), see below, p. 678. B.

**— 7. σύνθετον—καὶ τὸ ἐκ πάντων ἡ ψυχὴ—γίνεται (composite—and the soul becomes that which is from all)]** Ficinus, for the phrase "that which is from all," supplied by thinking [the word] "composite" (*σύνθετον*). I mention this because Engelhardt is "stuck" (*haeret aqua*) on these points. However, it does not seem that this opinion should be confused with the Aristotelian one. For the Stagirite in *On the Soul* III. 8. p. 62. Sylburg [says]: "Now, summarizing what has been said about the soul, let us say again that the soul is in a certain way all existing things." For the subsequent points about the separation of the soul from the body and other things that adhere to it, Engelhardt compares a passage of the pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite in *Mystical Theology* § 1. I have brought together more on this matter in Plotinus *On Beauty*, p. 55 (in annot. p. 302 sqq.), which I do not wish to repeat here. However, as Plotinus says here that only the composite [being] sins, he is severely rebuked on this account by Brucker in *Historia Critica Philosophiae*, Tom. II. p. 416; who exclaims thus: "Behold indeed a wretched foundation of moral philosophy! Which is the same as if you were to say that a steward of the royal treasury caught in theft is not punished with the noose, but only the 'thief' [is]." We shall not pass over in silence those things which are sometimes cast against Plotinus rather sharply and perhaps unfairly by some.

**— 11. θαλάττιον Γλαῦκον (the marine Glaucus)]** Plato, *Republic* X. 611. p. 497. Bekker: "we have seen it, however, situated just as those who see the marine Glaucus, etc." On which passage cf. Ast’s commentary p. 624, and the mythological Commentary of Moser on Nonnus’ *Dionysiaca* X. vs. 105. p. 237 cited there. Add Gottfried Hermann, *On the Glaucus-plays of Aeschylus*, and cf. Scholia on the cited passage of Plato, p. 196 sq. Ruhnken. Proclus also followed Plato's simile in *Alcibiades I*, ch. 76. p. 224. ed. Frankfurt.

**— 18. ἄλλου του ἀπ’ αὐτῆς γινομένου (of something else coming from it)]** A difficult passage, and it might seem that Ficinus had another reading before his eyes, although the Medicean books he used show no variation. Therefore, we did not wish to change anything. If you read *ἀπὸ* (from), it must be taken for *ὑπὸ* (by), a use not infrequent. See just now Viger, *De Idiotismis* IX. 1. 16. p. 580 sq. Regarding *νεῦσις* (inclination/nodding), we have collected more in the annotations to the book *On Beauty*, p. 265. ed. Heidelberg. Cf. Wyttenbach on Eunapius, page 30.

**p. 15, 1. Ἆρ’ οὖν ἀφίησι τὸ εἴδωλον (Does it then let go of the image?)]** With this passage should be compared those things discussed in the following IV. 5, especially ch. 7. p. 449 sq., from which I will excerpt only these: p. 480. A. above—"since even that which is in the mirror must be called an activity of that which is seen, acting upon that which is capable of being affected, not flowing out, etc." which are then applied to the soul, insofar as it imparts life to the body. And Ficinus also seems to have looked to this passage in his Commentary on our passage. The summary of this discussion, which Engelhardt also outlined, is this: The soul is not the cause of sin,

--- Page 13 ---
but rather that which is illuminated (*ἐλλάμπεται*) by the soul. Insofar as a certain communion intercedes between the soul and this illuminated thing (*τὸ ἐλλαμπόμενον*), the soul is said to descend, or to be carried by an inclination (*νεύσει*). From this communion is born the image (*τὸ εἴδωλον*), which the soul itself lets go (*ἀφίησι*) whenever that communion ceases. Nor indeed is this letting go (*ἄφεσις*) a separation or a tearing of that which was joined; but as soon as the soul has receded from that which received that image (*τὸ ὑποδεξάμενον*), the image itself ceases (vanishes); nor is this surprising, since this image itself had not arisen from elsewhere except from the communion itself of the illuminator with the illuminated (*τοῦ ἐλλάμποντος καὶ τοῦ ἐλλαμφθέντος*).—Furthermore, Stobaeus narrates the opinions of philosophers regarding the soul separated again from the body in *Eclogues* I. 52. § 39. p. 920 sqq. Heeren, where mention of Plotinus is also made.

**p. 15, 8. ἐὰν ἐκεῖ βλέπῃ ὅλῃ (if it should look "there" with its whole [self])]** That *ἐκεῖ* (there) and *ἐκεῖσε* (thither), very frequent in the *Enneads*, designates the intelligible world, and all divine things that are above, [and] God. I wanted this to be noted once.

**ibid. ὁ ποιητὴς—ἐπὶ τοῦ Ἡρακλέους (the poet—on Hercules)]** Eustathius [notes] more on that passage of Homer, p. 460. Basel. There were some, however, who said these verses were inserted by Onomacritus. See Porson’s *Excerpts from the Scholia of the Harleian Codex* on that passage. Hemsterhuis well says on Lucian Vol. II. p. 492. Bipont: "The Platonists, however, were so far from rejecting those verses of Homer that they thought a mystery of secret discipline, not common, resided there." Then he praises Proclus on Plato's *Republic*, p. 382, and others. What Proclus has, however, flowed from this passage of Plotinus. Add Davies’ and our annotations on Cicero’s *On the Nature of the Gods* III. 16. p. 551. of our edition. Tully had touched on the same matter in the books *On the Republic*. See Fragment of the third book no. XXVIII from Augustine, *City of God* XXII. 4.—What follows: *τὸ εἴδωλον—διδοὺς—αὑτὸν—δὲ—εἶναι* (granting the image... but that he himself is...), argues for an imitator of Plato, who similarly uses *διδόναι* (to give/grant) for *tradere* (to hand down/represent). See Ast’s *Commentary on the Republic* (II. 7. p. 364. Steph.) p. 406. Therefore, it properly ought to be translated thus: "handing down his image (viz. singing/making it) among the shades, but that he himself dwells among the Gods." Plotinus touched on the same fable below, IV. 3. 27. p. 392 sq.

**-> BOOK II. <-**
**-> P. 22, 7. ΠΕΡΙ ἈΡΕΤΩΝ (ON VIRTUES)]** The argument of this second book is connected with several dialogues of Plato, and the beginning itself is born from the *Theaetetus*, as we shall see in the annotation to chapter 1. Certain passages of the *Phaedo* also pertain here, on which (p. 42) Wyttenbach in his Annotation placed these [words] (p. 216): "Moreover, *civil virtue* is on the lowest grade, since there are four grades of virtues in all; at least as the later Platonists described them, *with Plotinus as the leader*, Enn. I. lib. II.: starting from which, those who followed mentioned them everywhere: e.g., Porphyry *On the Grades* p. 34; Marinus measuring the life of Proclus by them; Macrobius translating that passage of Plotinus into Latin, *On the Dream of Scipio* I. 8.: '*Plotinus, a leader among the professors of philosophy along with Plato, in the book on Virtues, arranged their grades according to a true and natural ratio of division in order. There are four, he says, kinds of fourfold virtues: of these, the first are called political, the second purgatorial, the third of the soul already purified, the fourth exemplary*'—let the rest be read in his own work, worthy of knowledge, but too long to be placed here. Moreover, Vincent of Beauvais excerpted Macrobius’ passage in the *Speculum Historiale*, lib. V. cap. 9." Thus Wyttenbach. Regarding Porphyry, you should consult the *Second Part of the Aids to the Intelligible*, which now appears for the first time from the Vatican Codex from the edition of Lucas Holstenius, Rome 1630, and again Cambridge 1655, p. 235 sqq. That part is entitled *Περὶ Ἀρετῶν*, On Virtues, and is mostly excerpted from the books of Plotinus, in the judgment even of Holstenius in *On the Life and Writings of Porphyry* page 53. On which account also *Thomas Taylor*, who in the book *Select Works of Plotinus*, Lond. 1817, presented this second Plotinian book in the English tongue, in the added notes p. 566, usefully converted not a few excerpts from that Porphyrian writing into an explanation of the Plotinian book. Moreover, not a few of these opinions of Porphyry are read in Stobaeus’ *Florilegium*, Tit. I. p. 54. ed. Gaisford, whose entire title *Περὶ Ἀρετῆς* (On Virtue) provides very many collected decrees of other philosophers also, starting from the Pythagoreans. Michael Psellus, however, plundered Porphyry in *Omnifaria Doctrina* § 55. p. 110. Finally, *George Gemistos’ Little Book on Virtue and its Parts* must be referred to here, which Angelus Maius recently edited in Greek and Latin from the Codices, Milan 1816; which writing is assigned to Philo in the Ambrosian Codex.

--- Page 14 ---
Simplicius also touched upon some of the more notable opinions of this Plotinian book in [his commentary on] Aristotle’s *Physics*; e.g., page 249. a. ed. Aldine, where it says: "For the passions, as Plotinus says, are sensations, or not without sensations. And having spoken previously in general about the habits of the soul, that these too are perfections and consist in certain symmetries and asymmetries in relation to something; and that they arise when the sensory part is altered, he finally divides the psychical virtues into ethical and intellectual. And in both cases he shows how they are in relation to something, and how they are not alterations, nor is there an alteration of them, but they arise when certain things are altered. And he shows that ethical virtue arises when the sensory part is altered, from the fact that all ethical virtue is concerned with bodily pleasures and pains, as has been demonstrated in the *Ethics*. But bodily pleasures and pains arise when the sensory part is altered by sensory objects. So ethical virtue arises when the sensory part is altered by sensory objects. And that pleasures and pains arise when the sensory part is altered, he shows from division, etc." Concerning what is written about Marinus, you should see J. A. Fabricius noting the same thing on Porphyry’s *Life of Plotinus* p. 140. note c., and especially the excellently discussed points by the same man on the fourfold number of virtues from the doctrine of the Greek philosophers, in the *Prolegomena* to Marinus’ *Life of Proclus* page 38 sqq. ed. Boissonade. Moreover, Marinus praises Proclus for the fourfold number of virtues, just as Julius Firmicus [praises] Plotinus himself, and others others. See Fabricius *Bibl. Graec.* Tom. V. p. 695. ed. Harles. Also pertaining to the argument of this book which we are treating are three chapters from Alcinous’ *Introduction to Plato*, namely chapter XXVII on Goods and the Highest Good and Virtues; ch. XXVIII Definition of Virtue and Distinction, and ch. XXIX On Virtues and Vice and how each are distinguished. Plotinus himself repeatedly touched on the same argument in other books, e.g., *On Beauty* page 55, which passage I cited for this reason, because in the annotation to the edition of this book (Heidelberg 1814, 8vo. p. 284 sqq.) I partly praised and partly employed other passages of other philosophers and of our author himself. How Proclus and Olympiodorus shaped this same doctrine of virtues for themselves and declared it in words, he will be able to know well enough who is willing to unroll the passages under the title *περὶ ἀρετῆς* page 348 of the Index in [our] *Institutes of Philosophy and Theology Derived from Platonic Fountains* (Frankfurt am Main 1820–1822, 8vo.) noted by us; to which add Brucker’s discussions in *Historia Critica Philosophiae* Tom. II. p. 460 sq. and Tennemann in the German book *History of Philosophy* VI. 47 sqq., who, as he compares the entire system of Plato and Plotinus, so compares the decrees of both concerning the virtues on page 48 sq. and page 159 sqq.

**— 8. ἐξ ἀνάγκης (by necessity)]** Plato in *Theaetetus* p. 176. a. b. p. 247. Bekker: "But it is not possible that evils be destroyed, O Theodorus; for there must always be something contrary to the good; nor can they be established among the gods, but they haunt mortal nature and this place by necessity. Wherefore one must also try to flee from here to there as quickly as possible. And flight is a likeness to God (*ὁμοίωσις θεῷ*) as far as possible. And likeness is becoming just and holy with wisdom." The same philosopher has similar things about *ὁμοίωσις θεῷ* everywhere, e.g., *Republic* X. p. 613. A. collated with VI. p. 500. C.; *Laws* IV. p. 716. B. C. Cf. on these passages Morgenstern, *On Plato’s Republic*, p. 153 sqq.; Heindorf on *Theaetetus* l. l. p. 400; Wyttenbach on *Phaedo* p. 285 sq. The same on Plutarch *de S. N. V.* p. 15 and p. 27 and on *Sept. Sapientt. Conviv.* p. 975. ed. Oxon. minor. where the same learned man shows that Suidas compiled from this passage of Plotinus and also from ch. 3. p. 13 the things which this Lexicographer exhibits in *φευκτέον* (to be fled). I will omit here other passages of other writers which I myself touched upon in the annotations to Plotinus *On Beauty* p. 289 sq.: I will bring forth two here not praised elsewhere: Porphyry *On Virtue* in Stobaeus *Florilegium* Tit. I. p. 55. Gaisford: "The disposition according to the political virtues is seen in moderation of the passions (*μετριοπαθείᾳ*), having as its end living as a man according to nature; but that according to the theoretical [virtues] is in impassivity (*ἀπαθείᾳ*), whose end is likeness to God; but since purification (*κάθαρσις*), etc." Alcinous, *On the Doctrine of Plato* ch. 27. p. 515 sq. ed. Dan. Heinsius, Leiden 1614: "to all of which he (Plato) set as a consequent end likeness to God as far as possible. And he handles this in various ways. For sometimes he says likeness to God is being prudent and just and holy, as in the *Theaetetus*; wherefore one must try to flee from here to there as quickly as possible; and flight is likeness to God as far as possible, and likeness is becoming just and holy with wisdom. But sometimes [he says] it is only being just, as in the last part of the *Republic*—And in the *Phaedo* he calls likeness to God becoming temperate as well as just, in this way, etc." Concerning this tenet of *likeness* (*ὁμοιώσεως*), by which

--- Page 15 ---
a man becomes similar to God through virtue, cf. also the following chapters and Ezechiel Spanheim’s *Sur les Césars de l’Empereur Julien* p. 254, who did not forget Plotinus. In the immediately preceding, that [phrase] *τόνδε τὸν τόπον* (this place) has been correctly interpreted from Plato’s system by Taylor as *this [terrestrial] place*. Cf. Julian’s *Oration V*, p. 175. B.: "For the earth is the last of existing things. And here, says Plato, even after being driven away [Wyttenbach deleted 'even' in the cited place], evils turn about, etc."

**p. 23, 1. οἷον σώφρονι (as to a temperate one)]** Proclus refers to these in Plato’s *Timaeus* p. 112, writing thus: "why is it not possible to hear many saying every day, 'God is good.' But the name 'God' is without virtue, as Plotinus says." Cf. above I. 1. 12. p. 7. where [it speaks] of Hercules.

**— 6. πολιτικὰς—ἀρετὰς (political virtues)]** Anonymous, *On Virtues* at the end of Andronicus of Rhodes’ *Paraphrase of the Nicomachean Ethics* ed. Dan. Heinsius, Leiden 1617. p. 754. thus:
**-> Practical Virtues: <-**
**-> Wisdom. Temperance. Courage. Justice. <-**
He calls them therefore "practical virtues," which the Platonists and Plotinus himself called "political." Then he explains the individual virtues and contrary vices partly from Aristotle. See his *Rhetoric* I. 9. p. 32 sq. Sylburg, p. 66 sqq. ed. Oxon. 1822, from which Psellus also profited in *Omnifar. Doctr.* § 51 sqq. Add *Nicomachean Ethics* VI. 5. p. 102 sqq. Sylburg and Plato's passages *Laws* III. 129, 172; *Republic* IV. p. 346 sqq. and p. 430 sqq. From those "practical virtues" the same Anonymous distinguishes others thus:
**-> Theoretical Virtues: <-**
**-> physical, and theological, which is above nature. <-**
Olympiodorus in *Alcibiades I* distinguishes virtues threefold, p. 155: physical, political, ethical.

**p. 25, 10. ὁμοίωσις διττὴ (likeness is twofold)]** Suidas in *ὁμοίωσις* T. II. p. 694. Kuster: "likeness is twofold. One is 'the same'; the other is 'different'" (which must be filled in from our passage). What he immediately subjoins: "When Plotinus says, likeness to God; it must be taken in another way," pertains to the following chapter III on the next page.

**— 11. ὅσα—ἀπὸ τοῦ αὐτοῦ (as many things as [are] from the same)]** Engelhardt takes these last words for *κατὰ τὸ αὐτὸ*, translating: "which are in all parts equally assimilated to the exemplar." Taylor followed Marsilio [Ficino]. Just below, you might translate *οὐκ ἀντιστρέφειν* with Tully (*Orator* ch. 32): "not to respond from the other part [reciprocate]." Regarding this formula, especially of the Platonists and Peripatetics, see Ast on Plato’s *Republic* VII. p. 564; Stallbaum on *Philebus* § 86. p. 120 and especially Wyttenbach on Plutarch’s *Moralia* Vol. I. p. 197 and the interpreters on Aristotle’s *Rhetoric* I. 1. p. 2–8. *Animadvv.* ed. Gaisford; finally cf. our annotation to Proclus in *Alcibiades* p. 339, collated with Olympiodorus p. 114, 118.

**p. 26, 2. καὶ ἀμείνους ποιοῦσιν (and they make [us] better)]** Marinus excerpted this passage in the *Life of Proclus* p. 42, which Boissonade amended from our passage p. 104.

**— 3. τὰ πάθη μετροῦσαι (measuring/limiting the passions)]** Plotinus wanted the preceding *ὁρίζουσαι* (defining) and the repeated *μετροῦσαι* here to be taken with the power of *restraining, limiting* and *moderating*; to which things that the most learned Seager recently appended to Stephanus’ *Thesaurus* p. 6111, add Lambert Bos’ *Observations on the New Testament* and indeed on 2 Cor. X. 12; Wetstein on the N.T. Tom. II. p. 204. Even Theodoretus Tom. IV. p. 1119 ed. Schulze said *μετρῆσαι τῇ πίστει τὴν ἀθυμίαν*, i.e., to diminish, to restrain despondency. In the words *τῷ ὅλως ἀμείνονι*, Marsilio [Ficino] is shown to have hesitated by his Commentary, which see, where however "by a better way" (*meliore modo*) should perhaps be corrected for "by our better" (*meliori nostro*). Taylor: "and taking away false opinions FROM A MORE EXCELLENT NATURE." But even if the comma after *ἀφαιροῦσαι* were deleted, one would still ask what *ὅλως* (entirely/at all) is, which Engelhardt also did not express, though otherwise he interpreted this passage excellently. If the reading is genuine, "altogether" or "entirely" should have been added. Perhaps this sentence is joined with that which Olympiodorus in *Alcibiades I* p. 155 touched upon, "that the political virtues reciprocate among themselves." Furthermore, Macrobius eloquently praised these civil virtues in the place cited above in *On the Dream of Scipio* I. 7.

**— 11. μὴ τὸ πᾶν θεοῦ τοῦτο ᾖ (lest this be entirely of God)]** Ficinus in his Commentary teaches that this can be taken in two ways: either that such a constitution of the soul is total divinity, or that it pertains entirely to God. To me, Engelhardt seems to have explained the meaning of this passage well in this way: Because the soul, being very close to God, has many qualities which are likewise in God, there is a danger lest he who thinks about the necessity [of a link] between God and the soul might opine that the essence of God is nothing other than the substance of the soul itself.

**— 16. Λέγων δὴ ὁ Πλάτων (Plato saying indeed)]** In the *Theaetetus* p. 176. b. c. "Wherefore one must try to flee from here as quickly as possible. And flight is likeness to God as far as possible." Cf. Plotinus I. 6. 8. p. 56. G. where we placed more

--- Page 16 ---
in the special edition p. 346. Ezechiel Spanheim touched on this opinion in *Remarques sur les Césars de l’Empereur Julien* p. 258 and at the bottom of page 112, and everywhere Clement of Alexandria and other Platonic doctors of the Church. See Segaar on Clement of Alexandria, *Quis Dives salvetur* p. 166.

**p. 27, 1. καθάρσεις λέγων (calling them purifications)]** In the *Phaedo* p. 69. c. p. 21. Wyttenbach. Furthermore, concerning the purgatorial virtues, cf. this interpreter on the same dialogue p. 172. We shall add here a passage of Iamblichus, from the book *On the Soul*, in Stobaeus *Eclogues* I. 52. p. 1056. Heeren: "Plotinus and most of the Platonists suppose that the final purification is the setting aside of the passions and of the formative discernments, the contempt of all opinion and the renunciation of material thoughts, the filling from the mind and from being, and the assimilation of the thing understood to the understanding [mind]." Olympiodorus, however, in *Alcibiades I* p. 54 and p. 145 distinguishes several modes of *κάθαρσις* (purification), among these the Pythagorean, Socratic, Peripatetic, (Stoic). Add also Marinus’ *Life of Proclus* p. 42, on which Boissonade did not neglect these Plotinian points. Furthermore, in all places where *καθαίρειν* (to purify) and *κάθαρσις* are mentioned, the proper force of the word must be held, which is to cast out filth. Hence Perseus and Hercules are said to have been born for the purification of evils (*ἐπὶ καθάρσει τῶν κακῶν*). Olympiodorus in *Alcibiades I* p. 156 sq. Regarding this force of the word, Baguet, a student of my Bekker, learnedly noted on Dion Chrysostom’s *Oration VIII*, p. 136 sq.

**— 4. συμπεφυρμένη (mingled together)]** He seems to have taken this word, used frequently by Plato, here from the *Phaedo* p. 17. Wyttenbach. We have dealt with it more fully at Plotinus *On Beauty* p. 246 sq.—*Ὁμοπαθὴς* (sympathetic/of like passion) is itself used by Plato, as in *Republic* V. p. 464 where Ast gave *ὁμοιοπαθεῖς* (see *Addit. ad Commentar.* p. 520), but Bekker restored *ὁμοπαθεῖς*. Wyttenbach briefly but accurately explained the distinction in Plutarch *On Distinguishing a Flatterer from a Friend* p. 539. Cf. Alberti’s *Philological Observations on the N.T.* p. 454 and Wetstein’s *N.T.* II. p. 454.—*Ὁμοπάθεια* (sympathy) is read below IV. 2. before the middle and IV. 7. 3. at the beginning; *ὁμοπαθεῖν* IV. 9. 1 and 2; *ὁμοπαθὴς* VI. 4. 1; *ὁμοιοπαθὴς* IV. 4. 23., at least in the Basel edition.

**p. 28, 1. μίμημα τοῦ ἐν ψυχῇ (an imitation of that which is in the soul)]** Plato, *Republic* II. p. 382. p. 103. Bekker: "since the imitation in words is a certain imitation of the affection in the soul and an image born afterwards, etc." on which passage Ast p. 437 both praises these points of Plotinus and Isocrates *To Nicocles* Orat. III. § 3. p. 24. ed. Coray.

**— 2. ὁ ἐν προφορᾷ (the [speech] in utterance)]** Concerning "uttered speech" (*λόγῳ προφορικῷ*), add a passage of Proclus in *Alcibiades* p. 286, and our *Meletemata* cited there. "Articulate voice" is joined to uttered speech. For *προφορὰ* is pronunciation, according to Wyttenbach’s teaching on Plutarch *On Hearing the Poets* p. 342. From uttered speech is distinguished the *internal* (*ὁ ἐνδιάθετος*). See the same learned man on Plutarch *On the Right Way of Hearing* p. 378 sq. I subjoin a passage of Philo Judaeus especially relevant to the understanding of our passage. For he thus says in *On the Life of Moses* III. p. 154. Mangey: "For speech is twofold, both in the universe and in the nature of man: in the universe, it is that which concerns the incorporeal and paradigmatic ideas, from which the intelligible world was built, and that which concerns the visible things, which are imitations and representations of those ideas, from which this sensory world was completed. But in man, one is internal, the other uttered; and one is like a certain fountain, the other flowing from it. And the place of the one is the ruling faculty (*ἡγεμονικὸν*), while of the one in utterance it is the tongue and mouth and all the other organ-construction of the voice." *Προφορὰ* will return below in II. 9. 1. [and] V. 1. 3.

**— 7. ἀτελεστέρα—ἤδη (more imperfect—already)]** Marsilio [Ficino] filled this in by interpreting, as he did six hundred other things, which for that very reason we do not touch upon. Otherwise there would be no end to laborious annotation, such as Engelhardt has applied here and elsewhere.

**— 12. οὐδὲ τὸ ἀγαθὸν (nor the good)]** Plato *Republic* VI. p. 509. A.—"but knowledge and truth, just as there it is right to think that light and sight are sun-like, but it is not right to think they are the sun; so here it is right to think these both are good-like, but it is not right to think either of them is the Good." From which passage Plotinus and the rest of the Platonists—Hermes (as he is called) Trismegistus, Dionysius (who wishes to be seen as the Areopagite)—took the occasion for using this word; their passages I touched upon in our *Studies* I. p. 101 and on Plotinus *On Beauty* p. XCV, p. 231 sq., p. 268 sq., and p. 385. These are Plotinian: III. 8. 10; V. 3. 3 and 16; V. 6. 4 and 5; VI. 7. 15.

**p. 29, 2. ἐκ τῆς ἐπιστροφῆς (from the conversion)]** In purification (*τῇ καθάρσει*), Plotinus had previously posited the "removal of foreign things" (*τὴν ἀφαίρεσιν ἀλλοτρίων*). Here follows "conversion" (*ἡ ἐπιστροφή*). A few words must now be said about this notion. Let Gale speak first, who [on]

--- Page 17 ---
Iamblichus *On the Mysteries* p. 291 [says] thus: "Regarding what he hints here about *ἐπιστροφή* (conversion), it should be understood thus: According to the Platonists, *ἐπιστροφή* is the correction of an internal state (*ἐνστάσεως*). For since all things are 'from the one,' therefore all things pant toward their principle, and strive to return to it as much as they can. There are, however, three principal conversions: according to essence, according to life, according to knowledge. Finally, in every principle (or superior) there is found permanence (*μονὴ*), procession (*πρόοδος*), and conversion (*ἐπιστροφή*)." See Porphyry *Sentences* 30 (viz. p. 230 sq.). Moreover, *ἔνστασις* is a "counter-struggle," or an adversarial contention, an opposition, if you wish to use the Tertullian term. Proclus treats *ἐπιστροφὴ* accurately and especially in *Elements of Theology* ch. XXXV sq. p. 61. sqq. of our edition and ch. CLVIII. p. 235 sq.; and no less in the *Commentary on Alcibiades I* p. 16, 30 sqq., 92, 194. Olympiodorus p. 9 sq. In the former place I noted: Proclus frequently uses in what follows "conversion toward (or into) themselves," i.e., the care of oneself, when we return to ourselves and convert the mind. One arrives at it through "attention" (*προσοχὴν*) or through diligent attention and consideration of each thing. Both words are familiar also to the Stoics; see Upton on Epictetus vol. III. p. 333 and p. 433. Schweighäuser and Gataker on Marcus Antoninus IV. 32. p. 119. From the Platonists it suffices to have praised Porphyry in *Sentences* § 34. p. 237 and Proclus in Plato’s *Timaeus* p. 64. Compare now these Plotinian points I. 4. 11, where there is both "to be converted toward the interior" and "to convert the will toward the interior," and VI. 5. 12, where the other form is found, *ἐπιστρωφάω*. Nicolaus of Methone also uses it frequently against Proclus p. 31 sqq. ed. Vömel and p. 113. Dionysius the Areopagite, *Divine Names* ch. 4. § 6, 10, 12. Synesius, *Epistle 57*: "for at the same time he turns away from matter and is converted toward God." On the word *ἔνστασις* we shall add more to our author’s IV. 5. 2.—Just below, *θέα* (sight) is "the vision," or that which the soul now looks upon, while *τύπος* (type) is the form and figuration signed from the impression of the vision, to use Apuleius’ words on the *Doctrine of Plato* p. 4. Elmenhorst, p. 193. Bosscha. Concerning this word, notice was given above at I. 1. 9. In what follows, Engelhardt distinguishes *τύπους* used in the plural from *τύπῳ* designated in the singular, such that by the former something lower and more ignoble is declared than by this unique form of the One.—Presently, *ἀποκείμενα* (laid aside) has a certain significance of neglect and contempt, on which see Steph. *Thes.* p. 4919. London.—*προσβάλλειν* (to strike against) and *ἐπιβάλλειν* (to cast upon) are frequently used of "mixture" and "conjunction," or of sight according to Platonic doctrine; whence also *ἐπιβολὴ* and *προσβολή*. See Wyttenbach and our *Annotation on Plotinus On Beauty* p. 383 and his animadversions on Plutarch p. 285 sq. Finally, at the last word of the chapter *ἀλλότριαι* (foreign), Engelhardt hesitates. He prefers *ἀλλότριοι* (masculine), understanding "we"; for even from the sciences "we are alien" unless we work according to them. Taylor: "For sciences also are foreign" etc. But since our best books exhibit *ἀλλότρια* (neuter), this must apparently be accepted, provided you think of or write *ἐν* (in) before *ταῖς ἐπιστήμαις* (the sciences), in this sense: "Since even in the sciences, if we work in no way according to them, they are foreign (to us)."

**p. 29, 13. καὶ ἡ ταυτότης (and the identity)]** Plotinus frequently uses this word. See III. 7. 1; IV. 4. 15; V. 1. 4; V. 3. 10; V. 9. 5; VI. 1. 6; VI. 2. 8; VI. 2. 15; VI. 7. 39 and everywhere. It flowed from Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics* VIII. 12. p. 150. Sylburg, p. 377. Zell, where he speaks of brothers and sisters who are born from the same parents: "for the identity toward those [parents] makes them the same as each other." Whence I wonder that Alberti calls this word "barbaric," on Hesychius II. 1354 sq. I wonder more at Lexicographers, who have either entirely neglected it or placed it without authority of passages, when nonetheless both Suidas and Suicer have it, and they not without the light of examples. To these join now Zonaras in *Lex. Gr.* p. 712, who discriminates three powers of the word in a sufficiently clear passage. By Proclus in *Inst. Theol.* ch. 171. p. 254, "eternal identity of activity" is attributed to the mind. Dionysius the Areopagite, *Divine Names* II. 4. p. 494 above, piling up similar things as he is accustomed to do—which I am weary to transcribe—[says] thus: "—identity of the whole property beyond all things." Theodoretus also uses it frequently. See *Index Graecitatis* Schulze edition. Marinus had the following points before his eyes in the *Life of Proclus*, where Boissonade designated the details in the notes p. 103 sqq.

**— 16. συνάγουσαν πρὸς ἑαυτὴν (gathering to itself)]** Cf. Boissonade on Marinus in the *Life of Proclus* p. 111.

**p. 30, 1. ἀπαλλαγὰς πόνων (release from pains)]** Taylor translates "pains," and cites Aristotle’s *Ethics*. You look at Book VII. ch. 11 sqq. p. 129 sqq. Sylburg.

**— 5. αὐτὴν συναρμοζομένην (joining itself)]** What this "itself" (*αὐτὴν*) is, the imitation of Marinus in the *Life*

of Proclus p. 50. ed. Fabricius, p. 17. Boissonade, clearly declares: "and he chastened his anger, as far as was possible, so that either it was not moved at all, or the rational soul was not the one joined (*συναρμοζομένην*) [to it]." Therefore the rational soul must be understood here.

**—16. γειτνιάσεως (of proximity)]** Plato *Laws* VIII. p. 842. e. p. 103. Bekker: "being a neighbor to another stranger—he will neighbor." Lucian *Conviv.* 33. p. 440. ed. Hemsterhuis-Reitz. *γειτνίασις* is in Plutarch *Pericles* ch. 19. p. 301. Coray. Regarding the forms of that verb see Lobeck on Phrynichus’ *Eclogae* p. 82. Regarding the word *γειτόνημα* (neighborhood), which Plato also uses, we shall speak at V. 1. 3. p. 484. **p. 31, 7. θεὸς—καὶ δαίμων (God—and daemon)]** These pertain to the distinctions between Gods and geniuses: on which matter since Empedocles (see Plutarch *On the Obsolescence of Oracles* p. 418. E. and Sturz on Empedocles p. 296 sqq.) different people have posited different things. Proclus and Olympiodorus discuss this argument copiously in *Alcibiades I*. See e.g., Proclus p. 31, 67 sqq., p. 90, 123 and Olympiodorus p. 15 sqq.—What follows, "but God, of those who follow the first," pertains to the doctrine concerning the choir or retinue of Jupiter’s gods, which his followers fashioned from the most noble passage of Plato’s *Phaedrus* (p. 246. c. 247.). No less did the same Platonists add to each of the mundane Gods a choir of geniuses (Plutarch *On the Obsolescence of Oracles* p. 421. p. 724. Wyttenbach; Proclus in *Alcibiades I* p. 68: "for every cosmic god leads a certain daemonic order, which immediately gives his own power, etc." For the following things must also be read.)

**— 11. συνῳκίσθη (was made to dwell with/united)]** Regarding the use of this verb, compare what has been collected at Stephanus’ *Thesaurus* p. 6626. Add Wyttenbach on Plutarch’s *Conjugal Precepts* p. 893 sq.; Locella on Xenophon of Ephesus p. 213. collated with p. 160. ed. Peerlkamp; Valckenaer *Scholl. in N.T.* I. p. 39, II. p. 209. For as *συνοικεῖν* (to dwell together) is said chastely of the coitus of spouses, so *συνοικίζειν* is said of a father, or of one in the place of a father, giving a daughter in marriage, then it is transferred by metaphor to other kinds of coupling (Jacobs on Achilles Tatius 12. p. 433.). The contrary is *διοικίζειν* (to separate/un-house). Justin Martyr *Apology I* p. 313. A woman having offered a bill of divorce to Caesar: "she requested that it be permitted to her to separate (*διοικίσασθαι*) her own [affairs/property]." I shall add a passage of Longinus, who, being a contemporary and friend of Plotinus, in *On the Sublime* XLIV. 7 [says]: "For luxury, joined to and stepping equally with immoderate and unbridled wealth, as they say, follows it, and at the same time as the latter opens the entrances of cities and houses, the former enters and dwells together (*συνοικίζεται*) [there]." Ficinus, therefore, ought to have translated in our passage "dwells together" (or cohabits or is associated) rather than "adheres."

**— 14. τῷ δεσπότῃ (to the master)]** Cf. ch. V at the end.

**p. 32, 1. αὐτοδικαιοσύνη (justice-itself)]** See critical annotation. The word *αὐτοσωφροσύνη* (temperance-itself) is to be added to Lexicons, and no less *αὐτοδικαιοσύνη* is to be confirmed by this example. Proclus has *Αὐτοδίκαιον* (the just-itself) in *Alcibiades I* § 40. p. 118 above of our edition, which passage is also to be compared with ours for the sake of the argument.—*Οἰκοπραγία* (doing one's own business) in what follows came from Plato’s *Republic* IV. 11. p. 434 sq. p. 192 sqq., where the contrary is *πολυπραγμοσύνη* (meddling), and it also treats of justice. The whole passage is therefore to be applied to ours.

**— 8. ἡ εἴσω πρὸς νοῦν στροφή (the inward turning toward the mind)]** Marinus in *Life of Proclus* 21. p. 51. p. 17: "For he no longer had thinking such as political [thinking], the doing well regarding contingent and otherwise-capable things, but it itself according to itself purely the intuiting, and the being turned toward itself, in no way sharing opinions with the body," where Boissonade reminds of our passage. Add Proclus in *Alcibiades I* p. 17 bottom and p. 21: "and the turning (*στροφήν*) that will lead himself back toward the better." In primary importance, however, the whole fifty-fifth chapter of the same Marinus (p. 59, 60. p. 20.) should be compared with our whole passage, as it was in a certain way described from our passage, on which what Boissonade p. 117 sq. appended, I will not describe myself.

**— 14. ἡ ἀϋλότης (immateriality)]** This vocabulary is to be added to Lexicons. Hierocles and Proclus in *Inst. Theol.* ch. 197 use *ἀϋλία*. see ibid. annot. p. 294. A little after *δυνάμει*, "by potentiality," must be distinguished from *ἐνεργείᾳ*, "by act"; on which difference Plotinus treats in a specific book, *Enneads* II. lib. 5.

**p. 33, 11. τῆς φρονήσεως κινηθείσης (wisdom having been moved)]** See the passage of Marinus from ch. 21 above at the end of ch. 5 and indeed appended to the word *στροφὴ*. Closely, *περιστατικῶς* means "circumstantially" or "as the occasion arises," as surrounding matters bring themselves, which often present business and trouble, and even danger. See Upton in the *Index of Epictetus* on *περιστασις* p. 421. Schweighäuser-Rhoer on Porphyry’s *On Abstinence* I. § 55. p. 95.

--- Page 19 ---
Gataker on M. Antoninus p. 15 and p. 174 and Wyttenbach on Plutarch’s *Moralia* p. 1025. Olympiodorus in *Alcibiades I* p. 77: "and he takes here all the circumstances (*περιστατικὰ*), such as the person, in what manner—in what land—at what time." cf. below I. 4. 13. p. 37. B. "circumstantial activities" (*ἐνέργειαι—περιστατικαί*).

**p. 33, 18. πρὸς ἀνθρώπους ἀγαθοὺς (toward good men)]** Marinus in *Life of Proclus* c. 25. p. 59. p. 20: "and living entirely according to Plotinus, not the life of a man, that of the 'good [man]' which political virtue thinks worthy to live out, but leaving this one, and exchanging it for another, that of the gods; for his likeness was toward these, not toward good men." He seems to recite this passage from memory; for the written books show no variation in Plotinus’ speech.

**-> BOOK III. <-**
**p. 39, 7. ΠΕΡΙ ΔΙΑΛΕΚΤΙΚΗΣ (ON DIALECTIC)]** This Plotinian book is the twentieth in the order in which individual ones are mentioned to have been written by Porphyry in *Life of Plotinus* ch. IV. p. 100. ed. Fabricius; but it is joined with the superior one on virtues not by time alone but also by argument. It is inscribed, however, "On Dialectic." Because this appellation is used by most philosophers with a clearly different meaning on the authority of Aristotle, a few words must be said about it. And first, what *Dialectic* is for Aristotle and the old Peripatetics and very many other philosophers, no one can doubt who has only inspected these passages: *Topics* I. 2. p. 272. Sylburg; *Sophistical Refutations* I. 11. p. 439, II. 8, 9. p. 466 sqq. *Rhetoric* I. 1. 1. with interpreters p. 6 sqq. ed. Oxon. 1820. Hence rightly G. J. Vossius *On Logic* I. 2. p. 206. *Opera* Tom. III: "But for the Peripatetics the word *διαλέγεσθαι* (to discourse) does not extend so widely, but denotes to argue probably. And similarly the word *Dialectic* is always taken by Aristotle and the old Peripatetics for that part of Logic which teaches how to argue probably, and by another name it is called *Topics*." Plato also understands Metaphysics by Dialectic [Add Tac. Facciolati *Institutiones Logicae Peripatet.* Venice 1729. p. 13 and 19 and his *Logicae Disciplinae Rudimenta*, ibid. 1728. p. 7 and 9 sq.]: let us see about Plato. Who indeed in the *Sophist* p. 253. d. p. 206. Bekker [says]: "To divide according to kinds and not to think the same form is another, nor another to be the same, shall we not say this is of the science of dialectic?" (cf. the same in *Phaedrus* p. 266. c. and Heindorf there page 314.) Then in the same place he proceeds: "But indeed you will grant the dialectical [skill] to no other, I think, except to the one who philosophizes purely and justly." Which is now closer to that use of the term which for the most part Plato and the Platonists and Plotinus himself use. Nevertheless, the passage in *Republic* VII. 12 and 13 especially serves to open the Platonic appellation of Dialectic, from which I shall transfer only these things (p. 533. Steph. p. 361. Bekker): "Is it not then, I said, that the dialectical method alone proceeds in this way, destroying hypotheses toward the principle itself, that it may be confirmed, and it gently draws and leads upward the eye of the soul, which is truly buried in a certain barbaric mud, using as assistants and companions those arts which we went through." After G. Vossius placed these words in *On Logic* lib. IV. cap. 12. p. 226, he thus proceeds: "Which things cannot be understood except of Metaphysics. He who knows this will not at all wonder that Plato in VII of the *Republic* wants five years to be spent on dialectic, and indeed 'doing nothing else but being exercised conversely to the exercises concerning the body.' Nay, he does not even open the school of Dialectic to youths, but only to 'those of thirty years,' those who were thirty years of age. Furthermore, unless Plato used the word Dialectic in this way, we could scarcely excuse the fact that his *Parmenides* is called 'dialectical': where it treats 'of being,' and those things are referred which pertain 'to being, insofar as it is being': such as the one, the many, the finite, the infinite, the whole, the part, the divisible, the indivisible, and others. Someone might say the mode of treating is dialectical. But this is not a sufficient reason, since Plato discusses similarly in other books also. Therefore either I am greatly deceived, or rather this book is so inscribed from its argument itself, which is 'dialectical,' but with this word accepted loosely, so that it comprehends *Logic and Metaphysics*." Caelius Rhodiginus saw this in lib. XVI of *Ancient Readings* ch. XXXX.; nay, before him *Marsilio [Ficino]* in the Commentary on Plotinus *Enneads* I. lib. III. p. 18. ed. Basel. an. 1580. Nay, it is clearly evident also from Plotinus’ lib. III itself, where it is asked (p. 21) what Dialectic is; and it is answered that it encompasses the whole breadth of those things which are, and proceeds even beyond: since it also considers *τὰ μὴ ὄντα*, "those which are not," to consider in addition

--- Page 20 ---
to these also *τί τὸ ἀΐδιον, καὶ τὸ μὴ τοιοῦτον*, "what is eternal and what is not so." After some more it is asked: *ἢ ταὐτὸν φιλοσοφία καὶ διαλεκτική;* "is philosophy and dialectic the same thing?" and it is answered that Dialectic is *φιλοσοφίας μέρος τὸ τιμιώτατον*, "the most precious part of philosophy." Afterwards the same author adds: "For dialectic and wisdom are still universal, and it brings everything into use for prudence immaterially," *Dialectica vero et sapientia etiam universali et immateriali ratione omnia in usum prudentiae profert*. And you may read more in this vein in the same place. Thus far Vossius; who also says of Mathematics lib. III. ch. 2. p. 61: "By which (Dialectic) Plato understands not Topics, or the art of discussing probably in both directions, as Aristotle uses this word; but *Metaphysics*, not simply indeed, but insofar as it uses the same instrument of *Logic*: so that altogether this name for Plato comprehends Metaphysics and Logic. And similarly the *Platonists* are accustomed to use that word." I thought these latter points should be added all the more because, to say nothing of other more recent [authors], J. A. Fabricius himself on Porphyry’s *Life of Plotinus* ch. 24. p. 140. says less accurately that *Metaphysics alone* is used by Plato and Plotinus under this name of Dialectic. That explanation is confirmed by a passage of Proclus, who in *Platonic Theology* II. 11. p. 110 [says] thus: "And after these things, descending again to reasonings from the intellectual hymnody, and putting forward the unrefutable science of dialectic, let us contemplate, following the vision of the first causes, how the first God of all is exempt." And after these things, again descending to *reasonings from the intellectual hymnody and putting forward the invincible science of Dialectic* (after we have proposed them), *following the first contemplation of causes*, let us contemplate how that first God is exempt from these universals. Nor indeed is it not to be held that the younger Platonists—who, when they speak in the usage of their own school, according to the example of the master, use the name of Dialectic for Logic and Metaphysics—sometimes use this latter name such that they understand the Peripatetic opinion, and even with a certain sort of contempt. A witness is the same Proclus in the same work I. 4. p. 18: "For such a kind of speech is not proper to the hypothesis concerning 'beings as beings,' nor is the notion of 'obscure and' (from all matter) 'separated causes' adapted to dialectical exercises." For neither does the argument about truly Beings suit such a kind of words (and of speaking), nor does the notion itself of *obscure and separated* causes suit dialectical exercises. Where, however, in the added "exercises" (*γυμνασίοις*) some force also resides. The same Proclus in *Scholl. in Cratylum* § 4. p. 2. sq. Boissonade: "And again he (Plato) rejects the dialectic of Aristotle as eristic, but loves the dialectic that sees the principles of beings, as a part of philosophy." *Et rursus Aristotelis Dialecticam ut litigiosam ejicit a se Plato, illam vero dialecticam, quae entium principia videt, amat tanquam partem philosophiae*. Nevertheless, he treats the same argument much more accurately in the *Commentary on the Parmenides* in a longer passage than can be transferred here; nor is this necessary, since Thomas Taylor in *Select Works of Plotinus* for our current book p. 18 sq. and again p. 577 sqq. applied this discussion of Proclus to Plotinus. Moreover, it is read on p. 46 sqq. of the fourth volume of Proclus’ *Works* ed. Cousin, Paris 1821. And as there that interpreter of Plato injects mention of passages met with in the *Phaedrus* and *Sophist*: namely, those which we praised above: so on p. 9 sq. he places these: "Parmenides advises Socrates to exercise himself in dialectic before the whole contemplation, if indeed he is a lover of the truth of beings, calling that dialectic about which Socrates himself also taught us in other places, as in the *Republic* (see above), as in the *Sophist*, as in the *Philebus*." Proclus discusses in the same vein at the beginning of the *Commentary on Alcibiades I* ch. 10. p. 27. sqq. of our edition, where he commemorates the three disciplines of Socrates: *midwifery, amatory, dialectical*—"and he leads one up through the erotic [art], another he moves to recollection of the eternal reasons of the soul through the obstetric [art], and another he leads around to the contemplation of beings according to the dialectical method," where you should hold "leads around" (*περιάγει*) as the proper [action] of dialectic, which has "turnings" (*ἐκτροπὰς*) and "windings" (*ελιγμοὺς*). Then he reminds of the passages in the *Republic* and *Phaedrus* which we touched upon above. And from all these things, which we have set forth a little more copiously, it is possible to judge to what extent Ficinus correctly pronounced above on page 16, when he says: "they would have more correctly inscribed this book 'On the return of souls to the Divine,'" which title he himself also prefixed to this book, obviously so that [he might help] the understanding of more recent readers.

...might assist. For to the Greeks, and especially to those skilled in Platonic philosophy, nothing at all was obscure in that second inscription concerning *Dialectic*. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 39, 11. ὅπου μὲν [where indeed]] Ficino, and Taylor following him, took these words to mean "since" or "inasmuch as," a usage not infrequent elsewhere ([[abbrev: vid. → see]] Tensen and Reiz on Lucian’s *Aetion*, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 832; Leopold on Plutarch’s *Romulus* 24. 3. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 150, cf. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 154); but the following ὡς ἐπὶ τὰγ. [as if towards the Good] prevents us from taking it thus. To that ὅπου μὲν [where indeed] there corresponds later in this place [[abbrev: h. l. → hoc loco]] τίνα δὲ δεῖ εἶναι τ. ἀ. [who must be the one led up?]; for ὅπου δὲ [where however] does not necessarily follow in the apodosis (as taught by Schaefer on Viger’s *De Idiotismis* VII. 10. 4. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 432). The entire passage should therefore be translated thus: "For to what place ([[abbrev: s. → scilicet]] namely, to what destination) one must go, as if towards the Good and the first Principle (i.e., that we may be persuaded that we shall come to the Good etc.), let it be placed among the things conceded—But who is it that ought to be led back?"

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 40, 8. ἐπ᾿ ἄκρῳ — τῷ νοητῷ [at the summit of the intelligible]] [[abbrev: Cf. → Compare]] Plato’s *Phaedrus* [[abbrev: c. → chapter]] 26, and on him Hermias and Ast in their *Commentaries* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 301.
