— 14. φθόγγους [sounds]] Marsilio [Ficino] translates as *sonos harmonicos* [harmonic sounds], clearly to distinguish them more significantly from the preceding ψόφοις [noises]. The word φθόγγος, properly used of the human voice, then also of the cithara, [[abbrev: cet. → etc.]], is illustrated by the writers cited in Stephanus’ *Thesaurus* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 10084 of the London [[abbrev: ed. → edition]]; to which add Schleusner’s *Lexicon of the New Testament* under the [[abbrev: voc. → word]] and Valckenaer’s *Scholia on the New Testament* I. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 344. Furthermore, turn your mind to the repetition of the word ἕτοιμον [ready] used in different senses. The Lycopolitan philosopher [Plotinus] is accustomed to indulge himself in such things, being more intent on matters than on words. I suspect the reading of the Vatican Codex εὔηχον [sweet-sounding] proceeded from a scribe who referred it to τοῖς φθομένοις [the sounds] and did not look back to σχήματα [figures], which are mentioned shortly after. It is well known that σχήματα belong to both rhetoricians and dancers. To those things which Stephanus and the editors collected in the London *Thesaurus* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 3944, add the discussions of Ernesti in the *Lexicon of Greek Rhetorical Technology* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 338 [[abbrev: sqq. → following]]. For the rest, consult Plato’s *Laws* II. 664 [[abbrev: sq. → following]], [[abbrev: p. → page]] 256 Bekker; Aristotle’s *Rhetoric* III. 1. 4. with the [[abbrev: interpr. → interpreter]]; Longinus’ *Fragments* III. 5; Theon of Smyrna’s *Music* [[abbrev: cap. → chapter]] 1 and Bullialdus there; and [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] Plotinus himself, II. 3. 13 and V. 9. 11.

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 41, 4. ὕστερον λεκτέον [must be told later]] For the sentiment of this first chapter, Aristides Quintilianus *On Music* I. 2. should be consulted: "Dialectic and its [[abbrev: sic → thus in text]] counterpart [rhetoric] benefit the soul toward prudence, if music should take it up already purified." Proclus discusses the power of music for forming the souls of the young in *On the Alcibiades* [[abbrev: pr. p. → especially page]] 194 [[abbrev: sqq. → following]]. I shall append the words of John Chrysostom, which also pertain to the beginning of the following chapter, in *On Psalm xli*, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 146: "Nothing so raises the soul, and gives it wings and frees it from the earth, and releases it from the bonds of the body, and makes it philosophize, and mock all worldly things, as the melody of a symphony and a divine song composed in rhythm." [Compare C. Anne den Tex, *Disputation on the Power of Music for Cultivating Man*, Utrecht, 1816, 170 [[abbrev: pp. → pages]] Mr.]

— 6. ἢ παρέλθοι [or let him pass by]] i.e., or let him ascend higher above that place where the μουσικὸς [musician] is. Plotinus refers [[abbrev: h. l. → in this place]] to the doctrine of the degrees toward higher things, which, handed down by the prince Plato, was more fully explained by the junior Platonists. We [[abbrev: h. l. → in this place]] merely mention the *Symposium*, from whose primary speech—that of Socrates—this entire chapter on educating the amatory man is taken. [[abbrev: Vid. → See]] [[abbrev: p. → page]] 210 [[abbrev: sq. → following]] Stephanus, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 442 [[abbrev: sqq. → following]] Bekker, where among other things are these: "For this is the right way to approach erotic matters or to be led by another, beginning from these beautiful things for the sake of that Beauty itself, always ascending, as if using steps, from one to two, and from two to all beautiful bodies, and from beautiful bodies to beautiful practices [[abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → and so forth]]." From the same source our author [Plotinus] drew in I. 6, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 48 G.: "until one, passing by in the ascent [[abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → and so forth]]." Just as...

...there we gave [the reading] from the [[abbrev: Codd. → Codices]] instead of ἀπελθών [departing]. The next phrase χωρὶς δὲ ζῶν [but living apart] pertains to these lower things into which the soul of the Amatory man has fallen, and thus to the Body in which it is enclosed.

— 9. πεσόντα ἐπτοῆσθαι [having fallen to be fluttered/excited]] This reading, which we have restored on the authority of the books, is itself Platonic. [[abbrev: Vid. → See]] *Symposium* 206 [[abbrev: infr. → below]], [[abbrev: p. → page]] 436 Bekker; *Cratylus* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 464 A.; *Phaedo* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 82. Plotinus had these passages before his eyes elsewhere as well, [[abbrev: v. c. → for example]] [[abbrev: p. → page]] 73 B. D., [[abbrev: p. → page]] 714, [[abbrev: c. → chapter]] 22 A. From these same passages it is clear that περὶ [about] depends upon ἐπτοῆσθαι [to be excited]. Therefore πεσόντα [having fallen] must be taken by itself, as if it were προπετετηκότα [having fallen forward], which word Gregory Nazianzen uses for the verb προεῖσθαι [to let go] in *Oratio Stelittica in Julianum* I. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 7.

— 12. ἐν ἀσωμάτοις — τοῦ ἐρασμίου ἤδη [already in incorporeal things—of the lovely]] For in incorporeal things there is already a familiarity with that which is lovely; i.e., the Amatory man already becomes accustomed to the lovely in incorporeal things. Our philosopher takes the word Ἐράσμιον [lovely] from his Plato. [[abbrev: Vid. → See]] *Phaedrus* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 250 [[abbrev: d. → d.]]; *Republic* III. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 620 B. He defines it more accurately below at [[abbrev: p. → page]] 724 [[abbrev: sq. → following]].

— 14. εἶτα ἓν ποιητέον [then one must make it one]] Lest anyone should by chance confuse this [[abbrev: èv → ἐν]] with περὶ ἓν σῶμα [around one body], he must be warned by a word that in this place τὸ ἓν [the One] is the same as the τὸ ἐν πᾶσι ταὐτὸν [the same in all things] mentioned above; [[abbrev: h. e. → that is]], it must be demonstrated that even the beautiful things that exist in incorporeal matters are in reality a certain single "beautiful."

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 42, 3. τὰ μαθήματα δοτέον [mathematics must be given]] [[abbrev: h. l. → In this place]] μαθήματα are not, as elsewhere in Plato and Plotinus, the disciplines of literature in general, but mathematics, arithmetic, geometry, and the rest; which is understood even from the passage of Plato that Plotinus followed here, namely *Republic* VII. 523 [[abbrev: sq. → following]], [[abbrev: p. → page]] 341 [[abbrev: sqq. → following]] Bekker. The use of διδόναι for *to hand over/teach* is likewise Platonic. [[abbrev: Vid. → See]] *Republic* II. 364 and [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] Ast’s *Commentaries* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 406; and joined with διδάσκειν [to teach] at [[abbrev: p. → page]] 196, 197, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 416 Bekker. From this perhaps someone might conjecture a little above, looking especially at the traces in the [[abbrev: codd. → codices]], δεικτέον οὖν καὶ διδακτέον [one must show and teach] instead of λυτέον [must be loosed].

— 4. πρὸς συνεθισμὸν — καὶ πίστεως ἀσωμάτου [for the sake of habituation—and of incorporeal faith/certainty]] A passage memorable for the history of the Plotinian text. For although none of our codices nor Ficino have it otherwise, it is nevertheless cited in a completely different way by several writers. For this sentiment of our Plotinus, like many others of his, attained a certain proverbial force. First, the Scholiast of Plato on book VI of the *Republic*, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 172 Ruhnken: "And Plotinus says such a thing, that mathematics must be handed over to the young for the habituation of the incorporeal nature." John Philoponus cites this passage no differently in his commentary on Aristotle’s *On the Soul*, fol. 1 A. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 2. Gerhard Vossius also put it plainly thus in *On Mathematics* III. 2. 7. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 61, having received these words from some unknown source. Likewise David the Armenian philosopher in his *Commentary on the Five Voices of Porphyry* in the Paris Codex [[abbrev: nr. → number]] 1939. But indeed Iamblichus in *On the Common Mathematical Science* in Villoison’s *Anecdota Graeca* II. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 207, says this of mathematical science: — "For it prepares and encourages a readiness and suitability for theology, and provides a likeness to it, and an ascent, and a purification, releasing the intellectual organs from their bonds and cleansing them, and joining them to Being, approaching in a way the intelligibles through the beauty and good order of the things contemplated in mathematics, and being assimilated through the contemplation of the unchangeable and immovable to the stable and the same and likewise intelligible and determined things, habituating also the discursive reason to gently apply itself to the light of Being, leading it away from bodies, and instilling faith concerning the essence of incorporeal things, and providing scientific certainty and precision." I have added more [[abbrev: ex → from]] the primary passage and the one which most especially pertains to our text. As for the reading, it is established that Iamblichus encountered the common reading in his copy. Whence it would not be absurd to suspect that the discrepancy flowed from a double recension. This common reading was less to be contested by us and is recommended by Platonic usage, which similarly employed πίστιν [faith/certainty]; [[abbrev: v. c. → for example]] in the *Phaedo* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 70 [[abbrev: b. → b.]]; and κατανόησις [understanding], or the thought of intelligible things, is prepared by faith, or trust, that there are incorporeal things; for he who does not believe they exist must necessarily be sluggish in undertaking the thought of them. Concerning the power of mathematics for the knowledge of intelligible things, Vossius cited many things from the ancients in the [[abbrev: l. l. → place cited]], as did Bullialdus on Theon of Smyrna’s *Mathematics for the Reading of Plato*, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 194, who also used the words of Plotinus. To these add Proclus, *On Providence and Fate*, [[abbrev: cap. → chapter]] 12; the same on Plato’s *Cratylus* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 1 Boissonade; on the *Alcibiades* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 194 [[abbrev: sq. → following]] of our edition; in Cousin’s *On the Parmenides* I. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 49 [[abbrev: sq. → following]]. — Soon after: καὶ φύσει ἐνάρετον τὸ πρὸς τελείωσιν ἀρετῶν ἀκτέον [and the one naturally virtuous must be led to the perfection of virtues] either the καὶ τὸ φύσει ἐνάρ. [and the naturally virtuous] must be transposed or the τὸ after ἐνάρ. must be deleted. However, the word ἐνάρετος [virtuous] is more recent and was introduced and frequented by the Stoics; others wish to use σπου-

— 9. λογικὴν πραγματείαν [logical treatment]] *Logical treatment*, clearly in the opinion of the Peripatetics, who were the first to introduce the name of λογικῆς, *Logic*. [[abbrev: Vid. → See]] Cicero, *De Finibus* I. 7. 22. 23. and Goerenz there; [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] G. Vossius on Logic [[abbrev: p. → page]] 206 [[abbrev: sq. → following]] and Wyttenbach’s *Precepts of Logical Philosophy*, Prolegomena §. 8. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 6. [Add Facciolati, *Institutes of Peripatetic Logic* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 13 [[abbrev: sq. → following]] and especially his *Rudiments of Logical Discipline* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 7 [[abbrev: sqq. → following]]. Moreover, with this entire Plotinian description of rest [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] the twin passage of Proclus in *On the Parmenides* I. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 47 Cousin: "and another [dialectical method] already resting the mind in the most proper contemplation of beings [[abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → and so forth]]"; for it is too long to be placed here.

[[abbrev: ib. → ibid.]] προτάσεων [propositions]] [[abbrev: Vid. → See]] Aristotle, *Prior Analytics* I. 1. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 79 Sylburg: "A proposition, therefore, is a statement affirming or denying something of something [[abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → and so forth]]"; [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] *Posterior Analytics* I. 2. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 200; Suidas under πρότασις III. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 208 [[abbrev: sq. → following]] Kuster, where a "dialectical proposition" is distinguished from a "problem"; and Olympiodorus on Plato’s *Alcibiades* [[abbrev: pr. c. → especially chapter]] 14. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 123. Often it is a proposition of that which is proposed for debate. Concerning the προτάσει ῥητορικῇ [rhetorical proposition] [[abbrev: vid. → see]] Aristotle’s *Rhetoric* I. 3. 7. and the [[abbrev: interprr. → interpreters]] there [[abbrev: p. → page]] 64 Oxford. Furthermore, both πρότασις and προτάσεις are frequently read in Plotinus, as in IV. 4. 44, V. 5. 1, VI. 8. 3.

— 15. Εἶτα — συντίθησι [Then — it composes]] Ficino, and following him Engelhardt and Taylor, make the subject of this verb and the following ones "the soul." I decide nothing; I only ask whether it might not be more convenient to have "dialectic" as the subject. Soon after: ἔστι γάρ, φησιν [for it is, says] [[abbrev: sc. → namely]] Plato. [[abbrev: Vid. → See]] the passages which we cited above in the [[abbrev: annot. → annotations]] to the Inscription of this book.

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 44, 1. τί οὖν ἡ φιλοσοφία; [What then is philosophy?]] Regarding the sentiment, consult Aristotle’s *Metaphysics* I. 2. where there are other things about philosophy and these: [[abbrev: p. → page]] 6 [[abbrev: ed. → edition]] Sylburg: "nor should one consider any other [science] more honorable than this. For it is the most divine and most honorable." Because Plotinus does not wish Dialectic to be an instrument of philosophy, but a part, and the most excellent part, in this he follows Plato. For so Plato says in the *Republic* VII. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 534 end, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 368 Bekker: "Does it seem to you then, I said, that dialectic lies above us like a coping-stone (apex, culmen. [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] Ast’s *Commentaries* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 574.) to the mathematical sciences, and that no other science can correctly be placed higher than this, but that the mathematical sciences already have their end? It seems so to me, he said." What he adds immediately: "for indeed it must not be thought — and rules," with these he touches upon the Peripatetics and other philosophers who held Logic as an instrument of Philosophy: [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] the [[abbrev: annot. → annotations]] above on the inscription of the book, and Ammonius’ *Preface to Aristotle’s Categories*. And [[abbrev: h. l. → in this place]] it must be held universally that *Philosophy* is almost never named by Plotinus unless it is Platonic, and *Philosophers* almost never unless they are *Platonists*, or if someone of another sect agrees with the Platonists. This was noted before me by Wyttenbach, who cites many passages for that purpose in these Enneads: [[abbrev: p. → page]] 2. D. E. 6. G. 19. A. B. 20. C. F. and likewise our passage; then [[abbrev: p. → page]] 203. F. 204. E. 212. F. 213. D. 291. A. C. 293. A. 325. C. 330. A. 423. D. 469. A. 556. A. 760. B. [[abbrev: Vid. → See]] *Epistles of the Socratic Companions* in the [[abbrev: ed. → edition]] of G. L. Mahne, Zierikzee, 1813, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 172 [[abbrev: sq. → following]]. ->BOOK III. FIRST ENNEAD. p. 43—45. 17<-

...Moreover, [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] Marsilio’s *Commentary* on this chapter and Heusde’s *Introduction to Platonic Philosophy*, Utrecht, 1827, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 48 [[abbrev: sqq. → following]]. Among more recent philosophers, Hegel judges concerning Dialectic (Logic) in a manner similar to Plotinus. This was also seen by Steinhart in *On Plotinian Dialectic* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 15 [[abbrev: not. → note]] 25.

— 8. ὅτι παρὰ τὸν κανόνα [because [it is] against the rule]] Ficino: *as if it were beside the rule of truth*. Better, Engelhardt and Taylor: *because it opposes the rule of truth*. Furthermore, if the books supported it, you could also write ὅ, τι, so that it would be: *that which is against the rule of truth*.

— 12. καὶ εἰ ἑτέρα, ἢ [[abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → and so forth]] [and if different, or...]] Again, E. wishes "removes and establishes" to be understood, taking the whole passage thus: "whether the soul affirms or denies that which is brought to it from without, just as the senses do when they judge external things." Conversely, Taylor translates thus: *likewise, whether different or the same things are adduced; applying itself to them in a way resembling sense*; adding this little note: *i. e. by intuition, so as to come into immediate contact with the objects of its knowledge. It does this, however, so far as its energy is purely intellectual*. This reasoning seems more true. For in this entire passage he opposes Platonic Metaphysics ([[abbrev: s. → or]] Dialectic) to the logical operations of the Peripatetics.

— 15. ἔχει γὰρ καὶ ἄλλα [[abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → and so forth]] [for it has also other...]] Plotinus follows the distribution of philosophy into these three parts: physical matters, ethical matters, and intelligible matters (concerning these last see [[abbrev: cap. → chapter]] 4 and 5 of the *Dialectic*), which some attributed to Socrates and others to Plato as the author. [[abbrev: Vid. → See]] Fabricius on Sextus Empiricus, *Outlines of Pyrrhonism* II. 2, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 69 and the citations there; and *Against the Mathematicians* VII. 6–10, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 370 [[abbrev: sq. → following]].

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 45, 1. κομίζεται [it derives/receives]] It perceives, as an aid (as before "having taken help"), a fruit. [[abbrev: Vid. → See]] Thomas Magister [[abbrev: p. → page]] 543 [[abbrev: sq. → following]] and the [[abbrev: interprr. → interpreters]] there; Sturz, *Xenophontic Lexicon* II. 768; Schleusner, *Lexicon of the New Testament* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 768. He wishes it to be understood that the connection between dialectic and the remaining parts of philosophy is much closer than that between arithmetic and the remaining arts.

[[abbrev: ib. → ibid.]] Καὶ περὶ ἠθῶν [And concerning morals]] ([[abbrev: sc. → namely]] philosophy, from the preceding) "contemplating indeed from there" ([[abbrev: sc. → namely]] deriving or receiving help).

— 3. Ἴσχουσι δὲ καὶ αἱ λογικαὶ ἕξεις [And the logical states/habits also hold]] Either Ficino read ἀρεταὶ [virtues] in his codex, or he supplied it by thought from what follows. Taylor followed him. Our books vary nothing, except between ἤδη [already] and εἴδη [forms]. However you decide on this passage—for I do not wish to determine it—this is certain: ἐκεῖθεν [from there] here also refers to Dialectic; as if Plotinus were saying this: even the rational habits or virtues trace their principles back to Metaphysics.

— 4. καὶ γὰρ μετὰ τῆς ὕλης [for also with matter]] These words and the phrase τὰ πλεῖστα [the most part] Taylor did not translate. Engelhardt supplies ἔχει (ἴσχει) [holds/has] to τὰ πλεῖστα, with this meaning: "reason and indeed the rational virtues, which are proper to themselves, derive from Dialectic, as it is kindred to reason; yet for the most part these same virtues have things in common with matter, as things which handle and moderate sensibles." Then the same [[abbrev: vir doctus → learned man]] entered upon another reasoning, this one: that you should supply after τὰ πλεῖστα this sentiment: "it has principles from Dialectic": many things together with matter depend on Dialectic, so much so that the principles of Dialectic have force even over matter. The former reasoning, if only it is [possible], seems preferable. Regarding what follows, the same [learned man] wishes it to be completed thus: "but prudence is a certain reflection, and considers the universal more, and the reasonings follow one another, it teaches (?), and it commands (?) if it is necessary now to refrain or later, and in general it gives (?) another better thing." He who knows the Thucydidean brevity of Plotinus will not have missed these things. For ἐπιλογισμὸς [reflection] must be thought of in relation to the following ἐπιλογίζεται [reflects]. Furthermore, the word ἐπιλογισμὸς is among those which Dionysius notes as obsolete and generally obscure in Thucydides (in *Epist. II to Ammaeus* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 793 Reiske, where Hudson had introduced περιλογισμός; the former was restored [[abbrev: ex → from]] two [[abbrev: Codd. → Codices]] by Krueger in Dionysius of Halicarnassus’ *Historiographies* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 224; and it is worth mentioning that even the word περιωπὴ [lookout/watch], criticized in Thucydides in the same place, is read in Plotinus’ Enneads. [[abbrev: Vid. → See]] II. 9. 14. end). Because ἐπιλογισμὸς is more often *reputation*, *thought*, and the meaning of some symbol which we extract from it after it has been presented (as [[abbrev: explic. → explained]] by Iamblichus in *Protreptic on the Symbols* XI. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 336 Kiessling): in Plotinus it is opposed to τοῖς λογισμοῖς [reasonings], which are attributed to the remaining virtues, and is something superior, which is claimed as proper to prudence alone, and thus is *a more august and loftier, as it were, kind of reasoning*. Zonaras’ *Greek Lexicon* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 793: Ἐπιλογισμός· that which has gone back...

[[language: Latin with Greek passages]]

18 ->ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS<-

...to the first reason and fights for or stands against the things before; regarding which [[abbrev: vi → sense]] of the word I find no more noted than in other Lexicons, which can therefore be supplemented from here. Theodorus Metochita also uses the word in [[abbrev: cap. → chapter]] 70, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 454 and [[abbrev: cap. → chapter]] 110, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 729 of the *Miscellanea* in the [[abbrev: ed. → edition]] of Müller and Kiessling.

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 45, 9. εἰς χρῆσιν προσφέρει τῇ φρονήσει [brings forward to prudence for use]] Marsilio [Ficino] with his two Medicean [codices] reads προφέρει [brings forth]. Both Porphyry and Alcinous furnish passages pertaining to this and what follows. For the former, in the *Sentences* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 237, where he deals with the four kinds of virtues—political, purificatory, intellectual, and exemplary—says: "There is therefore another third genus of virtues after the purificatory and political ones, when the soul acts intellectually. Wisdom indeed and prudence consist in the contemplation of what the mind holds. Justice and proper action consist in following the mind and acting toward the mind. Temperance is the turning inward toward the mind. Fortitude is apathy; according to the likeness of that which it looks upon, being apathetic by nature; and these indeed follow each other reciprocally just as the others do." Alcinous, *On the Doctrine of Plato* [[abbrev: cap. → chapter]] 28, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 518; [[abbrev: cap. → chapter]] 29, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 521: "of its forms (of virtue) some are rational, others irrational. — whence one must also think that the virtues follow one another. For fortitude, being preservative of lawful dogma, is preservative of right reason; for lawful dogma is a certain right reason, and right reason comes from prudence. And indeed prudence also exists with fortitude. For it is the knowledge of good things. For no one can see the good while obscured by cowardice and the passions that follow cowardice." Therefore the virtues are said to ἀντακολουθεῖν [follow each other reciprocally], of which in turn one follows from the other; and their ἀντακολούθησις [reciprocal following] is their mutual consequence, so that if this one exists, that one also exists, and if that one, also this one. Synesius uses the noun in *Dion* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 49 d. Petavius; and Proclus in *On the Alcibiades* [[abbrev: cap. → chapter]] 97, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 319, where in the annotations I also noted that this was the opinion of the Stoics: that the virtues follow each other reciprocally, citing also Schweighäuser on Epictetus III. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 243.

— 16. Ὅλως γὰρ ἡ φυσικὴ ἀρετὴ, καὶ ὄμμα ἀτελὲς καὶ ἦθος ἔχει [For in general natural virtue has both an imperfect eye and character]] Proclus cites these words verbatim in *On the Alcibiades* [[abbrev: pr. §. → especially section]] 46, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 133 of our [[abbrev: ed. → edition]]. David the Armenian philosopher also refers to these Plotinian words in his *Commentary on Aristotle’s Categories* [[abbrev: cap. → chapter]] VI. §. 7 in several Paris and Munich [[abbrev: msscrr. → manuscript]] [[abbrev: codd. → codices]]. "In which (i.e. in those things sought concerning power, Krabinger) the second chapter, in which it is shown that both power and weakness have passed through both soul and body and the composite. Through the soul, as in the case of natural and ethical virtues; for these themselves are in labor with the political ones, and he who has one of these through the addition of reason (others read 'pre-position') easily acquires the political ones, about which it has been said. Concerning the natural ones, for that which is naturally most powerless (others read 'most powerful'); concerning the ethical ones: for it has something even in being well-reared; and that Plato says they are slavish, but Plotinus says they are imperfect."

->BOOK IV.<-

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 55, 7. ΠΕΡΙ ΕΥΔΑΙΜΟΝΙΑΣ [ON HAPPINESS]] Porphyry reports in *On the Life of Plotinus* [[abbrev: cap. → chapter]] six, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 103 Fabricius, that this book is among those five sent to him by Plotinus while he was staying in Sicily around the fifteenth year of the reign of Gallienus. As for the order in which they were written, one and all, this one holds the forty-sixth place, and is to be numbered among those which were published by the philosopher when he was already aging. The argument is of such a kind that it has been treated by many in competition since the birth of philosophy. For, to omit barbarian philosophers, the Greeks since Pythagoras labored in explaining it, and according to the difference of schools, they defined that "Blessedness" in various ways. Nor were there lacking peculiar books of philosophers inscribed "On Happiness" or similarly, among which, to use this example, that lost work of Theophrastus was not the least. And from many sources, Aristotle (*Nicomachean Ethics* I. 3 [[abbrev: sqq. → following]]), Cicero (especially in the books *On the Ends*, *On the Nature of the Gods*, and in the *Tusculan Disputations*), Seneca, Plutarch, Diogenes Laertius, and others down to John Stobaeus, have recorded more notable decrees in their commentaries. Stobaeus indeed, both scattered in the books of the *Eclogues*, especially [[abbrev: libr. → book]] II. [[abbrev: cap. → chapter]] VII. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 54 [[abbrev: sqq. → following]] Heeren, and in the hundred and third title of the *Florilegium* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 552 [[abbrev: sqq. → following]], [[abbrev: p. → page]] 333 [[abbrev: sqq. → following]] Gaisford [[abbrev: ed. → edition]], received not a few sentiments of ancient writers, especially philosophers. And since Plotinus follows this custom of touching upon the opinions of other philosophers while omitting the names of the authors, we shall subsequently advise on the more important ones at individual places, as far as can be done in this brevity of annotation. Here, however, in advance, I shall...

— 8. *De Beatitudine* [On Blessedness]] Ficino used the indulgence which Cicero in *On the Nature of the Gods* I. 34 grants to those translating Greek in this noun. Εὐδαιμονία is *beatitas* [[abbrev: s. → or]] *beatitudo* [blessedness], or *Beatum* [the Blessed]; which last Cicero also uses substantively (Goerenz on *De Finibus* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 637): *εὐτυχία* is *Felicitas* [good fortune], and *εὐτυχὴς* is properly *Fortunatus* [fortunate], as opposed to *ὄλβιος* [prosperous], which is the same as *εὐδαίμων* [blessed/happy]. [[abbrev: Vid. → See]] Herodotus I. 32; Eustathius on *Odyssey* VI. 187; Valckenaer on Theocritus’ *Adoniazusae* [[abbrev: v. → verse]] 24. The same on Euripides’ *Hippolytus* 750, and Elmsley on the *Medea* 1197. For the usage of the philosophers’ speech, Aristotle’s *Nicomachean Ethics* VII. 13. 4 and his interpreters on I. 4. 2 should be consulted.

— 11. ἐν εὐζωΐᾳ—εἶναι [to consist in living well]] Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics* I. 8. 4: "living well and acting well agree with the definition of the happy man; for he is said to be almost a certain 'living-well' and 'acting-well'." [[abbrev: Cf. → Compare]] Thomas Gataker on Marcus Antoninus III. 12, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 87. A Stoic in Stobaeus likewise uses this noun twice in *Eclogues* II. 7, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 171, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 130 [[abbrev: sqq. → following]] Heeren; which passage Wyttenbach correctly vindicated from Heeren’s changes and restored especially according to Canter’s method in *Consolatio ad Apollonium* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 739 [[abbrev: sq. → following]] of the [[abbrev: ed. → edition]] [[abbrev: min. → minor]]. Moreover, [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] [[abbrev: infr. → below]] [[abbrev: cap. → chapter]] 14 and Proclus on the *Alcibiades* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 100 [[abbrev: sub. fin. → near the end]] and the Scholiast on Dionysius Thrax [[abbrev: ibid. → ibid.]] [[abbrev: p. → page]] 332 [[abbrev: lin. ult. → last line]].

— 15. οἷον καὶ τὰ μουσικὰ τῶν ζώων—τὴν ζωὴν ἔχει [as even musical animals—possess life]] If you again consider ἐνδέχοιτο [it might be possible], the reading ἔχειν [to have] is not bad, which could easily have been corrupted by scribes who did not consider this. Aristotle also professes that some animals are delighted by song in *Politics* VIII. 6. 4; Plutarch, *Symposium* [[abbrev: lib. → book]] VII, Problem 5, [[abbrev: cap. → chapter]] 2, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 704 [[abbrev: sq. → following]], [[abbrev: p. → page]] 902 Wyttenbach: "It seems to me that not even Aristotle by just cause releases the pleasures concerning sight and hearing from incontinence, as being only human. For we see that other beasts also use and share in these by having a nature. For we see that many irrational animals are charmed by music, just as stags by pipes [[abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → and so forth]]." [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] Gellius, [[abbrev: N. A. → Attic Nights]] XIX. 2; Muretus on Aristotle’s *Nicomachean Ethics* III. 10. 7, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 110 [[abbrev: sq. → following]] Zell; and Gerhard Vossius *On Music* §. 11, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 14. But as the construction varies in this period, so no less in the following αὑτοῖς ἀφικνουμένων [arriving for themselves] (for so we corrected it, or you may prefer ἀφικομένων [having arrived]). After this word we have placed a major punctuation mark, deleting the comma after ἐλθοῦσιν [to those having come], following Ficino and Engelhardt.

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 56, 7. ζωὴν ἐξελιττομένην εἰς τέλος ἔχουσι [they have a life unfolding toward an end]] Elegantly said of plants, which by maturing are subsequently unfolded more and more. Concerning the various use of the verb, I add to those things which learned men collected in H. Stephanus’ *Thesaurus*, Zonaras’ *Lexicon* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 771 and Jacobs on Callistratus’ *Statues* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 728. Plotinus, however, frequents it. [[abbrev: Vid. → See]] [[abbrev: v. c. → for example]] III. 7. 5, III. 7. 10, III. 8. 7, IV. 8. 6, V. 3. 3, VI. 8. 18; and ἐξέλιξις [unfolding] V. 7. 3. In the [[abbrev: seqq. → following]], Ficino did not express that καὶ μὴ [and not] after ἐπὶ—εὖ παθεῖν [upon—faring well], although it appears in one Medicean codex. It is more lucid, however: εὖ παθεῖν, καὶ μὴ, καὶ καρπὸν αὑ [[abbrev: φ. κ. μ. φ. → φέρειν καὶ μὴ φέρειν]] [to fare well, and not, and to bear fruit and not bear]. Regarding the argument of this entire passage, there pertain those things which our philosopher discusses elsewhere concerning animals and plants, as in III. 4. 2, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 283 [[abbrev: sq. → following]], III. 8. 1, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 344 and IV. 4. 27 [[abbrev: sq. → following]], [[abbrev: p. → page]] 419 [[abbrev: sqq. → following]]; and what Marsilio [Ficino] appended here and there in his *Commentaries*, [[abbrev: v. c. → for example]] on this very book [[abbrev: p. → page]] 22, 23, 27 and [[abbrev: p. → page]] 340, where he also speaks everywhere concerning the sex of plants. Porphyry, *On Abstinence* I. [[abbrev: sect. → section]] 18, hesitantly says: "If, as they say, even plants have a soul," which was the opinion of the Egyptians; [[abbrev: vid. → see]] Rhoer on the [[abbrev: l. l. → place cited]] [[abbrev: p. → page]] 30. Likewise III. 19, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 258: "yet indeed to compare plants with animals is altogether forced; for the latter are by nature capable of sensation, and feeling pain, and fearing, and being harmed; therefore also of being treated unjustly; but for the former there is nothing sensible [[abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → and so forth]]." [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] III. 27, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 287. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 56, 15. ἀταραξία [imperturbability]] Epicurus said he sought this: "Wisdom, which vindicates us from the impulse of lusts and from the *terror of fears*." Cicero, *De Finibus* I. 14. 46 and Goerenz there; [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] I. 15. 49, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 68. Bake on the *Remains of Posidonius* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 225; and Baguet on Chrysippus [[abbrev: p. → page]] 316 [[abbrev: sq. → following]].

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 57, 5. καὶ ὅτι ἡδὺ—εἶναι [and that it is pleasant...]] He changed the order of the members not inelegantly. Because Ficino added: *before you perceive that it is sweet*, I would not therefore conclude that it is likewise found added in some [[abbrev: cod. → codex]]: τὸ ἡδὺ πρὸ τοῦ μὴ λανθάνειν [the pleasant before not being hidden]; but, as he very often does, he expanded Plotinian density even [[abbrev: h. l. → in this place]]. For neither the Medicean [codices] which Marsilio used acknowledge this addition. The next words ὥστε ἀγαθοῦ—τὸ ἔχον [so that of the good—the one having] word for word sound thus: "Therefore, when this good is and is present, already the possessor is in the 'well' (well-being)" (because he has that [[abbrev: sc. → namely]] good).

— 11. ἀντιλαμβανομένοις [perceiving/grasping]] A proper word for the senses, therefore now meaning *to feel, to perceive*, now *to enjoy*, to become a participant. Scholiast on Thucydides VII. 66: ἀντιλάβεσθε· instead of αἰσθάνεσθε [perceive]. Theodoret, [[abbrev: lib. → book]] V *On Providence*, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 458 in the [[abbrev: ed. → edition]] of Schulz: "and he perceives (ἀντιλαμβάνεται) smells." [[abbrev: Vid. → See]] also Fischer’s *Index to Aeschines’ Dialogues* under the word; Wetstein’s *New Testament* T. II, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 347. Add Proclus on the *Alcibiades* [[abbrev: pr. p. → especially page]] 300: "as many as rejoice in changes, in no way perceiving (ἀντιλαμβανόμενοι) the stable nature." Add furthermore these very Enneads IV. 3. 24 and 30, IV. 4. 23, VI. 9. 1. Because Engelhardt suspects a lacuna in the [[abbrev: seqq. → following]] οἷον αἰσθήσεως τοιούτου [as if of such a sensation], there is no trace in the [[abbrev: Codd. → Codices]], and Ficino rendered the passage clear enough by paraphrasing. He explains it thus in his Commentary: "But if they further say that the good is mixed from the condition (or essence) itself and the perception of this through the senses." Use Ficino’s Commentary for what follows as well. For we do not write philosophical commentaries on these Enneads—certainly not an *Iliad* after Homer—but, as far as can be prepared with the help of codices, we have instituted to help Plotinus by opening up the use of words and the character of his speech, and finally by designating sources and the opinions of other philosophers.

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 58, 9. ἐν τρανωτέρᾳ ζωῇ [in a clearer life]] Marsilio translates as *in a more whole life*. It ought to be *in a clearer (more articulate, more effective) life*. For τρανὸς is the same as τορὸς [piercing], διάτορος [distinct]. We have put more concerning [[abbrev: h. v. → this word]] in the notes to Proclus’ *Institutes of Theology* 145, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 214–216, these words, which we append because they pertain to our passage: "and the stone indeed participates in the purificatory power, only bodily; but the plant, even more clearly (τρανώτερον), according to life; but the animal has this form also according to impulse; the rational soul, rationally; the mind, intellectually; but the gods, super-essentially and unitarily."

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 60, 13. ἀντιδιῃρημένου—πρότερον—ὕστερον [divided against—prior—posterior]] Aristotle’s *Categories* [[abbrev: cap. → chapter]] 13 ([[abbrev: cap. → chapter]] 10 [[abbrev: al. → otherwise]]) §. 3: "And those things divided against each other from the same genus are said to be simultaneous in nature; and those are said to be divided against each other which are according to the same division. Such as the winged with the pedestrian and the aquatic. For these are divided against each other, being from the same genus; for animal is divided into these: the winged, the pedestrian, and the aquatic. And none of these is prior or posterior, but such things seem to be simultaneous in nature. And each of these might again be divided into forms, as the winged, the pedestrian, and the aquatic. Therefore those things also will be simultaneous in nature, as many as are from the same genus according to the same division." “And also those things which are subject to the same genus, as parts of it opposed among themselves, are said to be simultaneous by nature: as...

--- Page 28 ---
[[language: Latin with Greek passages]]

->BOOK IV. FIRST ENNEAD. p. 56—63. 21<-

...parts subject to a genus correspond to each other in turn; those which have proceeded from the same division of it; just as the volatile corresponds from the opposite side to the terrestrial and the aquatic: for since these are from the same genus, they are opposed among themselves in that division; for a living thing is divided into these, into volatile, terrestrial, and aquatic: nor is any of these prior to the others or posterior, but by nature such things seem to be simultaneous. Indeed, those individual things, as volatile, as terrestrial, as aquatic, can again be divided into certain species. Therefore it is evident that those things also are simultaneous by nature which, being subject to the same genus, are from the same division.” These are the words of the Stagirite [Aristotle], and it will be obscure to no one who reads this that he is being referred to by Plotinus in this place. [[abbrev: Cf. → Compare]] Aristotle, *Topics* 6; Stobaeus, *Eclogues* II. 7, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 54 Heeren; and Plotinus VI. 3. 10, VI. 3. 20; and ἀντιδιαίρεσις [reciprocal division] IV. 4. 28 end, VI. 3. 10.

— 17. τρανότητι—ἀμυδρότητι [by clarity—by obscurity]] More properly: *claritate—obscuritate*. Plotinus uses the adjective quite often. [[abbrev: Vid. → See]] [[abbrev: v. c. → for example]] [[abbrev: p. → page]] 54 D. ἀμυδρά τις ζωή [a certain dim life]; [[abbrev: p. → page]] 724, [[abbrev: cap. → chapter]] 33 [[abbrev: a. → a.]], [[abbrev: p. → page]] 725 A. ἀμυδρῶς [dimly], [[abbrev: p. → page]] 169 A. I have said more about this word in the notes to the book *On Beauty*, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 247 [[abbrev: sq. → following]]. Now I will add an example of the noun from another philosopher of this family. Proclus on the *Alcibiades* [[abbrev: pr. p. → especially page]] 96: "the 'almost' seems to me to signify the obscurity (ἀμυδρότητά) of the natural virtues."

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 61, 2. ἐπιλείπει τὸ εὐδαιμονεῖν [happiness fails]] Ficino placed the last two little words outside the parenthesis, with Engelhardt’s approval. We do not change such things without books. The same man hesitates at μηδενὶ [in nothing], which all the books acknowledge, but by their command we have given ἐλλείπει [is deficient] instead of ἐπιλείπει [fails].

— 5. ἐπακτὸν [brought in/adventitious]] Concerning the use of this word, it was spoken above at I. 2. 1. Furthermore, because at the end of the chapter ἰνδάλματα [images/apparitions] is used just like the verb ἰνδάλλεσθαι [to appear] (Ruhnken on Timaeus’ *Platonic Lexicon* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 150), it is very frequently used by philosophers of this family. Look only at the *Greek Index to Plotinus* and the *Greek Index of the Principles of Platonic Philosophy and Theology* of our [[abbrev: ed. → edition]]. To this entire chapter apply the Commentary of Ficino.

— 16. τὸ εὐδαιμονεῖν [to be happy]] *Felicitatem* Ficino. Rather: *to be blessed*. [[abbrev: Vid. → See]] the beginning of the book.

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 62, 10. περικεῖσθαι δ᾿ αὐτῷ [and to be placed around him]] A locution transferred from the matter of clothing and used especially by the Stoics, by which they wish it declared that the body and other external things indeed surround us, but do not properly pertain to our soul. Hence Marcus Antoninus XII. 3: περικείμενον σωμάτιον, *the little body surrounding you*, and similarly elsewhere. [[abbrev: Vid. → See]] Gataker on VIII. 27, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 247. Seneca, *Epistle* 92: "Nature has surrounded the soul with the body as with a garment. It is its covering." Paul, *Epistle to the Hebrews* [since he himself also is surrounded with weakness [[abbrev: C. 5. v. 2. → Chapter 5 verse 2]]]. Schleusner did not correctly take this in his *Lexicon of the New Testament*. You should consult Valckenaer’s *Epistle to Roever* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 54 and his *Scholae on the New Testament* II, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 486. More expressively Proclus on the *Alcibiades* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 257: "having put on such bodies and having been surrounded by such bonds and having been hedged in by such change," where [[abbrev: vid. → see]] our [[abbrev: annot. → notes]].

— 14. Μαρτύριον δὲ τούτου [And a testimony of this]] Engelhardt wishes it punctuated thus: "And a testimony of this, is its being," [[abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → and so forth]] *The testimony of what we say is the very being* (or condition of this man). Not bad. You might nevertheless also take it as if it were written: "the being of this thing is a testimony": *The condition/status of this man is the argument*.

— 17. ὁ βίος—ζωὴν ἔχοντι [the life—to one having life]] Here you would gain nothing from the common distinctions of the Grammarians, of Ammonius under βίος [[abbrev: p. → page]] 32 ([[abbrev: p. → page]] 30), of the Antiatticist in Bekker’s *Greek Anecdotes* I, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 83. [[abbrev: Vid. → See]] however Valckenaer on Ammonius and the [[abbrev: interprr. → interpreters]] on Thomas Magister under βιοῦν [to live] [[abbrev: p. → page]] 153. In this place βίος [life/way of life] is the condition as a form, which refers to ζωὴν [biological life] as a genus. To be held for this passage and for the preceding things concerning τελειότητι [perfection] is the definition of blessedness among the Platonic ones which are found in the *Definitions* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 412 D: "Happiness, a good composed from all good things; a power self-sufficient for living well; perfection according to virtue, the self-sufficient utility of a living thing." Engelhardt however hesitates at the words: κἂν σπουδαῖος ᾖ [even if he be excellent]. The codices vary nothing.

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 63, 2. σώματι, τὰ αὑτοῦ ζῶντι [to the body, living its own things]] To the body, which lives its own life for itself. Because Ficino translates τοῦ τοιούτου ἀνθρώπου [of such a man] as *of the inner man*, he seems to have done it for the sake of clarity, and thus far not badly. In the manuscript books there is no variant reading.

— 7. οἶδε τὸν θάνατον, ὅ, τι ἐστίν [he knows death, what it is]] *On attraction*, it being common, it would be trite to speak. For the argument compare Plato’s *Gorgias* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 524 [[abbrev: b. → b.]]; *Phaedo* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 64 [[abbrev: c. → c.]].

— 11. Ἀλγηδόνες [Pains]] In this chapter Plotinus refers especially to the Peripatetic opinions concerning the...

--- Page 29 ---
[[language: Latin with Greek passages]]

22 ->ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS<-

...blessed life, with whom a part of the Academics and Pythagoreans agreed. Regarding these, see [[abbrev: v. c. → for example]] the passages of Archytas in Stobaeus’ *Florilegium* Title I. 70–81, [[abbrev: vol. → volume]] I, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 38–47 Gaisford. Concerning the Academics [[abbrev: vid. → see]] Cicero, *Academics* II (IV) 42 § 131. The primary place for the Peripatetics is provided by Aristotle himself in *Nicomachean Ethics* VII. 13. Sextus Empiricus, *Outlines of Pyrrhonism* III. 180, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 171 Fabricius: "some of the philosophers say there are three kinds of goods, such as the Peripatetics; for of these some are around the soul, such as virtues; others around the body, such as health and the like; others are external, such as friends, wealth, and similar things." Add Stobaeus’ *Eclogues* II. 7. Moreover, ἀλγηδὼν [pain] was frequented especially by Epicurus, as was ἀλγεῖν [to be in pain], yet not unknown to the Socratics. Xenophon, *Memorabilia* I. 2. 5; Plato in the *Philebus* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 42, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 126 Stallbaum; Menage on Diogenes Laertius X § 139; and hence solemn in designating this matter. To the places cited in Stephanus’ *Thesaurus*, add Theodorus Metochita’s *Miscellanea* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 212, 246, 276, 284, 365; Proclus on the *Alcibiades* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 58 of our [[abbrev: ed. → edition]]: "for just as we are trained toward pleasures, so also toward pains (ἀλγηδόνας)."

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 63, 15. τὰς πολυθρυλλήτους Πριαμικὰς τύχας [the much-talked-of Priam-like fortunes]] Priam was frequented in tragic personages and in stage matters. Hesychius II. 1020 and Alberti there. But Plotinus refers to Aristotle, who in the *Nicomachean Ethics* I. 10. 14 says: "but if it is so, the happy man would never become wretched, yet not indeed blessed, if he should fall into Priam-like fortunes." And that word πολυθρυλλήτους [much-talked-of] sufficiently proves that the fates of Priam were no less a common trope in the books of philosophers than the bull of Phalaris, mentioned below. A passage of Cicero on the last days of Priam, which appears in the *Tusculans* I. 35, also serves as an argument. A Scholion of the Marcian Codex B indicated the proverbial force which had grown in the name of Priam. He who desires more may consult the learned animadversion of Wyttenbach in Plutarch’s *Consolatio ad Apollonium* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 758 [[abbrev: sq. → following]] of the Oxford [[abbrev: ed. → edition]] in octavo [[abbrev: form. → format]].

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 64, 3. ψυχὴν τοιάνδε—σώματος φύσιν [such a soul—nature of the body]] The Peripatetics were not the first to insist on this, but before them the Pythagoreans also. Archytas [[abbrev: ap. → in]] Stobaeus’ *Florilegium* Title I § 76, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 43 Gaisford: "but man is not soul alone, but also body; for the living thing from both, and the man from such things. For even if the body is by nature the organ of the soul, yet it is also a part for the man, both this and the soul [[abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → and so forth]]."

— 5. αἱ—πείσεις [the—affections/experiences]] Gataker teaches that this is quite frequently used simply for the word πάθη [passions/affections] in Marcus Antoninus [[abbrev: p. → page]] 76 [[abbrev: sq. → following]] and [[abbrev: p. → page]] 202. [[abbrev: Cf. → Compare]] the Plotinian passages II. 9. 14, III. 1. 4, V. 9. 10, and everywhere.

[[abbrev: ib. → ibid.]] πρὸς αὑτὸν ἀναφέρονται [they are referred to himself]] Ficino translates: "they are transferred to the *soul* itself"; and so also Taylor. But then it ought to have been read αὑτὴν [to herself], which appears in no book. Therefore it must be referred to the man. Hippodamus of Thurii also compares the blessedness of the gods with the condition of men in a fragment *On Happiness* in Stobaeus’ *Florilegium* Title 103 § 26, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 339 [[abbrev: sq. → following]] Gaisford.

— 10. προσθήκην—λαβοῦσι [having taken—an addition]] We touched on this above at I. I. 4.

— 11. ὃ—καὶ θάτερον καὶ κρεῖττον [which—is both other and better]] These later words are added by epegenesis, as if Plotinus were saying: although it is different and more excellent. Ficino studied to help the more hindered construction by a transposition of the members.

— 16. Ἀλλ᾿ εἰ μὲν [[abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → and so forth]] [But if indeed...]] After Plotinus has set forth the opinions of his adversaries, he now proceeds to refute them. Which a learned reader wished indicated in the margin of Marcian Codex B. [[abbrev: Cf. → Compare]] also Ficino’s Commentary.

— 18. ἐν τῇ τοῦ ἀληθινοῦ ἀγαθοῦ κτήσει [[abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → in the possession of the true good...]] You may recognize a follower of Plato in these. For he professes this everywhere. [[abbrev: Vide → See]] only book VIII of the *Laws*, from which Stobaeus took a passage for the title on blessedness (*Florilegium* T. 103 § 30, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 347 Gaisf. cf. Plato’s *Laws* VIII, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 829, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 76 Bekker); the *Philebus* (for which consult Baumgarten-Crusius’ *Dissertation on the Platonic Philebus*, Leipzig, 1816, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 4 [[abbrev: sqq. → following]] and Stallbaum’s *Prolegomena to the Philebus* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 23 [[abbrev: sq. → following]]). To τοῦτο [this] understand τὸ εὐδαιμονεῖν [to be happy].

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 65, 1. κρίνειν—ζητεῖν [to judge—to seek]] Engelhardt translates: "to command the happy man to seek other things," which is not necessary, and I would believe that if the writer had wished this, he would rather have given τῷ εὐδαίμονι—ζητητέον εἶναι [it must be sought by the happy man]. Taylor expressed these things less accurately.

— 2. Εἰ μὲν γὰρ συμφόρησις [[abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → For if indeed an accumulation...]] These words were to be translated verbatim thus: "For if blessedness were an accumulation of goods both necessary and not necessary, but which are nevertheless themselves called good, it would be necessary to study to prepare these things also ([[abbrev: s. → namely]] it would be necessary for us to give labor so that these things also might be present)."

— 4. τὸ τέλος ἔν τι—οὐ πολλά [the end is one thing—not many]] [[abbrev: Cf. → Compare]] Cicero, *De*...

[[language: Latin with Greek passages]]

->BOOK IV. FIRST ENNEAD. p. 63—67. 23<-

...*Finibus* everywhere, and [[abbrev: vid. → see]] Goerenz on him [[abbrev: p. → page]] 582.

— 7. ἐγκολπίσασθαι [to take into the bosom/embrace]] [[abbrev: Vid. → See]] Alciphron’s *Epistles* I. 18, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 95 Wagner; Sylburg on Dionysius of Halicarnassus T. VI, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 964; Schaefer in the *Index to Dionysius on Composition* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 149; Plutarch, *On Garrulity* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 508 D, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 48 Wyttenbach [[abbrev: ed. → edition]] [[abbrev: minor. → minor]]: "—rather indeed, just as reptiles having taken secret words into the bosom." [[abbrev: Vid. → See]] also Suicer’s *Ecclesiastical Thesaurus* under ἐγκόλπιος. Plotinus however [[abbrev: h. l. → in this place]] uses it of intimate appropriation and conjunction, and indeed metaphorically of the soul, which meaning of the word is to be recorded in the Lexicons.

[[abbrev: ib. → ibid.]] Ἡ δὲ ζήτησις αὕτη—ἢ καὶ προσλαμβάνων (ζητεῖ) [And this seeking—or also taking in (he seeks)]] As I did not grasp the passage, I left it intact. Engelhardt goes on to explain it thus: The will, which tends toward common goods, does not therefore reject the study of true blessedness (so that it might be in the happy man himself—ἐν τούτῳ εἶναι). For the inner nature of man always desires and follows the highest things; but reason, reflecting, turns away that which displeases it and hinders him, while conversely it chooses and adopts for itself that which pleases and agrees with it—He adds that ζήτησιν [seeking] and βούλησιν [willing] in [[abbrev: h. l. → this place]] are the study of common goods, as opposed to ἔφεσιν [appetition], the seeking of the end (τοῦ τέλους, the supreme good).

— 9. ἀποικονομούμενος [disposing/ridding oneself of]] In most books it is explained in the margin as ἀποσκευαζόμενος [[abbrev: i. e. → that is]], turning away from oneself, rejecting, repudiating. For it is opposed [[abbrev: h. l. → in this place]] to προσλαμβάνων [taking in], elsewhere to προσιέμενος [admitting]. Concerning the verb ἀποσκευάζεσθαι, which is properly to lay down vessels, to remove instruments or utensils, to make oneself unencumbered, and thus to throw away or reject, I have spoken in Proclus’ *On the Alcibiades* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 38, who uses it quite often, even in this sense. [[abbrev: Vid. → See]] [[abbrev: ibid. → ibid.]] [[abbrev: p. → page]] 41, 44 and *Institutes of Theology* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 312. Lexicographer in Bekker’s *Anecdotes*: ἀποσκευαζόμενος· throwing away, casting off, stripping. [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] Hesychius [[abbrev: in voc. → under the word]]; Schleusner’s *Lexicon of the New Testament* [[abbrev: in voc. → under the word]] and Valckenaer on the New Testament I, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 584. ἀποικονομεῖσθαι is rarer. Yet philosophers use it: [[abbrev: v. c. → for example]] [[abbrev: ap. → in]] Stobaeus’ *Eclogues* II. 7, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 214 Heeren: "—as far as he honored this (virtue), he would rid himself (ἀπῳκονομεῖτο) of vice." Plotinus himself, V. 9. 1, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 555 B: "and pursuing the one, they lived ridding themselves (ἀποικονούμενοι) of the other." And Alexander of Aphrodisias, *On the Soul* II, opposes τὴν ἐκλογὴν [selection] and τὴν ἀποικονομίαν [ridding/disposal]. Whence it is established that the Lexicographers do not correctly doubt this power of the verb, which we have just confirmed with examples.

— 12. οὐ βούλησις [not will]] Clearly according to the *Definitions* attributed to Plato [[abbrev: p. → page]] 413 C: "Will is a desire with right reason; a reasonable appetite; a natural appetite with reason." These things seem by no means to favor Engelhardt’s explanation, which we leave for now in the middle [undecided].

— 17. ἀνωδυνίᾳ [freedom from pain]] Because Ficino translates this word as *indolentiam*, in that he followed the authority of Tully [Cicero]. [[abbrev: Vid. → See]] *De Officiis* III. 3; *De Finibus* II. 4, II. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 128 Goerenz and the [[abbrev: interprr. → interpreters]] there.

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 66, 1. *Ἃ δὲ παρόντα [[abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → And those things which being present...]] The construction would become smoother if it were written—ζητεῖται. Εὔλογον οὖν ἀναγκ. [is sought. Reasonable therefore necessary]. Marsilio expressed that.

— 6. Διὰ τὰ—ταῦτα [Because of—these things]] [[abbrev: sc. → namely]] τὰ ἀναγκαῖα [the necessary things], which Plotinus just now distinguished from *goods* (ἀγαθοῖς).

— 7. οὐχ ὅτι πρὸς τὸ εὐδαιμονεῖν [not that for the sake of being happy]] Engelhardt conjectured: παρὸν πρὸς τ. ε. [present for...]. But παρὸν is altogether of no value [[abbrev: h. l. → in this place]], nor did Ficino express it, whom Taylor followed, as he is accustomed.

— 11. ἢ ὃ ὅταν παρῇ [or that which when it is present]] It seems that from these words our philosopher begins the refutation of those thinking otherwise, whose arguments he had hitherto set forth. So also Engelhardt and Taylor seem to take the passage. Therefore, from the traces of the codices you might conjecture ἤτοι [surely] or rather καίτοι (*but indeed*, *but truly*, or *and yet*) ὅταν παρῇ.

— 16. οὐδέν τι [not at all]] *Nothing whatever, not in the least*, regarding which Xenophontic and also Platonic use [[abbrev: vid. → see]] Heindorf on Plato’s *Phaedo* § 28, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 42 and *Xenophontic Lexicon* III, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 356. Krabinger on Synesius’ *On the Kingdom* [[abbrev: cap. → chapter]] 3, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 146. Similarly οὐδέν τι μᾶλλον [nothing more] is joined. [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] Heindorf on the *Phaedo* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 137.

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 67, 1. καὶ οὐδενὸς—ἐξηρτημένον [and suspended from nothing]] *Nor suspended any longer from any of the lower things*. Concerning this force of the words ἀπαρτᾶσθαι and ἐξαρτᾶσθαι [[abbrev: v. → see]] Wyttenbach on Plutarch [[abbrev: p. → page]] 717 of the [[abbrev: ed. → edition]] [[abbrev: min. → minor]].

— 4. οὐδ᾿ εἰ ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ γ. [nor if it happened by him]] Even if he himself be the author of the same things. There was no reason why Engelhardt should hesitate at these, or why Taylor should omit them. Soon after: πόλεως αὐτοῦ κατασκαφὴν [the razing of his city] Ficino ought to have translated: *the razing of his (native) city*. Aeschylus, *Seven against Thebes* 46: "or having placed razings upon the city." Aeschines *Against Ctesiphon* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 76, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 544 Reiske. **ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

[original page 24]

**p. 67, 8. καὶ, νὴ Διὰ, θανάτους θνητῶν**] i.e., *and even more so the deaths of mortals.* A formula placed at the end of several nouns or verbs intends to intensify their force, as in **καὶ δὲ, καὶ γε δὴ**, according to the teaching of Wyttenb. [Wyttenbach] ad Plut. Mor. p. 506. ed. min. [minor edition].

— **9. δόγμα περὶ—ζωῆς—εἶναι**] Cic. Tuscc. I. 47 and 48. The judgments of the immortal gods are often brought forward in the schools concerning death—*that not being born is by far the best thing for man, and the next best is to die as soon as possible*, where see [vid.] Davis. Herodotus I. 31. **διέδεξέ τε ἐν τούτοισι ὁ θεὸς, ὡς ἄμεινον εἴη ἀνθρώπῳ τεθνάναι μᾶλλον ἢ ζώειν.** [And the god showed in these things that it was better for a man to be dead than to live.] Cf. [compare] the interpreters [interprr.] of Sext. Empir. Pyrrh. Hypotyp. III. 24. 231. p. 186. **ἔνιοι δὲ καὶ βέλτιον εἶναι τὸ ἀποθανεῖν τοῦ ζῆν ἡμᾶς ὑπολαμβάνουσιν.** [Some also suppose that to die is better for us than to live.] Fabricius will provide more on this passage. Add Plutarch. Consol. ad Apollon. p. 106, 108 and Wyttenb. Animadvv. on him, p. 726–730. ed. min. and the recently edited Theod. Metochita, who in chapter 58 of his *Miscellanea*, p. 339 sqq. [and following] ed. Müller and Kiessling, disputes in the opposite direction.

— **11. ἀλλ’ εἰ μὴ—σαπείη**] Plotinus may seem to have looked back to that saying of Theodorus of Cyrene in Plut. de Vitios. p. 499. D. p. 9. ed. Wytt. **καὶ τί Θεοδώρῳ μέλει, πότερον ὑπὲρ γῆς ἢ ὑπὸ γῆς σήπεται;** [And what does it matter to Theodorus whether he rots above ground or under the ground?] Which Seneca expressed thus in *de Tranquill.* cap. 14: “O foolish you, if you think it matters whether I putrefy above the earth or beneath it.” Cicero is slightly different in *Tuscc.* I. 43, where see Davis. Aristotle attributes a similar saying to Anaxarchus the physicist in his *Chriae* according to Stob. Flor. Tit. VII. p. 88. § 30. p. 207. Gaisford: **ἐμοὶ δὲ οὐδὲν διαφέρει ὑπὲρ γῆς ἢ κατὰ γῆς σήπεσθαι.** [To me it makes no difference whether I rot above the earth or beneath it.] I have also set these down so that the variety in the use of prepositions might be understood.

— **13. τῆς μικρολογίας**] Ficinus [Fic.] took this as an exclamation, as if the philosopher added it indignantly. He who recently appended **ὑπὸ** in Cod. Mon. C. [Codex Monacensis] joined it with **οὐκ ἀξιωθείς.** This reasoning also pleased Engelhardt, provided, however, that he believed an ellipsis of the particle **ἕνεκα** was present. Taylor followed Ficinus. For the rest, concerning the size of sepulchral monuments being restricted by laws among both the Greeks and Romans, see Cicero *de Legg.* II. 26. 64. 65. and the interpreters there, p. 363. sq. ed. Moser. and our own. But if it be credible that in the following parts Plotinus expressed a saying of some ancient Philosopher, it would be proper to read **πάρ τοι** for **πάρεστί σοι.** For the former is read twice in good books in Diog. Laërt. III. 22. in the Doric epistle of Archytas. See Bast and Schäfer on Greg. de Dialect. § 20. p. 258. sq. Then the interpretation would be **πάντῃ ἐστὶν ὁδὸς**, transferred from the margin into the text. Now, however, "hand off the tablet" [meaning: I shall stop here].

— **14. ἐξιέναι**] Taylor correctly: *he possesses a power of freeing himself by death.* For the philosophers, especially and primarily the Stoics, use **ἐξιέναι, ἐξελθεῖν, ἀπελθεῖν** simply for "to die." See Gataker on M. Antonin. V. 29. p. 164. Our author used the last verb below, and in this passage he must be thought to speak entirely according to the mind of the Stoics. This sentiment pertains to the doctrine of **εὐλόγῳ ἐξαγωγῇ**, or the rational exit from this life, when reason suggests that the wise man should inflict death upon himself. We shall see concerning this matter in the ninth book of this Ennead, which was written on this subject. To this also belongs that phrase at the end of this chapter **ἀπελθεῖν καὶ εὐλόγως vel ἀλόγως μένειν.** [To depart reasonably or to stay unreasonably.] Next, Ficinus ought to have translated **υνοὶ** [likely an OCR error for *nurus* or similar Greek] as *daughters-in-law*. The following parts bring to mind Cicero, who in *Tuscc.* I. 36 says: “These things are escaped by death, even if they have not happened, yet because they can happen; but men do not think that these things can happen to them.”

**p. 68, 10. ἀναρτήσεται**] To Engelhardt, it seems that Ficinus read **ἀναχήσεται.** But in none of our codices is there a trace of that reading, and we have even compared those which Ficinus used. He gave this, doubtless, for the sake of elegance. Properly it ought to be: He will not be rendered suspended by the prosperity or adversity of others.

— **13. οἷον ἐν λαμπτῆρι φῶς**] Assume **ἔσται** from the preceding. Ficinus, according to his custom, expanded it, translating *it will shine continually*. This passage reminds one of the Empedoclean verses in Aristotle *de Sensu* cap. 2: [Greek passage describing a lantern protecting a flame from winds, allowing the light to shine through]. See *Empedocl.* Sturzii p. 525 and p. 618. sqq. A **Λαμπτὴρ** [lampter], moreover, was a lantern, sometimes bronze, iron, or wood, sometimes horn, which would contain a torch and other things shining from afar, and thus was also suspended in harbors and city towers to provide a wide prospect. See Timæus *Lex. Platon.* p. 172. and Ruhnk. there. Pollux X. 116. and Hemsterh. there. Toup. on Longinus...

**BOOK IV. OF THE FIRST ENNEAD. p. 67—69.**

I wished to advise on this word, since I lack examples of its use (**ὅμως with μὴ**) in Hoogeveen himself *de Particulis* p. 416. sqq. ed. Schutz.

**p. 69, 3. Καὶ τοῦτο μαρτυρεῖ κ. τ. λ.**] Engelhardt thinks the passage, which he calls very difficult, should be restored thus: [Greek textual reconstruction]. But truly he ought to have moved away from the footsteps of Ficinus, who, by not attending to the force of the tenses in **ἀποθανόντων**, caused confusion. There is no need for us to expound on the different meaning of the tenses of this verb after Wyttenbach's discussions on Plato's *Phaedo* p. 142. sqq. The main point is that Plotinus does not mean imminent death, but that which has already occurred. Nor did Plotinus write **τεθνηκότων**, which would also pertain to those who had been dead for a long time, but **ἀποθανόντων**, which signifies those who have just now ceased to live. Simplicius in *Aristotel. Phys.* VI. p. 129. b. **σημαίνει δὲ τὸ μὲν ἀπέθανε τὴν πρώτην ἀπὸ τοῦ ζῆν μεταβολήν.** [The word 'died' signifies the first change from living.] Which meaning is more significant here. For our philosopher means: provided those sad things do not fall within the span of our life, if they follow immediately upon our death, this pertains nothing to us. Furthermore, the sudden change of construction between **ὅταν ἡγώμεθα** and **τιθεμένων** should not seem strange in this writer at least. The whole passage, based on the trust of the best books and with the punctuation slightly changed, should be translated thus: “which very thing (namely, the weakness of our mind) this proves: if we consider it a gain that (those mournful things) are hidden from us, and likewise if we count it a gain provided those things (mournful events) happen after we have departed our day, certainly not looking to (caring for) what concerns them (who suffer as survivors), but what concerns ourselves (**τὸ αὑτῶν**), so that we are not afflicted. But this is our weakness, which it behooves us (**δεῖ**) to prune away, and not, by neglecting it (and thus allowing it to grow strong), to fear lest (something inconvenient) happen.” Well known are the poems of the Tragedians proclaiming those happy who by their death anticipated both their own and others' adversities, as in Aeschylus *Sept. adv. Theb.* 327. sq. where Blomfield will provide more. Cicero says much on the same matter in *Tuscc.* I. 35. sqq., who says there of Pompey: “Who, if he had died then, would have died in the most ample fortune; what great and incredible calamities he drank in by the extension of his life.” Yet Plotinus seems to touch primarily on those philosophers who follow that saying of Epicharmus or Sophron: **ἀπῇ θανεῖν ἢ τεθνάν᾽ οὐ μοι διαφέρει** (*I do not wish to die, but to be dead I count as nothing*): in Sext. Empir. *adv. Math.* I. 273. and § 283. and in Cic. in *Tuscull.* I. 8. where see Davis; among which followers Epicurus was prominent, who, placing the blessed life in tranquility and pleasure, likewise contended **ὅτι ὁ θάνατος οὐδὲν πρὸς ἡμᾶς** [that death is nothing to us], or as Lucretius sings III. 842: “Nothing, therefore, is death, nor does it concern us a bit.” In which matter Plotinus notes especially that vice which commonly goes by the name of **φιλαυτίας** [self-love], when, as contemners of other men, we use that celebrated French saying: *Après moi le déluge.*

Nor are these metaphors or similes unknown to the sacred writers. See the interpreters on the Epistle of Paul to Timothy...

I have disputed more on the use of these words in the more extensive *Annott. in Plotin. de Pulcrit.* (at p. 57. A. Univers.* vol. I. p. 646. ed. alter. and Tiedemann *de Artium Magicarum Origine* p. 33. sqq. [add C. F. de Cauz. de Cultibus Magicis. Platon. *Alcib.* I. p. 122. and others—And after both the name and the arts of the **μάγων** had occupied the Roman world, writers declared almost nothing of enchantments and deceptions except by this word. Hence those explanations of the Lexicographers, such as Zonaras: **γόης· ὁ πλάνης, ὁ ἀπατεὼν, ὁ φαρμακεύς.** [A wizard: a wanderer, a cheat, a poisoner/sorcerer.] Thus **μάγος** is used indefinitely everywhere in Lucian, as in *Necyom.* p. 28. Bip. cf. also interpreters on *Acts of the Apostles* XIII. 6. Moreover, later writers also taught more subtly about the distinction between **μαγείας, γοητείας** and **φαρμακείας** in Eudocia in the *Violetum* p. 284.” Add the Venetian Scholia on the *Iliad* **α.** v. 86. For the rest, concerning Plotinus himself thinking he was being tested by magic arts, there is a remarkable passage in his *Life* written by Porphyry c. 10. p. 110. Fabric. For almost all Platonists were addicted to these opinions, just as were many most learned men who lived from the rebirth of letters up to the sixteenth century; and thus, if any are to be noted, certainly the Platonists are not the only ones to be noted.

Our passage is to be translated thus: *But all [the actions of a man endowed with virtue] are equally beautiful, and perhaps more beautiful the more they are surrounded by adverse fortunes.* For an honorable deed should be judged more honorable the more he who has undertaken to perform it must struggle against obstacles which adverse fortune throws in his way. [original page 29]

...17. “I could answer what Epicurus says, that the Wise Man, if he is scorched in the bull of Phalaris, will exclaim: It is sweet, and pertains nothing to me.” cf. Aristot. *Eth.* VII. 13 and Tully in *Tuscull.* V. 9. where concerning Theophrastus' saying: *that the blessed life does not mount the wheel*, and vid. Olympiodor. in *Alcib.* pr. p. 230. Engelhardt considers the following parts to be lacunose. In the written books there is no trace that anything has fallen out here. No one will deny that the passage is obscure, yet it seems it can be rendered somewhat clearer by this one observation alone: that in this whole book Plotinus distinguishes as much as possible between men as they usually are, who place that Blessed state even in external things, and those whom he calls **σπουδαίους** [virtuous/earnest], and who have separated their mind (i.e., *themselves*, as he said at the end of cap. 9) from all external things. Those common men, therefore, are present, for example, in the bull of Phalaris, and when they judge the state of him who is included in it; these (i.e., those endowed with virtue) are absent.

**p. 75, 1. συναμφότερον**] Namely **ψυχὴν καὶ σῶμα** [soul and body], about which there was discussion above at I. 1. in the Question: *what is the animal, what is the man.*

**ib. ἡ τῶν λεγομένων**] Which are commonly called, but truly are not. — **3. Τὸ δὲ καθόσον ἀξιοῦν**] Engelh. thinks Ficinus read **τὸ δὲ ἀξιοῦν ἐν τῷ ζῴῳ τὴν εὐδ. ε.** omitting **καθόσον**, which he himself could not digest; and so he also omitted it. But our books all acknowledge it to a man, and the passage is to be explained thus: As to what pertains *to the extent that*, i.e., But if it is asked *to what extent* happiness exists, namely in quantum it pertains (whether to the body, or to the soul, or to both, or to the animal), it would be ridiculous for the same to pertain to the soul.

— **7. τὸ εὐδαιμονεῖν τοῦτο**] That being blessed is already known to us, or about which it is already agreed between us. Cf. Heindorf on Platon. *Phædon.* § 38. p. 60. That Plotinus immediately scorns the **εὐεξίαν** [fitness] and the size of the body, he treats more fully in III. 4. 2. p. 284, where he discusses the conversion of men into beasts. Which passage Philoponus touched upon in *Aristot. de Anima* I. 4: [Greek quote: "Wherefore Plotinus said most divinely that those who act madly according to the nutritive powers run the risk of being turned into trees."] As we Germans use *baumstarke Menschen* [strong as a tree]. This Plotinian point is congruent with the Pythagorean discipline, about which Porphyry says much in *de Abstinentia* and *de Vita Pythagorica*. For the rest, in this Plotinian passage which I just cited, **φυτικὸν** is also read, which confirms our emendation.

— **9. Ἀντισηκώσεως**] It is a medical term. Foësius in *Œcon. Hippocr.* p. 41: **ἀντισήκωσις** is also **ἀντιστάθμησις**, *equal weighing*, where there are also more things about the verb **ἀντισηκῶσαι.** Zonaras *Lex. Gr.*: **Ἀντισήκωσις, ἡ ἀνταπόδοσις, διόρθωσις, ἰατρεία**, where see Tittmann p. 185. Other things are supplied by Lennep on *Phalarid.* p. 187 and Blomfield on Aeschylus' *Persae* v. 443.

**p. 76, 2. νέος ὤν**] Cf. Our author I. 6. p. 52. E.

— **3. προσηνὲς**] here it is that which is **ἡδύ** [pleasant]. cf. Annot. on the cited passage of Plotinus in the singular edition of the book *de Pulcritudine* p. 192. Hesych. II. p. 1045., Zonar. *Lex. Gr.* p. 223. Foësii *Œcon. Hippocr.* p. 322. and other places.

— **16. οὐδὲ γὰρ ἂν πρὸς αὐλητικὸν τέλος κ. τ. λ.**] I have written thus on the authority of the MSS books. As for the meaning, Plotinus might have wished to touch upon the proverb: **αὐλητοῦ βίον ζῇς** [you live the life of a flute-player], which was said of those who lived off others according to Diogenianus *Center.* III. 14. p. 199 and Suidas I. p. 380. Nor would this sentiment be entirely alien to the mind of Plotinus, who would say the goal or end of flute-players belongs to those men who falsely persuade themselves that happiness is to be placed in alien or external things which are not contained in the mind itself. Engelhard...

--- Page 37 ---
**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

[original page 30]

...tus furthermore reminded of the verses read in Athenæus VIII. 337. e. p. 245. Schwgh: **ἀνδρὶ μὲν αὐλητῆρι θεοὶ νόον οὐκ ἐνέφυσαν** (vulg. **οὐκ ἐνεφ.** Casaub. **εἰσενεφ.**) **ἀλλ’ ἅμα τῷ φυσῇν χὠ νόος ἐκπέταται.** [To a flute-player the gods did not implant a mind, but at the same time as the blowing, the mind also flies out.] so that consequently men who attribute no value to the mind are said to follow the *flute-player's end*. It could also be that Plotinus had before his eyes the disputes of the philosophers, such as those of Taurus and Aristotle. Gellius XX. 4: “A wealthy young man, a disciple of the philosopher Taurus, kept as favorites and delights comedians, tragedians, and *flute-players*, free men. But artists of that kind are called in Greek **οἱ περὶ Διόνυσον τεχνῖται.** Taurus, wishing to lead the young man away from the fellowships and company of stage-folk, sent him these words copied from Aristotle's book, which is inscribed **προβλήματα ἐγκύκλια**; and ordered him to read them daily: *Why are the Dionysian artists for the most part wicked? etc.*” See Aristotle's *Problem.* XXX. 10. p. 220. Sylb. And that flute-players were in contempt among most Greeks, as they often had Phrygian and servile names (Athen. XIV. p. 624. b.), there is no need to show laboriously. And Plato wished the flute to be separated from education. Following his example, Platonic philosophers mostly condemned this instrument, as one which snatched away the mind and stirred various motions of the soul. See Platon. *de Republ.* III. p. 398. sq. *de Legg.* II. p. 669. sq. and cf. Proclus' disputes in Platonis *Alcib.* 68. p. 197. sq. ed. Francof. Someone might wish to take that **αὐλητικὸν τέλος** in such a way as those who have proposed for themselves to exhibit pleasure to others; on which matter a passage of Plutarch *An seni sit ger. resp.* p. 786. A. B. might apply. But the simplest, in my judgment at least, would be if we explain it thus: that that abundance of external goods does not contribute even to the end of those men who are at the furthest distance from the gravity of wise men: or, as Engelh. expressed it, they do not even contribute to carelessness, or a life entirely free from cares.

**p. 76, 17. μετὰ τῆς ἡμετέρας ἀσθενείας**] *From or for*, in designating an affect or form in which something is done or even the source from which something flows. See Schweigh. *Lex. Polyb.* p. 382. Schleusner's *Lex. N. T.* under **μετὰ** and Valcken. *Scholl. in N. T.* I. p. 575. coll. 366.

**p. 77, 3. οὕτω γὰρ καὶ ἀδεὴς ἔσται κ. τ. λ.**] These and the following remind one of the Chrysippean tenet in Plutarch *de Repugn. Stoic.* § 27. p. 1446. F. sq. A. p. 266. Wytt.: **οὐκ ἀεὶ ἀνδρίζεσθαι τὸν ἀστεῖον, οὐδὲ δειλαίνειν τὸν φαῦλον, τὸν μὲν ἐμμένειν ταῖς κρίμασιν (κρίμασι), τὸν δὲ ἀφίστασθαι :** “that a good man does not always act bravely, nor a vicious man always timidly: for it happens that when certain visions are presented, one persists in his judgment, the other does not.” Under which name Plutarch initiates a lawsuit against him there.

— **7. καὶ τὸν ἐν αὐτῷ—παῖδα**] Plotinus took this from Plato, who in the *Phaedo* p. 77. Steph. p. 45. Bekker. says: **ἀλλ’ ἴσως ἔνι τις ἐν ἡμῖν παῖς, ὅστις τὰ τοιαῦτα φοβεῖται, τοῦτον οὖν πειρώμεθα πείθειν μὴ δεδιέναι τὸν θάνατον ὥσπερ τὰ μορμολύκεια·** [But perhaps there is a child in us who fears such things; let us therefore try to persuade him not to fear death like bugbears.] what imitators and how many this passage found has been indicated by Ruhnken on *Tim. Lex. Plat.* p. 181 and Wyttenbach in *Annott. in Phædon.* p. 192. sq., who also in *Philomathia* III. p. 93, adding our passage, already saw that **παῖδα** should be read, where however **καταπαύσεις** is written incorrectly. That Ficinus recently added *majorem*, there is no trace of it in the books. Hence he must be thought to have added it by **περιφράζων** [periphrasing], as he often does.

— **9. οὐ μὴν—ἄφιλος οὐδὲ ἀγνώμων**] This latter Ficinus expressed as *alien from gratitude*, and Taylor follows him. On the contrary, Engelh. took it so that it is *harsh, rough*. To me, the force of it being *unjust* seems to fall best into this place. Moreover, those three meanings are used by good writers. See Pollux IV. 10. Hesych. I. 59. Alb. with the interpreters. *Lexicon Xenophont.* I. 38. Scholiast and interpreters on Sophocles' *Oedip. Colon.* 86 and Heyne on Epictetus' *Enchir.* XXIV. 3.

— **13. ἆρας θήσειε**] Opposites here respond to one another: **ἆρας θήσειε** and **κατάγοι.** “But if anyone should not place a good man *sublimely* (i.e., exalted) in the mind, but should *bring him down* to fortunes, etc.” Since some scribe did not follow this, he corrected it with an unlucky hand to **ἀριθμήσειε.** Nor did Engelh. follow the force of the passage.

— **15. οὔτε σπουδαῖον τηρήσει**] “Nor will he keep a good...

...man (i.e., endowed with virtue) reserved (i.e., he will keep him unhurt and intact).”

**p. 78, 1. ἐν τῷ κοινῷ**] In the common or mixed condition. Engelh. reminds of those things which Plotinus had disputed above in I. 1. 8. I. 1. 9. I. 1. 10.
