— **7. ἀλλ’ ὡς στοχαζόμενος κ. τ. λ.**] Engelh. thus: “but as one who has been turned to higher things, he will lead his life while external things are merely poured around him.” Taylor: *In every circumstance of being he will conjecture what is right.* This is indeed better. Attention must be paid to **καὶ**, which Ficinus did not neglect. The sense of the passage is this: “That good man, although he has a single and highest end, nonetheless, whenever a change in his affairs brings it about, will attend even to those things which are offered to him from without, and are as if poured around him.”

— **9. οὐ κωλυόμενος κ. τ. λ.**] This is “although a good man has been brought into this or that place and has a soul joined to the body, yet he does not have it enslaved to the same, but uses free will toward the body, in such a way, however, that he separates himself from it only at the just time of nature.” We shall place more on that sentiment below on I. 9 or on the little book **περὶ ἐξαγωγῆς** [on the exit/suicide].

— **14. οἷον εἰ μουσικὸς λύρας κ. τ. λ.**] Philosophers and the Fathers of the Church frequent this simile of the body and a musical instrument. Plutarch *Sept. Sapp. Conviv.* p. 163. E.: **ψυχῆς γὰρ ὄργανον τὸ σῶμα, θεοῦ δὲ ἡ ψυχὴ...** [For the body is the instrument of the soul, and the soul of God...] To which place Wyttenbach in *Animadvv.* p. 988. ed. min. contributed more. Marc. Antonin. X. 38. p. 315. sq. **καὶ τὰ ὄργανα ταῦτα τὰ περιπεπλασμένα** [and these instruments molded around us], to which Gataker gathered both other things and the words of the Apostle *Epist. Rom.* VI. 13 and indeed these of Gregory of Nyssa *de homin. opific.* cap. 12: **Καθάπερ τι μουσικὸν ὄργανον ἅπαν τὸ σῶμα δεδημιούργηται.** [Just as a musical instrument, the whole body has been created.] I shall add some passages, especially those which approach closer to the Plotinian simile. Therefore I omit many, such as that of Theodoret T. IV. p. 516. *Opp.* ed. Schulz, where man is called an **ὄργανον ἀρχέτυπον** [archetypal instrument] and T. V. 102. where he says **λύραν ἐκκλησιαστικὴν** [an ecclesiastical lyre]. I shall rather transcribe a passage from Nemesius *de Natura Hominis* p. 91 sq. Matthæi: [Greek passage comparing the soul's use of the body to a musician's use of a lyre; if the lyre is out of tune, the musician must correct it]. Jo. Chrysostomus *in Psalm.* XLI. p. 150. ed. Francof.: **ἐνταῦθα οὐ χρεία κιθάρας...** [Here there is no need of a kithara, nor of stretched strings, nor of a plectrum and art... but if you wish, you shall make yourself a kithara, having put to death the members of the flesh and having made much harmony for the body with the soul.]

**P. 84, 6. *Liber V.***] Since this book is the thirty-sixth in order, while the previous one or the fourth of this Ennead is the forty-sixth; a not so small interval of time seems to separate both. This inscription it has in Porphyry's Catalog *de Vita Plotini* cap. 24: **Εἰ μὲν παρατάσει χρόνου τὸ εὐδαιμονεῖν;** [Whether happiness consists in duration of time?] To which place, because I. A. Fabricius adds in our title: *al.* **ἐπίτασιν**, namely for **ἐπίδοσιν**: our MSS books are indeed ignorant of this variation. It seems to have crept into the memory of the most learned man from Diogenes Laërtius X. 121, where there is **εὐδαιμονία ἐπίτασιν οὐκ ἔχουσα.** Caspar Barth, however, in *Adversarr.* lib. L. cap. 8. p. 2347, prefixed these words to his own translation: “To me, a twelve-year-old boy among the exercises of Greek interpretation, there fell a translation of the most acute and subtle little book *Whether happiness is increased by time* in Plotinus; a most noble philosopher among those who, joining Platonic and Pythagorean wisdom in the last times of Rome, fashioned a certain new sect from the two mixed. I shall transcribe that translation here, lest it perish among the...

**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

[original page 32]

...sheets of papers, not because it is of great importance that it be preserved, but because even childish attempts delight us in a more advanced age. I shall not, however, guarantee the flaws of the work if anyone comes to accuse it; because I attribute so little to it that I would rather cast it away for the rest than defend it.” Thus says Barth, who seems not to have compared Ficinus' version with his own. Otherwise, in the inscription of the book, he would certainly have put *beatitude* for *happiness*. But not even Marsilius himself, as we saw above, is consistently constant with himself in using these words.—As for the argument of this book, no one is ignorant that this question, which the philosopher of Lycopolis treats in this book, was agitated already in antiquity. Ancient fame held that the Seven Sages had disputed on this matter. See Suidas and Photius in **Μᾶλλον Φρύξ.** Herodotus copiously exposed Solon's especially famed colloquy with Croesus (I. 32.), and Stobaeus inserted it into his *Florilegium* (Tit. 105. al. 103. p. 564. sq. p. 365. sqq. Gaisford.). Not a few passages of poets since Theognis fall closer to the opinion of Solon, some passages of which Jos. Barnes collected on Euripides' *Andromache* v. 100. See furthermore Pindar in *Pyth.* III. 189. and the Scholia on that place. The philosophers everywhere silently respect passages of the same colloquy, as Plato for example in *Hippia maj.* p. 291. D. and *de Legg.* VII. p. 802. a. p. 29. Bekk. Which things we do not dwell upon: those things ought rather to draw us, as being more closely joined with these Plotinian matters, which Aristotle brings forward for the sake of weakening Solon's opinion, who in *Eth. Eudem.* II. 1. p. 90 sq. Sylb. says thus: [Greek passage arguing that happiness is an activity and actuality, and cannot be a child or a single day; thus Solon's view that one should not be called happy until the end is wrong, because nothing incomplete is happy]. The same in the *Nicomachean Ethics*, in a copious passage on Goods and the Blessed I. 10, more fully examined the Athenian legislator's saying: which dispute should be read in his own work. Because Plotinus examines different tenets of the Philosophers in these questions, which Cicero also does in his books *de Finibus*, it will not be alien to transcribe a notable passage of his here: “No one therefore (he says II. 27. § 87. 88.) can be happy; *for a blessed life is not usually called so in some part, but in the perpetuity of time*: nor is it called a blessed life at all, unless finished and absolute, nor can anyone be happy at one time and miserable at another: for he who thinks he can be miserable will not be happy. For when a blessed life has once been undertaken, it remains as long as that wisdom itself, the effectress of the blessed life: nor does it wait for the last time of age; which Herodotus writes was taught to Croesus by Solon. But indeed, just as you were saying, *Epicurus denies that even duration of time brings anything to living blessedly, and that no less pleasure is perceived in brevity of time than if it were eternal.* These things are said most inconsistently. For since he places the highest good in pleasure, he denies that pleasure becomes greater in an infinite time of age than in a finite and moderate one. *He who places all good in virtue can say that a blessed life is perfected by the perfection of virtue. For he denies that a day brings increment to the highest good. But he who thinks that life is made blessed by pleasure, how will he be consistent with himself if he denies that pleasure grows with length of time? etc.*” Disputes of this kind were before the mind of Plotinus, as the argument of these Questions shows, although he never makes mention of Tully [Cicero]; for other sources were not lacking from which he might draw. For the rest, consult also Marsilius' Commentary.

**84, 10. Εἰ—λαμβάνει**] Cf. the Inscription **Περὶ τοῦ εἰ—λαμβάνει.** [Concerning whether...] It should be held once and for all for the use of Plotinus and other philosophers, especially of a later age, that **εἰ** is frequented among them both in oblique interrogation and indeed in direct interrogation. See Hoogeveen *de Particul.* p. 173. ed. Schutz. alt. cf. Eustath. on *Odyss.* A. 158 and Ast on Plat. *Remp.* V. 21. p. 478 in the comment, p. 532. Schweigh. where it is: **Εἰ ἔχομεν δεῖξαι;** [If we are able to show?] Similarly Plotinus IV. 8. 1. **Εἰ πᾶσαι αἱ ψυχαὶ μία;** [If all souls are one?]...

**BOOK V. OF THE FIRST ENNEAD. p. 84—86.**

[original page 33]

...and very often. That Latin writers imitate this in oblique speech, H. Stephanus already noted in the *Thesaurus*, with a Horatian example provided. You add these Ciceronian ones: *De Divinat.* II. 34. *Dícito, si pascuntur aves.* [Tell me if the birds are feeding.] The same in *Topicis* 22: “It is asked, *si* [if] riches are to be sought, *si* [if] poverty is to be fled.”

**p. 84, 12. καὶ ἡ ἐνέργεια τῆς ζωῆς**] Barth: “For the sum of Blessedness consists not in memory, but in affect. But the affect is found placed only in that which one enjoys in the present, and the action of life is occupied about the same.” Toward the same mind Engelh.: *These authorities, however, and the activity of life in general, have their real existence only in the present*: namely in such a way that we do not separate the last member from the previous ones, nor think: **καὶ ἡ ἐνέργειά ἐστι τῆς ζωῆς**, but that we join them: **ἡ δὲ διάθεσις καὶ ἡ ἐνέργεια τῆς ζωῆς ἐστιν ἐν τῷ παρεῖναι.** [But the disposition and activity of life is in the being present.] Correctly.

— **13. Εἰ δ’ ὅτι ἐφιέμεθα—μᾶλλον**] Barth: “On the contrary, if anyone, from the fact that a certain *hope and expectation(?)* of a *blessed(?) as if future* life always holds us, should say that it is *completed* in the future, we feel thus.” The former part is poorly done. Nor does any book confirm a sentiment of that kind: this latter part is better as to the sense. For, as Engelhardt correctly warns, who nevertheless is ignorant of Barth's interpretation, that **τυγχάνειν** of Plotinus has an attached force of *time, continuation*. For Plotinus denies that a good man *becomes* blessed: he says he *is* blessed.

— **16. ἔπειτα καὶ οἱ θεοὶ—οὐδέποτε τέλεον**] Epicurus distinguished the blessedness of gods and men by this very difference. Diog. Laërt. X. 121: **τὴν εὐδαιμονίαν διχῇ νοεῖσθαι...** “That happiness is understood in two ways: that supreme kind, such as belongs to god, which does not admit of increase (nor decrease); and the human kind, which has both addition and subtraction of pleasures.” Cf. below Quest. VII. p. 45. A. where our philosopher similarly on blessedness: **οὐκ ἄρα ἀριθμητέα χρόνῳ ἀλλ’ αἰῶνι.** [Therefore it must be numbered not by time but by eternity.] on which place I shall contribute more. Next, it differs nothing greatly as to the meaning whether you read **τεύξιν** [attainment] or **τοῦ εἶναι ἔξιν** [the possession of being], even in the judgment of Engelh. What pleased Barth can hardly be figured out; so much did he obscure both this passage and the next with many words. But we saw that the great man himself did not attribute much to this translation.

**p. 85, 5. τὸ ἐφεξῆς θέλει**] In this place Plotinus took a dish from his Plato's *Symposium*. For so Socrates says there: p. 200. p. 423. Bekker:—**ἴσως γὰρ ἄν τις ταῦτα οἰηθείη...** [For perhaps someone might think... "You, O man, possessing wealth and health and strength, wish also to possess these for the time to come, since in the present, whether you wish it or not, you have them."]

— **9. εἰ—τὸ ἀκριβέστατον εἶδε**] Barth: “By Pollux, if that longer time was given to him, in which according to his vow he had the sight and the completion. etc.” Engelh.: *If in the longer time he has seen something clearer and more distinct etc.* Which I wish to have noted because Ficinus' translation is ambiguous.

— **13. τὴν ἐνέργειαν τὴν ἀνεμπόδιστον**] Both Fic. and Barth translate: “the unimpeded action *of intelligence*,” namely so that they might render this passage more suitable for the Plotinian opinion concerning blessedness and more clear. Which very blessedness (**τὴν εὐδαιμονίαν**) he here accurately distinguishes from pleasure (**τῇ ἡδονῇ**).

— **15. πλέον**] Coraes on Heliodorus' *Ethiop.* VI. p. 198 wants the form **πλεῖον** to be used substantively and adjectivally, and **πλέον** adverbially for the most part.

**p. 86, 6. πλεονεκτεῖν αὐτοὺς τῷ παρόντι**] This construction of the word is rarer and perhaps unheard of among the ancients. Paul the Apostle uses it several times, but nevertheless with a different meaning, namely *of deceiving, of committing fraud*. See Bud. *Comm. L. Gr.* p. 838 and Schleusn. *Lex. N. T.* under **πλεονεκτεῖν.** There is however a place where with the force of *surpassing*, as here, it takes an accusative, e.g., in Heliodor. II. 44. p. 103. Coraii. **ἡ δὲ νῦν θεωρία καὶ πλεονεκτεῖ τὰς ἄλλας** [And the present contemplation even surpasses the others], where I wonder that nothing was warned by the editor; no more than at the passage of Plutarch in *Marcellus* p. 279 Francof. p. 466 Reisk. that the soldiers of Marcellus **διεστρατήγουν ὅσα πλεονεκτήσουσι τοὺς πολεμίους**, how much they excelled the enemies (or what great opportunities they were going to snatch). Suidas touched on that distinction III. p. 128 Kuster.

### PAGE 41
**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

**Πλεονεκτῶ** [I have more/prevail]: *to have more, with the genitive*; **Πλεονεκτῶ δὲ** [but I act unjustly] | p. 87, 3. **τὸ δὲ τῆς εὐδαιμονίας** [that which pertains to happiness]: i.e., happiness. A periphrasis especially familiar to Thucydides and Plato. Duker on Thucydides IV. 54, | **τὸ ἀδικῶ** [I do wrong], *with the accusative*. Furthermore, as Engelhardt rightly advises, Plotinus deliberately added these last words—Φ [from]—"in the present," to remove the error of those who, when they add *past* things to the notion of blessedness, believe it is increased. He urges, therefore, that only *presence* falls within the notion of beatitude. And Barthius, whose remaining remarks on this passage I do not dwell upon, expressed these final points more weightily thus: "this indeed which it has, is neither in the past, nor in the future, but in the present."

p. 86, 7. **Τί οὖν ὁ κακοδαίμων** [What then of the wretched man?]: With these and the following should be compared the arguments of Tullius [Cicero], especially against the Epicureans, in *De Finibus* II. 17. 88; II. 28. 92 sq.; II. 29. 94 sq. "Is any longest pain the most wretched, while it does not make pleasure more desirable than lasting ones?—What shall we say of pain? whose torments are so great that in them a blessed life cannot exist, if only pain is the highest evil. etc.—A method of neglecting pain is handed down by Epicurus. Now it is absurd itself that the greatest evil be neglected. etc.—If it is heavy, it is short; if it is long, it is light, are the dictates. Pain is accustomed to be mitigated by the remedies of virtue, greatness of soul, patience, and fortitude."

— 14. **ἡ τὸν μὲν χρόνον—μηκέτι ὄντα** [the time which... is no longer]: Ficinus translates: "time even not yet existing"; Barthius: "time not yet existing or that which has passed." Engelhardt also in this place: "time which is *no longer*, and that is more suited to what follows."

— 17. **τὸ μὲν γὰρ εὐδαιμονεῖν συμβεβηκέναι ἀξιῶ** [for I deem that being happy is a contingency/attribute]: Engelhardt: *For happiness must absolutely happen in order to be there.* Incorrect. For it ought to have been written *συμβαίνειν* [to happen], and *ἀξιῶ* [I deem] must be referred to the adversary who posed the preceding points. Ficinus is correct: "for he would judge that beatitude happened" (*censet* [he judges]). Nor is Barthius bad: "For thus he will record a happiness equal under time and contingency." In German you might explain it: *For he wants to apply the measure of the past event to happiness.*

— 18. **ὁ δὲ χρόνος—τὸ μηκέτι εἶναι** [but time... being no longer]: Again, not yet Ficinus [or] Barthius: "but time, which is imminent, you cannot define otherwise than that which it will happen to come." Better, in my judgment regarding the meaning of this passage, is Engelhardt: *A longer time, however, outside the present is a not-yet-being, or a no-longer-being*, unless perhaps by these words the philosopher wished to declare only the past time.

p. 88, 1. **Διὸ καὶ εἰκὼν αἰῶνος κ. τ. λ.** [Wherefore also the image of eternity, etc.]: Sc. *time* from the preceding. Thus without doubt Ficinus understood the place, and Engelhardt expressed it explicitly. Barthius, on the contrary: "And by that reasoning, beatitude is rightly called the image of eternity." He allowed himself to be deceived, like a little boy, when he made this interpretation, by the following feminines **αὐτῆς—αὐτῆς** [of her/it].

— 4. **ἀπώλεσεν αὐτὸ κ. τ. λ.** [it destroyed it, etc.]: Marsilius [Ficino] seems to me to have expressed the passage correctly. I will add, as it is a more obscure passage, also the Barthian version: "For if you take away from eternity that it will always be the same and remain in its own state, perpetuity itself will expire: wherefore that which remains always, makes eternity perpetual, and is preserved by it in its state; but it will vanish immediately when you subject it to successions, and thus as it were emancipate it to time."

### PAGE 42
**BOOK VI. ENNEAD I. p. 86—89.**

Furthermore, Plutarch sets out the opinions of several ancient philosophers concerning time in *Platonic Questions* IV. p. 1007. [p. 98 sq. Wytt.]. Cf. Cudworth, *The True Intellectual System of the Universe* IV. 21. p. 467. ed. Mosheim. Concerning eternity and time, our philosopher himself treats in a specific book, Ennead II. 7. p. 325 sqq.; likewise Proclus in *Elements of Theology* c. LVIII sqq. p. 82 sqq. of our edition.

p. 88, 7. **οὐκ ἄρα ἀριθμητέα χρόνῳ, ἀλλ' αἰῶνι** [therefore not to be numbered by time, but by eternity]: Just as they did not attain this sublime Platonic doctrine, so the Epicureans seem to have followed such things when they placed in describing the Gods those things which are read in Diogenes Laërtius X. 123: "First, indeed, regarding the god as an incorruptible and blessed living being, as the common notion of the god was outlined, etc." where see Menage. Hence that so often repeated phrase **τὸ μακάριον καὶ ἄφθαρτον** [the blessed and incorruptible], Diog. Laërt. X. 139; "eternal and blessed" Cicero, *De Natura Deorum* I. 17.

— 13. **ἀλλὰ τὴν ἐκ παντὸς χρόνου πᾶσαν ὁμοῦ** [but the whole [life] from all time together]: Barthius translates: "but that which is simultaneously one and whole from all ages." Engelhardt: *but (life) which emerges whole from the entire time.* This last is to be feared lest it might produce error. For Plotinus does not contend that eternity is born out of any time: he wants it understood that eternal life, if you refer it to the measure of time (which properly ought not to be done), is whole and complete starting from all time; namely, by that very fact that it shrinks entirely from the notion of time.

— 17. **καὶ οὐκ ἂν τηροῖ τὴν ὑπόθεσιν** [and he would not keep his hypothesis]: Barthius: "neither will he hold that purpose which he has." Namely, he is not consistent with himself in that he now posits as less wise the same man whom he had called blessed and therefore most wise. Regarding the various meanings of the word **ὑπόθεσις** [hypothesis/supposition], see the classic passage of Sextus Empiricus *Against the Professors* I. 1. 3. p. 310. and Fabricius there.

— 18. **περιαιρεῖσθαι** [to take away/strip]: Compare above I. 4. 12. and the annotation there.

p. 89, 2. **ὅτι ἐχθὲς ἐπὶ ὄψῳ ἤσθη** [that yesterday he was pleased with a relish]: Xenophon, *Memorabilia* I. 5. 4. — "rejoicing in relish and wine more than in friends," where some take it simply for *food*; which opinion would not be foreign to the Plotinian passage; and thus Engelhardt understood the word. Nor is there any reason, however, why we should recede in this place from the common meaning, in which Ficinus took it. Barthius thus: "as if someone should recall today the sensation of what he ate yesterday of an excellent taste." Phavorinus is relevant here: **ὄψα λέγονται τὰ τοῦ σίτου ἡδύσματα** [relishes are called the seasonings of food]. I have quoted the whole passage of Tullius [Cicero], since it deals with the same argument as Plotinus. Properly **ὄψα** are opposed to **ἡδύσμασι** or seasonings.

### PAGE 43
**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

p. 89, 4. **Εἰ δὲ—πῶς οὐκ ἐνταῦθα λέγοι ἄν τι** [But if—how would he not say something here?]: Barthius: "But why, you say, does the recollection of honorable and excellent things make the soul more blessed?" Engelhardt supplies by thought—**ἄν τι sc. παρέχεσθαι ταύτην τὴν μνήμην τῷ εὐδαίμονι** [that this memory provides something to the blessed man]. It is not necessary: provided you supply **τις** [someone], which must be supplied a thousand times. For **λέγειν τι** is to say something which is of importance for finishing the matter.

— 17. **αἱ διαθέσεις** [the dispositions]: A word frequently occurring in these Enneads: e.g., I. 1. 2; III. 1. 9; IV. 4. 28. In this place it is distinguished from **πράξεσι** [actions], and designates *dispositions of the soul* or *affections of the soul*. Zonaras in his Lexicon p. 512 conveniently explains: "Disposition is the relation of the soul toward something, or again the movement of the soul in a certain way toward something. Disposition is also the quality of each thing according to accident. Disposition is not only sciences and arts, but also virtues."

See regarding the Philosophers: Arrian in the *Discourses of Epictetus* III. 23. 20: "Behold the disposition (of a man) who is to benefit men": "Behold the soul of a man (or the affection of the soul of a man) who is about to help men." Zeno in Stobaeus *Eclogues* II. 7. p. 100: "All vices are dispositions, but only the proclivities are habits, etc." In Plotinus in this place, **αἱ διαθέσεις** are what are called in our vernacular *inner characteristics, states of mind* [innere Beschaffenheiten, Geisteszustände].

p. 90, 3. **καὶ ἄλλου πράξαντος** [even if another has acted]: Ficinus, Barthius, and Engelhardt render: "even while doing *something else*." I do not wish to oppose them precisely; I only ask: whether perhaps it can be understood so that it is **καὶ ἄλλου σώσαντος** i.e., "when even *another* has saved the fatherland"—?

**BOOK VI.**

p. 97, 7. **ΠΕΡΙ ΤΟΥ ΚΑΛΟΥ** [ON THE BEAUTIFUL]: This book is the first of all that Plotinus ever composed. Certainly it is placed in the first position by Porphyry (*Life of Plotinus* Chapter IV. p. 99. ed. Fabricius) in the enumeration of those books which he records Plotinus had already written (twenty-one) at the time he himself first came to know him.

### PAGE 44
**BOOK VI. ENNEAD I. p. 89—97.**

We gave that very book to the public separately under this title: *Plotinus’s Book on Beauty*. Fridericus Creuzer emended it according to the trust of the Codices and added a continuous Annotation, with notes by *Daniel Wyttenbach* interspersed, and an epistle to the same and a preparation both for this book and for the others etc. Heidelberg 1814. 8vo. From that edition, I thought the notes of Wyttenbach should be transferred here in their entirety: of my own, only those which seemed adapted to this shorter mode of commentary. For in that singular book, I had then wandered more widely and deliberately, namely to show in that example how much the monuments of this family of philosophers contributed both to universal philosophy and to theology, and no less to the accurate treatment of Greek literature. Here, however, in illustrating the entire Enneads, another method had to be entered upon, lest the work grow to a great mass and cause trouble to students of letters.

The English [*Angelica*] translation of this book, which is inscribed thus: *Concerning the Beautiful, or a paraphrase translation from the Greek of Plotinus, Enn. I. book 6. by Thomas Taylor*, Lond. 1787. 8vo. is now no more at hand for me than it was then when I was explaining that book separately from the others. I shall make mention of the Engelhardtian translation in this book more rarely, since the most kind man himself professes on p. 300 that he used my edition most of all.

Now to see about those who have touched upon this topic *on Beauty*, it becomes credible from history itself as well as from the remains of the secret discipline of the Greeks, that this question, *what is this beautiful itself*, began to be discussed early. From which it is permitted to gather that the *Pythagoreans* especially, the more they applied themselves to that discipline, the less they would have neglected so grave and copious a topic. But yet, as far as what is produced in writing, the *Sophists* competed in laboring on the same argument, as other things testify, and especially Plato’s *Hippias Major*. Nor indeed in the schools of those who preferred to be called *Rhetoricians* was such a fertile material for displaying eloquence omitted. Which both Plato’s *Phaedrus*, and the speech of Lysias included in it, teaches, and even more clearly the *Encomium of Helen* by *Isocrates*. Who, flourishing with authority, found many imitators even to the end of the age, among these *Dio Chrysostom* in speech XXI **περὶ κάλλους** [on beauty].

...*Socrates*, as far as is established from Xenophon’s books (*Memorabilia* III. 8. 4; IV. 6. 9), had begun that doctrine of the Beautiful, [and] *Plato* refined it with the most polished art... In many dialogues that philosopher touched upon what is **τὸ καλὸν** [the beautiful], as in the *First Alcibiades*, in the *Greater Hippias*, in the *Sophist, Gorgias, Phaedo, Philebus, Phaedrus, Symposium*. But in not a few he deals with it only in passing and briefly. In the *Greater Hippias* also nothing certain is posited on this matter. On the contrary, in the *Philebus* this very question is repeated from its causes and explained more subtly.

### PAGE 45
**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

...out of the three dialogues, *Philebus, Phaedrus, Symposium*, especially the two which I placed last, *Plotinus converted not a few things to his own purpose in this very book*. — No one is ignorant that the Stoics included the notion of the honorable [honestum] in the term **τοῦ καλοῦ** [the beautiful], as for instance Cleanthes in his *Hymn to Zeus*. And the philosophers before Zeno the Stoic, who first used the word **καθῆκον** for *duty* [officium], declared duty by other names, among them both the words **καλοῦ** and **ἀγαθοῦ** [good]. Chrysippus indeed had embraced this most grave doctrine in several books. (**Χρύσιππος ἐν τοῖς περὶ τοῦ καλοῦ** [Chrysippus in his writings on the beautiful]).

That Stoic dictum *Only the wise man is beautiful* (Cicero, *De Finibus* III. 22) is declared in his own words by Clement of Alexandria, *The Instructor* [Paedagogus] II. p. 243: "wherefore also only the excellent man is truly beautiful and good." ... The writers of the *New Testament* agree with the usage of the Stoics and Platonists in using this word, namely in that they say **τὸ καλὸν** for the *Honorable* [Honestum]. Thus, to use this example, the *Apostle Paul*, plainly like Plotinus, opposes to it **τὸ κακὸν** [the evil] in Romans VII. 21.

...That the later Platonists were wonderfully delighted by this same argument of the beautiful is proved by the Enneads of Plotinus himself. He, the parent of the family, made room for the discussions of Porphyry, Iamblichus, and Proclus. It is no wonder, therefore, that this same place *on the Beautiful* itself was very pleasing to the fathers of the *Christian Church*. Thus, to use this, Clement of Alexandria touched upon it in the *Paedagogus* especially... *Aurelius Augustine* likewise recurs to the mention of beauty in various books. Now we shall bring forth a classic passage of his... *Confessions* lib. IV. cap. 13: "These things I did not then know, and I loved inferior *beautiful things*... and I said to my friends: do we love anything except the beautiful? What is it that allures and reconciles us to the things we love? For unless there were in them a grace and form [decus et species], they would in no way move us to themselves. And I noticed and saw in the bodies themselves something like a whole and therefore *beautiful*; but another thing, which would therefore *be fitting, because it was aptly accommodated to something*, like a part of the body to its whole... and I wrote books *On the Beautiful and the Fitting* [de Pulcro et Apto], I think two or three. You know, O God, for it has escaped me." Which books if we had, we would have them as if Latin Plotinian works written on the same argument.

### PAGE 46
**BOOK VI. ENNEAD I. p. 97.**

...Augustine, in *Against the Academics* book III. 18, says Plotinus is so similar to Plato that he should be thought to have lived again in him.

...Plotinus had taught in the book *On Dialectic* (p. 19—21. Basil.), following Plato, that three ways lie open for returning to the higher things from which we have fallen: the first through *music* (**μουσικὴν**), the second through *love* (**ἐρωτικὴν**), the third through *dialectic* or *metaphysics* (**διαλεκτικήν**). Now Plotinus reveals that second way to the highest Good in this very book *On Beauty*. It is therefore entirely of *moral argument*, and for that reason was grouped by Porphyry into this first Ennead. The philosopher acts from the book to show how through the contemplation of the *Beautiful* a man is gradually recalled to the author of that Beauty, God, or the highest Good.

...This same book is *purgatory* (**καθάρσιος**) insofar as it opens the way to *Philosophy*... it is also *exhortatory* (**προτρεπτικός**) and so far consistent in purpose and argument with the *Hortensius* of Cicero.

p. 97, 9. **Τὸ καλὸν κ. τ. λ.** [The beautiful, etc.]: For this universal enumeration of the kinds of beauty, apply Plato’s *Phaedrus* p. 250d, *Hippias Major* p. 295d... and *Gorgias* p. 474d, e.

— 10. **καὶ—μέλη καὶ ῥυθμοί** [and melodies and rhythms]: For the argument apply the copious passage of Plato, *Laws* II. p. 665. Plotinus wished the sweetness of odors, which Plato however counts among beautiful things in the *Philebus*, to be excluded; and indeed he kept the definition of beauty within sight and hearing in the *Hippias Major*.

— 11. **ἔστι δὲ καὶ—ἐπιτηδεύματα καλὰ καὶ πράξεις** [there are also beautiful pursuits and actions]: Concerning the singular verb [ἔστι] joined to several plural subjects collected into one notion... Perhaps, however, in this and similar places the singular *ἔστι* depends on the first noun.

### PAGE 47
**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

...The Latin formula is derived from this: *the matter will show* [res indicabit]. ... Furthermore, in these words we are treating, there is a declaration of the purpose which Plotinus proposed for himself in this book, as Engelhardt rightly notes.

p. 97, 14. **τί οὖν δὴ τὸ πεποιηκὸς κ. τ. λ.** [what then is it that has made...]: Plotinus asks this more briefly on p. 556c: **τί οὖν τὸ ποιῆσαν σῶμα καλόν;** [What then is it that made the body beautiful?]. — **Φαντάζεσθαι** [to appear/be imagined] in this place is *to appear, to seem*.

p. 98, 3. **τὰ μὲν γὰρ—τὰ σώματα μεθέξει** [for some things... bodies will participate in]: Regarding this communion, see Wyttenbach on Plato’s *Phaedo*... and cf. Proclus, *Elements of Theology* c. LXII sqq.

— 5. **ἀρετῆς ἡ φύσις** [the nature of virtue]: i.e., *virtue*. A periphrasis familiar to Plato and his imitators. ... Thus Cicero, *De Natura Deorum* II. 54, *natura alvi* [the nature of the belly] for *alvus* [the belly].

— 9. **ἐπιστρέφει καὶ ἕλκει** [it turns and draws]: Plato, *Gorgias* p. 474... Hence the etymology **τὸ καλὸν παρὰ τὸ καλεῖν εἰς ἑαυτό** [the beautiful (kalon) from its calling (kalein) to itself]. Petronius, *Satyricon* c. 132: "Drawn by the very beauty of the body calling me to itself."

— 10. **ἐπιβάθρᾳ** [on a stepping-stone/ladder]: Refers to Plato’s **ἐπαναβαθμοῖς χρώμενον** [using stepping stones] *Symposium* p. 331. ... Others in this argument have placed **ἐπιβάθραν**, e.g., Origen *Against Celsus* VII... "as if to use them as a stepping-stone toward the understanding of the nature of intelligible things."

p. 99, 1. **καὶ ἔστιν αὐτοῖς—ὑπάρχειν** [and it is for them... to belong]: To be ended with a period, as Ficinus: the sense to be rendered more accurately: "and in the judgment of these, they themselves are beautiful and the remaining things, if they are harmonious and exact to the equality of measure." *D.W.*

— 10. **ἢ ἄστρα ὁρᾶσθαι τῷ καλῷ** [or stars to be seen by the beautiful]: "Perhaps it should be read **πῶς καλὰ**, how the stars are beautiful to the sight." *D.W.* I had conjectured **τῷ καλά**... This passage reminds one of the Pindaric opening of *Olympian I*. Cicero in *Hortensius*... "They watch the admirable order of the signs of heaven and the insatiable beauty more."

— 12. **ἑκάστου φθόγγου** [of each sound/note]: Aristoxenus in *Harmonic Elements* book I: "The sound is the falling of the voice upon one tension."

— 14. **πᾶς οὐκ ἄλλο δεῖ ἐπὶ τῷ συμμέτρῳ κ. τ. λ.** [Does it not need anything else besides the symmetrical?]: Ficinus: "Must not something else be in that *which* is commensurate." I should believe: "Why should not something else *besides* that which is commensurate be called beauty."

### PAGE 48
**BOOK VI. ENNEAD I. p. 97—100.**

p. 99, 17. **καὶ τοὺς λόγους τοὺς καλούς** [and beautiful discourses]: Plato, *Symposium* p. 210d... Expressed by Lucian in *Charidemus*.

ib. **τὸ σύμμετρον καὶ ἐπ' αὐτῶν αἰτιῶντο** [they would blame/attribute the symmetrical even in these]: i.e., if indeed even in these things they should say symmetry was *in the cause* why they were beautiful.

p. 100, 1. **θεωρήματα γὰρ κ. τ. λ.** [for theorems, etc.]: ... Marsilius [Ficino] translates **θεωρήματα** as *speculations* [speculationes]... He could have, or rather ought to have, if he wished to follow Tullius [Cicero], used *percepts* [percepta]; Cicero, *De Fato* cap. 6: "I call *percepta* those things which the Greeks call **θεωρήματα**." We Germans: *scientific propositions* [wissenschaftliche Sätze].

— 4. **τὴν δικαιοσύνην—εἶναι εὐθεῖαν** [justice... to be straight/simple]: It is in Plato’s *Republic* I... Thucydides III. 82: "and the temperate was thought a screen for the unmanly." Xenophon, *Anabasis* II. 6. 22: "and the simple and true he thought the same as the foolish."

— 5. **κάλλος—ψυχῆς—κάλλος ἀληθινώτερον ἢ τὰ πρόσθεν** [beauty of the soul... a truer beauty than the former]: Plutarch in Stobaeus... seems to feel otherwise, writing: "And how is it not wonderful to speak of the beauties of the soul, looking down on those of the body": in reality he does not dissent. ... "But, as I said, no beautiful thing, unless it belongs to the body, is a cause of dangers. For the beauties of the soul contain at the same time the hope of safety."

— 7. **οὔτε ὡς μεγέθη οὔτε ὡς ἀριθμὸς σύμμετρα** [neither as magnitudes nor as number symmetrical]: By these words the Stoics are touched upon again, who *assigned numbers to virtue*.

— 8. **ἢ ἡ κράσις** [or the mixture/temperament]: "Cf. Plotinus’s Discussion *on the mixture through the whole*: Enn. II. 7. p. 184—187. The division of the ancients concerning the composition of bodies is treated by us at Plutarch *Moralia* p. 142d." *D.W.*

— 12. **καὶ βολῇ τῇ πρώτῃ** [and at the first glance]: Thus very often **βολὴ** [glance] and **βολαὶ** [glances], with **ὀφθαλμῶν, ὀμμάτων, βλέμματος** [of eyes, of sights, of look] sometimes added.

### PAGE 49
**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

p. 101, 14. **ἀνύλλεται—ἀλλοτριουμένη** [it shrinks/shrivels... becoming alienated]: ... Porphyry used the same word in the *Life of Plotinus*... The Scholion flowed from the same source as Suidas and Zonaras... Plotinus had in view Plato’s *Symposium* p. 206d: "whenever it approaches the beautiful, that which is pregnant becomes gracious and, being delighted, is poured out and brings forth and generates; but whenever it approaches the ugly, it becomes gloomy and, being pained, it curls up and turns away and **ἀνύλλεται** [shrivels] and does not generate."

— 15. **ἀνανεύει ἀπ' αὐτοῦ** [it denies/recedes from it]: Cf. Hesychius: "it does not agree with something." It is therefore in this place: *The soul denies that it has anything in common with the ugly*.

p. 101, 1. **φαμὲν δέ—καὶ πρὸς τῆς κρείττονος οὐσίας** [and we say... and from the better essence]: ... Plotinus contemplates the soul here in two ways: first by itself, insofar as it is soul and what it is by nature (**τὴν φύσιν οὖσα ὅπερ ἐστὶ**); then insofar as it stands from the better essence which is found among beings (**πρὸς τῆς κρείττονος ἐν τοῖς οὖσιν οὐσίας**). That better essence is the Intellect (**ὁ νοῦς**).

— 2. **ἢ ἴχνος** [or a trace]: A formula frequent in Plato and the Platonic philosophers. ... Plotinus, *Against the Gnostics* p. 215e: "those who behold bodily beauty in pictures, they as it were are thrown into turmoil and come into a recollection of the true (beauty)."

— 6. **μετοχῇ εἴδους** [by participation in form]: Let the force of the words **εἶδος** and **μορφὴ** be held in this place for *idea*, which usage has Plato as its author.

— 8. **καὶ τὸ πάντη αἰσχρὸν—μορφῆς καὶ λόγου** [and that which is entirely ugly... [devoid] of form and reason]: i.e., "and this is that which is altogether ugly; but ugly also is that which is not entirely contained by form and reason." *D.W.*

— 9. **οὔκ ἀνασχομένης τῆς ὕλης τὸ—μορφοῦσθαι** [the matter not enduring to be formed]: ... Plotinus, to avoid an excessive concurrence of participles, preferred to join an infinitive to the verb **ἀνέχεσθαι** [to endure]. This is a classic passage of Plotinus on the origin and nature of deformity. ... Deformity of bodies is not born from a certain idea of deformity, but from the weakness of matter not being strong enough to receive the form flowing down from above from the soul and intellect to be impressed upon bodies.

### PAGE 50
**BOOK VI. ENNEAD I. p. 101, 102.**

— 14. **Ἵδρυται** [It is established/seated]: Concerning the verb **ἵδρυται, ἐνίδρυται** and similar ones, which are very frequent in the monuments of the Platonic philosophers...

— 16. **ἐς ὅλον δίδωσι τὸ αὐτό** [it gives the same into the whole]: *It gives itself and the same into the whole*. Ficinus. You might say he read in his books **ἑαυτὸ καὶ τὸ αὐτό** [itself and the same]. ... But yet that reading must be attended to, and explained thus: The Species gives *itself and the One* (**τὸ ἓν**) into the whole.

p. 102, 3. **ὑπὸ θείων** [by divine things]: ... "The sense is: *a beautiful body becomes so by the communion of reason coming from the divine power*." *D.W.*

— 4. **ἢ ἐπ' αὐτὸ δύν. τεταγμένη** [or the power appointed over it]: ... Concerning the soul judging truly, see Plato, *Gorgias*...

— 6. **τάχα δὲ καὶ αὕτη λέγει** [and perhaps it also says]: "There are two ways of knowing the beautiful: one sudden *through the sense of the beautiful itself*; the other *proceeding gradually through judgment and comparison of some external beautiful thing with the internal example of beauty*." *D.W.*

— 7. **ὥσπερ κανόνι τοῦ εὐθέος** [as if by a rule/standard of the straight]: Cf. Plotinus p. 416d, where it should be read thus: "for the rule [kanon], joining the straight which is in the soul and that which is in the wood, being placed in between, gave the craftsman the ability to judge the artifact."

— 8. **τὴν ἔξω οἰκίαν τῷ ἔνδον οἰκίας εἴδει ὁ οἰκοδομικός συναρμόσας** [the builder having fitted the outer house to the inner form of the house]: The Grammarians are greatly deceived who think **οἰκοδομικός** [builder/architectural] is restricted to the Attics: [and that] **οἰκοδόμος** [builder] is unknown to them. ... Regarding the meaning, see Aristotle, *Metaphysics* II. 4. p. 41.

->BOOK VI. ENNEAD ONE. pages 89—97. 37<-

In the enumeration of those books, of which [Porphyry] records that [Plotinus] had already composed twenty-one at the time he first came to his acquaintance. We have published that very book separately under this title: *Plotinus's Book on Beauty*. *Friedrich Creuzer* amended it according to the reliability of the Manuscripts and added a continuous Commentary, interspersing the notes of *Daniel Wyttenbach*, and added a letter to the same as well as a preparation both for this book and for the rest, etc. Added are Greek Unpublished Works: *Proclus's Disputation on Unity and Beauty*, *Nicephorus Nathanael's Antithetic against Plotinus on the Soul*; likewise *Platonic Readings* noted down for the most part from Manuscript Codices. Heidelberg 1814. 8vo. From that edition, I thought it necessary to transfer Wyttenbach's complete Notes here: from my own, only those which seemed suited to this shorter method of commenting. For in that individual book I had then wandered more widely and by design, namely so that I might show in that example how much the monuments of this family of philosophers <note>The Neoplatonists</note> contributed both to universal philosophy and to theology, and no less to the accurate treatment of Greek literature. Here, however, in illustrating the Enneads as a whole, another method had to be undertaken, lest the work grow into a great mass and cause trouble to students of literature. The English interpretation of this book, which is inscribed thus: *Concerning the Beautiful, or a paraphrase translation from the Greek of Plotinus, Enn. I. book 6. by Thomas Taylor*, London 1787. 8vo. is no more at hand for me now than it was then, when I was explaining that book separated from the rest. Moreover, I shall make mention of Engelhardt’s translation more rarely in this book, since that most refined man himself professes on page 300 that he used my edition most of all. In revising my own notes, I have so conducted myself that I might silently change and complete not a few things both in the practice of criticism and in the addition of explanation.

Now, so that we may look at those who have touched upon this topic *on Beauty*, it becomes credible from history itself and likewise from the remains of the secret discipline of the Greeks, that this question, *what this very thing "the beautiful" is*, began to be discussed early on (See our Preparation to the book on Beauty §. 8. ff. p. XXV. ff. of that separate edition). From which it is possible to gather that the *Pythagoreans* <note>Followers of Pythagoras who emphasized numbers and harmony</note> especially, the more they applied themselves to that discipline, the less they would have neglected so grave and copious a topic. But nevertheless, as far as what stands recorded in writing, the *Sophists* <note>Professional teachers of rhetoric and virtue in ancient Greece</note> labored in competition on the same argument, as other things give proof, but especially Plato’s *Greater Hippias*. Nor indeed in the schools of those who preferred to be called *Rhetoricians* was such a fertile material for displaying eloquence omitted. This both Plato’s *Phaedrus* and the speech of Lysias included in it teaches, and even more clearly *Isocrates’s* Encomium of Helen. He, flourishing in authority, obtained not a few imitators even to the latest age, among these *Dio Chrysostom* in Oration XXI **on beauty** <note>original: "περὶ κάλλους"</note>, and in the *Melancomas* or Oration XXIX. (cf. Stobaeus, Sermon 65. (63) p. 495. ed. Gaisford); likewise *Lucian* in the *Charidemus*, if indeed that short exercise is by Lucian, patched together for the most part in a childish way no less from Plato’s *Symposium* than from Isocrates’s *Encomium of Helen*. More ample treatments existed in the spaces of the Academy and in the porch of Zeno <note>The Stoic school</note>. And first, after *Socrates*—as far as is established from Xenophon’s books (*Memorabilia* III. 8. 4 and IV. 6. 9)—had begun that doctrine of the Beautiful, *Plato* polished it with the most refined art, yet in such a way that he thereafter offered to other philosophers a most full topic both for new discovery and for demanding and increasing the things handed down by himself. Moreover, in very many dialogues that philosopher touched upon this very thing, what **the beautiful** <note>original: "τὸ καλὸν"</note> is, as in the *First Alcibiades*, in the *Greater Hippias*, in the *Sophist*, *Gorgias*, *Phaedo*, *Philebus*, *Phaedrus*, and *Symposium*. But in not a few he acts only in passing and briefly. In the *Greater Hippias* also, nothing certain is placed concerning this matter. On the contrary, in the *Philebus* this very question is repeated from its causes and explained more subtly. No less in the *Phaedrus* are many things treated which seem to place in a clearer light what this very thing "the beautiful" is. In the *Symposium*, however, and especially in Diotima’s conversation with Socrates, the same argument is explained seriously and sublimely, or rather, lest I seem to have said too little, divinely. You have the summary of the Platonic disputations in the *Greater Hippias* in Diogenes Laertius III. 89. Antipater, according to the testimony of Clement of Alexandria in the *Stromata* V. p. 705 Potter, had set forth in three books the primary opinion of Plato, teaching that the beautiful itself is nothing other than the good itself. From three...

<meta>This page continues the scholarly annotations on Plotinus’s treatise on Beauty, specifically tracing the historical and philosophical lineage of the concept of "the Beautiful" (to kalon) from Plato through the Stoics to the Church Fathers.</meta>

->38 ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINIUS<-

Moreover, in the dialogues *Philebus, Phaedrus, and the Symposium*—especially the two I have placed last—*Plotinus converted not a few elements to his own purpose in this very book*.—Everyone knows that the Stoics included the notion of the morally honorable in the term **the beautiful** <note>original: "τοῦ καλοῦ"</note>, as, for example, Cleanthes does in his hymn to Jupiter. And philosophers before Zeno the Stoic (who was the first to use the word **duty** <note>original: "καθῆκον"; literally "the fitting"</note> for moral obligation), declared "duty" by various other names, including these terms **the beautiful** <note>original: "καλοῦ"</note> and **the good** <note>original: "ἀγαθοῦ"</note> (see van Lynden in his *Disputation on Panaetius*, p. 89). Indeed, Chrysippus had embraced this most weighty doctrine in several books. (Diogenes Laërtius VII. 110. **Chrysippus in his writings on the beautiful**, cf. Baguet’s *Commentary on the Life, Doctrine, and Remains of Chrysippus* §. LIV. and especially §. CVII. p. 259. ff.). However, the followers of that school explained **the beautiful** in various ways, as is understood from the primary passage of Diogenes Laërtius on Zeno VII. 100. and from there in Suidas II. p. 233. Kust. and Zonaras’s Lexicon p. 1159. That maxim of the Stoics, *that only the wise man is beautiful* (Cicero, *On Ends* III. 22.), Clement of Alexandria declares in his own words in *The Instructor* II. p. 243. Pott.: **wherefore also only the serious man is truly beautiful and good**. <note>original: "διὸ καὶ μόνος ὁ σπουδαῖος καλὸς κἀγαθὸς ὄντως ἐστίν"</note> Cf. *Miscellanies* II. p. 440. These ideas flowed from Plato. See *Protagoras* p. 309. C.—Likewise, very close to the decrees of Plato and the Platonists is that Stoic decree: that through beauty, the souls of mortals are reconciled with God. Iamblichus indeed attributes this to them in *On the Soul*, found in Stobaeus’s *Selections* Vol. I. p. 918. Moreover, several passages of *Plutarch* concerning beauty exist in Stobaeus’s *Anthology* under the titles **on beauty** and **against beauty** (LXIII. and LXIV. p. 408. cf. 410. p. 496. and 502. Gaisford.) and from there in Plutarch’s *Fragments* p. 857. ff. ed. Wyttenbach, minor Oxford edition. Wyttenbach notes that it is uncertain whether this name signifies a specific small book by Plutarch, or merely the subject matter of this particular place from the title of Stobaeus’s discourse. The writers of the *New Testament* agree with the usage of the Stoics and Platonists in employing this word; namely, in that they say **the beautiful** <note>original: "τὸ καλὸν"</note> for *the Honorable*. Thus, to use this example, *Paul the Apostle*, plainly as Plotinus does, opposes it to **the evil** <note>original: "τὸ κακὸν"</note> in Romans VII. 21. compared with verse 18. The same author in the *Epistle to the Galatians* IV. 18. elegantly joins **beautiful to beautiful** <note>original: "καλὸν καλῷ"</note> in the same sense. Regarding a similar usage by the Greek translators of the Old Testament <note>The Septuagint</note>, Brelius will provide more in *Thesaurus* II. p. 102. The teachers of the Church followed the same path even to the latest age.—The Enneads of Plotinus himself prove that the later Platonists were wonderfully delighted by this very argument of the beautiful. He, as the father of the family of Porphyry, Iamblichus, and Proclus, made room for their disputations, some of which will be mentioned in the annotations to this very book. It is no wonder, therefore, that this same topic *on Beauty* was very pleasing to the fathers of the *Christian Church* themselves—at least those who had associated themselves with the Greek philosophers. Thus, to use this example, Clement of Alexandria touched upon it, especially in *The Instructor*, at the beginning of the third book, which is inscribed **on true beauty**. Although Clement does not explain this doctrine with the subtlety or in the manner of the philosophers, he nevertheless possesses some insights that are more recondite and pertain greatly to the sacred monuments of the Jews. Nor indeed should he be said to have touched upon the fables of the Pagans in a Plotinian manner any less than Plotinus himself. *Aurelius Augustine*, however, recurs again and again to the mention of beauty in various books. We shall now bring forward a classic passage of his, from which it is established that the same material was set forth by him in certain *specific books*. For he says thus in the *Confessions*, book IV. chapter 13. Vol. I. p. 104. Paris ed.: “These things I did not then know, and I loved the lower *beautiful things*, and I was going into the depths, and I said to my friends: do we love anything unless it is beautiful? What is it, then, that attracts us and reconciles us to the things we love? For unless there were in them a grace and a form, they would in no way move us toward themselves. And I observed and saw in bodies themselves something like a whole, and therefore *beautiful*; and another thing, which was *fitting, because it was aptly adapted to something*, like a part of the body to its whole, or a shoe to a foot and such like. And so this consideration gushed up in my mind from my inmost heart, and *I wrote books on the Beautiful and the Fitting*, I think two or three. You know, O God, for it has escaped me. For we do not have them; they have strayed from us, I know not how.” If we had those books, we would certainly have, in a Latin form as it were, a great part of the Plotinian writings on the same subject. For how much Augustine valued Plotinus, and how vehemently he followed him as an authority, is evidenced by the passages in which he honors him by name, and others which he took from the Enneads...

<summary>This page traces the philosophical development of "the Beautiful" (to kalon) from Plato and the Stoics through to Christian authors like Clement of Alexandria and St. Augustine, highlighting the lost work of Augustine "On the Beautiful and the Fitting."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the scholarly commentary on Plotinus’s Enneads, specifically focusing on the First Ennead, Sixth Book, which deals with Beauty. The text draws heavily on the relationship between Plotinus and Plato.</meta>

->BOOK VI. ENNEAD THE FIRST. p. 97. 39<-

He drew from a most abundant spring. Regarding this, Augustine in *Against the Academics*, Book III, 18, p. 294, says that Plotinus is so similar to Plato that the latter should be thought to have lived again in the former. <note>Augustine suggests a "reincarnation" of Platonic thought in Plotinus.</note>

But if we truly ask about the purpose and argument of this book, the matter can now be explained in a few words, after we have seen the remaining books of this Ennead which precede this one. Indeed, with Plato as his authority, Plotinus had taught in the book *On Dialectic* (p. 19—21, Basel edition) that three ways lie open for returning to the higher realms from which we have fallen: the first through *music* (**mousikē**), the second through the *amatory* (**erōtikē**), and the third through *dialectic* or *metaphysics* (**dialektikē**). Now, Plotinus opens that second path to the highest Good in this very book *On Beauty*.

The book is therefore entirely of a *moral argument*, and for that reason, it was grouped into this first Ennead by Porphyry. <note>Porphyry was Plotinus's student and editor who organized his works into "Enneads" or groups of nine.</note> The philosopher certainly acts in this book to show how, through the contemplation of the *Beautiful*, a person is gradually called back to God, the author of that Beauty, or to the highest Good (p. 80. D. Basel). Now, the nature of the musical man, as well as that of the one who *loves Beauty itself*, looks especially toward sublime things and strives for a return, provided that both are rightly educated and instructed.

And yet, this very book *On Beauty* is dedicated to this instruction, and it pertains no less to the **erōtikon**, or *lover of Beauty*, than to the **mousikon**, the *lover of harmony*; and indeed for this reason: because the latter is sometimes transformed into the former (see our author *On Dialectic* p. 20. D.), that is, because he who loves the Beauty found in the harmony of voices and sounds very easily becomes a lover of beauty itself. This same book is occupied for a large part with warnings and precepts for the flight from those things which strike the senses, especially those which either tickle them with the sweetness of sounds or flatter them with the charm and softness of forms.

Therefore, this book is so far purely *purgatory* (**katharsios** <note>original: "καθάρσιος", meaning purifying</note>), and it opens the way to *Philosophy*, as something which itself belongs in a way to *purification* (**katharsin**), but nevertheless no less achieves *release* (**lysin**) and even *perfection* (**teleiōsin**). The same book is *exhortatory* (**protreptikos**) and thus far consistent in purpose and argument with Cicero’s *Hortensius*, in which book, as Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> himself professes in *On Ends* I. 2., he had *exhorted his fellow citizens to the study of philosophy*.—Furthermore, Hermias seems to have had this very book of Plotinus before his eyes in his commentary on Plato’s *Phaedrus* p. 65 when he wrote: **"that the aim [of the Platonic Dialogue Phaedrus] is concerning every kind of beauty: first that in sensation and nature, then that in reason, and higher that in intellect, and finally that in the gods."**

*Wyttenbach*, however, says of this Plotinian book: "This is an explanation of the Platonic passage in the *Symposium* p. 331 ff. delivered from the persona of Diotima; it also refers to the part of the *Phaedrus* p. 344 ff." This same passage from Plato’s own writings was recently illustrated by *Philip Willem van Heusde*, a most excellent man, in *Beginnings of Platonic Philosophy*, part I. p. 96 ff.

p. 97, 9. **The Beautiful etc.**] For this entire enumeration of the kinds of beauty, consult Plato’s *Phaedrus* p. 250. d., *Greater Hippias* p. 295. d. (from which Laërtius took III. 89.), and *Gorgias* p. 474. d. e.

— 10. **and—melodies and rhythms**] For the argument, consult the copious passage of Plato in *Laws* II. p. 665. Compare *Philebus* p. 17. d. and the passages I praised above. Add Lennep on the *Epistles of Phalaris* p. 99 ff., Ernesti’s *Lexicon of Greek Rhetorical Technology* p. 208 ff., p. 303 ff., Cicero’s *The Orator* 64, and Quintilian’s *Institutes of Oratory* IX. 4. p. 554, edited by Spalding. Furthermore, the sweetness of odors, which Plato nevertheless numbers among beautiful things in the *Philebus* p. 51, Plotinus wished to be excluded. And indeed, that same man in the *Greater Hippias* p. 298 confined the definition of beauty to sight and hearing. Also Aristotle in *Topics* VI. 3. p. 377, Sylburg edition, places this among the examples of definitions: **"the beautiful is that which is pleasant through sight or through hearing."**

— 11. **there are also—beautiful pursuits and actions**] Regarding the singular verb **esti** <note>original: "ἔστι", meaning "there is"</note> joined to several plural subjects of different kinds collected into one notion, see *Grammatical Excerpts* in Villoison’s *Greek Anecdotes* II. p. 95 and cf. Ast on Plato’s *Phaedrus* p. 370 and Heindorf on the *Euthydemus* p. 403. Perhaps, however, in this place and similar ones, the singular **esti** depends on the first substantive. So Ludolph Dissen, a man of great learning, wishes me to think in a letter given to me. As for the meaning, see Plato’s *Symposium* chapters 28 and 29; cf. also Plotinus p. 556. A. B. and Themistius’s *Oration* XIII. p. 168. C. p. 177. B—D. Harduin edition.

— 13. **and if there is anything even before these, it will show itself**] He took this formula from his Plato, who in the *Theaetetus* p. 200 E. says: **"the one leading the way through the river, O Theaetetus—"**

Wagner on Alciphron III. 1. p. 5. and Boissonade on Philostratus' *Heroicus* p. 547. ff.
p. 101, 14. **shrivels up—becoming estranged**] <note>original: "ἀνύλλεται—ἀλλοτριουμένη"</note> “The Vossian Manuscript [Codex Vossianus] follows the marginal reading of the Edition. [See the various readings.] In this reading, the words preceding the verb **shrivels up** are indeed a Scholion <note>A marginal explanatory note by an ancient scholar</note>. Porphyry used the same [verb] in the *Life of Plotinus* p. 116 in Fabricius' edition, and one should consult Ruhnken on Timaeus p. 35.” *D. W.*—and Tib. Hemsterhuis in the same work p. 68. ff. as well as Valckenaer on Theocritus' *Adoniazusae* p. 248. ff. Moreover, the Scholion flowed from the same source from which Suidas and Zonaras drew for the entry **to shrivel up** <note>original: "ἀνύλλεσθαι"</note>, of whom the former has **to reject/disdain** and the latter **to deem worthy**. Plotinus had in mind Plato’s *Symposium* p. 206. D. p. 435. Bekker: **whenever that which is pregnant approaches the beautiful, it becomes gentle and, being filled with delight, it overflows and brings forth and procreates; but whenever it approaches the ugly, it becomes sullen and, being pained, it curls up and turns away and shrivels up and does not procreate.** In this passage, there might also seem to be support for the conjecture of **rejoices** instead of **says**. Olympiodorus in *Alcibiades* p. 48: **those who shrivel up at punishments.**
— 15. **it denies it**] <note>original: "ἀνανεύει ἀπ' αὐτοῦ"</note> Cf. Hesychius I. p. 132: **to deny is to not agree to something.** See the same under **to emerge/withdraw** p. 320 and the interpreters there. Therefore, in this place: *The soul denies that it has anything in common with the ugly.* Regarding the sentiment, cf. Plato’s *Lysis* p. 216. C. Muretus' *Variae Lectiones* IV. 4. Barnes on Euripides' *Bacchae* 879. 899. Valckenaer on *Phoenissae* 821. ff. Lucian’s *Charidemus* IX. p. 291. Bipontine ed. cf. 293. Dio Chrysostom XXIX. p. 539. Reiske, to whom from Stobaeus' *Sermon* 63 should be restored **to be hidden** instead of **to escape notice** and **furthermore** instead of **if indeed**. Basil the Great, *Homily on Isaiah* 5. p. 505. B. and Augustine, *On Music* VI. 38. p. 513. B. C.
p. 101, 1. **But we say—and toward the better essence**] <note>original: "φαμὲν δέ—καὶ πρὸς τῆς κρείττονος οὐσίας"</note> Ficino also reads it thus, and my friend Rinck saw that it should be read this way. For in this place Plotinus contemplates the soul in two ways: first by itself, insofar as it is soul and such as its nature is (**being in its nature that which it is**); secondly, insofar as it stands toward the better essence which is found among beings (**toward the better essence among the things that are**. Regarding this construction of the preposition **toward** <note>original: "πρὸς"</note> see Matthiae's *Greek Grammar* §. 590.) That better essence, however, is the Mind (**the Intellect** <note>original: "ὁ νοῦς"</note>); cf. below 55. C. **the soul led up toward the Mind**, p. 15. C. **it was joined with the Mind**. Add p. 5. A. and p. 73. A. And so both that soul, such as its nature is, and when it is turned toward the more excellent Mind, whatever (**whatever**) kindred thing or trace of a kindred thing it perceives, it rejoices etc. Unless you prefer **whenever it sees**, which Ficino seems to have expressed by translating *whenever*.
— 2. **or a trace**] <note>original: "ἡ ἴχνος"</note> A formula frequently used by Plato and Platonic philosophers. See my friend Heusde’s *Specimen Criticum on Plato* p. 137. Hemsterhuis on Lucian’s *Dialogues of the Gods* p. 331. Wetstein on the *Second Epistle of Peter* II. 21. and cf. Plotinus p. 393. p. 439. A. p. 710. C. p. 713. B. 711. A. 725. A. above.
— 4. **and it remembers itself and its own things**] <note>original: "καὶ ἀναμιμνήσκεται ἑαυτῆς καὶ τῶν ἑαυτῆς"</note> These things pertain to the doctrine of **recollection** <note>original: "ἀναμνήσεως"</note> see *Meno* p. 81. ff. [p. 58. ff. Stallbaum, whom see especially p. 60—62.] *Phaedo* p. 72. E. p. 27. Wyttenbach. *Phaedrus* p. 249. C. and the many things I have collected in the special edition of this book p. 166—168. Plotinus *Against the Gnostics*, p. 215. E.: “those who behold bodily beauty in paintings, they **are as it were agitated and come into a recollection of the true (beauty)**. The same on p. 714. C. *the soul warmed by divine heat* **as if fluttering with memory is rather lightened**.
ib. **what likeness then is there to the things here**] <note>original: "τίς οὖν ὁμοιότης τοῖς τῇδε"</note> “The Vossian Manuscript has **of this [beauty]** <note>original: "τῆσδε"</note>, which is less good.” *D. W.* For the argument of the passage, compare Clement of Alexandria *Stromata* IV. p. 616. and Augustine in *Confessions* X. 53. p. 188.
— 6. **by participation in form**] <note>original: "μετοχῇ εἴδους"</note> Let the force of the words **form** <note>original: "εἶδος"</note> and **shape** <note>original: "μορφή"</note> be held in this place for *idea*, a usage which has Plato as its author, although he is not everywhere consistent in it, as Wyttenbach teaches on the *Phaedo* p. 274. ff., not forgetting this Plotinian passage. I have added more in the special Edition p. 169. ff.
— 8. **and that which is entirely ugly—of shape and reason**] <note>original: "καὶ τὸ πάντη αἰσχρὸν—μορφῆς καὶ λόγου"</note> i.e. “*and this is that which is altogether ugly; but it is also ugly, that which is not inwardly contained by form and reason.*” *D. W.* However, Wilhelm Rinck wants the **and** <note>original: "καὶ"</note> after **ugly** deleted because **the entirely ugly** or *absolutely ugly* and *simply ugly* are in this place contrary to each other and similarly distinguished on p. 76. C. **the good** and **good**, likewise **essence** and **the essence**, of which those with the article are taken absolutely: those without the article, relatively, as they say today. Several good books favor this reasoning, which do not recognize the **and** in this place. Wyttenbach on Eunapius p. 103 compares the formula **outside of divine reason** with the other **outside the divine choir**, cf. below at p. 316. B.

->BOOK VI. ENNEAD FIRST. pages 101, 102. 43<-

In this place, Plotinus, in order to avoid an excessive concurrence of Participles, preferred to join the infinitive to the verb **to endure** <note>original: *ἀνέχεσθαι*</note>, rather than the more customary Participle. See Valckenaer on Herodotus V. 19. and compare Olympiodorus on the *Alcibiades* p. 101 ff. and p. 226 and our notes there. Moreover, this passage of Plotinus is a classic one concerning the origin and nature of deformity. Regarding this matter, which I have explained more fully in the singular Commentary on this book in the edition pages 171—177, I omit most of those points here out of a desire for brevity; I will also add some things to Ennead III. book 2. chapter 5. p. 259. C. In this place let it suffice to have indicated the source of the doctrine and to have declared Plotinus's opinion. See therefore Plato's *Sophist* p. 228. B. p. 150. Bekker edition. Aristotle *Metaphysics* II. 3. Varro in Cicero's *Academic Questions* I. 40. and Davies's notes there. Plutarch *On Stoic Self-Contradictions* p. 1054. A. p. 295. Wyttenbach small Oxford edition. Proclus on Plato's *Alcibiades I* p. 326. ff. our edition. Hermias on the *Phaedrus* p. 88. Plotinus in the place just cited and p. 216. C. p. 260. A. B. p. 556. B—D. p. 719. (chapter 28.) A. B. and p. 757. C. Syrianus, however, writes thus on folio 6 of the Venice edition of 1558 regarding the cited passage of Aristotle: “We say indeed,” he says, “that of shameful and imperfect and evil things there are no Ideas <note>The Platonic 'Ideas' or 'Forms' are the perfect archetypes of things; Syrianus argues evil has no such divine blueprint.</note> at all. For these things subsist in the furthest reaches of nature through a falling away, namely because the particular soul is weak, since it does not overcome the infinity of the subject matter.” Thus Syrianus. From the same source, no small light is shed upon the opinion of Plotinus, which posits this: that the deformity of bodies is not born from some idea of deformity, but from the weakness of matter which is not strong enough to receive the form flowing from above from the soul and mind and intended to be impressed upon bodies.
— 14. **Is established**] <note>original: *Ἵδρυται*</note> Concerning the verb **is established**, **is seated within** <note>original: *ἐνίδρυται*</note> and similar words, which are most frequent in the monuments of the Platonic philosophers, see Wesseling on Diodorus XI. 49. Wyttenbach on Julian's *Oration I* p. 193. Leipzig edition. Add Proclus on Plato's *Timaeus* p. 75. where correct to **establishing within** <note>original: *ἐνιδρύουσα*</note>. The same in *Alcibiades I* p. 43. often, and in the *Elements* chapter 27. p. 52. our edition. and chapter 170. p. 252. finally Dionysius the Areopagite *On Divine Names* IV. 12. Plotinus IV. 7. 4. Hence also **establishment** <note>original: *ἵδρυσις*</note> III. 5. 2. VI. 4. 8. VI. 9. 6. and **establishments** <note>original: *ἱδρύσεις*</note> VII. 7. 36.
— 16. **it gives the same to the whole**] <note>original: *ἐς ὅλον δίδωσι τὸ αὐτό*</note> *It hands over itself and the same thing into the whole*. Ficino. You might say he read in his books **itself and the same** <note>original: *ἑαυτὸ καὶ τὸ αὐτό*</note>. Yet neither the Medicean Manuscripts nor the others support this. But nevertheless, that reading must be attended to, and explained thus: The Species <note>The 'Form' or 'Idea'</note> hands over *itself and the one* (**the One** <note>original: *τὸ ἓν*</note>) into the whole.
p. 102, 3. **by divine things**] <note>original: *ὑπὸ θείων*</note> “So the Basel edition. But **from the divine** <note>original: *ἀπὸ θείου*</note> in the Vossian Manuscript is correct. It signifies **divine reason** <note>original: *θεῖον λόγον*</note> namely **the god in the whole**. See *Bibliotheca Critica* Part IX. p. 20. Notes on the *Phaedo* p. 228. (and there Heraclitus and Cicero *On the Nature of the Gods* I. 15.). The sense is: *a beautiful body is made by the communion of reason coming from the divine power*.” *D. W.* <note>Likely Daniel Wyttenbach</note> Concerning the passage of Plato in the *Phaedo* I have advised more in the special edition p. 179. You should furthermore compare the *Parmenides* p. 134. C. Juncus in Stobaeus's *Sermons* Title 115. p. 588. p. 424. Gaisford edition. and Plotinus himself above p. 52. A. p. 566. C. and p. 714. A.
— 4. **or the power appointed over it**] <note>original: *ἢ ἐπ' αὐτὸ δύν. τεταγμένη*</note> Polybius V. 63. 4. **those appointed over this part**. The same author joins it with the dative. See *Lexicon to Polybius* p. 613.
ibid. **than which nothing is more sovereign—to the soul**] <note>original: *ῆς οὐδὲν κυριώτερον—ψυχῇ*</note> “Ficino: *other, translate the rest*. Thus **others** <note>original: *ἄλλα*</note> *alia* and **the others/the rest** <note>original: *τὰ ἄλλα*</note> *reliqua* differ. Notes on *Selections from the Principal Historians* p. 342. The contrary is in love: **not to do things decreed by the whole mind** in Plato's *Phaedrus* p. 349. A. [p. 256. C. Stephanus edition] whence Synesius *On Kingship* p. 10. C. D. Epistle 57. p. 200. C.” *D. W.* You compare Krabinger's notes on the passage of Synesius *On Kingship* p. 206. Concerning the soul judging truly, see Plato's *Gorgias* p. 465. and the Scholia there p. 107. Ruhnken edition. and compare Valckenaer *Diatribe on Euripides* p. 244. ff.
— 6. **and perhaps it even says itself**] <note>original: *τάχα δὲ καὶ αὕτη λέγει*</note> “*But perhaps it even pronounces*: There are two ways of knowing the beautiful: one sudden *through the sense of the beautiful itself*; **the power appointed over it**: the other *proceeding gradually through judgment and comparison of some external beautiful thing with the internal pattern of beauty.*” *D. W.*
— 7. **as if by a rule of the straight**] <note>original: *ὥσπερ κανόνι τοῦ εὐθέος*</note> Compare Plotinus p. 416. D. where it should be read thus: **for the rule, having joined the straightness in the soul and that in the wood, being placed in between, gave to the craftsman the ability to judge the thing crafted**.
— 8. **the builder having fitted the outer house to the form of the house within**] <note>original: *τὴν ἔξω οἰκίαν τῷ ἔνδον οἰκίας εἴδει ὁ οἰκοδομικὸς συναρμόσας*</note> The Grammarians are greatly deceived who go about claiming **architectural/builder** <note>original: *οἰκοδομικὸς*</note> for the Attics: they pronounce **builder** <note>original: *οἰκοδόμος*</note> unknown to the same. You see Oudendorp on Thomas Magister p. 645. and Lobeck's *Parerga* p. 487. ff. As for the sentiment, see Aristotle *Metaphysics* II. 4. p. 41.

It also discusses the soul's internal "rule" or "standard" used to recognize beauty in the physical world.</summary>

-> ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS <-

Sylburg p. 52. ed. Brandis. Syrianus on him [Plotinus] p. 6. a. b. Venice edition: "*nevertheless, the nature of constant substances existing throughout the universe consists of fabricatory species [forms], just as artificial things exist in art itself; but even he (Aristotle) concedes those things which are according to art. For in many places he says that the material is perfected by an immaterial gift,*" etc. cf. the same [Syrianus] p. 29. b. where he praises Parmenides, Iamblichus on him, and Plotinus himself. See *Enneads* V. 9. p. 559. sq. where our author [Plotinus] treats of the intellect, the species, and *of being*. Moreover, Augustus [Augustine] follows the footsteps of Plotinus in *De vera relig.* cap. 38. p. 768. sq.; likewise Hermias in *Platon. Phaedrum* p. 109. and the Grammarian in Bast. in *comment. palaeogr.* at the end of Gregory of Corinth p. 813.

p. 102, 12. **συνδησάμενον καὶ κρατῆσαν** [binding together and prevailing]] "συγκροτῆσαν is a worse reading." *D. W.* [Daniel Wyttenbach]. Concerning this verb see the interpreters on Julian's *Caesars* p. 308. D. Spanheim; Dorville on Chariton p. 251. Leipzig edition; and others whom I have praised in my specific Edition p. 189. sq. where I judged these two readings ought to be joined, so that we read: **συνδησάμενον καὶ συγκροτῆσαν καὶ κρατῆσαν**. In this way, a truly elegant gradation arises: *binding together* (i.e., joining from without), *fusing* (making to coalesce inwardly), and *subduing* (namely, the nature adverse to itself). Thus these three would most aptly correspond to the three: *binding together, fusing,* and *prevailing*, and *consonant, harmonizing,* and *friendly*. For *syndêsamenon* and *sygkrotêsan*, the accusative must be supplied from the following genitives. Marcus Antoninus V. 1. **συγκοσμούσας κόσμον** [arranging the world]; codex Darmstadt: **συγκροτούσας κόσμον** [striking/fusing the world together]. Eustathius on *Odyssey* IV. 230. concerning man — "composed [**συγκροτουμένου**] of certain good things." Himerius *Orat.* XXI. 10. p. 746. "the beauty of nature now tempered [**σύγκρατον**] by variety." Read **συγκροτοῦν**, "consonant in its variety of forms."

— 15. **ἀνήνεγκέ τε καὶ εἰσήγαγεν εἰς τὸ εἴσω** [[he brought up and introduced to the interior]] Whether Ficinus read it otherwise, I could not say. In the books [manuscripts] there is no variation. However, it ought to be: "*he carries forth (brings out) and introduces to that which is impartible within.*" *Anapherein* is to carry forth to a *higher* (or more noble) level. Suidas I. p. 201. Kuster edition; Zonaras p. 107. Schweighäuser *Lex. Polyb.* p. 42. sq.

p. 103, 1. **οἷα ἀνδρὶ ἀγαθῷ κ. τ. λ.** [[as to a good man etc.]] We have removed the commas after *prosênes* and *alêthei*. "Just as a trace of virtue appearing in a youth is pleasing to a virtuous man, because it accords with the true virtue which is within." Concerning the word *prosênes* [pleasing], we advised above at I. 4. 14. p. 38. D.

— 3. **τὸ δὲ τῆς χρόας κάλλος—φωτὸς** [[the beauty of color—light]] The beauty of color *is a simple form and will overcome the darkness in matter by the presence of light.* See Plato's *Timaeus* p. 31. a., *Philebus* p. 29. C. Aristotle *De Anima* II. 36. [likely 418b], *De Sensu et Sensib.* III. 7. Plotinus p. 166. A. 711. c. 18. A. Iamblichus *De Myst.* p. 45. ibid. Gale. Moreover, Plotinus posits matter as devoid of quality (**ἄποιον**, see Lennep on *Phalaris* p. 149; our notes to Proclus *Inst. Theol.* cap. 80. p. 124.). See Plotinus p. 166. sq. Proclus in *Tim.* p. 141.

— 4. **φωτὸς, ἀσωμάτου καὶ λόγου καὶ εἴδους ὄντος** [[light, being incorporeal and reason and form]] Cf. p. 101. sq. p. 704. A. where, just as light is in this passage, so he says fire *is life and reason and endowed with soul.* See also Philo *De Vit. Mosis* p. 676 sqq. pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite *De coelest. hier.* p. 193 sq. Augustine *Confessions* X. 51. p. 188.

— 5. **τὸ πῦρ—τάξιν—εἴδους ἔχει** [[fire has the rank of form]] Hence Heraclitus, Hippasus, Metapontinus, and the Stoics derived the origin of things from fire. Plato *Cratylus* p. 413. C. Stobaeus *Eclogg.* I. p. 312. 314. Heeren edition.

ib. **πῦρ—ἄνω μὲν τῇ θέσει** [[fire—upward by position]] These things agree with the tenets of Pythagoras and Empedocles. See Proclus in *Tim.* p. 141. and Sturz’s Empedocles p. 307. Hence *pyr anôpheres* and *anôphoron* [upward-tending fire]. Achilles Tatius in *Arati Phaenom. Isag.* p. 126. sq. Gregory of Thessalonica in *Matthaei Lectt. Mosquenss.* II. p. 23. cf. Aristotle *Topic.* V. p. 342. Sylburg edition.

— 8. **οὐκ εἰσδεχόμενον κ. τ. λ.** [[not receiving etc.]] Dionysius the Areopagite expressed these things almost word-for-word in *De coelesti hier.* 15. p. 193. And very often that man [pseudo-Dionysius] is accustomed to incrust his "Areopagite wall" with the tesserae of Plotinus, Proclus, and other Platonists. Away then with Nicolaus of Methone in Proclus *Instit. Theol.* p. 150. ed. Voemel and similar doctors of the Church who would persuade us that Plotinus, Proclus, and the rest of that school took many things from Dionysius and corrupted them.

— 9. **θερμαίνεται—οὐ ψύχεται** [[it is heated—not cooled]] cf. Our author [Plotinus] on the immortality of the soul p. 465.

ib. **κέχρωσται** [[it is colored]] Cf. Plotinus p. 715. c. 22. where most codices agree in this reading. Add Hermias in *Plat. Phaedr.* p. 141.

ib. **τὰ δὲ ἄλλα—τὸ εἶδος τῆς χρόας λαμβάνει** [[but the others receive the form of color]]
