-> LIB. VI. ENNEAD. FIRST. p. 102—104. <-

More correctly in this place, Ficinus translates **Cætera** [The rest]. Thus it should also be in the following for *alia* [others]. See above. Let us see what **εἶδος χρόας** [form of color] might be. A manuscript Grammarian: *chroma* [color]; properly that which is with matter, such as ochre, cinnabar [read **κιννάβαρι**]; but *chroa* and *chroia* is the form itself of the color. Similarly Chalcidius in Plato's *Tim.* p. 454. Meursius edition calls colors "**sylvam**" [matter/wood/forest]: "But an image made by art, and fashioned according to an archetypal species, unless it has *sylvam*, if indeed it be a painting, *that is*, colors—will lack a certain perfection." Yet for Plotinus, **τὸ εἶδος τῆς χρόας** is the universal species of color (or color universally), the cause and source of which is fire; thus the species of color itself is the source and origin of individual colors. Cf. our author himself p. 711. cap. 18. a.

— 11. **ἐξίτηλον** [[faded/evanescent]] Hesychius II. 82. and Alberti there. *Photii Lex. Gr.* p. 90. The contrary is *deusopoios* [fast-dyed]. *Lex. Rhet.* in Bekker's *Anecd. Grr.* I. p. 252. Wyttenbach on *Selecta Historr.* p. 340. It is used of light, color, dye, and the characters of letters. A Doric fragment in Iamblichus *De vit. Pythag.* XVII. 76. "so that (the garments) might drink up the dye so as to be unwashed out, and never become **ἐξίταλον** [faded]." Artemidorus *Onirocrit.* IV. 47. p. 360. Reiff edition uses this word figuratively; likewise Plotinus p. 347.—"Codex Vossianus reads **οὐ μετέχον** [not participating], as in the margin of the Basel edition, which is more correct." *D. W.*

— 13. **αἱ δὲ ἁρμονίαι—δέξασαι** [[the harmonies—having received]] The passage, unless it is lacunose, seems to be weighed thus: "but the hidden harmonies which are in sounds, having produced manifest harmonies, they themselves also produced as it were... having received": "But the hidden harmonies, which are in voices, and produce (elicit) manifest harmonies, *themselves* imbue the soul with the knowledge of the beautiful, *inasmuch as* they demonstrate this very thing in another genus." Furthermore cf. Augustine *De Musica* VI. 38. p. 531. E.

— 15. **Παρακολουθεῖ—εἰς τὸ κρατεῖν** [[It follows—unto prevailing]] In this passage, hidden harmonies of sounds are compared with apparent ones. The latter are measured by numbers; the former are not. Nor is just any ratio suitable for measuring these numbers to produce a fitting or beautiful concord, but only that which obeys, which allows itself to be tempered to produce a species, so that this victorious Idea subdues the as-it-were unformed matter of sounds. Cf. Ficino's *Argumentum*; **ποίησις** in this place is to be taken actively, as for example in Plato's *Symposium* p. 205. b. and very often; **εἰς** before *poiêsin* signifies the end or *purpose*; the second **εἰς** before *to kratein* signifies *consequence* or *effect*, in this sense: but only that ratio is to be applied to those numbers which is able to procreate an idea; *whereby it happens* that this idea, as if a conqueror, subdues the matter.

— 17. **εἴδωλα καὶ σκιαὶ** [[idols/images and shadows]] Cf. below p. 56. F. "images and traces and shadows," likewise concerning corporeal beauty. These are Platonic formulas and vocabulary. See *Phaedr.* p. 255. d. Heindorf on *Theæt.* p. 499. Wyttenbach on *Phædon.* p. 171. and the many others I have collected in my specific edition p. 203. and in Proclus *Inst. Theol.* p. 101.

p. 104, 1. **ἐκόσμησαν** [[they adorned]] Correctly Ficino referred this word to **ὕλην** [matter], and *dieptoêsan* [they fluttered/excited] to the senses of men who are moved by corporeal beauty; as the context wishes them to be understood. Sappho uses the simple active **ἐπτόασεν** for amatory affection in that Ode in Longinus *De Subl.* X. p. 42. where see Toup. Plato *Legg.* VI. p. 783. **ἀφροδισίων διαπτοήσω** [fluttering of sexual desires] concerning the vehement lust of lovers. In this place, I would prefer it to be taken universally for *stunning and exciting desire*.

— 3. **περὶ μὲν τῶν προτέρω καλῶν κ.τ.λ.** [[concerning the former beauties etc.]] These are drawn from Plato's *Symposium* p. 210. a. b. Our author [Plotinus] has the same before his eyes p. 556. A.B. cf. also *Timaeus* p. 31. c. and Proclus on it p. 128. Soon after, **ἀντειλημμένοις** [seized upon] was faultily written in the Basel edition, regarding which Wyttenbach says: "Codex Vossianus reads **ἀντειλημμένοις**, which is more correct." We have corrected it thus. Conversely, in Dionysius p. 76, Clement of Alexandria *Pædagog.* II. p. 219, we rendered **ἐνειλημμένον** [wrapped in] for **ἐνηιλημμένον**.

— 7. **οἷον εἴ τινες—τυφλοὶ γεγονότες** [[as if some—having become blind]] You may take these as if separated by a parenthesis. Ficino, in translating, completed the sentence. Furthermore, these things recall the Aristotelian saying in Stobaeus *Floril. Tit.* 65. p. 408. p. 496. Gaisford edition: "Why is there love for the beautiful? He said it was the question of a blind man." Cf. Dio Chrysostom *Orat.* 29. p. 539. Reiske edition and Basil the Great *Homil. in Psalm.* XLIV. p. 505. A.

— 11. **ὡς καλὸν τὸ τῆς δικαιοσύνης καὶ σωφροσύνης πρόσωπον** [[how beautiful is the face of justice and temperance]] "**καὶ σωφροσύνης** is absent from Codex Leidensis. It refers to the saying of the poet: 'the golden face of justice,' which Aristoxenus has in Athenaeus XII. p. 546. b. [p. 529. Schweigh.] cf. also Heyne on Pindar *Fragg. incert.* LXIII. [p. 114.] *D. W.*—Gellius *N. A.* XIV. 4: "Worthily indeed and decorously *Chrysippus*, in the first of the books inscribed *On the Beautiful and Pleasure*,

[[vocabulary: Ficinus, Plotinus, Chalcidius, idea, materia [matter], harmonia [harmony], pulcritudo [beauty], Justitia [Justice], Sapientia [Wisdom]]]

p. 104, 11. **καὶ οὔτε ἕσπερος οὔτε ἑῷος οὕτω καλὰ** [[and neither the evening nor the morning star is so beautiful]] Which signs, however, are commonly celebrated as the most beautiful. And in ancient times, beautiful things were accustomed to be compared to the stars. *Iliad* VI. 295. XXII. 317. *Odyssey* XV. 108. Virgil *Aen.* VIII. 590. and Heyne there. Perictyone in Stobaeus *Serm.* 78. p. 458. p. 118. Gaisford edition: "For the sight of parents is divine and beautiful—as much as neither the sun nor all the stars, which the heaven having kindled dances around," where see Gaisford, who rightly defends the common reading in the last word. Aristotle *Ethic. Nicom.* V. 1. 15. p. 79. Sylburg edition p. 210. Zell edition: "and for this reason justice often seems to be the greatest of virtues, and neither the evening star nor the morning star is so marvelous," etc. My friend Zell, in the *Comment. ad Aristot.* T. II. p. 164. sq. to the cited passage, taught me that this proverbial senarius [line of verse] is assigned to Euripides by Acciaiolus and Argyropylus. Furthermore cf. Andronicus' *Paraphrase of Aristot. Ethic. Nicom.* p. 261. ed. Dan. Heinsius. Similar things are read, certainly in sentiment, in Cicero's *De Offic.* Bk. I. cap. 7. §. 1. Moreover, the Venerable Bede in *Sententt. Aristotell.* Tom. II. p. 245. Basel edition, expressed it word for word. A sepulchral title in the Schoepslin Museum p. 75. praises a certain Crescentina thus:
*She who among the living rose like the morning star [Eous],*
*Now sets beneath the earth as the evening star [Hesperus] among the dead.*

— 12. **ἀλλὰ δεῖ ἰδόντας μὲν εἶναι, ᾗ ψυχὴ τὰ τοιαῦτα βλέπει** [[but it is necessary for those seeing to be such that the soul sees these things]] "ἰδ. μὲν εἶναι, perhaps read **νοεῖν** [to perceive/think]." *D.W.* The codices and Ficino persevere in the common reading; and it has that by which it may defend itself. The philosopher had just shown that as those who lack the sense of the eyes cannot judge corporeal beauty, so neither can the beauty of pursuits etc. be pronounced upon by those who have never beheld it with the internal vision of the mind. Now he proceeds: *Yet it is necessary that we see by that with which the soul beholds such things.* Concerning the construction see Fischer on Weller III. 6. p. 4. sqq. and in the meaning of *sight* itself. Aeschylus *Ag.* 1189. "will be seeing." Euripides *Hecuba* 658. "if seeing the light." Plotinus moreover respects Plato's *Symposium* p. 94. Wolf edition p. 80. Ast edition: "seeing with that by which the beautiful is visible." We will place more below p. 57. B.

— 13. **ἠσθῆναι καὶ ἔκπλ. λαβεῖν** [[to be delighted and struck with awe]] "They are plainly Platonic in words and things." *D. W.* See *Phaedrus* p. 250. A. *Sympos.* c. 29. p. 93. Wolf edition. Dio Chrysostom *Orat.* 21. p. 506. Reiske edition. Proclus in *Theol. Plat.* III. 18. 51. Plotinus below p. 55. G. p. 56. A. and p. 722.

ib. **καὶ πτοηθῆναι** [[and to be fluttered/excited]] Cf. above at p. 53. B. The source of the locution is again in Plato's *Symposium* p. 206. p. 436. Bekker edition: "much fluttering [**πτόησις**] has occurred concerning the beautiful," where others read **πτοίησις**, for no one today would doubt Abresch's masterful emendation for *poiêsis*. Cf. also *Phaedon.* p. 82. *Cratylus* p. 404. A. Plutarch *De occulte vivendo* p. 1128. Plotinus above p. 20. B—D. p. 714. c. 22 A. and the many others I have compared in my specific edition.

— 16. **καὶ πόθον καὶ ἔρωτα** [[and longing and love]] See *Symposium* p. 191. a. p. 197. 3. *Cratylus* p. 420. A. Ammonius p. 59. Valckenaer. Coray on Heliodorus *Aeth.* p. 370. sq. and cf. John Chrysostom *De Sacerd.* III. 11. p. 150. Roman edition.

p. 105, 1. **καὶ τὰ μὴ ὁρώμενα** [[and things not seen]] Guil. Rinck conjectured **ἐρώμενα** [loved things], comparing Plato *Phaedr.* p. 237. d. p. 221. Heindorf edition: "and those not loving." I was unwilling to change without manuscripts. But just now my friend Rinck persuaded me to correct **πάντες μὲν ὁρῶσι** [all indeed see], which reading had long pleased me and is confirmed by the authority of Ficino and all the manuscripts. Conversely, I left the following **κινοῦνται** [they are moved] untouched, although **κεντοῦνται** [they are pricked] tempts us. See Plato *Republic* V. p. 474. d. Plotinus p. 215. E. 430. C. 770. B. Proclus *Theol. Plat.* p. 60. Michael Psellus *In omnifar. doctrina* §. 82. p. 128.

— 3. **ἀλλ' εἰσὶν οἳ μάλιστα** [[but there are those who most...]] "namely **κινοῦνται**, but there are those who are moved most." *D.W.* Rinck formerly defended **οἳ**, namely **κινούμενοι**: "But those are most incited, who are also said to love." I thought Wyttenbach should be obeyed, nor is manuscript authority lacking.

— 4. **Τῶν δὴ καὶ** [[Of those indeed also]] Rinck wishes to read **τῶν δὲ καί**. Certainly *kai* should not be cast away. For these things respect those which were sought above in ch. 2 from the lover of beauty which falls upon the senses.

ib. **τὰ ἐν οὐκ αἰσθήσει** [[things not in sense]] For this Plato in *Hipp. maj.* p. 298. has: "being outside of sense." Furthermore, the Batavian censor of the specific edition of this book wishes this passage to be translated thus: "Moreover, even from those who are held by the love of things rising above sense, it is necessary to inquire, what do you suffer etc."

— 5. **καὶ τρόπους καλοὺς** [[and beautiful characters]] See Alcibiades' speech in Plato's *Symposium* p. 216. D. and *Charmides* p. 159. D.

— 7. **ἑαυτοὺς ἰδόντες τὰ ἔνδον καλούς** [[seeing themselves beautiful within]] Socrates prays in Plato's *Phaedrus* p. 279. B.: "grant me to become beautiful within," whence Himerius *Orat.* 4. 4. p. 464. and Clement of Alexandria *Strom.* V. p. 595. B. drew the same formula. Cf. our author p. 216. E. F. where he uses the other form, **τἄνδον**, and p. 543. D. E.

— 8. **καὶ πῶς ἀναβακχεύεσθε** [[and how you are driven to Bacchic frenzy]] Plato *Phaedrus* p. 249. a.: "possession and madness—awakening the soul and driving it to Bacchic frenzy," which passage many have expressed. See praises in the specific edition. Plotinus p. 714. A.: "the soul is moved and driven to Bacchic frenzy and filled with a gadfly [sting]."

ib. **καὶ ἑαυτοῖς συνεῖναι ποθεῖτε** [[and you long to be with yourselves]] See Plato *Symposium* cap. 27. p. 86. Wolf edition and concerning similar formulas, such as "to be in oneself," Valckenaer at the end of Hemsterhuis and Valckenaer *Oratt.* p. 383. Plotinus below p. 57. D.: "and you have been purely with yourself"; p. 759. D.: "to be with oneself." Hermias in *Phaedrum* p. 170.: "becoming in himself." Persius *Satir.* IV. 53.: *Live with yourself.* Moreover, Proclus had our passage before his eyes in *Tim.* p. 173.

— 11. **οὐ σχῆμα—ἔχουσαν** [[not having a figure]] Plato *Symposium* c. 29. p. 92. 94. Wolf edition. *Phaedrus* p. 247. c. *Republic* V. p. 476. b. *Gorgias* p. 465. b. Plotinus *De intellig. pulcrit.* p. 543. D. E.: "and beauty is not in magnitude"; cf. especially our author p. 722. sq. I have compared more to our passage in the specific edition p. 221—227.

— 13. **ὅταν—θεάσησθε—ψυχῆς—ἦθος δίκαιον καὶ σωφροσύνην** [[whenever you behold in the soul a just character and temperance]] Plato *Symposium* p. 209. b. p. 88. Wolf edition. *Republic* III. p. 402. and thence in Stobaeus *Serm.* 63. p. 409. p. 499. Gaisford edition: "whenever beautiful characters in the soul happen to coincide and harmonize with the form of that person, participating in the same type, this would be the most beautiful sight for one able to behold it." Cf. Menander in Stobaeus *Serm.* 64. p. 407. p. 493. nr. 2. Gaisford edition.

— 15. **καὶ ἀνδρίαν βλοσυρὸν—πρόσωπον—σεμνότητα** [[and courage [with] a grave face—dignity]] Concerning the spelling **ἀνδρία** and **ἀνδρεία** see those I praised in the specific edition. Plato *Republic* VII. p. 535.: "for the most steadfast and courageous—not only noble and grave [**βλοσυροὺς**] etc." Aelian *V. H.* XII. 21.: "to behold [one] dignified and grave." Moreover, **σεμνὸς** [dignified/august] is also said of beauty. See Isocrates *Encomium of Helen* §. 25. In Plotinus in this place, **βλοσυρὸς** is *grave, venerable*. Ficino translates not inconveniently: "*with a noble countenance, modest.*" I have appended more in the specific edition p. 229. At this place, I will advise Aristotle's *Rhetor.* I. 9. 3. p. 67. Oxford edition: "The beautiful, therefore, is that which, being desirable for its own sake, is praiseworthy; or that which, being good, is pleasant because it is good." p. 68 follows concerning justice, courage, temperance, and the rest of the virtues.

ib. **αἰδῶ** [[shame/modesty]] Concerning this form of the accusative add to those things which I placed in the specific edition p. 230, Stephanus *Thesaurus* London edition p. 1459—1463 and Buttmann *Grammat. maj.* p. 187. sq. You find the same also in the context of the Oxford edition of Aristotle *Rhetor.* II. 6. p. 132.

— 16. **ἐπιθέουσαν** [[running upon/supervening]] Plotinus *De intelligib. pulcrit.* p. 551. C.: "or that which runs upon all things around its entire magnitude, as it were." Cf. p. 709. A. 714. A. 715. A. "grace supervening [**ἐπιθέουσα**] upon beauty," p. 722. D. where we restored from the books **ἐπιθέον** for **ἐπιθετέον**.

ib. **ἐν ἀτρεμεῖ—διαθέσει** [[in an immovable disposition]] Plato *Phaedrus* p. 250. C. cf. Hermias p. 158. Plotinus p. 770. B.: "it has become quietly in a solitary state, immovable in its own essence, inclining nowhere."

ib. **ἀκύμονι—διαθέσει** [[in a waveless/calm disposition]] "Synesius imitates this in *De Regno* p. 10. C." *D. W.* See now the annotations of the learned Krabinger on this oration of Synesius p. 205. and Wyttenbach cited there on Plutarch *Morall.* p. 112. sq. minor Oxford edition.

p. 106, 1. **τὸν θεοειδῆ νοῦν ἐπιλάμποντα** [[the godlike mind shining upon]] Plato *Phaedrus* p. 251. a.: "whenever he sees a godlike face [or] beauty well imitated," where cf. Hermias p. 159. Dionysius the Areopagite *Coel. Hier.* I. 3. p. 4. Elsewhere our author calls the mind the "son" and "beautiful youth" [**κόρον**] of the Good, as at p. 353. B. cf. Plato *Rep.* VI. p. 506. e. Naturally, in the *Good itself* is the first source of beauty, but the *mind* flowing from it imparts beauty to the *soul*, and the soul to all other things. Plato used *lampein* [to shine] concerning beauty in *Phaedrus* p. 250. D., which many have imitated, whom I praised in the specific edition. Maximus Tyrius *Diss.* 25. p. 8.: "the flower of the soul implanted in a beautiful body is made bright by it and shines out and is transparent." Cf. Isidore Pelusiota *Epist.* IV. 71. p. 450. sq. and our author himself *De intellig. pulcrit.* p. 543. A. and *Against the Gnostics* p. 201. C.

— 3. **ἄλλο τι φήσει** [[will he say anything else]] Which many books offer as **φῆ** (they intended **φῇ**), nor is this unusual after *ou mê*. Xenophon *Hiero* XI. 15.: "enemies will not be able to hold out against you."

Plato *Rep.* p. 341. b. p. 31. Bekker edition: "but you will certainly not be able." The reasoning of that passage, however, is different. However you read it, our passage ought to be added to the places collected by those who have treated this construction. Valckenaer on Euripides *Hippol.* 607. Dawes *Miscell. Critt.* p. 221. sq. Wyttenbach on *Selectt. Historr.* p. 343. and 446. and Heindorf on Plato *Phaedon.* p. 44.

p. 106, 4. **τί ὄντως ὄντα; ἢ καλὰ** [[what are truly existing things? or beautiful?]] These must be distinguished either thus: "What truly existing things are other than beautiful?" understanding *allo* [other]; concerning which ellipsis see Zeun. on Viger p. 409: "What truly existing things are others than beautiful?" or with Codex Vindobonensis C. one should read **ἦ**, *certainly*. This is pleasing.

ib. **τί ὄντα πεποίηκε—οἷον φῶς** [[what has made them beings—like light]] Plato *Republic* III. p. 620. b.: "and indeed the most beautiful is most lovely." The same *Phaedr.* p. 250. D. Augustine in *Psalmm.* p. 56. 7. E. Plotinus posited a definition of the *erasmios* [lovely] p. 724. sq.

— 6. **βούλει δὲ—αἰσχρὰ—ἀναπαραθεῖναι** [[and do you wish—ugly things—to compare/set beside]] Plato *Republic* VI. p. 506. c. p. 315. Bekker edition: "Do you wish then to behold ugly things?" The other form **εἰ δὲ βούλει** [if you wish] also has an aorist infinitive attached in the same author in *Sympos.* p. 177. a. p. 378. Bekker edition: "if you wish again to consider the good sophists."

— 7. **ἀντιπαραθεῖναι** [[to set beside/compare]] "Codex Leidensis [and] Vossianus read **ἀντιπεριθεῖναι** [to place around], badly." *D. W.*

— 8. **διότι φαμέν** [[because we say]] **φανὲν** [appearing] in Codex Vossianus [and many others]. Ficino omitted it. Let the common reading be translated: "and why we say what is ugly." *D.W.* But if the reading of most codices prevails, it should be translated: "what is ugly and for what reason, let it be made manifest (appear)."

ib. **Ἔστω δὴ ψυχὴ—αἰσχος** [[Let there be indeed a soul—ugliness]] We have corrected the punctuation of this passage.

— 10. **μικροπρέπειαν** [[meanness/pettiness]] Ficino could and perhaps ought to have translated: *illiberalitatem* [illiberalness]. Aristotle *Rhetor.* I. 9. 12. p. 33. Sylburg edition p. 68. Gaisford edition: "magnificence is a virtue productive of greatness in expenditures; but smallness of soul and meanness are the opposites." Cf. Aristotle *Ethic.* II. 7. IV. 2. Concerning *envy*, Demosthenes does not greatly differ from Plotinus, who in *Against Leptines* p. 121. sq. Wolf edition: "that envy is altogether a sign of a wicked nature."

— 12. **σκολιὰ πανταχοῦ** [[crooked everywhere]] Similarly in Plato, *orthos* [straight], *euthys* [direct] and *skolios* [crooked] are opposites. *Gorgias* p. 524. c. concerning the vicious soul; "and all things crooked by falsehood and boastfulness, and nothing straight." Cf. *Phaedrus* p. 253. c.; *Republic* II. p. 368. (from Pindar, see *Fragg. incerta* IV. p. 81. Heyne edition); ibid. VI. p. 506. C. cf. Athenaeus XV. p. 540. Schweighäuser edition and Maximus Tyrius XVIII. p. 338.

ib. **ζῶσα ζωὴν τοῦ** [[living the life of...]] "Perhaps read **ἑαυτῆς** [her own], or something omitted." *D.W.* Our codices exhibit nothing more, and Ficino expressed the same reading.

ib. **ὅ, τι ἂν πάθοι—αἶσχος** [[whatever it might suffer—ugliness]] "*Whatever it may suffer through the body, taking that for sweet ugliness.*" *D. W.* We have given, however, **πάθη** [it suffers], with the persuasion also of the learned Dissen, Professor at Göttingen.

— 13. **αὐτὸ τοῦτο—ἐπακτὸν καλὸν φήσομεν** [[this very thing—we shall call acquired beauty]] I removed the comma after *autê*. Ficino might seem to have found somewhat more in his codices. Which is otherwise. For the Medicean excerpts do not differ from the common reading. To Rinck, it seemed necessary to substitute *kakon* [evil] for *kalon* [beautiful], but we do not wish to innovate without manuscripts, nor do I see, if you accept this conjecture, what it would mean in the following, "and mixed with much evil."

— 14. **ἆρα οὐ—φήσομεν** [[Shall we not—say?]] *Nonne dicemus?* See Hoogev. on *Particull.* p. 74. ed. Schutz. alt. Hermann on Viger p. 824. Heindorf on Plato *Cratylus* p. 18. sq.; on *Phaedon.* p. 36.

ib. **προσγεγονέναι** [[to have been added/accrued]] Plato *Hipp. maj.* p. 289. d.: "whenever that species is added to the beautiful." Concerning the word **ἐπακτὸν** [acquired/added] I have placed many things in the specific edition, which I omit here; nor is it necessary for more to be added after Wyttenbach's discussion on Plutarch I. p. 319. sq. minor Oxford edition; I will confine myself to Platonic and Plotinian things. (See p. 56. B. p. 556. B. "beauty acquired for bodies." Suidas I. p. 785. cf. Zonaras p. 808.) *Epakton*: brought in; foreign; violent; Plotinus says *epakton* to the soul is virtue, etc. The passage is I. 2. 1. where see our Annot. p. 12. C. Basel edition. In Cicero, the opposites in *De Harusp.* are *domesticus nativusque luctus* [domestic and native grief]. The same in *De Republ.* II. 4. says: *merces adventiciæ* [foreign goods], and ibid. II. 15. *transmarinis et importatis artibus* [by overseas and imported arts]. Regarding the sentiment on the ugliness of the soul, cf. the same in *De Legg.* I. 19. 52. sqq. Concerning natural beauty, and that which is placed opposite to it, *acquired* [quæsita], it will be helpful to have read Philostratus' fortieth Epistle. Moreover, the discussion of Plato in *Philebus* p. 51. c. d. p. 161. sqq. Stallbaum edition, pertains primarily to the philosophical notion of both beauties. Add *Hipp. maj.* p. 295. c. d. *Gorgias* p. 474. sq. To the words of this Plotinian passage belong these of Philo Judæus in *De no-*

p. 107. 11. **καὶ ἔργον αὐτῷ** [[and it is a work for him/it is his task]] Ficino: *it will be worth the effort*. I prefer: *there is need of work*. See Xenophon *Cyrop.* II. 3. 5.; *Agesil.* X. 1. ib. **ἀπονιψαμένῳ καὶ καθαραμένῳ** [[having washed off and purified]] One must think of *aponimmata* [washings] and *katharsia* [purifications], i.e., purgations and washings and expiations, by which shames were expiated. Stobaeus *Eclogg.* T. I. p. 342. Heeren edition: "Plato [says] that nothing is either heavy or light by nature existing in its own place. Stallbaum; *Phaedon.* p. 16. Wyttenbach edition and the annotation there. Valckenaer *Scholl. in N. T.* on 1. Cor. V. 8. p. 181. sq. and Plotinus p. 721. c. 30. C.

ib. **ὥσπερ χρυσῷ—γεώδους—ἀφέλοι—χρυσὸς—καλὸς—μονούμενος** [[as if for gold—earthy—he should take away—gold—beautiful—being left alone]] In the specific edition p. 267. sqq. I set forth more things, by which the reason might be opened why Plotinus, both in this place and others, e.g., *De intelligib. pulcr.* p. 544. B., transferred the simile of purified gold to declare the nature and excellence of the soul. You see Plato *Phaedon.* p. 81. c.; *Symposium* p. 216.; *Sophist* p. 228. c—e. Apollo concerning Augustus in Julian's *Caesars* p. 309.: "For I, delivering him to this Zeno, will immediately show him to you as pure gold [**χρυσὸν ἀκήρατον**]," where see Spanheim's *Epreuve de Remarques* p. 24. add Plutarch *De Discrim. p. 108, 3. **καθαρθεῖσα ἃ ἔχει σωματωθεῖσα** [[purified of what she has having been embodied]] "*Purified from those things which she had received by habit of the body.*" Ficino reads otherwise; perhaps he read something else in his book." *D. Phaedr.* p. 167. and Plotinus p. 378. F.

*Phaedon.* p. 64. p. 40. Wyttenbach edition and *Gorgias* p. 524. B.

p. 108, 13. **μεγαλοψυχία δὲ δὴ ὑπεροψία τῶν τῇδε** [[magnanimity indeed is the disdain for things here]] Plato *Alcib.* I. 140. c.; Aristotle *Rhet.* I. 33.; *Eth. Nicom.* I. 10. IV. 3. Its opposite is *mikropsychia* [smallness of soul], *an abject and lowly mind*. cf. Graevius on Cicero *Epist. ad Att.* IX. 11. p. 65. where he shows that what codices commonly exhibit, *makropsychia* [long-suffering/patience], is not Greek. See also above at p. 54. C. To "turning away from things below" cf. below p. 56. E. and what I placed above at I. 2. 4. p. 14. B.

p. 109, 2. **νοῦς δὲ—τὸ κάλλος αὐτῇ οἰκεῖον κ.τ.λ.** [[the mind indeed—beauty is its own to her etc.]] Cicero *Acadd.* II. 12. "*that which appears accommodated to nature (the Greeks call it oikeion).*". Cf. the notes annotated above at p. 54. D.

— 4. **ὁμοιωθῆναι εἶναι θεῷ, ὅτι—τῶν ὄντων** [[to be made like to be God, because—of beings]] "Codex Vossianus adds **εἶναι** [to be] before God, well." *D.W.* We received it from most of our codices, and from Ficino, who adopted it from the Medicean books and rendered it by translating. For the sentiment cf. Plotinus *De Bono et Uno* p. 768. A. Augustine in *Epist. ad Marcellum* 138. p. 412. and in *Confessions* X. 53. cf. also above p. 51. G.

— 6. **ἡ δὲ ἑτέρα φύσις, τὸ αἰσχρὸν** [[the other nature, the ugly]] These flowed from Plato's doctrine of the *heteron* [other] or *thateron* [the other]. See *Timaeus* 35. sq.; Plutarch *De virtutib.* p. 441. sq.; Pollux V. 169. sq. and cf. Ast on Plato *Phaedr.* p. 290. add Plotinus above p. 54. F. p. 463. A. p. 559. A.

— 7. **ὥστε κἀκεῖνο ταὐτὸν** [[so that that also is the same]] "Codex Vossianus [and three others, and those good ones, see var. lectt.] read **κἀκείνῳ**. Perhaps one should read **κἀκείνως**, i.e., also in that way." *D.W.* Guil. Rinck defends the common reading in this little word. Moreover, he orders the passage to be punctuated and read thus: "the ugly, and the same and first evil; so that that also is the same and good and beautiful, or etc." I have held it a religious duty to change such places. The same Rinck likes *oun* [therefore] before *au* and *dê*. And Ficino expressed that. We have obeyed the better books.

— 9. **καὶ τὸ πρῶτον θετέον τὴν καλλονὴν—τὰ δὲ ἄλλα ἤδη καλά** [[and the first is to be posited as beauty—but the others already beautiful]] This is a primary passage. Plato himself sometimes touches strictly upon this decree, by which *the Beautiful itself is posited as the same as the Good*, now brings it forth doubtingly, now indeed confirms it more surely and confidently when repeated from its own causes. You go to *Lysis* p. 216. D.; *Hipp. maj.* p. 296. sq.; *Alcib. pr.* p. 115. sq. and especially *Philebus* p. 64. sq. Plotinus also returns very often to this passage which is *on the Good and the same as the first beautiful, and on the degrees of beauty*. See p. 291. D. E. p. 556. C. D. p. 557. sq. p. 714. sq. especially p. 724. sq. I treated these passages in the specific edition p. 294—298.

— 12. **Καὶ τὰ σώματα—ψυχὴ ἤδη ποιεῖ** [[And bodies—the soul already makes]] "The soul makes bodies beautiful." Plutarch explains this sentiment in a fragment of a lost book *For Beauty*, in Stobaeus *Serm.* 63. p. 408. p. 496. Gaisford edition, which passage I praised above. Cf. also Plotinus p. 715. C. Moreover, this decree is joined with the other Platonic one: *the body is begotten by the soul*; regarding which see *Tim.* p. 107. sq. and Plutarch in *Quaest. Platonn.* p. 1002. F.

— 13. **ὧν ἂν ἐφάψηται** [[whatever it might touch]] Aristaenetus *Epist.* I. 12. 3. p. 57. Boissonade edition: "and it touches upon beauty." Alciphron *Epist.* III. 12. p. 50. Wagner edition: "to touch upon music." And very often figuratively in Plato, as in *Phaedr.* p. 273. A.; *Phaedon.* p. 18. Wyttenbach edition; *Symposium* p. 212. p. 446. Bekker edition. Plutarch in *Numa* c. 8.: "to touch upon God," *to attain God with the mind*. Hermias in *Phaedrum* p. 75.: "to touch upon generation." cf. Plotinus I. 1. p. 5. and VI. 2. 20. VI. 2. 22.

— 15. **ἀναβατέον—καλόν** [[one must ascend—beautiful]] Plotinus p. 708. c. 16.: "it is necessary not always to remain in this much beauty, but to pass over further toward the upward, having darted forth and left this behind."

p. 110, 1. **εἴ τις οὖν εἶδεν αὐτὸ, οἶδεν** [[if anyone therefore saw it, he knows]] "If anyone indeed saw, he has known." Thus I have now thought it should be written, first moved by the authority of most of our books, then because Plotinus teaches that the greatest force consists in beholding beauty and in the preceding p. 53. C. had already said, he who has not seen the beautiful, cannot speak of it, then because at p. 56. A. he repeats the same, "if anyone should see this." My friend Rinck also persuaded me that it should be corrected thus. Furthermore, concerning these forms *eiden, oiden* see *Etymol. M.* p. 296. Sylburg edition and Wyttenbach on Posidonius' *Reliquiae* p. 277.

ib. **ἐφετὸν—ἡ ἔφεσις πρὸς τοῦτο** [[desirable—the desire toward this]] Plotinus p. 712. A. below. "Shall we say then the Good is desirable?" cf. 714. A. Dionysius the Areopagite *De Divinn. nomm.* 4. p. 567. The source is in Plato. Hermias in *Phaedrum* p. 111.: "divine souls—desiring divine beauty." Proclus *Inst. Theol.* c. 8. The same in *Alc. I.* p. 328. 336. our edition. Olympiodorus ibid. p. 117. 121. where these interpreters of Plato conclude thus: "If therefore every good is desirable, every desirable is lovable, every lovable however is beautiful: consequently every beautiful is good." Moreover, another Plotinian passage, *De intelligib. pulcrit.* p. 551. A., is to be compared with our entire passage.

— 2. **τεύξις δὲ αὐτοῦ** [[attainment of it]] See above I. 5. 2. and what I placed there at p. 43.

— 3. **καὶ ἀποδυομένοις ἠμφιέσμεθα** [[and stripping off we have been clothed]] Plato *Gorgias* p. 523.: "many then—having wicked souls have been clothed in beautiful bodies etc." Concerning the figurative use of the word *chitôn* [tunic/garment] and similar ones see Wyttenbach *Epist. Crit.* p. 49. sq. Porphyry *De Abstin.* I. 31. p. 52. Rhoer edition; Proclus in *Inst. Theol.* §. 208. p. 312. agree with our passage, where see our Annot. Justin Martyr *Dial. cum Tryphone* p. 385.

ib. **ἠμφιέσμεθα· οἷον ἐπὶ τὰ ἅγια—καὶ τὸ γυμνοῖς ἀνιέναι** [[we have been clothed; as if toward the holy places—and to go up naked]] Although confusion of the members of a sentence is not unusual in Plotinus: nevertheless in this place Rinck saw well that the construction can be looked to thus, so that a colon is replaced for a comma before *heôs*, so that the words *hoion anienai* are taken as a parenthesis. Therefore we have punctuated it so.

— 4. **ἐπὶ τὰ ἅγια τῶν ἱερῶν τοῖς ἀνιοῦσι** [[unto the holy of holies for those ascending]] Cf. p. 56. e. "remaining within in holy sanctuaries." Whence also in our passage Ficino translates: "*he penetrates into the holy of holies*." To which interpretation another passage of our author p. 770 seems to favor somewhat. But although you take it as referring to a temple, one must necessarily think in our passage of holy arcana or mysteries. And since Plotinus placed *epi ta hagia* [unto the holy things], not *eis ta hagia* [into the holy things], it seems more advisable for the passage to be taken as referring to arcane sacrifices. Now if anyone should object that before sacrifices were performed the garments were laid aside, I wish him advised that one should not think in this place of legal sacrifices, by which victims are slaughtered, but of that kind of offerings where flowers, wreaths, and fruits are presented to the Gods. And that sacrifices of this kind were rather often administered by naked men, so many images conspicuous on the painted vases of the Greeks argue. Moreover, those who wished to be initiated into the Eleusinian Mysteries ascended through degrees to the highest; of which the first is *katharmos* [purification]. Hence our *katharseis* [purifications]. No less were the garments laid aside in the same Mysteries. Whence likewise Plotinus [says] "the putting away of garments — to go up naked." As for Plotinus saying "for those ascending" [**τοῖς ἀνιοῦσι**] and "to go up" [**ἀναβαίνειν**]: these are the solemn words in this matter, as *anerchesthai* [to go up]. Cf. also our author p. 720. c. 28. We have set these things forth more fully, with passages of the ancients added, in the specific edition p. 305—309.

— 5. **ἕως ἄν τις παρελθὼν—ἴδῃ** [[until someone having passed—sees]] "Codex Leidensis [and] Vossianus read **ἀνελθών** [having ascended]. In the same **ἀλλότριον** [foreign/alien] is missing. Perhaps correctly." *D. W.* Ficino must be thought either to have indulged himself too much, or to have read thus: "having gone away—casting off everything as much as is foreign to God."—I, who had found *parelthôn* [having passed/surpassed] and *allotrion* [foreign] in most books, which depends on it, did not hesitate to introduce it into the order. Lucian T. IX. p. 382. Bipontine edition: "to surpass [**παρελθεῖν**] all in happiness." Plotinus *De anima in multitudinem prolapsa* p. 761.: "she surpasses [**παρέρχεται**] therefore the one, having come into number and multitude." Cf. Matthiae *Gramm.* §. 518. 522. Add Eudocia's *Violetum*: p. 291.: "until he should pass the punishments." Therefore our passage is to be translated thus: "Until, with all things *surpassed* in the ascent, *which are foreign to God.*" For the sentiment cf. Plato *Symp.* c. 29. *Politicum* p. 158. c. 26. Proclus *Alc. pr.* 249. our edition. Furthermore, concerning the word *apothesis* [putting away], of rarer use, and familiar to sacred and ecclesiastical writers, *concerning the laying aside of the vices of the soul or body*, Wyttenbach advised on Plutarch p. 789. minor Oxford edition.

— 7. **ἀφ' οὗ πάντα ἐξήρτηται** [[from whom all things depend]] See Suidas I. p. 771. Kuster edition, where also concerning the construction with the preposition *ek*. Cf. also Budaeus *Comm. Ling. Gr.* p. 739. Interpreters on Thomas Magister p. 327.

p. 110, 8. *καὶ ζῇ καὶ νοεῖ—καὶ τοῦ εἶναι* [and it lives and thinks—and of being]] [[abbrev: Cf. → Compare]] **Plotinus, *On Numbers*, p. 690. B. sq. Proclus, *In Alcibiadem prima*, p. 249.** "See life boiling and a sleepless intellect, lacking nothing for the sake of living."
— 9. *τοῦτο εἴ τις ἴδοι* [if someone should see this]] “This refers to the saying of Plato in **Phaedrus p. 346. E. [p. 251. Steph.]** as in the Ciceronian **Offices I. 5. [and] Ends II. 16.**” *D. W. [Dissen?]*
— 10. *βουλόμενος αὑτῷ συγκαθῆναι* [wishing to sit down with oneself]] Interpreters on **Herodotus IV. 152. end. Valckenaer on Euripides, *Hippolytus* 253. the same on Hebrews IV. 2. in *Scholae in N. T.* II. p. 473. sq. Timaeus of Locri, *On the Soul of the World* p. 548. Galen. Plato, *Laws* X. p. 324.** Moreover, it possesses the force of an intimate conjunction, or declares that mixture from which one thing entirely emerges. **Pollux VIII. 151.** "to be unified; to be mixed; to be blended." **Proclus, *In Alcibiadem prima*, p. 321. sq. in our edition.** "And the beautiful is perfect and good and altogether just, and the just is mixed with the beautiful and the good; and the subject is one, though the definitions differ." **Origen, *On Prayer*, p. n. Wetstein.** "to be blended with the spirit." **Gregory Nazianzen, Oration XXXV. p. 575. A.** "man was blended with God." [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] **Oration I. p. 11. C. Plotinus IV. 2. end; V. 5. 2. beginning; VI. 6. 18; VI. 7. 35.**
— 12. *τῷ—ἰδόντι—ἐπὶ καλῷ ἀγασθαι* [to the one seeing—to wonder at the beautiful]] Properly, *the power arises, it happens*. Thus *ὑπάρχει* [it belongs/exists] is used rather frequently. **Plato, *Greater Hippias*, p. 292. d.** "(the beautiful) to whatever it may be added, it belongs to that thing to be beautiful." [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] ***Symposium* c. 29. and see Wyttenbach on *Select Historical Texts*, p. 381. Dio Chrysostom 29. p. 538.** "Complete and true beauty [wondrous] thus belonged (adding *τῷ* with Reiske) (*had not yet been present to anyone*) as it does to this one."
— 13. *καὶ ἐκπλήττεσθαι ἀβλαβῶς* [and to be struck without harm]] **Plato, *Greater Hippias*, p. 303. c.** Concerning the pleasures involved in beauty, "that these are the most harmless of pleasures and the best." **Marcus Antoninus IV. 8.** "it does not make a man worse than himself, nor does it harm him (the Darmstadt book adds) etc." **Plutarch, *On Beauty*, in Stobaeus, *Sermon* 63. p. 410. p. 501. Gaisford.** "For the beauties of the soul are also hopes of salvation (perhaps *καὶ σώματι σωτηρίας* [and salvation for the body], Wyttenbach) etc."
ib. *καὶ ἐρᾶν ἀληθῆ ἔρωτα* [and to love with a true love] etc.]] In the Latin edition of Florence, it is argued that the comma was not placed after *πόθους* [longings] in the Greek. Incorrectly. **Ficino:** “let him be affected by a true and supreme love: let him mock sharp passions and other loves etc.” We, with Dissen's approval, have changed the punctuation and joined the two members: *καὶ ἐρᾶν ἀλ. ἔρωτα καὶ δριμ. πόθους* [and to love with a true love and sharp longings], with this sense: “*and to burn with true love and sharp affections, but to mock the remaining loves.*” Moreover, the word *Δριμὺς* [sharp/keen] is a *medium* term [of neutral connotation], and not rarely designates *prudent, sagacious*. **Aristophanes the Grammarian in Eustathius on *Odyssey* γ'. p. 110. Basel edition. [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] Gataker on Marcus Antoninus V. 5. p. 142. (p. 187.)** And indeed, **Plutarch** joined the word to love itself in a good sense, ***Numa* XVI. 2.** "a keen love of peace." **Proclus** expressed our passage in ***In Alcibiadem prima* 100. p. 330. in our edition:** "and if anyone is conscious of himself, he surely knows that this good has keener loves than the beauties in perception; therefore the good is beautiful." This sentiment is due to **Plato in *Symposium* p. 210. sq. p. 443. sq. Bekker. Add Plotinus, *On Intelligible Beauty* p. 549. B. C. and p. 556. A. B.**
— 16. *ὅσοι, θεῶν εἴδεσιν ἢ δαιμόνων* [as many as, by the forms of gods or daemons] etc.]] i.e. *met by chance, happening upon gods etc.* Here first must be brought to mind what the ancient Greeks commonly accepted as tradition concerning the *epiphaneiai* [manifestations] of Gods and Goddesses. See Interpreters on **Homeric Hymn to Ceres v. 275; Heyne, Excursus IX on the *Iliad*, Vol. IV. p. 191. sqq.** Next, regarding the Philosophers, see **Plato, *Epinomis* p. 1010; Cicero, *De Natura Deorum* I. 18. 27; II. 23; Oration of Julian VII. p. 408. sq.; Iamblichus, *On the Mysteries* I. 17.** Plotinus should be compared with **Marcus Antoninus III. 6. p. 76.** from which I shall subscribe only the conclusion: "if you see anything better than this (of these, Darmstadt Codex), turning to it with the whole soul, enjoy the best that is found (plainly as Plotinus does in the following: *remaining in the vision—and enjoying it*); but if nothing better appears than the daemon dwelling within you—if all other things are smaller and cheaper than this, give no place to any other."
p. 111, 1. *τί δῆτα οἰόμεθα εἴ τις* [what then do we think if someone] etc.]] These and the following are taken almost word for word from the **Symposium** of Plato, p. 211. d. e. p. 244. sq. Bekker. [[abbrev: Cf. → Compare]] furthermore **Phaedo p. 70. Wyttenbach; Parmenides p. 212. Heindorf; *Republic* V. p. 476; Cratylus p. 439. e.** On the distinction between *τὸ αὐτὸ καλὸν* [the beautiful itself] and *τὸ ἀεὶ καλὸν* [the eternally beautiful], see **Proclus on *Timaeus* p. 73.** The Darmstadt Codex recognizes this in **Marcus Antoninus V. 3.** instead of *ἀλλὰ ἔκαλον* [but I was beautiful], where Gataker conjectured in the margin *ἀλλὰ εἰ καλόν* [but if beautiful].

ib. *ἵνα τις καὶ βέβηλος ἴδῃ* [so that someone even profane might see]] He again took an Orphic expression from the ***Symposium* p. 33.** On it see **Ruhnken on Timaeus p. 60; Wesseling at the end of Valckenaer, *On Aristobulus the Jew* p. 130; and Valperga in *Epistola Critica* p. 15. sqq.**
— 4. *εἰς τὰς προτέρας ἀγλαΐας σωμάτων* [into the former splendors of bodies]] On this word more in the specialized edition. Now I shall summon **Homer, *Odyssey* XVII. 244.** *ἀγλαΐας—ἁπάσας*, "all splendors," i.e., "insolence spreading widely." [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] **XIX. 82.** and **Apollonius, *Homeric Lexicon* p. 13. Tollius, and the interpreters there. Plotinus p. 299.** "the garden of Zeus or his statues and splendors (*ἀγλαΐσματα*)." Nor is the plural placed in our passage by accident. For the philosopher wishes it to be understood: *the charms and ornaments of beautiful bodies and the delights born therefrom: All the pomp and all the sensual charms of beautiful bodies.* Plotinus's imitator, the so-called **Dionysius the Areopagite**, imitated the plural in ***On Mystical Theology* I. 1. p. 2.:** "of the exceedingly beautiful splendors (*ἀγλαϊῶν*)."
— 6. *προστρέχειν* [to run toward]] Lest anyone think of *προσέχειν* [to pay attention], we have argued more in the specialized edition. To these passages add now **Plutarch, *On Listening to Poets* p. 40. A. p. 151. Wyttenbach.** "running toward and flocking together with those who blame." In a similar sense *ὑποτρέχειν* [to run under/flatter] is used with the Dative and with the Accusative; see **Plutarch, *Sayings of Kings* p. 185. E. p. 736. Wyttenbach. Plato, *Laws* XI. p. 923. b.** By which the common reading is also confirmed in **Hesychius I. page 915. Alberti.** In our passage, regarding *μήτι προστρέχειν*, *αὐτοῖς* [to them] must be supplied, with this sense: “*For though he should behold bodily beauties, yet in no way ought he to apply himself to them or be held by their allurements.*” The opposite is the following *φεύγειν* [to flee], and it is followed by *ἐπιδράμοι λαβεῖν βουλόμενος* [he might run over wishing to seize]. Immediately **Ficino** expressed *γνόντα* [recognizing], and this seems necessary after *ἰδόντα* [seeing]. But since neither the Medicean codices nor any other of ours have the plural, I felt a religious scruple about changing it, especially in this writer, who rather frequently uses a sudden conversion of speech. For the sentiment compare **Galen, *Protrepticus* c. 8; Dio Chrysostom, Oration 29. p. 543. E. F. collected 216.**, with whom **Augustine** agrees in ***On True Religion* c. 41. p. 741. D.**
— 7. *εἰ γάρ τις ἐπιδράμοι* [for if anyone should run over] etc.]] For *δοκῶ μοι* [I seem to myself] one should write *δοκεῖ μοι* [it seems to me] [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] p. 57. **A.** p. 383. "as is reasonable that even the myth should enigmatically signify." A formula of modesty, by which Plotinus is accustomed to introduce his interpretations of myths. Next, either *δ λαβεῖν βουληθεὶς* [he who wished to seize] must be corrected for *οὗ* [where], or the words *οὗ λαβ. βουλ. —ἀφανὴς ἐγένετο* [wishing to seize... he vanished] must be included in parentheses, with this sense: “*For if anyone should snatch the shadow of beauty as true beauty, just as when an image appeared in water (which someone, as the myth, I believe, signifies, desiring to capture, fell headlong into the stream and vanished): so too he who embraces beautiful bodies, and does not let go, will be cast down—not indeed in body, but in soul—into the depth;*” so that accordingly *λαβεῖν* for *to grasp, to snatch*, is joined with the accusative case: with the genitive for *to desire to capture, to hunt for, to wish to possess*. Writers of prose are usually accustomed to declare that by the *middle* verb and the genitive. **Heindorf on Plato, *Protagoras* p. 602. Wyttenbach on Plutarch, *Moralia* p. 560.** See however **Aelian, *Various History* I. 30. and Gospel of Luke V. 5.** and the interpreters there.
— 8. *ἐφ’ ὕδατος ὀχουμένου* [carried upon the water]] Above p. 52. **E.** "a form carried upon other forms." In our passage it means *to appear*. For the rest see the specialized edition, and there **Hemsterhuis on Lucian, *Prometheus* I. p. 216. Bipont; Coray on Heliodorus p. 252; Wyttenbach on Plato, *Phaedo* p. 227. and on Plutarch, *De Sera Numinis Vindicta* p. 86. p. 271. new edition and cf. Plotinus p. 387.**
— 9. *ὥς που τὶς μῦθος* [as some myth, I believe]] **Aelian, *Various History* X. 18.** "as Homer also somewhere says." **Paul, Hebrews II. 6.** "But someone somewhere testified saying," where see **Valckenaer in *Scholae* II. p. 427.** Therefore the reading of some of our books *ὥσπερ τις μ.* is of no value.

D.** works excellently for our passage. — 8. *Τὸ δὲ ἐπέκεινα* [But that which is beyond]] Regarding the subject, we saw most recently at the words *ἥξει πρῶτον ἐπὶ τὸν νοῦν* [he will come first to the intellect]. **Origen**, though otherwise a Platonist, had differed from Plotinus and the rest of the Platonists in this matter, whom **Proclus** attacks in ***Platonic Theology* Book II. c. 9. p. 40.** And Plotinus in *On Intelligible Beauty p. 581. A.* calls this very *Good the father of intelligible beauty, who is superior to intellect*. **Proclus, *On Providence and Fate* in Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Graeca* IX. p. 375. c. 5. thus:** “For this (*the good*) alone is more divine than intellect, because even intellect, which is greatly praised, desires the Good and is with all things and before all things.”
— 9. *προβεβλημένον* [projected/put forward]] “These things in certain places seem entangled and should be thus explained: *προβεβλημένον τὸ καλὸν πρὸ αὑτῆς ἔχουσαν κ.τ.λ. i.e., holding the Beautiful projected before itself, so that, simply stated, the first thing that offers itself to us is the beautiful. The rest as in Ficino.*” *D. W.* See various reading. The word agrees with **Iamblichus, *On the Soul* in Stobaeus, *Physical Eclogues* I. p. 926. Heeren. "ethereal coverings surrounding the intellectual life, projected before itself (the soul)."** **Proclus on *Alcibiades prima* p. 257.** "many having projected some other form of irrational things," where however other books have *περιβεβλημένον* [having wrapped around]. Not badly either. [[abbrev: Cf. → Compare]] the same **in Plato's *Republic* p. 380. and Gregory Nazianzen, *Invectives against Julian* p. 75.**

W.* See various readings. [[abbrev: Cf. → Compare]] **Plotinus p. 555.** where likewise **Codex Cizensis** falsely has *σκόπον* [aim] for *τόπον*. **Zonaras, *Lexicon* p. 1502.** "in the soul in a higher and incomparable and more beautiful manner (*τρόπῳ*)." Correct to *τόπῳ* [place], and see **Suidas III. p. 29.** On the subject see **Plato, *Republic* VI. p. 509.; Hermias on *Phaedrus* p. 142. and p. 169.; and Plotinus, *On Intelligible Beauty* p. 555. B.**

C.** "both spring and principle of activities." [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] **p. 770. C.** For the sentiment apply **Plato, *Greater Hippias* p. 289. D.** and **Plotinus himself p. 711. c. 18. A. and p. 723. c. 32. ib. *ἢ ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ τὸ ἀγαθὸν—ἐκεῖ τὸ καλόν* [or the good in the same—there the beautiful]] “These things are mutilated and seem to be thus integrated: *ἢ ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ τὸ ἀγαθὸν καὶ καλὸν θήσεται, πλὴν πρῶτον τὸ ἀγαθὸν, ἑξῆς δὲ καλόν, i.e., or he will place the good and the beautiful in the same place, yet so that he places the good first, and next the beautiful.*” *D. W.* No remedy was offered by the Codices in this place. Therefore we accept **Wyttenbach's** reasoning with a grateful mind, yet so that we leave the context untouched.

-> LIB. VII. ENNEAD. FIRST. p. 115—120. <-

Because **Rinck** objects to **Wyttenbach's** reasoning on the grounds that in this way the notion of *time* is transferred to the supreme Good, from which it is most foreign: the learned man did not see that philosophers very often speak thus, so as to accommodate their speech to *our grasp*, while the same men profess nothing more foreign to the notion of God than the notion of *time, succession* and other things of that kind. For the rest, the same **Rinck** thinks these things should be distinguished in Plotinus: first, *τὸ ἀγαθὸν* [the good], or *τὸ πρῶτον ἀγαθὸν* [the first good], or *τὴν καλλονὴν* [beauty], next *τὸ καλὸν* [the beautiful] or *τὸ νοητὸν καλὸν* [the intelligible beautiful], then *ἀγαθὸν* without the article simply, which also falls upon the soul and even sensible things. These are the views of **our Rinck**.—Moreover, these final points of Plotinus are joined with the doctrine of the Platonists concerning the *steps* or the *ascent* of man *through steps to God*. Certainly Plotinus, dealing with this, discusses more things apposite to our passage in the **final Ennead p. 770.**; by which the wise and blessed man is described: "not even turning around himself, standing altogether and becoming as it were a station—but already over-running the beautiful, having already surpassed even the chorus of virtues."

-> **LIB. VII.** <-

**p. 120, 7. *Περὶ τοῦ πρώτου ἀγαθοῦ, καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἀγαθῶν.* [On the First Good, and Other Goods.]]** This book is, if we consider the order of writing, the last of all Plotinian works, as being the final one of those four which he had sent to **Porphyry** shortly before his death. See the latter on the life of Plotinus chap. 6., where however he entitles it otherwise: ***περὶ τοῦ πρώτου ἀγαθοῦ, ἢ περὶ εὐδαιμονίας* [On the First Good, or On Happiness]**, whereas on the contrary the same chap. 24 refers to the same inscription which the books themselves present in this exordium; and indeed the fourth book of this first Ennead has the title: ***περὶ εὐδαιμονίας* [On Happiness]**. Moreover, this book, to which we now preface, is most of all to be compared with the ninth book of the **sixth Ennead: *περὶ τἀγαθοῦ ἢ τοῦ ἑνὸς* [On the Good or the One]**, likewise with the seventh book of the **sixth Ennead: *περὶ τοῦ πῶς τὸ πλῆθος τῶν ἰδεῶν ὑπέστη, καὶ περὶ τἀγαθοῦ* [On how the multitude of ideas subsists, and on the Good]**, in which book he repeats the doctrine of the *Good* joined with the passage on *numbers and ideas* more deeply from its own causes, following the example of Plato. Who indeed, after he had begun and sketched these primary passages of his philosophy in the ***Sophist, Philebus, Timaeus*** and in the books ***On the Republic***, especially the eighth, had followed them out more copiously in his schools and so brought them to an end. And these disputations of the master his disciple **Aristotle** had examined and explained in the books ***περὶ ἀγαθοῦ* [On the Good]** or ***περὶ φιλοσοφίας* [On Philosophy]** (**Suidas in *ἀγαθοῦ δαίμονος* Vol. I. p. 17. Kuster; John Philoponus on Aristotle, *On the Soul* I. 2. c. 2.; Alexander of Aphrodisias in Simplicius on Aristotle, *Physics* Fol. 32. B.**) **Xenocrates**, a hearer of Speusippus, had likewise written ***περὶ τἀγαθοῦ* [On the Good]**. (**Diogenes Laertius IV. 13.**) Moreover, the books of Speusippus and other Platonists entitled ***περὶ φιλοσοφίας* [On Philosophy]** (**Diogenes Laertius IV. 4.**) seem to have been of the same argument as that Aristotelian one on the Good or on Philosophy. Regarding which matter ***Chr. Aug. Brandis*** recently disputed at length in ***Diatribe Academica* on the lost books of Aristotle *On Ideas* and *On the Good* or *Philosophy*. Bonn 1823. p. 4. sqq. [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] p. 49.**—Moreover, Plato had referred the Good (*τὸ ἀγαθόν*) to the highest unity. (**Aristotle, *Metaphysics* XIII. 8. XIV. 4. p. 246. p. 301. ed. Brandis. : "Of those saying there are immovable substances, some say that the one itself is the good itself. They thought however that the one was its substance most of all."**) In which **Speusippus** had separated his judgment from Plato's authority (**Aristotle in the place cited p. 247. and the Pseudo-Alexander on him; Stobaeus, *Eclogues* I. 28. p. 58. Heeren.**) Moreover, Plato had distinguished that first and supreme being, which he called *τὸ ἀγαθὸν*, the Good, from the unities which are in numbers (**Aristotle, *Metaphysics* XIV. 4. [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] the cited Diatribe of Brandis p. 65. sq.**) We shall add other things concerning these decrees below at the beginning of the seventh book of the sixth Ennead p. 692. In this place it will not be out of place to have reminded of those things which **Diogenes Laertius III. 101.** reports from Plato's doctrines concerning the Good, narrating thus: that by Plato the Good was divided into four genera (*γένη*) or forms, species (*εἴδη*): one being endowed with virtue, another being virtue itself, a third being useful (or convenient) foods and exercises, a fourth being the skill of playing flutes, acting, poetry and similar things. And I would believe that Plotinus had such decrees of Plato before his eyes in several places of this little book. Moreover, how Aristotle and the Peripatetics were accustomed to divide *Goods* variously, we learn from the copious excerpts in **Stobaeus, *Ethical Eclogues* II. 7. p. 286. sqq. ed. Heeren.** What the rest of the philosophers thought about the *Good* and *Goods* is both long to explain and does not greatly serve the argument of this little book. Of the Stoi-

cs, to add this one thing, you have the matters disputed on this subject reduced to an epitome in **Diogenes Laertius VII. 94. and 101.** Moreover, those things which Plotinus touched upon in the third chapter of this little book concerning death are joined with an argument competed for by Greek philosophers; from whose schools Cicero brought many things into the first of the *Tusculan Disputations*. See only **book I. c. 7. sqq.** and what **Davies** applied there in the annotation from the sources. For books of philosophers ***περὶ θανάτου* [on death]** are mentioned, such as those of **Xenocrates (Diogenes Laertius IV. 12.), Diogenes the Cynic (Diogenes Laertius VI. 80.), Aeschines, and others**. Hither also pertains the argument of the *Consolations*, in which the most noble Greek writers labored. Regarding whom **Wyttenbach's** learning and diligence in the *Animadversions on Plutarch's Consolatory Letter to Apollonius* has spared us the trouble of speaking. Consult him, especially at the beginning p. 697. sqq. of the Oxford octavo edition, and the present passage on the goods that are in death p. 758—770.
— 12. *Εἰ δὲ—ἀρίστη οὖσα* [But if—being the best] etc.]] In the edition it was incorrectly printed *οὔση*. **Engelhardt** explains the meaning well, namely thus: The natural action of life is the Good for each one; consequently also for the soul. But besides natural action, the soul also has another action, which strives toward the best; by which second action it (the soul) itself becomes the best. And this Best is not only Good in respect to the soul (*πρὸς αὑτήν*), but is Good simply and through itself.—For the rest, that *τὸ κατὰ φύσιν ζῆν* [to live according to nature] or *ὁμολογουμένως τῇ φύσει ζῆν* [to live consistently with nature] was among the ethical principles of the Stoics is argued by those things which are disputed in Cicero, *De Finibus* III. 5. and 6. where consult **Davies**, and in **Diogenes Laertius VII. 85—87 ; to whom Menagius contributed more.**
p. 121, 2. *τὰ δὲ ἄλλα διχῶς ἂν ἔχοι ὅσα* [but the other things, as many as, would have it in two ways]] *ὅσα* [as many as] placed after *ἄλλα* [others] with several words intervening will trouble no one who knows Greek usage.
— 5. *ἐφιέμενον—οὖσαν* [desiring—being]] The feminine in *οὖσαν* [being] after *ἐφιέμενον* [desiring (neut.)] must be explained by the use of what they call Attraction. The force of that Attraction should be said to extend to the end of the period. For instead of *ἀλλ’ αὑτῇ μόνῃ τἀγαθὸν εἶναι* [but that the good exists for it alone], you would have expected *ἀλλ’ αὑτῷ μόνῳ* [but for it (neut.) alone]. Which would be very harsh. Accordingly I did not hesitate to receive into the text *αὑτῇ τῇ μονῇ*, by the very *abiding*. Which conjecture is confirmed both by the earlier *ἐν ἡσύχῳ οὖσαν* [being in quiet], and the following: *δεῖ οὖν μένειν αὐτὸ* [it must therefore remain], and indeed by the passage of Proclus in ***Platonic Theology***, which we have added at the end of this chapter. This *μονὴ* [abiding/permanence] of the Good itself is opposed to *ἐνεργείᾳ* [activity] and to *ἐφέσει* [striving] and no less to *νοήσει* [intellection]. For the sentiment of our passage apply **Proclus on *Alcibiades prima* p. 16.** where the perfect form is likewise said to be "one and the same remaining in itself." Similarly **Theodoret III. p. 470. Schütz** uses *μονὴν παρὰ τῷ πατρὶ* [abiding with the Father], so that the Word was from eternity with the Father, which use of the word **Suicer** neglected in the *Thesaurus Ecclesiasticus*, nor do the Lexica have it noted. **Engelhardt** incorrectly understood the beginning of the period; which we do not dwell upon. We touched upon the Platonic formula "spring and principle" (*πηγὴν καὶ ἀρχὴν*) above on **I. 6. p. 58. A.** What moreover moved **Ficino**, that after "spring" and "principle" he should infer "origin," I cannot fathom. There is no trace in the books. **Tennemann** excerpted this passage in ***History of Philosophy* VI. p. 141. sq.**
— 7. *ἀγαθοειδῆ* [good-form/boniform]] Likewise Platonic. Moreover, by Platonic philosophers the soul was said to be by nature *ἀγαθοειδὴς* (good-form). **Proclus on *Alcibiades prima* p. 280. in our edition:** "for it (the soul) is by nature good-form." [[abbrev: Cf. → Compare]] **Hermes, *The Key* p. 11. ed. Franciscus Patritius.** But especially this other passage of **Proclus in *Elements of Theology* CXIX. p. 174. in our edition** agrees with our passage: **"But in that it is a Unity, it is Goodness; and in that it is Goodness, it is a Unity; and as those who come after the first have proceeded from the first, they are good-form and unit-form; if indeed that is the One and the Good etc."** ubi in annot. et nostri loci et aliorum admonui. In the same book ***Elements of Theology* VIII. p. 14. Proclus teaches that the first good is called both the Good, and that other: *τὸ ἁπλῶς ἀγαθὸν* is that which all beings desire.** “Simply Good is that which all beings desire.” Which sentiments seem to be drawn from this passage of Plotinus.
— 12. *Οὕτω—καὶ ἀληθὲς, τὸ, οὗ πάντα ἐφίεται* [Thus—it is also true, that which all things desire]] As the words are now, **Ficino** translates correctly. **Engelhardt**, without noting the reader, translates: “*For thus it is the True, for which all things yearn.*” [German: “*Denn so ist es das Wahre, nach welchem Alles sich sehnet.*”]

as if it were written: *οὕτω γὰρ τἀληθὲς οὗ π. ἐφ*. For the rest **Proclus on *Alcibiades prima* p. 51.** posits three monads, faith, truth, and love (*πίστιν, ἀλήθειαν καὶ ἔρωτα*). The first (faith) establishing all things and settling them in the good, the second (truth) manifesting the knowledge in all beings, the third (love) turning all things back and gathering them into the nature of the beautiful. For the rest, the distribution of the Good which **Aristotle and the Peripatetics** posited serves the universal passage of Plotinus. See **Aristotle, *Magna Moralia* I. 1. and I. 2. and Stobaeus, *Eclogues* II. p. 286. sqq. Heeren.** from which I shall subscribe only these:—they say (the good) is spoken of in three ways: for it is the cause of salvation for all beings, and that which is predicated of every good, and the divisible; of which the first, which is pleasing:), the genus of goods, the end to which we refer all things, which is happiness. Whence you might conjecture that that other inscription of this Plotinian little book: ***περὶ εὐδαιμονίας* [On Happiness]** proceeded from some Peripatetic. Moreover, the twin passage **III. 9. 3. p. 358. E. F.** ought to be compared with our passage, where Plotinus explains these things more fully.
p. 121, 13. *ὥσπερ κύκλον πρὸς κέντρον—τὸ φῶς* [like a circle to a center—the light]] [[abbrev: Cf. → Compare]] **Plotinus IV. 1. "a line in the center." IV. 2. beginning** "lines in a circle from the center to the circumference." **IV. 7. 6.** "lines meeting from the circumference of a circle." [[abbrev: Cf. → Compare]] **IV. 4. 23.; VI. 5. 11.; VI. 6. 17.** from which it is sufficiently understood how frequent Plotinus is in using this mathematical example. **Proclus** took the same example from this very passage of Plotinus in ***Platonic Theology* XXIII. p. 58.: "Therefore all things remain because of the desirability of goodness, and it begets—and again the third, the perfect, is that which turns all things back and is collective toward the causes in a circle, of which one is the divine, another the intellectual, another the psychic, another the physical etc."** **Emperor Julian, Oration IV. p. 145.** after he set forth *on Goods*, of which the supreme God makes the remaining Gods participants, having crossed over to the mention of the *Beautiful*, proceeds: "to which he also distributes the perfect intellect, just as if putting vision into the eyes through light.—another activity besides these appears around the king of all things, the sun, the portion granted to the superior genera." Moreover, no one is ignorant of how diligently Julian read Plotinus.
p. 122, 1. *Τὰ δ’ ἄλλα πάντα—διχῶς καὶ ἐπ’ αὐτό* [All other things—doubly and to it]] Because in this place he uses the words *εἰδώλου—εἴδωλα* [of an image—images], in that he follows the usage of Plato, who opposes the image to the true thing. See above **on p. 50. B. and cf. Proclus on *Alcibiades prima* p. 33. 49. 136. 152. sqq. 155. in our edition.** Especially, however, these and the following are illustrated by the passage of our philosopher in ***Enneads* V. book 1. c. 6. p. 487. F. G. "What then must be said about the most perfect? Nothing from it except the greatest things after it. But the greatest after it is intellect, and it is second. For indeed intellect sees it, and has need of it alone. But it has no need of intellect. And that which is begotten from a superior intellect is itself intellect. And intellect is superior to all, because other things are after it, such as also the soul, the speech (*logos*) of intellect, and a certain activity, just as it is of that one. But the speech of the soul is dim, for as an image of intellect, it must thus look to intellect, and intellect likewise toward that one, so that it might be intellect."** Which things **Theodoret in *Therapeutica* II. p. 750. Schütz and Cyril *Against Julian* VIII. p. 173. B. C. Spanheim** touched upon. Cf. **Cyril ibid. IV. p. 145.** where he says Plotinus explains no more his own opinion than Plato's:—"For Plotinus says thus about him, and explains not so much his own opinion as that of Plato; moreover he says that the father of the causal intellect is the Good, and that which is beyond intellect, and beyond substance; and in many places he calls being, and intellect, the idea; so that Plato knew intellect was from the good; and from intellect, the soul." We shall add more to the passage of Plotinus, which we just summoned from the fifth Ennead. In what follows we have given from good books *ψυχῇ δὲ τὸ ζῆν* [for the soul to live] instead of *ψυχὴ* [soul], then we have amended the punctuation, as the sense demanded, and likewise in the Latin of Ficino we have corrected from the first edition: “if it should *gaze upon* [suspiciat] the good itself,” instead of the faulty "should receive" [suscipiat].
— 9. *διχῶς καὶ ἐπ’ αὐτό* [doubly and to it]] To these words one must think: *ἐστὶ τὸ ἀγαθόν* [the good is]. Doubly also *the good is in its power*. For the rest, he sets forth *on Goods* concerning the *soul* from the character of his universal system in **Aristotle in *Magna Moralia* I. 3.** which passage **Stobaeus** brought into the *Ethical Eclogues* **II. 7. p. 290. 299. Heeren.**
— 10. *χωλεύει γὰρ ἡ ζωὴ τῷ φαύλῳ* [for life limps for the wicked man]] In imitation of Plato, who uses *χωλὸς* [lame] and *χωλεύειν* [to limp] of things which fail in one of two parts, and transfers it metaphorically to the soul and other things. **Wyttenbach** teaches this on **Plutarch, *On the Education of Children* p. 74. and on Plato, *Phaedo* p. 178.** As for the fact that Ficino translates *claudicat* [limps], in that he has Cicero as his authority, who used it similarly in the *Brutus* c. 59.

<meta>This page continues the philological commentary on Plotinus, specifically focusing on the treatise "On Beauty" (Ennead I.6). The author compares Plotinus's Greek phrasing with other Neoplatonic, Patristic, and Classical sources.</meta>

# ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS

The word is very frequently joined to the noun *beauty* <note>original: "κάλλος" (kallos)</note>. **Plotinus, *On Intellectual Beauty*, "unfathomable beauty (of the gods)" p. 544. C. compare 549. D. John Chrysostom, *Homily VI on Hebrews*, p. 467. p. 666. Cyril of Alexandria, *Exposition of the Orthodox Faith*, p. 430.** However, our passage has a certain sweetness of its own, arising from a type of oxymoron <note>A figure of speech in which apparently contradictory terms appear in conjunction.</note> found in the words *device—deviceless* <note>original: "μηχανὴ—ἀμήχανον" (mechane—amechanon); a play on finding a way where there is no way.</note>. Similarly **Isidore of Pelusium, *Letters*, Book III, 160, p. 321:** "and he finds devices out of devicelessness." Plainly so **Cyril of Alexandria, *On Haggai* I, p. 630.**

p. 112, 2. *as if remaining inside in the holy sanctuaries* <note>original: "οἷον ἔνδον ἐν ἁγίοις ἱεροῖς μένον"</note>] Whereas **Wyttenbach in *Critical Epistle*, p. 250** had conjectured "established" <note>original: "ἱδρυμένον" (idrymenon)</note>, he has now passed over that in silence in this annotation; and the following words prove the common reading to be correct: "nor proceeding to the outside."

ibid. *so that even one who is profane may see* <note>original: "ἵνα τις καὶ βέβηλος ἴδῃ"</note>] He has again borrowed an Orphic expression from the **Symposium, p. 33.** Regarding this, see **Ruhnken on Timaeus, p. 60. Wesseling at the end of Valckenaer, *On Aristobulus the Jew*, p. 130, and Valperga in *Critical Epistle*, p. 15 and following.**

— 4. *into the former splendors of bodies* <note>original: "εἰς τὰς προτέρας ἀγλαΐας σωμάτων"</note>] More on this word in the Special Edition. For now I will cite **Homer, *Odyssey* XVII, 244:** "all splendors" <note>original: "ἀγλαΐας—ἁπάσας"</note>, meaning "widely spreading insolence." Compare **XIX. 82.** and **Apollonius, *Homeric Lexicon*, p. 13, edited by Tollius, and the interpreters there. Plotinus p. 299:** "the garden of Zeus or his statues and his splendors." Nor is the plural placed in our passage without reason. For the philosopher wishes it to be understood as: *the charms and ornaments of beautiful bodies and the delights born from them: All the magnificence and all the sensory charms of beautiful bodies.* **Dionysius**, commonly called the **Areopagite**, a mimic of Plotinus, imitated the plural in ***On Mystical Theology* I. 1. p. 2:** "of the beyond-beautiful splendors."

— 6. *to run toward* <note>original: "προστρέχειν" (prostrechein)</note>] Lest anyone think of "to pay attention to" <note>original: "προσέχειν" (prosechein)</note>, we have discussed this more fully in the Special Edition. To those passages add now **Plutarch, *On Listening to the Poets*, p. 40. A. p. 151 Wyttenbach:** "running toward and herding together with those who find fault." In a similar sense, "to run under" <note>original: "ὑποτρέχειν"</note> is used with the Dative and with the Accusative; see **Plutarch, *Sayings of Kings*, p. 185. E. p. 736 Wyttenbach. Plato, *Laws* XI, p. 923. b.** By which the common reading in **Hesychius I, page 915, edited by Alberti**, is also confirmed. In our passage, "not to run toward" must be understood as referring to *them* <note>the beautiful bodies</note>, with this meaning: "*For though he may look at bodily beauties, he must in no way apply himself to them or be held by their allurements.*" The opposite is the following "to flee," and there follows "he might run to catch them, wishing to seize them." Immediately **Ficinus** <note>Marsilio Ficino, the 15th-century translator of Plotinus.</note> rendered "having recognized" <note>original: "γνόντα"</note> and this seems necessary after "having seen." But since neither the Medicean manuscripts nor any other of ours has the plural, I was reluctant to change it, especially in an author who quite often uses a sudden shift in the style of speech. For the sentiment, compare **Galen in *Exhortation*, ch. 8. Dio Chrysostom, *Oration* 29, p. 543. E. F. collected 216.**, with whom **Augustine** agrees in ***On True Religion*, ch. 41, p. 741. D.**

— 7. *For if anyone should run toward, etc.*] For "it seems to me" <note>original: "δοκῶ μοι"</note> one should write "it seems to me" <note>original: "δοκεῖ μοι"</note> compare p. 57. **A.** p. 383. "as is likely that even the myth hints at." A formula of modesty by which Plotinus is accustomed to introduce his interpretations of fables. Then, either "he who wished to seize" <note>original: "δ λαβεῖν βουληθεὶς"</note> should be corrected for "of which" <note>original: "οὗ"</note>, or the words "wishing to seize which—he vanished" should be included in a parenthesis, with this meaning: "*For if anyone should snatch at the shadow of beauty as if it were true beauty, just as when an image appeared in the water, (which someone, as the myth, I believe, signifies, desiring to catch, fell headlong into the stream and vanished): so also he who embraces beautiful bodies, and does not let go, will be plunged—not in body, but in soul—into the depths;*" so that "to seize" <note>original: "λαβεῖν"</note> for *to grasp, to snatch*, is joined with the fourth case <note>Accusative</note>: while with the second <note>Genitive</note> it means *to strive for, to hunt, to wish to possess*. Writers of prose usually declare the latter with the *middle* voice and the genitive. **Heindorf on Plato's *Protagoras*, p. 602. Wyttenbach on Plutarch's *Moralia*, p. 560.** See, however, **Aelian, *Various History* I. 30. and the Gospel of Luke V. 5.** and the interpreters there.

— 8. *borne upon the water*] Above p. 52. **E.** "a form borne upon other forms." In our passage it means *to appear*. For the rest, see the Special Edition and there **Hemsterhuis on Lucian's *Prometheus* I, p. 216 Bipontine edition. Coray on Heliodorus, p. 252. Wyttenbach on Plato's *Phaedo*, p. 227. and on Plutarch's *On the Delay of Divine Vengeance* V, p. 86. p. 271 new edition, and compare Plotinus p. 387.**

— 9. *as a certain myth somewhere says*] **Aelian, *Various History* X. 18.** "as Homer also says somewhere." **Paul, *Hebrews* II. 6.** "But someone somewhere testified, saying," where see **Valckenaer in *Scholae* II, p. 427.** Therefore, the reading of some of our books "just as a certain myth" <note>original: "ὥσπερ τις μ."</note> is worthless.

ibid. *a certain myth*] "Namely, of Narcissus." *D. W.* Regarding this fable, as it pertains to the universal doctrine of the Beautiful, I have set forth more fully in the *Preparation*,

# BOOK VI. ENNEAD ONE. p. 112, 113.

-> <note>This section refers to the</note> preface to the special edition §. 10. p. XLV. and following, where see the praises in **Ovid's Metamorphoses VIII. 342; Nonnus's Dionysiaca XI. 322. and following, XV. 352, XLVIII. 582. and following; Pausanias IX. 31. 6; Eustathius on the Iliad II. 498; Anonymous on Incredible Tales ch. 9. p. 88. in Gale's edition** etc. etc. At this point I will add—what is not found there—that the fable of Narcissus is touched upon and applied as a stern warning by **John of Salisbury in the *Policraticus* <note>A 12th-century work on government and philosophy</note> book 8. chapter 5. F. G.** A mention of a similar fable in the poem of Antar, celebrated among the Eastern peoples, is made by **Tholuck in the book *Sufism*, p. 118. and following.**

p. 112, 9. <gloss>sinking into the depths of the stream</gloss>] **Philostratus, *Images* I. 23.** concerning the same Narcissus: <gloss>he went down into the spring.</gloss> More in the *Preparation* at the cited place and in the *Annotations* p. 343 and following of the special edition.

10. <gloss>he became vanished/invisible</gloss>] This is to be understood in a sinister sense, with this meaning: Narcissus, who chased the empty shadow of beauty, was himself reduced to emptiness. The indefinite phrase <gloss>he became vanished</gloss> serves this meaning better than the definite <gloss>he was drowned</gloss> or <gloss>suffocated</gloss>, which several writers use in this narrative. For Plotinus does not acknowledge the youth being turned into a flower.

— 12. <gloss>depths, where blind etc.</gloss>] These words seem to be arranged thus: *“depths, where remaining blind both here and there in Hades, he will dwell with shadows.”* “He who pursues the shadow of beauty, and thus falls into the dark and mentally horrific deep, is blind; and whether he *does this* (in *this life*) or descends into the underworld, he will live among shadows in both places.” Moreover, he touched upon the common <term>etymology of Hades<note>The Greek word for the underworld, 'Haides', was often anciently explained as 'a-ides', meaning 'the unseen' or 'not seeing'.</note></term> from *not seeing*.—Furthermore, *True Beauty* in this passage is opposed to *Apparent Beauty*, meaning true beauty joined with the goods of the soul.

ibid. <gloss>remaining blind in Hades</gloss>] “From Plato somewhere.” *D. W.* Compare this passage with its twin on p. 55. **A.**

— 13. <gloss>Let us fly then to our dear fatherland</gloss>] “Homer, **Iliad book 2, line 140.**” *D. W.* Compare **Iliad book 9, line 27 and Odyssey book 10, line 269.** and see **Plotinus** above p. 13. **C.** p. 724. **A.** ch. 33.

— 15. <gloss>how shall we be carried up?</gloss>] “that is, *how are we carried out to sea.* <note>original: "quomodo provehemur in altum"</note> Ficino omitted this; the **Leiden Vossian Manuscript** [and others] have <gloss>we shall endure</gloss>, which is incorrect.” *D. W.* This nautical verb in Plotinus was also read by the **Scholiast on Plato p. 129. Ruhnken edition**, a passage I shall produce next. Its opposite is <gloss>to be brought down</gloss>, meaning *to return to port*.

VOL. III.

See also **Wetstein on the New Testament Vol. I. p. 708.**

ibid. <gloss>as if from the sorceress Circe—or Calypso; Odysseus—not being pleased</gloss>] I have punctuated this according to the books and as reason itself suggests; “—just as from the sorceress Circe or Calypso, Odysseus says, signifying secretly, as I believe, not wishing to remain, although etc.” **Ficino** translates this passage more freely. Regarding the Homeric passages pertaining to the fable, such as **Odyssey V. 150 and following; VII. 254 and following; X. 470 and following;** likewise **Xenophon's *Memorabilia of Socrates* I. 3. 7; Cicero's *On Duties* I. 31. 8; Maximus of Tyre XXXIV. 8; Athenaeus I. 18. p. 34. and p. 39. LXX. and following. Add **Proclus on the *Alcibiades* preface p. 257. our edition.**

ibid. <gloss>sorceress</gloss>] See the notes above on our author **I. 4. 9. p. 35. D. and compare below p. 382, p. 434. A, 438. B, 479. A.**

— 16. <gloss>not being pleased to remain</gloss>] **Thucydides I. 35. beginning** likewise joined an infinitive to this verb. For the rest, compare **Fischer on Weller III. 1. p. 41; Koen on Gregorius p. 66. Schaefer edition; Hemsterhuis on Lucian's *Hermotimus* IV. p. 27. Bipont edition; Wesseling and Valckenaer on Herodotus p. 579; Bergler on Alciphron II. 51. p. 165. and there Wagner.**

ibid. <gloss>although having pleasures through the eyes</gloss>] “Although he uses or looks upon pleasurable things with the sense of the eyes.” Concerning this <term>periphrasis<note>A roundabout way of speaking</note></term> see **Valckenaer on Euripides' *Phoenician Women* 1554; Bergler on Alciphron I. 26.** Regarding the sentiment, compare **Plotinus p. 723. chapter 32.**

p. 113, 1. <gloss>Fatherland—from whence we came</gloss>] A conjecture in the margin of the **Vatican Manuscript** argues for a not unlearned reader. However, there is no reason why we should depart from the authority of the majority of the books. On the word <gloss>fatherland</gloss>, **Eustathius on Odyssey I. 55.** says: —<gloss>of the intelligible world; which is, according to the Platonists, the true fatherland of souls.</gloss> Compare the *Preparation* p. LXXXVI. and following, and see **Plotinus p. 556. A; Porphyry in the *Sentences* Section 34. p. 237; Paul's Epistle to the Hebrews XI. 14; and the many other things we cited in the special edition.**

— 2. <gloss>and Father</gloss>] A Platonic designation. See, to name but one, the **Timaeus p. 28. c.** **Plotinus** himself uses it for God on **p. 76. D.** and for Saturn in the same chapter 12.
