**p. 553. and following.** Another passage agrees with our text: **Plotinus p. 723: "Where is the one who created beauty—and gave birth to true being?"** <note>original: "ποῦ ὁ ποιήσας κάλλος—καὶ γεννήσας οὐσίαν;"</note>

p. 113, 2. **What then is this voyage?** <note>original: "Τίς οὖν ὁ στόλος;"</note>] See above *what then is this flight*, and *how shall we be carried up?* Therefore, in this place, *stolos* is not a "fleet," as Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the influential Renaissance translator of Plotinus.</note> translates it, but a **navigation or a maritime journey**. See **Orus in the Great Etymological Dictionary p. 728. 13. Wesseling on Herodotus I. 21. Ruhnken on Timaeus p. 43. Compare below I. 8. 6. p. 76. A. B. and the annotations there.**

ibid. **one must not travel it on foot** <note>original: "οὐ ποσὶ δεῖ διανύσαι"</note>] **Scholiast <note>An ancient commentator.</note> on Plato p. 129. Ruhnken on the Gorgias p. 507. D.** *as one has feet*: thus: instead of "as much as we are able, we ought to flee from evil deeds—let us therefore flee from evils by our way of life, not with our feet, since Plotinus also says that souls are carried up, not by foot, but by life."

— 5. **but as if closing the eyes** <note>original: "ἀλλ’ οἷον μύσαντα"</note>] “A Platonic expression.” *D. W.* <note>Likely Daniel Wyttenbach, a noted scholar.</note> **Plato in the Gorgias p. 480. C.** "not to be cowardly, but to offer oneself with eyes closed and bravely, etc." Compare **Phaedrus p. 251. Aristides' Orations Vol. I. p. 547.** "and this is indeed the saying: to endure with closed eyes." **Philo the Jew Vol. II. p. 464.** "the closed eye of the soul having looked up, etc." For the argument, consult **Hemsterhuis on Lucian Vol. II. p. 498. Bipont edition. Plotinus p. 724. A.** "Therefore, whenever beauty is spoken of, one must rather flee from such a form... but it must not be placed before the eyes." Compare also **p. 543.**

— 6. **and to awaken** <note>original: "καὶ ἀνεγεῖραι"</note>] “*anageirai* in the **Basel edition and the Leiden Vossianus manuscript**. *anegeirai*: more correctly.” *D. W.* See the various readings.

— 7. **What then is that eye, which looks within?** <note>original: "Τί οὖν ἐκεῖνη, ἢ ἔνδον βλέπει;"</note>] *What then must be done with that eye, which looks inside?* I have punctuated it thus, relying on the authority of the good manuscripts. For Plotinus wants it understood as the method by which that eye, dull and weak from the beginning, ought to be gradually sharpened and accustomed to discerning higher things. Our colleague **Rinck** noted this, adding that **Ficino** did not translate these words correctly.

ibid. **it is not at all able to look at bright things** <note>original: "οὐ πάνυ τὰ λαμπρὰ δύναται βλέπειν"</note>] Compare below **p. 57. F.** *not being able to look at very bright things.* These passages and similar ones pertain to the doctrine of that vision which **Plato** calls "the eye of the soul." See **The Republic VII. p. 533. p. 361. Bekker edition.** or "the sight of the intellect." **Symposium p. 219. A. p. 460. Bekker. Compare Marcus Aurelius III. 15. p. 80. and Gataker's notes there. Compare p. 228. Wyttenbach on Plutarch's Observations p. 1013. Add Proclus on the Alcibiades pr. p. 37. and p. 194. and our annotations there, and Plotinus on Intelligible Beauty ch. 10. p. 551. B.** The next parts are again taken from **Plato’s Symposium ch. 28.** Compare the notes above for p. 50. A.

— 10. **then look at the soul** <note>original: "εἶτα ψυχὴν ἰδὲ"</note>] In such cases, the good manuscripts should be followed, which here and in the next part, and even elsewhere, adapt the accent to the Attic custom; this should have been rejected if you consider the age of Plotinus: *íde* <note>The author is debating the placement of the Greek accent on the word for "look."</note>, as was done, for example, in **Epictetus I. 17. 6. II. 16. 31. II. 18. 22.** and likewise in the **New Testament, as in John I. 29.** Compare **Gregory of Corinth p. 121. Schaefer edition, and Bast's notes there.** I have cited more in my Special Edition. Add the annotation to **Olympiodorus p. 217. where, as the manuscripts commanded, we retained *íde*.**

— 11. **How then might you see the soul?** <note>original: "Πῶς ἂν οὖν ἴδοις ψυχήν"</note>] “**Vossianus manuscript** *an oun*, more correctly: as in the margin of the **Basel edition**. [The printed edition has *oun an*]” *D. W.* This is very frequent: however, the other is also correct and confirmed by reliable manuscripts: **for example, Plato's Greater Hippias p. 237. A. p. 382. Bekker.** *what then would such a speech seem to us?* More in the Special Edition and compare **Stallbaum in the Errata to the Philebus p. 169.** We have, however, followed the best manuscripts in this place.

— 12. **and if you do not yet see yourself as beautiful—of a statue** <note>original: "κἂν μήπω σαυτὸν ἴδῃς καλὸν—ἀγάλματος"</note>] Dius the Pythagorean in **Stobaeus' Sermons 63. p. 408. and following, p. 498. Gaisford edition, in the book On Beauty:** "For beauty provides pleasures to those who approach it, creeping toward them like a statue or a painting or some other hand-crafted work." Compare **Socrates in the same place, Sermon I. p. 4. p. 18. Gaisford no. 33.** After the words *on the one hand he removes* <note>original: "τὸ μὲν ἀφαιρεῖ"</note> **Ficino** (by conjecture, it seems; for the Medici manuscripts have no more) added: *partly also he directs*, so that this member of the sentence exactly corresponds to the one below: *and he straightened whatever was crooked.*

— 14. **on the one hand he removes** <note>original: "τὸ μὲν ἀφαιρεῖ"</note>] Compare **Cicero, On Divination II. 21:** “for those very things (the heads by Praxiteles) are produced by **removal**, nor is anything added there by Praxiteles; **but when many things have been removed**, and the lines of the face have been reached, then you may understand that what has now been **polished** was already inside.”

ibid. **and on the other hand he scraped away** <note>original: "τὸ δὲ ἀπέξεσε"</note>] Regarding the spelling, see **Zonaras' Lexicon p. 275. and the Interpreters on Thomas Magister p. 641.** Regarding the use of the word, which is specific to a sculptor who polishes statues, see **Hemsterhuis on Lucian's Dialogues of the Dead p. 351. Bipont edition, and F. A. Wolf’s Prolegomena to Homer p. 74. and following.** Regarding the metaphorical use, see **Hesychius I. p. 437. Suidas I. p. 254. Pollux VI. 141. Gregory Nazianzen in his Praise of Basil** regarding the stability and firmness and polished nature of his character—

# ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS

**Sextus Empiricus, *Against the Mathematicians* I. 13. §. 303. <note>original: "Empir. adv. Math."</note> Compare Proclus, *Commentary on the First Alcibiades* p. 247.** and the notes we placed there. Regarding the term *to apply the mind* <note>original: "ἐπιβάλλειν" (epiballein) — a technical term for intuitive apprehension</note> consult **Suidas Vol. I. p. 803, and Proclus, *Commentary on the First Alcibiades* p. 8 and 246.** Plato and Plotinus use the term *assault* or *the assault of the eyes* <note>original: "προσβολὴ" (prosbolē) — used here to mean a direct, forceful application of the senses or intellect</note> in a similar sense. See **Plotinus p. 352. B. 552. B.**

p. 115, 2. *For it would never have seen etc.*] From **Plato’s *Republic* VI. p. 508. ff.** Compare the most recent notes and see **Julian’s *Oration* IV. p. 133. C.** who praises this very passage of Plotinus. Compare also **Spanheim, *Essays of Remarks on the Caesars of Julian* p. 23.** add **Galen, *On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato* VII. 5. and Plotinus p. 552. A. C. and p. 709. C. D.** Most recently, **Rinck** wishes to read: *“Let it become—if it intends to behold both God and the Beautiful.”* This is recognized by the **Leiden Manuscript** and I have already indicated my approval in the *Special Edition* p. 384. ff. where I discussed this passage at length. **Ficino** also seems to have read it this way. Regarding the construction *if it intends to become* <note>original: "εἰ μέλλει γενέσθαι"</note> see **Matthiæ’s *Greek Grammar* §. 502. and Fischer on Weller III. 6. p. 19.** Regarding the sentiment, see **Plato’s *Phaedrus* p. 246.** and there **Hermias p. 132. ff. and the *Phaedo* p. 153. p. 70. Wyttenbach.** I have presented and partly examined passages from other writers in the *Special Edition* at the cited location.

— 5. *He will come first, ascending etc.*] The source is in **Plato’s *Philebus* p. 64.** Moreover, a twin passage of Plotinus **on the Mind p. 536. D.** fits our passage excellently. Add **Iamblichus, *On the General Mathematical Science*** in **Villoison’s *Anecdota* II. p. 191, Proclus in *Platonic Theology* III. 18. p. 151, and Damascius, *On First Principles* p. 233. edited by I. C. Wolf.**

ibid. *and there—the forms—the ideas*] This passage must be kept in mind regarding the Platonic doctrine of *Ideas*, on which see the ***Parmenides***, especially p. 56. F. p. 132. **A.** Compare **Aristotle’s *Metaphysics* XII. 4. and consult Wyttenbach on the *Phaedo* p. 270. and there Plotinus p. 119. G. and p. 356. A.** add **Enneads III. 2. 2. compared with II. 3. 17. III. 6, 7. VI. 3. 9.** and compare **Proclus, *Commentary on the First Alcibiades* p. 36. 49. 50. Olympiodorus on the same p. 74. 77. and Proclus, *Elements of Theology* p. 290. our edition.**

— 8. *That which is beyond*] Regarding this matter, we saw just above at the words *he will come first to the mind*. **Origen** had disagreed with Plotinus and the rest of the Platonists on this point—though he was otherwise a Platonist himself—whom **Proclus** attacks in ***Platonic Theology* Book II. c. 9. p. 40.** And Plotinus, in *On Intelligible Beauty p. 581. A.* says this very *Good is the father of intelligible beauty, who is superior to the mind*. **Proclus, *On Providence and Fate* in Fabricius’ *Greek Library* IX. p. 375. c. 5. puts it thus:** “For this (*the good*) alone is more divine than the intellect, because even the intellect, which is greatly praised, desires the Good and is with all things and before all things.”

— 9. *having been put forward* <note>original: "προβεβλημένον" (probeblēmenon)</note>] “These passages, which are hindered in certain places, seem to be resolved thus: *having the beautiful put forward before itself etc., that is, holding the Beautiful stretched out before it, so that, to speak summarily, the first thing that offers itself to us is the beautiful. The rest as Ficino.*” — *Daniel Wyttenbach.* See the variant readings. The word agrees with **Iamblichus, *On the Soul* in Stobaeus’ *Physical Eclogues* I. p. 926. Heeren: *ethereal coverings surrounding the intellectual life, having been put forward before itself (the soul).* Proclus, *Commentary on the First Alcibiades* p. 257.** *many having put forward some other form of irrational things*, where, however, other books have *having been clothed in*, which is not bad. Compare the same in **Plato’s *Republic* p. 380. and Gregory of Nazianzus, *Invectives against Julian* p. 75.**

— 11. *he will call it the place of forms*] “**Basle edition** reads *manner* <note>original: "τρόπον" (tropon)</note>. But the **Voss** manuscript rightly reads *place* <note>original: "τόπον" (topon)</note>, as does the margin of the edition.” — *Daniel Wyttenbach.* See the variant readings. Compare **Plotinus p. 555.** where likewise the **Zeitz Manuscript** falsely has *aim* <note>original: "σκόπον"</note> instead of *place*. **Zonaras’ *Lexicon* p. 1502.** *and to the soul in a higher and incomparable and more beautiful manner.* Correct this to *place*, and see **Suidas III. p. 29.** Regarding the matter, see **Plato’s *Republic* VI. p. 509. Hermias on the *Phaedrus* p. 142. and p. 169. and Plotinus, *On Intelligible Beauty* p. 555. B.**

— 12. *both the fountain and the principle of the beautiful*] A Platonic expression. See, for example, ***Phaedrus* p. 245. E. Plotinus p. 21. C.** *both the fountain and the principle of activities.* Compare **p. 770. C.** Regarding the sentiment, consult **Plato’s *Greater Hippias* p. 289. D.** and **Plotinus himself p. 711. c. 18. A. and p. 723. c. 32. E.** Moreover, **Proclus** seems to touch upon our passage in ***Platonic Theology* II. 11. p. 106: “Whence I think even Plotinus did not hesitate to call the first god the fountain of the beautiful.”** Or rather, he should be thought to have respected the three passages which we are currently treating.

ibid. *or in the same [place] the good—there the beautiful*] “These words are mutilated and seem to be integrated thus: *or he will place the good and the beautiful in the same [place], except the good first, and the beautiful next; that is, he will place the good and the beautiful in the same location, yet in such a way that he places the good first, and the beautiful thereafter.*” — *Daniel Wyttenbach.* No remedy has been offered for this passage from the Manuscripts. Therefore, we accept **Wyttenbach’s** reasoning with a grateful mind, yet in such a way that we leave the context untouched.

-> BOOK VII. FIRST ENNEAD. p. 115—120. <-

As for the fact that **Rinck** <note>Friedrich Rinck, a 19th-century scholar</note> opposes **Wyttenbach’s** reasoning on the grounds that, by this method, the notion of *time* is transferred into the Supreme Good—from which it is most foreign—the learned man failed to see that philosophers very often speak in such a way as to accommodate their discourse to *our understanding*, even while they themselves profess that nothing is more foreign to the notion of God than the notion of *time, succession*, and other things of that kind. Furthermore, this same **Rinck** believes these distinctions should be made in Plotinus: first, *the good* <note>original: "τὸ ἀγαθὸν"</note>, or *the primary good*, or *beauty*; second, *the beautiful* or *the intelligible beautiful*; then *good* simply without the article, which applies even to the soul and to sensible things. These are the views of **our Rinck**.—Moreover, these final points of Plotinus are connected with the Platonic doctrine of *stages* or of the *ascent* of man *through stages to God*. Certainly, Plotinus, dealing with this in a way appropriate to our passage, discusses several points in the **final Ennead p. 770.**; in which the wise and blessed man is described: *not even turning around himself, standing entirely still and becoming as it were a state of rest—but already overshooting the beautiful, having already even surpassed the choir of the virtues.* <note>original: "οὐδὲ περὶ αὑτὸν στρεφόμενος... τὸν τῶν ἀρετῶν χορόν."</note>

-> **BOOK VII.** <-

**p. 120, 7. On the primary good, and other goods.]** <note>original: "Περὶ τοῦ πρώτου ἀγαθοῦ, καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἀγαθῶν."</note> This book is, if we look at the order of writing, the last of all Plotinus's works, being the final one of those four which he had sent to **Porphyry** <note>Plotinus's student and editor</note> shortly before his death. See the latter's work *On the Life of Plotinus* chapter 6, where, however, he titles it differently: ***On the primary good, or on happiness*** <note>original: "περὶ τοῦ πρώτου ἀγαθοῦ, ἢ περὶ εὐδαιμονίας"</note>; whereas, on the other hand, the same chapter 24 records the same title which the books themselves present at this opening; and indeed the fourth book of this first Ennead has the title: ***On happiness***. This book, however, for which we are now providing a preface, is especially to be compared with the ninth book of the **sixth Ennead: *On the Good or the One***, and likewise with the seventh book of the **sixth Ennead: *On how the multitude of ideas came into existence, and on the Good***, in which book he repeats the doctrine of the *Good* joined with the passage on *numbers and ideas* more deeply from its causes, following the example of Plato. Indeed, after Plato had begun and sketched out these primary topics of his philosophy in the ***Sophist, Philebus, Timaeus*** and in the books ***On the Republic***, especially the eighth, he had pursued them more copiously in his schools and thus brought them to completion. And these discussions of the master were examined and explained by his disciple **Aristotle** in the books ***On the Good*** or ***On Philosophy*** (**Suidas in *Agathou Daimonos* Vol. I. p. 17. Kust. John Philoponus on Aristotle's *On the Soul* I. 2. c. 2. Alexander of Aphrodisias in Simplicius's commentary on Aristotle's *Physics* Fol. 32. B.**) **Xenocrates**, a listener of **Speusippus**, had likewise written ***On the Good***. **(Diogenes Laërtius IV. 13.)** It seems, moreover, that the books of Speusippus and other Platonists titled ***On Philosophy*** **(Diogenes Laërtius IV. 4.)** were of the same subject matter as that Aristotelian work *On the Good* or *On Philosophy*. Concerning this matter, ***Chr. Aug. Brandis*** has recently argued at greater length in his *Academic Diatribe on the lost books of Aristotle on Ideas and on the Good or Philosophy*. Bonn 1823. p. 4. ff. compare p. 49.—Plato, moreover, had referred the Good (*to agathon*) to the supreme unity. (**Aristotle, Metaphysics XIII. 8. XIV. 4. p. 246. p. 301. ed. Brandis: *Of those who say that there are unchangeable substances, some say that the One itself is the Good itself. They thought, however, that its substance was primarily the One.***) In this matter, **Speusippus** had separated his own judgment from Plato's authority **(Aristotle in the place cited p. 247. and Pseudo-Alexander on the same; Stobaeus, *Ethical Eclogues* I. 28. p. 58. Heeren.)** Plato, however, had distinguished that first and supreme being, which he called *to agathon*, the Good, from the unities which are in numbers (**Aristotle, Metaphysics XIV. 4. compare Brandis's cited Diatribe p. 65. ff.**) We shall add other things concerning these decrees below at the beginning of the seventh book of the sixth Ennead, p. 692. In this place, it will not be irrelevant to have advised of those things which **Diogenes Laërtius** records from Plato's doctrines in **III. 101.** relating thus concerning the Good: that the Good was divided by Plato into four kinds (*genē*) or forms, species (*eidē*): one endowed with virtue, the second, virtue itself, the third, useful (or convenient) foods and exercises, the fourth, skill in playing the pipes, acting, poetry, and similar things. And I would believe that Plotinus had such decrees of Plato before his eyes in several passages of this short book. How Aristotle and the Peripatetics were accustomed to divide *Goods* in various ways, we learn from the copious excerpts in **Stobaeus's *Ethical Eclogues* II. 7. p. 286. ff. ed. Heeren.** What the remaining philosophers felt about the *Good* and *Goods* is both a long story to explain, and does not greatly contribute to the argument of this short book. The Stoi-

-> ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS <-

...of them, so that I may add this one thing: you have a summary of this disputed matter in **Diogenes Laërtius, Book VII, sections 94 and 101.** Furthermore, what Plotinus touched upon in the third chapter of this booklet concerning death is connected with an argument eagerly treated by Greek philosophers; Cicero brought many things from their schools into the first of his *Tusculan Disputations*. See especially **Book I, chapter 7 and following**, and what **Davis** <note>John Davis (1679–1732), a scholar known for editing Cicero</note> applied there in his annotation from the original sources. For the books of the philosophers *On Death* <note>original: "περὶ θανάτου"</note> are mentioned, such as those by **Xenocrates (Diogenes Laërtius IV. 12), Diogenes the Cynic (Diogenes Laërtius VI. 80), Aeschines, and others**. To this also belongs the subject of *Consolations*, upon which the most noble Greek writers labored. Regarding these, the learning and diligence of my dear **Wyttenbach** <note>Daniel Wyttenbach (1746–1820), a Swiss-Dutch philologist</note> in his *Observations on Plutarch’s Consolation to Apollonius* has spared us the trouble of speaking. Consult him, especially near the beginning on page 697 and following of the Oxford octavo edition, and on the present passage regarding the good things that are found in death, pages 758–770.

— 12. *But if—being the best etc.* <note>original: "Εἰ δὲ—ἀρίστη οὖσα κ. τ. λ."</note>] In the Edition, it was incorrectly printed as *being* <note>original: "οὔση" (dative) instead of "οὔσα" (nominative)</note>. **Engelhardt** explains the meaning well, namely thus: The natural action of life is the Good for each thing; therefore also for the soul. But besides natural action, the soul also has another action which strives toward the best; by which second action the soul itself becomes best. And this "Best" is not only the Good with respect to the soul itself (*toward itself* <note>original: "πρὸς αὑτήν"</note>), but is the Good simply and in itself. — Moreover, that "living according to nature" <note>original: "τὸ κατὰ φύσιν ζῆν"</note> or "living in agreement with nature" <note>original: "ὁμολογουμένως τῇ φύσει ζῆν"</note> was among the ethical principles of the Stoics is proved by those things discussed in Cicero’s *On Ends*, Book III, chapters 5 and 6, where you should consult **Davis**, and in **Diogenes Laërtius VII. 85–87; to whom Menagius contributed many notes.**

p. 121, 2. *and the other things would be in two ways, as many as* <note>original: "τὰ δὲ ἄλλα διχῶς ἂν ἔχοι ὅσα"</note>] The word *as many as* <note>original: "ὅσα"</note> being placed after *other things* <note>original: "ἄλλα"</note> with several words in between will delay no one who knows Greek usage.

— 5. *desiring—being* <note>original: "ἐφιέμενον—οὖσαν"</note>] The feminine form in *being* <note>original: "οὖσαν"</note> after the neuter *desiring* <note>original: "ἐφιέμενον"</note> is to be explained by the usage of what they call "Attraction" <note>A grammatical term where a word takes the gender/case of a nearby word rather than its logical subject</note>. **Ficinus** <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the famous Renaissance Platonist</note> studied to provide clarity by changing the word order. However, the force of that Attraction should be said to extend to the end of the period. For instead of *but that the good is for itself alone* <note>original: "ἀλλ’ αὑτῇ μόνῃ τἀγαθὸν εἶναι"</note> (feminine), you would have expected *for itself alone* <note>original: "ἀλλ’ αὑτῷ μόνῳ"</note> (neuter). This would be very harsh. Therefore, I did not hesitate to restore to the text *by the very remaining* <note>original: "αὑτῇ τῇ μονῇ"</note>, that is, by *permanence*. This conjecture is confirmed both by the preceding words, *being in quiet*, and by the following: *it is necessary therefore that it remain*, and indeed by a passage of Proclus in the *Theology of Plato*, which we have placed at the end of this chapter. This *permanence* <note>original: "μονὴ"</note> of the Good itself is opposed to *activity* and to *desire*, and no less to *intellection*. For the meaning of our passage, apply **Proclus in Alcibiades I, page 16**, where the *perfect form* is likewise called *one and the same, remaining in itself*. Similarly, **Theodoret, Volume III, page 470 of Schutz’s edition**, uses *permanence* <note>original: "μονὴν"</note> with the Father, to mean that the Word was from eternity with the Father; **Suicer** neglected this use of the word in his *Ecclesiastical Thesaurus*, nor do the Lexicons have it noted. **Engelhardt** incorrectly understood the beginning of the period; we shall not dwell on that. We touched upon the Platonic formula *fountain and principle* <note>original: "πηγὴν καὶ ἀρχὴν"</note> above at **I. 6. p. 58. A.** What moved **Ficinus**, however, to introduce *origin* <note>original: "exordium"</note> after *fountain* and *principle*, I do not know. There is no trace of it in the books. **Tennemann** excerpted this passage in his *History of Philosophy, Vol. VI, p. 141 and following.*

— 7. *good-form* <note>original: "ἀγαθοειδῆ"</note>] Also Platonic. To Platonic philosophers, the soul was said to be by nature *good-form* (boniformis). **Proclus in Alcibiades I, page 280 of our edition:** "For by nature (the soul) is good-form." <note>original: "φύσει γάρ ἐστιν (ἡ ψυχὴ) ἀγαθοειδής"</note> [[Compare: → See]] **Hermes’s *Key*, page 11 of Francesco Patrizi’s edition.** But this second passage of **Proclus in *Elements of Theology*, CXIX, page 174 of our edition**, especially agrees with our passage: "But insofar as it is Unity, it is Goodness, and insofar as it is Goodness, it is Unity; and as those who come after the First proceeded from that First, they are *good-like* and *one-like*; if indeed that One is also the Good itself, etc." <note>original: "‘Αλλ’ ᾗ ἑνὰς, ταύτῃ ἀγαθότης... εἴπερ ἐκεῖνο ἓν καὶ τἀγαθόν κ. τ. λ."</note> where in the annotation I noted both our passage and others. In the same book, *Elements of Theology*, VIII, page 14, **Proclus teaches that the first good is called "The Good," and that other point: "The simply Good is that which all beings desire."** <note>original: "τὸ ἁπλῶς ἀγαθὸν esse illud οὗ πάντα τὰ ὄντα ἐφίεται"</note> These opinions seem to be drawn from this passage of Plotinus.

— 12. *Thus—and true, that which all things desire* <note>original: "Οὕτω—καὶ ἀληθὲς, τὸ, οὗ πάντα ἐφίεται"</note>] As the words now stand, **Ficinus** translates correctly. **Engelhardt**, without warning the reader, translates: "*For thus it is the Truth, after which everything longs.*"

-> BOOK VII. FIRST ENNEAD. p. 121, 122. <-

as if it were written: <note>original: "οὕτω γὰρ τἀληθὲς οὗ π. ἐφ."</note> *for thus the truth is what they desire.* Furthermore, **Proclus in his commentary on the First Alcibiades, p. 51**, posits three monads <note>monads: fundamental, indivisible units or principles</note>: faith, truth, and love. The first (faith) **establishes all things and settles them in the Good**; the second (truth) **reveals the knowledge present in all beings**; the third (love) **turns all things back and gathers them into the nature of the Beautiful**. Moreover, the distribution of the Good, which **Aristotle and the Peripatetics** <note>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle's philosophy</note> used to propose, is relevant to this entire passage of Plotinus. See **Aristotle, Magna Moralia I. 1. and I. 2. and Stobaeus, Eclogues II. p. 286. ff. Heeren.** from which I shall transcribe only these points:—they say that (the Good) is spoken of in three ways: that which is the cause of preservation for all beings, that which is predicated of every good thing, and that which is desirable in itself; of which the first <insert>which is pleasing :)</insert>, the second is the genus of goods, and the third is the end toward which we refer all things, which is happiness. From this you might conjecture that the other title of this Plotinian treatise, **On Happiness**, originated from some Peripatetic. However, a twin passage, **III. 9. 3. p. 358. E. F.**, where Plotinus explains these things more fully, ought to be compared with our current passage.

p. 121, 13. *just as a circle toward a center—the light*] Compare **Plotinus IV. 1. a line in the center. IV. 2. beginning.** lines in a circle from the center to the circumference. **IV. 7. 6.** lines converging from the circumference of a circle. Compare **IV. 4. 23. VI. 5. 11. VI. 6. 17.** from which it is sufficiently understood how frequent Plotinus is in employing this mathematical example. **Proclus, in Plato’s Theology XXIII. p. 58**, took the same example from this very passage of Plotinus: **All things remain, therefore, because of the desirability of goodness, and it generates—and the third, in turn, the perfect, is that which turns all things back and gathers them toward their causes in a circle: here the divine, there the intellectual, there the psychic, there the physical, etc.** **The Emperor Julian, Oration IV. p. 145**, after he set forth *concerning the Goods* of which the highest God makes the other Gods participants, having moved on to the mention of the *Beautiful*, continues: **to which he also distributes the perfect mind, just as if granting sight to the eyes through the light.**—another activity besides these, wonderful to behold, appears around the Sun, the King of all, which is the portion granted to the higher races. No one, however, is unaware of how diligently Julian used to read Plotinus.

p. 122, 1. *But all other things—in two ways and toward it*] In using the words *image*—*images* <note>original: "εἰδώλου—εἴδωλα"</note> in this place, he follows the usage of Plato, who opposes the likeness to the true thing. See above **at p. 50. B. and cf. Proclus in Alcibiades I, p. 33. 49. 136. 152. ff. 155. of our edition.** But this and the following are especially illustrated by a passage of our philosopher in **Ennead V. book 1. c. 6. p. 487. F. G. What then must be said concerning the most perfect? Nothing comes from it except the greatest things after it. And the greatest after it is Mind, and it is second. For Mind sees that one, and needs it alone. But that one needs this Mind not at all. And that which is generated from a superior Mind is itself Mind. And Mind is superior to all things, because other things come after it, such as the Soul, which is the word of Mind, and a certain activity, just as Mind is of that one. But the word of the Soul is dim, for as it is an image of Mind, for this reason it must look toward Mind; and Mind likewise looks toward that one, so that it may be Mind.** **Theodoret in his Remedy for Greek Maladies II. p. 750. Schulz.** and **Cyril against Julian VIII. p. 173. B. C. Spanheim** touched upon these things. Compare **Cyril in the same work IV. p. 145.** where he says that Plotinus is explaining Plato’s opinion no less than his own:—**For Plotinus says this about him, and interprets not so much his own view as that of Plato: for he says the Good is the father of the Mind which is the cause, and that which is beyond Mind, and beyond essence; and in many places he calls Being and Mind the "Idea"; so that Plato knew the Mind comes from the Good, and the Soul from the Mind.** We shall add more to the passage of Plotinus which we just cited from the fifth Ennead. In the following, we have given *to the soul, living* <note>original: "ψυχῇ δὲ τὸ ζῆν"</note> instead of *the soul* from good manuscripts; then we corrected the punctuation as the sense required, and likewise corrected the Latin of Ficino from the first edition: "if it should *look up to* the good," instead of the faulty "should *receive*."

— 9. *in two ways and toward it*] At these words one must think: *the Good is*. Also, in a twofold way, *the good is in its own power*. Furthermore, **Aristotle in Magna Moralia I. 3.** explains *concerning the Goods* regarding the *soul* according to the character of his entire system; **Stobaeus** included this passage in his ethical Eclogues **II. 7. p. 290. 299. Heeren.**

— 10. *for life limps for the wicked*] In imitation of Plato, who uses *lame* and *to limp* regarding things that fail in one of two parts, and transfers it metaphorically to the soul and other things. **Wyttenbach** teaches this **on Plutarch’s On the Education of Children p. 74. and on Plato’s Phaedo p. 178.** As for Ficino translating it as *claudicat* (limps), he has Cicero as his authority, who used it similarly in *Brutus* ch. 59.

**p. 122, l. 11. ὄμματι μὴ καθαρῶς ὁρῶντι]** [with an eye not seeing clearly] There is no need for this to be explained by us in this place [[abbrev: h. l. → hoc loco]] after those things which we set down at p. 57. **F. λημῶν κακίας, καὶ οὐ κεκαθαρμένος** [bleary-eyed with vice, and not purified]. Cf. these words of Proclus in *Alcib. pr.* p. 281: **λημῶντος αὐτοῖς τοῦ ὄμματος ὑπὸ τῆς γενεσιουργοῦ λήθης καὶ τῶν ἐκ τῆς λήθης ἐπεισκωμασάντων ἐπ' αὐτὰς παθῶν** [their eye being bleary with the rheum of generative forgetfulness and the passions that have burst in upon them from that forgetfulness]. For indeed **λῆμαι** [rheum/eye-discharges] are the impurities flowing out from the eyes, as Hesychius explains, II. p. 464. Albert.

— **12. ἡ ζωὴ—κακὸν ἀγαθόν]** [life—an evil good] This has the appearance of an oxymoron. For elsewhere Plotinus says: **τὸ κακὸν ἔλλειψις ἀγαθοῦ** [evil is a deficiency of good] III. 2. 5. and **κακὸν οὐδὲν τῷ ἀγαθῷ** [nothing is evil to the good] II. 2. 6.

— **14. οὐδ' οὕτω κακὸν τῷ λίθῳ]** [not even thus an evil to the stone] This bears, in a way, the appearance of a proverb, as in that which is among the proverbs in the *Append. Vatic.* in Andr. Schott. II. §. 56: **λίθου ἔψεις** [the boiledings of a stone]. To the same effect is that saying of Aristippus in Diog. Laërt. II. 72: **ἐν γοῦν θεάτρῳ οὐ καθεδήσεται λίθος ἐπὶ λίθῳ** [in the theater, at least, one stone will not sit upon another stone], in which there is the common sentiment of *lacking sensation*, or of that which happens at random or cannot happen. Cf. the *Adagia* of Erasmus and others, p. 322. near the end. Moreover, the decree is joined with the disputations of Plato and other philosophers, the sum of which Tullius [Cicero] recounted in dialogue form in the first book of the *Tusculans*, chapter 5 and following; and in these that saying of Epicharmus was frequent, as found in Sext. Empir. *adv. Math.* I. §. 273: 'Αποθανεῖν ἢ τεθνάναι, οὔ μοι διαφέρει· "*Emori nolo: sed me esse mortuum nihil aestumo.*" [I do not wish to die, but to be dead I count as nothing.] In which you see the Latin does not agree with the Greek. On this matter cf. [Fabricius on Sext. Emp. l. c.] Davis on *Tuscc.* I. 8. and Wyttenbach on Plato’s *Phaedo* p. 143. sq.

— **15. εἰ δ' ἔστι ζωὴ καὶ ψυχὴ κ. τ. λ.]** [But if there is life and soul, etc.] Everyone knows that these very things are drawn from the decrees of Plato in the *Apology*, *Phaedo*, and other books; whence also are drawn those things which are read in Cicero, *Tuscull.* I. 8. sqq.

**p. 123, 1. Εἰ δὲ τῆς ὅλης γίνεται]** [But if it becomes part of the whole] I suspect Marsilius [Ficino] did not translate this accurately enough: "For if it escapes as a companion of the whole soul." I should prefer: "For if it becomes part of the whole soul." For it is established that some of the Platonists taught that our soul after death and the following purification is joined again with the universal soul of the world, and thus is poured back into it.

— **5. ὅτι μὴ ζωή]** "Because it is not life." You might suspect these words were added by a Christian, or certainly by one who had read the books of the New Testament. For no one is ignorant that **ζωὴ** [life] is often taken there to mean a life undefiled and uncorrupted by the contagion of vices; which the Apostle explains more clearly in the *Epist. to the Romans* VIII. 10. opposing **τὸ πνεῦμα, ζωὴν διὰ δικαιοσύνην τῷ σώματι νεκρῷ δι' ἁμαρτίαν** [the spirit, which is life because of righteousness, to the body which is dead because of sin].

**ib. Εἰ δὲ καὶ ἐν ᾅδου δίκαι]** [And if there are judgments in Hades] This passage is also frequent in the philosophers' disputations concerning death. Cic. *Tuscull.* I. 5. "Tell me, I pray, do those things terrify you? The three-headed Cerberus in the underworld? The roar of Cocytus? The crossing of Acheron? Tantalus dying of thirst, touching the top of the water with his chin?—Sisyphus?" etc.

— **10. ὁ δὲ θάνατος, μᾶλλον ἀγαθόν]** [But death is rather a good] Handed down in histories no less than in the schools as a most ancient oracle of the Gods or certainly of the Demigods. See Herodot. I. 31. Aristotle in Plutarch, *Consolat. ad Apollon.* p. 115. C. D. p. 454. Wytt.: **'Ως ἄρα μὴ γίνεσθαι μὲν, ἄριστον πάντων, τὸ δὲ τεθνάναι τοῦ ζῆν ἐστὶ κρεῖττον** [That not to be born is best of all, but to have died is better than living]. Cic. *Tuscull.* I. 47. "*Non nasci homini longe optimum esse, proximum autem quam primum mori.*" [Not to be born is by far the best for man, but the next best is to die as soon as possible.] Cf. Davis on that passage and Wyttenbach on Plutarch *l. l.* [in the places cited] *Animadvv.* p. 765. sq. How the Platonists and indeed Plotinus himself accommodated this sentiment to their own system of moral philosophy, both the preceding and following things prove.

— **12. οὐ σώζουσαν τὸ σύνθετον, ἀλλ' ἤδη χωρίζουσαν ἑαυτήν]** [not preserving the composite, but already separating itself] These things themselves pertain to the essence of Pythagorean and Platonic doctrine. I do not wish to take up here [[abbrev: h. l.]] things which the following books of Plotinus will exhibit. It will not be irrelevant to add here that the ancient Chinese philosopher **Laot-seu** [Laozi] clearly followed Pythagoras and Plato in this decree as in others: namely, to teach that the human soul flowed from a divine and ethereal nature, and is poured back into it after death, provided it has spent its life in virtue; for the wicked and those polluted by the filth of vices are kept away from that happiness, so that they may be restored to their original seat as if by the right of *postliminium* [recovery of rights]. See *Abel—Rémusat* in *Mélanges Asiatiques* Tom. I. p. 95. sq. who elegantly explains these tenets of the Chinese philosopher and goes on to prove from the vestiges of monuments that the seeds of Pythagorean and Platonic philosophy were studiously received and propagated by that oriental philosopher. Furthermore, *pro ut servat* [for as it preserves], Ficino might perhaps have more conveniently written *quatenus servat* [insofar as it preserves].—

--- Page 72 ---
[[language: Latin with Greek passages]]

**BOOK VII. OF THE FIRST ENNEAD. p. 122—136.**

But if you consider that these are the final words of the final book of Plotinus (about which warning was given above), you cannot but profess that this philosopher remained consistent with himself throughout, and laid down both his pen and his soul with the same sentiment. For it is found in Porphyry's *Life of Plotinus* c. II. p. 94. that at the very point of approaching death he said to Eustochius: **ὅτι σὲ ἔτι περιμένω, καὶ φήσας πειρᾶσθαι τὸν ἐν ἡμῖν θεὸν** (most books and Synesius read **τὸ ἐν ἡμῖν θεῖον**) **ἀνάγειν πρὸς τὸ ἐν τῷ παντὶ θεῖον—ἀφῆκε τὸ πνεῦμα** ["I am still waiting for you," and having said he was trying to lead the god in us back to the god in the universe, he gave up the spirit]. Synesius adapted these words as a commendation of philosophy in *Epist.* 138, but in such a way that he changed them slightly for a Christian purpose: **ἐῤῥῶσο καὶ φιλοσόφει. καὶ τὸ ἐν σαυτῷ θεῖον ἀναγε ἐπὶ τὸ πρωτόγονον (al. πρόγονον) θεῖον.** "Farewell and philosophize: and that which is divine in you, lead up to that primordial divine."

### BOOK VIII.

**p. 136, 7. περὶ τοῦ τίνα καὶ πόθεν τὰ κακά]** [On what are evils and whence they come] This eighth book is itself to be referred to the final ones, as having been written by Plotinus near the end of his life (Porphyr. *de Vita Plotini* c. 6.). Moreover, the inscription which the edition of Plotinus exhibits is composed of two parts, since in the cited passage of Porphyry we read: **τίνα τὰ κακά;** [What are evils?]; but in the same author in another place, c. 24: **πόθεν τὰ κακά;** [Whence are evils?]. The Greek philosophers snatched the occasion for the question *what and whence are evils* from Homer himself, specifically from the celebrated passage of *Odyss.* I. 33: **ἐξ ἡμέων γάρ φασι κάκ' ἔμμεναι· οἱ δὲ καὶ αὐτοὶ σφῇσιν ἀτασθαλίῃσιν ὑπέρμορον ἄλγε' ἔχουσιν.** [For they say that evils come from us; but they themselves, through their own follies, have sorrows beyond their lot.] See, to use this as an example, Hierocles in Stobaeus, *Eclogg. eth.* II. 9. p. 420—422. Heeren. And those Homeric words are in a way interpreted by Democritus in the same author p. 408, who himself professed: "The Gods provide all good things to men both of old and now, but not those things which are evil and harmful and useless: these the Gods bestow on men neither of old nor now, but they themselves procure these through blindness of mind and ignorance." Plato generally adapted his own reasoning to this sentiment, severely noting the poets, Homer and Aeschylus, who sometimes seemed to say the contrary, and adding: **κακῶν δὲ αἴτιον φάναι θεόν τινι γίγνεσθαι ἀγαθὸν ὄντα, διαμαχετέον παντὶ τρόπῳ** κ. τ. λ. [But that God, being good, is the cause of evils to anyone—this must be fought in every way, etc.] (*de Rep.* II. p. 379. sq. p. 97—100. Bekk.). But since that divine philosopher could not rest satisfied with such pious sayings of the ancients, such as Democritus, but descended deeper into investigating the origin of evil itself, he returned more frequently in his dialogues to this most difficult topic of philosophy, as in the *Theaetetus* p. 176. a. b., *Statesman* p. 273. (cf. Stob. *Eclogg.* II. 9. p. 422. sqq.), *Timaeus* p. 41. sq. These passages we shall apply individually below to the chapters 2. sqq. of this Plotinian book; here in the proem it will not be out of place to have mentioned both Aristotle and Plutarch. For the former, in *Metaphysics* XII. p. 209. sq. Sylb. p. 256. Brandis, and XIV. p. 247. Sylb. p. 302. Br., touched upon the opinions of previous philosophers concerning evil. But Plutarch, after he had contended that Zoroaster, the Chaldeans, Pythagoras, Anaxagoras, Heraclitus, Empedocles, Plato, and Aristotle had placed two separate principles of Good and Evil in the world (*de Isid. et Osir.* p. 369, on which passage cf. Wyttenb. *Animadvv.* p. 234. sq.), in another place (*de Animarum procreat. in Timaeo* p. 1015. B.C.D. p. 133. sq. Wytt.) sets down these things: "But the same did not happen to Plato as to those who came later; nor did he, overlooking as they did the third principle and power between matter and God, admit that most absurd of arguments, which makes the nature of evils an accident, creeping in I know not how, by chance. — Plato was not so; but while freeing matter from all distinction, and placing the cause of evils as far as possible from God, he wrote these things about the world in the *Statesman*: 'For from him who composed it, it has acquired all beautiful things,'" etc. (the passage from the *Statesman* follows, which we cited above; where the true reading, correctly restored by Bekker instead of the corrupt **κέκληται**, is also recognized by the most excellent Bodleian Codex of Clark): "Otherwise, it did not happen to Plato as to later men, nor having neglected, as happened in their use, the third faculty and principle which is in the middle place between matter and God, did he admit that most absurd fiction, which feigns that the nature of evils crept in from elsewhere by accident and chance. — Not so Plato. But when he had freed matter from every distinction, and had placed God as far as possible from the cause of evils, he wrote these things in the *Statesman* concerning the world: 'For it has obtained all good things from him who composed it.'" This passage was thus understood by Cudworth in *Syst. intell. univ.* IV. 13. p. 236. sqq. Mosh.: that Plato, according to Plutarch's faulty interpretation, referred Evil to the soul or 

VOL. III. -> K <-

--- Page 73 ---
[[language: Latin with Greek passages]]

**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

to a demon lacking reason and moving matter with disordered motion, whereas on the contrary Plato taught: "That God himself properly and directly produced and procreated nothing except things naturally good and useful; but through the nature of inferior and less perfect things, it could in no way happen that evils would not be born and fill the nature of things." To Mosheim, however, Plutarch's explanation seems truer. To examine this in this place is long, nor does it matter. The **Stoics**, to touch on this, Plutarch mentioned in the same place: **τὸ κακὸν ἐκ τοῦ μὴ ὄντος ἀναιτίως καὶ ἀγεννήτως ἐπεισάγοντας** ["introducing evil from non-being without cause and without generation"]. He who desires to know the tenets of Zeno and other Stoics concerning Evil should consult Stobaeus, *Eclogg. Phys. et Eth.* II. 7. p. 90. sqq. and Gataker on Marc. Antonin. II. 1. p. 37. the sum of which comes to this: That nothing is good except what is honorable, nothing evil except what is base (Cic. *ad Att.* X. 4.). Stobaeus in *Eclogg.* I. 42. p. 896—898. Heer. likewise enumerates the decrees of the Platonists, Peripatetics, and Stoics concerning the Evil of the soul, where concerning Plotinus he says: **προστιθέντων ὁπωσοῦν τῇ ψυχῇ, τὸ κακὸν ἀπὸ τῆς φύσεως καὶ τῆς ἀλόγου ζωῆς Πλωτίνου** (correct to **Πλωτίνου**) **καὶ Πορφυρίου ὡς τὰ πολλά** [attributing it somehow to the soul, the evil [comes] from nature and the irrational life of Plotinus and Porphyry for the most part]. Nevertheless, the Sceptics again attacked the decrees of those philosophers, and no less of others who are commonly called dogmatic, denying that anything is **φύσει ἀγαθὸν ἢ φύσει κακόν** ["naturally good or naturally evil"] (Sext. Empir. *adv. Ethicos*, XI. §. 110. sqq. p. 711. sqq. Fabric.). Plotinus, to return here, insofar as he sides with his Plato and contributes to both the understanding and strengthening of his decrees, is taught by the reading of this very book to the more learned. Moreover, Dionysius the so-called Areopagite diligently despoiled the works of Plotinus and other more recent Platonists, as in other places, so also in this (*de Divinis nomm.* IV. §. 18. sqq.) in a long enough disputation, the sum of which we shall add in these few words, which it is helpful to add here from the Scholia of St. Maximus p. 619:—**δεικνὺς ὡς οὔτε ἐνυπόστατον τὸ κακὸν, οὔτε ἐν φύσει, ἀλλὰ κατὰ στέρησιν ἀγαθοῦ γινόμενον, οὔτε ὂν, οὔτε ὡς μὴ ὂν λογιζόμενον.** "By showing that Evil has neither a substantial existence nor is it in the nature of things, but happens according to a privation of good, being neither a being, nor reckoned as a non-being:" he adds the passage of Psalm XXXVI. v. 35. and 36. and that Dionysius answers the Manichaeans especially. Furthermore, how much this question was celebrated is proved by these words of Tertullian, *de Praescript. Haeret.* cap. 7: "The same materials are rolled about among *heretics and philosophers*, the same retractions are entangled: *whence is Evil and why?*" Likewise Eusebius, *Hist. Eccles.* V. 27: **πολυθρύλλητον παρὰ τοῖς αἱρεσιώταις τὸ πόθεν ἡ κακία;** [The "whence is wickedness?" is much-chattered among the heresiarchs]. Surely the Gnostics and Manichaeans were especially agitating this question. Tennemann provides the more significant excerpts of this Plotinian book in his *History of Philosophy* written in German, Vol. VI. p. 143. sqq. Thomas Taylor translated it entire into English in: *Five Books of Plotinus*, Lond. 1794. p. 57. sqq.

**136, 14. τῆς γνώσεως ἑκάστων δι' ὁμοιότητος γιγνομένης]** [knowledge of each thing occurring through similarity] Hence Porphyry in *Sententt.* XXVI. p. 129: **τῷ γὰρ ὁμοίῳ τὸ ὅμοιον γιγνώσκεται** [for like is known by like], and Proclus in *Alc. pr.* p. 247. our edition: **τῷ γὰρ ὁμοίῳ τὸ ὅμοιον πανταχοῦ κατάληπτον, τὰ μὲν ἐπιστητὰ τῇ ἐπιστήμῃ, τὰ δὲ νοητὰ τῷ νῷ, τὰ δὲ ἑνικώτατα μέτρα τῶν ὄντων τῷ ἑνὶ τῇ ψυχῇ** (or **τῆς ψυχῆς**) [for everywhere like is grasped by like: things known by knowledge, things thought by the mind, and the most unified measures of beings by the 'one' of the soul]. And what Plotinus sets down here [[abbrev: h. l.]] as an **ἀξίωμα** [axiom] universally, he applies individually above at I. 6. 9. p. 57. G. thus: **οὐ γὰρ ἂν πώποτε εἶδεν ὁ ὀφθαλμὸς ἥλιον, ἡλιοειδὴς μὴ γεγενημένος** [for never would the eye have seen the sun, had it not become sun-like], where see our note. Add Proclus on Plato's *Tim.* p. 332, Themistius on Aristotle’s *de Anima* I. fol. 66. b., Philoponus on the same fol. 34. b., and more often, which interpreters emulously praise the Empedoclean verses in which they taught this same **ἀξίωμα** was contained: **γαίῃ μὲν γὰρ γαῖαν ὀπώπαμεν, ὕδατι δ' ὕδωρ** κ. τ. λ. [For by earth we see earth, by water water, etc.] See Empedocles' *Carmina* v. 318—320. and Sturz's *Annott.* on those verses p. 634. sq.

**17. Εἶδος δὲ τὸ κακὸν—ἰνδαλλόμενον]** [But evil is a form... appearing as an image] In these Plotinus denies that a form can be attributed to evil, since it consists in the absence of good; and these things are understood partly from those things which he had disputed above in the sixth book concerning Beauty, and partly become clearer from this very book and those following.

**p. 137, 3. ἤπερ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ καὶ τοῦ κακοῦ ἔσται]** I should believe Ficino read **ἤπερ**, who translates: "therefore the knowledge of good and evil will be the same:" namely, with the word **ἐπιστήμη** [knowledge] understood from the preceding. Taylor: *On this account we obtain a knowledge of good and evil*; Engelhardt: *und sonach die Kenntniss des Guten die Kenntniss des Boesen mitbrachte*. I like **εἴ-**
