[[language: Latin with Greek passages]]

**BOOK VIII. OF THE FIRST ENNEAD. p. 136—138.**

**περ** [if indeed] referred to the higher **εἰ** [if] and the lower **ἐπείπερ** [since indeed].

— **4. προηγούμενα]** Properly *antecedentia* [antecedents], but here [[abbrev: h. l.]] and elsewhere *praecipua, praestantiora* [principal, superior], they ought not to be confused with the Stoics' **προηγμένοις** [preferred things]. See Wyttenb. on Plutarch p. 779. 780. Concerning these (**προηγμένοις, productis, promotis**), see Cic. *de Finn.* III. 15. 16. and the interpreters there, and Stobaeus *Eclogg.* II. 7. p. 144. sq. ed. Heer. cf. annot. on Procl. *Alc. pr.* p. 235. sq. Plotinus II. 3. 16. p. 146. E: **προηγούμενα οὖν καὶ ἐπακολουθοῦντα πάντως καὶ πάλιν ἐπὶ τούτοις τὰ ἐφεξῆς προηγούμενα ὡς ἐκ τῶν παρόντων· ὅθεν ἴσως ἀεὶ χείρω τὰ ἐφεξῆς.** II. 3. 18. p. 147. G: **'Αρ' οὖν τὰ κακὰ τὰ ἐν τῷ παντὶ ἀναγκαῖα, ὅτι ἕπεται τοῖς προηγουμένοις** κ. τ. λ. cf. IV. 4. 8. and III. 8. 3. IV. 4. 39. (where it is **προηγουμένως, praecipue** [principally],) VI. 6. 9. where there is the infinitive **προηγεῖσθαι** [to lead/precede].

— **5. καὶ εἴδη, τὰ δὲ οὔ]** [and forms, but the others not] Engelhardt hesitates on these and says it must necessarily be written: **καὶ εἴδη, τῶν δὲ οὐ sc. εἴδη ὄντων (?)**, and he opines that Marsilius read it thus in his books. We, who know Marsilius' Codices from the Florentine books, would rather say that he, as often elsewhere, translated somewhat freely; and since no written book varies anything in these words, let us accept the passage so that we supply by thinking: **καὶ τὰ μὲν εἴδη, τὰ δὲ οὔ sc. ἐστί**: *and since these (Better things) are forms, those (Worse things) are not.* Which ellipsis, not unusual even to Xenophon, has nothing of wonder in Plotinus.

— **12. μέτρον πάντων καὶ πέρας (τὸ ἀγαθόν)]** [the Good is the measure and limit of all things] A decree of Plato. For he says in *Laws* IV. 716. e. p. 355. Bekk.: **ὁ δὴ θεὸς ἡμῖν πάντων χρημάτων μέτρον ἂν εἴη μάλιστα, καὶ πολὺ μᾶλλον ἢ πού τις, ὥς φασιν, ἄνθρωπος.** [God would be for us the measure of all things in the highest degree, and much more so than, as they say, any man.] By which words he touches upon that Protagorean saying: **πάντων χρημάτων μέτρον ἄνθρωπον εἶναι** [man is the measure of all things]. cf. Platon. *Theaet.* p. 152. a. *Cratyl.* p. 385. where apply Proclus' *Scholia* p. 14. sq. Boisson. Aristotle also set out to refute the same tenet of Protagoras, *Metaphys.* III. 5. p. 61. Sylb. cf. Sext. Empir. *Pyrrhon. Hypotyp.* I. §. 216. and Fabricius there p. 55. Proclus more fully explains the opinion of Plato and Plotinus in *Inst. Theol.* c. 117. p. 172, our edition: **πᾶς θεὸς μέτρον ἐστὶ τῶν ὄντων. εἰ γάρ ἐστιν ἑνιαῖος ἅπας θεὸς, τὰ πλήθη πάντα ἀφορίζει καὶ μετρεῖ· πάντα μὲν γὰρ τὰ πλήθη, τῇ ἑαυτῶν φύσει ἀόριστα ὄντα, διὰ τὸ ἓν ὁρίζεται. τὸ δὲ ἑνιαῖον μετροῦν καὶ περατοῦν οἷς ἂν παρῇ, βούλεται περιάγειν εἰς ὅρον τὸ μὴ τοιοῦτον κατὰ τὴν αὑτοῦ δύναμιν.** [Every god is a measure of beings. For if every god is unitary, he defines and measures all multiplicities; for all multiplicities, being indefinite by their own nature, are defined through the One. And the unitary, measuring and limiting those things in which it is present, wishes to lead back into a bound that which is not such, according to its own power.]

— **14. αὐτός τε γὰρ ὑπέρκαλος]** [for he himself is beyond beauty] From these words begins the description of the Mind [Nous].

— **15. βασιλεύων ἐν τῷ νοητῷ]** [reigning in the intelligible] An expression proper to the Mind. The source is in Plato’s *Philebus* p. 28: **ὡς νοῦς ἐστι βασιλεὺς ἡμῖν οὐρανοῦ τε καὶ γῆς** [that Mind is our king of both heaven and earth], where likewise Stallbaum p. 76. cf. Plotin. V. 3. 3; where likewise **νοῦς βασιλεύς** [Mind is king]. Hence Proclus uses **νοερὰς βασιλείας** [intellectual kingdoms] in *Alc. pr.* p. 249; cf. what we set down at Porphyry's *de Vit. Plotini* III. p. 98. Fabric.

— **17. τοὺς ἐκ προτάσεων κ. τ. λ.]** [those from premises, etc.] See above I. 3. 4. p. 21. C: **τὴν λεγομένην λογικὴν πραγματείαν περὶ προτάσεων καὶ συλλογισμῶν** [the so-called logical treatise concerning premises and syllogisms] and what I added there.

**p. 138, 4. ἀλλ' ἔχει πάντα, καὶ ἔστι πάντα]** [but it has all things, and is all things] Cf. *Enn.* VI. 9. 2. end: **τοῦ νοῦ τὰ πάντα ὄντος** [Mind being all things].

— **11. Ἡ δὲ ἔξωθεν περὶ τοῦτον χορεύουσα ψυχὴ κ. τ. λ.]** [And the soul dancing outside around this, etc.] I am mistaken or the philosopher of Lycopolis [Plotinus] thought of mystical dances when he used this word. For it was a received custom among the ancients, **σὺν ῥυθμῷ καὶ ὀρχήσει μυεῖσθαι** [to be initiated with rhythm and dancing], as is in Lucian, *de Saltatione* chapter 15. The passage of Plato in the *Euthydemus* p. 277. d. could lead him to this similarity: **καὶ γὰρ ἐκεῖ χορεία τίς ἐστι καὶ παιδιά, εἰ ἄρα καὶ τετέλεσαι· καὶ νῦν τούτῳ οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἢ χορεύετον περὶ σὲ καὶ οἷον ὀρχεῖσθον ὡς μετὰ τοῦτο τελοῦντε.** [for there is a certain dancing and play there, if you have indeed been initiated; and now these two are doing nothing other than dancing around you and as it were performing a dance, as if intending to initiate you after this.] where see Heindorf p. 320. Proclus touched on that passage in *Platonis Theolog.* VI. 14. p. 382. I have collected more on the matter in *Symbolica et Mythologia*, which there is no need to add here.

— **13. θεῶν ἀπήμων καὶ μακάριος ὁ βίος]** [the life of the gods is free from harm and blessed] Translated from the Homeric epithet of the Gods into the disputations of the philosophers. Cf. Herodot. I. 32. where a man: **ἄλλο μὲν ἔχει· ἄλλου δὲ ἐνδεής ἐστι.** [has one thing, but lacks another.] Hence the notions of **ὄλβιου** [happy] and thus **μακαρίου** [blessed] as if opposite to human felicities. Hence **μακαρίζειν** [to call blessed] (Herodot. I. 31. cf. Zonar. Lex. p. 704.) and **μακάριος** (Wyttenbach on Plutarch p. 767. sq. cf. p. 602.), which is sometimes even transferred to those who are compared to the Gods, cf. Plotin. III. 2. 1. III. 7. 3. Olympiodor. in *Alc. pr.* p. 171: **μακάριον δὲ αὐτόν φησιν, ὡς μέλλων αὐτὸν συνάπτειν θεοῖς. ἐν τούτοις γὰρ ἡ μακαριότης διὰ τὴν στέρησιν τοῦ κηρός.** κ. τ. λ. [He calls him blessed, as being about to join him to the gods. for among these blessedness is through the privation of fate/death.] Procl. in *Platonis Theol.* XV. p. 41: **οὐ γὰρ ἐθέλει χραίνεσθαι τὸ μακάριον αὐτῶν (τῶν θεῶν), ἐπεὶ καὶ τοῖς παρ' ἡμῖν**

--- Page 75 ---
[[language: Latin with Greek passages]]

**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

**ἀγαθοῖς μετὰ ῥᾳστώνης ὁ βίος καὶ ἀπράγμων καὶ ἄλυπος.** [For their blessedness (the gods') does not wish to be defiled, since even with our good things, life is with ease and free from business and pain.] Moreover, regarding the sentiment: that the Gods and those things which belong to the Gods are in every part best disposed, cf. Plato's own disputations in *Republ.* II. 20. p. 381.

**p. 139, 3. Λείπεται τοίνυν κ. τ. λ.]** [It remains therefore, etc.] Tiedemann disputes concerning these and following decrees in *Geist der specul. Philosophie* III. p. 330. sqq. comparing III. 2. 5. and 11. III. 2. 11. III. 3. 3. Similar things to the Plotinian decrees concerning evil are brought forward from the **Persian** books **Ssucicis** [Sufi], likewise from **Indian** writings by Tholuck in the book: *Ssufismus, sive Theosophia Persarum Pantheistica*, p. 254. sqq. nor did he forget Dionysius the so-called Areopagite, who says at page 494. ed. Coterierius: **οὐκ ἄρα οὔτε ἐν δαίμοσι οὔτε ἐν ἡμῖν τὸ κακὸν, ὡς ὂν κακὸν, ἀλλ' ὡς ἔλλειψις καὶ ἐρημία τῆς τῶν οἰκείων ἀρετῶν τελειότητος.** [Therefore evil is neither in demons nor in us as a being evil, but as a deficiency and desertion of the perfection of proper virtues.] Cf. ib. p. 497.

— **5. Μὴ ὂν—οὔ τι τὸ παντελῶς μὴ ὄν]** [Non-being—not that which is entirely non-existent] A primary decree and taken from the heart of the doctrine of the ancient philosophers, about which Plato in the *Parmenides* and other Dialogues, Aristotle in the *Physics* and *Metaphysics* dispute. But what *Non-being* is, is understood only from its contrary, *Being*; concerning which Plotinus explains copiously elsewhere. See, for example, III. 8. 9. IV. 7. 14. VI. 4. 2. VI. 9. 2. Proclus in *Alcib. pr.* p. 22: **καὶ μὴν καὶ ὁ Τίμαιος, ἀνάλογον τοῖς οὖσι τὰς γνώσεις διελόμενος, νοήσει μὲν ἡμᾶς καὶ λόγῳ παρακελεύεται τὰ ὄντα κρίνειν, δόξῃ δὲ καὶ αἰσθήσει τὰ μὴ ὄντα γινόμενα, καὶ ἀπολλύμενα.** [And indeed the Timaeus, having divided kinds of knowledge in proportion to beings, exhorts us to judge beings by intellection and reason, but things becoming and perishing (non-beings) by opinion and sensation.] Mosheim does well in *Dissert. de Creatione ex nihilo* §. 7. p. 164: "**τὸ ὂν** [the Being] was called by the most ancient Greek philosophers that which is *immutable, constant, perennial, fixed and defined*: **τὸ μὴ ὂν** [the non-being] truly, that which is not endowed with a certain and constant nature, but perpetually flows, changes, slips away, and is converted." Moreover, how Plotinus wishes **μὴ ὂν** to be taken here [[abbrev: h. l.]], he himself explains immediately.

— **17. Τίνι οὖν ὑποστάσει κ. τ. λ.]** [In what hypostasis, etc.] Ficino translates *fundamento* [foundation]; Engelh. *Substanz*; Taylor *receptacle*. I have decided nothing. For the rest, see Diodor. XIII. 82. p. 203. where it is the *foundation of a temple*. Cf. Polyb. I. 5. 3. and the interpreters there and I. A. Ernesti in *Lex. Polyb.* p. 640. Schweigh. Suid. III. p. 560. sq. whence Zonaras has it. Add Wetsten in *N. T.* Vol. II. p. 200. and Suicer's *Thes. Eccles.* II. p. 1398.

**140, 10. τὴν τοῦ κακοῦ]** [that of evil] Engelhardt and Taylor also expressed **κακοῦ** [evil] instead of **καλοῦ** [beautiful/good]. This same confusion of these words is frequent both in other writers and in these very Enneads, e.g., below p. 715. B. above p. 55. D. at which place in the Heidelberg edition of the book *On Beauty* p. 293. I cited more examples. Add Olympiodor. in *Alcib. pr.* p. 115. where likewise **κακὸν** must be restored for **καλόν.**

— **12. Τὴν δὴ ὑποκειμένην]** [The underlying...] Ficino translates: *naturam subditam* [subjected nature], yet we do not read **φύσιν** [nature] in the books. Engelhardt supplied *Materie* [Matter], and he himself without the books, none of which exhibit **ὕλην** [matter]. Perhaps Plotinus thought of **οὐσίαν** [essence/substance] from the following things, unless he looked back to **φύσιν** in the preceding.

— **17. Σωμάτων δὲ φύσις—δεύτερον κακόν.]** [The nature of bodies—a secondary evil.] Engelhardt hesitated at this passage, rightly advising that Plotinus had two subjects in mind here, to which he would bind individual members: **φύσιν** [nature] and **σώματα** [bodies]. Thus, however, he changes and translates: "*But the nature of bodies, insofar as it participates in matter, would be an evil, but not the first, for it has a certain, though not true, form, and is not (?) deprived of life. But the individuals in it destroy one another through the disordered motion proceeding from themselves (**φορᾷ—ἀτάκτῳ**), and are an obstacle to the soul in its own proper activity (namely **σώματα**), they flee as a Second Evil, eternally flowing, the essence.*" I, partly by the authority of the Codices, partly by conjecture, would read: **Σωμάτων δὲ φύσις—εἴη. ἔχει μὲν γὰρ εἶδός τι οὐκ ἀληθινὸν, ἐστέρηται δὲ ζωῆς. φθείρει (sc. σώματα) τε ἄλληλα· φορά τε παρ' αὐτῶν (sc. σωμάτων) ἄτακτος (sc. ἐστί) ἐμπόδιά τε ψυχῆς (sc. σώματά ἐστι)—κ. τ. λ.** [But the nature of bodies... would be. for it has a certain untrue form, and is deprived of life. and they (the bodies) destroy each other; and the motion from them (the bodies) is disordered; and they (the bodies) are obstacles to the soul—etc.] Taylor in this place [[abbrev: h. l.]], as for the most part, applied himself closely to Ficino; and therefore followed the reading **ἐστέρηταί τε ζωῆς** better than Engelhardt, translating: *It is, besides this, destitute of life*.

**p. 141, 3. 'Αλλὰ τίς ἡ κακή; κ. τ. λ.]** [But what is wickedness? etc.] Ficino might seem to have read **δουλωσαμένη** [having enslaved]. You might also read: **'Αλλὰ τίς ἡ κάκη;** "But what is the *depravity*? Of what sort is it in a servile man, in whom depravity of soul is usually ingrained by nature." (Concerning **κάκη** for **κακία** [wickedness/vice] see above at p. 55. A.) Yet nevertheless the vulgate reading has a suitable explanation, if after **οἷον** [such as] you think:

--- Page 76 ---
[[language: Latin with Greek passages]]

**BOOK VIII. OF THE FIRST ENNEAD. p. 139—143.**

**ἐστὶ ψυχὴ**, such as the soul *is* to one who has been enslaved. Moreover, Plato, whom Plotinus praises here with his word **φησὶ** [he says], mentions a *servile mind* in more than one place. It suffices to have cited one from *Alcib. pr.* p. 17. Etwall. p. 144. Buttm. cf. Olympiod. on the same p. 148. sqq. where we placed more in the annotation.

— **10. οὐδὲ κατ' αὐτὴν]** [not according to itself] Ficino seems to have read **καθ' αὑτήν.** Engelhardt, on the contrary, reads **κατ' αὐτὴν**, taking these things thus: First, the soul is not outside matter, nor indeed is it determined by it (matter) in every way. Perhaps, if **εἶναι** [to be] is correct, this is the sense of the passage: The soul is neither outside matter, nor is it such (i.e. wicked), insofar as it is itself (i.e. according to its own and proper nature). For in such a place I decide nothing.

— **14. καὶ τῷ ἐπισκοτεῖσθαι τῇ ὕλῃ]** [and by being obscured by matter] This verb is used in various ways. For it is said both of celestial bodies, which by their splendor stand in the way of sight and pour darkness over the eyes, and are themselves obscured by other bodies. See Dorville on Chariton p. 636. sq. ed. Lips. [p. 713. ed. Amst.] where the construction of this verb is also discussed. Cf. Longinus, *de Subl.* XXXV. 4. Hence it is transferred to various metaphors. It will suffice to have brought forward one example very similar to our passage. Iamblichus in Stobaeus, *Ecl. Physs.* I. 51. p. 792. Heer.: **Οἱ δ' ἀπὸ Πλάτωνος καὶ Πυθαγόρου παρεῖναι μὲν καὶ ἐν τοῖς ἀρτιγενέσι φασὶ τὸν λόγον, ἐπισκοτεῖσθαί γε μὴν ἐν τοῖς ἔξωθεν, καὶ μὴ ἐνεργεῖν τὴν οἰκείαν ἐνέργειαν, ἀλλ' ἡσυχάζειν.** [Those from Plato and Pythagoras say that reason is present even in those newly born, but it is obscured by external things, and does not perform its proper activity, but keeps quiet.] At the end of the chapter, Engelhardt studied to disentangle the more difficult words thus: **ἡ δὲ μὴ μείνασα τοῦτο, ἀλλ' ἐξ αὐτῆς προελθοῦσα, τῷ μὴ τελείῳ μηδὲ πρώτῳ (μεμιγμένη sc. ἡ ψυχὴ οὐ μείνασα) οἷον ἴνδαλμα ἐκείνης (sc. τῆς τελείας ψυχῆς) τῷ ἐλλείμματι (potius ἐλλείμματι).** [But that which did not remain there, but went forth from itself, (being mixed) with that which is not perfect nor first, is like an image of that (perfect soul) by deficiency.] Well done, if I see anything; and the books partly support it. But at the words **τῷ μὴ τελείῳ μηδὲ πρώτῳ** I for my part would prefer that **ὁρισθεῖσα** [having been defined] be supplied, which participle had immediately preceded: "a soul which did not allow itself to be defined by the perfect nor that which is first." For the rest, what Ficino added: *existing in a certain degree*: there is no trace of those words in the books. As to what is read in the following, **τῷ σκότει** and **τῷ σκότῳ** [by darkness], the latter is more Attic, the former more common, as Coray teaches on Heliodorus, *Aethiop.* p. 198. cf. Gregor. Corinth. p. 22. and p. 615. Schäfer.

**p. 143, 1. Οὐδὲ γὰρ τὸ εἶναι ἔχει ἡ ὕλη—αὐτὸ μὴ εἶναι]** [For matter does not have being... itself non-being] Ficino did not express the final words **ὡς ἀληθῶς—αὐτὸ μὴ εἶναι**, but they nevertheless appear in the Medicean books. Nor did Taylor express them. The difficult passage, in which even Engelhardt hesitated, I should believe is to be disentangled thus: "For matter does not have 'to be' itself, otherwise it would be a participant in the Good by this very thing (**ταύτῃ**, by this reason, i.e., by 'to be'); (Well Taylor: *By means of which it might be invested with good.*) But for it (in matter itself) the word *being* is equivocal; so that it is truly said (namely of matter) to be itself non-being." (I would read either **ὡς ἀληθῶς**, which everyone knows is used six hundred times for **ἀληθῶς**, though some scribes did not know it, and **λέγειν** [to say], and I would join **ὡς ἀληθῶς λέγειν** [to speak truly], and in the final place: **αὐτὸ τὸ μὴ εἶναι** [the non-being itself]). These things remind one of the passage of Diogenes Laertius in *Pyrrho*, IX. 77: **Μόνον οὖν διακόνοις ἐχρῶντο τοῖς λόγοις· οὐ γὰρ οἷόν τε ἦν μὴ λόγῳ** (see Kühn in annot.) **λόγον ἀνελεῖν· καθ' ὃν τρόπον εἰώθαμεν λέγειν τόπον μὴ εἶναι, καὶ δεῖ πάντως τὸν τόπον εἰπεῖν. ἀλλ' οὐ δογματικῶς, ἀποδεικτικῶς δέ. καὶ μηδὲν γενέσθαι κατ' ἀνάγκην, καὶ δεῖ τὴν ἀνάγκην εἰπεῖν.** [They used words only as servants; for it was not possible to abolish reason except by reason; just as we are accustomed to say there is no place, and one must necessarily say 'place'. But not dogmatically, but demonstratively. And that nothing happens by necessity, and one must say 'necessity'.] Moreover, Porphyry describes matter in *Sententt.* XXI. p. 227 thus:—**ἔλλειψις παντὸς τοῦ ὄντος· δι' ὃ πᾶν ὃ ἐπαγγέλλεται, ψεύδεται· κἂν μέγα φαντασθῇ ναι, μικρόν ἐστιν· οἷον γὰρ παίγνιόν ἐστι, φεῦγον εἰς τὸ μὴ ὄν· ἡ δὲ φυγὴ οὐ τόπῳ, ἀλλα τῇ ἐκ τοῦ ὄντος ἀπολείψει** κ. τ. λ. [a deficiency of all being; because of which everything it promises, it lies; and if it appears to be great, it is small; for it is like a plaything, fleeing into non-being; and its flight is not in place, but in the desertion from being, etc.] Cf. Proclus in *Alc. pr.* p. 108. where **ὕλη** [matter] is called both **ψεῦδος** [a lie] and **αἰτία πονηρίας** [cause of wickedness]. Add Plotinus himself below IV. 2. 1. beginning, where we shall give other things p. 159.

— **6. ἀλλ' ἐκεῖνο δ' οὐδὲν κ. τ. λ.]** [but that is nothing yet...] The reading of several books is pleasing: **ἀλλ' ἐκεῖνο δ' οὐδὲν μέν πω τούτων**: "but that which *is as yet none of these things.*" Thus also Ficino read in this place [[abbrev: h. l.]] and Taylor following him. Thus the following **δὲ** has that to which it may be referred. **πονηρίαν** [wickedness] also seems sound immediately because of the preceding: **ἀδικίαν—κακίαν** [unrighteousness—vice]. In the following, from the vestiges of the Codices you might conjecture: **ἡ ὕλη**, so that it responds to **τοῖς μέρεσι.** Yet nevertheless such sudden changes of construction are very frequent in Plotinus. Then by the authority of all books we have placed **ὁρμᾷν** [to rush/strive] for **ὁρᾷν** [to see]. Taylor and Engelhardt also expressed the former.

— **11. νόσον μὲν ἔλλειψιν καὶ ὑπερβολὴν]** [disease as deficiency and excess] Cf. Hippocrat. *de Flatibus* p. 296. Foes. who says **ἰατρικὴν** [medicine] is **ἀφαίρεσιν μὲν τῶν ὑπερβαλλόντων, πρόσ-**

--- Page 77 ---
[[language: Latin with Greek passages]]

**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

**θεσιν δὲ τῶν ἐλλειπόντων** [the removal of what is excessive, and the addition of what is lacking], which Eryximachus the physician explains slightly differently in Plato’s *Symposium* p. 187. p. 396. Bekk., where see Sydenham's note. Olympiodorus also touches on the Hippocratic passage in *Alc. pr.* p. 6. The same author in the same place p. 124 explains **αἶσχος** [ugliness/shame] and **νόσον ψυχῆς** [disease of the soul]: cf. Plotinus above p. 54. D—F.

**143, 14. ὕλην—χρησμοσύνην]** [matter—indigence] This is a Heraclitean and Stoic word. For Heraclitus and his followers in this matter, the Stoics, used to call the state of the burned world, or of its destruction and emptying, **χρησμοσύνην** [indigence/need], but the state of its restoration and adornment **κόρον** [satiety]. Philo, *Leg. Allegor.* III. 89. Mangey. cf. p. 839. Wyttenbach on Plutarch, *de ei Delph.* p. 283. Our author therefore transferred this appellation to *matter*, to declare its indigence. On which matter I have disputed at greater length below p. 317. C. D.

— **17. ἃ δ' ἂν—κατέχειν οὐχ ἑκόντας]** [which things... they hold unwillingly] Concerning the **ἑκουσίῳ** [voluntary] and **ἀκουσίῳ** [involuntary] nature of those things which men do wickedly, the philosopher disputes copiously in *Magn. Morall.* I. 14. sqq. p. 16. sqq. ed. Sylb.

**p. 144, 4. ἀμείνους—καὶ τούτῳ]** [better—and by this] Ficino undoubtedly read: **ἀμείνους—καὶ τοῦτο.** Yet no codex confirms this. The vulgate reading is to be explained thus: they are better *by this very thing*, that in them there is no necessity of overcoming depravity. For the rest, how much this sentiment of our philosopher contradicts the sayings of the Apostles, there is no one who does not know.

— **6. 'Επισκεπτέον δὲ κ. τ. λ.]** [But it must be considered, etc.] The passage in the *Theaetetus* p. 176. p. 247. Bekk. reads thus: **Σωκρ. 'Αλλ' οὔτ' ἀπολέσθαι τὰ κακὰ δυνατόν, ὦ Θεόδωρε· ὑπεναντίον γάρ τι τῷ ἀγαθῷ ἀεὶ εἶναι ἀνάγκη· οὔτε ἐν θεοῖς αὐτὰ ἱδρύσθαι, τὴν δὲ θνητὴν φύσιν καὶ τόνδε τὸν τόπον περιπολεῖ ἐξ ἀνάγκης.** [Socr. But it is not possible for evils to be destroyed, O Theodorus; for there must always be something contrary to the good; nor are they established among the gods, but of necessity they haunt mortal nature and this region.] Plotinus respects the same passage below III. 2. 5. end p. 259. D. To the second sentiment of this passage corresponds this in the books of the *Republic* II. p. 379. p. 98. Bekk.: **Οὐκ ἄρα πάντων γε αἴτιον τὸ ἀγαθὸν, ἀλλὰ τῶν μὲν εὖ ἐχόντων αἴτιον, τῶν δὲ κακῶν ἀναίτιον.** [The Good therefore is not the cause of all things, but the cause of things that are well, and not the cause of evils.] At which passage Ast calls Plotinus our author to his side, as well as other writers, in *Comment.* p. 432. You should besides cf. the passage in the *Statesman* p. 273. p. 281. Bekk. which I touched on at the beginning of this book, and Hierocles in Stobaeus, *Ecl. Eth.* II. 9. p. 420. sqq. Heer. Cyril also touched on this most celebrated sentiment, *adv. Julian.* p. 145. B. For the next things, cf. the Anonymous *Life of Pythagoras* §. 11. ed. Kuster:—**τὴν δὲ τάξιν μέχρι σελήνης σώζεσθαι, τὰ δὲ ὑπὸ σελήνην οὐκέτι ὁμοίως· ἐξ ἀνάγκης δὲ ἔστι καὶ ἡ κακία εἰς τὸν περὶ γῆς τόπον.** [order is preserved as far as the moon, but below the moon no longer similarly; and of necessity wickedness exists in the region about the earth.] Cicero, *de Republ.* VI. 17. (in *Somn. Scip.* c. 4.): "Below the moon, however, now there is nothing except what is mortal and perishable, except for the souls given to the race of men by the gift of the Gods: above the moon all things are eternal:" where Moser p. 488 conveniently compares the passage from the *Academics* II. 39. Wyttenbach collected other things in Plutarch, *de Isid. et Osirid.* p. 234.

— **13. 'Αλλὰ τὸ ἐντεῦθεν φεύγειν δεῖν—φυγὴ γὰρ, φησίν κ. τ. λ.]** [But it is necessary to flee from here—for flight, he says, etc.] Again he has Plato in the *Theaetetus* before his eyes, *l. l.*: **διὸ καὶ πειρᾶσθαι χρὴ ἐνθένδε ἐκεῖσε φεύγειν ὅτι τάχιστα. φυγὴ δὲ ὁμοίωσις θεῷ κατὰ τὸ δυνατόν. ὁμοίωσις δὲ δίκαιον καὶ ὅσιον μετὰ φρονήσεως γενέσθαι.** [wherefore one must try to flee from here to there as quickly as possible. and flight is becoming like God as far as possible. and becoming like is to become just and holy with wisdom.]

— **17. καὶ τοῦ προσδιαλεγομένου κ. τ. λ.]** [and the one conversing with him, etc.] In these Plotinus respects those things which precede in that Dialogue: **Θεόδωρος. Εἰ πάντας, ὦ Σώκρατες, πείθοις ἃ λέγεις, ὥσπερ ἐμὲ, πλείων ἂν εἰρήνη, καὶ κακὰ ἐλάττω κατ' ἀνθρώπους εἴη. Σωκρ. 'Αλλ' οὔτ' ἀπολέσθαι—ἀνάγκη.** [Theodorus: If, O Socrates, you persuaded everyone of what you say, as you do me, there would be more peace, and fewer evils among men. Socr.: But neither to be destroyed—is necessary.] See the things I placed entire from that passage above. But those things concerning **ὁμοιώσει** [likeness] I have already treated above at I. 2. 1—3. Cf. also what is handed down above I. 6. 8. p. 57. A. concerning the flight to be undertaken neither by land nor sea, and what I annotated there. Moreover, Vincent of Beauvais joined these passages, who in *Speculo Historiali* lib. V. cap. 8. set down these things: "There was also another Platonist, about whom the same Augustine in the aforementioned book (*de Civ. Dei*), whose notable sentiment he also recites. *One must flee*, he says, *to the clearest fatherland, and there all things are open to you.* What fleet or flight, then, is to become like God?"

**p. 145, 10. *Ἡ οὐκ ἀνάγκη λέγειν αὐτὸν]** [Or is it not necessary for him to say] Thus we have given it as the sense demands (for Plotinus interprets Plato in this place [[abbrev: h. l.]]) and as the books command. But the passage, if I see anything, ought to have been translated thus: "or it is not necessary for him to say (Plato, namely, in the passage of the *Theaetetus*) that this is truly said of every opposite (namely, given one opposite, the other is also given): but (for Plato to say) that this is truly said of the Good?" In the vernacular: "*Or is it not necessary that Plato asserts that this is correctly stated of every contrast, but (that he asserts) that it is only correctly stated of the Good.*" Taylor and Engelhardt followed Ficino.

--- Page 78 ---
[[language: Latin with Greek passages]]

**BOOK VIII. OF THE FIRST ENNEAD. p. 143—146.**

— **13. τὸ μὲν οὖν μὴ εἶναι—ἐστὶ πιστόν]** [that it is not, therefore... is trustworthy] i.e. it is true, certain, indubitable. See Hesych. in v. **πιστά.** Ez. Spanhem. on Julian. *Opp.* p. 174. and Wetsten’s *N. T.* II. p. 538. because namely it has been demonstrated by induction.

— **14. ὅλως δὲ οὐσία οὐκ ἔστι δεδειγμένον]** [and generally it has not been shown in substance] You might set out to disentangle these things by conjecturing **ὅλως δὲ ἐπ' οὐσίας**, universally concerning essence (or in essence). But Simplicius leads us elsewhere in Aristotle’s *Categories* fol. 27. a.: **ἡ μὲν οὖν δόξα, ἀφ' ἧς ὁρμώμενοι ἄλλοι τινὲς καὶ ὁ μέγας Πλωτῖνος ἀντιλέγουσιν, ἔστι τοιαύτη. χρῶνται δὲ λόγοις τοιούτοις· τὸ μὴ εἶναι μηδὲν οὐσίᾳ ἐναντίον ἐπὶ τῶν καθ' ἕκαστα οὐσιῶν ἐστὶ πιστὸν, τῆς τε ἀτόμου καὶ τῆς εἰδικῆς καὶ γενικῆς, τῇ ἐπαγωγῇ δεδειγμένον, ὅλως δὲ οὐκ ἔστι δεδειγμένον.** [The opinion, therefore, starting from which certain others and the great Plotinus speak against it, is such. and they use such arguments: that there being nothing contrary to essence/substance is trustworthy in the case of individual substances, both the atomic and the specific and the generic, shown by induction, but generally it has not been shown.] You see he did not read that troublesome **οὐσία** [substance] in his code, and it is likely that it was wrongly transferred here from the following line. Therefore we have included it in brackets. Whether he added those words **τῆς τε ἀτόμου—γενικῆς** of his own accord, or Simplicius likewise read them in his book, I have not figured out. In our Codd. certainly there is no trace: but they serve excellently for interpretation. Simplicius continues: "Against this, one way of counter-argument would be to remind of the teaching concerning the universal." Then with many things interjected, by which these decrees of Plotinus are examined, he thus continues: **'Αλλὰ δὴ καθόλου, φησὶν ὁ Πλωτῖνος, τῇ οὐσίᾳ ἡ μὴ οὐσία ἀντίκειται, τῇ δὲ ἀγαθοῦ φύσει, ἡ κακοῦ φύσις, καὶ τῇ ἀρχῇ τῶν βελτιόνων ἡ ἀρχὴ τῶν χειρόνων ἐστὶν ἐναντία.** [But indeed universally, says Plotinus, non-substance is opposed to substance, and the nature of evil to the nature of good, and the principle of the worse is contrary to the principle of the better.] No trace of these final words appears in our books. Then Simplicius, after he had disputed copiously and acutely concerning these sentiments, thus continues: **πᾶσι μὲν οὖν ταῦτα τὰ ἐναντιώματα ἐπακολουθεῖ τοῖς ἐν ἀρχῇ τὸ κακὸν καὶ τὸ μὴ ὂν ἀφοριζομένοις, μάλιστα δὲ Πλωτίνῳ καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις τοῖς ἀπὸ τῆς ἑνώσεως ἀρχομένοις. οὗτοι γὰρ τὸ ἓν καὶ τἀγαθὸν ἐν ἀρχῇ προτιθέντες, ἐπεισοδιῶδες ὀφείλουσι ποιεῖν τὸ ἀπὸ τῆς διαιρέσεως πλῆθος, καὶ τὸ κακὸν κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς ἐπιγινόμενον καὶ μηδαμῶς προηγούμενον ἀποφαίνεσθαι. ὡς δὲ νυνὶ λέγεται καὶ πρὸς ἑαυτὸ ἐναντίως ἀφώρισται.** [Therefore all these oppositions follow those who define evil and non-being in the beginning, especially Plotinus and the others who begin from unification. For these, placing the One and the Good in the beginning, must make the multiplicity from division episodic, and declare that evil comes about by accident and is in no way primary. but as it is now said, it is defined as contrary even to itself.] The following things, since they are longer, those who desire to inquire more accurately into these decrees must read in Simplicius himself.

**146, 4. ὅσα δὲ—συμπληρώσει τοῦδ' ἐστι—ἐστὶ]** Word for word: *By the complement/completion of that which they are.* Moreover, he uses this word frequently. Cf. e.g. III. 2. 5. VI. 3. 15. Engelhardt: "*But what is entirely separated from one another, so indeed, that the different nature of the One through its transition into the Other appears precisely as the opposite of this Other—*"

— **7. πέρατι δὴ (vel δὲ) καὶ μέτρῳ—ἐν τῇ θείᾳ φύσει, ἀπειρίᾳ καὶ ἀμετρίᾳ]** [by limit and measure... in the divine nature, by infinity and immoderation] This sentiment concerning limit and measure in the nature of the Gods, and the infinite and immoderate in contrary natures, drawn from the decrees of the Pythagoreans, Plato explained especially in the *Philebus* as well as elsewhere, and exhibited copious material for disputation to the remaining philosophers. See *Phileb.* p. 23. c. p. 59. sqq. Stallbaum (which interpreter Rudelbach contradicts in *Disquis. de Ethices principiis*. Copenhagen, 1822. p. 109. sq.) cf. Aristotel. *Metaphys.* I. 5. XII. 4. XIII. 4. *Magna Moralia* I. 1. Proclus in *Theol. Platon.* III. 7. the same in *Inst. Theol.* c. 86. sqq.—89. where he defines to what extent every true being is from the end (**ἐκ τοῦ πέρατος**) and the infinite (**ἐκ τοῦ ἀπείρου**): See p. 134. our edition.

— **10. ψευδόμενον—ψεῦδος]** [lying... a lie] To these things recall what we cited above at cap. 5. p. 75. C. concerning *lying matter* from Porphyry and Proclus.

— **13. τὸ μὴ πανταχοῦ οὐσίαν]** [not everywhere substance] Ficino undoubtedly thought **οὐσίᾳ μηδὲν εἶναι ἐναντίον** [nothing is contrary to substance] should be read, and we have complied with him the more because our books have vestiges of his reading. Construe: **ἀναπέφανται τὸ μὴ πανταχοῦ μηδὲν εἶναι ἐναντίον οὐσίᾳ.** [it has appeared that it is not everywhere the case that nothing is contrary to substance.] Taylor and Engelhardt followed Marsilius. — David the Armenian, a philosopher in ms. on Porphyry's *Isagoge* (in codd. Pariss. Regg. 1937. and 1938. likewise in Monacc. 99. and 399.): **῞Ωσπερ ἀληθείας προϊστάμενοι οἱ τὰ Πλάτωνος πρεσβεύοντες δόγματα τῆς 'Αριστοτελικῆς διαιρέσεως ἐπιλαμβάνεσθαι σπουδάζουσι. φασὶ γὰρ ὅτι ἐναντία αὐτῷ καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις φθέγγεται ὁ 'Αριστοτέλης φάσκων τὴν οὐσίαν διαιρεῖσθαι εἰς ἐναντιότητα, εἴγε ἐν κατηγορίαις φησὶ μὴ ἔχειν αὐτὴν ἐναντιότητα. Πλωτῖνος δὲ καὶ τὴν αἰτίαν ἔλεγε. φησὶ γὰρ δικαίως οὐκ ἔχει ἡ οὐσία ἐναντία τὰ καθόλου· οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν ὑποκειμένῳ, αὐτὴ γὰρ ὑποκείμενον ὑπάρ-** [Just as those presiding over truth who honor the dogmas of Plato hasten to take hold of the Aristotelian division. for they say that Aristotle utters things contrary to himself and others by saying that substance is divided into contrariety, if indeed in the Categories he says it has no contrariety. and Plotinus also used to state the cause. for he says that rightly substance has no universal contraries; it is not in a subject, for it itself is the subject...]

--- Page 79 ---
[[language: Latin with Greek passages]]

**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

**χει. Τὰ γοῦν ἐναντία πάντως ἐν ὑποκειμένῳ ὄντα τὴν μάχην ποιεῖται· οὕτω γὰρ τὸ ψυχρὸν καὶ θερμὸν ἕνεκεν ὑποκειμένου μάχονται. βούλεται γὰρ ἐὰν καὶ ἕκαστον τοῦ ἄλλου τὸ ὑποκείμενον λαβεῖν· τὸ ψυχρὸν σπεύδει μεταβάλλειν τὸ θερμὸν εἰς ψυχρόν.** [...For contraries, being altogether in a subject, make the battle; for thus cold and hot fight for the sake of the subject. for each wishes to take the subject of the other; the cold hastens to change the hot into cold.] David also touched on these same things elsewhere, as in the *Scholia on Aristot. Categg.* cap. III. §. 18. and cap. VIII. §. 14. sqq. and those things which Plotinus disputes against Aristotle concerning the *Categories* are to be compared, e.g., VI. 1. 27. VI. 6. 3. sqq.

**147, 11. οὕτω κοσμηθεῖσαν εἰ θεῷτο]** [if he should see it so adorned] Ficino expanded these final words translating: "if only it were looked upon at that level." Taylor omitted these entirely; Engelhardt, with no warning to the reader: *die von dem Gotte noch nicht geordnet.* [which was not yet ordered by the God.] An old wound seems to lie hidden here. I should read **ἐκ θεοῦ** [from God], which has not yet been adorned by any God.

— **12. τόνδε τὸν τόπον]** [this place] Without hesitation we have received **τόπον** [place] into the order from the margin instead of **τρόπον** [manner/way]. For he refers again to the words of Plato quoted from the *Theaetetus* p. 176: **τὴν δὲ θνητὴν φύσιν, καὶ τόνδε τὸν τόπον (τὰ κακὰ) περιπολεῖ ἐξ ἀνάγκης.** [but evils haunt mortal nature and this region by necessity.]

— **13. ἢ τὸ, 'Αλλ' ἐπείπερ ἐγένεσθε κ. τ. λ.]** [Or the "But since indeed you were born" etc.] In these he touches on the words of the Creator of the world in Plato's *Timaeus* p. 41. a. b. p. 43. Bekk.: **θεοὶ θεῶν, ὧν ἐγὼ δημιουργὸς πατήρ τε ἔργων, ἃ δι' ἐμοῦ γενόμενα ἄλυτα ἐμοῦ γ' ἐθέλοντος. τὸ μὲν οὖν δὴ δεθὲν πᾶν λυτόν, τόγε μὴν καλῶς ἁρμοσθὲν καὶ ἔχον εὖ λύειν ἐθέλειν κακοῦ. δι' ἃ καὶ ἐπείπερ γεγένησθε, ἀθάνατοι μὲν οὐκ ἐστὲ οὐδ' ἄλυτοι τὸ πάμπαν, οὔτι μὲν δὴ λυθήσεσθέ γε οὐδὲ τεύξεσθε θανάτου μοίρας, τῆς ἐμῆς βουλήσεως μείζονος ἔτι δεσμοῦ καὶ κυριωτέρου λαχόντες ἐκείνων οἷς, ὅτ' ἐγίγνεσθε, ξυνεδεῖσθε.** κ. τ. λ. [Gods of gods, of whom I am the demiurge and father of works, which having come into being through me are indissoluble if I so will. Now everything bound is dissolvable, but to wish to dissolve that which is well fitted and in good condition is the mark of an evil one. wherefore, since you have been born, you are not immortal nor altogether indissoluble, yet you shall not be dissolved nor meet the fate of death, having obtained in my will a bond even greater and more sovereign than those with which you were bound when you came into being, etc.] What follow in the Plotinian passage pertain again to the words of the *Theaetetus*. See what I quoted above *concerning the flight to be undertaken not by feet but by the mind*, at cap. 6. p. 76. a. b.

**p. 148, 1. δηλῶν που καὶ αὐτὸς ποιεῖ]** [somewhat showing that he himself makes...] So also Ficino and Taylor following him. For he respects Plato's **μετὰ θεῶν εἶναι** [to be with the gods]. Engelhardt expressed **αὐτὸν** [him], thinking of **ἄνθρωπον** [man]: "That separating oneself or not separating from matter reveals the man" (i.e. the character of the man).

— **3. ἀνάγκη τῇ ἐκβάσει—[ὑποστάσει]]** [necessity by the departure—(hypostasis)] We have included the final word in brackets, nor does Ficino seem to have read it; and it could have crept in from the following line, in which **ὑποβάσει** [descent] occurs. For the rest, Taylor circumscribed these with more words. **ἔκβασις** moreover is *digressio* [digression], as Ficino rightly took it: elsewhere *evasio, transgressio* [escape, transgression] etc. cf. Steph. *Thesaur.* p. 2538. ed. Valpy. What **ὑπόβασις** is, I explained at these words of Proclus in *Inst. Theol.* c. 97. p. 144: '**'Απ' ἐκείνου ἄρα τὴν ἰδιότητα τῆς ἐκείνου ὑποστάσεως πᾶσα δέχεται ἡ σειρά. Εἰ δ' ἀπ' ἐκείνου, φανερὸν ὅτι μετὰ ὑφέσεως καὶ τῆς προσηκούσης τοῖς δευτέροις ὑποβάσεως.** [From that one, then, every series receives the character of that one's hypostasis. and if from that one, it is clear that it is with a remission and the descent proper to the secondary things.] (Cf. also Proclus in *Alcib. pr.* p. 31.) **Ὑπόβασις** is *descensus, diminutio, detrimentum* [descent, diminution, detriment]. Plato, *de Legg.* VI. p. 775. a. p. 457. Bekk.: **καθάπερ ὑποβέβηκεν ἑκάστῳ τὸ τίμημα** [just as the assessment has descended/decreased for each]. Ficino. It is therefore also *decrescentia* [decreasing]—*die Abnahme, Verminderung*. Hence to Dionysius the Areopagite, *de caelesti hierarch.* cap. 5. and elsewhere, **τὰ ὑποβεβηκότα** are *inferiora* [lower things], which are subject to the rest. **ἀποστάσει** [by departure/rebellion] likewise here [[abbrev: h. l.]] is rather *defectione* [by defection/revolt], in which sense both **ἀπόστασις** and especially among more recent writers **ἀποστασία** [apostasy] are often used. (Irmisch. *Indic. in Herodianum* in **ὑπόστασις**. Lobeck on Phrynichus p. 528. Schleusner, *Lex. Nov. Test.* in **ἀποστασία**.) That form is familiar to Plotinus. See II. 8. 1. VI. 2. 5. VI. 6. 1. VI. 7. 42.

— **11. εἰ διὰ σώματος κακίαν ἡ σύστασις γένοιτο]** [if through the wickedness of the body the constitution/conspiracy should occur] The word **στάσις** [sedition/standing], which appears here [[abbrev: h. l.]] in good books, seems rather, although **σύστασις** [constitution/conjunction] is frequent enough, but in another sense, e.g., in Plato’s *Phileb.* p. 47. p. 142. Stallbaum, whom see (where nevertheless the Clark codex confirms the Bekkerian reading **σύντασις** [tension/arrangement]). Cf. Monck on Eurip. *Hippolyt.* 987. Proclus in *Alc. pr.* p. 75: **(ὁ δαίμων) ἄνωθεν ἀρχόμενος ἐπιτροπεύει πᾶσαν τὴν σύστασιν ἡμῶν.** [(the demon) beginning from above oversees our whole constitution.] On the contrary the same author page 210: **πρῶτον μὲν, ὅτι διττῆς ἐν ψυχῇ πονηρίας οὔσης, ὡς αὐτὸς ἐν Σοφιστῇ διεῖλε, καὶ τῆς μὲν κατὰ τὴν ἀγνοίαν ὑφισταμένης τοῦ λόγου, τῆς δὲ κατὰ τὴν στάσιν τοῦ ἀλόγου πρὸς τὸν λόγον νόσος μὲν ἐστὶ ψυχῆς ἡ τοιαύτη στάσις, αἶσχος δὲ ἡ ἄγνοια.** [firstly, that wickedness in the soul being twofold, as he himself divided in the Sophist, the one consisting in ignorance of reason, the other in the sedition of the irrational against reason; such sedition is a disease of the soul, and ignorance is ugliness.] cf. ibid. p. 222. 264. 273. Olympiodor. in *Alc. pr.* p. 92. 134. But nevertheless since Plutarch in *Pyrrhus* cap. 23. p. 465 thus: **ἀποστάσεις δ' ὁρῶν ἅπαντα καὶ νεωτερισμοὺς καὶ σύστασιν ἰσχυρὰν ἐπ' αὐτὸν** ["seeing defections everywhere and innovations and a strong conspiracy against him"] (cf. Baehr on that passage p. 218.): I did not wish to depart from the vulgate reading. If you hold this, translate: *a conspiracy occurs*; if

--- Page 80 ---
[[language: Latin with Greek passages]]

**BOOK VIII. OF THE FIRST ENNEAD. p. 147—150.**

you prefer **στάσις**: *let a faction come together, let a sedition occur.* Plotinus uses **συστασίαν** [conspiracy/standing together] in another sense below VI. 7. 20. beginning, and **σύστασιν** and **συστάσεις** [constitutions] in VI. 3. 25. VI. 7. 11. We shall touch upon another use of the word **στάσις**, for **κατάστασις** [settled state], below at II. 1. 2. p. 97. F.

**p. 149, 7. Γενομένη γὰρ κυρία—ἐμφαντασθέντος]** [For having become mistress... of that which was imaged in her] This verb often governs the dative. Marc. Antonin. II. 12: **τὰ ἐμφανταζόμενα αὐτῷ** [the things appearing in him], where concerning the power of the verb see Gatak. p. 49. Synes. *de insomn.* p. 139. c. Petav.: **γένη δαιμόνων—εἰδωλικά τε ὄντα καὶ τοῖς γινομένοις ἐμφανταζόμενα.** [kinds of demons, being both idol-like and appearing in things that happen.] Plotinus VI. 7. 22. p. 714: **τοῦ ἐμφανταζομένου κάλλους ἐπ' αὐτοῖς.** [of the beauty appearing in them.] Moreover, just as our philosopher frequents the simple verb **φαντάζεσθαι** [to appear/imagine] after the example of Plato (concerning which I warned at p. 50. B. and added more examples in the special edition of the book *On Beauty* p. 135. 137.), so no less is he delighted by the compound verb. See V. c. III. 6. 7. III. 6. 14. III. 6. 17. III. 6. 18. VI. 4. 4. In the third place is also read the noun **ἐμφάντασις** [internal appearance], which Lexicons lack.

— **16. 'Αλλὰ κρατεῖν ἔδει—'Αλλ' οὐ καθαρὸν]** [But she ought to have ruled—But she is not pure] Note the use of the repeated particle, clearly Platonic, which many thereafter adopted. Wyttenbach provides a wealth of passages in *Phaedon.* p. 142. Concerning the force and power of that particle in objections, it is not altogether agreed among more recent Grammarians. See Hoogev. *de Particull.* p. 4. IX. ed. Schütz. alt. Viger. *de Idiotism.* p. 470. and Hermann on him. Add Wess. Alb. van Hengel *Annott. in loca nonnulla Novi Test.* Amsterdam 1824. p. 138. sq. In both places here [[abbrev: h. l.]] it was to be translated *At* [But/Yet]; since it properly has the force of *response*. But he who would wish to correct such things everywhere in Ficino's version would never see the finish. Wherefore it suffices to have warned students of the Greek language here and there of these minutiae.

**p. 150, 1. κράσει τοιᾷδε σωμάτων]** [by such a mixture of bodies] Ficino translates: *by a certain complexion of bodies*. Perhaps this pronoun is to be referred to those things which he had already warned about the mixed body from Platonic use of that pronoun, by which it serves the declaration of the subject. See Wyttenb. on Plutarch, *de audd. Poëtis* (15. B.) p. 173. and on the *Phaedo* p. 148. Nevertheless, it can also be referred to the following things here [[abbrev: h. l.]].

— **2. ἀμβλύτεροι—καὶ ἐμπεποδισμένοι]** [duller... and hindered] *But they are also duller for judging on account of the depravity of bodies, cooled and hindered.* These things are already hindered enough themselves even if you place them in parenthesis; nevertheless, the following are either faulty or certainly lacunose: **αἱ δ' ἐναντίαι, κούφους ἀνερματίστους** κ. τ. λ. [the opposite ones (desires?), light and unballasted, etc.] The Codices exhibit no protection. Ficino provided a suitable enough sentiment by translating: *but others on the contrary are carried by a certain unbridled levity.* But there is **αἱ δ' ἐναντίαι**, which you cannot conveniently refer to anything other than **ἐπιθυμίαι** [desires], which is read above, unless from the preceding **κράσει** you wish to repeat **κράσεις** [mixtures] here by thinking. Perhaps you may fill the lacuna with the one word **ποιοῦσι** [they make], so that the sense is: *but contrary desires (or mixtures) render men light and inconstant.*

— **3. κατεψυγμένοι]** [chilled] The same verb recurs below IV. 4. 28. Moreover, he borrowed the word **ἀνερματίστους** [unballasted] from the same source as many others, from Plato, who in *Theaetet.* p. 144. a. thus: **ἀλλ' οἵ τε ὀξεῖς ὥσπερ οὗτος καὶ ἀγχίνοι καὶ μνήμονες ὡς τὰ πολλὰ καὶ πρὸς τὰς ὀργὰς ὀξυῤῥοποί εἰσι καὶ ᾄττοντες φέρονται ὥσπερ τὰ ἀνερμάτιστα πλοῖα** ["but those who are sharp like this one and quick-witted and mindful are for the most part also quick-tempered towards anger and are carried rushing along like unballasted ships"], *as ships not ballasted with sand*; whence the reason for the metaphor is understood. Cf. Heindorf on *l. l.* p. 289. Ruhnken and Toup on Longinus, *de Subl.* II. 2. p. 229. sq. Weisk. Boissonade on Nicet. Eugenian. IX. 35. p. 381. sq. Zonaras p. 191 of the Lexicon serves the explanation, whence a confirmation is also added to the Ruhnkenian emendation established in Suidas. *Lexicon. Sangerm.* in Bekker's *Anecdd.* p. 398. p. 401. where in the second place **ἀνερμάτιστος ναῦς· κούφη σάβουρος, οὐκ ἔχουσα ἕρμα.** [an unballasted ship: light in ballast, not having ballast/sand.] *Glossarium Graeco-barbarum* in Cangius in **σαβούρα** thus: **ἀνερμάτιστος ναῦς, κούφη σαβούρας, ἐλαφρὴ διὰ τῆς σαβούρας.** [unballasted ship, light of ballast, light because of the ballast.] Correct from *Lex. Sangerm.* **κούφη σάβουρος**, which it is strange Cangius did not see, since in **σάβουρος** he himself both brings forward other things, and indeed from Gregory M. **πλοῖον σάβουρον**, i. e. *an empty ship*. You see, moreover, that this very adjective **κοῦφος** [light] is joined with **ἀνερμάτιστος** by our philosopher. Concerning the word **σαβοῦραι** cf. Coray in *'Ατάκτοις* Tom. I. p. 271. 272. Philo Jud. gracefully in *de Provident.* II. in Eusebius *P. E.* VIII. 14. and in the Armenian edition of Venice p. 55: **κἂν οἱ πολλοὶ σφαλλόμενοι κρίσεως ἀληθοῦς νομίζωσι, δεκασθέντες ὑπὸ κακοῦ διδύμου, τύφου καὶ κενῆς δόξης, δεῖν παρασαλεῦσαι καὶ παραγαγεῖν ἀνερματίστους ψυχὰς περὶ ἃ κηραίνει γένος τὸ πλεῖστον ἀνθρώπων.** ["even if the many, failing of true judgment, think, having been bribed by a twin evil, pride and empty opinion, that they ought to shake and lead astray unballasted souls concerning those things about which the greatest part of the human race is anxious."]

— **13. Τίνι οὖν ἐγνωρίσαμεν κ. τ. λ.]** [By what then did we recognize, etc.] He returns...

[[original page: 74]]

-> ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS <-

Plotinus addresses the question established in the first chapter: *By what power among those in us might we know the nature of evil, since the knowledge of each thing arises through likeness? This would be a difficulty.* In the following, Ficinus [Fic.] reads: *for [the soul] knows it through prudence (phronēsei).* For when prudence knows virtue, virtue knows itself, provided that prudence itself is one of the virtues. See what our philosopher had previously handed down concerning the opinion of Plato on p. 55. B., where cf. the annotation.

p. 150, 17. **᾿Αφαιρέσει οὖν τὸ μηδαμοῦ τοῦτο**] From the preceding, it seems *know* (gnōrizomen) must be understood: *We know by separation (ablation) that which is by no means "this."* "This" (*touto*) designates virtue (*aretē*), according to the usage of Plotinus, who often subjects a Neuter to Substantives of different genders. Ficinus, and the German and British translators following him, sought to assist the meaning through periphrasis. I did not wish to innovate in the reading of the next words. What Plotinus intends to be understood is sufficiently clear from the subsequent words: *part... having been left behind* (meros—kataleipontes). In the following, the use of *houtō* [thus] placed after the Participles—and even interposed in this very place—marks a reader of Plato. See just now Heindorf on *Phaedo* §. 13. p. 23. and Wyttenbach [Wyttenb.] on the same, p. 164 sq. Proclus and Olympiodorus adopted the same usage. See their Commentaries on the first *Alcibiades* p. 163. 304. and p. 5.

p. 151, 2. **λαμβάνοντες**] This is in this place *positing, supposing, or suspecting*, as Ficinus not badly [rendered it]. Regarding this usage, see Budé’s *Comm. L. Gr.* 144. 197; Stephanus’ *Thesaurus* p. 5553. sq. London ed. Bæhr noted similar things on Plutarch's *Alcibiades* 18. p. 168.

— 6. **αἰσχρὸν φανταζόμεθα**] We form an image of matter as something base (i.e., we imagine it) through the defect of form [species].

— 7. **ἢ τὸ παράπαν εἶδος ἀφαιροῦντες. Πᾶν εἶδος κ. τ. λ.**] This second *eidos* [form] is inconvenient. Feeling this, Ficinus softened it by translating as if *leiloipos* [failing/left] were written. There is no help in the Codices [manuscripts].

— 9. **εἰ ἐμέλλομεν θεάσασθαι**] Cf. above I. 6. 9. p. 57. G. *if he is to behold*, and the annotation there.

— 11. **ὥσπερ ὄμμα**] Engelhardt [Engelh.] wandered from the meaning of the passage; Taylor more prudently attached himself to Ficinus. Furthermore, cf. II. 4. 12. p. 166. G.: *it would much rather be matter, even if it were not clearly desirable, being invisible to the senses, for it is not seen by eyes, being colorless, etc.*

p. 152, 1. **῎Αποιος δὲ οὖσα (ἡ ὕλη) πῶς κακή;**] "That the Stoics established matter as without quality (*apoion*), we know from Diogenes Laertius VII. 134, Plutarch *Against the Stoics* p. 1085. B.C.F. 1086. A., and others: and that this especially hindered the Stoics in *explaining the origin of evil*, since they could not refer it to matter as being soulless and without quality; Plutarch teaches that it fell more correctly to Plato (*On the Procreation of the Soul in the Timaeus* p. 1015. 1016), although he himself left matter without quality, he did not, however, make it soulless." Wyttenbach *Animadvv. in Plutarch. de Isid. et Osirid.* (p. 369. A.) p. 232. Regarding matter *devoid of qualities*, *apoiō*, cf. Stobaeus *Eclogg.* I. 12. 3. p. 318. Heeren; Alcinous *On the Doctrine of Plato* c. 8. p. 473. Heinsius; Hemsterhuis on Hesychius I. p. 463. sq.; Lennep on the *Epistles of Phalaris* p. 149; Plotinus himself in the book *On Matter* II. 4. 1, II. 4. 7, and IV. 7. 3, VI. 1. 26; Proclus on the first *Alcibiades* p. 317. sq. and in *Theol. Inst.* c. 72. p. 112. In the same [Proclus], *apoion sōma* [body without quality] is taken in another sense, namely, as *inert*, cap. 80. p. 124. Porphyry *Sententt.* XXI. p. 226. sq.

— 2. **ἃς δέχεται, καὶ ἐν αὐτῇ—ἔσονται**] Viz. *autai* [they themselves]. See Hermann on Viger p. 708.

— 11. **᾿Ορθῶς ἄρα λέγοιτο**] I have retained the optative: cf. the twin passage below III. 6. 11. at the end: *So that if someone says matter is evil, he would speak the truth.* The end of this chapter—*lest it perhaps be evil as form, but rather as a nature opposed to form*—I interpret with Engelhardt thus: lest perhaps it be evil insofar as it is a form, but rather it is evil as a nature which is adversarial to form [species].

p. 153, 1. **ἐπεὶ—τὴν ὕλην ὅλως ἀναιρεῖν ἀξιοῦσιν.**] See below, c. 15 of this book.

—4. **᾿Αλλ᾿ εἰ ἡ στέρησις ἐπιβάλλοντός ἐστι παρεῖναι εἴδους τινός**] Without doubt, Ficinus also read *ei* [if], which we have added. Engelhardt, who noted nothing regarding this lacuna [gap], believing another to lie beneath in the following, supplied the passage thus: *all’ hē sterēsis apousia eidous t. e. epiballontos pareinai*: "But if privation is contained in the *defect* of form, *which tends toward being*" (or which desires *to einai*). Badly. Taylor attached himself better to Ficinus, translating: *But if privation of form respects being*. Nor does any book [manuscript] exhibit *apousia* [absence]. It is a Confusion [Synchysis] for: *But if it is the privation of some form that ought to be present* (viz. the form). *But if it is the privation of a certain form in that which desires to be present* (viz. that...

[[vocabulary: prudence, virtue, aphairesis (separation/ablation), apoios (without quality/formless), sterēsis (privation)]]

-> BOOK VIII. FIRST ENNEAD. p. 150—154. <-

*form*). No one is ignorant of how variedly the verb *epiballein* is understood. See now Stephanus’ *Thesaurus* p. 2613—2617. ed. Valpy. and add Schleusner’s *Lex. N. T.* under the word. Jacobs on Philostratus’ *Imagg.* p. 578. Scholia on Aristides p. 107. ed. Frommel. and Wyttenbach and our own annot. on Plotinus *On Beauty* special ed. (p. 57. F.) p. 387. In this place, however, *epiballein* is what is more usually *epiballesthai*, i.e., to look toward something as toward an end, to aim at a mark, and even to desire something. Hesychius p. 1341: *epiballomenos*: having an aim and purpose, desiring; where see the Note. Cf. Upton on Arrian’s *Dissertt.* I. 4. 14. and Upton and Schweighäuser in the *Greek Index to Epictetus* p. 327. sq. Photius *Lex. Græc.* p. 313. p. 364. Porson. *ophthalmisai* (Suidas and Zonaras *Ophthalmiaisai*): to envy; to cast a look desirously. Cf. the following: *Ophthalmon epiballein*: to behold curiously, from which the reason for this meaning appears.

— 5. **τὴν δὲ κακίαν ἐν αὐτῇ ποιεῖ**] You might conjecture *en autē* [in itself], and so Engelhardt. The words *logō tō heautēs* [by its own reason] Taylor did not express. Next: *hōste ou sterēsin—par’ autēs* [so that not privation—from itself] it likewise seems *par’ autēs* should be read, and so Ficinus: and soon again. Such things hereafter, to avoid the weariness of readers, I shall omit.

— 12. **παντελῇ στέρησιν**] Ficinus translates *universal privation*. He would have rendered it more clearly as *absolute*, by which word Tully [Cicero] himself expresses *pantelē*. See H. Stephanus in *Thes. L. Gr.* p. 7225. ed. Valpy. and Cicero *de Finib.* III. 7. 26. and Goerenz there p. 343.

— 14. **τὸ μὲν ἔχουσα, τὸ δὲ ἐστερημένη**] Ficinus also expressed this, and this alone is the genuine reading. For the philosopher describes that which he had recently called *tinā sterēsin agathou*, "a certain privation of good," i.e., that which is contrary to *absolute privation of good*.

154, 1. **Εἰ μὴ ἄρα τούτῳ κακὸν ᾖ ἐμπόδιον**] Regarding *ei* with the Subjunctive, it was discussed above at I. 4. 2. p. 30. F. G. Engelhardt referred *toutō* to *agathon* [the good], taking it thus: "Perhaps Evil shall have been an impediment to the Good." Taylor, on the contrary: — *that evil is an impediment to the soul*. Correctly. See just now what follows after a few words: *if then vice is an impediment to the soul*. Engelhardt was led into error by the usage of Plotinus, who quite often tends to subject a pronoun of the neuter gender, as in this place *toutō*, to Masculines and Feminines.

— 2. **ἀλλ᾿ οὕτω ποιητικὸν — τὸ κακὸν αὐτῆς**] So also Ficinus, and Taylor and Engelhardt following him. But if, following the faith of the most approved books [manuscripts], you read *autois* [to them], this Pronoun must be referred to those who say these things, with this meaning: "But in this way, to *them* (i.e., according to the opinion of those who contend that evil is only an impediment to the soul) evil will be the efficient cause of evil for the soul." Nevertheless, I did not wish to change it.

— 6. **Εἶτα καὶ ἡ ἀρετὴ — οὐδ᾿ αὐταγαθόν**] See the Various Readings. Certainly, we did not wish to change the accent of the last word without the consensus of the best books. For it varies in these. Thus, to use this example, in Simplicius on Epictetus I. 1. p. 12. p. 22. Schweighäuser [Schweigh.] ed. *autagatha*, Schweighäuser *autoagatha* (cf. the notes of Schweighäuser p. 201). Similarly in Plotinus VI. 6. 10. in the middle, the edition has *auto agathon*: three manuscripts have *autoagathon*. On the other hand, in Nicolaus of Methone’s *Refutation of Proclus*, *autagathos* and *autagathon* are read more often. See p. 17 and Vömel’s note there. Similarly *autoagathos* and *autoagathon* by others. Cf. Stephanus’ *Thes. L. Gr.* p. 146. ed. Valpy. Furthermore, the form *autagathos* and *autagathon* is not in the Lexicons. Concerning the word *autokalos* and *autokalon* [the Beautiful-itself], we advised in Proclus on the first *Alcibiades* p. 28. cf. p. 118.

— 12. **ἀρξαμένῳ μὲν ἀπὸ τῆς κακίας**] These have the appearance of a scholium, by which someone in the margin intended to explain the words *descending from vice* (apo tēs kakias katabainonti). But nonetheless, all the Codices recognize those words which, if they are genuine, are to be taken thus: *and first indeed (he will encounter) depravity*; regarding this use of the Participle *arxamenos* [beginning], see Heusde *Spec. Crit. in Platon.* p. 39. sq., Heindorf on *Gorgias* p. 83. sq., and Buttmann’s Index in the first *Alcibiades* under *archesthai*.

— ib. **θεωροῦντι μὲν ἡ θεωρία ἥτις ἐστί**] You might say Ficinus corrected it to *ei tis esti* [if there is any]. The Codices vary nothing. Moreover, to the participle *theōrounti* [to one contemplating] is subjected *ginomenō* [to one becoming/being in], he who contemplates evil itself: to him who has just now been in it. To which light is added by the immediately following: *for it becomes—in the place of dissimilarity*, in which words is contained the description of matter and evil, when from the doctrine of Plato *the dissimilar* (to anomoion) is contrary to the Good and to the ideas. See just now *Symposium* p. 211. p. 444. Bekker [Bekk.]. Hence, in the mention of matter, the word *anomoiotēs* [dissimilarity] recurs below in VI. 3. 2., which passage should be compared: likewise another in VI. 9. 5.

154, 15. **ἐπεὶ καὶ εἰ παντελῶς ἴοι—εἰς παντελῆ κακίαν**] For if the soul should go even altogether (or thoroughly) into absolute depravity. See above at the beginning of the twelfth chapter.

— 17. **ἔτι γὰρ ἀνθρωπικὸν ἡ κακία**] Below in II. 9. 9. our author distinguishes *the more human* (hoi anthrōpikōteroi) and *the excellent* (hoi spoudaioi), where Ficinus translates the former as "more humble." For our passage, Pollux II. 131 might be applied, who joins *light, easy in the human*, and adds *things which one might not bear*, and similar things; therefore *human* in this sense, that it falls into the nature of man and thus is to be tolerated in man. For these forms are used promiscuously. Pollux II. 5.: — *anthrōpos, anthrōpinon, anthrōpiskos, anthrōpion, anthrōpikon, etc.* Cf. also Ammonius p. 147 and Oudendorp there. Hence scattered variations in readings, such as Xenophon *Cyrop.* III. 1. 40: *you seem to me to have sinned in human fashion (anthrōpina)—pardon your father*, where others read *anthrōpika*, a variation I see neglected in the Xenophontic Lexicon. Plutarch frequents the former form more in the *Lives*, and this latter in the *Moralia*. Phrynichus *Soph. Prep.* in Bekker *Anecdott. Græcc.* I. p. 21: *anthrōpikos mythos*: one concerning human affairs. Synesius *Epistol.* 139. at the beginning p. 176: *of loves, some walking on the ground and having human (anthrōpikas) origins—others over whom a god presides and judges, etc.*

Franc. Patric.: *baptize yourself in this crater.* The same in the same place a little after, but with a different meaning: *as many as—baptized themselves in the mind (nous).*

Regarding the Attic form *epikatadarthein*, see Dorville on Chariton p. 415. Leipzig [p. 353. Amsterdam edition].

Add Theodoret IV. p. 140. where from Ambrose the *synkatathesis* of the holy virgin is the obedience of the holy virgin permitting herself to God. Just as Arrian in Epictetus III. 22. 104 joined the adjective *propetēs* [rash] to the word *synkatathesis*, so our author uses *rashness toward assents*, which in this place are *reconciliations* opposed to anger.

Bekk.: *some are indeed strange and ill-omened because of various spirits and solar heats (dieilēseis), others because of waters*, where likewise Ficinus had translated "whirlwinds," as in this passage of Plotinus, from which and from Galen Vol. I. p. 389. ...Bekker expressed the rough breathing, and, although Wyttenbach in a similar passage of Plutarch’s *Symposs.* VI. 2. p. 688. A. p. 824. The same reason applies to *psychē* [soul] instead of *psychēs*. That reading is more elegant and fortified by the authority of the codices.

— 14. **εἰ μὴ ταύτῃ εἰς τὸ αὐτὸ αἴτιον ἡ ὕλη τῆς ἀσθενείας**] All books recognize that *eis to auto*. It is, moreover, *equally, in the same way, auf dieselbe Weise*. Similar examples of this use of the preposition *eis* you may find (see Viger *de Idiotismm.* IX. 2. 11. sqq. and Hermann there on p. 597; Schäfer in Stephanus’ *Thes.* p. 3638. sq.): of the same formula you will hardly find [an example]. The passage, however, is to be interpreted thus: unless here (i.e., in the soul) matter is equally (viz. as in the body) the cause of weakness.

p. 156, 5. **καὶ τὸ λεγόμενον ἐπτερωμέναι καὶ τέλειοι**] He touches upon that of Plato in the *Phaedrus* p. 246. c.: *the soul, being perfect and winged (epterōmenē), traverses the heights and governs the whole world, etc.* where see the interpreters. Add Proclus on the first *Alcibiades* p. 20. sqq., Olympiodorus on the same p. 5. and *Præparat. ad Plotin. de Pulcrit.* p. XXXVI. sqq. special ed.

p. 157, 1. **ὕλη δὲ παροῦσα προσαιτεῖ οἷον καὶ ἐνοχλεῖ**] Thus we have given it from good books, and Plotinus refers to the passage of the *Symposium* p. 203: *after the gods had dined, Penia (Poverty), intending to beg (prosaitēsousa) as if there were a feast, arrived and was around the doors.* Which fable he explains more fully below in III. 5. 5, 6, 7, 8, 9; III. 6. 14. Moreover, some thought that matter was signified by Penia.

— 4. **οὐ γὰρ ἀνέχεται — διὰ κάκην**] It is surprising how much Engelhardt disturbed things here, which we shall not dwell upon. Taylor more prudently followed the footsteps of Ficinus.

— 6. **τὴν γένεσιν αὐτῇ παρασχοῦσα κ. τ. λ.**] Engelhardt translates *genesis* as "Daseyn" [existence]. Taylor more highly adorned this passage: — *by opposing the waters of generation she (the matter) occasions the soul's entrance into the rapid stream, and by this means renders her light, in itself vigorous and pure, polluted and feeble, like the faint glimmerings from a watch-tower beheld in a storm*. Beautiful, and not remote from the speech of Platonic philosophers as to the meaning; but legitimate interpretation bids us descend a little deeper into the individual words. First, *autē* [herself/itself] is uniquely true, for it is in this place *of its own accord, or spontaneously*; then, if a single book offered *tēn gennēsin*, I would receive it, i.e., *paidopoiian*, the procreation, viz. the business of procreating; regarding which distinction between the two words Wyttenbach briefly but well explained on Plutarch *de puerorr. educ.* p. 67. sq. In this way Plotinus would continue the fable of Penia (i.e., Matter); concerning which Plato speaks thus in the praised passage of the *Symposium*: *Penia then, plotting because of her own poverty to have a child from Poros, lies down beside him* (see a little before the Plotinian *matter subjecting herself*, viz. to the soul) *etc.* However, this is not necessary. For *genesis* to Platonic philosophers is more often *the birth and nature of flowing things*, with the added meaning of weakness and mortality. Hence *genesis* and *mortal nature* are frequently joined, likewise *genesis* and *destruction*, and no less *generation-working oblivion*, *generation-working passion* (see just now Proclus on the first *Alcibiades* p. 7. 36. 108. 250; Olympiodorus on the same p. 2.).

— 7. **οὐ γὰρ ἂν ἦλθε τῷ μὴ παρόντι**] It is of Plotinian brevity, for this meaning: unless matter were present and thus ready to receive the soul, the latter would not approach it. Therefore the meaning of the whole passage is this: Matter paves an easy path for the soul to approach itself (matter), and offers every opportunity to the same, so that she may exist together with matter as the parent and procreatress of flowing and mortal things.

— 11. **καὶ οἷον συσπειραθῆναι**] See the various readings. Add Plato in the *Symposium* p. 206. p. 435. Bekk.: *whenever the pregnant one (approaches) the ugly, it becomes gloomy and pained, and it contracts (syspeiratai) and turns away and rolls up.* Proclus in *Inst. Theol.* LXXXXVI. p. 130: *and the impartibility, binding and contracting (syspeirōsa), maintains it inexhaustible and undiminished in itself*: where consult our annotation.

— 14. **καὶ γὰρ εἰ αὐτὴ ἡ ψυχή**] Ficinus in the Commentary on this chapter: "Remember," he says, "that Plotinus here and elsewhere hints to us that matter is generated by nature, that is, by the lowest power of the soul; by the soul, I say, *whether suffering* [patiente], as it is read in some places, *or present* [præsente], which I think is more correctly read." He preferred, therefore, *parousa* [present] in this place. But, fortunately, he added the other as well: *suffering*; and Taylor and Engelhardt also expressed that. Nor does any MS. book give *parousa*. But if you nevertheless accept it, you ought to explain it so that it is "progressed," i.e., after the soul had rushed forth from the place of the Gods and was already looking at external things. If you hold to the former, the *prōton pathos psychēs* [first passion of the soul] must be thought of, or that first affection of the soul by which it is made forgetful of its primeval origin and virtue. This is pleasing.

157, 16. **μὴ τῇ παρουσίᾳ αὐτῆς τὴν γένεσιν λαβοῦσα**] i.e., unless the soul, by the presence of matter, had adopted a desire for things which *become*, not truly *are*, and thus for a nature flowing and destined to die. See what we said a little above regarding the word *genesis*.

p. 158, 1. **ἐκ τῶν περὶ ὕλης λόγων—εἰρημένου**] Plotinus sends the readers in this place to the fourth book of the second Ennead, which, although commonly praised as *On Matter*, is inscribed in the title itself *On the Two Matters*. We shall say more at the beginning of this book.

— 5. **ἡ γὰρ ὄρεξις ἀγαθοῦ**] Proclus *Inst. Theolog.* XXXXIX. p. 66 distinguishes a triple *orexis* [desire]: *and desire then belongs to some according to being alone, being a fitness for the participation of causes; to others according to life, being a motion toward better things; to others according to knowledge, being a co-sensation of the goodness of the causes.* Hence Dionysius the Areopagite calls this *orexis* itself "good" in *On Divine Names* IV. 19. p. 571.

— 6. **ἡ δὲ νόησις—ἀγαθοῦ ἐστι καὶ κακοῦ**] Proclus on the first *Alcibiades* p. 22: *and indeed the Timaeus—exhorts us to judge beings by intellection and reason, but things which are not, but are becoming and perishing, by opinion and sensation.*

— 9. **ἤδη καὶ αὐτὸ—ὅλον κακόν**] Ficinus seems to have conjectured *ekeinō ho holon kakon*, "and indeed that *en tō* could have arisen from an erroneously repeated *ekeinō* and the *ho* before *holon* suppressed." You could also: *ekeinō en hō holon kakon*, no less than *ekeinō en tō holō* (as several codices) *kakō*. Regarding the verb *syntelein*, add to those things which the Lexicographers have collected our Bæhr's Annotations on Plutarch’s *Compar. Philop. and Flamin.* 1. p. 136: for the construction of this verb with the Dative, hold these passages: Polybius IV. 60. 4: *to contribute (syntelein) common taxes to the Achaeans.* cf. Plutarch’s *Arat.* c. 34. Pausanias X. 8. 2: *that the Magnetes and Malieans and Aenianes and Phthiotians contribute (syntelein) to the Thessalians.* Our author no less uses the more common construction, as in VI. 1. 21: *to contribute to essence (syntelein eis ousian).* cf. VI. 7. 13. at the end. Next: *elattonos* (viz. *metalabōn* [having partaken] from the preceding) *de hē ēlattōtai tō agathō* (viz. *syntelesan*), "but because it is a participant in a smaller evil, by the proportion in which it has less, it is reckoned to the good."

— 15. **Φαντασία δὲ κ. τ. λ.**] In the preceding, Plotinus had explained the evils of the soul by the fact that it did not remain pure, but was mixed with matter. Now he begins to explain from the same source both imagination and false opinion: *phantasia de, plēgē alogou hōs exōthen* [imagination is a strike of the irrational as if from without]. Instead of *hōs* [as if], which is absent from most books, Ficinus seems to have read *zōou* [of a living thing]. Perhaps there lies hidden in *alogou hōs* the phrase *alogou physeōs* [of an irrational nature] or *alogou zōēs* [of an irrational life]. Be that as it may, Iamblichus in Stobaeus *Eclogg.* I. 52. p. 896. Heeren, reviewing the decrees of some more recent Platonists concerning the *origin of Evil*, narrates thus: *of those again differing from these, and adding evils to the soul from things growing to it from without in whatever way: from matter, Numenius and Cronius, often; from these bodies themselves, sometimes even Harpocration; from nature and the irrational life, Plotinus and Porphyry for the most part.* Therefore, Plotinus says the evil of the soul approaches from *a nature and life devoid of reason*. Proclus in the first *Alcibiades* p. 280: *for every evil is from without and adventitious to the soul, but the good is from within.—Because of this indeed everything which it receives from without remains lying outside it like phantasms and sensible things etc.* But nonetheless I have left the common reading untouched, which could also be explained such that it is "as if from the outside," and so Engelhardt translates.

— 16. **καὶ δόξα δὴ ψευδὴς ἔωθεν—ἀληθοῦς αὐτοῦ**] Ficinus seems to have read *k. doxai dē pseudeis exō genomenē* (viz. *psychē*) *tou alēthous autou*: "and indeed false opinions for [the soul] having become outside the true itself." Not badly, and for the most part with the books approving. Furthermore, these things are to be compared with those which Plato in the *Sophist* p. 263, *Rep.* III. 4. 13. and elsewhere, and Aristotle *On the Soul* III. 3. and thence Stobaeus I. 58. 59. p. 1114. sqq. teach concerning *imagination, sensation, opinion, and intellection*.

p. 159, 2. **συνεῖναι—καὶ ἐν αὐτῷ ἱδρυμένην**] Regarding the verb *hidryesthai* [to be established], which the Platonists frequent so much concerning stability and permanence in intelligible and thus divine things, I have said more in...

-> BOOK IX. <-

P. 163, 7. **ΠΕΡΙ ΕΞΑΓΩΓΗΣ**] Porphyry *Life of Plotinus* c. 4: *On the reasonable exit (peri eulogou exagōgēs).* The same chapter 24: *On the reasonable exit from life.* Olympiodorus on Plato’s *Phaedo* ed. Venice, which Mustoxydes first recently published, page 5: *On the reasonable exit.* A Scholion in the Vatican Codex soon to be praised: *On the irrational (Correct: reasonable) exit.* No one will wonder at these and similar variations in the titles of the Plotinian books, who has learned from the same writing of Porphyry c. 4 that since Plotinus did not himself initially entitle his books, others entitled them differently. This little book, moreover, belongs to those which Plotinus had composed before Porphyry had come to him, who then took up this duty of review and entitling. For it is the sixteenth. See Porphyry l. l. And this matter is joined with the narration of Eunapius in *Porphyry* p. 17. p. 9. ed. Boissonade who indeed, after he related how Plotinus averted Porphyry from suicide (*autocheiria*) (which matter he himself had touched upon in the life of his master; see Porphyry *Life of Plotinus* c. 11), thus proceeds: *and he indeed was inspired and rose up, but the other set down the spoken words into a book of those written.* To which Wyttenbach in the Annotations p. 33: "The first part indeed (of Eunapius’ words) has a sufficiently clear meaning: *And Porphyry indeed breathed again and arose. Plotinus, however, referred the sermons spoken by himself into a certain little book from the number of those he wrote.* It would be easy to establish that this was the book *On the Reasonable Exit*, which now exists as I. 9., unless Porphyry himself had revealed that this book was written before his arrival in Plotinus’ school: *Life of Plotinus* V. (rather IV.) p. 100. Therefore Fabricius, on Porphyry’s *Life of Plotinus* XI. p. 113, suspects that Eunapius signifies Ennead III. book II. *On Providence*, since in it is disputed *that it is permitted for souls to be happy in this world too, and that they must not succumb to calamities, but must fight against them strenuously, so that you may attain the rewards set forth for virtue.* Yet the argument of the book *On Happiness* I. 4. seems even more convenient to that sermon, likewise sent to Porphyry in Sicily, as is clear from the *Life of Plotinus* VI. p. 103. What also prevents those sermons from being contributed into the book *On the Reasonable Exit* already written; for which *bibliōn tōn gegrammenōn* [of the books written] seems to hold value, afterwards corrected and polished by Porphyry along with the rest of Plotinus’ books: of which duty of his he is himself a witness, in the same place XXIV. p. 139—147." Thus Wyttenbach. One could also think of the book *Against the Gnostics* II. 9., likewise written before Porphyry’s departure to Sicily. Certainly, there are in that book, especially toward the end p. 216 sqq., things which pertain to the same argument. But, to say what I feel, those arguments mentioned by Eunapius seem to me to have been referred to Plotinus’ book *On the Reasonable Exit*, much larger and fuller than this one itself which we are now treating; which indeed ought to be regarded as a fragment of a book, inasmuch as it is finished with only a few sentences, rather than as a proper book. And this very thing perhaps might be one of the traces (of which several exist, see Fabricius *Bibl. Gr.* V. p. 696. Harles) of the double recension [edition] of Plotinian works, the...

-> ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS <-

...Eustochian and the Porphyrian. I would add this: it is not credible that Porphyry, in his recension, sent out such a naked and contracted little book as this one we now have, but rather a proper book, certainly furnished with all those arguments by which he himself had been averted by his teacher Plotinus from bringing death upon himself. But this little book has the appearance of a *sciagraphia* [outline], from which finally, by a second care, a book complete in its parts could be made. These things, if they are posed probably, are at the same time an indication that we today possess in our Codices a mixed recension, evidently composed from the Porphyrian and the Eustochian.

As for the matter of the little book, many discussions of philosophers—Pythagoreans, Plato, Aristotle, Stoics, Cyrenaics—provided the occasion for this dispute; to speak of which in this place is both long and unnecessary after so many cares of other men. You see Lambinus’ commentary on Horace’s *Epist.* I. 16. at the end; Petrus Victorius *Varr. Lectt.* VI. 11; M. A. Muretus *Varr. Lectt.* IV. 2. p. 80. ed. Ruhnken; Justus Lipsius *Manuduction. ad Philos. Stoic.* III. 23. sq.; Thomas Gataker on Marcus Aurelius II. 47. p. 58. and especially III. 1. p. 62. sq.; Jo. Davies on Cicero’s *Tuscull.* I. 30; Wyttenbach on Plato’s *Phaedo* p. 130. sqq. and those whom he praises; finally Carolus Beier on Cicero’s *de Offic.* p. 350—355 [certainly in excursion XV. Vol. I. to I. 31. 112. and 43. 153. Add Tiedemann *System der Stoischen Philosophie* Vol. III. p. 308—321]. For Plotinus’ sake, we contain ourselves in one passage of Plato, from which, as our Philosopher is accustomed, he undoubtedly found the occasion for this question; which would be more clearly understood if we had a larger book of Plotinus in hand. For in the *Phaedo* p. 61. D. E. p. 62. B. this opinion of Philolaus the Pythagorean is explained: *to mē themiton einai heauton biazesthai*: *that it is not lawful to do violence to oneself*. Of which decree two reasons are subjected, one: *the word said in secret (aporrhētois) concerning them, that we humans are as if in a certain garrison (phroura), and one must not indeed loose oneself from this nor run away*: the other: *that god is he who cares for us, and we are his possessions.* And some took the former reason thus: that we are in the protections and station of life, like soldiers on guard (Cicero *Cato the Elder* cap. 20), which metaphor the Stoics subsequently especially fashioned (see Gataker on Aurelius II. 47). But the opinion of Philolaus and Plato was this: that we are in *prison and bonds* (Cicero *Tuscull.* I. 30. *Dream of Scipio* c. 3. or *de Republ.* VI. 14. p. 478. sq. ed. Moser and our own. cf. Aug. Boeckh’s *Philolaus* p. 178.). Regarding both arguments, Olympiodorus in the *Scholia on the Phaedo* p. 1. sqq. ed. pr. Mustoxyd.: *and the text shows this through two arguments, one mythical and Orphic (mystical and Orphic?), the other dialectical.* Now Olympiodorus explains that mythical or fabulous argument with many words, the sum of which comes to this: *that we ought not to lead ourselves out, since our body is Dionysian*: i.e., since we are particles of the Bacchic body. For after Bacchus was torn apart and devoured by the Titans and the Titans were burned, the human body was fashioned from there. Then he comes to the dialectical argument. And that we may leave aside the fabulous argument, this is certain: in the Orphic mysteries it was especially handed down that we are enclosed in this body as if in a prison for the sake of paying a penalty, and therefore it is not permitted by religious laws to depart from there earlier and free ourselves, than by the command of God, the same being our master. (Plato in the *Cratylus* p. 400 where in the Orphic manner *sōma* [body] is called *sēma* [tomb], the body being the tomb of the soul.) And that in Thrace anciently opinions of this kind flourished, and were handed down through the hands of priests and ministers of mysteries and reached the Pythagorean philosophers, who wished to seem Orphic, and were more fully explained by them—there is very little reason for us to call into doubt. (See just now Herodotus V. 4. II. 81. and conf. more things which I myself contributed to that matter in the *Studies* written in German Vol. II. p. 234. sqq. and p. 321. sqq. and Boeckh *Philolaus* p. 180. sqq.) Which things I touched upon because Wyttenbach on the *Phaedo* p. 134. sqq. and in *Philomath.* III. p. 86. did not correctly take those things of Plato in the *secret doctrines* (aporrhētois), and Heindorf also on Plato’s *Gorgias* p. 493, after Meiners—who was wonderfully blind in such matters—dared to pronounce those decrees about the soul enclosed in a prison, and not to be sent out from there without the master's order, as unworthy of an ancient Pythagorean philosopher such as Philolaus was. *Furthermore, that opinion from which Plotinus proceeds in this dispute...*

[[vocabulary: sciagraphia (outline/sketch), Recensio Eustochiana, Recensio Porphyriana, phroura (watch/guard/garrison), sōma-sēma (body-tomb), aporrhēta (secret doctrines)]]
