[[original page: 81]]

-> BOOK IX. FIRST ENNEAD. p. 163. <-

...could also be that of the ancient Zoroaster, if we look at the argument, since ancient writers produce Zoroaster as having somehow held the torch before Pythagoras; it *could*, I say, if you look at the matter, for no one more learned will deny that that verse from the magic oracles, which are carried under the name of Zoroaster, must be held as belonging to a later age and manufacture.

Moreover, many of the later writers knew this Plotinian dispute, among these David the Armenian, whose passage I shall add at the end, Olympiodorus, Macrobius, and John of Salisbury, although he undoubtedly owes his knowledge to Macrobius. And the former [Olympiodorus], in those arguments which he brings forward to protect the "exit" (*exagōgē*), placed this not unpleasantly: in the *Phaedo* p. 5: *third argument: if it has been written by Plotinus concerning the reasonable exit, then one must sometimes lead oneself out.* Then he adds more concerning the arguments of the Stoics; from which, to sample this on this given occasion, Wyttenbach on Plutarch’s *Apophthegmm. Lacænarum* p. 1222 thus: "By the word *exēgagen heautēn* [she led herself out], she killed herself, the *eulogos exagōgē* [reasonable exit] of the Stoics is signified, in whose disputes concerning this argument the Laconian example seems to have been frequent from Epictetus *Dissert.* I. 2. p. 12, 13. ed. Schweighäuser." Macrobius, however, seized the occasion for disputing from the passage of Cicero (*Dream of Scipio* III. or *de Republ.* VI. p. 478—483. ed. Moser), which we touched upon above, in *Somn. Scipionis* I. 13: "This is the sect and precept of Plato, who in the *Phaedo* defines that a man must not die by his own accord.—Plotinus follows these seeds of the Platonic sect more deeply." John of Salisbury, however, in the *Policraticus* lib. II. c. 26 (in *Max. Bibliotheca Patrum* Vol. XXIII. p. 278) thus: "Granted he erred in this also, that he cast away the gift of life by his own authority. Which is established as prohibited not only by the institutes of the faithful, but by the constitutions of nations and the edicts of the wisest men. The ancient princes of Philosophy indeed, Pythagoras and Plotinus, are not so much the authors of this prohibition as the heralds, saying it is altogether illicit for anyone serving in the military to depart from the protection and the station committed to him without the order of the leader or prince. Clearly they used an elegant example, because the life of man upon earth is a warfare." You see that John both explained that Pythagorean opinion concerning the *garrison* [phroura] in the manner of Cicero and also attached the same to Plotinus. Furthermore, the things which Marsilio Ficino explained in the Commentary on this little book were for the most part taken from Olympiodorus and from Macrobius. That he says Olympiodorus and Macrobius disagree with each other in this cause, the former pronouncing it licit, the latter denying it—he did not report accurately. For Olympiodorus explained the arguments of this cause on both sides. Theodosius Metochites touched on the same question in *Miscellan.* c. 90. p. 582. ed. Müller and Kiessling: *For it is not possible nor truly lawful to be cut before the given limits, and as if to stand out and depart from this unfortunate conjunction (the yoke by which the soul and body are coupled).*

163, 9. **Οὐκ ἐξάξει**] See the various readings. We have received the reading of almost all books and the margin. For no book offers *Mē exaxēs*. In the published magic oracles of Zoroaster p. 78. ed. Gale v. 15 this passage is read thus: *Mē exaxēs, hina mē exiousa echē ti*, and it is translated: "*Do not lead out the soul, lest exiting from the body it have something of danger.*" This is bad. He ought to have either omitted the last word or substituted *sordium* [filth/sordes]. But the Vatican Codex n. 1416, excerpted for my use by Hieron. Amatius p. 94, has it thus: *Chaldaean oracle: Do not lead out [the soul], lest it exit having something.* Plainly as the margin of the Cizensis codex and the Plotinian books in the context. Those: *for it shall go forth*, and *so that it may also go forth*, were added by Plotinus for the sake of completing the meaning. Furthermore, as in this place for *exaxei* and *exaxēs* "the soul" must be thought of, so elsewhere it must be supplied by thinking "yourself," "himself," or "from life" or "from living"; so, however, that the ellipsis is more usual than the full locution. The fragments of Protichus IX. p. 52: *some lead themselves out by poppy, others by hemlock*, one could write: "Soon someone might prefer: they lead [themselves] out *from living*." Nor did he deal altogether accurately with this usage in the same place. As for what Reiske adds in the Index to Plutarch’s *Lives* p. 231 to *heauton exēgagen*: "viz. from the body," whether it is ever found in a full locution in an author, I would not say. I shall add some passages from my Adversaria [notebooks], from which either the variety of the formula or the diversity of the philosophers' thinking may be known: Zeno the Stoic in Diogenes Laertius VII. 130: — *and they say the wise man will reasonably lead himself out of life both for country and for friends; even if he be in harder pain, or maimings, or incurable diseases.* Olympiodorus in the *Phaedo*: — *the Stoics said there were five ways of the reasonable exit.* On the other hand, Theodorus the Cyrenaic in Diog. L. II. 98: *he said it was also reasonable that the excellent man not lead himself out for the sake of his country. etc.* Plutarch *Against the Stoics* p. 1060. p. 326. Wyttenbach: *to lead themselves out of living reasonably and to renounce life.* Arrian *Dissert.* II. 15. 10: *you lead a friend out from living for us.* The same IV. 1. 105: *whenever [God] leads you out.* Marcus Aurelius III. 1. p. 62: *if it is already to be led out.* Synesius *Epist.* 79: *I would have led myself out having been overcome by the passion.* Similarly Appian *On the Civil Wars* IV. 135. p. 707. Schweighäuser. On the other hand, the same *On the Spanish War* VI. 96. p. 707 more fully: *and they wish to lead themselves out of life.* Athenaeus IV. p. 157. b: *I would advise you, according to the Socratic Antisthenes, to lead yourselves out of life.* Nor otherwise Porphyry *Life of Plotinus* p. 113 Fabricius. — *of me thinking to lead myself out of life.* A singular meaning of the formula is in Xenophon of Ephesus V. p. 35: *they led themselves out of life* concerning *old men* who hastened death for themselves by too much indulging in grief. See Peerlkamp on that passage p. 359. In the Greek translators of the Bible and in the N. T. *hypagein* is quite often used simply for *to die*, which there is no reason to confirm by examples after those which Schleusner collected in the *Lex. N. T.* under the word. — These things concerning the formulas. The meaning of the Plotinian passage agrees with Hierocles 160: *And it shall be pure, if it should contribute nothing to irrationality, nor to the mortal body (perhaps 'kindred' is missing), but as one thing caring for others, bestowing on them as much care as the divine law commands, not permitting to try to lead it (Medic. Codex: himself) out, but to wait until God himself releases us.* Macrobius in *Somn. Scip.* I. 13 from Plotinus: "Nor is there a light difference between dissolving life by nature or by one's own accord; for the soul, when it is deserted by the body, can retain in itself nothing of the guilty, if it instituted itself purely while it was in this life; but when it is itself violently thrust out from the body, because it exits with the bond not loosed, that very necessity becomes an occasion of passion for it, and it is infected with evils while it breaks the bond." Furthermore, Plotinus' words *hina kai exelthē* were to be translated: *wherever it may have gone out*. Regarding the argument cf. below *Against the Gnostics* II. 9. 18. p. 217. D.

p. 163, 13. **ἀδυνατοῦντος ἔτι τοῦ σώματος—συνδεῖν τῆς ἁρμονίας αὐτοῦ οὐκέτι οὔσης**] This opinion also pleased the Pythagoreans, or a similar one certainly: Clearchus in Athenaeus IV. 157. c. p. 112. Schweighäuser: *Euxitheus the Pythagorean—said that the souls of all were bound in the body and in life here for the sake of punishment. And god has declared that if they do not remain in these until he himself willingly looses them, they will then fall into more and greater outrages. Wherefore all, being cautious, fear the threat of the masters to exit life willingly, and they welcome only the death in old age, being persuaded that the release of the soul happens with the mind of the masters.* With Plotinus’ words another passage of the same [Plotinus] II. 9. 18. p. 217. B. C. D. agrees more, where the body is compared with a house skillfully built; from which I shall add only these things in this place: — *it is necessary to remain in houses while having a body fashioned by a good sister soul.* Especially see Diogenes Laertius VIII. 29 where from the doctrine of Pythagoras the body of an infant is said *to be held together according to the ratios of harmony.* Cf. Censorinus *de die natali* c. 9. Macrobius l.l.: "He (Plotinus) also adds that that alone is a natural death, where the body leaves the soul, not the soul the body. For it is established that a certain and constituted ratio of numbers associates souls with bodies; as long as these numbers remain, the body perseveres in being animated; but when they fail, soon that secret force is dissolved, by which society itself consisted: and this is what we call fate and the fatal times of life. The soul therefore itself does not fail, since it is immortal and perpetual; but the numbers being filled, the body faints: nor is the soul weary of animating; but the body deserts its duty when it can no longer be animated. Hence is that of the most learned seer (Virgil *Aen.* VI. 545): *I shall fill the number, and be returned to the shadows.* This is therefore a truly natural death, when the defect of its numbers alone brings the end of the body: not when life is extorted from a body still fit for the continuation of bearing it." Brucker praises these words of Plotinus in *Hist. Crit. Philos.* II. p. 418 using Ficinus' version, as he is accustomed, and adds: "Behold indeed a *pre-established harmony* between the soul and the body, already partially known to Plotinus!"

<note>original: "τὸν σοφὸν καὶ ὑπὲρ πατρίδος..."</note> ...the wise man [should act] both for the sake of his fatherland and for his friends, even if he should find himself in the harshest pain, or in cases of mutilation, or incurable diseases. Olympiodorus in his commentary on the *Phaedo*:—The Stoics spoke of five ways of "reasonable exit" <note>original: εὐλόγου ἐξαγωγῆς; a technical term for justified suicide</note>. On the other hand, Theodorus of Cyrene, according to Diogenes Laertius II. 98, said: "It is reasonable that the man of high character should not sacrifice himself for his fatherland," etc. Plutarch, *Against the Stoics*, p. 1060 (p. 326 in Wyttenbach's edition): "to reasonably lead themselves out of living and to renounce life." Arrian, *Discourses of Epictetus* II. 15. 10: "you lead a man, a friend, out of life." The same author, IV. 1. 105: "whenever He (God) leads you out." Marcus Aurelius III. 1. p. 62: "if it is already time for him to be led out." Synesius, *Epistle* 79: "I would have led myself out, overcome by my suffering." Similarly, Appian, *The Civil Wars* IV. 135 (p. 707 in Schweighäuser): and in the same author's *Spanish Wars* VI. 96, more fully: "and they wish to lead themselves out of life." Athenaeus IV. p. 157. b: "I would advise you, according to the Socratic Antisthenes, to lead yourselves out of life." Likewise Porphyry in his *Life of Plotinus*, p. 113 in Fabricius:—"thinking of leading myself out of life." A singular meaning of this formula is found in Xenophon of Ephesus V. p. 35: "they led themselves out of life," referring to *the elderly* who hastened their own deaths by indulging too much in grief. See Peerlkamp on that passage, p. 359. Among the Greek translators of the Bible and in the New Testament, the word "to go away" <note>original: ὑπάγειν</note> is used quite frequently simply to mean *to die*; there is no need to confirm this with examples after the collection made by Schleusner in his *Lexicon of the New Testament* under that entry.—So much for the formulas. The sentiment of the passage in Plotinus agrees with Hierocles, p. 160: "The soul will be pure if it is not carried away with irrationality or the mortal body (perhaps 'kinship' is missing here), but as one thing caring for another, it grants them only as much care as the divine law commands, not permitting it to try to lead itself out (the Medici Manuscript reads 'himself'), but to wait until God Himself releases us." Macrobius, in his *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio* I. 13, drawing from Plotinus: "Nor is there a slight difference between dissolving life by nature or by one's own will; for the soul, when it is deserted by the body, can retain nothing of guilt in itself if it conducted itself purely while in this life; but when it is violently thrust out of the body, because it exits while the bond is not yet loosened, that very necessity becomes an occasion for passion, and it is stained by evils while it breaks the bond." Furthermore, Plotinus's words "so that it may also go out" should be translated: *wherever it may depart*. Regarding the argument, compare below *Against the Gnostics* II. 9. 18. p. 217. D.

p. 163, 13. **the body being no longer able—to bind it together, its harmony being no more**] This sentiment was also pleasing to the Pythagoreans, or at least a similar one: Clearchus in Athenaeus IV. 157. c. p. 112 in Schweighäuser: "Euxitheus the Pythagorean—said that the souls of all are bound in the body and in this life for the sake of punishment. And God has proclaimed that if they do not remain in these conditions until He willingly releases them, they will then fall into more and greater outrages. Therefore, all, being cautious of the threats of their masters, fear to exit life willingly, and only welcome death in old age, being persuaded that the release of the soul occurs with the consent of the masters." Another passage from the same author (Plotinus) II. 9. 18. p. 217. B. C. D. agrees more with these words, where the body is compared to a skillfully built house; from which I will set down only these words here:—"it is necessary to remain in the houses, having a body prepared by a good sister-soul." See especially Diogenes Laertius VIII. 29, where from the doctrine of Pythagoras the body of an infant is said to be "held together according to the ratios of harmony." Compare Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, ch. 9. Macrobius, in the place cited above: "He (Plotinus) also adds that that alone is a natural death where the body leaves the soul, not the soul the body. For it is established that a certain and fixed ratio of numbers <note>original: numerorum... rationem</note> associates souls with bodies; while these numbers remain, the body continues to be animated; but when they fail, that secret force is soon dissolved, which consisted of the association itself: and this is what we call fate and the fated times of life. Therefore, the soul itself does not fail, since it is immortal and perpetual; but when the numbers are fulfilled, the body faints: nor does the soul grow weary of animating; but the body deserts its duty when it can no longer be animated. Hence that line of the most learned poet (Virgil, *Aeneid* VI. 545): *I shall complete the number, and be returned to the shadows.* This, therefore, is the truly natural death, when the failure of its own numbers alone brings an end to the body: not when life is twisted out of a body still fit for the continuation of endurance." Brucker praises these words of Plotinus in his *Critical History of Philosophy* II. p. 418, using Ficino's translation as he usually does, and adds: "Behold indeed a *pre-established harmony* between soul and body, already partially known to Plotinus!"

p. 163, 14. **Τί οὖν εἰ μηχανήσαιτό τις—μηδὲν πράττειν**] Macrobius l. l.: "It is necessary," he says (Plotinus), "that the soul after man be found free from corporeal passions; which he, who violently thrusts it from the body, does not permit to be free. For he who prepares slaughter for himself of his own accord, either descends to this having been weary of necessity or by the fear of someone or by hatred; all of which are held among the passions. Therefore even if it was previously pure from these sordes [filth], nonetheless by this very fact by which it exits having been extorted, it becomes sordid."

p. 164, 3. **Εἰ οὖν ἀρχὴν αἴσθοιτο τοῦ ληρεῖν—αἱρετοῖς**] This was the very opinion of the Stoics. For the Stoics had compared life with a Banquet. Olympiodorus in the *Phaedo* p. 6: — *But also because of drunkenness the banquet is dissolved, so also one must dissolve life (perhaps 'because of' should be added) the silliness (lēron) following the body, for silliness is a natural drunkenness, but also because of the things set before us being diseased, life is to be dissolved because of the body being held by incurable diseases, and unfit for ministering to the soul.* Plotinus himself touched upon the same evils above in the book *On Happiness* I. 4. where see especially c. 5. p. 32: *But pains and diseases, and things altogether preventing acting; if indeed he should not even follow himself; etc.* i.e., if indeed a man should not be consistent with himself in mind: or, if indeed he should even be captured in mind [insane], where cf. the annotation.

— 6. **Καὶ γὰρ ἡ τῶν φαρμάκων προσαγωγή**] See the various readings. Six Codices and the margin of the Edition: *prosexagōgē*. An unheard-of word. You might suspect Plotinus wrote: *for indeed the leading out (proexagōgē) of the soul through drugs before it is time*, and that *pros exodon* [toward exit] is an interpretation brought from the margin into the speech. Certainly Polybius XXX. 7. 8 uses: *to lead oneself out (proexagein) from living* before it is necessary, to commit suicide. See Schweighäuser *Lex. Polyb.* But neither is the word *proexagōgē* in use; nor does the common reading exhibit a convenient sense.

— 7. **ψυχῇ οὐ πρόσφορος—οὐκ εὐτυχές**] Perhaps Macrobius amplified these. For he says thus: "Then he (Plotinus) says that death ought to be a solution of the soul from the body, not a bond: but by a forced exit the soul is bound more and more around the body and indeed for that reason souls thus extorted wander for a long time around the body or its burial or the place in which the hand was injected. When on the contrary those souls, which dissolve themselves in this life from corporeal bonds by the death of philosophy, with the body still standing are inserted into the heaven and stars, and therefore he signifies that alone of voluntary deaths to be laudable, which is prepared, as we said, by the reason of philosophy, not by iron: by prudence, not by poison." But perhaps someone might say that these seem to be able to be taken from a more complete book of Plotinus, about which we conjectured above, since several sentences are not found in this little book *On the Exit*, which Macrobius brings into the midst in this chapter. Personally, I would not have believed it. These are taken partly from Plato’s *Phaedo*, partly from other books of Plotinus himself, e.g., *On Dialectic*. And universally, he who compares these Macrobian things with the Plotinian things, would immediately understand that the Roman philosopher acted so as to dilate the dense and contracted sentences of the Egyptian philosopher, and to make them readier for his readers. These things also, continuously joined, will teach each one. For what Plotinus adds at the end of the little book: *But if he is such—there being an accession, he must not be led out*, Macrobius adorns thus: "He (Plotinus) also adds this reason to the superior ones for not perishing of one's own accord. Since it is established," he says, "that remuneration is to be rendered to souls there, according to the measure of perfection to which each one arrived in this life: the end of life is not to be precipitated, when an accession of profiting can still be possible. Nor was this said in vain. For in the secret disputes concerning the return of the soul it is said &c." Marsilio inserted the rest into his Commentary. From which it appears that Macrobius interposed even some of his own arguments in these Plotinian sentences, and altogether, as I signified above, wrote a sort of Periphrasis of this little book. — At the end of this dispute it is helpful to add a passage of David the Armenian *Prolegg. Commentar. in Porphyrii Quinque Voces* from the Royal Paris ms. cod. nr. 1939. fol. 117: *Plotinus however, writing on the reasonable exit, accepts none of these five ways (David had enumerated in the preceding the five reasons which other philosophers established), saying not to neglect the body altogether through the care of the soul, but to make the fitting providence for it, until that, having become unfit, should separate itself from the communion (koinōnia) with the soul, for it is absurd to lead oneself out before the time.*

**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

#### BOOK I [II] OF THE SECOND ENNEAD.

**p. 178, 7. *Περί οὐρανοῦ* [On the Heaven]**] This book is the fortieth according to the order in which individual works were written by Plotinus. See Porphyry, *On the Life of Plotinus*, p. 141, Fabricius edition (ch. 24), where, however, it is titled *περί κόσμου* [On the World]. Philoponus, Simplicius, and others employ the same title, as we shall see hereafter. Our manuscripts [MSS] do not vary in this place. The cause of this diversity lies in the custom of the ancients, who used *κόσμον* [world] and *οὐρανὸν* [heaven] interchangeably. Plato in the *Timaeus*, p. 28 (p. 23 Bekker): "Now the whole heaven or world—or whatever other name it might most properly receive, let it be called by us by that name." On which passage Proclus says (p. 83): "For this very thing must be known, that these names have much ambiguity among the ancients, etc." Thus Aristotle, *Meteorology* I. 2 and 3: "the world encompassing the earth," where consequently *κόσμος* [world] is *cælum* [heaven]. The same author, in *De Cælo* ch. 9, 10, 24 (Sylburg ed.), distinguishes a triple meaning of the word *οὐρανοῦ*. Cf. also Philo Judaeus, *On the Incorruptibility of the World*, and Mangey there (p. 488), from which it is understood that Pythagoras first called either the heaven or this universality of things *κόσμον*. Hence the dual usage of Roman writers, as Pliny, *Natural History* II. 1: "The world, and this which it has pleased us to call by another name, the heaven, by whose bending all things are covered," where cf. Hardouin (p. 69 and p. 126). Conversely, the Latins sometimes used *cælum* for *mundus* [world]. Cicero in the *Hortensius*, cited by Servius on *Aeneid* I. 335: "The Epicureans, who wish there to be many *cælos* [heavens]," i.e., *mundos* [worlds]. Regarding this usage, see those whom Harles praises in Fabricius, *Bibl. Gr.* III, p. 230, note; Io. Christ. Kapp on Aristotle’s *De Mundo* II, p. 18 sq.; and Jan Bake on Cleomedes’ *Meteora* I. 1, p. 258. Cf. below at p. 384 D. — Furthermore, the argument of this Plotinian book is connected with the discussions of Plato in various Dialogues, but especially in the *Timaeus*. Next, with several books of Aristotle, particularly *On the Heaven*. Nor should the philosopher of Lycopolis [Plotinus] be thought to have ignored the tenets of the Epicureans, Stoics, and other philosophers in this dispute. He who desires to know their decrees concerning the world should consult Philo Judaeus’ book *On the Incorruptibility of the World*, as well as Proclus’ commentaries on Plato’s *Timaeus*, where the opinions of the Pythagoreans, Plato, Aristotle, Crantor, Plutarch, Atticus, Plotinus himself, Porphyry, Iamblichus, and others are reviewed—especially concerning whether the world is eternal or not (p. 84 sqq.). Cf. the same Proclus in *Theol. Platonis* II. 11, p. 107; III. 1, p. 126 sq.; and III. 16, p. 147; and his *Inst. Theol.* c. 48 sqq., p. 78 sqq. (our edition). Io. Philoponus attacked Proclus' tenet on the eternal world in a specific book, from which we shall borrow somewhat in our annotation. From these same disputes Nicolaus Methonensis took material for censuring Proclus in his *Refutation of Proclus’ Theological Elements*, p. 71 sqq. (Voemel ed.). Cf. also Dionysius the Areopagite, *On Divine Names* V. 4, p. 690, with the Scholia of Maximus, p. 705 sq. Finally, Nicephorus Blemmida inserted a chapter into his *Physical Epitome* titled "On the Heaven, and that the world is not eternal." See ch. 24, p. 179 sqq. (Wegelin ed., Augsburg, 1605). I have touched upon the opinions of some more recent writers on that tenet below at our author’s *Ennead* III. 2. 1, p. 255 A. B.

— **11. *πρῶτον μὲν ἀληθὲς μὲν ἂν ἴσως*** [first, it might perhaps be true]] That some scribes hesitated at this place is no wonder, since even learned critics have stumbled at this rock. See Dorville on these words of Chariton VI. 5: "*Καλλιῤῥόη μὲν τὸ μὲν πρῶτον ὥρμησεν*" in *Animadvv.* p. 543 (Leipzig ed.) [p. 560 sq. Amsterdam ed.], where the arguments Weiske disputed to the contrary regarding pleonasms (p. 193 sq.) do not diminish the force of many examples. Next, I do not doubt that *ἂν* should be added after *οὐδεμίαν* from almost all our manuscripts. Plato, *Symposium* p. 176 (p. 377 Bekker): "*ἴσως ἂν ἐγὼ... ἧττον ἂν εἴην ἀηδής*" [Perhaps I... might be less unpleasant]. Proclus, *Inst. Theol.* c. 115, p. 168 (our ed.): "*ἓν ἂν οὐκ ἂν εἴη μόνον*" [One would not be one alone]. Regarding this repetition, see Gregory of Corinth, p. 18 (Koen); p. 42 (Schæfer); Hermann on Viger, p. 814 sqq.; and Dissen, *Dissquiss. philoll.* I, p. 28 sq. To add this one point, perhaps the reading of the Basel Codex in Thucydides III. 53 (beginning) should not be neglected: "*ἡγούμενοι τὸ ἴσον ἂν μάλιστ’ ἂν φέρεσθαι*." Shortly thereafter, so that he might consult clarity, Ficinus expressed the doubt

### PAGE 92 ###

**BOOK I [II]. SECOND ENNEAD. p. 178—181. 85**

contained in the sentence *μήποτε τοῦτο—ἀξιώσοι γίγνεσθαι* [lest this should be thought to happen] (for I change nothing). Concerning this force of the particle, consult Hoogeveen, *On Particles*, p. 391 (Schutz 2nd ed.), especially p. 394 sq. Next, **it is not** necessary to laboriously show that **κατὰ τὸ εἶδος** [according to the species/form] and **κατὰ τόδε** [according to this particular thing] are opposed to one another—the latter meaning according to individual things, or, as it is commonly said, according to *individuals*.

**p. 179, 4. *Εἰ δὲ τῷ πάντα συνειληφέναι (τὸν κόσμον)—ποιήσεται*** [But if, by having comprehended all things (the world)... it shall be made]] These things are connected with the decree that *the world is unique*; which some attribute to Heraclitus, as Diogenes Laërtius IX. 8: "that the whole is finite and that the world is one." Plato certainly pronounces this explicitly in the *Timaeus* p. 31 and in several other places. No less so does Aristotle in *De Cælo* I. 8. 9. These decrees are discussed at length in Philo, *On the Incorruptibility of the World*, Vol. II, p. 488 sq. (Mangey ed.); Plutarch, *On the Obsolescence of Oracles*, p. 422 sq. (p. 725 Wyttenbach); cf. also Plutarch, *On the E at Delphi*, p. 389 F, and Wyttenbach on him, p. 285 in *Animadvv.* Vol. III, and the additional material I have brought to this matter regarding Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II. 46, p. 401.

**p. 180, 14. *τὸν μὲν οὐρανὸν—ἔχειν τὸ ἀεί*** [the heaven... to have the 'always']] Proclus on Plato's *Timaeus* p. 166: "The celestial things remain immutable, just as the ancients Proclus of Mallus and Philonides said, and of the more recent, all the Platonists from Plotinus." That ancient Proclus is a Cilician Stoic philosopher. See Fabricius, *Bibl. Gr.* Vol. III, p. 574 sq. (Harles ed.) and Vol. IX, p. 365 sq. Cf. another passage of the same Proclus of Lycia in *Plat. Tim.* p. 73, where he touches upon these Plotinian matters again. — Ioannes Philoponus cites the following in *Against Proclus on the Eternity of the World* XIII. 15; which passage, without the author's name, Immanuel Bekker also inserted from the Parisian Royal Codex 1832 among the *Scholia on the Timaeus*, p. 439 sq. It reads thus: "Where shall we place the great Plotinus, who, if anyone else claimed to belong to the school of Plato, did not himself accept the fifth body introduced by Aristotle into the universe, from which that man [Aristotle] composed the heavens? Speaking in harmony with Plato’s opinion, he [Plotinus] also composes the celestial body from the four elements and declares this to be Plato’s opinion. He says, at any rate, in the discourse *On the World*: 'And yet, while the nature of the body is always flowing, it must...'" There follows the passage of Plotinus up to the words **ἔτι δὲ μᾶλλον πῶς ἥλιος** [and still more, how the sun]. Simplicius also cites the next part concerning Aristotle in his commentary on Aristotle’s *De Cælo*, and indeed in three places: p. 3. b., p. 5. b., and p. 26 (Venice, Aldine ed.). And in the first place thus: "Of these hypotheses Plotinus also makes mention in his *On the World*. For wishing to show the eternity of the heaven according to Plato, he says: 'For Aristotle there would be no labor, etc.'" In the second place he begins: "And the great Plotinus and Xenarchus in their difficulties against the fifth essence, etc." Apuleius, *On the World* p. 708 (p. 291 Bosscha ed.) says of the Heaven: "An element, not one of the four which are known to all, but far another, *fifth* in number, first in order, divine and inviolable in kind."

**p. 181, 2. *τῆς φύσεως τοῦ σώματος ῥεούσης ἀεὶ κ. τ. λ.*** [the nature of the body always flowing, etc.]] Regarding the first sentence, it is the well-known decree of Heraclitus **that all things move and nothing remains—as you could not step into the same river twice**. These are the words of Plato in the *Cratylus* p. 402. a. Aristotle (or the author of *De Mundo*) expresses the same tenet: "all things flow like rivers" IV. 25. On this matter see the material collected by Wyttenbach on Plutarch’s *De S. N. V.* p. 76 sq. (minor ed.), p. 398 (Oxford ed.); and on Plutarch’s *On the Multitude of Friends* in *Animadvv.* p. 660 sq.; likewise in *Animadvv.* on *Consol. to Apollonius* p. 721 sq. and p. 791 sq.; and what I myself have gathered on this matter in Dionysius p. 79 sqq. That second point is more memorable, but it has Plato himself, Aristotle, and other very grave authors. For he says in *Republic* VI, p. 498. b. (p. 300 Bekker): "toward old age, except for some few, they are extinguished far more than the Heraclitean sun, insofar as they are not rekindled." And more explicitly Aristotle in *Meteorology* II. 2, p. 39 (Sylburg): "it is clear that the sun is not only, as Heraclitus says, new every day, but is always continuously new." Which Alexander of Aphrodisias in *Meteorol.* fol. 93. a. explains: "another being rekindled each day as the former is extinguished in the west," that is, so that a new sun is lit every single day once the prior one is extinguished at its setting. Others have understood it differently. Plutarch preserved for us a decree of Heraclitus concerning the sun in *On Exile* p. 604. A: "For the sun will not overstep its measures; says Heraclitus; if it does, the Erinyes, the handmaids of justice, will find it out." Likewise in *On Isis and Osiris* p. 370. D, on which passage see Wyttenbach in *Animadvv.* p. 238; cf. Diogenes Laërtius IX. 1; Proclus on Plato’s *Timaeus* p. 334; Stobaeus, *Eclogues* I. 26.

### PAGE 93 ###

**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

p. 524 sqq. (Heeren ed.) where a similar sentiment is attributed to Hecataeus, whom they said was a listener of Heraclitus. Schleiermacher has explained these Heraclitean tenets at length in Wolf and Buttmann's *Museum der Alterthumswissenschaft* p. 392—399. Cf. also Baguet, *On Chrysippus* p. 176 sq.

**181, 7. *Ἀριστοτέλει—τὰς ὑποθέσεις τοῦ πέμπτου—σώματος*** [To Aristotle—the hypotheses of the fifth body]] Namely, Aristotle—contrary to what other philosophers and, according to Plotinus, Plato himself had done—did not wish the body of heaven to be composed of the remaining four elements, but had attributed to it a certain fifth element, proper to it and more excellent than the others. Furthermore, he attributed perpetual motion to the Heaven. For thus he says in *De Cælo* II. 3, p. 40 (Sylburg): "Everything that has a function exists for the sake of the function. The activity of God is immortality; and this is eternal life. Thus it is necessary for a divine thing to have eternal motion. Since the heaven is such a thing—for it is a divine body—for this reason it has the circular body, which by nature moves in a circle always." And just as he calls the body of heaven divine in this place, so in another place (*De Cælo* I. 3) he calls the same body "unaging, unalterable, impassive," and "the first of bodies." The ancient interpreters of Aristotle themselves establish that Plotinus touched upon these passages, whose testimonies we have cited above.

— **16. *πρὸς ζώου σύστασιν*** [toward the composition of a living thing]] The [printed] edition reads *στάσιν* [standing/position] with two manuscripts. And indeed *στάσις* is sometimes used transitively, so that in this place it could mean "constitution." See only Stephanus’ *Thesaurus* p. 4543 sqq. (London ed.). For other meanings gathered there, add Upton and Schweighäuser on Epictetus III, p. 443; Wyttenbach on Eunapius 302; Proclus on *Alcibiades* p. 273 (our ed.). We encounter the same permutation of these two words above in I. 8. 8, p. 77. F. But nevertheless, just as we retained *σύστασις* [composition] in the context there, so in this place, on the authority of many of our manuscripts, we have judged that *σύστασιν* should be introduced. Marsilio [Ficino] correctly renders: "*ad animal constituendum*" [to constitute the animal]; there was no reason for him to add "itself."

**p. 182, 2. *ἀλλὰ πρόσφορον—προσήκει*** [but suitable... it is fitting]] Wyttenbach on Plato’s *Phaedo* p. 232: "i.e., it is necessary that the matter also be adapted to the will of the effectuation; indeed the meaning is, *to the effectuation of the will: πρὸς τὸ τοῦ βουλήματος ἀποτέλεσμα*." Similarly in Plato he takes "*τὴν φύσιν τῆς ἀσθενείας*" [the nature of the weakness] for "*τὴν ἀσθένειαν τῆς φύσεως*" [the weakness of the nature] (cf. the same in *Philomath.* III, p. 98) and offers more examples of this permutation of the Genitive with the governing case, citing also Markland on Maximus Tyrius XVIII. 1, p. 566, who exhibits others, including this from Plutarch Vol. II, p. 500. B: "*τὰ θνητὰ τῶν ζώων γένη*" [the mortal kinds of animals] for "*τὰ τῶν θνητῶν ζώων γένη*." The writers of the New Testament by a similar enallage say sometimes "*ἐν πυρὶ φλογὸς*" [in fire of flame], sometimes "*ἐν φλογὶ πυρὸς*" [in flame of fire], as Valckenaer teaches in *Scholia on Acts* VII. 30, p. 426.

— **9. *ὕδατος φύσις*** [the nature of water]] Regarding this formula, see Wyttenbach on *Phaedo* p. 233, and ourselves on Plotinus’ *On Beauty* above p. 50. C. (in the special edition p. 139 sqq.).

— **14. *πῦρ δὲ, ὀξὺ μὲν καὶ ταχὺ—στάσιν ἐπ’ ἄμφω ζητεῖν*** [fire, being sharp and fast... to seek a standing in both]] One who has not inspected the manuscripts might easily persuade himself that Marsilio [Ficino] had a fuller text of this passage before his eyes. But the extra words he has are to be attributed to his paraphrasing, as he strives a thousand times to consult clarity. You might say he read "*καὶ γῆ τῇ μὴ ἐν ἄλλῳ*" [and earth in that which is not in another] and then "*ἔκτασιν ἐπ’ ἄμφω ζητεῖν*" [to seek extension in both]. But of these readings not a trace nor a footstep appears in the Medici Codices which he used. Therefore, these things are probably to be attributed to conjecture alone; let him see to it himself.

**p. 183, 5. *Τὰ μὲν οὖν ἡμέτερα μέρη—οὐ στέγοντα αὐτῶν (vel potius αὑτῶν) τὴν σύστασιν*** [Our parts, therefore... not containing/sustaining their composition]] Ficinus does not render this badly. The primary force of the verb is best understood from these words of Plato, *Republic* X, p. 621. A: "*οὐ τὸ ὕδωρ ἀγγεῖον οὐδὲν στέγει*" [no vessel holds the water]. Plato uses it often and variedly; Cf. *Republic* IX, 586, p. 454 (Bekker), and Ast in his *Commentary* p. 604, who was not unmindful of this Plotinian passage. Cf. the same on Plato’s *Laws* IV. 6, p. 213. Plutarch often uses it with this power, so that "*μὴ στέγειν*" means "not to contain, not to sustain, to allow to flow out and perish," as Wyttenbach teaches on the book *On Virtue and Vice*, p. 689. Another meaning is that touched upon by Zonaras in his *Lexicon* p. 1679: "*Στέγει: ὑπομένει*" [holds: endures], where see Tittmann. Learned men have occupied themselves with other meanings in Stephanus’ *Thesaurus* (recent London ed.). Moreover, here and in the following, Plotinus touches upon those vicissitudes of natural things (*ἀμοιβάς* [exchanges]) so much frequented by Heraclitus and the Stoics. See our author below, *Ennead* IV, book 8, p. 468, where more will be said.

**p. 184, 2. *πάγιόν ἂν τὴν δόξαν—λάβοι*** [he would take a firm opinion]] He would assume a certain and firm sentiment. The opposite is "*τῷ ἐπαμφοτερίζοντι*" [to one who wavers/doubts]. See Ruhnken on Timaeus' *Lexicon of Plato*, p. 108. Phrynichus, *Prep. Soph.* in

### PAGE 94 ###

**BOOK I [II]. SECOND ENNEAD. p. 181—186. 87**

Bekker, *Anecd. Grt.* II, p. 41; and Heindorf on Plato’s *Theaetetus* §. 36, p. 333: "*παγιῶσαι*" [to make firm]. Theodoret III, p. 759 (Schulz) uses it of plants which are fixed deeper in the soil. "*Παγίωσις*" is read in Olympiodorus on the *Phaedo*. This should be added to the lexicons. Regarding what is praised of Aristotle on flame in the next part, mention of it is frequent in his *Physics*. It seems to agree most with what is read in *Meteorology* I. 4, p. 8 (Sylburg): "for flame is the boiling of dry breath, etc." For the rest satisfies Plotinus’ meaning. Nicephorus Blemmida, as is his wont, pillaged Aristotelian points in his *Physical Epitome* p. 101 (Wegelin ed.). Plotinus, however, in these matters also looked to Plato discussing the kinds of fire, flame, and light in the *Timaeus* p. 58 (p. 76 Bekker).

— **5. *τὴν ψυχὴν—κινουμένην—κειμένην*** [the soul... moving... situated]] You might say Ficinus conjectured "*δυνάμει θαυμαστῇ κοσμουμένην*" [adorned with wonderful power], omitting the preceding "*κινουμένην*" [moving]. Another might think the words should be transposed: "*ἐφεξῆς τοῖς ἀρίστοις κειμένην—δυνάμει μεγίστη κινουμένην*" [situated next to the best things... moving with the greatest power]. The manuscripts seem to indicate that this passage is not intact. I find nothing else.

**p. 185, 1. *Ἡ δὲ μετάνοια τῆς ψυχῆς ὅτι κενόν ἐστι δέδεικται*** [That the 'repentance' of the soul is a void has been shown]] Namely, in the book against the Gnostics, as it is called, written before this one of ours. See II. 9. 6, p. 203. E: "But what must we say of the other hypostases which they introduce, the 'sojourn-places' and 'counter-types' and 'repentances'? For if they call these the passions of the soul when it is in repentance, and 'counter-types' when it contemplates images of beings as if they were not yet beings themselves, they are innovators in the constitution of their own heresy" (al. [reading] "speakers of vanities... composition") where I shall add certain other things.

— **6. *ἣ φησὶν ὁ Πλάτων*** [which Plato says]] Plato in the *Timaeus* p. 69 (p. 97 Bekker): "Then from these he composed this whole, one living thing having all living things within itself, mortal and immortal; and of the divine things he himself became the craftsman, but he commanded his own offspring to craft the birth of mortals, etc."

— **8. *Τοῦτο δὲ ταὐτὸν τῷ ἐφεξῆς—τὴν οὐρανίαν*** [This is the same as the next... the celestial]] Plato, *Phaedo* p. 109 (p. 110 Bekker): "*τὸ δὲ εἶναι ταὐτὸν, ὑπ’ ἀσθενείας καὶ βραδυτῆτος οὐχ οἵους τε εἶναι ἡμᾶς διεξελθεῖν ἐπ’ ἔσχατον τὸν ἀέρα*." Thus Bekker ordered the passage to be repeated. Heindorf conjectured (p. 229): "*τὸ δὲ εἶναι τοιοῦτον ὑπ’ ἀσθενείας:*" "since the matter is so, that on account of weakness." Wyttenbach (p. 301): i.e., "that this is the same as our not being able." "Although in this composition I would prefer either that *ταὐτὸν* [the same] be absent, or that *ᾖ* be added to it, which is often found removed from the preceding *ᾖ*, as we shall show on Plutarch *Mor.* p. 96. A. (See *Animadvv. on Plutarch* p. 652 sq., minor Oxford ed.) or that *τῷ* be added, as Plotinus spoke in a similar construction"— There follow the words of Plotinus, which Wyttenbach thus rendered into Latin: "This however is the same as if it were said, that the celestial soul is the next after the creator of the world, etc." Ficinus rendered it no differently.

— **15. *ὡς ἂν ἄλλης ψυχῆς αὐτῶν προσεχῶς ἀρχούσης*** [as if another soul were ruling them closely]] The adverb *προσεχῶς* [closely/immediately] is of very rare use, and thus neglected in common Lexicons. The new Stephanus (Valpy ed., p. 3978) offers a few things. As for Hesychius (II. 1045, Albert) explaining it as *σπουδαίως* [earnestly/diligently], no example of its use is noted by the editors. Therefore, someone might ask whether this force of the word fits our passage. If you accept it, it would be the same here as *προσεχόντως*, i.e., attentively, *diligently, seriously*. Nevertheless, Marsilio [Ficino] embraced the other [meaning], and it seems more appropriate. Pseudo-Plutarch, *On the Opinions of the Philosophers* III. 18, p. 897 (p. 617 Wyttenbach): "which circle being visible is called a halo, because it is a halo by the phantom appearing there *closely* [proxime] where the thickness of the sight now fell." Reiske, conjecturing "*ὅτι ἐστὶν ἅλωνι προσφερὴς*" [that it is similar to a halo], replaces a very rare adverb with a common adjective; as if very rare things were so readily at hand for scribes. Wyttenbach charmingly: "*ὅτι ἐστὶν ἅλως τῆς ὄψεως προσεχῶς ἐκεῖ δοκοῦντος τοῦ φάσματος γίνεσθαι, ἔνθα συνέπεσε κ. τ. λ.*" Whatever it be, in that place it means *closely/immediately*. Similarly in these words of Porphyry’s *Introduction to the Five Voices of Aristotle*, ch. II. §. 24, p. 378 (Buhl): "*καὶ πᾶν τὸ πρὸ τῶν ἀτόμων προσεχῶς κατηγορουμένων εἶδος ἂν εἴη μόνον:*" "and whatever is predicated *immediately* [proxime] above individuals would be a species only." To these places we also add this Plotinian one.

**p. 186, 7. *Τῷ μὲν οὖν Τιμαίῳ*** [In the Timaeus then]] Plato in *Tim.* p. 31 (p. 27 Bekker): "That which comes to be must be bodily and visible and tangible. But nothing could ever become visible separated from fire, nor tangible without some solid, and solid not without earth. Wherefore God, beginning to compose the body of the whole from fire and earth, labored." Io. Philoponus described these Plotinian things from those words up to the words: "*εἰ καὶ ἐν φυσικοῖς οὕτως*" [if even in physical things thus] in *Against Proclus on the Eternity of the World* XIII. 15, in the edition and in the Parisian Scholium

### PAGE 95 ###

**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

on *Tim.* p. 440 (Bekker ed.), adding these: "And Plotinus thus clearly spoke against Aristotle's assumption concerning the fifth body, and judged Plato’s to be well-held, saying that the heaven is composed of the same elements as the animals here. And in the following parts Plotinus again taught that the celestial bodies should not be thought to be anything other than of fire and the rest of the elements, nor should we, hearing 'earth' in those things, be carried away to the worse part of earth, or think the fire is flame." (There follows the passage of Plotinus treated by us above, namely **ch. 4. p. 99. A.**) "For the most pure and unmixed portion of the elements was separated into the composition of the celestial system, so that the nature of the celestial body is neither alien nor foreign to the elements among us, nor is the fire there or the earth or any of the others exactly such [as here]; but among us the dreggy and, as it were, the sediment of the elements flowed down, while there the most fine-parted and better portion was distinguished; since also in other animals, says Plotinus, nature selects the better parts especially in their most sovereign organs." Then he adds that this was the true opinion of Plato, which can be proved from elsewhere, and by the testimony of Aristotle himself, who, attributing it to him, spoke against it. Aristotle also seems to have been the first to introduce the opinion about the fifth body.

**p. 186, 9. *στερεόν*** [solid]] It is confirmed by Plato’s own books. Those who wrote *στἐῤῥον* seem to have wanted *στεῤῥόν* [stiff/solid]. It varies in different ways in this word. Cf. Jacobs on Achilles Tatius p. 850 sq. Longinus in Eusebius, *P. E.* XV, p. 825 (Longinus, *Fragg.* VII. 3) opposes "*στερεὸν σῶμα*" [solid body], the human body, to the soul, which according to the Stoics' opinion is an "*ἀναθυμίασις*" [exhalation] of the solid body. Plato himself teaches what "*τὸ στερεὸν*" is for mathematicians in *Republic* VII, p. 528. a.; cf. also *Philebus* p. 51 and Stallbaum there, p. 161.

— **11. *φαίνεται ἔχοντα*** [appearing to have]] It ought to have been translated *it appears to have* [habere apparet], and conversely in what follows "*ἔχειν φαίνεται*" as *it seems to have* [habere videtur]. (See F. A. Wolf on Demosthenes' *Against Leptines* p. 259.) But in such matters it is a long task to undertake to amend Ficinus, otherwise the best interpreter of Plotinus. In the following, we have wiped away several manifest faults by the help of Philoponus and good manuscripts. The same interpreter [Ficinus] contributes very much to the understanding of this entire dispute, as is shown by what we have just set down. Moreover, Plotinus had before his eyes in this whole passage what Plato discusses in the *Timaeus* from p. 58 sqq. (Stephanus) p. 76 sqq. (Bekker).

**p. 188, 10. *Περὶ δὲ πυρὸς—διάστατον τριχῇ*** [Concerning fire... extended in three ways]] Plato in the *Timaeus* p. 56. B: "Let it be then, according to right reason and probability, that the solid form of the pyramid has become the element and seed of fire; and let us call the second according to birth that of air, and the third of water, etc. Cf. *Theolog. Arithmet.* p. 20 (p. 19 Ast): "that in the first tetrad is the smallest and most seed-like embodiment, if indeed fire is the most elementary of bodies and has the smallest parts, and the shape of this very thing as a body is the pyramid named after it, etc." Next, after **διάστατον τριχῇ** [extended in three ways] Ficinus read **ἢ φυσικὸν σῶμα (sc. ἐστὶ)** [or it is a physical body]; but he did not read **διά τι—φυσ. σῶμα;** [for what reason... a physical body?]. Of this variation there is no trace in our manuscripts. After the second *σῶμα* I placed a question mark, which is found correctly placed in the following after **διά τι**.

— **14. *τῷ χρυσῷ ὕδατι ὄντι*** [gold, being water]] Plato, *Tim.* p. 59 (p. 77 Bekker): "Of all these things which we have called 'fluid waters,' that which is formed from the finest and most uniform parts, the densest, a unique kind, colored with a glittering and yellow hue, the most precious possession, is gold, which has been strained through rock and solidified." Aristotle, *On Colors* III, p. 241 (Sylburg): "The gold-like color comes about when the yellow and the sun-like, being strongly condensed, glitters. Wherefore the necks of pigeons and the drops of water appear gold-like, the light being reflected." These points do not pertain more to Plato’s opinion on the nature of gold than those regarding "apyron" [unfired] gold found in Paeonia after rains in *Mirabil. Auscultt.* XLV, p. 87 (Beckmann). These words of Philo Judaeus in *Who is the Heir of Divine Things* p. 503 (Mangey) come somewhat closer to Plato’s words: "Those who praise gold say many other things in its praise, but two are supreme. One, that it does not admit rust; another, that it can be beaten and poured into the thinnest membranes while remaining unbroken. It has thus reasonably become a symbol of a greater nature, which, being stretched and poured and reaching everywhere, is full of all things throughout, having woven the rest together harmoniously." Other sayings of the ancients regarding gold as the most beautiful of all things, and likewise regarding the sincerity of the human soul declared through the likeness of gold, we have displayed on the book *On Beauty* p. 54 F. G., especially in the special Heidelberg edition p. 267 sqq.

— **17. *καὶ ζῶα—πυρινὰ—δαιμόνων*** [and fiery animals... of daimons]] Concerning the bodies

### PAGE 96 ###

**BOOK I [II]. SECOND ENNEAD. p. 186—190. 89**

of Daimons, many have said many things, especially among the Alexandrian philosophers who came after Plotinus. Some spoke hesitantly, as of a difficult matter, like Iamblichus and others. See Iamblichus, *On the Mysteries of the Egyptians* V. 10, p. 125; V. 11, p. 127; and Gale in the notes, p. 267. Cf. Proclus on *Alcibiades* (beg.) p. 83 sq.; Olympiodorus on the same, p. 15 sqq. To Plato, or certainly to the author of the *Epinomis* (p. 984), daimons are called an "*ἀέριον γένος*" [airy kind]; from which passage, as a primary source, many have benefited. Apuleius calls daimons *Animalia corpore aërea* [animals of airy body] in *On the God of Socrates* p. 108. Similarly Porphyry, *On Abstinence* II. 39 and 42, p. 172 and 182 (Rhoer), whom you should consult. Psellus, however, in *On the Operation of Daimons*, wishes a "cognate light" (*σύμφυον φῶς*) to be attributed to Daimons (p. 49, Kiel ed.).

**p. 188, 17. *ἀλλὰ κινήσωμεν—ἔχειν*** [but let us move... to have]] This is of Plotinian brevity. Understand *λέγοντες* [saying]. But such things are met on almost every page in these Enneads: and it would be tedious to repeat it too often, especially since Ficinus is accustomed to consult understanding with a not inconvenient paraphrase.

**p. 189, 2. *συμπεριάγειν—γεηρὰ σώματα*** [to carry around with them... earthly bodies]] Epicurus taught identical things, as is clear from his fragments of the books *On Nature*, observed also by the editor Rosini in *Volumm. Herculanens.* Vol. I, p. 62. To which also pertain those things in Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I. 18, concerning the Gods: "Yet that species is not a body, but as if a body, etc." And: "Epicurus teaches that such is the power and nature of the Gods, that first it is perceived not by sense, but by mind; not by some solidity nor by number, like those things which he calls *στερέμνια* [solid/compact] on account of their firmness, but by images perceived by similarity and transition."

— **5. *Πλάτωνος λέγοντος*** [Plato saying]] In the *Timaeus* p. 31, p. 43, p. 51 sq.

— **6. *τὸ ἀντίτυπον*** [the counter-type/resistance]] Plotinus uses this frequently with various meanings, also concerning souls; likewise the substantive *ἀντιτυπία* [resistance]. See II. 6. 2; II. 9. 6; III. 6. 6; IV. 4. 29; V. 8. 4; VI. 1. 26; VI. 1. 28, where there is another form *ἀντιτυπές*. VI. 7. 29; VI. 8. 7. In this place the word comes closer to the meaning of "*τοῦ σκληροῦ*" [of the hard]. See Ruhnken on Timaeus p. 157; Wyttenbach on Plutarch’s *On Superstition* p. 999; and what I have placed in *Commentt. Herodott.* p. 299. Proclus on Plato’s *Alcibiades* (beg.) 55, p. 154: "that passions are of a hard and resisting nature, since they are material and earthly, all of them so to speak, but especially the spirited ones." I have placed other things below on the word *ἀντιτυπίας* p. 180. G. Cf. also Hermann and Erfurdt on Sophocles’ *Antigone* 134; and Schleusner’s *Lex N. T.* under the word, who correctly vindicated the meaning of "likeness" in many places. Regarding the word *ἐπιβάθρα* [stepping-stone/ladder] it was discussed above on I. 6. 1, particularly in the special edition p. 143. In this place it is the foundation.

**p. 190, 4. *Μαρτυρεῖ δὲ καὶ αὐτὸς τούτοις*** [He himself also bears witness to these things]] Plato in the *Timaeus* p. 39: "God kindled a light in the second of the orbits relative to the earth, which we have now called the sun, etc."

— **8. *τὸ φῶς—ἕτερον φλογὸς εἶναι*** [that light is different from flame]] Cf. above ch. 4 and the annotations there to p. 99. A., and consult Plato’s discussions on the sun, light, and truth in Book VI of the *Republic* p. 507 sq.

— **9. *τοῦτο δὲ τὸ φῶς σῶμα εἶναι κ. τ. λ.*** [that this light is a body, etc.]] The Emperor Julian explains this opinion with more words in *Oration* IV, p. 133 sq. He speaks of a triple sun: "But this third visible disk (of the sun) is clearly the cause of salvation for sensible things. And just as much as we said the great sun is to the intellectual gods, so much is this visible one to the manifest gods. Come now, is not light itself an incorporeal and divine form of things transparent in activity? — and of light itself being incorporeal, the rays would be a certain peak and as it were a flower. Now the opinion of the wise and knowledgeable Phoenicians said that the radiance proceeding everywhere was an undefiled activity of pure intellect itself. Nor is the account discordant. If anyone should suppose that light itself is incorporeal, even if its source is not a body, etc." (Regarding the Phoenicians' Ether and the Intelligible God, cf. Damascius *On First Principles* p. 385, Kopp ed.). Moreover, Marsilio Ficino undertook to illustrate those tenets about *incorporeal light* both in his commentary on this book of Plotinus (p. 87 sq. and p. 93) and on the seventh book of Plato’s *Republic* (p. 690, Frankfurt ed.) and on the *Symposium* (p. 1151 sq.). Because our author immediately uses "*ἄνθος*" [flower] for light, we saw Julian use the same word in the words just cited. I have noted more on this usage at Plotinus, *On Beauty* p. 54. A (in the special edition p. 233) and on Olympiodorus, on *Alcibiades* (beg.) p. 109, at the words: "*διὸ καὶ ἀφρὸς καὶ ἄνθος τοῦ εἴδους ἐστὶ τὸ κάλλος*" [wherefore beauty is the foam and flower of the form]. Proclus on the same, p. 247: "*ἄνθος τῆς οὐσίας ἡμῶν*" [the flower of our essence]. The same, ibid. p. 240: "*ἄνθος τοῦ νοῦ*" [the flower of the intellect].

— **12. *καὶ στιλπνότητα,—τὸ ὄντως λευκόν*** [and brightness—the truly white]] These things remind one of those Ennian words in Cicero’s *On the Nature of the Gods* II.

2. 25. III. 4: "sublimely glowing." Ez. Spanheim collected others in *Remarques sur les Césars de Julien* p. 16, who also praised this Plotinian passage. Cf. furthermore below p. 711. c. 18. A.

**p. 190, 13. *ὃ δὴ εἶναι—λευκὸν σῶμα*** [which indeed is... a white body]] Ezechiel Spanheim (loc. cit. p. 16) compared these with Julian’s words in the *Caesars*, "brighter than silver, whiter than gold," taking it for *splendid (brilliant)* yet not referring to the Plotinian text accurately enough.

— **18. *φλόγα—ἀνελθοῦσαν—μετὰ γῆς ῥίπτεσθαι κάτω*** [flame... having ascended... to be thrown down with earth]] Ficinus understands this as lightning. Regarding the causes of which the ancients disputed, read in Aristotle (attributed), *On the World* II. 10, IV. 3, IV. 17; Io. Laur. Lydus, *On the Months* III. 15, p. 53 sq. (Schow); the same *On Omens* p. 86, 164, 174 (Hase).

**p. 191, 3. *κάτω δὲ τῆς σελήνης ἵστασθαι—ἀέρα*** [and air to stand below the moon]] The same Marsilio [Ficino] refers this to comets. Compare Aristotle, *Meteorology* I. 7; Seneca, *Natural Questions* I. 15; and those many whom Kapp praised on Aristotle’s *De Mundo* II. 9, p. 42 sqq.; IV. 22, p. 141 sq. Add Io. Laur. Lydus, *On the Months* II. 13, p. 51; and the same *On Omens* p. 36, and Hase’s *Annott.* p. 299.

— **4. *φλόγα—ζέσω*** [flame... boiling]] Cf. Annot. above to ch. 4, p. 99. A. Moreover, cf. Plutarch, *On the Face in the Orb of the Moon* p. 923. E, p. 738 (Wyttenbach): "the whole upper region, even if it receives something earthly thrown up by force, immediately squeezes it out hither, or rather lets it go falling down by its own proper weight."

— **7. *Τὸ δὲ φῶς ἐκεῖ—ἐν λόγοις τοῖς ἄστροις*** [The light there... in the reasons/words which are the stars]] I fear Ficinus did not translate these things accurately. Plotinus seems to mean that the **stars** themselves are **λόγοι** [reasons/words], as if you said thoughts and thus uttered words: namely, that the primary celestial light is like the *λόγος ἐνδιάθετος* [internal reason], the reason hidden within, while the stars are the *λόγοι προφορικοί* [expressed reasons], i.e., reasons and thoughts brought forth in speech; and that the primary light, being one in itself, becomes varied through the varieties of the stars, just as one speech becomes varied through the variety of men. Certainly, no one more learned is ignorant that such an opinion is not far from the mind of the Alexandrian Philosophers and Plotinus himself, as the following books of Plotinus argue. Accordingly, I would translate: "**But the light which is there is partly variegated in the stars, as if in utterances.**"

— **16. *πᾶν δὲ σῶμα μετὰ ψυχῆς—τοιούτου δὲ τὸ ἐκεῖ*** [every body with soul... such is the one there]] Pseudo-Plato in the *Epinomis* p. 983 (p. 358 Bekker): "It is not possible for the earth and heaven and all the stars and the masses of all these to proceed thus with precision through the year without a soul being present at each or in each, etc." In what follows, you might say Ficinus read "*πῦρ δὲ οὐδ’ ἂν ἐναρμόσειε*" [and fire would not fit]. But the codices do not vary, and the place can be cleared if you think of *τὶ* [something] with the word "*πυρός*" [fire]. However, I do not wish to pronounce on the passage, as the variation of the books in the next part indicates it is undoubtedly corrupt. For the rest, *ποιεῖν* [to make] differs from *δρᾷν* [to do] as it does from *πράττειν* [to act].

**p. 192, 1. *ῥύμη*** [impetus/momentum]] From the margin we have restored this in place of *ῥώμη* [strength], which had succeeded into its place. Regarding this confusion, Lobeck recently warned with examples added in *On Phrynichus’ Eclogues* p. 404; Jacobs in *Additamm. Animadvv. in Athenaeum* p. 209; the same on Achilles Tatius p. 426 and on Philostratus’ *Images* p. 650 and 655; and Bähr on Plutarch’s *Philopoemen* p. 44 and on *Pyrrhus* p. 216; Tittmann on Zonaras’ *Lex.* p. 774, note 72. Among the Attics, it is the same as *ὁρμή* [impulse]. Phrynichus (loc. cit.), Suidas, and Zonaras (under the word); and when it designates *impetus of rotation*, it is interchanged with *δίνη* [whirl], as in Plutarch’s *De S. N. V.*, observed by Wyttenbach, p. 120. It is used, however, of the motion of elements and worldly bodies, and of the stars, and thence also of others, and is translated also to other things. Pseudo-Plato in the *Epinomis* p. 983 (p. 358 Bekker) concerning the bodies of the world, stars, etc.: "if anyone shall speak of certain *ῥύμας* [impulses] of bodies, or natures, or something of that sort, he will say nothing clear." Plutarch, *On the Face in the Orb of the Moon* p. 922. C, p. 733 (Wyttenbach): "the *ῥύμη* [momentum] kindles even the air in stones and that in cold lead, much more so that which is whirled in fire with such speed." The same, ibid. p. 924. A, concerning heavy masses falling downward—"but you, being carried down by the *ῥύμη*, might overpass the center, then turn back again and be bent back by them." But that whole discussion should be compared with Plotinus’ passage. Aristotle in Stobaeus, *Eclogg. Physs.* I. 33, p. 624 (Heeren): "and the winds from the clouds, when being carried all at once and densely into themselves, it dissolves more of the cloud by the vehemence of the *ῥύμη*." Io. Chrysostom, *Homily* II, p. 84 (Matthaei ed.): "just as a sudden *ῥύμη* [blast] of wind falling upon it drives away the troublesome dust," where the editor supplies more passages from the same sacred orator. The same, ibid. p. 118, used metaphorically

### PAGE 98 ###

**BOOK II. SECOND ENNEAD. p. 190—199. 91**

of the force of the Christian religion which no one can resist: "nor will he be able to bear its unspeakable *ῥύμην* [force]."

**p. 192, 7. *κατὰ φύσιν ἡ περιφορά—ἡ κατὰ φύσιν —φορά*** [rotation according to nature... the according to nature motion]] Consult Ez. Spanheim on these, *Epreuves de Remarques sur les Césars de Julien* p. 15, where he teaches that the word *περιφορᾶς* [rotation/circuit] is used by Plotinus with a double power: both for the circular motion of the stars and of the heaven itself, and for the globe of the sun, moon, and other stars.

— **10. *Οὐ τοίνυν οὐδὲ τροφῆς δεῖσθαι φατέον τὰ ἐκεῖ*** [One must not say, then, that those things there need nourishment]] He contradicts Heraclitus and the Stoics, who had contended that the stars and the moon were nourished either by the exhalations of the earth or by waters and the sea. Stobaeus I. 25, p. 510 (Heeren) on Heraclitus’ opinion: "that the stars are nourished from the exhalation from the earth." Ibid. p. 556 (I. 27) from Chrysippus’ doctrine: "wherefore also the moon is nourished by these fresh waters." Plutarch’s *Symposiacc.* VIII, p. 728: "for the gods are not nourished from it (the sea) as the Stoics suppose the stars to be." Cf. Diogenes Laërtius VII. 145, and Menage there, and Baguet’s commentary on Chrysippus §. LXXX. p. 177. [Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II. 15, p. 265 sq. coll. p. 747.]

— **13. *συγκρίματα*** [concretions/complexes]] Properly *concretiones*, whence also "concrete bodies." A word frequented by physicians: cf. Stephanus’ *Thesaurus* p. 5348 (Valpy). Add Plutarch IX, p. 499 (Reiske) and Vol. X, p. 592 (below). Plotinus clearly V. 9. 3, p. 557. B, after he has explained things composed by art, proceeds thus: "and indeed even those things which have been composed by nature, their many-compounded things called *συγκρίματα*, you dissolve into the form which is over all the things compounded, as man into soul and body, and the body into the four [elements]."

**ib. *τὴν τε μεταβολὴν τῶν τῇδε σωμάτων ἀφ’ ἑαυτῶν μεταβάλλειν*** [and that the change of the bodies here changes from themselves]] I repeat *φατέον* [it must be said] from the preceding, and thus translate: *And it must be said that the change of the bodies which are here (on earth) happens from themselves (i.e., from their own nature).*

#### BOOK II. [II. 2]

**P. 199, 7. *ΠΕΡΙ ΚΙΝΗΣΕΩΣ ΟΥΡΑΝΟΥ* [ON THE MOVEMENT OF THE HEAVEN]**] This is the second of all Plotinus' books according to the time of writing, inscribed elsewhere *περὶ κυκλοφορίας* [On Circular Motion]. See Porphyry, *Life of Plotinus* ch. 24, p. 141 (Fabricius). The argument arose for our philosopher primarily from the Platonic *Timaeus*, especially what is read in p. 34 sq. (Bekker): "for he assigned to it the motion proper to its body, which of the seven [motions] is most of all concerned with intellect and wisdom. Wherefore, leading it around in the same way, in the same place and within itself, he made it move turning in a circle, and he took away from it all the six motions and made it unerring from them, etc." Furthermore, cf. also *Epinomis* p. 982 sq. (p. 356 sqq. Bekker). In explaining that passage of the *Timaeus*, the Platonic philosophers especially labored in competition. Proclus in particular examined the diverse opinions of the ancients concerning the movement of heaven at length (p. 167 sqq.). Aristotle’s tenets on this matter, which Proclus and others touch upon, are read in the books *De Cælo* II. 2, IV. 1; in *Meteorology* I. 2; and also in the booklet circulated among Aristotle's works, *De Mundo* II. 3, where Kapp has set down some things regarding this matter (p. 25 sqq.). Others have partly reported and partly adorned Plato’s opinions on the motion of heaven. See Alcinous, *On the Doctrine of Plato* ch. XIV, p. 488 sqq. (Dan. Heinsius ed.), where among others these words are read (p. 490): "for the motion of the heaven encompassing all things, being unerring, is one and ordered. However, that of the things outside is varied, and different in its risings and settings; wherefore it is called 'wandering' [planet], etc." Chalcidius in Plato’s *Timaeus* p. 213 (Meursius) [p. 322 I. A. Fabricius ed. at the end of the works of S. Hippolytus]: "Where however the use of moving was seen to be necessary, he [Plato says God] gave the world two principal ones out of all motions: one by accident, by which he snatches the fixed stars [aplanes] toward the west, which motion he now calls 'going before'; the other indeed principal, which is the circumaction, and it turns about itself, similar to the motion of the deliberative soul, the other five ceasing. For the locular motions are seven, I believe; two indeed along the length, i.e., before and after; two others likewise through the breadth, to the right and to the left; and two others along the depth, upward and downward, and the last similar to the above-mentioned circumaction, which flies around a fixed hinge. Since then out of those seven motions he gave the stars the use of only two... he rightly said the other five motions were vacant. Then he concludes by mentioning that he has discussed the motions of the wandering stars."

### PAGE 99 ###

**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

"And the heaven indeed is thus adorned, with wise and eternal animals as its inhabitants." Cf. also Apuleius, *On the Doctrine of Plato* p. 578 sqq. (p. 198 sqq. Bosscha). The same, *On the World* p. 707 (p. 289 sqq. Bosscha). Just as in ancient times they used to call Heraclitus and his followers *τοὺς ῥέοντας* [the flowing ones], because they contended that all things flow and change continually; so they used to call those who thought the universe was moved *τοὺς τὸ πᾶν κινοῦντας* [those who move the all]; from whom were distinguished those who said it was immobile, *οἱ τοῦ ὅλου στασιῶται* [the partisans of the stillness of the whole]. (Plato, *Theaetetus* p. 180 sq., p. 256 sqq. Bekker; cf. regarding these tenets Brandis’ *Commentt. Eleatt.* I, p. 142 and Plotinus himself, p. 489 sq.). Plato himself posited two kinds of motion, calling one *ἀλλοίωσιν* [alteration] and the other *περιφοράν* [rotation]. *Theaetetus* (loc. cit.) where Heindorf preferred *φορὰν* [motion/carrying] with the support of Baguet (*On Chrysippus* p. 179). Nevertheless, Bekker did not change it, nor does the Darmstadt Codex support it, nor any other, and it appears Proclus (whose words the next annotation will display) read *περιφοράν*. The same variation appears in a clear passage of Philo Judaeus, where he treats the double motion of fixed and wandering stars, in *On the Cherubim* p. 12 (Vol. II, Pfeiffer): "Perhaps then he introduces the *περιφορὰν* [rotation] of the whole heaven through under-meanings?" (others [read] *φορὰὶ*, Codex A *φορὰν*); but the whole passage should be compared with Plato and Plotinus. Aristotle lists three: "according to place, according to quality, according to quantity (*φορὰ, ἀλλοίωσις, αὔξησις καὶ φθίσις* [locomotion, alteration, growth and decay])." Aristotle, *Physics* VII. 2; cf. Heindorf on Plato’s *Theaetetus* (loc. cit.) p. 421. Sextus Empiricus, *Against the Mathematicians* X. 52, and Fabricius there, p. 142. The Stoics labored more than the rest in defining motion and examined subtly every point said to the contrary; yet they did not sufficiently take care to avoid falling often into the errors of the Epicureans whom they were attacking. See Plutarch’s excerpts from the books of Chrysippus *On Motion* in the writing *On Stoic Self-Contradictions* p. 1053 sq.; Stobaeus, *Eclogues* I, p. 404 (Heeren); and cf. Bake’s *Animadvv.* on Cleomedes’ *Meteora* I. 1, p. 275 sq. and Baguet, *On Chrysippus* §. LXXXI, p. 178—180. Regarding the motion of the heaven and the world, what Platonists, Peripatetics, and other philosophers had established, the same Cleomedes (I. 3) touched upon, where Balforeus and Bake (whom I just cited) p. 297 sqq. should be consulted. No less did Nicephorus Blemmida include the sum of the doctrine of Plato, Aristotle, and other physicists *On Motion* in his little work. See e.g. p. 13, 39, 43, especially ch. 24, p. 179 (Wegelin ed., Augsburg, 1605). The same (ibid. p. 183) even makes mention of our Plotinus: — "for the straight-line motion of the elements belongs to them while they are still coming to be and when they are in a place contrary to nature, but have not yet taken the one according to nature, as Ptolemy, Plotinus, Xenarchus, and certain others of the physicists agree." If you ask where Nicephorus took this doctrine, consult the most learned interpreter of Aristotle on the book *On the Heaven* fol. 5 verso (Aldine ed.): "It must be known that Ptolemy in his book *On the Elements* and in the *Optics*, and the great Plotinus, and Xenarchus in his difficulties against the fifth essence, supposed the straight-line motions of the elements to occur while they are still coming to be and are in a place contrary to nature, and not yet in the one according to nature; and Aristotle seems to have thought this as well, etc." (For I cannot provide the whole excellent discussion excerpted here) and a few words later: "but as the aforementioned men Ptolemy, Xenarchus, and Plotinus say, being according to nature and existing in their own places, the elements either remain or move in a circle. The earth obviously remains, as does the water and the stabilized part of the air; but fire and the easily-moved part of the air move in a circle, being carried around with the heaven, insofar as it is fitting for them." The same opinion was touched upon several times by Proclus in *Tim.*, as on p. 142 and 274, where he likewise appeals to the authority of Ptolemy and Plotinus. Cf. Plotinus below p. 328. B. C. Xenarchus, whom Simplicius cites quite often, is that Cilician, and thus a fellow citizen of Simplicius, a teacher of Strabo, who had become famous among the Peripatetics in the age of Augustus both for his excellence of doctrine and the favor of that Prince. See Strabo XIV, p. 670 (Casaubon) p. 683—685 (Tzschucke). Alexander of Aphrodisias praises the same in Aristotle’s *On the Soul*, fol. 154 sqq. Simplicius returns to the argument of Plotinus’ book in the same place, fol. 9 verso, — "Even if Ptolemy and Plotinus and Proclus, and even Aristotle himself, say that the fuel [sub-lunar fire] is moved, not with this motion as its own, because of its rising together with the outermost sphere, but nevertheless it is naturally inclined toward it, so that it is not dragged by force but moved with the other, just as the planets are moved with the fixed sphere; for this motion is not its own; nor indeed is it violent, but above nature." And from Sim-

### PAGE 100 ###

**BOOK II. SECOND ENNEAD. p. 199. 93**

plicius alone it is understood by how many and how various disputes this place *On the Motion of the Heaven* was treated by various schools of philosophers. In the conclusion of this Introduction, I will append a passage from Macrobius’ *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio* I. 17, where he exhibits a part of the Plotinian diatribe in his own words: — "The nature and power and reason of the world-soul teaches that the heaven turns, whose eternity is in motion; because motion never leaves what life does not desert: nor does life depart from that in which always-agitated vigor thrives. Therefore also the celestial body, which the soul of the world fabricated for itself as a sharer of immortality, lest it ever fail in living, is always in motion and knows not how to stand; because the soul by which it is impelled does not itself stand. For since the essence of the soul, which is incorporeal, is in motion; and the soul fabricated the body of the heaven first of all: without doubt the nature of motion migrated from incorporeal things into this first body. Whose power, whole and incorrupt, does not desert what it first began to move. Therefore, the motion of the heaven is necessarily revolving; because since it is necessary for it always to move, and there is no place beyond it to which it might tend to go further, it is agitated by the continuation of a perpetual return into itself. Therefore, it runs in that in which it can or must, and its going forward is to be revolved: because the one course of a sphere encompassing all spaces and places is to rotate. But thus it seems to follow the soul always, which runs throughout the universality itself. We shall say, therefore, that it finds the soul, if it follows it always; indeed, it always finds it, because it is everywhere whole, everywhere perfect. Why then, if it finds what it seeks, does it not rest? Because that soul also is unacquainted with rest. For it [the heaven] would stand if it found the soul standing anywhere. But since that soul, by the appetite for which it is drawn, always pours itself into the universe, the body also always turns itself back into it and through it. These few things out of many found with *Plotinus* as the author regarding the secret of celestial revolution may suffice."

**p. 199, 9. *Διὰ τί κύκλῳ κινεῖται; ὅτι νοῦν μιμεῖται*** [Why does it move in a circle? Because it imitates Intellect]] Sc. *ὁ οὐρανός* [the heaven], from the title of the book. The source of the sentiment is in the passage of the Platonic *Timaeus* cited in the next note. Many have touched upon the same. Apuleius, *On the Doctrine of Plato* p. 198 (Bosscha): — "this one thing was left to the world as proper to its wisdom and prudence, *that it should be revolved rationally*." Chalcidius in the *Timaeus* p. 213: "the other indeed (motion) principal, which is the circumaction, and it turns about itself similar to the motion of the deliberative soul." Sallust the philosopher almost expressed Plotinus word-for-word in *On the Gods and the World*, ch. VIII, p. 24 (Io. Conr. Orell ed.): "*τῶν δὲ ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ σωμάτων τὰ μὲν νοῦν μιμεῖται καὶ κύκλῳ κινεῖται, τὰ δὲ ψυχὴν, καὶ ἐπ’ εὐθείας, πῦρ μὲν καὶ ἀὴρ ἄνω, γῆ δὲ καὶ ὕδωρ κάτω. τῶν δὲ κύκλῳ, ἡ μὲν ἀπλανὴς ἀπ’ ἀνατολῆς, αἱ δὲ ἑπτὰ ἐκ δύσεως φέρονται*" [Of the bodies in the world, some imitate Intellect and move in a circle, others Soul and in a straight line: fire and air upward, earth and water downward. Of those in a circle, the fixed sphere moves from the east, the seven from the west]. Clearly Proclus in *Theology of Plato* XIII, p. 35 (below): "Add also, if you wish, the presence of the intellectual radiance into the body; for from where is this whole heaven either spherical, or carried in a circle and recirculated about the same according to one fixed order? For how did it always obtain the same form and power immutably according to nature, if it did not participate in the formation according to intellect? For soul is the provider of motion, but the cause of the stable state—which leads back the unsettled variation of moved things into identity, and the life which is finite according to one reason and the rotation which holds itself likewise—is clearly beyond soul." The same V. 36, p. 324. — "for because of this the heaven is said to dance eternally... for because they move in a circle, they represent the intellect and the intellectual rotation." No one fails to recognize the Pythagorean source of these dogmas. It will suffice to have touched upon one passage. Hippodamus the Pythagorean in Gale’s *Opuscc. Mythol.* p. 664: "*ἔστι γὰρ ἁ μὲν ἁρμονία ἀρετὰ κόσμῳ*" [for harmony is the virtue of the world]. I have set down more on Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* III. 11, p. 531. Proclus, however, to return there, explained these things elsewhere, as in the *Timaeus* p. 167 sqq. and in *Inst. Theol.* ch. 33 and 34, p. 58—60 (our ed.). Ioannes Philoponus, who disputed against Proclus in *On the Eternity of the World* XIII. 2, writes thus: "Plato also wishes the heaven to be ensouled and moved by soul. It is clear then that as a living thing he defines for it circular motion according to nature. For if he says circular motion is especially about intellect, and as Plotinus says, 'it moves in a circle because it imitates intellect,' it is clear he wishes circular motion to come to it from the soul, moving its own body into an imitation of intellectual activity." The same in Aristotle’s *Meteorology* p. 78. b.: "Why it moves in a circle, Plotinus says, is because it imitates intellect. For as the divine and demiurgic intellect, turning back into itself, contemplates all things and itself in those things, so he says this [perhaps 'this' should be deleted] celestial thing [turns] into itself the...
