-> BOOK II. ENNEAD TWO. pages 178—181. 85 <-

The force which is present in the sentence <note>original: "μήποτε τοῦτο—ἀξιώσοι γίγνεσθαι"</note> *lest he should ever think this... to happen* (for I change nothing) is clearly expressed. Regarding the power of this particle, consult Hoogeveen on *Particles* p. 391, second edition by Schutz, especially p. 394 and following. Next, **there is no need** to laboriously demonstrate that **according to the form** <note>original: "κατὰ τὸ εἶδος"</note>, meaning according to the *species*, and **according to this** <note>original: "κατὰ τόδε"</note>, meaning according to *individual things*, or as is commonly said, according to *individuals*, are set in opposition to one another.

**p. 179, 4. But if by having embraced all things (the world)—it will be made**] These words are connected with the decree that *the world is unique*; which some attribute to Heraclitus, as in Diogenes Laërtius IX. 8: <note>original: "πεπεράσθαι τε τὸ πᾶν καὶ ἕνα εἶναι κόσμον"</note> *that the universe is finite and that the world is one*. Plato certainly pronounces this clearly in the *Timaeus* p. 31 and in several other places. No less does Aristotle in *On the Heavens* I. 8. 9. These decrees are discussed at length in Philo’s *On the Incorruptibility of the World* Vol. II p. 488 and following, edited by Mangey; Plutarch’s *On the Obsolescence of Oracles* p. 422 and following, p. 725 in Wyttenbach; see also Plutarch’s *On the 'E' at Delphi* p. 389 F. and Wyttenbach’s notes on it p. 285 in *Observations* Vol. III, and the further material I have collected on this matter regarding Cicero’s *On the Nature of the Gods* II. 46. p. 401.

**p. 180, 14. the heaven indeed—to have eternity**] Proclus in his commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus* p. 166: “*The celestial things therefore remain unchangeable, just as the ancients Proclus of Mallus and Philonides have said, and of the more recent, all the Platonists following Plotinus.*” That ancient Proclus is the Cilician Stoic philosopher. See Fabricius, *Greek Library* Vol. III p. 574 and following, edited by Harles, and Vol. IX p. 365 and following. Compare another passage of the same Proclus the Lycian in his commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus* p. 73, where he touches upon these Plotinian matters again.—The next part is praised by John Philoponus in *Against Proclus on the Eternity of the World* XIII. 15; Immanuel Bekker also inserted this passage without the author's name from the Royal Parisian Codex of Plato 1832 among the *Scholia on the Timaeus* p. 439 and following. It holds as follows: <note>original: "ποῦ δὲ καὶ τὸν πολὺν Πλωτῖνον θήσομεν..."</note> *Where shall we place the great Plotinus, who, if anyone else claimed to belong to the sect of Plato, did not himself accept the 'fifth body' introduced into the universe by Aristotle, from which that man composed the celestial things; but speaking in harmony with the opinion of Plato, he himself composes the celestial body from the four elements, and declares this to be the opinion of Plato. At any rate, he says in his discourse On the World: 'And yet, while the nature of the body is always flowing, it must...'* There follows the passage of Plotinus up to the words **and even more, how the sun**. The next part concerning Aristotle is also praised by Simplicius in his commentary on Aristotle’s *On the Heavens*, and indeed in three places: p. 3b, p. 5b, and p. 26 of the Venetian Aldine edition. And in the first place thus: *Plotinus also mentions these hypotheses in his work On the World. For wishing to show the eternity of the heaven according to Plato, he says: 'For Aristotle there would be no labor,' etc.* In the second place he begins thus: *Both the great Plotinus and Xenarchus in their doubts regarding the fifth essence, etc.* Apuleius in *On the World* p. 708, p. 291 edited by Bosscha, says of the Heaven: “An element, not one of the four which are known to all, but something far different, *fifth* in number, first in order, divine and inviolable in kind.”

**p. 181, 2. the nature of the body always flowing, etc.**] Regarding the first sentiment, the most famous decree is that of Heraclitus: <note>original: "ὅτι πάντα χωρεῖ καὶ οὐδὲν μένει"</note> **that all things move and nothing remains—as you could not step twice into the same river**. These are the words of Plato in the *Cratylus* p. 402a. Aristotle (or the author of the work attributed to him, *On the World*) expresses the same tenet thus: *all things flow like rivers* IV. 25. On this matter see what Wyttenbach collected on Plutarch’s *On the Late Vengeance of the Deity* p. 76 and following, and on Plutarch’s *On Having Many Friends* in his *Observations* p. 660 and following, as well as in his *Observations on the Consolation to Apollonius* p. 721 and following, and p. 791 and following, and what I myself have gathered on this matter in *Dionysius* p. 79 and following. That second point is more remarkable, but it has Plato himself, Aristotle, and other very weighty authors as sources. For Plato in *The Republic* VI. p. 498b: *toward old age, except for some few, they are extinguished much more than the Heraclitean sun, insofar as they are not rekindled again.* And more explicitly Aristotle in *Meteorology* II. 2. p. 39: *it is clear that the sun is not only, as Heraclitus says, new every day, but is always continuously new.* Which Alexander of Aphrodisias in his commentary on the *Meteorology* fol. 93a explains: *each day another sun is kindled while the first is extinguished at its setting*, that is, so that every single day a new sun is lit, the previous one having died out at sunset. Others have understood it differently. Plutarch preserved for us a certain decree of Heraclitus himself concerning the sun in *On Exile* p. 604A: *For the sun will not overstep his measures; says Heraclitus; otherwise, the Furies, the helpers of Justice, will find him out.* Likewise in *On Isis and Osiris* p. 370D, on which passage see Wyttenbach in *Observations* p. 238; cf. Diogenes Laërtius IX. 1, Proclus on Plato’s *Timaeus* p. 334, and Stobaeus’s *Anthology* I. 26.

p. 524. and following. Heeren. where a double opinion is attributed to Hecataeus, whom they used to say was a pupil of Heraclitus. Schleiermacher has explained these Heraclitean doctrines at length in Wolf and Buttmann’s *Museum of Antiquity*, p. 392—399. See also Baguet on Chrysippus <note>A Stoic philosopher</note> p. 176 and following.

**181, 7. To Aristotle—the hypotheses of the fifth—body**] <note>original: "Ἀριστοτέλει—τὰς ὑποθέσεις τοῦ πέμπτου—σώματος"</note> To be sure, Aristotle—contrary to what other philosophers and, according to Plotinus, Plato himself had done—did not want the body of the heavens to be composed of the four remaining elements, but had attributed to it a certain fifth body, unique and more excellent than the others <note>The "quintessence" or aether</note>. Furthermore, he attributed perpetual motion to the Heaven. For he says in *On the Heavens* II. 3. p. 40. Sylburg edition: "*Each thing exists for the sake of its work, for those things which have a work. The activity of a god is immortality; and this is eternal life. Therefore, it is necessary for a divine being to have eternal motion. Since the heaven is such a thing—for it is a certain divine body—for this reason it possesses the circular body, which by nature moves in a circle forever.*" <note>original Greek: "ἕκαστόν ἐστιν... κινεῖται κύκλῳ ἀεί"</note> And just as in this passage he calls the body of the heaven divine, so in another place in *On the Heavens* I. 3. he calls the same body *unaging and unalterable and impassive* and *the first of bodies*. <note>original: "ἀγήρατον καὶ ἀναλλοίωτον καὶ ἀπαθὲς" and "τὸ πρῶτον τῶν σωμάτων"</note> The ancient interpreters of Aristotle, whose testimonies we have cited above, themselves establish that Plotinus touched upon these passages.

— **16. for the constitution of a living being**] <note>original: "πρὸς ζώου σύστασιν"</note> The Edition, along with two written manuscripts, has *standing/position* <note>original: "στάσιν"</note>. And indeed *stasis* is sometimes used transitively, so that in this place it can mean "constitution." See just now Stephanus's *Thesaurus* p. 4543 and following, London edition. Regarding other meanings collected there, add to them Upton and Schweighäuser on Epictetus III. p. 443; Wyttenbach on Eunapius 302; Proclus in *On the Alcibiades* p. 273. above in our edition. We encounter the same exchange of both words above in I. 8. 8. p. 77. F. But nevertheless, just as we retained *constitution* <note>original: "σύστασις"</note> in the context there, so in this place, with our many manuscripts commanding it, we judged that *constitution* <note>original: "σύστασιν"</note> should be introduced. Marsilio <note>Marsilio Ficino, the Renaissance translator of Plotinus</note> did well: "*for the purpose of constituting the animal*"; there was no reason for him to add "itself."

**p. 182, 2. but suitable—it is fitting**] <note>original: "ἀλλὰ πρόσφορον—προσήκει"</note> Wyttenbach on Plato’s *Phaedo* p. 232: "i.e., it is necessary that the matter also be adapted to the will of the effect; indeed the meaning is, *toward the completion of the will: πρὸς τὸ τοῦ βουλήματος ἀποτέλεσμα*." Similarly in Plato he takes *the nature of the weakness* for *the weakness of nature* (cf. the same author in *Philomathia* III. p. 98.) and brings forward several examples of the same exchange of the Genitive case with the governing case, praising also Markland on Maximus Tyrius XVIII. 1. p. 566, who shows others, including this from Plutarch vol. II. p. 500. B: *the mortal kinds of animals* for *the kinds of mortal animals*. <note>original: "τὰ θνητὰ τῶν ζώων γένη" for "τὰ τῶν θνητῶν ζώων γένη"</note> Moreover, the writers of the New Testament, by a similar grammatical shift, say sometimes *in fire of flame*, and other times *in flame of fire*, as Valckenaer teaches in his *Scholia on the Acts of the Apostles* VII. 30. p. 426.

— **9. nature of water**] <note>original: "ὕδατος φύσις"</note> Regarding this formula see Wyttenbach on the *Phaedo* p. 233. and our notes on Plotinus *On Beauty* above p. 50. C. in the special edition p. 139 and following.

— **14. but fire, sharp and fast—to seek a state in both**] <note>original: "πῦρ δὲ, ὀξὺ μὲν καὶ ταχὺ—στάσιν ἐπ’ ἄμφω ζητεῖν"</note> He who has not inspected the books might easily persuade himself that Marsilio had a fuller version of this passage before his eyes. But the extra things he has are to be attributed to Paraphrase, which he strives for six hundred times for the sake of clarity. You might say, however, that he read *and earth by not being in another* and then *to seek extension in both*. <note>original: "καὶ γῆ τῇ μὴ ἐν ἄλλῳ" and "ἔκτασιν ἐπ’ ἄμφω ζητεῖν"</note> But of these readings also, not a trace nor a footprint appears in the Medicean Codices which he used. Therefore, these things are probably to be attributed to conjecture alone, about which he himself may see to it.

**p. 183, 5. Our parts then—not containing (or rather of them) the constitution**] <note>original: "Τὰ μὲν οὖν ἡμέτερα μέρη—οὐ στέγοντα αὐτῶν (vel potius αὐτῶν) τὴν σύστασιν"</note> Ficino translated this not badly. The primary force of the verb is best understood from these words of Plato in *The Republic* X. p. 621. A. *no vessel contains the water*. <note>original: "οὐ τὸ ὕδωρ ἀγγεῖον οὐδὲν στέγει"</note> Plato uses it quite often and in various ways; cf. *Republic* IX. 586. p. 454. Bekker edition, and on that passage Ast in his *Commentary* p. 604, who was not unmindful of this passage in Plotinus. Cf. the same on Plato’s *Laws* IV. 6. p. 213. Plutarch also often uses it with this power, so that *not to contain* <note>original: "μὴ στέγειν"</note> means *not to hold together, not to sustain, to allow to flow out and perish*, as Wyttenbach teaches on the book *On Virtue and Vice* p. 689. There is another meaning which Zonaras touched upon in his *Lexicon* p. 1679: *Stegei means he endures*, where see Tittmann. Learned men have occupied themselves with other meanings in the recent London edition of Stephanus's *Thesaurus*. For the rest, here and in what follows, Plotinus touches upon those successions of natural things (*changes*) <note>original: "ἀμοιβάς"</note> so frequently mentioned by Heraclitus and the Stoics. See our notes below on Ennead IV. book 8. p. 468. where more will be said.

**p. 184, 2. he would take a firm opinion**] <note>original: "πάγιόν ἂν τὴν δόξαν—λάβοι"</note> He would assume a certain and firm opinion. The opposite is *to one who wavers*. See Ruhnken on Timaeus's *Platonic Lexicon* p. 108. Phrynichus in the *Preparation for Sophistry* in...

Bekker’s *Greek Anecdotes* II. p. 41. and Heindorf on Plato’s *Theaetetus* § 36. p. 333. *to make firm* <note>original: "παγιῶσαι"</note>. Theodoret III. p. 759. Schulz. regarding plants that are fixed more deeply in the soil. *Fixation* <note>original: "Παγίωσις"</note> is read in Olympiodorus’s commentary on the *Phaedo*. This should be added to the lexicons. Regarding the flame, which is praised in the nearby passages of Aristotle, mention of it is frequent in his *Physics*. These seem to agree most with what is read in *Meteorology* I. 4. p. 8. Sylb. *for flame is the boiling of a dry breath, etc.* <note>original: "ἔστι γὰρ ἡ φλὸξ πνεύματος ξηροῦ ζέσις κ. τ. λ."</note>. For the rest satisfies the opinion of Plotinus. Nicephorus Blemmida, in his *Physical Epitome* p. 101 ed. Wegelin, plundered Aristotelian ideas, as is his custom. Plotinus, however, also looked to Plato in these matters, who discusses the types of fire, flame, and light in the *Timaeus* p. 58. p. 76. Bekker.

— **5. the soul—being moved—being situated** <note>original: "τὴν ψυχὴν—κινουμένην—κειμένην"</note>] You might say Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino, the famous Renaissance translator of Plotinus</note> conjectured *adorned with a wonderful power* <note>original: "δυνάμει θαυμαστῇ κοσμουμένην"</note>, omitting the preceding *being moved*. Another might think the words should be transposed: *situated next to the best things—moved by the greatest power*. The manuscript books seem to indicate that this passage is not intact. I find no other readings.

**p. 185, 1. That the repentance of the soul is an empty thing has been shown** <note>original: "Ἡ δὲ μετάνοια τῆς ψυχῆς ὅτι κενόν ἐστι δέδεικται"</note>] Doubtless in the book *Against the Gnostics*, as it is called, written before this one of ours. See Ennead II. 9. 6. p. 203. E. *What need is there to speak of the other substances which they introduce, such as "dwellings nearby," and "impressions," and "repentances"? For if they say these are passions of the soul when it is in repentance, and "impressions" when it contemplates as it were images of beings but not yet the beings themselves, they are using new-fangled terms to establish their own sect* <note>original: "τὰς δὲ ἄλλας ὑποστάσεις... εἰς στάσιν τῆς ἰδίας αἱρέσεως"</note> (others read: *empty talk—composition*) where I shall add certain other things.

— **6. which Plato says** <note>original: "ἣ φησὶν ὁ Πλάτων"</note>] Plato in the *Timaeus* p. 69. p. 97. Bekk. *Then from these he constructed this whole, one living being containing all living beings within itself, both mortal and immortal; and of the divine things he himself becomes the craftsman, but the birth of the mortals he ordered his own offspring to fashion, etc.* <note>original: "ἔπειτα ἐκ τούτων πᾶν τόδε ξυνεστήσατο... κ. τ. λ."</note>

— **8. This is the same as the following—the heavenly [soul]** <note>original: "Τοῦτο δὲ ταὐτὸν τῷ ἐφεξῆς—τὴν οὐρανίαν"</note>] Plato in the *Phaedo* p. 109. p. 110. Bekk. *But the fact is the same, that through weakness and slowness we are not able to pass through to the furthest limit of the air.* <note>original: "τὸ δὲ εἶναι ταὐτὸν... τὸν ἀέρα"</note> Thus Bekker ordered the passage to be repeated. Heindorf conjectured p. 229: *but the fact being such through weakness:* <note>original: "τὸ δὲ εἶναι τοιοῦτον ὑπ’ ἀσθενείας"</note> “since however the matter stands so, that on account of powerlessness.” Wyttenbach p. 301: i.e., this is the same as saying that we—are not able. “Although in this specific composition I would prefer either that *the same* <note>original: "ταὐτὸν"</note> be absent, or that *it be* <note>original: "ᾖ"</note> be joined to it, which is often found removed from the preceding *it be*, as we shall show regarding Plutarch’s *Moralia* p. 96. A. (See *Observations on Plutarch* p. 652 sq. Oxford minor edition) or that *to the* <note>original: "τῷ"</note> be added, as Plotinus spoke in a similar construction” — The words of Plotinus follow, which Wyttenbach rendered into Latin thus: “*But that is the same as if it were said, that the heavenly soul is the one immediately following after the creator of the world, etc.*” Ficino rendered it no differently.

— **15. as if another soul were ruling them closely** <note>original: "ὡς ἂν ἄλλης ψυχῆς αὐτῶν προσεχῶς ἀρχούσης"</note>] The adverb *closely/immediately* <note>original: "προσεχῶς"</note> is of very rare use, and for that reason neglected in common Lexicons. The new Stephanus edition by Valpy p. 3978 provides a few examples. As for Hesychius II. 1045 Albert. explaining it as *earnestly* <note>original: "σπουδαίως"</note>, no example of its use is noted by the editors. Therefore, someone might perhaps ask whether this sense of the word fits our passage. If you accept it, it would be the same here as *attentively*, i.e., carefully, *diligently, seriously*. But nevertheless, Marsilio [Ficino] embraced the other meaning, and it seems more appropriate. Plutarch (attributed), *On the Opinions of the Philosophers* III. 18. p. 897. p. 617. Wytt. *which circle being visible is called a halo, because a halo appears to happen closely there, where the thickness of the sight now falls.* <note>original: "ὃς κύκλος φαινόμενος ἅλως καλεῖται... ἔνθα νῦν ἔπεσε τὸ πάχος τῆς ὄψεως"</note> Reiske, conjecturing: *because it is similar to a halo* <note>original: "ὅτι ἐστὶν ἅλωνι προσφερὴς"</note>, suppresses a very rare adverb with a common adjective; as if very rare things were so readily available to scribes. Wyttenbach gracefully: *because it is a halo of the sight, the appearance seeming to happen closely there, where it coincided, etc.* However it may be, in that place it signifies *immediately* or *closely*. Similarly in these words of Porphyry’s *Introduction to the five terms of Aristotle* ch. II. § 24. p. 378. Buhle: *and everything before the individuals predicated closely would be a species only*: “and whatever is predicated *immediately* above the individuals.” To these places, therefore, we also add this passage of Plotinus.

**p. 186, 7. To Timaeus then** <note>original: "Τῷ μὲν οὖν Τιμαίῳ"</note>] Plato in the *Timaeus* p. 31. p. 27. Bekk.: *That which comes into being must be bodily, and visible and tangible. But nothing could ever become visible apart from fire, nor tangible without something solid, and nothing is solid without earth. Whence God, beginning to compose the body of the universe, made it out of fire and earth.* <note>original: "σωματοειδὲς δὲ δὴ... ὁ θεὸς ἐπόνει"</note> John Philoponus described these Plotinian matters from those words down to the words: *if even in physical things it is so* in *Against Proclus on the Eternity of the World* XIII. 15. in the edition and in the Paris Scholia.

88 -> ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS <-

<note>The author is quoting John Philoponus' commentary</note> on the *Timaeus* p. 440 ed. Bekker, adding these words: *“And Plotinus, therefore, clearly spoke against Aristotle’s assumption regarding the fifth body <note>The 'ether' or quintessence</note>, and judged Plato’s view to be correct, which says that the heaven is composed of the same elements from which the living beings here on earth are constituted. And in the following sections, Plotinus again taught that one should not think the heavenly bodies are anything other than fire and the remaining elements, nor should we think of 'earth' in those regions as being carried down toward the lower nature of earth, or think of that fire as a mere flame.”* (There follows the passage of Plotinus treated by us above, namely **chapter 4, page 99 A.**) *“For the most pure and unmixed portion of the elements was set apart for the composition of the heavenly system, so that the nature of the heavenly body is neither foreign nor alien to the elements among us, nor is the fire or earth or anything else there exactly the same as here; rather, among us the dregs and, as it were, the sediment of the elements flowed down, while there the most fine-grained and better portion of them was separated out; since even in other living beings,” says Plotinus, “nature selects the better parts for their most sovereign organs.”* Then he adds that this was the true opinion of Plato, which can be proved from other sources as well as by the testimony of Aristotle himself, who, by attributing this view to Plato, spoke against him. It also seems that Aristotle was the first to introduce the doctrine of the fifth body.

**p. 186, 9. solid** <note>original: *στερεόν*</note>] This is confirmed by the books of Plato himself. Those who wrote *sterron* <note>original: *στἐῤῥον*</note> seem to have intended *sterron* <note>original: *στεῤῥόν*, meaning rigid or stiff</note>. However, there are various readings for this word. Cf. Jacobs on Achilles Tatius p. 850 f. Longinus in Eusebius *P.E.* XV p. 825 (Longinus Fragments VII. 3) contrasts the **solid body** <note>original: *στερεὸν σῶμα*</note>, the human body, with the soul, which according to the Stoic opinion is an *anathymiasis* <note>original: *ἀναθυμίασις*</note>, or exhalation, of the solid body. Plato himself teaches what **the solid** <note>original: *τὸ στερεὸν*</note> is for mathematicians in *Republic* VII p. 528 a.; cf. also *Philebus* p. 51 and Stallbaum there, p. 161.

— **11. they appear to have** <note>original: *φαίνεται ἔχοντα*</note>] This ought to have been translated *it appears they have*, and conversely in what follows *it seems they have* <note>original: *ἔχειν φαίνεται*</note>. (See F. A. Wolf on Demosthenes' *Against Leptines* p. 259.) But in such matters, it would be a long task to begin correcting Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino, the famous Renaissance translator of Plotinus</note>, who is otherwise an excellent interpreter of Plotinus. In the following parts, we have wiped away several manifest errors with the help of Philoponus and good manuscripts. The same interpreter contributes greatly to the understanding of this entire dispute, as shown by the things we just cited. Moreover, in this whole passage, Plotinus had before his eyes the arguments Plato makes in the *Timaeus* from p. 58 ff. Stephanus, p. 76 ff. Bekker.

**p. 188, 10. Concerning fire—three-dimensionally extended** <note>original: *Περὶ δὲ πυρὸς—διάστατον τριχῇ*</note>] Plato in *Timaeus* p. 56 B.: *“Let it be, then, according to right reason and probability, that the solid form which has become a pyramid is the element and seed of fire; and let us say the second in order of generation belongs to air, the third to water, etc.”* Cf. *Theology of Arithmetic* p. 20, p. 19 Ast: *“that in the first tetrad there is the smallest and most seed-like embodiment, since fire is the most elemental of bodies and the most fine-grained, and the shape of this very thing as a body is the pyramid, named accordingly, etc.”* Next, after **three-dimensionally extended**, Ficino reads **or it is a physical body** <note>original: *ἢ φυσικὸν σῶμα (sc. ἐστὶ)*</note>; however, those words: **why... a physical body?** <note>original: *διά τι—φυσ. σῶμα;*</note> he does not read. Of this variation, there is no trace in our manuscripts. After the second *body* <note>original: *σῶμα*</note> I have placed a question mark, which is found correctly placed in the following after **why** <note>original: *διά τι*</note>.

— **14. to gold, which is water** <note>original: *τῷ χρυσῷ ὕδατι ὄντι*</note>] Plato *Timaeus* p. 59, p. 77 Bekker: *“Of all these which we have called fluid waters, that which becomes densest from the finest and most uniform parts, a unique kind, endowed with a glittering and yellow color, is that most precious possession, gold, which has been strained through rock and solidified.”* Aristotle *On Colors* III p. 241 Sylburg: *“The gold-like color occurs when the yellow and the sun-like color, being strongly condensed, glitters. Therefore, the necks of pigeons and drops of water appear gold-colored when the light is refracted.”* These remarks pertain no more to Plato’s opinion on the nature of gold than those concerning "unfired gold" found in Paeonia after rains in *On Marvelous Things Heard* XLV p. 87 Beckmann. Somewhat closer to Plato’s words are these of Philo the Jew in the book *Who is the Heir of Divine Things* p. 503 Mangey: *“Those who praise gold say many other things in its favor, but two are supreme: one, that it does not admit rust; the other, that it can be beaten and poured into the thinnest membranes while remaining unbroken. It has therefore reasonably become a symbol of a greater nature, which, being stretched and poured out and reaching everywhere, is full of all things through and through, having harmoniously woven together the rest.”* Other sayings of the ancients concerning gold as the most beautiful of all things, and likewise concerning the sincerity of the human soul declared through the likeness of gold, we have presented in the book *On Beauty* p. 54 F. G., especially in the special Heidelberg edition p. 267 ff.

-> BOOK I. ENNEAD TWO. pages 186—190. 89 <-

Many authors, especially among the Alexandrian philosophers who came after Plotinus, have written much concerning the nature of **Demons**. Some spoke with hesitation, as if dealing with a difficult matter, such as Iamblichus and others. See Iamblichus, *On the Egyptian Mysteries*, V. 10. p. 125; V. 11. p. 127; and Gale in the notes, p. 267. Compare Proclus on the *First Alcibiades*, p. 83 ff.; Olympiodorus on the same, p. 15 ff. By Plato, or certainly by the author of the *Epinomis* (p. 984 below), demons are called an <note>original: "ἀέριον γένος"</note> *aerial race*; from which passage, as a primary source, many have drawn. *Animals with aerial bodies*, Apuleius calls demons in *On the God of Socrates*, p. 108. Similarly Porphyry in *On Abstinence*, II. 39 and 42, pp. 172 and 182 in Rhoer’s edition, whom you should consult. Psellus, moreover, in *On the Operation of Demons*, wishes to attribute a <note>original: "σύμφυον φῶς"</note> *connatural light* to Demons, p. 49 of the Kiel edition.

**p. 188, 17. but let us move—to have**] This is an instance of Plotinian brevity. Understand it as *saying*. But such things are encountered on almost every page in these Enneads: and it would be tedious to point them out too often, especially since Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino, the famous Renaissance translator of Plotinus.</note> usually provides for the reader's understanding with a helpful paraphrase.

**p. 189, 2. to carry around with them—earthly bodies**] Epicurus taught similar things, as is evident from the fragments of his books *On Nature*, as noted also by the editor Rosini in the *Herculaneum Papyri*, Vol. I, p. 62. To this also belong those words in Cicero’s *On the Nature of the Gods*, I. 18, concerning the Gods: “Yet that form is not a body, but as it were a body, etc.” And: “Epicurus teaches that the power and nature of the Gods is such that, first, it is perceived not by the senses but by the mind; not by any solidity or numerical distinctness, like those things which he calls <note>original: "στερέμνια"</note> *solid* on account of their firmness, but by images perceived through similarity and transition.”

— **5. Plato saying**] In the *Timaeus*, p. 31, p. 43, p. 51 ff.

— **6. the resistance**] <note>original: "τὸ ἀντίτυπον"</note> Plotinus uses this term frequently with various meanings, even regarding souls; he also uses the noun <note>original: "ἀντιτυπία"</note> *resistance* or *solidity*. See II. 6. 2; II. 9. 6; III. 6. 6; IV. 4. 29; V. 8. 4; VI. 1. 26; VI. 1. 28, where the other form <note>original: "ἀντιτυπές"</note> *resistant* appears; VI. 7. 29; VI. 8. 7. In this passage, the word comes closer to the meaning of *hardness*. See Ruhnken on Timaeus, p. 157; Wyttenbach on Plutarch’s *On Superstition*, p. 999; and what I have placed in the *Commentaries on Herodotus*, p. 299. Proclus in his commentary on Plato’s *First Alcibiades*, 55, p. 154: *that the passions belong to the hard and resistant nature, being material and earthly—all of them, so to speak, but especially the spirited ones.* I have placed other notes below at the word *resistance*, p. 180 G. Compare also Hermann and Erfurdt on Sophocles’ *Antigone*, 134; and Schleusner’s *Lexicon of the New Testament* under this word, who correctly defended the meaning of "likeness" in many places. Regarding the word <note>original: "ἐπιβάθρα"</note> *stepping-stone* or *foundation*, it was discussed above at I. 6. 1, especially in the special edition, p. 143. In this place, it means *foundation*.

**p. 190, 4. And he himself bears witness to these things**] Plato in the *Timaeus*, p. 39: *God kindled a light in the second of the orbits relative to the earth, which we have now called the sun, etc.*

— **8. that light—is different from flame**] Compare above, chapter 4, and the annotations there for p. 99 A; and apply Plato’s arguments concerning the sun, light, and truth in the sixth book of the *Republic*, p. 507 ff.

— **9. and that this light is a body, etc.**] The Emperor Julian explains this opinion in more words in *Oration IV*, p. 133 ff. He speaks of a triple sun: *But also this third visible disk (of the sun) is clearly the cause of salvation for sensible things. And as much as we said the great sun is to the intellectual gods, so much is this visible sun to the manifest ones. Come then, first, is not light itself an incorporeal and divine form of things that are transparent in their activity? — and light itself being incorporeal, its summit and, as it were, its flower, would be the rays. Now the opinion of the Phoenicians, wise and knowledgeable in divine matters, said that the rays proceeding everywhere are the pure activity of the pure mind itself. Nor is this account discordant. If light itself is incorporeal, provided one does not suppose its source to be a body, etc.* (Concerning the Ether of the Phoenicians and the Intelligible God, cf. Damascius *On First Principles*, p. 385, ed. Kopp.) Furthermore, Marsilio Ficino undertook to illustrate these dogmas concerning *incorporeal light* both in his commentary on this book of Plotinus (p. 87 ff. and p. 93) and on the seventh book of Plato’s *Republic* (p. 690, Frankfurt ed.) and on the *Symposium* (p. 1151 ff.). Because our author immediately uses <note>original: "ἄνθος"</note> *flower* in relation to light, we have seen Julian use the same word in the words just praised. I have noted more on this usage in *Plotinus on Beauty*, p. 54 A (in the special edition, p. 233) and in Olympiodorus on the *First Alcibiades*, p. 109, at the words: *wherefore beauty is the foam and flower of form*. Proclus in the same, p. 247: *the flower of our essence*. The same, ibid. p. 240: *the flower of the mind*.

— **12. and brightness,—that which is truly white**] These things remind one of that passage of Ennius in Cicero’s *On the Nature of the Gods*, II.

90 -> ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS <-

**2. 25. III. 4. “sublimely white.”** <note>original: "sublime candens"</note> Ezekiel Spanheim collected other examples in *Remarks on the Caesars of Julian*, p. 16, where he also praised this passage from Plotinus. Cf. furthermore below, p. 711. c. 18. A.

**p. 190, 13. which is indeed—a white body** <note>original: ὃ δὴ εἶναι—λευκὸν σῶμα</note>] Ezekiel Spanheim, in the place cited above (p. 16), compared these words with Julian’s phrasing in *The Caesars*—"brighter than silver, but whiter than gold"—taking the meaning to be **splendid (brilliant)**, though he did not report Plotinus’s words with sufficient accuracy.

— **18. a flame—ascending—to be thrown down with the earth** <note>original: φλόγα—ἀνελθοῦσαν—μετὰ γῆς ῥίπτεσθαι κάτω</note>] Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the first to translate Plotinus into Latin</note> understands this as referring to lightning bolts. Regarding the causes of these, which the ancients debated, read the author attributed to Aristotle, *On the Universe* II. 10, IV. 3, IV. 17; also Johannes Laurentius Lydus, *On the Months* III. 15, p. 53 ff. (Schow edition); and the same author, *On Omens* p. 86, 164, 174 (Hasii edition).

**p. 191, 3. to stand below the moon—the air** <note>original: κάτω δὲ τῆς σελήνης ἵστασθαι—ἀέρα</note>] The same Marsilio [Ficino] refers this to comets. You should compare Aristotle, *Meteorology* I. 7; Seneca, *Natural Questions* I. 15; and the many others cited by Kapp in his edition of Aristotle’s *On the Universe* II. 9, p. 42 ff., IV. 22, p. 141 ff. Add Lydus, *On the Months* II. 13, p. 51, and *On Omens* p. 36, as well as Hasii’s *Annotations*, p. 299.

— **4. flame—boiling** <note>original: φλόγα—ζέσω</note>] Cf. the Annotation above for chapter 4, p. 99. A. Furthermore, cf. Plutarch, *On the Face in the Moon's Orb* p. 923. E. (p. 738 in Wyttenbach’s edition): *“But the entire upper region, even if it receives something earthy thrown up by force, immediately squeezes it out here, or rather lets it go as it is carried down by its own natural weight.”*

— **7. But the light there—in the reasons of the stars** <note>original: Τὸ δὲ φῶς ἐκεῖ—ἐν λόγοις τοῖς ἄστροις</note>] I fear Ficino has not translated this accurately. Plotinus seems to mean that the **stars** themselves are **reasons** <note>original: λόγοι (logoi)</note>, as if you were to say "thoughts" and thus "spoken words." Specifically, the original celestial light is like the *internal reason* <note>original: ὁ λόγος ἐνδιάθετος (ho logos endiathetos), the unspoken thought</note>, the hidden inner logic; whereas the stars are the *uttered reasons* <note>original: οἱ λόγοι προφορικοί (hoi logoi prophorikoi)</note>, or the reasons and thoughts brought forth into speech. Thus, that original light, which is one in itself, becomes varied through the variety of the stars, just as a single speech becomes varied through the variety of men. Certainly, no learned person is unaware that such a sentiment is consistent with the mind of the Alexandrian Philosophers and Plotinus himself, as the following books of Plotinus prove. Therefore, I would translate it: “**But the light which is there, is partly variegated in the stars, as if in uttered words.**”

— **16. every body with a soul—and such is the one there** <note>original: πᾶν δὲ σῶμα μετὰ ψυχῆς—τοιούτου δὲ τὸ ἐκεῖ</note>] The author attributed to Plato, in the *Epinomis* p. 983 (p. 358 in Bekker’s edition): *“It is impossible for the earth and heaven and all the stars and their entire masses to proceed so accurately year by year unless a soul were present with each or in each.”* In what follows, one might say Ficino read *fire would not even fit in* <note>original: πῦρ δὲ οὐδ’ ἂν ἐναρμόσειε</note>. But the manuscripts show no variation, and the passage can be resolved if you supply the word *something* <note>original: τὶ (ti)</note> to the word *fire*. However, I do not wish to pronounce judgment on the passage, as the variation of the books in the following parts indicates it is undoubtedly corrupt. Furthermore, *to make* <note>original: ποιεῖν (poiein)</note> differs from *to act* <note>original: δρᾷν (dran)</note> in the same way it differs from *to do/practice* <note>original: πράττειν (prattein)</note>.

**p. 192, 1. rush/impetus** <note>original: ῥύμη (rhume)</note>] We have restored this from the margin in place of *strength/force* <note>original: ῥώμη (rhome)</note>, which had taken its place. Regarding this confusion, Lobeck recently warned with examples in his notes on Phrynichus’s *Eclogae* p. 404; also Jacobs in his *Additional Observations on Athenaeus* p. 209; the same in *Achilles Tatius* p. 426 and *Philostratus’s Images* p. 650 and 655; and Bähr on Plutarch’s *Philopoemen* p. 44 and *Pyrrhus* p. 216; and Tittmann on *Zonaras’s Lexicon* p. 774, note 72. Among the Attics, it is the same as *impulse* <note>original: ὁρμή (horme)</note>. See Phrynichus in the place cited, and Suidas and Zonaras under the entry; and, when it designates the *impetus of rotation*, it is exchanged with *whirl/vortex* <note>original: δίνη (dine)</note>, as in Plutarch’s *On the Divine Vengeance* as observed by Wyttenbach p. 120. It is used regarding the motion of the elements and mundane bodies, the stars, and thence also others, and is also applied metaphorically to other things. The author attributed to Plato, in the *Epinomis* p. 983 (p. 358 Bekker) regarding the bodies of the world, stars, etc.: *“If anyone calls certain causes of bodies 'rushes' [rhumas], or 'natures,' or something of that sort, he will say nothing clear.”* Plutarch, *On the Face in the Moon's Orb* p. 922. C. (p. 733 Wyttenbach): *“But the rush [rhume] even ignites the air in stones and in cold lead, let alone that which is whirled in fire with such great speed.”* The same, ibid. p. 924. A. regarding heavy masses falling downward: *“But if, being carried down by the rush [rhume], they should overshoot the center, they would turn back again and be bent upward by them.”* But that entire discussion should be compared with the passage in Plotinus. Aristotle in Stobaeus, *Physical Selections* I. 33. p. 624 (Heeren edition): *“As for the storm-winds, when they are carried along in a mass and densely upon themselves, the greater part of the cloud is dissolved by the violence of the rush [rhume].”* John Chrysostom, *Homily II*, p. 84 (Matthaei edition): *“Just as a sudden rush [rhume] of wind falling upon it drives away the annoying dust,”* where the editor provides several more passages from the same sacred orator. The same, ibid. p. 118, used metaphorically—

concerning the power of the Christian religion which no one can resist: <note>original: "καὶ οὐδὲ ἐνεγκεῖν δυνήσεται ἄφατον αὐτοῦ ῥύμην"</note> *and it shall not be able to bear its unspeakable rush.*

**p. 192, 7. the revolution according to nature—the movement according to nature**] To these points, consult Ezechiel Spanheim’s *Essays of Remarks on Julian’s Caesars* p. 15, where he teaches that the word <term>periphora<note>original: "περιφορᾶς"</note></term> (revolution) is used by Plotinus with a double meaning: both for the circular motion of the stars and the heaven itself, and for the globe of the sun, moon, and other stars.

— **10. Therefore it must not be said that the things there require nourishment**] He speaks against Heraclitus and the Stoics, who contended that the stars and the moon were nourished either by the exhalations of the earth or by the waters and the sea. Stobaeus Book I. 25. p. 510. Heeren, on the opinion of Heraclitus: <note>original: "τρέφεσθαι δὲ τοὺς ἀστέρας ἐκ τῆς ἀπὸ γῆς ἀναθυμιάσεως"</note> *that the stars are nourished from the evaporation from the earth.* In the same work p. 556. (I. 27.) from the doctrine of Chrysippus: <note>original: "διὸ καὶ τούτοις τρέφεσθαι (sc.) ποτίμοις ὕδασι τὴν σελήνην"</note> *wherefore the moon is also nourished by these (namely) drinkable waters.* Plutarch’s *Table Talk* VIII. p. 728. *for the gods are not nourished from it (the sea) as the Stoics suppose the stars to be.* Compare Diogenes Laërtius VII. 145. and there the commentaries of Menage and Baguet on Chrysippus §. LXXX. p. 177. [Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II. 15. p. 265. sq. compared with p. 747.]

— **13. compositions**] Properly <term>concretions<note>original: "συγκρίματα"</note></term>, from which also *concrete bodies*. A word frequently used by physicians: cf. Stephanus’s *Thesaurus* p. 5348. Valpy. Add Plutarch IX. p. 499. Reiske and vol. X. p. 592. below. Plotinus explains this brilliantly in V. 9. 3. p. 557. B. after he has set forth things composed by art, he continues thus: <note>original: "καὶ μὴν καὶ τὰ φύσει συνεστῶτα..."</note> *and indeed also those things established by nature, their many-compounded parts and what are called "compositions," are resolved into the form that is over all the things composed, such as man into soul and body, and the body into the four elements.*

**ibid. and that the change of the bodies here comes from themselves**] I repeat the word *it must be said* from the preceding, and thus I translate: *And it must be said that the change of the bodies which are here (on earth) happens from themselves (i.e., from their own nature).*

### BOOK II.

**P. 199, 7. ON THE MOTION OF THE HEAVEN**] This is the second book of all Plotinus’s works according to the time of writing, elsewhere inscribed *On Circular Motion*. See Porphyry’s *Life of Plotinus* ch. 24. p. 141. Fabricius. Moreover, the argument arose for our philosopher chiefly from Plato’s *Timaeus*, especially those things read on p. 34. sq. Bekker: <note>original: "κίνησιν γὰρ ἀπένειμεν αὐτῷ..."</note> *for he assigned to it the motion proper to its body, which of the seven motions is most related to mind and intelligence. Therefore, leading it around in the same way, in the same place, and within itself, he made it move turning in a circle, but he took away the other six motions and made it wanderless from them, etc.* For the rest, compare also *Epinomis* p. 982. sq. p. 356. sqq. Bekker. In explaining that passage of the *Timaeus*, the Platonic philosophers especially worked in competition. Proclus, in particular, copiously examined the various opinions of the ancients regarding the motion of the heaven in his commentary on the *Timaeus* p. 167. sqq. Aristotle’s views on this matter, which Proclus and others touch upon, are read in the books *On the Heavens* II. 2. IV. 1. in the *Meteorology* I. 2. and likewise in the booklet circulated among Aristotle’s works, *On the Universe* II. 3. where Kapp added several notes on this matter p. 25. sqq. Others have partly reported and partly embellished Plato’s opinions on the motion of the heaven. See Alcinous *On the Doctrine of Plato* ch. XIV. p. 488. sqq. ed. Daniel Heinsius, where among other things these are read on p. 490.: <note>original: "ἡ μὲν γὰρ τοῦ πάντα περιέχοντος..."</note> *for the motion of the heaven which contains all things, being wanderless, is one and ordered. However, the motion of the things outside is varied, and different in its risings and settings; wherefore it is also called a planet, etc.* Chalcidius in his commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus* p. 213. Meursius [p. 322. ed. I. A. Fabricius at the end of the Works of St. Hippolytus]: “Where however the use of moving was seen to be necessary, out of all motions he (Plato says God) attributed these two principal ones to the world: one by accident, by which he carries the fixed stars <note>original: "aplanes"</note> toward the west, which motion he now calls 'in precedence'; the other truly principal, which is the revolution, and it turns around itself, similar to the motion of a deliberative soul, with the five other motions ceasing. For the local motions are seven, I believe; two indeed according to length, that is, forward and backward; two others likewise through breadth, to the right and to the left; and two others according to depth, upward and downward, and the last similar to the above-mentioned revolution, which flies around a fixed axis. Since therefore out of those seven motions God attributed the use of only two to the individual established stars—the principal one being revolution, and by accident that which is carried to the right—he rightly said that the five other motions were besides idle.” Then he concludes by mentioning that he has disputed concerning the motions of the wandering stars.

92 -> ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS <-

"And the heaven is indeed so adorned, inhabited by wise and eternal living beings." <note>original Latin: *animalibus inquilinis*. This refers to the stars and celestial bodies, which Neoplatonists viewed as divine living entities.</note> Cf. also Apuleius, *On the Doctrines of Plato* p. 578 ff. p. 198 ff. ed. Bosscha. The same author, *On the World* p. 707. p. 289 ff. Bossch. Just as in ancient times they bitterly called Heraclitus and his followers **the flowing ones** <note>Greek: *τοὺς ῥέοντας*</note>, because they contended that all things continually flow and change; so they used to call those who thought the universe was moved **those who move the whole** <note>Greek: *τοὺς τὸ πᾶν κινοῦντας*</note>; from whom were distinguished those who said it was immobile, **the partisans of the whole's rest** <note>Greek: *οἱ τοῦ ὅλου στασιῶται*</note>. (Plato, *Theaetetus* p. 180 f. p. 256 ff. Bekker; cf. on these decrees Brandis, *Commentaries on the Eleatics* I. p. 142. and Plotinus himself, p. 489 f.) Plato himself, however, established two kinds of motion, calling one **alteration** <note>Greek: *ἀλλοίωσιν* — qualitative change</note> and the other **revolution** <note>Greek: *περιφοράν* — circular motion</note>. *Theaetetus* in the place cited, where Heindorf preferred **locomotion** <note>Greek: *φορὰν*</note> with the support of Baguet on Chrysippus p. 179. Nevertheless, Bekker did not change it, nor does the Darmstadt Manuscript support it, nor any other; and it appears that Proclus, whose words the next note will show, read **revolution** <note>Greek: *περιφοράν*</note>. The same variation occurs in a brilliant passage of Philo the Jew, where he treats the double motion of the fixed and wandering stars <note>The "erratic" stars are the planets.</note>, in *On the Cherubim* p. 12. Vol. II. Pfeiffer: "Does he not then introduce the **revolution** <note>Greek: *περιφοράν* (others read *φορὰὶ*, Manuscript A reads *φορὰν*)</note> of the whole heaven through allegories?" but the whole passage ought to be compared with Plato and Plotinus. Aristotle established three: **according to place, according to quality, according to quantity (locomotion, alteration, growth and decay)**. <note>Greek: *κατὰ τόπον, κατὰ τὸ ποῖον, κατὰ τὸ πόσον (φορὰ, ἀλλοίωσις, αὔξησις καὶ φθίσις)*</note> Aristotle, *Physics* VII. 2. cf. Heindorf on Plato's *Theaetetus* in the place cited p. 421. Sextus Empiricus, *Against the Mathematicians* X. 52. and Fabricius there p. 142. The Stoics labored above all others in defining motion, and examined with subtlety every point said to the contrary; yet they did not sufficiently take care to avoid falling frequently into the errors of the Epicureans, whom they were attacking. See Plutarch’s *Excerpts from the books of Chrysippus* **on motion** <note>Greek: *περὶ κινήσεως*</note> in the treatise *On Stoic Self-Contradictions* p. 1053 f. Stobaeus, *Eclogues* I. p. 404. Heeren. and cf. Bak’s *Observations on Cleomedes' Meteora* I. 1. p. 275 f. and Baguet on Chrysippus §. LXXXI. p. 178—180. Regarding the motion of the heaven and the world, which the Platonists, Peripatetics, and many other philosophers had established, the same Cleomedes touched upon it in I. 3., where Balforeus and Bak (whom I just cited) p. 297 ff. should be consulted. No less did Nicephorus Blemmydes include a summary of the doctrine of Plato, Aristotle, and other physicists **on Motion** in his small work *Epitome of Physics*. See for example p. 13. 39. 43., especially chapter 24. p. 179. ed. Wegelin. Augsburg, 1605. The same author on p. 183 also makes mention of our Plotinus: — "**For the straight-line motion of the elements belongs to them while they are still coming into being and are in a place contrary to their nature, but have not yet reached the place according to their nature, as Ptolemy, Plotinus, Xenarchus, and certain other natural philosophers agree.**" <note>Greek: *ἡ γὰρ ἐπ’ εὐθείας κίνησις...*</note> If you ask where Nicephorus took this doctrine from, go to the most learned interpreter of Aristotle <note>Likely Simplicius.</note> on the book *On the Heavens* folio 5 verso, Aldine edition: "**It should be known that Ptolemy, in his book on the elements and in his Optics, and the great Plotinus, and Xenarchus in his doubts against the 'fifth essence,' supposed that the straight-line motions of the elements occur while they are still coming into being and are in a place contrary to nature, and not yet in the place according to nature; and Aristotle also seems to have understood this, etc.**" (For I cannot provide the whole excellent dispute excerpted here) and after a few words: "**But as the aforementioned men Ptolemy, Xenarchus, and Plotinus say, when the elements are in their natural state and exist in their proper places, they either remain still or move in a circle. The earth and water and the settled part of the air clearly remain still; but fire and the easily-led part of the air move in a circle, being carried around with the heaven, insofar as it is fitting for them.**" Proclus touched upon the same opinion several times in his commentary on the *Timaeus*, as on p. 142 and 274, where he likewise appeals to the authority of Ptolemy and Plotinus. You may compare Plotinus below, p. 328. B. C. Xenarchus, however, whom Simplicius praises quite often, is that Cilician—and therefore a fellow countryman of Simplicius—a teacher of Strabo, who had become famous among the Peripatetics in the age of Augustus, both for the excellence of his teaching and the favor of that Prince. See Strabo XIV. p. 670. Casaubon. p. 683—685. Tzschucke. Alexander of Aphrodisias praises the same man in his commentary on Aristotle’s *On the Soul*, folio 154 ff. Simplicius returns to the argument of Plotinus's book in the same place, folio 9 verso: — "**Even if Ptolemy, Plotinus, and Proclus, and even Aristotle himself say that the 'kindling' <note>Greek: *ὑπέκκαυμα* — the sphere of fire just below the moon</note> is moved, this motion is not its own, because it follows along with the outermost sphere; yet it is disposed toward it by nature, so as not to be dragged by force, but to move with another, just as the wandering stars move with the fixed sphere; for that motion is not its own; yet it is not forced, but above nature.**" And from this one Sim-

-> BOOK II. SECOND ENNEAD. p. 199. 93 <-

From this summary, it is understood through how many and how varied discussions this topic *On the Motion of the Heaven* has been treated by various schools of philosophers. At the conclusion of this Introduction, I will subjoin a passage from Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Roman provincial and Neoplatonist author</note> from his *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio* I. 17., where he presents a portion of the Plotinian discourse in his own words: — “The nature, power, and reason of the world-soul teach that the heaven revolves, for its eternity is in motion; because motion never leaves that which life does not desert: nor does life depart from that in which a constant agitation flourishes. Therefore, the celestial body—which the soul of the world fabricated for itself to be a participant in immortality so that it might never fail in living—is always in motion and knows not how to stand still; because the soul itself by which it is driven does not stand still. For since the essence of the soul, which is incorporeal, is in motion, and the soul fabricated the body of the heaven first of all things: without doubt the nature of motion migrated from the incorporeal into this first body. Its power, whole and uncorrupted, does not desert that which it first began to move. Therefore, the motion of the heaven is necessarily revolving; because since it is necessary to be moved always, and there is no further place toward which an addition might extend, it is agitated by the continuation of a perpetual returning into itself. Therefore, it runs in that which it can or has, and for it to approach is to be revolved: because for a sphere embracing all spaces and places, there is but one course: to rotate. But even so, it seems always to follow the soul, which runs through the whole universe. We shall say, therefore, that it finds the soul if it always follows it; or rather, it always finds it, because the soul is whole everywhere and perfect everywhere. Why then, if it finds what it seeks, does it not rest? Because the soul also is ignorant of rest. For the heaven would stand still if it found the soul standing still anywhere. But since that soul, toward whose desire the heaven is drawn, always pours itself through the universe, the body also always turns itself back into it and through it. Let these few points out of many, discovered with *Plotinus* as the author, suffice concerning the secret of celestial revolution.”

**p. 199, 9. Why does it move in a circle? Because it imitates Intellect** <note>original Greek: Διὰ τί κύκλῳ κινεῖται; ὅτι νοῦν μιμεῖται</note>] Namely *the heaven* <note>Latin: ὁ οὐρανός</note>, from the title of the book. The source of this sentiment is in the passage of Plato’s *Timaeus* cited in the nearest note. Many others have touched upon the same. Apuleius in *On the Doctrines of Plato* p. 198. Bossch.: — “this one thing was left to the world as proper to wisdom and prudence, *that it should be revolved rationally*.” Chalcidius in his commentary on the *Timaeus* p. 213.: “but the other (motion) is the principal one, which is a turning around, and it turns about itself similar to the motion of the deliberative soul.” Indeed, the philosopher Sallustius almost expressed Plotinus word-for-word in *On the Gods and the World* chapter VIII. p. 24. ed. Io. Conr. Orellii: *Of the bodies in the cosmos, some imitate Intellect and move in a circle, while others imitate Soul and move in a straight line—fire and air upward, earth and water downward. Of those moving in a circle, the fixed sphere moves from the east, and the seven planets are carried from the west.* <note>original Greek: τῶν δὲ ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ σωμάτων τὰ μὲν νοῦν μιμεῖται καὶ κύκλῳ κινεῖται... κ.τ.λ.</note> Proclus speaks brilliantly in *On the Theology of Plato* XIII. p. 35. below: *Add, if you wish, the presence of the intellectual illumination into the body; for from where does this whole heaven get its spherical shape, or why is it carried in a circle and recycled around the same point according to one fixed order? For how did it always obtain the same form and power unchangeably according to nature, unless it participated in the formalizing power of the Intellect? For while the Soul is the provider of motion, that which is the cause of the stable state—bringing back the restless variation of moving things into identity, and into a life limited by one reason and a revolution that stays the same—is clearly something beyond the Soul.* <note>original Greek: Πρόσθες δὲ, εἰ βούλει... κ.τ.λ.</note> The same author in V. 36. p. 324. — *for because of this the heaven is also said to dance eternally.—for because they move in a circle, they model themselves after the Intellect and the intellectual revolution.* Everyone recognizes the Pythagorean source of these dogmas. It will suffice to have touched upon one place. Hippodamus the Pythagorean in Gale’s *Mythological Opuscula* p. 664. *For harmony is the virtue in the cosmos.* <note>original Greek: ἔστι γὰρ ἁ μὲν ἁρμονία ἀρετὰ κόσμῳ</note> I have set down more at Cicero’s *On the Nature of the Gods* III. 11. p. 531. Moreover, Proclus, to return to that point, explained these things elsewhere, as in the *Timaeus* p. 167. ff. and in *Elements of Theology* chapters 33. and 34. p. 58—60. of our edition. John Philoponus, who argued against Proclus in *On the Eternity of the World* XIII. 2., writes thus: *Plato also wants the heaven to be ensouled and to be moved by a soul. It is clear then that he defines the circular motion for it as for a living being according to nature. For if he says that circular motion is especially concerned with Intellect, and as Plotinus says, it moves in a circle because it imitates Intellect, it is clear that he wants the circular motion to reach it from the soul, moving its own body toward an imitation of the intellectual activity.* <note>original Greek: καὶ τὸν οὐρανὸν δὲ ὁ Πλάτων ἔμψυχον εἶναι... κ.τ.λ.</note> The same author in Aristotle’s *Meteorology* p. 78. b. *Plotinus says: Why does it move in a circle? Because it imitates Intellect. For just as the divine and demiurgic Intellect, turning back into itself, contemplates all things and itself in those things, so he says that as far as possible this (perhaps "this" should be deleted) celestial matter [turns] toward itself...* <note>The sentence breaks off at the end of the page</note>

**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

...makes a conversion. And as that one [the One/Intellect] is nowhere in essence but everywhere in activities (repeat *everywhere*), so also the heaven, being a body and unable to be everywhere at once, becomes everywhere by its parts. And that it governs all things by its own activities while being set apart in essence from the things within, etc. To the same class of passages belongs also this passage of the same Philoponus in *Aristotle’s On the Soul*, B. 5. a.: "Plotinus also (incorrectly Suidas, who reports these things under the entry *physikos logos*, wrote 'Plato,' as Kuster noted) renders [the cause] from the relation which it has toward the things before it." *“Plotinus also gives the cause of this figure (the spherical, σφαιρικῆς), sought from the relation which the heaven has toward those things which are above itself.”* I have set down these somewhat more numerous remarks so that the fame of this Platonic and Plotinian passage might be understood, and so that light might be shed upon this decree from the ancient interpreters.

**p. 199, 10. ὅτι ψυχὴ ἐν αὐτῇ ἐστι—ἀεὶ ἰέναι [that the soul is in itself—to go always]**
One might say that Ficinus read *ὅτι ψυχὴ ἐν σφαίρᾳ ἐστὶ* [that the soul is in a sphere], and *αὕτη πρὸς αὑτὴν σπεύδει ἰέναι* [this hastens to go toward itself], with *ἀεὶ* [always] omitted. The latter indeed has the authority of the books [manuscripts], the former two preceding readings very little; and altogether it is better in such a passage to keep one's hand back [from emending].

**p. 200, 17. ἢ—ὥσπερ περιολισθάνων ἀνακάμπτει [or—as if slipping around it bends back]**
No book exhibits *περιολισθαίνων*. Thucydides VII. 65 has *ἀπολισθάνοι*, likewise with the agreement of the MSS. Lucian, *Dialogues of the Sea* XV. 2, similarly, where however Tib. Hemsterhuis (p. 326) demanded *ἀπολισθαίνοι* by usage. Nor do I see that form noted in the Polybian Lexicon, although in IV. 32. 2. p. 80 all books offer *διωλίσθανον*. But Porson, contradicting Hemsterhuis (on Euripides, *Phoenissae* v. 1398), vindicated this ancient form of the verb for more recent prose writers as well. Cf. also Fischer on Weller III. p. 141; with whom compare Lobeck on Phrynichus p. 74. 2 sq. regarding the forms of the Tenses. Therefore, let this very Plotinian example be added to the Lexicons as an instance of the ancient form, and likewise below in II. 6. 1. and III. 6. 14, where three books have *ἀπολισθάνειν*. I have dealt with the usage of the verb *ὀλισθαίνω* and *ὀλίσθησις* [slipping] figuratively in [the notes on] Proclus, *On the First Alcibiades* p. 139. Add now Wyttenbach, *Annotations on Eunapius* p. 90 sq. ed. Boissonade. The compound verb *περιολισθαίνω* [to slip around] is frequent enough in Plutarch alone, who also in the *Lives* Vol. II. p. 551 Reiske uses *περιολισθήσεις τῶν γεωδῶν* [slipping around of earthy things], and this kind of verb is often encountered concerning mundane bodies and elements, as in this passage of Plotinus; who, in adding *ἀνακάμπτει* [it bends back], reminds us of the two kinds of signs of the Zodiac, namely *τῶν καμπτομένων* [those that bend] and *τῶν ὀλισθηρῶν* [those that slip]. Concerning these and others, Dorville noted on Chariton II. 1. p. 293 ed. Leipzig [p. 154 ed. Amsterdam].

**p. 201, 2. θεῖ οὖν ἐν ᾧ ἔχει—οὐκ ἵνα μένῃ—ἀλλ’ ἵνα φέρηται [It runs therefore in that which it has—not so that it might remain—but so that it might be carried]**
So we have written instead of *μένοι—φέροιτο* [optative forms]; the former on the authority of the best books, the latter so that the logic of the Moods might be consistent with itself, and because that *φέρηται* could have been suppressed by the following *καὶ* [and], both moreover being required by the laws of the language. Furthermore, Macrobius in *Saturnalia* I. 17, which passage I set down in full above, seems to have had these words of Plotinus before his eyes when he writes: — "because since it is necessary to be moved always, *and moreover there is no place* toward which an approach might tend, it is driven by the continuation of a perpetual returning into itself. Therefore *it runs in that in which it is or which it has, and its approaching is to be revolved, because for a sphere embracing all spaces and places there is but one course: to be rotated.*"

**— 14. νῦν δὲ ἐπειδὴ πᾶσά ἐστιν αὐτῆς, παντὸς ἐφίεται [but now since she is all of herself, she desires all]**
We have received *πᾶσα* [all] instead of *ταῦτα* [these things] from almost all our books. But the passage does not yet seem fully healed. Ficinus translates it as if he conjectured: *Νῦν δὲ, ἐπειδὴ ἧς ἐφίεται πᾶσά ἐστι παντός* [But now, since that which she desires is all of the whole]. This pleases, provided you fill in the missing Apodosis, as the same translator did. Such an Ellipsis after *νῦν δὲ* is very frequent in Attic writers. Plato, *Symposium* c. 8: "For if Eros were one, it would be well; but now—for he is not one." Cf. *Laws* IX. p. 875 c. d., *Laches* p. 184, and the more numerous examples provided by Heusde, *Specimen criticum in Platonem* p. 286, and Heindorf on *Charmides* p. 114 and *Theaetetus* p. 286. Macrobius in *Dream of Scipio* (loc. cit.), who rather transcribed these words of Plotinus than translated them (unless perhaps you say he used the Eustochian recension of these Enneads), nevertheless expressed this passage thus: — "for it would stand still, if it found the soul standing still anywhere. *But since that soul, by whose appetite it is drawn, always pours itself into the universe*, always the body also turns itself back into her and through her." Furthermore, this entire chapter has contracted various blemishes, which we have striven to wipe away by the aid of both reason and the books, as far as is possible. To explain the meaning in passages so impeded as this one is, the version of Marsilio [Ficino] is, for the most part, wonderfully helpful. He indeed at the end translates as if he read, or

**p. 202, 11. ἢ ὅτι μὴ μόνον ἐκεῖ [or because not only there]**
For the sake of aiding understanding, Ficinus dilated the extreme brevity of Plotinus in this place, as in six hundred others; lest perhaps you believe he found more in his books.

**— 13. ἀφ’ οὗ ἡ ἄλλη [from which the other]**
So we have given from several books. As for what Ficinus adds, *vitae* [of life], no trace of the word *ζωὴ* appears in the MSS. In the immediately preceding words, *φύσεως ψυχῆς* [of the nature of the soul] is the same as *ψυχῆς* [of the soul] alone. Concerning which usage a warning was given above at I. 6. 1. You can unravel the next parts in no other way than by distinguishing thus: *Εἰ δὲ ψυχῆς ἐστι (sc. τὸ μέσον) περιθέουσα τὸν θεὸν ἀμφαγαπάζεται* [If it is of the soul (sc. the center), running around God she is cherished], or if with the Vatican [MS] you read: *εἰ δὲ ψυχή ἐστι περιθ. τ. θεὸν, ἀμφ.* [if it is the soul running around God, she is cherished].

**p. 203, 11. Καὶ Πλάτων κ. τ. λ. [And Plato, etc.]**
In *Timaeus* p. 34 and p. 40. Cf. Cleomedes, *Meteora* I. 3, and Balfour there, p. 297 sqq.

**— 17. ἡ δὲ αἰσθάνεσθαι πεφυκυῖα [and that which is by nature capable of perceiving]**
Sc. the power of the soul (*ψυχῆς δύναμις*). From Plato’s doctrine in the *Timaeus* concerning the rational soul and the inferior soul, subject to the senses and opinions. See p. 37, p. 44.

**p. 204, 2. ἐποχουμένη καὶ τῇ προτέρᾳ [riding upon also the former]**
*Incubans inferiori* [leaning upon the inferior], Ficinus; whence you might believe he conjectured *τῇ ποῤῥωτέρω* [the one further off], which is *more remote*, sc. from the superior. Or perhaps he translated it as if Plotinus, beginning from the lowest things, calls the *prior* that which is inferior. Concerning the use and construction of the verb *ἐποχεῖσθαι* [to ride upon], I have dealt at length in Plotinus I. 6. 56. F. in the special edition p. 340 sq.; cf. p. 52. E. *μορφὴν ἐπὶ ἄλλαις μορφαῖς ἐποχουμένην* [a form riding upon other forms], as if *equitant*, carried: a locution drawn from a ship, a chariot, or a beast of burden. Cf. Wyttenbach on Plutarch, *On the Delay of Divine Vengeance* p. 86, p. 271 of the new edition, and on the book *On the Fortune of Alexander* p. 126, and Coray on Hippocrates, *On Airs, Waters, and Places* p. 330. Moreover, the argument of this Plotinian chapter gains light from those things which he disputes elsewhere, especially in the book *On the Three Hypostases*. See, to use this, below V. 1. 8. p. 490 and p. 494. Furthermore, Brucker disputes concerning this passage, which we are now treating, in *Hist. Crit. Philos.* p. 409 sq.

**— 5. Κύκλῳ οὖν ἐκείνης περιεχούσης, συννεύουσα ἐπιστρέφεται κ. τ. λ. [While she encompasses in a circle, it turns, inclining toward her]**
Tiedemann, in the book *Geist der speculativen Philosophie* III. p. 293, notes Plotinus and Plato himself by this name, because they undertake to explain all things—even the motion and order of mundane bodies—from the powers and operations of the soul, adding, however, that the first traces of the doctrine of *Attraction*, learned many centuries later, lie hidden in these. But indeed, much more illustrious beginnings of this doctrine, which they call Attraction and even *Gravity*, appear in the *Phaedo* c. 60, in Aristotle, *On the Heavens* II. 13, and others, concerning which Wyttenbach has learnedly explained, refuting the errors of other more recent writers, both in his *Annotations on the Remains of Posidonius* p. 272 sq. ed. Bake, and in Plato’s *Phaedo* (loc. cit.) p. 296—298. Furthermore, very recently the most skillful man of arts, Inghirami, employed this passage of Plotinus in the work entitled *Monumenti Etruschi*, at table 33, in that part where he treats of earthenware vessels, p. 365.

**BOOK III.**

**P. 242, 7. ΠΕΡΙ ΤΟΥ ΕΙ ΠΟΙΕΙ ΤΑ ΑΣΤΡΑ [WHETHER THE STARS EFFECT ANYTHING]**
The fifty-second book, and accordingly one of the last which Plotinus composed, joined by its argument with his books *On Fate* and *On Providence*. See Porphyry, *Life of Plotinus* c. 24; who also in another place testifies that our philosopher, having detected that the predictions of astrologers were not worthy of belief, did not loathe to refute their presages in his writings (c. 15). You may compare, besides this book itself, these passages of Plotinus: p. 211 sq., 232, 263, 245, 275. Almost every philosopher, however, has touched upon this very opinion concerning either the power of the stars over human affairs or their impotence; as even Cicero’s books *On Divination* and *On Fate* can teach anyone. In which matter, members of the same family often differed from one another. Thus, to use this [example], among the Stoics, who otherwise attributed much to fatal necessity, Panaetius doubted concerning universal Divination. Cicero, *On Divination* I. 3: “But even the leader of this discipline—Panaetius—degenerated from the Stoics: yet he did not dare to deny that there was a power of divining, but said he doubted.” Cf. van Lynden, *On Panaetius* p. 70 sqq., and regarding the decrees of other Stoics on these matters, Baguet, *On Chrysippus* § XXXIX. sq. p. 94 sqq. But Cudworth has spared us the leisure of speaking universally about these views of the ancient philosophers in his excellent dispute...

...in the first chapter of his *Intellectual System* p. 2 sqq. ed. Mosheim. Eusebius preserved for us a fragment of Bardesanes the Syrian in *Praeparatio Evangelica* VI. 10. He no less attacks the astrologers. Hugo Grotius translated it into Latin, and Io. Conr. Orellius recently edited it with others, Leipzig 1824. And the translator Marsilio himself prefixed a copious diatribe to this Plotinian book, in which many things most worthy of reading are contained, although he also sprinkled other things which must be judged according to the character of that age, namely the fifteenth century. He profited most, however, from that brilliant *Oration against the Astrologers* by Favorinus the philosopher in Gellius, Book XIV. c. 1. Which is to be compared with Geminius of Rhodes, *Elements of Astronomy* cap. XIV. in Petavius’ *Uranologion* p. 55 sqq. (whom Delambre, in *Biographie Universelle* under *Geminus*, rightly praises by this name as a contemporary of Sulla, because he attempted to overthrow the faith of Astrology); and likewise with the learned dispute of Sextus Empiricus, *Against the Mathematicians*, fifth book, p. 337—355 Fabricius. Furthermore, Plotinus’ fellow-student Origen Adamantius, from the passage of Genesis I. 14, *that the lights were made for signs* (*εἰς σημεῖα γεγονέναι τοὺς φωστῆρας*), seized the handle for a prolix discussion; a great part of whose *Commentaries*, preserved by Eusebius in *Praeparatio Evangelica*, we now read with great profit in his *Works* Vol. II. p. 3 sqq. ed. Rue. In which place, attend primarily to these words 10. p. 15: "Let us see also a second argument, how the stars cannot be causative (*ποιητικοὶ*), but if anything, signifying (*σημαντικοὶ*), etc." and compare Huet p. 13 there, who says: “Whether the stars are *ποιητικὰ* or *ἀποτελεσματικὰ* [effective] of human affairs, or only *σημαντικὰ* [signifying], Plato doubted, and Seneca doubted. *Origen and his contemporary Plotinus embraced the latter opinion.*” Furthermore, cf. also the doubts which Lucian touched upon concerning the decrees of the astrologers in the book *On Astrology* § 27 sqq. p. 371 sqq. ed. Reitz, Amsterdam; no less what *Letronne* recently warned about the origins and vicissitudes of this system in the booklet: *Observations sur les Representations Zodiacales*, Paris 1824, p. 72 sqq. [There exists also a book by *I. M. Maraviglia, entitled Pseudomantia veterum et recentiorum explosa* (Ancient and Modern False Divination Exploded), Venice 1662, folio max., in which astrology is disputed in a special discussion of 80 pages.] — Augustine attacks this doctrine in *City of God* book V. c. 1. And in fact in this book Plotinus speaks several times in such a way that you might say he had either read Origen or certainly had him in view. Concerning which matter it will be spoken of in the annotation. But Philo Judaeus, before Origen and Plotinus, had touched upon the same passage of Moses in Genesis in his book *On the Creation of the World*, where both other things regarding this matter and that [passage are found] Vol. I. p. 36 Pfeiff.: "And now some have signaled by conjecture the commotion and earthquake of the earth from the motions in heaven, and ten thousand other things as most true, so that it might be said as most unerringly, that the stars were made for signs, and furthermore for seasons, etc." From which his opinion is already understood. Plotinus, however, to return here, undoubtedly looked primarily to the passage in Plato’s *Timaeus* p. 40, p. 41 Bekk., where concerning the stars [it says]: — "after which ones, which being in front of one another and to us at certain times, each are hidden, and appearing again send fears and signs of things to happen afterward to those capable of calculating—etc." We shall designate other passages in the annotation. Very many afterward applied themselves to the Platonic and accordingly Plotinian opinion. For, although Julius Firmicus in Book I of *Mathesis* blamed Plotinus on this account, because he was unwilling to acknowledge the power of the stars, others nevertheless went over to his side. Among whom Macrobius also makes mention of Plotinus, writing thus in Book I. c. 18 of the *Saturnalia*: — "the course of the stars themselves disposes the order of human affairs by power, as it seems to some, or, as it is certain pleased Plotinus, signifies it." And more clearly in *Dream of Scipio* c. XIX. end: “And Plotinus indeed in the book entitled *Whether the stars effect anything*, pronounces that nothing happens to men by their force or power; but those things which the necessity of the decree sanctions for each person are shown through the passage, station, or retreat of these seven, just as birds signify future things by their wings or voice while flying by or standing, being themselves ignorant: yet thus he shall rightly be called 'the salutary' or 'the terrible,' when through the former prosperous things, and through the latter inconveniences, are signified.” There is also the dispute of Nemesius of Emesa *concerning fate through the stars*, namely the thirty-sixth, p. 294—298 ed. Matthaei. Sallustius the Platonic philosopher also profited from this book in *On the Gods and the World*, chapter nine. Moreover, John of Salisbury in the *Policraticus* II. 19 (in *Max. Bibl. Patrum* Tom. XXIII. p. 267. D.) seems to touch upon this diatribe of Plotinus.

...where these things are read: — "But the Genethliaci [casters of horoscopes] insist too much on the divination of the knowledge of celestial things, and have lost the knowledge of the celestial things themselves as much as of God. Who nevertheless among them seem to excuse their error more suitably, since they do not withdraw from *Plotinus* the author of the works the authority for the creator, but assert that a law was instituted by him once and for all, which no effort ever voids, since all things which he disposed are to be, as he predicts." Yet I would not have conjectured from this (as *Frid. Christoph. Schlosser* does in the book entitled: *Vincent of Beauvais: Handbook and Textbook for Royal Princes and their Teachers* II. p. 68) that Plotinus himself was read by John, when the notice of this opinion could have been drawn from the cited passages of Macrobius, of whose books no one is ignorant how much they were frequented by the use of reading through the Middle Ages. In the fourteenth century another writer became famous, who likewise, when the evil of Astrology was recrudescing (as happens), deserved excellently by writing *Against the Astrologers*. Namely, *Henry of Hesse the elder*, who again brought the saner disciplines of Mathematics back into Germany. See Fabr. *Bibl. Lat.* lib. VIII. p. 656. B. Furthermore, in this doctrine for the most part Ptolemy and Plotinus agree very well, as Marsilio [Ficino] showed here and there in the Commentary on this book and as Augustinus Niphus also taught in the book *On Auguries*, Basel 1534, L. II. p. 107. *It is established that Ioannes Kepler*, that countryman of ours, said *that Astrology is the foolish daughter of a wise mother.*

**p. 242, 10. εἴρηται μὲν πρότερον ἐν ἄλλοις [it has been said before in other places]**
Namely in the books *On Fate* III. 1 and *On the Soul* IV. 3 and IV. 4. Origen begins a similar dispute thus in *Genesis* § 9. p. 13 Rue: "Come now, let us also contend concerning the fact that the stars are in no way causative of things in men, but only signifying." Augustine, *City of God* V. 1: “But if the Stars are said to *signify* those things rather than to *effect* them, so that that position is as it were a certain speech, predicting future things, not acting (for this was the opinion of men of no mediocre learning), the Mathematicians are not indeed accustomed to speak thus, as, for example, they might say 'Mars thus positioned signifies a murderer,' but 'effects a murderer.'” Etc. Where Augustine seems to have before his eyes Origen and Plotinus, whom he often praises. That the "Mathematicians" in such passages are the *Genethliaci*, there is no need for us to show laboriously. Sallustius the Platonic, *On the Gods and the World* c. 9. p. 34 Orellius: "teaching that the stars do not effect all things, but signify some only."

**p. 243, 7. κέντρων—καὶ ἀποκλίναντας [of centers—and those declining]**
Hence the *κέντρα* [centers/cardinal points] and *ἀποκλίματα* [declinations] of the Genethliaci. Those centers or hinges were the four above, from which they prepared predictions especially in births. The preceding sign (*προάγον*) of each of these hinges they called the declination (*ἀπόκλιμα*). See Sextus Empiricus, *Against the Mathematicians* V. 12—14 p. 340 and Fabricius there, who also added a diagram of the horoscope. Cf. also Fabricius’ *Prolegomena* to Marinus’ *Life of Proclus* p. XXIV ed. Boissonade, where the natal theme of Proclus is exhibited. Furthermore, consult especially Ptolemy’s *Tetrabiblos* lib. IV. near the end, and Porphyry’s *Introduction* to that book p. 197 ed. Basel 1559 folio.

**p. 245, 1. Ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἑκόντες—καὶ τοῖς σχήμασιν [But not willingly—and by the figures]**
Sallustius, *On the Gods and the World*: "If they speak of triangles and squares, it is absurd that the virtue of men remains the same, while the gods change according to their places." At that passage, Io. Conr. Orellius in the annotations (to which add Nicephorus Blemmydes, *Epitom. Physic.* c. 25 p. 204) p. 235 employed our passage. I would wish the readers of Plotinus to be warned of this: both in this entire book and in this chapter many things are touched upon which are read in Ptolemy’s *Tetrabiblos*. Thus, to use this, those things which were said in the previous chapter (the second) concerning the heat and coldness of the stars, compare those both with Ptolemy I. p. 17 sqq. ed. Basel Oporin 1535 8vo concerning the power of the planets. No less are other things of this chapter to be explained from the same astronomer’s cited book. For what Plotinus says a few words later: *οὐ γὰρ δὴ τοτὲ μὲν ἥδεται, τοτὲ δὲ λυπεῖται* [for surely it is not sometimes pleased and sometimes pained], and at the end of the page: *ὅλως δὲ οὐδὲ λυπεῖσθαι, οὐδὲ ἐπὶ καιροῦ χαίρειν αὐτοῖς δοτέον* [and altogether it must not be granted to them to be pained, nor to rejoice at a specific time]; and likewise at the end of the following chapter p. 139 C. *τὸ δὲ τόνδε μὲν χαίρειν κ. τ. λ.* [and that this one rejoices, etc.], compare Ptolemy in the cited book I. p. 51: "And they say that they (the planets) rejoice when, even if the familiarity of the surrounding signs is not toward them, nevertheless it happens thus through sympathy toward those of the same sects from of old." Which things the Anonymous Greek Interpreter, or rather Proclus, explains thus p. 49 ed. Basel Henr. Petr. 1559 folio: *λέγονται δὲ παρὰ ταῦτα πάντα χαίρειν, ὅταν ἐν ἀλλοτρίοις μὲν οἴκοις εὑρεθῶσιν, οὐ παντάπασι δὲ ἀλλοτρίοι*... [They are said besides all these things to rejoice, when they are found in alien houses indeed, but are not altogether alien to the places...]

...[they share in the same sect, as when Venus happens to be found in the house of Mars and vice versa Mars in the house of Venus.
