For unless they were found thus, they are not said to rejoice.”*

**p. 246, 6. εἰ ὥσπερ ὄρνισι κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς τὸ σημαίνειν [if as with birds signifying is by coincidence]**
Salmasius, *On Climacteric Years and Ancient Astrology*, Leiden 1648 p. 804 sq. thus: “More clearly Plotinus in the book, *Whether the stars effect anything*, pronounces, etc.” There follow the words of Macrobius in *Dream of Scipio* I. c. 19 end, which we exhibited above as far as the word *nescientes* [unknowing]; then Salmasius proceeds: “Thus Macrobius. Today this treatise is found in the books of Plotinus, *Whether the stars effect anything*. But other things which Macrobius has are not found there. He only says that they are *σημαντικὰ* [signifying], as divination happens from birds and other animals. Neither indeed is it true that the stars have that which Plotinus gives them, *τὸ σημαντικόν* [the signifying quality]. And by a certain prevarication it is certain that this is attributed to them.” Thus Salmasius. Justus Lipsius set down the same words of Macrobius in *Physiology of the Stoics* book II. c. 14 end (p. 587 *Opp.*), adding: “For it may rather be that the stars signify than effect, and Plotinus' assertion is more modest (than Manilius')—More modest, I said, not truer.” Origen also mentions birds in *Genesis* § 10. p. 17 Rue, disputing clearly in the opinion of Plotinus. The passage is rather long, wherefore I shall set down only the ends: "Why rather will things that happen be from the stars than from birds? — these things indeed will suffice for the present for the removal of the stars being causative of human things." Our author himself touches upon auspices below III. 1. 5. p. 232 B.: "likewise the birds would be causative of the things which they signify." Iamblichus, *On the Egyptian Mysteries* III. 16. p. 80 Gale, disputing concerning both the signs of birds and stars, proceeds thus: "It has therefore become clear through all the things said also this, that the gods, using many middle instruments, send the signs to men, etc." Eustathius in the *Odyssey* (3. 153. p. 83 Bas. cf. Gale loc. cit. p. 236) also uses the authority of Iamblichus regarding augural birds.

**— 10. τρίγωνος μὲν ὁρῶν—τετράγωνος [looking as a triangle—square]**
See concerning these aspects Ptolemy’s *Tetrabiblos* L. IV near the end and Porphyry in that book p. 201 ed. Basel 1559. Sallustius also touched upon these in *On the Gods and the World* chapter IX. p. 34. We transcribed the words above in the annotation on the beginning of cap. 3. At this place let it suffice to have added this: in a fragment of the Astrological Vettius Valens, of which there is a transcript in my books, one chapter is inscribed thus and begins thus: *περὶ ἀκουόντων καὶ βλεπόντων ζωδίων* [concerning signs that hear and see]. — "Likewise also concerning hearing and seeing signs it must be known from the ascensions; as follows etc."

**p. 248, 6. Οὐκ ἐπικουροῦντος κ. τ. λ. [Not helping, etc.]**
Concerning the double sense of this passage and concerning the probable opinion, so far indeed as can be seen in these shadows, Ficinus spoke in the Commentary above p. 116.

**— 12. Διὰ δὲ ὃν λέγουσιν κ. τ. λ. [And through whom they say, etc.]**
We have designated a remarkable transposition occurring in this place in the *Var. Lect.* Whether this is due to a confused double recension I would not say: but such things are detected in almost all writers. Ficinus explained the meaning of the passage, so far as was possible, both in the version and in the Commentary. Concerning the Planets universally, see Cleomedes, *Meteor.* I. 3. p. 21 sqq. ed. Bake with the interpreters p. 306 sqq. Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II. 20 and the annotation there p. 286 of our edition and Moser’s.

**—13. Πρὸς δὲ τὸν πυρόεντα καλούμενον τῇ κράσει [And toward the one called fiery by temperament]**
Perhaps *σύμφορος* [advantageous] has fallen out, or certainly it must be understood; as Ficinus also received it. Furthermore, Cicero (loc. cit.) thus: “But the next lower sphere to this one is held by *πυρόεις* [the fiery one], which is called the star of Mars etc.” Instead of *ἀλλοτρίως* [alienly], it seems *ἀλλότριος* [alien] should be read, if only on account of the following words.

**—14. Ἑρμῆς—πρὸς ἅπαντας—ὁμοιούμενος [Hermes—likened—to all]**
These respond exactly to these words of Ptolemy in the *Tetrabiblos* II. p. 87: "and he who has taken the lordship of Hermes, altogether being compared to whomever he is with, is made familiar to each of the others by their natures." To that passage the Interpreter thus p. 73: "For it has been found concerning Hermes that being common in nature he imitates the quality of those configured with him." It seems *συσχηματιζομένων* [configured with] should be corrected. Cf. also Porphyry’s *Introduction* to the same book p. 199.

**— 15. ἀναφορὰς ζωδίων ἀναμένει [awaits the ascensions of the signs]**
Sextus Empiricus, *Against the Mathematicians* V. 20. p. 341. — "for they do not think the stars have the same power for doing evil, or not, when viewed at the centers and...

...[upon the ascensions and the declinations, etc.] *“For they judge that the stars do not have the same power for acting badly or otherwise, if they are considered in the hinges and in the successions and in the declinations:”* where Fabricius rightly protected the common reading against Salmasius, who had introduced *ἐπαναφοραῖς* [successions] into the text, praising Sextus V. § 52, 53, 73 etc. And this passage of Plotinus, in which no book varies, argues that the ancient Astrologers used both [terms] concerning the same matter. Stephanus, from Budaeus p. 10010 ed. Valp. (to which these passages of Sextus and Plotinus must be added), explains thus: “That part of the heaven which is distant thirty parts from the Horoscope, existing in the second sign from that in which the horoscope begins, is called *ἀναφορὰ* [ascension], and sometimes *ἐπαναφορά*, as if a part just about to emerge.” Georg. Henisch on Proclus’ *Sphere*, Augsburg 1619 p. 201: “Astronomers [call] the ascents *ἀναφορὰς* in Greek, and descents *καταφοράς*.” Moreover, a chapter of Vettius Valens’ *Anthology* is inscribed exactly as we read in Plotinus: *περὶ ἀναφορᾶς τῶν ζωδίων* [concerning the ascension of the signs]. I shall transcribe the beginning from the transcript of Gronovius, which the late (*ὁ μακαρίτης*) Wyttenbach gave me as a gift. For it begins thus: "How many hours each sign ascends must be known from the ascension of each." The other fragment begins thus: "And to find the mid-heaven from the hand taking from the setting one according to the ascensions of the climate, until half of the diameter of these etc." And Valens frequents the word *ἀναφορᾶς* in these fragments of the *Genethliacal or Astrological Florilegium*, which Roether added from that transcript at the end of his edition of Io. Laurentius Lydus, *On the Months*, Darmstadt and Leipzig 1827 p. 334. Ptolemy frequents it no less in his Astrological books. Cf. only, to use this, sect. 25 of the *Karpos* or *Centiloquium*, which passage ought to be compared with the passages of Vettius Valens, and Porphyry in the *Introduction to the Tetrabiblos*, where also the Adverb *ἀναφορικῶς* [ascensionally] is used. See only p. 201. There exists also a book of Hypsicles of Alexandria, which is entitled *Anaphorikos*.

**p. 250, 3. τὸ αὑτοῦ περαίνειν καὶ ἐνεργεῖν τὰ αὑτοῦ [to accomplish its own and to act its own]**
After these words, Ficinus introduced these in the Latin: *“in which thereafter all things are similarly coordinated.”* Of which words no trace exists even in the Medicean books. And it is probable that he wished to express by these words the following *συντεταγμένον αὖ μετ’ αὐτοῦ* [coordinated again with it], but afterward, when he saw that those things were rather to be joined with the words *λύοντός ἐστι* [is of one releasing], he translated otherwise, and rightly indeed: *“in which he himself is counted.”* Wherefore we also ejected the comma before *λύοντος*, and included those prior Ficinic words in brackets.

**— 8. οὐ γὰρ ἂν ἐσημαίνετο τεταγμένως μὴ [for it would not be signaled in an orderly way unless]**
See *var. lect.* Furthermore, I ejected the comma between *τεταγμένως* [orderly] and *μὴ* [not], as Ficinus had also done, in whose first edition no comma exists between *procederet* and *singula*, which the Basel edition has.

**— 9. Ἔστω τοίνυν ὥσπερ γράμματα—σημασία [Let there be therefore as it were letters—signification]**
A passage in Geminius III. 1. 6. p. 233 B. brings light. — "But rather that these (the stars) are carried for the safety of the whole, but they also provide another use, that of looking into them as into letters so that those knowing such literature might read the future, from the figures according to the analogy methodizing the thing signaled." *“Or rather (it is better to say) the stars run for the safety of all (this is what Plotinus designates in our passage by these words—'and being moved, doing a certain work and another': namely the stars are moved so that they may provide varied use both for the whole and for individuals), but nevertheless they also provide another use, so that as they are skilled in such literature, they may look upon those as it were letters, and read future things, tracing the meaning from the figures according to analogy.”* (In our passage the Philosopher wishes these things to be understood by these words: *ἐπακολουθεῖτο δὲ τῷδε ἡ παρ’ αὐτῶν σημασία* [and let the signification from them follow this].) Sextus calls those figures or *σχήματα* in *Against the Mathematicians* V. 95 p. 353 *τοὺς τῶν ζωδίων τύπους* [the types of the signs]. In place of which images, as Fabricius observes on Sextus (loc. cit.), the masters of the Jews seemed to have found for themselves the characters of Hebrew letters. Plotinus is far from that perversity, who rather in this matter reflects in a certain way the character of Egyptian religions. For Thoth or Hermes of the Egyptians, who was believed to dispose and order the stars in heaven, and was held as the first master of astronomy, was said to be a sacred scribe himself, and accordingly to describe the sacred figures of letters (Hieroglyphs) in heaven, when he described the logic and order of the stars. Concerning which matter I said more in *Commentt. Herodot.* I. p. 353 sqq. and in *Symbolica et Mythologia* I. p. 373 sqq. second ed. But I said *in a certain way*, nor should that *ὥσπερ γράμματα* [as if letters] be neglected.

**100**
**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

Indeed, he only accommodates to his own purpose what was reported from antiquity, like a true *philosopher*. Moreover, those things which Origen in *Genesis* § 9. p. 15 Rue speaks thus are very similar: "For as we showed before, that nothing harms the argument concerning what is in our power that God foreknows the things to be done by each, so also the signs, which God appointed for signifying, do not impede what is in our power; but similarly to a book containing future things prophetically, the whole heaven can, being as it were the book of God, contain future things. Wherefore in the prayer of Joseph that which is said by Jacob can be understood thus, 'for I read in the tablets of heaven whatever will happen to you among your sons.' And perhaps also that, 'the heaven shall be rolled up as a book' (Isaiah 34. 4) indicates the signifying words contained of things to be, being about to be completed, and if I may say so, about to be fulfilled, just as prophecies are said to have been fulfilled by having come to pass. And thus the stars will be for signs according to the voice saying 'let them be for signs'." Before Origen and Plotinus, Geminius of Rhodes, as I warned above, had denied that the stars *effect* terrestrial things, events, character, and other human things; he had affirmed that they *signify*. I shall set down his passage here. For he [says] thus in the *Elements of Astronomy* (in Petavius’ *Uranologion*) p. 56: — "whence with the risings of the stars defined according to the seasons the changes of the air happen, not as the stars having power toward the change of winds and rains, but as being taken for the sake of a sign for us to foreknow the circumstances concerning the air. And as the torch itself is not the cause of the warlike circumstance, but is a sign of a warlike time; in the same way also the risings of the stars themselves are not the causes of the changes concerning the air, but are set out as signs of such circumstances." Then he excellently explains how ancient men were led to observe and record the prognostics of the weather. A writer also, either Platonic or Christian, in Fabricius’ *Bibl. Gr.* Vol. II. p. 516 sq. in the dialogue entitled *Hermippus*, denies that events are effected by the stars: he contends they are *pre-signified*; which opinion he also accommodates to the star seen by the Magi and to the eclipse at the death of Jesus Christ. Cf. also *Frid. Münter’s book: Der Stern der Weisen* p. 28 sq. Furthermore, *Tiedemann* in the book entitled: *Geist der speculativen Philosophie* III. p. 334 sqq. judges that Plotinus is not quite consistent with himself, who, while he acknowledges the universal power of the stars, nevertheless goes on to deny their power over the souls of men, namely so that he may vindicate free will for men as safe. Concerning which matter there is no need to dispute in this place.

**p. 250, 17. Τίς οὖν ἡ σύνταξις ἡ μία κ. τ. λ. [What then is the one coordination, etc.]**
In these, until the end of the Chapter, whoever does not feel that there is an accurate both understanding and description of that which today philosophers call *organic body* and *organic unity*, he would seem to be about to feel nothing at all, to use Cicero’s words in a not dissimilar place, where he speaks of the constancy and order of celestial bodies, *On the Nature of the Gods* II. 20. Yet I would not dare to pronounce that any philosopher before Plotinus penetrated so deeply into the nature and power of the *Organic*.

**p. 251, 12. Καὶ δὴ καὶ ψυχὴ—τοῦ κρατοῦντος [And indeed also the soul—of the one ruling]**
In this impeded passage, first that must be held, that the soul of the world is distinguished from the mind of the universe, the Gods, and the stars. These are moved in a circle, or always return to themselves through an orbit (cf. above II. 1. 1. p. 107 A. and the Annotation there): the soul of the world already is carried straight, i.e., she already leaves the orbit of the Gods, and proceeds to the procreation of external things. Hence she can also be *παράγεσθαι* [led aside], or driven transversely, and deflect from the right way. But nevertheless Justice (perhaps *ἕπεται* [follows] should be read with *καὶ—Δίκη* [and Justice] omitted) follows those things which are done in the Universe, unless it (the Universe) be dissolved. But it (the Universe) remains always as being ordered by the order and power of him who presides over it. Ficinus interpreted these later things otherwise, and it can be doubted which interpretation is true: that cannot be doubted which I put at the beginning, namely that circular motion is attributed to the universal Mind by the Platonists: to the Soul of the universe motion in a straight line, or motion tending outward.

**p. 252, 1. ποιεῖ δὲ—φανερῶς ποιεῖ [it effects—manifestly it effects]**
That is, the stars do not operate in a certain hidden way, e.g., so that they have power over the character of men, in the vicissitudes of states, etc., but they operate manifestly; for example, they have power over the temperature of the air, for stirring up winds, rains, etc. (which very thing however Geminius of Rhodes denied. See the passages cited above), and in moving the sea, as the moon, etc.

**— 7. Ἀλλὰ—ἐν ἄλλοις εἴρηται [But—it has been said in others]**
Namely II. 9, III. 1 (on Fate), VI. 8 (*περὶ τοῦ ἑκουσίου* [concerning the voluntary]).

**p. 252, 8. Νῦν δὲ ἀναμνησθέντες κ. τ. λ. [But now having remembered, etc.]**
Plotinus explains at length in c. 15. p. 145 sq. the same tokens (*tesseras*) of Plato described in book X of the *Republic* p. 616 sq., p. 506 sqq. Bekk. For the passage of Plato, employ Ast’s Commentary p. 630, who nevertheless does not mention Plotinus, and what I myself disputed in *Symbol. et Mythologia* I. p. 464 sqq. In this place let it suffice to have warned that these tokens were drawn by Plato from the books of the Egyptians or Pythagoreors. Mosheim, in *Cudworth’s Intellectual System* p. 7 note 5, received the Plotinian explanation no more favorably than he did the Platonic myth itself: “Plotinus, he says, wished to bring some light to this myth. But he himself clearly declares that it was unknown to him what it meant. Nor would I think anyone can declare its power and meaning firmly enough. For Plato’s entire opinion on fate is open to so many questions and doubts that it is incredible to say.” Thus he. The Homeric verb *ἐπικλώθουσι* [they spin/allot] (*Odyssey* γ. 208, α. 17), and not unknown to Plato (*Theaetetus* p. 169 C. p. 233 Bekk.: "by all means it is necessary to endure the fate concerning these things, which you might spin out, while being refuted"), was treated by Eustathius at this passage of the Odyssey p. 11 Bas. cf. the same at η. 197. p. 280 sq., Apollonius’ *Lex. Hom.* p. 385 Tollius and Jacobs. *Addit. ad Antholog. Palat.* p. XCV. But Tzetzes disputes about these Homeric things in his own way in *Exeges. in Iliad.* p. 33 sq. Porphyry in Stobaeus’ *Eclogues* II. 8. p. 366, looking to the same passage of Plato: "Atropos, she who makes the things spun out unchangeable."

**— 12. Ἔν τε Τιμαίῳ [And in the Timaeus]**
Namely p. 42 Steph. whence let us now hold these things also on account of the following: "first indeed it would be necessary for one perception to be born in all as innate from violent sufferings, second indeed love mixed with pleasure and pain, etc. Having bound all these things to them (the god did), so that he might thereafter be guiltless of the vice of each." Cf. *Republic* II. p. 379: "Neither then would God, since he is good, be the cause of all things, as the many say, but the cause of few things to men, and guiltless of many." We have already employed the passage in the *Theaetetus* p. 176 above for I. 8. 6. p. 70 sq. And that opinion of free will, established from Homer onward (*Odyssey* α. 37) by the common opinion of men, and handed down through the Pythagoreans (*Golden Verses* vs. 54, Hierocles there p. 184 Needh.) had reached Plato and his followers; while on the contrary the Stoics, because they were said to make God the author both of the good things that happened and the bad, were most sharply censured by their adversaries. (Plutarch, *Repugn. Stoicc.* p. 1064 C. seqq. Cf. Baguet, *On Chrysippus* p. 99 sqq.) Concerning Plato’s opinion, Plutarch speaks briefly in *On the Opinions of the Philosophers* I. 27. p. 884 extr. p. 560 Wyttenb.: "Plato admits fate indeed over human souls and lives, but he also introduces a cause from us." Nemesius treats it more diffusely in *On the Nature of Man* p. 303 sqq. ed. Matth. whence let us excerpt this decree of Plotinus: "For the things according to fate are not defined from eternity, but follow upon those things that preceded which are in our power; and this also agrees with 'the cause is of the one choosing, God is guiltless,' and 'virtue is without a master,' and that 'there is prophecy.'" Josephus is the author that the Pharisees established the same. For he [says] thus in *Antiquities of the Jews* XIII. 5. 9. p. 649 Havercamp: "the Pharisees indeed say that some things and not all are the work of fate, but some things are in our own power, and happen and do not come to be." No less among the philosophers of the Persians not a few acted with Plato in this cause. See *Sylvestre de Sacy, Notes sur Pend—Namèh ou le livre des conseils de Férid—Eddin Attar* p. 73, where that most learned interpreter rightly employed the passage of Plato from the *Timaeus*. I have thought these things should be sketched in few words, so that the sources and streams of the Platonic and Plotinian response in this most grave question, and indeed the similarities with the decrees of some oriental philosophers, might be recognized.

**p. 253, 1. ἢ ὅπερ ἐσμὲν κατ’ ἀλήθειαν ἡμεῖς [or that which we are in truth]**
These things are clearly diverse from the common opinion in these [lines] of *Iliad* α. 3 sq. "souls—but themselves [as] prey, etc." where bodies are "themselves." Nor is that of Plotinus in the following—*ὁ δὲ αὐτός* [but he himself]—any less diverse from the Homeric. On the contrary, both the reason and speech of the Indians is congruent with the Platonic. For to them the body is *Deha*, as you might say "contaminated," as those who teach that divine souls are polluted and contaminated in origin by the contagion of the body. See *Aug. Guil. Schlegel* in *Indische Bibliothek* II. 2. p. 230.

**— 3. ἀδέσποτον ἀρετὴν [virtue without a master]**
The most noble saying of Plato in *Rep.* X. p. 617 near the end p. 509 Bekk., and celebrated by the mention of many. See the passage of Nemesius in the preceding annotation, and cf. Apollonius of Tyana, *Epistle* XV. p. 390 Olear. and others, whom Ast summoned in the Commentary on Plato (loc. cit.)...

...p. 632; to which add Olympiodorus, *On the First Alcibiades* p. 226: "the ancient word saying that virtue is without a master and free. — wherefore the soul also is free as self-moving and by nature ruling." To which must be joined those things which are preached concerning virtue in Cicero’s *Paradoxes* III. 1. 22; and concerning the nobler soul not subject to the body, Aristotle, *On the Soul* I. p. 3 Sylb. and especially III. 4. p. 57 sq. should be consulted. Furthermore, Brucker at these things in *Hist. Crit. Philos.* II. p. 425: “Thus, he says, these inept philosophers corrupted all the heads of natural philosophy with their ideal trifles.” If such things are to be called trifles, then Plato, the God of philosophers, must no less be said to trifle. For my part, I shall set down such judgments of men here and there, lest I seem to fail in the duty of an interpreter. And given this occasion I shall add this besides. That Plotinus is obscure no one would deny, but it must be no less confessed that he was obscured by the fault of scribes. This very chapter proves it, which undoubtedly has several latent ulcers, into which we were unwilling to proceed by burning and cutting: and accordingly we have left most things untouched.

**p. 254, 9. τὰ δὲ δυσχερῆ, διὰ τὴν μίξιν—δαίμων, φησὶ, μέγας κ. τ. λ. [but the difficult things, through the mixture—a great daemon, he says, etc.]**
See Plato’s *Symposium* p. 202 Steph. p. 428 Bekk. "A great daemon. through this also all divination proceeds, and concerning all prophecy." Cf. also *Timaeus* p. 89 sq. and especially employ the twin passage of Plotinus III. 4. 3. p. 284, where there are more things concerning the daemon and concerning the power of the Gods and genii over us.

**— 255, 13. ἡ πανουργία ἐθέλει νοῦς εἶναι [all-craftiness wishes to be intellect]**
Porphyry in Proclus, *On the Timaeus* p. 335: "for Plotinus says that all-craftiness becomes an outflow of intellect for the one who receives it." Cf. the same in Plato’s *Republic* p. 378 where he praises the same words: likewise in *Alcib. I.* c. 12. p. 34 of our Frankfurt edition, where we praised Plato in *Phaedrus* c. 28. p. 248 p. 45 Bekker, and in that Hermias p. 151.

**— 256, 4. συνεργὸς δὲ ἥλιος [the sun is a helper]**
Anonymous in Hase, *Animadvv. in Io. Laur. Lydum de Ostentis* p. 313: "for this (the sun) has in itself the essence of all things, and for this reason some thought it to be mixed even with the nature of the four elements. It is the leader of the whole world, and generative of all things; generating moreover again it dissolves and takes back to the seminal logic (*σπερματικὸν λόγον*), giving to matter essence almost and life, but taking back in return the existence from above."

**—257, 2. ἄψυχα τῶν ἐν αὐτῷ πάντη ὄργανα [altogether soulless instruments of the things in it]**
Ez. Spanheim touched upon this opinion of several philosophers in the notes and in *Epreuves de Remarques in Julian’s Caesars* p. 234 and p. 100 at the end, not forgetful of the Plotinian passage.

**— 16. ὥσπερ στρατιώτας στρατηγῷ [as soldiers to a general]**
Plato in the *Phaedrus* p. 246 extr.: "Indeed the great leader in heaven, Zeus, driving a winged chariot, goes first, ordering all things and caring for them; and a host of gods and daemons follows him, ordered according to eleven parts."

**p. 258, 11. Περὶ δὲ πενίας, καὶ πλούτους, καὶ δόξας κ. τ. λ. [Concerning poverty, and riches, and glories, etc.]**
Similarly the philosopher of Lycopolis [Plotinus] below p. 231 sq. (III. 1. 5.) in a longer passage; whence I shall transcribe only these things: "How then does the relation of each toward the stars effect those things which are already said to be thus from fathers? For either those prior things will be the effecting ones, or if those do not effect, neither do these." Sallustius also treats this same argument more copiously in *On the Gods and the World* c. 9. p. 34 Orell.: "and to foretell the nobility or ignobility of fathers, as teaching that the stars do not effect all things, but only signify some." Cf. Chalcidius in Plato’s *Timaeus* p. 218: [p. 324 ed. I. A. Fabricius:] “From which it is given to be understood, not that the stars effect the things that come to pass, but that they announce future things.”

**p. 259, 7. συνεργὸν τὸ περιέχον γεγενημένον [the surrounding having become a helper]**
Concerning the accent of the word *συνεργὸς*, which there are those who write *σύνεργος*, see Bast’s *Epistle Crit.* p. 208 sq. and Reiz there cited *On Greek Prosody* p. 110, where you see there were those who believed these two words to be and to differ from one another. *τὸ περιέχον* is the heaven, the air, and its temperature. Cf. Schweigh. in *Lex. Polyb.* p. 466. Below at the end of this chapter *τοῦ περιέχοντος* is either to be accepted similarly, or explained concerning the matrix receiving the seed and containing the fetus. Which latter Ficinus seems to have felt.

**p. 260, 4. Ὁ δὲ Πλάτων [And Plato]**
See Book X of the *Republic* p. 616 Steph. and cf. annotation above at the beginning of cap. IX. p. 141. F.

**— 15. ὥσπερ γοητευθέντες [as if bewitched]**
Cf. IV. 4. 30., IV. 4. 40. and 43. and 44., II. 9. 14., V. 1, 2. Porphyry, *On Abstinence* I. 27. p. 44.: "the bewitchment of our stay here."

...Cf. Proclus in *Tim.* p. 44 and p. 330 and what I put at Plotinus above p. 57 and at Proclus in *Alcib. prior.* p. 257. For these Alexandrian Philosophers are wonderfully delighted by these metaphors and locutions, where they wish to describe souls enticed and corrupted by the allurements of earthly and sensible things. In the next parts Ficinus did not express the words *καὶ ἐκτὸς* [and outside], which nevertheless appear in the books: and I accept it so, that they refer to the preceding *τῶν τοῦ ὅλου καὶ ἔξω* [of the things of the whole and outside], in this sense: those nobler men raising themselves to sublime things and emancipating themselves from that mundane series of external things.

**p. 262, 12. Προηγούμενα [Things preceding/Principle things]**
Cf. below II. 3. 18. init. p. 147 G. and Annot. in I. 8. 1. p. 72 C.

**p. 264, 1. ὥστε ἓν ἐκ πάντων—ἐν τοῖς λόγοις [so that one from all—in the reasons]**
In this place I think a fault lies hidden, which Ficinus seems to have felt also, translating: *“otherwise they result from the matter itself.”* In the books there is no help. I suspect it should be read: *ἄλλως ἐκ θατέρων γιγνομένων*: “when things happen otherwise from the other [evil] things.” That *τὸ θάτερον* [the other] quite often, and especially among philosophers, has the significance of inconvenience, loss, or evil, Valckenaer taught in *Eurip. Fragmm. Diatrib.* p. 112; cf. also Heindorf at Plato’s *Euthydemus* § 24. p. 329. Furthermore, because Plotinus uses the word *σεισμοῦ* [earthquake] in the immediately preceding parts, there are examples of its use, not those indeed obvious to me in many places, but nevertheless I remember finding such in the writings of the philosophers. And, to use this, see the passage of Io. Chrysostom translated by Wesseling to Diodorus Siculus XIII. 97. p. 621, where *σεισμὸς* is figuratively used of goods dissipated as if by an earthquake. Also Theodoret in *Ezekiel* 38. 19. Vol. II. p. 1011 ed. Schulz: "he calls the magnitude of the thing a *σεισμὸν*" and says it can be accepted for a huge conversion of things, although he afterward prefers an earthquake to be understood. In such places, as here in Plotinus, that "Titanic" thing (*τιτανικόν*) must be thought of, which philosophers of this formula quite often use, when they undertake to describe the blind impetus of resistant *Matter*. See only Proclus in *Alcib. pr.* p. 43 sq. Concerning the figurative use of the word *σεισμὸς*, Schleusner also warned in the *Lexicon of the New Testament* under the word.

**— 4. ὁ γὰρ λόγος ἐν ὕλῃ [for the reason is in matter]**
Concerning these things Brucker in *Hist. Crit. Philos.* II. p. 425: “From this source Cudworth, loving this philosophy beyond measure, drew his generative nature.” Behold a charming critic, who in things exceeding the measure of his own wit, thinks he can prescribe the measure of love and study to such a great man!

**p. 265, 7. ὑποστάθμης—πικρᾶς, καὶ πικρὰ ποιούσης [of a bitter dregs/sediment, and making bitter things]**
Of a heavy, or bitter bilge, and rendering bitter things. Whenever the Platonists wish to describe the vices of matter and bodies, they often use metaphors repeated from the sea. *Πικρὸς* [bitter] however or *ἁλμυρὸς* [salty] is properly used of sea water. *Odyssey* ε’. 322. "bitter brine." Alcibiades in the Scholiast on Aristides in *Oratt. Platonn.* p. 162 ed. Frommel. — "by the waves of the sea—by most bitter streams." Plato, *Laws* IV. p. 704 Steph. concerning the sea "a salty and bitter neighborhood." Cf. Alcman’s *Fragments*, nr. 62 p. 66 sq. Welcker. Theodorus Prodromus imitated this in *To Manuel Commenus* vs. 12: "Scarcely having left the sea of salty cares." Cf. Coray in *Atakt.* at that page 110. Nilus the Ascetic or Ioannes Geometra *kephal. parain.* nr. XXIX. concerning life and the sea: "bitter breeders of beasts." Cf. Hemsterh. at Lucian, *Diall. Marinn.* III. p. 353 sq. Bip. Wyttenbach in *Bibl. Crit.* VII. p. 17 and what I myself gathered in the special edition of Plotinus, *On Beauty*, in the Appendix p. 79, p. 455 and especially p. 465 sq. Furthermore, in this place that it is the same as *κακὸς, πονηρὸς* [bad, wicked], the connection of the meanings argues; nor are examples lacking where both are joined. Thus, to use this, Theodoret in *Isaiah* XXX. 6. Tom. II. p. 305 Schulz: "for through the lion and the cub he has shown the bold; through the asps the wicked and bitter."

**— 12. οἷα τὰ τῶν ἰοβόλων [such as those of the venomous]**
There is added now *ζῴων* [of animals], now *θηρίων* [of beasts], yet often the word is used more elegantly without a substantive. Dioscorides, *Theriac.* init. p. 415 ed. Wechel: "concerning venomous animals (*ἰοβόλων ζῴων*) and deadly drugs." Cf. ibid. p. 417, where however perspicuity demanded *ζῴων*. For elsewhere the same Physician is accustomed to use *ἰοβόλα* elliptically, as ibid.: "and the one concerning venomous things is called theriac." Cf. p. 422 above: "but upon the venomous." Herodian moreover III. 9, 10. p. 649 sq. Irmisch uses the formula "venomous beasts" (*ἰοβόλων θηρίων*). Theodoret in *Isaiah* XXX. 6. Tom. II. p. 305 Schulz: "the prophetic word hinting at their great wickedness compared them not to cattle, but to venomous beasts." But Socrates in the *Eclogues* of Antonius and Maximus in Stobaeus p. 565 Gesn. and in...

   **P. 242, 7. ON WHETHER THE STARS ACT]**
The fifty-second book, and accordingly among the last which Plotinus wrote, but joined in argument with his books *On Fate* and *On Providence*. See Porphyry's *Life of Plotinus* ch. 24; who also testifies in another place that when our philosopher had discovered that the predictions of **Astrologers** were not worthy of trust, he did not hesitate to refute their omens in his writings (ch. 15). You may compare, besides this very book, these passages of Plotinus: p. 211 f., 232, 263, 245, 275. Moreover, almost every single philosopher has touched upon this same opinion regarding either the power or the impotence of the stars over human affairs; as even Cicero's books *On Divination* and *On Fate* can teach anyone. In which matter, members of the same school often diverged from one another. Thus, to use this example, among the Stoics, who otherwise attributed much to fatal necessity, Panaetius doubted universal Divination. Cicero, *On Divination* I. 3: "But even the leader of this discipline—Panaetius—deviated from the Stoics: yet he did not dare to deny that there was a power of divining; but said that he doubted." Cf. van Lynden on Panaetius p. 70 ff. and, regarding the decrees of other Stoics on these matters, Baguet on Chrysippus § XXXIX f. p. 94 ff. But Cudworth, in his excellent disquisition, has spared us the leisure of speaking universally about these views of the ancient philosophers...

A fragment of Bardesanes the Syrian <note>A Gnostic teacher from the 2nd century who wrote on fate</note> has been preserved for us by Eusebius in *Preparation for the Gospel* VI. 10. He likewise attacks the Astrologers. Hugo Grotius translated it into Latin, and it was recently edited with others by Johann Conrad Orellius, Leipzig, 1824. Furthermore, the translator Marsilio [Ficino] himself prefixed a copious <term>diatribe</term> <note>A lengthy scholarly discourse or critical discussion</note> to this book of Plotinus, in which there are many things most worthy of reading, although he also sprinkled in other things which must be judged according to the character of that age—namely, the fifteenth century. Moreover, he profited greatly from that brilliant "Oration against the Astrologers" by the philosopher Favorinus found in [Aulus] Gellius, Book XIV, chapter 1. This should be compared with Geminus of Rhodes’ *Elements of Astronomy*, chapter XIV, in Petavius’ *Uranologion* page 55 and following (whom Delambre, in the *Universal Biography* under the entry *Geminus*, rightly praises by this name because he was equal to Sulla and attempted to overthrow the credibility of Astrology); likewise with the learned disputation of Sextus Empiricus *Against the Mathematicians*, fifth book, pages 337–355, Fabricius edition. Furthermore, Plotinus’ fellow-student, Origen Adamantius, took the opportunity to discuss at length the passage from Genesis 1:14: <note>original: "εἰς σημεῖα γεγονέναι τοὺς φωστῆρας"</note> "let the lights be for signs"; a large part of his Commentary was preserved by Eusebius in *Preparation for the Gospel*, which we now read with great profit in his *Works*, Volume II, page 3 and following, edited by De la Rue. In that place, pay particular attention to these words in section 10, page 15: <note>original: "Ἴδωμεν καὶ δεύτερον ἐπιχείρημα, πῶς οὐ δύνανται οἱ ἀστέρες εἶναι ποιητικοὶ, ἀλλ’ εἰ ἄρα σημαντικοὶ κ. τ. λ."</note> "Let us see also a second argument, how the stars cannot be causative, but if anything, only significant [of future events], etc." and compare Huet on page 13 of the same work, who says: "Whether the stars are <term>poetic</term> <note>From the Greek 'poietika', meaning 'productive' or 'causative'</note> or <term>effective</term> <note>From 'apotelesmatika', referring to the completion of an influence</note> regarding human affairs, or only <term>significant</term>, Plato doubted, and Seneca doubted. *The later opinion was embraced by Origen and his contemporary Plotinus.*" For the rest, compare also the doubts Lucian touched upon regarding the decrees of the Astrologers in his book *On Astrology*, section 27 and following, page 371, Reitz edition, Amsterdam; no less the things which *Letronne* recently advised concerning the origins and changes of this reasoning in the booklet: *Observations on Zodiacal Representations*, Paris, 1824, page 72 and following. [There also exists a book by *I. M. Maraviglia, entitled "The False Divination of the Ancients and Moderns Exploded,"* Venice, 1662, in large folio, in which he disputes against Astrology in a specific discussion of 80 pages.]—Furthermore, Augustine attacks this doctrine in *The City of God*, Book V, chapter 1. And indeed, in this book Plotinus speaks several times in such a way that you might say he either read Origen frequently or certainly has him in mind. This matter will be discussed in the annotation. However, Philo the Jew, in his book *On the Creation of the World*, had touched upon that same passage of Moses in Genesis before Origen and Plotinus, where among other things on this subject he says (Volume I, page 36, Pfeiffer edition): <note>original: "ἤδη δὲ καὶ κλόνον καὶ σεισμὸν γῆς... εἰς σημεῖα γεγονόσι οἱ ἀστέρες..."</note> "already some have predicted by conjecture even the shaking and earthquake of the earth from the movements in heaven... it has been said most truly that the stars were made for signs, and furthermore for seasons, etc." From which his opinion is already understood. Plotinus, however, to return to the point, undoubtedly looked primarily to the passage in Plato’s *Timaeus*, page 40 and 41, Bekker edition, where concerning the stars it says: <note>original: "μεθ’ οὓς τινάς τε ἐπίπροσθεν ἀλλήλοις... φόβους καὶ σημεῖα τῶν μετὰ ταῦτα γενησομένων..."</note> "after which, as they come in front of one another... they send fears and signs of things that will happen hereafter to those who are able to calculate them—etc." We shall point out other passages in the annotation. Indeed, very many later writers applied themselves to the Platonic and thus Plotinian opinion. For although Julius Firmicus, in Book I of his *Mathesis*, reproached Plotinus on this account—that he refused to acknowledge the power of the stars—others nevertheless went over to his side. Among these, Macrobius even makes mention of Plotinus, writing thus in Book I, chapter 18 of the *Saturnalia*: "the courses of the stars themselves dispose the order of human affairs by their power, as it seems to some; or, as is established to have pleased Plotinus, they merely signify them." And more clearly in the *Dream of Scipio*, chapter XIX, at the end: "And Plotinus indeed, in the book entitled *If the Stars Act*, pronounces that nothing happens to men by their force or power; but those things which the necessity of decree sanctions for individuals are shown through the transit, station, or retreat of these seven [planets], just as birds, either by flying past or standing still, signify future things with their feathers or voice without knowing it: yet in this way, that one will rightly be called 'salutary' and that one 'terrible,' since through the former prosperous things, and through the latter inconveniences, are signified." There is also the disputation of Nemesius of Emesa *On Fate through the Stars*, namely the thirty-sixth, pages 294–298, Matthaei edition. Sallust the Platonic Philosopher also profited from this book in *On the Gods and the World*, chapter nine. Finally, John of Salisbury also seems to touch upon this diatribe of Plotinus in *Policraticus* II. 19. (in the *Great Library of the Fathers*, Volume XXIII, page 267. D.)

where these words are read:—"But the Astrologers <note>original: *Genethliaci*, those who cast birth charts</note> insist too much on the divination of celestial science; they have lost the knowledge of both the celestial beings themselves and of God. Yet among them, those seem to excuse their error more suitably who do not take away the authority of works from the creator with *Plotinus*, but assert that a law was instituted by him once and for all, which no effort ever voids, since all things which he disposed are to happen as he predicts." However, I would not conclude from this (as *Friedrich Christoph Schlosser* does in the book entitled: *Vincent of Beauvais: Handbook and Textbook for Royal Princes and their Teachers* II. p. 68.) that Plotinus himself was frequently read by John <note>referring to John of Salisbury</note>, since the latter could have drawn his knowledge of this opinion from the cited passages of Macrobius, whose books everyone knows were very frequently used for reading throughout the Middle Ages. In the fourteenth century, another writer became famous who likewise, as the evil of Astrology was recurring (as often happens), earned great merit by writing *Against the Astrologers*. Namely, *Henry of Hesse the Elder*, who brought the healthier disciplines of Mathematics back to Germany. See Fabricius, *Latin Library* book VIII. p. 656. B. Book II. p. 107. Moreover, it is well known that our countryman *Johannes Kepler* said that *Astrology is the foolish daughter of a wise mother.* <note>Kepler meant that the "foolish" astrology supported the "wise" astronomy financially.</note>
   **p. 242, 10. It has been said before in other places]** Namely in the books *On Fate* (III. 1.) and *On the Soul* (IV. 3. and IV. 4.). Origen begins a similar dispute in his commentary *On Genesis* §. 9. p. 13. edited by Rue: "Come now, let us also contend concerning the fact that the stars are in no way the causes <note>original: *poietikous*, 'makers' or 'producers'</note> of human affairs, but are only signs <note>original: *semantikous*</note>." Augustine, in *The City of God* V. 1. says: "But if the stars are said to *signify* those things rather than to *cause* them, so that this position is like a kind of speech, predicting the future but not acting (for this was the opinion of men of no small learning), the Mathematicians <note>Astrologers</note> are not indeed accustomed to speak in this way, as for example, to say 'Mars so positioned signifies a murderer,' but rather 'it makes a murderer.'" etc. Where Augustine seems to have before his eyes Origen and Plotinus, whom he often praises. That "Mathematicians" in such passages refers to Astrologers <note>original: *Genethliacos*</note>, we need not laboriously demonstrate. Sallustius the Platonist, in *On the Gods and the World* ch. 9. p. 34. edited by Orelli: "He teaches that the stars do not cause everything, but only signify some things."
   **p. 243, 7. centers—and declining]** Hence the "centers" <note>original: *kentra*</note> and "declinations" <note>original: *apoklimata*</note> of the Astrologers. Those centers or "hinges" <note>original: *cardines*</note> were the four points above from which they chiefly prepared predictions in birth charts. The sign preceding each of these hinges they called a declination. See Sextus Empiricus, *Against the Mathematicians* V. 12—14. p. 340. and there Fabricius, who also added a diagram of a horoscope. Cf. also Fabricius's Prolegomena to Marinus's *Life of Proclus* p. XXIV. edited by Boissonade, where Proclus's birth chart is displayed. Furthermore, consult especially Ptolemy's *Tetrabiblos* book IV. near the end, and Porphyry's *Introduction* to that book p. 197. Basel edition 1559. folio.
   **p. 245, 1. But not willingly—and by the figures]** Sallustius, *On the Gods and the World*: "If they speak of triangles and squares, it is absurd that the virtue of men remains the same, while the gods change according to their positions." To that passage, Johann Conrad Orelli in his notes (to which add Nicephorus Blemmydes, *Epitome of Physics* ch. 25. p. 204.) p. 235. applied our passage. I would wish the readers of Plotinus to be advised of this: both in this whole book and in this chapter, many things are touched upon which are read in Ptolemy's *Tetrabiblos*. Thus, to use this example, what was said in the previous chapter (the second) about the heat and coldness of the stars, compare those with Ptolemy I. p. 17. ff. Basel edition by Oporinus 1535. octavo, concerning the power of the planets. No less are other things in this chapter to be explained from the same Astronomer's cited book. For what Plotinus says a few lines later: "for surely it is not sometimes pleased and sometimes pained," and at the end of the page: "generally, we must not grant them either to be pained or to rejoice at a specific time"; and likewise at the end of the following chapter p. 139. C. Which the anonymous Greek interpreter, or rather Proclus, explains thus on p. 49. of the Basel edition by Heinrich Petri 1559. folio: "they are said, besides all these things, to rejoice when they are found in the houses of others, but not entirely alien..."

   **p. 246, 6. if, just as with birds, the signaling is accidental]** Salmasius in *On Climacteric Years and Ancient Astrology*, Leiden 1648, p. 804 ff. writes: “Plotinus speaks more clearly in the book *If the stars act*, etc.” There follow the words of Macrobius in *Commentary on Cicero's Dream of Scipio* I. ch. 19 at the end, which we provided above up to the word *unknowing*; then Salmasius continues: “Thus Macrobius. He only says that they are significant <note>original: *semantika*</note>, just as divination is made from birds and other animals.    **p. 248, 6. Not helping, etc.]** Concerning the double sense of this passage and the probable meaning, as far as can be seen in these shadows, Ficino spoke in his Commentary above on p. 116.

Ficino explained the meaning of the passage, as far as was possible, both in his translation and in his Commentary. On the planets in general, see Cleomedes’ *Meteors* I. 3. p. 21 ff. -> BOOK III. ENNEAD TWO. p. 246—250. <-
-> 99 <-

**concerning the risings and the declinations etc.** <note>original: "ἐπὶ ταῖς ἀναφοραῖς καὶ τοῖς ἀποκλίμασι"</note>
“For they [the astrologers] believe that the stars do not have the same power for doing good or otherwise, if they are considered in the cardines <note>The four 'hinge' points of a horoscope: Ascendant, Descendant, Midheaven, and Imum Coeli.</note>, in the successions, and in the declinations:” where Fabricius rightly defended the common reading against Salmasius, who had introduced "ascensions" <note>original: "ἐπαναφοραῖς"</note> into the text, citing Sextus [Empiricus] V. §. 52, 53. 73. etc. And this passage of Plotinus, in which no manuscript varies, proves that the ancient Astrologers used both terms for the same thing. Stephanus, following Budé p. 10010. ed. Valp. (to which these passages of Sextus and Plotinus should be added) explains it thus: “That part of the sky which is thirty degrees distant from the Horoscope, existing in the second sign from that in which the horoscope begins, is called the *rising* <note>original: "ἀναφορά" (anaphora)</note>, and sometimes the *ascension* <note>original: "ἐπαναφορά" (epanaphora)</note>, as if it were a part just about to emerge.” Georg Henisch in *On the Sphere of Proclus*, Augsburg 1619. p. 201.: “Astronomical ascents, in Greek *anaphoras*, and descents, in Greek *kataphoras*.” Moreover, the chapter of Vettius Valens's *Anthologies* is inscribed exactly as we read in Plotinus: *concerning the rising of the zodiac signs*. I will add the beginning from the transcript of Gronovius, which the late <note>original: "ὁ μακαρίτης" (the blessed/deceased)</note> Wyttenbach gave to me as a gift. For it begins thus: *how many hours each sign takes to rise must be known from the rising of each.* The other fragment begins thus: *to find the midheaven by hand, taking it from the setting sign according to the risings of the climate, until half of the diameter of these, etc.* And Valens frequently uses the word *rising* in these fragments of the *Genethliacal* <note>Relating to the casting of birth charts.</note> or astrological Florilegium, which Roether added from that transcript at the end of his edition of John Lydus's *On the Months*, Darmstadt and Leipzig 1827. p. 334. Ptolemy uses it no less frequently in his Astrological books. Compare also, to use this example, section 25 of the *Fruit* or *The Hundred Sayings*, which passage ought to be compared with the passages of Vettius Valens, and Porphyry in his *Introduction to the Tetrabiblos*, where the adverb *ascensionally* <note>original: "ἀναφορικῶς"</note> is also employed. See also p. 201. There also exists a book by Hypsicles of Alexandria titled *The Ascensional*.

**p. 250, 3. to accomplish its own and to act its own]** <note>original: "τὸ αὑτοῦ περαίνειν καὶ ἐνεργεῖν τὰ αὑτοῦ"</note> After these words, Ficino introduced these in the Latin: “*in which thereafter all things are similarly coordinated.*” Of these words, not even in the Medicean manuscripts does any trace exist. It is probable that he wished to express the following words with this phrase: *ordered again with it*, but then, when he saw that those words should rather be joined with the words *it is of one loosening*, he translated it differently, and indeed correctly: “*in which he himself is counted.*” For this reason, we have both removed the comma before *loosening*, and enclosed those earlier words of Ficino in brackets.

**— 8. for it would not be signified in an orderly way unless]** <note>original: "οὐ γὰρ ἂν ἐσημαίνετο τεταγμένως μὴ"</note> See the various readings. Otherwise, I have removed the comma between *orderly* and *unless*, as Ficino had also done, in whose first edition no comma exists between *procederet* and *singula*, which the Basel edition has.

**— 9. Let it be, therefore, just like letters—signification]** <note>original: "Ἔστω τοίνυν ὥσπερ γράμματα—σημασία"</note> Light is shed by a passage in Geminus III. 1. 6. p. 233. B.—*But rather as these (the stars) are carried along for the safety of the whole, they also provide another use: that those who know such 'grammar,' looking at them as if they were letters, may read the things to come, tracking the meaning from the figures according to analogy.* “Or rather (it is better to say) the stars run their course for the salvation of the universe (this is what Plotinus designates in our passage with these words—*and being moved, performing some work and another*: namely, the stars move to provide various uses for both the whole and the individuals), but nevertheless they provide another use, by which, as they are skilled in that kind of literature, they look up at them as if they were letters, and read future things, investigating the meaning from the figures according to analogy.” (In our passage, the Philosopher wants this to be understood by these words: *and the signification from them followed this.*) Sextus calls those figures or *schemata* in *Against the Mathematicians* V. 95. p. 353. *the types of the zodiac signs*. In place of these images, as Fabricius observed on the cited passage of Sextus, the masters of the Jews seemed to have found for themselves the characters of the Hebrew letters. Plotinus is far from such perversity; rather, in this matter, he reflects in a certain way the character of the Egyptian religions. For Thoth or Hermes of the Egyptians, who was believed to arrange and order the stars in the heaven, and was held to be the first master of astronomy, was himself said to be a sacred scribe, and thus to describe the sacred figures of letters (Hieroglyphs) in the heaven when he described the proportion and order of the stars. Regarding this matter, I have said more in *Commentaries on Herodotus* I. p. 353 ff. and in *Symbolism and Mythology* I. p. 373 ff. second edition. But I said *in a certain way*, nor should that phrase *just like letters* be neglected.

<meta>This page continues the scholarly annotations on Plotinus, specifically focusing on the distinction between the stars as "signs" versus "causes" of earthly events, and the nature of the "organic body" of the universe.</meta>

[[original page: 100]]

-> ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS <-

To be sure, as a true *philosopher*, he merely adapts to his own purpose those things which were handed down from antiquity. Moreover, the things which Origen says in his commentary on Genesis (§ 9. p. 15. Ruæus edition) are very similar, speaking thus: <note>original: "ὥσπερ γὰρ προαποδειξαμεν..."</note> "For just as we have previously demonstrated that God’s foreknowledge of what will be done by each person does not harm the argument concerning our free will, so neither do the signs which God appointed for signifying interfere with what is in our power; but similarly to a book containing future events prophetically, the whole heaven, being as it were a book of God, can contain the things to come. Therefore, in the *Prayer of Joseph*, what is said by Jacob can be understood in this way: 'For I read in the tablets of heaven whatever shall happen to you and your sons.' And perhaps also the phrase, 'the heaven shall be rolled up like a book' (Isaiah 34:4), indicates that the words contained therein, which signify things to come, will be completed and, so to speak, fulfilled, just as prophecies are said to be fulfilled by their outcome. And thus the stars will have been made for signs according to the voice saying: 'Let them be for signs.'" But before Origen and Plotinus, Geminus of Rhodes, as I mentioned above, had denied that the stars *produce* terrestrial things, events, character, and other human affairs; he affirmed that they *signify* them. I will set down his passage here. For he says thus in the *Elements of Astronomy* (in Petavius’s *Uranologion*) p. 56: <note>original: "ὅθεν ταῖς τῶν ἄστρων..."</note> "Whence, at the rising of the stars at defined seasons, changes in the air occur, not because the stars have power over the change of winds and rains, but because they are taken as signs for the sake of our foreknowing the circumstances concerning the air. And just as a signal-fire is not itself the cause of a state of war, but is a sign of a time of war; in the same way, the risings of the stars are not themselves the causes of changes in the air, but are set forth as signs of such circumstances." Then he excellently explains how ancient men were led to observe and record the prognostics of the weather. Also, a writer—either Platonic or Christian—in Fabricius’s *Greek Library* Vol. II. p. 516 ff., in the dialogue titled *Hermippus*, denies that the events of things are produced by the stars: he contends they are "foreshown" <note>original: "προσημαίνεσθαι"</note>; which opinion he also adapts to the star seen by the Magi and to the eclipse at the death of Jesus Christ. Cf. also *Friedrich Münter’s book: The Star of the Wise* p. 28 ff. Furthermore, *Tiedemann* in the book titled: *Spirit of Speculative Philosophy* III. p. 334 ff. judges that Plotinus is inconsistent with himself, since, while he acknowledges the universal force of the stars, he nevertheless goes on to deny their force over the souls of men, clearly so that he may preserve the free will of men. Concerning this matter, there is no need to dispute in this place.

**p. 250, 17. What then is the one coordination etc.]** In these lines, up to the end of the Chapter, there is an accurate understanding and description of what philosophers today call the *organic body* <term>organicum corpus: a system where parts work together for a whole</term> and *organic unity*. He who does not perceive this would seem to perceive nothing at all, to use Cicero’s words in a not dissimilar passage where he speaks of the constancy and order of the celestial bodies, in *On the Nature of the Gods* II. 20. Nor would I dare to declare that any philosopher before Plotinus penetrated so deeply into the nature and power of the *Organic*.

**p. 251, 12. And indeed the soul—of the ruler]** In this difficult passage, it must first be held that the soul of the world is distinguished from the mind of the universe, the Gods, and the stars. These move in a circle, or always return to themselves through an orbit (cf. above II. 1. 1. p. 107. A. and the Annotations there): the soul of the world now moves in a straight line, i.e., it now leaves the orbit of the Gods and proceeds to procreate external things. Hence it can even be "led aside" <note>original: "παράγεσθαι"</note>, or driven crosswise, and deflect from the right path. But nevertheless Justice (perhaps it should be read "follows" <note>original: "ἕπεται"</note> omitting "and Justice" <note>original: "καὶ—Δίκη"</note>) follows those things which are done in the Universe, unless the Universe be dissolved. But it remains always ordered by the order and power of him who presides over it. Ficino interpreted these later words differently, and it can be doubted which interpretation is true: but it cannot be doubted, as I stated at the beginning, that circular motion is attributed by the Platonists to the Universal Mind: and to the Soul of the universe, motion in a straight line, or motion tending outward.

**p. 252, 1. it acts—it acts manifestly]** That is, the stars do not work in some hidden way, for example, as if they had power over the morals of men, the vicissitudes of states, etc., but they work manifestly; for example, they have power over the temperature of the air, for stirring up winds, rains, etc. (which very thing, however, Geminus of Rhodes denied. See the passages praised above), and in moving the sea, as the moon does, etc.

**— 7. But—it has been said in other places]** Namely in II. 9., III. 1. (on Fate), and VI. 8. (on the voluntary).

-> BOOK III. ENNEAD TWO. p. 250—253. <-

   **p. 252, 8. Now having remembered, etc.]** <note>original: "Νῦν δὲ ἀναμνησθέντες"</note> Plotinus explains at length in chapter 15, p. 145 ff., these same "tokens" <term>tesseras: small tablets or tokens used as lots or identification</term> of Plato, which were described in the tenth book of the *Republic*, p. 616 ff. and p. 506 ff. in Bekker's edition. For the passage in Plato, consult Ast’s *Commentary*, p. 630—who, however, makes no mention of Plotinus—and the arguments I myself set forth in *Symbols and Mythology* Vol. I, p. 464 ff. At this point, it suffices to advise that these tokens were drawn by Plato from the books of the Egyptians or the Pythagoreans. Mosheim, in his notes on Cudworth’s *Intellectual System* (p. 7, note 5), was not as favorable toward the Plotinian explanation as he was toward the Platonic fable itself: “Plotinus,” he says, “wished to bring some light to this fable. But he himself clearly declares that he did not know what it meant. Nor do I think anyone can declare its force and meaning with sufficient firmness. Indeed, Plato’s entire opinion on fate lies open to so many questions and doubts that it is incredible to say.” So he writes. Furthermore, the word "spin upon" <note>original: "ἐπικλώθουσι" — referring to the Fates spinning the thread of destiny</note> is Homeric (*Odyssey* 3.208, 1.17), and was not unknown to Plato (*Theaetetus* p. 169 C, p. 233 Bekker: "In every way, one must endure the fate concerning these things, whatever you may spin out, while being tested"). Eustathius treated this in his commentary on this passage of the *Odyssey* (p. 11, Basel edition; cf. the same at 7.197, p. 280 ff.). See also Apollonius’s *Homeric Lexicon* p. 385 by Tollius, and Jacobs’ *Additions to the Palatine Anthology* p. XCV. Tzetzes, however, discusses these Homeric matters in his own fashion in *Exegesis on the Iliad* p. 33 ff. Porphyry, in Stobaeus’s *Eclogues* II. 8, p. 366, looking back at the same passage of Plato, speaks of: "Atropos, she who makes the things spun out unchangeable." <note>Atropos is the Fate who cuts the thread; her name literally means "unturnable" or "inflexible."</note>

   **— 12. And in the Timaeus]** <note>original: "Ἔν τε Τιμαίῳ"</note> Namely at p. 42 Stephanus, from which we should now hold these points even for the sake of what follows: "First, it would be necessary for one sensation to be innate to all from violent passions; second, love mixed with pleasure and pain, etc." And: "Having bound all these things together, [God] might then be blameless for the wickedness of each individual." Cf. *Republic* II, p. 379: "Therefore God, since he is good, would not be the cause of all things, as the many say, but the cause of few things for men, and blameless for many." We already applied the passage in the *Theaetetus* p. 176 above to I. 8. 6, p. 70 ff. And that sentiment of free will <term>liberi arbitrii</term>, established by the common opinion of men since Homer (*Odyssey* 1.37) and handed down through the Pythagoreans (*Golden Verses* line 54; Hierocles on the same, p. 184 Needham), had reached Plato and his followers; whereas, on the contrary, the Stoics were most sharply criticized by their adversaries because they were said to make God the author of both the good things that happened and the bad. (Plutarch, *On Stoic Self-Contradictions* p. 1064 C ff. Cf. Baguet on Chrysippus p. 99 ff.) On Plato’s opinion, Plutarch speaks briefly in *On the Opinions of the Philosophers* I. 27, p. 884: "Plato admits fate in regard to human souls and lives, but he also introduces a cause from ourselves." Nemesius treats this more diffusely in *On the Nature of Man* p. 303 ff. ed. Matthaei, from which we may excerpt this decree of Plotinus: "For what is according to fate is not determined from eternity, but follows upon those things which are first in our power; and this agrees with the saying: 'The cause is in the chooser, God is blameless,' and that 'virtue has no master,' and that there is prophecy." Josephus is the authority that the Pharisees decided the same. For so he says in *Antiquities of the Jews* XIII. 5. 9, p. 649 Havercamp: "The Pharisees say that some things, but not all, are the work of fate; but some things exist in our own power, to happen or not to happen." No less among the philosophers of the Persians did quite a few act with Plato in this cause. See *Sylvestre de Sacy, Notes on the Pand-Namah, or the Book of Counsels by Farid al-Din Attar*, p. 73, where that most learned interpreter rightly applied the passage of Plato from the *Timaeus*. I have chosen to sketch these things in a few words so that the sources and streams of the Platonic and Plotinian answer to this most serious question—and indeed the similarities with the decrees of some Oriental philosophers—might be recognized.

   **p. 253, 1. Or that which we are in truth]** <note>original: "ἢ ὅπερ ἐσμὲν κατ’ ἀλήθειαν ἡμεῖς"</note> These things are plainly different from the common opinion in these lines of the *Iliad* 1. 3 ff.: "souls—but themselves as prey, etc." where the bodies are "themselves." No less different from the Homeric view is that of Plotinus in the following—"but he himself." On the other hand, both the reasoning and the language of the Indians <note>referring to Hindu/Vedic philosophy</note> are congruent with the Platonic. For to them the body is *Deha*, as if you were to say "contaminated," inasmuch as they teach that souls, divine in origin, are polluted and contaminated by the contagion of the body. See *August Wilhelm Schlegel* in *Indian Library* II. 2, p. 230.

   **— 3. Virtue has no master]** <note>original: "ἀδέσποτον ἀρετὴν"</note> A most noble saying of Plato in *Republic* X, p. 617 near the end, p. 509 Bekker, and celebrated by the mention of many. See the passage of Nemesius in the preceding note, and cf. Apollonius of Tyana, *Epistle XV*, p. 390 Olearius, and others whom Ast cites in his *Commentary on Plato* at the same place.

To which add Olympiodorus in his *Commentary on the First Alcibiades*, p. 226: <note>original: "τοῦ παλαιοῦ λόγου λέγοντος τὴν ἀρετὴν ἀδέσποτον καὶ ἐλευθέραν.—διὸ καὶ ἡ ψυχὴ ἐλευθέρα ἐστὶν ὡς αὐτοκίνητος καὶ φύσει ἀρχική."</note> "the ancient saying that virtue has no master and is free.—wherefore the soul also is free, as it is self-moving and by nature fit for command." To these should be joined the things preached concerning virtue in Cicero’s *Paradoxes* III. 1. 22.; and regarding the nobler soul not being subject to the body, one should consult Aristotle’s *On the Soul* I. p. 3. (Sylburg edition) and especially III. 4. p. 57. and following. Furthermore, on these matters Brucker says in his *Critical History of Philosophy* II. p. 425: "Thus," he says, "these foolish philosophers have corrupted all the main points of natural philosophy with their ideal trifles." If such things are to be called trifles, then Plato, the God of philosophers, must no less be said to trifle. For my part, I shall place the judgments of men of that sort here and there, lest I seem to fail in my duty as a translator. And having this opportunity, I will add this besides: no one would deny that Plotinus is obscure, but it must be equally confessed that he has been obscured by the fault of the copyists. This very chapter proves it, for it undoubtedly has several hidden "ulcers" <note>A metaphor for textual corruptions or errors in the manuscript.</note> which we were unwilling to attack by burning or cutting; and accordingly, we have left many things untouched.

**p. 254, 9. But the difficult things, because of the mixture—a great spirit, he says, etc.]** See Plato’s *Symposium* p. 202. (Stephanus ed.) p. 428. (Bekker ed.). <note>original: "Δαίμων μέγας. διὰ τούτου καὶ ἡ μαντικὴ πᾶσα χωρεῖ, καὶ περὶ τὴν μαντείαν πᾶσαν."</note> "A great spirit <term>daemon: a mediating spirit between gods and men</term>. Through this all divination proceeds, and everything concerning prophecy." Cf. also the *Timaeus* p. 89. and following, and especially apply the twin passage of Plotinus III. 4. 3. p. 284. where there is more concerning the spirit and the power of the Gods and geniuses over us.

**— 255, 13. knavery wishes to be intellect]** Porphyry in Proclus’s *Commentary on the Timaeus* p. 335: <note>original: "καὶ γὰρ νοῦ φησιν ὁ Πλωτῖνος ἀπόῤῥοια γίγνεται πανουργία τοῦ δεξαμένου."</note> "For Plotinus says that knavery <term>panurgia: cleverness used for evil</term> becomes an outflow of the intellect in the one who receives it." Cf. the same in Plato’s *Republic* p. 378. where he praises the same words: likewise in *Alcibiades I* ch. 12. p. 34. of our Frankfurt edition, where we praised Plato in the *Phaedrus* ch. 28. p. 248. p. 45. **— 256, 4. and the sun is a co-worker]** An anonymous author in Hasium’s *Observations on John Lydus's On Omens* p. 313: <note>original: "οὗτος γὰρ (ἥλιος) ἔχει μὲν ἐν ἑαυτῷ τὴν τῶν ὅλων οὐσίαν... διδούς μὲν τῇ ὕλῃ οὐσίαν σχεδὸν καὶ ζωὴν, ἀνταπολαμβάνων δὲ τὴν ἄνωθεν ὕπαρξιν."</note> "For this (the sun) has in itself the essence of all things, and for this reason some thought it was mixed with the nature of the four elements. It is the leader of the whole cosmos, and the generator of all things; generating them, it again dissolves them and takes them back to the seminal reason, giving to matter almost its essence and life, and receiving back in return the existence from above."

**— 257, 2. entirely soulless instruments of the things within it]** Ezekiel Spanheim touched upon this opinion of several philosophers in his notes and in *Essays of Remarks on Julian’s Caesars* p. 234. and p. 100. at the end, not forgetting the passage in Plotinus.

**— 16. just as soldiers to a general]** Plato in the *Phaedrus* p. 246. at the end: <note>original: "ὁ μὲν δὴ μέγας ἡγεμὼν ἐν οὐρανῷ Ζεὺς... τῷ δ’ ἕπεται στρατιὰ θεῶν τε καὶ δαιμόνων..."</note> "The great leader in heaven, Zeus, driving a winged chariot, goes first, ordering all things and caring for them; and he is followed by an army of gods and spirits, ordered in eleven parts."

**p. 258, 11. Concerning poverty, and wealth, and reputations, etc.]** Similarly the philosopher of Lycopolis <note>Plotinus</note> below on p. 231. and following (III. 1. 5.) in a longer passage; from which I shall write down only this: <note>original: "πῶς ἂν οὖν ἡ ἑκάστου σχέσις ἐπὶ τῶν ἄστρων ποιεῖ ἃ ἤδη ἐκ πατέρων οὕτως ἔξειν λέγεται;..."</note> "How then does the relation of each person to the stars produce those things which are said to be held thus from one's fathers? (De la Rue ed.), clearly in the opinion of his fellow student. Sallustius also touched on these in *On the Gods and the World* ch. 9. p. 34. Cf. Chalcidius in Plato’s *Timaeus* p. 218: [p. 324. ed. I. A. Fabricius:] "From which it is given to be understood, that the stars do not make the things that happen, but foretell future things."

Cf. Schweighäuser in the *Lexicon to Polybius* p. 466. Below at the end of this chapter, "of the surrounding" is either to be understood similarly, or explained as the matrix receiving the seed and containing the fetus. Ficino seems to have felt the latter.

our delay in this place. <note>original: "ἐνταῦθ’ ἡμῶν διατριβῆς" (our delay here)</note> Compare Proclus in *On the Timaeus* page 44 and page 330, and what I have set down regarding Plotinus above on page 57, and regarding Proclus in *On the First Alcibiades* page 257. For these Alexandrian Philosophers are wonderfully delighted by these metaphors and expressions when they wish to describe souls that have been charmed and corrupted by the allurements of earthly and sensible things. In the following passage, Ficinus <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the influential Italian scholar who first translated Plotinus into Latin.</note> did not express the words "and outside," <note>original: "καὶ ἐκτὸς"</note> which nevertheless appear in the manuscripts; and I understand them as referring to the preceding words "of the whole and outside," <note>original: "τῶν τοῦ ὅλου καὶ ἔξω"</note> in this sense: those nobler men raising themselves to sublime heights and emancipating themselves from that worldly series of external things.
   **page 262, 12. Primary things]** <note>original: "Προηγούμενα" (Proēgoumena) - a Stoic term for preferred things.</note> Compare below II. 3. 18. at the beginning, page 147 G. and the Annotations on I. 8. 1. page 72 C.
   **page 264, 1. so that one from all—in the reasons]** <note>original: "ὥστε ἓν ἐκ πάντων—ἐν τοῖς λόγοις"</note> I believe a fault lies hidden in this passage, which Ficinus also seems to have sensed when translating: "otherwise they result from the matter itself." There is no help in the manuscripts. I suspect the reading should be: "when things happen otherwise from the other [evils]": <note>original: "ἄλλως ἐκ θατέρων γιγνομένων"</note> "when things happen otherwise from evils." Valckenaer, in *Diatribe on the Fragments of Euripides* page 112, taught that "the other" <note>original: "τὸ θάτερον" (to thateron)</note> quite often, and especially among philosophers, has the meaning of inconvenience, loss, or evil; see also Heindorf on Plato's *Euthydemus* § 24, page 329. Furthermore, as for Plotinus using the word "shaking" <note>original: "σεισμοῦ" (seismou)</note> in the immediately preceding lines, examples of its use are not many that I have come across, but I remember finding such things in the writings of philosophers. And, to use this example, see the passage of John Chrysostom translated by Wesseling in Diodorus Siculus XIII. 97. page 621, where "shaking" is used metaphorically for goods being squandered as if by an earthquake. Also Theodoret on Ezekiel 38:19, Vol. II. page 1011, Schulz edition: "he calls the magnitude of the matter a shaking" and says it can be taken for a huge revolution of affairs, although he later prefers it to be understood as an earthquake. In such places, as here in Plotinus, one must think of that "Titanic" element <note>original: "τιτανικόν" (titanikon)</note> which philosophers of this school quite often employ when they set out to describe the blind impulse of resisting *Matter*. See only Proclus in *On the First Alcibiades* page 43 ff. Regarding the metaphorical use of the word "shaking," Schleusner also noted this in his *Lexicon of the New Testament* under that word.
   **— 4. for the reason is in matter]** <note>original: "ὁ γὰρ λόγος ἐν ὕλῃ" (ho gar logos en hylē)</note> Concerning these things, Brucker says in *Critical History of Philosophy* II. page 425: "From this source Cudworth <note>Ralph Cudworth (1617–1688), an English Cambridge Platonist.</note> drew his 'plastic nature,' being excessively fond of this philosophy." Behold a charming critic, who imagines he can prescribe the limit of love and zeal to such a great man in matters exceeding the measure of his own intellect!
   **page 265, 7. of a bitter dregs—and making bitter]** <note>original: "ὑποστάθμης—πικρᾶς, καὶ πικρὰ ποιούσης"</note> Of a heavy, or bitter, bilge-water, and rendering things bitter. Whenever the Platonists wish to describe the vices of matter and bodies, they often use metaphors drawn from the sea. For "Bitter" <note>original: "Πικρὸς" (Pikros)</note> or "Salty" <note>original: "ἁλμυρὸς" (halmyros)</note> is properly used of seawater. *Odyssey* book 5, line 322: "bitter brine." <note>original: "ἅλμην πικρήν"</note> Alcibiades in the Scholiast on Aristides' *Platonic Orations* page 162, Frommel edition: "—by the waves of the sea—by the most bitter streams." Plato in *Laws* IV. page 704, Stephanus edition, says of the sea: "a salty and bitter neighbor." Compare *Fragments of Alcman*, no. 62, page 66 ff. Welcker. Theodorus Prodromus imitated this in his work to Manuel Comnenus, verse 12: "Having barely left the sea of salty cares." Compare Coray in *Atakta* on that page 110. Nilus the Ascetic or John Geometra in *Paradigmatic Chapters* no. XXIX, concerning life and the sea: "bitter breeders of beasts." Compare Hemsterhuis on Lucian's *Marine Dialogues* III. page 353 ff. Bipont edition; Wyttenbach in *Bibliotheca Critica* VII. page 17; and more which I myself gathered in the special edition of Plotinus *On Beauty* in the Appendix page 79, page 455, and especially page 465 ff. Furthermore, the connection of thoughts proves that in this place it is the same as "bad" or "wicked"; nor are examples lacking where both are joined. Thus, to use this, Theodoret on Isaiah 30:6, Vol. II. page 305, Schulz: "for through the lion and the cub he showed boldness; through the asps, the wicked and the bitter."
   **— 12. such as those of the venomous ones]** <note>original: "οἷα τὰ τῶν ἰοβόλων" (iobolōn)</note> Sometimes "animals" <note>original: "ζῴων"</note> is added, sometimes "beasts," <note>original: "θηρίων"</note> yet often the word is used more elegantly without a noun. Dioscorides in *Theriaca* at the beginning, page 415, Wechel edition: "concerning venomous animals and deadly drugs." Compare ibid. page 417, where however clarity demanded "animals." For elsewhere the same Physician is accustomed to use "venomous" elliptically, as ibid.: "and the one concerning the venomous is called the theriac [treatise]." Compare page 422 above: "but in the case of the venomous." Herodian, however, III. 9, 10. page 649 ff. Irmisch edition, uses the formula "venomous beasts." Theodoret on Isaiah 30:6, Vol. II. page 305, Schulz: "the prophetic word, hinting at their great wickedness, compared them not to cattle, but to venomous beasts."
