p. 266, 6. **ἐπὶ πᾶσι δὲ νοῦς δημιουργός** [And upon all is the demiurgic intellect]: Proclus in *Plat. Timæum* p. 93 sq.: "Plotinus the philosopher posits a double demiurge: one in the intelligible [realm], the other in the governing principle of the universe. And he speaks rightly." Next, he says that Amelius added a third artificer and posited three intellects (*τρεῖς νοῦς*) or three kings (*τρεῖς βασιλέας*). This he [Proclus] disapproves. No less does he disapprove that, after Amelius, Porphyrius—who thought himself to agree with Plotinus—called the super-mundane soul (*τὴν ψυχὴν τὴν ὑπερκόσμον*) the artificer (*δημιουργόν*), adding: "In which [works] does Plotinus make the soul the demiurge?" He argues that this can no more be reconciled with the decrees of Plato, who always calls God and intellect the artificer, but the soul never. Regarding the difference between the writings of Plotinus and Amelius, see Longinus in Porphyry's *Life of Plotinus* c. 20, p. 130 sq., ed. Fabricius. Cudworth, in *Systemat. Intell.* p. 637, ed. Mosheim, introduces the following words of Plotinus—**εἰκότως οὖν—καὶ κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς κινουμένου**—in this way: "Nor is Plotinus at variance with these (namely, Harpocation, Atticus, and Amelius, who had posited three Gods, vid. the cited passage of Proclus), who calls one of these three principles, namely *νοῦν*, or the first mind and intelligence, *δεύτερον θεὸν*, a second God:" (the passage of Plotinus V. 5. 3. p. 522 follows. Then Cudworth proceeds thus:) "In another place he makes mention of three Gods at once, and establishes that this world is the image of all these." (Our passage follows. From this, however, it is understood that Cudworth separates his own opinion from the authority of Proclus. For the rest, cf. VI. 9, 10 below, p. 769).

-> BOOK IV. <-

p. 282, 7. **ΠΕΡΙ ΥΛΗΣ** [ON MATTER]: This is the twelfth of all the books which Plotinus had written in succession, and it is praised in Porphyry's *Commentary on the Life of Plotinus* c. 24 under the title *περὶ τῶν δύο ὕλων* [on the two matters], with Fabricius also observing the diversity of the title in the aforementioned place, p. 141. Porphyry himself, however, had written six books *περὶ ὕλης* [on matter], as Suidas testifies in *Πορφυρ.* III. p. 158, ed. Kuster, which time has nevertheless snatched from us. That these served for explaining this very book of Plotinus is argued by a passage of Aeneas of Gaza in *Theophrastus* p. 56, ed. Casp. Barth: "and opening the book of Plotinus, where he says somewhere concerning nature, that matter is indeed unbegotten, and that to place it among the first principles is a doctrine to be rejected as atheistic." Concerning this passage, besides Barth, Lucas Holstenius had advised in *De Vit. et Scriptis Porphyrii* c. IX, p. 56, ed. Cambridge, and Io. Laur. Mosheim in *Dissert. de Creatione Mundi ex Nihilo* at the end of Cudworth's *Syst. Intell.* p. 995. A summary of those six books on Matter is exhibited by the same Porphyry's *Ἀφορμαὶ πρὸς τὰ νοητὰ* [Sentences leading to the Intelligibles], especially in sentence XXI. See what we have brought together on this matter above regarding *Enn.* I. 8. 5. init.

Indeed, there is no one who does not know that this passage concerning Matter has been treated in various ways since the origins of both so-called Barbarian and Greek philosophy down to the most recent times. On which matter we shall taste only a few things while simultaneously praising the writings from which lovers of ancient philosophy may seek more. And first, there is no need for me to explain here that the Indians, Chaldeans, and Persians disputed on this argument. You may best know the doctrine of the Indians from the most celebrated episode of the epic poem *Mahá-Bhárata*, which is titled *Bhagavad-Gítá*, specifically in the thirteenth song. See the edition of A. G. Schlegel and cf. the lecture of Wilhelm von Humboldt, Berlin 1826, p. 49. Porphyry, as Aeneas testifies in the cited place, had touched upon the decrees of the Chaldeans concerning Matter; nor is there any doubt that the same man touched upon the dogmas of other peoples as well. Among the Greeks, Timaeus Locrus (or whoever is the author of that booklet) p. 544 ed. Gale (p. 379 Bekker in *Platonis Operib.* P. III. Vol. III.): "ταύταν δὲ τὰν ὕλαν ἀΐδιον μὲν ἔφα, οὐ μὰν ἀκίνατον, ἀμόρφωτον δὲ καθ’ αὑτὰν καὶ ἀσχημάτιστον, δεχομέναν δὲ πᾶσαν μορφάν· τὰν δὲ περὶ τὰ σώματα μεριστὰν εἶμεν καὶ τᾶς θατέρω φύσιος. ποταγορεύοντι δὲ τὰν ὕλαν" [And he said that this matter is eternal, yet not motionless, and of itself formless and unshaped, but receiving every form; and that which is about bodies is divisible and of the nature of the Other. And they call matter...]

**τόπον καὶ χώραν** [place and space]. In these words are the seeds of many disputes which later occupied the families of philosophers. For this question was most vexed among the Platonists themselves: whether Matter is unbegotten (*ἀγέννητος*) or not. See above, Aeneas on the opinion of Porphyry. Add Gale on Iamblichus *De Myster.* p. 277: "If matter be unbegotten, there will be two first principles; if generated by God, whence comes what is base and evil?" Moreover, the primary passages of Plato on Matter are in the *Timaeus* p. 50 sq., p. 60 sqq. ed. Bekker, and likewise in the *Philebus* p. 24 and p. 25, p. 61 sqq. ed. Stallbaum; concerning which passages, as well as the opinion set forth in the *Sophist*, see Brandis's booklet on the lost books of Aristotle *On Ideas* and *On the Good*, p. 38 sq. and p. 63. Aristotle, in *De Generat. et Corrupt.* I. 1, accuses the obscurity of Plato no less than that of Timaeus Locrus: "ὡς δὲ ἐν Τιμαίῳ γέγραπται οὐδένα ἔχει διορισμόν" [As it is written in the Timaeus, it has no definition]. "What is written in the Timaeus (concerning Matter) has nothing certain and defined." Gale complains of the same in the cited place: "Furthermore, what Plato's opinion on matter was is certainly not clear enough in the Timaeus; for he seems to oppose matter to the Demiurge and distinguish it from him; yet in the Philebus he says explicitly that God showed 'the limit of beings, and the infinite' (τὸ μὲν πέρας δεῖξαι τῶν ὄντων, τὸ δὲ ἄπειρον). It is established that by 'the infinite' matter is understood. But that God of Plato is not the Demiurge, but of a higher order." Mosheim, on the contrary, in *Dissert. de Creatione Mundi ex Nihilo* at the end of Cudworth's *Syst. Intell.* p. 947, strives to defend Plato from Aristotle’s mark, adding: "Aristotle himself surely withdrew into the camps of those who would establish that matter is incorporeal (*ἀσώματον*), which this definition of his for Matter proves, which appears in *Metaphys.* VII. 3, p. 353: 'λέγω δὲ ὕλην ἣ καθ’ αὑτὴν, μήτε τι, μήτε πόσον, μήτε ἄλλο μηδὲν λέγεται, οἷς ὥρισται τὸ ὄν' [I call matter that which of itself is called neither a 'what', nor a 'how much', nor any other thing by which being is defined]." Cicero asserts that all philosophers after Plato held this very decree, that matter is incorporeal. For he says thus in *Acadd.* I. 7. 27, p. 45, ed. Goerenz: "But they think (the philosophers) that there is a certain matter subject to all things without any form of its own and lacking every quality, from which all things are expressed and fashioned: which can receive all things in their entirety and be changed in all ways and in every part: and therefore even perish, not into nothingness, but into its own parts, which can be cut and divided infinitely, since there is nothing at all in the nature of things so small that it cannot be divided," etc. Cf. Mosheim in the cited place, who says the same there concerning the decrees of Plotinus on Matter: "After Plato and Aristotle, innumerable philosophers embraced this dogma. Concerning the Stoics specifically, see Diogenes Laertius book VII, s. 134, p. 449. But especially the more recent Platonists, whom the contemplations of things secret from the body vehemently delighted, were diligent and laborious in polishing and adorning it. *Plotinus* ought to be read as the model for all in two very subtle booklets, *On matter* and *On the impassibility of things that are incorporeal*, the former of which is the *fourth* in the second Ennead, the latter the *sixth* in the third Ennead. Plotinus proves first in chapter 6 of the earlier book, p. 162: that there is a certain primary matter in all bodies: then in chapter 7 he refutes the opinions of others on matter: hence in chapter 8 he digresses to the affections of Matter to be explained, which in chapters 10, 11, 12 he proves to lack all quantity, in chapters 13, 14 to lack all quality—that is, to be incorporeal—and finally in chapter 15 he proves it to be *indeterminate*." Altogether, what Plotinus disputes below in III. c. 7 sqq. should be compared with this book, and we shall annotate there. Also contributing to the argument of this Plotinian book are the things Brucker disputes in *Historia Critica Philosophiæ* T. II, p. 426—431. To this join Tiedemann in the book: *Geist der speculativen Philosophie* III, p. 294, who, comparing *Ennead.* V. 1. 1. c. 2, opines that Plotinus, in embracing these opinions on Matter, departs from his own Plato and joins himself to Aristotle. Tennemann, however, in *Geschichte der Philosophie*, studied to reduce excerpts from the individual Enneads concerning the decrees on Matter into a certain order, Vol. VI, p. 119 sqq. Andreas Rudelbach also touched upon this tenet of the ancient philosophers concerning Matter in *Disquisitione de Ethices Principiis*, Copenhagen 1822, p. 107 sqq.; and finally no less Thomas Taylor, p. 41 of the English version of this Plotinian book in *Select Works of Plotinus*, Lond. 1817. For the rest, no one will repent comparing the *Expositionen der Physiologie* of Goerres (Landshut, 1805) with Plotinus regarding the decrees on Matter.

To these passages apply Schwebel on Lambert Bos, *De Ellips.* p. 52, p. 87 ed. Schaefer. The active *φέρειν* is used in similar sentences. Herodotus V. 118: "τούτου τοῦ ἀνδρὸς ἡ γνώμη ἔφερε" [the opinion of this man tended]. Cf. the *Lexic. Herodot.* of the venerable elder Schweighaeuser, p. 353. Dionys. Halic. *De Compos. Verbb.* p. 117 ed. Reiske, p. 238 ed. Schaefer: "ὡς ἡ ἐμὴ δόξα sc. φέρει" [as my opinion tends]. The same in *Judic. de Thucyd.* c. 35, p. 899, p. 164 ed. Krüger: "οὔτε πρότερον ὤκνησα τὰ δοκοῦντά μοι φέρειν εἰς μέσον" [nor did I previously hesitate to bring what seemed right to me into the middle]. The same in *Epist. ad Pompei.* p. 751, p. 5 ed. Krüger: "ὅσοι τὰς αὑτῶν ἐπινοίας εἰς τὴν κοινὴν φέρουσιν ὠφέλειαν" [as many as bring their own thoughts to the common utility]. Herodotus VIII. 100: "τοῦ στρατηγοῦ ταύτῃ ὁ νόος ἔφερε" [the mind of the general tended this way]. Moreover, that "τὴν αὐτὴν" signifies an imitator of Plato. For the philosopher says in the *Politicus* p. 277a: "νῦν δὲ κατὰ τὴν ἐμὴν οὕτω φαίνεται" [but now it appears so according to mine]. *Phileb.* p. 41a: "ἀλλ’, ὦ Πρώταρχε, εἰσὶ κατά γε τὴν ἐμήν" [but, O Protarchus, they are at least according to mine]. The same in the same place fully, p. 32: "κατά γε τὴν ἐμὴν δόξαν" [at least according to my opinion]. Concerning which ellipsis my [friend] Heusde treated learnedly, as is his wont, in *Specim. Crit. in Platon.* p. 102, and after him Stallbaum on the earlier passage of the *Philebus*, p. 121 sq. Therefore, in the words of Plotinus you might no less conveniently supply *δόξαν* (or *ψῆφον* [vote]. Cf. Fischer on Plato's *Politic.* 19, note 1) or from what precedes *ἔννοιαν* [notion]. Furthermore, the universal formula "τὴν αὐτὴν φέρεσθαι" should be recorded in Lexicons. Latinity offers an example of a similar ellipsis in these [words] of Cicero, *Verrin.* II. 2. 23. §. 74: "Verres refert illam suam Syracusanam;" where one should not add *rationem* [account] with Hotoman or Lambinus, but understand it.

p. 283, 1. **Καὶ δὴ καὶ τολμῶσι καὶ μέχρι θεῶν αὐτὴν ἄγειν. κ. τ. λ.** [And they even dare to lead it as far as the gods etc.]: Taylor, on this passage from the interpretation of Ficinus, conjectures that **καὶ ἀκρότατον αὐτῶν τὸν θεόν** [and the highest of them, God] should be read, a not ungraceful suspicion, yet not probable. For to say nothing of the testimony of the Manuscripts, which, as they vary somewhat, yet do not recognize "ἀκρότατον", Marsilius is accustomed to add such things six hundred times for the sake of clarity alone. And "ὁ τῶν θεῶν Θεὸς" is the highest God or Jupiter. Moreover, Plotinus touches here upon the Stoics and whatever other philosophers established nothing but the corporeal. For the Stoics both celebrated "ἄποιον τὴν ὕλην" [quality-less matter] (Diogen. Laert. VII. 134; Cic. *Acad.* I. 2; Senec. *Epist.* 65; Gell. *N. A.* V. 12; Lactant. *Div. Inst.* VII. 3) and reckoned not only Matter but God himself among bodies (Diog. in the cited place; Aristocles in Eusebius *P. E.* XV. 14, p. 816, who distinguishes the Stoic system from Plato thus: "the Stoics say fire is the element of beings, just as Heraclitus did, and the principles of this are matter and god, as Plato said. But these say both are bodies, both the agent and the patient [i.e., matter], whereas that former one [Plato] said the first efficient cause is incorporeal." Cf. also Cic. *De N. D.* I. 15, where he also treats the Jupiter of the Stoics, and see what we have placed there p. 67 sqq. Add Casaubon and Menage on the cited passage of Diogenes; Lipsius *Physiol. Stoicorr.* I. 4, II. 2, XV. 5, and the book of the learned Baguet on Chrysippus II. 31, p. 78, 87, 204 sqq. For the rest, Simplicius touched upon these and the following points of the Plotinian dispute in Aristotle's *Physics* p. 50b, ed. Venet. Aldin: "ἔτι δὲ καὶ τῷ αὐτὸ καθ’ αὑτὸ σκοποῦντι τὸ πρόβλημα ἀδύνατον δόξει τὴν πρώτην ὕλην τὸ ἄποιον εἶναι σῶμα, ὡς καὶ Πλωτῖνος ἐπέδειξεν" (perhaps *ἀπέδειξεν*) [and furthermore to one considering the problem itself by itself, it will seem impossible that primary matter is a quality-less body, as Plotinus also demonstrated]. Immediately following, where those who think quite differently are introduced with these words: **Οἱ δὲ ἀσωμάτου λέγοντες** [But those saying it is incorporeal], you will be able to think of the Pythagoreans, Peripatetics, and also the Platonists, as Marsilius also judges in his Commentary on this chapter.

p. 284, 5. **Ἔν τε τοῖς νοητοῖς τὸ σύνθετον ἑτέρως, οὐχ ὡς τὰ σώματα** [In the intelligibles the composite is otherwise, not as bodies]: Wyttenbach on Plato's *Phaedo* p. 197 sq.: "Moreover, what the Platonists mean by *σύνθετον*, a composite made of *parts placed outside parts*, as they are commonly called, filling space and extended, is understood from the frequency of examples: e.g., Plutarch *De Anim. Procreat.* p. 1022 E, *Adv. Stoicc.* p. 1085 C, Plotinus p. 160 C, D, E. (These are the very places) 161 C, D, 162 D, 163 E, 165 A, 166 E, 310 C, 313 E, 457 A, D, 466 A, C, 557 A; Albinus *Doctrin. Plat.* p. 372 D; Aeneas Gaz. p. 59, 66; Zachar. Mityl. p. 175; Olympiodorus in *Phaedon.* Cod. III. p. 40 and elsewhere often Cod. I. p. 63, 183. The reasoning is different when they call the soul a *σύνθετον*, a composite, from three parts: *λόγῳ, θυμῷ, ἐπιθυμίᾳ* [reason, spirit, desire], as the manuscript Hermias on the *Phaedrus* p. 437; or the whole man from *σώματι, ψυχῇ, νῷ* [body, soul, mind], as Plutarch *De Vultu Lunae* p. 943 A." Add Proclus *Inst. Theol.* §. 58 and 59, p. 92 sqq. our edition, where we cited both Aristotle's *Metaphys.* VII. 17, p. 132 ed. Sylburg, and Plotinus p. 604, and Proclus in *Platon. Theol.* VII. 12. Taylor translates the next word **λόγοι** as

p. 285, 6. **μὴ ὕλην εἰς εἶδος ἰδών** [not seeing matter into form]: Taylor attached himself to Ficinus, except that he did not express "εἴδη" [forms]. I have chosen to change nothing in this variety of readings, since the reading of the edition can be explained from the singular brevity of Plotinian speech, as if the writer had thought **εἰς εἶδος ἰοῦσαν**, matter going into forms. But nevertheless, since this reading does not have the certain authority of the written books, either **μὴ εἰς εἶδος ἰδών** or **μὴ εἰς εἴδη ἰδών** must be read. For that "εἶδος" or "εἴδη" ought not to be expunged is argued by what follows: **πῶς δὲ εἶδος**.

— 10. **Εἰ δὲ πολλὰ ὂν ἀμέριστόν ἐστι** [But if being many it is indivisible]: Taylor deems it necessary to write: **εἰ δὲ πολλὰ ἐν ὃν ἀμ. ἐ.** doubtless following the version of Ficinus, who has it thus: "*unum ens impartibile*" [one indivisible being]. But no Manuscript supports this, and Ficinus could have added this for the sake of clarity alone.

— 11. **ἐν ὕλῃ ἐστὶ ἑνὶ** [it is in one matter]: In this place, where most books have: **ἐστὶ τῷ ἑνὶ**, I would read with the same Ficinus **ἐστὶν ὡς ἑνί**. Next **πρὸ τοῦ ποικίλου**, which the margin with many Manuscripts has, is to be filled in such a way that you understand **εἶναι**. — Tennemann touched upon the argument of this chapter in *Hist. Philosoph.* VI, p. 105. Tiedemann, however, thinking he could refute these Plotinian points, strives against them in *Geist der specul. Philosophie* III, p. 409 sq. To me, for opening the mind of Plotinus, those things which Rudelbach placed in *De Ethices Principiis* p. 108, note 19, seem very appropriate: "'Ὕλη according to the mind of the ancient philosophers, is that which is discerned as the substratum of all things, or the primary, still unformed foundation from which the formation of things proceeds (Aristot. *Phys.* I. 8: 'τὸ πρῶτον ὑποκείμενον ἑκάστῳ, ἐξ οὗ γίνεται τι ἐνεργείᾳ ἀλλὰ δυνάμει' [the primary substratum for each thing, from which it comes to be in actuality but not in potentiality]), which just like the generative form is not generated (Aristot. *Metaphys.* XII. 3). In this sense, Timaeus Locrus called the Monad *γόνην* [offspring], but Anatolius called it *ὕλην* (*Theologum. Arithm.* p. 8). Matter, therefore, is never opposed to the mind, but always to the form, both being eternal dynamic principles of things. Giordano Bruno also, as we may note in passing, following the ancients, embraced this reasoning. (Vid. *Frid. Henr. Iacobi Werke* IV. 2. p. 19 sqq.)" For the rest, what Plotinus's own opinion on Matter is, some things from the earlier books signify, and what follows will declare. Iamblichus agrees with Plotinus in matter being attributed to the intellectual world, who says thus in *De Mysteriis* V. 23, p. 138 Gale: "Let no one wonder if we also say there is a certain pure and divine matter; for being generated from the father and creator of all things, it has acquired its own perfection suitable for the reception of gods," etc.

p. 288, 2. **παραγυμνωθέντα** [laid bare]: Cod. Ciz. **παραγυμνασθέντα**, whence perhaps you might conjecture **παραγυμνοσθέντα**. Certainly Dorville on Chariton IV. 5 init., p. 445 Leipzig [p. 403 ed. Amst.] preferred **παραγυμνωσθείς** to **παραγυμνωθείς**, where he disputes concerning this double form, but yet in the same place says that the former is more usual, nor do the rest of our books depart from the common reading. Examples of the proper meaning are at hand. See, to use these, Diodorus XVII. 60, p. 207 Wesseling; Herodian *Hist.* III. 9, 10; Dio Cassius XLIX. 6, p. 574 Reimar; Chariton IV. 1, where it is *not altogether to bare*; vid. Dorville p. 419 [p. 361]; add Moeris in *Δωριάζειν* and Pierson there p. 126. Herodotus frequently uses the figurative sense, as in I. 126: **παρεγύμνου τὸν πάντα λόγον** [he laid bare the whole account]. Cf. VIII. 19 and IX. 45; Polyb. I. 80. 9. The same in *Fragg. Grammatt.* 113 p. 97 Schweighaeuser: "ἡ δὲ τύχη—παρεγύμωσε τὰς ἀληθεῖς ἐπινοίας": "Fortune indeed laid bare true counsels." Chariton in the earlier place (II. 5, p. 96 Leipzig, p. 71 Amst.): "παραγυμνωθεὶς αὐτῷ καὶ τὸν ἴδιον ἔρωτα": "having made him privy to his own love." Cf. also Arrian's *Dissert. Epictett.* IV. 8. 32, p. 636 Schweighaeuser. Therefore, you might express the meaning of our passage thus: "And as for the points which, more than was relevant, were disclosed (or declared) concerning Matter in intelligible things, let these suffice thus far."

— 7. **ἐκ τοῦ παντελῶς μὴ ὄντος** [from that which is completely non-existent]: Brucker in *Hist. Crit. Philos.* II, p. 428: "For those (the Christians), being entirely different from the enunciative system and abhorring the impious dogma, established that matter was generated from no subject at all, neither internal nor external, and thus not even from the essence of God, but from absolutely no thing, by the free will and power of God; while on the contrary, the school of Ammonius, by necessary reason and the law of emanation, derived matter from the bosom of God, as all things else. For thus, if we follow Plotinus, who heard Ammonius himself, he thought it must be established: *From nothing, nothing is made*, (*which indeed*

p. 288, 10. **εἰ δὲ τοῦτο—ἕκαστον** [if indeed this—each]: Ficinus: "—from matter and form is *each perishable thing*." To be sure, in his thinking he repeats the adjective *φθαρτόν* [perishable] from the preceding *φθορὰ* [perishing]. For in the books this does not appear. Taylor translates: "*each sensible thing*." Moreover, the sentiment is to be compared with these in Plato's *Phaedo* c. 26, p. 36 ed. Wyttenbach: "ἆρ’ οὖν τῷ μὲν συντεθέντι τε καὶ συνθέτῳ ὄντι φύσει προσήκει τοῦτο πάσχειν, διαιρεθῆναι ταύτῃ ᾗπερ συνετέθη" [Is it not then fitting for that which has been put together and is by nature composite to suffer this, namely to be divided in the same way it was put together?].

— 12. **οἷον εἰ ἡ φιάλη εἰς τὸν χρυσὸν—ὕδωρ** [as if the bowl into gold—water]: Taylor advises that Plato and Aristotle also taught thus, namely that all metals can be resolved into water, and he praises these words of Albertus Magnus in Becher, *Physica subterranea* p. 319, 4to: "That no elemental thing is given in whose ultimate substantiation gold is not found."

p. 289, 1. **Ἐμπεδοκλῆς—αὐτῶν** [Empedocles—of them]: Our author in *Ennead.* V. 1. 9: "In Empedocles, strife indeed divides, but friendship unifies the one (*leg.* ἑνοῖ); and he himself also posits this (sc. the one) as incorporeal. But the elements [he posits] as matter." Cf. Io. Philoponus in *Aristotel. de Generat. et Corrupt.* I. p. 3a, p. 4a, b, II. 47a, 57b, 58a sq. and in *Aristot. de Anima* lib. I. fol. 41b and fol. 42a, and Aristotle himself *De Generat. et Corrupt.* II. 3, *Metaphys.* I. 4. Sturz gave more in *Empedocles* p. 227 sqq., p. 250 sqq. Who also p. 171 says thus: "For since the opinion stood for the philosopher (Empedocles) that all things arose from one, not from many, he thought the nature of one element, not many, should be attributed to that one. But to which element's nature he should most primarily attribute to that one, i.e., to the rude matter, a Pythagorean man could not much doubt. He said therefore that it has the nature of fire, so that *τὸ ἓν, χάος, ὕλη, πῦρ* [the one, chaos, matter, fire] *are to be held almost as synonyms*."

— 2. **Ἀναξαγόρας δὲ τὸ μίγμα ὕδωρ ποιῶν—νοῦν ἀναιρεῖ** [But Anaxagoras, making the mixture water—destroys mind]: We have given **Ἀναιρεῖ** [destroys] from the best book instead of *ἀναιρεῖν*, although even this could be defended. See only Sturz *Lex. Xenoph.* I. p. 194. — As to what is to be held regarding the matter, Plato noted this same inconsistency in these philosophers in *Laws* XII, p. 967, and especially rebuked Anaxagoras in the classic passage of the *Phaedo* p. 98a, at which passage Wyttenbach in his notes p. 258 sq. summoned Aristotle *Metaph.* I. 4

and other witnesses, and did not forget Plotinus; to which Ed. Schaubach in *Anaxagoræ Fragmm.* p. 106 added Proclus in *Tim.* p. 1, Simplicius in *Aristot. Phys.* p. 73, and others. Who in the same place p. 104—109 disputes thus: "For some think that air or ether, from the opinion of Anaxagoras, is the mind, and therefore it is called the most subtle (*λεπτότατον*) and the purest (*καθαρώτατον*) of all things. — But first, this does not follow from the passages — brought forward, then the passages cited above stand in the way, and finally Anaxagoras is often blamed by the ancients *because in explaining the nature of things he is inconsistent with himself, he uses mind only in individual cases, but otherwise calls on other causes, such as ether and air; whence it is clear that mind is distinguished from those*." Cf. what the same man p. 109 advised against Ritter (in: *Geschichte der Ionischen Philosophie* p. 250 sq.). Aeneas of Gaza, however, had our passage before his eyes in *Theophrastus* p. 57 sq. C. Barth: "but it is impossible to assume matter together with the Demiurge. Plotinus, investigating this matter very clearly, foretells this, and mocks Anaxagoras, because he did not foretell but introduced the Demiurge and matter together; but it is impossible [to be] together; for it is necessary that the maker be older than the thing made." For the rest, concerning the *νῷ* or mind of Anaxagoras, cf. Our author V. 1. 9. p. 480 A, which passage Schaubach in the cited place ought to have employed.

— 9. **διὰ πραγμάτων ἀνυνύτων** [through unachieved affairs]: "Through business that cannot be completed, and therefore is done in vain." In the form all our books agree, nor in Plato's *Gorg.* 507e, p. 133 Bekker, does any codex have the other **ἀνήνυστον**, but all have **ἀνήνυτον κακόν** [an unachieved/endless evil]. But both are obvious in the writings of later Greeks, as Lennep teaches on *Phalarid. Epist.* 96, p. 278. Plutarch *Pompei.* 30, p. 768: "φεῦ τῶν ἀνηνύτων ἄθλων": Alas for the unachieved/endless struggles! Dionys. Halic. *A. R.* VI. 5, p. 1046 Reiske: "τοῖς δὲ κάτωθεν ἐπιοῦσιν οὐδὲν ὅ τι μὴ πολλὰς πάνυ πληγὰς καὶ πόνους ἀνηνύτους ἔφερε": vain labors. Theodor. Metochit. *Miscellan.* c. 110, p. 726 sq.: "ἀλλ’ ὅστις ἆρα καὶ πεπείραται, ἢ κακῶς ἀπήλλαξεν ἢ ὡς ἀνήλυτα πονῶν ἠλέγχθη" (Read with Cod. Paris. **ἀνήνυτα**). Sext. Empir. III. 56, p. 143 Fabricius: "ἀνήνυτοί εἰσι παρὰ τοῖς δογματικοῖς στάσεις" [the disputes among the dogmatists are endless/unachieved].

— 12. **καὶ εἰ οὕτως ἄπειρον, ὡς ἀδιεξίτητον** [and if so infinite as to be unpassable]: This last word is read quite often in these Enneads, as VI. 6. 17, VI. 9. 6. Proclus *Inst. Theol.*

§. 94. p. 140 ed. nostr. Frankfurt: "καὶ εἴτι ἄλλο τοιοῦτον, ἢ διὰ τὸ ἀδιεξίτητον ἄπειρον ὑπάρχον, ἢ διὰ τὸ ἀόριστον τῆς οὐσίας" [and if there be any other such thing, either being infinite through being unpassable, or through the indeterminacy of its essence]; where I have placed these [notes]: "Aristotle in *Phys. Auscultt.* III. 7, p. 58 Sylburg: 'οὐκ ἀφαιρεῖται δὲ ὁ λόγος οὐδὲ τοὺς μαθηματικοὺς τὴν θεωρίαν, ἀναιρῶν οὕτως εἶναι τὸ ἄπειρον, ὥστε ἐνεργείᾳ εἶναι ἐπὶ τὴν αὔξησιν, ὡς ἀδιεξίτητον' [the argument does not deprive mathematicians of their theory, by denying that the infinite is such as to be in actuality in the direction of increase, as something unpassable]. For thus philosophers distinguished the infinite, so that **τὸ ἄπειρον** was either **ἀδιεξίτητον**, or **ποσὸν ὡρισμένον**, i.e., a quantity which either could not be penetrated, and thus not defined and circumscribed, or which could be circumscribed. Cf. Themistius in *Physs.* I. Hence Suidas I. p. 53 explains **ἀδιεξίτητος** as **ἀδιεξέλευστος**. Zonaras *L. Gr.* p. 47 adds **τὸ ἀπόρευτον** [the untraversable]."

p. 289, 17. **οὐδὲ αἱ ἄτομοι—αἱ τοπαράπαν οὐκ οὖσαι** [neither the atoms—which are altogether non-existent]: These agree word-for-word with Cicero's [words] in *De Nat. D.* I. 23: "You abuse the kingdom and license of atoms for all things; hence whatever comes into your mind, as they say, you fashion and effect. Which things primarily *are nothing.*" Where in the notes p. 103 we have placed these Plotinian points.

p. 290, 2. **ἄλλην τε φύσιν—δημιουργεῖν οὐχ οἷόν τε** [and another nature—it is not possible to fabricate]: Taylor translates thus: "*Again, it is not possible to fabricate any other nature, besides atoms from atoms.*"

— 7. **Τίς οὖν ἡ μία αὕτη καὶ συνεχὴς κ. τ. λ.** [What then is this one and continuous (matter) etc.]: In these and the next points, Tiedemann says in *Geist der speculativen Philosophie* III, p. 295, that Plotinus agrees with Aristotle and the Stoics, comparing the passage *Enn.* III. 6. 17 sqq. Taylor, however, at this place, separates his own opinion on Matter from Plotinus and joins him to Simplicius in Aristotle's *Physics*.

— 16. **μεμεγεθυσμένῳ** [magnified]: Eustathius on *Iliad* ν’. 588: "λέξεσι μεμεγεθυσμέναις" [with magnified words]. For it is also a word used by Grammarians. *Etymol. M.* p. 330 Heidelberg, p. 299 Leipzig, and p. 820. p. 743 Scholia on Dionys. Thrac. *Gramm.* (*Anecd.* Bekker, Vol. II, p. 928). To the passages of other writers add both this one of Plotinus and these from Theodorus Metochita c. 45, p. 272: "ὄγκοῖ δ’ ὅμως καὶ μεγεθύνει συγκιρνάμενον τὸ μεγαλοφυὲς καὶ τίμον. καὶ αἰδοῖον καὶ μηδόλως ὑπ’ εὐκολίας εὐπεριφρόνητον" [it swells and magnifies when the noble and precious is mixed, and reverend and not at all easily despised by ease].

p. 292, 4. **ἀσώματος δὲ καὶ ἡ ὕλη** [but matter is also incorporeal]: You might believe these are opposed to the Stoics. Stobaeus *Eclogg. Physs.* I. 12. 5, p. 324 Heeren: "οἱ Στωϊκοὶ σῶμα τὴν ὕλην ἀποφαίνονται" [the Stoics declare matter to be a body]. Cudworth touched upon this passage of Plotinus in *Syst. intellect.* p. 59, and Mosheim in his note 2 there.

p. 293, 5. **ὁ Πλάτων** [Plato]: In the *Timaeus* p. 52, p. 64 Bekker; where the philosopher, after he says that that which is always the same without origin and destruction can be known by intelligence (*νοήσει*), but the generated and sensible [can be known] by opinion together with the senses (*δόξῃ μετ’ αἰσθήσεως*), proceeds thus: "τρίτον δὲ αὖ γένος ὂν τὸ τῆς χώρας ἀεὶ, φθορὰν οὐ προσδεχόμενον, ἕδραν δὲ παρέχον ὅσα ἔχει γένεσιν πᾶσιν, αὐτὸ δὲ μετ’ ἀναισθησίας ἁπτὸν λογισμῷ τινι νόθῳ, μόγις πιστὸν, πρὸς ὃ δὴ καὶ ὀνειροπολοῦμεν βλέποντες κ. τ. λ." [and a third kind is that of space, which is always, not admitting destruction, but providing a seat for all things that have birth, itself being grasped without sensation by a certain bastard reasoning, hardly trustworthy, looking toward which we also dream, etc.]. But that entire passage from p. 50 all the way to p. 53 ought to be compared with our book, which indeed serves as an excellent commentary on it. For the rest, I will not gather from our passage that Plotinus read **ληπτὸν** [grasped] instead of **ἁπτόν** [touched] in his Plato. Alcinous also touched upon these in *De Doctrina Platonis* VIII, p. 472 sq.: "ταύτην (τὴν ὕλην) τοίνυν ἐκμαγεῖον τε καὶ πανδεχὲς καὶ τιθήνην καὶ μητέρα καὶ χώραν ὀνομάζει, καὶ ὑποκείμενον ἁπτὸν τε μετὰ ἀναισθησίας καὶ νόθῳ λογισμῷ ληπτόν" [This (matter) therefore he calls a molded mass, and all-receiving, and a nurse, and a mother, and space, and a substratum both touched with lack of sensation and grasped by a bastard reasoning]. Whence you might conjecture either that the passage of Alcinous was expanded from Plato, and that he wrote **ὑποκείμενον μετ’ ἀναισθησίας νόθῳ λογισμῷ ληπτόν** (like Plotinus), or that in Plato it should be read **μετ’ ἀναισθησίας ἁπτὸν λογισμῷ τέ τινι νόθῳ ληπτόν**. For the rest, cf. *Plat. Tim.* p. 28a.

— 7. **ἢ ἐν καταφάσει κ. τ. λ.** [either in affirmation etc.]: Taylor says it appears from the version of Ficinus that one should read: **ἢ ἐν ἀποφάσει τινὶ οὐν καταφάσει**, and that this emendation is required by the sense. When I consider the preceding things and that the *contraries of ignorance* (**τῇ ἀγνοίᾳ**) are joined here, I would think otherwise. Nor does any book confirm the suspicion. For the rest, concerning affirmation (*καταφάσει*) and negation (*ἀποφάσει*), see Aristot. *Analyt. poster.* I. 2, p. 200 Sylburg; the same *περὶ Ἑρμην.* c. 7, p. 61; Sext. Empir. *Pyrrh. Hypotyp.* I. 5 and there Fabricius p. 201 below; Suidas II. p. 268; Ernesti *Lex. Technol. Gr. Rhet.* p. 41 and p. 176; and cf. Proclus in *Alc.* I. p. 284 and p. 330, and Olympiodorus in the same p. 118, and Our author himself VI. 3. 19, p. 634 B, C.

p. 295, 11. **Εἰ δ’ ὅτι—κἀκεῖ ἀπαιτεῖ** [But if because—there also it requires]: Ficinus had translated *simply*, more to the sense. More closely to the words Taylor: "*if however because—some one should also this require in matter.*" We have rendered word for word. To the immediately

p. 296, 10. **Καὶ γὰρ τῶν μὲν ἄλλων ἀμεγέθων κ. τ. λ.** [For indeed of the other sizeless things etc.]: Brucker touched upon these in *Hist. Crit. Philos.* II, p. 420, advising: "Be careful not to confuse matter with body. For Plotinus acts here as a metaphysician, not a physicist, as does Porphyry who follows him in *De antro nympharum* p. m. 110 ed. Roman." See Porphyry, cited book, c. p. 297, 17. **καὶ οὐ κενὸν ὄνομα, ἀλλ’ ἔστι τι ὑποκείμενον** [and it is not an empty name, but there is a certain substratum]: Tholuck, in the book titled *Ssufismus* p. 184 sqq., teaching that these tenets of Plotinus on matter are to be properly distinguished from the mystic opinions of the Persians, writes thus: "For Fludd and the Platonists called matter *Nothing* or *Non-being* only in that respect that it lacked all qualities whatsoever; on the contrary, the Sufis declare without ambiguity that the *Deprived*, as they call it, is neither matter nor the place of matter." The same man in a note added in the same place: "Indeed, Plotinus deprives matter of all qualities, even extension, and maintains it only as the cause of the world: the dynamic presence (*πρὸς δυναμικὴν*) of all things in the divine intellect; nevertheless, one must distrust his Idealism. For although during the course of argument he places the origin of matter in the Deity, this seems to have been done more for the sake of consistent logic than by persuasion. For he pronounces matter to be not *Nothing*, but a substratum (*ὑποκείμενον*), both in other places and in *Enn.* II. 4. 12: 'ἔσται τοίνυν ἡ ὕλη—ὑποκείμενον—ἀμέγεθες' [Matter will therefore be a sizeless substratum]. How few genuine Idealists we have in antiquity besides the Eleatic discipline!"

p. 299, 11. **αὐτοετερότης** [self-otherness]: Analogy supports this word. Thus, to use this, in Dionysius Areopagite, *De Divinn. Nomm.* XII. 1, is read **αὐτοαγιότης** [self-holiness] and II. 1 **αὐτοαγαθότης** [self-goodness], to pass over others. Therefore, let it be added to the Lexicons.

— 15. **Ἄρσις γὰρ ἡ στέρησις** [For privation is a removal]: In parentheses I have added *sublatio* [removal], so that I might render it word for word; but the following **κατάφασις** [affirmation] argues that Plotinus wrote **ἄρνησις** [negation], which Ficinus also expressed and Taylor followed: *privation* (*privation*).

— 16. **τὸ γὰρ μὴ ποιὰ εἶναι** [for to not be qualified]: The reading of some good books **τῷ γὰρ κ. τ. λ.** is pleasing. For one must think **ὕλη ἐστίν**. "*Matter is this very thing, that it is not of a certain quality nor has form.*"

p. 300, 11. **τῆς μὲν ὕλης—τῆς τε αὖ στερήσεως ὡσαύτως** [of matter—and of privation likewise]: Taylor well: "*and to the definition of matter, indeed, he should adapt nothing of privation, and to the definition of privation, nothing of matter.*" I wonder that Ficinus in this place departed from his custom, by which he strives to serve clarity. Supply therefore by thinking: Likewise the account of Privation, which defines it, touching nothing of Matter (in the definition).

p. 301, 1. **ῥὶς ἡ σιμὴ καὶ τὸ σιμόν** [a snub nose and snubness]: Aristotle uses the same example in *Metaphys.* V. 1, p. 99 Sylburg. Our author himself uses the noun below in V. 9. 12.

— 15. **Εἰ μέντοι τῷ ἀορίστῳ εἶναι—εἶναι τῇ ὕλῃ ταὐτόν** [If however by being indefinite—it is the same as matter]: Lest perhaps you conjecture **τὸ ἀορίστῳ εἶναι—ταὐτόν**, supply to this **ἡ στέρησις** [privation], as Taylor did, who translates: "*But if privation, in consequence of being indefinite, infinite and without quality, is the same with matter, how will there be any longer two definitions?*"

p. 302, 14. **ἀπολεῖ αὐτοῦ τὴν φύσιν** [it will destroy its nature]: Taylor seems to have wanted **αὑτοῦ** [its own]. The same man advises on the next points of a passage of Proclus in *Theol. [For as much as Being is more akin to the One, so much more does it hide the multitude, and is defined only according to the Union itself. Plotinus and his followers seem to me to show these things often, making Being a multitude from form and from intelligible matter through the One and existence, but subjecting power by a corresponding proportion to matter]. For the more Being itself is near in kinship to the One, the more it conceals the multitude itself, and is defined according to the Unity itself only. These things Plotinus also seems to me to demonstrate quite often, making Being out of form and out of intelligible matter, subjecting multitude to the One and to substance, but the power, responding in proportion, to matter.

Taylor: "*to be infinite is not here.*" Word for word it is thus to be rendered: *to be for the infinite is not here.* The same translates and explains the next points thus: "*For it would be reason in order that it might be infinite, [i. e. would have a productive and forming*

P. 310, 7. **ΠΕΡΙ ΤΟΥ Ὁ ΔΥΝΑΜΕΙ ΚΑΙ ΕΝΕΡΓΕΙΑΙ** [ON THAT WHICH IS IN POTENTIALITY AND ACTUALITY]: The twenty-fifth book. See Porphyry's *De Vita Plot.* c. 24, p. 142 ed. Fabricius, where in the edited works it is titled thus: **περὶ τοῦ δυνάμει καὶ ἐνεργείᾳ**, with the **ὁ** omitted, which in this place is also absent from some of our books and from the passage of Simplicius which we shall soon summon. Plato quite often touches upon the notion of power (*δυνάμεως*), as in the *Sophist* p. 247 d, e; *De Rep.* V. p. 477 C. But the true source of the doctrine is in the Aristotelian writings, especially in *Metaphys.* VIII. 6 sqq. p. 147 sqq. Sylburg, p. 181 sqq. Brandis. For the use of students of philosophy, I will write down the clear words of Alcinous from *De Doctr. Platonis* c. 26, p. 511 ed. Heinsius, Lugd. Bat. 1614: "ὃ δὲ δυνάμει, τοῦτ’ ἔστι, τοῦ καθ’ ἕξιν καὶ κατ’ ἐνέργειαν λεγομένου διήνεγκε (perhaps **δυνάμει τοῦτ’ ἔστιν ὁ τοῦ καθ’ ἕξιν κ. τ. λ.**) τὸ μὲν γὰρ δυνάμει ἐπιτηδειότητά τινα ἀποσημαίνει πρὸς τινα οὕτω τὴν ἕξιν ἔχοντα· ὡς ὁ παῖς δυνάμει ῥηθήσεται, καὶ γραμματικὸς καὶ αὐλητὴς καὶ τέκτων, ἔσται δὲ τὸ τηνικάδε ἐν ἕξει, ἑνός τινος, ἢ δυοῖν τούτοιν, ὁπόταν μάθῃ καὶ κτήσεταί τινα τῶν ἕξεων· κατ’ ἐνέργειαν δὲ, ὁπόταν ἐνεργῇ ἀπὸ τῆς ἕξεως ἐκείνης, ἣν κέκτηται. τὸ δὲ δυνατὸν οὐδὲν τούτων. ἀόριστον δὲ ὃν τὸ ἐφ’ ἡμῖν, κατὰ τὴν ἐφ’ ὁπότερον ῥοπὴν λαμβάνει τὸ ἀληθεύειν ἢ μή." [But that which is in potentiality differs from that which is said to be according to habit and according to actuality... for the potential signifies a certain suitability toward someone having a habit thus; as a boy will be called potentially both a grammarian and a flute-player and a carpenter, and he will then be in the habit of one or two of these when he learns and acquires some of the habits; but in actuality, whenever he acts from that habit which he has acquired. But the possible is none of these. The 'in our power', being indeterminate, takes on being true or not according to the inclination toward either side]. Cf. also Proclus *Inst. Theol.* c. 77, p. 120 ed. nostr. and Nicolaus of Methone's *Refutation of the Inst. Theol. of Proclus* c. 77, p. 103 sqq. All these progressed from the Aristotelian passages cited. — For the rest, instead of **ἐνεργείᾳ** [in actuality], the Greek philosophers now use **συντελείᾳ** [completion], now **ἐντελεχείᾳ** [entelechy], now **ἀποτελέσματι** [effect]. Ocellus Lucanus c. 2 (in Gale's *Opuscc. Mytholl.* p. 517): "δυνάμει οὖν πάντα ἐν τούτῳ πρὸ τῆς γενέσεως, συντελείᾳ δὲ γενόμενα καὶ λαβόντα φύσιν" [therefore all things were in this in potentiality before birth, but in completion they have come to be and received nature]. Aristotle's *Metaphys.* III, p. 73 ed. Brandis: "τὸ γὰρ δυνάμει ὂν, καὶ μὴ ἐντελεχείᾳ, τὸ ἀόριστόν ἐστιν" [for that which is in potentiality, and not in entelechy, is the indeterminate]; and so very often in the same books. Sextus Empiricus *adv. Mathem.* X. 2. §. 340, p. 689 ed. Fabricius: "καὶ τὸ ὠὸν κατὰ δύναμιν μέν ἐστι νεοσσός, κατ’ ἐντελέχειαν δὲ οὐκ ἔστιν" [and the egg is a chick according to power, but according to entelechy it is not]; where cf. Fabricius. I would have believed that Cassiodorus imitated these things, who says thus in *De Anima* p. 342, ed. Paris. 1600: "It is produced like a parturial egg, where the life of the future bird and the pleasing variety of feathers are contained." Philo Judaeus, *Legg. Allegorr.* I, p. 64 ed. Mangey (p. 178 ed. Pfeiffer): "ὥσπερ γὰρ ἐν τῷ κηρῷ δυνάμει μέν εἰσι πᾶσαι αἱ σφραγῖδες, ἐντελεχείᾳ δὲ μόνη ἡ τετυπωμένη, οὕτω καὶ ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ κηροειδεῖ ὑπαρχούσῃ πάντες οἱ τύποι περιέχονται δυνάμει, ἀποτελέσματι δὲ κρατεῖ ὁ εἰς χαραχθεὶς ἐν αὐτῷ, ἕως μὴ ἀπαλείφεται (Mangey: "μὴ videtur redundare, aut forsan legendum οὗ vel ἄν." Nothing is to be attempted, and if you write *ἕως ἂν*, you must also [write] *ἀπαλείφηται*) ὑφ’ ἑτέρου ἐνεργέστερον (Cod. M. **ἐναργέστερον**) καὶ ἐκδήλως μᾶλλον ἐπιχαράξαντος (perhaps **ἐπιχαραχθέντος**)." [For just as in wax all the seals are there in potentiality, but in entelechy only the one stamped, so too in the soul, being like wax, all the types are contained in potentiality, but in effect the one engraved in it prevails, as long as it is not blotted out by another engraving more effectively and more clearly]. Concerning the Soul as entelechy according to Aristotle, see below IV. 2 init. p. 361 A.

p. 311, 1. **οὐ—ἐξείργεσθαι** [not—to be excluded]: Without doubt to be read with Ficinus **τῷ οὐ χρόνῳ ἐξείργασθαι** [by not having been worked out by time]. Otherwise it ought to have been written **τῷ (deleto οὐ) χρόνον ἐξείργεσθαι**: by that which is excluded by time, i.e., by that which time has no power over.

— 7. **Δεῖ τοίνυν—λέγεσθαι** [It must therefore—be said]: Ficinus seems to have read: **δεῖ τοίνυν ὃ δυνάμει τί ὂν—μεθ’ αὑτὸ δύναται—μετὰ τὸ ἐκεῖνο ποιεῖν—δυνάμει λέγεσθαι**. Simplicius in Aristotle's *Physics* p. 90b ed. Ald. Venet., after he had exhibited these and the preceding points, proceeds thus: "He who said these things says at the end of the book that matter is in potentiality only, being nothing in actuality of things that are. But perhaps, wishing the first being to be form, he wishes being to reach as far as the forms. Wherefore matter, having fallen out from the forms, is also cast out from being; and for this reason, being non-being, it is in potentiality only what it is, although both the potential and the so non-being has not yet completely fallen out from being. Entirely, if it were in potentiality such as to change into actuality, as water into stars, matter would perish; which he does not wish." For the rest, Aristotle uses the same examples in part, as of bronze, a statue, etc. in the cited place *Metaphys.* VIII. 7, p. 149 Sylburg.

p. 323, 7. **ΠΕΡΙ ΟΥΣΙΑΣ ΚΑΙ ΠΟΙΟΤΗΤΟΣ** [ON ESSENCE AND QUALITY]: The seventeenth book, but joined by argument with those that precede in this Ennead. It is titled variously. In Porphyry's *De Vita Plot.* c. 4, the edition only recognizes: **περὶ ποιότητος** [on quality]: but in chapter 24 the same has: **περὶ ποιότητος καὶ εἴδους** [on quality and form]. The title of our book in the edition exhibits: **περὶ οὐσίας καὶ ποιότητος** [on essence and quality]: some books have: **περὶ οὐσίας ἢ περὶ ποιότητος**. The word **οὐσίας** [essence] was already known to the ancient Italian philosophers, as Archytas in Stobaeus *Eclogg.* I. 43, p. 712 Heeren: "καὶ τὸ καθ’ ὅλῳ ὠσίας τε καὶ εἶδος μεταδίδομεν" [and we impart essence and form according to the whole]. Ocellus in the same place p. 424: "ἅ τε μὰν ὠσία τῶν πραγμάτων ἀνέκβατος καὶ ἀμετάβλατος" [the essence of things is indeed without exit and unchangeable]. Plato had this passage before his eyes in the *Cratylus* p. 401 C, where he simultaneously pursues the etymology of essence (*οὐσίας*) in two ways. Plato was the first to innovate the word quality (**Ποιότητος**). For he says thus in the *Theaetetus* p. 182a: "Ἴσως οὖν ἡ ποιότης ἅμα ἀλλόκοτόν τε φαίνεται ὄνομα, καὶ οὐ μανθάνεις ἀθρόον λεγόμενον" [Perhaps then quality seems at once a strange name, and you do not understand it when spoken all at once]. Whence Cicero in *Acadd.* I. 7. 26: "*I have therefore called them qualities, which the Greeks call ποιότητας: which word among the Greeks is not a word for the common people, but for philosophers.*" Cf. Schol. on the cited passage of Plato; Ruhnken on Timaeus's *Lex. Platon.* p. 24 and Heindorf on the cited passage of the *Theaet.* p. 423. The passages of Plato, both the cited and others, provided the occasion for Plotinus to dispute, among them this one in the *Epistles* (VII) p. 343, p. 463 ed. Bekker: "τὸ δὲ μέγιστον, ὅπερ εἴπομεν ὀλίγον ἔμπροσθεν, ὅτι δυοῖν ὄντοιν, τοῦ τε ὄντος καὶ τοῦ ποιοῦ τινος, οὐ τὸ ποιόν τι, τὸ δὲ τί ζητούσης εἰδέναι τῆς ψυχῆς, τὸ μὴ ζητούμενον ἕκαστον τῶν τεττάρων προτεῖνον τῇ ψυχῇ λόγῳ τε καὶ κατ’ ἔργα, αἰσθήσεσιν εὐέλεγκτον τό τε λεγόμενον καὶ δεικνύμενον ἀεὶ παρεχόμενον ἕκαστον, ἀπορίας τε καὶ ἀσαφείας ἐμπίπλησι πάσης ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν πάντ’ ἄνδρα κ. τ. λ." [But the greatest thing, which we said a little before, that whereas there are two things, being and a certain 'what sort', and the soul seeks to know not the 'what sort' but the 'what', each of the four offering to the soul what is not sought by word and by deeds, providing each thing always easily refuted by the senses both when spoken and shown, fills every man, so to speak, with every doubt and obscurity, etc.]. For that whole passage is to be compared. Alcinous also, in *De Doctrina Platonis* c. 11, p. 481 sq., posits and explains that qualities are incorporeal, as a decree of Plato; it begins thus: "Καὶ μὴν καὶ αἱ ποιότητες τούτου τὸν τρόπον δεικνύοιντ’ ἂν ἀσώματοι" [And indeed qualities also would be shown to be incorporeal in this way]. There are quite a few passages of Aristotle concerning Essence (**οὐσίᾳ**) both in purely physical books, like *De Generatione et Corruptione* I. 2, *De Sensu et Sensibili* c. 4, and in metaphysical ones, like IV. 5, VII. 8, XIV. 2 and 3; and concerning Qualities, the classic passage is in the *Categories* c. 6, p. 40 sqq. where he posits four kinds of quality: One, habit and affection (disposition, **ἕξις καὶ διάθεσις**); the second, containing all those things which are named from natural power or faculty and its contrary (from **δυνάμει ἢ ἀδυναμίᾳ φυσικῇ**); the third kind, in which are found passive qualities and disturbances, affections (**παθητικαὶ ποιότητες καὶ πάθη**); the fourth kind of quality, he adds, is figure and the form which is in each thing, likewise straightness, crookedness, and similar things (**σχῆμα, μορφὴ, εὐθύτης, καμπυλότης καὶ εἴ τι τούτοις ὅμοιον**). Simplicius, in his Commentary, injects a mention of Plotinus at this passage of the Stagirite. For thus on folio 19b he advises: "Both Plotinus and those around Nicostratus raise a doubt regarding the account of essence: how is essence one genus? For if there were something common to both the intelligible and the sensible, it will be before both and will be predicated of both, and it is clear that it will be neither body nor incorporeal, so that body does not become incorporeal, and the incorporeal become body." The same on folio 20b: "the name of matter and form and the things signified by these were not familiar to the common people, but some say matter, and others form is essence rather. How then does Plotinus say that the three are equally called essences? etc. For this reason (**διὰ τοῦτο**) Archytas also characterized essence by being 'according to itself'." Cicero also, in *Academics* I. 5 sqq., reduces the doctrine of form, matter, and qualities from the books of the Greek philosophers into a shorter summary; which he begins thus (c. 5 §. 24): "*Concerning nature, however—they spoke thus (the ancients), so that they divided it into two things: so that one was the efficient cause, but the other as if offering itself to this, and from it something was effected. In that which effected, they thought there was force; in that which was effected, a certain matter: yet in both, both. For neither could matter itself have cohered if it were not contained by some force, nor force without some matter—for there is nothing which is not compelled to be somewhere. — But that which [arose] from both, they already called body and a certain sort of quality.*" etc. Then he adds more concerning qualities. I shall not add more here, but I wish the readers to be summoned to Cudworth's *Systema intellectuale*, where on p. 10 sq., p. 58 sq., and p. 907 sq. ed. Mosheim many things from the disputes of the ancients are brought forward and examined. You may find what later philosophers down to the Scholastics discussed concerning qualities, partly following Aristotle

and other authors, partly by themselves, briefly indicated in Morhof's *Polyhistor* Tom. II. lib. II. part II. c. 7 and 8, p. 299—312 ed. Fabricius. For the rest, this booklet of Plotinus should be compared not only with the previous one, especially p. 167, where he had said that matter is neither quality nor has it, but also with others, especially, as Ficinus already saw, with that which is titled *On the Genera of Being.* Compare especially VI. 3. 16, p. 631 sq.

— 9. **ἀπηρημαμένων τῶν ἄλλων** [deprived of others]: He took this from Plato, who says thus in *Sophist* p. 237d, p. 171 ed. Bekker: "and this is now clear to us, that we also speak this word 'something' regarding a being each time; for to speak it alone, as if naked and deprived of all beings, is impossible." Which passage is altogether to be compared with our own. Plutarch *Lycurg.* cap. 9, p. 80 ed. Alberti: **ἀπερημάσαι· ἀπῳκῆσαι** [to be deprived: to have been removed], where Abresch reads **ἀπερημῶσαι. ἀποικίσαι** [to deprive: to remove]. In our author this verb recurs soon after in II. 6. 3 and below in VI. 8. 11. med.

p. 325, 11. **ὅθεν καὶ ἀμαρτάνειν ἡμᾶς ἀεὶ κ. τ. λ.** [whence also we always err etc.]: The dissertation in the Epistles usually attributed to Plato (VII, p. 342 sq.) pertains here; whence I added a small piece above at the Inscription of this book. For the rest, for these and the following points, which are more difficult, apply Ficinus's Commentary.

p. 326, 17. **καὶ ἀντιτυπίας** [and resistance]: i.e., renitency, which arises from the greater or lesser hardness of bodies. See what I have advised above concerning the word **ἀντίτυπος** at II. 1. 7, p. 101 C. For the understanding of our passage, these [words] of Sextus Empiricus in *Pyrrhon. For they say a point is that of which there is no part; but a line is length without breadth; but a surface is length with breadth. Such are—both whiteness and blackness—and the body is called white by having received whiteness.—Whiteness and blackness and other colors are not called affective qualities in the same manner as those mentioned, but by the fact that they themselves have arisen from an affection.” On these matters, compare Simplicius fol. 66. ### LIB. VII. [BOOK VII]

P. 333, 7. **ΠΕΡΙ ΤΗΣ ΔΙ’ ΟΛΩΝ ΚΡΑΣΕΩΣ** [On Mixture Through All]: The thirty-seventh book (Porphyry, *On the Life of Plotinus*, ch. 24, p. 142, Fabricius), but correctly placed in this location by Porphyry, as it approaches closely in argument to the preceding ones. The doctrine of *Mixtio* [Mixture] and *Temperatio* [Tempering], however, was treated early in the schools of the Greek philosophers, as those who began philosophizing did so from the question of the origin and destruction of things, with which that other [question of mixture] is most closely joined. Wherefore, from Thales onwards, philosophers eagerly investigated *Mixture and Tempering*; their decrees are found in the work attributed to Plutarch, *On the Opinions of the Philosophers* [De Placitis Philosophorum], I. 17, p. 554, ed. Wyttenbach, and in Stobaeus’s *Eclogues*, I. 18, p. 368 ff., ed. Heeren. Cf. also Empedoclean verses 130, 133, and Sturz p. 575; and Parmenidean passages (in Brandis’s *Commentaries on the Eleatics*) p. 129. Yet it seems that Plato, especially in the *Timaeus* p. 56, p. 71 ff., ed. Bekker, as well as Aristotle, the Stoics, and indeed no less the Sceptics, provided Plotinus the occasion to touch upon this matter. And first, Aristotle in the *Topics*, IV. 2, p. 323, ed. Sylburg, says: “...further, if he has placed the genus into the species; as for example *synapsis* [joining] as *synochē* [continuity]; or *mixis* [mixing] as *krasis* [tempering]; or as Plato defines *phora* [locomotion] as movement according to place; for it is not necessary for joining to be continuity; but on the contrary, continuity is joining; for not everything that touches is held together, but that which is held together touches. Likewise also in other cases; for not every mixing is tempering. For the mixing of dry things is not tempering. Nor is every change according to place locomotion.” The classic passage of the Stagirite is *On Generation and Corruption*, I. 10, where (p. 32, ed. Sylburg) these are distinguished: *synthesis* [composition], *auxēsis* [growth], *krasis* [tempering], *mixis* [mixing], and this definition of mixture is subjoined (p. 33): “Mixture is the union of mixed things which have been altered.” The Stoics later followed these traces, teaching thus (as found in Stobaeus, l. l.): **Διαφέρειν παράθεσιν, μίξιν, κρᾶσιν, σύγχυσιν** [That apposition, mixing, tempering, and confusion differ]. They called *Appositio* [Apposition] the contact of bodies at their surfaces, as in heaps of grain; *Mixtio* [Mixture], the diffusion of two or more bodies through the whole while their qualities remain, as in fire and glowing iron; *Temperatio* [Tempering], the mutual and corresponding extension of two or more bodies, their qualities likewise remaining; and finally, *Confusio* [Confusion], such a transmutation of two or more bodily qualities that a new thing is born therefrom, different from those qualities, as in the composition of ointments and medicines. **This** is the sum of the arguments by the

--- Page 122 ---
**BOOK VII. OF THE SECOND ENNEAD. p. 327—334.**

Stoics in Stobaeus (l. l.). And the mention just made of medicines reminds me also of Galenus; who indeed, both in his books *On Temperaments* [De temperamentis] and *On Distemper* [De dyscrasia], as well as in his writing *On the Opinions of Plato and Hippocrates*, has not a few things pertaining to this doctrine of Mixture and Tempering and its history. Chrysippus taught in such a way that *mixis* was broader than *krasis*: a reasoning also followed by Sextus Empiricus. For the latter, in *Pyrrhonian Outlines*, III. 6. § 56 (which chapter is inscribed *On Tempering*), says: “How then do they say that composites are even formed from the first elements, when there is neither touching nor contact, nor tempering nor mixture at all?” Cf. ibid. § 62; and regarding Chrysippus’s opinion, see Alexander of Aphrodisias, *On Mixture*, p. 141. For this very philosopher whom I named last not only composed a book *On Mixture*, but another also *On Tempering and Growth*. See Fabricius’s annotations to Sextus (l. l.), p. 143. Finally, he who wishes to learn the opinions of more recent authors, from the Middle Ages down to the beginning of the previous century, regarding mixtures, should consult Morhof’s *Polyhistor*, Book II, Part II, ch. 13, § 6—10.

— 12. **Οἱ μὲν γὰρ τῇ παραθέσει διδόντες—ἑαυτοῖς** [For those who grant it to apposition...]: We have spoken [lit: *lived*] concerning apposition (*parathesis*) at the Inscription of this chapter. He touches upon Anaxagoras and Democritus. Plutarch, *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*, I. 17, p. 554, ed. Wyttenbach: “Those around Anaxagoras and Democritus [say it is] according to apposition.” Stobaeus, *Eclogues*, I. 18, p. 368, ed. Heeren: “Anaxagoras [says] that temperings occur according to the apposition of elements.” Sextus also touches on this, III. 62, p. 145: “...if the so-called elements, being placed next to one another (*paratitheména*) not according to touch... are able to be productive of mixtures, etc.” Galenus, as is commonly attributed, has the same in *History of Philosophy*, ch. 10. Perhaps Plotinus also looked back to Aristotle. For Stobaeus (p. 368 f.): “Aristotle and those after him say that bodies are broken, and the small parts are placed next to one another.”

— 15. **Οἱ μὲν οὖν τὰς ποιότητας μόνας κιρνάντες—καὶ ἐπ’ αὐτῶν** [Those, therefore, who mix the qualities alone...]: To these, think of “of the matters” (*tōn hylōn*) from the preceding “the matter of each body.” Sextus also touches on this opinion, like several others, III. 6. 57, p. 143 ff. I will set down the more notable parts: “They say that those things being mixed are composed of substance and qualities. Either, then, someone says the substances of them are mixed, but the qualities not at all; or that the qualities are mixed, but no longer the substances; or that neither is mixed with the other, or both are unified with each other.” Then, after he has striven to refute all these opinions, he concludes his reasoning thus: “If tempering can occur neither when only the substances are mixed with each other, nor only the qualities, nor both, nor neither; and beyond these it is possible to conceive of nothing; the mode of tempering and of mixture in general is inconceivable.” Finally, he adds: “Physiology according to the dogmatists is inconceivable.” Without a doubt, Plotinus knew these negations of the Sceptics when he turned himself anew to moving this stone [i.e., tackling this difficult problem].

p. 334, 12. **Οἱ δ’ αὖ οἱ τὴν δι’ ὅλων κρᾶσιν εἰσάγοντες** [But those, again, who introduce mixture through the whole]: Among these was Zeno the Stoic. Stobaeus, *Eclogues*, I. p. 370—372: “But Zeno declares thus explicitly... that mixture becomes tempering by the change of elements into one another, one whole body passing through another whole body.”

— 14. **τοὺς ἱδρῶτας οὐ τοῦ σώματος τομὰς ποιεῖν οὐδ’ αὖ κατατετρῆσθαι κ. τ. λ.** [That sweats do not make cuts in the body nor, again, are they bored through, etc.]: Relevant here is a passage of Plutarch, *Symposiacs* [Table Talk], VI. 3. 2, p. 689, p. 830 f., ed. Wyttenbach: “For even if someone,” I said, “by those pores which some hold and love, should bore through the flesh, making it flabby and trembling and unsound, at least these parts of the body would not receive the drink and the food, but would flow down and be secreted as if through sieves, which is entirely absurd and strange; for this mixing with the liquid, breaking down the food and taking the internal heat and the spirit as cooperators, thins the nourishment by all cuts and divisions most accurately of all instruments.” The next words of Plotinus, if they are well-healed [emended] in our text, must be taken as Ficinus took them, and the words **τὸ ὑγρὸν δεύοντα αὐτὰ** [the liquid wetting them] explained: they receive the moisture into themselves. Perhaps, however, Plotinus had written: **τὸ ὑγρὸν δι’ ὅλου δεῦον αὐτὰ καὶ διαῤῥεῖν ἐπὶ θάτερα** [the liquid wetting them through the whole and flowing through to the other side], deleting the second instance of *to hygron*. As for the fact that Ficinus, at this place, positioned the example of ivory and horn plates as well as membranes through which oil penetrates, it is not inept; but perhaps Plotinus, when writing **ἐπὶ τεχνητῶν** [regarding artificial things], thought of those “softeners of ivory” who softened ivory with barley beer and mandrake. Plutarch, in *On whether vice is sufficient for unhappiness*, p. 499. e. p. 9.

Wyttenbach: “and they bend and reshape the ivory, which has become soft and yielding by the beer.” Cf. Dioscorides, IV. 46.

p. 335, 3. **Τὰς—αὔξας—τὴν—αὔξην** [The growths—the growth]: He borrowed this form from Plato in the *Theaetetus*, p. 173. a., p. 388, ed. Heindorf, who, with Ruhnken leading, indicates other imitators of that form. Regarding the accent, see Bekker’s *Anecdota Graeca*, p. 464 and p. 1347; and cf. our Author [Plotinus], IV. 7. 5; V. 1. 4 (where commonly *auxein* is used); and VI. 3. 13.

p. 336, 12. **διὰ τοῦ ἐρίου ῥέῃ τὸ ὕδωρ** [water flows through the wool]: If the Critics knew this passage, they could have spared themselves conjectures on these words of Plato in the *Symposium*, p. 175, p. 375, ed. Bekker: “...that it would be well, Agathon said (quoting Socrates), if wisdom were such as to flow from the fuller of us into the emptier, if we touch one another, just as the water in cups flowing through wool from the fuller into the emptier, etc.” where Sydenham, however, and Wolf, and those who have recently followed him, have defended the vulgate [standard reading]; nor is there more disagreement in the Platonic MSS than in the Plotinian ones. But since we have stumbled upon this passage of Plato: read for me against these things in the *Theages*, p. 130, p. 279, ed. Bekker, where Aristides narrates both other things—when and how he himself profited most from Socrates—and indeed these very things: “but I made by far the most progress whenever I sat next to you (he means Socrates), holding on and touching you.” And those things Socrates speaks out no less as if his own opinion; therefore, read those things to me, and compare them with these words from the *Symposium*. What do you seek? A philosopher of the Alexandrian family made the *Theages*—not indeed a primary one, like Plotinus, but from those secondary ones who thought divine power could be transmitted through contact, and who imitated Plato more successfully in words and style than in decrees and opinions. I suspect an Alexandrian of the first age, and one who preceded Plutarch by several centuries.

p. 337, 2. **Εἰ δὲ πανταχοῦ ἡ ὕλη μετὰ τῆς ποιότητος κ. τ. λ.** [But if matter is everywhere with quality, etc.]: At this place Plotinus again seems to look back at the arguments of the Sceptics. For Sextus, p. 144, says: “If someone should say that qualities are mixed, but substances not at all, he will say impossible things. For the subsistence of qualities is in the substances. Wherefore it would be ridiculous to say that some qualities, having been separated from the substances [the word *and* seems to be deleted], mix with each other in their own place, while the substances are left behind without quality. It remains to say that both the qualities of the things mixed and the substances pass through each other and, by being mixed, produce the tempering; which is [perhaps *yet*] more absurd than the things previously said. For such a tempering is impossible.” This he strives to prove by the example of someone mixing one *cotyla* [approx. 1/2 pint] of hemlock juice with ten *cotylae* of water.

— 15. **ἢ ὅτι ἀσώματοι (αἱ ποιότητες) τῆς ὕλης ἀσωμάτου οὔσης** [Or because qualities are incorporeal, matter being incorporeal]: Cf. below ch. 3. G: “it is necessary for the reason of this—not to have included matter.” Stobaeus, *Eclogues*, I. p. 370: “...the incorporeal reasons (*logoi*) which are reasons to be combined.” Heeren, having wondered that these things were attributed to Aristotle, notes that the mention of incorporeal reasons is found neither in him nor in his interpreter Alexander of Aphrodisias. The same man thinks the words “if some are reasons” (he gave *ei tines* from Cod. A instead of *hoitines*) are due to a glossator, and therefore included them in brackets. For my part, since this fragment exists in the section *On Tempering and Mixture* in Stobaeus, and since they agree with the Plotinian opinions set forth here, I would believe they were wrongly added to the Aristotelian ones. And if it is permitted to guess, the whole passage should be constituted thus: “...placed next to one another; (With these words the excerpt from Aristotle’s writing ends) There are some who say that the incorporeal reasons are combined.”

### LIB. VIII. [BOOK VIII]

P. 343, 7. **ΠΕΡΙ ΟΡΑΣΕΩΣ κ. τ. λ.** [On Sight, etc.]: The thirty-fifth according to the chronological order in which the Plotinian books were written. In Porphyry’s edition of the *Life of Plotinus*, however, the words “On Sight or” are missing (see ch. 24, p. 142, and Fabricius there). But that the conjunction of this book with the one immediately preceding may be understood, I will subjoin a passage of Plutarch in the *Symposiacs*, I. 8. 4, p. 626. C., p. 532, ed. Wyttenbach: “But we, having guarded the Platonic principle, say that a light-like spirit falling out from the eyes is mixed with the light which is around bodies, and takes on a solidification, so that from both there becomes one body entirely sympathetic; and one is tempered with the other by a reasoning of symmetry and quantity; for it is not necessary for one to be abolished by being mastered by the other, but from both being brought together into some middle state by harmony and communion, one power is completed.” “But we, following the Platonic principle, shall say that a spirit similar to light falls out from the eyes and is mixed with the light which is around the body, and with it

--- Page 124 ---
**BOOK VIII. OF THE SECOND ENNEAD. p. 335—343.**

grows together, so that from both one consenting body is made. Furthermore, that mixture of one with the other occurs by the reasoning of a certain proportion and fixed quantity: for one must not be abolished by being overcome by the other, but from both, reduced into a certain middle by harmony and communion, one force is produced.” From this it is clear, from the doctrine of the Platonists, that this passage on *Sight* pertains to the topic of *Mixture* and *Tempering*. The meeting of the light emitted from the eyes with the kindred air is called here the “Platonic *synaugeia*” [confluence of light], as Plutarch (as is attributed) testifies in *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*, IV. 13, p. 634, ed. Wyttenbach. See also Nemesius, *On the Nature of Man*, ch. VII, p. 180, ed. Matthaei, and cf. Schneider’s *Animadversions* written in German on the *Physical Eclogues*, p. 188 f. and p. 246. Both of them, however—Plutarch (l. l.) in *On the Opinions* and Nemesius, and indeed Aristotle in *On the Senses and Sensibles*, ch. 2, p. 3 f., ed. Sylburg; *On the Soul*, II. 7, p. 34 ff.; in *Problems*, XV. 5, p. 118 f., and XXXI, p. 222 f.; Theophrastus, *On the Senses*, p. 18 f., p. 548 ff., ed. Schneider; Galenus, both in the *Fragments on Plato’s Timaeus*, Vol. V, p. 275 ff., ed. Charterius, and in Book X of *On the Use of the Parts of the Human Body*, p. 273 ff., Basel; Sextus Empiricus, in *Pyrrhonian Outlines*, I. 14, p. 13 ff., Fabricius; Euclid and others who composed *Optics*, *Catoptrics*, and *Dioptrics*; Diogenes Laertius X. 48—51 (Cf. Ign. Rossi, *Commentary on Laertius*, p. 262); Stobaeus in *Physical Eclogues*, I. 56, p. 1110 ff., ed. Heeren; Nicephorus Blemmides in *Epitome of Physics*, ch. XXI, p. 155 ff., ed. Wegelin; among the Latins, Lucretius, IV. 380 ff.; Cicero in *Academics*, IV. (II.) 25. 79 ff., p. 145 ff., ed. Goerenz, and *On the Nature of the Gods*, I. 43 and II. 30; Seneca in *Natural Questions*, I. 7; Pliny, *Natural History*, VII. 2, XXXVII. 5 and elsewhere; Macrobius in *Saturnalia*, VII. 14; and finally Vincent of Beauvais in *Speculum Naturale*, II. 77 and XXV. 25—all these, then, either strived to illustrate the doctrine of Sight themselves, or narrated and partially judged what had been pronounced on that matter by Physicists from Pythagoras onwards. As for the passages of Plato himself, they are of two kinds: some in which he explains his opinion on *Sight* in general, others where he touches specifically upon this proposition: *that things far away seem small*. And those former passages are especially in the *Timaeus*, p. 45. a., p. 50 ff., ed. Bekker, and p. 67, p. 93 f., ed. Bekker, with which are to be used, besides the works of Galenus, Plutarch, and Stobaeus cited above, Alcinous, *On the Doctrine of Plato*, ch. XVIII, p. 497, and Chalcidius, *On the Timaeus*, p. 329 ff. [p. 363 ff., ed. Fabricius]. The second point he uses quite frequently and adapts variously to the proposed question. We shall indicate the passages: *Republic*, X. 602, p. 480, ed. Bekker: “The same magnitude does not appear equal to us through sight from near and from far.” *Philebus*, p. 42. A, p. 198, ed. Bekker: “In sight, seeing magnitudes from far and near obscures the truth.” *Protagoras*, p. 356. C, p. 237, ed. Bekker: “Do the same magnitudes appear larger to us from near and smaller from far, or not?” Cf. also *Phaedo*, p. 102. a. ff., and especially the memorable discussion in the *Sophist*, p. 235 f., p. 167 ff., ed. Bekker. Chalcidius, moreover (l. l.), p. 330 f., also touches upon these very things, writing thus: “And because all nature is moved by mode and measure, there is also a convenience of space and magnitude: and those things which are neither very close to the sight nor too distant are seen clearly as visible things. Certainly the cone itself is increased according to the mode and measure of the intention [of the gaze], and as its base will be either direct or bent, and will fall upon the contemplatable species, so the things that are seen will appear. Thus a merchant ship seen from a distance appears very tiny, the spirit not spreading itself through all the parts of the ship. Likewise a square tower simulates the roundness of a cylinder, and a portico seen from an angle fails into a thin line, by a depravation of the eyes. So also the fire of the stars appears small, and the sun itself, many parts larger than the earth, is discerned within the ambit of a two-foot diameter.” These agree exactly with the Euclidean *Optics* and with those things which Heliodorus of Larissa discusses at the beginning of the second book. Schneider supplies the passage in *German Animadversions on the Physical Eclogues*, p. 215 f.

— 11. **ὅτι συναιρεῖσθαι — ἐθέλει — τὸ φῶς** [that the light—wants/tends—to be contracted]: I do not find fault, at least in Plotinus, with what Ficinus translates as *desiderat* [desires], but, as in an inanimate thing, it is properly in this place the same as *mellei* [is about to] and has the force of a periphrastic future, unless you prefer *is accustomed* [solet] here. Concerning that usage, Coray explained in Isocrates’ oration *On the Exchange*, p. 244 f.; Schweighäuser, *Herodotus Lexicon*, p. 182; and concerning the other more elegant usage of the verb *thelein*, Hoogeveen and Zeune on Viger, V. 8. 10; Wyttenbach on Plato’s *Phaedo*, p. 272; Ast on the
