**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

*Phaedrus*, p. 235, and on the *Republic*, p. 443 and p. 548.

p. 343. 16. **ἐν διεξόδῳ καὶ ἐπελεύσει** [in passage and progression]: I have corrected the version of Ficinus, who otherwise well added: *made step by step* [gradatim facta]. Herodotus, II. 24: *diexodos hēliou*, the course of the sun; but the same metaphorically, III. 156, VII. 234: *hai diexodoi tōn bouleumatōn*, the ways and reasons of counsels: cf. Schweighäuser, *Herodotus Lexicon*, p. 166. Our Author [Plotinus] often uses this word. See III. 7. 10; III. 8. 8; IV. 3. 12; IV. 4. 1; IV. 4. 8; V. 3. 7; III. 7. 12: *diexodos aidios* [eternal passage]; IV. 4. 35: *diexodos tēs zōēs* [passage of life]. Cf. Plutarch, *Dinner of the Seven Wise Men*, p. 158. D: “life is a certain conduct of a man’s actions having a *diexodos* [passage/tract]”; and *biou diexagōgē*, the transaction of life, Hierocles in Stobaeus, p. 414 f. Consult Wyttenbach on the passage of Plutarch cited above, p. 973, minor Oxford edition, who says: “*diexodos* is the handling of life, action, or doctrine. It is also a continuous speech in teaching.” Proclus in *On the First Alcibiades*, p. 248 f., our Frankfurt edition, on the powers of the soul: “...and their perfection not being eternal nor standing all together, but unfolding according to time, and subsisting in *diexodoi* [passages/successions],” where the qualities, parts, and powers that are in the soul *are said to explain themselves not simultaneously and in a moment of time, but successively and by degrees*; which passage I decided to employ here because *diexodos* is said there regarding *time*, just as in our passage it is said regarding *space*. In the same place I praised the classic passage of Plotinus, III. 8. 8, p. 351. A (from which let us now hold these: “by the *diexodos* not passing through but having passed through”) and in addition Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation*, IV. 25, and Iamblichus, *Exhortation*, p. 96.

p. 346, 1. **τὸ δὲ κατὰ τὰς τῆς ὄψεως γωνίας κ. τ. λ.** [the matter concerning the angles of sight, etc.]: Just as Aristotle in *On Sense and the Sensible*, ch. 2, strives to refute Plato’s *synaugeia*, or the meeting of rays exiting from the eyes with the rays of light (saying: “it is entirely irrational for sight to see by something going out and to stretch out as far as the stars or, going out, to grow together with something as far as a certain point”): so in this place Plotinus seems to speak against Aristotle. For read what the Stagirite discusses concerning angles, *gōniais*, and their power in the action of seeing in *Problems*, XV, especially § 5, and compare Schneider’s *Animadversions* written in the vernacular [German] on the *Physical Eclogues*, p. 208 (cf. 206) and p. 217 f.

— 9. **εἰ δὲ δὴ καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ θεωροῖ** [if indeed he should observe even upon the heavens]: These things remind one of Democritus’s comment about an ant being visible to us even in the sky, which Aristotle refutes in *On the Soul*, II. 7: “For Democritus does not say this well, thinking that if the intermediate space became empty, one would see accurately, even if an ant were in the sky. For this is impossible, etc.” The ant had passed into a proverb because of its smallness. Lucian, *Saturnalian Letters*, 19, p. 401 f., ed. Wetstein: “as we are now, an ant or a camel, as the proverb says,” i.e., regarding most unequal things, where previously in the first place *ē* [or] was also wrongly read. Whence Erasmus, in *Adages*, in “an ant is a camel,” p. 187, explains less correctly. Jensius’s emendation is confirmed by the *Synagōgē lex. chrēs.* from Lucian in Bachmann’s *Anecdota Graeca*, II, p. 346. Concerning the camel as a token of magnitude, see the interpreters on the Gospel of Mark X. 25 and Luke XVIII. 25, among them Valckenaer in *Scholion* I, p. 243 f.

### LIB. IX. [BOOK IX]

P. 358, 7. **ΠΡΟΣ ΤΟΥΣ ΓΝΩΣΤΙΚΟΥΣ.** [Against the Gnostics]: Not only do the MSS books vary here, but also in Porphyry’s *Life of Plotinus*, where mention of this book occurs, and indeed in several places, ch. 5, ch. 15, ch. 24; and in that place, the Basel edition and the rest of the Codices have: “against those saying that the creator of the world and the world itself are evil”; but two books have: “against the *gnōstous* [known ones].” Finally, in the index of Plotinian books, which the Codices Marciani A. B. C. repeat at the end of that life: A has “against the *gnōstous*,” B has “about the *gnōstikous*,” and C has “against the *gnōstikous*.” Regarding the first reading, no one, I believe, will actually think of *gnōstous* here, i.e., *philous*, friends, familiars (Suidas I, p. 489, ed. Kuster), nor will anyone attempt *gnōstas*, i.e., *manteis*, soothsayers, diviners, seers (Biel, *Thes. Vet.* Vol. I, p. 335; cf. Paris Scholion in Boissonade on Eunapius, p. 445): but rather he will allow himself to be persuaded that *gnōstous*, as happens six hundred times [i.e., very often], was thrust upon us from a single omitted line [over the letter] (*gnōstous* [abbreviation for *gnōstikous*]), and thus a poorly explained writing shorthand, instead of the genuine *gnōstikous*. What should draw our attention more is that in cod. Marc. Venet. A and Monacensis C, there is read above the line: “that the Christians are also called *gnōstoi* (read *gnōstikoi*),” especially when we consider the primary force of *gnōsis* as true intelligence, from which *gnōstikos* is universally explained as “he who is made perfect in truth” (Zonaras, *Lex. Gr.*, p. 443), in which sense no one is unaware of how often Clement of Alexandria uses *gnōstikous*. And there were learned men who thought that *Christians* were attacked by Plotinus both elsewhere and in this book.

--- Page 126 ---
**BOOK IX. OF THE SECOND ENNEAD. p. 343—358.**

Ficinus went in an entirely different direction, who in his commentary on this book thinks it can be understood even from this that Plotinus was not alienated from the Christian law, because he was always a disciple of Ammonius, a Christian, and a friend of the “most Christian” Origen (p. 191 and cf. p. 196, Basel edition). Marsilio [Ficino] confuses Origen the Church Father with the Platonic Origen, the fellow-student of Plotinus; moreover, whether Ammonius Saccas was ever a Christian is questioned. Regarding this matter, we noted above on Porphyry’s *Life of Plotinus*, ch. 3, p. 96, Fabricius, which it is not necessary to repeat here. Plotinus himself, however, no more calls them *Gnostics* than he calls them *Christians*. We do not know what title Eustochius may have given to this book in his recension of Plotinus’s works—perhaps that longer one, which we mentioned above from some Codices: “against those saying the Creator is evil”; this shorter one, which is preserved in most books, “Against the Gnostics,” is due to Porphyry. He himself explains the reasons for this in the *Life of Plotinus*, ch. 16, p. 118 f., Fabricius, a classic passage, from which we may set down the more notable parts: “There were in his time many Christians, both others and heretics led out from the ancient philosophy, those around Adelphius... they deceived many and were themselves deceived, as if Plato had not approached the depth of the intelligible essence. Wherefore he himself, making many refutations in his gatherings, also having written a book, which we inscribed *Against the Gnostics*, left the rest for us to judge.” “There were Christians at that time many both others and heretics having gone out from the ancient philosophy, followers of Adelphius, and they deceived many, and they themselves had already been deceived: asserting that Plato had minutely penetrated the depth of the intelligible essence. For which reason Plotinus brought many arguments against them in his discussions, and wrote a book against them, *which we inscribed against the Gnostics*, and committed to us the task of discussing and judging the rest.” Now, if you ask whether Porphyry correctly gave this title to the book or not: the piety of the disciple toward the master does not allow us to doubt that he acted correctly and in the best faith, nor shall we doubt that in familiar conversation between them mention of the Gnostics was quite often made; and indeed Plotinus himself, in the sixth chapter of his book, plainly agrees with Porphyry (l. l.), writing on p. 203. F: “For in general, some things have been taken by them from Plato, but others, as many as they innovate so that they may establish a philosophy of their own, have been said outside the truth.” No one is so blind as not to see that these things could have been said not against *Christians*, but against *Gnostics*, especially those who, having profited greatly from Plato, twisted the decrees of this philosopher to their own reasoning. And since the question of the *origin of evil* occupies a primary place in this book, we have already understood above that this question was primarily agitated by the heretics. See the end of our Annotation on the Inscription of *Ennead* I. 8, p. 72. Furthermore, I would not deny on that account that Porphyry, and perhaps also Amelius and others, in their books against the Gnostics, often included Christians as well, and discussed many things with a mind hostile to the Christian religion. *But let us maintain that Plotinus, at least in this book, does not campaign so much against Christians as against Gnostics*. It remains for us to discern which family of Gnostics the Lycopolitan philosopher [Plotinus] seems primarily to touch upon. And no one is ignorant that the Gnosis of these heretics flowed from various sources, and that into it were fused Indic, Persian, Jewish, Platonic, and finally Christian doctrines. Nor is the reasoning and sect of the Manichaeans to be separated from the Gnostics. We know the opinions of the Manichaeans to the life [vividly] from the formula of execration of those who returned to the Catholic doctrine in Jacob Tollius, *Insignia Itinerarii Italici*, Vol. I, p. 134: “I anathematize those who say that Zaradas [Zoroaster], and Buddas [Buddha], and Christ, and Manichaeus, and the sun are one and the same.” For the doctrine of these men came to this: that it held Christ as well as Buddha, Zoroaster, and Mani in a certain way for sons of the sun or for those in whom the power and majesty of the sun had rendered itself conspicuous in a certain wondrous way. Concerning Buddha, this passage of Clement of Alexandria is to be held, *Stromata*, I, p. 359, ed. Potter: “There are some of the Indians who obey the commands of Boutta [Buddha]. Whom, on account of the excess of his solemnity, they have honored as (or like) a god.” And the leaders of the Manichaeans boasted this: Scythianus [boasted] that he was the Father; Buddhas or Terebinthus [boasted] that he was the son of God born of a virgin; Mani finally [boasted] that he was the Paraclete or the Holy Spirit (Photius *Against the Manichaeans*, Book I, p. 47, in Wolf’s *Anecdota Graeca* I). The religions of the Indian Buddha

--- Page 127 ---
**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

I myself touched upon in *Symbolica and Mythologia* I, p. 577, 2nd ed. (cf. *Guigniaut, Religions de l’Antiquité*, I, p. 288 ff.) and indeed recently the most learned *Abel-Rémusat* has brought much light to the affairs of Buddha and the Buddhists from the monuments of oriental writers in *Mélanges Asiatiques*, Paris, 1825, p. 100—151. As for the fact that *Neander*, a most illustrious man, denies that the Manichaeans mixed the decrees of oriental philosophy with Platonic opinions (see his *General History of the Christian Religion and Church*, I. 2, p. 813), someone might oppose this opinion with the words of Photius from the cited book, p. 38 f., mentioning that Scythianus, the leader of the Manichaeans, both lived in Alexandria (where we know Platonic philosophy flourished) and profited from Aristotelian books and corrupted their meaning (“this man, having become practiced in tongue from misunderstandings of the Aristotelian [works], etc.”). But indeed it is established among all how many false things Western and Greek writers, especially later ones, produced about the Manichaeans; and therefore it is better to follow oriental sources, an abundance of which is available in *Hyde*’s *On the Religion of the Ancient Persians*, p. 276, Herbelot in *Bibliothèque Orientale*, I, p. 549—551, ed. Hague, and *Silvestre de Sacy* in *Mémoires sur diverses antiquités de la Perse*, p. 42 ff.; cf. also Is. Jac. Schmidt, *On the Relationship of the Gnostic-Theosophical Teachings with the Religious Systems of the Orient, especially Buddhism*, Leipzig, 1828: from which we can gather these as certain: first, that Mani’s opinions and precepts were mixed from Zoroastrian decrees of the Magi and doctrines of the Christians; second: that the primary opinion in that doctrine was that of two principles, God and Matter. This later Manichaean opinion was also touched upon by Nicolaus of Methone in *Refutation of Proclus’s Theological Institution*, recently edited by my friend Voemel, p. 72. Now, to set down that for the sake of which these things about the Manichaeans were sketched: although Porphyry, in the classic passage cited above, applied the name of no one who is explicitly enumerated among the Manichaeans; yet since he says in the same place that those Gnostics carried with them the “revelations” (*apokalypseis*) of Zoroaster, and Plotinus himself composed this book of his at that time when the Manichaeans had already grown powerful in the Roman world (concerning which matter cf. *Heyne’s Commentary on Alexander Severus approving miscellaneous religions*; and the six excursions added to that Commentary in *Opuscula Academica*, Vol. VI, p. 169—281), and in the same book he discusses many things concerning two Principles: I indeed would not deny that he also thought of the Manichaeans when he reduced his arguments into the form of this book. Gnostics are divided variously by various people, especially since recently learned men through Germany have inquired more accurately into the opinions of those heretics. See *Ferd. Christ. Baur*’s Commentary I, *On the Ideal Christianity of the Gnostics*, Tübingen 1827, p. 33 ff., who, as a learned man himself, formed for himself three genera of Gnostics: “1. Those in which Ethnicism [Paganism] mixed with Christianity so prevailed that it hardly gave room even to Christianity; of which genus were Simon and the Simonians, the Ophites, and the Manichaeans, by no means to be separated from the Gnostics. 2. Those who established a closer necessity of relationship to intervene between Judaism and Christianity, such as Basilides, Valentinus, Bardesanes, and others. 3. Those who so extolled Christianity that it seemed set in opposition to Judaism, in which matter we know Marcion was singular.” Concerning the Manichaeans we have seen. But if we ask which of the remaining Gnostics Plotinus especially touched in this book: certain singular opinions must be weighed. Among which the first is that which says they introduce transmigrations (*paroikēseis*, ch. 6, init.), which we are taught by Irenaeus, Book I, ch. 7, was a decree of the Valentinians, as they said many things about the duty of transmigrating and about souls to be transferred to higher things; second, that they are said to have inculcated *metensōmatōsis* [reincarnation] taken from Plato (Plotinus, ibid.). Now listen to Origen for me in the *Epistle to the Romans*, Vol. IV, p. 549, ed. Ruaeus: “But Basilides, not noticing that these things ought to be understood regarding natural law, dragged the Apostolic discourse (Rom. VII. 9) to inept and impious fables and strives to build from this Apostolic saying the dogma of *metensōmatōsis*, that is, that souls are poured into one body after another.” Nor did the same Basilides and his followers less frequent in their discussions *antitypoi* or images of the lower life, reflected from the supreme life or from the first ogdoad (*ek tēs prōtēs ogdoados*. Irenaeus I. 24, II. 16; Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, IV, p. 637, ed. Potter). Now indeed, since the reasoning of the Ophites

--- Page 128 ---
**BOOK IX. OF THE SECOND ENNEAD. p. 358, 359.**

was similar to the reasoning of the Valentinians, perhaps it is not a vain conjecture if you judge that these also were attacked here and there by Plotinus. Moreover, the Egyptian Philosopher [Plotinus] could have known the Basilidians and Valentinians as well as the Ophites all the more because these had indeed arisen in Egypt, and indeed long before Plotinus’s age. Basilides and Valentinus had arisen in Alexandria one century earlier than he himself had worked under Ammonius Saccas in this city. This book, however, according to the order of all Plotinus’s books, is the thirty-third. See Porphyry, *Life of Plotinus*, ch. 5, p. 102, ed. Fabricius, and ch. 24, p. 142. *Thomas Taylor* translated this book into English in *Select Works of Plotinus*, p. 64 ff.

And from these things which I have discussed, or rather sketched, in this small preparation for this book, the learned reader will understand to what extent I can agree with the illustrious *Matter*, who in his excellent work, *Critical History of Gnosticism*, Paris 1828, Vol. I, p. 55, judges thus: “*It is this which explains to us, for example, the position of Plotinus, who is full of ideas analogous to those of the Gnostics, and who nevertheless refutes them in a particular treatise, because he is the enemy of everything that pertains to Christianity.*” Which judgment he strives to confirm in Vol. II, p. 460 ff., adding: “*Ammonius, who shared in a certain way the singular destiny of Constantine the Great, of being venerated by two contrary parties (by Christians and by Pagans), seems to have impressed upon his disciples in Alexandria a profound antipathy for the Gnostics. It is true that history, which has preserved so few facts on Ammonius, reports none which could attest to this direction; but the direction itself exists, it manifests itself in the most illustrious of Ammonius’s pupils, in Plotinus, whose tender and mystic soul would hardly have conceived this passion of itself, and who moreover had fewer occasions than his master to meet with the Gnostics.*” The same man, p. 462: “*This is that writing which Porphyry found among the other manuscripts of Plotinus, which he arranged and corrected, doubtless, like the others, and which he entitled* AGAINST THE GNOSTICS (*kata tōn Gnōstikōn*. He should have written: *pros tous Gnōstikous*.) *As the only monument which has been preserved of the polemic of the Platonists and the Gnostics, it is without doubt very curious: but it is far from being worth the treatises of the Irenaeuses, the Clements of Alexandria, or the Tertullians against Gnosticism. It hardly exposes the doctrine which it refutes; it supposes it so present to minds that it attacks it, so to speak, without recognizing it.*” Finally, p. 464 ff., Matter declares that in this cause Plotinus saw the truth more acutely than the Gnostics (p. 466: “*and in general his mysticism, we say it without any reserve, is often superior to that of Gnosis.*”). Which the most learned writer strives to demonstrate by applying examples, yet in such a way that he himself circumscribes his own opinion in this manner (p. 467): “*But it must still be remembered that we no longer know Gnosis by itself; we only have it such as the polemic, that is to say, hatred, has made it.*” Which I leave placed in the middle [unjudged], as one who has undertaken the patronage of neither party: I have undertaken to emend and explain the works of Plotinus as far as can be done.

p. 358, 9. **ΕΠΕΙΔΗ τοίνυν** [Since therefore]: A longer period [sentence], which pertains from *epeidē toinun* all the way to *hōs hoion te*, Ficinus, as he quite often does, dissected into several shorter sentences, so that before *ouden echon* he repeated *ephanē* by thinking it. Taylor better described the ambit of the universal period in translating, beginning the apodosis thus: “*This being the case, when we say* THE ONE, *&c.*”

p. 359, 7. **εἴτε γὰρ ἐλάττω** [for whether fewer]: Gemistus in Cod. Vat. nr. 1416, p. 156, in the *Epistle to Bessarion on the Maker of Heaven*: “Proclus, dragging the dogmas of Plato into the myths of Orpheus, places a fourth cause from the first. But Plotinus, looking toward the many of the poets, [places] a third.” See Proclus *On Plato’s Timaeus*, p. 93, and Cyril *Against Julian*, VIII, p. 384. Brucker discusses these opinions of Plotinus, Proclus, and others in *Critical History of Philosophy*, II, p. 398 f., whence I decided these should be subjoined: “Following whom (Ammonius Saccas), Plotinus admitted the same trinity of primary hypostases, so that he might have something not only to oppose to the Gnostics, but also to the Christians: whose doctrine this sect vehemently and with all zeal strived to show its own philosophy was not inferior to. Theodoretus saw this (*Therap. Serm.* II, Vol. II, opp. p. 496), who clearly noticed this imitation of the Christians,

**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

although he is greatly mistaken, having thought that the trinity of Numenius and Plotinus was the same as that of the Christians.” The passage of Theodoretus has it thus, Vol. IV, p. 750 f., ed. Schulz: “...immediately, therefore, unfolding the thought of Plato, both Plotinus and Numenius say that he spoke of three things surpassing and eternal: the Good, and Mind [Intellect], and the Soul of the universe; naming the Good that which we call Father; and Mind, that which we call Son and Word [Logos]; and naming Soul that power which inspires and gives life to all things, which the divine words call the Holy Spirit. And all things, as I said, have been plundered from the philosophy and theology of the Hebrews—” and a little later: “and indeed both Plutarch and Plotinus listened to the divine gospels.” He repeats the same in book VI, p. 868 f., where Plotinus is even said to have been imbued with the discipline of the fishermen [apostles] and Paul. You see, therefore, just as the more recent Platonists said the Christians profited from Plato, so the Fathers of the Church assert that the opinions of the Platonists flowed from the philosophy of the Hebrews and indeed, as far as recent things pertain, from the Gospel and the books of the apostles. Concerning which matter there is no reason for us to discuss; nor shall I repeat here what might serve to judge Brucker’s opinion, as it has already been explained above in the annotation to the title of this book.

p. 359, 11. **Τῆς τε γὰρ λεχθείσης κ. τ. λ.** [For of the mentioned...]: For that which we say the principle of the universes has itself thus, no one will find anything simpler nor more excellent than it. Taylor applied himself to Ficinus here. *Phēsousi* [they will say] is to be referred to the Gnostics, whom Plotinus, being studious of brevity, does not name, as one who knew they would be named by Porphyry in the title of the book. See the annotation on the inscription of this book.

360, 1. **κίνησις δὲ πρὸς αὐτὸν** [but movement toward him]: Proclus, *Theological Institution*, ch. 169, p. 250, our edition: “For if the mind is immobile, it would not be measured by time, neither according to being, nor according to activity; and these things being likewise, its power is also eternal.” cf. ibid. ch. 170—172.

— 4. **καὶ γὰρ εἰ ἄλλο** [for even if another]: Again Proclus profited from this in *Theological Institution*, ch. 168, p. 248: “Every mind knows according to activity that it thinks, and it is not one thing to think, and another to think that it thinks.” But the whole chapter ought to be compared with these discussions of Plotinus.

— 11. **εἰ καὶ—εἶεν—ἔχοιεν** [even if—they should be—they should have]: You might say Ficinus, whom Taylor follows, read: *eimen—echoimen* [if we should be/have]. But since no book supports it, it seems rather that these are referred to *hormas* [impulses] and *dianoēseis* [thoughts]: *even if the impulses and counsels are moderately good*. Proclus again expressed the following in the cited place [l. l.]: “For if there is a mind according to activity, and it thinks itself being no other than the thing thought, it knows itself and sees itself.” This flowed from the most noble opinion of Epicharmus: “mind sees, and mind hears; the rest are deaf and blind,” celebrated by many of the ancients. See only Plutarch, *On Fortune*, p. 98. B, and Wyttenbach’s *Animadversions* on him, p. 671, minor Oxford edition, and on the book *On the Fortune of Alexander the Great*, p. 125. Add these Plotinian passages: III. 9. 1; V. 1. 6; V. 3. 8; V. 5. 7; V. 8. 3; VI. 6. 17; VI. 7. 35. Moreover, this very opinion, “the mind sees itself,” recurs below V. 3. 4; cf. what is read below on p. 204. A. Joined with the passage of Epicharmus, however, is the discussion of Plato in the *Theaetetus*, p. 184. C. D: “For consider, which answer is more correct, that that by which we see is eyes, and through which we see, and by which we hear, ears, or through which we hear... but not into some one idea, whether soul, or whatever it is necessary to call all these things, they all tend together, etc.” Which question Aristotle pursued in *On the Soul*, book III, ch. 1 and 2, and our Author himself below, p. 363. E; cf. also 374. C. D. Cf. also Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, I. 20, who has both other things and these: “Therefore often, hindered either by thought or by some force of disease, with open and healthy eyes and ears, we neither see nor hear: so that it can easily be understood that the soul both sees and hears, not those parts which are as if windows of the soul; by which, nevertheless, the mind can perceive nothing unless it acts and is present. What? That by the same mind we comprehend most dissimilar things, as color, taste, heat, smell, sound; which the soul would never know by five messengers unless all things were referred to it, and it alone were the judge of all.” From the same source perhaps Theodorus Metochita drew in ch. 89, p. 577, those things: “that the perceptions of sensibles—contribute very much to the inner council-chambers of the mind—and nature seems to have placed the senses before the doors like certain messengers for the master mind, etc.” For the passage is longer than can be conveniently placed here. To the next parts, use Proclus, *Theological Institution*, ch. 174, p. 258, where both other things and these are read: “For if the intelligible and mind are the same, also the being of each is the same as the intelligence in itself.”

**BOOK IX. OF THE SECOND ENNEAD. p. 359—364.**

If for the intelligible and the mind is the same, also the very being of each is the same and the intelligence which is in it.

p. 362, 1. **ψυχῆς δὲ ἡμῶν τὸ μὲν ἀεὶ** [but of our soul, one part always...]: Correctly here Taylor reminds one of Proclus, who in the *Theological Institution*, last chapter (p. 314—316, our edition), speaking against Plotinus, says: “every partial soul, descending into generation, descends as a whole, and not one part of it remains above, while the other descends, etc.” The learned Briton whom I just praised exhibited the whole passage in English. Here, since our edition of Proclus might not be at hand for all readers, I shall write down what I placed there: “Concerning the descent of the soul into bodies, some have handed down some things, others others. Nor did the Platonists themselves agree among themselves. (See Stobaeus, *Eclogues*, I, ch. 52, p. 902 f., 908 ff.; and cf. Wyttenbach’s annotations on Plato’s *Phaedo*, p. 210 ff.). In which disagreement there was also this, that some contended the soul descends as a whole: others denied it. Hermias, *Commentary on Plato’s Phaedrus*, ch. 28, p. 147, ed. Ast: ‘You might take from here that according to Plato the whole soul descends—and not, as Plotinus says, that one part of it descends, while the other remains above.’ You see, therefore, that in this matter it was not agreed between Plato and Plotinus. You may compare Plotinus p. 416. A and elsewhere. Proclus, however, sides with Plato, as is understood from this very passage. On the contrary, Damascius had embraced Plotinus’s opinion. For he says thus in the MS commentary on Plato’s *Parmenides* in Cod. Monacensis, fol. 308. verso: ‘so that Plotinus’s reasoning is true, that the whole soul descends, etc.’ Also Iamblichus, in *On the Migration of the Soul from the Body*, had placed one genus of souls: ‘which even descending into generation nevertheless does not descend,’ as Damascius reveals in the same place, fol. 311. verso.”

— 12. **καὶ ὥσπερ ἐλλάμπουσα—ἐλλάμπεται** [and as if shining—it is shone upon]: Cf. I. 1. 8 and the Annotation there, p. 5. B. Add to these and the following Damascius on Plato’s *Parmenides*, p. 314, ed. Kopp: “Double is also the illumination (*ellampsis*), one suspended from the illuminator and being with that one according to one continuity, the other implanted in the thing illuminated and becoming of that thing, and subsisting in the subject itself.” Cf. Olympiodorus on Plato’s *Alcibiades*, sect. VI, p. 59, and the annotation A there. Dionysius the Areopagite borrowed these formulas from the Platonists in *Celestial Hierarchy*, ch. 1, and elsewhere; by whom *ellampsis* is also called the *Holy Scripture* of the Christians. See Annotation on Proclus’s *Theological Institution*, ch. 98, p. 145.

— 15. **καὶ ἄρδεται—τῷ φωτί** [and it is watered—by the light]: This passage of Plotinus is to be added as a singular use to the many passages which learned men have collected. See Wyttenbach on Plutarch, *De S. N. V.*, p. 117, and the London Stephanus *Thesaurus*, ed. Valpy, p. 2238. For it is properly “to irrigate.” It is, however, quite often joined or confused with the verb *auxetai* [it grows], as in Proclus on the *First Alcibiades*, p. 29, our edition: “for by these the wing of the soul is nourished and watered,” where one book has *auxetai*. The source is in Plato’s *Phaedrus*, p. 246. e., p. 250, ed. Heindorf.

p. 363, 12. **ἐλλαμφθήσεται** [it will be shone upon]: Namely, *matter by higher things*, as Taylor correctly took it; who nevertheless adds *perpetually*, and thinks *aei* is missing: in the MSS books there is neither bird nor track [i.e., not a trace] of this little word.

— 14. **πτεροῤῥυήσασαν** [having shed its wings]: Cf. IV. 3. 7; IV. 8. 1 (where there is *pterorrhuesis* [shedding of wings]); IV. 8. 4; VI. 9. 9; and see Plato, *Phaedrus*, ch. 25, 55, 60, and Ast on that dialogue, p. 293; Proclus on *Alcibiades* I, p. 20, and the annotation there, p. 20; Olympiodorus on the same with the annotation, p. 5, our Frankfurt edition; cf. on this passage our Neander, *Genetic Development of Gnostic Systems*, p. 213.

p. 364, 4. **οὐδὲ γὰρ ἀμυδρῶς ἔχει, εἰ οὐ μᾶλλον νεύει ἐκεῖ κ. τ. λ.** [for it does not have it dimly, if it does not rather incline there, etc.]: Ficinus expressed the reading of the margin, which I myself also restored, commended by the faith of the books, except that from Medicean A I corrected *neuei* [inclines]. Taylor: “*For it does not possess nor see them obscurely, if it is without this tendency.*” He omitted, therefore, the last parts: **ἵνα—ἴδῃ** [so that—it may see]. A double *neusis* [inclination] seems to be signified here: first, that inclination which happens downwards toward sensibles and the transitory; then, that which happens backwards and upwards toward the divine and the perennial. This latter is the inclination of the Maker, when he began to make the world, in which he looks at the patterns of ideas in the world, which he then expresses in his making of the world. Plato, *Timaeus*, p. 28, p. 23, ed. Bekker: “This, again, must be considered about him (the Demiurge), toward which of the patterns the builder worked it (the world), whether toward that which is according to the same and likewise, or toward that which has become. If indeed this world is beautiful and the maker good, it is clear that he looked toward the eternal, etc.” The next question: whether for the sake of his own glory the Maker made the world, already agitated of old and today frequent in the discussions of Theologians. Which Cudworth also touched upon, not forgetful of the Plotinian passage in *Intellectual System*, V. 5. 20, p. 1184 f., and his editor [Mosheim]...

As for what follows: εἰ δὲ τὰς καθ’ ἑκάστου ψυχὰς ἀναμένει [and so forth], Valentinus taught that the world endures until the end for the reason that *Wisdom* (ἡ Σοφία) waited until all souls should arrive for whom it was destined that they be instructed in this world until they might pass into the Fullness (εἰς τὸ πλήρωμα). Cf. *Neander, Entw. d. Gnost. Systeme* p. 212.

p. 365, 10. τὴν παρ’ αὐτοῖς δύναμιν μὴ ἀτιμάζειν] i.e., to judge their own faculty not to be unequal [to the task], as Wyttenbach interprets it in *ad Phædon.* p. 81. In *Annot.* p. 284, regarding these words τὴν ἀνθρωπίνην ἀσθένειαν ἀτιμάζων, i.e., judging human weakness *to be unequal* to the reasoning required for perceiving such magnitude; this most excellent man [Wyttenbach] thinks this passage was expressed by Plotinus. Next, καὶ διὰ τοσοῦτον κωλυομένων τῶν ἀπατώντων, which Ficinus translates: "and we are hindered by innumerable fallacies," I have corrected by writing καὶ διὰ τοσοῦτον κωλυομένων τῶν ἀπαντώντων, partly from the books [manuscripts], partly from Ficinus. It is a synchysis for καὶ κωλυομένων διὰ τοσοῦτον τῶν ἀπαντώντων, and ἀπαντᾷν itself sometimes has the force of "hindering." Soon I suspect it should be written: οὐδὲ δεῖ τὴν μὲν αὐτῶν ψυχὴν [etc.], which Ficinus also expressed.

p. 366, 6. ἀντιπαρεισαγωγή] This word, if indeed it be sound, is to be added to the Lexicons. It possesses, however, the authority of the manuscript books.

p. 367, 8. Τὰς δὲ ἄλλας ὑποστάσεις—παροικήσεις καὶ ἀντιτύπους καὶ μετανοίας] Regarding the adjective ἀντίτυπος, we saw above on p. 180. G. In this place it is used substantively concerning the ἀντιτύπῳ [antitype] of Basilides the Gnostic, who placed seven powers after the first principle, from which the various life of souls arose, so that the lower was always an image (ὁ ἀντίτυπος) of the higher. See Irenæus I. c. 24. II. 16. Clement of Alexandria, *Strom.* IV. p. 539. and cf. *Neander in Allgem. Gesch. d. Christ. Relig. u. Kirche* I. 2. p. 681 sq. Regarding μετανοίας [repentance/after-thought], Plotinus above in II. 1. 4. p. 99. C. refers to our book (which was written prior to that one) with these words: Ἡ δὲ μετάνοια τῆς ψυχῆς ὅτι κενόν ἐστι δέδεικται [It has been shown that the 'repentance' of the soul is a void].

— 12. τῆς ἀρχαίας ‘Ελληνικῆς οὐχ ἁπτόμενοι [etc.]] As for the following verb σκευωροῦνται, understand it as *they scheme, they architect*. Concerning this verb and the related substantives σκευωρία and σκευώρημα, see the Scholiast on Plato’s *Philebus* p. 42, where it is employed to explain the Platonic τευτάζειν. Cf. Ruhnken on *Tim. Lex.* p. 254. (whose doubt concerning the use of the middle τευτάζεσθαι was removed by Bast in *Epist. Crit.* p. 152. Latin ed.) *Photius’ Lex. Græc.* p. 447. Dobree’s ed. Leipzig. Tiberius Hemsterhuis on *Pollux* IX. 133. p. 1118. sq. Reiske’s *Indic. Demosth.* p. 686. Theodoret, *Epist.* 145. p. 1257. joins μηχανήματα [contrivances] and σκευωρήματα. Next, I should prefer καὶ ἀτύφως λεγόντων [and speaking without vanity]. Regarding the matter itself, a distinction must be made among the Gnostics. For there were some who wished to acknowledge nothing at all received from the Greeks, and therefore, whatever they had borrowed from them, they either concealed—such as the Basilidians, with whom and the Valentinians Plotinus seems to have the greatest discord *in this book*. Others, on the contrary, such as the Carpocratians, honored the philosophers of the Greeks to such an extent that they set up icons of Pythagoras, Plato, and Aristotle together with the image of Christ. Irenæus I. 25. 6. cf. *Frid. Münter, über die kirchlichen Alterthumer der Gnostiker* c. 5. p. 231. sqq. and Ern. Ant. *Lewald’s Commentat. de Doctrina Gnostica*, Heidelberg. 1818. c. 4. p. 81. sq.

— 18. καὶ αἱ μετενσωματώσεις] Cf. I. 1. 12. IV. 3. 9. p. 378. F. Wyttenbach on Plato’s *Phædo* p. 210: “Metempsychosis, which is called the migration of the soul into other bodies, ought rather to have been called μετενσωμάτωσιν [re-embodiment]; for μετεμψύχωσιν [re-animation], according to grammatical reason, signifies that kind of migration of souls by which other souls successively migrate into the same body: Olympiodorus rightly advises in *Cod.* III. p. 27.” Nevertheless, several ecclesiastical writers use it here and there. Thus, to use this example, Nicolaus Methonensis against Proclus p. 200. Voemel ed.: ἢ πρὸς τὴν πρεσβευομένην σοι μετεμψύχωσιν καταφεύγῃ [or you flee to the metempsychosis you advocate], etc. cf. ibid. p. 209. Yet the more ancient and learned, such as Clement, Origen, and Theodoret, know both the verb μετενσωματοῦσθαι and the substantive μετενσωμάτωσις. [On this matter and these names see the discussion by *Irhovius, de Palingenesia veterum* p. I. and p. 414. sq. and the citations there, Amsterdam, 1733, 4to.] Ez. Spanheim touched upon this passage of Plotinus in *Remarques sur les Césars de l’Empéreur Julien* p. 47. and 49; Cudworth in *System. Intellect.* p. 1055. sqq. *Moshemius and Tenemann* in *Hist. Philos.* VI. p. 192. sqq. whom I do not dwell upon now: I shall inquire into this, which of the Gnostics established the transmigration of the human soul into bodies. I have thought these final points worthy of mention because they serve to judge the question of whether Plotinus says correctly that the Gnostics borrowed this doctrine from Plato, or not. In which matter, to state briefly what I feel, it again seems to me that a distinction must be made between the various families of Gnostics. For those Gnostics who lived in Alexandria, or had set out from the Alexandrian school, I should believe to have had knowledge of Platonic μετενσωματώσεως; others, on the contrary, who were dispersed through Syria and other lands of the East, could have drawn the same doctrine from elsewhere—from the books and discourses of Eastern men. For it cannot be universally denied that much is present in the decrees of the Gnostics that savors of Persian, Indian, and Chaldaic origin, etc. Nor must it be forgotten that Plotinus and the remaining Platonists somewhat too often act as patrons for their Plato, especially in this cause, being—as is just—offended by the arrogance of many Gnostics who fastidiously spurn all things Greek. Look only at what follows on p. 204. D. E. [Relevant to the matter is Irhovius, whom I cited above, *de Palingenesia vett.*, who discusses the Indians p. 273—299; the Chaldeans and Persians p. 251—272; the Egyptians p. 188—224; the northern peoples p. 300. sqq.]

p. 368, 4. ἐν τῷ ὃ ἔστι ζῶον καθορᾷ] A passage of Plato in the *Timaeus* p. 39. end, has it thus: ᾗπερ οὖν νοῦς ἐνούσας ἰδέας τῷ ὃ ἔστι ζῶον, οἷαί τε καὶ ὅσαι, καθορᾷ [Just as, then, the Mind perceives the ideas existing in 'that which is the Living Being,' both of what kind and how many they are], this reading is therefore confirmed by the consensus of the codices of Plotinus) τοσαύτας καὶ τοιαύτας διενοήθη δεῖν καὶ τόδε σχεῖν. — 5. ὡς οὐκ ἄμεινον τῇ ψυχῇ] For οὐκ ἀγαθὸν, *it is not well for the soul, it does not profit the soul*: this formula, or similar ones, has been frequent among the best writers since Homer. See Eustathius on *Odyssey* VII. 159; Herodotus I. 27. II. 46; and Valckenaer on him p. 176; and cf. Henr. Stephanus *de Dialectis* p. 38 and 58; Musgrave on *Eurip. — 9. ἐνδεδεμένη] I have restored the reading of the books. Koen on *Gregor. de Dialect.* p. 188 advised that he found the verb δέω [to bind] frequently corrupted in ancient monuments. δέω, ἐνδέω and other compounds are especially used in the sense of fate. Herodotus I. 11: μή μιν ἀναγκαίῃ ἐνδεῖν [lest he bind him by necessity]. Hence the necessity of things is called ἔνδεσις, *a binding/illigation*. Seneca, *Epistle* 77: "An unconquerable and in no way changeable series binds and drags [us]." Concerning which use Gataker also advised on *Marcus Antoninus* X. 28. and I myself have collected more in *Dionyso* p. 73. sqq. using the verb Monceae; therefore in our passage you may translate ἐνδεδεμένη as *illigata* [bound]. Our philosopher refers here especially to bodies. See what follows, in which the words συνδεῖ δ’ ἂν περιλάβῃ remind one of Plato in the *Symposium* p. 202. end: ὥστε τὸ πᾶν αὐτὸ αὑτῷ ξυνδεδέσθαι [so that the whole is bound together with itself].

p. 371, 10. ἐνταῦθα δὲ, ὡς ὑπεκφεύγοντα, εἰς τὴν τάξιν τὴν ἑαυτῶν δέδ. δ. δ.] I have followed the punctuation of Ficinus. In the Edition it is printed: ἐ. δὲ ὡς ὑπεκφεύγοντα εἰς τ. τ. τ. ἑαυτῶν δ. δ. δ., which reasoning caused a second hand in one Codex to strike out that εἰς. Taylor correctly has: “*in their* PROPER *order*,” and I myself have corrected the translation. Next, I have retained the reading of the edition, πιέζουσαν. It pertains to δεῖ (τὴν ψυχήν). For in this place is described the clearly different care by which the universal soul from one side disposes and retains the higher order of things: from the other side it compels and restrains the lower; the former by will alone, the latter by force and necessity. The participle πιέζουσαν [pressing/crushing] serves this meaning. Concerning the power of this verb, add various things to those which are collected in the new Valpy London *Thesaurus* p. 7562, Wyttenbach’s *Animadvv. in Plutarch.* Vol. I. p. 272, and what I myself placed with my friend Bekker in his specimen in *Philostratus’ Vit. Apollonii* p. 52. sq.

p. 372, 15. ἄγαλμα—τῶν νοητῶν θεῶν] Casp. Barth applied this passage to *Zacharias Mytilenæus’ Dialog.* p. 178. in *nott.* p. 282, where he mentions various formulas for praising this world. Ruhnken also ought to have added our passage to his excellent discussion on the word ἄγαλμα in *Timæi Lex Platon.* p. 6, where he says: “For he (Plato) calls *the whole universe of created things* the ἄγαλμα [statue/image] of God. *Tim.* p. 529. C. ὡς δὲ κινηθέν τε αὐτὸ καὶ ζῶν ἐνενόησε τῶν ἀϊδίων θεῶν γεγονὸς ἄγαλμα ὁ γεννήσας πατήρ [when the father who begat it perceived it moved and living, having become an image of the eternal gods]. Which Julian imitated in *Ep.* 51. p. 434. *Epinom.* p. 701. H. Proclus in *Tim.* lib. I. p. 4. II. p. 83. IV. p. 239.” But Ruhnken in those notes very rarely employed passages of Plotinus. From passages of this sort Platonic writers here and there have drawn their color, as Proclus in *Alcib. pr.* p. 92: Λέγοιτο δ’ ἂν, ὅτι καὶ οἷον ἀγάλματι τοῦ νοητοῦ κάλλους πρόσεισιν ὁ Σωκράτης τῷ ἐμφανεῖ κάλλει [It might be said that Socrates approaches visible beauty as if it were an image of intelligible beauty].

p. 373, 7. ὁ τὸ μίμημα ἀποσώζων ἐκείνου] Cf. IV. 7. 5. p. 460. τὸ ταὐτὸν ἀποσώζειν δύναται [it is able to preserve the same]. Concerning this verb consult *Lexic. Xenophont.* I. p. 370. Unique is the use in Plato’s *Epist.* VII. p. 336. p. 450. But the books do not vary, and that use can be conveniently explained from the nature of this verb.

p. 375, 14. πολὺ δὲ μᾶλλον θεοὺς—τοῦτ’ ἔστι δύναμιν θεοῦ εἰδότων [etc.]] Cyril against Julian p. 23. A. Spanheim ed.: καὶ ὅτι πῶς οὐχ ἅπασι ἐναργὲς, ὅτι καὶ τοῖς τὰ ‘Ελλήνων φιλοσοφεῖν εἰωθόσιν ἕνα μὲν ἐδόκει θεὸν εἶναι συνομολογεῖν, τὸν τῶν ὅλων δημιουργὸν, καὶ πάντων ἐπέκεινα κατὰ φύσιν, πεποιῆσθαι δὲ παρ’ αὐτοῦ καὶ παρῆχθαι πρὸς γένεσιν ἑτέρους τινὰς θεοὺς, καθά φασιν αὐτοὶ, νοητούς τε καὶ αἰσθητούς [And how is it not clear to all that even to those accustomed to philosophize in the manner of the Greeks, it seemed right to agree that there is one God, the demiurge of all things and beyond all by nature, but that there have been made by him and brought forth into generation certain other gods, as they say, both intelligible and sensible]. Then he cites passages from Plato. Cudworth, using this and similar passages in *System. Intellect.* c. IV. §. 26. p. 529, argues thus: “Now those who attained glory by philosophizing after the Christian religion was introduced into the world, whether they joined themselves to Plato or Aristotle, although most of them established that the world is eternal, nevertheless with one voice professed the supreme God, the parent and cause both of the whole world and of all the other gods. I pass over Numenius, Plotinus, Amelius, Porphyry, Proclus, Damascius, and others, that they also divided the divinity into three natures, and I mention this one thing, that some among these philosophers discussed God so skillfully that one could not easily find anything to reprehend in their discourses. *Plotinus* yields to no one in the weight and gravity of his opinions. And yet even he, while he contends that matter itself and all things simultaneously were begotten from one principle, is wonderfully copious in commending the worship of many gods.” Then he subjoins this very passage. He who desires to learn what Bayle opposed to these things, with more show than truth, may consult Mosheim’s *annott.* p. 530. sq. Regarding Proclus, consult his *Instit. Theolog.* cap. 114. p. 166. sqq. cap. 164. sqq. p. 242 sqq.

p. 376, 12. ὥσπερ ὀνείρασι πέτεσθαι] It has the appearance of a proverb, yet it is not noted by the Parœmiographists. The color of this entire passage is not unlike the Platonic passage in *Republ.* VII. p. 518—521.—In the next part, those words draw our attention: καὶ ὅσον ἐστὶ δυνατὸν ψυχῇ ἀνθρώπου θεῷ γενέσθαι—τὸ δὲ ὑπὲρ νοῦν—τὸ πεσεῖν—that it is possible to become God for one born a man, and indeed by the constant exercise of segregating the soul from the senses by an intimate conversion of the mind, and one that gradually transcends the mind itself and erases the action of thinking: that, therefore (they call this *junction* or *yoga*), the philosophers of the Indians taught. The poem *Bhagavad-Gita* VI. 19. 27 speaks of this; which passage, like all of that poem, *Guil. de Humboldt* excellently explained in his vernacular dissertation on that poem in *Dissertatt. Acad. Scientt. Berolinens.* 1826. p. 33. sqq.

— 17. πολλὴ γὰρ ἐν ἀνθρώποις ἡ αὐθάδεια—σὺ εἶ θεοῦ παῖς—σὺ δὲ κρείττων καὶ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ.] Paul the Apostle to the Corinthians I. 8. 1: ἡ γνῶσις φυσιοῖ [knowledge puffs up]. On which passage Valckenaer says in his *Scholis* p. 227: “Paul undoubtedly notes here the *Gnostics*, or those semi-Christians who boasted in the name of *the learned* (γνωστικῶν), and who under the pretext of Christian liberty committed many things contrary to the laws of Christ.” Thus that greatest of men. From there, Clement of Alexandria in *Pædag.* I. 6. p. 112. Potter ed., took οἱ εἰς γνῶσιν πεφυσιωμένοι, *those puffed up in knowledge*. The same author, ibid. p. 128. sq.: Ἐμοὶ δὲ καὶ θαυμάζειν ἔπεισιν, ὅπως σφᾶς τελείους τινὲς τολμῶσι καλεῖν καὶ Γνωστικοὺς, ὑπὲρ τῶν Ἀποστόλων φρονοῦντες φυσιούμενοί τε καὶ φρυαττόμενοι [It also occurs to me to wonder how some dare call themselves perfect and Gnostics, thinking themselves above the Apostles, being puffed up and swaggering]. Cf. Irenæus III. 21 and 15. Theodoret concerning the same in 1 *Timoth.* VI. p. 490 thus: Ἡ σεσίγηκέ, φασιν, ἡ θεία γραφή, ταῦτα ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῖν ἀπεκάλυψε [What holy scripture has kept silent, they say, God has revealed these things to us]. These same Gnostics used to call themselves alone πνευματικοὺς [spiritual], to omit other things that the Fathers of the Church everywhere complain about regarding them, since these will suffice for understanding how well Plotinus agrees with the Apostle and the primary Doctors of the Christian Church in describing this pride and superciliousness. Therefore I should not believe that in these Plotinian words there is anything that could be seen as thrown against the *Christians* themselves. Ficino also denies this above on p. 196. at the end: *Neander* leaves it in suspense in *Allgem. Geschichte der Christ. Relig. und Kirche* I. 2. Lect. IV. p. 668. sq. Yet I would not deny that some things are discussed in this book by Plotinus which are also adverse to the decrees of Christ and the Apostles: e.g., what he placed on p. 207. F. G. for the sake of strengthening polytheism, and other things of that sort elsewhere. For the rest, regarding the final part in the Plotinus passage, *Taylor* in the annotation to his version, in order to approve the pride of Bentley, appended that man’s words from his eighth *Sermon at Boyle’s Lectures*, the end of which is: “*That the soul of one virtuous and religious man is of greater worth and excellency than the sun and his planets, and all the stars in the world.*” Which nevertheless ought to be freed from the crime of pride, if you consider that Bentley

was not a Platonist, nor consequently did he hold the sun and stars to be among the number of animated beings and thus of gods. Soon συνεπηχοῦσιν, *they sound together, they agree*. Taylor: *vociferate the same things*: properly said of a choir which joins the song led by the leader with a universal voice. See *Lex. Xenoph.* IV. p. 179. Plutarch *de Audit.* p. 44. A. Pseudo-Aristotle *de Mundo* 6, 15. p. 246. sq. Kapp ed.: Καθάπερ δὲ ἐν χορῷ κορυφαίου κατάρξαντος, συνεπηχεῖ πᾶς ὁ χορὸς ἀνδρῶν ἔσθ’ ὅτε καὶ γυναικῶν ἐν διαφόροις φωναῖς ὀξυτέραις καὶ βαρυτέραις μίαν ἁρμονίαν ἐμμελῆ κεραννύντων [Just as in a choir when the leader has begun, the whole choir of men and sometimes women joins in, blending one tuneful harmony in different voices, higher and lower]. where see Kapp. Dio Cassius XXXIX. 19. p. 199. Reimar ed.: κἀκ τούτου τῶν μὲν ἐξαρχόντων, τῶν δὲ συνεπηχούντων σφίσιν. Cf. the same p. 834. 1095.

p. 377, 15. πρὸς τὸ ἑκάστῳ καταθύμιον] *Odyssey* X. 392. *Iliad* κ’. 383. where Apollonius’ *Lex. Homer.* p. 388. Toll ed. explains it as κατὰ ψυχήν [according to the soul]. Zonaras *Lex.* p. 1160: κατὰ νοῦν [according to the mind]. Herodotus V. 39. IX. 45. From the former passage Pausanias III. 3. 7, a follower of Herodotus, fashioned his ἀρεστὴν [pleasing], certainly from the Herodotian καταθυμίη, if indeed Bergler saw the truth, whose conjecture Wesseling approves at that passage p. 390. No one fails to see that this meaning falls into our passage, such that it is *what is according to the mind's opinion*.

p. 378, 9. πρός τινας τῶν φίλων—μένουσιν] A memorable passage. As for Taylor's suspicion at this place that Origen the Church Father is touched upon, who had previously been one of the disciples of Plotinus, the logic of chronology refutes it. Plotinus' fellow student was that Origen Adamantius, and no less another Origen must be carefully distinguished from that Christian Origen. See what we have placed regarding Porphyry's *Life of Plotinus* c. 3 and especially chapter 14 p. 116. Fabricius ed.

p. 379, 4. Ψυχὴν γὰρ εἰπόντες νεῦσαι κάτω [For saying that the soul inclined downward]—to the end of the chapter—ἐπ’ ἔσχατα εἰδώλων [to the extremes of images]. The source of these decrees, primarily put forward by the Valentinians, is in the passages of Irenæus I. 2. 3. and 4. I. 4. 1. with which passages *Neander* compared these Plotinian ones in the book *Genet. Entwickelung der vornehmst. gnostischen Systeme* p. 211. sq., from which I shall subjoin the primary points: ψυχὴν κάτω καὶ σοφίαν τινὰ i.e., the *Sophia* of the Valentinians, Achamoth (Ἀχαμὼθ, Chachimuth), Soul, Aeon Sophia. For, according to Valentinian teaching, Achamoth held enclosed in herself all spiritual seeds (σπέρματα πνευματικὰ), whence afterwards, through a conjunction entered into with souls, spiritual natures (φύσεις πνευματικαὶ) were born which did not depend on anything else.—ἐκείνην—ἐλλάμψαι τῷ σκότῳ [that she shone into the darkness]—namely Sophia, who again ascended upward into the fullness (πλήρωμα)—εἴ τ’ ἐκεῖθεν εἴδωλον ἐν τῇ ὕλῃ γεγονέναι (Achamoth as the ἐνθύμησις [thought] of Sophia)—εἶτα τοῦ εἰδώλου εἴδωλον πλάσαντες (making the Demiurge as an image of the divine Sophia-Enthymesis, which itself is an image of the higher Sophia)—ἐνταῦθα—ἀποστάντα τῆς μητρὸς (namely the Demiurge, son of Enthymesis, but who was ignorant of her and of the origin of the higher world) ποιήσαντες—ἐπ’ ἔσχατα εἰδώλων (animated natures, ψυχικαὶ, just as the Maker, ὁ Δημιουργὸς, are psychic images which matter, having been illuminated, makes. On the contrary, αἱ φύσεις πνευματικαὶ are true souls. The Maker [or ὁ Δημιουργὸς] consists of matter and an image.) And from these things it is understood why Plotinus above in chapter 6 faults these men because they introduce generations and corruptions entirely.

— 13. οὐ λέγουσιν εἰς ἐπισκότησιν] Taylor, following Ficinus: “*For the purpose of rendering what they say obscure.*” We saw the verb used above concerning the soul which, immersed in matter, is obscured. See I. 8. 4. p. 74. F. where see the annotation. For the rest, the substantive is of rarer use, Zonaras *Lex. Gr.* p. 804. Ἐπισκότησις: *that which is placed over something and walls off the light*. Tittmann cites Demosthenes *contr. Mid.* p. 565 there; in him not the substantive but the verb is read. The final words ἵνα σφόδρα λοιδορήσηται ὁ τοῦτο γράψας Taylor omitted in the context, denying in a subjoined note that he knew what the words meant in this place: “*In order that he who writes this may be more vehemently reprehended.*” But Ficinus took it actively: *should revile*, and seems to have thought of some one Gnostic who wrote a book full of revilings. Correctly. But if it be allowed to take it passively, I should read πράξας instead of γράψας. For no one is unaware that this was a common error of the Gnostics, that they looked down upon and vituperated the Maker of this world. I would therefore translate: “so that he who did this (the business of founding the world) may be cut down with revilings (by the Gnostics).” But I would not wish to guess, and prefer to seek protection from the books, which nevertheless are silent here.

p. 381, 10. μόλις καὶ ἀγαπητῶς] Plato, *Lysis* p. 218. C. Καὶ δὴ καὶ αὐτὸς ἐγὼ πάνυ ἔχαιρον, ὥσπερ θηρευτής τις ἔχων ἀγαπητῶς ὃ ἐθηρευόμην [And indeed I myself was very glad, just like a hunter having with contentment that which I hunted].

*scarcely holding, hardly holding well*. See Heindorf at that passage p. 40. cf. Ast on *de Legg.* IV. 1. p. 200. and V. 7. p. 251. also Locella and Pearlcamp on *Xenoph. Ephes.* p. 335. Jacobs, *Additamm. Animadd. in Athen.* p. 289. Then writers join ἀγαπητῶς καὶ μόλις [contentedly and scarcely], as Aristides I. p. 616. (p. 293.) Ælian, *H. X. p. 294.—Next, Ficinus translates as if he read both ἐκταθεῖσα and ἐξεραθεῖσα, as is in the manuscript books except one and in the edition. Taylor did not express the latter. But what follows shows that only ἐξετασθεῖσα [having been examined] is true, and perhaps, as is usual, Marsilius translated more copiously. Near the end I have thought it should be punctuated and written thus: οὐκ ἦν δῆλον, ὅτι, ὅπου ἂν ἔνευσεν (instead of ἀνένευσεν). In δῆλον, ὅτι almost all books agree and see Ast, *Additamm. ad Platon. Phædri Comment.* at the end of *Reipubl.* p. 635. and Stallbaum on *Platon. Phileb.* p. 102. and the citations there. Regarding the argument, *Neander* touched upon this passage in the vernacular book on the reasonings of the Gnostics p. 212. sq., where he says regarding these words of Plotinus: εἰ δ’ αὐτὴν—ὅπου ἂν ἔνευσεν [if it (the soul)... where it inclined] that the Valentinians could have responded from their principles: “Alienation or separation from Being (τοῦ Ὄντος) itself procreated Non-being (τὸ μὴ Ὄν).” Finally he adds that some Valentinians actually taught: darkness was begotten from the very nature of the soul.

p. 383, 15. καὶ ὡς οὐ λοιδορητέον τοῖς χείροσι τῶν πρώτων] From where Ficinus has those words: *or to accuse the lower of being the supreme things*, I do not know. Certainly our books offer nothing. Therefore we have enclosed them in brackets. The other, *or to improvise the subsequent things of the supreme*, responds well enough to the Greek words. I should prefer, however: *things worse than the supreme*. Taylor: “*And from not considering that subordinate beings ought not to revile such as are first.*” Concerning which he himself may see.

p. 383, 18. αἳ δὴ πάντα μείλιχα τεύχουσιν αὐτοῖς] He had before his eyes these words of Pindar, *Olymp.* I. 48. (30.): Χάρις δ’ ἅπερ ἅπαντα τεύχει τὰ μείλιχα θνατοῖς [Grace, which fashions all things that are sweet for mortals].

p. 384, 9. ταῦτα οὐ τυραννίδος ἕνεκα ἐν τῷ παντὶ ὄντα] For there were among the Gnostics, especially the Ophites, those who taught that the maker of the world (τὸν δημιουργὸν), whom they called *Ialdabaoth* (Ἰαλδαβαὼθ), and whom they called the supreme prince of the planets, was proud and malevolent. (See Origen *contra Cels.* lib. VI. p. 296. sqq. Spencer ed. and confer Gieseler in *Lehrbuch der Kirchengeschichte*, Darmstadt and Bonn, 1824. I. Period. I. Sect. 2. §. 42. p. 125. But if you compare the next part: ἃ δὲ λέγεται γίνεσθαι παρ’ αὐτῶν, σημεῖα νομίζειν τῶν ἐσομένων εἶναι [and those things said to happen by them, consider them to be signs of things to come], and if you remember what Plotinus discussed above in II. 3, in the book *whether the stars act*, you might rather think that in this place he deals with those who placed the power of the stars over human affairs and actions. (Cf. also Origen's *Philocalia*, cap. XXIII. p. 75. Spencer ed.: φέρε δὴ, ἀγωνισώμεθα καὶ περὶ τοῦ τοὺς ἀστέρας μηδαμῶς εἶναι ποιητικοὺς τῶν ἐν ἀνθρώποις, σημαντικοὺς δὲ μόνον [Come then, let us also contend concerning this, that the stars are in no way causative of things among men, but only significant], etc.) There were, however, among the Gnostics those who were dedicated to astrology, i.e., the science of divining the future from the stars. An epigram against Marcus the Gnostic in Irenæus *advers. Hæres.* I. c. 15 shows this. Which dreams, however, other Gnostics rejected, among them Bardesanes, who vehemently attacked that opinion on the power of the stars in the actions of men; see his discussions in Eusebius, *P. Evang.* VI. 10. at the end. Cf. *Frid. Münter* in the book: *Der Stern der Weisen* p. 61. and citations there; in these Hahn’s *Bardesanes* p. 24.

p. 385, 6. οὐκ ἀκήρατα] Cf. III. 5. 2. and V. 1. 14. where there is ἀκήρατος νοῦς [undefiled mind]. It is a Platonic word and frequent as far as Synesius and later writers. See Ruhnken on *Tim. Lex.* p. 17. and the annotation of the learned Krabinger, my very dear friend, on Synesius *de Regno* p. 194. Regarding the argument of this entire passage, no one is unaware that Paul the Apostle attacked these evil arts already spreading in Ephesus (*Acts* XIX. 19. τὰ περίεργα [curious arts]). Concerning which passage see, besides the others, Valckenaer's *Scholas in N. T.* I. p. 564. sq. Mercer and Schurzfleisch on *Aristænet.* XVIII. p. 711. Boissonade ed.

**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

That many of the Gnostics gave their effort to these incantations and other magical arts is spoken of by gems (Abraxas, although not all these things are to be attributed to Gnostics), plates and other amulets, also songs, remains of which are preserved. See, lest I mention more, Routh's *Reliquiæ Sacræ* I. p. 57. and p. 65. and *Fr. Münter’s* Gnostic Odes in Thebaic [Coptic] and Latin, Copenhagen 1822.

p. 386, 1. ὑποστησάμενοι τὰς νόσους δαιμόνια εἶναι] A memorable passage, and one which ought to be compared by interpreters of the N. T. (unless perhaps someone among so many learned men has already done so.) Δαιμόνια in this place must be taken as Jewish Hellenists and sacred writers take it, for *evil spirits*, from whom the Jews were accustomed to trace whatever calamities or more serious diseases happened to men. Concerning which use of the word see, lest I rouse many, Schleusner's *Nov. Thesaur. Philolog.—crit. in LXX.* T. II. p. 48. sq. Wetstein's *N. T.* Vol. I. p. 279. sq. and L. C. Valckenaer's *Scholas in N. T.* Vol. I. p. 131. and II. p. 264. Nor is it at all surprising that those of the Gnostics who applied themselves more closely to the doctrines and institutions of the Jews—such as Valentinus, Heracleon, Marcus, Ptolemæus, Theodotus, Bardesanes and their followers—retained those dogmas on the power of evil spirits in the bodies of mortals, and according to their pride and supreme arrogance, took it upon themselves to call themselves the superiors of these spirits and to promise their most effective aid to the sick.

p. 387, 8. καὶ πλείστης περιωπῆς ἔχουσα] See Apollonius *Lex. Hom.* p. 547. Toll ed. Zonaras *Lex.* p. 1534 and Tittmann there. But there σκοπιᾷ, a watchtower. Thucydides IV. 86. had turned the use of this word into another meaning, namely περισκέψεως, *providence/foresight*, reprehended by this name by Dionysius of Halicarnassus *Epist.* II. ad Ann. cap. III. Tom. V. p. 793. Reiske ed. See Wasse on the cited passage of Thucydides and Krüger on Dionysius of Halicarnassus’ *Historiographica* p. 224. Plotinus uses the word in clearly the same way as Thucydides in this place. Proclus uses the same word in *Platon. Alcib.* I. p. 19. p. 21. p. 83. where there is περιωπὴ νοερά [intellectual watchtower]. Cf. Annotations above p. 22. B. and Philostratus’ *Imagg.* p. 89. and p. 133. and Jacobs at that passage p. 656. Concerning the construction of the passage: instead of μεταδιώκουσα and ἔχουσα, you would expect μεταδιώκον and ἔχον after εἶδος φιλοσοφίας in the preceding words. But Plotinus indulges himself six hundred times in joining the members of his speech through an enallage. The final words of the chapter: τὰ δ’ ἄλλα—ἡμῖν ἂν πρέποι Taylor entirely omitted, alleging that these things were too obscure for him to wish to risk translating them. Nor perhaps should we take the risk, but let us try nonetheless. The next part: τὰ δ’ ἄλλα τῷ τοιούτῳ παραβάλλειν are to be joined with the higher καταλείπω, from which the remaining infinitives also hung, in this sense: *But these other things, i.e., contrary to this our reasoning of philosophy, I leave to you (who read the Gnostic writings) to be compared with this (our) kind of philosophizing. But whatever is handed down by these others (Gnostics) is instituted in all things in a most diverse way. For you would not profit anything. (For a comparison of this sort is of no use, since the Gnostics seem in no way able to be corrected.) For thus it may become us to speak of these (Gnostics).* You see Plotinus, after he had said in the preceding words that he left the reading of the Gnostic books to his friends so that they could compare the Platonic reasoning with the Gnostic reasoning: in the final words he retracts his statements, because he is persuaded that nothing is gained by this labor spent in reading the Gnostic books. The formula οὐδὲν γὰρ ἂν πλέον [for there would be nothing more] sc. ἦν [it was], Plotinus has from Plato. For he says in the *Symposium* p. 217. C. p. 456. Bekker ed. οὐδὲν γάρ μοι πλέον ἦν. Likewise *Republ.* I. p. 341. p. 31. Bekker: οὐδέν γέ σοι πλέον ἦν. See Valckenaer in *Diatr. Euripid.* p. 150. Ast on *Platon. Phædr.* p. 386. on *Rempubl.* p. 363. Without ἦν, like Plotinus, Xenophon *Cyrop.* V. 5. 34: τί γὰρ ἐμοὶ πλέον τὸ τὴν γῆν πλατύνεσθαι, αὐτὸν δὲ ἀτιμάζεσθαι. *What does it help me? What does it profit me?*

p. 388, 1. Ὁ μὲν Ἐπίκουρος τὴν πρόνοιαν ἀνελὼν, τὴν ἡδονὴν—διώκειν παρακελεύεται] In these things Plotinus proves himself a genuine Platonist. Look at Plato, *de Legg.* X. p. 885. b. and p. 900. sqq. The Pythagorean Hippodamus also, in Stobæus *Floril.* XLIII. p. 127. Gaisford ed., argues to the same effect. Origen also says beautifully against Celsus VI. p. 293. Spencer: καὶ ὥσπερ οὐ καθήκει τοῖς τὰ Πλάτωνος φιλοσοφοῦσιν ἀπολογεῖσθαι περὶ Ἐπικούρου καὶ τῶν ἀσεβῶν αὐτοῦ δογμάτων [And just as it is not fitting for those who philosophize the things of Plato to apologize for Epicurus and his impious dogmas]. That Epicurus removed Providence and commended pleasure was commonly believed by the ancients. See only Cicero, *de N. D.*

**BOOK IX. ENNEAD SECOND. p. 386—392.**

I. 17. and I. 40.; whence that witty saying of Taurus the philosopher against him in A. Gellius IX. 5.: "‘Pleasure is the end’ is a dogma of a harlot. There is no providence; not even a dogma of a harlot." Cf. our annotations to Cicero l. l. p. 181. Plotinus continues: ὁ δὲ λόγος οὗτος. Ficinus: *But the discourse of the Gnostics*. Correct as to the sentiment, but not as to the words. For our philosopher does not name the Gnostics. See I. A. Fabricius on *Porphyr. de Vit. Plotini* c. 24. and our annotations to the title of this Plotinian book.

p. 388, 3. ἔτι νεανικώτερον] Ficinus is better here than Taylor. For the former: *even more insolently*: the latter: *as still more juvenile than this*. A Platonic formula. See examples collected by Heindorf on *Lysis* p. 7; add *Suidas* II. p. 603. Zonaras *Lex.* p. 1392: νεανικώτερον: τολμηρότερον [more daringly]. Cf. Hemsterhuis on *Aristoph. Plutum* vs. 1183. Casaubon on *Athen.* IV. p. 606. sq. and Schweighäuser there. Valckenaer *Scholl. in N. T.* I. p. 335. sq. Locella on *Xenoph. Ephes.* p. 326. Peerlkamp ed. Matthæi on *Io. Chrysost. — 4. καὶ τὴν ἀρετὴν τὴν ἐκ παντὸς τοῦ χρόνου ἀνευρημένην] These words of Plotinus remind one of Herodotus I. 8: πάλαι δὲ τὰ καλὰ ἀνθρώποισι ἐξεύρηται, ἐκ τῶν μανθάνειν δεῖ [and long ago beautiful things have been discovered for men, from which one must learn].

— 5. τό, τε σωφρονεῖν τοῦτο ἐν γέλωτι θέμενος—τὴν ἡδονὴν [etc.]] These things correspond exactly to what the Fathers of the Church complain about regarding the Gnostics. Clement of Alexandria, *Strom.* II. p. 490. Potter ed.: οἶδα ἐγὼ αἱρέσει τινὶ ἐντυχών· καὶ ὁ ταύτης προϊστάμενος, διὰ τῆς χρήσεως ἔφασκεν τῆς ἡδονῆς ἡδονῇ μάχεσθαι. αὐτομολῶν πρὸς ἡδονὴν διὰ προσποιητοῦ μάχης ὁ γενναῖος οὗτος Γνωστικός· ἔφασκε γὰρ δὴ αὑτὸν καὶ Γνωστικὸν εἶναι [I know I have encountered a certain sect; and the leader of it said that through the use of pleasure he fought pleasure. This noble Gnostic, deserting to pleasure through a feigned battle; for he even claimed to be a Gnostic], etc. Then Clement reminds us of Aristippus of Cyrene, just as Plotinus here reminds us of Epicurus. Plotinus' disciple Porphyry records clearly similar dogmas and institutions of men of this kind in *De Abstinentia* I. 40. sqq. p. 69—72. Rhoer ed. Cf. Clement l. l. where this decree of the Nicolaitans is also castigated: τὸ δεῖν παραχρῆσθαι τῇ σαρκί [that one must abuse the flesh]. Add Clement *Strom.* III. I. p. 510, where the perverse things which the followers of Basilides repeated from the arguments of their reasoning are recounted, and cf. Lewald’s *Comment. de Doctrina Gnostica* p. 55. sq. and Neander’s *Allg. Geschichte der Christl. Relig. u. Kirche* I. 2. Sect. IV. p. 658. sq. and p. 776. Certainly these Gnostics whom Plotinus, Clement, and Porphyry note, abused the sayings of Paul the Apostle in I Corinthians 6, 12 and 8, 9 concerning liberty (ἐξουσίᾳ), and stubbornly denied that they, as spiritual men (πνευματικοὺς), could be contaminated by pleasures and crimes, though they might immerse themselves entirely in them. Which perversity was not only vituperated by the doctors of the Christian religion, but was fundamentally overturned by the ethnic philosopher Plotinus. The final parts of the page and p. 214. Α. καὶ τὸ οὐ κοινὸν πρὸς ἄλλους ἀνθρώπους [and what is not common with other men] could therefore be said more justly against the Gnostics than against the Christians, to whom nevertheless *hatred of the human race* was given as a crime and recorded in the memory of Roman historians as well. See Tacitus *Annales* XV. 44. *Historr.* V. 6. Pliny *Epist.* X. 97. Tertullian *Apologet.* c. 7. 21. and cf. I. A. Fabricius’ *Bibliograph. Antiquar.* p. 756. and Tillemont, *Histoire des Empéreurs Romains* T. I. p. 297. sqq.

p. 389, 12. ἄνευ δὲ ἀρετῆς ἀληθινῆς θεὸς λεγόμενος ὄνομά ἐστιν.] An outstanding passage, and one which reminds us of similar sayings in the N. T.

p. 392, 10. Καί τοι εἰ καὶ μισεῖν—ἐπήει τὴν τοῦ σώματος φύσιν.] Everyone perceives that the sentence is harsher if you read with the Edition ἐποίει. And through Itacism, the parent of so many vices, the more elegant reading ἐπήει could have been obscured. Concerning this formula ἔπεισι and ἐπήει with the dative and infinitive, regarding thoughts entering the mind, see Tib. Hemsterhuis on *Lucian's Prometheus* Vol. I. p. 26; Valckenaer on *Eurip. Phœniss.* 1378; Wyttenbach on *Selecta Historr.* p. 346; Bast on *Gregor. Cor.* p. 375; and regarding the elliptical formula ἐπήει αὐτῷ ὅτι, Bak on *Cleomedes’ Meteor.* p. 421.—Next, ὅτι [that] must be thought with εἶπε [he said]. Plato’s primary passage is in the *Phaedo* p. 65. a. c. 11. p. 15. Wyttenbach ed.: τί δὲ δὴ περὶ αὐτὴν τὴν τῆς φρονήσεως κτῆσιν; πότερον ἐμπόδιον τὸ σῶμα ἢ οὐ, ἐάν τις αὐτὸ ἐν τῇ ζητήσει κοινωνὸν συμπαραλαμβάνῃ; [And what about the acquisition of wisdom? Is the body an obstacle or not, if one takes it as a partner in the search?], etc. at which passage Wyttenbach has not forgotten our passage, nor another IV. 9. 386. C. ἐμπόδιον γὰρ τοῦτο εἴ τις αὐτῷ ἐν ταῖς σκέψεσι προσχρῷτο [for this is an obstacle if one should use it in his investigations], and p. 153. the same learned man: “Plotinus pronounces (II. 9. p. 215. F. G.) that the Gnostics, interpreting the Platonic reprehension of the body incorrectly, deceived themselves.”

— 14. ψυχὰς ἐν τάξει ἄνευ τῶν σωμάτων] In these (where in the following, instead of κατὰ τὸ, perhaps καὶ κατὰ τὸ should be read), those words ἐν τάξει [in order] and κατὰ

**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

τὸ νοητὸν [according to the intelligible] must be held, lest you think anything sinister in the word διαστάσεως [separation/extension]. For elsewhere διάστασις signifies a degenerate departure. Proclus in *Alcib. pr.* p. 57: ὥσπερ οὖν τὸ ἄλλοι τὴν διάστασιν αὐτῶν ἐδήλου καὶ τὴν διεσπαρμένην ζωὴν, οὕτω καὶ τῷ δι’ ὄχλου γίνεσθαι τῷ νεανίσκῳ τὴν εἰς αὐτὸν ἀπ’ ἐκείνων ἥκουσαν ἐπήρειαν ἐνδείκνυται [Just as then 'others' showed their separation and scattered life, so too the influence coming to the youth from them is indicated by happening through the crowd]. Generally, however, διάστασις is sometimes *an interval*, as in Plato in the *Timæus*. See Plutarch *de animorr. generat. in Timæo* p. 1020. A. and *dimension* (see above p. 101. A. and cf. p. 331, 332. and below p. 360. B. which passage is entirely to be compared with ours. Cf. also Aristotle in Stobæus *Eclogg. Phys.* I. p. 344. Heeren ed.); sometimes *secretion* (division) the contrary of which is μίξις, mixture; Plutarch *de Placc. Philos.* I. 30. p. 885. p. 562. sq. Wyttenbach ed. Ἐμπεδοκλῆς φύσιν μηδὲν εἶναι, μίξιν δὲ τῶν στοιχείων καὶ διάστασιν (Empedocles said that nature is nothing, but a mixture of elements and a separation). Hermes in Stobæus *Eclogg.* I. 52. p. 968. Heeren ed.: εἶπε καὶ εὐθέως κοσμικῶς τῆς ἔτι μελαίνης ἑνώσεως διάστασις ἐγένετο, καὶ ἐφάνη μὲν ὁ οὐρανὸς ἄνω [He spoke, and immediately a separation occurred of the still dark cosmic union, and the heaven appeared above]. In which passage Heeren restored μελαίνης from *cod. A.* instead of μελένης, but Ruhnken on *Longinus de Sublim.* p. 280. Toup, p. 277. Weiske ed., shows: κοσμικῆς τῆς ἔτι γενέσεως διαστ. ἐγεν. Longinus himself *de Subl.* IX. 6. p. 30. Weiske ed.: ἀνατροπὴν δὲ ὅλου (Ruhnken corrects ἂν: δὲ δι’ ὅλου) καὶ διάστασιν τοῦ κόσμου λαβόντος [taking the overthrow and separation of the whole world].

p. 393, 6. ὅτι μὴ θέμις φθόνον ἐν τοῖς θεοῖς εἶναι.] See Plato *Timæus* p. 29. D. Most especially, these words from the *Phaedrus* p. 247. a.: φθόνος γὰρ ἔξω χοροῦ θείου ἵσταται [for envy stands outside the divine choir], are celebrated by the imitation of writers. See Tib. Hemsterhuis on *Lucian, Prometheus* §. 18. tom. I. p. 201; Heindorf on *Phædr.* l. l. p. 251; and Wyttenbach on *Eunap.* p. 102. sq., who compared another formula there, which Plotinus used in I. 6. 2. p. 52. A. (for thus it is to be corrected): ἔξω θείου λόγου [outside divine reason]; with that one.

— 11. αἰσχρὰ καὶ καλὰ ὁρᾷν σώματα—ἐπιτηδεύματα—μαθήματα [etc.]] He has before his eyes the words of Diotima in Plato’s *Symposium* p. 210. A. B. p. 442. Bekker ed.—

— 13. οὐδὲ θεωρίας τοίνυν] Ficinus seems to have read θεωρίαν, which is pleasing, as being more suited to the Platonic passage. For Plato, immediately after ἐπιτηδεύματα [practices], places τὰς ἐπιστήμας [sciences]: Plotinus τὰ μαθήματα [studies]. Then Plato subjoins τινὰ ἐπιστήμην μίαν [a certain single science], which τὸ καλὸν αὐτὸ καθ’ αὑτό [beauty itself according to itself] immediately follows: Plotinus: θεωρίας and finally θεόν [God]. You see therefore that the singular θεωρίαν [contemplation] responds better to the τῇ ἐπιστήμῃ μιᾷ of Plato than the plural.

p. 395, 14. ἀγνοῶν, ὅτι τῷ μὴ φέρειν τὰ ἀναγκαῖα διαφέρει—των λίθων] I have changed nothing in a passage of this sort, which I should think could be resolved thus: *Not knowing that he differs from another (only) in this, that he himself does not bear (patiently) necessary things*, if indeed he does not even say (profess, claim for himself, as Plotinus uses this word with a gentle irony) *that he bears it with difficulty* (departure from that building) *who is moderately delighted by the beauty of the stones*. Namely ποιεῖται instead of περιποιεῖται (Viger X. 14. p. 288. and Hoogeveen there) and then ὁ ἀγαπῶν. But nevertheless this reasoning has something harsh about it. Therefore another must be entered upon, so that you either conjecture πονεῖται for ποιεῖται, and say δυσχεραίνειν was born from a gloss, or: εἴπερ καὶ μὴ δυσχεραίνων πορεύεται ὁ ἀγαπῶν [etc.]. Since *neither will he who loves... depart with difficulty*, etc.; and certainly Ficinus seems to have read this or something very similar. Regarding the argument, see above the booklet *on rational departure*, and what I placed there p. 85.

— 17. ὑπὸ ψυχῆς ἀδελφῆς ἀγαθῆς—τὴν κόσμου ψυχήν] It is helpful to append what *Tholuck* discusses in the book *Ssufismus* p. 232. sq.: “For they are not far from that (decree) which the *Indians* have concerning *Pur-Atma* and *Dschiv-Atma*. The former among the Indians is equated to divine omniscience; it is quiet and free from all change; the latter penetrates the world, making man, animals, and plants living, and joins itself by a close necessity to the human mind and senses. See *Ayeen Akbari* trans. *Gladwin*, London 1800. T. VI. p. 389. and *Dow, History of Hindostan* 1772, 4to. And since the Sufis so studiously inculcate that the soul of the world is connected and coupled with the divinity by the closest kinship and necessity, it would not be inept to return to those fathers of the Christian church who were persuaded that, besides the Holy Spirit, wrongly snatched into this matter, there is another mundane soul, though in no way different from God, to whom the dispensation and sustenance of all things is committed. The testimonies of this invention were collected by the most learned Moshemius on Cudworth p. 688.” This same Tholuck adds in a subjoined annotation: “As I was writing this, *Plotinus*

came to mind, who calls the universal soul the human soul’s πρεσβυτέραν ἀδελφὴν, *the elder sister*. See Cudworth in *System. Intell.* p. 700. Mosheim ed.” Thus Tholuck. But Philo Judæus also denies that the soul of the world is different from God, *Leg. Allegoriarr.* I. p. 172. Α. thus: Ἀρ’ οὖν ἡ βελτίστη γυμναστικὴ ἀδελφή τις ἂν εἴη τῆς ἁπλῆς μουσικῆς, ἣν ὀλίγον πρότερον διῇμεν; [Would not then the best gymnastics be a certain sister to the simple music which we discussed a little before?].
