H.* X. 14.: ἡ ἀργία ἀδελφὴ τῆς ἐλευθερίας [idleness is the sister of liberty]. cf. X. 18. Sometimes it is conveniently translated as *similar*. cf. Koen on *Gregor. Corinth.* p. 269. On the use of the adjective: ἀδελφὰ τούτων [sisters to these] or τούτοις, add Valckenaer *Scholl. in N. T.* II. p. 33.

p. 395, 18. ἢ ἀδελφοὺς μὲν καὶ τοὺς φαυλοτάτους ἀξιοῦσι προσειπεῖν [etc.]] These things might seem to pertain to the Christians; for no one is unaware that they once called themselves *brothers and sisters*. Hence ἀδελφοὶ often means *Christians*, in the Gospel of *Matthew* XXV. 40; *Acts* VI. 3; 1 *Cor.* v. 11. and everywhere in the N. T. and in the writings of the fathers of the church. See Suicer, *Thesaur. Ecclesiast.* T. I. p. 86. and Vorstius, *Philol. Sacra* c. 3. p. 67. Fischer ed. Nevertheless, since the word ἀδελφοὶ is used by ancient writers in this sense as well, such as of φίλων, *friends*, and includes a similar force: see Price on *Appuleius’ Metam.* I. 44. Tom. III. p. 157. Bosscha ed., Dorville on *Chariton.* IV. 3. p. 433. Leipzig ed. [p. 384. Amsterdam ed.] and Sturz’s *Lex. Xenoph.* I. p. 51.) nor is it improbable that this appellation among the Gnostics also had the significance of mutual love. But the final words στόματι μαινομένῳ [with a raving mouth] is an epithet of Bacchic fury. See only Clement of Alexandria *Cohortat.* p. 3. above and p. 30. middle, Potter ed., and it reminds us of similar formulas, such as ἀχάλινον [unbridled], ἀκρατὲς [unrestrained], ἀθύρωπον [un-doored], ἀπύλωτον στόμα [un-gated mouth], likewise ἀθυροστομίας [opening the mouth without a door]. Regarding this see Wyttenbach on *Plutarch de Educat. puer.* p. 132. Oxford ed. Perhaps Plotinus also had before his eyes Plato's passage in *Rep.* VIII. 13. p. 562. sq.

p. 396, 6. Ἔστι δὲ τοῦτο, τὸ μὴ κρούειν] We have received the reading of the margin and of all our books. And Ficinus also read it, translating: “*That however is not to be cast down from one's step.*” Taylor: “*This however, consists* IN BEING FREE FROM IMPULSION:” and the verb πλήττεσθαι [to be struck] in the following seems to respond to that verb. But I should believe that in this place, regarding κρούειν [to strike/push], πρύμναν [the stern] must be thought of, i.e., to push the stern, i.e., to retreat little by little κατ’ ὀλίγον ἀναχωρεῖν, or to stop the ship’s course such that you press it with oars and drive it back little by little. (See Thucydides I. 51. III. 78. V. 17. and the Scholiast and interpreters there.) Which significance was afterwards transferred by metaphor to those who, when an attack is made upon them, do not resist but recede a little, or perhaps even to those who turn themselves in the opposite direction. But another similar expression, διπλᾶ κρούειν [to strike double], is taken from musical affairs, if one trusts the Marcian Scholiast on *Aristides* T. II. p. 402. Jebb ed.: τὸ διπλᾶ κρούειν: a proverb applied to those who are double-minded. It was taken from musical instruments which have strings on both sides, etc. It is used, however, of a man *who is not consistent with himself*. See Cognatus and Jacob Morell on *Aristides’ Leptin.* p. 162. sq.

— 9. ἀρετῇ τὰς πληγὰς ἀπωθοίμεθ’ ἂν] To this formula apply what Wyttenbach collected on *Julian’s Orat.* I. p. 18. p. 177. sq. Leipzig ed.—Next, Ficinus did not express ἢ ὁρωμένοις [or things seen]. I have added it in the version, just as Taylor also did. I suspect nevertheless that more has fallen out after ὁρωμένοις, which would pertain to the remaining senses of the body, hearing, and smell. Soon with the *Vatican Codex* and Marsilio, whom Taylor also followed, we have written ἐν θέᾳ [in sight/spectacle] instead of ἔνθεα [divinely inspired]. Recognize the necessity of the correction from these words which are read a little after: οὐδὲ εἰ μόνοι λέγοιεν θεωρεῖν δύνασθαι [nor if they alone should say they were able to contemplate], etc.

p. 397, 3. ἔξεστιν οὖν καὶ μὴ φιλοσωματεῖν—καὶ τοῦ θανάτου καταφρονεῖν] These have Plato as their author. For thus he says in the *Phaedo* c. 13. p. 68. B.: οὐκοῦν ἱκανόν σοι τεκμήριον, ἔφη, τοῦτο ἀνδρὸς ὃν ἂν ἴδῃς ἀγανακτοῦντα μέλλοντα ἀποθανεῖσθαι, ὅτι οὐκ ἄρ’ ἦν φιλόσοφος, ἀλλὰ τις φιλο- [Is not this then a sufficient proof for you, he said, of a man whom you see being vexed when about to die, that he was not then a philosopher, but some lover of (the body/money)...]

**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

**σώματος [of the body].** Aristides, *Orationes Platonicae*, p. 312: “One might call the others 'body-lovers' (*philosomatoi*), but not 'philosophers,' in the language of Plato.” Wyttenbach presents more on the passage of the *Phaedo* at pp. 166–168. I shall add certain other things. Philo Judaeus, *Legis Allegoriae* I, p. 140 (Pfeiffer ed.), distinguishes between "the earth-born and body-loving mind" (*ton gegenē kai philosomaton noun*) and "that which has come into being according to the Idea." Hierocles, *In aurea carmina Pythagoreorum*, p. 123 (London ed.): “And you will find what the human essence is, never supposing it to be the body, nor the things outside it, nor struggling for these as if for yourself, lest you be dragged down toward body-loving (*philosomatia*) and money-loving.” Porphyry, *Epistola ad Marcellam* XXV, p. 44 (editio princeps), p. 305 (Orellius ed.): “But the law of nature is transgressed by those who, through vain opinions, are ignorant and devoted to an excessive love of the body (*philosomatia*).” Thus Orellius correctly for the portentous [OCR error] *agaphilosomatia*. The word seems rather rare. However, Pollux has it in *Onomasticon* III. 137, p. 337 (Hemsterhuis ed.): “and the verbs *deilian* [to be afraid], *apodeilian* [to shrink back], *oknein* [to hesitate]—*philopsychein* [to love life/soul], *philosomatein* [to love the body]”—and after a few interjections: “*philopsychon, philosomaton, oknon*,” etc. Accordingly, in this verb, the significance of soul (*psyche*) and body (*soma*) corresponds. Regarding the verb *philopsychein*, see Gataker on Marcus Aurelius VII. 46, p. 222 sq.

***

**BOOK I. ENNEAD THREE.**

**p. 411, 7. ΠΕΡΙ ΕΙΜΑΡΜΕΝΗΣ [ON FATE]** This is the third book in number, and consequently among those from which Plotinus began his writing (Porphyry, *Life of Plotinus*, c. 4 and c. 24). Moreover, that "astrological fate," as it is usually called, was held sacred in the religions of the most ancient peoples, no one can doubt. For even if the name of the Chaldeans is widespread among writers after Alexander the Great, it cannot be doubted that the Babylonians and other nations who worshipped the stars believed from antiquity that human affairs were contained and disposed by the power of the constellations. Philo Judaeus, *On the Migration of Abraham*, p. 464 (Mangey ed.): “The Chaldeans seem to have labored exceptionally more than other men in astronomy and genethlialogy [horoscopy]... These men imagined this visible world to be the only thing among existing things, either being God itself, or containing God within it as the soul of the whole; having deified Fate and Necessity, they overspread human life with much impiety, teaching that, apart from the visible [stars], there is no cause of anything at all, but the circuits of the sun, moon, and other stars dispense both good and its opposite to each of the things that exist.” Sextus Empiricus argues to the same effect in *Against the Mathematicians* V. 2 sqq., p. 338 (Fabricius ed.), where in that same place, based on Philo (loc. cit.), *genethlialogian* should be restored instead of *genealogian*, which I am surprised Fabricius did not admit into the text, having seen the fault. The Jewish philosophers had to decide differently regarding fate; among them, the Pharisees (if Josephus is trusted in *Jewish War* II. 7) made all things depend on God and Fate, since they themselves were far removed from that cult of the stars such as existed among the Chaldeans. But what they specifically taught is a long matter to inquire into, and not necessary in this place.

The Greek philosophers, as soon as they began to inquire into the occult causes of things, Cicero reports, decided in two ways. For he says thus in *On Fate*, c. 17: “And it seems to me, indeed, that since there had been two opinions of the ancient philosophers—one of those who thought that all things happened by fate in such a way that fate brought the force of necessity (in which opinion Democritus, Heraclitus, Empedocles, and Aristotle were); the other of those to whom the voluntary motions of minds seemed to exist without any fate—Chrysippus, as an honorary arbiter, wished to strike a middle path; but he attaches himself rather to those who want the motions of minds to be freed from necessity.” On this, see Davies and the rest of the interpreters, whose collected observations are best provided by our edition of Cicero’s *On Divination* and *On Fate*, i.e., the Frankfurt edition of 1828, adorned chiefly by the care of Moser. I have treated the decrees of Heraclitus on Fate elsewhere in the commentary titled: *Passages of Ancient Philosophers on Divine Providence and Likewise on Fate are Emended and Explained*, Heidelberg 1806, 4to, and in my *Dionysius* p. 71 sqq., where I touched upon other matters and showed how much the Stoics profited in this doctrine from Heraclitus.

--- Page 142 ---
**BOOK I. ENNEAD THREE. p. 411.**

I have also endeavored to explain the passages of the Stoics, and especially Chrysippus, on Fate in the annotations to Cicero’s *On the Nature of the Gods* I. 15, p. 67 sqq.; cf. ibid. the excerpts from Wyttenbach’s *Scholae* for Book III, ch. 6, p. 778 sq. To these now add the arguments of the most learned **Baguet** in his *Disputation on the Life, Doctrine, and Remains of Chrysippus*, p. 94 sqq. and p. 218 sqq. Also, Diodorus of Tarsus had written *Against the Astronomers and Astrologers and Fate*, as Suidas testifies (I, p. 594, Kuster ed.), and likewise *On Providence*. See Suidas (loc. cit.) and cf. Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Graeca* IX, p. 278 (Harles ed.) and Lucas Holstenius, *Epistolae*, p. 95, 100, and 106 (Boissonade ed.) and his annotations. Cf. also the booklet of Sallustius *On the Gods and the World*, c. 9, which chapter is inscribed: *On Providence, Fate, and Fortune*. But some things regarding the decrees of these philosophers will be added below at various passages of this Plotinian book.

Here I will subjoin a few things which seem to pertain generally to the argument of this book, in which an indication of the books or passages from which the opinions of the Pythagoreans, Platonists, and Peripatetics on Fate can be known will be especially expected. Conveniently, there offers itself to me the explanation of **Tiberius Hemsterhuis** from MS notes on Iamblichus’s *Protrepticus*, which the most distinguished and friendly man **Jacobus Geel** communicated to me, and which at another time I will apply in their entirety, if God permits, to the book of Iamblichus. Thus, however, he says on the passage of Iamblichus p. 7 (Arceerius ed.): “For the Pythagoreans thought this: that nothing in this universe is immoderate, but all things happen by fixed laws and a tempered tenor; indeed, even the stars, which they call by the common name 'wanderers,' keep constant and fixed motions, so that the circuit goes around in like manner (*periphoran hōsautōs periousan*), as Davies taught on Cicero’s *Tusculan Disputations* I. 25.

The question was asked whether human will was inherent in, and subject and bound to, the laws and order of nature, or rather free and surpassing the force and necessity of fate. This question was tossed and debated with various disagreements of minds among philosophers of every family. But see how the Pythagoreans, at least the more recent ones, by introducing a twofold mind, strive to extricate themselves from this. All things that exist are contained by a certain common bond, as if linked by little chains; the human race is placed in the middle, distant equally from both boundaries, the highest and the lowest. It has, therefore, both that by which it may be raised to eternal things and divine cognition, and that by which it may be depressed and incline toward these fluxional things and the earthly condition of life. The ancients also pass these things down with great consensus, as I shall say elsewhere: above the force of natural law and order stands the more divine and free mind, which preserves affinity with the first deity, and in which, perfected and modeled after the likeness of God as far as it can be, the total happiness of men consists. This is that 'God-viewing' (*theoptikē*) part of the soul, which participates in the first intelligible and the power of the intelligible. The other part, which descends into us derived from the uniform circuit of the heavens, obeys the fixed and settled laws of its own origin, inasmuch as it has obtained a 'generative nature' (*physin genesiourgon*), and is thus servile and subject to the order of nature. This opinion flowed from the Egyptians, as Iamblichus shows in *On the Mysteries*, Sect. VIII, 6, 7, and Thomas Gale on him. From the source of the same opinion flowed Astrology, which especially professes the science of establishing nativities [horoscopes], which Porphyry shows in more detail in *On Things in Our Power* in Stobaeus, *Eclogae Physicae*, p. 203; cf. also Manetho in *Apotelesmata*, Book I and passim. Even the demons of a lower order, when they have come into these regions of the sky which are revolved by an immutable ratio of motions, obey the necessity of nature. Philoponus, in *On the Creation of the World* IV. 20, preserved an excellent fragment of Porphyry from *On Philosophy from Oracles* on this matter. The opinion of the Stoics inclined in the same direction, when they divided the things and actions of human life into 'things in our power' (*ta eph’ hēmin*) and 'things not in our power' (*ta ouk eph’ hēmin*). In the latter category were placed all events which hung upon the fatal law of natural motions; whence that saying of Epictetus: 'If someone attempts to incline the mind toward these things, and to persuade himself to willingly receive necessary things (*ta anankaia*), he will live his life quite moderately and harmoniously.' Simplicius shows to what extent the 'fated circuit' (*hē heimarmenē periphora*) dominates in men on Epictetus p. 24, 26. Rightly indeed are 'necessary things' (*ta anankaia*), which happen naturally and 'by necessity' (*kat’ anankēn*) in our author, [traced back] to the necessary laws of nature: for that this is necessity and *anankē* was sometimes learnedly noted by that great man, **I. Fr. Gronovius**, *Observationes* II. 2. **Gassendi** observes the same in *On the Physiology of Epicurus*, p. 711. It is from this that Euripides calls Jupiter 'the necessity of nature' (*physeōs anankēn*) in *Troades*, v. 886. See **Spanheim** on Callimachus, *Hymn to Delos* 122.”

--- Page 143 ---
**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

“...and a certain ancient epigram calls the fixed motions of this Universe 'the ever-whirling necessities of the world' (*kosmoio aeidinētous anankas*). Among the Pythagorean people, therefore, the mind is said 'to serve the necessities of nature' (*douleuein tais tēs physeōs anankais*) when it submits its immutable and eternal nature—the author of its innate motion—to the necessary laws of the lower world and makes it compliant; nevertheless, in this very condition of the inferior life, there is some place for 'the life according to the mind that clings to the gods' (*tō kata noun biō tōn theōn echomenō*), which is of its own accord; which path if anyone follows, he asserts into liberty 'the masterless authority of the soul' (*tēn adispoton tēs psychēs exousian*) and, to use their words, 'is released from necessary things' (*tōn anankaiōn apolyetai*). Iamblichus to Macedonius and others hand down these and more of this kind. Those words of Democritus in Stobaeus, *Sermo* CVI (for they are wrongly ascribed to Demetrius), must be understood in the same sense: 'it is folly not to yield to the necessities of life'—that is, to those things that seem to happen by chance and without order, although in truth they are tempered by a certain plan; wherefore no sane person, having weighed the order of things and necessity, 'grows wild against necessity' (*pros tēn anankēn agriainetai*), as that which is defined and circumscribed by the unmoved limits of nature. Read the most elegant Hierocles and cf. Plutarch Vol. II, p. 926 sq., Diogenes Laertius IX. 45, and especially Aristides Quintilianus p. 161 sqq.”

Thus Tib. Hemsterhuis. How much these things pertain to the disputations of Plato and Plotinus does not need to be laboriously demonstrated. Moreover, what Plato’s opinion was concerning Fate and free will is best known from several primary passages in the books *On Laws*, in the *Phaedrus*, *Phaedo*, and in the *Timaeus*, which we find for the most part included in the booklet—alas, truncated—of Plutarch, *On Fate*, Vol. III, p. 289 sqq. and especially p. 309 sqq. (Wyttenbach ed.). Photius preserved the arguments of the philosopher Hierocles *On Providence and Fate and that which is in our power* etc. in his *Bibliotheca*, Cod. CCXXIV and CCLI, from which they were presented in the editions of **Pearson** (London 1673) and the Cambridge edition which Needham cared for in 1709. Other disputations on this topic, including this one of Plotinus himself, you will find collected in this little work: “*What remains of Alexander of Aphrodisias, Ammonius son of Hermias, Plotinus, Bardesanes the Syrian, and George Gemistos Plethon On Fate, in Greek etc. reviewed by—Jo. Conr. **Orellius**. Inserted are the Observations of Jo. Casp. **Orellius**. Zurich 1824, 8vo.*” In the review of this Plotinian book, J. Conr. Orellius, *of blessed memory*, used no MS codices, nor did Jo. Casp. Orellius, a most learned man; the former added Hugo Grotius’s Latin version. For Grotius presented this book of Plotinus in Latin in this booklet: “*Opinions of the Philosophers on Fate and on That which is in our Power, collected in part and translated from the Greek by Hugo Grotius. Amsterdam, at Lud. Elzevir, 1648.*” Among the more recent Greek philosophers, **Nemesius of Emesa** also dealt with Fate in chapter XXXIV, *On Fate*, and ch. XXXVI, *On Fate through the Stars*. **Proclus** touches upon these books of Plotinus on Fate and Providence, as well as the Porphyrian and Iamblichean disputations, in the book: “*On Providence and Fate and that which is in us*,” which Fabricius had first published in the *Bibliotheca Graeca* as translated into Latin by William of Moerbeke; but recently **Victor Cousin**, a most discerning man, published a more emended version in the *Works of Proclus*, specifically in the first volume, Paris 1820. Alcinous, in *On the Doctrine of Plato* ch. XXVI, reduced Plato's opinions on Fate and free will into a compendium: *On Fate and Liberty*. Finally, Jacobus Carpentarius compared the decrees of Plato and Aristotle on Fate and free will in that rarest book: “*A comparison of Plato with Aristotle in universal philosophy*,” Paris 1573, 4to, part II, p. 73–86.

**p. 412, 3. Τάς τε ἐνεργείας ἑκάστων ἀποδιδούς τις—ἀποδιδόναι [Rendering the activities of each... to render]** Ficinus expressed the force of this passage not badly. Moreover, the use of the verb *apodidonai* is Platonic. *Phaedrus* § 29, p. 237 C: “as if they knew, they do not agree at the beginning of the inquiry, but as they proceed, they *render* (*apodidoasin*) the likelihood,” i.e., they exhibit or produce what might be expected. *Theaetetus* p. 175 D: “again they *render* (*apodidoasin*) the converse,” they present a similar spectacle; see Heindorf there, p. 398. Aristotle, *On the Generation of Animals* I. 18, p. 176 (Sylburg ed.): “for the resemblances *render* (*apodidoasin*) through many generations, as in Elis the woman who lay with the Ethiopian; for her daughter was not born [an Ethiopian], but the son from her was,” where it is neuter: the resemblances return or revert (namely, those you expected from the beginning). In all these, one must hold to these words of Wyttenbach on Julian’s *Oration* I, p. 57 sq. (Leipzig ed., p. 210): “It would not be foreign to advise that this meaning of which we now treat (namely *to explain, to relate, to narrate*) proceeded from the proper force of *rendering* [giving back], by which he who completes an undertaken speech is thought to *pay back as a debt to his auditors*.” He then subjoins several examples, including Plato, *Republic* X, p. 518 A: “will you not *render* (*apodōsete*) to me what you borrowed in the argument?” and *Politicus* p. 173 G.

--- Page 144 ---
**BOOK I. ENNEAD THREE. p. 412–414.**

**p. 412, 7. οὔτε παρεγκλίσεσι κεναῖς χώραν διδόντα—ἐμπλήκτῳ [neither giving space to empty swerves... impulsive]** Our author touches upon Epicurus, and I hope this passage of Plotinus will hereafter be held as a classic and applied to the twin passages of Cicero. *On Ends* I. 6. 19: “Then in the same place that sharp man (Epicurus), when this occurred to him: if all things were carried downward from their region and, as I said, in a line, it would never be that one atom could touch another: therefore he brought in a *fictitious thing; he said the atom swerves a very little, than which nothing less can be made*.” Especially *On the Nature of the Gods* I. 25, p. 110 (our and Moser's ed.): “just as Epicurus, when he saw that if atoms were carried to a lower place by their own weight, *nothing would be in our power, because their motion would be certain and necessary*, found a way to escape necessity, which had evidently escaped Democritus: he says *the atom, while it is carried straight downward by weight and gravity, swerves a little*.” Lucretius II. 288— “*but lest the mind itself have an internal necessity in all things to be done, and be conquered as if forced to bear and suffer, this is done by the tiny swerve [clinamen] of the principles at no fixed part of space nor at any fixed time*.” Cf. Cicero, *On Fate* ch. 20, where he speaks of *fictitious swerves* (*commenticias declinationes*). Plutarch, *Why the Pythia now does not render oracles in verse*, p. 398 B (Wyttenbach ed. p. 631 sq.): “Then, I said, does it seem to you that each of such things is like chance and the spontaneous, and is it plausible that the atoms slip and dissolve and *swerve* (*parenklinai*) neither earlier nor later but at that time in which each of those who dedicated them was going to fare either worse or better? And Epicurus helps you now, as it seems, from what he said or wrote three hundred years ago.” Plotinus also uses the verb *parenklinein* in VI. 6. 3, but from our passage we gain the Substantive, and that undoubtedly used properly in this matter by the Epicureans. The new Stephano-Valpy *Thesaurus* presents only one example of this substantive from Galen and only in the opinion of physicians. Moreover, the Plotinian *parenklisesi kenais* [empty swerves] corresponds exactly to the Ciceronian *commenticias declinationes* [fictitious swerves].

**p. 412, 9. ὁρμῇ ἐμπλήκτῳ [by an impulsive/rash movement]** *By a reckless impulse and one that impels without counsel or reason.* Wyttenbach noted on the use of this adjective in Plutarch p. 927 and p. 1033. Cf. also the most learned Baguet on Dio Chrysostom, *Oration* VIII, p. 58 sq. Add Proclus on Plato’s *Alcibiades* pr. c. 64, p. 186, and our annotation there, where we noted that the word is Platonic.

**p. 413, 8. εὔρους εἰς παιδοποιΐαν ἡ γυνὴ, ἐπιτήδειος εἰς τόκους [the woman having facility for child-bearing, suited for births]** Thus I have written both on the authority of good books and of Plato, whom Plotinus has before his eyes. For he says in *Laws* VI, p. 784 a (Bekker p. 474): “let the child-bearing and the guarding of those bearing children be for ten years, and no longer time, whenever there is *facility* (*euroia*) of generation.” The vulgar reading arose from the same confusion whence *euroein* [to flow well] and *heurein* [to find] are often permuted, as Boissonade also observes on Eunapius p. 140 sq. Hippocrates, *Aphorisms* II. 9: “to make the bodies *euroa* [well-flowing/supple],” which Galen explains. See Foesius, *Oeconomia Hippocratis* under the word *euroun*, and cf. Lennep on Phalaris’s *Epistles* XVII, p. 86 sq. That our philosopher joined *paidopoiian* [child-bearing] in the singular with the plural *tokous* [births], the matter itself teaches, and the passage of Plato confirms.

**— 11. καὶ οὐ κατακούοντος τῶν—ἀνιόντων [and of one not clearly hearing/understanding those things coming up]** And of one who does not clearly and deeply perceive. The author of the *Erastae* in Plato’s dialogues p. 133 b: “speaking with a great voice, so that his beloved might *clearly hear* (*katakouoi*) him.” Plato, *Sophist* p. 248 b: “Perhaps then, O Theaetetus, you do not *clearly hear* (*katakoueis*) their answer to these things,” where see Heindorf p. 388. Lucian, *Necyomantia* 7, Vol. I, p. 465 (Amsterdam/Wetstein ed.): “he says some long thing as he reads, which I did not very much *hear clearly* (*katēkouon*),” where only one MS codex has *ēn*. I wanted to add these things concerning construction and meaning, as they are not sufficiently explained in recent Lexicons.

**— 17. οἱ μὲν ἀρχὰς σωματικὰς θέμενοι, οἷον ἀτόμους [those who posit bodily principles, such as atoms]** Plato touches on these same philosophers in the *Sophist* p. 246 sq. (Bekker 190), namely Leucippus, Democritus, Aristippus; see Heindorf on that passage p. 381; cf. *Theaetetus* p. 155 e. Add Cicero, *On Ends* I. 6, *On the Nature of the Gods* I. 25, where I also touched on this passage of Plotinus p. 111 and praised other writers. Cf. also below p. 309 B. C.

**p. 414, 6. Οἱ δὲ ἐπὶ τὴν τοῦ παντὸς ἀρχὴν ἐλθόντες—καὶ ταύτην οὐ μόνον κινοῦσαν [Others having come to the principle of the whole... and this not only moving]** In the commentary...

...on Fate and Providence I have already shown p. 23 (cf. *Dionysius* p. 77) that *kinein* [to move] and *kinēsis* [motion] are quite often used in the sense of Fate. **p. 414, 12. ἀλλοιδὲ—τῶν ἄστρων—σχηματισμοῖς—προῤῥήσεως κ. τ. λ. [others... the stars... by configurations... of prediction, etc.]** See what we have placed above both on the title of the book *Whether the stars act*, and on the inscription of this very book, where I touched upon "astrological Fate," as it is called. Otherwise, Conr. Orellius first received from the version of Grotius into the text *dia tēn ek toutōn prorrhēsin* [through the prediction from these], then he thinks Ficinus read *kai tē ek toutōn prorrhēsei* [and by the prediction from these]. **— 17. καὶ τὸν ἄνωθεν εἱρμὸν [and the chain/series from above]** Cicero, *On Divination* I. 55: “But I call Fate that which the Greeks call *heimarmenē*, that is, the order and series of causes, when cause linked to cause *generates a thing from itself*.” Hence this same link is also called *contagio* [contact/contagion] in Cicero’s *On Fate* ch. IV, and *contagium* in Lucretius III. 346. Cf. our annotation in Cicero’s *On the Nature of the Gods* I. 20, p. 92. Add Plutarch, *On Fate* IV, p. 570 B (Wyttenbach ed. p. 297): “it is also called *heimarmenē*, as if being a certain stringing together (*eiromenē*). It exists as both ordinance and law, because subsequent things are politically subordinated to those that happen.” From which John Lydus drew his rivulets in *On the Months of the Romans* IV. 7, p. 156: “*Heimarmenē*, as it were *eiromenē* [strung], because it needs time and distance, so that the *heirmos* [series/chain] of underlying things might be saved”; where cf. Roether’s annotation. Proclus, *On Providence and Fate and that which is in us*, from the version of William of Moerbeke (Proclus, *Works*, ed. Victor Cousin I, p. 10): “It is worthy of lenient indulgence if, looking at all kinds of tragic and comic or other connections of human affairs, you estimated that one founder and maker of such colligations alone resides in the universe, and you called him Fate, *or rather 'heirmos,' that is, the connection of ropes itself and the consequent generation*... you alone thought such dramaturgy, that is, operation, to be directed by some inevitable necessity, and you hymned him as Providence, and thought that he alone exists as *autexousion*, that is, of free will and mistress of all.”

**p. 415, 3. Διττοὺς δὲ ἄν τις θέμενος κ. τ. λ. **p. 417, 1. ’Αλλ’ ἆρα μία τις ψυχὴ διὰ παντὸς διήκουσα—εἶναι λέγοι; [But could it be said that one soul pervading through all... exists?]** Cf. above ch. 2 and below ch. 7. In both places he touches upon Heraclitus and the Stoics, who had borrowed their decrees on Fate from him. Cicero, *On Divination* I. 55, p. 273 sq. **BOOK I. ENNEAD THREE. p. 414–423.**

**p. 419, 5. λίθοις φερομένοις—εἶναι, ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἀνθρώποις [to be stones being carried... but not men]** Unless I am mistaken, there was before Plotinus's mind as he wrote this a passage of Plato in the *Greater Hippias* p. 292 D: “or if you sat by me as a stone, and a millstone (*mylias*) at that, having neither ears nor brain.” *Millstone* corresponds perfectly to *lithō pheromenō* [a stone being carried]. Aristides says not dissimilarly in the *Platonic Oration on Pericles*: “what if the sons of Pericles had become stones?” Hence Erasmus included it in the *Adages* p. 268. Frommel collected more on another proverb, “stones and sticks,” on the Scholiast of Aristides p. 418 sq. I shall transcribe the passage of Philo Judaeus using the same similarity in the same cause in the recently discovered books *On Providence*, Armenian version (Aucher ed., Venice 1822); for he says thus in Discourse I, p. 36: “—so that someone might wish to deprive himself of free will, and prepare for himself a pretext against the rebukes for the iniquities perpetrated by him. *A stone found to be hard would certainly not say that the will it carried with it in its depravity was the work of its own counsel, but of the stars revolved in heaven, which necessarily effect the qualities of motions in individual souls.*”

**p. 420, 3. οἱ ὄρνεις ποιητικοὶ ὧν σημαίνουσιν [the birds are makers of what they signify]** See Origen on Genesis, Vol. I, p. 17 (De la Rue ed.) and Huet there; cf. above II. 3. 3. end, p. 139 A, and the annotation there.

**p. 422, 3. ἀναγιγνώσκειν τὰ μέλλοντα κ. τ. λ. [to read the things that are to be...]** To these, in the margin of the edition, this scholion is written: "how he says that future things are revealed through the configurations of the stars."

**— 8. λόγους σπερματικοὺς [seminal reasons/principles]** Compare our annotation to p. 230 F, or to the beginning of the fourth chapter, where we showed that Heraclitus and his followers the Stoics used in this matter the words "seed of generation" (*sperma tēs geneseōs*), "seed of the cosmic order" (*sp. t. diakosmēseōs*), and "to generate" (*gignere*). Add that in this place, near the end of the chapter, Plotinus uses "the impulse... being generated" (*tēs hormēs... gennōmenēs*), and in the following chapter, at the beginning: "it not being produced like other things from seeds." By these very things, the Orellian conjecture *pragmatikous* [practical] is refuted.

**— 12. εἰλημμένων—εἴληπται [having been taken... is taken]** Compare from ch. 9, "all the causes having been taken" (*pantōn de lēphthentōn tōn aitiōn*). In both places it is: "the causes having been grasped/comprehended," and thus *lambanein* [to take/grasp] is very often used of fate. Herodotus uses "a god takes someone" (*theos lambanei tina*) in the same sense, I. 31, 108, IV. 79—lest perhaps someone should conjecture *eilēmenōn*: "all causes having been closely shut in" and as if "constricted," from the verb *eileō*, which otherwise is not absent from the signification of fate. See my *Dionysius* p. 76, where I brought forward several examples of the confusion between *eilēmenon* [shut in] and *eilēmmenos* [taken].

**— 16. ὅπη ἂν ἐκεῖνα ὠθῇ [wherever those things push]** Cf. above ch. 3, "pushing us like soulless animals," and read these words of Plato in the *Cratylus*, where mention of Heraclitus himself is made, p. 401 D: “but as many as say *ōsia* [essence], these again would think, according to Heraclitus, that all things go and nothing remains; therefore the cause and the leader of them is the *pushing* (*to ōthoun*), whence it is well that it has been named *Ōsia*.”

**p. 423, 2. τοιοῦτόν τε τὸ ἡμέτερον ἔσται κ. τ. λ. —Τοῦτο δὲ καὶ πάντες ὁρῶντες [and such will be our part... and all seeing this...]** Plotinus seems to speak against the Stoics. See Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II. 22, where we wanted p. 293 of our and Moser's edition to be compared with Plutarch’s *On Stoic Self-Contradictions* p. 1050 sq. (Wyttenbach ed. p. 279 sqq.). Moreover, hold these words of Tully [Cicero]: “Thus the nature of the world has all voluntary motions, and endeavors, and appetitions, which the Greeks call *hormas*.”

**— 5. αἱ πυρὸς ὁρμαὶ [the impulses of fire]** The impetus of fire, in our passage, pertains to the conversion of nature and thus to Jupiter himself according to the decrees of the Stoics, who converts all things into himself. Moreover, the formula *nē Dia* [by Zeus] is placed in this passage for "and indeed," "and even," and has this power so that, when placed before the last of several nouns or verbs, it intensifies the force of this, as Wyttenbach teaches on Plutarch’s *Morals* p. 506. In this place, however, we see it placed before the penultimate member.

**— 9. Τίς οὖν ἄλλη αἰτία κ. τ. λ. [What other cause then...]** Tiedemann disputes these in *On the Causes of Contemplative Philosophy* III, p. 360, yet he does not believe...

**p. 425, 17. ὅταν μόνοι ὦμεν [whenever we are alone]** This doctrine of moral solitude flowed from the Pythagoreans. See Eustathius on *Odyssey* XIII. 33, p. 653 (Basel ed.). **BOOK II.**

**P. 453, 7. ΠΕΡΙ ΠΡΟΝΟΙΑΣ ΠΡΩΤΟΣ [ON PROVIDENCE, THE FIRST]** These books on Providence are among the last of Plotinus, being the forty-seventh and forty-eighth. See Porphyry, *Life of Plotinus*, c. 6 and 24, p. 103 and p. 142 (Fabricius ed.). Casp. Barth makes a judgment on them in *Adversaria* Book LIII, c. 13, p. 2513, saying: “These little books of Plotinus, a philosopher so close to the truth that he even refuted some Heretics, written on Providence, are golden”; and in the same place he enumerates other writers who treated the same argument. To which I will add some things here, both what I had touched upon in the little commentary inscribed *Passages of Ancient Philosophers on Providence*, etc., and other things pertaining here that I have placed in my notes.

And first, as Favorinus in Diogenes Laertius III. 24 says that Plato was the very first to use the term "Providence of God" (*Pronoias theou*), Davies shows on Cicero’s *On the Nature of the Gods* II. 31 (end) that this had already been done by Euripides. Moreover, the nascent philosophy of the Greeks used to call Providence into doubt or deny it altogether. Evidence for this are the things that Antiphon the sophist had taught, not fearing to remove Providence (Suidas under *adeētos*, I, p. 49, Kuster ed.; Origen, *Against Celsus* IV, p. 179, Spencer ed.; cf. Ruhnken’s *Dissertation on Antiphon* in *Opuscula* p. 252). The Socratics attacked such decrees, especially Plato, who has other passages on Providence (see Plutarch, *On Fate* p. 573, p. 308 sqq., Wyttenbach ed.) and the primary ones in *Laws* X, p. 885 b and especially p. 900 sqq. (Bekker p. 208 sqq.). Aristotle seems to some to pronounce on these things only doubtingly, although these words of his in *Nicomachean Ethics* X. 9: “For if any care for human things comes from the gods, as it seems,” etc. Andronicus of Rhodes, or perhaps rather Heliodorus of Prusa in the paraphrase of those books, wishes it to be taken in a better sense (see **Sainte-Croix**, *Examen Critique des Historiens d’Alexandre le Grand*, p. 524, note 1). Certainly, that the care of the gods regarding human affairs was undermined by many is argued even by the saying of Hippodamus the Pythagorean in Stobaeus, *Florilegium* T. XLIII, p. 250 (Vol. II, p. 127, Gaisford ed.). To this also pertain the arguments of Hierocles both in *On the Golden Verses of the Pythagoreans*, p. 105 sqq. (London ed.), and in the booklet *On Providence and Fate*. But none attacked the Providence of the gods more sharply than Epicurus and his followers. We already touched above on those words of Taurus the philosopher in Gellius IX. 5, where he touches upon Epicurus: “there is no providence; not even the decree of a harlot.” Among these philosophers, that saying is also frequented in the mention of many writers (Diogenes Laertius X, § 139; cf. Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I. 17, and Davies there): “the blessed and incorruptible being neither has troubles itself, nor provides them for another.” In the same sense you may take that which is in the epigram of Philodemus the Epicurean: “the immortals sleep.” (*Anthologia Graeca* Vol. II, nr. XXXII, p. 144, Brunck ed.; p. 79, Jacobs ed.; and Rosini in *Herculaneum Volumes* Vol. I, § 6, p. 6). The reasoning of Epicurus is most revealed by these words which Lactantius preserved in *On the Anger of God* ch. XIII, p. 1063 sq. (Bunemann ed.): “God, says [Epicurus], either wants to remove evils and cannot; or he can and does not want to; or he neither wants to nor can; or he both wants to and can. If he wants to and cannot, he is weak, which does not fall upon God; if he can and does not want to, he is envious, which is equally alien to God; if he neither wants to nor can, he is both envious and weak, and therefore not God; if he both wants to and can, which alone is suitable for God;—whence then are evils? Or...

--- Page 148 ---
**BOOK II. ENNEAD THREE. p. 425–453.**

...why does he not remove them?” Whether the leaders of the Stoics, whose books on Providence are praised here and there (as those of Chrysippus: Diogenes Laertius VII. 138), wanted the gods themselves to be enslaved to Fate, or Providence to be exempt from Fate, is not something we should inquire into here. Justus Lipsius in *Physiologia Stoica* I. 11, 12, endeavored to claim this latter opinion for the Stoics, with others tending to the contrary. You may know the decrees of the more recent Stoics—Arrian, Seneca, and others—partly from Stobaeus, *Eclogae* Vol. I, p. 70, 132 (Heeren ed.), and partly from their own writings that remain, such as Arrian’s *Dissertations* Vol. I, p. 86, 426 (Schweighäuser ed.). Plutarch, an adversary of the Epicureans and no less a supporter of the Stoics throughout, posited a triple Providence in the books *On Fate* ch. IX, p. 572 sq., p. 307 sqq. (Wyttenbach ed.). Those who sought to pull down the decrees of the Epicureans were joined also by Aelian of Praeneste, who did this primarily so that he might exhibit documents of divine providence collected into one from universal history. The fragments preserved chiefly by Suidas argue this. (Cf. Perizonius in the preface to Aelian’s *Fragments* prefixed to Vol. II, p. 316, C. G. Kühn ed.). The Platonic philosophers thereafter followed the footsteps of their master even to the last. Very many both before and after Plotinus sought to illustrate this doctrine either in separate books *On Providence and Fate*, or certainly copiously in others. Thus, to use this example, Theodoret in *Therapeutica* VI, p. 868 (Schulz ed.), praises this opinion of Atticus the Platonist: “so that the rejection of providence is a thing ready for injustice.” Nor is Iamblichus to be thought to have treated this topic less diligently. There also remain several disputations of Proclus, both *On Providence and Fate and That which is in us*, and *Ten Doubts regarding Providence*, and no less *On the Subsistence of Evils*, though converted into the Latin language by the barbarous interpretation of William of Moerbeke. In these booklets, mention of our Plotinus is injected here and there. And first ch. I (p. 9, Victor Cousin ed., *Works of Proclus*, Paris 1820, Vol. I): “But you ask (Theodorus) things said a thousand times and which will never have rest in my opinion, because the soul is provoked to the business that consists around itself, when it has already given many directions, and things elaborated by those *Plotinians and Iamblichians* and written before us by the divine *Plato*, and if it is not a heavy thing to say, heralded before him by the Theologians with a prophetic mouth (*maniaco ore*), such as Plato alone explained with demonstrations.” Likewise ch. IV, p. 13: “Since those three problems are therefore necessary and well-discussed by the ancients, Iamblichus indeed in those which he elaborated with a thousand approaches on Providence and Fate, and all lovers of Plato divulging the twofold soul, and Plotinus in many places indeed, and Porphyry in many, distinguishing speculation and speculative virtue: but Plato follows all these for those who are able.” ch. X, p. 25: “—Plotinus also correctly saying that all passions are either sensations or not without sensation.” Finally ch. XLIII, p. 64: “And more perseveringly struggling toward that Plotinus, Iamblichus, [and] your namesake (namely Theodorus of Asine, see Fabricius on this place).” Recently this doctrine of divine Providence was also increased by several books of Philo Judaeus. See *Philo Judaeus’s Three Discourses Hitherto Unpublished, I and II On Providence, and III On Animals. Now for the first time faithfully translated from the Armenian version into Latin by P. Jo. Bapt. **Aucher**, of Ankara, Venice, 1822, 4to.* That the Doctors of the Christian Church, considering the force and weight of this topic of Providence, vied with each other in elaborating on its illustration, is not something I need to explain at length. For there exist ten disputations of Theodoret on Providence, three of the most eloquent John Chrysostom to Stagirius, and likewise three of Nemesius of Emesa *On the Nature of Man*, namely chapters XLII, XLIII, and XLIV. And that this cause, passed down as if by hand in the Christian Church, found its patrons until the end of the Byzantine Empire, is shown by the example of Theodorus Metochita and Gennadius, of whom the former, in a turgid and inflated style, noted the levity and inconstancy of men in judging Providence in ch. LXVI, p. 405–412 (Müller and Kiessling ed.); while Gennadius Scholarius of Constantinople, in the fifteenth century, explained this doctrine in five dissertations. The first of these, *On Divine Providence and Predestination*, was recently first published by the most learned B. Thorlacius at Copenhagen in the year 1825. That the character of this booklet may be known, I will add these few things from the end. For...

**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

...Gennadius says thus, p. 22: “—the sacred histories are full of such things; and the polytheists also record many such, even if they have wandered regarding their causes and modes, they themselves also blaming some deity for such things, and providence and necessity. Distributing the deity, not piously, to the creations of the only God, being deceived toward their causality... and speaking of providence either not of all things or not correctly, and establishing necessity where they should not, with no necessity of arguments, and what is greater, being consistent neither with themselves nor with each other.” Thus far. Moreover, **Tennemann**, in the *History of Philosophy* written in German (Vol. VI, p. 149 sqq.), excerpted the more notable parts of this book and examined them in his own way according to the rule of Kantian philosophy. **Taylor** translated it into English in the book titled: *Five Books of Plotinus*, Lond. 1794, p. 113 sqq.

**p. 453, 9. Τὸ μὲν τῷ αὐτομάτῳ κ. τ. λ. [That it is by the spontaneous...]** Theodoret introduces these thus in *Therapeutica* VI, p. 868 (Schulz ed.): “And Plotinus, prominent also among philosophers in [his writings], has set this proem to his discourses on providence.” Then he adds and strives to show by the calculation of times: Plotinus borrowed these from the sacred books of the New Testament just as Plato had previously profited from the writings of the Hebrews. We do not delay on these things. Cf. Sainte-Croix, the note recently praised by me. Here let us add a very similar passage of Philo Judaeus, *Legis Allegoriae* III, p. 93 (Mangey ed. p. 260, Pfeiffer ed.): “It is said indeed among many that all things in the world are carried without a leader, happening spontaneously (*apantomatizonta*), and that arts and pursuits and laws and customs and political and private and common rights toward both men and toward irrational animals, the human mind alone established. But you see, O soul, the irrationality (*paralogon*) of these opinions. For the one, leaving the partial, generated, and mortal, is inscribed truly to the one of all things, ungenerated and incorruptible; while the other again, rejecting God, improperly draws in the mind as an ally, which is not even sufficient to help itself.” Where Mangeius prefers *apantomatisthenta* [having happened spontaneously], it is not necessary; where in Suidas these: *apantomatistheisa*, "not perfected from itself" [changed by him to]: "not from a cause," it is no more necessary; the reading of Suidas is confirmed by the *Lexicon Rhetoricum* of Bekker p. 419 and Zonaras p. 258. Read in the gloss: "not happened spontaneously." Cf. Tittmann p. 259, note 31. Worse, however, the same Mangeius in *On the Creation of the World* p. 36 (p. 102 Pfeiffer ed.) gave *ina apantomatisē tas theseis* instead of *apantomatisē*, as the edited books and Cod. A exhibit. The same in what follows conjectured *to diaphoron* [the difference] for *to paralogon* [the irrational/unexpected]. Gentler was: *to parallasson* or *to parallatton*, which is the same as *to diaphoron*. Correctly, however, if I am not mistaken, he recently conjectures *deontos* [of what is fitting] for *ontōs* [really]. Otherwise, because the same man suspects the Epicureans and Sadducees are noted by Philo in those words, Plotinus is also to be thought to touch on the Epicureans in this place. Regarding the decrees of the Sadducees pertaining here, consult Josephus in *Jewish Antiquities* XIII. 5. 9 and *Jewish War* II. 8. 2. Moreover, Plotinus, in the following words: "but to others it has been generated as if by an evil demiurge," rebukes the Gnostics, as we saw above in the book *Against the Gnostics*, II. 9.

**p. 454, 13. τὸ κατὰ νοῦν αὐτὸν εἶναι [it being according to mind itself]** Here Wyttenbach on Plato’s *Phaedo* p. 257 orders *tō—autō* to be read, who thinks this passage of Plato is signified by Plotinus. The passage of Plato is in the *Phaedo* p. 97 (Part II, Vol. III, p. 86, Bekker ed.). Mosheim on Cudworth’s *Intellectual System* p. 219 and Brucker in *Critical History of Philosophy* II, p. 420 dispute the argument; the latter indeed thus: “A most celebrated dogma born in the Alexandrian School from the study of reconciling Plato and Aristotle, since the former said the world was generated, while the latter asserted an eternal world without generation. To bring them into concord, they departed from the opinion of both and asserted a certain eternal generation of the world, distinguishing the origin of the world 'according to cause' (*kat’ aitian*) from that which is 'according to time' (*kata chronon*). In which matter, the passage of Plotinus sufficiently shows that Ammonius showed the way to the rest, from which we learn that this dogma was already received in the Alexandrian School in the age of Plotinus... The followers thereafter pressed the footsteps of Plotinus: Porphyry (*On the Cave of the Nymphs* p. 131), Iamblichus (*On the Mysteries of the Egyptians* p. 159, VIII. 3), Proclus (*On Plato’s Timaeus*), and others, whose philosophizings on this matter Zacharias of Mytilene exposes (*On the Creation of the World* p. 209). Indeed, the emanative system demanded such an eternal generation, since all things are to be derived from the simplest supreme source of all things: for in this system nothing is voluntary, but all things flow from the necessity of essence, whence the architect of the world could not be admitted as approaching with free will to adorn matter, although that had pleased...

=== PAGE 143 [Repeat of previous context for flow] ===

...Plato. Perhaps it is also not to be denied that the Alexandrian Platonic philosophers applied this distinction to elude the weapons of the Epicureans against the Platonic origin of the world in time.” Thus Brucker. You should compare Proclus on the *Timaeus* p. 85 and Proclus, *Theological Elements* ch. 48, p. 78 sqq., and those whom we praised there, Plotinus p. 96 sqq., p. 553 sq., Proclus in *Theology of Plato* II. 11, p. 107, III. 1, p. 126 sq., III. 16, p. 147; Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, *On the Divine Names* V. 4, p. 690, with the Scholia of Maximus p. 705 sq., and Stobaeus in *Eclogae* I. 22, p. 438 sqq. (Heeren ed.). For what follows, cf. Tennemann, *History of Philosophy* VI, p. 100 sq., who moreover compared *Ennead* V, Book I, ch. 4. Moreover, **Neander**, in *General History of the Christian Religion and Church*, I. 2, p. 688, compares with this decree on providence a similar decree of Basilides the Gnostic (in Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* IV, p. 509).

**p. 455, 13. Τὸ δὲ πολυπραγμονεῖν οὐκ ἀσφαλὲς [But to be meddlesome/over-curious is not safe]** A decree of Plato, the Stoics, and other wise men, whose sayings Ez. **Spanheim** briefly touches in *Proofs of the Remarks on the Caesars of Julian*, p. 40. Cf. Plato, *Gorgias* p. 566 c and Heindorf on that passage p. 273.

**p. 457, 1. Οὕτω δὴ καὶ ἐξ ἑνὸς νοῦ καὶ τοῦ κ. τ. λ. [Thus indeed also from one mind and the...]** Theodoret, *Therapeutica* Book VI, p. 868 (Schulz ed.), praises these "Thus indeed... it stood apart," adding: “he has plundered these things also from the sacred oracles.”

**p. 458, 6. ὅλον γάρ τι ἐποίησε [for he made it some whole]** Theodoret cites this (loc. cit.) p. 869 up to p. sq. B "nature." **Cudworth** also praises and treats it in the *Intellectual System* p. 1178 sq., whom see; Tennemann, moreover, in *History of Philosophy* VI, p. 149, says that in these things which Plotinus places in this and the previous chapter, clear traces of the Leibnizian Theodicy exist; while Theodoret, to return thither, says that Plotinus snatched these from David (Psalm XVIII. 2).

**p. 459, 6. δαιμόνων δῆμοι [crowds of demons]** Similarly Arnobius: *plebs numinum* [the common people of the deities]; Martianus Capella: *heroum populus* [the people of the heroes]; with which passages Ez. Spanheim compares our author in *Proofs of the Remarks on the Caesars of Julian*, p. 35.

**— 16. καὶ τὰ μὲν τοῦ εἶναι—δοκεῖ μόνον [and while the things of being... only seem]** Theodoret likewise inserted these into his sixth Disputation of the *Therapeutica* p. 870 sq. until the end of the chapter—"and to have its own." The translator of Theodoret expressed these last things thus: “—and of the finger, I think, it is one thing to be a finger, and another to have those things which are its own.” To which words **Acciaiolus** advises: "*To be a finger* signifies the 'substance of the finger.'" **Sylburgius**, having followed other readings (see Var. Lect.), adds p. 196: “The Greek sounds more thus word-for-word: *Of the finger, however, think another thing sc. to be sought; namely to be a finger, and to have what is its own, or what is suitable for it.*” He therefore read *autou* [his/its own] for *autou*. Nor did Ficinus do otherwise. We have followed these. **Taylor** thus: *while another purpose is desired in the finger, which can, I think, be no other than that it remains a finger, and performs its peculiar office.*

**p. 460, 3. Πῦρ δὲ—μὴ θαυμάσῃς [And fire... do not wonder]** Again Theodoret has these, p. 871. In the following: “and [fire] came into being from the destruction of another,” he seems to follow the Heraclitean decree, by which all elements arose from fire and would perish again into fire by perpetual conversions. See the primary fragment of Heraclitus in Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* V, p. 712: “conversions of fire: first sea; and of sea, half is earth, half lightning-storm. For he says (Heraclitus) that fire, by the reason (*logos*) and god that administers the universe, is turned through air into liquid, like the seed of the cosmic order which he calls sea; and from this again arise earth and heaven and the things contained in them. How it is again taken up and consumed by fire, he shows clearly through these: 'Sea is poured out and is measured into the same reason as it was before it became earth.' Similarly regarding the other elements.” These vicissitudes of the world and this conflagration, *ekpyrōsis*, the Stoics borrowed from Heraclitus. Cf. my commentary *On Providence and Fate* p. 26 and the citations there: Marcus Aurelius III. 3 with **Gataker’s** annotations; Diogenes Laertius IX. 8; **Muretus’s** Scholia on Seneca’s *Epistle* 9; and **Sturz** on Empedocles p. 274. [Add **Iac. Thomasius’s** *Exercise on the Stoic Burning of the World*, prefixed to his *Dissertations on the History of Stoic Philosophy*, Leipzig 1682, 4to.]

**p. 461, 2. Ἀνθρώπων—εἰς ἀλλήλους ἀδικίαι—ἔφεσιν τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ κ. τ. λ. [The injustices of men toward each other... a desire for the good, etc.]** Somewhat a Democritean opinion. For he says thus in Stobaeus, *Eclogae* II. 9: “Human evils are born from good things, whenever someone does not know how to guide or carry the good things easily.” Sallustius, *On the Gods and the World*...

# BOOK II. ENNEAD THREE. pages 453—461.

**Regarding Plato.** It should perhaps not be denied that the Alexandrian Platonic philosophers also employed this distinction to evade the weapons of the Epicureans <note>The Epicureans argued against a world created in time, suggesting it would imply a change in God's nature.</note> against the Platonic origin of the world in time. So says Brucker. You should compare Proclus's *Commentary on the Timaeus* p. 85, and Proclus's *Elements of Theology* ch. 48, p. 78 and following, and those we have praised there: Plotinus p. 96 and following, p. 553 and following; Proclus in *Platonic Theology* II. 11. p. 107, III. 1. p. 126 and following, III. 16. p. 147; the so-called Dionysius the Areopagite, *On Divine Names* V. 4. p. 690, with the Scholia of Maximus p. 705 and following; and Stobaeus in *Eclogues* I. 22. p. 438 and following, edited by Heeren. For what follows, cf. Tennemann's *History of Philosophy* VI. p. 100 and following, who additionally compared Ennead V, book I, ch. 4. Moreover, *Neander, in General History of the Christian Religion and Church, I. 2. p. 688*, compares this doctrine of providence with a similar doctrine of the Gnostic Basilides (found in Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* IV. p. 509).

**p. 455, 13.** <note>original: "Τὸ δὲ πολυπραγμονεῖν οὐκ ἀσφαλὲς"</note> **"But to be meddlesome is not safe"**] A doctrine of Plato, the Stoics, and other wise men, whose sayings Ezekiel *Spanheim briefly touches upon in Proofs of Remarks on the Caesars of Julian, p. 40.* You should compare Plato's *Gorgias*, p. 566. c. and Heindorf on that passage, p. 273.

**p. 457, 1.** <note>original: "Οὕτω δὴ καὶ ἐξ ἑνὸς νοῦ καὶ τοῦ κ. τ. λ."</note> **"Thus indeed also from one Mind and the..." etc.**] Theodoret praises these words—"thus indeed... it stood apart"—in *Cure for Greek Maladies* Book VI, p. 868, edited by Schulz, adding: "these things he [Plotinus] also has plundered from the sacred oracles <note>Theodoret, a Christian bishop, frequently claimed that Greek philosophers stole their best ideas from the Bible.</note>."

**p. 458, 6.** <note>original: "ὅλον γάρ τι ἐποίησε"</note> **"For he made a certain whole"**] Quoted by Theodoret in the place cited above, p. 869, up to the word "nature" on the following page. *Cudworth* also praises and treats this in *The True Intellectual System of the Universe*, p. 1178 and following, whom you should see. *Tennemann*, however, in *History of Philosophy* VI. p. 149, says that in these things which Plotinus posits in this and the preceding chapter, there are clear traces of the Leibnizian Theodicy <note>The attempt to justify God's goodness in the face of evil.</note>; but Theodoret, to return to him, says Plotinus snatched these things from David (Psalm 18:2).

**p. 459, 6.** <note>original: "δαιμόνων δῆμοι"</note> **"tribes of spirits"**] Similarly Arnobius uses the phrase *plebs numinum* <note>the common people of the divinities</note>; Martianus Capella uses *heroum populus* <note>the people of heroes</note>. Ezekiel Spanheim compares our author with these passages in *Proofs of Remarks on the Caesars of Julian, p. 35.*

— **16.** <note>original: "καὶ τὰ μὲν τοῦ εἶναι—δοκεῖ μόνον"</note> **"and on the one hand, of being... it only seems"**] Theodoret likewise inserted these words into his sixth Disputation of the *Cure for Greek Maladies*, p. 870 and following, up to the end of the chapter—"and to have its own." The translator of Theodoret expressed these last words thus:
-> "and of the finger, I think, it is one thing for the finger to be, and another to have those things which belong to it." <-
Regarding these words, *Acciaiolus* advises: *To be a finger* signifies "the substance of the finger." *Sylburg*, having followed other readings (see Various Readings), adds on p. 196: "The Greek sounds more literal this way: *But for the finger, think that something else is required; namely, to be a finger, and to have what is its own, or what is suitable to itself.*" He therefore read *autou* <note>of it</note> instead of *hautou* <note>of itself</note>. Ficino did no differently. We have followed them. *Taylor* translates it thus: **"while another purpose is desired in the finger, which can, I think, be no other than that it remains a finger, and performs its peculiar office."**

**p. 460, 3.** <note>original: "Πῦρ δὲ—μὴ θαυμάσῃς"</note> **"But fire... do not wonder"**] Theodoret again has these words on p. 871. In the next part: "and [fire] came into being by the destruction of another," he seems to follow the Heraclitean doctrine, by which all elements arise from fire and perish again into fire in perpetual cycles. See the primary fragment of Heraclitus in Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* V. p. 712: <note>original: "πυρὸς τροπαὶ..."</note> **"The turnings of fire: first sea; and of sea, half is earth, half is fire-wind. For he [Heraclitus] says in effect that fire, by the Word [Logos] and God that governs all things, is turned through air into liquid, as the seed of the world-order, which he calls sea; and from this again arise earth and heaven and the things contained therein. But how it is taken back and turned to fire again, he clearly shows through these words: The sea is poured out and measured into the same proportion [Logos] as it was before it became earth."** The same is said regarding the other elements. The Stoics borrowed these world-vicissitudes and this "conflagration" <term>ekpyrosis: the Stoic belief that the universe is periodically consumed by fire and reborn</term> from Heraclitus. Cf. my commentary *On Providence and Fate* p. 26, and the authorities cited there: Marcus Aurelius III. 3. with *Gataker's* notes; Diogenes Laertius IX. 8; *Muretus's* Scholia on Seneca's *Epistle 9*; and *Sturz* on Empedocles p. 274. [Add *Jakob Thomasius's* Exercise on the Stoic Burning of the World, placed before his Dissertations on the History of Stoic Philosophy. Leipzig 1682. 4to.]

**p. 461, 2.** <note>original: "Ἀνθρώπων—εἰς ἀλλήλους ἀδικίαι—ἔφεσιν τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ κ. τ. λ."</note> **"The injustices of men toward one another—the desire for the good," etc.**] A somewhat Democritean sentiment. For he says in Stobaeus, *Eclogues* II. 9: **"Human evils grow out of goods, whenever one does not know how to guide or carry the goods easily."** Sallustius, *On the Gods and the World*...

-> ANNOTATIONS UPON PLOTINUS <-

**cap. XII. [Greek passage from Plotinus, Enneads III.2.12]: "That there is therefore nothing in the world evil by nature, is to be seen from these things. Concerning the actions of men, and not all of these, nor always, do evils appear. These things, if men sinned because of evil itself, nature itself would be evil—but he who treats an enemy badly, the treating badly is evil, but the repelling of the enemy is good; and thus the soul sins in all things, and through goodness evils arise (just as through the absence of light darkness arises, not being so by nature). The soul sins, therefore, because it desires the good, but it wanders concerning the good because it is not the primary essence."** That these things have been taken from Plotinus there is no one who does not see, and Holstenius has conveniently placed this passage of Plotinus in his annotations on Sallustius at this place [h. l. = *hoc loco*], moreover praising the one called Dionysius the Areopagite, *On the Divine Names*, ch. IV, and Proclus in his commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus*, p. 115 sq., from which I shall write out only the end: [Greek passage]: "By which it is clear that all evil exists by way of a 'pre-substantial' occurrence [*parhypostasis*], and yet this exists as something colored by the good, so that all things are good through the will of God, and nothing is destitute of good according to its power, even if evil exists in whatever manner. For it was not possible, generation being what it is, that this should not also subsist alongside it, being necessary for the perfection of the whole." See the notes of Holstenius and Orellius on Sallustius, book 1, pp. 152–154, edition of Jo. Conr. Orellius.

**p. 461, 15. [Greek]: "And many things it suffers by others etc."** Theodoretus has this in his *Therapeutica* VI, p. 871 sq., up to the words of the following chapter: [Greek]: "unto the fulfillment of the whole."

**p. 462, 15. [Greek]: "Poverty and diseases [are] nothing to the good,"** These and the following things, discussed according to the mind of Plato in the *Republic*, bring to mind the *Gnomes* of Theognis, line 526 (518 in Brunck):
-> [Greek]: "Poverty is a burden for a bad man to bear." <-
Otherwise, at this passage of our Plotinus, *Proclus in his commentaries on these Enneads* had made mention of that famous Epictetus. For he, the slave of Epaphroditus, who was among the intimates of Nero (Arrian, *Discourses of Epictetus* I.1; Suidas I. p. 817, ed. Kuster; Justus Lipsius on Tacitus, *Annals* XV.55), had endured both poverty and disease and the other things which a hard and bitter servitude entails. Moreover, mention of those commentaries of Proclus exists in the manuscript books of Arrian, both the Parisian and the Vatican. See Schweighäuser on Arrian’s Epictetus, book 1, p. 21. Furthermore, the Vatican Codices, the notice of which we owe to Hieronymus Amatius, nr. 328 and 1374, have it thus: [Greek]: "From the commentaries of the philosopher Proclus on Plotinus: I was born a slave, Epictetus, etc." There follows an epigram which is read today in the Greek Anthology, edited Tom. IV, p. 238, by Jacobs. — For the rest, *Tiedemann* in the book: *Geist der speculativen Philosophie* [Spirit of Speculative Philosophy], Vol. III, p. 329 sq., strives to turn the blame of inconsistency upon Plotinus from these three chapters (3, 4, 5). Concerning which, let him see to it himself. For the rest, apply to the argument those things discussed by our author below, III.3.16, p. 384.

**p. 463, 8. [Greek]: "But vice"** Theodoretus has this in *Therapeutica* VI, p. 872 sq., up to the words [Greek]: "must be placed as a failure of the good."

**— 11. [Greek]: "by the ways of wickedness"** This formula reminds one of Psalm CXIX. 1, 9, 101: [Greek]: "from every evil way I have restrained my feet," and the Epistle of James V. 8 [actually V. 20/V. 8 context]: "from the error of his way," and similar things through the sacred monuments [scriptures]. But examples are not lacking in other writers where [Greek: *hodos*] "way" designates a manner of acting, a reason, institutions, or morals. Concerning which usage learned men have instructed: Abresch on Aeschylus II. 108; Kuster on Aristophanes, *Knights* 1012; Brunck on Sophocles, *Oedipus Rex* 311. Nor otherwise do the Latins, Cicero *Paradoxes* V.1: *vivendi via* [the way of living]. Cf. Livy II. 24. Consult also Alberti on Hesychius I. p. 1252; Schleusner’s Lexicon of the New Testament under *hodos*; and Valckenaer’s *Scholia* on the New Testament I. p. 446. Add the little book of Gennadius Scholarius *On Providence*, p. 11, first edition by Thorlacius: — [Greek]: "nor is there anything defined in the way of vice." I judged that the color of this formula should be rendered in the Latin version, yet in such a way that I might leave the Ficinion [translation] placed alongside it.

**— 13. [Greek]: "And evils have not happened because of these things etc."** Cf. Synesius, *Epistle* 57, p. 192, ed. Petavius: — [Greek]: "but especially those things, to achieve some good and useful end through evils devised for honor, and to use profitably things that seem base." To which Petavius in his notes, p. 51 bottom and p. 52 top, applied both the passage of Plotinus from Theodoretus and Augustine's *City of God*. Moreover, that Plotinus calls evil a defect of the good, that is a consequence of the opinion that *there are no ideas of evils*. Concerning which matter Syrianus thus speaks in [commentary on] Aristotle’s *Metaphysics* II. 3 sqq., folio 6, Venice edition 1558: "We say indeed that there are no ideas of shameful and imperfect and evil things. For through withdrawal these things subsist in the furthest parts of nature, namely because the particular soul is weak, because it does not overcome the subject's infinity—"

--- Page 152 ---
[[original page: 145]]

-> BOOK II. OF THE THIRD ENNEAD. p. 462—465. 145 <-

—"infinity." Where the same author praises Plotinus and Iamblichus. That other Platonists thought otherwise is proved by this passage of Proclus in Plato’s *Parmenides*, Book III, p. 63, ed. Cousin, Paris: [Greek]: "For if we speak thus, we shall not introduce ideas of evils, as some of the Platonists do, etc." I have compared other things in the book of Plotinus *On Beauty*, pp. 172–175 sq. In the place of Theodoretus cited above, Hoeschelius applied these other words of Augustine from the *Commentary on the Gospel of John*: "A good man using evils well and doing good things from evils for the sake of making good men out of evil ones and discerning the good from the evil." Moreover, Gennadius of Constantinople in *On Providence*, p. 11, ed. princeps Thorlacius, comes close enough to the opinion of Plotinus concerning the nature of Evil: [Greek]: "But if the truth must be told, neither is vice anything, but only a privation of virtue." Altogether, this writer seems to have silently borrowed several things from our Plotinus.

**p. 464. l. 4. [Greek]: "Wherefore neither [can] evils be destroyed."** He touches upon the opinion of Plato in the *Theaetetus*, p. 176, p. 247 ed. Bekker; which I brought forward above at I. 8. 6. p. 75 G., which passage is to be compared entirely with ours, as well as the things I placed there. As for what follows immediately: [Greek]: **"but what is contrary to desert, whenever the good have evils, and the base have the opposite, etc."**—concerning these things, then: Philo Judaeus especially labored diligently on this argument in *Sermon II on Providence* to Alexander. For he thus begins in Eusebius, *Praeparatio Evangelica* VIII. 14, p. 386: [Greek]: "Do you say there is providence in such great turmoil and confusion of affairs? For what of the things according to human life has been ordered? What is not full of disorder and destruction? Or are you the only one ignorant that for the most wicked and evil men, good things abound—wealth, reputation, honors among the masses, leadership, and again health, keen perception, beauty, strength, unhindered enjoyment of pleasures through the abundance of resources and the most peaceful good-fortune of the body? But the lovers and practitioners of prudence and all virtue are all, I might almost say, poor, obscure, without reputation, and lowly." — Which the most eloquent writer then pursues more fully; Eusebius does not have them, but the recently edited Armenian version has them whole, p. 46 sqq., from which we understand that Philo treated these things copiously, and illustrated them with the applied examples of Polycrates, the Dionysiuses, and on the other side, Zeno of Elea, Anaxarchus, and others.

**p. 465, 6. [Greek]: "but also the parts are rightly [ordered]—and especially when they are ensouled"** I have written [Greek]: *en deonti autōn* (instead of *autō*) with some books and Ficinus, even because of the things following immediately. Moreover, the sentence: [Greek]: **"and that providence—reaches [all things]"** depends likewise on the antecedent "rightly ordered," nor ought Ficinus to have interposed "it is probable." For doubts are mentioned in this place and it is shown what befits providence, if it wishes to be worthy of this name. For the rest, Gennadius in *On Providence*, p. 4 sqq., strives to explain more copiously this reason of Providence, which extends itself through all things, and cares for even the smallest, yet for each individually in a different way, arguing thus: [Greek]: "For providence is of the unceasing movement of this whole and of its parts... distributed impartially to each by an excess of knowledge and power... reaching even to the last things... according to the strength given to each to participate... with the harmony of all things in the whole. In a more particular way, it provides for those individuals which are ordered immediately toward it... such as the individuals of a rational nature. And because of this, in some places of the holy oracles it is said that without the divine will not even a sparrow falls into a snare, and in others that God has no care for oxen, both being entirely true. — Such care does God have for them (the beasts), but beyond that nothing, because there is no end beyond the life here for such things. — But the affair of men does not stand similarly to the other generated and perishable things, but man is composed from the beginning of the mortal and the immortal, etc."

**— 12. [Greek]: "First therefore—if nothing of this is lacking"** Theodoretus has these things in the place cited above, p. 873. *All* our books have [Greek]: *lēpteon* ["it must be taken"]. On the contrary, all those of Theodoretus have [Greek]: *lektēon* ["it must be said"]. Beware of correcting it. For it has Platonic authority, and rather the context of Theodoretus should be emended from ours. For thus in the *Phaedrus*, p. 246 d: [Greek]: "Let us take [*labōmen*] the cause of the loss of the wings, through which it flows away from the soul," where see Heindorf, p. 250. Elsewhere he says [Greek]: *logō lambanein* for "to think, to remember," as in *Laws* I. 10, where see Ast’s *Animadversions*, p. 58. Elsewhere also [Greek]: *lambanein nō, dianoia* [to take in mind or thought]. But yet more often even without such substan-

**p. 470, 8. **— 16. Ficinus understood the passage otherwise. But the nearest things argue that this is the opinion of Plotinus.

[Greek]: she who has seized and holds together the stings of all the laws at once in herself uniquely, this is the goddess, called Adrastea for this reason, because the things placed and legislated by her are inescapable. Heeren: [Greek]: "A sharp-sighted goddess Adrastea will therefore be the overseer of the order of the whole." Neither indeed is Hermias to be corrected from Plutarch and Apollodorus, as the little verse argues: **[Greek]: Ide the beautiful-formed etc.** What do you seek? Especially from the religions of the Egyptians, through the Orphics, the notion of the Goddess had been transferred to the Greeks, who was called by the Egyptians Athor, by the Greeks Night, by the Attics *Rhamnusian Nemesis* and perhaps also *Adra*, the same as *Adrastea* [Greek: *Adrasteia*], whom they worshipped as the inspector and *Fate (or pronouncer) of divine laws and of all this Universe. He who looks back to and preserves these laws, he beholds the most beautiful order of things and cultivates justice.* Therefore in sacred fables *Phanes* is sometimes joined to Adrastea, who procreated the beauty and harmony of visible things; sometimes the Sister *Ida* [Greek: *Idē*] is added, named from *seeing and inspecting* [Greek: *idein*], who is the same called *Eide*, from *eidos* or from *beautiful form*, which makes all the members of this world conspicuous and decorous; sometimes even *Dike*, or *Justice*, is added, who executes the laws of the universe. From this I think it can be understood why Plotinus in our passage passes from *Adrastea*, or *the inevitable power of divine laws*, to the mention of the *order of things* which are seen in this universe [Greek: *tōn dromenōn en tō panti*], why then he descends to the *beautiful forms* [Greek: *to eueides*] and *variety* [Greek: *to poikilon*] of animals and plants, and why finally in describing the divine essence he joins both *that beautiful and just thing* [Greek: *to kalon kai to dikaion*].

They <note>original: οἱ Στωϊκοὶ; the Stoics</note> call her **Adrastea** <note>A Greek name for the goddess of inescapable destiny, often identified with Nemesis</note> because she imposes a forced limit upon causes, being inescapable and unavoidable. Compare Chrysippus in Plutarch’s *On Stoic Contradictions* page 1056. C. page 304. Wyttenbach; and see Wyttenbach on Plutarch’s *On the Delay of Divine Vengeance* page 107, and Baguet on the *Fragments of Chrysippus* XC. page 224. Ammianus Marcellinus XIV. 11: "These and countless other similar things are sometimes performed by **Adrastea**, the *avenger of crimes and the rewarder of good deeds*—whom we also call by the double name **Nemesis**." Not a few authors partly look back to and partly describe the passage in Plato, among them Plutarch in *On Fate* page 570. A. page 296. Wyttenbach; Proclus in *Platonic Theology* page 186, page 205 and following, in a classic passage where he discusses many things concerning Adrastea according to the mind of Plato: compare the same work page 298, and *On the Timaeus* IV. page 206 (collected with V. page 206) where he presents a memorable Orphic fragment; with which should be compared the Orphic verse in the *Prayer to Musaeus*, 36. page 254. I will, however, add the words of Hermias in the passage of Plato’s *Phaedrus* page 148. Ast, which are connected with this passage of Plotinus. For that interpreter says: "And Adrastea is herself one of the goddesses who abide in the Night, born of Melisseus and Amalthea; Melisseus is taken to represent the care and providence over secondary things, while Amalthea represents the unswerving and 'not-softening' <note>A wordplay on 'Amalthea' and 'malthasso' (to soften)</note> quality. From this unswerving Providence, then, was born Adrastea, who is the sister of Ide:
-> And fair-formed Ide and her sister Adrastea; <-
she who holds together and contains in herself the stings <note>or 'points'</note> of all the laws at once in a unified way—this is the goddess called Adrastea for this reason: because the things established and legislated by her are inescapable <note>original: ἀναπόδραστα; anapodrasta, a pun on Adrastea</note>. Wherefore she is also said to resound before the cave of Night.—For inside, in the sanctuary of Night, sits Phanes; in the middle is Night, prophesying to the gods; and Adrastea is at the thresholds, legislating the divine decrees to all." Moreover, Adrastea, together with her sister Ida, was the nurse of Zeus. Apollodorus I. 2. 6: "And she gives him (Zeus) to be reared by the Curetes and the daughters of Melisseus, the Nymphs Adrastea and Ida." Plutarch’s *Table Talk* III. 9. page 657. E. page 680 and following. Wyttenbach: "Because even the Ancients seem to him to make two nurses for Zeus, Ide and Adrastea." So Wyttenbach from all the books; Xylander reads: *Iden*. You might suggest *Eide* in Plutarch and Apollodorus from the passage of Hermias cited above. Yet in Adrastea herself there is the notion of seeing <note>original: τοῦ ἰδεῖν; to see</note>. Hermes in Stobaeus’s *Physical Selections* I. 52. page 966. Heeren: "Therefore the sharp-sighted goddess Adrastea shall be the overseer of the arrangement of the whole." Nor does the verse **"And fair-formed Ide etc."** prove that Hermias should be corrected from Plutarch and Apollodorus. What more do you seek? The notion of the Goddess was transferred to the Greeks through the Orphics, chiefly from the religions of the Egyptians; she was called Athor by the Egyptians, Night by the Greeks, *Rhamnusian Nemesis* by the Athenians, and perhaps also *Adra*, the same as *Adrastea*, whom they worshipped as the overseer and *Fate (or the proclaimer) of the divine laws and of this entire Universe. He who respects and keeps these laws beholds the most beautiful order of things and cultivates justice.* For this reason, in the sacred myths, Adrastea is sometimes joined with **Phanes**, who brought forth the beauty and harmony of visible things; sometimes her sister **Ida** (Ide) is added, named from *seeing and inspecting* <note>original: Ἴδη from ἰδεῖν</note>, who is also called *Eide*, from *eidos* or *beautiful form*, which makes all the members of this world conspicuous and decorous; sometimes also **Dike**, or *Justice*, is added, *who executes the laws of the universe.* From this, I believe it can be understood why Plotinus, in our passage, moves from *Adrastea*, or the *inevitable power of divine laws*, to the mention of the *order of things* which are seen in the universe, why he then descends to the *beautiful forms* and *variety* of animals and plants, and why finally, in describing the divine essence, he joins together *the beautiful and the just*.

**page 476, line 6. For the whole divine... where would it be?]** See Cudworth, *True Intellectual System of the Universe*, page 1167.

**page 477, line 1. as to this one that it lacks horns etc.]** This passage brings to mind the little song in the *Anacreontea* (2): "Nature gave horns to bulls—to men, wisdom." Compare

<summary>This page provides a philological and mythological commentary on the goddess Adrastea, linking her to the Stoic and Platonic concepts of inescapable divine law and cosmic order. It explores her genealogy as a nurse of Zeus and her symbolic connection to sight, beauty, and justice in the works of ancient authors like Hermias and Plotinus.</summary>
