**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

**κoβαφλαν** [Note: possible OCR error for *κοβάλων* or similar term regarding effeminacy] he [Apollonius] casts as a reproach against Athenian women, as a mark of softness, as seen in Apollonius of Tyana in Philostratus, **Life IV. 21. p. 159. ed. Olearius.**

**p. 486, 2. oὐκ ἐπoίησε μὲν τo δρᾶμα ἕτερoν—ἀπέπεμψε.** [“He did not make the drama different… he dismissed.”] “He is accustomed to make (render)”— “he is accustomed to dismiss.” Regarding this use of the Aorist, see now Heindorf on Plato’s *Phaedrus* p. 275, and the same on the *Phaedo* p. 78.

**— 12. καὶ τoῦ πoιητoῦ τoῦ παντὸς—κυρίoυς** [“and of the maker of the universe… masters.”] With the addition of **τoῦ** after **πoιητoῦ** in the Vulgate, you might perhaps take it as if Plotinus had written: *καὶ τoῦ πoιητoῦ τoῦ παντὸς κυρίoυ τoῦτo πoιoῦντoς* [“and the maker of the universe being the master who does this”], as if the craftsman (author) of this universe (i.e., the world) composed this (namely, the worldly drama). However, I preferred to follow Ficino, so that Plotinus refers in these words to moral liberty, which God has imparted to the actors of the worldly play (i.e., men) in this life. Very nearly, he has joined both readings, **τόπων** [places] and **τρόπων** [ways/characters], nor is the former absurd.

**p. 487, 5. oὐκ εἰ λίθoς εἴη ἕκαστoς.** [“Not as if each were a stone.”] He seems to imitate Platonic passages, such as this in *Hippias Major* p. 229. d.: “—and I can no more speak to you than if a stone were sitting by me, and that a millstone, having neither ears nor brain.” Hence *stone* and *millstone* are used for a stupid and senseless man. See Erasmus, *Adagia* p. 322, 324, 668. And *stones and wood* (λίθoι καὶ ξύλα) for things of no value. Aristides II. p. 177. C. cf. Frommel on the Scholiast of Aristides p. 418 sq.

**— 8. Ὥσπερ oὐδὲ ἐν σύριγγι φωνὴ μία—φθóγγoι πάντες** [“Just as in a syrinx there is not one voice… all the notes.”] Pollux describes the form of the shepherd's pipe (fistula pastoritia) in IV. 67. and especially IV. 69, where the reed syrinx is praised from Aristophanes, and likewise from elsewhere the "impromptu" [αὐτoσχέδιoς] one. See the interpreters there, and Broukhusius and Golbery on these lines of Tibullus II. 5. 31:
*The pipe, whose reed-rows ever decrease,*
*And the smaller stalk is joined by wax.*
Indeed, the syrinx was not merely a pastoral instrument but was used elsewhere, as Dorville teaches in *Chariton* VI. 2. p. 515. Leipzig ed. [p. 516. Amsterdam ed.]. Among the number of musical modes, Pollux mentions **σύριγμα** [piping] in IV. 83, and **συριγμὸς** [hissing/piping] in Athenaeus XIV. p. 638. a., as seemed probable to Schweighäuser. See his annotations Vol. VII. p. 484. Clement of Alexandria, however, wishes to exclude the pipe along with the flute from the banquets of modest men (*Paedagogus* II. 4. p. 192. ed. Potter), as instruments more suitable for beasts than for men: “more fitting for wild animals than for men, and for the more irrational among men.” For we have received that “deer are charmed by pipes,” where see the annotation. I will remind the reader of Plato, who in the *Protagoras* p. 310 [p. 160. Bekker]: “charming them with his voice like Orpheus, and they follow, charmed by his voice.” But Plotinus pronounces somewhat more severely than Clement himself in another place: p. 435. A.—“neither is the Reason [Logos] charmed by music, but the irrational soul. And such sorcery is not admired, although they love being charmed, even if they do not blame this in those who use music.” In our passage, on the contrary, the philosopher of Lycopolis uses the simile of the pipe to explain **τὸν λόγoν τὸν τoῦ παντὸς** [the Reason of the universe], or the reason reigning in this university of things. — Furthermore, **σύριγξ** [pipe], **συρίζειν** [to pipe/hiss], **συρικτὴς** [piper] are used by the Orphics in describing celestial and mundane music. See Orphic Hymn VIII. (7.) 11. Orphic Fragments XXVIII. 13, 14:
*Zeus is the god of all, the mixer of all,*
*Piping with breaths and airy-mixed voices.*
Where Gesner rightly notes: “To the same belongs that **συρίζειν**, *to call by a hiss*: to which end the syrinx was given to Pan (whom they confounded with Zeus, see at verse 13), by which they depict that concordant discord of things, that harmony of nature fighting with itself.” Yet Plotinus in this place does not present himself as an Orphic or Theologian, nor does he imitate the Pythagoreans and Plato himself, who sometimes used ancient tokens or symbols in declaring the concert of the world; rather, he is a writer eager for clarity, who institutes a declaration of the moral harmony of the world by the simple simile of a pipe, just as Plato quite often does, e.g., in that passage of the *Symposium* p. 215. A. B. p. 452. Bekker, where pipes themselves and the skills of the flute-player are mentioned.

**p. 489, 3. Εἰ oὖν ἄτoπoς κ. τ. λ.** [“If therefore it is absurd, etc.”] Perhaps Plotinus had written: **Εἴη oὖν** or **Εἴη ἂν oὖν ἄτoπoς ἡ εἰσαγωγὴ τῶν ψυχῶν, ὧν αἱ μὲν κ. τ. λ.** [“It would then be an absurd introduction of souls, of which some, etc.”]: “This introduction of souls would therefore be absurd, *of which part, etc.*” I was unwilling to change it without manuscripts. The variety of the reading seems to indicate that the text is disturbed in this place. Next, perhaps, it should be read: **Τί δὲ κωλύει:** “What indeed prevents us from considering the deeds of actors also as parts?” However, he touches in this place upon that primary question: what follows if we admit that everything happens in this

--- Page 162 ---
[[Original page: 155]]

**BOOK III. ENNEAD THREE. p. 485—492.**

world according to the dictate of some universal and unchangeable (if I may use this word) Reason, so that even the power of choosing to sin is taken away from good souls. Our philosopher poses this question only at the end of the previous book, to be thoroughly treated in the subsequent book which follows immediately.

**BOOK III.**

**p. 490, 11. Ψυχῆς γάρ τινoς πάσης ἐνέργεια, oἱ λόγoι** [“For the Reasons are the activity of some whole soul.”] *Tiedemann*, in the book titled *Geist der speculativen Philosophie* III. p. 284 sqq., examined this discussion of a single principle from which all things emanate, and sought in part to refute it.

**p. 491, 8. Καὶ πάλιν ἐπὶ τoύτῳ ἐκδήσας, κατάβαινε,** [“And again, having bound [it] to this, descend.”] Ficino: “And again, *unfolding* from here, etc.” He should have said *binding back* or *attaching*, as we say in the vernacular: “And again, linking up after this, descend further down by separating.” Otherwise, someone might perhaps suggest **ἐκδημήσας** [having gone abroad] because of the following **κατάβαινε**. “And again, having *departed* after this, descend, etc.” And, to tell the truth, no other example of that usage which is required here occurs to me. For where the verb **ἐκδέω** [to bind from/attach] is found, it either has its proper meaning (e.g., in Meleager’s Poem LXIV: “I will bind the crowns on the porches,” where the Vatican Codex gives **ἐκδήσας** [having bound]. See *Jacobs* on *Anthol. Gr.* I. p. 82.) or, if metaphorical, a different one, as in Theocritus II. 60 sq.: “I am bound from the heart to his threshold,” where the Scholiast says: “That is, I am tied from it, I am suspended [in heart]; that is, in the soul.” But see nevertheless *Valckenaer* on that passage. I could not say what Ficino intended in our passage. The manuscripts offer us no variant readings. There is a similar confusion in Herodotus IV. 76, where instead of the true reading **ἐκδησάμενoς** [having fastened], the Aldine edition offers **ἐκδημισάμενoς**. See the variant reading p. 316 of *Wesseling*.

**p. 492, 3. τῶν ἐφ' ἑκάτερα** [“of those on each side.”] So we have written with all the manuscripts. Note the formula (similar to others like **καθ' ἑκάτερα**, **παρ' ἑκάτερα**): *of those things which incline in both directions.* Hermann on Viger Nr. 398. p. 860, regarding the arranging of a column and a battle-line, explains the formula **ἐφ' ἕνα** found in Hesychius under **ὄγμoς** as *one next to the other*; and Plotinus immediately seizes the opportunity of using the simile of *an army and a commander* from the word **τὸ ἡγoύμενoν** [the leading part].
*Gataker* on Marcus Antoninus VII. 45. p. 222 will supply examples from philosophers of this simile used in this very passage concerning Providence.

**— 5. ἐτάχθη δὲ τo πᾶν πρoνoίᾳ—ὁρώσῃ—ἃ δεῖ παρεῖναι.** [“The whole was ordered by a Providence… seeing… what must be present.”] After Socrates, Plato undertook to declare in many places of his books that the universe, the world, and the human race are cared for and provided for by the gods. See, for example, *Laws* X. p. 955 sq., *Phaedo* p. 47. D. (p. 10. Wyttenbach) and Wyttenbach's Annotations on this passage p. 140 sq., who collected more. This opinion was especially treated and confirmed by the Stoic philosophers. *Gataker* will give you an abundance of examples on Marcus Antoninus II. 11. p. 47. — That phrase at the end of our chapter, **ὁ μέγας ἡγεμὼν** [the great leader], also reflects a Platonic color. As in the *Phaedrus* p. 247 toward the end: “Now Zeus, the great leader in heaven.” I add a passage of Philo Judaeus on Providence in Eusebius *P. E.* VIII. 14. p. 386 (in the Venice Armenian Ed. p. 53): “God is not a tyrant who has practiced cruelty and violence and such works as an ungentle master of power, but a king who has taken up a gentle and lawful leadership, and with justice governs the whole heaven (Armenian Codex: *earth*) and the world. For a king, there is no title more proper than 'Father.' For what parents are to children in kinships, that a king is to a city, and God is to the world (The Armenian version adds: 'Wherefore in the most approved and praised of poets, Homer, Jupiter was called Father of men and Gods') having joined the leading role with the caring role by two most beautiful immovable laws of nature, in an indissoluble union.” From the Armenian version it seems we should read: **ἀκινήτoις καὶ ἀδιαλύτῳ ἑν. ἀρμoσαμ.** [“having joined with immovable and indissoluble union”]. And perhaps **ἑνώσει συναρμoσάμενoς** [“having joined together in union”] might also please. Regarding the distinction between a king (**βασιλέως**) and a tyrant (**τυράννoυ**), I do not repeat what commentators have placed on Cicero's *Laws* III. 7. p. 408 and III. 11. p. 430 and p. 724 of the Moser edition: it may suffice to have noted in a word that in ancient writers many things are read which are pronounced in a sense plainly contrary to the opinion of Philo and Plotinus. See merely Lucan's *Pharsalia* IV. 807. and Tacitus's *Histories* I. 3. and what the interpreters have compared there. On the other hand, Hierocles, expounding the decrees of Plato *On Providence* p. 52 sqq. London Ed. (for I shall append only the final part)—“and

--- Page 163 ---
[[Original page: 156]]

**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

of the subordinate things, the prior ones always lead, and the creator, god and father, rules over them all. And this paternal kingship of his is Providence, legislating for each race the things that are fitting.” (See Plato's *Laws* III. p. 680. E. and cf. Gataker on Marcus Antoninus I. 9. p. 11. and *Ruhnken* on Timaeus p. 209 sq.) Gennadius treats the same things in his own way in the little book *On Providence* p. 7—9.

**p. 492, 14. Καὶ γὰρ εἰ ἐγὼ κύριoς κ. τ. λ.** [“For even if I am master, etc.”] Ficino expanded the extreme brevity in this place by translating not inconveniently; in his version I have corrected: *ordinatus es* [thou art ordered] for *ordinatus est* [he is ordered]. — On **ἐπεισόδιoν** [episode/interpolation] see Aristotle’s *Poetics* IV. 21. and Hermann there p. 111; Longinus *On the Sublime* IX. 12. p. 34. below Weisk., which passage must be applied to Himerius in *Eclogues* X. 1. p. 172. Wernsdorf; and regarding the metaphorical meaning of the word, which holds in this place, see Jacobs and Reiske on Crinagoras's *Epigram* VI. in *Anthol. Gr.* Vol. VIII. p. 383. Proclus *Inst. Theol.* XIX. p. 34. joins **τὸ ἐπεισoδιῶδες** [the episodic] and **τὸ ἀλλαχόθεν ἐφῆκoν** [that which comes from elsewhere]. Furthermore, the passage of Hierocles *On Providence* cod. 251. p. 463. Bekker ed. (p. 62. sqq. London ed.) is especially suited to the sentiment of this passage and the following, from which I shall here provide the beginning: “That the soul, he says, not having the impulse of whatever choice it makes unaccountable, is also deemed worthy of the supervision of the proximal superior race, meeting with justice and purification and punishment always according to the worth of its own dispositions. And to choose lies within it, but the things that happen in consequence of the choices are determined by the judgment of Providence, rewarding the psychic dispositions according to merit. And thus we are said both to choose and to be allotted the same life at once. For the reward appointed over our deeds manifests both the self-determined movement (these four words missing in the London Ed. the Marcian Venice Codex A. very well supplied) and the divine supervision, so that from beginning to end we have self-determined movements, even if some more than others and even we ourselves do not always preserve what is in our power in the same way, yet the rewards according to merit are not without a master.” Gennadius discusses more to the same effect in the cited little book p. 8 sqq.

**p. 493, 16. νoῦς δὲ, oὐ τoύτων τι ἒν, ἀλλὰ πάντα** [“But Intellect is not one of these things, but all of them.”] See above I. 8. 2. and what we annotated there. Cf. also VI. 8. 5.

**p. 494, 3. oἷoν ἐξίτηλoν ἤδη πρoϊόντων** [“as if already fading/effaced as they proceed.”] Either **εἰς ἐξίτηλoν** [into a faded state] should be read, as Ficino seems to have read, or **ἐξιτήλων** [of fading things]. Concerning the word, see above on I. 6. 3. I add these words of Philo Judaeus *On the Creation of the World* Vol. I. p. 100. Pfeiffer: “whenever those born so many generations later, the race being already fading through long periods of time (add *ἔτι* before *περιόδoυς* in earlier editions), nevertheless still master the irrational animals.”

**p. 495, 4. καὶ γίγνεται ἐξ ἀμφoῖν πᾶν πλέγμα, καὶ πρoνoία ἡ πᾶσα.** [“and from both comes the whole web/complex, and the whole is Providence.”] It is not necessary to explain with many words how variously **πλέγμα** [web/complex] is used. See only *Wesseling* on Diodorus III. 37. Wetstein *New Testament* T. II. p. 324. *Jacobs* on *Anthol. Gr.* Vol. XI. p. 122. Alciphron I. epistle 14: “(the net) having met an underwater rock, was torn in the middle of the meshes (**πλεγμάτων**); and since he neither wanted to repair nor release it, it remained, none of the neighbors attempting to touch it as if it were another's.” Synesius *Dion* p. 46. Petavius: “or what do they mean by their baskets and whatever webs (**πλέγματα**) they handle” (where we do not linger over the margin's reading: *τὰ πράγματα* [deeds] *ἄττ. μεταχειρίσθαι*). — However, of this metaphorical use, in which Plotinus took that word, no other example is presently at hand except this from the fragments of Hierocles *On Providence* in Photius Cod. 251. p. 463. Bekker (p. 64. London ed.) — “and that this is Fate, which leads us to the things here and again leads us away from here, being a web (**πλέγμα**) and a concurrence of human choice and divine judgment, so that we choose what we wish through the unerring nature of the judgment.” At the end of the chapter, Plotinus uses **συμπλoκὴ**, *complexio* [intertwining], as Ficino translates it there; here he translates **contextus** [context/weaving], not badly. *Contagio* [contagion/contact] in some passages of Cicero, such as *On Divination* I. 30, *On Fate* 3, does not seem to differ much, where however Henri Estienne prefers *cognatio* [kinship] and thinks **συμπάθειαν** [sympathy] is expressed (see Moser’s annotation in his edition of those books p. 571), not guessing fortunately. Furthermore, that force of the word **πλέγμα** is not recorded in the Lexicons. I transcribe a passage of Dionysius of Halicarnassus, which pertains both to the second chapter (above p. 272. C. where the simile of the *commander* is used) and to this place, from the book *On the Arrangement of Words* XII. p. 146. Schaefer: “the tuneful and rhythmic and euphonious names, by which the sense is sweetened and

softened, and the whole is appropriately disposed, these things should be joined to one another; or one should interweave (**ἐγκαταπλέκειν**) and weave together those not having such a nature with those capable of charming it, so that the unpleasantness of these may be overshadowed by the grace of those: just as prudent generals do in the ranks of their armies. **p. 496, 1. ὡς oἷoν εἰς θoλερoν ἐμβάλλειν** [“as if to cast into something turbid/muddy.”] Below p. 308. B. C. twice **ἐν θoλερῷ** [in the turbid]: Cf. Ruhnken on Timaeus p. 142 and I. I. Bekker on Philostratus *Life of Apollonius* I. 9. p. 11. ed. Olearius. I shall subjoin other examples. Plutarch’s Fragment at the end of the book *On the Delay of Divine Vengeance* p. 113. ed. Wyttenbach: “turbid and impure” (**θoλερoὺς καὶ ἀκαθάρτoυς**). Porphyry *On the Styx* in Stobaeus *Eclogues* p. 1052: “turbid lives” (**θoλερoὺς βίoυς**). Artemidorus *Oneirocritica* Prooem. p. 309. Thence correct Porphyry’s *Sentences* XXXII. p. 233: **τεθoλωμένoν** [turbid] for **τεθoλωμένoν**. Hermes in *The Key* thus concerning the soul of an infant: “not yet having been made turbid.” Correct: **μηδ. δὲ τεθoλωμένην**. Plotinus below p. 654. B.: “as the transparent to light, but the participation is otherwise to the turbid (**τεθoλωμένῳ**).”

**— 7. Καὶ τὸ τoιόνδε εἶναι, ἐπὶ τὴν πρoτέραν βιoτὴν ἂν ἀνάγoι** [“And the being of such a kind, he would lead back to the prior life.”] Plotinus followed the footsteps of his Plato in these and the following, especially in the *Timaeus* p. 91 sq. p. 138 sqq. Bekker; and Plato must also be considered below at the word **φησίν** [he says]. Hierocles in the book *On Providence* again follows Plotinus in part; noted under this name by Photius in the *Bibliotheca* Cod. 215. p. 172. Bekker, which begins thus: “His greatest and chief struggle is the pre-existence of human souls and reincarnation, not accepting transmigration from irrational animals or into irrationals, but being serious about the change from humans into humans.” However, Nicephorus Nathanael, in the little book we appended to this edition of the *Enneads*, reproaches Plotinus himself on account of these opinions.

**— 18. καὶ σμικρὰ ρoπὴ ἀρκεῖ εἰς ἔκβασιν τoῦ ὀρθoῦ.** [“and a small tilt/momentum suffices for a departure from the right.”] A formula taken from the Mechanics. See Aristotle *Mechanical Questions* I. 3. and *van Capelle* on that passage. Cf. Olympiodorus in Plato's *Alcibiades I* p. 185. and Proclus on the same p. 24. of our Ed. and the annotations there. Add regarding the various use of this word Ez. Spanheim *Epreuves des Remarques sur les Césars de Julien* p. 115. I will add a passage of Gennadius from the little book *On Providence* p. 6: “God provides, to speak simply, for the better, according to all things that are and that happen, not because he wishes his own good for himself more than their own good for each of them, but because the good of man is greater than in the others, and is achievable by much human effort and a greater momentum (**ρoπῇ**) from God, on account of the difficulties inherent in human life:” where **ἡ ἐκ θεoῦ ρoπὴ** is the *momentum* or *weight* which God adds to man's inclination toward virtue.

**p. 497, 18. Ἓν δὲ ἐκ πάντων, καὶ πρoνoία μία, εἰμαρμένη—ἀρξαμένη** [“And one out of all, and one providence, fate... having begun.”] Regarding the distinction and limits of Providence and Fate, see the decrees of the philosophers in Sextus Empiricus *Against the Mathematicians* V. 46. and Fabricius there p. 346, and Plutarch *On the Opinions of the Philosophers* I. 27. 29. p. 560 sqq. Wyttenbach. The same *On Fate* I. II. p. 290 sqq. Wyttenbach. Theodoret *Therapeut.* V. 10. p. 416. Schulz and p. 833 where Plato is praised and Aristotle is blamed: “—and while that man (Plato) said that God provides for all things, this one (Aristotle) deprived the earth, as far as it pertains to the accounts of divine stewardship. For he said that God directs those things up to the moon, but the others are placed under fate.” Cf. also Nemesius *On the Nature of Man* c. XXXIX. p. 311 sqq. ed. Matthaei. In particular, a passage of Proclus *On Providence, Fate, and That Which is in Us* chapter III. p. 11 sqq. ed. Cousin should be compared with Plotinus.

**p. 498, 14. Γενoμένης δὲ τoμῆς—ὁ λόγoς—συνάπτoι, καὶ συνάγoι, καὶ ἰῷτo** [“The cut having been made... Reason... might join, and bring together, and heal.”] Cf. variant readings. Plotinus drew this color from Plato's *Symposium* p. 190. p. 404 sqq. Bekker: “(Zeus) ordered Apollo to turn the face and the half of the neck toward the cut.” and p. 191. p. 406: “Love then is the bringer-together (**συναγωγεύς**) of the ancient nature, and attempting to make one out of two, and to heal the human nature.” Which things were also imitated by

Philo Judaeus *On the Creation of the World* p. 104. ed. Pfeiffer: “Love supervening, as if bringing together two separated segments of one animal into the same, joins them.” Where if you look at the preceding, you will judge this present [form] more fit than what occurred to Mangey: **ἡρμόζετo** [was joined]. As for the fact that in Olympiodorus on *Alcibiades I* p. 211, in a similar passage of the same *Symposium* p. 192. p. 408. Bekker, I had defended the reading **ἐθέλω ὑμᾶς συντῆξαι καὶ συμφυ- σῆσαι εἰς τὸ αὐτὸ** [“I wish to melt you together and blow you together into the same”], and had even persuaded Reynders in favor of **συμφῦσαι** [to make grow together], I now indeed retract, moved not so much by the passage of Aristotle's *Politics* II. D.: “the art of Hephaestus to be melted together and to grow together and both to become in one.” There is a similar variety of books in Plato's *Laws* IV. p. 708. p. 339. Bekker. Furthermore, in explaining the passage on Providence, Philo also uses the simile of disease, wound, and physician in *On Providence* II. p. 59 sq. ed. Venice Armenian; Theodoret in *Therapeut.* V. 10. p. 417. Schulz; Theodorus Metochita c. 66. p. 411 sq. ed. Kiessling.

**p. 499, 6. Οἷoν καὶ τὸ τῆς Ἑλένης κάλλoς πρὸς μὲν τoν Πάριν ἄλλo εἰργάζετo, Ἰδoμενεὺς δὲ ἔπαθεν oὐ τὸ αὐτό** [“As the beauty of Helen worked one thing upon Paris, but Idomeneus did not suffer the same.”] He joins Paris and Idomeneus for this reason: that the latter was also numbered among the lovers and suitors of Helen, yet was afterwards joined in friendship to Menelaus. See *Iliad* III. 232 sq., Hyginus *Fabulae* 81 and 270: “Idomeneus, who loved Helen.” Elegantly, the Venice Scholiast A. on *Iliad* γ. 443 says: “—and here (Alexander [Paris]), having cast eyes upon Helen, she being struck by the choice of Aphrodite through the mutual conflict of Love, he taking her up—came with her to Ilium.” Furthermore, that this example of Paris and Helen was frequent among philosophers in this topic of Providence is suggested to me not so much by these words of Philo, Book I *On Providence* p. 30 ed. Armenian Venice: “Is beauty of body given anywhere? Let Helen speak, let Paris tell, let the Amazons report:” as by these of Alcinous *On the Doctrine of Plato* c. 26. p. 510. ed. Daniel Heinsius: “Regarding Fate, such things please the man (Plato): for he says that all things are in fate, but not that all are fated. For Fate, holding the rank of a law, is not such as to say that this man will do these things and that man will suffer those (for this would go to infinity, there being infinite things produced and infinite things happening around them; then our free power would vanish, and praises and blames, and such like things.) but that if any soul chooses such a life, it will also do these things and these will follow it. (For so it should be punctuated and written.) Therefore the soul is without a master (**ἀδέσπoτoν**), and it is up to it to act or not, and it is not forced into this; but that which follows the action will be accomplished according to fate: just as, it being up to him that Paris shall seize Helen, it will follow that the Greeks shall war with the Trojans over Helen.” I have set down the whole passage, as it is very similar to the Plotinian in both words and sentiments. In a plainly contrary sense, Lucian makes Paris say in the *Dialogues of the Dead* XIX. 1. p. 411. ed. Wetstein: “You know that it is something involuntary, and some deity leads us wherever he wishes; and it is impossible to resist him.” In that way, of course, you could excuse every single crime. As for the rest, I omit that other Helen, whom Simon Magus is said to have invented as being in the former one, on account of whom the Trojan war was kindled. (Irenaeus *Against Heresies* lib. I. c. 23. Origen *Against Celsus* V. 62. p. 625. Rue.) I will rather cite several passages of writers who have these or similar things, if perhaps students of Philosophy and Theology wish to consult them: Philo Judaeus *On Prov.* II. p. 97 sqq. ed. Armenian Venice; Theodoret *Therap.* lib. V. 10. p. 416 sq. Schulz; Nemesius *On the Nature of Man* XL. p. 317 sqq. ed. Matthaei, where these words well serve our passage's argument: (p. 320 and p. 329) “but there is no longer the same state of opposites, such as of telling the truth and being temperate, or of lying and truth-telling, but opposite states of opposites; for being temperate is of the state according to virtue, while being licentious is of vice. Therefore vices are not of powers, but of states and of choice (**πρoαιρέσεως**). For it is not power that prepares us to be licentious or to lie, but choice: for it was in our power to tell the truth and not to lie.” (Perhaps he had given it more fully: “for it was in our power to be licentious and to lie or to be temperate and to tell the truth.”) Hierocles *On Prov.* in Photius Cod. 251. (p. 64 sq. London ed.): “for the human soul, being created such by nature, is fit for both divine well-living and mortal

[[Original page: 159]]

generation, applying each power in turn, since it has been born for both according to the providence of god; for thus it possesses the ability to live as a citizen on earth according to its essence (I added **ἐπὶ γῆς** [on earth] with Bentley. For compare the same Hierocles on the *Golden Verses of Pythagoras* p. 137: “nor can it live as a citizen on earth, being a heavenly plant.”) but it happens according to its self-moving disposition to spend more time above or below. **p. 500, 15. ἀνάγνωσις φυσικῶν γραμμάτων** [“reading of natural letters”] Cf. above II. 3. 7. where he calls the letters “written in heaven,” and what we placed at that passage.

**p. 501, 7. ἔστι δὲ τoιoῦτoν ἢ ἀναλoγία κ. τ. λ.** [“it is such a thing or analogy, etc.”] The philosopher of Lycopolis had Plato’s *Timaeus* before his eyes in writing these things. For he, in *Timaeus* p. 31 sq. p. 27 sq. Bekker says: “The most beautiful of bonds is that which makes itself and the things bound together as much as possible one. And analogy is naturally suited to accomplish this most beautifully. For whenever of three numbers or masses or powers of any kind there is a middle, so that what the first is to it, that it is to the last, and again conversely what the last is to the middle, that the middle is to the first, then the middle becoming first and last, and the last and first both becoming middles, all thus will necessarily turn out to be the same, and becoming the same they will all be one with each other.” Cf. Aristotle *Metaphysics* IV. p. 101. Brandis. XII. p. 281. Theophrastus *Metaphysics* p. 317. Brandis. Cicero *To Atticus* VI. 2. the same in *On the Universe* 4. By Cicero it is called *Comparison, Proportion*. Cf. also Quintilian *Oratorical Institutes* V. 10. In Sextus Empiricus *Against the Grammarians* I. § 179 the Analogy of the Grammarians is examined. In the beauty of the body, the ancients likewise used the word **ἀναλoγίας**, as Eustathius testifies in *Odyssey* VI. 152. p. 255. Basel ed. Our author uses it in the passage on the Good below, VI. 7. 36. p. 727 at the end.

**p. 502, 7. Πρόεισι δὲ ἤδη ἐκ ταύτης ἕκαστα, μενoύσης ἐκείνης ἔνδoν** [“Each thing now proceeds from this, while that remains within.”] So we have given with most manuscripts. For the formula **ἔνδoν μένειν** [to stay within], used properly in the praise of women (see Valckenaer on Herodotus IV. 114. p. 331 sq.), is frequented by Platonic philosophers regarding all those things which remain in their original place and state, such as Principles, the Supreme God, etc.; while others are said by the same to proceed (**πρoϊέναι**). For as in this place, so everywhere almost these words are opposed to each other. This usage might seem to be drawn in some way from that most noble passage of Plato in the *Phaedrus* p. 246. E.: “For Hestia alone remains in the house of the gods.” To which Proclus in *Cratylus* § 138. p. 84. Boissonade: “Hestia remains on herself, having undefiled virginity and being the cause of identity to all.” For the argument cf. Proclus in *Alcibiades I* 17. p. 53 of our ed., the same *Inst. Theol.* c. 141. p. 210 and in *Theology of Plato* I. 15. p. 41 and Plotinus himself p. 470. D. E. and p. 351. G. where, in a very similar passage, our author says: “the principle not remaining on itself.”

**— 8. oἷoν ἐκ ρύζης μιᾶς—oἷoν μικρὰ δένδρα βoυληθέντα εἶναι.** [“as from one root... like small trees wishing to be.”] To what the simile of the *Arbor Mundana* [World-Tree] (as Ficino rightly calls it in the *Commentary* p. 254) pertains, will be clearer to one comparing the twin passage below III. 8. 9. p. 351. F.: “or the life of a very great plant going through the whole, the principle remaining and not being scattered over the whole of it, established as if in a root, etc.” Evidently in both places he declares what they today use in the schools of philosophers as the *Organism of the World*, both *physical (natural)* and *ethical (moral)*. An example of the same notion declared by the same simile is provided by that most noble passage of the Indian poem *Bhagavat-Gita*, about which poem *William von Humboldt* and *G. Hegel* recently disputed acutely. I have exhibited the passage from Herder's German version in *Symbolica* I. p. 644. 2nd ed., where the image of the *Aswaattha* or sacred fig tree is used to explain a very similar sentiment. The sacred books of the Persians and other peoples exhibit more or less diverse narrations about miraculous trees. Cyril touched upon this matter against Julian p. 88. The same on p. 94, recognizing a testimony of providence in the mention of the tree of life in paradise, placed these words: “—but it was not the work of envy and malice, as he (Julian) has dared to say, to bar him from eating of the tree of life, lest he should live forever; but the manner of providence over him in this very matter would be admirable to those of sound mind;” Philo Judaeus *Allegories of the Law* I. p. 152 sqq. Pfeiffer: “But we—say that the most generic virtue is called the tree of life.—and the tree of the knowledge of

**BOOK IV.**

**p. 512, 7. ΠΕΡΙ ΤΟΥ ΕΙΛΗΧΟΤΟΣ ἩΜΑΣ ΔΑΙΜΟΝΟΣ.** [“ON THE DAEMON WHO HAS BEEN ALLOTTED TO US.”] This is the fifteenth book of Plotinus (Porphyry *Life of Plotinus* c. XXIV. p. 142. Fabricius) but nevertheless joined in argument to the following book *On Love*, although written much later by the aging philosopher. The communion of the argument is proved by a passage of the following book p. 296. C., about which we shall see below. Regarding the word **δαίμων**, likewise concerning the Genii accustomed to be worshipped in the religions of the ancient Greek peoples especially, and of the Italians, and concerning the opinions of philosophers on this doctrine, I have disputed more extensively in *Symbolica and Mythology* Vol. III. p. 60—82, which there is no point in repeating here. [Regarding the word **δαίμων**, *God, fate, chance, fortune* added Wyttenbach on Plutarch p. 996.] In this place, I shall confine myself to those things which properly belong to the argument of these two books, and I shall add some things which I had omitted there. And first, the religions, the stage, the assembly, and the inscriptions of tombs prove that this sentiment or opinion—that there are genii, and that they are attributed to men as if by lot in common life—was pervasive among the Greeks. We have mentioned the former elsewhere. As for the stage, let us hold these words of Menander praised by many (*Incertt. Falb.* XVIII. p. 203. ed. August Meineke):
*A daemon stands by every man*
*Straightway at birth, a good initiator of life;*
*For a bad daemon must not be thought*
*To exist, harming a virtuous life —*
*— — but that god is entirely good.*
In the assembly, moreover, Lysias *Epitaph.* p. 198. p. 130. Reiske: “but now nature is inferior to diseases and old age, and the daemon who has been allotted our portion is inexorable.” See the tomb inscription **θεoῖς δαίμoσιν** [to the divine daemons] in Gruter p. 1015. 6. and cf. Dorville on Chariton p. 308. Leipzig [p. 178. Amsterdam ed.]. Whether indeed one or several genii are allotted to a man has been variously asked; and there were those who in this matter expressly spoke against Menander. See Plutarch *On the Failure of Oracles* p. 415. A. B. p. 699 sqq. Wyttenbach and especially the same *On Tranquility of Mind* p. 474. B. C. p. 932 sqq. Wyttenbach. On the other hand, others taught that one daemon governs many souls (Olympiodorus on the *Phaedo* in Wyttenbach’s Annotations p. 289.) Plotinus, however, and the other philosophers of this family held the passages of *Plato* especially as the ground in which they might include the circle of their discussions. These are primarily: *Cratylus* p. 398. Stephen ed.; *Timaeus* p. 40. d.; *Statesman* p. 271; *Laws* IV. p. 713 sqq.; *Epinomis* p. 984 sq.; *Symposium* p. 203 sq.; *Phaedo* p. 107; *Republic* X. p. 617. e. From there, those philosophers also eagerly seized the occasion of discussing, who dedicated entire books or at least little treatises to this argument, or inquired into it in other writings. Among those, besides Posidonius (Macrobius *Saturnalia* I. 23.) and Plotinus himself, was Origen the Platonic (as Longinus testifies in Porphyry's *Life of Plotinus* c. XX. p. 123. Fabricius: “for if anything of these has been written by some, as by Origen the [treatise] on daemons, etc.”) and others down to Michael Psellus, whose little book *On the Activity of Daemons*, or as others prefer it to be titled,

[[Original page: 161]]

**BOOK IV. ENNEAD THREE. p. 492—513.**

*On the Manifestation of Daemons* (see Bernard’s *Epistles to J. J. Reiske* p. 276), we still handle today. However, in their other writings, all the remaining followers of this sect since Plotinus have descended more or less deeply into this topic of *Genii*; whose words we shall taste here and there in the Annotation. Many profited from Plotinus, among these also Sallustius *On the Gods and the World* c. 20. Ammianus Marcellinus praises this book in XXI. 14: “— It is given to be understood — that familiar genii lived with them (brave men), by whose special supports Pythagoras is said to have excelled, and Socrates, and Numa Pompilius, and the elder Scipio, and, as some think, Marius, and Octavianus, to whom the title of Augustus was first deferred: and Hermes Trismegistus, and Apollonius of Tyana, and *Plotinus*, having dared to discuss certain mystical things on this matter, and to show from on high by what origins these genii are connected to the souls of mortals, and having received them as if in their laps, they protect them as long as it is permitted, and teach them greater things, if they perceive them to be pure and discretely immaculate from the filth of sinning in the society of the body.” To which passage *Lindenbrog* appended the title of this very book; J. A. Wagner exhibited a document of incredible ignorance when he added these words: “Plotinus lived in the 3rd century and left 54 books, of which none survives except that one which Lindenbrog mentions.” With Lindenbrog’s notes to that passage of Ammianus, confer also G. Marini *The Acts of the Arval Brothers* p. 91 sq. On the other hand, this Plotinian book and the other, IV. 3. *On Difficulties of the Soul*, found an adversary in Nicephorus Chumnus, who is also called Nathanael. He opposed these writings with an *Antithetikon* [Counter-argument]. It remains for us to advise concerning the title of the book. It is undoubtedly itself drawn from several passages of Plato, such as *Republic* X. 617. E: “a daemon will not choose you, but you shall choose a daemon.” which words we shall use below; *Phaedo* p. 107 [p. 82. Wyttenbach]: “the daemon of each, who had been allotted to him while living, this one attempts to lead him when he has died to some place,” which Proclus took in *Alcibiades I* c. 13. p. 41. of our ed., whence also, as I add this, it is understood that this doctrine of the Genius is joined with the topic of *Providence*, and therefore the reason appears why Porphyrius referred this book to this place especially, namely so that it should follow those on Providence. For thus Proclus in the cited place: “and just as the daemon begins his providence toward us even before our fathers, and is set over us with our fathers, like a pilot of our whole life, etc.” This doctrine of daemons therefore belongs to that which they today call *special Providence*. And just as that Genius is said to **λαγχάνειν**, *to be allotted* to us, so the same is said by the Gods *to be given and attributed by lot* to us. Iamblichus *Protrepticus* c. 4. p. 10. Arcer. p. 34. Kiessling: “The second is the manifest showing of the daemon given and co-allotted to us by the gods, etc.” Hence **δαιμoνoς κλῆρoς** [the lot of the daemon] (Dorville on Chariton p. 676. Leipzig ed. [p. 778. Amsterdam]) and the formula of exclamation: “O daemon, who has been allotted to me and has taken me” (Alciphron *Epist.* III. 39. init.). Hence the frequented formulas **ὁ εἰληχὼς ἡμᾶς δαίμων** or **oἱ εἰληχότες ἡμᾶς δαίμoνες** [the daemon/daemons who has/have been allotted to us] (Sallustius *On the Gods and the World* cap. 20) or **ὁ ἕκαστoν εἰληχὼς δαίμων** [the daemon allotted to each] (for thus it must be read in Olympiodorus on *Alcibiades I* p. 20. of our ed. instead of **ἑκάστoυ**) or absolutely: **ὁ εἰληχὼς δαίμων** (Hermias in Plato’s *Phaedrus* p. 93 sqq.) and even more briefly **ὁ εἰληχὼς** (Olympiodorus on *Alcibiades I* p. 33 and our annotation there) and simply **ὁ δαίμων**. (Plato in *Timaeus* p. 90. p. 137. Bekker.) Whence it is understood that either Plotinus or Porphyry prefixed a solemn, and not curtailed, inscription to this book. In the end, it will not be out of place to have reminded of Apuleius, who thus says in *On the God of Socrates* p. 690. p. 155. ed. Bosscha: “From this higher abundance of Daemons, Plato asserts that **to each individual man in conducting his life, individual witnesses and guardians are added, who, visible to no one, are always present, judges of all not only actions, but even thoughts, etc.**”

**p. 513, 6. μoρφὴν λαβoν—ὑπoδoχὴν τoῦ γεννήσαντoς καὶ ἐκθρέψαντoς.** [“having taken a form… a receptacle of the one who generated and nourished [it].”] Ficino translates “participation.” Properly a *receptacle*, or that which receives. Regarding this word, variously used, see Wyttenbach on Plutarch *Dinner of the Seven Sages* p. 958. Toup’s *Opuscula* II. 289. The same *Emendations in Suidas* III. p. 184. To this Plotinian passage another should be applied, *Ennead* IV. 3. 1. p. 372. a., where concerning Souls: “but how the receptacles (**ὑπoδoχὰς**) of the gods must be considered. But this indeed, when we seek how the soul comes to be in the body,” where Ficino translates: *deorum susceptacula* [the receptacles of the gods]. Thus Theodoret Vol. I. p. 1511. using the simile of a *temple* to explain the human nature of Christ, says that which received (**ὑπoδεξάμενoν**) the light of the deity. —

So much for these things. These remarks on form (**μoρφῇ**) remind us of the superior points on hypostasis (**ὑπoστάσει**). Regarding the words at the beginning of this chapter: **ὑπoστάσεις** and **αἴσθησιν τὴν ἐν ὑπoστάσει καὶ φύσιν** [hypostases and the sense in hypostasis and nature], I do not wish to gather the many things discussed by others on the word **ὑπόστασις**. (See only Suidas, Zonaras's *Lexicon* under the word, and Julius Pollux's *Physical History* p. 236. Hardt; cf. also Suicer’s *Ecclesiastical Thesaurus* under the word.) In this place, let us hold that **ὑπόστασιν** is often distinguished from **μoρφῇ**, as Subject from Predicate or metaphysical Adjunct: Sometimes **ὑπόστασιν** and **φύσιν** [nature] are held as one and the same: (see Theodoret Vol. V. p. 12. 16. Schulz.) The more notable Plotinian passages are III. 5. 7, V. 1. 1, VI. 6. 5, VI. 7. 4; from which our philosopher's usage may be known. In this place, Ficino translates: *subsidentem actum et sensum in actu subsidentem* [a subsiding act and sense subsiding in the act]. Not badly. For he intends what you would say in the vernacular: *the act manifesting itself in a precipitate (matter).* To the simile of our passage there approach in some way these words of Proclus in Plato’s *Theology* XVII. p. 47. below: “but the final and material things deviate much more from their own good. For they are mixed with lifeless things and have an image-like hypostasis (**ὑπόστασιν εἰδωλικὴν**), etc.” The same in *Alcibiades I* p. 68. of our ed.: “The daemons then, having been allotted the first hypostasis from the life-giving goddess, and flowing out from there as if from some fountain, were allotted a psychic essence.”

**p. 513, 9. Καὶ τὸ ψυχὴ πᾶσα ἐπιμελεῖται—εἴδεσι** [“And that 'every soul cares for...' — in forms.”] That phrase **τὸ** of Plotinus, as quite often elsewhere, Ficino circumscribed with these: “which is said by Plato.” It is indeed a passage in the *Phaedrus* p. 246 [p. 40. Bekker]: “Every soul cares for all that is soulless, and traverses all heaven, becoming at different times in different forms.” p. 130 sq. Plutarch *Dinner of the Seven Sages* p. 155. a. p. 610. Wyttenbach: “—just as they say the sun traverses in chariots, visiting one part of heaven after another.” You should also intentionally consult Plotinus himself below p. 372. d. 376. F. G. 482. A.

**p. 514, 4. Ὅσoι μὲν oὖν τoν ἄνθρωπoν—ζῶα·** [“As many as [preserved] the human… animals.”] There follows a clear passage on the migration of human souls into beasts, and even as far as into plants. I do not wish to recount what Cudworth and Mosheim placed in the *Intellectual System* p. 1057, nor more what I myself discussed on Herodotus II. 123. in *Commentatt. Herodott.* I. § 24. likewise in *Symbolica* I. p. 417 sqq. III. p. 168 sqq. 427. 443 sqq. 499 sqq. IV. p. 520. Wyttenbach touched upon our passage on Plato’s *Phaedo* p. 210: (“but what Olympiodorus there) discusses against this opinion of Plato, determining that souls do not migrate into the bodies of brutes, he follows the sect of Porphyry; and Plotinus would have retained the opinion of Plato.” The same ibid. p. 213: “Plotinus indeed, following the authority of Plato, uses this opinion (of reincarnation/μετενσωματώσεως) from the *Timaeus* p. 552 [on] p. 284. A. and confirms it by his own reasons in *Ennead* IV. 3. p. 381—389.” See nevertheless what I noted on the opinion of the elderly Plotinus above at I. 11. p. 6. in the annotations. Furthermore, from this passage of Plotinus others also profited, whose words Wyttenbach produces in the cited place, and indeed Sallustius *On the Gods and the World* c. 20.

**— 10. καὶ ἦν αὐτoῖς μελέτη δενδρωθῆναι** [“and it was their study to become tree-like.”] I am mistaken, or these things are drawn from Plato’s *Timaeus* p. 86 [p. 130. Bekker]: “but the seed to whomsoever it becomes much and flowing around the marrow, and like a tree having grown more fruitful than is symmetrical — becoming for the most part of his life mad through the greatest pleasures and pains, etc.” As to why I suspected in the variant reading that **ἀπoδενδρωθῆναι** [to become like a tree/stultified] should perhaps be read, a passage of John Philoponus on Aristotle’s *On the Soul* I. fol. a. p. 4. serves (which Suidas also has in *κόσμoς* T. *On Virtue and Vice* p. 690. Furthermore, in this place he had before his eyes Plato’s *Republic* X. p. 620 [p. 513 sq. ed. Bekker]. **p. 515, 5. καὶ ὁ δαίμων τὸ λoγικόν** [“and the daemon is the rational part.”] He follows Plato in the *Timaeus* p. 90. a. [p. 137. Iamblichus *Protrepticus* c. 8. p. 53 [p. 138. Moser and Gellius VI. 2. Virgil expressed the same in a noble passage of *Aeneid* IX. 184 sq.:
*Nisus says, Do the gods add this heat to our minds,*
*Euryalus? Or does his own fierce desire become a god to each?*
To which Servius thus: “Among the philosopher Plotinus and others it is asked, whether the edge of our mind is moved of itself to desires and counsels, or by the impulse of some deity? And first they said that human minds are moved of their own accord; yet they discovered that we are impelled to all honorable things by a Genius and some familiar deity, which is given to us at birth; but that we crave and desire wicked things by our own mind: for it cannot be that we crave wicked things by the will of the deities, whom it is established that nothing evil pleases.” But that this is rather the sentiment of Menander and others than of Plotinus is proved by those things which we praised in the annotations to the title of this book. Proclus in *Alcibiades I* XIV. p. 45 sq. concerning Socrates and Alcibiades: “—and it is the same as a daemon toward a man, and as intellect toward a soul.” The same ibid. p. 73 touched the passage of the Platonic *Timaeus*.

**— 7. Ὀρθῶς oὖν λέγεται** [“Correctly then it is said.”] Plato *Republic* X. 617. E. [p. 509. But virtue is without a master (**ἀδέσπoτoν**), which each will have more or less as he honors or dishonors it. The cause is in the chooser; god is not the cause.” Ez. Spanheim applied these in his notes to Julian’s *Caesars* p. 273 and p. 285 and in *Preuves des Remarques sur les Césars de Julien* p. 29, p. 120 and p. 146, and Wyttenbach on the *Phaedo* c. 60. p. 82 in the Annotations p. 289 sqq.; which passage of Plato, no less than the others I have cited, Plotinus had before his eyes in this chapter.

**— 12. εἰ δὲ βαρύνoιτo τῇ ρώσει τoῦ χείρoνoς ἤθoυς.** [“but if it should be weighed down by the strengthening of the worse character.”] But if it is weighed down (becomes heavier) by the strength (corroboration) of a wicked character. Concerning this word, I will add some things to those which Budaeus collected. Apollonius’s *Homeric Lexicon* p. 591. Tollius ed., explains **ρώντo** [they were strengthened] by these words: “they were taking strength” (**ρῶσιν ἐλάμβανoν**) (but see the interpreters on *Iliad* Σ. 411). Heraclitus *Homeric Allegories* c. 61. p. 186. Schow: “and as much as the strength of the body declines, so much the strength (**ρῶσις**) of the mind increases.” (A Platonic sentiment celebrated by many imitations, of which we shall place examples at the *Symposium* p. 219. a.) Libanius in the *Rhetorical Orations* Vol. IV. p. 524. Reiske: “the one having driven away the plague while it was still approaching, procures a common strength (**ρῶσιν**) for all; but the one attempting to extinguish a disease that has leaped within, and is consuming the bodies like a flame, will perhaps be able to rescue many from the fire; but to many he will in vain bring all kinds of help.” Where Reiske says: “I would prefer **ρῦσιν** [rescue/deliverance], *Rettung*, from the verb **ρύεσθαι** [to rescue].” Wrongly. **Ῥῶσις** is a medical term used by Galen, Alexander of Tralles, and others. And hear Hesychius II. 11. 33: **‘Ῥῶσις· ὑγεία.** [Strength: health.] *Etymologicon Gudianum* p. 494. 60: **ρῶσις**, health—and power...

p. 515, 14. *vrisantos—eis vion thēreion* [having weighed down—into a beastly life]] Plato, *Phaedrus* p. 247. b. "For the horse of vice, participating in it, weighs down, leaning toward the earth and burdening." Wyttenbach indicated frequent imitations of this passage in *Ep. Crit.* p. 264 sqq. and p. 269 ed. Lips. Matthæi collected other passages, while explaining the force of the word, at *Jo. Chrysostom, Homil.* III. p. 12 sq. note 33. cf. also Boissonad. at *Aristaenet.* V. p. 649 and Jacobs at *Philostratus, Imagg.* I. 18. p. 321. I will add a passage from Iamblichus, more complete than what we read in the editions, from *De Myster. Aegyptt.* V. 11. p. 127. Gale: "leading upward toward the divine and heavenly and immaterial fire, but not weighing down [vrisousa] toward matter and generation; for if it were some sweetness of matter or [reading *ē* for *hē*] a delight enticing [sc. the daemons] through vapors from matter (I have completed these from the manuscript *Codex Gothanus*, whose variant readings I report through the service of Frid. Jacobs), the matter ought to be pure (*akeraion* Cod. Goth.)."

p. 516, 3. *pepedēmetha tō katō* [we are fettered by the lower]] Hesychius: *pepedēmenos*: bound; consider the Homeric passages, such as *Iliad* Δ. 517: "Fate fettered him." Χ. 5. "Destructive Fate fettered Hector to remain there." *Odyssey* Δ. 580: "Whoever of the immortals fetters me and binds me from the path." and similar things.

— 9. *ouch enochloumenou de parechon merimnas* [not being disturbed, yet providing anxieties]] Ficinus rendered these more freely. If the reading is sound, one must think according to the *parechon merimnas*. Since he is not disturbed by it, because he exhibits troubles (solicitudes). For the following, apply Plato’s *Timaeus* p. 30 sqq.—The word *hēremēsis* [quietude] toward the end of the chapter also reminds one of Plato. See *Sophist* p. 248. p. 195. Bekk. where that which is quiet (*to hēremoun*) is taught to neither be moved nor suffer. Hence *hēremein* [to be quiet] is used by the same author in *Gorgias* p. 575. p. 171. Bekk. even of firm reasons and principles, which can be disturbed by no doubt and no argument.

p. 517, 2. *ē kai hē hairesis ekei—tēn tēs psychēs proairesin kai diathesin—ainittetai* [or even the choice there—hints at the purpose and disposition of the soul]] Where Ficinus had translated both as *electio* [choice], I have, for the sake of clarity, appended to the latter once: *propositum* [purpose]. Regarding the same sentiment, Proclus in *Alc. pr.* LVII. p. 163 of our edition (Frankfurt) says: "By which it is clear that it does not [reading *hoti ouk ek pantos apaitei*] require that a daemon moves us toward actions, but when our purpose is good-like, the fact that we are not turned away nor hindered is a sign of that which is our duty (*tou kathēkein*)." In the following: "and the daemon, he says, is not changed;" and "when it is said that the lots were first," he again looks back to the very famous fable of Plato at the end of *Republic* Book X. p. 617 sq. p. 508 sq. Bekk. Cf. also Xenocrates in Aristotle, *Topicor.* II. 2. p. 299. Sylb.—To those words, however, "the body is no longer the cause of any evil to him," the Egyptian philosopher [Plotinus] partly objects to the Egyptians. Plutarch, *De esu carn.* p. 996. E. p. 54. Wytt.: "Since it would be well, just as the Egyptians, having removed the stomach of the dead and splitting it open toward the sun, cast it out as the cause of everything the human has sinned, so we ourselves, cutting out gluttony and blood-lust, might keep the rest of life pure." Regarding this custom, I have collected more in *Commentt. Herodott.* I. 3. p. 30 sqq. Truly, these words of Porphyry in the *Epistle to Marcella* c. 29. p. 50. ed. Ang. Maii show the disciple worthy of the master: "Neither let us blame the flesh as the cause of great evils, nor let us turn our frustrations toward things, but let us rather seek the causes of these within the soul."

— 11. *epei kai hai—tychai tēn holēn proairesin ouk ekvivazousin* [since even fortunes do not drive out the whole purpose]] Ficinus had translated: *transgrediuntur* (rather he ought to have said *transgredi faciunt, expellunt* [make to step across, expel]). Therefore, he himself also read *ekvivazousin*. And we have retained this reading all the more since Platonic usage commends it and a suitable sense arises from it. The confusion between the two verbs is frequent. See Dorvill. at *Chariton* VI. 2. p. 605. Lips. [p. 662. Amst.] Especially relevant here is Arrian in *Dissertt. Epict.* I. 18. 21. p. 102. Schwgh. "Who then is the invincible? He whom nothing outside the choice disturbs... then finally approaching each of the circumstances I learn, as in the case of the athlete; this one *exevlase* [cast out] the first lot." Schweigh. in the Index prefers: *exeviasato* [forced out]. But many books there offer: *exevivase*. Regarding this reading, Upton says: "But Meibomius’s reading *exevivase* is not displeasing. For *ekvivazō* is 'I make to go out.' They were said 'to go out' whose names, inscribed on lots and cast into an urn, were then ex-

p. 518, 2. *martyrei ta en tō Timaiō* [the things in the Timaeus testify]] Plato, *Tim.* p. 90. p. 137 sq. Bekk. Cf. also the passage of Proclus in *Alcib. pr.*, the more notable parts of which I placed in the first note on this very chapter.

— 10. *kai daimōn toutō theos* [and a daemon is a god to this one]] Cf. below p. 296. B. C. To this pertains the narrative of Porphyry regarding the *Life of Plotinus* X. p. 111. Fabr., where an Egyptian calls Plotinus blessed, who has a God for a genius [guardian spirit]: "blessed are you having a god as your daemon." — 16. *Ho mentoi daimōn—agōgon legetai eis haidou; ouketi ho autos menei* [The daemon, however—is said to be a leader to Hades; he no longer remains the same]] He inquires about the passage of Plato in *Phaedo* p. 107. E. p. 82. Wytt. p. 107. Bekk.: "It is said thus, that after each person dies, the daemon of each, which had fallen to him while living, this one attempts to lead him to a certain place, where those gathered must be judged and travel to Hades with that leader, to whom it has been commanded to journey those from here to there; having obtained there what they must obtain, and remained as long as is necessary, another leader brings them back here again in many times and long periods." Wyttenbach illustrated these copiously in *Annott.* p. 289—292.

p. 519, 2. *to dē agagein eis tēn krisin—kolazomenais paresti—dikē* [to lead to judgment—is present for those being punished—justice]] See Plato’s *Gorgias* p. 523 sqq. p. 185. Bekk. where at the words p. 523. b. "both Pluto and the overseers" in the Clarkian Bodleian Codex p. 93. Gaisf. this scholion is appended: "there are punishing, purifying, and perfecting daemons."

— 6. *elatton ē daimōn, ē ponēros ge, ē euēthēs* [less than a daemon, or at least a wicked one, or a simpleton]] Regarding the kinds of Daemons and their varied nature and character, see, to name but a few, Iamblichus, *De Myster. Aegypt.* I. 6 sqq. p. 10 sqq. ed. Gal. Proclus in *Alcib. pr.* p. 68 sqq. Olympiodorus in the same, page 15 sqq. and annotations there. That same Proclus in *Alcib. pr.* p. 73 distinguishes thus: the daemon *by essence* (*ho ousia* or *kat’ ousian*), who by certain proper and unique powers has the essence of a genius (daemon) separate from divine and human essence; the daemon *by analogy* (*ho kat’ analogian*), who attentively looks out for someone, whether that be a god or one placed in the second rank after the gods; the daemon *by relation* (*ho kata schesin*), who exhibits greater powers than human ones, and being more like daemons than men, renders his life entirely suspended from the geniuses.

— 14. *kai apallageisas (tēs psychēs) ekei gignesthai* [and having been released (the soul) to come to be there]] Cf. *Enn.* IV. 3. 12. IV. 9. 4. Regarding the return of souls to higher things (*anodō*), there was a specific book by Porphyry (Augustine, *De C. D.* X. 29.) Virgil applied himself to this doctrine of the ancients in *Aeneid* VI. 735 sqq. "Nay even, when with the last light life has left," etc. Consult Heyne’s *Excursus* XIII on these. Iamblichus in *Protrept.* III. p. 34. Kiessling: "for otherwise no one would be able to run back to the most divine part of himself, unless he used such a daemon (add after *daimoni* from ed. Arc. and MSS: *hēgemoni* [as a leader]) whom it is necessary for every lover of the gods to genuinely purify. From which first [reading *prōtē*] there is a pause from the evils joined to us from birth; then true knowledge will be present to us of the daemonic and blessed life, what it is and of what kind; with which, ascending, we shall look upon the primary divine race of men, and being established in it, we shall have as an end the most blessed life proposed by the gods for men; at the end, therefore, it exhorts toward the migration (*metastasin*) of the soul and its life according to itself, by which it is released from the body and the natures joined to the body." I omit many other things which I placed in *Symbolica* III p. 432 sqq. regarding the return of souls from the decrees of ancient religions and philosophy.

p. 520, 17. *eita paralavousa hē tou atraktou legomenē physis.* [then the so-called nature of the spindle, having taken over.]] Plato, *De Republ.* X. p. 616. p. 506. Bekk. "and from the extremities is stretched the spindle of Necessity, through which all the turnings are made," etc. Proclus, *On the Theology of Plato* VI. 23. p. 409: "—and just as he said the whole spindle itself turns in the knees of Necessity, so indeed the myth attaches the providence concerning partial souls to the knees of Lachesis; with the hands, as higher powers, moving the whole eternally, but in the knees subordinately having the causes of the psychic periods." Moreover, I have tried to explain the reason for the *Fusi* [spindles] from the ancient signs of the Goddesses in *Symbolica* III. p. 433. second ed.

p. 527, 7. **ON LOVE [PERI ERŌTOS].** In the chronological order in which the individual books were written, this is the fiftieth (see Porphyry, *Life of Plot.* c. XXV. p. 143. cf. cap. VI. p. 103. Fabric.), and therefore to be recorded among the last, but in subject matter most closely joined with the preceding one on the Genius [daemon], and no less with the books *On the Beautiful* and *On the Intelligible Beauty*. Plotinus professes at the very beginning of this book that he seized the occasion and material for disputing about love especially from the writings of Plato. And although mention of love is made in many of the divine philosopher's dialogues, yet the *Symposium* along with the *Phaedrus* and *Philebus* were observed by Plotinus above the others in composing this writing. And that *Symposium* was treated in the schools at that time is proved by Porphyry’s narrative in *Life of Plot.* c. XV. p. 117. Fabr. That many after Plato down to the latest Platonists elaborated on the same subject, and that there were many books, such as Plutarch's *Erotikos*, is not something I need to demonstrate laboriously here; nor is it necessary to descend deeper into the sources of this passage *on Love*, and the changes after those things we placed above at the title of Book I. 6. (on the Beautiful) and in the annotation to the same, likewise to the book on *Dialectic* p. 19—21. nor less those things we disputed in many places of the *Symbolica*, especially Volume three, chapter VI. p. 536—579. second ed., and finally what my dear Heusde elegantly, as is his wont, set forth on this entire subject in the first part of the book entitled: *Initia Philosophiae Platonicae* [Beginnings of Platonic Philosophy]. I. Utrecht 1827.

— 13. *hos dē (Platōn)—peri erōtos egrapsen—kai daimona phēsin auton kai, peri geneseōs autou diexēlthen* [he who (Plato)—wrote about love—and says it is a daemon and went through its generation]] There is a most famous passage in the *Symposium* p. 202 sq. p. 428 sqq. Bekk. celebrated by the explanations and imitations of many, such as Origen *Against Celsus* book IV. p. 189 sq. Spencer, p. 532 sq. Ruæus, who compares that narrative with the history of Paradise in Genesis. Aristides *Oratt.* Vol. II. p. 106. Jebb. Plutarch *De Isid. et Osir.* p. 361. B. and p. 374. C. D. p. 480. and p. 532, 533. Wytt. Maximus of Tyre *Dissertat.* X. 4. XIV. 8. Porphyry *De Nymph. Antr.* §. 16. The same in *Sententt.* at the end p. 248. Cantabr. Proclus *In Plat. Theol.* c. 28. p. 233. Jo. Laurentius Lydus in fragments of *De Mensibus* p. 282. ed. Hasii. Themistius *Orat.* XIII. p. 162. B. Also Proclus in *Timaeum* p. 287. and p. 305. and in *Cratyl.* p. 75 sq. Boisson. and in *Alc. pr.* p. 190 sq. collected p. 233. Hermes Trismegistus in Stobaeus *Eclogg. Phys.* p. 118. Apuleius *De Deo Socratis* p. 674. p. 133. ed. Bosschae. Eusebius in *Praep. Evang.* XII. p. 584. Moreover, *van Heusde* recently illustrated the decrees of Plato on love from his own writings in *Initiis Philosophiae Platonicae* I. p. 120 sq. Regarding Plotinus's own passages, we have seen some above at p. 142. G., and we shall see some below. Next, the reading *symplakēnai* [to be entwined] can be defended by the authority of Plato in the *Symposium* itself p. 191. p. 405. Bekk.: "the remaining part sought the other and was entwined."

p. 528, 13. *hotō de tis agatai* [by whatever someone is admired]] I embrace this reading as the more difficult and Platonic: *Sympos.* p. 179. p. 383. Bekk. "admired for the deed." Regarding this construction see Ruhnken at *Timaei Lex. Plat.* p. 8. Pierson at *Moer.* p. 1 sq. and *Lex. Seguier.* in Bekker's *Anecdott. grr.* I. p. 335. bottom.

— 16. *Kai gar outoi tiktein voulontai en tō kalō; epeiper atopon—en aischrō gennan voulesthai k. t. l.* [For these also wish to give birth in the beautiful; since it is out of place—to wish to beget in the ugly, etc.]] Plato *Sympos.* p. 206. p. 435 sq. Bekk.—"because of these, whenever the pregnant approaches the beautiful, it becomes cheerful and, rejoicing, is poured out and gives birth and begets; but whenever it approaches the ugly, frowning and grieving, it curls up and turns away and is squeezed and does not beget. For Love is not, O Socrates, as you think, of the beautiful. But what then? Of generation and birth in the beautiful." Plotinus has the rest of this dispute before his eyes in what follows. Furthermore, regarding the origin of friendship and love, which the philosopher of Lycopolis [Plotinus] touches upon here with a word, Aristotle says in *Eth. Nicom.* IX. 5. 3.: "The beginning of friendship seems to be like that of loving: the pleasure through sight; for no one loves without first being pleased by the form. But he who rejoices in the form does not love more for it, but only when he also longs for the absent one and desires the presence."

p. 529, 9. *Hotō de memiktai kai allē tou athanatou einai hōs en thnētō epithymia k. t. l.* [To whomever there is mixed also another desire of being immortal as if in a mortal, etc.]] Plato *Sympos.* p. 208. p. 439. Bekk. after he made mention of Alcestis, Achilles, Codrus, proceeds thus:—"but, I think, for the sake of immortal virtue and such glorious reputation all do all things, and the better they are, the more so; for they love the immortal; those then who are pregnant in body, she said, turn more toward women, and in this way are erotic, through child-bearing, providing for themselves immortality and memory and happiness, as they think, for the time to come."

p. 529, 19. *genomenoi paraphoroi* [having become carried away]] You might say: *after they have become inebriated*. For Plato uses this word for a drunkard in *Laws* VI. 13. p. 775. But yet it signifies generally those who have been cast down from a sound mind, a usage repeated from sailing or from vehicles or from horses which carry their riders sideways. Bähr set this word out accurately in our *Meletemata* III. p. 5 sq. cf. the same on *parapherein* [to carry past/distract] at Plutarch *Pyrrh.* XVII. p. 195. The force of the verb *ekpherein* [to carry out] is sometimes not dissimilar. See Budaeus *Comm. L. Gr.* p. 508 sq. Viger. p. 602. b. and Cattierius’s *Gazophylac.* p. 79. Add Plato *Cratyl.* p. 386. a. Regarding the word *paraphoros* consult also Jacobs at *Callistratus, Statues* p. 690. (p. 148, 31.) Proclus in *Alc. pr.* p. 210: "but ugliness [comes] from being mastered and being asymmetrical [perhaps *tou as.*] and rendering its own activities *paraphorous* [erratic]." where see the annotation. Plotinus below VIII. 8. 6. has the word *paraphora*.

p. 530, 3. *All’ oun, hoi te sōmatōn kalōn kai dia mixin erōntes.* [But then, those loving beautiful bodies even through mingling.]] Ficinus, who translates: "*not for the sake of mingling*," seems to have corrected it to *kai dicha mixeōs* [and without mingling]. Soon, with the same author, the words seem to be transposed thus: *sōphronousi men amphō, hoi de ameinon* [both are temperate, but the others better], or if you follow most books, *hoi de ameinous*, sc. *eisi* [but they are better]. For the sentiment, apply both the cited passage of the Platonic *Symposium* and this one p. 192. p. 407.—"but it is enough for them to live together with each other unmarried." Concerning this matter, it is disputed in a contrary sense in Plutarch’s *Amatorius* p. 750 sq. p. 9 sqq. Wytt., from which I will give only these excerpts:—"but true Love has not even the slightest part in the women's quarters, nor do I say that you love who are attached to women or virgins, etc." For the rest, although celibates are mentioned among the most famous Philosophers before Plato, yet it cannot be doubted that both the celibacy of Plato himself and truly sentiments of this kind found in his writings were the reason why the later Platonists especially shunned marriages. Marinus in the life of Proclus c. 17. (p. 39.) p. 14. Boisson: "For never having taken trial of marriages or children (Proclus), etc." In which matter Proclus followed the example of Plotinus. See Porphyry *Life of Plot.* IX. p. 108. Fabric. Heineccius on the *lex Julia et Papia Poppaea* book I. c. 2. p. 38: "Hence, as formerly Thales, Pythagoras, Democritus, Plato, Zeno of Citium, Epicurus judged celibacy to be most friendly to the study of wisdom; so, after the Lex Julia was passed, Epictetus, Apollonius of Tyana, Plotinus, Porphyry, Proclus held tenaciously to the same opinion." In the case of Porphyry, Heineccius has not reported the truth in every respect. For this philosopher himself writes thus at the beginning of the epistle to his wife Marcella: "I chose you, Marcella, to have as a companion—not for the sake of child-begetting from the body—but rather for a twofold reasonable cause: one according to which, having decided to appease the gods of birth, etc." Mentions of preserved virginity from the inscriptions of tombs were exhibited by *G. Marini* in the book *Gli Atti E Monumenti Degli Fratelli Arvali* Vol. I. p. 41. That Plotinus in the following mentions "the beauty here" [*to tēde kallos*] and "the beauty there" [*to ekei kallos*] reminds one of Diotima herself in Plato's *Symposium*; where among many other things there is this, to take only the end, p. 211. p. 444 sq. "starting from these beautiful things for the sake of that beauty always to ascend, etc." Cf. Plotin. above p. 50 and annotations there.

— 13. *alla kai theologoi* [but also theologians]] Thus these philosophers for the most part call the Orphics. And in the Orphic Hymns and Fragments the praises of Love are celebrated. See *Hymn.* LVIII. (57.) *Fragg.* VI. 19. VIII. 2. and XXII.

— 14. *kai Platōn pollachou* [and Plato in many places]] To these apply just now the *Phaedrus* p. 252. p. 52. Bekk. and especially the classic passage, which Plotinus then explains, from the *Symposium* p. 202. p. 427. Bekk.: "and she, laughing, said, And how, O Socrates, could he be agreed to be a great god by those who say he is not even a god, etc." Which reminds one of the words of Alexis in the *Phaedrus* at Athenaeus XIII. p. 562. b. p. 89. Schwgh. "For (Eros) is neither female nor male; again neither god nor man." In what follows Plotinus looks back to the speech of Pausanias in the same *Symposium* (p. 180. p. 385.): "For all

we know that Aphrodite is not without Love. If there were one, there would be one Love. But since there are two, there must also be two Loves. How could the goddesses not be two? One indeed older and motherless, daughter of Uranus, whom we call Heavenly; the second of Zeus and Dione, whom we call Common." Many have treated this passage; whence I shall praise only the most recent: *Jo. Bapt. Vico* in *Principles of the New Science* p. 362. German transl. *Weber*. *Tiedemann* in *Geist der Spekulat. Philosophie* III. p. 415. and *Heusde* in *Initia Philosophiae Platonicae* I. p. 112 sq.

p. 530, 17. *kai dē kai hosa en Symposiō eirētai paralēpteon, en hois ouk Aphroditēs genethliois, ek—tou Porou* [and indeed whatever has been said in the Symposium must be taken up, in which not on the birthday of Aphrodite, from—Porus]] You might fill the lacunose passage thus: —*en hois ouk oid' Aphroditēs genethliois ek—tou Porou Erōta gegonenai* [in which I know not on the birthday of Aphrodite from Porus Love was born]. Furthermore, those things should be joined which are said in the *Symposium*, that on I know not what birthdays of Venus, Love was begotten from Penia and Porus. Ficinus, however, in his interpretation filled the passage otherwise: *en hois en Aphroditēs genethliois—Porou gegonenai legetai Erōs*. And, to hide nothing, this way seems truer because in citing testimonies of writers the formula is accustomed to be used; *en hois legetai* [in which it is said]. For the rest, what the edition has in the context, *pornou* [of a harlot]: there has frequently been an error in this name. See the interpreters at *Orig. c. Celsum* IV. p. 532 where *Pōros* is similar as in Porphyry *De antro Nymph.* p. 107. where see Goens. In the same author's books *De Abstin.* III. p. 289 Rhoer might prefer to protect the vulgar reading *ton koron* [satiety]. In his *Sententiis* p. 248. Cantabr. end, it is undoubtedly to be read: *tēn men eikotōs Penian; tēn de Poron (pro koron)* [the one appropriately Poverty; the other Plenty (instead of satiety)], those who first knew this hinted at the fullness of the soul. Below p. 317. C. we likewise corrected the false reading *tō Porrhō*.

p. 231, 8. *hoti mēde en ouranō gamoi* [that there are not even marriages in heaven]] These remind one of those words in *Evang. Marci* XII. 25: "for when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage but are like angels in the heavens." Cudworth disputes this passage in *System. Intellect.* p. 660. 679. and Mosheim ibid. p. 680. 681. 682. Brucker in *Hist. Crit. Philos.* II. p. 405 sq.:—"That Proclus (in *Tim.* p. 92 sq.) indicates that not only Amelius and Porphyry, but also Plotinus, had already [postulated] a Supramundane soul. In which words, although Proclus doubts about Plotinus, Cudworth rightly advised that faith is not to be denied to Porphyry in this matter, who clearly held the mind of his teacher to a hair. Nor is it far from probability that Ammonius, when he adorned the Platonic triad according to the norm of the Christian triad, seeing that the mundane soul—partaking no less of the divisible than of the indivisible, and of the other as much as of the same—did not at all correspond to the dignity of the divine principles, devised this distinction. For what seemed to Cudworth, that it is found already in Plato, is entirely false, and was devised only to excuse the Platonists, whom that most acute man greatly favored." I have placed this entire passage both because this question is primary concerning the double soul of the world, and so that it may be understood by this example how *Mosheim* and *Brucker* for the most part received the decrees of the recent Platonists and their British interpreter. To confess candidly what I feel, I think both, both *Mosheim* and *Brucker*, lacked that quality of genius and sagacity of mind to be able to penetrate everywhere into the inner sanctuaries of these philosophers, and thus to rightly estimate the merits of Cudworth. Nor is it to be pronounced otherwise concerning *Tiedemann*, who touched upon these very things and those following in the book *Geist der Spekulat. Philosophie* III. p. 410 sq. although here he is much fairer in judging the merits of Plotinus. See ibid. p. 431—433. Cf. also *Tennemann’s* Histor. Philos. VI. p. 105 sqq. *Neander* compares this passage with Valentinian decrees in: *Genetische Entwickelung der vornehmsten Gnostischen Systeme* p. 213 sq.

— 9. *ek Kronou, nou ontos ekeinou* [from Kronos, he being Intellect]] The source of this decree is in Plato's *Cratylus* p. 396. b. at which Proclus in *Scholiis* §. 104. p. 60. Boisson: "But when Kronos is called Intellect, Zeus occupies the rank of thought, and when again Kronos is thought, we shall say he is called thus entirely in relation to some other higher Intellect by analogy." Where he disputes many things in what follows. I gave other things in our *Meletemm.* I. p. 44 sq. p. 533, 6. *kai ek tou oion aporrheontos apo tou horōmenou—Erōs egento* [and from as it were the outflowing from the seen—Love was born]] Our author below p. 714. B. "and therefore the soul, having received into itself [adding *tēn* perhaps] an outflow from there, is moved and is maddened and is filled with gadflies, and love is born." Plato *Phaedrus* p. 251. b. p. 49. Bekk.: "for having received the outflow of beauty through the eyes he was warmed." Many imitations of this passage were indicated by Wyttenb. in *Bibl. Which sentiment the fathers of the Church for the most part attacked. See Theodoret Vol. III. p. 743 and 993 ed. Schulz.

— 8. *tacha pou kai tēs prosēgorias enteuthen mallon autō gegennēmenēs k. t. l.* [perhaps also the appellation having been born to it from there more, etc.]] Plato *Cratylus* p. 420. a. "Love [erōs] flows in from outside and this flow is not proper to the possessor but imported through the eyes; for these reasons from the flowing-in [*esrein*] it was then called *esros* anciently—for we used *ou* instead of *ō*—but now it is called *erōs* through the exchange of *ō* for *ou*." Sight was therefore used by Plato himself in pursuing the etymology of Love. Plotinus, however, differently, a trace of whose etymology exists in *Etymol. Magn.* p. 379. p. 344. Lips. *Erōs*—that from *horō* (I see), the desire arising in men through the sense of sight, where he will find many other things too, who is held by delights of that kind. Plotinus, however, only tentatively risks that etymology. For the rest, the first edition of Ficinus at this place gives: "*who perhaps from this is called hero, since from horaseōs, i.e., vision, he has substance.*"

Ciz. Mon. A. Vat.* is to be constituted thus: *epei toge pathos hypo toutou eran legetai, eiper proteron ousia mē ousias, kai eiper erōs auton achei toude*. In this place for *auton* Ficinus reads *autēn*, perhaps thinking of the *soul*. I rest in the books [manuscripts]. Plotinus could write *auton* for *tina* [someone]. However it is: this is certain, that these words of the *Symposium* p. 299. p. 421. Bekk. were before our philosopher: "is he such a one as to be Love *of* something, or of nothing?—tell me this much, whether Love desires that of which it is the love or not. Certainly, he said." Those things truly remind one of Dio Chrysostom. Which excellent writer thus in *De Regno*, or *Orat.* III. p. 52. p. 132 sq. Reisk.: "for are not even these sexual matters most pleasant and least insulting, as many as happen with the friendship of those together? and as many as seek goodwill for men, it comes from boys, or from women. for there are many appellations of friendship, as surely there are also uses. but that friendship happening with beauty and ripeness is rightly named love, and seems the most beautiful of the gods." That the passage is lacunose was seen by Is. Casaubon and Reiskius; what they attempted, I pass over in silence. I read: *kai hosa* (so the margin of Morellius) *masteuousin eunoian anthrōpoi, anthrōpois epēlthe charis para paidikōn ē para gynaikōn*: "and what things men zealously seek as goodwill, come to men of their own accord (or are given) as grace from beloved boys or from women." *masteuein* [to seek] and *epelthein* [to come upon] are opposed to each other. *charis* [grace] and *eunoia* [goodwill] are joined also by Plutarch in *Amatorius* p. 751. C. p. 13. Wytt.: "for if the unnatural intercourse with males does not destroy erotic goodwill nor harm it, much more is it likely that the Love of women or men (so rightly Wytt.) using nature arrives at friendship through grace." That sexual compliance was called *charita* and *charitas* [grace/favors] by the Ancients is not something we need laboriously demonstrate after Ruhnken at *Tim. Lex. Plat.* The word *charis* in Dio’s passage was drawn from the following *para*.
