p. 542, 18. *kēpos—kai ploutou egkallōpisma* [a garden—and an adornment of wealth]] To the last word is added: *of the soul* in the Excerpts of Christopher Contoleon from Plotinus in *Cod. Vat. nr. 2141*. I doubt whether correctly. Next, I did not fear to replace *aglaïzetai kai tō tou Dios logō* [it is made bright also by the reason of Zeus] for *ta*. Moreover, Ez. Spanheim looked back to our passage in the notes to the French version of Julian’s *Caesars* p. 228 note 778: "*Plotinus in some place calls the* GARDENS OF JUPITER, *the splendor, which, issuing from his understanding, goes to shine in the soul of man.*"

p. 543, 5. *kai ho ploutos tōn kalōn, en ekphansei ēdē* [and the wealth of beautiful things, already in manifestation]] Aristobulus in Eusebius *P. E.* VIII. p. 378. A.: "by the manifestation [ekphansei] of fire like lightning—because those looking together apprehend each thing manifestly." Cf. Wyttenb. at *Plutarch.* p. 714 who says *emphantikōs* [emphatically/manifestly] is more Plutarchan, and places this distinction: that *emphainein* is: *to signify anything at all, to make clear and known*, *ekphainein* *to bring a thing from the occult into light*. Add Proclus in *Alc. pr.* p. 51. 52. 71 and *Instit. Theol.* III. 186.

— 6. *kai touto esti to methyein tō nektari* [and this is to be drunk with nectar]] Porphyry *De Antro Nymph.* XVI. p. 16. Goens. After he had said that nectar and ambrosia are taken for honey by some, he proceeds thus: "but in Orpheus Kronos is ambushed by Zeus with honey, for having been filled with honey he is drunk, and is darkened as if from wine and sleeps. as in Plato Porus having been filled with nectar. for there was not yet wine;" Proclus looked back to the antecedent things in *Theology of Plato* c. 13. p. 38: "For (intellect) has twofold activities, as Plotinus says, some indeed as intellect, others as being drunk with nectar." Next, you might opine that Ficinus read: "intellect indeed having itself in satiety [korō] is at rest." Yet the books vary nothing.

— 11. *Dei de tous mythous—hopou kai hoi logoi—diairousi* [It is necessary that myths—where also the reasons—divide]] Truly golden words, and which deeply open the entire nature of fables and their difference from doctrinal reason (system). Moreover, because he says reasons (*logous*) and that they themselves introduce generations of those things which were not begotten: the cosmogonies of the ancient philosophers, and of Plato himself, especially in the *Timaeus*, must be thought of, in which generations [*geneai*] and births [*geneseis*] are mentioned even in metaphysical and moral matters. In the last words Plotinus expressed the passage of Plato in *Politicus* p. 269. p. 272. Bekk. where likewise concerning ancient fables: "—but through the fullness of time some of them have been extinguished, but others having been scattered are spoken of each apart from each other."

**-> LIB. VI. <-**

p. 551, 7. **ON THE IMPASSIBILITY OF INCORPOREAL THINGS [PERI TĒS APATHEIAS TŌN ASŌMATŌN].** The twenty-sixth book (see Porphyry *Life of Plot.* c. 5 and c. 24. and Fabricius there) and therefore written immediately before the three books on the doubts of the soul. Just as this book is a prelude to the books *On the Soul*: so its argument is most closely joined with the two immediately preceding; since in the place concerning daemons it was also primarily sought, whether they are endowed with a body and therefore can suffer [be acted upon], or not. See above p. 295. G. and what we placed there; which question was especially repeated in *Love*, since the ancients distinguished *energetic* [active] Love from *pathetic* [passive]. Proclus thus begins that distinction in *Alc. pr.* §. 39. p. 117, so that he reminds one by his very words of the argument in which this book of Plotinus is engaged: "For it is proper to incorporeal things to act, but to corporeal things to suffer [be acted upon]; but then Loves are opposed to each other if—one is active, the other passive, and one is immaterial, the other material, etc." Thence enough, I think, can be understood why Porphyry added this book to those. Moreover, how variously *Incorporeal*, or *to asōmaton*, which Cicero himself also used in Greek in *de N. D.* I. 12, is said, is not something we should seek here after the disputes of *Cudworth* and *Mosheim* in *System. Intell.* I. 26. p. 36 sq. IV. 24. p. 491. V. 3. p. 1014 sqq. (in which places, however, *Cudworth* descended deeper than *Mosheim* into the mind of Plato and certainly of the Platonic philosophers); let it suffice to have advised by a word: *asōmaton* [incorporeal] is found in the writings of the Pythagoreans. Ocellus Lucanus *On the Nature of the Universe* II. p. 519. Gal.: "But the powers are neither destroyed nor born. For they happen to be the incorporeal reasons [*logoi asōmatoi*] of these." Plato, however, and the philosophers who followed him, defined the account of the *Incorporeal* more subtly, and applied it to establishing the notion of soul, god, daemon, etc., nor for that reason were they able to persuade other philosophers everywhere. To this pertain those words of Lucian in *Hermotimus* §. 36. p. 779 ed. Wetsten.: "Plato thinks there is something incorporeal among beings," likewise in *Icaromenippus* §. 9. p. 760: "moreover some thought the divine to be incorporeal and formless,"

*οἱ δὲ ὡς περὶ σώματος αὐτοῦ διενοοῦντο* [But others thought of it as a body]. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 108 [[abbrev: sq. → following]] De la Rue); in *Phaedo* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 78, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 46 [[abbrev: sqq. → following]] Bekker (at which place consult Wyttenbach’s annotations [[abbrev: p. → page]] 195—198); in *Timaeus* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 43, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 46 [[abbrev: sqq. → following]] Bekker ([[abbrev: cf. → compare]] Plutarch’s *Platonic Questions* III, IV [[abbrev: p. → page]] 1001 [[abbrev: sq. → following]], [[abbrev: p. → page]] 75 [[abbrev: sqq. → following]] Wyttenbach, and Alcinous *On the Doctrines of Plato* [[abbrev: c. → chapter]] XXV); *De Republica* X [[abbrev: p. → page]] 609, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 492 [[abbrev: sqq. → following]] Bekker; *De Legibus* X [[abbrev: p. → page]] 894 [[abbrev: sqq. → following]], [[abbrev: p. → page]] 193 [[abbrev: sqq. → following]] Bekker; of Aristotle in *Metaphysics* II. 4, IV. 2, VII. 1 [[abbrev: sqq. → following]], [[abbrev: p. → page]] 133 [[abbrev: sqq. → following]] Sylburg; *De Anima* I. 2 (where the Stagirite reviews the opinions of the ancient philosophers) and II. 1; *De Generatione et Corruptione* I. 2, I. 5, I. 6, 7, 8. Furthermore, the primary opinions of this Plotinian book are to be compared with other books, especially in these places [[abbrev: p. → page]] 645, 656, 667, 764, and with the entire book *On Matter*. Porphyry diligently reduced the Plotinian decrees into a compendium in the *Sententiae* [[abbrev: Cap. → Chapter]] XIX (which begins thus: *Ἄλλο τὸ πάσχειν τῶν σωμάτων, ἄλλο τῶν ἀσωμάτων* [The affection of bodies is one thing, that of the incorporeal is another] [[abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → etc.]]) up to [[abbrev: Cap. → Chapter]] XXIX, and again XXXVI (which places Cudworth employed for his discussion in *The True Intellectual System of the Universe* V. 3. 11, 12. Finally, see Alexander of Aphrodisias in his commentary on Aristotle’s *Metaphysics* I. 20; Simplicius on *Physics* book IV and on the books *De Anima* folio 7: Thomas Taylor translated this book into English: *Select Works of Plotinus*, London 1817, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 122 [[abbrev: sqq. → following]].

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 552, 12. *καὶ δοξῶν ψευδῶν καὶ ἀνοίας οἰκειώσεις*] So in the [[abbrev: Ed. → Edition]]. But [[abbrev: Fic. → Ficinus]] expressed it as *καὶ ἀγνοίας* [and of ignorance]. *Οἰκειώσεις* [[abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → etc.]]: "and of ignorance. There are generated in it (the soul) also conformities and deformities etc.," so that you should again understand *ἐγγίγνονται* [are produced] from the preceding. This reading and punctuation is pleasing, and Taylor also embraced it: we have decided that the same must be done.

— 15. *Ἀλλ' εἰ μὲν σῶμά ἐστιν ἡ ψυχή*] [But if the soul is a body]. Anaxagoras, Heraclitus, Democritus, Epicurus, and the Stoics had taught this, as the author of the little book *On the Opinions of the Philosophers* indeed discloses, in the works of Plutarch IV. 3 [[abbrev: p. → page]] 898 C. D., [[abbrev: p. → page]] 622 [[abbrev: sq. → following]] Wyttenbach. Moreover, Porphyry has this entire chapter of Plotinus before his eyes in the *Sententiae* [[abbrev: c. → chapter]] XIX [[abbrev: p. → page]] 225 [[abbrev: sq. → following]] Cambridge edition. For the rest, [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] below at the beginning of the book *On the Essence of the Soul* IV. 2. 1 [[abbrev: p. → page]] 361 A, where our philosopher likewise denies that the soul is a body.

— 19. *αὐτῇ πάθη διδόναι—αὐτὴν φθαρτὴν εἶναι διδόντες*] *To attribute such affections to it—conceding that it is corruptible*. The repetition of the same word (the Verb) used with a different force is not infrequent, nor is it unknown to Latin writers. An example of the same verb conveniently comes to mind. Cicero, *De Officiis* I. 21. 71: "**Wherefore it should perhaps be conceded (*concedendum*) to those who, having excellent talent, have dedicated themselves to learning and do not take up public affairs; and to those who, hindered by weakness of health or some more serious cause, have withdrawn from the state, since they were conceding (*concederent*) to others the power and praise of administering it:**" where see Heusinger [[abbrev: p. → page]] 172. [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] also Beier on *De Officiis* I. 39 [[abbrev: p. → page]] 284. There is another reason for passages of this sort, where the same word but of a different origin is repeated, as in these words of Philo Judaeus, *De Mundi Opificio* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 118 [[abbrev: ed. → edition]] Pfeiffer: *εἰσὶ γὰρ οἱ πλείους παραλαμβάνοντες κόσμους εἶναι, οἱ δὲ καὶ ἀπείρους, ἄπειροι καὶ ἀνεπιστήμονες αὐτοὶ πρὸς ἀλήθειαν ὄντες, ὧν καλὸν ἐπιστήμην ἔχειν* [For there are many who assume there are worlds, and some even infinite worlds, being themselves infinite (inexperienced) and ignorant regarding the truth, of which it is good to have knowledge]. Moreover, Plato has the verb *διδόναι* [to grant/give] twice in one place with the meaning of "to concede," after he had used *συγχωρεῖν* [to agree] a little earlier, in *Charmides* §. 44 [[abbrev: p. → page]] 172. [[abbrev: c. → chapter]]. Phalaris similarly adds an Accusative with Infinitive as Plotinus does, *Epistulae* V [[abbrev: p. → page]] 26 Lennep: *ἐγὼ δὲ οὔπω δίδωμι, τὴν τιμωρίαν πεπράχθαι ἄδικον* [But I do not yet concede that the punishment was unjustly carried out]. Regarding another force of this verb, we saw above at I. 1. 12 [[abbrev: p. → page]] 7 B.

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 553, 1. *εἴτε ἀριθμὸς—ἡ οὐσία αὐτῆς*] [Whether its essence is number]. This was the opinion of Pythagoras and Xenocrates. Plutarch *De Placitis Philosophorum* IV. 2 [[abbrev: p. → page]] 898 C, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 621 Wyttenbach: *Πυθαγόρας (ἀπεφήνατο) τὴν ψυχὴν ἀριθμὸν ἑαυτὸν κινοῦντα. τὸν δὲ ἀριθμὸν ἀντὶ τοῦ νοῦ παραλαμβάνει* [Pythagoras (declared) the soul to be a self-moving number. And he takes number in place of intellect]. The same man said that number was the wisest of all things. Iamblichus *On the Pythagorean Life* §. 146 [[abbrev: p. → page]] 122 Kuster and §. 162 [[abbrev: p. → page]] 138. The adjective *σαθρὸς* [unsound/rotten] is familiar to Plato. *Theaetetus* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 179 [[abbrev: d. → column]] ([[abbrev: ib. → ibid.]] Heindorf [[abbrev: p. → page]] 413); *Philebus* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 55 ([[abbrev: ib. → ibid.]] Stallbaum [[abbrev: p. → page]] 177); *Euthyphro* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 5 [[abbrev: c. → chapter]] ([[abbrev: p. → page]] 35 Stallbaum); *Laws* V. 8 ([[abbrev: ib. → ibid.]] Ast [[abbrev: p. → page]] 254). *μεν τὴν αἱρετικὴν, ἕως οὗ τὰ τῆς αἱρέσεως ἤρτηται*: "**For it is absurd to say that the stronger obligation—I mean the pure one—is pressed down by the weak; and I call the conditional one weak, as long as the event of the condition is pending.**" Ibid. IV. 6. 130: *τὰ σαθρὰ τοῦ ἀντιδίκου* are the faulty rights of the opponent. But to return to Plotinus: Demosthenes used the Adjective regarding the human body, *Olynthiac* II [[abbrev: p. → page]] 7 (on which passage [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] Voemel’s Annotations [[abbrev: pag. → page]] 93 [[abbrev: sq. → following]]). And Plutarch *De Sanitate Tuenda* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 137 C: *τὰ σαθρὰ καὶ ὕπουλα τοῦ σώματος* [the unsound and ulcerous parts of the body]. However, the use of the Substantive is very rare, and accordingly this place in Plotinus is to be added to the single instance in Chrysostom (which they praise from Homily 93 [[abbrev: p. → page]] 628: *τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων πραγμάτων τὴν σαθρότητα* [the unsoundness of human affairs]). For the rest, the argument of this entire Plotinian discussion is joined with a passage of Aristotle *De Anima* I. 1, which ends thus: *ἐλέγομεν δὲ ὅτι τὰ πάθη τῆς ψυχῆς ἀχώριστα τῆς φυσικῆς ὕλης τῶν ζώων, ᾗ γε τοιαῦθ' ὑπάρχει, θυμὸς καὶ φόβος, καὶ οὐχ ὥσπερ γραμμὴ καὶ ἐπίπεδον* [We were saying that the affections of the soul are inseparable from the natural matter of living beings, insofar as such things exist as anger and fear, and not like a line and a surface].

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 557, 1. *ὡς εἰ τὴν ψυχὴν λέγομεν ἐρυθριᾶν—ἀλλ' ἡ μὲν αἰσχύνη ἐν ψυχῇ* [[abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → etc.]] [As if we say the soul blushes... but the shame is in the soul etc.]. Tertullian *De Anima* [[abbrev: c. → chapter]] 5 [[abbrev: p. → page]] 267 Rigaltius, reporting the opinion of Cleanthes the Stoic on the Soul, says thus: "**Moreover, both that the soul sympathizes with the body, for which it feels pain when it is hurt by blows, wounds, and ulcers; and the body with the soul, for which it grows ill through the affliction of care, anguish, and love, namely through the loss of vigor, whose shame or fear it may witness by redness and pallor.**" The same [[abbrev: cap. → chapter]] IX [[abbrev: p. → page]] 270: "**He allowed himself to be so moved by the sight of some woman, that he strives to persuade us that the soul, as a breath and spirit, is an offspring of an airy and bright color.**" Concerning which he may see for himself.

— 14. *οὐ σαλευομένην αὐτὴν*] [It not being shaken]. Above [[abbrev: p. → page]] 287 C: *ἡ παρὰ τοῦ σάλου τῆς νεὼς ἢ παρ' αὐτοῦ κινηθέντος ὁρμῇ οἰκείᾳ* [[abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → etc.]] [that which is from the tossing of the ship or from itself being moved by its own impulse etc.] and *σάλος* regarding the tossing of the sea and ships, from which also *σαλεύεσθαι* is used for both. Then both substantive and verb are variously transferred. [[abbrev: Vid. → See]] *Monk* on Euripides *Hippolytus* [[abbrev: vs. → verse]] 824. *Blomfield* in the Glossary on Aeschylus *Prometheus* 1170. *Baehr* on Plutarch’s *Pyrrhus* [[abbrev: c. → chapter]] 24 [[abbrev: p. → page]] 248 [[abbrev: sq. → following]] and my annotation on John Laurentius Lydus *De Mensibus* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 253 [[abbrev: sq. → following]] Roether’s [[abbrev: ed. → edition]].

— 18. *οὐ τύπους ἐναποσφραγιζομένους* [[abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → etc.]] [Not impressions being sealed within etc.]. [[abbrev: Cf. → Compare]] above [[abbrev: p. → page]] 305 A *οὐ σφραγῖδος ἔνδον γενομένης* and the annotation there. Ast on Plato’s *Laws* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 681 (in *Animadversiones* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 151) compares our verb with the Platonic *ἀποτυποῦσθαι* [to be modeled]. Philo *De Mundi Opificio* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 10 Pfeiffer: *εἴθ' ὥσπερ ἐν κηρῷ τινι τῇ ἑαυτοῦ ψυχῇ τοὺς ἑκάστου (al. ἑκάστων) δεξάμενος τύπους, ἀγαλματοφορεῖ νοητὴν πόλιν, ἧς ἀνακινήσας τὰ εἴδωλα μνήμῃ τῇ συμφύτῳ, καὶ τοὺς χαρακτῆρας ἔτι μᾶλλον ἐνσφραγισάμενος, οἷα δημιουργὸς ἀγαθὸς, ἀποβλέπων εἰς τὸ παράδειγμα, τὴν ἐκ λίθων καὶ ξύλων ἄρχεται κατασκευάζειν (εὐκρασίαν* should be rejected as having arisen from a preceding word. For *πόλιν* must be understood from the antecedents), *ἑκάστῃ τῶν ἀσωμάτων ἰδεῶν τὰς σωματικὰς ἐξομοιῶν οὐσίας* [then, as if in some wax in his own soul, having received the impressions of each, he carries as a statue an intelligible city, whose images having stirred by innate memory, and having sealed the characters even more, as a good demiurge, looking towards the model, begins to construct it from stones and wood... likening the bodily essences to each of the incorporeal ideas]. [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] *Allegories of the Laws* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 154. The same in *De Mundi Opificio* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 56: — *οὐρανὸν πολλὰς ἐν αὑτῷ φύσεις ἀστεροειδεῖς ἀγαλματοφοροῦντα* [the heaven carrying many star-like natures in itself]. To the examples of this verb cited by Ruhnken on Timaeus [[abbrev: p. → page]] 7, I will add this from the letters of Michael Psellus recently edited by me. For thus he says in epistle 22 [[abbrev: p. → page]] 615: — *ἤδη σε καὶ ἀγαλματοφορῶ ἐν ταῖς τῆς καρδίας θαλάμοις καὶ περιφέρω διαπαντὸς, καὶ ὥσπερ εἰκόσι τισι στηλογραφίαις (Leg. στηλογραφικαῖς) τοῖς ἀποκομιζομένοις γράμμασι διοπτρίζομαι* [Already I carry you as a statue in the chambers of my heart and carry you about always, and I look through you as if by certain stelar images in the letters brought to me]. Moreover, the verb *ἐναποσφραγίζομαι* [to seal into] and things derived from it are especially proper to the Stoics, which they are accustomed to use when they want the impressions of things in the soul to be signified: Sextus Empiricus *Pyrrhonic Hypotyposes* II. 4: *εἰ μὲν γὰρ καταλαμβάνειν εἶναί λέγουσιν ἐν τῷ λόγῳ τῷ καταληπτικῇ φαντασίᾳ συγκατατίθεσθαι, τῆς καταληπτικῆς φαντασίας οὔσης ἀπὸ ὑπάρχοντος, κατ' αὐτὸ τὸ ὑπάρχον ἐναπομεμαγμένης καὶ ἐναπεσφραγισμένης, οἵα οὐκ ἂν γένοιτο ἀπὸ μὴ ὑπάρχοντος* [[abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → etc.]] [For if they say that to apprehend is to assent in reason to an apprehensive representation, the apprehensive representation being from an existing thing, having been molded and sealed according to that very existing thing, such as could not come from a non-existing thing etc.]. For that entire place is to be compared with the Plotinian discussion. Sextus often joins those two Stoic verbs, as in *Against the Mathematicians* VII. 248, 250, 255; no less the Adverbs in *Against the Mathematicians* XI. 183: *πρὸς τούτοις ἡ καταληπτικὴ φαντασία κρίνεται κατὰ τοὺς Στωϊκοὺς, ὅτι καταληπτική ἐστι, τῷ ἀπὸ ὑπάρχοντος γενέσθαι, καὶ κατ' αὐτὸ τὸ ὑπάρχον ἐναπομεμαγμένως καὶ ἐναπεσφραγισμένως* [In addition to these, the apprehensive representation is judged according to the Stoics... by being from an existing thing and molded and sealed according to that very existing thing]. Clement of Alexandria *Protrepticus* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 84 Potter: *ταύτας οἶμαι τὰς θείας γραφὰς ἐναποσφραγισαμένους χρὴ τῇ ψυχῇ καλὸν ἀφετήριον σοφίας (σοφίαν maluit Potter. ex Codd.) ἡγεῖσθαι* [[abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → etc.]] [Having sealed these divine scriptures in the soul, I think one should lead it to a good starting point of wisdom]. The same in *Paedagogus* II [[abbrev: p. → page]] 240: *ὡς ἂν—τὸ ἑταιρικὸν τοῦ φρονήματος ἐκ τοῦ βαθίσματος ἐναποσφραγίσωνται* [so that they might seal the harlot-like mind from their gait]. The same in *Stromata* II [[abbrev: p. → page]] 487 uses the Substantive: *ἐναποσφραγίσματα τῶν πνευματικῶν δυνάμεων* [sealings of spiritual powers]. But regarding these Clementine

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 559, 4. *οἷον δόξα καὶ ἀνεπίκριτος φαντασία* [[abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → etc.]] [Such as opinion and unjudged imagination etc.]. Ficinus took it passively, "**indiscreta imaginatio,**" and this word is used passively quite often. Sextus Empiricus *Pyrrhonic Hypotyposes* I. 98: *διαφωνίας τοσαύτης ἀνεπικρίτου παρὰ τοῖς δογματικοῖς οὔσης* [there being so much unjudged disagreement among the dogmatists], a passage which should be used in its entirety. Ibid. II. 210 *ἀνεπίκριτοι ὅροι*, definitions that cannot be decided. *Against the Mathematicians* II. 110 *ἀνεπίκριτος μάχη* [an undecided battle]. Scholiast on Lucian in *Hermotimus* §. 53 Vol. I [[abbrev: p. → page]] 794 regarding the Sceptics: *ἀκαταληψίαν ἀνεπίκριτον* [an unjudged incomprehensibility]. But Thomas Taylor seems to have better grasped the sense of this passage: "**It is evident however, that the phantasy is in the soul, both the first, which we call opinion, and the second, which is derived from the first, and is no longer opinion [truly so called] but is conversant with that which is beneath, being as it were obscure opinion, AND AN UNADVISED AND RASH IMAGINATION, such as the energy which is said to be inherent in nature, according to which it produces every thing without phantasy.**" At the end of this period, I suspect: *δῆλον ἂν τῷ γίνοιτο* [[abbrev: i. e. → that is]] *τινὶ* [it would be clear to someone], from Plotinus’s usage. Taylor appended this annotation to those words: "**The phantasy or imagination is the highest of the gnostic irrational powers of the soul. But this in its summit is united to OPINION, or that gnostic rational power which knows THAT a thing is, but does not know WHY it is; and in its other extremity it is conjoined with sense. So far therefore, as it is united to opinion, it may be said to be the same with it.**—See my *Introduction* to a translation of Aristotle's treatise *On the Soul*."

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 560, 4. *ἔσται τοίνυν τὸ παθητικὸν—ἢ καὶ ἄνευ φαντασίας*] [Therefore the passive part will be... or even without imagination]. Proclus *On Providence and Fate* [[abbrev: c. → chapter]] X [[abbrev: p. → page]] 25, translated by William of Moerbeke, edition Cousin; "**Rightly also Plotinus saying that all passions are either senses, or not without sense.**"

— 7. *αὐτὸ δὲ μένον ἐν ἁρμονίας εἴδει—μὴ τῆς ἁρμονίας τοῦτο λεγούσης*] [But it remaining in the form of harmony... the harmony not saying this]. Let us join with this passage another in *Ennead* IV book 2 [[abbrev: cap. → chapter]] 1 [[abbrev: p. → page]] 361: *σῶμα οὐδὲν αὐτὴν δείξαντες εἶναι (sc. τὴν τῆς ψυχῆς οὐσίαν) οὐδὲ ἐν ἀσωμάτοις αὖ ἁρμονίαν* [Having shown that it (namely the essence of the soul) is no body, nor again a harmony among incorporeal things]. In which matter our philosopher follows his Plato, who in the *Phaedo* thus concludes his discussion against the then-common opinion of many ancients, and later of Aristoxenus and also Dicaearchus [[abbrev: p. → page]] 94 [[abbrev: fin. → end]], [[abbrev: p. → page]] 80 Bekker: *οὐκ ἄρα, ὦ ἄριστε, ἡμῖν οὐδαμῇ καλῶς ἔχει ψυχὴν ἁρμονίαν τινὰ φάναι εἶναι* [Therefore, my friend, it is in no way well for us to say that the soul is a certain harmony]. To which place I will here subjoin those things which *Wyttenbach* added as relevant to Plotinus’s passages in his Annotations [[abbrev: p. → page]] 248, and I will add a few of my own: "**What harmony Plato understands is clear: that which is composed externally, and sounds nothing other than what it can sound through the necessity of composition and striking: on the contrary, the Soul composes itself internally, brings its dissenting parts into consensus, and resists and moderates them when they are repugnant to it. Nor does this opinion conflict with that which he hands down in the *Timaeus*, that the Soul was made by God from different materials, according to a certain ratio and proportion [[abbrev: p. → page]] 528, which Proclus rightly notes in *On the Timaeus* III [[abbrev: p. → page]] 178 and in *On the Republic* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 392 [[abbrev: fin. → end]]. For the wise man ought to establish a harmony of the soul with the body, and accommodate it to the harmony of the universe, as Plato teaches in *Republic* IX [[abbrev: p. → page]] 510 [[abbrev: d. → column]]. And virtue itself is contained in harmony (I have placed the passage above at the beginning of chapter II [[abbrev: p. → page]] 304).**" For this is, as Iamblichus says in Stobaeus *Eclogae Physicae* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 864 (Heeren), *mathematical harmony*, which many Pythagoreans and Platonists variously handed down: Timaeus, Moderatus, Plotinus, Porphyry, Amelius. For Aristoxenus seems to have thought of a bodily harmony like that of a musical instrument, as did many others before him. For כך the passage of Cicero *Tusculan Disputations* I. 10 is to be understood." Thus far Wyttenbach. [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] Mahn’s *Diatribe on Aristoxenus the Peripatetic Philosopher* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 200 [[abbrev: sqq. → following]]. For the sake of Plotinus, I will transcribe the words of Iamblichus in the [[abbrev: l. l. → place cited]]: "*Ἔτι τοίνυν τὴν ἁρμονίαν ἴδωμεν, οὐ τὴν ἐν σώμασιν ἐνιδρυμένην ἀλλ' ἥ τις ἐστὶ μαθηματική. ταύτην τοίνυν ὡς μὲν ἁπλῶς εἰπεῖν, τὴν τὰ διαφέροντα ὁπωσοῦν σύμμετρα καὶ προσήγορα ἀπεργαζομένην, ἀναφέρει εἰς τὴν ψυχὴν Μοδέρατος—τὴν δὲ ὡς ἐν λόγοις τοῖς κατ' οὐσίαν προϋπάρχουσιν Πλωτῖνος καὶ Πορφύριος καὶ Ἀμέλιος παραδεδώκασιν*: [[abbrev: i. e. → that is]] that Plotinus, Porphyry, and Amelius have handed down that harmony exists in ratios pre-existing in essence. Moreover, Porphyry had our passage before his eyes and exhibits it partly word-for-word in *Sententiae* XIX [[abbrev: p. → page]] 225 [[abbrev: sq. → following]]: *ὅταν γὰρ τὸ ζῶον αἰσθάνηται, ἔοικεν ἡ μὲν ψυχὴ ἁρμονίᾳ (leg. ἁρμονίᾳ) χωριστῇ, ἐξ ἑαυτῆς τὰς χορδὰς κινούσῃ ἡρμοσμένας˙ τῇ δὲ ἐν ταῖς*

-> 178 ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS <-

*χορδαῖς ἁρμονίᾳ ἀχωρίστῳ, τὸ σῶμα˙ τὸ δ' αἴτιον τοῦ κινῆσαι τὸ ζῶον, διὰ τὸ εἶναι ἔμψυχον. Ἀνάλογον δὲ τῷ μουσικῷ˙ διὰ τὸ εἶναι ἐναρμόνιον. τὰ δὲ πληγέντα σώματα διὰ πάθος αἰσθητικὸν ταῖς ἡρμοσμέναις χορδαῖς, καὶ γὰρ ἐκεῖ οὐχ ἡ ἁρμονία πέπονθεν ἡ χωριστὴ, ἀλλ' ἡ χορδή. καὶ κινεῖ μὲν ὁ μουσικὸς κατὰ τὴν ἐν αὐτῷ ἁρμονίαν˙ οὐ μὴν ἐκινήθη ἂν ἡ χορδὴ μουσικῶς, εἰ καὶ ὁ μουσικὸς ἐβούλετο, μὴ τῆς ἁρμονίας τοῦτο λεγούσης.* [For when the living being perceives, the soul is like a separate harmony moving the tuned strings of itself; but the body is like the inseparable harmony in the strings; and the cause of moving the living being is because it is ensouled. Analogous to the musician: because of being harmonious. But the struck bodies through sensible affection are like the tuned strings, for there it is not the separate harmony that has been affected, but the string. And the musician moves according to the harmony within him; yet the string would not have been moved musically, even if the musician wished it, if the harmony did not say so.] These things contribute not only to the explanation but also to the reading of this passage. Olympiodorus on the *Phaedo*, Codex I [[abbrev: p. → page]] 88: *ἐνδεικνύμενος ὅτι ἐστὶ νοεῖν καὶ χωριστὴν ἁρμονίαν—οὕτω γάρ πως καὶ ἡ ψυχὴ λέγοιτο ἂν ἁρμονία, κατὰ τὸν Τίμαιον.* [Pointing out that it is possible to conceive even a separate harmony... for in this way the soul might also be called a harmony, according to the *Timaeus*.] Cassiodorus *De Anima* [[abbrev: cap. → chapter]] 8: "**All immortal things are simple: however, the soul is not harmonic, nor does it consist of several parts, but is a simple nature; therefore the soul is immortal.**"

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 561, 1. *οἷον εἴ τις—ἐν ἐγρηγόρσει τὴν ψυχὴν—ποιοῖ*] [As if someone... should make the soul in a state of waking]. Philo Judaeus *Allegories of the Laws* I [[abbrev: p. → page]] 200 Pfeiffer: *τῷ γὰρ ὄντι ὑπνώσαντος νοῦ γίνεται (Mang. vult: κινεῖται) αἴσθησις. καὶ γὰρ ἔμπαλιν ἐγρηγορότος νοῦ, σβέννυται*. [For in reality, when the mind sleeps, sense arises (Mangey wants: is moved). For on the contrary, when the mind is awake, it is extinguished.] Ibid. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 202: *Οὐκοῦν ἥτε τῶν αἰσθήσεων ἐγρήγορσις ὕπνος ἐστὶ νοῦ˙ ἥτε τοῦ νοῦ ἐγρήγορσις, ἀπραξία τῶν αἰσθήσεων.* [Therefore the waking of the senses is the sleep of the mind; and the waking of the mind is the inactivity of the senses.] Clement of Alexandria *Paedagogus* II [[abbrev: p. → page]] 202 Potter: *ὑπνώδης γὰρ πᾶς ὁ μὴ εἰς σοφίαν ἐγρηγορῶν, ἀλλὰ ὑπὸ μέθης βαπτιζόμενος εἰς ὕπνον.* [For everyone is sleepy who is not awake unto wisdom, but is immersed into sleep by drunkenness.] Theodoret *On Providence* VI Vol. IV [[abbrev: p. → page]] 566 Schulz: *οὐκοῦν φρόνησις μέν ἐστι τοῦ ἐν ἡμῖν λογικοῦ ἡ ἐγρήγορσις, ὥσπερ ἀμέλει παραφροσύνη καὶ ἀφροσύνη πάλιν, ἡ τούτου μέθη ἐκ τῶν παθῶν τικτομένη, καὶ οἷόν τις νεφέλη γενομένη, καὶ πυκνουμένη καὶ ἐπιπροσθοῦσα, καὶ συνορᾶν αὐτὸν οὐκ ἐῶσα τὸ δέον.* [Therefore waking is the wisdom of the rational part in us, just as indeed madness and again folly is the drunkenness of this, born from the passions, and becoming like a certain cloud, thickening and obstructing, and not allowing it to see clearly what is necessary.] Plotinus himself below [[abbrev: p. → page]] 310 A.—*οἱ παραπλήσιον τοῖς ὀνειρώττουσι ποιοῦσι ταῦτα ἐνεργῆ νομίζουσιν, ἃ δρῶσιν εἶναι ἐνύπνια ὄντα. καὶ γὰρ τὸ τῆς αἰσθήσεως ψυχῆς ἐστιν εὑδούσης˙ ὅσον γὰρ ἐν σώματι ψυχῆς, τοῦτο εὕδει˙ ἡ δ' ἀληθινὴ ἐγρήγορσις, ἀληθινὴ ἀπὸ σώματος, οὐ μετὰ σώματος, ἀνάστασις.* [Those who do things similar to dreamers think that the things they do are actual, being but dreams. For the state of sensation belongs to a sleeping soul; as much of the soul as is in the body, this sleeps; but true waking is a true resurrection from the body, not with the body.] [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] below III. 8. 3 [[abbrev: p. → page]] 345 F and above II. 6. 3 [[abbrev: p. → page]] 175 C. To this place I have added the primary passage of Plato from the *Timaeus* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 52, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 64 Bekker. Now Xenophon in *Cyropaedia* I. 4. 20, simply, as being far removed from Plato's genius, joins *ἐφρόνει καὶ ἐγρηγόρει* [he was wise and awake], which only serves as an argument that common usage joined these words. Closer to these Platonic and Plotinian ideas come these of Aristotle *De Anima* II. 1 [[abbrev: p. → page]] 22 Sylburg: *ἐν γὰρ τῷ ὑπάρχειν τὴν ψυχὴν ὕπνος καὶ ἐγρήγορσίς ἐστιν. ἀνάλογον δ' ἡ μὲν ἐγρήγορσις τῷ θεωρεῖν˙ ὁ δὲ ὕπνος, τῷ ἔχειν καὶ μὴ ἐνεργεῖν˙ προτέρα δὲ τῇ γενέσει ἐπὶ τοῦ αὐτοῦ, ἡ ἐπιστήμη.* [For in the soul’s existence there is sleep and waking. And waking is analogous to contemplating; but sleep to having and not acting; but knowledge is prior in generation in the same thing.] Philo Judaeus *Who is the Heir of Divine Things* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 524 B, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 510 Mangey: "*Ὕπνος γὰρ νοῦ γρήγορσίς ἐστιν αἰσθήσεως, καὶ γὰρ αἱ γρηγόρσεις τῆς διανοίας, αἰσθήσεως ἀπραξία.*" [For the sleep of the mind is the waking of sense, and indeed the wakings of the intellect are the inactivity of sense.] Philo is accustomed sometimes to repeat primary opinions word for word. Hence one may suspect that from those cited above one should read *ἐγρήγορσις* and *ἐγρηγόρσεις*. But *γρήγορσις* is read [[abbrev: ap. → in]] Eumathius *De Ismeniae Amoribus* IX. 396 and Lobeck on Phrynichus [[abbrev: p. → page]] 294 [[abbrev: sq. → following]], whom consult, thinks it should be added to the Lexicons. Dio Chrysostom *Oration* VIII [[abbrev: p. → page]] 134 D: *τῆς ἡδονῆς—διαφθεῖραι πειρωμένης ὁμοίως μὲν ἐγρηγορότας, ὁμοίως δὲ κοιμωμένους.* [Pleasure... trying to corrupt equally those who are awake and those who are asleep.] To which place the most diligent Baguet in his annotations [[abbrev: p. → page]] 94 [[abbrev: sq. → following]] collected similar examples of this use in which these words are opposed to each other.

— 18. *ὡς ἐπ' αὐτοῦ ὀχεῖσθαι ἡσυχῇ*] Taylor more word-for-word: "**so that it may be quietly carried in it.**" Namely, so that the soul may use this vehicle more safely. For the body is the vehicle of the soul: if indeed I rightly grasp the sense of this passage, which no one, I think, will deny is obscure, and perhaps even too corrupt for one to pronounce with certainty. Regarding the verb *ἐποχεῖσθαι* [to be carried upon] see above [[abbrev: p. → page]] 52 E, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 56 F, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 109. Regarding *καθάρσει* [purification] [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] I. 2. 3. 4; I. 6. 7; VI. 7. 36.

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 562, 1. *Τὴν μὲν δὲ οὐσίαν τὴν νοητὴν*] [The intelligible essence indeed]. Because Plotinus denies that matter also is affected in the following, he is rebuked on this account by Petrus Petitus in *Miscellanea Observationes* II. 11; *Tiedemann* also discusses these decrees of our philosopher in *Geist der spekulativen Philosophie* III [[abbrev: p. → page]] 286 [[abbrev: sq. → following]]. Aristotle reviews the opinions of philosophers regarding *being and non-being* in *De Generatione et Corruptione* I. 1 and chapter III; *Physicorum Auscultationes* I. 5; *De Caelo* [[abbrev: c. → chapter]] 1. As far as Plato's opinions are concerned, they are contained mostly in the *Parmenides*, *Sophist*, and *Timaeus*. Proclus *Elements of Theology* [[abbrev: c. → chapter]] XIV [[abbrev: sq. → following]]. [[abbrev: Cf. → Compare]] also the discussion of Hermes [[abbrev: ap. → in]] Stobaeus *Eclogae Physicae* I. 43 [[abbrev: p. → page]] 750 [[abbrev: ed. → edition]] Heeren. Mosheim must be consulted regarding these at the end of *Cudworth’s Intellectual System* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 964 [[abbrev: sqq. → following]].

— 10. *τοῦτο δὲ, ὃ μηδὲν ἀποστατεῖ τοῦ εἶναι*] [This indeed, which departs in nothing from being]. I would not say whether Ficinus read *ᾧ*. The Vulgate

one may express thus: *Hoc vero, quod nihilo abest (recedit) ab esse.* [But this, which is nothing away (recedes) from being.] To the examples which Stephanus’s *Thesaurus* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 4569 [[abbrev: ed. → edition]] Valpy exhibits, add Plutarch *Symposiacs* I. 1 [[abbrev: p. → page]] 613 B, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 475 [[abbrev: sq. → following]] Wyttenbach: *ἣν (φιλοσοφίαν) οὔτε τινὸς παιδιᾶς οὔτε τινὸς ἡδονῆς ἀποστατεῖν εἰκὸς, ἀλλα πᾶσι παρεῖναι*. Plutarch *Amatorius* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 758 B, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 39 Wyttenbach: *οὐ μὴν οὐδὲ νοσοῦντος ἀνθρώπου θεὸς ἀποστατεῖ—ἀλλ' οὐδὲ ἀποθανόντος*. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 563, 9. *ἀλλ' εἶναι τούτοις τὸ εἶναι, τὸ μὴ οὖσιν εἶναι*] [But being for these is to be being-not-being]. Similarly Proclus *Elements of Theology* [[abbrev: c. → chapter]] L [[abbrev: p. → page]] 80: *τοῦτο δέ ἐστιν ἐν τῷ μὴ εἶναι τὸ εἶναι ἔχειν.* [And this is to have being in not being.]

— 9. *ἡ τῶν σωμάτων φύσις*] [The nature of bodies]. Regarding this periphrasis, it was spoken of above [[abbrev: ad pag. → at page]] 50 C. Now I add this one thing: that formula *τὸ χρῆμα τῆς ἀρετῆς—τῆς ἡδονῆς* [the matter of virtue—of pleasure] and similar ones do not differ much from this; concerning which the most learned Baguet explained on Dion Chrysostom VIII [[abbrev: p. → page]] 92 [[abbrev: sq. → following]]. In the following, Plotinus drew his color from Plato’s *Sophist* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 246 a, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 190 Bekker: *οἱ μὲν εἰς γῆν ἐξ οὐρανοῦ καὶ τοῦ ἀοράτου πάντα ἕλκουσι, ταῖς χερσὶν ἀτεχνῶς πέτρας καὶ δρῦς περιλαμβάνοντες˙ τῶν γὰρ τοιούτων ἐφαπτόμενοι πάντων διισχυρίζονται τοῦτο εἶναι μόνον ὃ παρέχει προσβολὴν καὶ ἐπαφήν τινα, ταὐτὸν σῶμα καὶ οὐσίαν ὁριζόμενοι, τῶν δ' ἄλλων εἴ τίς φησι μὴ σῶμα ἔχον εἶναι, καταφρονοῦντες τοπαράπαν καὶ οὐδὲν ἐθέλοντες ἄλλο ἀκούειν.* [Some drag everything down from heaven and the invisible to earth, literally grasping rocks and oaks with their hands; for touching all such things they maintain that this alone is which provides some resistance and touch, defining body and essence as the same thing; and if anyone says that something of the others does not have a body, they despise them altogether and wish to hear nothing else.] [[abbrev: Cf. → Compare]] also *Theaetetus* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 155 e, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 204 Bekker and Plotinus above [[abbrev: p. → page]] 229 C. D. and Porphyry *Sententiae* XXXV, XXXVI.

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 564, 3. *ἀηδέστερα—εὐχαριστότερα*] [Less pleasant—more agreeable]. Opposed to each other. On this [[abbrev: v. → see]] Pierson on *Herodianus Grammaticus* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 441. Phrynichus [[abbrev: p. → page]] 18 [[abbrev: ib. → ibid.]] Lobeck. Sturz *Lexicon Xenophonteum* II [[abbrev: p. → page]] 424 [[abbrev: sq. → following]]. Schleusner *Lexicon N. T.* under *εὐχάριστος* and Valckenaer’s *Scholia in N. T.* II [[abbrev: p. → page]] 44.

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 565, 4. *Καὶ γὰρ τὸ τῆς αἰσθήσεως ψυχῆς ἐστιν εὑδούσης.*] [For indeed sensation belongs to a sleeping soul.] [[abbrev: Cf. → Compare]] above [[abbrev: p. → page]] 175 C and the annotation there [[abbrev: et ad p. → and at page]] 307 G. For the rest, regarding our passage [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] *Variae Lectiones*. If you retain *ἐνεργῆ* [active] or *ἐνεργεῖν* [to act], these must be translated thus: *They think those things efficient (or to act, to work) which seem to be, when they are dreams.* I fear the passage is not sound.

— 12. *Ἀλλ' ἐπανιτέον ἐπὶ τὴν ὕλην*] [But one must return to Matter]. Because [[abbrev: Fic. → Ficinus]] in the Lemma of this chapter praises Porphyry, it must be noted that it is a passage from the *Sententiae* [[abbrev: c. → chapter]] XXI. You may compare what we set down above at the beginning of the book *On Matter* II. 4. 1 [[abbrev: p. → page]] 159. But the source of this entire discussion regarding Matter is in the most noble passage of the Platonic *Timaeus* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 49 [[abbrev: sqq. → following]], [[abbrev: p. → page]] 57 [[abbrev: sqq. → following]] Bekker.

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 566, 18. *ἀμεννηνὰ γὰρ καὶ ἀσθενῆ*] [For they are fleeting and weak]. [[abbrev: Cf. → Compare]] VI. 6. 8; VI. 6. 18. Olympiodorus on the *Alcibiades* [[abbrev: pr. → preface]] [[abbrev: p. → page]] 217 [[abbrev: sq. → following]]: *Οὐ γὰρ οἴεται αὐτὸς ὁ Πλάτων ἀμεννηνὰ καὶ ἀσθενεῖς καὶ ἀδρανεῖς, ἀλλ' ὑποστάσεις βούλεται αὐτὰς εἶναι.* [For Plato himself does not think them fleeting and weak and powerless, but wants them to be hypostases.] Where I have placed these things, which likewise apply to Plotinus: "**Proclus in this Dialogue [[abbrev: p. → page]] 164: πᾶν γὰρ τὸ ἔνυλον ἀδρανές ἐστι καὶ ἀσθενὲς (i. e. sluggish, having no nerves and infirm.) *ἀμενηνὴς* or *ἀμεννηνὸς* and it is explained thus: weak. Hesychius I [[abbrev: p. → page]] 271 Albert: 'Ἀμενηνὰ: weak, according to a deprivation of power; for *μένος* is power. Or soulless.* Add the same on *ἀμενήνωσεν*, where Heliodorus on *Odyssey* κ. 521 explains *ἀμενηνὰ* as *ἀδιανόητα* [unthinkable]. [[abbrev: Cf. → Compare]] the interpreters of Apollonius’s *Homeric Lexicon* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 104 [[abbrev: et p. → and page]] 228 Tollius; Heyne’s Observations on *Iliad* ε. 887. In *Odyssey* τ. 562, for *ἀμενηνῶν ὀνείρων* [fleeting dreams] Suidas and Photius exhibit *ψευστάνων* [deceitful]. [[abbrev: Vid. → See]] Porson on that place. Add Orion’s *Etymologicon* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 28. Zonaras’s Lexicon [[abbrev: p. → page]] 142. But simpler and more suited to all passages of Homer and others is the other etymology, which the *Etymologicon Magnum* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 81, 83 reports: *ἢ παρὰ τὸ μένω μενηνός, ὡς πέτω πετηνός* [either from *meno* (to remain) *menenos*, as from *peto* (to fly) *petenos*]. In which matter my friend *Doederlein* clearly makes me agree with him, who has learnedly pursued the origins and meanings of this kind of words in *Lectionum Homericarum Specimen* III [[abbrev: pag. → page]] 3—8. Hence the names of the Palic Gods among the Sicilians. For one of them is *Amenanus*, the other *Adranus*. [[abbrev: Vid. → See]] Plutarch’s *Timoleon* 12. my Annotations on Cicero *De Natura Deorum* III. 22 [[abbrev: p. → page]] 601—603 and *Phil. Car. Hess’s* Observations on Plutarch’s *Timoleon* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 59 [[abbrev: sq. → following]]. Philostratus Junior XVII [[abbrev: p. → page]] 139 [[abbrev: ed. → edition]] Jacobs and Welcker on Philoctetes—*ξυννεφῆ ὀφρὺν ἐπὶ τῷ ὀφθαλμῷ ἐφέλκων, κάτω που καὶ ἐν βάθει ὄντας καὶ ἀμενηνὸν ὁρῶντας.* [drawing a clouded brow over the eyes, being somewhere below and in depth and seeing fleetingly.]

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 568, 3. *Μαρτυρεῖ δὲ καὶ ἡ λεγομένη πυρὸς φθορὰ—εἰς στοιχεῖον ἄλλο*] [The so-called destruction of fire... into another element also bears witness]. Theophrastus *De Igne* I [[abbrev: p. → page]] 705 Schneider: *τὸ δὲ πῦρ γεννᾶν καὶ φθείρειν πέφυκεν αὑτό˙ γεννᾶν μὲν, τὸ ἔλαττον τὸ πλέον, φθείρειν δὲ, τὸ πλέον τὸ ἔλαττον* [[abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → etc.]] [Fire is by nature such as to generate and destroy itself; to generate, the smaller the larger; to destroy, the larger the smaller].

Moreover, those *πυρὸς τροπαὶ* [turnings of fire] are attributed to Heraclitus as the author of that reasoning, and from there transferred to the Stoics. Regarding fire as the principle according to Heraclitus [[abbrev: vid. → see]] Plato *Cratylus* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 413 b. Aristotle *Metaphysics* I. 3 [[abbrev: p. → page]] 8 Sylburg. Diogenes Laertius IX. 7. 8 and Menage there. Add Wyttenbach on Plutarch *On Having Many Friends* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 661 [[abbrev: sq. → following]], who on [[abbrev: p. → page]] 662 in Diogenes [[abbrev: l. l. → in the place cited]] emends: *πυκνούμενον γὰρ τὸ πῦρ ἐξαεροῦσθαι* [[abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → etc.]] [For fire being thickened becomes air etc.]. Cicero *De Natura Deorum* III. 14 thus: "**But all your people (the Stoics), Balbus, are accustomed to refer everything to fiery force, following Heraclitus, I believe.—But you say thus, that all force is fire: and so also living things, when the heat fails, then perish; and in all nature, that lives and thrives which is warm.**" Stobaeus *Eclogae Physicae* I [[abbrev: p. → page]] 314 Heeren: *Τριχῶς δὲ λεγομένου κατὰ Χρύσιππον τοῦ στοιχείου, καθ' ἕνα μὲν τρόπον τοῦ πυρὸς, διὰ τὸ ἐξ αὐτοῦ τὰ λοιπά συνίστασθαι κατὰ μεταβολὴν, καὶ εἰς αὐτὸ λαμβάνειν τὴν ἀνάλυσιν.* [According to Chrysippus the element is spoken of in three ways, in one way of fire, because from it the rest are constituted according to change, and into it they receive their dissolution.]

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 568, 6. *καὶ τούτῳ τὸ φθείρεσθαι, ᾧ καὶ τὸ πάσχειν. Τὴν δὲ ὕλην φθείρεσθαι, οὐχ οἷόν τε* [[abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → etc.]] [And for this to be destroyed, for which also to be affected. But for Matter to be destroyed is not possible etc.]. Apply to this entire discussion Aristotle *De Generatione et Corruptione* I. 7. 8, who says thus [[abbrev: ib. → ibid.]] [[abbrev: p. → page]] 24 Sylburg: *ἡ δὲ ὕλη, ᾗ ὕλη, παθητικόν˙ τὸ μὲν οὖν πῦρ ἔχει ἐν ὕλῃ τὸ θερμόν˙ εἰ δέ τι εἴη χωριστὸν θερμόν, τοῦτο οὐδὲν ἂν πάσχοι˙ τοῦτο μὲν οὖν ἴσως ἀδύνατον εἶναι χωριστόν.* [Matter, insofar as it is matter, is passive; therefore fire has heat in matter; but if there were some separate heat, this would suffer nothing; therefore this is perhaps impossible to be separate.] Porphyry *Sententiae* XXII [[abbrev: p. → page]] 227: *οὔτε οὖν ἴσως ἡ ὕλη πάσχει, ἄποιος γὰρ καθ' ἑαυτήν.* [Neither therefore perhaps does matter suffer, for it is without quality in itself.] On the contrary, Alexander of Aphrodisias in Aristotle *De Anima* I [[abbrev: c. → chapter]] 29 says that Matter in all things is that which suffers. From this it is understood that in these and the following things quite a few points are argued by Plotinus against the Peripatetics.

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 569, 8. *Τί δ' ἂν γραμμὴ πάθοι ὑπὸ χρώματος;*] [What would a line suffer from a color?]. Aristotle *De Generatione et Corruptione* [[abbrev: c. → chapter]] 7 [[abbrev: p. → page]] 22 Sylburg: *οὐδὲν γὰρ ἂν πάθοι λευκότης ὑπὸ γραμμῆς, ἢ γραμμὴ ὑπὸ λευκότητος, πλὴν εἰ μή που κατὰ συμβεβηκός, οἷον εἰ συμβέβηκε, λευκὴν ἢ μέλαιναν εἶναι τὴν γραμμήν* [[abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → etc.]] [For whiteness would suffer nothing from a line, or a line from whiteness, unless perhaps by accident, as if it happened that the line was white or black etc.]. For many things in those Aristotelian works apply to this book of Plotinus, and if I wished to describe them all, there would be no limit to the annotation. And once I wish the readers to be warned: that the *sources* are indicated by us at the threshold of each book of Plotinus so that we may not be compelled to cite passages of writers individually everywhere, which in many books, as I have said, would be infinite.

— 11. *Εἰ δέ τις καὶ τὰ κάτοπτρα λέγοι καὶ ὅλως τὰ διαφανῆ ὑπὸ τῶν ἐνορωμένων—πάσχειν* [[abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → etc.]] [But if someone should say that mirrors and generally transparent things are affected by the things seen in them etc.]. Plato in *Timaeus* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 46 A, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 52 Bekker: *τὸ δὲ περὶ τὴν τῶν κατόπτρων εἰδωλοποιΐαν, καὶ πάντα ὅσα ἐμφανῆ καὶ λεῖα, κατιδεῖν οὐδὲν ἔτι χαλεπόν* [[abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → etc.]] [But concerning the image-making of mirrors, and everything that is bright and smooth, it is no longer difficult to see etc.]. To which place apply Alcinous *On the Doctrines of Plato* 18 [[abbrev: p. → page]] 498 and Chalcidius *On the Timaeus* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 333 [[abbrev: sq. → following]] ([[abbrev: p. → page]] 365 [[abbrev: sq. → following]] [[abbrev: ed. → edition]] Fabricius). *Jac. Carpentarius* on Alcinous [[abbrev: p. → page]] 416: "**Although not all admit this reason for those things which appear in mirrors: but, as Seneca says [[abbrev: c. → chapter]] 5 book I of *Natural Questions*, there are entirely two opinions about them. For some think that images are seen in them, i.e. the figures of our bodies scattered from our bodies through the air and received in them. Others say with Plato that no images are in reality in the mirror, just as neither are there colors in the rainbow, but that the bodies themselves are looked upon, the sight of the eyes being turned back and reflected in itself again.**" Which opinion Alexander follows in *Problems* 129 book I. "**Then he reports on the passage of Aristotle *Meteorology* [[abbrev: c. → chapter]] IV book III.**" Theophrastus, Iamblichus, Proclus, and Priscian were explaining Plato's opinion in the same sense. [[abbrev: Cf. → Compare]] Ficinus on the cited passage of the *Timaeus* [[abbrev: cap. → chapter]] 30. Against them rises Olympiodorus on the *Alcibiades* [[abbrev: pr. → preface]] [[abbrev: p. → page]] 217: *ἀλλ' ἐπειδὴ περὶ τῶν ἐν τοῖς κατόπτροις φαινομένων εἰδώλων γέγονεν ὁ λόγος, οὐ δεῖ οἰηθῆναι, καθὼς ὁ φιλόσοφος Πρόκλος οἴεται, τὸν Πλάτωνα δοξάζειν, ὅτι ἀνακλάσεις εἰσίν. Αὗται γὰρ Περιπατητικαὶ καὶ μηχανικαί εἰσιν ἔννοιαι, τὸ λέγειν τὰς σκιὰς δι' ἐπιπρόσθησιν σώματος γίνεσθαι.* [But since the discussion has been about the images appearing in mirrors, it should not be thought, as the philosopher Proclus thinks, that Plato believes they are reflections. For these are Peripatetic and mechanical notions, to say that shadows happen because of the obstruction of a body.] Then he strives to show: *τὰς σκιὰς [that shadows] are hypostases, and that they happen through out-flows (*ἀποῤῥοιῶν*) proceeding or flowing out *ἐκ τῶν αἰσθητῶν* [from sensible things]*, and he cites Damascius the philosopher as a patron of his opinion. But you see from these that Olympiodorus is rather unfair towards the Peripatetics. On the other hand, Alcinous in the [[abbrev: l. l. → cited passage]] himself also acknowledges *ἀνακλάσεις* [reflections] in this matter.—Our philosopher again uses the simile of mirrors at [[abbrev: p. → page]] 316 D and below VI. 2. 22 [[abbrev: p. → page]] 615 C (where likewise mention of matter is made); for which passage we shall add other things. However, the entire passage below [[abbrev: p. → page]] 316 D.—G. is to be compared with our passage. Schneider explained the words *κλάσις* [breaking/refraction], *ἀνάκλασις* [reflection], *διάκλασις* [refraction] [[abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → etc.]] on the *Eclogae Physicae* II [[abbrev: p. → page]] 243 [[abbrev: sq. → following]] and consult there Euclid’s *Catoptrics* Vol. I [[abbrev: p. → page]] 391 [[abbrev: sqq. → following]].

— 14. *ἔτι μᾶλλον ἀπαθέστερον*] [Still more unaffected/impassive]. Regarding this redundancy, I remember that I warned elsewhere in Plotinus

and on Proclus in *Alcibiades* [[abbrev: pr. → preface]] [[abbrev: p. → page]] 225, on Olympiodorus in the same [[abbrev: p. → page]] 97, and on Proclus’s *Elements of Theology* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 74. [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] [[abbrev: p. → page]] 244. However, this Pleonasm seems to be more familiar to these Platonic writers. Nor is it unknown to Plato himself. [[abbrev: Vid. → See]] Heindorf on *Charmides* §. 15 [[abbrev: p. → page]] 81 [[abbrev: sq. → following]].

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 570, 1. *Τί γὰρ εὐωδία γλυκύτητα ἐργάσαιτο;* [[abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → etc.]] [For what sweetness would a fragrance produce? etc.]. These examples recur below VI. 7. 12 [[abbrev: p. → page]] 705 C. D. And the Armenian philosopher David seems to regard these passages in his manuscript commentary on Aristotle’s *Categories* (excerpts of which from the Vatican [[abbrev: cod. → codex]] [[abbrev: nr. → number]] 1023 Hieronymus Amati communicated with me, from the Munich [[abbrev: codd. → codices]] [[abbrev: nr. → number]] 99 and 399 Krabinger, and from the Parisian Royal ones [[abbrev: nr. → number]] 1937, 1938, 1939 Sahunius). For thus he says: *Εἶτα φασὶν (alii φησίν) ὅτι (al. καὶ ὅτι) δύναται χωρὶς ὑποστῆναι (ἀποστῆναι al. male) συμβεβηκός. Ἰδοὺ γὰρ ἡ εὐωδία τοῦ μήλου συμβεβηκὸς οὖσα καταλείψασα τὸ μῆλον μένει ἐν τῷ αἰσθητηρίῳ ἢ τῷ κιβωτίῳ. Λύουσι τοῦτο διάφοροι˙ ὁ μὲν Πλάτων, ὅτι οὐκ ἐχωρίσθη τοῦ ὑποκειμένου˙ μετά τινων γὰρ λεπτῶν ἀποῤῥοιῶν χωρεῖ πρὸς ἡμᾶς, ὡς δηλοῖ ἡ κατὰ μέρος αὐτοῦ ἴσχνανσις (al. ἴσχανσις) ἐν γὰρ τῷ δένδρῳ οὐκ ἰσχναίνεται (al. ἰσχνεύεται. al. neglexerunt οὐκ, male.), διὰ τὸ πλείονα εἶναι τὴν εἰσροὴν τῆς ἐκροῆς. Ὁ δὲ Ἀριστοτέλης τὸ διακονικὸν αἰτιᾶται τοῦ ἀέρος, ὅτι ᾧ λόγου ἐστὶ διορατικὸς καὶ διηχὴς, τουτῷ καὶ δίοσμος (al. καὶ διοχὴς al. καὶ εἰδεχθεὶς al. διοιχὲς itemque al. ἡδίοσμος, al. ἡδυοσμός.) Ὁ δὲ Πλωτῖνος τὰ Ἀριστοτέλους καὶ Πλάτωνος συναγαγών φησιν, ὅτι μεταβάλλεται μέρος τοῦ ἀέρος ἐν τῇ εὐωδίᾳ˙ ἡ γὰρ εὐωδία μείνασα ἐν τῷ μήλῳ γεννᾷ ὁμοίαν (al. ὁμοίως) ἑαυτῇ ἑτέραν ποιότητα μεταβάλλουσαν μέρος τοῦ ἀέρος ἧς αἰσθανόμεθα.*—[Then they say (others "he says") that (others "and that") an accident can subsist without (the subject). For behold, the fragrance of the apple, being an accident, having left the apple, remains in the sense organ or the box. Various people solve this: Plato, that it was not separated from the subject; for it moves towards us with certain thin outflows, as the gradual thinning of it shows; for on the tree it does not thin, because the inflow is greater than the outflow. But Aristotle blames the instrumental nature of the air, that by the same reason it is transparent and resonant, by this it also carries smell. But Plotinus, bringing together the views of Aristotle and Plato, says that part of the air is changed by the fragrance; for the fragrance remaining in the apple generates another quality similar to itself changing part of the air which we perceive.]—Next, after he said that neither Plato’s nor Aristotle’s opinion alone was true, he proceeds thus: *Οὐδὲ τὸ τοῦ Πλωτίνου (al. οὐδὲ τοῦ Πλ. al. οὐδὲ τὸ Πλ. al. Πλουτίνου sic.) μόνον ἀληθὲς, τὸ ποιοῦσθαι ὅλον τὸν ἀέρα. Πλασματῶδες (πλαστόδες al.) γὰρ τὸ λέγειν ὅλον τὸν ἐν μέσῳ ἀέρα ποιοῦσθαι ἐπὶ τῶν γυπῶν τῶν αἰσθανομένων τῶν ἐν ἄλλαις πόλεσιν ἀτάφων σωμάτων.* [Nor is Plotinus's only true, that the whole air is qualified. For it is fabricated to say the whole intervening air is qualified in the case of vultures perceiving unburied bodies in other cities.]

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 572, 1. *ἀναλλοίωτον αὐτὸ τὸ εἶδος*] [The form itself unchangeable]. Nicolaus of Methone [[abbrev: adversus → against]] Proclus’s *Elements of Theology* [[abbrev: c. → chapter]] 15 [[abbrev: p. → page]] 30: *ἡ ἀναλλοίωτος καὶ ὑπερούσιος ἐξουσία.* [the unchangeable and super-essential power.] Others were collected by Suicer in *Thesaurus Ecclesiasticus* I [[abbrev: p. → page]] 283.

— 3. *Ὅθεν δὴ καὶ τὸν Πλάτωνα—τὰ δὲ εἰσιόντα καὶ ἐξιόντα τῶν ὄντων μιμήματα μὴ μάτην εἰρηκέναι*] [Whence indeed that Plato... did not say in vain that the things entering and exiting were imitations of beings]. Plato in *Timaeus* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 50, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 60 Bekker: *ὁ αὐτὸς δὴ λόγος καὶ περὶ τῆς τὰ πάντα δεχομένης σώματα φύσεως˙ ταὐτὸν αὐτὴν ἀεὶ προσρητέον˙ ἐκ γὰρ τῆς ἑαυτῆς τοπαράπαν οὐκ ἐξίσταται δυνάμεως˙ δέχεται τε γὰρ ἀεὶ τὰ πάντα καὶ μορφὴν οὐδεμίαν ποτὲ οὐδενὶ τῶν εἰσιόντων ὁμοίαν εἴληφεν οὐδαμῇ οὐδαμῶς˙ ἐκμαγεῖον γὰρ φύσει παντὶ κεῖται, κινούμενόν τε καὶ διασχηματιζόμενον ὑπὸ τῶν εἰσιόντων˙ φαίνεται δὲ δι' ἐκεῖνα ἄλλοτε ἀλλοῖον˙ τὰ δὲ εἰσιόντα καὶ ἐξιόντα τῶν ὄντων ἀεὶ μιμήματα, τυπωθέντα ἀπ' αὐτῶν τρόπον τινὰ δύσφραστον καὶ θαυμαστόν, ὃν εἰσαὖθις μέτιμεν.* [The same account indeed also about the nature that receives all bodies; it must always be called the same; for it does not stand apart from its own power at all; for it always receives all things and has nowhere in any way taken a form similar to any of the things entering; for it lies by nature as a mold for everything, being moved and reshaped by the things entering; and through those things it appears different at different times; but the things entering and exiting are always imitations of beings, having been modeled from them in a certain way difficult to describe and wonderful, which we shall follow up hereafter.]

— 5. *ἀλλὰ βουλόμενον ἡμᾶς συνεῖναι ἐπιστήσαντας τῷ τρόπῳ τῆς μεταλήψεως*] *ἀπιστήσαντας* [distrusting], which the [[abbrev: Vat. → Vatican]] manuscript has, is plausible but not necessary. I translate: *But wishing us to understand, applying our mind (or directing our mind) to the manner of participation.* For in *ἐπιστήσαντας* [directing attention] there is the force of more intent diligence which we apply to some matter, whence almost joined to that word is the force of *pausing, doubting*. [[abbrev: Vid. → See]] Schneider in the Lexicon under *ἐφίστημι* and in *ἐπίσταμαι* explaining accurately, and those things which I placed above [[abbrev: p. → page]] 265 F at the words *ἐπίστασιν* and *ἀπορίαν* [attention and difficulty]. And in our passage, *τὸ ἄπορον* [the difficulty] follows immediately, which reading gains support from there also. Moreover, the form *συνεῖναι* [to understand] for *συνιέναι* is not unknown to Plato himself. [[abbrev: Vid. → See]] *Laws* III [[abbrev: p. → page]] 683 b: *εἴ τι ξυνείναι δυνάμεθα*. *Cratylus* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 413 D: *μηδ' ἂν ἕνα ἀνθρώπων συνεῖναι, ὅ,τι ποτὲ βούλεται τὸ ὄνομα.* Codex Darmstadt in my notes: *ἄνθρωπον συνιέναι τὰ ὀνόματα.* But see regarding that form of the Verb Heindorf at the [[abbrev: l. l. → cited passage]] [[abbrev: p. → page]] 105 and lauded by him Dorville on Chariton [[abbrev: p. → page]] 278 Amsterdam.

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 573, 9. *ὥστε οὐκ οὕτως ἡ μετάληψις, ὡς οἷόν τε παθούσης˙ ἀλλ' ἕτερος τρόπος οἷον δοκεῖν.* [So that participation is not thus, as if it had suffered; but another manner as if appearing.] Only [[abbrev: Cod. → Codex]] Ciz. and that from correction has *ὡς οἷόνται* [as they think]. A likelihood might seem to approach this reading from the antecedents [[abbrev: p. → page]] 313 D: *ὃ οἱ πολλοὶ ᾠήθησαν* [which the many thought], and Ficinus expressed that, and Taylor followed him, who renders this passage thus: "**Hence it does not participate in such a way as some fancy it does, viz. by being passive, but after another manner, which is that of appearing to participate.**" I think Plotinus wrote: *ὡς οἷόν τι παθούσης*, "**as if as something having suffered.**" To which the other member responds: *οἷον δοκεῖν* [as if to appear], unless you pre-

Plato *De Republica* IV [[abbrev: p. → page]] 442, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 208 Bekker: *μή πῃ ἡμῖν ἀπαμβλύνεται (al. ἀπαμβλύνεται) ἄλλο τι δικαιοσύνη (al. δικαιοσύνην) δοκεῖν (al. δεῖν, al. δεῖ, al. δὴ, Ast. δοκοῦν) εἶναι ἢ ὅπερ ἐν τῇ πόλει ἐφάνη;* [Does justice in any way seem to us to be blunted into being something else than what it appeared in the city?]. Schneider following Suidas (explaining *ἀπαμβλύνει˙ ἐκκαθαίρει σκότους καὶ ἀλλοιώσεως* [blunts: clears from darkness and change]) translates: "**Lest justice evolved from darkness and placed in light appear now to be different from that which we saw in the republic.**" Ast speaks against this in his Commentary [[abbrev: p. → page]] 503, translating: "**Whether anything in us is so blind and doubtful etc.**" Ficinus: "**Is there something which disturbs this our opinion to such an extent.**" It is asked, therefore, whether the power of privation or of perfection and intention exists in that word. And this seems to be asked more in the passage of Plotinus, because Suidas perhaps looked back at the same [[abbrev: l. l. → cited passage]] and follows *δηλοῖ τε (vel fortasse δηλοῖ δὲ)* [and it shows]. Yet I would believe neither: but I hold Ficinus's interpretation true, which Taylor also adopted, translating: "**mitigates.**" That Verb occurs quite often with the same meaning, [[abbrev: v. → see]] the [[abbrev: cap. → chapter]] [[abbrev: ap. → in]] Plutarch II [[abbrev: p. → page]] 786 E: *τὰς περὶ πόσιν καὶ βρῶσιν ἐπιθυμίας ἀπημβλυμένας τὰ πολλὰ καὶ νωδάς*, desires regarding drinking and eating mostly blunted and toothless. [Cicero at any rate, being carried towards public life full of hopes, was blunted in his impulse by a certain oracle.] And since mention of Cicero was made, in the books *De Republica* Tully had the cited passage of Plato before his eyes, as I noted at [[abbrev: cap. → chapter]] 38 of book I [[abbrev: p. → page]] 155 [[abbrev: ed. → edition]] Moser. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 578, 8. *οἷον καὶ εἰς τὸ κάτοπτρον*] [As also into the mirror]. [[abbrev: Cf. → Compare]] above [[abbrev: p. → page]] 312 and below [[abbrev: p. → page]] 615 C, and what we have annotated there. Porphyry reduced this whole passage into a compendium in *Sententiae* XXI: *οἷον γὰρ παίγνιόν ἐστι φεῦγον εἰς τὸ μὴ ὄν. ἡ γὰρ φυγὴ οὐ τόπῳ, ἀλλὰ τῇ ἐκ τοῦ ὄντος ἀπολείψει. ὅθεν καὶ τὰ ἐν αὐτῇ εἴδωλα ἔστιν ἐν εἰδώλῳ χείρονι, ὥσπερ ἐν κατόπτρῳ τὸ ἀλλαχοῦ ἱδρυμένον, ἀλλαχοῦ φανταζόμενον.* [For it is like a plaything fleeing into non-being. For the flight is not in place, but in the abandonment of being. Whence also the images in it are in a worse image, as in a mirror that which is established elsewhere is imagined elsewhere.]

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 579, 3. *αἰτιωμένους τῆς φαντάσεως τὴν τῶν ὄντων ὑπόστασιν.*] [Blaming/ascribing the hypostasis of beings for the appearance.] Taylor following Ficinus translates: "**The cause of this appearance, likewise, must be ascribed to the hypostasis of beings.**" But perhaps Ficinus had written *substantia* [substance]. Certainly the sense of the passage is this: When we say that the cause of the substance of things (why things subsist) exists in appearance. *Αἰτιᾶσθαι* for philosophers and for Plato himself is often simply to posit something as the cause of some thing, to attribute something to someone, to predicate something of someone. [[abbrev: Vid. → See]] Valckenaer on Herodotus VI. 115. Heindorf on Plato’s *Gorgias* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 194. Ast’s Commentary on the *Republic* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 613. Moreover, the word *φάντασις* [appearance], which recurs below [[abbrev: p. → page]] 319 D, must be added to the Lexicons. For the rest, those things should be applied to the sense of our passage which I placed above at [[abbrev: p. → page]] 312 B in the Annotation.

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 579, 7. *Τί οὖν μὴ οὔσης οὐδὲν ὑπέστη ἂν;*] [What then, if it did not exist, would nothing have subsisted?]. Ficinus adds: *Nihil praeter entia* [Nothing except beings]: and Taylor: "**Nothing except beings.**" And here he thinks the words *οὐδὲν παρὰ τὰ ὄντα* [nothing besides beings] have fallen out of order. Our [[abbrev: MSS. → Manuscript]] books supply nothing more.

— 12. *τῷ οὐκ ἐλθόντι*] [To that which has not come]. I have received this writing from the good books, for *τῷ οὐκ ἐθέλοντι* [to that which is not willing], and Ficinus expressed the former. But because, undoubtedly moved by Ficinus's version, Taylor says it is necessary to read: *παρέχων τῷ ὄντως οὐκ ἐλθόντι* [providing for that which has not truly come]: the books exhibited *παρέχον* [providing], they do not exhibit *ὄντως* [truly], and we have often warned that Ficinus's version of many passages is too full for one to be able to refashion the text from it without the support of manuscripts.

— 15. *ὁ μὲν μῦθος* [[abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → etc.]] [The myth etc.]. In Plato in the *Symposium* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 203 [[abbrev: sq. → following]] Bekker. Which fable Plotinus treated above [[abbrev: p. → page]] 296 [[abbrev: sqq. → following]]. With the nearest things compare these words of Porphyry *Sententiae* XXI [[abbrev: fin. → end]]: *καὶ πιμπλάμενον, ὡς δοκεῖ, καὶ ἔχον οὐδὲν, καὶ δοκοῦν τὰ πάντα.* [and being filled, as it seems, and having nothing, and seeming to be all things.] Because our author then makes mention of *πόρου* [Poros/Resource] likewise *κόρου* [Koros/Satiety], he here warns of Heraclitus’s opinion. Philo Judaeus *Allegories of the Laws* III [[abbrev: p. → page]] 89 Mangey, [[abbrev: p. → page]] 248 Pfeiffer: *Ἡρακλειτείου δόξης ἑταῖρος, κόρον καὶ χρησμοσύνην καὶ ἓν τὸ πᾶν καὶ πάντα ἀμοιβῇ (Mang.: fort. ἀμοιβήν. Jer. Markland πᾶν τὸ ἓν ἀμοιβῇ) εἰσάγων.* [A companion of Heraclitean opinion, introducing satiety and want and that all is one and all things by exchange.] In which decree *κόρος* [satiety] corresponds to *Πόρῳ* [Resource]: *χρησμοσύνη* [want] to *Πενίᾳ* [Poverty] in Plato, although no one would have said that the opinion of Heraclitus and Plato was entirely the same. We mentioned these Heraclitean things above at [[abbrev: ad p. → at page]] 75 E.

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 580, 1. *τὸ—συγγίγνεσθαι—τῇ σοφίᾳ τοῦ φαντάσματος*] [To be united... with the wisdom of the appearance]. Someone might compare these word-for-word with the decrees of the Gnostics *περὶ Σοφίας* [concerning Sophia/Wisdom]: as to the sense, let no one begin to compare things so very disparate. For he who has read the book of Plotinus against the Gnostics, he at least must understand by how great an interval this Philosopher's system stands apart from the system of the Gnostics.

— 8. *γειτνιάσεως*] [Of proximity]. [[abbrev: Cf. → Compare]] above [[abbrev: ad p. → at page]] 15 A.—To *ἀπολισθαίνει* [it slips away] [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] *Variae Lectiones* and [[abbrev: vid. → see]] above [[abbrev: ad pag. → at page]] 108 B.

This passage is to be added to those which exist in ancient writers concerning burning mirrors. [[abbrev: Vid. → See]] the fragment of Anthemius *On Paradoxical Machines* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 8—16 (in Schneider’s *Eclogae Physicae* I. 19 [[abbrev: p. → page]] 402 [[abbrev: sqq. → following]] where concerning the mirrors of Archimedes, and from there in Tzetzes *Chiliads* II. 35 [[abbrev: sqq. → following]]; Zonaras’s *Annals* Vol. III [[abbrev: p. → page]] 46 where concerning the mirror of Proclus. This is provided by this passage of Lactantius *On the Anger of God* [[abbrev: c. → chapter]] X §. 19 [[abbrev: p. → page]] 1073 [[abbrev: ed. → edition]] Bunemann: "**If you hold a glass orb full of water in the sun, fire is kindled from the light which is reflected from the water, even in the hardest cold. Is it even to be believed that there is fire in the water? And yet fire cannot be kindled from the sun even in summer.**" Similar things were attempted by more recent men as you may find reported both elsewhere and in *Mémoires de Paris* for the [[abbrev: ann. → year]] 1774 [[abbrev: p. → page]] 62.

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 582, 8. *ὡς ἐγὼ ἐνταῦθα.*] [As I am here]. Because Ficinus adds: "**although I may not seem to be at all,**" since it is not read in the Greek, Taylor included it in brackets. Many more things would have to be included in brackets if you wished to distinguish what that interpreter interposed in the Latin context for the sake of clarity.

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 583, 14. *πῶς οὐκ ἔχον μέγεθος μέγα ἔσται* [[abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → etc.]] [How will that which has no magnitude be great? etc.]. Also in the following chapter: *εἶδος γὰρ τὸ μέγεθος.* [For magnitude is a form.] Compare with this discussion those which Plotinus placed above in II. 4. 8; II. 4. 10; II. 4. 11 and 12, Porphyry’s *Sententiae* XXI on Matter: *εἴδωλον καὶ φάντασμα ὄγκου, ὅτι τὸ πρώτως ἐν ὄγκῳ, τὸ ἀδύναμον καὶ ἔφεσις ὑποστάσεως, καὶ ἑστὼς οὐκ ἐν στάσει. καὶ τὸ ἐναντίον ἀεὶ ἑαυτοῦ φανταζόμενον˙ μικρὸν, καὶ μέγα˙ καὶ ἧττον, καὶ μᾶλλον˙ ἐλλεῖπον καὶ ὑπερέχον.* [An image and phantom of bulk, because that which is primarily in bulk, the powerless and the desire for hypostasis, and standing not in a stance; and always imagining the opposite of itself: small and great; and less and more; deficient and exceeding.] And at this place let me warn in a word, that there were among philosophers those to whom that Proteus (*Πρωτεὺς*) seemed to be nothing other than *ἡ πρωτόγονος ὕλη* [first-born matter], Eustathius reporting on *Odyssey* δ. 417 [[abbrev: sq. → following]], where concerning Proteus:
*Πάντα δὲ γιγνόμενος πειρήσεται, ὅσσ' ἐπὶ γαῖαν*
*ἑρπετὰ γίγνονται, καὶ ὕδωρ καὶ θεσπιδαὲς πῦρ.*
[And becoming all things he will try, as many as on earth are born as creeping things, and water and divine-blazing fire.]
Which passage Plato gracefully employs in another sense in the *Euthydemus* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 288 C. Moreover, the primary passage of Apuleius *On the Doctrine of Plato* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 572 [[abbrev: sq. → following]], [[abbrev: p. → page]] 191 [[abbrev: sq. → following]] [[abbrev: ed. → edition]] Bosscha applies to this entire Plotinian discussion on Matter: "**He relates that Matter is indeed unbegotten and incorruptible (Plato [[abbrev: sc. → namely]]. **ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

...universal. Indeed, infinite for the reason that its magnitude is unbounded (*interminata*). For that which is infinite has an indistinct limit of magnitude, and thus, since it is deprived of a limit, it can rightly be seen as "unfinishable" (*infinibilis*). *But he grants that it is neither corporeal nor incorporeal.* However, he does not think it is a body for the reason that every body is not lacking in some species or quality. Yet he cannot say it is without a body, because nothing incorporeal [by itself] manifests a body: but it seems to him to be corporeal by force and reason, and therefore understood neither by act alone, nor yet by the mere opinion of thought. For bodies, on account of their remarkable evidence of themselves, are recognized by a similar indicator. But those things which do not have a corporeal substance are seen by thoughts, whence by an adulterated opinion *this quality of matter is understood as ambiguous*: regarding this, consult the annotations of Elmenhorst. As far as the boundaries of matter are concerned: the Platonists, as we have learned, contended that matter was infinite; the Stoics, on the contrary, [contended it was] a "finite substance" (Diog. Laërt. VII. 150.). How Justus Lipsius strove to reconcile this diversity among themselves, he who wishes may see in his *Physiologia Stoicorum* book II. c. 2. (Works Vol. IV. p. 569.) nor will it repent anyone to read what Baguet collected on this matter in *de Chrysippo* p. 155. sq. Moreover, there is no need for me to demonstrate laboriously that the *figures* which Appuleius says (in the place cited) are the *eidē* [forms]: let it be permitted to add on this occasion that some philosophers explained that Idothea, daughter of Proteus (Odyss. δ. 365. sq.), was *Eidothea*, as if it were "Matter rushing into form" (*tēn hylēn eis eidos theousan*): *Matter rushing into forms*. See Eustathius at the cited place.

p. 584, 5. [Greek text: *kai eiti mimēma autōn*] Taylor, moved by the interpretation of Ficinus: *of beings* [entium], orders it to be read [Greek: *ontōn*]. Our books do not recede at all from the common reading.

p. 585, 7. [Greek text: *kai hē poiotēs hē entautha hē ex ou poiotētos esche tēn epōnymian*] Wyttenbach on Plato’s *Phaedo* p. 271. sq.: “Moreover, from this communion of the idea with sensible and singular things comes the surname [cognomen] of that thing, *epōnymia*: regarding which twice elsewhere in the *Phaedo*, p. 59. and 75. and *Phaedrus* p. 341. B... [Greek quote omitted] ... ibid. p. 346. E. 358. A. *Theaet.* 132. E.” Then this very passage of Plotinus is praised.

— 17. [Greek text: *Hylē gar esti kai touto kai ou toutou ti*] Thus in the edition. But Ficinus reads [Greek: *hylē gar esti kai toutou kai ou touti*]. Taylor expressed the same: “*Matter, however, being compelled to concur with this attraction, at once imparts itself wholly and every where; for it is the matter of the universe, and not some particular matter.*” I have corrected the passage from our books.

p. 586, 8. [Greek text: *ou dynatai to allo chōrēsai mega*] Ficinus expressed: [Greek: *ou—chōrēsai touto to mega*]. Taylor also: “*nothing else [besides matter] is able to receive this magnitude.*” Our books vary nothing. The common reading is to be translated:—“*the rest cannot contain the great.*”

— 15. [Greek text: *prosēlthe te*] From the traces of good books, restore: [Greek: *prosēlthe theon te*], and so Ficinus seems to have read; who in the apodosis seems not to have read [Greek: *kai*], which surely disturbs the construction.

p. 588, 4. [Greek text: *Zōou gar hylē—ton logon.*] Taylor: “*For the matter of the animal nature is distributed in conjunction with the division of the animal into parts. For if this were not to be the case, nothing would have been produced besides reason.*”

p. 589, 3. [Greek text: *hē de mētēr—epei kai hoson sōma tou ginomenou, ek tēs trophēs—all’ hoti kai eidos.*] Thus we have restored it from our books and the version of Ficinus. To understand the meaning of this passage and those things read toward the end of the chapter, it must be held that this question was agitated among the ancient philosophers, which it is helpful to declare in the words of Censorinus (*De Die Natali* c. 5. p. 26. ed. Havercamp.): “whether the offspring is born from the seed of the father only, or also from the mother, which was the view of Anaxagoras and Alcmaeon, and also of Parmenides, Empedocles, and Epicurus.” As far as Empedocles is concerned, Aristotle says in *De Generatione Animalium* I. 18: ‘Empedocles—says that in the male and the female there is as it were a tally [symbolon], but the whole comes from neither;’

but the nature of the limbs is torn apart, part in the man's— in another place (of the same book IV.) he adds: part in the woman's. And as the Stagirite [Aristotle] does not approve this opinion in every part, he nevertheless judges it universally truer than the others. Cf. also Galen *de Semine* II. 7. p. 241. ed. Basil. Moreover, from the commentary of Joannes Philoponus on Aristotle *De Animalium Generatione* I. fol. 161. a. we learn what...

[[vocabulary: magnitude, incorporeal, matter, of beings, seed]]

### PAGE 192 ###
**BOOK VI. ENNEAD THREE. p. 584—589.**

...what Plato's opinion also was on this cause:—for indeed Empedocles said that parts come away both from the father and from the mother, but not as those others (he means Plato and others here). For those others [say] that from the father come all things which constitute the animal, and from the mother likewise all the same things. But Empedocles said that some come from the father, and some from the mother, etc. Cf. *Empedocles Agrigentinus* ed. Sturz. p. 390—393. Now as far as Plotinus is concerned, he does not precisely and eloquently set out to settle this dispute in this place: yet it is obscure to no one that he inclines toward assigning efficient parts and generating powers to the mother as much as to the father in generating offspring, and accordingly in this argument also he applies his opinion to Plato.

p. 589, 8. [Greek text: *Monon gar to eidos gonimon—Hermēn—ton archaion k. t. l.*] A memorable passage; about which we shall see individually. And first, what those words mean: *mystically and in the rites hinting at the ancient Hermes etc.* the Father of History [Herodotus] himself teaches us in II. 51. who says several things in the same place and these: "The Athenians, being the first of the Greeks to learn from the Pelasgians, made the statues of Hermes with upright genitals. But the Pelasgians told a certain sacred story about him, which is revealed in the mysteries in Samothrace." This ancient and Pelasgian Mercury, to whom Herodotus refers his readers regarding the Samothracian Mysteries, is the same as he whom Cicero mentions in *De Natura Deorum* III. 22. 56: “*Mercury, born of Father Heaven and Mother Dia, whose nature is handed down as having been more obscenely excited, because he was moved by the sight of Proserpina.*” It is the Ithyphallic Mercury, of whom there are many traces throughout the monuments of ancient writers. Pausanias VI. 26. p. 519. p. 124. Siebelis. on the gods of the Cyllenians: "the statue of Hermes, whom those people worship exceedingly, is an upright genital on a pedestal." The same is mentioned by Lucian in *Jov. Tragoed.* Vol. VI. p. 275. Bip.: "the Cyllenians sacrificing to Phales," which passage critics have tempted with unfortunate conjectures. Plutarch recognizes the same Mercury in *De rep. gerend.* p. 797. F., which passage Cornutus *de Nat. Deorr.* c. 16 and Eudocia in her *Violarium* p. 155 described. But attend to how purely and chastely our philosopher expresses this; [Greek: *to tēs geneseōs organon aei echonta pros ergasian*] [always having the organ of generation ready for work]. No less modestly does his pupil Porphyry in Eusebius *Praep. Evang.* III. p. 114 say: "Mercury is the representative of the reason [logos] that is productive and interpretive of all things; but the stretched-out Hermes [Mercury] shows vigor; and it also shows the seminal reason [spermatikos logos] which pervades all things... etc." In which place Kuhn, on the cited passage of Pausanias, at the word *entetamenos* [stretched], correctly supplied: "in his members," i.e., with an erect phallus, or *excited nature*. Moreover, Vigerius badly understood the entire passage of Porphyry. Therefore, I have emended the punctuation. As for the argument, let us first hold these things from Proclus in Joannes Lydus *de Mensibus Romanis* p. 101. To him, Mercury is called "the reason pervading all things." In the same place, to Aquilinus, Mercury is "the reason naturally pervading all things." He also says Hermes is the son of "intelligible matter" (*noētēs hylēs*), and that all things consist of Matter (*hylēs*) and species/*form* (*eidous*). I add nothing else that I could to the cited passage of Cicero, except these things, which pertain to the following words of our Plotinus: *showing that the one generating sensible things is the intelligible reason*, and likewise to the words of Porphyry just cited. Clearly, the Ithyphallic Mercury is the seminal reason (*spermatikos logos* Porphyry l. l.) and effector, both in the generation of things, plants, animals, etc., and in thought and speech. In either business, Mercury provides the perfected perennial forms or ideas of things. Now this seminal and effective reason adopts for itself a receptive and generative reason. The former is male; the latter female: the former the sun; the latter the moon. For, says Plutarch in *de Iside et Osiride* p. 367. D. and *De facie in orbe lunae* p. 943. B., they mythologize that Mercury is located in the moon, because the things the moon effects are similar to the works of reason and wisdom. The vegetating force and seminal reason is of the sun, and whatever of its reason is imparted to the moon, that is signified as having been imparted to it by the sun. Let these suffice for explaining the fable in Cicero and others regarding the nature of Mercury *excited by the sight of Proserpina (the Moon)*. I gave more at the cited passage of Cicero. —Plotinus, however, to return thither, who says Mercury is always excited, accepts him universally *for the seminal reason (the formative and law-giving Idea, the concept of reason expressing itself in forms:)* and thus opposes to him Matter (*tēn heteran physin*), that receiver of forms, yet sterile and least fit for begetting.
