...and least fit for begetting. For thus he continues: [Greek quote: *to de agonon tēs hylēs menousēs to auto aei dia tōn peri autēn agonōn dēlountes.*] Ficinus: “*showing the sterility of matter always remaining the same through those sterile things which are disposed around it.*” Taylor likewise: “*But they indicated the unprolific nature of matter, which always remains the same, **by the barren substances which were placed about it**.*” For my part, I do not know which sterile things are placed around matter, or which are sterile substances: this I know and signaled above, that Plotinus is accustomed to use a modest kind of speaking in obscene matters, such as these tokens [tesserae] of ancient religions and fables are; nor do I think those words should be separated from these, which the philosopher immediately joins and connects through a causal particle with the same: "making her the mother of all things" etc. Accordingly, Plotinus designates those who exhibited and worshipped *hylēn rheustēn* (flowing and unstable matter) as Rhea (*Rheia*), the *mother* of all. But by the age of Plotinus, the rites of Rhea had long since merged with the rites of Cybele (*Kybebe*). Now those who were the minor priests [sacrificuli] around Cybele or Rhea, and worshipped her with the sound of drums and horns, with dances and other things performed with fury (cf. Wyttenbach on Plutarch *de discr. amic. et adul.* p. 457—459.) were Galli (*Galloi*), that is, *eunuchoi apokopoi* or "those whose genitals have been cut off," *spadones* (*spadontes*. see Phrynichus *Epit.* p. 272. sq. ib. Lobeck. and Thomas Magister p. 138. sq. and the interpreters there. Ruhnken on Timaeus' *Lexicon Platonicum* p. 11.) of whom Manetho says in *Apotelesm.* VI. 297:
"for they cut off the useless shame from their body."
and thus *agonoi* i. e. *sterile for begetting*; in which sense Plato in *Theaet.* p. 150. c. and others use this word (see Hesychius at the word and I. Fr. Fischer's Index in Aeschines Socraticus under the same word.) Now hold the following: "nonetheless from afar, as they were able, they showed that she was both sterile and not entirely female" (*hē hylē* without *hē mētēr tōn pantōn*): “*from a distance indeed* (and thus obscurely) they signified that matter (or that mother) was sterile nor in every way a female.” Think also of the extremes of the chapter: "being cut off from all power of begetting." The servants of the Great Mother wished this to be signified by their own excision, or those Galli who are themselves described as "those whose genitals have been cut off." Therefore, the *Galliambics* of these sounded plainly contrary to the *Ithyphallica* of the prophets of Mercury. The latter celebrated the Pelasgian Mercury *with nature excited*, and always ready for begetting: the former, on the contrary, the Mother Goddess, yet not entirely a mother, but only a receiver and *agonos* h. e. unfit for begetting. These contraries were signified among themselves by those fables, tokens, and rites. And accordingly I think it is a matter of doubt to no one that those words from which we set out are to be accepted thus: “*But the sterility of matter always remaining the same they signify **through the sterile ones who are occupied around it**.*” I did not wish to interrupt these mythological matters. It remains that I should advise briefly on the words: "always having the organ of generation ready for work." But *ergasia* in this place is coitus itself, which elsewhere is *ergon* [work], as in Attic laws: "to catch an adulterer in the act" (*en ergō*), i. e. to catch an adulterer in the venereal act itself; or in the very turpitude. See Brisson on *Leg. Jul. de Adulteriis* c. 3. (in Gronovius *Thess. Antiqq. Graecc.* Vol. VIII. p. 1363.) Petit. *de Legg. Attic.* p. 562. ed. Wesseling. Hence *en ergō gignesthai* or *e. e. einai*. T. Hemsterhuis on Lucian *Deorr. Dialogg.* XVII. 2. p. 246. ed. Wetst. Elsewhere *ergasia* is used of meretricious gain. Fully, however, Demosthenes thus against Neaera Vol. II. p. 1357. Reiske. "as if the work [ergasia] from her body did not provide sufficient wealth." Since, however, elsewhere coitus is called "the work of Aphrodite" (*ergon Aphroditēs*) or "the Aphrodisian work" (*ergon Aphrodision*) (Antonin. Liberal. XXXVII. and XXXVIII. p. 246. 256. Verheyk.) it seems advisable that locutions which have *ergon* alone should be ascribed to Ellipses, and accordingly added to the book of Lamb. Bos.

...must return to the religions of Oriental peoples, and the beginnings of what is commonly called barbarian philosophy. For anciently this question of *eternity and time* was joined among the Indians, Chaldeans, Persians, and Phoenicians with the cult of divinities which are called by the Greeks by the name of *Aeon* and *Kronos*. These religions persisted alongside the families of philosophers through various vicissitudes until the final times of the Roman Empire, yet in such a way that from time to time not a few things from the decrees of philosophers were mixed into them. On these matters, *Heyne* should be consulted in *Opuscull. Bassirilievi antichi di Roma* at table 59, which has the image of *Aenis* [sic, likely Aeon] Vol. II. p. 32. sqq. Boettiger in *Ideen zur Kunstmythologie* I. p. 40 and 219 and what I myself have collected and disputed in *Meletematt. e discipl. antiquitatis* I. p. 44 and in the review of Boettiger's cited book in *Annalibus literarr. Heidelberg.* year 1827. nr. 34. p. 538—p. 543. Moreover, that there is actually no difference between the words *Kronos* and *Chronos*, it would be offensive to wish to explain laboriously. From there, partly satires and proverbs were translated into common speech (see Plato's *Cratylus* p. 396. b. p. 45. Heindf. and *Euthydemus* p. 287. b. p. 351. Pherecydis *Fragg.* p. 42. ed. Sturz.) Pherecydes the Syrian, the most ancient philosopher, had placed time among the principles of things. After him, no philosopher wished this question of time and eternity to be separated from his own system. At which place Menagius makes mention also of the Plotinian book; which same book Casp. Barth. praises in *Adversarr.* LIII. 12. p. 2504. Philo Judaeus expressed the passage of Plato in *Legis Alleg.* I. after the beginning p. 122—124. Pfeiff. From both, Plato and Aristotle, subsequent Platonic and Peripatetic philosophers borrowed the argument for a wealth of disputations, for they clearly saw what force this question had both for other areas of philosophy, and especially for the topic of the World and likewise of the Soul. p. 618, 3. **If then someone should say that time—is life passing from one state of life to another**] Taylor, following Ficinus, wanted the word "activity" <note>original: *ἐνέργειαν* (energeian)</note>, as the act of the giver. Furthermore, this definition is more easily handled by the Greeks, who distinguished between "life" as a biological principle <note>original: *ζωὴν* (zōēn)</note> and "life" as a career or way of living <note>original: *βίον* (bion)</note>, than by the Latins or ourselves. Cf. Ammonius p. 30. p. 32. one must return to the religions of the Eastern peoples and the origins of what is commonly called "barbarian philosophy" <note>The author refers to non-Greek systems, such as those of the Persians or Indians, which Greeks often labeled 'barbaric'.</note>. For in ancient times, this question concerning *eternity and time* was linked among the Indians, Chaldeans, Persians, and Phoenicians with the worship of deities who are called by the names *Aion* <note>original: Αἰῶνος; personified Eternity</note> and *Kronos* <note>original: Κρόνου; the Titan associated with time</note> by the Greeks. These religious traditions persisted alongside the schools of the philosophers through various shifts until the final days of the Roman Empire, though in such a way that, from time to time, many elements from the decrees of the philosophers were mixed into them. On these matters, one should consult *Heyne* in his *Short Works*, "Ancient Bas-reliefs of Rome" at table 59, which contains an image of *Aion* <note>original: Aenis</note> in Volume II, page 32 and following; Boettiger in *Ideas for Art Mythology* I, pages 40 and 219; and what I myself have collected and discussed in *Inquiries into the Discipline of Antiquity* I, page 44, and in the review of Boettiger’s aforementioned book in the *Heidelberg Literary Annals*, year 1827, number 34, pages 538–543. Furthermore, it would be a tedious task to explain laboriously that there is actually no difference between the words *Kronos* <note>The deity</note> and *Chronos* <note>The word for time</note>. From this source, partly, jokes and proverbs were brought into common speech (see Plato’s *Cratylus* page 396b, page 45 in Heindorf’s edition, and *Euthydemus* page 287b, page 351 in Heindorf and his notes on it), and partly the very material of philosophizing was born (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II. 25: “*For he is called Kronos (Saturn); who is the same as chronos, that is, a space of time:*” etc.). And according to the testimony of Damascius (*On First Principles* chapter 124, page 384, edited by Kopp; compare the fragments of Pherecydes, page 42, edited by Sturz), Pherecydes of Syros, the most ancient philosopher, had placed *Time* <note>original: χρόνον</note> among the first principles of things. After him, no philosopher wanted this question of time and eternity to be separated from his own system of reasoning. This is proven by the opinions of philosophers excerpted since Thales and Pythagoras, which Plotinus touches upon in part on page 331 and following, and which the pseudo-Plutarch summarized in *On the Opinions of the Philosophers* I. 21 and 22, page 884 (page 556 in Wyttenbach’s edition), and more accurately Stobaeus in *Physical Extracts* I. 40–45, pages 248–268 in Heeren’s edition. Add to this John Laurentius Lydus’s little book *On the Roman Months*, page 2, page 110, and page 208 in Roether’s edition, from which we gain a fragment of the Pythagorean Philolaus. The opinions of Chrysippus and other Stoics were examined by *Justus Lipsius* in *Stoic Physiology* book II, Dissertation 24 (Works, Volume IV, page 603) and F. N. G. *Baguet on Chrysippus*, pages 170–172. Regarding the doctrine of Posidonius, consult the *Remains of the Doctrines of Posidonius of Rhodes*, page 51, edited by J. Bake. However, if you seek the primary sources of this book by Plotinus: they are found chiefly in Plato’s *Timaeus* page 37 and following (page 36 in Bekker), and likewise in Aristotle’s books on *Physics* IV. 10–14, page 80 and following in Sylburg’s edition. He also touches upon the notion of time in the *Categories* IV, page 31, and in the *Topics* III, page 318. Diogenes Laertius III. 73 uses these words:—*that time was born as an image of the eternal, and that the motion of the heavens is time; for night and day, and the month and all such things are parts of time; therefore without the nature of the world time does not exist; for it exists simultaneously with the world.* Regarding this passage, Menagius also mentions the book of Plotinus; Caspar Barth also praises the same in *Adversaria* LIII. 12, page 2504. Philo the Jew expressed Plato’s passage in *Allegorical Interpretation of the Law* I, after the beginning, pages 122–124 in Pfeiffer. From both Plato and Aristotle, the later Platonic and Peripatetic philosophers borrowed the substance of their copious discussions, as they clearly perceived what weight this question carried both for other areas of philosophy and especially for the topics of the World and the Soul. Indeed, even the Grammarians profited from the schools of the leading philosophers. Thus, to use this example, many have applied themselves to that saying of Aristotle in *On the Heavens* I. 9, page 25 in Sylburg: *Aion [Eternity] is so named from "always being" [aei einai], immortal and divine.* See the *Great Etymological Dictionary* page 540 (where Chrysippus is also praised); the *Gudian Etymological Dictionary* page 24; Zonaras’s *Lexicon* page 63 and following, and Tittmann’s notes there; Maximus’s *Scholia on Dionysius the Areopagite’s Divine Names* V. 4, page 705; and Proclus’s *Theological Institutes* chapter 52, page 82 of our edition. Many discussions by this same Proclus are read concerning this topic of Eternity and Time, such as in the commentary on the *Timaeus* (at the place cited), in the *Parmenides* throughout and on page 98 and following of Volume VI in Cousin’s edition (compare also Damascius *On Principles* chapter 91 and following, page 277 in Kopp’s edition), in the *First Alcibiades* 73, page 236 of our edition, and especially in the *Theological Institutes* chapter 48 and following, *on the eternal*, page 78 of our edition; chapter 53, *on eternity and eternal things*, page 82; and chapter 198, page 294; finally in *Platonic Theology* I. 13, page 37; III. 16 and following, page 146; V. 30, page 311, where the decrees of both Plotinus and Theodorus are touched upon, and page 330. Suicer exhibits the passages of the Fathers of the Christian Church—

I submit two testimonies concerning this book by Plotinus, one from Proclus, the other from Simplicius. The former, in *Platonic Theology* III. 18. p. 149, says: <note>original: "καὶ ὅ γε Πλωτῖνος..."</note> "And Plotinus, most divinely manifesting the eternity of the age according to the theology of Plato, defines eternity as infinite life, at once displaying itself in its entirety and revealing itself and being as its own." p. 596, 2. **in different ways, and perhaps even the same things in different ways**] I did not hesitate to embrace the Munich reading <note>original: "ἄλλως ἄλλας"</note> instead of "another" <note>original: "ἄλλος"</note> which Ficino has with the rest. Next, one should observe the redundancy: **resting upon these things, and deeming them self-sufficient—being content.** Regarding the verb "to be content" <note>original: "ἀγαπᾶν"</note> constructed in various ways, add to those collected in the new London *Thesaurus* of Stephanus, Leopold’s *Index to the Lives of Plutarch* and Jacobs on Philostratus’s *Images* p. 393. In our passage, it must be taken absolutely: *content*. Regarding the adverb "contentedly" <note>original: "ἀγαπητῶς"</note>, notice was given above at II. 9. 12. Presently, **certain of the ancient and blessed philosophers**, whose decrees he had shortly before called "the pronouncements of the ancients," you may rightly take to mean those philosophers who from antiquity, starting with Pherecydes and Pythagoras, have debated this Question. Regarding the expression **blessed**, we saw above at p. 204. B. regarding the words "of that man (Plato) and of the other blessed men."

— 10. **and the image of it (eternity), which they indeed say is time**] Regarding the construction, there is no need to say much. See only Stallbaum on Plato’s *Philebus* p. 118 and what we have set down regarding these words of Cicero in *On the Laws* I. 7. 22: "this provident, shrewd animal—*whom* we call man." Moreover, in this place Plotinus expressed the words of the Platonic *Timaeus* p. 37 near the end: <note>original: "εἰκὼ δ’ ἐπινοεῖ..."</note> "He resolved to create a moving image of eternity, and while bringing order to the heaven, he made an eternal image, moving according to number, while eternity remains in unity, this very thing which we have named time." Boethius, *On the Consolation of Philosophy* V. 6: "For that infinite motion of temporal things imitates this present state of immobile life, and since it cannot reproduce or equal it, it falls from immobility into motion—which (temporal presence), because it bears a certain image of that remaining presence, grants to whatever it touches the appearance of being."

— 17. **as if someone were to say that time is the entire heaven and the cosmos**] This opinion is attributed to Pythagoras and the Pythagoreans. Simplicius in *Aristotle’s Physics* p. 165: "Some say that time is the motion of the whole... others that it is the sphere of the heaven itself, as they record the Pythagoreans saying, having perhaps misheard Archytas when he said that time is generally the interval of the nature of the universe." And from Simplicius’s words, it is understood why Plotinus immediately reports this opinion only with hesitation. Pseudo-Plutarch in *Opinions of the Philosophers* I. 21 and Stobaeus in *Eclogues* I. p. 248, 250 (where see Heeren’s annotation) transmit these Pythagorean views less accurately.

p. 597, 6. **for one says—eternal**] See Plato’s *Timaeus* p. 37 f.

— 16. **first—then—furthermore**] Plato, in formulas of enumeration, is accustomed to use "then" <note>original: "ἔπειτα"</note> in the third place as well, or instead of it "and still further" <note>original: "ἔτι δὲ καί"</note>. See Heindorf on Plato’s *Phaedo* § 86.

p. 598, 11. **of the age and everlasting**] <term>aeternus and ἀΐδιος (aïdios): terms for eternal duration</term>. Cf. below p. 328. G. and consult Olympiodorus on Aristotle’s *Meteorology* 4. p. 32; which passage Wyttenbach provides in *Observations on Plutarch* Vol. V. p. 438 f., who called upon these two passages of Plotinus.

p. 599, 8. **eternity—a remaining life**] Proclus refers to these words, and those read below on p. 336, in his commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus* p. 127; compare also Proclus in *Platonic Theology* V. 27. p. 305 and p. 311.

Plotinus calls eternity "life," the one and the whole. <note>original: "ὁ Πλωτῖνος μὲν ζωὴν ἀποκαλεῖ τὸν αἰῶνα, τὴν μίαν καὶ ὅλην."</note> Add page 330: since eternity, arranged according to the intelligible wholeness, is a complete life, and every life according to Plotinus. <note>original: "ἐπεὶ καὶ ὁ αἰὼν κατὰ τὴν ὁλότητα τὴν νοητὴν τεταγμένος ζωὴ παντελής ἐστι, καὶ πᾶσα ζωὴ κατὰ τὸν Πλωτῖνον."</note> Furthermore, *Tiedemann* strives to refute these points in the book: *Spirit of Speculative Philosophy* III. page 287 and following.

page 599, 13. **because nothing of it has passed away, nor will it ever come to be—it being always]** Boethius in *The Consolation of Philosophy* V. 6: “That which, therefore, grasps and possesses the whole fullness of an unending life all at once, to which nothing of the future is absent, nor has anything of the past flowed away, is rightly held to be eternal: and it is necessary that it, being master of itself, always stands present to itself and holds the weakness of moving time as a present moment.” <note>original Latin: "Quod igitur interminabilis vitae plenitudinem..."</note> How these words differ from Plotinus's words, everyone understands.

page 601, 2. **and truth is not a harmony etc.]** *Tiedemann* touched upon these in the book: *Spirit of Speculative Philosophy* III. page 382 and following.

page 602, 11. **for eternity [Aeon] comes from "always being" [aei on]]** See Aristotle, *On the Heavens* I. 9. page 25. Sylburg edition. I have praised this passage and others derived from it above in the notes to the title of this book.

— 12. **And this, whenever someone applying the soul to it etc.]** Taylor translates thus: “*He, however, will know, that eternity thus subsists, who by the projecting energies of intellect is able to speak concerning it.*” <note>Thomas Taylor (1758–1835) was a famous English translator of Neoplatonist texts.</note> Doubtless he bids us read "to eternity" <term>aioni</term> instead of "to someone" <term>tini</term>. None of our manuscript books support this: and in this place Plotinus speaks universally thus: If anyone should direct the sharp edge of the mind and soul toward any thing whatever, and do this again, and yet find it in no way changed, he may infer from this that it is everlasting. Regarding the word "applying" <term>prosbalon</term>, the same author placed this note: “*The visive energy is an immediate darting forth as it were to the object of its intuition.*”

page 603, 2. **admiring the nature]** A construction familiar to Plato. See Ruhnken on Timaeus page 8. Pierson on Moeris page 1. compare Ast on Plato's *Laws* page 554.

— ibid. **by an unwearied nature]** Compare Ennead V. 8. 4. Proclus in *Platonic Theology* III. 18. page 149: for eternity belongs to the "unfailing life, and the unwearied power, and the untiring activity." <note>original: "τῆς γὰρ ἀνεκλείπτου ζωῆς, καὶ τῆς ἀτρύτου δυνάμεως καὶ τῆς ἀόκνου —ἐνεργείας ὁ αἰών."</note> Olympiodorus in *Commentary on First Alcibiades* page 40: Third, he admires the power, saying: "being present most carefully wherever I may be" (these are Plato's words in that dialogue). This belongs to a "sleepless and unwearied power; whence also Athena is called Atrytone [The Unwearied]" <note>original: "Ἀτρυτώνη ἡ Ἀθηνᾶ"</note> (Iliad book 2, line 157. Apollonius, *Homeric Lexicon* page 174. Tollius edition.) From this, another passage of Proclus should be corrected, in *Commentary on the Parmenides* Vol. VI. page 100. Cousin edition: for the soul, thinking transitionally, has the power of "unfailing motion, and is unmoved, joining the periods to one another, and making its activity unwearied [reading <term>atryton</term> for <term>atroton</term>, 'unwounded'], and always one and unfailing."

— 8. **such is everlastingness—but eternity—whence eternity is a solemn thing—eternity is a god etc.]** He had before his eyes here not only Plato in the cited passages of the *Timaeus*, but also Aristotle in these lines from *On the Heavens* I. 9. page 25. Sylburg edition: —"wherefore the things there are not in a place, nor does time make them grow old, nor is there any change in any of the things stationed above the outermost motion, but they continue unchanged and impassive, having the best and most self-sufficient life for all eternity; for this name has been divinely uttered by the ancients: for the limit which contains the time of each life, outside of which nothing exists according to nature, is called the eternity [Aeon] of each. By the same reasoning, the limit of the whole heaven, and the limit containing the infinite time of all things and infinity, is eternity, taking its name from 'always being' [aei einai], immortal and divine." Proclus in *Plato's Parmenides* Vol. VI. page 100 and following. Cousin edition: —"and the infinite does not stop at these alone, but even before the Intellect, that much-hymned Eternity itself is infinite, which also contains all intellectual infinity; for from where does the Intellect get its eternal life, if not from Eternity? This, then, is infinite before the Intellect according to power; or rather, other things are infinite according to power, but Eternity is Power itself; for the first Eternity is nothing other than Power: —For Eternity, even if it is infinite because of the 'always,' is surely the measure and limit of eternal things." Compare Proclus's *Elements of Theology* chapters 48—54 and in *Platonic Theology* III. 16. who, just like Boethius in *Consolation of Philosophy* V. 6, looks back to the cited passage of Aristotle. Compare also Taylor page 189 in the notes. Because Plotinus in this place beautifully says that the Aeon is perhaps called a god, he seems to be modestly referring to those religions of his age which had fashioned Aeons as gods and images and had established sacred worship. Consult what we have advised on this matter above in the annotations to the title of this book on page 325.

They discuss these things clearly because they are proper to philosophy. For sophistry and dialectic revolve around the same genus as philosophy. So indeed—creeping under the true lover, etc." You see that this author also imitated these passages of Plato and Aristotle in both words and sentiments.

# BOOK VII. OF THE THIRD ENNEAD. pages 605—614.

Proclus in his commentary on Plato's *Alcibiades* (p. 126) holds this view. These words of Boethius in *The Consolation of Philosophy* (V. 6) are relevant to Plotinus:
> "Hence some are not right who, when they hear it was Plato's view that this world neither had a beginning in time nor will have an end, think that in this way the created world becomes co-eternal with the creator. For it is one thing to be led through an endless life, which Plato attributes to the world; it is another to have embraced the whole presence of an endless life all at once, which is manifest as the property of the Divine Mind. Nor should God be seen as more ancient than created things by a quantity of time, but rather by the property of His simple nature." <note>original: "Unde non recte quidam..." Boethius is distinguishing between the "everlasting" duration of the universe and the "eternal" now of God.</note>

p. 606, 14. *signifying by the whole that which is beyond* <note>original Greek: σημαίνων τῷ ἐπέκεινα παντὶ</note>] Ficinus <note>Marsilio Ficino, the famous Renaissance translator of Plotinus</note> seems to have read "of the whole." Our manuscripts show no variation. Regarding the statement that Plato is said to "find fault later" with that phrase "was" etc., consult the words in the *Timaeus* p. 38 at the beginning.

p. 608, 3. *Of those who say it is motion—or of the ordered kind*] So that it may be immediately understood which philosophers' opinions Plotinus is touching upon in this place, I will add the Excerpts of Stobaeus in the *Physical Eclogues* (I. 248—256): **Pythagoras** (says time is) the sphere of that which surrounds.—The **Stoics**, that the essence of time is motion itself.—**Xenocrates**, a measure of things generated and eternal motion. **Chrysippus** said it is the measure of slowness and speed. **Epicurus** called it an accident [of accidents], that is, a consequence of motions. **Antiphanes** and **Critolaus** called time a thought or a measure, not a self-existing substance.—The **Aristotelians**—that time is not motion, yet not without motion.—**Zeno** said that time is the interval of motion, and this is both the measure and the criterion of speed and slowness, as the case may be.—**Apollodorus** in his *Art of Physics* defines time thus: Time is the interval of the motion of the cosmos, etc. I have touched upon the views of other philosophers here and there and at the title of this book (p. 325). **Taylor** <note>Thomas Taylor "The Platonist," 1758–1835</note> mentions the opinions of Archytas, Aristotle, and several other philosophers concerning time in his notes to the English version of this passage (p. 195).

p. 610, 5. *just as water flowing again and again*] A common simile. Marcus Aurelius (V. 23) says "like a river." Others very frequently say: "in the manner of a river." I did not recall this passage of Plotinus when, regarding the words in Cicero's *On the Nature of the Gods* (I. 39): "Such is the impunity of babbling. But how licentiously! A transition of visions frequently occurs as if they were flowing"—I conjectured: "of babbling. *Like waters flowing continually* (this following Davis) a transition of visions occurs." See our Dionysius (I. p. 82 f.). To those places this Plotinian one may now be added. We praised another below at p. 351. E. in the same work.

p. 611, 9. *and you might say—being of both*] Our manuscripts show no variation. The end is to be rendered literally as if it were clearly one thing for both. **Taylor** puts it thus: "*And you may say that the time of each is the same, though its relation to the one is different from its relation to the other.*"

— 13. *Number of motion or measure*] Stobaeus, *Physical Eclogues* (I. p. 252): **Aristotle** (says) that time is the number of motion according to before and after, having neither beginning nor end, but always being, and always becoming; and that it is continuous and divisible, for its "before" and "after" are taken, and the "now" exists as a limit, for this is conceived as the end of the past and the beginning of the future. (Compare Aristotle, *Physics* IV. 11—13.) Stobaeus continues: The **Aristotelians** say time is of the motions defined according to the "now." And the "now" is a unit of rest within motion.

p. 614, 5. *but nevertheless measuring according to the before and after, whether by a point etc.*] **Posidonius** the Stoic in Stobaeus (as above, p. 258):—that the distinction is point-like <note>original: σημειώδη</note>, i.e., of the three times—present, past, and future—it is like a point. To the same Posidonius and also to **Chrysippus** (p. 260) this definition of time is attributed: that time is the interval of motion.

— 6. *This time therefore will be etc.*] **Taylor** thinks it is necessary to read "this *number*" <note>original: ὁ ἀριθμὸς</note>. No manuscript supports this conjecture, nor does Aristotle's definition necessarily require it. For he had said that *time* is the number of motion (to which Plotinus adds "or measure." See above p. 332. G. and the note there) according to before and after. Therefore, one can ask about *time* as the measurer; and in this place Plotinus describes that "now" <note>original: νῦν</note> of Aristotle, which is connected by the "before" and "after" to the whole of time. Furthermore, the same learned man [Taylor] says in that place that Aristotle's definition of time agrees with the Platonic one, adding: "*In short, time is properly the measure of motion according to the flux of being, which is the peculiarity of* GENE- <meta>catchword: GENERATION</meta>

<summary>This page provides a scholarly apparatus for Plotinus's Enneads, comparing his definitions of time and motion with those of Plato, Aristotle, the Stoics, and later commentators like Boethius and Thomas Taylor. It specifically examines the concept of the "now" (nunc/vun) as a boundary between past and future.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the scholarly commentary on Plotinus’s treatise regarding Time and Eternity, specifically focusing on the transition from eternal being to temporal becoming.</meta>

<page-num>192</page-num>
<header>192 ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS</header>

**RELATION OF BECOMING TO BE.**" <note>original: "RATION OF BECOMING TO BE." This appears to be a partial English heading or quote within the Latin commentary.</note> Indeed, you should compare this passage of Plotinus with these words of Hermes in Stobaeus, page 256, edited by Heeren, where he speaks of the three times—present, past, and future: "For since time does not stand still, having a shifting weight <note>or 'inclination'</note> nor a fixed point of rest, how can it be said to be 'present' when it is unable even to stand? And again, the past, joining with the present, and the present, joining with the future, becomes one; for they are not apart from one another in their identity, their unity, and their continuity. Thus time becomes both continuous and divided, being one and the same."

p. 615, 10. *To call it the accompaniment of motion*] Our philosopher <note>Plotinus</note> comes here to judge the definition of **Epicurus**. See above at page 331. B.

p. 616, 5. *into that disposition which we said belonged to eternity*] See above, chapter IV, page 328 and following. Compare Proclus in *Platonic Theology* III. 18. p. 149, where there are other points we touched upon above, and these: — "rather, eternity is characterized by the infinite; for it contains infinite time within itself," etc. Compare V. 30. p. 311. I provided this passage above at the end of the annotations to the title of this book at page 325. A. The same author in his commentary on the *Parmenides*, Volume VI, page 102, edited by Cousin: "and eternity is infinite because of the fountain of infinity, which supplies the inexhaustible from above to all essences, powers, activities, cycles, and generations; and the order of infinite things ascends to this and descends from it." Boethius in *The Consolation of Philosophy* V. 6. after the beginning: "**Eternity, therefore, is the total, simultaneous, and perfect possession of an unending life.**"

— 8. (*time—at least was not*)] I have decided these words should be included in a parenthesis, so that what follows—*about to be generated*, etc.—might be closely connected with the preceding words *we must lead ourselves back to—*. Furthermore, it is helpful to place here the annotation of **Taylor**: "*'Time,' he says, 'as well as the world, is said to have been generated, not because it once was not, for it always existed, but because it depends for its subsistence on causes naturally prior to itself.'*"

— 10. *how—time fell out*] Whoever reads the subsequent parts in order will have no doubt that in the word *ekpiptein* <note>to fall out/away</note> there is the power of "falling away" and ***degenerating*** in this passage. Regarding this meaning, Palairetus says more in *Philological and Critical Observations*, page 522 (on Revelation 2:5: "remember from whence thou art fallen.") Philostratus in *Life of Apollonius* V. 7. p. 193, edited by Olearius, concerning Nero: — "to fall away from himself and the Romans so far as to sing songs instead of making laws, and to beg <note>Olear. from the Manuscripts instead of 'to philosophize'. In the Schellershem Manuscript, whose readings I have noted, a second hand wrote 'to beg', deleting 'to philosophize'. This passage should therefore be added to those collected by Ruhnken in his Lexicon to Timaeus, page 10.</note>." Our author himself uses "To fall away from happiness" in I. 4. 7. and similar phrases elsewhere, which Coraes touched upon in *Atakta* II. page 263 and following.

— 11. *but perhaps, if the Muses were also then*] If the reading is true, perhaps after the "but" one should think "it happened." Yet even so, a convenient sense does not arise. Perhaps it should read: *but perhaps again*, that is: *But on the contrary, perhaps* he will call upon the Muses not inaptly, if indeed the Muses existed even then. I need not explain that the invocation of the Muses is mentioned here because Homer and the rest of the poets affirmed they could sing of the Creation of the World and the things that preceded it by the help of the Muses, the daughters of Memory. **Taylor** says on this passage: The Muses, insofar as they are in Apollo, or in the intellectual order of things, exist before time; but insofar as time is said to take a beginning, the Muses, according to their mundane substance, do not exist before time is generated.

p. 617, 11. *first it made itself temporal <note>added to the Lexicons</note>, and then it gave to that which was created (that is, the sensible world) to be a slave to time, etc.*] To these and the following points Proclus contributes in *Elements of Theology* LV. p. 86: "that which 'at some time' is not truly 'being' is the same as that which is 'generated'; therefore the 'at some time being' is not a middle term. It remains, then, that the 'always becoming' is the middle between both: by 'becoming' it joins itself <note>original: "se jungens"</note> to the lower things, but by 'always' it imitates the eternal nature. From these things it is clear that eternity was twofold (Aristotle, *On the Heavens* II. 1. p. 36, edited by Sylburg): one is eternal, the other is according to time. One is a standing eternity, the other a becoming one. And the one has its being gathered together and all at once; the other is poured out and spread out according to temporal extension <note>reading 'parataxis' for 'parastasis'</note> and the one is whole in itself, the other consists of parts, each of which is separate according to 'before' and 'after'." Boethius in *The Consolation of Philosophy* V. 6. after the beginning: "**For whatever lives in time, that being present proceeds from the past into the future—**"

# BOOK VII. ENNEAD THREE. p. 615—624.

it passes away, and nothing is established in time that can embrace the whole span of its life at once; but it has not yet grasped tomorrow, and it has already lost yesterday. Even in today's life, you live no more than in that moving and transitory moment. Therefore, that which suffers the condition of time—even if, as Aristotle judged regarding the world, it never began to be nor shall ever cease, and its common life is extended into infinity <note>original: *παρατείνεται* (parateinetai), see the note immediately following regarding the word *παράτασιν* (paratasin, meaning "extension")</note>—is nevertheless not yet of such a kind that it may rightly be believed to be eternal. For it does not comprehend and embrace the whole span of an infinite life all at once; rather, it no longer possesses the past and does not yet have the future." cf. above chapter II of this book p. 327. A.

p. 618, 3. **If, then, someone should say that time—is life from one life to another**] Taylor, following Ficinus <note>Marsilio Ficino, the 15th-century Platonist</note>, wanted the word "activity" <note>original: *ἐνέργειαν* (energeian)</note>, the act of the giver. Three manuscript books provide the true reading along with the false one which occupies the edition: "time is life" <note>original: *χρόνον ζωὴν* (chronon zōēn)</note>. We have deleted the former and retained the latter. This is confirmed by Simplicius in his commentary on Aristotle's *Physics* p. 187. b. Aldine edition, who, presenting these words of Plotinus verbatim, has "life" <note>original: *ζωὴν* (zōēn)</note>, and in the following passages refers to this place in Plotinus thus:—"in these matters he (Plotinus) thinks time is the transitive life of the soul." <note>original: *τὴν μεταβατικὴν τῆς ψυχῆς ζωήν*</note>. Furthermore, this definition was more easily handled by the Greeks, who distinguished between "life" as a principle <note>original: *ζωὴν* (zōēn)</note> and "life" as a career or way of living <note>original: *βίον* (bion)</note>, than by the Latins or ourselves. Cf. Ammonius p. 30. p. 32. Schaefer; perhaps you might clarify the difference in this passage if you translate:—"that time is the life of the soul <note>original: *ζωὴν*</note>, and in transitory motion it passes from one action of life to another <note>original: *βίον*</note>." Simplicius presents these words of Plotinus intact until the end of the chapter in the place cited, prefacing them thus: "It is perhaps better to hear the intellectual words of Plotinus himself." <note>original: *Κάλλιον δὲ ἴσως αὐτῶν ἀκοῦσαι τῶν νοερῶν τοῦ Πλωτίνου ῥημάτων*</note>. Proclus also looked back at these Plotinian passages in *On the Theology of Plato* III. 18. p. 149, whose passages we praised above at p. 325. 328. 333. Taylor himself touches upon this passage of Proclus here, adding: "*This definition of time by Proclus appears to me to be uncommonly beautiful and accurate.*"

p. 619, 4. **silently** <note>original: *ἀψοφητὶ* (apsophēti)</note>] Plato *Timaeus* p. 37. p. 35. Bekker.—"moving without sound or echo." <note>original: *φερόμενος ἄνευ φθόγγου καὶ ἠχῆς*</note>. Our author uses "silently" quite often, as in III. 8. 4. IV. 4. 14. V. 8. 7. V. 8. 11. Olympiodorus in *On the Alcibiades* p. 29. where I have directed readers to Hesychius I. p. 98. note; Etymologicum Gudianum p. 101. Dorville on Chariton p. 260. Leipzig [p. 101. Amsterdam ed.] and Theodoret Vol. I. p. 1104. Schulz. "Silence" <note>original: *Ἀψοφία*</note> is read above in II. 1. 6. p. 100.

p. 620, 2. **Wherefore it is also said**] In Plato's *Timaeus* p. 37. end. p. 36. sq. Bekker.
— 5. **that times are spoken of by him, as well as the circuits of the stars, etc.**] Plato in the *Timaeus* p. 38. and p. 39. p. 37. sqq. Bekker.

p. 621, 5. **That, therefore, which is measured by the revolution, etc.**] Simplicius in Aristotle's *Physics* p. 187. b. Aldine: "And (Plotinus) also proposes that time does not measure motion, but motion measures time, since time is indeed invisible, but motion is visible; and from things that are manifest, things that are invisible are known and measured. He says, therefore, that what is measured by the revolution, etc." <note>original: *προτίθησι δὲ καὶ (ὁ Πλωτῖνος) ὅτι οὐχ ὁ χρόνος μετρεῖ τὴν κίνησιν...*</note>. For he adds the words of Plotinus up to "having been made manifest" <note>original: *δηλωθεὶς*</note> without any variation in the reading.

p. 622, 4. **Wherefore also of motion—it is measured by motion**] Found in Simplicius on Aristotle's *Physics* p. 187. b.

p. 624, 1. **But if someone should say that time is not in a substance** <note>original: *ἐν οὐχ ὑποστάσει*</note>] He seems in this place to touch upon the opinions of Antiphanes and Critolaus. See above at page 331. B.

— 16. **Is time, then, also in us?**] It would be worthwhile to compare these decrees of Plotinus concerning Time with the decrees of Kant, the philosopher of Königsberg, who taught that both time and space are forms of human intuition. Concerning this opinion, as it is well known to the public, there is no reason for me to add more. Proclus in *On the Alcibiades* p. 236. sq.: "Wherefore Socrates also demands that he state the time of his thinking that he did not know. For just as before, it is necessary that all such changes be measured by time. Wherefore the divine Aristotle in this matter at least admits motion in the soul and change according to time." (See Aristotle *On the Soul* I. 3. III. 10. *Categories* p. 55. sqq. Sylburg. *Topics* II. p. 296.) "But that the soul which is joined to a body and is changing from vice to virtue needs time, is surely manifest to everyone. But already some say that the soul, being by itself, does not need time in its activity, but on the contrary, that the soul itself generates time. This, I think, requires some explanation, etc." <note>original: *Διὸ καὶ ὁ Σωκράτης ἀπαιτεῖ χρόνον...*</note>. Cf. the same author in *Elements of Theology* c. 197—200. and in *On the Parmenides* Vol. IV. p. 103. Cousin. These final parts, however, from the words "is [time] then" <note>original: *ἆρ' οὖν*</note> until the end of the book, are again presented by Simplicius in the place cited.

->BOOK VIII.<-
**p. 630, 7. ΠΕΡΙ ΦΥΣΕΩΣ ΚΑΙ ΘΕΩΡΙΑΣ ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥ ΕΝΟΣ [On Nature, Contemplation, and the One]** Thus this book is also titled in Porphyry’s *Life of Plotinus* ch. 24, but in the same work in another place, ch. 5, simply: *περὶ θεωρίας* [On Contemplation]. See Fabricius at page 143. Moreover, in chronological order, it is the thirtieth. See ibid. Regarding the term *Theoria* [Contemplation], to begin here, it extends widely through the monuments of Greek writers. It is not pertinent to pursue every variety; the primary usages of the philosophers must be maintained. And since [abbrev: ꝙ → quod] Plutarch in *De Musica* p. 1140. E. p. 663 Wytt. says: *καὶ τὸ θεωρεῖν—ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ τὴν προσηγορίαν ἔλαβε* [and contemplation took its name from God], this subsequently pertained even to the latest Grammarians. Thomas Magister p. 446 Bernard.: *λέγεται δὲ θεωρία καὶ ἡ περὶ τὸν θεὸν σχολὴ, καὶ διηνεκὴς αὐτοῦ φαντασία* [the leisure concerning God and the constant imagination of Him is called contemplation]. He adds: *ἡ πράγματός τινος κατανόησις* [the understanding of a certain thing]. And in these words, the principal meanings of the voice among philosophers are touched upon. For by the Pythagoreans, *theorein* is used for the accurate knowledge of the nature of the universe and those things which pertain to wisdom, as in Perictyone in Stobaeus, *Florilegium* T. I. p. 7. p. 24 ed. Gaisford.: *γέγονε δὲ συνέστα ὁ ἄνθρωπος ποττὸ θεωρῆσαι τὸν λόγον τᾶς τῶν ὅλων φύσιος καὶ τᾶς σοφίας κ. τ. λ.* [man was constituted for the purpose of contemplating the reason of the nature of the whole and of wisdom, etc.]. Hence *epistemonike theoria* [scientific contemplation] is mentioned in the history of the Pythagorean discipline by Iamblichus XVI, *De Vita Pythagorae* p. 56 Kust., and *mathemata kai theoria* [studies and contemplation] ibid. p. 62: *καὶ ἄνευ μαθημάτων καὶ θεωρίας* [even without studies and contemplation], where however *kai* [and] is absent from the second place in one of the books from which I have excerpts. And since these same philosophers devoted effort to geometry, mathematical disciplines, and astronomy (as we call it today), hence *theoria* in their writings is also used for contemplation (properly so called) and consideration, or for the knowledge of the stars, as a sublime study worthy of philosophers: Perictyone in Stobaeus, *Floril.* Tit. 79. p. 457. p. 118 Gaisf. [Greek passage describes the sight of parents as a divine and beautiful vision, exceeding even that of the sun and stars]. (Jacobs on *Anthol. Gr.* IX. p. 293: *ἀμφιχορεύεται*) and if anyone thinks any other thing is greater and is a *theoria* of existing things (Jacobs l. l. and more divine than existing things, which [abbrev: ꝙ → quod] Conr. Orellius received in *Opuscull. Graecorr. sententioss.* II. p. 350, though Jacobs does not mention it in *Lection. Stobensibus*. Cod. A. at Gaisford has *μεῖζον ἐόντων καὶ θεωρίην* [greater of existing things and contemplation]. From this and the common reading, you might more smoothly derive: *μεῖζον εἶναι τῶν κατὰ θεωρίην ἐόντων* [to be greater than those things existing according to contemplation]: and if anyone should judge a work greater among those things which pertain to contemplation.) But regarding Plato, to cross over to that point, no one is ignorant that he uses *theorein*, *theorian*, and *theorias* no less when dealing with the higher investigation of things which this world and heaven contain, than with the subtler knowledge of human nature, morals, and laws, but truly also regarding the higher spectacle of that world in which perennial ideas shine. Hence these are very frequent through his dialogues: *nous theates* [intellect as spectator], *theasthai* [to behold], *theorein* [to contemplate], *ho theoron* [the one contemplating] (or *ho theomenos* [the one beholding]) the beautiful itself, the good itself, and similar things. I will add one place, since more are not needed, from the books *De Rep.* [The Republic] VII. p. 517. near the end p. 332 Bekk.: [Greek passage describes the confusion of one who returns from divine contemplations to human evils, still blinking in the darkness]. Themistius looked to this in *Orat. de Praefectura* c. 30. p. 72 ed. prc. Mediol.:—that Plato in the *Republic* refers to those descending from divine contemplation to human contemplation by this word, etc. Porphyry expressed the same place in *De Vita Plot.* c. XXIII. p. 138. Alcinous in *De Doctr. Plat.* ch. III. p. 453: "The zeal of the philosopher according to Plato seems to be in three things: in the vision and knowledge of existing things, in the practice of beautiful things, and in the contemplation of reason itself"; cf. the same ch. VII. Aristotle also distinguishes *theoria* as *speculation*, as we say today, and the speculative life (*theoretiken*) from *praxis*, action, and the active life. Read only *Ethicc. ad Nicom.* X. 7. 8. p. 183. sqq. Sylb. Similarly Eudorus the Academic in Stobaeus' *Eclogg. Physs. et Eth.* II. p. 48 Heeren. places these three as distinct from one another: *theorian*, or inspection; *horman*, appetite; and *praxin*, action. And this distinction of *theoria* and *praxis* pertained to later philosophers as well, such as Philo Judaeus. See *Leg. Allegorr.* I. p. 152 Pfeiff. Yet that same Stagirite [Aristotle] in the books *De Anima* II. 1. p. 22 Sylb. separates *epistemen*, science, from *theoria*, speculation. For he says thus in *De Anima*: "matter is potentiality; form is entelechy; and this in two ways: one as science, the other as contemplating." But the whole place must be inspected—

->BOOK VIII. ENNEAD III. p. 630—631. 195<-

—Also, a subtle disputation concerning any matter, and even a writing on the same, is called *theoria*. Cicero *ad Att.* XII. 6. cf. I. A. Ernesti *Indic. Graecit. Cicer.* in voc. It is also a purpose or subject, for example, of a writing, a book, etc., as Toup teaches on Longinus *De Sublim.* XXXIX. 1. and just as *contemplatio* [contemplation] and *visio* [vision] are sometimes used by the Latins for *species* [appearance] and *similitudo* [likeness]; so also for the Greeks *theoria*, and *thoria* for more recent ones. Whence it is no wonder that it sometimes even signifies *color*. See Salmasius’ *Exercitatt. Plin.* p. 169. 322. 541. and Boissonade on Herodian’s *Epimerismm.* p. 45. Truly, those philosophers who subsequently applied themselves to Plato: they for the most part recalled *theoria* and related words to Platonic usage, and use it for the contemplation of divine, eternal, and universally sublime things. It is a long task, and not necessary, to pursue these individually. The books of Philo Judaeus, Origen, and Clement of Alexandria speak of this. I will set down one place from Theodore Abucara *De Unione et Incarnatione* p. 71, with which I may wipe away a blemish: [Greek passage describes the intellect having another specific vision beyond the eyes, which we call contemplation]. (διαθροῦσαν corrected: rightly). Other places were gathered by Suicer in *Thes. Eccles.* under the words *theoreo*, *theoria*, among them those where "contemplation of the spiritual sense" and the "allegorical sense" itself is called *theoria*. Hence the word takes on the force of *hyponoias* [under-meaning] and *allegorias* [allegory]. For which reason, frequently the interpretation "according to anagoge," "according to allegory," or "according to contemplation" is opposed to the interpretation "according to history" and "according to the text." Rittershusius teaches this on Amphilochius in the metrical Epistle to Seleucus v. 244. p. 768 ed. Orell. Matthaei in annot. 69 to *Quatuor Homilias Joannis Chrysostomi* IV. p. 107. Hence Dionysius the Areopagite titled that part of the books *De Hierarchia* which deals with the allegorical interpretation of the Sacraments as *theoria*. On the other hand, those philosophers who followed Plato but also retained ethnic religions, take the word *theoria* partly universally for contemplation or science (See e.g., Plotin. II. 9. 17. p. 216. C.), partly for the mental vision of forms (*ton ideon* cf. I. 1. 7. p. 4. F.), partly for the science of divine things, or Theology, especially that which Plato handed down (Proclus in *Platonis Theol.* I. 1. p. 1. inf. cf. Longin. apud Porphyr. *De Vita Plotini* p. 14.) and they turn the force of the word into other parts as well, which are joined with contemplation and speculation, as we call it. Now if you ask how Plotinus accepts this word in this very book, since he recognizes even a *theoria* of the earth, plants, and trees: I would be doing what has already been done if I wished to reconsider this matter after Marsilio Ficino’s Commentary. I will set down other things in the Annotations. **THOMAS TAYLOR** translated this book into English in the book *Five Books of Plotinus*. Lond. 1794. p. 199. sqq. I myself translated it into German and presented it with annotation in the book: *STUDIEN edited by C. Daub and Fr. Creuzer* Vol. I. p. 30—103. (Furthermore, because [abbrev: ꝙ → quod] in that translation I had everywhere interpreted *theoria*, *theorein* as *Betrachtung, betrachen* [contemplation, contemplate]: now I would prefer: *Anschauung, schauen* or *anschauen* [intuition, behold].) Tennemann, in *Geschichte der Philosophie* Vol. VI. p. 108. sqq., reduced the argument of this Plotinian book into the number of individual propositions and (as must be observed in all the writings of this man) examined it according to the measure of Kantian philosophy.

**p. 630, 9. ΠΑΙΖΟΝΤΕΣ δὴ—σπουδάζειν [Playing indeed—to be serious]** Worthy of comparison are those things which Our Author [Plotinus] explains in a certain higher sense regarding these mutually opposed things in III. 2. 15. coll. Platon. *Phaedr.* p. 348. Heindf. It must be held, however, that in Plotinus the *spoudaios* [serious/virtuous man] is the same as the *kalos kagathos* [noble and good] for the Socratics, and the *sophos* [wise man] for the Stoics. Cf. Lucian *Icaromenipp.* c. 4. Altogether compare Courier on Longus' *Pastorall.* p. 206. sq. and Simner in *Auctar. Animadverss. ad Long.* p. 171.

**p. 631, 11. ἣν ἀφάνταστόν φασι καὶ ἄλογον εἶναι [which they say is without imagination and without reason]** In what sense the word *aphantastos* is to be understood you will best learn from there, if you consider what *phantasia* [imagination] is for Plato. Regarding which matter see Plat. *Sophist.* p. 296.

**— 13. Ὅτι μὲν οὖν οὔτε χεῖρες ἐνταῦθα κ. τ. λ. [That therefore neither hands are here etc.]** In this chapter Plotinus attacks the opinions of those philosophers who thought that whatever was produced in the nature of things was produced by elements and a certain motion, over which no superior intelligent force and nature presided. He himself contends that whatever happens in bodies or is moved, is produced by a certain incorporeal nature or form, to which those things are subjected, but which itself does not depend from elsewhere.

**p. 631,13. ἐπακτὸν ἢ σύμφυτον [adventitious or innate]** Herodotus opposes *epakton* and *syntrophon* [innate] to each other. VII. 102. cf. also Pindar *Olymp.* X. 107. and the Scholia there. On the whole passage see Cudworth *Syst. int.* p. 164 ed. Mosh. I have placed other things below at p. 380. B.

**— 17. ἢ κοροπλάσται [or puppet-makers]** The Attic form of this word is *koroplathoi*, which Plato himself uses. See Ruhnken on Tim. *Lex. Plat.* p. 149. coll. p. 166. They are also called *peloplathoi*, as in Demosthenes in *Or. Philipp.* I. see Wieland *Att. Museum* III. p. 468. Ezech. Spanheim on Julian *Caes.* (*Preuves des remarques*) p. 107.

**p. 632, 5. καὶ συνεῖναι ὡς μένειν δεῖ [and to be with as it must remain]** Perhaps read *synienai* [to understand]. Wesseling thus corrected it in Herodotus V. 80. p. 412 from the Manuscripts, where it was *syneinai*. cf. his annot. p. 11. But *syneinai* is found in Plat. in *Cratylo* 28. and in Antonin. Philos. [Marcus Aurelius] V. 6. where cf. Gataker. Below however in ch. 3 *synienai* is read twice.

**— 8. οὐκ ἔσται τὸ κινοῦν πρώτως [there will not be the primary mover]** You will learn the meaning of the word *kinesis* [motion] in Plato, which is not always one and the same, by comparing the passages *Theaet.* p. 132. sq. where you have our author; *Tim.* p. 301. sq. 348. *De Rep.* X. p. 298. sq. where it signifies the change of qualities, as they say; as in Plotin. I. 1. 6. where *aisthesis* [sensation] is called *kinesis somatos* [motion of the body], and likewise *alloiosis* [alteration] is said to be a genus of motion: v. *Enn.* VI. 3. 21. coll. 23.—Furthermore, in the words *αὐτῆς δὲ οὐδὲν κινούμενον* [but of itself nothing being moved] our philosopher seems to look back to Plato in *Phaedrus* p. 38 Bekk. p. 244 ed. Heindf., which passage Cicero received into the first book of the *Tusculans* ch. 23. 53—55 [and with a few changes into the 6th book *De Rep.* ch. 25. 26. (*Somn. Scip.* VIII.)] where see the annot. of Moser p. 504. coll. p. 557—560.] where see Davies with the annotation of Heindorf to the *Phaedrus* compared.

**— 12. Καὶ γὰρ εἶδος αὐτὴν δεῖ εἶναι [For indeed it must be a form]** What *eidos* [form] is for our author you will learn from Plato, whom Plotinus follows in the meanings of this word, as everywhere. See Platon. *Sophist.* p. 253 Steph. *Parmenid.* p. 135. *Politic.* p. 285. (cf. Diog. Laert. II. 19. Aristot. *Metaph.* I. 6.) *Phaedon.* p. 100. but go also to our author himself *Enn.* VI. 3. 9. II. 3. 17. coll. III. 2. 2. and 22. On the word *hyle* [matter] see *Enn.* III. 6. 7. and 9. 10. coll. Plat. *Phileb.* p. 23. sqq. *Tim.* p. 50. sqq. From matter universally thought, our author distinguishes *ἡ ὑποκειμένη καὶ δημιουργουμένη* [the underlying and fashioned]. *Enn.* III. 6. 6. sq. IV. 7. 11.

**— 17. ἐν τοῖς φυτοῖς τοὺς λόγους εἶναι τοὺς ποιοῦντας [the reasons in plants are those which act]** Thus Zeno the Stoic in Diog. Laert. VII. 134. "that which acts (is) the reason in it (matter), God—fashioning each thing." Whence also §. 136 it is called *logos spermatikos* [seminal reason]. Cf. Gataker on Antonin. p. 141. There is also in Plotinus *logos ho en spermati* [the reason in the seed]. *Enn.* III. 2. 2.

**p. 633, 2. ἔσχατος ἤδη καὶ νεκρὸς [already last and dead]** You have *nekron* [dead] in the same sense in Clem. Alex. *Strom.* IV. p. 633. Even the most ancient philosophers, and especially Aristotle, distinguished between *eidos* and *morphe* [shape], whose passages Tülleborn collected on the *Fragments of Parmenides* in the book titled *Beiträge Zur Geschichte der Philosophie* VI. 80.

**p. 634, 7. Καὶ εἴ τις δὲ αὐτὴν κ. τ. λ. [And if someone indeed... her etc.]** Those things which Iamblichus produces from Plotinus in Stobaeus' *Eclogae* I. 52. p. 880. 882. seem to Heeren to pertain here. see ib. p. 881. his note. Furthermore, Tiedemann in *Geist d. spekulat. Philosophie* III. p. 323. sqq. examined these dogmas concerning the efficacy of the world soul in his own way and indeed set out to explode them.

**— 12. ἔχειν—ὑπάρχει [to have—it is present]** You have the same construction in Xenophon in *Cyrop.* IV. 5. 31. cf. Wyttenb. on *Eclog. Hist.* p. 199. sqq. I have corrected *καὶ μοὶ γενομένῃ*. For *γενομένη* was without sense.

**— 15. καὶ μοὶ τὸ τῆς μητρὸς κ. τ. λ. [and for me that of the mother etc.]** Cf. *Enn.* II. 9. 2. On the words *γεωμέτραι θεωροῦντες* [geometers contemplating] in the preceding things cf. Diog. Laert. III. §. 84.

**p. 635, 7. καὶ οὐκέτι ἐζήτησεν, ἀλλὰ θεώρημα ἀποτελέσασα [and no longer sought, but having completed the theorem]** Someone might perhaps wish it written: *οὐκέτι ἐζήτησεν ἄλλα, θεώρημα ἀποτελέσασα* [sought no other things]. But neither do the Manuscripts support this, nor is the use of the Participle for the Indicative rare (see Dorville on Chariton p. 624 ed. Lips. Raphel on *Acts of the Apostles* XXIV. 5.) and Plotinus elsewhere also uses the verb *zetein* [to seek] absolutely, as they say, and without an object.

**— 10. τὴν τοῦ ὕπνου τοῦ ἐγρηγορότος [that of the waking sleep]** Plotinus seems to look back to his Plato in *Tim.* p. 52. Compare our author *Enn.* II. 5. 3. and the annotation there p. 175. C. Lucian *Hermotim.* c. 1. Alciphron *Epist.* III. 38. and the interpreters there. Add Plotin. *Enn.* III. 6. 6. p. 310. coll. Ficin. p. 340, where I touched upon the same matter. Compare also at p. 307. G. (III. 6. 5.)

**— 19. ἐφιέμενοι δὲ αὐτὸ ἰδεῖν—ὃ μὴ νῷ ἐδύναντο [desiring to see it—what they could not by intellect]** A similar difference is established by the reasoning of the Indian phi-

[[vocabulary: σύμφυτον (innate), κίνησις (motion), εἶδος (species/form), ὕλη (matter), λόγος (reason/word)]]

--- Page 204 ---
[[language: Latin]]

->BOOK VIII. ENNEAD III. p. 634—644. 197<-

—losophers, which is explained in the poem *Bhagavad-Gita*. For there (XIV. 5—8.) *Radschas*, i.e., the terrestrial habit, is said to be of those who (since they cannot reach *Sattwa* or the true essence and therefore the knowledge of truth and pure virtue) fall down to individual things, and the shadows and appearances of things, and are distracted into various parts by the zeal for acting. See Guil. de Humboldt’s vernacular disputation on the Poem *Bhagavad-Gita* in *Actis. Societ. Regiae Berolin.* 1826. p. 29. sq.

**p. 636, 12. τὴν ψυχὴν τὴν πρὸ ταύτης [the soul before this one]** Plotinus places three principles: first *τὸ ἀγαθὸν* [the good], second *τὸν νοῦν* [the intellect], third *τὴν ψυχὴν τοῦ παντὸς s. τῶν ὅλων* [the soul of the universe or of the whole]. Regarding which matter see especially *Enn.* II. 9. 1. p. 199. C. coll. III. 5. 3. V. 2. 1. V. 1. 6. V. 1. 3. This is that Plotinian Trinity, which among many has earned for our author the name of a friend of Christians and Christianity: although from the same reasoning others accused him of Tritheism. Furthermore, compare what we have placed in the *Prolegomena* 127. V. lit. 6. concerning the Principles of Plotinus.

**— 13. καὶ ἡ ἐξ ὧν ἐγνώκει ὠδὶς [and the birth-pang from what she had known]** Not once does Our Author use this simile. Thus *Enn.* IV. 7. 13. It is Platonic. See *Sympos.* p. 70. Ast. and cited there *Republ.* VI. p. 490. p. 285. Bekk.

**— 16. ἐν παιδίῳ, ἴνδαλμα ἔχοντι ἁπάντων [in a child, having the image of all things]** Plotinus seems to look back to the Platonic doctrine of recollection or reminiscence, namely that learning is nothing other than to remember (*anamnesin*). See Plat. *Phaedon.* p. 72. sq.

**p 637, 1. πρώτῃ μεταλήψει μεταλαμβάνον [partaking in the first participation]** Concerning this use of the verb *metalambanein* see Jacobs on Stobaeus p. 256. To the following *πρόεισιν ἡ ζωή* [life proceeds] cf. *Enn.* II. 9. 2. where the same locution is found. Furthermore, all these are Platonic: see only *De Rep.* IV. p. 431. a. cf. Cicer. *Tuscc.* I. 10. Philon. Jud. *De victim. offer.* p. 858.

**— 12. τῷ ἐξίτηλον καταβαῖνον γίνεσθαι [by the fact that it becomes fading as it descends]** On the various use of the word *exitylos* see Stephanus' *Thes. L. Gr.* s. v. Sturz in *Lex. Xenoph.* Wyttenbach in *Selectt. Historr.* p. 349. and ourselves above on I. 6. 3. Moreover, Basil Sel. in *De vita S. Theclae* p. 293 joined it with the word *amydron* [faint]. cf. Boissonade's *Anecdott. grr.* I. page 288. On the word *asyphēti* [silently] v. above on III. 7. 11. p. 336. F.

**— 14. Καὶ ψυχὴ δὲ ἡ θεωροῦσα [And the soul indeed which contemplates]** Ficino might seem to have had a fuller version of this passage, if indeed a conjecture can be made from his version.

**— 17. ἢ καὶ διὰ τοῦτο πανταχοῦ [or also because of this everywhere]** Ficino seems to have read this passage differently. Perhaps it should be read *διὰ τούτου* [through this].

**p. 638, 1. Διὸ ὁ ἡνίοχος τοῖς Ἵπποις δίδωσιν [Wherefore the charioteer gives to the horses]** Plotinus looks back to that very common place of Plato in *Phaedrus* p. 272. Heindf. concerning the charioteer and the two different horses. And that occurs in other places in Our Author and *Enn.* I. 6. 8. and 9. on which places see Wyttenbach in *Epist. Crit.* p. 250 ed. Schaefer.

**— 11. τοῦτο δὲ ποῦ; ἐν ψυχῇ [and where is this? in the soul]** Cf. Platon. *Phaedon.* p. 96. p. 83. Bekk. and there Wyttenb. p. 254.

**— 16. εἴσω κεῖται. [it lies within]** This use of the word *eiso* is familiar to more recent writers. See Valckenaer on Eurip. *Phoeniss.* p. 727.

**p. 639, 16. εἶτ᾽ ἐπανιοῦσα, πάλιν θεωρεῖ [then returning, she contemplates again]** Cf. *Enn.* V. 8. 10. I. 6. 9. where it is *opsis ede genomenos* [having already become sight]. But the whole passage should be compared.

**p. 640, 3. ἤδη γὰρ οὗτος πρὸς τὸ ἓν [for already this one is toward the one]** Cf. Clem. Alex. *Strom.* IV. 23. where it concerns the Pythagorean precept *ἕνα—μοναδικὸν γενέσθαι* [to become one—monadic].

**— 11. ποιοῦντα δεικνύσι [showing them acting]** Ed. *δείκνυσι*. I corrected it, referring it to the *hypostaseis* [hypostases].

**p. 642, 4. ἡ δὲ ἐναργεστέρα αὕτη [and this clearer one]** I thus corrected it, moved by the third chapter of this book p. 346. A.

**— 18. ὡς βέλτιον αὐτῷ [as better for it]** Ficino seems to have read *ᾧ βέλτιον*, with *αὐτῷ* omitted. which [abbrev: ꝙ → quod] is convenient for the meaning.

**p. 643, 8. καὶ σωρός τις συμφορητὸς ἔσται [and it will be a certain collected heap]** Plotinus' disciple, Porphyry, uses the word *soros* in the same sense in Stob. *Eclogg.* p. 823 Heeren.

**p. 644, 1. δεῖ τὸ πρὸ τοῦ δύο λαβεῖν [it is necessary to take that which is before the two]** Tiedemann in *Geist. der spekul. Philosophie* III. p. 374. sqq. and p. 386 tried to examine these and the following things, saying that Plotinus took this dogma of unity from Pythagoras and Plato.

**— 7. Τί οὖν τοῦτο, καὶ ποῖόν τι κ. τ. λ. [What then is this, and of what kind etc.]** How *ho nous* [the intellect] and *to on* [being] agree and what they differ in according to Plotinus' opinion v. *Enn.* V. 9. 2. D. coll. V. 2. 1. V. 3. 13.

**— 14. ἁλίσκοιτο ἐπιβολῇ ἀθρόᾳ: [it might be grasped by a sudden intuition:]** what [abbrev: ꝙ → quod] is here *epibole* is for Plato *epereisis* [resting upon]: which our author himself uses also a little above when he says: *ἐρείδοντες τὴν διάνοιαν* [resting the thought]. Cf. Ign. Rossi *Commentat. Laert.* p. 277. Which is the use of the Epicureans.

198 ->ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS<-

On the Stoics' use of the same word see at Stob. *Eclogg.* p. 120.

**p. 644, 17. ὥσπερ εἰ φωνῆς [as if of a voice]** Nicol. Methonensis also followed the simile of the voice in Proclus *Inst. Theol.* c. 23. p. 43.

**p. 645, 8. διέξοδος [discourse/passage]** We treated this word above p. 189. B. Add Clem. Alex. *Strom.* IV. 25.

**— 9. ἀκριβῶς, καὶ οὐκ ὁλοσχερῶς [accurately, and not generally]** See on this use of the word *holoscheros* Gataker on Antonin. p. 11. who is also to be compared on the word *adiarthrotos* [inarticulately] p. 83.

**— 11. καὶ ἀρχὴ ζωῆς [and the principle of life]** These are drawn from Platonic springs. See *Cratyl.* p. 396 Steph. *Phileb.* p. 26. sq. Cf. Clem. Alex. Vol. I. p. 638 Potter.

**p. 646, 15. ἀφήσουσιν αὐτῶν τὰ ῥεύματα [they will let go of their streams]** Ficino did not rightly understand the word *rheumata*. Ammonius shows the true meaning under the word *rheithron* [stream] p. 122. Therefore we corrected it.

**— 17. οἷον ἐν ῥίζῃ ἱδρυμένης [as if fixed in a root]** Our author uses the same comparison also in *Enn.* III. 3. 7. Hence I corrected in the following things *ἔμεινε δὲ αὐτὴ* for *αὐτη*. In that place truly, from our author, even without manuscripts, *μενούσης* [remaining] should have been corrected for *ἐνούσης* [being in]. See what we annotated there p. 277. B. C. and below IV. 3. 4. p. 375. B. and annott. to p. 390. c. 25. A.

**p. 647, 4. ὃ μὴ πλῆθος ἦν. [which was not a multitude]** Brucker in *Hist. Crit. Philos.* II. p. 395. from this place thus: "The principle of all things is not all things, but above all things and the power of all things, which if it indeed were not, the rest would not be. Namely, above-being, which [abbrev: ꝙ → quod] is neither moved nor divided, nor multiplied, although all things proceed from it." Then he orders Plotinus' passages V. 1. 7. p. 489. V. 2. 1. p. 493. VI. 2. 9. p. 603 to be compared. Then he disputes concerning the passage of Iamblichus *De Mysterr.* VIII. 2. p. 158, partly contradicting Cudworth in *Syst. Intell.* c. IV. §. 36. p. 732—734. partly agreeing with him. Cf. the same Brucker p. 403. sq.

**— 7. καὶ ἐφ᾽—εἰς ὃ ἀνάξει [and toward—into which it will lead back]** These smell of a gloss: wherefore I included them in brackets; as in the following words *τοῦτο δὲ ἡ ἀρχὴ μένουσα* [and this the remaining principle].

**— 12. καὶ τὸ τίμιον [and the honorable]** Cf. Platon. *Politic.* p. 286.

**— 15. μὴ ὄντος, μὴ οὐσίας, μὴ ζωῆς [not being, not essence, not life]** He looks back to Plato *De Rep.* VI. p. 509 Steph. p. 320 Bekk.

**p. 648, 1. τῇ προσβολῇ [by the application/vision]** The Scholiast of Euripides on *Medea* p. 271 ed. Beck explains this word with the word *thea* [vision]. In this sense Plato in the *Theaetetus* and Philo Judaeus use the same word, although the former adds *ton ommaton* [of the eyes], the latter *tes opseos* [of the sight]. Just as in this place it returns in our author *Enn.* V. 8. 10.

**— 2. μετ᾽ αὐτὸ δι᾽ αὐτὸ οὐσιν [after it and because of it being]** It seems *δι᾽ αὐτοῦ* should be read.

**— 5. Ὕλη δὲ ἐν νοητοῖς [And matter in the intelligibles]** Before these perhaps a part of the sentence fell out, in which *men* [indeed] was contained, and which pertained to the *eidos nou* [form of intellect].—Plotinus explains the nature *του νοῦ* [of the intellect] by a simile drawn from seeing in the same way *Enn.* V. 3. 5. p. 500. "Intellect sees" was already the opinion of Epicharmus. V. Davis on Cic. *Tuscc.* I. 20. Jacobs on Eurip. *Helen. Animadverss.* c. X. p. 139.—Tiedemann disputes concerning these in the book *Geist der spekul. Philos.* III. p. 381. sq. Moreover, these Plotinian decrees agree with the decrees of the "Unitarians," as they call them, among the philosophers of India, that is, those who in Metaphysics do not admit a highest principle which [abbrev: ꝙ → quod] is double, and in ethics are subject neither to love nor hate, nor joy nor pain, *are not double, nor occupied in double things;* which unity the *Bhagavad-Gita* places as the first virtue of all. See Eugen. Burnouf’s annot. in Abel-Rémusat *Mélanges Asiatiques* Tom. I. p. 454.

**— 12. Φθεγξάμενος οὖν κ. τ. λ. [Having spoken then etc.]** Cf. Annot. to Proclus *Inst. Theol.* c. 8. p. 16.

**— 16. ἀγαθοειδὲς [good-form]** The word *agathoeides*, joined to the intellect, is Platonic, *De Rep.* p. 509. a. p. 236 Ast. Cf. Plotin. *Enn.* VI. 7. 18.

**p. 649, 7. Τοῦ δὴ νοῦ καλοῦ ὄντος [Indeed the intellect being beautiful]** It is Platonic: *De Rep.* VI. p. 508 Steph. p. 319 Bekk.

**— 8. ἐν φωτὶ καθαρῷ [in pure light]** He looks back to Plato *De Rep.* X. p. 616 St. Coll. Plotin. *Enn.* V. 3. 8. IV. 5. 7. Philon. Jud. *De Victim. off.* p. 859.

**— 9. ὁ καλὸς οὗτος κόσμος [this beautiful world]** Pythagoras is said to have been the author of this name in Diog. Laert. VIII. Photius *Bibliothec.* Cod. 659.—Cf. Platon. in *Gorg.* p. 508. a. especially in *Tim.* p. 29. a. from where the words of our passage were drawn.

**— 11. μηδ᾽ ἄμετρον [nor immoderate]** Platon. *Phileb.* p. 66. a. —"but first indeed concerning measure and the moderate and timely etc."

**— 12. Θάμβος—ἔχοι [Awe—might hold]** It is Homeric. *Iliad* γ. 342. and more often.

**— 13. καὶ αὐτοῦ γενόμενον ἕνα [and having become one with it]** Lest anyone should wish it corrected to *αὐτῷ*, I remark with a word that another reasoning for this place

is different from those where Our Author joins the verb *henousthai* [to be united] with the Dative; Clem. Alex. Vol. I. p. 635. is *ἑνούμενον ἐν αὐτῷ* [being united in it].

**p. 649, 16. τὸν κἀκείνου ποιητὴν [and the maker of that one]** This is Platonic from *Rep.* VI. p. 506 St. p. 315 Bekk. and p. 508 p. 318.

**p. 650, 1. κόρου—κόρος—κεκορέσθαι [of satiety—satiety—to have been satiated]** You may understand that Plotinus intentionally plays with these words by comparing these passages of the same author: III. 6. 14. V. 1. 4. V. 1. 7. V. 9. 8. Add on the words *koros*, *kore* [satiety, girl] Coray’s *Atakta* I. p. 87. sq.

**— 3. τοῦ ἀνενδεοῦς [of the one needing nothing]** The oldest philosophers (physiologists) attributed "needing nothing" to the whole and to being, e.g., Parmenides. See Tülleborn l. c. VI. p. 73 and Simplicius there.

->BOOK IX.<-
**p. 655, 7. ΕΠΙΣΚΕΨΕΙΣ ΔΙΑΦΟΡΟΙ [Different Considerations]** To be referred among the earlier books of Plotinus, if you consider the time in which each was written in order. For it holds the thirteenth place. See Porphyry *De Vita Plotini* ch. IV and ch. XXIV p. 100 and p. 143 ed. Fabric. Concerning the individual questions which our philosopher handles here, Ficino gave us the leisure for speaking in his commentary. Moreover, Proclus praises this very book; whose words will be added in the annotation to the beginning of the first chapter.

**— 10. Νοῦς, φησιν, ὁρᾷ ἐνούσας ἰδέας [Intellect, he says, sees the ideas being within]** Plato in *Timaeus* p. 39. p. 40 Bekk.—"as therefore intellect beholds the ideas being within the 'living being that is,' such kinds and as many as are in it, so he thought this one also must have such and so many." Plotinus touched upon the passage twice above, p. 200. E. where we touched upon that saying of Epicharmus, though somewhat different, "Intellect sees" etc.; and p. 204. A. But what he calls *ideas* here, he next calls *eide* [forms]. Concerning which see Wyttenb. on Platon. *Phaedon.* p. 270 and above p. 58. A.

**— 14. τὸ τοίνυν ζῶον αὐτὸ, οὐ νοῦς, ἀλλὰ νοητὸν, αὐτὸ φήσομεν [the living being itself therefore, we shall say is not intellect, but intelligible itself]** Read this to me in the book *On Numbers* ch. VIII below p. 678. A: "since therefore it is also primarily a living being, and because of this 'autozoon' [animal-itself] and is intellect and essence or truly." Which diversity Proclus also indicates in *Platonis Timaeum* p. 130: "Plotinus supposes 'autozoon' in two ways, sometimes better than intellect, as in the 'Different Considerations,' sometimes more inferior, as in the book 'On Numbers,' whenever he says that being is first, then intellect (perhaps *τὸν νοῦν*), then 'autozoon'." Thus he says in that place. I will add other things below at the cited place of the book *On Numbers*.

**— 17. ἐκεῖ γὰρ καὶ τὴν ἀλήθειάν φησιν εἶναι ἐν τῷ ὄντι [for there he says truth also is in being]** Platon. *Tim.* p. 28. p. 22. sqq. Bekk. *Phileb.* p. 64. *De Republ.* VI. p. 486.

**p. 656, 2. Ὁ γὰρ καθορᾷ—ἐν αὑτῷ κ. τ. λ. [For what he beholds—in himself etc.]** Cf. below p. 526. E: "so indeed also intellect—will behold not another light in another thing, but—itself by itself alone, pure by itself suddenly appearing." Furthermore, in these things also you may recognize certain seeds, as it were, of the *Kantian* system and those which have recently followed it in Germany, although, besides *Schelling* and *Hegel*, men of the greatest talent, I believe none of these philosophers have read these Enneads.

**p. 657, 13. διὸ οὐκ ἐν τῷ σώματι—ἀλλὰ τὸ σῶμα εἰς αὐτὴν [wherefore not in the body—but the body into her]** Alcinous in *De Doctrina Platonis* produces this opinion of this philosopher concerning the soul of the world in ch. XIV p. 489 ed. Lugd. Bat. 1614: "but with the soul (of the world) being stretched from the middle to the extremities, it happened that it contained the body of the world in a circle through the whole and covered it; so as to extend it through the whole world, and in this way bind and contain it." Furthermore, Christoph. Contoleon in the Plotinian Excerpts in Cod. Vat. n. 2141. produces these thus: "Wherefore also Plato well, not having placed the soul in the body in the case of the universe, but the body in the soul."

**p. 658, 3. οἷον κενεμβατοῦσα, καὶ ἀοριστοτέρα γινομένη [as if walking in the void, and becoming more indefinite]** On the verb *kenembatein* add to those things which were recently cited in Steph. *Thes. Valpyano*—Londin. Hesych. Phot. Suid. Zonar. *Etymol. Magn.* *Etymol. Gud.* in the word. Alex. More *Comment. ad Coloss.* II. 18. I will add a charming place of Plutarch *De Fortun. Alex. The place was treated by Wyttenb. in *Animadvv. in Plutarchi Apophthegmm. Regg.* p. 1074: he remarked nothing about that verb; to understand whose use this very Plotinian place must be held. ->BOOK I. ENNEAD IV.<-

**P. 667, 7. ΠΕΡΙ ΟΥΣΙΑΣ ΨΥΧΗΣ [On the Essence of the Soul]** The books *On the Soul* follow, all of which Porphyry included in this fourth Ennead. See *De Vita Plotini* c. 25. p. 143. sq. Fabric. This first little book is fourth in the order of time. See ibid. and ch. 4. p. 100. Moreover, the Manuscripts argue that these books are disturbed. See *Var. Lect.* at the end of book IX *Enn.* III. p. 359. B. That more things were read in them in ancient times than today appear in the MSS and in the Edition, seemingly taken from the other edition of Plotinian works, namely that of Eustochius, we will indicate next at the title of the second book p. 361.

Concerning the argument of these nine books, it [abbrev: ꝙ → quod] is joined with the primary passages of Plato both in other dialogues and in the *Phaedrus* p. 247 and in the *Timaeus* p. 34. sqq. (from which later one Plutarch also took the occasion for writing the book *On the Procreation of the Soul*,) with the decrees of Aristotle *De Anima*, especially books II and III. Nor indeed did Plotinus not look back at the opinions of the remaining philosophers. And to touch briefly only upon what the principal philosophers placed in this doctrine, the Father of History [Herodotus] himself produces the opinion of the Egyptians II. 123. whose opinion those things which Pausanias mentions in *Messen.* c. 32 concerning the wise men of the Indians and Chaldeans do not contradict, as I have taught elsewhere, in *Commentt. Herodott.* I. p. 315. sqq. Iamblichus *De Mysterr.* VIII. 6. p. 162 Gal. testifies that the Egyptians handed down that the soul is twofold. And just as other things, so you might say this doctrine is common to them with the doctrine of the Pythagoreans. For Crito or Damippus in Stobaeus' *Florileg.* Tit. III. p. 75. p. 106 Gaisf. thus: "in man the harmony of the irrational part of the soul with that having reason is virtue." More on the decrees of the Pythagoreans in this matter see in Cic. *De N. D.* I. 11. cf. Diog. Laert. VIII. 27. and especially Alcinous *De Doctrina Platonis*, who in three chapters especially, XXIII—XXV, reduced Plato’s dogmas on the soul into a compendium. The same Tully [Cicero] in the *Tusculans* I. 10. likewise *De Divinat.* I. 29. touched upon Plato’s distinction (against whom Aristotle in *De Anima* is rather unfair in reviewing the opinions of the ancients) of the *triple soul: reason, anger, and desire*, as he translates. Concerning Aristotle’s *entelechy*, we will see next at the beginning of the following book. Alexander of Aphrodisias applied himself to him in most things in the two books *De Anima*; concerning which consult Fabricius’ *Bibliothec. Gr.* Vol. V. p. 660. sqq. ed. *Harles.*—The Stoics distinguished various parts of the human soul, and to that which they judged most excellent, they deferred the primacy under the name of *to hegemonikon* [the ruling part]. And Chrysippus is said to have enumerated eight parts of the soul (Galen *De Hippocrat. et Platon. Decretis* p. 275 ed. Basil. Marcus Antonin. II. 2. Diog. Laert. VII. 50 and 110. Tertullian *De Anima* c. XVI. Cf. also the learned Baguet’s *Commentat. de Chrysippo* p. 89. sq. p. 181. sqq.) But either the dreams and opinions of the old philosophers concerning the Soul, or their sen-

[[vocabulary: ἐνέργειαι (acts/operations), οὐσία (essence), ἐντελέχεια (entelechy), ἡγεμονικόν (ruling part)]]
