—tences and subtly thought-out dogmas, which are infinite, were primarily handed down by those writers who composed books *On the Soul*. Among these the first is Aristotle’s three, in which we said the decrees of the ancient philosophers are judged. Theophrastus, Dicaearchus, Alexander of Aphrodisias, and other Peripatetics follow. Twelve and perhaps more of Chrysippus’ volumes *on the soul* seem to have existed (*Baguet* l. l.). Cicero touches upon this place of Philosophical History both elsewhere and especially in the ninth and tenth chapters of the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*. From the Platonic family, many of whom had commented on the Soul, those are to be thought to have remembered the decrees of previous philosophers as well, such as Porphyry in the books *on the powers of the soul* and *on the immortality of the soul*. (See Heeren *De Fontibus Eclogarum Jo. Stobaei* §. 53. p. 211.) Iamblichus especially, whose book *on the soul* the same learned man considers merely historical (§. 44. p. 203.). And from these and other writings Plutarch (so-called) patched together all his own things in *De Placitis Philosophorum* IV. 2—23, and, who is found much more diligent and copious in this place, John Stobaeus in the *Eclogae Physicae* I. 52. when the opinions collected by him concerning the Soul occupy the fourth part of the whole book of Physics. (Heeren to Stob. I. p. 794.). The same man makes mention of Plotinus p. 866. 880. 886. 894. 896. (where *Πλοτίνου* is erroneously printed) 902. 924. 1056 of Heeren. The same Stobaeus ibid. I. 52. §. 13. sqq. exhibits excerpts of the Porphyrian *aphormai pros ta noeta* [starting points toward the intelligibles]; which are read in the Opuscules of Porphyry sent out by Holstenius in Rome 1630 and in the Cambridge edition §. 15—23. §. 39. p. 222—228. p. 246. sq. and, like the rest of the same book, contain the sum of the Plotinian disputations. Tertullian also has not a few things *on the Soul*, whence you may learn the pronouncements of earlier philosophers, no less than Nemesius in the second chapter of the book *De Natura Hominis*, which [abbrev: ꝙ → quod] is inscribed *on the soul* p. 67. sqq. ed. Matthaei. Cassiodorus finally, although having mostly used the authority of the sacred writers, yet himself has nothing which [abbrev: ꝙ → quod] might seem to make in some way for the doctrine of the old philosophers. Above I set out from the mention of Plato and Aristotle, since Plotinus primarily looks back at the opinions of these two men in these books on the Soul. I also warned our readers of the Stoics, because [abbrev: ꝙ → quod] he sub-refutes them frequently. For Eusebius in *P. E.* XV. 22. p. 824. titled a longer passage, which he took from the Plotinian books (below p. 456. sqq.), thus: "Against the Stoics, that the soul cannot be corporeal, from Plotinus’ book on (immortality) of the soul." *Justus Lipsius* also mentions these Eusebian things in *Physiologia Stoicorum* lib. III. Dissert. 13. p. 617 of his Works. Several again spoke against Plotinus, such as Nicephorus Chumnus or Nathanaël, who in his *Antitheticum* strives to destroy the primary opinions of Plotinus concerning the Soul; and likewise an Anonymous author on the Soul. We have added these little books with Excerpts of others to this Corpus of Enneads. And from the writings of Plotinus, Proclus, and other Platonists, Christian writers everywhere repeat the false opinions of Heretics concerning the Soul. On this account Nicolaus Methonensis often complains about Proclus, whom our Voemelius recently edited. Concerning Plotinus, Nemesius has this in *De Natura Hominis* p. 9. p. 36 ed. Matthaei: "Some indeed, of whom Plotinus is also one, dogmatizing that the soul is one thing and the intellect another, wish man to be composed of three things: body, soul, and intellect. Whom Apollinarius, who became Bishop of Laodicea, also followed." Michael Glycas *Annall.* Part. I. p. 70 ed. Paris. p. 54 Venet. likewise explaining the opinion of Apollinarius *that there are two souls in man* thus proceeds: "but also Plotinus the wise, whom Apollinarius of Laodicea indeed followed." Then by the decree of Basil the Great concerning the Soul and the passage of Genesis: "and man became a living soul," he strives to confute that opinion concerning the triple soul. From places of this kind it is allowed to conjecture that Plotinus was at that time more often read than Plato himself; since this god of philosophers was not immune from the same fault.

->BOOK II.<-
**p. 667, 7. ΠΕΡΙ ΟΥΣΙΑΣ ΨΥΧΗΣ [ΟΣ—ΑΝΑΓΙΓΝΩΣΚΕΣΘΑΙ] [On the Essence of the Soul (Which... to be read)]** The twentieth and first book according to chronological order. Porphyry *De Vita Plotini* ch. 25 thus inscribes it: *περὶ οὐσίας ψυχῆς δεύτερον* [On the Essence of the Soul, the Second]. In another place, ch. 4, thus: *πῶς ἡ ψυχὴ τῆς ἀμερίστου καὶ μεριστῆς οὐσίας μέση εἶναι λέγεται* [How the soul is said to be the middle of indivisible and divisible essence]. Truly, in neither does he recognize the words which we have included in brackets, which are not read in several MSS books. Nevertheless, it seems this very gloss was the cause why the order of these prior books of the fourth Ennead was disturbed in several Codd. Concerning which matter it was warned in the *Varia Lectio* at the end of the last book of the third Ennead. But in the beginning of this second book itself, unless we are altogether mistaken, a trace appears of a double recension of these Enneads, the Eustochian (of which a Scholia below p. 423. B placed in most Manuscripts makes mention) and the Porphyrian. For Eusebius, in *Praeparatione Evang.* XV. 10. p. 811 ed. Colon. exhibits a longer passage under Plotinus’ name, which, since it deals with the Aristotelian Entelechy, seems to be referred to the beginning of this second book, yet it does not agree with those things which exist in the Plotinian MSS and edition. The same Eusebian things are also read in the Vindobonn. Codd. XI and XIV. (See Fabricius’ *Bibl. Gr.* Vol. V. p. 698 and Harles there.) This is added also because [abbrev: ꝙ → quod] Eusebius introduces those Plotinian things thus: "Of Plotinus, from the second book *on the immortality of the soul*, against Aristotle, who said the soul is an entelechy." The place itself begins thus: "And someone might thus examine the matter of entelechy, how it is said concerning the soul." An accurate disquisition of the Aristotelian dogma itself follows, which [abbrev: ꝙ → quod] in this place of the Enneads on the contrary is passed over in few words as false and not fit for declaring the soul. Now since there does not exist a second book of Plotinus *on the immortality of the soul*: deservedly this matter was a wonder both to Fr. Vigerus in the Notes on Euseb. p. 77 and to J. A. Fabricius in *Annott. in Porphyr. de Vita Plotini* p. 144 lit. u. I, to explain my own opinion such as it is, believed the matter could be expedited thus: Plotinus had in reality written what are read in Eusebius disputed against Entelechy, which Eustochius providently received into his recension, whence Eusebius took them. Porphyry on the contrary, more hostile to that doctrine, either later persuaded Plotinus, or took this upon himself, so that instead of that Disquisition which Eusebius has, he might put back that formula of omission which we read in our place of the Enneads, especially since he could believe that Entelechy had been fundamentally overturned by himself. Read the following chapter (XVI) of Eusebius, where Porphyry himself rises against Entelechy, in these words: (p. 812. C.) "for how is the account not disgraceful which places Entelechy etc.?" but as for the fact that Eusebius cites "the second book on immortality," which does not exist among the Plotinian ones: first it is asked, whether Eusebius truly wrote:—*ἐκ τοῦ περὶ ἀθανασίας ψυχῆς δευτέρου*: or rather: *ε. τ. π. οὐσίας ψ. β.* [from the second on the essence of the soul]. But either Eustochius or Eusebius could also title this book "on immortality," because all these books of this Ennead, certainly most, and this second one itself pertain to the question concerning the immortality of the soul. And we saw above (at the title of the first book p. 360. A.) that the same Eusebius simply praises Plotinus’ book "on the immortality of the soul" (*P. E.* XV. 22.): *περὶ ψυχῆς* [on the soul]. Nor indeed would I allow myself to be persuaded that the Porphyrian recension lacked some Plotinian book which the Eustochian had: However it be: We have judged that those things which are read in Eusebius are to be joined with this book, lest the Readers should miss anything which [abbrev: ꝙ → quod] might have proceeded from Plotinus. Thomas Taylor exhibits this book translated into English in *Select Works of Plotinus* p. 309. sqq.

**p. 667, 11. οὐδὲ ἐν ἀσωμάτοις αὐτὴν ἁρμονίαν [nor in the incorporeals is she harmony]** We treated these above at page 307. E.

**p. 668, 2. Λέγομεν δὴ [We say indeed]** Tiedemann, in the book: *Geist der spekulat. Tennemann, however, in *Geschichte der Philosophie* VI. p. 182. sqq., says that Plotinus explained more clearly than Plato himself that the soul is altogether immune from matter, or segregated from every mortal concretion, and first of all showed clearly by certain reasons how the natures of the mind and body differ from each other: but yet that the philosopher from Lycopolis could teach these things more by denying than by affirming. And lest I seem to wish to suppress contrary judgments in silence, Heeren at Stobaeus' *Eclogg. Physs. et Eth.* I. p. 866 thinks that Plotinus fluctuates in those things which he disputes concerning the nature of the soul.

**p. 670, 10. ἡ δ᾽ ὁμοῦ μεριστή τε—φύσις, ἣν δὴ—Καὶ ὁ—τὴν δύναμιν αὐτῆς κατιδὼν [and the nature at once divisible—which indeed—And he—having seen its power]** Porphyry in *Sententt.* XXXXIX. p. 246 Cantabr. and in Stobaeus' *Eclogg. Heer.: "For the nature of the soul is of infinite power, and according to each part of it that happens, it is soul, and all are one; and again the whole is other than all. For as bodies being cut to infinity do not end in the incorporeal (Stob. *ἀσώματα*, which Heeren should not have received) taking the difference of the parts according to bulk alone (missing from Stob.), so the soul, being a vital form, is comprised to infinity according to forms, having formal variations, and being whole with these, and without these." You cf. Proclus *Instit. Theol.* ch. 195. 196. p. 290. sqq. To these and the following things of Plotinus pertain these of Iamblichus at Stob. *Eclogg. Physs.* I. 52. 33. p. 888: "for those extending one and the same soul everywhere, either in genus or form, as it seems to Plotinus, or even in number, as Amelius youthfully contends not a few times, will say it is exactly what it acts." Proclus moreover in *Alcib. pr.* p. 211 says the soul is "the most honorable thing." cf. the same p. 250. sq.

**p. 671, 15. ὡς διαδόσει ἐπὶ τὸ ἡγεμονοῦν ἴασιν αἱ αἰσθήσεις [as by transmission the senses go to the ruling part]** Thus all our books. See *Var. Lect.* Cf. these of Cicero *Tuscull.* I. 20: "What? because by the same mind we comprehend very dissimilar things, as color, taste, heat, smell, sound, which the mind would never know through five messengers, unless *all things were referred* to it, and it alone were the judge of all." We have gathered more in this opinion above p. 200. E to illustrate that: "Intellect sees, intellect hears" etc. Moreover, *diadosis* is "tradition" [transmission], when the senses, what they have perceived, *hand over* to the mind, and Theodore Metochita in a twin passage p. 577 mentions the things "given" by the senses. But why do I require other testimonies? Plotinus illustrates Plotinus. For thus below in a twin passage p. 462. B: "and the whole soul suffers it. How then does this happen? by transmission they will say, with the psychic pneuma around the finger having suffered primarily, and having handed it over to the next, and this to another, until it should arrive at the ruling part. It is necessary therefore, if the first part in pain felt it, that the sensation of the second be another, if sensation is according to transmission etc." And below on this very page the verb *diadidonai* [to transmit] is read.

### BOOK III.

**page 687, 7. ΠΕΡΙ ΨΥΨΗΣ ΑΠΟΡΙΩΝ ΠΡΩΤΟΝ [First on Problems of the Soul]** This is the twenty-seventh book according to the chronological order. In the earlier place of Porphyry’s books *On the Life of Plotinus*, specifically in chapter five, none of these three following books has the word *ἀποριῶν* [problems/doubts] in the title. On the contrary, in another place (chapter 25), this little word appears in both the manuscripts and the printed editions. You might conjecture that this word was taken by some Grammarian or scribe from the beginning of this very book: *περὶ ψυχῆς ὅσα ἀπορήσαντας — ἢ καὶ ἐν αὐταῖς ταῖς ἀπορίαις στάντες* [concerning the soul, as many as have doubted—or even standing in the doubts themselves]. St. Augustine praises this book, or rather a certain passage of it, below in chapter XII, page 381. D. *The City of God*, Book IX, chapter 18: "Plotinus certainly, in times near to our memory, is praised for having understood Plato more excellently than the rest. He, when treating of human souls, says, 'The Merciful Father,' etc." We shall append the remainder below at the passage cited. This same passage and others, both in these books *On the Problems of the Soul* and in that titled *On Our Allotted Daemon*, and several other later ones, provided an occasion for criticizing Plotinus. We have joined two of this kind with this edition of the *Enneads*, namely, Nicephorus Chumnus’s *Antithetic against Plotinus*, already edited by us previously, and an Anonymous *Dialogue* of similar argument not yet edited, by the same author, as Hieronymus Amatius thinks. Nathanaël especially attacks the tenet of the *pre-existence of souls*, as they call it. Which very thing, since the famous Origen in his books *On First Principles* (taken from the Platonic philosophers) sought to maintain, [Gregory of] Nyssa and other writers of the Christian church sought to refute. See Fabricius’s *Select Arguments for the Truth of the Christian Religion*, page 445.—Thomas Taylor translated this book of Plotinus into English in *Select Works of Plotinus*, page 319 ff.

— 15. *τῷ τοῦ θεοῦ παρακελεύσματι, αὑτοὺς γιγνώσκειν* [by the command of the god, to know themselves] Compare VI. 7. 41. page 733. B. and the annotations there.

**page 688, 4. Ἦν γὰρ καὶ ἐν τῷ παντὶ νῷ τὸ διττόν. [For there was also in the universal mind the twofold.]** Namely, the intelligible and the intellectual. Taylor. Next: *τὰς ὑποδοχὰς τῶν θεῶν* [the receptions of the gods] we touched upon above at page 283. C.

"...it might be a work most beautiful according to nature and best. Thus, therefore, according to likely reasoning, one must say that this world became a living being, ensouled and truly intelligent, through the providence of God." Compare page 34 following, and Proclus’s *Elements of Theology*, chapter CXX, page 174 ff., and those whom I have praised there. *Philebus* page 29, page 81 Stallbaum. "Whether, then, our body is nourished by that body [of the universe], or that from ours, and all those things we just said about them, it has received and holds." Compare the preceding in the same place, page 29, page 79 Stallbaum, and the following page 30, pages 83–86 Stallbaum, whom compare also for the citations praised by him: Xenophon, *Memorabilia of Socrates* I. 4. 8; Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II. 6. 7, III. 11; Seneca, *Epistle* 69; Marcus Antoninus [Aurelius] IV. 4.

**page 689, 3. Καὶ τὸ, ψυχῇ δὲ πᾶσα παντὸς ἐπιμελεῖται τοῦ ἀψύχου. [And that, 'The whole soul takes care of all that is soulless.']** These words of Plato in the *Phaedrus*, page 246, page 40 Bekker, Plotinus already praised above in III. 4. 1, page 283. C. D.; compare page 376. F. G. where Our Author [Plotinus] expressly names the *Phaedrus*, page 482. A. Consult also Atticus in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* XV. 9, page 809. B., cited by Ast with the Plotinian passages at page 293. Next, *καὶ οὐκ ἄλλο τι ἔξωθεν ψυχῆς καταλείποντος* [and leaving nothing else outside of soul], these are to be referred to Plato with an understood *ἔστι* [it is], unless perhaps it should be read: *καὶ ἔστιν οὐκ—ἄλλο τι—καταλείποντος*: "and it is the [saying or tenet] of him who leaves nothing of the soul further after the soul of the universe."

— 9. *ἔξω ποιοῦσι τοῦ μέρος εἶναι.* [they make it outside of being a part.] Boissonade, in his notes on Philostratus's *Heroica* page 552, and Jacobs on the *Images* page 382, have collected examples of this construction with the Genitive and Infinitive. The latter, praising Philostratus's *Life of Apollonius* II. 28—"and not outside of being serious." (Next, Codex Schellersheimianus: *παῖς γάρ τις ὡς ὁ τῶν ὀρχηστρίδων κ. τ. λ.* [for a certain boy like that of the dancers, etc.]) Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Excerpts from Roman Antiquities* XV. 1, page 66 editio princeps: *ὥστε τὸν Κέλτον ἔξω γίνεσθαι τῶν φρενῶν* [so that the Celt became outside of his mind]. Hoogeveen and Zeunius, in their notes on Viger's *Greek Idioms* V. 10. 6, page 283, have gathered examples of the formulas *ἔξω ποιεῖν* [to make outside] and *ἔσω ποιεῖν* [to make inside] and similar ones. *Acts of the Apostles* V. 34: "he ordered to make the apostles (rather 'the men') outside for a little while." Where, whether you understand "themselves," Gamaliel ordered *the men to withdraw*, or simply: *he dismissed the men, ordered the men to withdraw*. See Valckenar's

**page 691, 6. καὶ ὄνομα μόνον ἔσται [and it will be a name only]** A sufficiently frequent formula, not unknown to Plato. *Laws* I. page 626. A. page 482 Bekker: "For what most men call peace, this is only a name; but in deed—there is an unproclaimed war according to nature." Compare *Theaetetus* page 177. D. page 250 Bekker; *Symposium* page 189 toward the end, page 402 Bekker. Lennep collected many similar examples in his notes on the *Epistles of Phalaris* LXVIII, page 208 ff., and recently Boissonade on Eunapius page 420 f. and page 424, which Krabinger used for his Synesius (*On Kingship* page 19. D.) at page 272. In a passage of Iamblichus *On the Life of Pythagoras* III. 16, page 44 Kiessling, it is now correctly read: *καὶ σεμνοτέροις ἥπερ* [and with more venerable ones than] (formerly *εἴπερ*. Codex Cizensis *ἡ περὶ*, whence the most recent Editor, clearly following Boissonade's mind, made *ἥπερ*, and so Codex Memmianus, the excerpts of which I have in my possession) *εἰώθεσαν ὀνόμασί τε καὶ πράγμασιν* [they were accustomed to names and deeds] (several manuscripts have *γράμμασιν* [letters/writings], which escaped Kiessling, but Codex Monacensis A correctly maintains *πράγμασιν*) "they used toward each other and toward him." Theodoret in *Epistle to the Ephesians* I. 22, page 408: "and he seeks to show names capable of expressing the paradox of the deed." Instead of "only a name" (*ὄνομα μόνον*), Thucydides uses "a name otherwise" (*ὄνομα ἄλλως*) in book VIII, chapter 78—"but waiting for the Phoenician ships from Tissaphernes, a name otherwise and not a deed, to run the risk of wasting time." (Codex Casselanus and several most excellent ones correctly read *κινδυνεύσειν*). On which see Duker and compare C. G. Krüger on Dionysius of Halicarnassus’s *Historiographica* pages 263, 265. Similarly "a word otherwise" (*λόγος ἄλλως*). Aristides *Against Leptines* page 88 ed. Jacob Morelli: —"I think all these things will seem a word otherwise [a mere tale], being disbelieved by the rest of wickedness": "*The pious deeds of the ancients will seem nothing but a fable, not believed because of our own wickedness.*" Compare Ruhnken on Timaeus's *Platonic Lexicon* page 199, and Boissonade on Basil's *Scholia on Gregory Nazianzen* in *Notices et Extraits* Tom. XI, page 78 f. Sometimes "only" (*μόνον*) must be understood with the word "name" (*ὄνομα*). Eunapius in *Proaeresius* page 79 Boissonade: "when these had been elected, the humbler ones had the name"—"*that is*, the poorer ones were Sophists *in name only*." To which Wyttenbach, page 293 ed. Boissonade, teaches that first "only" (*μόνον*), then from the following words "fact" or "deed" (*πρᾶγμα* or *ἔργον*) is to be understood. Compare also below page 459. B.—"and everything is a name." In the next parts, the Various Readings argue that there is much variation. Having left Ficinus’s interpretation, we have added a second version. If one may hazard a guess, you might conjecture: *εἰ δὴ ἀρχὴν τίς ποτε ἦν οὖσα* [if indeed she ever were existing at the start]: "For they will destroy the whole soul, and only the name will remain, *if indeed she was at all ever existing*"; so that you may take these added words ironically.

**page 692, 15. πάσας μέντοι—εἰς—μορφοῦσθαι [all however—into—to be formed]** If with several books you read *ὡς* [as] for *εἰς* [into], this sense emerges: "since form (idea) can be formed into all things." Ficinus understood from the following in this place: *καὶ ἰέναι εἰς εἶδος—μορφοῦσθαι* [and to go into form—to be formed]. Taylor follows him. For the following: "but the judgment from the same, as from a judge—who has perceived," or rather for this whole passage, consult Plato in the *Theaetetus* page 184. C. D. and Aristotle *On the Soul* III. 1, 2, 3, page 48 ff. Sylburg, where at page 53 these things are read: "Since they define the soul by two differences especially, movement according to place and thinking, and judging, and perceiving; and it seems that thinking and being prudent are like a kind of perceiving; for in both of these the soul judges and recognizes something of beings. And the ancients say that being prudent and perceiving are the same." Passages of Empedocles and Homer follow. Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I. 20: "What? Is it not with the same mind that we comprehend the most dissimilar things, as color, taste, heat, smell, sound; which the soul would never recognize with five messengers unless all things were referred to it, and it alone were the judge of all." This is not the only passage in which Plotinus agrees almost in sense with Cicero. Which is evidence, not that the latter was read by the former, but that both frequently drew from the same sources. I applied the Tullian [Ciceronian] passage above to page 200. E. (where I gathered more on this opinion) and to page 363. E. For the rest, compare below page 388.

**page 693, 10. Οὐ γὰρ ὥσπερ ἡ ἡμετέρα (ψυχὴ) λέγεται, καταλείπειν τὸ σῶμα κ. τ. λ. [For it is not as ours (soul) is said, to leave the body, etc.]** From this passage and another below at page 639, Cudworth brings a dispute against Plotinus in *Intellectual System* V. 3. 15. page 1025 Mosheim, because he absurdly attributes a double life to the soul, and because he is unmindful of the precept of his own school placed in our passage: "That our soul, although it leaves its body,

**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

will never be entirely separated from every body whatsoever." Consequently, Porphyry also contradicts his own teacher in the *Sentences*, page 232. Mosheim defends Plotinus in the same place in his annotations, who says, among other things: "There were therefore two opinions among the Platonists on this matter, if these words are viewed absolutely. For while some wanted the soul departing the body to be stripped of every body entirely, others on the contrary thought some body always remained joined to the soul, even though it laid aside this earthly body composed of natural principles. Plotinus himself seems to have wanted to join neither family. But he will err, I think, regarding the meaning of Plotinus's words, who attributes this force to them. It was agreed among all Platonists that the soul was always clothed in a certain celestial body, and girt with such a body it descended into this concrete body, and took that same body away again upon departing. What then does the philosopher mean? It seems to me he speaks only of the body which the philosophers called the *eidolon* [image/phantom], which he says some think is never entirely freed and released from the soul."

**page 694, 9. Τῆς μὲν ἐοικυίας τῇ ἐμφυτῷ μεγάλῳ ψυχῇ—τῆς ψυχῆς τοῦ παντός. [Of that which is similar to the great innate soul—of the soul of the universe.]** Taylor correctly included in brackets those words in the edition of Ficinus (Basle): "*it governs the plant, that is, just as worms arise in wounds.*" He could have struck them out, as we have done. For they do not appear in the Florentine *editio princeps* of 1492, and therefore are not Ficinus's. Moreover, in the Greek also, this passage is rugged. The manuscripts do not offer much help. The sum of the discussion, however, is sufficiently clear. Our philosopher uses the image of the plant and the tree above at page 277. B. C., and, in a even more similar argument, at page 351. F. In the same place, page 350. F., he likewise used the similarity of the voice, and in this place the similarity of light.

— 14. *καὶ ταῖς μεριμναῖς πρὸς τῷ φυτῷ γίγνοιτο* [and it might be in its cares for the plant] We have given *πρὸς* [at/by] in place of the preposition *πρὸ* [before], from several of our books, and next we read: *πρὸς ἐκείνοις εἶναι, πρὸς οἷς ἐστιν* [to be near those things, near which it is], and *πρὸς ταῖς τοῦ σώματος θεραπείαις ὄντος* [being at the ministrations of the body], and likewise *πρὸς τῷ σώματι εἶναι* [to be at the body]. Our passage is therefore, if any other, frequent in the use of this construction. Plato uses the same in the *Phaedrus* page 249. C.: "for it is always near those things in memory" (so Schleiermacher; vulgate *μνήμη* [memory—dative vs. nominative]. See Heindorf page 160, and our own passage supports that reasoning) "according to power." The same in the *Phaedo* page 84. c.: "and Socrates himself was near [intent upon] the spoken word": "*he himself was fixed in the contemplation of those things which had been discussed*": or: "*and he himself was considering in his mind the discussion held.*" Compare Wyttenbach on this passage page 223 and Heindorf page 122. He cited other very similar examples from Plutarch *On the Right Way of Hearing* page 40. A: "being near none of the things said" Wyttenbach in *Animadversions* page 330. Indeed, no one delights more in this construction than Philostratus. To use this example, *Life of Apollonius* V. 31, page 213 Olearius: "they said that he had long been awake and was at his letters [busy with correspondence]." Boissonade collected more examples from this writer in *Heroica*, and indeed for words very similar to the Plotinian, *πρὸς τοῖς φυτοῖς εἶ* [you are at the plants], which the Scholiast explains as "you are devoted to the plants," page 310. Similarly Plato and others join the verb *διατρίβειν* [to spend time] and others with the Dative and *πρὸς*. See ibid. page 660. Add Schäfer to Julian page IV, where he teaches it is used equally: *εἶναι πρός τι* and *εἶναι πρός τινι*. The same learned man touched on this matter regarding these words of Dionysius of Halicarnassus *On Composition*, section 83, page 142 f.: "and not to remain in the same figures." Sylburg wanted: "to remain within." Upton maintained the vulgate; Schäfer conjectured: "to remain additionally." Codex Darmstadt has it thus: "and not to always remain upon the same figures." Finally, quite like Plotinus, Arrian in the *Discourses of Epictetus* II. 18. 21 and II. 19. 6 uses *γίνεσθαι πρός τινι*, as: "I have not become near this thing," "I have not labored in this matter," I have not given effort to that thing.

**page 695, 4. ἢ ἀπολεῖται οὐδὲν τῶν ὄντων—οἱ νόες οὐκ ἀπολοῦνται. [or nothing of beings will perish—minds will not perish.]** Codex Marcianus A. has *οἱ νοῖ* in the older form; concerning that more recent one see Buttmann's *Larger Grammar*, section 36, page 156; Matthiä's *Greek Grammar*, section 90, second edition, and those things which I have cited more fully in Proclus's *Elements of Theology*, chapter XXI, page 40, which passage is also to be applied to the meaning of our passage. This was especially the opinion of Plato, and likewise of the Platonists, that nothing of entities perishes, but only takes another form. Compare Casaubon's *Exercitations on Baronius*, page 63. Indeed, our passage and many similar Plotinian ones thoroughly refute the opinions of those "Zoili" [hostile critics], who, since they have never read Plotinus, dare to attribute to him some sort of doctrine, which they call Indian, concerning the All and the One (*All-Eins-Lehre*). But we do not delay over those men, who hate what they do not understand.

**page 697, 2. τὸ γὰρ δευτέρας καὶ τρίτας—ὑπονοητέον εἰρῆσθαι [for 'second and third'—must be understood as having been said]** Plato in *Timaeus* page 41, page 44 Bekker: "he said these things, and again into the former mixing bowl, in which he had blended the soul of the universe, he poured the remains of the previous things, mixing them in a certain way the same, but no longer unmixed in the same way, but second and third." Whence perhaps in Plotinus *δεύτερα καὶ τρίτα* [second and third things] should be corrected, and so Our Author below, page 377. D. I have explained the mythologumena of the ancient peoples concerning the mixing bowl, or rather mixing bowls, in *Dionysus* page 26 ff., which should be joined with those things which the most learned editor of the excellent Warton's work, *The History of English Poetry*, London 1824, copiously compared in the Preface page 76 ff. from the poets and writers of the middle ages, likewise those things which the most celebrated *de Hammer* discussed on this subject in the work: *Fundgruben des Orients* [Mines of the East] Vol. VI, page 18 ff. and page 80 ff.

— 4. *οὐχ ὁμοίως πάσαις ψυχαῖς ὑπάρχει τὰ πρὸς τὰ ἐκεῖ* [the things toward those there do not belong to all souls in the same way] To all souls the power of those things which are above is not given equally. For *ὑπάρχειν* is more often "to happen," and even more often "to be available." Compare Plato, *Hippias Major* page 292. — 9. *Ἀλλὰ τὸ ἐν Φιλήβῳ λεχθὲν—ἀλλ᾽ ὅπερ ἦν χρήσιμον αὐτῷ τότε (so I would read with Ficinus for τότε)—ἀψύχου τοῦ παντὸς ὄντος.* [But what was said in the Philebus—but whatever was useful to him then—the universe being soulless.] Plato, *Philebus* page 30. A. page 81 Stallbaum: "Socrates: Shall we not say that the body among us has a soul? Protarchus: It is clear that we shall say so. Socrates: Whence, O friend Protarchus, did it take it, if indeed the body of the universe did not happen to be ensouled, having the same things as this and even more beautiful?" This passage of Plotinus is memorable because our philosopher teaches that we ought to look at the purposes of the individual dialogues of Plato or even the parts of a single dialogue if we wish to judge rightly concerning the true opinion of Plato. And yet none of the recent interpreters, as far as I know, has applied this passage of Plotinus. Our philosopher touched on another part of this Platonic passage above, page 372. B. C.

— 15. *δῆλον δὲ—ἐν Τιμαίῳ ποιεῖ—ἐκ τοῦ αὐτοῦ μιγνύων κρατῆρος—την δὲ διαφορὰν, δευτέροις καὶ τρίτοις διδούς.* [it is clear—he makes in the Timaeus—mixing from the same bowl—giving the difference by second and third.] The passage of the *Timaeus*, page 41, I just placed at the end of the preceding chapter. Lindau on Plato's *Timaeus* at the passage cited page 65, after he praised the words of Plotinus, adds this: "The man would surely have spoken less obscurely: *ὁμοειδεῖς* [of the same form], *that is*, the other souls, making them like the other, *that is*, the soul of the universe, and soon *δευτέρας καὶ τρίτης* [of the second and third], *that is*, of the rank or portion." Compare Lambert Bos, *Greek Ellipses* page 305 f. Below, Our Author makes mention of the mixture from the second cup *ἐκ τοῦ ὑστέρου κρατῆρος* [from the later bowl], page 473. A. Plato, *Philebus* page 61, page 203 Stallbaum: "whether it be Dionysus or Hephaestus or whichever of the gods has received this honor of blending." To which words Olympiodorus (or Strato, as it is said in Codex Monacensis, according to Kopp on Damascius page 174) says: "That gods are over the blending, Hephaestus over the physical and mundane, Dionysus over the psychic and supramundane. For the blending quality begins from above from the gods themselves, and proceeds down to the last existences; just as Hephaestus, leading the physical blending, first put forth the characteristic in himself; then in the mind that reigns and traverses all nature (Thus I would think this lacuna could be filled), then in the soul likewise of such a kind, and finally in the physical world according to existence, but also Dionysus likewise—" Then after several intermediate things he continues: "Zeus is over the intellectual blending, etc." and from here that *mixing bowl of mind* (*ὁ κρατὴρ τοῦ νοός*) of the so-called Hermes takes its origin. **page 698, 7. Ἱκανὴ γὰρ ψυχὴ καὶ παρὰ φύσεως τόπων πολλὰ ἀπομάττεσθαι. [For the soul is capable of receiving many impressions even from the nature of places.]** Ficinus, translating *propulsare* [to drive away/repel], took *ἀπομάττεσθαι* in this place for *ἐκβάλλειν* [to cast out], *abstergere* [to wipe away]; and no one will deny that this verb has this force in many passages. On the other hand, Taylor says: "*The soul is sufficiently able to represent many things in itself, from the nature of places, and water, and air.*" Which reasoning seems truer to me, both because *καὶ παρὰ φύσεως τόπων* [and from the nature of places] preceded, and because only in the following words does he mention that other force, namely, resisting natural things: *ἀλλ᾽ ἀντετίθεμεν ἄλλην ψυχὴν κ. τ. λ.* [but we oppose another soul, etc.]. Concerning both powers of that verb, it was discussed above regarding the book *On Beauty* page 54. F. It is better, however, to say with Proclus, that as nature does nothing in vain, the presence of the rational soul to the fetus in the womb would be useless, as it could not then energize; but that it becomes united to the irrational soul in the very moment, in which the infant leaves the womb."

**page 702, 5. Δεῖ δὴ τῷ λόγῳ—διδασκαλίας καὶ τοῦ σαφοῦς χάριν, γίγνεσθαι νομίζειν κ. τ. λ. [It is necessary indeed in the discussion—for the sake of teaching and clarity, to think that it happens, etc.]** The meaning of this passage is: One must believe that the entry of the soul (of the world) into the body (of the world) and its animation are explained here in words only for the sake of doctrine and clarity: in reality, such an entry and animation have occurred at no time [i.e., they are eternal]. It is to be compared with a similar passage in VI. 5. 8. page 665. A., where in explaining the conjunction of form (or species) and matter, Plotinus similarly warns his readers that they should not be thought of as separated in reality by place and time, but are separated only by words in doctrine, so that the understanding of students might be aided. Admonitions of this kind must be held by all who intend to apply themselves correctly to Metaphysics. Compare our annotation to page 473. B. above. For the rest, Brucker, in *Critical History of Philosophy* II. page 407, after he cited this opinion in Ficinus's words, continues thus: "Here Plotinus begins to fall away from Plato with bolder steps, so that he might the more bolster the syncretistic System. For from Plato's system it is known that it pleased him that matter lay unformed and animated by an inordinate and brute motion, until God the demiurge established it by a voluntary accession, and having sent in a soul, formed it and impressed an orderly motion. This was strongly opposed to Aristotle, who conceived a world eternal for himself without any generation or formation, but much more to the System of the Christians, who greatly attacked and defeated the double principle that Plato supposed; the Platonic doctrine had to be tempered to both by the counsel of Ammonius, Plotinus, and the rest of the founders of the Alexandrian philosophy; it had therefore to be reformed, and that double principle indeed abandoned, while matter was to be pronounced as having emanated from god from eternity by divine generation.—Thus indeed most triflers hoped that a desired concord could be entered into." It pleased us to append such things here and there by way of example, both for the sake of students of the history of philosophy, and lest we seem to study these Alexandrian philosophers too much if we pass over such reproaches of the moderns in silence. For the rest, Tiedemann also discusses these and the following in the book: *Geist der spekulativen Philosophie* [Spirit of Speculative Philosophy] III. page 309 ff., comparing the passage *Ennead* IV. book 5 chapter 7, IV. 4. 23. 24, IV. 4. 26. He also in the same place page 312 compares the Plotinian decree concerning the essence of the soul with the Cartesian. Compare the same page 320 ff. where in his own way he subjects these Plotinian decrees to examination.—For the rest, concerning the Eternal World, see the opinions of the philosophers in Wyttenbach before the *Phaedo* page XXII.

— 7. *οὐδ᾽ ἐνῆν ὅτε—ὑφεστήκει* [nor was there when—it existed] This construction of the verb *ἐνεῖναι* [to be in/at] is to be added to those which learned men have elsewhere collected of this verb in Stephens's *Thesaurus*, London-Valpy edition page 3585 f., and recently Krüger in the *Greek Index to Dionysius's Historiographical works* page 475. That opinion, however, reminds one of the passage of Plato in the *Cratylus* page 399. E: "I think those who named the soul meant something like this, that this, when it is present in the body, is the cause of its living, providing the power of breathing and cooling; and as soon as the cooling element fails, the body perishes and ends. Whence indeed they seem to me to have called it *psyche* [soul]." Chrysippus follows the same etymology in Plutarch's *On Stoic Contradictions* page 1052. F. page 290 Wyttenbach. Baguet seems to have thought Chrysippus sided with Anaxagoras concerning the essence of the soul in *Fragments of Chrysippus* page 182. Compare also Plotinus below *On the Immortality of the Soul* in Eusebius, there the annotations to IV. 7.—Plutarch expressed those same words of Plato in the fragment *On the Soul* page 133 at the end of *On the Divine Vengeance*; compare Plutarch's *Moralia* Tom. V. part II. page 427, Wyttenbach edition. Origen, *On Principles* Book II. chapter 8: "It must be seen, therefore, lest perhaps, just as we said is declared by the name itself, it was called *psyche*, *that is, anima* [soul], *from that which has cooled from the fervor of the just and participation in the divine fire*." You see that this zeal for etymology runs out into a completely different direction. Compare the same Origen in *Exhortation to Martyrdom* T. I. page 282. B. Rue edition, and Tertullian, *On the Soul* chapter XXV. page 283 Rigalt edition.

— 15. *ὅπερ ἰδοῦσα ἡ ψυχὴ—ἐμόρφωσεν αὐτό* [which the soul seeing—formed it] This passage is noteworthy: for from it we think it becomes clear that Ammonius and Plotinus took this Genesis of the world from the soul from the Egyptian discipline, such as flourished at that time when the Jews also received it and fashioned the Cabbalistic system, etc.

— 18. *γενόμενος δὴ οἷον οἶκός τις καλὸς καὶ* [becoming indeed like a certain beautiful and...]

**...variegated house,]** Compare Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I. 8 and 9: "But what was it that God would desire to adorn the world with signs and lights, like an aedile? Was it so that [the god] himself might live better, etc." where see Davies and the rest of the interpreters. Philo Judaeus, *On Dreams* page 648 Mangey: "But this shown and visible thing, this sensible world, is therefore nothing else but the house of god, one of the powers of the truly existing god (Read from the manuscripts of Mangey: 'of one of the powers of Being') according to which he was good." The same in *On Monarchy* I. page 217: "Must not he who has arrived at the truly great city, this world—take up a conception of the father and maker and leader, more by necessity than by likelihood? For none of the works of art are made by chance; and the world is the most artistic work, as having been fashioned by someone absolutely good and most perfect in knowledge." Dio Chrysostom, *Borysthenitic Oration* (XXXVI.) page 448. page 91 Reiske —: "so that in this way they do not seem to me to have hesitated to declare the whole world the house of Zeus; if indeed he is their father in himself (Reiske's reading is not bad: 'father of all those in himself')." The same at the end of the oration (page 454. page 100.): "the whole heaven and world, when it was first completed, having been adorned by the wisest and best art, just released from the hands of the creator, bright and translucent, and shining in all its parts." I appended these last words also so that support might come to the conjecture of Markland, who in a corrupt passage of Philo (page 648 Mangey) concerning the Intelligible World, for: "the intelligible world composed from ideas in that which was chosen according to divine bounties," saw that it should be read: "fashioned by hand according to divine handicrafts." When Mangey referred this emendation as received by the benefit of that great Critic, as he often does, he himself nevertheless preferred to think of something else.

**page 703, 5. Κεῖται γὰρ ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ [For it lies in the soul]** Taylor compares to this place the verses concerning human souls from the *Chaldaean Oracles*, which begin thus:

*Ἐν δὲ θεῷ κεῖνται—* [And in god they lie—]

For I omit the rest, as doing nothing for this place in which the reason of the *Mundane Soul* is explained. For the rest, consult Psellus's *Scholia on the Chaldaean Oracles* Tom. I. page 104, Gallaeus edition, for the meaning of those verses.

**page 704, 15. μηχαναῖς πολλαῖς εἰς εἰδώλων φύσιν προσχρωμένη [using many machines for the nature of images]** It might seem that Ficinus read *ποίησιν* [making/creation]: but the books vary in nothing. Philosophers and our author himself often compare the workmanship of Nature with the workmanship of artisans in such a way that they seek to demonstrate the difference of each. Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I. 8. page 32 f.: "For with what eyes could your Plato gaze upon that workshop of so great a work, by which he makes the world to be constructed and built by god? What construction? What iron tools? What levers? What machines? What ministers of so great a work were there?" Compare Musonius Rufus's fragment in Wyttenbach's *Philomathia* II. page 5, and the annotation of the latter there. Our passage is a classic on this matter. III. 8. 1. end page 344. A. compare V. 9. 6. page 560. D. "(nature) —formed matter, not pushing it, nor using those much-fabled lever-actions, but having given of the reasons (or 'the reason')."

**page 705, 13. ὧν τοὺς λόγους ἔχει· ἔχει δὲ καὶ θεῶν. [of which it has the reasons; and it has also those of gods.]** Taylor: "Soul, likewise, comprehends in itself the productive principles of Gods"—and in a note: *that is*, of divine souls, each of which is a God according to participation. Then he praises his translation of Proclus on Plato's *Theology* book I.—With those things which Plotinus thinks in this chapter and the following concerning the images of the Gods, compare Iamblichus, *On the Mysteries* I. 19. page 33 Gale: "I say then, that from the intelligible paradigms of the gods are generated the visible statues of the gods, and having become so, are entirely established in them, and have their image resulting from them reaching back to them themselves. In another way the same things have been fashioned into another arrangement, and the things here are continuous with those according to a single union; and the present divine intellectual forms exist prior to the seen bodies of the gods separately. But their unmixed and super-celestial intelligible paradigms remain by themselves, all things together in one (Codex Vindobonensis 'in one,' correctly) according to their eternal excellence." How much these agree with the next parts of Plotinus in chapter XI, there is no need to demonstrate. Indeed, the same Iamblichus had written a specific book *On Statues*, the purpose and summary of which Joannes Philoponus opens to us in Photius, Codex CCXV. page 173 Bekker edition. Which passage likewise ought to be compared with the Plotinian. I omit others, whom I indicated in the annotation on Cicero's *On the Nature of the Gods* II. 17. page 273. Here I shall add some other things pertaining hereto: Proclus in *Scholia on the Cratylus*, section 51. page 21 Boissonade:

**BOOK III. OF THE FOURTH ENNEAD. pages 703—707. -> 211 <-**

"that there is indeed in the soul a certain representational power, is clear (for painting and such [perhaps 'arts' should be added] are suspended from this power), being assimilative of the second things to the better, and of the forms carried in composition to the simpler.—but it also assimilates the second things from itself or by itself to itself through the same power, and further to the things better than itself; wherefore it creates statues of gods and daemons.—and just as the telestic art [ritual/initiatory] through certain symbols and secret tokens assimilates the statues here to the gods, and makes them suitable for the reception of divine illuminations, so also etc." Whence that purpose of Iamblichus in Photius at the passage cited is understood: "the goal for Iamblichus is to show both that the images are divine (for these things he suggests by the name of statue) and full of divine participation." Nor was Plotinus alien to that opinion, from the nature of the imitation, which is easily affected by a soul kindred to itself, that the power of the gods can be received in a certain way from their likenesses. Which opinion Julian, Iamblichus, Proclus, Marinus, and others thereafter adorned in a greater way. The Fathers of the Church and the teachers of the Jews sought to overturn it. See Clement of Alexandria's *Protrepticus* page 49 ff. Potter. Whence Richard Bentley excites a passage in the *Epistles* page 163 London, page 136 Leipzig, as if taken from the *Paedagogus*. It exists in the *Protrepticus* page 51 below, Potter edition.

**page 706, 1. προσπαθές τι—προσπαθές [something sympathetic—sympathetic]** For the repeated *προσπαθές* at the beginning of this chapter, where it is attributed even to inanimate things, Proclus’s *Scholion* from the *Commentaries on Plato’s and Aristotle’s Politics* in Wyttenbach to Plutarch’s *On the Multitude of Friends* page 645 is to be applied, where *προσπάθεια* [sympathy/passion] is attributed to brute animals: friendship to the Gods: both to humans, as being constituted in the middle between Gods and beasts.

**page 707, 3. Ἀνθρώπων δὲ ψυχαὶ, εἴδωλα αὑτῶν ἰδοῦσαι, οἷον Διονύσου ἐν κατόπτρῳ κ. τ. λ. [But human souls, seeing images of themselves, as that of Dionysus in a mirror, etc.]** Several passages of Plato must be held as the sources of this entire discussion. The first is in the *Timaeus* page 43 f. page 46 f. Bekker; to which Proclus on the *Timaeus* page 338 ff. is to be applied. The same in the same place page 163 below: "and of old the mirror has been taken by theologians as a symbol of suitability, for the intellectual fulfillment of the whole. Wherefore they say Hephaestus made it for Dionysus, looking into which the god, and having seen the image of himself, proceeded into the whole divided creation." It had been handed down, therefore, in the ancient cosmogonies that Dionysus, delighted by his own form which he had seen in the mirror, procreated this nature of things as an imitator of this form. Whence it followed that human souls themselves were said to have seen their own image in this mirror of Dionysus and, delighted by their own beauty, to have taken the impulse to put on bodies and to have fallen from above. That this fable is joined with the fate of Narcissus, I have shown elsewhere at page 56. F. That the Dionysian mirror is an ancient token [tessera] not only Proclus is witness, at the passage cited, but even the monuments of ancient art speak, especially the painted Vases of the Greeks and the mirrors themselves accustomed to be used in religions with both the Etruscans and the Greeks; concerning which I myself have discussed more in *Symbolics and Mythology* III. page 301, page 392 f. page 425 ff. page 497 ff. page 556 f. second edition, and recently the most learned *Francesco Inghirami* explained in *Monumenti Etruschi* [Etruscan Monuments] throughout, and with this Plotinian passage applied, page 383 and page 425. Hence many passages of the Platonists are to be explained. Thus, to use this: Proclus on the *First Alcibiades* page 108 our edition: "that the first cause of opinion and of vanity and of deceit for souls is the body and matter, and the imagistic sketching of the forms around it." Olympiodorus on the same page 217. Thomas Taylor, most knowledgeable of the decrees of the Platonists, applied another passage of the same Olympiodorus from the *Commentary on the Phaedo* to these Plotinian points, whence I shall transcribe the beginning of this place: "In order to the soul's descent it is necessary, that she should first establish an image of herself in the body; and in the second place, that she should sympathize with the image according to a similitude of form. For every form hastens into a sameness with itself, through an innate convergency to itself." For the rest, the Emperor Julian touched on these things concerning the lapse of souls and the flow of lives in *Oration IV* page 222 Spanheim, where he says the same things concerning these fables and tokens according to the mind of Plato and Plotinus, likewise Porphyry and Iamblichus:

— 6. *κάρα δὲ αὐταῖς ἐστήρικται ὑπεράνω τοῦ οὐρανοῦ* [their head is fixed above the heaven] *Iliad* δ. 443. concerning Eris:

"With her head she is fixed in heaven, and walks upon the earth."

But our manuscripts all have *κάρα* [head], by which form the *Scholia Minora* on the *Iliad* π. 392: "The poet never says *κάρα*." However, he says it in the *Hymn to Ceres* verse 12, but in the plural number; and you might take it as *heads* even in Plotinus. Nevertheless, I should rather believe that he followed the Attic form. See Apollonius, *Homeric Lexicon* on *κάρη* page 383 Tollius.

**page 707, 9. Ζεὺς δὲ πατὴρ ἐλεήσας πονουμένας θνητὰ αὑτῶν τὰ δέσμα ποιῶν περὶ ἃ πονοῦνται [But Father Zeus, having pitied them being in toil, making their bonds mortal about which they toil]** The beginning of this period has a Platonic color. *Symposium* page 191. page 405 Bekker: " Zeus, having pitied them, provides another device." As to the fact that Zeus is called "father" in this place: these things of Proclus on Plato's *Cratylus* section 149, page 90 Boissonade are to be held —: "and Zeus having the reason of a father, who indeed through the union with the whole demiurgic mind attained the same name—" and section 151, page 92: "Therefore Zeus oversees the life of souls before generation." The source, however, of this Plotinian passage concerning mercy and leniency, concerning the loosened bonds of souls, etc., is in these passages of Plato: in the *Cratylus* page 403 (which Plutarch also regards in *On Isis and Osiris* page 362. page 485 f. Wyttenbach, likewise Proclus in Plato's *Theology* V. 3. page 253 and VI. 11. page 371); in the *Timaeus* page 44. page 48 ff. Bekker; and in the *Phaedo* page 82 f. page 54 ff. Bekker. Augustine praises our passage in *The City of God* VIII. 10: "Plotinus certainly, in times near to our memory, is praised for having understood Plato more excellently than the rest. He, when treating of human souls, says: 'The Father,' he said, 'being merciful, made mortal bonds for them.' Thus he thought this very thing, that men are mortal in body, pertained to the mercy of God the father, lest they be held forever by the misery of this life, etc." For the rest, for this whole passage concerning the lapse of souls and their descent, consult Wyttenbach on Plutarch’s *On the Divine Vengeance* page 113. page 444 f. Oxford edition (in which repeated edition that most excellent man also makes mention of this Plotinian passage).

**page 708, 3. καὶ μίαν συμφωνίαν πρὸς τὴν περιφορὰν ποιουμένων, καὶ οἷον μίαν τινὰ φωνὴν ἐμμελῶς ἀφιέναι [and making one symphony toward the revolution, and as if sending forth one certain voice harmoniously]** I have deleted with Ficinus *οὐκ* [not] before *ἐμμελῶς* [harmoniously], and in the following things I have also corrected several items. See the *Various Readings*. He has before his eyes those things of Plato in the tenth book of the *Republic* page 616 f. page 506–508 Bekker, from which I transcribe these: "and upon its circles above each one a Siren stood, being carried round with it, sending forth one voice, one tone. And from all eight there being one harmony sounding together." Concerning the Sirens in the underworld, another passage in the *Cratylus* page 403. d. is to be compared. I have discussed more on these fables and tokens in *Commentaries on Herodotus* page 311 and page 347 ff.

**page 709, 1. Τὸ γὰρ ἀναπόδραστον καὶ ἡ δίκη οὕτως ἐν φύσει κρατούσῃ. [For the inescapable and justice are thus in a ruling nature.]** Above, page 264. E: "Whence also the divine rumor Adrasteia, for this arrangement is truly Adrasteia and truly Justice." Compare page 284. F. G. and page 389. B. below: —"for the divine law is inescapable." On which passages consult what we have placed in the annotations.

— 9. *οἷον δυνάμεσι μάγων* [as if by the powers of magi] Compare II. 9. 14. IV. 4. 26. IV. 4. 40 and 43. IV. 9. 3. and consult the sayings at I. 4. 9. beginning.

— 12. *ὁρμὰς καὶ ἐπανθήσεις,* [impulses and flowerings/efflorescences] Our Author, following Plato *On the Laws* IV. 827. F. (173), uses the verb *ἐπανθεῖν* [to bloom/flower] several times, of flowers, light, beauty. See, for example, V. 8. 10. VI. 2. 21. Similarly Proclus on Plato's *Alcibiades* page 111. Rhetoricians especially delight in this verb. Dionysius of Halicarnassus *On Composition* page 268 Schäfer: "and many graces perhaps bloomed upon Isocrates himself (Codex Palatinus 'to many' [male: badly]) hiding this deformity": where Schäfer collected more. Jacobs on Callistratus’s *Statues* page 708 teaches that it is used even of internal affects; add Boissonade's *Annotation on Eunapius* page 227. Iamblichus in *Protrepticus* page 153 Arcerius page 362 Kiessling: "he named laughter above all passions, because it alone is most clearly signaled, existing like a certain efflorescence (so all my books. Codex Parisiensis 'sub-flowering' [male: badly]) and an inflammation (also 'epiphthegma' in one of mine, no better) up to the face of the disposition." In Lexicons, however, which show *ἐπάνθησις* [flowering] without authority, this passage of Plotinus should be added.

— 16. *ἢ πρὸς γάμων φυσικὰς προθεσμίας* [or toward the natural appointed times of marriages] A little before: "in fixed appointed times." The Greek Orators use it properly, as Demosthenes page 269 and more often Lysias page 140 and 264 and Plato himself *On the Laws* XII. page 954 end, concerning the prescribed day, or the term established by law. Compare Ast at the passage cited in the *Commentary* page 562. Wesseling on Diodorus XXXVI. 1. page 530. G. O. Reiz's *Glossary of Theophilus* page 1289 and Dorville on Chariton page 348 Leipzig [page 245 Amsterdam]. Then it is transferred to natural things. Phalaris, *Epistle* 105: "for it reminds me (the sickness) to consider the present day the last appointed time of life for a man." The same *Epistle* 97 uses "the appointed time of death." See Lennep on the former place page 301. Chariton III. 2. page 59 Leipzig [page 43 Amsterdam]: —"and I shall persuade the father-in-law more by this, that I am not unworthy of marriage; endure, soul, a short appointed time, so that you may enjoy pleasure safely for the longer time." From our reading this sense exists: or just as we are accustomed to hasten toward the natural terms of marriages, *that is*, when the age for entering marriage (*ὥρα γάμου*) is present. In which sense Clearchus in Athenaeus XIII. page 556. d. (page 5 Schweighäuser) says "to approach marriages in the season [hour]." Nevertheless, the other reading, expressed also by Ficinus, *προθυμίας* [eagernesses], has something by which it seems to be able to defend itself. For first *προθεσμίας* [appointed times] could be said to have been brought here from the superior *προθεσμίας*. Then natural eagernesses for marriages might seem to be opposed to "actions of beautiful things" in the other member of the sentence, so that the meaning is: they are carried by a certain instinct either toward fulfilling the desires for marriage, or toward honest actions; although it would have been better to say *ἀφροδισίων* [sexual matters] than *γάμων* [marriages]. Next, Ficinus seems to have read "certain actions" (*πράξεις τινές*). The books, however, vary in nothing.

**page 710, 13. οἷον εἰκὸς καὶ τὸν μῦθον αἰνίττεσθαι, ἃς, πλάσαντος τοῦ Προμηθέως τὴν γυναῖκα. [as it is likely also the myth enigmatically tells, those which Prometheus having fashioned the woman.]** No one who knows how much writers differ among themselves in handing down this fable will wonder at Plotinus himself, although he touches upon the Hesiodic passage, departing nevertheless from this poet and from others. Concerning that variety see Heyne’s *Observations on Apollodorus* page 37. Schütz’s *Excursus on Aeschylus’s Prometheus* and Wernsdorf on Himerius’s *Eclogues* page 745 ff. The most celebrated narration of that fable is Plato’s in the *Protagoras* page 320 f. page 170 ff. Bekker, whom other Philosophers then followed, whom Wernsdorf brings in at the passage cited. And first, these words "Prometheus having fashioned the woman" deviate from the vulgate form, which said the woman was fashioned by Vulcan at the command of Jove; but nevertheless traces of even this diversity exist elsewhere. See the passages cited—"and the other gods." Therefore, for Plotinus also, Prometheus is a god, as for Sophocles in *Oedipus at Colonus* 54 f.: "and in it the fire-bearing god, the Titan Prometheus." Himerius however, *Eclogues* XXI, makes mention of "those two daemons," Prometheus and Epimetheus, with the added name. Tiberius Hemsterhuis collected other things on Lucian Vol. I. page 196 f. and Fr. G. Welcker discussed this matter copiously in the book: *Die Aeschyleische Trilogie* [The Aeschylean Trilogy] page 69 ff., who nevertheless, if he had first mentioned the testimony of Plato in the *Statesman* page 274. page 283 Bekker and others, would have pronounced somewhat more leniently concerning this passage of Plotinus.

— 15. *γαῖαν ὕδει (or ὕδατι) φύρειν κ. τ. λ.* [to mix earth with water, etc.] We touched on these in the *Various Readings*.

— 18. *τῷ πλάσματι, παρὰ προμηθείας τινὸς γενομένῳ* [to the fashioned thing, having come from a certain providence] Everywhere Philosophers take Prometheus for providence, which looks out for the world and human affairs (*προμηθείᾳ* or *τῷ προνοητικῷ τῆς φύσεως*) and for "pronoia" [forethought]. (See the Greek Interpreters on Hesiod’s *Works and Days* 49 ff. and Nicephorus on Synesius’s *On Dreams* page 404.)

**page 711, 1. Ὁ δὲ Ἐπιμηθεὺς (Edition 'Prometheus' or Various Reading) ἀποποιούμενος τὸ δῶρον αὐτοῦ—ἀμείνω εἶναι [But Epimetheus rejecting his gift—to be better]** These earlier things Ficinus translates thus: "*But as for the fact that Epimetheus gave him no gift, what else does it signify, etc.*" Taylor, having noted Ficinus, and followed the reading of the Edition, says: "*But what else is signified by Prometheus warning his brother Epimetheus not to accept the gift (Pandora), than that the choice of that which is in the intelligible, is more excellent [than of that which is in the sensible world ?]*" Then he praises Hesiod at the passage cited. But this is rather to be called a paraphrase than a translation, nor is it less to be held that Plotinus does not follow the authority of Hesiod in these things throughout. Consequently, our philosopher does not consider Epimetheus as a fool or one who is wise too late, but as one who knows how to estimate the work fashioned by his brother Prometheus and sent to him as a gift in the right way, nor does he deign to retain it; similarly as in Himerius's narration both Prometheus and Epimetheus are called wise. Therefore, if we follow the authority of several books and Ficinus, this passage is to be understood thus: Epimetheus however *rejected* (scorned) his gift (*that is*, Prometheus’s, unless perhaps you prefer "of his brother" for *αὐτοῦ*). The next things also speak: *δέδεται καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ ποιήσας* [he himself who made it is also bound]: "He who made (that Pandora) etc. is himself bound." *Ἀποποιεῖσθαι*, *to put away, scorn, reject, repel*, is frequently met with this power. See the passages in Stephens's *Thesaurus*, London-Valpy—page 7787; add Schleusner's *New Thesaurus of the Septuagint Interpreters* I. page 186 and Wyttenbach on Plutarch's *Seven Sages*.

<meta>This page continues the philological annotations on Plotinus’s Ennead IV, specifically commenting on the descent of the soul, textual variants in Greek manuscripts, and comparisons with other Neoplatonic and classical authors.</meta>

# NOTES ON PLOTINUS

**Symposium p. 947:** <note>original: "Conviv."</note> a passage which the Scholiast of Hesiod in the Schellershemian Codex plundered, without any variant reading, except that he omitted **entirely** <note>original: "ὅλως"</note> between **all** <note>original: "πάντα"</note> and **external things** <note>original: "τὰ ἐκτός"</note>. Theophylactus, in Meursius’s *Works*, Vol. VIII. p. 981, even uses it actively; if the passage is sound: **why do you hold your tongue and reject your ancestral customs?** <note>original: "τί τὴν γλῶτταν ἐπέχεις καὶ ἀποποιεῖς σοῦ τὰ πάτρια;"</note>. Furthermore, that this myth was also used by others to explain the nature and vicissitudes of souls is shown by the Greek scholia on Hesiod’s *Works and Days* line 47 and following. See just now p. 64 of Gaisford’s edition. Others attempted different explanations, such as Plutarch in *On Listening to the Poets* p. 23. F. p. 88. sqq. Wyttenbach edition; Julian in *Oration VI* p. 194; Themistius in *Oration XXVII* p. 338; Olympiodorus in Plato’s *Gorgias* (who also understands it as referring to Souls. Taylor provided the passage turned into English at this place in Plotinus), and others. However, you may understand that Plotinus’s explanation is new from the epilogue at the end of this chapter.

**p. 711, 8. They go out, having peered forth from the intelligible.** <note>original: "Ἴασι δὲ ἐκκύψασαι τοῦ νοητοῦ."</note>] In a riddle in Athenaeus, Book X, p. 455. E. p. 171 Schweighäuser edition: **eyes peering out and peering in.** <note>original: "ὄμματα τ᾽ ἐκκύπτοντα κ᾽ εἰσκύπτοντα."</note> It means to look out of doors, to thrust out the head and eyes, and to project. And just as souls are said **to look up** <note>original: "ἀνακύπτειν"</note> when they raise themselves on high out of this darkness of sensible things and, as it were, thrust out their heads into the light of truth (as Wyttenbach teaches on Plato’s *Phaedo* p. 302; add Eustathius on the *Odyssey* book 22, line 235 f. p. 393 f. Basel edition—: **weighed down and unable to look up** <note>original: "κάτω βρίθοντας καὶ ἀνακύπτειν οὐκ ἔχοντας"</note>): so, by a sufficiently rare usage of the same word, they are said **to peer out** <note>original: "ἐκκύπτειν"</note> when they look out as if from the sanctuary of the divine dwelling in which they live, and even proceed forth; which latter meaning is to be attributed to our passage. Regarding the argument, compare Enneads III. 9. 2., IV. 2. 1., IV. 3. 20., V. 7. 12. Our author used **having leaned forward** <note>original: "προκύψασα"</note> with the same meaning below in IV. 4. 3. See Annotations p. 399. A. Furthermore, Tennemann, in *History of Philosophy* Vol. VI, p. 185 f., examines these and the following parts of our passage according to the standard of Kantian philosophy.

**— 12. through heaviness and forgetfulness** <note>original: "διὰ βάρυνσιν καὶ λήθην"</note>] Artemidorus in *The Interpretation of Dreams* Book I, ch. 18, p. 21. p. 32 Reiff edition, joins **heavinesses and outrages.** <note>original: "βαρύνσεις καὶ ὕβρεις."</note> Concerning souls, however, **heaviness** <note>original: "βάρυνσις"</note> is the same as **weight** or **heaviness** <note>original: "βρίθος seu βριθοσύνη"</note>, a gravity, the weight of matter by which they are dragged downward. See the recently cited passage of Eustathius, where **to be weighed down** <note>original: "κάτω βρίθειν"</note> and **to look up** <note>original: "ἀνακύπτειν"</note> are opposites.

**— 13. or of the bodies into which they were admitted** <note>original: "ἢ σωμάτων εἰς ἃ ἐνεκρίθησαν"</note>] Above he had said **being admitted into bodies.** <note>original: "εἰς σώματα εἰσκρινόμεναι."</note> In both places, however, it means to enter and be received into bodies. Sometimes that word is found corrupted. See Reiske and Leopold on Plutarch’s *Lycurgus* XVIII. 3. p. 226. A corruption seems also to have occurred in this passage of Philo Judaeus, *Allegorical Interpretation* III, p. 384 Pfeiffer: **Phinehas — taking the spear <note>literally "siphon-breaker," a type of spear</note>, that is the zealous word, will not stop until he has pierced through the Midianite woman, the nature admitted <note>or "hidden"</note> into the divine choir, through her womb, so that no plant or seed of wickedness may ever be able to rise.** <note>original: "Φινεὲς — τὸν σειρομάστην τουτέστι τὸν ζηλωτικὸν λόγον λαβὼν οὐκ ἀποστήσεται, πρὶν ἢ ἐκκεντῆσαι τὴν Μαδιανῖτιν τὴν ἐγκεκρυμμένην θείῳ χορῷ φύσιν, διὰ τῆς μήτρας αὐτῆς, ἵνα μηδέποτε ἰσχύσῃ φυτὸν ἢ σπέρμα κακίας ἀνατεῖλαι."</note> Mangey wants **enrolled** <note>original: "ἐγγεγραμμένην"</note>, but both from the traces of the writing and more suited to the word **choir** <note>original: "χορῷ"</note> seems to be **admitted** <note>original: "ἐγκεκρυμμένην"</note>, which has been accepted.

**p. 712, 10. poverties or diseases** <note>original: "πενίαι, ἢ νόσοι"</note>] Cf. II. 3. 8. and especially III. 2. 5. and the note there p. 258. F.

**— 18. from those things previously having justification** <note>original: "ἐκ τῶν πρόσθεν ἐχόντων τὴν δικαίωσιν"</note>] Since they have an opinion of justice (or an excuse of justice) from the preceding things, i.e., they can be defended as if they were done justly. Concerning the force of the word **justification** <note>original: "δικαίωσις"</note>, Wyttenbach has spared us the trouble of speaking; read him in *Observations on Plutarch’s On Fortune* p. 679. sqq.

**p. 713, 1. to be relaxed** <note>original: "κεχαλάσθαι"</note>] On this verb, add to those things which the Valpy edition of Stephanus’s *Thesaurus* has (p. 10400 f.), our own note on Proclus in *On the First Alcibiades* p. 41 f.; cf. Proclus’s *Elements of Theology* ch. 122, p. 179. The noun **relaxation** <note>original: "χάλασις"</note> is read below in IV. 4. 45.

**— 11. That from the intelligible to the realm of heaven the souls at first [take their] place** <note>original: "Ὅτι δὲ ἐκ τοῦ νοητοῦ εἰς τὴν οὐρανοῦ ἴασιν αἱ ψυχαὶ τὸ πρῶτον χώραν"</note>] Many and the best of our Manuscripts showed the Singular. And where the manuscript books do not compel otherwise, in Platonic writings and in Plotinus himself, the Singular **heaven** <note>original: "οὐρανὸς"</note> seems to be preferred. In the Septuagint, the New Testament, and Ecclesiastical writers, the Plural is more frequent. Concerning the words **heaven** <note>original: "οὐρανὸς"</note> and **world** <note>original: "κόσμος"</note>, it was discussed above at p. 96. A. To which add Dorville on Chariton p. 664 f. Leipzig [p. 759 Amsterdam]; Valckenaer’s *Scholia on the New Testament* Vol. II. p. 91 f. p. 406 f. and p. 573. *Bibliotheca Critica Amstelodamensis* X. p. 98. and Suicer’s *Thesaurus Ecclesiasticus* II. p. 519 sqq.—For the argument of our passage, apply these other places: V. 5. 7. VI. 7. 41. VI. 8. 18. Brucker seized the opportunity from our passage for criticizing the Platonists, towards whom this man is generally quite unfair, repeatedly stating in *Critical History of Philosophy* II. p. 399, that these eclectic philosophers neither agree among themselves in principles, nor in the remaining hypostas—

# BOOK III. FOURTH ENNEAD. pages 711—717.

...that they differ greatly among themselves in ordering these matters. Tiedemann, in his book: *The Spirit of Speculative Philosophy*, Vol. III, p. 415, compares these Plotinian decrees concerning souls with Cabbalistic doctrines. Tennemann also touched upon our passage in his *History of Philosophy*, Vol. VI, p. 94.

p. 714, 3. <note>original: "ἔστι γάρ τι οἷον κέντρον—αὐγῆς ἀλλοτρίας"</note> **"For there is something like a center—of a foreign light"**] Traces of Eleatic doctrine <note>A pre-Socratic school of philosophy that argued for the unity and unchangeability of the universe</note> are present in these words. See what, for example, Cicero reports concerning Parmenides in *On the Nature of the Gods*, I. 11. p. 49. sq. and the annotations there in our edition and Moser's. Cf. Brandis's *Commentaries on the Eleatics*, p. 160. sqq. How these and similar ideas of the Eleatics and Platonists were later variously transformed by the Gnostics and others has been shown by that most learned man and my very dear friend, **Joseph von Hammer**, not unmindful of our passage, in the work: *Treasures of the Orient* (*Mines de l'Orient*) Vol. VI. p. 51. sqq. and p. 110.—Regarding the words **"light from light"** <note>original: "φῶς ἐκ φωτὸς"</note> our colleague Moser compares these lines of Nonnus in his *Paraphrase of the Gospel of John*, I. 3:
> and the Word of the self-begotten God, light, light from light.

Cf. also below, VI. 4. 9.

— 12. <note>original: "ὥσπερ χειμαζομένων πλοίων κυβερνῆται ἐναπερείδονται"</note> **"just as the pilots of storm-tossed ships brace themselves."**] Below, p. 389. A: "there it was necessary, as it were, for that power of the craftsman to brace itself," and p. 524. C. "as if the speaker braced himself in the sound." Plutarch, *Moralia*, p. 236. D. "to lean upon the spear." The same author in *Precepts of Health*, p. 126. E. p. 497. Wyttenbach: "bracing ourselves by memory," we struggle against memory, where Meziriacus preferred "bracing ourselves against." See Wyttenbach's *Observations*, p. 823. Stephanus has other examples in the *Thesaurus of the Greek Language*. But the term <term>enapereisis</term> <note>a "bracing" or "pressing into"</note>, which is read below in Plotinus IV. 4. 1., no one, as far as I know, has recorded in the Lexicons. Furthermore, metaphors of steering and navigation were frequent in the dialogues of Socrates and the Socratics. See for instance Xenophon, *Memorabilia*, I. 7. 3., III. 6. 38., III. 3. 9., and *Oeconomicus*, VIII. 14. Plato, or whoever the author of that dialogue may be, *Alcibiades I*, p. 125. C. No less frequent are expressions taken from nautical matters throughout the writings of Plato, for example in the *Symposium*, p. 197. p. 418. Bekker, concerning Love: **pilot, passenger, helper, savior**;—in the *Laches*, p. 194. p. 237. Bekker: **"help men who are friends and storm-tossed in speech"**; in the *Parmenides*, p. 137. p. 24. Bekker; and in the *Laws*, XI. p. 919. A. Ruhnken collected other examples both from Plato and from other writers in his notes to *Timaeus's Lexicon*, p. 79. Add Philo Judaeus, *On the Cherubim*, Vol. II. p. 22. Pfeiffer, and Proclus on *Alcibiades I*, p. 140. sq.

p. 716, 4. <note>original: "περὶ δὲ δαιμόνων καὶ ψυχῶν ἐν ἀέρι φωνῇ χρῆσθαι, οὐκ ἄτοπον"</note> **"concerning spirits and souls using a voice in the air, it is not absurd"**] Namely, "to believe so," following Plotinus's typical brevity. Hermias, in his commentary on Plato's *Phaedrus*, p. 94. Ast edition, praises our passage from memory: "Whence Plotinus, in the first book on the difficulties of the soul, says it is not at all absurd for spirits dwelling in the air to emit a voice; for such a striking of the air is voice." Then he follows this with more detail. Pythagoras himself is said to have recognized the voice of spirits, according to Porphyry in the *Life of Pythagoras*, §. 41. p. 42. Kuster edition. Later, the Spirit <note>Daimon</note> of Socrates gave occasion for discussions of this kind. Plutarch, in *On the Spirit of Socrates*, p. 589. C. D.—I have added the entire beautiful passage in the notes to Olympiodorus on *Alcibiades I*, p. 21. Here, however, it says: "Thirdly, that (Socrates) seemed to hear it as his (the spirit's) voice; not that the spirit spoke, but a kind of illumination from it occurred around the organs of hearing, and he thought it was a voice," etc. Michael Psellus touched upon the same question in *On the Operation of Daemons*, p. 73. Kiel edition.

— 10. <note>original: "᾿Αμέριστον μὲν οὖν ἁπλῶς εἴρηται αὐτῷ—γιγνομένην μεριστὴν"</note> **"That which is simply indivisible has been said by him—becoming divisible"**] Plato in the *Timaeus*, p. 35. p. 32. Bekker: "From the indivisible and eternally unchanging essence, and from that which becomes divisible in bodies, he compounded a third form of essence in the middle between both, concerning the nature of the Same and the nature of the Other, and thus he established it in the middle between the indivisible and that which is divided among bodies." Furthermore, Porphyry reduced these and the following Plotinian thoughts into a compendium in his *Sentences* or *On the Degrees*, chapters XXVIII. sqq. and XXXIX. p. 229. sqq. 246. sqq. Cambridge edition. Plutarch also touched upon this Platonic doctrine of the three principles and the soul in *On Isis and Osiris*, p. 370. E., for which passage Wyttenbach, in his *Observations*, both applied those words of Plato and cited others, p. 240. Oxford octavo edition.

p. 717, 8. <note>original: "ἐμπόδιον γὰρ τοῦτο (τὸ σῶμα) εἴ τις αὐτῷ ἐν ταῖς σκέψεσι προσχρῷτο"</note> **"for this (the body) is a hindrance if one were to use it in contemplations"**] Concerning this opinion, cf. what Plotinus said above on p. 215. F. and our notes there.

— 16. <note>original: "Εἰ δὲ καὶ ἐν τόπῳ ταὐτά τε καὶ τὰ ἄλλα τῆς ψυχῆς λεγόμενα μέρη κ. τ. λ."</note> **"But if also in a place these same and the other so-called parts of the soul..."** etc.] Iamblichus touched upon these and the following points in Stobaeus, *Physical Selections*, I. 52. 36.
