# ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS

**p. 908. Heeren:** <note>original: "Οὐχ ἡ αὐτὴ ἔστι πασῶν τῶν ψυχῶν κοινωνία πρὸς τὰ σώματα..."</note> "The communion of all souls with bodies is not the same; rather, the whole soul—as it also seems to Plotinus—holds the body approaching it within itself, but does not itself approach the body, nor is it contained by it. But partial souls approach bodies and become 'of the bodies,' and presently, as the bodies are mastered by the nature of the universe, they take up residence in them, etc." But indeed, the following chapters of this book prove that this is not entirely the opinion of Plotinus himself. Cf. also Porphyry, *On the Degrees of the Soul*, XXIX. p. 230.

**p. 718, 11.** <note>original: "οὐ μὴν οὐδ’ ὡς ἐν ἀγγείῳ"</note> "certainly not as if in a vessel, etc."] Porphyry, *On the Degrees*, ch. XXIX. p. 230: "If the incorporeal is held within a body, it must not be shut up like wild beasts in a cage. For nothing can shut it in or encompass a body in that way. Nor is it like a wineskin drawing in liquid or air. Rather, it must itself establish powers leaning outward from its own internal union, through which, descending, it becomes entwined with the body. Therefore, the connection into the body occurs through an ineffable extension. Thus, nothing else binds it, but it binds itself. Nor, then, does it dissolve when the body is broken and destroyed, but it releases itself by turning away from its attachment." Plotinus, however, seems to be touching upon the **Epicureans**, who taught that the body contains the soul like a vessel contains another material, according to the testimony of Diogenes Laertius X. 64; on which consult Menagius p. 463. cf. Annotations to our next page, 387. E.

**p. 720, 2.** <note>original: "οὐκ ἂν ἔφαμεν τὴν ψυχὴν ἐν τῷ σώματι εἶναι."</note> "We would not say that the soul is in the body."] Cf. annotations to the preceding page 386. F. Achilles Tatius, *Introduction to the Phenomena of Aratus*, ch. 13: "Posidonius said the Epicureans were ignorant that bodies do not hold souls together, but souls hold bodies together; just as glue holds both itself and external things." See *The Remains of Posidonius*, Ed. Bake, p. 65, which Wyttenbach translates and illustrates in the same place, p. 273 ff.:

> "i.e., bodies do not contain souls, but souls contain bodies. And the word <term>synechein</term> <note>original: "συνέχειν"</note> is proper in this matter, meaning *to preserve, contain, or sustain, lest they fall apart*: and this view, being truly Platonic, is celebrated by the Platonists. Maximus Tyrius XV. 5. p. 169: 'For if the soul provides the body (which is by nature perishable) with the ability not to perish whenever it is with it, it is far from being perished itself. In the constitution of a being, the body is held together, while the soul does the holding. If something else held the soul together, and not the soul itself, what would that be, and who could conceive of a soul of a soul?' etc."

There follows here this very passage of Plotinus; to which are added Porphyry and Numenius in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* XI. p. 556 and XV. p. 819; Plutarch, *Platonic Questions* p. 1002. B. Olympiodorus on Plato’s *Phaedo*, Book I. p. 74. Augustine, *On the Quantity of the Soul*, Vol. I. p. 322. etc.

**p. 720, 11.** <note>original: "Ὡς μὲν γὰρ πλωτὴρ—ὡς δὲ κυβερνήτης—ὥσπερ ἡ ψυχὴ ἐν τῷ σώματι."</note> "For as a passenger—as a pilot—just as the soul is in the body."] Taylor:

> "For the pilot, so far as he is a sailor, will be from accident a pilot in the ship. But if the soul is present with the body in the same manner as the pilot alone with the ship, how is this affected? For the pilot is not in all the ship, in the same manner as the soul is in all the ship."

From the approved books, I first gave <note>original: "ἐν αὐτῷ"</note> *in it* [masculine/neuter] instead of <note>original: "ἐν αὐτῇ"</note> *in it* [feminine]. And that very thing had been conjectured by the Dutch Censor of the special edition of Plotinus' *On Beauty*, which learned man sagacitously conjectures this passage could be restored: "For as a passenger, he would be in it (the body) by accident; but as a pilot, how? For the pilot is not in the whole ship, as the soul is in the body." I have indicated this reasoning in the Latin version, yet in such a way as to leave Ficino's version simultaneously intact. — Just as Aristotle enumerates those prior modes of the soul's conjunction with the body in the *Physics*, so he does in *On the Soul*, Book I, ch. 3, p. 9 of Sylburg's edition: "Everything that moves does so in two ways: either by another, or by itself. We say 'by another' for those things that move by being in something that is moving, such as passengers; for they do not move in the same way as the ship, for the ship moves by itself, but they move by being in the moving thing. This is clear in the parts of the body: the proper motion of the feet is walking, and this is also the motion of men; but it does not belong to the passengers then. Since 'to be moved' is said in two ways, we are now considering whether the soul is moved by itself and participates in motion." From this, the source of his example is understood. And the interpreters of Aristotle dispute much regarding this example. I will add this one thing from Simplicius, from the preface to his *Commentary on the Books on the Soul*: "But also the instrument is different from the user. Both the <term>entelechy</term> <note>The actualization or vital principle of a thing.</note> and the user are like the pilot of the ship. For the entelechy is twofold: one by which it is a ship, the other as the pilot." Iamblichus in Stobaeus, *Physical Eclogues* I. 52. 37. p. 916. Heeren, after mentioning Plotinus as one to be reckoned among the earlier Platonists, continues thus: "Now then, the use of the body—"

# BOOK III. ENNEAD FOUR. pages 718—722. 217

...requires much discernment. For some say that it <note>the soul</note> resembles a pilot <note>original: "κυβερνήσει" (kybernēsei) - the art of steering a ship</note> (Heeren suggests adding "of a ship") from which the pilot can also be separated without being destroyed. From this it is clear that this simile was frequently used in that doctrine. We have indicated the sources and examples of such similes above at page 385, A.

**p. 720, 15. Just as at the tiller—the tiller was.]** The source of the simile is in Plato's *Critias* page 109, page 150 in Bekker's edition.—"but as a most easily turned living being, directing it from the stern as if with a tiller, laying hold of their minds by the persuasion of the soul, thus leading the mortal element, they <note>the gods</note> governed the whole." <note>original: "πᾶν ἐκυβέρνων" (pan ekybernōn)</note> By the same formula, God is called the "steerer of the tiller" of men by Cyril of Alexandria in chapter IV of *Amos*, page 295. Likewise Philo the Jew in *On the Creation of the World*, Volume I, page 28, Pfeiffer edition: "For like a charioteer holding the reins, or a pilot holding the tillers, he leads each thing wherever he wishes according to law and justice, needing nothing else; for all things are possible for God." Compare *On the Migration of Abraham*, Volume III, page 412. In the same way, Theodoret now employs "tillers of the world," as in Volume II, page 468, Schulz edition; now "tillers of creation," Volume I, page 951. Other examples from the Church Fathers were collected by Matthæi in his notes on John Chrysostom's *Selected Orations*, III, page 6 and following. Proclus in *On the Alcibiades*, page 78, Frankfurt edition:—"and this one <note>the guardian spirit or 'daimon'</note> is the king of all things within us and around us, steering <note>original: "οἰακίζων" (oiakizōn)</note> our entire life." Regarding this passage, I have gathered more on the verb "to steer." Other material is supplied by the doctrine of the late Wyttenbach in his *Observations on Plutarch's On Studying the Poets*, page 284, where he illustrates the participle "being steered around." Himerius, *Oration* XIV, 32: "Just like a good pilot who, letting all the sailors be carried effortlessly upon the merchant ship, stands alone at the tillers and directs the vessel without a wave" (where I do not see why Wernsdorf prefers "without harm"). The same author in *Excerpts* XXXVI, 10, page 314: "A great city is at risk for me, and a whole continent is governed by the tillers." The same author, *Oration* VII, 15, page 536, Wernsdorf edition: "Therefore it is clear that it is an absolute necessity for one who is to sit at the rudders of the city to be a master of the tillers." Alciphron, Book I, Epistle 10: "Often, therefore, they are saved by being eager through safety to guard against danger. But there are those who, having once surrendered themselves to the sea, out of helplessness entrust the tillers to fortune to be carried along." See there Bergler and Wagner, page 60. Proclus also touches upon the passage in Plato in his commentary on the *Cratylus*, section 69, page 33, Boissonade edition, proceeding thus: "These rudders, then, and the tiller of the universe, by which the Creator being mounted arranges the whole, one must believe to be nothing other than symbols of the entire creation," etc.

**721, 12. Wherefore Plato also rightly did not place the soul in the body in the case of the universe]** See Plato's *Timaeus*, page 36 near the end, page 34 in Bekker, and page 42, page 45 and following in Bekker.

**p. 722, 6. The power in the eyes is the visual power—smell in the nostrils, etc.]** Aristotle discusses these senses and their powers and names, examining the opinions of the earlier natural philosophers, in *On the Soul*, III, 2, page 50, Sylburg edition. For the argument, compare Xenophon's *Memorabilia*, I, 4, 5; Cicero's *On Ends*, V, 11, 33; *On the Nature of the Gods*, II, 56; and Plotinus himself, IV, 6, 2; VI, 1, 12; VI, 3, 17; VI, 4, 11. Dio Chrysostom, *Oration* VIII, page 134, C. D., page 6, Baguet edition: "(of pleasure)—trying to corrupt through sight and hearing, or smell, or taste, or touch." Plutarch, *On Fortune*, page 98, F., page 387, Wyttenbach edition:—"but in all these things we are more unfortunate than the beasts. But by experience and memory and wisdom and art, according to Anaxagoras, we use them <note>the animals</note>, and we take their honey, and we milk them, and we carry and lead them, capturing them." In the preceding lines, Plutarch had mentioned the miraculous powers of individual animals, and what utility humans are accustomed to derive from them, in which place he also made mention of *dogs* accustomed to be used for the protection of men. Now he explains the opinion of Anaxagoras, who teaches how humans, although they possess less of those physical powers than beasts, nevertheless know how to use these very things by their own intelligence. However, those words are corrupt. Turnebus suggests: "with their vigor" or "by their wisdom." From the context of the thoughts and from the traces of the variant readings, I conjecture that instead of "their own" or "vigor" or "wisdom," we should read: "according to Anaxagoras, **we use their sense of smell**" <note>original: "ὀσφράνσει τε αὐτῶν χρώμεθα" (osphransei te autōn chrōmetha)</note>; and *we use their sense of smell* (namely in hunting, by which we catch wild beasts that we eat). And consider the following: "we take their honey," etc., each of which pertains to a part of the animals' bodies, except the last: "and we carry," which pertains to the whole body. Cicero also, in a passage very similar to Plutarch's, in *On the Nature of the Gods*, II, 60: "We impose burdens on certain beasts, we impose yokes..."

# ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS

"...we abuse the most acute senses of elephants and the sagacity of dogs for our own utility." <note>original Latin: "nos elephantorum acutissimis sensibus, nos sagacitate canum ad utilitatem nostram abutimur."</note>

p. 723, 6. **"For this reason it was placed by the ancients in the highest parts of the whole living being, upon the head."** <note>original Greek: ταύτῃ ἐτέθη τοῖς παλαιοῖς ἐν τοῖς ἄκροις τοῦ ζῴου παντὸς, ἐπὶ τῆς κεφαλῆς.</note>] This refers to Plato’s *Timaeus* p. 70. A. p. 98. Bekker edition: "That part of the soul, then, which partakes of courage and spirit, being contentious, they settled closer to the head, between the midriff and the neck, so that being obedient to reason, it might join with it in forcibly restraining the tribe of desires whenever they should refuse to obey the command and reason from the citadel." <note>original Greek: τὸ μετέχον οὖν τῆς ψυχῆς ἀνδρίας καὶ θυμοῦ... ἐκ τῆς ἀκροπόλεως.</note> Longinus, in *On the Sublime* XXXII. 5, cited this entire passage as an example of the divine style of speaking in which Plato excels. Alcinous, in *On the Doctrines of Plato* ch. XXIII, p. 503, Heinsius edition:—"The divine and immortal part of the soul they settled in the body, as if upon a citadel <note>perhaps: they settled it upon the citadel, as it were, of the body</note> declaring it the ruler and king, and assigning the head as its dwelling place, which has a shape mimicking that of the universe." Chalcidius, in his commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus* p. 327: "The rational part of the soul, as the wisest, holds the principal part, like the Capitol of the entire body." Cicero, in *On the Nature of the Gods* II. 56: "The senses, however, the interpreters and messengers of things, are marvelously formed and situated in the head, as if in a citadel, for necessary uses;" on which passage Davis provides further notes. To this, join the excellent remarks of Jacobs on *Philostratus' Images* p. 525 ff. —The following points in Plotinus regarding concupiscence, anger, the liver, and the heart agree perfectly with Plato’s description in the cited passage of the *Timaeus* p. 70. B. C. Compare Plutarch, *On the Generation of the Soul in the Timaeus* p. 1025 ff. and p. 174 ff. Wyttenbach edition, who has other remarks including these, pertaining to the words of Plotinus in the following: "for the sensory part is in a way critical and imaginative, like the intellectual, etc." <note>original Greek: αἰσθητικὸν γὰρ, κριτικόν πως καὶ φανταστικὸν, οἷον νοερὸν κ. τ. λ.</note>: "Indeed, one could not easily understand an emotion or a movement of the mind unless some desire or ambition, or something of joy or sorrow, were present. Therefore, some of the philosophers make the emotions into reasons, as if every desire, pain, and anger were judgments."

p. 724, 15. **"For the divine law is inescapable, etc."** <note>original Greek: Ἀναπόδραστος γὰρ ὁ θεῖος νόμος κ. τ. λ.</note>] The source is in Plato’s *Gorgias* p. 523. A. p. 163 ff. Bekker: "This law concerning men existed in the time of Cronus and always was and still is among the gods: that the man who has lived his life justly and holily, when he dies, goes to the Isles of the Blessed to dwell in all happiness far from evils; but he who has lived unjustly and godlessly goes to the prison-house of retribution and justice, which they call Tartarus." To this passage in the Bodleian Manuscript, four Scholia <note>ancient marginal commentaries</note> are added on p. 93 of Gaisford’s edition, undoubtedly taken from the commentaries of Proclus. Plutarch follows the same path, also following Plato, in *On the Late Revenge of the Deity* p. 564 ff. and p. 273 ff. Wyttenbach; cf. his observations p. 435 ff. The same Plutarch in Stobaeus, *Physical Eclogues* I. 19. p. 188. Heeren: "For this reason they call fate also 'Adrasteia' <note>The Inescapable One</note>, because it imposes a necessitated end upon causes, being unavoidable and inescapable." The same word is used by the author of *On the Universe* VII. 3 (attributed to Aristotle); likewise Hermias in Plato’s *Phaedrus* p. 149. Ast; from whence it passed into the Scholia p. 63. Siebenkees edition. No less does Eustathius in *Odyssey* 13. v. 839. p. 269. Basel edition, and our author himself above on p. 382. B. For the argument and summary of thoughts, apply what we noted above for p. 264. E. and p. 284. F. G. Proclus has these Plotinian passages before his eyes in his commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus* p. 323, where he copiously illustrates Plato’s decrees on the divine order in worldly affairs and the choices of lives: "because," he adds, "each choice (of lives, whether good or bad) is full of the laws of fate, and they lead themselves where the law speaking within them dictates, as Plotinus also says."

— 17. **"he is carried—and the sufferer himself—suspended everywhere in his wanderings by an unstable motion—having an involuntary element in his suffering."** <note>original Greek: φέρεται—καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ πάσχων—ἀστάτῳ μὲν τῇ φορᾷ πανταχοῦ αἰωρούμενος ταῖς πλάναις—τὸ ἀκούσιον εἰς τὸ παθεῖν ἔχων.</note>] A most significant passage that reflects the true character of the Platonic philosopher. Taylor, because Ficino translates it as "driven around by errors," says we should read *peri-agomenos* <note>led around</note> instead of *aioroumenos* <note>suspended/wavering</note>. I would not wish this to have escaped that excellent man. For first, the books (manuscripts), except for one which has a common confusion, show no variation; secondly, the verb *aioreisthai* <note>to be suspended or hover</note> fits perfectly with "unstable motion" and "wanderings." What more do you seek? Plotinus drew his coloring from Plato’s *Menexenus* p. 248. A: "For the man for whom all things leading to happiness depend on himself or nearly so, and do not hang suspended <note>aioreitai</note> upon other men, from whose good or ill fortune his own affairs are forced to wander, he is best prepared..."

# BOOK III. FOURTH ENNEAD. p. 723—727.

...to live, this is the man of self-control, the courageous, and the wise. <note>original: "ζῆν, οὑτός ἐστιν ὁ σώφρων καὶ οὗτος ὁ ἀνδρεῖος καὶ φρόνιμος."</note> Aristides touches upon this passage in his *Platonic Orations* Vol. II. p. 163. Jebb edition. Cicero also expressed this in *Tusculan Disputations* V. 12: “For the man for whom all things that lead to a happy life depend upon himself, and are not **suspended** from others or forced to **hang** upon the outcomes of another and **wander** by good or bad fortune,” etc. Consult Gottleber and Loers on the *Menexenus* at the cited location, p. 172. I will not repeat what learned men have recently gathered in the London edition of *Stephanus's Thesaurus* regarding this word; I will add a few other points. Plutarch in *On the Face in the Moon* p. 924. B. "a ceaseless flow and a suspension <term>aiora: a state of being suspended or balanced</term> ceaselessly suspended" <note>original: "ῥεῦμα ἄπαυστον αἰώραν καὶ ἀκατάπαυστον αἰωρούμενον"</note>: balanced by an unceasing oscillation. Compare Wyttenbach on Plato’s *Phaedo* p. 311—313, where he explains the term *aiora* regarding the interior motion of the Earth. See the same author on Plutarch p. 837, where he also discusses the alternative spelling *eora* (on which add G. O. Reiz on *Theophilus's Paraphrase of the Institutes* II. p. 733; Ast on Plato’s *Laws* p. 341; Jacobs in *Lectures on Stobaeus* p. 19—21; and Coray in *Atakta* II. p. 19.) Dionysius of Halicarnassus in *Excerpts of Antiquities* XII. 20. p. 19. Milan first edition, concerning Camillus: "then reflecting how the happiness of men is suspended <note>original: "αἰωρεῖται"</note> upon a small momentum and nothing of good remains stable"—he prayed. <note>original: "ἔπειτ’ ἐνθυμηθεὶς ὡς ἐπὶ μικρᾶς αἰωρεῖται ῥοπῆς ἡ τῶν ἀνθρώπων εὐδαιμονία καὶ βέβαιον οὐδὲν διαμένει τῶν ἀγαθῶν—ηὔξατο"</note> Angelo Mai translates: “Then considering that human happiness is raised up for a short time;” I would prefer: *to be balanced on a tiny moment, or to be suspended by a thin momentum*; although I would not deny that elsewhere it can also mean *to extol*. In Xenophon’s *On Hunting* IV. 4. dogs are said to have their "souls suspended" <note>original: "αἰωρεῖσθαι τὴν ψυχὴν"</note> when they almost reach the wild beast. But Herodian also spoke of being suspended regarding hope in *History* VI. 2. 9: "suspended by vain hopes." Plutarch in *Brutus* chapter 37. p. 212. Coray edition: "to you indeed the body, being naturally distressed, suspends and turns aside the intellect." <note>original: "σοὶ δὴ καὶ τὸ σῶμα ταλαιπωρούμενον φύσει τὴν διάνοιαν αἰωρεῖ καὶ παρατρέπει."</note> Hence "to be suspended" <note>original: "αἰωρεῖσθαι"</note> is used of those who, like ships, are tossed here and there and fluctuate in mind. On this use and others, C. F. Bæhr has collected more in his notes on Plutarch’s *Alcibiades* 28. p. 219 and following, and on *Philopoemen* c. 16. p. 58.

p. 725, 15. **Concerning memory, whether it belongs to the souls themselves—to remember, etc.**] <note>original: "Περὶ δὲ μνήμης, εἰ αὐταῖς ταῖς ψυχαῖς—μνημονεύειν ὑπάρχει κ. τ. λ."</note> To these and the following points belong what Porphyry posits in the booklet *On Degrees* found in Stobaeus's *Physical Eclogues* I. 52. 19. p. 820 and following. Heeren in the Cambridge edition of that booklet c. XXXIX. p. 246 and following; likewise the notes of Iamblichus in the same Stobaeus ibid. I. 52.

31. p. 880. who says: "Plotinus takes away from it (the soul) the irrational powers: the senses, the imaginations, the memories, the reasonings. He directs only pure reasoning toward its pure essence, as having a connatural power toward the very idea of essence. But those around Porphyry and Plotinus declare that the appropriate powers are projected by the soul into each part of the universe, and [the Platonic followers of Porphyry and Plotinus] define that the lives projected in any way are let go and no longer exist, much like things growing from a seed when the seed runs back into itself." <note>original: "Πλωτῖνος αὐτῆς (τῆς ψυχῆς) ἀφαιρεῖ τὰς ἀλόγους δυνάμεις... ὁπόταν εἰς ἑαυτὸ ἀναδραμῇ τὸ σπέρμα."</note> These last points pertain in part to the earlier passages of Plotinus p. 351. F. where you should consult the annotations and apply Porphyry’s *On Degrees* in Stobaeus at the cited location p. 824—826. and p. 247 below in the Cambridge edition.

p. 726, 2. **for what memory is, has been stated elsewhere.**] <note>original: "τὸ μὲν γάρ ἐστι μνήμη, εἴρηται ἐν ἄλλοις."</note> Namely in the book *On Sensation and Memory* below in IV. 6. But because this book *On Sensation and Memory* was written after these books *On the Doubts of the Soul*, Plotinus must be thought to refer here to other passages of these Enneads, which are not few. Taylor, in his Annotations to this place, wrote: “Memory is summarily **stability of knowledge**; just as immortality is stability of life, and eternity is stability of being.”

— 6. **certainly memory is not to be placed in God, nor in Being and Intellect**] <note>original: "μνήμην δὴ περὶ θεὸν, οὐδὲ περὶ τὸ ὂν καὶ νοῦν θετέον"</note> For "certainly not" <note>original: "μν. δὴ οὐ"</note> or "neither." See Schæfer on Lamb. Bos. *Ellipses* p. 777. and Matthiae’s *Greek Grammar* §. 609. p. 1227. second edition.

p. 727, 2. **and especially having come here**] <note>original: "καὶ μάλιστα ἐνταῦθα ἡκούσῃ"</note> Ficino translates: “and especially having traveled far to this place.” Taylor: “and especially when it has profoundly descended into body.” I think these words should rather be understood thus: and especially that which (*just now*, or *very recently*) arrived here. Plotinus seems to be speaking of the souls of infants born not so long ago, which, disturbed by their recent fall and as if intoxicated, are less able to unfold the higher powers of the mind but are more enslaved to matter and nutrition. See Proclus on the *First Alcibiades* p. 196. In this matter, Plotinus seems to teach the opposite of the so-called Hermes, who in the *Key* p. 11. a. b. edition of Francesco Patrizi, claims the infant's soul is purer, as it is not yet deeply stained by the filth of matter. Regarding the words "memory and recollection" <note>original: "μνήμην καὶ ἀνάμνησιν"</note> compare below p. 472. E.

<meta>This page continues the scholarly annotations on the works of Plotinus, specifically commenting on Book III of the Enneads. # NOTES ON PLOTINUS

**p. 728, l. 1. such as boring, and weaving]** <note>original: "οἷον τὸ τρυπᾶν, καὶ τὸ ὑφαίνειν"</note> Plotinus borrowed these similarities from Plato, who employed these very examples for a lengthy discussion in the *Cratylus* p. 388 and following. Compare the *Scholia* of Proclus on that passage, sections 47–50, pages 18–21 in the Boissonade edition.

**— 18. as if in a mixture of honey-wine]** <note>original: "ὥσπερ ἐν οἰνομέλιτος κράσει"</note> Aristotle in *Metaphysics* VII. 2. p. 134 and following in the Sylburg edition uses the phrase "just like a honey-water mixture" <note>original: "καθάπερ μελίκρατον"</note>. Sextus Empiricus in *Against the Physicists* IX. 154, p. 586 in the Fabricius edition, writes: "but not the one drinking honey-wine" <note>original: "ἀλλ’ οὐχ ὁ οἰνόμελι πίνων"</note>, where Fabricius did not forget our passage, yet mentioned nothing regarding the false reading which we have corrected from the better manuscripts. Moeris the Atticist <note>A 2nd-century grammarian who compared "pure" Attic Greek with common Greek</note> on page 254: "**Melikraton [honey-water mixture], in Attic Greek. Oinomeli [honey-wine] and hydromeli [honey-water], in common Greek**" <note>original: "Μελίκρατον, ’Αττικῶς. οἰνόμελι καὶ ὑδρόμελι, Ἑλληνικῶς"</note>: on which see Pierson. Eustathius in his commentary on *Odyssey* book 10, line 519: "**The ancients say that 'melikraton' is a mixture of honey and milk** <note>original: "Μελίκρατον δὲ οἱ παλαιοὶ μίγμα φασὶ μέλιτος καὶ γάλακτος"</note> (*compare Euripides' Orestes line 115 and the Scholiast there*) **in this context. However, those after Homer, even down to the latest writers, know 'melikraton' as a mixture of honey and water.**" Regarding this matter, see Palladius on *De Re Rustica* [On Agriculture] for October, XVII, p. 227 in Schneider’s edition: concerning *Enomelle* [Honey-wine] "You take unfermented wine from larger and excellent vines—you shall take, as others say—and if you mix in a fifth part of the best honey, not skimmed, previously ground vigorously until it turns white, etc." Compare Beckmann on Aristotle's *On Marvelous Things Heard* p. 52; Fabricius on Sextus at the place cited; Tib. Hemsterhuis on Lucian’s *Prometheus* chapter 5; and Jacobs on the poems of Meleager in the *Greek Anthology* Vol. VI. p. 51. The words of Aristotle and Sextus which we have cited prove that this comparison was pleasing to the philosophers. However, Porphyry had misused this same comparison—or certainly used it far too much—in explaining the Soul of the World, for which he was mocked by Proclus in his commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus* p. 218: "**Thus Porphyry, being carried away toward sensible things and material mixtures, prattles on up and down about honey-water and honey-wine.**" <note>original: "ὁ μὲν οὖν Πορφύριος ἐπὶ τὰ αἰσθητὰ φερόμενος καὶ ἐπὶ τὰς μίξεις τὰς ἐνύλας, τὸ μελίκρατον καὶ τὸ οἰνόμελι ἄνω καὶ κάτω θρυλλεῖ."</note> Olympiodorus also seems to touch upon this in Plato’s *Alcibiades* I, section XXV, p. 207: "**it remains then that the soul is the human being. As the argument proceeds in this way, some take hold of it saying, so far as this is concerned: since honey-water is water and honey, or honey and water; and it is not honey, nor (perhaps 'neither') indeed honey and water, it follows that it is water.**" Furthermore, the Ancients occasionally compared the character and speech of poets and writers to the sweetness or harshness of wines. Diogenes Laertius IV. 20. regarding Sophocles: "**and where he was, according to Phrynichus**"

<column-break/>

**not sweet, nor diluted, but Pramnian.** <note>Pramnian wine was famously strong and harsh, often associated with the older, more rugged style of poetry.</note>
Suidas erroneously referred these words to the philosopher Polemon in Vol. III, p. 264 of Kuster’s edition. You should see Salmasius in *Plinian Exercises* p. 261; the interpreters on Hesychius Vol. I, p. 839 in Alberti’s edition; Casaubon and Menage on Diogenes Laertius at the cited place; Casaubon and Schweighaeuser on Athenaeus Vol. I, p. 234; Valckenaer on *Acts of the Apostles* II. 13. (in the *Scholae* Vol. I, p. 353); and Boissonade in *Notices and Extracts* Vol. XI. p. 195.

**p. 729, 4. just like the seal-impressions]** <note>original: "ὥσπερ αἱ ἐνσφραγίσεις"</note> The verb **ensphragizo** [to seal or impress] is recorded by lexicographers (Add Lucian’s *Affairs of the Heart* §. 5. p. 403 in the Wetstein edition and §. 14. p. 412): but the substantive form is unknown to them. Nor is the substantive **antisphragisma** [a counter-seal] found, nor **apographon** [a copy] confirmed by a pressed seal; which the most learned *Letronne* also orders to be added to the lexicons in his pamphlet: *Critical Analysis of the Collection of Greek and Latin Inscriptions of Mr. the Count de Vidua. Paris. 1828. p. 39.* You may find **eksphragisma** used for "a copy" in the *Oxford Marbles* p. 130. Gregory Nazianzen in *On Holy Baptism* p. 245 in the Basel Hervagius edition: "**consider it thus: let there be gold, let there be iron; let both be rings, and let the same royal image be engraved on both, then let them make an impression in wax. How will this seal differ from that seal? In nothing. Recognize the material in the wax; even if you are the wisest of men, tell me, which is the impression of the iron, and which of the gold? And how is it that they are one? For the difference lies in the material, not in the character of the mark.**" Suidas and Zonaras explain **eksphragisma** [the impression] with the word **ektupoma** [a molded image]. The *Gudian Etymologicon* on p. 179 does the reverse, explaining **ektupoma** by that former word.

**p. 730, 7. Wherefore also this might be understood as the river of Lethe.]** <note>original: "Διὸ καὶ ὁ τῆς Λήθης ποταμὸς οὗτος ἂν ὑπονοοῖτο."</note> Macrobius in *The Dream of Scipio* I. 12: 
> "But the highest and purest part of it, by which divine things are either sustained or consist, is called nectar, and is believed to be the drink of the gods: the lower and more turbulent part, however, is the drink of souls. And this is what the ancients called the *River Lethe* [the river of forgetfulness]."

Hence the terms "**oblivion of the soul**" <note>original: "λήθη τῆς ψυχῆς"</note> and "**generative oblivion**" <note>original: "λήθη γενεσιουργός"</note>. Compare Proclus on *Alcibiades* I, pages 20, 41, 189, 250, 257, 281, and our *Symbolica* III, p. 394 and following. Some also referred Latona <note>The mother of Apollo and Artemis</note> to the meaning of oblivion. Proclus in Plato’s *Cratylus* § 178. p. 111 in the Boissonade edition: "**For memory leads toward the thing to be remembered, says Plotinus, and just as Mnemosyne [Memory] awakens the memory of the intelligible things, so also does...**"

<summary>This page contains scholarly commentary on Plotinus's metaphors, specifically discussing the mixtures of honey and wine as philosophical analogies for the soul, the linguistics of wax seal impressions, and the mythological river Lethe as a symbol for the soul's loss of divine memory.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the scholarly commentary on Plotinus’s Ennead III, specifically detailing textual variants and philosophical interpretations of the soul’s memory and its relation to material existence, following the discussion of metaphors and mixtures on the previous page.</meta>

# BOOK III, FOURTH ENNEAD, pages 728–736.

Leto bestows Oblivion upon material things. <note>original: "Λητὼ τὴν Λήθην δωρεῖται τῶν ἐνύλων." In Greek mythology, Leto was sometimes etymologically associated with 'lethe' (forgetfulness) to explain how the soul forgets its divine origin when entering the material world.</note> Furthermore, Plato discusses forgetfulness in several places, such as in the *Phaedo* ch. 20 p. 75. D. (on which see Wyttenbach’s *Annotations* p. 189 and in *Philomath* III. p. 92); in the *Philebus* p. 33; (see Stallbaum p. 95 ff.) in the *Symposium* p. 208. p. 438. in Bekker’s edition (a passage Stobaeus included in his *Florilegium* LXXV. p. 94. Gaisford edition); and in the *Laws* V. 732. p. 381. Bekker edition. Compare also Aristotle in the *Topics* VII. 2. Philo Judaeus, in *Allegorical Interpretation of the Law* III. p. 296. Pfeiffer edition—"**memory is better, but recollection is worse. For memory possesses perceptions that are present and clear, so as not to fail through ignorance; but forgetfulness always precedes recollection, which is a crippled and blind thing. The worse thing, recollection, is found to be older than memory, which is continuous and inseparable.**" <note>original: "ἀμείνων μὲν μνήμη..."</note> Mangey, recognizing a gap in the text, wishes to read: "**[older than] the superior [memory] <unclear>* * *</unclear> continuous and inseparable.**" Perhaps you might fill the gap and read: "**[older than] the superior [memory], since it is continuous and inseparable.**" Unless you prefer: "**the foundation (or support) of the superior thing, continuous and inseparable.**" For after a few intervening words he continues: "**for which reason also (memory) is younger, for it is late-born, arising out of recollection.**"

**p. 730, 14. The image of Heracles in Hades]** See above, I. 1. 12. p. 7. B. "**the poet seems to separate this in the case of Heracles, giving his image to Hades, while he himself is among the gods**" <note>Plotinus is interpreting the passage in the *Odyssey* where Odysseus sees the 'shade' or image of Heracles in the underworld, even though the true Heracles resides on Olympus.</note> : consult the annotations there. On this passage we are treating, Taylor noted: “i. e. the irrational, which is the image of the rational soul, is in the obscurity of the sensible life.” This is correct: but those things read above on p. 7. B. C. must also be kept in mind: "**that (Heracles) was active but not contemplative.**" <note>Plotinus suggests that the 'image' remains in the lower world because Heracles focused on physical labors rather than pure intellectual meditation.</note> Furthermore, see our author's third passage on this, below p. 396. C. D. Wyttenbach touched upon this in his commentary on Plutarch’s *On the Delay of Divine Vengeance* p. 99. p. 427. Oxford edition.

**p. 731, 5. for that which is attracted]** <note>original: "ἡ γὰρ ἐφελκομένη"</note> Ficino translates: “For the soul indeed, drawn together with this.” Better, Taylor: “For the soul, indeed, which is attracted by body.” I, thinking these words should be taken in the Middle voice, have revised the translation. For the opposite state is "**the soul having been set free.**"

— 9. **and what it did not have in memory here, it will recall.**] Plotinus takes this from Plato. *Philebus* p. 34. p. 180. Bekker: "**And indeed, whenever the soul, having lost the memory either of a perception or a lesson, again recovers**

<column-break/>

**this within itself, we call all these things recollections and memories.**" See Stallbaum’s annotations there, p. 97 ff. From this comes the phrase "**to take up a recollection**" <note>original: "ἀναπόλησιν λαβεῖν"</note> above p. 210. E. and "**to come into recollection**" <note>original: "εἰς ἀναπόλησιν ἔρχεσθαι"</note> below p. 455. D. Both passages help in understanding the argument of our own text.

**p. 732, 7. but so as to suffer without perceiving]** <note>original: "ἀλλ' ὥστε ἀπαρακολουθήτως παθεῖν"</note> That is, to experience something in such a way that it does not grasp it through understanding (or notice it). Taylor: “but so as to suffer without perceiving what it is.” The word "**unperceived**" <note>original: "Ἀπαρακολουθήτου"</note> is also taken passively, as "**that which one cannot follow.**" See Tzetzes on Lycophron v. 5. p. 279. Mueller edition. To "**act without perceiving**" and "**to do good**" <note>original: "Ἀπαρακολουθήτως ἐνεργεῖν et εὖ ποιεῖν"</note> means to act or do good to someone as if you did not know or did not notice what you were doing, and therefore at random or without a plan; see Casaubon and Gataker on Marcus Aurelius p. 56. and p. 145. This passage from Plotinus should be added to those references.

— 9. **as, if a shepherd seeing a wolf near the flock etc.**] These things bring to mind the proverb "**you have seen a wolf.**" <note>An ancient Greek belief suggested that if a wolf saw a person first, that person would lose their voice.</note> See Theocritus, *Idyll* XIV. 22. and the *Scholia* there p. 175. Gaisford edition, which Plato himself alludes to in the *Republic* I. p. 336. p. 22. Bekker. And the Socratics loved that fable of the dog and the wolf, "**the story of the dog.**" See Xenophon, *Memorabilia of Socrates* II. 7. 13. 14. cf. II. 9. 2. Therefore, it is no wonder that this simile occurred to Plotinus as well. Moreover, the "**faithful guardianship of dogs**" is also mentioned among the examples used by the Stoics in Cicero’s *On the Nature of the Gods* II. 63. I touched upon other matters regarding this above in my notes on chapter XXIII of this book, p. 388. A, below. In our passage, this dog might be said in a way to "**recognize through the eyes of others,**" as occurs in Pliny’s *Natural History* XXIX. 8. Furthermore, that a flock of sheep is intended is proven by the words "**shepherd**" and "**flock**" <note>original: "ποιμὴν et ποίμνιον"</note>, which are properly used for *sheep*. See my notes in the *Commentaries on Herodotus* p. 193.—Shortly after, I did not hesitate to adopt from the better manuscripts the word "**scent**" <note>original: "ὀδμῇ"</note> instead of "**impulse**" <note>original: "ὁρμῇ"</note>, as it is more suitable for this passage where "**noise**" and therefore "**hearing**" are mentioned. Nor did I hesitate to restore "**knowing**" <note>original: "εἰδυῖαν"</note> instead of "**pleasant**" <note>original: "ἡδεῖαν"</note> near the end of the chapter, even though our printed books persist in the common reading. For the connection of the ideas demands the former, and it is very likely that Ficino read it that way.

**p. 736, 7. and those things which even a refined man would not be out of place in remembering—and the refined aspects of the passions to the virtuous (soul) etc.**] On this and similar passages, see the *Rhetorical Lexicon* in Bekker’s *Greek Anecdotes*.

# ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS

I. p. 206. *Asteios*—means—also the one praised for their character <note>original: "Αστεῖος—σημαίνει—καὶ τὸν διὰ ἦθος ἐπαινούμενον." The term *asteios* originally meant "of the city" (urbane), but evolved to mean refined, virtuous, or beautiful.</note> that is, *approved for one's character, and thus good and upright.* The *Gudian Etymologicon*, somewhat more fully on p. 86: "the one praised for their excellent character." <note>original: "ὁ διὰ τὸ ἦθος χρηστὸν ἐπαινούμενος."</note> But because he nevertheless adds: "how the child was *asteios* to God" <note>original: "ὡς ἢ τὸ παιδίον ἀστεῖον τῷ θεῷ."</note> (which words are composed from Acts of the Apostles 7:20 and Hebrews 11:23) it means rather in that passage: *he was wonderfully charming.* Cf. *Etymologicon Magnum* p. 158. Zonaras p. 313. Suicer’s *Ecclesiastical Thesaurus* Vol. I p. 557 ff. and Valckenaer’s *Scholarly Notes on the New Testament* Vol. I p. 425. Furthermore, see Plato’s *Republic* I p. 349. B., *Lysis* p. 204, and Heindorf's notes there p. 5. Cf. another Lexicon in the same *Anecdota* of Bekker p. 453 ff. I do not wish to repeat what others have collected: I praise Wyttenbach’s *Observations on Plutarch’s Consolation to Apollonius* p. 760. I add a passage from Philo Judaeus, *Allegorical Interpretation of the Law*, Book III, p. 97 near the bottom of Mangey’s edition:—"For the soul of the wicked has no place where it may step, or upon which it may be established. For this reason, the wicked person is also said to be *atopos* <note>original: "ἄτοπος." Literally "out of place," but used to mean "absurd" or "strange." Philo plays on the word's root to suggest the wicked have no spiritual standing.</note>; and the *atopos* is an evil thing, difficult to place. Such is the man who is not *asteios* [refined/virtuous], always shaking and being tossed about, etc." Philostratus, *Life of Apollonius* VIII. 19. p. 362: "they have need of an *asteios* man," meaning: "they have need of an upright, good man." Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* III. p. 559 Potter edition: "For the tree of life, says the Prophet, is produced in good desire, teaching that the desires in the living Lord are *asteious* [noble] and pure." For which reason I would prefer Plotinus’s "the *asteia* of the passions" <note>original: "τὰ ἀστεῖα τῶν παθῶν."</note> to be translated: *the good, pure affections.* Taylor translates: "The passions as are of an elegant nature," which I fear may be ambiguous. Other details regarding the words *asteios* [refined], *astikos* [civil], *asteismos* [wit], and *asteizesthai* [to play the wit] were recently provided by Boissonade on Aristaenetus p. 441 ff. and Eunapius p. 404, and Jacobs on Philostratus’s *Images* p. 376. Cf. also Meineke’s *Menander* p. 97, 157, 205, 271. In Alciphron (Epistle II. 4. p. 325 Wagner edition) the Heidelberg Palatine Manuscript No. 132 retains *attikismois* [Atticisms] instead of *asteismois* [witticisms], which the most recent editor, following the authority of Hemsterhuis and Ruhnken, has restored to the text.

p. 737, 7. **Since it also flees from the many—for thus it is not with the many, but light and by itself.**] <note>original: "Ἐπεὶ καὶ φεύγει ἐκ τῶν πολλῶν... ἐλαφρὰ καὶ δι' αὐτῆς." This describes the soul's ascent and its separation from the "multitude" of material concerns.</note> How Marsilio Ficino might have weakened these final words is shown by his version. Taylor translates thus: "For thus it will not associate with multitude, but expelling it will live by itself." And I doubt whether Ficino correctly understood that word *elaphra* [light/alleviated]. Synesius, *On

<column-break/>

Dreams* p. 139 Petavius edition: "and philosophy agrees that the first lives are preparations for the second, with the best condition in souls *making light* [alleviating] it (the animal spirit) and wiping away the stain of the worse condition." <note>original: "τῆς ἀρίστης ἕξεως ἐν ψυχαῖς ἐλαφριζούσης..."</note> meaning: "when indeed the best habit of the soul makes the animal spirit more subtle." Moreover, this discussion by Synesius from p. 135–142 is entirely to be compared with that of Plotinus. Therefore, I would translate those words of Plotinus thus: "For in this way the soul is also not with the many; but *lightened* and by itself (alone)." Proclus pursues this argument at length in *On the Alcibiades*, beginning of Chapter 82, p. 245: "Therefore, for those beginning from below, one must flee the multitude of men who go in herds, as the oracle says, and one must share neither in their lives nor their peculiarities. And one must flee the many-formed desires, which divide us around the body, etc."

— 11. **And that famous Hercules might speak of his own fortitude—and having been transferred into a more sacred place**] Undoubtedly the immediately preceding words moved Ficino to add to the first part: *in the heavens.* Taylor does everything differently, translating thus: "And Hercules, indeed, [when in Hades,] may speak of his own fortitude; but in the intelligible world he will consider these things as trifling, being transferred into a more sacred place." I do not precisely object; and see above p. 7. B. and p. 392 at the bottom and 393. But nevertheless, in this passage, the words that immediately follow cast doubt: "therefore even there the things from here are few, and being in heaven they are more." If you follow Ficino's reasoning, Hercules must be placed in four locations: on earth, among the shades in the underworld, in the heavens, and in the intelligible world. <note>The "intelligible world" in Neoplatonism refers to the highest realm of pure thought and forms, above the physical heavens.</note>

## BOOK IV.

p. 738, 7. **ON DIFFICULTIES CONCERNING THE SOUL, THE SECOND [BOOK]**] <note>original: "ΠΕΡΙ ΨΥΧΗΣ ΑΠΟΡΙΩΝ, ΔΕΥΤΕΡΟΝ."</note> According to the chronological order, this is the twenty-eighth book, and is therefore joined with the one immediately preceding it in both order and subject matter. See the note on the title of that book, p. 371.

p. 739, 10. **for the part above—why shall it not be**] I have been sparing in correcting these and the following words, as they are not entirely clear to me. As for what follows:—"that the intellection becomes multifaceted and great at once, and the intellections many," <note>original: "ποικίλην καὶ πολλὴν τὴν νόησιν ἅμα γίγνεσθαι καὶ πολλὰς τὰς νοήσεις."</note> you may compare these passages from our author: III. 8. 7., III. 9. 3., V. 3. 5. Moreover, the source of these passages is in Plato’s *Timaeus* p. 28. A. (p. 22 Bekker) and p. 30. A.

### BOOK IV. OF THE FOURTH ENNEAD. pp. 737—744.

B. p. 25. Bekker. From this, Proclus, in his *Commentary* p. 74 (below) and p. 75 (in a classic passage, though too long to be included here), derived material for his discussion on the six kinds <note>He counts exactly six.</note> of **modes of thought** <note>original: "τῶν νοήσεων"</note>. Philo Judæus also seems to have benefited from these same Platonic passages in his *Allegorical Interpretation of the Law*, Book I, p. 41 (Mangey) / p. 122 (Pfeiffer), and Book II, p. 71 / p. 198.

**p. 741, 13. for he is all things, and both are one; but the soul]** <note>original: "πάντα γὰρ αὐτός ἐστι, καὶ ἄμφω ἕν· ἀλλ’ ἡ ψυχή"</note> I have provided this reading based on the authority of many books and because of what follows: **having come into the intellect she has been joined—but both are one and two.** <note>original: "εἰς τε νοῦν ἐλθοῦσα ἡρμοσταὶ—ἀλλ’ ἐν ἔστιν ἄμφω καὶ δύο"</note> The printed edition has: *for he is all things. and both are in another soul, being in the intelligible.* Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the Italian scholar who first translated Plotinus into Latin.</note> translates: “For he is indeed all things, and according to both, remaining through another soul in the intelligible world:” etc. The words at the beginning, **for he is all things**, are to be explained by that sentiment frequently met with in these *Enneads*, **that the intellect is all things.** <note>original: "ὅτι ὁ νοῦς, τὰ πάντα"</note> See Book I. 8. 2. p. 73. A; III. 3. 3. and the annotation there; and compare below, VI. 9. 3. p. 759. D. Furthermore, anyone who has followed the fluctuations of philosophy throughout Germany over the last forty years will find in these investigations of Plotinus the seeds of those doctrines which Kant and his followers brought forward, without even having consulted Plotinus.

**p. 742, 7. and as if looking forth]** <note>original: "καὶ οἷον προκύψασα"</note> Anyone who compares the earlier passage in IV. 3. 15. p. 383. D. will have no doubt that **peeping out** <note>original: "ἐκκύψασαι"</note> is used there with a similar meaning regarding souls that are prone to sinking downward. See the note there. A contrary sentiment is found in the Doric letter of Lysis in Iamblichus's *Life of Pythagoras*, XVII. 77. p. 64 (Kuster) / p. 166 (Kiessling): **for dense and thick thickets have grown around the minds and hearts of those who have not been purely initiated into the teachings, overshadowing everything gentle and mild and rational in their souls, and openly preventing the power of the intellect from increasing and peeping out.** <note>original: "πυκιναὶ γὰρ καὶ λάσιαι λόχμαι περὶ τὰς φρένας καὶ τὰν καρδίαν πεφύκαντι... προκύψαι τὸ νοητικόν."</note> See Kuster and Kiessling on this. From the manuscript books whose various readings I possess, the Vienna and Munich B manuscripts incorrectly read *lochma* <note>thicket</note>; then, the same Vienna manuscript confirms *pephykanti* <note>have grown</note>. Then Munich A reads *ameron* <note>gentle</note> erroneously; nor is the same manuscript or the Memmian any better with *tas psychas* <note>the souls</note>. Furthermore, all my sources read *prophanos auxethenmen* <note>openly increased</note>, omitting *men*. Finally, the same sources read *to notiakon*, for which Kiessling wishes to write *noatikon* <note>intellectual</note>. Shortly after, in the passage of Plotinus, the reading of several books, **it receives memory, as it seems, in succession** <note>original: "μνήμην, ὡς ἔοικε, ἐφεξῆς λαμβάνει"</note>, is somehow enticing. But Ficino

<column-break/>

also retained the common reading. Later, from the Vatican book and Mark’s A, I added **of those** <note>original: "τῶν"</note> before **in the heaven**.

**— 17. so as not to pass through into her.]** <note>original: "ὥστε μὴ διελθεῖν εἰς αὐτήν."</note> In this place, it seems one should read **into it** <note>original: "εἰς αὐτὸ"</note>, which also seemed correct to Taylor <note>Thomas Taylor (1758–1835), the "English Platonist" known for translating Greek philosophy.</note>, or the **into** <note>original: "εἰς"</note> should be deleted, so that **her** <note>original: "αὐτὴν"</note> refers to the soul (**psuchen**) and the thought is **into it**. Shortly after, instead of **into the three** <note>original: "εἰς τὰ τρία"</note>, Ficino seems to have read **into the last things** <note>original: "εἰς τὰ τελευταῖα"</note>. Perhaps Plotinus wrote **into the thirds** <note>original: "εἰς τὰ τρίτα"</note>, if you consider that Marsilio Ficino is not always accustomed to rendering word for word; thus, he could have taken "the thirds," according to the nature of Plotinian reasoning, for "the last things."—Taylor, in a letter sent to me, says this about this passage: “*In this place for* **her** <note>original: "αὐτὴν"</note> *it is requisite to read* **him/it** <note>original: "αὐτόν."</note> *For Plotinus is here speaking of the soul when in the intelligible world, and says that through intellect it perceives and proceeds to the good. And in line 4 of the same page for* **into the three** *it is necessary to read, conformably to the version of Ficinus,* **into the last things**. *For frequently in bodies the medium admits of a progression from things that are first to such as are last.*”

**p. 744, 5. but it is possible—to contemplate things there]** <note>original: "ἀλλ’ ἔστι—τὰ ἐκεῖ θεωρεῖν"</note> Edition: *and being here she is said...* <note>original: "καὶ ἐνθάδε οὖση τὸ αὐὸ λέγεται..."</note> I have joined the readings of the approved books and Ficino. Regarding our soul's duty to watch and perceive intelligible things, the Emperor Julian <note>Julian "the Apostate" (r. 361–363 AD), who attempted to revive Neoplatonic paganism.</note> argues similarly in his Fourth Oration. See p. 136. B. Spanheim / p. 162. Also p. 163. C.—**for it is not even necessary to grasp it by demonstration, but by intuition alone; for it concerns the first causes, or at least those of the same rank as the first** <note>original: "καὶ γὰρ οὐδὲ ἀποδείξει χρὴ λαβεῖν αὐτὸ, ἀλλὰ ἐπιβολῇ μόνον..."</note>, and p. 172. C. **it has been shown that the nature of the rays of the god (the Sun) is upward-leading, both through its manifest activity and its hidden activity; by which a great multitude of souls were led upward, having followed the senses to the brightest and most sun-like thing; for the divine Plato will sing of such a sense of the eyes not only as beloved, nor only as useful for life, but also as a guide to wisdom.** <note>original: "δέδεικται... ἀναγωγὸν φύσει τὸ τῶν ἀκτίνων τοῦ θεοῦ (Ἡλίου)..."</note> In this matter, however, one must also recognize a difference when comparing Plotinus's system, being more remote from the senses, with the coarser system of Julian.

**— 8. as if someone were raising his eye upon some high lookout]** <note>original: "οἷον εἴ τις ἀνάγων αὑτοῦ τὸν ὀφθαλμὸν ἐπί τινος ὑψηλῆς σκοπιᾶς"</note> The word **lookout** <note>original: "σκοπιά"</note> can mean both "speculation" <note>mental looking</note> and "watchtower." See Xenophon’s *Lexicon* IV. p. 56. But also *skope* <note>original: "σκοπὴ"</note> is found here and there for a watchtower. However, the word *skopia* is more common in this sense. See Hemsterhuys.

**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

[References to] Lucian, *Diall. Marinn.* I. 2. Wyttenbach on Plutarch, *Apophthegmm. Regg.* p. 1078. Car. Frid. Hermann on Lucian, *Quom. Histor. conscr. oport.* p. 188. Perictyone [apud: in] Stobaeus, *Floril.* Tit. I. p. 7. p. 25. Gaisford. (These are attributed to Archytas in Iamblichus, *Protrept.* ch. IV. p. 58. Kiessling.) "Whoever is able to resolve all genera into one and the same principle, and again from this to synthesize and enumerate them (cf. Gaisford, *Not. Iamblich.* 'to co-enumerate'), he seems to be both the wisest and the most truthful (Iamblichus: 'he seems to me to be both wise and most truthful'; well said: 'and most entirely truthful') and moreover to have discovered a beautiful vantage point (Iamblichus: 'to have found'), from which he will be able to behold God and all things that are distinguished in that order and rank of His (Iamblichus, ed. Kiessling: 'and all things in the order and rank of those things')." Aelian in *Fragm.* books *de Providentia* p. 363. ed. But in the words of Plotinus there remains something awkward, which the writer of the Vatican manuscript wished to remove by his *αὑτὸν* (read: *αὑτὸν*) for *αὑτοῦ*, if indeed you delete the words: *τὸν ὀφθαλμόν* [the eye]. And in the reading of Vindobonensis A. something seems to lie hidden. I suspect Plotinus wrote: "just as if someone, raising his eye from some—vantage point." Then I have given: *μηδεὶς τῶν οὐ σὺν αὐτῷ ἀναβεβηκότων* [none of those who have not ascended with him]. Compare the end with Lucian, *Hermotimus* 28: "having ascended upon some lookout to observe."

**Page 745, 10. *οὐδὲν δὲ κωλύει πάλιν ἐκδῦναι* [Nothing prevents unclothing/stripping again].** The source of this sentiment is in Plato's *Phaedo* ch. 29. p. 40. Wyttenbach, whose annotation you may consult p. 206. Item *Cratylus* p. 403. Consult also Plotinus above p. 381 and what I have collected more fully in *Commentatt. Herodott.* p. 310 ff. As for the fact that Ficinus, in the argument of this chapter, mentioned Porphyry, Iamblichus, and Julian: the passage of the former is in the book *de Styge* in Stobaeus, *Eclogg. Physs.* Vol. I. p. 1034. Heeren. Iamblichus in the same place p. 1056 ff. Finally Julian in *Oration* IV. p. 136. Spanheim.

**— 15. *ἄστρων δὲ περὶ ψυχῆς κ. τ. λ.* [And concerning the soul of the stars, etc.]** These and the following things pertain to that Pythagorean tenet which, learned from Plato and handed down as if through hands, reached the latest Platonists, and which Cicero explains thus in *Somn. Scip.* ch. III (de Republ. VI. 14. p. 481 f. ed. Moser): "**For men were generated under this law, to tend that globe which you see in the middle in this temple, which is called Earth: and to them a soul was given from those eternal fires which you call stars and constellations; which, being globular and round, animated by divine minds, complete their circles and orbits with marvelous speed:**" etc. To this apply Macrobius and Ang. Mai. Proclus included these decrees in his excellent hymn *To the Sun*, in *Anthol. Gr.* III. p. 148. ed. Jacobs, which hymn the venerable man Thomas Taylor translated into English and explained at the end of Sallust *On the Gods and the World*, London 1793; in which poem the poet also addresses the Sun thus in v. 34 f.:

*But, O best of the gods, encircled with crowns, blessed daemon,*
*Image of the all-generating God, uplifter of souls.*

On these consult Jacobs' *Animadvv.* Vol. X. p. 280. Julian pursues this doctrine more diffusely in the fourth Oration, which Zacharias Mytilenaeus strives to refute in a Dialogue. From there I shall give only these excerpts p. 178. ed. Casp. Barth: "whence, obeying His (God's) law, (the sun) circles this universe like a wheel, having a uniform motion and involuntary like a slave and soulless, and not being a rational animal at all, as those who theologize upon it suspect, or who gape at the wretched little dogmas of these men." On these compare Barth's notes p. 279—282. The following words of Plotinus: "to busy oneself with the memories of Zeus himself," are to be explained from those things which our author set down below in ch. IX. p. 403 f. concerning Jove as the ruler and caretaker of all things. And the Jovial order (*ἡ Διΐα τάξις*) according to the opinion of the ancient philosophers, is "the practical and the political." See Proclus on *Alcibiades* preface p. 196.

**Page 746, 9. *Ἄλλος — τρόπος τῆς εἰς τὸ πᾶν παρ’ αὐτῶν εὐθημοσύνης* [Another—way of the good order toward the whole from them].** Several books in this place [hoc loco] read *εὐθυμοσύνης* [cheerfulness]. Below p. 752. A: "that the logoi lie in the things present, standing in greater cheerfulness (*εὐθυμοσύνῃ*)." So the Edition and the Manuscripts, where likewise it should undoubtedly be read: *εὐθημοσύνῃ* [good order]. This Hesiodic word (see *Works and Days* 471 and cf. Pollux IX. 161 and Graevius' *Lectt. Hesiod.* p. 564) is now sound in Xenophon: *Cyrop.* VIII. 5. 4 (cf. Paul Leopard's *Emendatt.* V. 2. in Gruter's *Thes. Crit.* III. p. 88: "he took care of this good order" (*εὐθημοσύνης*): in others it is often corrupt. Plutarch, *Sympos.* VIII. 3. p. 701. B. p. 886. Wytt.: "those things striking the horns of oxen do not happen upon the best

***

### PAGE 232 ###

**BOOK IV. OF THE FOURTH ENNEAD. p. 746—749. 225**

good order (*εὐθημοσύνης*) according to Hesiod," where in his own manuscript Xylander likewise seems to have found *εὐθυμοσύνης*. This same error must be cleansed from Proclus on the *Timaeus* p. 28 above, where this philosopher says regarding the Apaturia: "that which is proper to deception, departing from the impartible and immaterial logoi for the sake of the mundane forms, and becoming appearances instead of the things that truly are. But the enrollment of the children mimics the assignments of the particular souls into their proper lots and their descents into various generations; and that which belongs to the festival mimics the eternal cheerfulness (*εὐθυμοσύνην*—read *εὐθημοσύνην* [good order]) in the world." I have set down almost the entire passage, since it is joined with the argument of the Plotinian passage. Concerning its argument I have spoken in *Symbolica* III. p. 510 f., which does not pertain here: I shall say more about the word below at our p. 752. A.

**Page 747, 15. *εἰ μή τις ἔργῳ οἰκονομοῖτό τι κ. τ. λ.* [unless someone should manage something by work, etc.]** The gods are often said "to manage" (*οἰκονομεῖν*) when they dispose of human affairs and order matter; whence it is also transferred to craftsmen. Alciphron, *Epist.* II. 4. near the end: — "but I have your love as wise and you are able to know these things. For you taught me, a gifted woman, to learn quickly from lovers, but the Loves manage (*οἰκονομοῦσιν*) [Cod. Palat. no. 132 reads *ὁρᾶτε*] while hastening; we revere Artemis [the same reads *μὰ τὴν Ἄρτεμιν* 'By Artemis'; excellently] lest we be unworthy of you by not learning faster." You see the conjecture of Herelius confirmed by our book, which Wagner wished to introduce into the text, as was proper. But the laborers did not obey. See *Epist.* II. 1. 35: "For from that time, by Artemis, many did not even send to me [Cod. Pal. cited reads *προσέβλεψαν* 'look at me']." Aristaenetus I. 10: "By Artemis, I am married to Acontius," where see Boissonade's *Annot.* p. 364. To return there, Lucian uses the Middle voice in *de conscrib. Histor.* ch. 51. p. 62. ed. Amst.: "and this was their art, to have managed (*οἰκονομήσασθαι*) the matter." Where our C. F. Hermann rightly defends that reading against D'Orville, in *Annot.* p. 306. Regarding God moderating all things, the Church writers frequently use the Word, whence I shall add two notable passages for the construction: Macarius *Homil.* XXVII: "God, knowing our weakness, manages (*οἰκονομεῖ*) you into tribulations," which Suicer well translates thus: — "**he so dispenses your affairs that you fall into afflictions.**" Theodoret on *1 Corinthians* 13. Vol. III. p. 253. Schulz: "(Love) does not grope for the measures of the essence of God, nor does it judge those things in which He manages (*οἰκονομεῖ*), as some were accustomed to do."

**Page 749, 17. *Καὶ μὴν εἰ καὶ χορείᾳ ἀπεικάσειέ τις τὴν κίνησιν αὐτῶν — ὥσπερ χορδαὶ ἐν λύρᾳ συμπαθῶς κινηθεῖσαι, μέλος ἂν ᾄσειαν ἐν φυσικῇ ἁρμονίᾳ* [And indeed, if one were to liken their movement to a dance—just as strings in a lyre moved sympathetically, they would sing a melody in natural harmony].** Cf. III. 2. 15 and IV. 4. 4: "one harmony in the universe." I remember indicating elsewhere and in Cicero *de N. D.* III. 11. p. 350 f. of our ed. and Moser's the Pythagorean origin of these notions and images, handed down from Plato thereafter to later thinkers. Proclus, *hymn to the Sun* 3. 4:

*— — — — — and in the material worlds*
*conducting from on high a rich stream of harmony.*

Ibid. verse 8 ff.:

*and the planets, girding themselves with your ever-blooming torches,*
*always in their mutual and untiring dances*
*send life-generating drops to those upon the earth.*

On which Jacobs in *Annot. in Antholog. Gr.* Vol. X. p. 274 f. collected many similar things even from the Platonic philosophers. To which I shall add a few. The same Proclus in *Alcib.* preface § 71. p. 204 f.: "The Heaven being full of symphony and of the rhythm in movements, then all the genera superior to us also enjoying the harmony proceeding from there, and according to these [other books read 'after these'] human life making its habits proportionate and receiving from there the whole well-fitted and rhythmic condition." From which it is understood how those philosophers applied this doctrine of the harmony of the World to the amendment of life and morals. Ecclesiastical writers put forward similar things, but accommodated to the norm of the sacred book and Christian reason: Theodoret, *Therapeut.* III. thus concerning the Angels p. 786. Schulz: — "wherefore we also call them holy, as having nothing earthly, but being freed from earthly passions, and having as their work the dance (*χορείαν*) in heaven, and the hymnody of the Creator." The same *de Provident.* I. p. 498: "Behold also the nature of the stars, their position, their order, the variety of their figures, their utility, their dance (*χορείαν*), their risings, their settings." Cf. the same in *1 Corinth.* p. 171 middle. Philo Judaeus, *de Mundi Opif.* p. 29 f. Mangey. p. 84. Pfeiffer, in praise of the number seven: "For the seven-stringed lyre, being analogous to the dance of the seven planets, completes the renowned harmonies, being as it were the leader of almost all musical instrument-making." Jo. Chrysostom *Homil.* III. p. 389. A. p. 16. ed. Mat-

**Page 750, 13. *Ὁ δὲ δὴ πάντα κοσμῶν Ζεὺς — ψυχὴν βασιλικὴν καὶ βασιλικὸν νοῦν ἔχων* [And Zeus, who orders all things—having a royal soul and a royal mind].** It is observed both in this place and others (see e.g. p. 551. A. middle) that the passage of Plato in the *Phaedrus*, frequented by the imitation of many, was used by Plotinus p. 246. E. p. 251. Heindf. p. 41. Bekk.: "Zeus indeed, the great leader [Eustathius omitted the last word in *Odyss.* μ. 63. p. 446. Basel. p. 15. Leipzig] in heaven, driving a winged chariot [Eust. and the rest: 'driving a winged chariot'] proceeds first, ordering all things and taking care of them." Our author drew the following from the *Philebus* p. 84. Stallb.: "will you not say that in the nature of Zeus there is a royal soul and a royal mind?" For Plotinus' sake I add the words of Onatas (or Onati) the Pythagorean in Stobaeus, *Eclogg.* I. p. 4. p. 94. Heeren: "It seems to me that God is not one, but one is the greatest and most superior [perhaps 'most supreme'], and the ruler of the universe, and the others are many, differing in power. But he reigns over all of them, who is greater in power, magnitude, and virtue, etc." Which passage seems to Heeren in the place cited [loco laudato] (cf. the same *de Fontibus Stobaei* § 49. p. 207) to be drawn from the passage in the Platonic *Phaedrus*; Wyttenbach on the other hand (on Plutarch *de S. N. V.* p. 27. prior ed. p. 336. alt. ed.) thinks the Platonic is from Onatas. However it is: Onatas in the place cited regards the stars as gods, and no less does he who supplied that addition to Eustathius: "which is the Sun." Zacharias Mytilenaeus, however, when he says p. 178 that the sun is subject to the one and eternal God and serves like a chattel (*δοῦλον*) and is without a soul (*ἄψυχον*), seems to have wished to touch upon those philosophers who, like Onatas, say Zeus—the Sun "reigns," or who, like Plato and Plotinus, attribute a royal soul and a royal mind to Jove.

**Page 751, 11. *καὶ τὸν Δία λέγοντες ὁτὲ μὲν — ὁτὲ δὲ ἐπὶ τὸ ἡγεμονοῦν τοῦ παντός* [and speaking of Zeus sometimes—sometimes as the governing principle of the universe].** Concerning the double Jove, or certainly the name of Jove, there exists Plato's testimony in the *Cratylus* p. 396. A. p. 29. Bekk. I shall transcribe the end, although the passage does not correspond in every way to Plotinus: — "for there is no one for us and for all others who is more the cause of living than the ruler and king of all. It happens therefore that this god is correctly named, through whom living always belongs to all living things. But the name is divided in two, as I say, between *Dia* and *Zena*." On which passage Proclus disputes many things in *Scholia* § 94—102. p. 51 ff. Boissonade. Ancient philosophers distinguished Joves in various ways. See the annot. of Davis and our own on Cicero *de N. D.* III. 21. p. 584. our ed. and Moser's.

**Page 753, 8. *αἱ δὲ ἕπονται — ὡς αἱ ἐν κλάδοις, τῇ τοῦ ὅλου φυτοῦ* (sc. *φύσει*) [but they follow—as those in the branches, the (nature) of the whole plant].** We have provided for this passage by punctuation. For unless a comma were interposed after *κλάδοις*, a Genitive would be required on account of *ἐξηρτημέναι* [dependent] and *ἐκφῦσαι* [growing out]. Regarding the argument of the passage and the example of the plant, which Plotinus uses rather frequently in this discussion, see above IV. 8. 9 and the Annot. there at page 351. F.

**Page 754, 1. *οἷον — γενείων, μαζῶν αὐξήσεις* [such as—increases of beards and breasts].** Plato *de Legg.* VIII. p. 833. C: "among children, among those without beards [beardless], among men." Whence it is understood that the "beardless" are middle between little boys and men. In this matter Plato is consistent with himself. Cf. *Sympos.* ch. 7. p. 17. Ast concerning Achilles: "and still beardless" (which passage several learned men have undeservedly brought into suspicion); cf. ibid. ch. 9. p. 20: "but when they already begin to have mind. And this is near to growing a beard." Plutarch, *de frat. amore* p. 484. A. p. 970. Wytt.: "But Athenodorus was still a youth not yet growing a beard." In *μαζῶν* [breasts] Plotinus also thought of men, if the Grammarians are to be believed. But their distinction between *μαζοὶ* and *μαστοὶ* is very slippery. See our annot. on Porphyry's *Life of Plotinus* ch. 3. p. 96. ed. Fabricius.

**— 12. *Ἔστι δὲ τοῦτο ἀνθρώπων — ἢ τὸ ἐφίεσθαι εὑρεῖν φρόνησιν* [This is of men—or to desire to find wisdom].** These are joined with these sentiments: "none of the gods philosophizes," as Diotima teaches in Plato's *Symposium* ch. 29. p. 64. Ast, and "philosophizing is not for the wise," as it is in Proclus on *Alcib.* preface p. 189. our ed. Cf. Musonius Rufus *Fragment* in Wyttenbach's *Philomathia* I. p. 161 f. and Plotinus himself VI. 7. 38 and VI. 9. 10 ff.

**Page 755, 15. *οὐδὲν ἀμφίβολον οὐδὲ ἀμφιγνοούμενον* [nothing doubtful nor disputed].** Cf. *Lexic. Xenoph.* under *ἀμφιγνοεῖν*. Vol. I. p. 168 and Zonaras' *Lex. Graec.* with Tittmann's *Annot.* p. 162.

**— 19. *οὐδὲ πρός τι βλέπων ποιήσει — ἢ ὡς οἷον* (Perhaps *τε* should be inserted, so that it is *ἢ ὡς οἷόν τε*) *τὸ ἐν αὑτῷ παράδειγμα ἔχει* [nor will he act looking toward something—but as far as possible he has the model in himself].** These are drawn from Plato's *Timaeus* p. 28. p. 23 f. **Page 756, 8. *οὐδ’ ἔχειν πράγματα ὥσπερ τινὲς ᾠήθησαν κ. τ. λ.* [nor to have troubles as some thought, etc.]** The Epicureans, whom Plotinus often touches upon by this name, as in *on Providence* III. 2 against the Gnostics, See p. 213. F. For it was in the *Principal Doctrines* of Epicurus: "**That which is eternal and blessed, neither has any business itself, nor exhibits any to another.**" *τὸ μακάριον καὶ ἄφθαρτον οὔτε αὐτὸ πράγματα ἔχει, οὐδὲ ἄλλῳ παρέχει*. Diog. Laert. X. § 139. cf. Cic. *de N. D.* I. 17. I. 30. I. 40 and 41 and what Davis and other interpreters have placed there, and what we ourselves placed both to those passages and to the Plotinian ones.

**Page 757, 5. *ὃ γὰρ ἔχει τῷ ἐφεξῆς διδοῦσα κ. τ. λ.* [for what it has, giving to the next, etc.]** Thus I have written with the Vatican book and Ficinus; but perhaps the reading of Mediceus B., omitting the *τὸ* before *ἐφεξῆς*, is better. Then it is: *with no delay interposed, not hesitating at all*, as if with a certain slight reproach, to which the following *ἀπροαιρέτως* [without choice] is suited. Datives follow after the word *δόσιν* [gift]. Concerning that meaning and others of the particle *ἐφεξῆς* Wyttenbach has well explained on Plutarch *de Aud. Poett.* p. 288—290. Oxford.

**Page 758, 5. *οἷον οὐ κιρνάμενος* [as if not being mixed].** Thus I have given with Ficinus, the sense demanding it, for *οἷον ὁ κιρνάμενος*, which is in the Edition.

**Page 759, 8. *περιέχειν γὰρ δεῖ τὸν χρόνον τὸ ἐν χρόνῳ, ὥσπερ, φησὶ, τὸ ἐν τόπῳ καὶ ἐν ἀριθμῷ* [for time must contain that which is in time, just as, he says, that which is in place and in number].** Plato in the *Timaeus*. Cf. Proclus on him p. 303; the same in *Theolog. Plat.* II. 11. p. 107; in *Institut. Theolog.* ch. 48 ff. p. 78 ff. and cf. Plotinus himself p. 96 ff. p. 325 ff. and p. 553 f.

**— 11. *κἂν εἰ — ποιεῖ καὶ νεύει* [even if—he acts and beckons].** The Edition has the Subjunctive in both places: I have restored the Indicative from many and very good books. In Plato's *Republic* IX. p. 579 near the end, in Bekker's Edition is read: *κἂν εἰ μή τῳ δοκῇ*, where one manuscript omitted *κἂν* (See *Varr. lectt.* Bekker ed. Vol. II. p. 99). Ast gave *δοκεῖ*. And indeed, if you listen to Stallbaum on the *Philebus* § 136. p. 193, *κἂν εἰ* is always joined either with the Indicative or Optative, never with the Subjunctive. Cf. Heindorf on the *Sophist* p. 386 and Buttmann on the *Meno* § 4. p. 313. Similarly in Proclus' *Commentary on Alcibiades* preface § 71. p. 217 our ed., manuscript E. has: *κἂν εἰ τὸ οἰκεῖον ἦν*; the rest *καὶ τὸ οἰκ. ἦν*. Where see Annot.

**Page 760, 11. *Οὕτω γὰρ ἔχει ἕκαστα· εἰ δὲ τἀγαθόν τις κατὰ κέντρον τάξειε, τὸν νοῦν κ. τ. λ.* [For each thing is so; but if someone should place the Good as the center, the mind, etc.]** Thus I have given from the best books. The margin of the Edition and two manuscripts have: *εἰ δὲ θᾶττόν τις* [but if someone more quickly], but in one it was corrected by a second hand. Cudworth in *System. Intell.* p. 698 f. ed. Mosheim: *οὕτω γὰρ ἔχει ἕκαστα εἰ τ’ ἀγαθόν* (incorrectly, as the Edition for *τἀγαθόν*) *τις καὶ τὸ κέντρον τάξειε*, with *δέ* omitted. The same learned man adds regarding the argument of this and the Platonic passage in the *Philebus* p. 30: "**Therefore if we weigh and consider all things rightly, those three hypostases of Plato seem to be nothing other than infinite goodness, infinite wisdom, and infinite active love or power. But these are least of all regarded as properties and qualities in this cause, but as consistent natures, or persons, which, although they differ in degree, nevertheless complete one thing jointly, the divine (*τὸ θεῖον*), one divinity, not otherwise than the middle point in a sphere, the immobile distance, and the mobile circumscription constitute one sphere.**" On which passage Mosheim, as he is accustomed, attacks the excellent Briton [Cudworth], because in this discussion he also used the authority of Plotinus. This indeed is to be wise!

**Page 761, 1. *τοῦτο δὲ περιπτύξασθαι, καὶ περιελθεῖν πάντη ἑαυτῷ* [but to embrace this, and to go around it entirely for itself].** I have placed a comma after *περιπτύξασθαι*, lest this word be joined to the following Dative, warned by the precepts of the great Hemsterhuis on Lucian *Diall. **Page 762, 9. *Καὶ ἔστιν ἐν μὲν τῷ φαυλοτάτῳ ἀνδρὶ τὸ κοινόν* [And there is in the most worthless man the common (element)].** Ficinus seems to have read *ἀνδρί τι κοινόν* [some common thing in the man]. The manuscripts do not vary. Soon I have retracted *κοινόν* [common] from the margin. The manuscripts do not vary. Soon I have retracted *κοινόν*. [from] nearly all the manuscripts *χρηστόν τι* [some good thing]. The Edition has *κρεῖττόν τι* [some better thing]. Finally: *τῆς μὲν ἄνω, τῆς δὲ τῶν κάτω* [of the things above, of the things below]. In another writer it was easy to say: *τῆς μὲν τῶν ἄνω*: in Plotinus, less studious of elegance, not so. The argument however and the examples of comparison are plainly drawn from the passages of Plato. See *Politicus* p. 300 ff. p. 341—346. Bekk. **— 16. *μέσον ἀνάλογον* [an analogous mean].** i.e. *ἀνὰ λόγον*, by the same proportion. So rather often Plato and the Platonists. Wyttenbach teaches on the *Phaedo* p. 307. Cf. Proclus *Inst. Theol.* ch. 164 and 185 and Annot. there p. 242. cf. also the celebrated Hase on Leo Diaconus p. 187 f. The same formula recurs below p. 440. D. p. 675. B. Eunapius in *Excerpts of History* in the affairs of Julian IX. (in the New Vatican Collection of Ancient Writers ed. Angelus Mai Vol. II. p. 257): "thus—the deeds proceeded for a long time and the crowd of those standing together followed the deeds proportionately (*ἀνάλογος*): — "**thus—more deeds were already being produced, and a crowd of conspirators followed the deeds equally.**" Rather *ἀνάλογον*, as it is written in the manuscript: "**so both things succeeded in a greater measure, and the multitude of conspirators followed the things by the same proportion,**" i.e. and the more the things to be done succeeded, the more there flowed together daily those who themselves wished to take part in the affairs.

**Page 773, 10. *Ὁ γὰρ κανὼν τῷ εὐθεῖ τῷ* (margin: *τὸ εὐθὺ τὸ*) *— καὶ τῷ ἐν τῷ ξύλῳ — τεθεὶς, τὸ κρίνειν τῷ τεχνίτῃ — ἔδωκεν* [For the rule (standard), being placed to the straight—and to that in the wood—gave to the craftsman (the power) to judge].** Thus from good books we have emended these words, interpolated here and there and corrupted. For the argument apply the former things I. 6. 3. p. 52. D. and the notes there.

**Page 775, 11. *ἀλλ’ ὀμμάτων, φησὶν, οὐκ ἐπεδεῖτο* [but of eyes, he says, it had no need].** Plato in the *Timaeus* p. 33. p. 30. Bekk.: "But it was finished entirely smooth in a circle from without, for many reasons; for it had no need of eyes [one manuscript reads 'needs', but the Plotinian ones confirm the common reading]: for nothing visible was left outside, nor of hearing, for neither was there anything audible [another manuscript adds 'left']." He wished for *ὑπελείπετο* [was left], as very many Plotinian books have. Lindau on Plato's *Tim.* p. 39, not forgetful of Plotinus, says thus concerning the nearest words of Plotinus: "to which (namely the preceding) the same (Plotinus) adds: *but indeed it was within and it hindered itself from seeing nothing.* Where these tend, you might guess. For the meaning of the verb *λείπειν* [to leave/lack] allows that its tenses be exchanged among themselves."

**Page 776, 8. *ἀλλ’ οὔτε ὄψιν — ἐνδεοῦς* [but neither sight—of the needy].** Ficinus
