**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

does not seem to have read *οὔτε*. The manuscripts in this place, which Marsilius already saw to be faulty, do not help. Soon *περιελκυσμοὺς* [distractions/drawings around] is to be held as a unique example of the Plural. The Singular is recorded from one place in Stephanus' *Thesaurus*, not in Schneider's *Lexicon*. — Soon *ὁρᾷν καὶ ἀκούειν δὲ* [to see and to hear] several of our manuscripts. Then in the margin: *εἰ δὲ δεῖ καὶ ἐπιστρέφεσθαι* [if it is necessary also to turn around], for *εἰ δὲ δὴ κ. ε.* [if indeed both himself]. But the Infinitive depends on the preceding *ἄν τις θείτο* [one would place].

**Page 777, 1. *καὶ ἐν ταῖς μάγων τέχναις* [and in the arts of the magi].** Cf. I. 4. 9. p. 35 and the annot. there. In the following things where Plotinus says of the body of the earth, "nor indeed immobile," beware lest you confuse this sentiment with the sentiment of some Pythagoreans and especially Philolaus: "that the earth is not immobile." (Plutarch in *Numa* ch. XI. *De Placitt. Philoss.* III. 13. Diog. Laert. VIII. 85. Cic. *Acadd.* IV. 39.) For Plotinus disputes in this place [hoc loco] whether the earth has sensation and thus can be affected (*κινεῖσθαι*). For that *κινεῖν* and *κινεῖσθαι* [to move/be moved] are often used by philosophers with this force, is not something we should confirm with great labor. Nor are those things which Plotinus sets down in the following things concerning "spirit" (*πνεύματι*) to be confused with the decree of the Pythagoreans, who attributed respiration to the world as to an animal. See Aristotle's *Physicc.* IV. 6 and Stobaeus, *Eclogg.* I. 19. 1. p. 380. Heeren: "And the Pythagoreans say there is a void, and that it enters into the heaven itself (i.e. the world) from the infinite spirit, as if it were breathing." Cf. Boeckh's *Philolaus* p. 108 ff.; although it is not useless to compare these and similar things with Plotinian ones, and in the universal decree, *that the world is an animal*, Plato and the Platonists and Plotinus himself altogether agree with the Pythagoreans.

**— 14. *κατὰ τὰς τῶν χυλῶν ὀσμάς* [according to the odors of the juices].** In the Vatican manuscript from the first hand was *χυμῶν* [of the flavors]. but this word is properly used of taste. Cf. Plutarch's *Quaestt. Naturr.* ch. 5 where he enumerates eight species of flavors p. 913. B. p. 690. Wytt. Regarding the distinction that exists between *χυλὸς* [juice] and *χυμὸς* [flavor/humor], there is Orion's passage in the *Etymolog.* p. 163 but rather corrupt. Cf. Schneider's *Indic.* to Theophrastus' *Works* p. 546 f. *Χυμοὶ* is read more often in Plotinus. See II. 4. 12. VI. 3. 17 and 18 and concerning taste in this very book IV. 4. 25. above p. 418. A: "and to taste flavors (*χυμῶν*)."

**Page 779, 11. *εἶτα τὴν ἄλλην ψυχὴν καὶ νοῦν, ἣν δὴ Ἑστίαν καὶ Δήμητραν ἐπονομάζουσιν ἄνθρωποι* [then the other soul and mind, which indeed men name Hestia and Demeter].** Cf. below p. 423. C: "as of Demeter and Hestia, being the earth." Proclus respects our passage in *on the Timaeus* p. 282: "but others looking at its (the earth's) fertility called it Demeter, just as Plotinus also, calling its mind Hestia, and its soul Demeter." You see therefore that Plotinus, with Proclus as interpreter, calls the mind of the earth Vesta: its soul Ceres in this place [hoc loco]. Correctly: and would that it were permitted today to use Proclus' commentaries on these Enneads! Philosophers have taken the argument of many discussions concerning Vesta and Ceres especially from two passages of Plato: in the *Timaeus* p. 40: "earth our nourisher etc." (for I have placed the rest above at page 414. B.) and in the *Phaedrus* p. 246 end: "for Hestia alone remains in the house of the gods." Chalcidius on the *Timaeus* p. 269. ed. Meursius (p. 344. ed. Fabricius): "**For he (Plato) says that Vesta alone remains in her seat; Vesta namely, the soul of the universal body, and the mind of its soul, moderating the reins of the starry sky, according to the law sanctioned by Providence.**" Philo Judaeus *de Cherubim* p. 143. Mangey. p. 14—16. Pfeiffer: "but she (the earth) alone of the parts of the world standing firmly has been aptly named Hestia by the ancients etc." Proclus *Theol. Platon.* VI. 21. p. 401: "But Hestia shines a fertile and unbending power upon all; although even Zeus remaining in himself is thus led back to the intelligible watch-tower, and Hestia because of the unbending and undefiled abiding in herself is joined to the first causes." The same says similar things in *Cratylum* § 138. p. 83 f. Boissonade. The same ibid. § 178. p. 109: comparing Demeter with Leto: "that Leto is a life-generating fountain contained in Demeter." But the same defines his own opinion in *on the Timaeus* in the place cited [loco laudato] thus, that he says the first causes of these goddesses are intellectual, genial and separate, from which illuminations and powers descend into the earth, and accordingly Demeter-Earth and Hestia arise etc. (*καὶ εἶναι Δήμητραν χθονίαν καὶ Ἑστίαν.*) Which things are to be compared with the other passage cited in the *Theology*, where he says that everything which is constant and immutable descends from that super-celestial Vesta to all mundane things (*ἐκ τῆς ὑπερουρανίου καθήκειν Ἑστίας.*) Other things are read in Hermias on Plato's *Phaedrus* p. 133. Dionys. Halic. II. 66. p. 376. Reiske: "They think that fire is dedicated to Hestia, because the goddess, being earth and occupying the middle

***

**BOOK IV. OF THE FOURTH ENNEAD. p. 777—786. 231**

place of the world, makes the kindlings of the high fire from herself." Euripides in Macrobius *Saturn.* I. 23. (Fragm. no. 178.):

*and Mother Earth; but the wise of mortals*
*call you Hestia, seated in the ether.*

Whence Ovid *Fastor.* VI. 267: "**Vesta is the same as the earth.**" cf. 460. The same vs. 291: "**Nor understand Vesta as anything other than a living flame.**" Plutarch in *Numa* ch. XI. p. 301. Leopold, remembering the rites of Vesta established at Rome by that king, refers to the opinion of the Pythagoreans concerning the fire constituted in the middle of the Universe, which they call Vesta. Other things which I myself have disputed concerning Vesta and Ceres in *Symbol.* and *Mythologia* Vol. II. p. 622. second ed., it is not pertinent to recall here.

**Page 779, 14. *καὶ περὶ τοῦ θυμοειδοῦς ζητητέον* [and it must be sought concerning the spirited part].** The ground on which this discussion is established is in Plato's *Timaeus* p. 70. A. ff. p. 89 ff. Bekk.

**Page 781, 17. *αὖ τὴν ψυχήν* [the soul further].** Thus I have given on the authority of good manuscripts. Edition: *αὐτήν* [itself]. Concerning this confusion more from Schaefer in *Meletemm.* p. 39 and p. 103.

**Page 782, 10. *ἧττον κινεῖσθαι πρὸς ὀργὰς* (I deleted *τὰς* with very many manuscripts) *καὶ ἀλόγῳ ἀπαθείᾳ* [less to be moved toward rages and with an irrational lack of passion].** Ficinus read *ἀλόγῳ πάθει* [irrational passion]. Manuscripts do not vary at all, except that one gives *ἀπαθίᾳ*. Without manuscripts I was unwilling to change, but Plotinus seems to have written *ἀλόγῳ εὐπαθείᾳ* [irrational well-feeling/sensitivity]. For although *εὐπάθεια* is for the most part almost the same as *ἡδυπάθεια*, or a sweet sensation either of the mind or body: (See the learned annot. of Wyttenbach on Plutarch *de Sanit. Tuend.* p. 846 f. Add Plotinus himself below p. 726. C.) it is nevertheless also where it acquires the force of *irritability* from the Adjective *εὐπαθὴς*. See Alexander of Aphrodisias' passage *Probl.* II. placed in Stephanus' London *Thes.* p. 7254.

**— 14. *ζέσις — καὶ ἀγανάκτησις* [seething—and irritation].** Cf. above p. 412. A. and the Annot. there.

**Page 784, 16. *τὴν δὲ ἀντιτυπίαν τὸ ἐκ πάντων οὖσαν μὴ μένειν* [and that the resistance, being from all things, does not remain].** Whether *τὸ ἐκ πάντων* is to be taken according to the analogy of the formulas *τὸ παράπαν*, *τὸ πάμπαν* [altogether], or whether *τὴν ἐκ πάντων* should be written? I would have preferred this on account of the following *οὖσαν*; I was unwilling to restore it without manuscripts. Concerning *ἀντιτυπίᾳ* [resistance] it was spoken above at p. 180. G. Next Ficinus seems to have read for *νόμῳ ὀρθῷ* [by right law], — *ὁμοίως νῷ ὁρᾷν* [similarly to see by mind]: and thus you may judge it should be read. Manuscripts help nothing.

**Page 786, 2. *καὶ εὐχῶν — ἃς πρὸς ἥλιον ποιούμεθα, καὶ δὴ καὶ πρὸς ἄστρα ἄλλοι τινὲς ἄνθρωποι* [and of prayers—which we make to the sun, and indeed also to the stars certain other men].** You might guess that the stars were also adored by the Greeks from ancient times from these words of Plato's *Cratylus* p. 397. C. D: "The first of men around Greece seem to me to have thought these only were gods, just as many of the barbarians do now: the sun, and moon, and earth, and stars, and heaven." Which things agree with the Herodotus' narration concerning the religions of the ancient Persians I. 131. The same man in *de Legg.* X. p. 887. E: "and at the rising of the sun and moon and as they go toward their settings, hearing and seeing the prostrations (*προκυλίσεις*) and adorations (*προσκυνήσεις*) of all Greeks and barbarians alike etc." Cf. ibid. XI. p. 931. A. And in the *Symposium* Socrates himself p. 220: — "he stood until it became dawn and the sun rose; then he went away after praying to the sun." Whether Plotinus attributed this Sun-cult to his own Platonists or to his citizens: and the cult of the other stars to certain other people. See Clement of Alex. *Protrept.* p. 22. Potter. Josephus *Antiqq. Judd.* XV. 10. *Zend-Avesta* II. 3. Caesar *de Bell. Gall.* VI. 21. Tacit. *German.* ch. 40. and compare Ficinus' argument of this chapter; Turnebus *Adversarr.* XXIV. 35. *Payne Knight Inquiry into the symbolic Language of anc. Art and Mythology* § 2. p. 1 and what I myself placed in *Symbolica* Vol. I. p. 4 f. second ed. To those things which Ficinus touched upon in the argument of this chapter regarding Plato's doctrine on the sun, these things of Ammianus Marcellinus XXI. 1. 11 pertain: "**For the Sun, as the Physicists say, the mind of the world, diffusing our minds from itself as if by sparks, when it has kindled them more vehemently, renders them conscious of the future.**" What follow, *καὶ πεπίστευται ὡς δι’ αὑτῶν αὑτοῖς πολλὰ τελεῖται, κ. τ. λ.* Villoison in *Anecdott. Grr.* II. p. 227 ff. exhibited from two Venetian manuscripts as unpublished with this inscription and this beginning: "Of Plotinus concerning how the celestial disposition looks into the terrestrial world. Since it has been believed, that through the stars many things are completed —"

**— 10. *καὶ ἀκολάστους συλλήψεις* [and unbridled conceptions/couplings].** Ficinus translates as *Concubitus* [intercourse]; in this place indeed not badly. Properly *conceptiones* [conceptions]. Plutarch's *Romul.* XI. 4. p. 113. Leopold: "that the conception (*σύλληψιν*) of Romulus occurred in his mother in the first year of the second olym-

For the rest, a writer studious of sophistic elegancies would have written: *θεοὺς συλλήπτορας γίγνεσθαι — πρὸς ἀκολάστους συλλήψεις* [gods become co-helpers—toward unbridled conceptions]. **Page 788, 12. *Ῥητορείαν δὲ καὶ μουσικὴν καὶ πᾶσαν ψυχαγωγίαν, ἢ πρὸς τὸ βέλτιον ἢ πρὸς τὸ χεῖρον ἄγειν ἀλλοιούσας* [And Rhetoric and music and all soul-leading (psychagogia), which leads either to the better or to the worse by altering].** Ficinus translates the last word thus: "**which especially differ among themselves.**" Perhaps this is the meaning: "**by the fact that they affect the souls of men in a different way, or because they affect them otherwise than the souls had been affected until now.**" For the rest, these Plotinian things prove him an alumnus of Plato in both words and sentiments. See Plato's *Gorgias* p. 453 ff. cf. Aristides' *Orat. Platon.* I. p. 47. Sext. Empir. II. 2. p. 288. Quintilian *Inst. Orat.* II. 15. 4. Plato *de Republ.* II. p. 365 end: "for there are teachers of persuasion, giving both political and forensic wisdom." For *ἡ ῥητορεία* [rhetoric] and *ἡ δημογορία* [public speaking] are often used as synonyms, and no less *ἡ σοφιστεία* [sophistry]. Diod. Sic. XX. beginning. Diogen. Laert. II. 20. Consult Chr. Theoph. Ernesti *Lexicon Technol. Graec. Rhetor.* p. 300 f. Krüger on Dionys. Halic. *Historiograph.* p. 518. Hence *ῥητορεύειν* [to speak rhetorically] and *ῥητορεία* also designate a futile and talkative discourse (*sermocinationatio*). See D'Orville on Chariton p. 507. Leipzig ed. and cf. C. Fr. Hermann on Lucian *de conscr. Hist.* p. 162. To understand the force of the word *ψυχαγωγία* [soul-leading] consult Plato *de Legg.* X. p. 908 end 909. A. and Ast's animadversions on that passage p. 505.

**Page 790, 9. *πρῶτον τοίνυν θετέον ζῶον ἓν κ. τ. λ.* [first therefore it must be placed as one animal, etc.]** Tiedemann judges that nothing of new argument is added to these by Plotinus in: *Spirit of speculative Philosophy* III. p. 289. Those things which follow thereafter, the same compares with the decrees of the Stoics and other more ancient philosophers ibid. p. 326 f.

**Page 791, 1. *Συμπαθὲς δὴ πᾶν τοῦτο τὸ ἕν* [Indeed this whole one is sympathetic].** Iamblichus treats the same argument in *de Myster.* IV. 8. p. 112; from where I set down these: "And indeed [and 'and indeed' Manuscript Vindobonensis adds] some (energy) descends into the parts from the wholes, one being sympathetic according to the likeness of the powers, the other a multi-formed acting according to the suitability of the agent toward the patient. If therefore [Goth. Monac. Vindob. read 'therefore not'] it happens by bodily necessities that some evils and destructions occur around the parts; as toward the wholes and the harmony of the universe being saving and good, they bring necessary destruction (*φθορὰν*) upon the parts [Mon. and Leid. Manuscripts read 'motion' (*φορὰν*). Vindob. 'bring a certain necessary destruction']. Add the participle *ἐπάγοντα* from Goth. and Monac. and you have the true reading] either by the inability to bear the energies of the wholes, or by some other mixture and blend of the weakness from themselves, or thirdly by the asymmetry of the parts toward one another."

**— 11. *καὶ οὐ προσήνως τὸ πάσχον ἴσχει* [and the patient does not hold it pleasantly].** See above p. 38. B. p. 52. E. and cf. Olympiodorus on *Alcib.* preface p. 122. — "wherefore also we say that those who are pleasant to us and wish us good things are well-disposed to us." — As for what is read next in some books: "since both bile and pushing another—presses and pricks," this reading reminds one of those things which are read above p. 205. F: "nor pushing from without to drive into the inside," where compare annot. For the rest, very many of our Manuscripts as well as two Venetian ones in Villoison's *Anecd. Grr.* II. p. 228 agree in the reading *ὁ θυμὸς* [anger], which is also confirmed by the nearest words.

**Page 794, 8. *καὶ τὰς διαφόρους αὐτῶν θέσεις ἐπόμενα καὶ τὰ ἄλλα, ὡς ζώου ἑνὸς κινουμένου παρέχεσθαι* [and the other things following their different positions, as provided by one animal moving].** The Lycopolite philosopher [Plotinus] used the same image of a dance to declare the harmonious motion of the world above p. 267. E. F. cf. also p. 372. B. C. and what I annotated there. For the source of this whole passage and similar ones is in Plato's *Timaeus* p. 30 end p. 26 f. Bekk.: "For God, wishing to liken it (the world) to the most beautiful of the intelligible things and perfect in all things, constituted it as one visible animal, having within itself all such animals as are by nature related to it." Diogenes Laertius

III. 71 places this in the tenets of Plato: "that it (the world) is ensouled because the ensouled is better than the soulless." To which passage Menage p. 164, applying our passage, says thus: "**Let Plotinus IV. 4. 33 be seen, where the world is said to be *one animal* dancing by musical reason and by dancing varying all things consequently together with itself.**" Cicero expressed the words of Plato thus in the *Fragment on the Universe* ch. 4: "**For what can be understood as most beautiful in the nature of things, and what is most absolute in every part, when God wished to make the world similar, he made it one animal for a spectacle in which (now my Manuscript adds, previously it was 'of the Uffenbachs') all animals were contained:**" in which passage, as he often does, Tully [Cicero] indulged himself in this, that he passed over an entire sentiment, namely in this place [hoc loco] that one: "as many as are by nature related to it." For the rest, cf. those things of Cicero or rather of the Stoic in Cicero *de N. D.* II. 12: — "**From which it is effected that the world is an animate being.**" Pomponius Mela III. 1. 15 ff.: "**Nor is it yet sufficiently known, whether the *World* effects this by its own panting (*anhelitu*), and draws back the wave and leads it back with its spirit from all sides, if (as it pleases the more learned) *it is one animal:***" to which Isaac Voss p. 780. third ed. Abr. Gronov. seeks patronage for the reading *unum* [one] instead of *vivum* [living] from the doctrine of Plato and from these very passages of our Plotinus. For the rest, Proclus on the *Timaeus* p. 131 ff. cf. p. 93 f. refers to and judges diffusely the opinions of Plotinus, Atticus, Amelius, Porphyry, and Iamblichus concerning the Soul of the world and the demiurge, and likewise concerning the animate world. But those things which our Plotinus adds in the continuous passage agree very much with the decree of the Indians, that the demiurge of the world passes through all mundane things. See Guil. von Humboldt *Dissert. de Bhagavad-gítá*. Berlin 1827. p. 26. and citations there and cf. Guigniaut in *Religions de l’Antiquité* IV. p. 4. no. 18.

**Page 795, 2. *ὥσπερ οἱ ἔμφρονες τῶν θητευόντων — ἅτε μὴ ἀνδράποδα ὄντες* [just as the prudent among the hirelings—inasmuch as they are not slaves].** The verb *θητεύειν* [to serve as a hireling] is found in Plato's *Euthyphro* p. 4. C. p. 26 f. Stallb.: "he was a certain client of mine, and as we were farming in Naxos he was a hireling (*ἐθήτευεν*) with us." To which passage apply Pollux III. 82. VI. 196. Ruhnken on Tim. *Lex. Platon.* p. 211 ff. Concerning the difference between mercenaries and slaves and the different condition of both among the Greeks and Romans, see Petit *Legg. Atticc.* p. 249 ff. ed. Wesseling. Cf. also Boeckh's *Oeconom. Athenienss.* I. p. 128 f.

**Page 796, 7. *οἱονχειρὸς τὰ συνθλιβόμενα* [as if bones of a hand being pressed together].** Manuscript Marc. reads *χεὶρ ὀστᾶ συνθλιβόμενα*. Whence perhaps you might conjecture that Plotinus wrote: *χειρὸς ὀστᾶ συνθλιβόμενα*.

**Page 797, 1. *ἡ διέξοδος τῆς ζωῆς* [the course/outlet of life].** Cf. above p. 189. B. *Enn.* II. 8. 1 where I explained it.

**Page 799, 13. *οἷον καὶ λίθων φύσεις καὶ βοτανῶν ἐνέργειαι θαυμαστὰ πολλά παρέχονται* [just as the natures of stones and the energies of herbs provide many marvelous things].** These and similar decrees supplied the argument for many writings of very different ages; which volumes, composed either in verse or prose, and everywhere ascribed to the most ancient priests, are circulated under the names of Hermes, Orpheus, Kyranus, and others. Thus, to use this example, here in our ancient Palatine library, now preserved in the Vatican at Rome, is "**The book of Hermes Trismegistus concerning the herbs of the seven planets to Asclepius**" as witnessed by Frid. Sylburg in the *Catalog of Greek Manuscripts of the Palatine Library of Heidelberg* no. 226. p. 69. bottom. But in Triarteus' *Greek Manuscripts of the Royal Library of Madrid* p. 431 f. while other notices of this kind exist, there is also this: "it was written in the book called *Kyranis* concerning 24 stones, and 24 birds, and 24 fish, and 24 herbs." Cf. Tyrwhitt on Orpheus' (falsely so called) *Lithica*, especially on the Greek argument p. 360. ed. Hermann. add Fabricius *Bibl. Gr.* Vol. I. p. 70 ff. ed. Harles and p. 156 ff. and our *Symbolica* Vol. I. p. 396. second ed. A similar little work, which likewise feigns the name of Hermes Trismegistus, we have quite recently added to the edition of Jo. Laurentius Lydus' *Fragments on the Months* by our Roether p. 312—339. It is inscribed however *concerning the juice of herbs*, and it has notices and precepts as to by which star plants should be collected and artificially treated for the use of medicine.

**Page 800, 10. *τῷ μὴ αἰσθητῶς παρ’ αὑτοῦ κινουμένους* [by the fact that they are not moved perceptibly by themselves].** Thus I have written by the authority of more Manuscripts and especially of the Marcian one. The Edition has it thus: *τὸ μὴ αἰσθητῶς παρ’ αὑτῷ κινούμενον*; Ficinus: "**because it does not appear to us to be moved manifestly by itself among these.**" The same Marcian book in the last words of this chapter gives: *διὸ καὶ πολλὰ δουλεύει αὐτοῦ ταῖς δυνάμεσιν*; which are perhaps to be translated thus: *Wherefore many things also serve its (namely the Universe's) powers*. And I know not how this sentiment pleases.

# BOOK IV. OF THE FOURTH ENNEAD. Pages 746—749. 225

Hesiod's "good order" <note>original: εὐθημοσύνης (*euthēmosynēs*)</note>, where in his own Manuscript Xylander <note>Wilhelm Holtzman (1532–1576), a humanist scholar</note> seems likewise to have found "cheerfulness" <note>original: εὐθυμοσύνης (*euthymosynēs*)</note>. This same error must be cleared away from Proclus's *Commentary on the Timaeus*, page 28 above, where this philosopher speaks thus concerning the Apaturia <note>An ancient Greek festival of "common fathers"</note>: "But the element of deception <note>original: ἀπάτης (*apatēs*), a pun on the festival name</note> is proper to the worldly forms as they depart <note>reading *existamenois* for *existamenēs*</note> from the indivisible and immaterial reasons, and become appearances instead of true beings. The enrollment of the children mimics the distribution of particular souls into their proper lots and their descents into various births; but the festive element mimics the eternal good order <note>original: εὐθημοσύνην (*euthēmosynēn*); the text notes a correction from "cheerfulness"</note> within the cosmos." I have set down almost the entire passage, as it is joined to the argument of the Plotinian passage. Concerning its argument, I spoke in *Symbolica* III, page 510 and following, which do not pertain here; I shall say more regarding the word below on our page 752. A.

Page 747, 15. *Unless one were to be managed by the work...* etc. The Gods are often said to **manage** <note><term>Oeconomo (οἰκονομεῖν)</term>: To administer or arrange, like a steward of a household</note> when they dispose of human affairs and even order matter; from which the term is also transferred to craftsmen. Alciphron, *Epistles* II. 4. near the end: — "But I have your love as a wise thing and you are able to know these things. For you taught me, a gifted woman, to learn quickly from lovers, but the Loves manage <note>The Palatine Manuscript number 132 reads: 'you see'</note> while hurrying; we revere Artemis <note>The same MS reads 'by Artemis,' which is excellent</note> that we are not unworthy of you by not learning faster." You see that the conjecture of Herelius is confirmed by our book, which Wagner wished to introduce into the text, as was right. But the workmen did not obey. See *Epistle* II. 1. 35: "For since then, by Artemis, many have not even sent to me" <note>The cited Palatine MS reads 'looked at me'</note>. Aristaenetus I. 10: "By Artemis, I shall be married to Acontius," where see Boissonade’s Annotations, page 364. To which Jacobs, in his *Annotations on the Greek Anthology* Vol. X, page 274 and following, collected many similar things even from the Platonic philosophers. To which I shall add a few. From this it is understood how those philosophers applied this doctrine of the Harmony of the World to the improvement of life and morals. Similar things, but adapted to the norm of the sacred book and Christian reasoning, are brought forth by Ecclesiastical writers: Theodoret, *Therapeutics* III, thus concerning the Angels, page 786, Schulz edition: — "Therefore we also call them holy, as having nothing earthly, but being freed from earthly passions, having as their work the dance in heaven, and the hymn-singing of the Creator." <note>original: "thæi: — δι’ ὃν οὐρανὸς ἐτάθη, καὶ ἥλιος ἀνήφθη, καὶ σελήνη τρέχει καὶ ποικίλος καταλάμπει χορός."</note> "...through whom the heaven was stretched out, and the sun was kindled, and the moon runs her course, and the varied choir of stars shines down." Where see Matthæi's 50th annotation.

Page 750, 13. <note>original: "Ὁ δὲ δὴ πάντα κοσμῶν Ζεὺς — ψυχὴν βασιλικὴν καὶ βασιλικὸν νοῦν ἔχων."</note> "And Zeus, who orders all things... having a royal soul and a royal mind."] It is observed both in this place and others (see, for example, page 551. A. middle) that Plotinus frequently imitates a passage from Plato's *Phaedrus* (page 246. E. page 251. Heindf. page 41. Bekk.): <note>original: "ὁ μὲν δὴ μέγας ἡγεμὼν... ἐν οὐρανῷ Ζεὺς... ἐλαύνων πτηνὸν ἅρμα... πρῶτος πορεύεται, διακοσμῶν πάντα καὶ ἐπιμελούμενος."</note> "The great leader in heaven, Zeus, driving a winged chariot, goes first, ordering all things and caring for them." (Eustathius omitted the last word in his commentary on the *Odyssey* book 12, line 63, page 446. Basil. page 15. Lips. The same author adds: "who is the Sun.") The following words our author <note>Plotinus</note> drew from the *Philebus* (page 84. Stallb.): <note>original: "οὐκοῦν ἐν μὲν τῇ τοῦ Διὸς ἐρεῖς φύσει βασιλικὴν μὲν ψυχὴν, βασιλικὸν δὲ νοῦν ἐγγίγνεσθαι."</note> "Therefore you will say that in the nature of Zeus there exists a royal soul and a royal mind." For the sake of Plotinus, I add the words of Onatas (or Onatus) the Pythagorean (found in Stobaeus's *Physical Selections* I. page 4. page 94. Heeren.): <note>original: "Δοκέη δέ μοι καὶ μὴ εἷς εἶμεν ὁ θεὸς, ἀλλ’ εἷς μὲν ὁ μέγιστος καὶ καθυπέρτερος... οἱ δ’ ἄλλοι πολλοὶ διαφέροντες κατὰ δύναμιν. βασιλεύει δὲ πάντων αὐτῶν, ὁ καὶ κράτει καὶ μεγέθει καὶ ἀρετᾷ μείζων..."</note> "It seems to me that God is not just one, but there is one who is greatest and highest, and who rules over the whole, while the others are many, differing in power. But he reigns over them all, being greater in power, magnitude, and virtue, etc." This passage seems to Heeren (in the place cited; compare also his work *On the Sources of Stobaeus* section 49, page 207) to be derived from the passage in Plato's *Phaedrus*; Wyttenbach, on the contrary (on Plutarch's *On the Late Vengeance of the Deity* page 27, first edition, page 336, second edition), thinks the Platonic passage is derived from Onatas. However it may be: Onatas, in the place cited, considers the stars to be gods, as does the one who supplied that addition to Eustathius: "who is the Sun." Zacharias of Mytilene, however, when he says (page 178) that the sun is subject to the one and eternal God and serves like a <term>mancipium</term> <note>a slave or piece of property</note> and is "soulless" (<note>original: "ἄψυχον"</note>), seems to have wanted to strike at those philosophers who, like Onatas, say that Jupiter-Sun "reigns," or who, like Plato and Plotinus, attribute a royal soul and a royal mind to Zeus.

Page 751, 11. <note>original: "καὶ τὸν Δία λέγοντες ὁτὲ μὲν — ὁτὲ δὲ ἐπὶ τὸ ἡγεμονοῦν τοῦ παντός"</note> "and speaking of Zeus sometimes as... and sometimes as the ruling principle of the universe."] Regarding the double Zeus, or at least the name of Zeus, there is testimony from Plato in the *Cratylus* (page 396. A. page 29. Bekk.). I will add the end of it, although the passage does not correspond in every respect to that of Plotinus: — "For there is no one who is more the cause of life for us and all others than the ruler and king of all. It happens, therefore, that this god is rightly named, through whom (<note>original: "di' hon"</note>) living (<note>original: "zēn"</note>) always belongs to all living things. But the name, though one, is divided in two, as I say: into *Dia* and *Zēna*." <note>A Greek wordplay on the names of Zeus and the verb 'to live'.</note> Proclus disputes many things regarding this passage in his *Scholia* (sections 94–102, page 51 and following, Boisson.). Ancient philosophers distinguished the "Zeuses" in various ways. See Davis's note and our own on Cicero's *On the Nature of the Gods* III. 21 (page 584 of our edition and Moser's).

Page 753, 8. <note>original: "αἱ δὲ ἕπονται — ὡς αἱ ἐν κλάδοις, τῇ τοῦ ὅλου φυτοῦ (sc. φύσει)"</note> "and they follow... as those in the branches [follow] the nature of the whole plant."] We have provided for this passage with punctuation. For unless a comma were placed after "branches," a Genitive case would be required because of the words "dependent upon" and "growing out of." Regarding the argument of the passage and the example of the plant, which Plotinus uses quite frequently in this discussion, see above IV. 8. 9. and the note there on page 351. F.

Page 754, 1. <note>original: "οἷον — γενείων, μαζῶν αὐξήσεις"</note> "such as... the growth of beards and breasts."] Plato in the *Laws* VIII (page 833. C.): "among boys, among the beardless, and among men." From which it is understood that the "beardless" (<note>original: "ageneioi"</note>) are midway between little boys and men. In this matter, Plato is consistent with himself. Compare the *Symposium* (chapter 7, page 17, Ast's edition) regarding Achilles: "and still beardless" (a passage which some learned men have unjustly brought under suspicion); compare also the same work (chapter 9, page 20): "but when they already begin to possess mind; and this is close to the time of growing a beard." Plutarch in *On Brotherly Love* (page 484. A. page 970. Wytt.): "But Athenodorus was still a youth, not yet growing a beard." In the mention of "breasts" (<note>original: "mazōn"</note>), Plotinus also thought of men, if the Grammarians are to be believed. But their distinction between *mazoi* and *mastoi* <note>different Greek terms for breasts/nipples</note> is very slippery. See our note on Porphyry's *Life of Plotinus* (chapter 3, page 96, Fabricius's edition).

— 12. <note>original: "Ἔστι δὲ τοῦτο ἀνθρώπων — ἢ τὸ ἐφίεσθαι εὑρεῖν φρόνησιν."</note> "This is characteristic of men... or the desiring to find wisdom."] These are connected with these sentiments: "none of the gods philosophizes," as Diotima teaches in Plato's *Symposium* (chapter 29, page 64. Ast.) and, "philosophizing does not belong to the wise man," as found in Proclus's commentary on the *Alcibiades* (preface, page 189 of our edition). Compare the *Fragments of Musonius Rufus* in Wyttenbach's *Philomathia* I (page 161 and following) and Plotinus himself VI. 7. 38. and VI. 9. 10. and following.

Page 755, 15. <note>original: "οὐδὲν ἀμφίβολον οὐδὲ ἀμφιγνοούμενον"</note> "nothing ambiguous nor doubtful."] Compare the *Xenophon Lexicon* under the word *amphignoein* (Volume I, page 168) and Zonaras's *Greek Lexicon* with Tittmann's notes (page 162).

— 19. <note>original: "οὐδὲ πρός τι βλέπων ποιήσει — ἢ ὡς οἷον (Fort. inserendum τε, ut sit ἢ ὡς οἷόν τε) τὸ ἐν αὑτῷ παράδειγμα ἔχει."</note> "nor will he create by looking toward something... but as if (Perhaps 'te' should be inserted, so it reads 'as far as possible') he has the <term>paradeigma</term> <note>the model or archetype</note> within himself."] These things are drawn from Plato's *Timaeus* (page 28. page 23 and following, Bekk.): — "and this then..."

"Again, it must be considered concerning it <note>The universe</note>, according to which of the models the one fashioning it <note>The Demiurge or Creator</note> worked: whether toward that which is always the same and in the same state, or toward that which has come into being. Concerning that meaning and others of the particle "next in order" <note>ἐφεξῆς</note>, Wyttenbach has explained well in Plutarch's *On Hearing the Poets*, pages 288—290. Oxford edition.

Page 759, 8. "For it is necessary for time to encompass that which is in time, just as, he says, that which is in place and in number." <note>original: περιέχειν γὰρ δεῖ τὸν χρόνον...</note> Plato in the *Timaeus*. — 11. "even if — he acts and nods" <note>original: κἂν εἰ — ποιεῖ καὶ νεύει</note>] The Edition has the Subjunctive in both places: I have restored the Indicative from many and the best manuscripts. In Plato's *Republic* IX. page 579. near the end, in Bekker's edition it reads: "even if it does not seem so to someone" <note>κἂν εἰ μή τῳ δοκῇ</note>, where one manuscript omitted "even if" <note>κἂν</note> (See Various Readings, Bekker edition Vol. II. page 99.). Page 760, 11. The ark of Osiris trembling: — <note>original: "ἀνοῖξαι τὴν λάρνακα, καὶ τῷ προσώπῳ τὸ πρόσωπον ἐπιθεῖσαν, ἀσπάσασθαι καὶ δακρύειν"</note> *to open the chest, and placing face against face, to embrace and weep.* The active voice is used in describing a similar scene by Bion, regarding Venus embracing the corpse of Adonis: *Idylls* A. v. 44: <note>original: "ὥς σε περιπτύξω καὶ χείλεα χείλεσι μίξω"</note> *so that I may fold you in my arms and mix my lips with yours.* An example of the passive will be given by our Author himself below in *Enneads* VI. 9. 9. page 768. Leopold edition: *the Lapiths turned toward defense.* Timaeus, *Platonic Lexicon*: **Defense** <term>Amyna: Ἄμυνα</term>. *Used both for recompense and for the exacting of a penalty.* If, therefore, you believe this lexicographer, Plato used this word. But you would **"seek it in vain in the most Attic Plato."** <note>Ruhnken refers here to the purity of the Athenian dialect; "Attic" was the gold standard for classical Greek.</note> Ruhnken on this passage, page 26. If he had remembered our passage and the other which we praised, he would undoubtedly have pronounced Timaeus to be interpolated from Plotinus, just as he suspects him to be interpolated from Porphyry in the Preface page XIII and following, and in the notes on page 202. Nor is that word better known to the rest of the Attic writers, although its seeds are found in Attica. See Ruhnken on Hesychius regarding "winter-defense" <note>original: "χειμάμυνα"</note> page 1546. (compare *Sophoclean Lexicon* Oxford edition 1826. II. page 150.) Interpreters on Moeris page 80—82; on Thomas Magister page 42. Wernsdorf on Himerius page 142. Lobeck on Phrynichus page 23. As for Havercamp praising "defense" <note>original: "ἀμύνη"</note> in the *Index of Josephus's Greek* from a passage in *The Jewish War* II. 13. 5. page 177: *and all the people voted for defense*: Josephus did not even dream of the Ionic form. *Etymologicum Gudianum* page 47. 6: *defense, the vengeance. This is from 'mune', the pretext, with the intensive 'a' prefix.* (perhaps "defense" <note>original: "ἀμύνη"</note>). Otherwise, however it may be, compare *Odyssey* book 21, verse 111, where Apollonius in the *Homeric Lexicon* page 465 explains "pretexts" <note>original: "μύνησι"</note> likewise as "excuses"; add Eustathius on that passage page 748. Basel edition.) Plutarch joined the noun with a similar verb as Plotinus in *Life of Caesar* chapter 44. page 305. Coray edition: *first he sees a certain man among the captains, faithful to him and experienced in wars, encouraging those under him and calling them forth to a defense of valor.* where some manuscripts and Reiske read: "summoning." The former is true, and perhaps someone might conjecture it should be written thus in Plotinus: "calling forth." Without the manuscripts, I was unwilling to change it.

page 762, 9. **And there is in the most base man the common element.** <note>original: "Καὶ ἔστιν ἐν μὲν τῷ φαυλοτάτῳ ἀνδρὶ τὸ κοινόν."</note>] Ficino seems to have read "some common thing in the man." The books do not vary. Presently I restored "common" <note>original: "κοινόν"</note> from the margin. The books do not vary. Presently I restored "common" from the margin <note>The text repeats this phrase in the original</note>... almost all books having "some good thing." The edition has "some better thing—." Then, instead of "giving to the better," you would expect "serving," but understand "himself" with "giving." Finally: "of the one above, of the other below." In another writer, it would be natural to say: "of those above": in Plotinus, who was less studious of elegance, it is not so. However, the argument and the examples of comparison are clearly drawn from passages in Plato. See *The Statesman* page 300 and following, pages 341—346. Bekker edition. (The Parisian Scholiast on Aeschines the Orator referred to this latter passage: *Aeschines did not correctly call tyranny a 'politeia' [constitution]; for a constitution consists of laws. But Plato says both two and five and seven.*) From *The Republic* VIII. page 562, from which Plotinus took that phrase "not being unmixed." From *The Laws* III. page 689, page 304 Bekker, and likewise page 699 and following, page 324 and following, Bekker edition; from which, regarding the Plotinian "those making an uproar and shouting," keep in mind page 325: *certain unmusical shouts of the multitude*: likewise from *The Laws* VI. page 773, page 454 Bekker. But especially relevant here are Plato's discussions in *The Republic* IV. page 440 and following, pages 203—206—208 Bekker; from which Cicero also profited in *On the Republic* I. 38: **"Therefore Archytas used to say that anger was a certain sedition of the soul, clearly disagreeing with reason, and he wished it to be calmed by counsel. Add greed, add the desire for power and glory, add lusts; and see this: if there is a royal power in the minds of men, it will be the dominion of one thing, namely of counsel: (for that is the best part of the soul:) and when counsel dominates, there is no place for lusts, none for anger, none for rashness."** —Scipio: **"Does it please you then that all parts of the soul be under a kingdom, and that they be ruled by counsel?"** — **"Why then do you doubt what you should feel about the commonwealth?"** pages 155—157. Moser edition. See also Proclus on Plato's *Alcibiades*, preface page 56 and following, especially page 255 and following: *but the common people are not born to possess knowledge, nor to live according to knowledge, so that not even a democracy would become...*

Page 764, line 18. **again moreover** <note>original: "πάλιν αὖ"</note>] Separately and in reverse order in Plato’s *Apology of Socrates*, page 27, page 111 in Bekker's edition: — "to say that I do not believe in gods, and then **again** to believe in **gods**." Sophocles in *Peleus* as cited by Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* VI, page 748: "for **again moreover** the aging man is a child" (compare Fragments, page 57, newest Oxford edition). Compare also Segaar on Clement of Alexandria’s *Who is the Rich Man that shall be Saved?*, section 27, page 259. Lucian, *Necyomantia*, section 4, Volume I, page 461, Amsterdam edition: "and someone else **again moreover** declared that wealth itself was a good." Compare Hoogeveen on *Particles*, page 518, second edition by Schutz. Weiske on *Pleonasms*, page 142. Rhoer on Porphyry’s *On Abstinence* II. 40, page 179, and Schaefer’s *Meletemata*, page 39. Plotinus again on page 414. B: "and **again moreover** saying," and very frequently in the remaining books, so that it would be tedious to accumulate examples of this redundancy. John Davies, on Maximus of Tyre XXV. 1, page 593, teaches that "again moreover" <note>original: "αὖθις αὖ"</note> is used in place of it by both poets and secular writers.

Page 765, line 3. **and the irritation according to the mass** <note>original: "ἡ δὲ ἀγανάκτησις κατὰ τὸν ὄγκον"</note>] Compare below, page 421. D: "there would only be a boiling and a sort of **irritation**" <term>Aganactesis: a physical tingling or vexation</term> from Plato’s *Phaedrus*, page 251. C: — "an itching and **irritation** about the gums — it boils and is **irritated** and tickles while growing feathers." If Pierson had known this other passage of Plotinus when commenting on Moeris, page 41, he certainly would have refrained from his conjecture on the Platonic passage: "it boils and bites."

Page 766, line 3. Concerning these matters and those that follow, Tiedemann discusses them in the German book *On the Causes of Contemplative Philosophy*, Volume III, page 348 and following.

Page 767, line 2. **the clear desire.**] Compare above I. 4. 2. and 3. Compare Proclus, *Elements of Theology*, chapter 145, page 216, and the annotations there.

Page 768, line 11. **as if overseeing it by that which is contrary to nature and according to nature**] I have corrected this from two Manuscripts. — The printed edition had "the" <note>original: "τὸ"</note>. See Matthiæ’s *Greek Grammar*, section 402. finally, Plotinus himself below, page 659: "overseeing nothing (the soul)": which passage should also be compared to the argument of our current passage.

Page 769, line 8. **Plato — or again moreover saying etc.**] Plato in the *Timaeus*, page 40, page 41 in Bekker's edition, concerning the earth: — "he devised it as a guardian and creator of night and day, the first and oldest of the gods who have been born within the heavens." For this passage, consult Proclus in his *Commentary*, page 281 and following; Chalcidius, page 214; Simplicius on Aristotle’s *On the Heavens*, folio 125 and following; Turnebus’s *Adversaria* XVI. 18; and Cudworth’s *Intellectual System*, page 483, Mosheim edition.

Page 771, line 11. Tiedemann also discusses these decrees of Plotinus in the book: *Spirit of Speculative Philosophy*, Volume III, page 348 and following.

Page 772, line 12. **sympathetic** <note>original: "ὁμοιοπαθὲς"</note>] See above at page 13.

— line 16. **mean proportional** <note>original: "μέσον ἀνάλογον"</note>] <term>Analogos: in the same proportion</term>. Thus Plato and the Platonists use it quite often. Wyttenbach teaches this on the *Phaedo*, page 307. Compare Proclus, *Elements of Theology*, chapters 164 and 185, and the annotations there, page 242. Compare also the celebrated Hase on Leo the Deacon, page 187 and following. The same formula recurs below on page 440. D. and page 675. B. Eunapius in the *Historical Excerpts* regarding the affairs of Julian, IX (in the *New Vatican Collection of Ancient Writers*, edited by Angelo Mai, Volume II, page 257): "thus — more deeds were now being put forth, and the crowd of those joining together followed the deeds **proportionately**." — "**so — more crimes were now being committed, and the crowd of conspirators followed the deeds as an equal.**" Indeed, "proportionately" <note>original: "ἀνάλογον"</note>, as it is written in the Manuscript: "**so both matters succeeded in a greater way, and the multitude of conspirators followed the matters in the same proportion,**" that is, the more the business at hand succeeded, the more people flocked there daily, desiring to take part in the affairs themselves.

Page 773, line 10. **For the rule applied to the straight (margin: the straight to the) — and to that in the wood — gave the craftsman the power to judge.**] Thus, from good books, we have emended these words which were interpolated and corrupted here and there. For the argument, consult the earlier passage I. 6. 3. page 52. D. and the notes there.

Page 775, line 11. **but of eyes, he says, it had no need.**] Plato in the *Timaeus*, page 33, page 30 in Bekker's edition: "And he finished it off smooth all round on the outside, for many reasons; for it had no need of eyes (one Manuscript reads 'needs', but the Plotinian ones confirm the common reading): for nothing visible was left outside, nor of hearing, for there was nothing audible (another Manuscript reads 'was left'). He intended 'was left', as in most Plotinian books." Lindau, in his commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus*, page 39, not forgetting Plotinus, says of Plotinus’s next words: "**to which (namely the preceding) the same (Plotinus) adds: 'but it was within and nothing prevented it from seeing itself.' You may guess what these words point toward.**" Indeed, the meaning of the verb "to leave" <note>original: "λείπειν"</note> allows its tenses to be exchanged with one another.

Page 776, line 8. **but neither sight — of the needy**] Ficino

-> 230 NOTES ON PLOTINUS <-

it does not seem so: he must have read <note>original: οὔτε</note> "neither." The manuscripts in this passage, which Marsilio Ficino <note>The famous Renaissance translator of Plotinus.</note> already saw was corrupt, are of no help. Next, the term <term>perielkysmos</term> <note>original: περιελκυσμοὺς; meaning "distractions" or "drawings away"</note> must be retained as a unique example of the plural. The singular is recorded from only one place in Stephanus’s *Thesaurus*, and not at all in Schneider’s *Lexicon*. — Next, several of our manuscripts read "to see and also to hear" <note>original: ὁρᾷν καὶ ἀκούειν δὲ</note>. Then in the margin: "if it is necessary also to turn back," instead of "if indeed <insert>and of himself</insert>." But the infinitive depends on the preceding phrase "one might suppose."

Page 777, line 1. *and in the arts of the magi.*] Compare Book I, 4, 9, page 35, and the notes there. In what follows, where Plotinus speaks of the body of the earth, saying it is *not indeed motionless*, beware lest you confuse this opinion with the opinion of some Pythagoreans and especially Philolaus: *that the earth is not motionless.* (See Plutarch in *Life of Numa*, chapter 11; *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*, III, 13; Diogenes Laërtius, VIII, 85; Cicero, *Academics*, IV, 39.) For Plotinus disputes in <term>this place</term> <note>original: hoc loco</note> whether the earth has sensation and thus is capable of being affected or "moved" <note>original: κινεῖσθαι</note>. For that "to move" and "to be moved" are often used with this meaning by philosophers is not something we need to laboriously prove. Nor should the things Plotinus later posits regarding the <term>spirit</term> <note>original: πνεύματι; pneuma</note> be confused with the decree of the Pythagoreans, who attributed respiration to the world as if it were a living animal. See Aristotle’s *Physics*, IV, 6, and Stobaeus’s *Eclogues*, I, 19, 1, page 380, edited by Heeren: "The Pythagoreans say there is a vacuum, and that it enters into the heaven (that is, the world) from the infinite spirit, as if it were breathing." Compare Boeckh’s *Philolaus*, page 108 and following; although it is not useless to compare these and similar things with Plotinus’s views, and in the general decree that *the world is a living animal*, Plato, the Platonists, and Plotinus himself agree everywhere with the Pythagoreans.

— 14. *according to the smells of the juices.*] In the Vatican Codex, the first hand had written <term>chymon</term> <note>original: χυμῶν; saps/flavors</note>, but this word is properly used regarding taste. Compare Plutarch’s *Natural Questions*, chapter 5, where he enumerates eight types of flavors, page 913 B, or page 690 in Wyttenbach's edition. Regarding the distinction that exists between <term>chylus</term> <note>original: χυλὸς; juice/extract</note> and <term>chymos</term>, there is a passage by Orion in the *Etymologicum*, page 163, but it is rather corrupt. Compare Schneider’s *Index to the Works of Theophrastus*, page 546 and following. The word <term>chymi</term> is read more frequently in Plotinus. See II, 4, 12; VI, 3, 17 and 18; and regarding taste in this very book, IV, 4, 25, above on page 418 A: "and to taste flavors."

Page 779, 11. *then the other soul and intellect, which indeed men name Hestia and Demeter.*] Compare below, page 423 C: "such as Demeter and Hestia, being the earth." Proclus, in his commentary on the *Timaeus*, page 282, refers to our passage: "But others, looking to her (the earth's) fertility, called her Demeter, just as Plotinus does, calling her intellect Hestia, and her soul Demeter." You see, therefore, that Plotinus—according to the interpretation of Proclus—calls the mind of the earth Vesta <note>Hestia</note> and its soul Ceres <note>Demeter</note> <term>in this place</term>. Correctly so: and would that we were permitted to use Proclus’s commentaries on these *Enneads* today! Regarding Vesta and Ceres, philosophers have taken the subject of many discussions chiefly from two passages of Plato: in the *Timaeus*, page 40: "the earth, our nurse..." etc. (for I have placed the rest above at page 414 B) and in the *Phaedrus*, page 246, at the end: "for Hestia alone remains in the house of the gods." Chalcidius, in his commentary on the *Timaeus*, page 269 in Meursius's edition (page 344 in Fabricius's): "**For he (Plato) says that Vesta alone remains in her seat; Vesta, namely, the soul of the universal body, and the mind of that soul, governing the reins of the starry sky, according to the law hallowed by Providence.**" Philo the Jew, in *On the Cherubim*, page 143 in Mangey's edition (pages 14–16 in Pfeiffer's): "But she (the earth) alone of the parts of the world, standing firmly, was aptly named Hestia by the ancients..." etc. Proclus, in *Platonic Theology*, VI, 21, page 401: "Hestia shines her fertile and unswerving power upon all; and yet Zeus, remaining in himself, is thus led back to the intellectual watchtower, and Hestia, through her unswerving and undefiled remaining in herself, is joined to the first causes." He says similar things in his commentary on the *Cratylus*, section 138, page 83 and following in Boissonade's edition. Also in the same work, section 178, page 109, comparing Ceres with Latona: "because Latona is a life-giving fountain contained within Demeter." Moreover, in the <term>cited place</term> of the *Timaeus*, he defines his own opinion such that he says the primary causes of these goddesses are intellectual, generative, and separate, from which illuminations and powers descend into the earth, and thus arise the Earthly Ceres and Vesta, etc. (and that there is an "earthly Demeter and Hestia.") These should be compared with the other passage cited in the *Theology*, where he says that everything which is constant and immutable in all worldly things descends from that super-celestial Vesta. Other things are read in Hermias’s commentary on Plato’s *Phaedrus*, page 133, and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, II, 66, page 376 in Reiske's edition: "They think that fire is consecrated to Hestia, because the goddess, being the earth and occupying the center—"

<note>The author is discussing the position of the Earth and the element of fire.</note> ...occupying the place of the world, it produces the kindlings of the celestial fire from itself. Euripides, as quoted in Macrobius's *Saturnalia* I. 23. (Fragment number 178.):

-> And Mother Earth; whom the wise among <-
-> mortals call Vesta, seated in the ether. <-
<note>original: "καὶ γαῖα μῆτερ· Ἑστίαν δέ σ’ οἱ σοφοὶ βροτῶν καλοῦσιν ἡμένην ἐν αἰθέρι."</note>

Hence Ovid in *Fasti* VI. 267: "**Vesta is the same as the earth.**" Compare page 460. Also at verse 291: "**Understand Vesta as nothing other than a living flame.**" Plutarch, in his *Life of Numa*, chapter XI, page 301 (Leopold edition), mentioning the sacred rites of Vesta established at Rome by that king, relates the opinion of the Pythagoreans concerning the fire situated in the middle of the Universe, which they call Vesta. Whether and to what extent these Pythagorean decrees—and especially those of Philolaus—influenced Plato’s *Phaedrus* in the cited passage, is examined by Boeckh in his book in the vernacular <note>German</note>: *The Doctrines of Philolaus the Pythagorean*, page 104 and following. Other matters which I myself have discussed regarding Vesta and Ceres in *Symbolism and Mythology*, Volume II, page 622 of the second edition, need not be revisited here.

Page 779, 14. **and concerning the spirited part, we must inquire** <note>original: "καὶ περὶ τοῦ θυμοειδοῦς ζητητέον"</note>] The foundation upon which this discussion is established is in Plato’s *Timaeus*, page 70. A. and following, and page 89 and following in Bekker's edition. <term>Thymoeides</term> <note>The "spirited" or "passionate" part of the soul in Platonic philosophy, associated with anger and courage.</note>

Page 781, 17. **again the soul** <note>original: "αὖ τὴν ψυχήν"</note>] I have given this on the authority of the good Manuscripts. The Edition has "itself" <note>original: "αὐτήν"</note>. Regarding this confusion, see more in Schaefer’s *Meletemata*, page 39 and page 103.

Page 782, 10. **to be less moved toward anger... and by irrational apathy.** <note>original: "ἧττον κινεῖσθαι πρὸς ὀργὰς... καὶ ἀλόγῳ ἀπαθείᾳ."</note>] <note>The author deleted the article "the" (τὰς) following the majority of manuscripts.</note> Ficinus reads "by irrational passion" <note>original: "ἀλόγῳ πάθει"</note>. The Manuscripts do not vary, except that one gives "insensibility" <note>original: "ἀπαθίᾳ"</note>. I was unwilling to change it without the books, but Plotinus seems to have written "by irrational well-being" <note>original: "ἀλόγῳ εὐπαθείᾳ"</note>. For although *eupatheia* is for the most part almost the same as "sensual indulgence," whether a pleasant sensation of the mind or body (See the learned note of Wyttenbach on Plutarch’s *On Preserving Health*, page 846 and following; add Plotinus himself below, page 726. C.), there are nevertheless instances where, from the adjective *eupathes*, it acquires the force of *irritability*. See the passage of Alexander of Aphrodisias, *Problems* II, cited in the London Stephanus *Thesaurus*, page 7254.

— 14. **seething — and indignation** <note>original: "ζέσις — καὶ ἀγανάκτησις"</note>] Compare above, page 412. A. and the Annotation there.

Page 784, 16. **and that the resistance, being from all things, does not remain** <note>original: "τὴν δὲ ἀντιτυπίαν τὸ ἐκ πάντων οὖσαν μὴ μένειν"</note>] Should "that from all" <note>original: "τὸ ἐκ πάντων"</note> be taken by analogy to the formulas "entirely" or "altogether," or should we write "the [resistance] from all" <note>original: "τὴν ἐκ πάντων"</note>? I should prefer the latter because of the following "being" <note>feminine: οὖσαν</note>; yet I was unwilling to restore it without the books. Regarding <term>Antitypia</term> <note>Resistance or solidity; the quality of matter that prevents other matter from occupying the same space.</note>, it was discussed above at page 180. G. Next, Ficinus seems to have read "to see with the mind in like manner" <note>original: "ὁμοίως νῷ ὁρᾷν"</note> instead of "by right law" <note>original: "νόμῳ ὀρθῷ"</note>; and you might judge it should be read thus. The books offer no help.

Page 786, 2. **and of prayers — which we make to the sun, and indeed even to the stars by certain other men.** <note>original: "καὶ εὐχῶν — ἃς πρὸς ἥλιον ποιούμεθα, καὶ δὴ καὶ πρὸς ἄστρα ἄλλοι τινὲς ἄνθρωποι."</note>] That the stars were also adored by the Greeks in ancient times you may conjecture from these words in Plato’s *Cratylus*, page 397. C. D: "It seems to me that the first of the men in Greece held these only to be gods, just as many of the barbarians do now: the sun, and the moon, and the earth, and the stars, and the sky." These agree with Herodotus’s account of the religions of the ancient Persians, I. 131. The same author in *Laws* X, page 887. E: "At the rising of the sun and moon, and as they go toward their setting, hearing and seeing the prostrations and <term>Proskynesis</term> <note>The act of bowing down or prostrating oneself in worship.</note> of all Greeks and barbarians alike, etc." Compare the same, XI, page 931. A. And in the *Symposium*, Socrates himself, page 220: "—he stood until it became morning and the sun rose; then he went away after offering a prayer to the sun." Does Plotinus attribute this sun-worship to his own followers, the Platonists, or to his fellow citizens? The worship of the other stars he attributes to "certain others." You may see Clement of Alexandria, *Protrepticus*, page 22 (Potter edition); Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, XV. 10; the *Zend-Avesta*, II. 3; Caesar, *Gallic War*, VI. 21; Tacitus, *Germania*, chapter 40; and compare Ficinus’s argument for this chapter; Turnebus’s *Adversaria*, XXIV. 35; *Payne Knight’s Inquiry into the Symbolic Language of Ancient Art and Mythology*, section 2, page 1; and what I myself have set down in *Symbolism*, Volume I, page 4 and following, second edition. To those things which Ficinus touched upon in the argument of this chapter concerning Plato’s doctrine on the sun, these words of Ammianus Marcellinus (XXI. 1. 11) pertain: "**For the Sun, as the Physicists say, the mind of the world, spreading our minds from himself like sparks, when he has kindled them more vehemently, renders them conscious of the future.**" What follows, "and it is believed that many things are accomplished by them for themselves, etc." Villoison, in *Greek Anecdotes*, II, page 227 and following, from two Venetian Manuscripts, presented as if unpublished under this title and with this beginning: *Plotinus on how the celestial disposition looks into the terrestrial world. Since it is believed that many things are accomplished through the stars—*

— 10. **and licentious unions** <note>original: "καὶ ἀκολάστους συλλήψεις"</note>] Ficinus translates this as "intercourse" <note>Latin: concubitus</note>; in this place, indeed, not badly. Properly, it means <term>Syllēpsis</term> <note>Conceptions or the act of taking together.</note>. Plutarch’s *Life of Romulus*, XI. 4, page 113 (Leopold edition): "that the conception of Romulus in his mother took place in the first year of the second Olym—"

-> 232 ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS <-

<note>original: "πιάδος"</note>. Thus frequently in the Septuagint <note>The Greek Old Testament</note>. See Biel, *Thesaurus of the Old Testament*, Vol. III, page 351. Regarding the verb, see Hesychius on <note>original: "συλλήψεσθαι"</note> <gloss>to conceive or seize</gloss>, page 1292; Thomas Magister, page 816; Hippocrates, *Aphorisms*, Book V, section 46. Boissonade on Philostratus's *Heroica*, page 385. The same author on Herodian’s *Epimerismi*, page 64 and following; also on Aristaenetus, page 497, where the words of Severus in the *Catena* <note>A "chain" of biblical interpretations</note> found in Wolf’s *Greek Anecdotes*, Vol. IV, page 57, more closely approach the similarity of the Plotinian passage: <note>original: "ἥτις διὰ τῆς ἀτοπωτάτης ὀρέξεως οἱονεὶ συλλαμβάνουσα καὶ κύουσα τὴν πρᾶξιν τῆς ἁμαρτίας ἀποτίκτει"</note> <gloss>which, through the most misplaced desire, as if conceiving and being pregnant with the act of sin, gives birth to it.</gloss> To this passage should be applied the learned arguments of my friend Georg Joseph Bekker in his *Specimen on Philostratus's Life of Apollonius*, page 17 and following. Furthermore, a writer fond of Sophistic elegances would have written: <note>original: "θεοὺς συλλήπτορας γίγνεσθαι — πρὸς ἀκολάστους συλλήψεις"</note> <gloss>that the gods become helpers—toward unrestrained conceptions.</gloss> But from such "little flowers" <note>rhetorical flourishes</note>, in which the followers of Gorgias delighted (such as Agathon, who was mocked by Socrates on this account), the severity of Plotinus is most distantly removed. Regarding the words "of Demeter and Hestia," compare the note to page 419, C.

Page 788, 12. **"But rhetoric and music and every form of soul-leading <term>Psychagōgia: the art of winning or leading souls through persuasion or enchantment</term>, which by altering the soul lead it toward the better or the worse."** Ficino translates the last word thus: "**which especially differ among themselves.**" Perhaps the meaning is: "**by the fact that they affect the minds of men in different ways, or because they affect minds differently than they had been affected until then.**" Moreover, these Plotinian ideas, in both words and sentiments, prove him a student of Plato. See Plato’s *Gorgias*, page 453 and following; compare Aristides, *Platonic Orations*, I, page 47; Sextus Empiricus, II. 2, page 288; Quintilian, *Institutes of Oratory*, II. 15. 4. Plato, *Republic*, Book II, page 365, end: <note>original: "εἰσὶ δὲ πειθοῦς διδάσκαλοι, σοφίαν δημογορικὴν τε καὶ δικανικὴν διδόντες"</note> <gloss>there are teachers of persuasion, giving wisdom for public speaking and the law courts.</gloss> For "rhetoric" and "public speaking" are often used as synonyms, as is "sophistry." Diodorus Siculus, Book XX, beginning; Diogenes Laërtius, II. 20. Consult Chr. Theoph. Ernesti, *Lexicon of Greek Rhetorical Technology*, page 300 and following; Krüger on Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Historiography*, page 518. Hence <note>original: "ῥητορεύειν"</note> <gloss>to practice rhetoric</gloss> and <note>original: "ῥητορεία"</gloss> <gloss>rhetoric</gloss> also designate futile and talkative <term>Sermocinatio: a style of dialogue or speech-making</term>. See Dorville on Chariton, page 507, Leipzig edition, and compare C. F. Hermann on Lucian’s *How to Write History*, page 162. To understand the force of the word <note>original: "ψυχαγωγία"</note> <gloss>soul-leading</gloss>, consult Plato, *Laws*, Book X, page 908 end, 909 A, and Ast’s observations on that passage, page 505.

Page 790, 9. **"First, then, we must posit one living being..."** <note>original: "πρῶτον τοίνυν θετέον ζῶον ἓν κ. τ. λ."</note> Tiedemann judges that no new argument is added here by Plotinus in *The Spirit of Speculative Philosophy*, Vol. III, page 289. The things that follow thereafter he compares with the decrees of the Stoics and other ancient philosophers in the same work, page 326 and following.

Page 791, 1. **"This whole 'One' is sympathetic."** <note>original: "Συμπαθὲς δὴ πᾶν τοῦτο τὸ ἕν."</note> Iamblichus treats the same argument in *On the Mysteries*, IV. 8, page 112; from which I append these remarks: "And indeed a certain energy descends from the wholes to the parts, one being <term>Sympathes: sharing a common feeling or cosmic connection</term> according to the similarity of powers, the other being a manifold action according to the fitness of the agent toward the patient. If, therefore, certain evils and destructions happen to the parts due to bodily necessities, these are—in relation to the wholes and the harmony of the universe—salutary and good, but they bring an inevitable <term>Phthora: destruction or decay</term> upon the parts, either through the inability to bear the energies of the wholes, or by some other mixture and temperament of their own weakness, or thirdly, by the asymmetry of the parts toward one another."

— 11. **"and the part affected does not hold it pleasantly"** <note>original: "καὶ οὐ προσήνως τὸ πάσχον ἴσχει"</note> See above, page 38. B, page 52. E, and compare Olympiodorus on the *Alcibiades*, preface, page 122. — "Wherefore we call those who are pleasant to us and wish us good things 'well-wishers' <note>original: "εὔνους"</note>." — As for what is read next in some books: "since both bile and a thrusting <note>original: "ὠθισμὸς"</note>... presses and stings," this reading reminds one of what was read above on page 205. F: "nor pressing from without to push toward the inside," where compare the note. Furthermore, most of our manuscripts, as well as two Venetian ones in Villoison’s *Greek Anecdotes*, Vol. II, page 228, agree on the reading <note>original: "ὁ θυμὸς"</note> <gloss>anger/spirit</gloss>, which is also confirmed by the words immediately following.

Page 794, 8. **"and their different positions following, and the rest, as if provided by a single living being in motion"** The philosopher of Lycopolis <note>Plotinus</note> used the same image of a dance to declare the harmonious motion of the world above on page 267. E. F. Compare also page 372. B. C. and my notes there. For the source of this entire passage and similar ones is in Plato’s *Timaeus*, page 30, end (page 26 and following in Bekker): "For God, wishing to make the world most like that which is fairest of the intelligible beings and perfect in all respects, constituted it as a single visible living being, containing within itself all living beings that are by nature akin to it." III. 71. He places this among the doctrines of Plato: <note>original: "ἔμψυχόν τε εἶναι (τὸν κόσμον) διὰ τὸ κρεῖττον εἶναι τὸ ἔμψυχον τοῦ ἀψύχου"</note> **that the world is an animate being because that which is animate is superior to that which is inanimate.** Regarding this passage, Menagius on page 164, applying our present text, says: "**See Plotinus IV. 4. 33. where the world is called *one animal* dancing to a musical rhythm, and by dancing, consequently varying all things in harmony with itself.**" Cicero expressed Plato's words thus in his *Fragment on the Universe*, chapter 4: "**For since God wished to make the world similar to that which can be understood as the most beautiful in the nature of things and most absolute in every part, He made it one animal, visible, in which** (my Manuscript now adds, formerly the Uffenbachs') **all animals are contained:**" in which passage, as he often does, Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> allowed himself to omit a complete phrase, namely this one: <note>original: "ὅσα αὐτοῦ κατὰ φύσιν ξυγγενῆ"</note> **as many as are by nature akin to it.** Furthermore, compare those words of Cicero, or rather of the Stoic in Cicero's *On the Nature of the Gods* II. 12: — "**From which it is concluded that the world is a living being.**" Pomponius Mela III. 1. 15. and following: "**Nor is it yet sufficiently known whether the *World* effects this by its own panting, and draws back the wave with its breath and then returns it from all sides, if (as pleases the more learned) *it is one animal:***" to which Isaac Vossius on page 780 of the third edition of Abraham Gronovius seeks support for the reading *one* instead of *living* from the doctrine of Plato and from these very passages of our Plotinus. Moreover, Proclus in his *Commentary on the Timaeus* page 131 and following (compare page 93 and following) reports and judges at length the opinions of Plotinus, Atticus, Amelius, Porphyry, and Iamblichus concerning the Soul of the world and its maker, and likewise concerning the world as a living being. Indeed, those things which our Plotinus adds in the continuous passage agree strongly with the decree of the Indians, that the maker of the world permeates all worldly things. See Wilhelm von Humboldt's *Dissertation on the Bhagavad-gítá*, Berlin 1827, page 26, and the citations there, and compare Guigniaut in *Religions of Antiquity* IV, page 4, number 18.

Page 795, 2. <note>original: "ὥσπερ οἱ ἔμφρονες τῶν θητευόντων — ἅτε μὴ ἀνδράποδα ὄντες"</note> **just as the sensible among those who serve for hire — inasmuch as they are not slaves.**] The verb <term>thēteuein</term> <note>to serve as a laborer for pay</note> is found in Plato's *Euthyphro* page 4. C. page 26 and following in Stallbaum's edition: <note>original: "πελάτης τις ἦν ἐμὸς, καὶ ὡς ἐγεωργοῦμεν ἐν Νάξῳ ἐθήτευεν παρ’ ἡμῖν"</note> **he was a certain dependent of mine, and when we were farming in Naxos, he worked for us for hire.** For this passage, consult Pollux III. 82, VI. 196, and Ruhnken on Timaeus's *Platonic Lexicon* page 211 and following. Regarding the difference between mercenaries and slaves and the diverse condition of both among the Greeks and Romans, see Petit's *Attic Laws* page 249 and following, Wesseling edition. Compare also Boeckh's *Public Economy of the Athenians* I, page 128 and following.

Page 796, 7. <note>original: "οἱονχειρὸς τὰ συνθλιβόμενα"</note> **as if the bones of a hand being pressed together**] The Marcian Manuscript reads <note>original: "χεὶρ ὀστᾶ συνθλιβόμενα"</note>. From which you might perhaps conjecture that Plotinus wrote: **the bones of a hand being pressed together.**

Page 797, 1. <note>original: "ἡ διέξοδος τῆς ζωῆς"</note> **the course of life**] Compare above page 189. B. Ennead II. 8. 1. where I have explained this.

Page 799, 13. <note>original: "οἷον καὶ λίθων φύσεις καὶ βοτανῶν ἐνέργειαι θαυμαστὰ πολλά παρέχονται"</note> **just as the natures of stones and the powers of herbs provide many wonderful things.**] These and similar doctrines have supplied the subject matter for many writings of very different ages; these volumes, composed either in verse or prose and widely ascribed to the most ancient priests, are circulated under the names of Hermes, Orpheus, Kyranus, and others. Thus, to use this example, here in our ancient Palatine library (now kept in the Vatican at Rome) is preserved "**Hermes Trismegistus's book on the herbs of the seven planets, addressed to Asclepius**" according to the testimony of Friedrich Sylburg in the *Catalogue of Greek Manuscripts of the Palatine Library of Heidelberg*, number 226, page 69, bottom. In Iriarte's *Greek Manuscripts of the Royal Library of Madrid*, page 431 and following, while other notices of this kind exist, there is also this: **in the book called the Kyranides, there were written accounts concerning 24 stones, 24 birds, 24 fish, and 24 herbs.** Compare Tyrwhitt on the *Lithica* falsely attributed to Orpheus, especially the Greek argument on page 360 of the Hermann edition; add Fabricius's *Greek Library* Vol. I, page 70 and following, Harles edition, and page 156 and following, and our own *Symbolica* Vol. I, page 396, second edition. A similar short work, which likewise falsely claims the name of Hermes Trismegistus, we recently added to the fragments of Joannes Laurentius Lydus's *On the Months* in our friend Roether's edition, pages 312—339. It is entitled **On the Juices of Herbs**, and contains information and instructions on which star should be present when plants are collected and skillfully treated for medicinal use.

Page 800, 10. <note>original: "τῷ μὴ αἰσθητῶς παρ’ αὑτοῦ κινουμένους"</note> **by the fact that they are not moved perceptibly by themselves.**] I have written this on the authority of several Manuscripts and especially the Marcian alone. The printed edition has: <note>original: "τὸ μὴ αἰσθητῶς παρ’ αὑτῷ κινούμενον"</note>; Ficino translates: "**because among these things it does not appear to us to be moved clearly by itself.**" The same Marcian book gives in the final words of this chapter: <note>original: "διὸ καὶ πολλὰ δουλεύει αὐτοῦ ταῖς δυνάμεσιν"</note>; which are perhaps to be translated thus: *Therefore many things also serve its (namely, the Universe's) powers*. And somehow this sentiment is pleasing.

**p. 803, 8. τὰ δὲ τὴν ὑποκειμένην φύσιν εἰσφέρεσθαι.]** I did not hesitate to restore *physis* [nature] with Ficino in place of *pistin* [faith]. The logic of the dispute demands this; and read a little earlier these words: *καὶ δεῖ καὶ τὸ πάσχον ὑποκειμένην τινὰ καὶ τοιάνδε φύσιν ἔχειν* [and it is necessary that the patient also have a certain underlying nature of this kind].
**— 11. ἀρετὴ δὲ ἀδέσποτον.]** See above II. 3. 9. and below VI. 8. 5. and 6. Olympiodorus in *Alcib. pr.* [Preface to the First Alcibiades] § 28. p. 226: *τοῦ παλαιοῦ λόγου λέγοντος τὴν ἀρετὴν ἀδέσποτον καὶ ἐλευθέραν* [the ancient saying stating that virtue is without a master and free]: where *cf.* [confer] the annotation. Soon after, the two Marcian [manuscripts] do not have the words: *τῶν ἐν τῷδε τῷ παντὶ τοῖς θειοτέροις*. If they are genuine, they are to be understood as Ficino understood them, namely so that you think of *τῶν ὄντων ἐν τοῖς θειοτέροις τοῖς οὖσι τῷδε τῷ παντί*.
**p. 804, 2. παρὰ τοὺς σπερματικοὺς αὐτοὺς λόγους·]** Marc. Antonin. IV. 14: *ἐναπέστης ὡς μέρος. ἐναφανισθήσῃ τῷ γεννήσαντι· μᾶλλον δὲ ἀναληφθήσῃ εἰς τὸν λόγον αὐτοῦ τὸν σπερματικὸν κατὰ μεταβολήν* [You existed as a part. You will disappear into that which produced you; or rather, you will be taken up into its seminal reason through change]. *Cf.* ibid. § 21. and 23. Diog. Laërt. VII. 136. concerning Zeno the Stoic: *ὥσπερ ἐν τῇ γονῇ τὸ σπέρμα περιέχεται, οὕτω καὶ τοῦτον σπερματικὸν λόγον ὄντα τοῦ κόσμου* [just as the seed is contained in the progeny, so this too being the seminal reason of the cosmos]. For this was primarily the doctrine and formula of speaking of the Stoics, later frequented by others and by our Plotinus himself; Meric Casaubon was not unmindful of this in his excellent annotation on Antoninus in the cited place p. 397, in the *Works of Th. Gataker* at the end of Antoninus, who allows me the leisure to speak more extensively on this formula. See also the annotations of Wyttenbach and our own in *Cic.* [Cicero] *de N. D.* [On the Nature of the Gods] II. 22. and 32. p. 291. and 757. *ed.* [edition] Moser, and *cf.* [confer] Baguet on the Fragments of Chrysippus p. 93.
**— 4. ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον ἂν ἐοίκοι ὁ λόγος τοῦ παντὸς κατὰ λόγον τιθέντα κόσμον πόλεως.]** This opinion especially pleased the Stoics. *Cic.* [Cicero] *de N. D.* II. 31. and likewise II. 62: “For the world is as it were the common house of Gods and men, or the city of both.” The same in *de Legg.* [On the Laws] I. 7. 23: “so that now this whole world is to be considered one common city of gods and men:” where see Wyttenbach p. 58. *ed.* Moser and Turnebus p. 551. and p. 758 *sq.* [following] [*add.* [added] from *Cic.* [Cicero] *de Rep.* [On the Republic] I. 13. p. 58. our edition Moser.] And *kosmos* [means] *order, disposition*. Herodotus VII. 36: *κόσμῳ θέντες τὴν ὕλλην* [arranging the timber in order]. II. 52. The Gods (*οἱ θεοὶ*) were named because *κόσμῳ θέντες τὰ πάντα πρήγματα* [they set all things in order]. Schweighäuser's *Lexicon of Herodotus* will give more under the word. *Cf.* [Confer] also Wyttenbach on Plutarch *de Sent. Profect. in Virt.* p. 558.—Then at the end of this period, let us hold the words *πάντων ὁδῷ οἷον αὐτομάτη εἰς συμφωνίαν χωρούντων* [all things proceeding by a path, as if spontaneously, into harmony]. Concerning the metaphorical use of the words *hodos* [path] and similar ones, there is nothing more for us to say after the most elegant Heusde in *Specim. Platon.* p. 130 *sq.* and Wyttenbach on the *Phaedo* p. 155 (and what I myself placed in *Cicero de N. D.* II. 22. at the beginning, on the words: *progredientem via* [proceeding by a path] (*ὁδῷ βαδίζοντα*). But the passage of Plato in the *Statesman* p. 170. (p. 258. Steph. p. 247. Bekk.) which he himself praised here: *τὴν οὖν πολιτικὴν ἀτραπὸν πῆ τις ἀνευρήσει;* [where will one find the political path?]; this reminds us of a passage of Plutarch at the beginning of the book *de Capienda ex inimic. Utilit.* p. 86. B. p. 331. Wytt.: *ὁρῶ μὲν ὅτι τὸν πραότατον, ὦ Κορνήλιε Πούλχερ, ἄτερ πολιτείας ᾕρησαι τρόπον...* [I see, O Cornelius Pulcher, that you have chosen the mildest manner without political life...]. All critics confess the place to be corrupt (see *varr. lectt.* [various readings] in Wyttenbach's edition and his remarks p. 614.) I am mistaken, or Plutarch had the praised passage of Plato before his eyes. Therefore, I would read: *ὁρῶ μὲν ὅτι τὴν πραοτάτην, ὦ Κορνήλιε Πούλχερ, ἀτραπὸν πολιτείας ᾕρησαι, ἐν ᾗ—* [I see, O Cornelius Pulcher, that you have chosen the mildest path of political life, in which—] with the word *tropon* expunged. Unless you prefer: *ὅτι τὴν πραοτάτην—ἀτραπὸν πολιτείας ᾕρησαι καὶ τρόπον, ἐν ᾧ μάλιστα κ. τ. λ.* [that you have chosen the mildest path and manner of political life, in which etc.]. Which interpretation of the word *atrapon* [path] introduced from the margin into the text gave place to the remaining changes. Furthermore, the adjective *praos* [mild] applied to the word *atrapos* [path] both logic admits and the author's usage protects, who elsewhere said: *πρᾷον βάδισμα* [a mild walk], *πραότης πορείας* [mildness of journey] and similar things. Proclus in Plato's *Parmenides* I. p. 47. *ed.* Cousin: *τὴν οἷον εὐθεῖαν ἀτραπὸν ἐπ’ αὐτὸ τὸ ἀληθὲς φέρουσαν* [the as it were straight path leading to the truth itself]. The same in *Alcib. pr.* p. 306 our edition uses *τὰς διαλεκτικὰς ἀτραπούς* [the dialectical paths].—But to return to Plotinus: I wrote *αὐτομάτη* [spontaneous, fem.] by the command of most *Codd.* [manuscripts] instead of *αὐτομάτῳ* [spontaneous, neut.], which is read in the Edition.

**p. 805, 14. καὶ γὰρ ὅτι ἐρᾶν πεφύκασι, καὶ τὰ ἐρᾶν ποιοῦντα ἕλκει πρὸς ἄλληλα, ἀλκῇ ἐρωτικῆς διὰ γοητείας τέχνης γεγένηται.]** The Marcian manuscripts in both places: *δρᾷν* [to do] for *ἐρᾷν* [to love], then the edition *ἐκεῖ* [there] for *ἕλκει* [draws]. The same *ἀλκῇ* [by strength], the Marcian *ἀλκῇ*. Medicean B. *ἀλκῆς*. Villoison ordered it to be read *ἀλκῇ ἐρωτικῇ*. I, with Ficino, have replaced it with *ἀλκῇ ἐρωτικῆς*. As for the words and meanings, compare below p. 438. B: *ἢ ἑλκόμενος οὐ μάγων τέχναις, ἀλλὰ τῆς φύσεως τῆς ἀπάτης δούσης καὶ συναψάσης ἄλλο πρὸς ἄλλο οὐ τοῖς τόποις, ἀλλ’ οἷς ἔδωκε φίλτροις;* [or being drawn not by the arts of magi, but of nature giving and joining one thing to another by deceit, not by places, but by the charms she gave?] and I. 4. 9. p. 35. D. and what I placed there.
