**— 13. Καὶ ὅσα λωβᾶται ἀνθρώποις]** The two Marcian manuscripts and other *Codd.* [manuscripts] have *ἀνθρώπους*. Concerning this discrepancy, notice was given above on p. 54. D.
**— 15. οἷον εἴ πῦρ τις ἐκ πυρὸς λαβὼν—μετηνέχθη]** I left the passage untouched, as it is undoubtedly disturbed. Ficino seems to have read *οὐ μηχανησάμενος* or *μὴ μηχαν.* and then *μετατεθέν τι*. Cod. Medicean gives *μεταθέντι*. The Marcian rejects the words *μὴ ἐλθεῖν* after the words *ἐκεῖνος ποιεῖ*. From which I think these should be thus emended: *οἷον εἴ πῦρ τις ἐκ πυρὸς λαβὼν ἔβλαψεν ἄλλον, ἢ ὁ μηχανησάμενος ἢ ὁ λαβὼν ἐκεῖνος ποιεῖ ἐλθεῖν, τῷ δεδωκέναι γοῦν τι οἷον μετατεθὲν ἐξ ἄλλου εἰς ἄλλο, καὶ τὸ ἐληλυθὸς δὲ (ποιεῖ sc.) εἰ μὴ μετηνέχθη:* Just as if someone, having taken fire from fire, has harmed another, either he who devised it (i.e. who first lit the fire) or he who took it (one fire from the other) makes it come (the fire) by having given something, as if translated one from another; but also the approaching fire acts (i.e. is the agent), if the one into whom it is transferred (the fire) is not able to receive it.
**p. 808, 7. ἀλλὰ καὶ μετ’ εὐχῆς γίγνεσθαί τι δοτέον, καὶ εὐχῆς ἄνευ κ. τ. λ.** Iamblichus *On the Mysteries* V. 26. p. 141: [Greek text describing the first kind of prayer as unifying, the second as connecting in harmonious communion, calling down gifts from the gods before reason and before understanding the whole works]. To which passage Gale from other writers, especially Platonists, placed in the notes things which belong here, p. 280. At which I wonder it did not come to his mind these Plotinian things; which also remind us of the Socratic dispute in the *Second Alcibiades*; in which dialogue Boeckh seems to have found traces of Stoic logic for himself (though not in the *First Alcibiades*, as I falsely wrote in the *Preface to Proclus' Commentary on Plato's Alcib. pr.* p. XIII.) In that second *Alcibiades* therefore, p. 143. A. p. 281. Bekk. those lines not unlike the poet's occur:
*King Zeus, give us good things both to those who pray and those who do not,*
*but keep away terrible things even from those who pray for them.*
Which the *Greek Anthology* shows slightly differently in the anonymous [epigrams] *nr.* [number] CCCCLXVI. p. 217. Jacobs; whom consult in *Animadvv.* Vol. XII. p. 137. Diodorus Siculus produces very similar precepts of Pythagoras in the *Excerpts* book VIII—X. *nr.* 39. in the *Collect. Vaticana ed.* Ang. Mai Vol. II. p. 32. I have placed more on this matter in *Symbolica* Vol. I. p. 164 *sqq. second ed.* But, what I did not place there, I will certainly touch upon here in one word. Namely, lest anyone doubt that in his genuine dialogues Plato prescribes such sound things concerning prayers and vows as those above, let him read *Cratylus* p. 400. D., *Theæt.* p. 112. C., *Philebus* p. 12. C. and *de Legg.* VII. p. 801. A—C; where Plato complains about common poets who write prayers unworthy of the gods for the use of public religions. Which healthiness both of mind and speech was recently approved also by that woman truly a philosopher and learned in Socratic writings, Wyttenbach, in that brilliant dialogue entitled *Theagenes*.—He who desires to learn the opinions of Christian doctors on prayers and vows, lest I produce more *h. l.* [in this place], should consult what Suicer gathered in the *Thesauro Ecclesiastico* under the word *Εὐχὴ* [Prayer]. **— 6. Τί γὰρ παθών τις πρὸς ἄλλο ἔχει;]** Someone might perhaps wonder that I left the reading of the Edition untouched, although five manuscripts of the best quality offer *mathon* [having learned], and Jacobs, a most ingenious man, pronounced on this passage in *Additamm. Animadvv. in Athenaeum* p. 327: “The most learned man in Greek, Villoison, fell into the same error in *Anecdott.* Vol. II. p. 235, who in Plotinus' *Diatrib.* corrects *τί γὰρ παθών τις πρὸς ἄλλο ἔχει* [for what having suffered does one have...] instead of *τί γὰρ μαθών*... which is entirely sincere.” Thus he. But Villoison did not know then that these chapters were already read in print; he did not know that in the edition from four MSS books *pathon* was read; he did not know that the Cizensis and Darmstadt books likewise retain *pathon*; he did not know that Ficino, who would have found *τί μαθών* in the two Medicean books, nevertheless replaced it with: “*quidnam passus* [what indeed having suffered].” —And rightly here. For in the whole passage it is discussed what indeed happens from without, so that by the allurements of prayers, vows, and incantations, men and genii are drawn; and the words *κινεῖσθαι* [to be moved] and *πάσχειν* [to suffer] are repeated multiple times. And immediately after those *τί παθών—ἔχει;* follow these: *ἢ ἑλκόμενος οὐ μάγων τέχναις* [or being drawn not by the arts of magi]. What more do you seek? The argument of the whole passage, where the difference between the suffering soul and the impassive mind is touched upon, requires, as Villoison rightly guessed, *τί παθών*: On the contrary, the same Jacobs very truly judged in the same place about the Philostratean passage in the *Life of Apollonius* I. 28. p. 36, where also Cod. Schellersh. shows *μαθών*. Wherefore also my Bekker in *Specim. Philostrat.* p. 90 rightly accommodated himself to Jacobs' authority. Which second formula, rare in Plato's writings, the most illustrious Heusde excellently, as is his custom, confirmed from the passages of the Comic poets in *Specim. Crit. in Platon.* p. 57.—The next *μάγων τέχναις* we touched on above at p. 434. **p. 812, 7. ὅσα γὰρ ἀνθρώπους δελεάζει, ἡδέα γενόμενα ταῖς ἐπιθυμίαις]** Xenophon *Memorabb.* II. 1. 4: [Greek text describing animals being enticed by their belly and led by desire for food to the bait]. Where these words are properly used. The metaphorical use extends very widely. Plato *Euthydem.* p. 272. D. p. 395 *sq.* Bekk.: *ἴσως δὲ δέλεαρ ἄξομεν αὐτοῖς τοὺς σοὺς υἱέας* [perhaps we shall bring your sons as bait for them], where the Bodleian Cod. and two others inspected by Bekker [read]: *αὐτοῖς ἔξομεν*. And there was a time when I thought this the better reading. For beasts are led (*ἄγονται*) to the bait, as in the passage of Xenophon, or men lead beasts by a sprout (*θάλλῳ*) or lead them around under a sprout (see Ruhnken on Timæus p. 136. and Euripides in *Erechtheus Fragm.* I. *v.* [verse] 18. p. 442 *sq.* Beck: *τῆς γε (vel τῆς γῆ) δέλεαρ ἔχοντες* [having a bait of the earth]. The same in *Andromache* v. 262. (264. *ed.* A. Matthiae) *τοιόνδ’ ἔχω σου δέλεαρ* [I have such a bait for you]. But yet in the passage of Plato, Socrates is eager to persuade Crito to frequent the Sophists with him: *καὶ σὺ τί συμφοίτα* [you also go with them], and lead his sons with him also, and bring them with him as bait to those sophists. Therefore that is well: *ἴσως δὲ δέλεαρ ἄξομεν αὐτοῖς τοὺς σοὺς υἱεῖς*, in almost the same way as Xenophon in *Hellenica* V. 4. 4. says: *γυναῖκας ὑπισχνούμενος ἄξειν αὐτοῖς καλλίστας* [promising to bring them most beautiful women], concerning prostitutes being led to men. I return to the word; on whose metaphorical use commentators have gathered not a few things for these [words] of James *Epistle* I. 14: *ὑπὸ τῆς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας ἐξελκόμενος καὶ δελεαζόμενος* [drawn away and enticed by his own desire]. The same Theodoret, or his interpolator, in *Religious History* or *Philotheus* p. 1114. Chalcidius on Plato's *Timaeus* p. 331. Moreover, confused and more fouled, it signifies black and dark things: and similar is the passion of those who grow numb by the contagion of the marine fish, since that poison creeps through the line and the reed and through the hands, and penetrates the innermost sense.” And perhaps Chalcidius, who used this similarity just as Plotinus in the passage on vision, had our philosopher before his eyes.
**p. 819, 14. εἰ καὶ νῦν—τὸ τῶν ὀμμάτων πρόσθεν κείμενον]** I left the passage untouched as perhaps not sound. How Ficino understood it, the version proves. I do not wish therefore to decide whether he translated correctly, or whether the ends should rather be translated: *what is placed before the eyes*. The next: *καὶ οἱ ἐκχέοντες δὲ τὰς ὄψεις* [and those pouring out their sights] recall the elegance of Platonic speech. For they are modeled on that [phrase] in the *Theaetetus* p. 181. a: *τοὺς ῥέοντας* [the flowing ones], those, "who contend for the flux of all things, but *οἱ τοῦ ὅλου στασιῶται*" “those who say the universe is immobile” and *τοὺς τὸ πᾶν κινοῦντας*, “those who think the universe is moved.” See Heindorf on that place p. 419. and, to add an example drawn from the same thing, Plutarch *Quæst. Symposiacc.* I. 8. 2. p. 529 Wytt.: *ἕτεροι δὲ τοῖς συμβάλλουσι τὰς αὐγὰς προσείχον.* “others conceded to the opinion of those who think the rays of sight concur:” i.e. who adopted the Platonic *sunaueia* [confluence of rays]. Plotinus offers an example of the same brevity, differing only in this, that instead of a Participle he has a Verb with a Pronoun, below V. 8. 12. p. 85. B: *διὸ καὶ οὐκ ὀρθῶς (sc. δοκοῦσιν) οἱ φθείρουσι (sc. τὸν κόσμον τὸν αἰσθητὸν) τοῦ νοητοῦ μένοντος, καὶ γεννῶσιν οὕτως κ. τ. λ.* i.e. those who say the sensible world is perishable—and thus think it was begotten.

See Budé and Stephanus in *Thes. L. Gr.* p. 4610. Valpy edition and *cf.* [confer] Schneider's *Index to Theophrastus' Works* p. 315. Plutarch *de Placitt. Philoss.* IV. 1. p. 621. This [passage] of the same Pseudo-Plutarch ibid. III. 15. p. 611. Which now are to be compared with J. L. Lydus' *Fragment on Earthquakes* in the book *On Ostents* chapter 53. p. 186—188. Hase. Plutarch in *Quæstionn. Platonn.* p. 1004. D. p. 88. X. 48: *καὶ γὰρ ῥεῦσις ἀπὸ τῆς τῶν σωμάτων ἐπιπολῆς συνεχὴς συμβαίνει* [for a continuous flow from the surface of bodies occurs]. The same brings forth similar things in the Herculaneum papyri p. 69; from which Rosini the editor not ineptly filled the lacunose passage thus p. 4: *περᾶν δὴ συνεχῆ τὸν ῥοῦν* [the flow passes through continuously]. (*cf.* [confer] our annotation in *Cicero de N. D.* I. 39. p. 178, where the typesetters erred in the passage of Diogenes.) Hence in Plotinus someone perhaps might have tried: *περῶσιν* [they pass through] for *πάρεισιν* [they are present], yet it is not necessary. Gellius V. 16: “But Epicurus thinks that certain images of the bodies themselves always flow off from all bodies, and these bring themselves into the eyes, and thus the sense of seeing happens.” Macrobius *Saturnn.* VII. 14: “Therefore Epicurus judges that from all bodies certain images flow in a constant stream; nor does even the smallest delay intervene, but that the sloughed skins of bodies, adhering in an empty figure, are carried forward, the receptacles of which are in our eyes: and thus the senses properly return to the seat assigned to them by nature.” Ign. Herodian IV. 15. p. 814 *sq.* Irmisch, on the funeral pyres of Roman emperors: [Greek text describing how the structure can be compared to beacon-towers (φρυκτωρίοις) which, placed over harbors, guide ships at night through fire, and many call them lighthouses (φάρους)]. where see the Editor's notes. Isidore *Origg.* XI. 1. “Pupilla: —It is called *pupula*, because it is a pure and unpolluted girl (*puella*).” I have praised these for the sake of Philo, who in *Leg. Allegorr.* II. p. 78. Mangey (p. 118. For just as in the eye the seeing part is black, so the visionary part of the soul is called an Ethiopian woman]. In which passage, after Mangey confessed that he did not perceive what is clearer than midday, he nevertheless makes a risk of conjecturing, wanting to thrust upon us *katapyron* [fiery] instead of *katakore*. But he who knows Philo's license for playing with words will not doubt that he wanted to allude with that *katakore* to the *koren* [pupil], which he then describes with these words: *ὡς γὰρ ὀφθαλμῷ τὸ βλέπον μέλαν ἐστὶν* [for as the seeing part in the eye is black], in which words the reason also exists why he drags the Ethiopian woman here, i.e., black. Then neither is that true, that *h. l.* [in this place] *gnomen* [opinion] and *physin* [nature] are synonyms. I should rather believe Philo wrote *phausin* [shining]: concerning which Alexandrian word see what I placed at Nathanael's *Antithet. advers. Plotin.* chapter 6. (p. 441. Heidelberg edition, which passage I would entirely wish to be compared with the Philonic one.) Thus these will respond excellently to each other: *τὴν ἀμετάβλητον καὶ κατακορῆ γνώμην* (the unchangeable and unpolluted). With the word *πεπυρωμένην* [fiery] Philo again refers to the *Ethiopian woman*, i.e., scorched as it were and blackish in face.—I return to Plotinus. **p. 826, 6. Ἐπεὶ καὶ τὸ τῆς νυκτὸς ὁρᾷν—χαλεπὸν ταύτῃ τῇ ὑποθέσει ἀπευθῦναι.]** To the passages gathered to illustrate the use of this Verb add Dionys. Halicarn. *de Compos.* XI. 80. p. 134. Schaef. and Photius' *Bibliotheca* Cod. 165. p. 108. b. below Bekker: and *cf.* [confer] P. Wesseling at Sophocles' *Ajax* v. 72. It is used more often by Plutarch in the *Moralia*; who thus in *de Pueror. Educat.* p. 2. D. p. 6. Wytt.: [Greek text where it is impossible to straighten (ἀπευθύνειν) the crooked staves of actors]. If you apply this to our passage, the force of the verb here is to be taken as *to make straight what is crooked*, or to direct and expedite what is tangled and hindered. See Scholiast of Sophocles on *Oedipus Rex* v. 104. Then this would be the meaning of our passage: Since that—seeing by night—is difficult to explain (*explicatu*) by this hypothesis (by this reasoning). But I do not know whether that other force makes more sense here, which the same Scholiast produces: *ἀπευθύνω, καὶ τὸ ἀπὸ εὐθύνης ποιῶ, ἤτοι ἀπεύθυνον* [I straighten, and I do it from an audit, i.e. I excuse/justify]. If you admit this, the ends are to be translated: *it would be difficult to excuse by this hypothesis* (or to render free from blame). Namely, ironically. And there are many traces of mockery in this dispute; which Ficino already saw.
**— 18. Περὶ δὲ τοῦ ἀκούειν κ. τ. λ.** For the sources of this Plotinian passage are to be held Plato's *Timaeus* p. 67. p. 92. *sq.* Bekk. Aristotle's second book *On the Soul* c. 8. p. 37 *sqq. cf.* [confer] Theophrastus *de Senss.* p. 19 *sqq.* Aristotle's *Problemm.* II. 6. p. 89 *sqq.* Sylburg and Alexander's *Probll.* p. 259. 268. Nor, as far as I know, have the other Physicists, as they are properly called today, compared Plotinus' decrees on vision, hearing, and the other senses with the discoveries or opinions of the more recent.
**p. 829, 2. ἀλλ’ εἰ μὲν ποιότης μόνον—ἀνάγκη, καὶ τὸ φῶς ζητεῖν, ἐν ᾧ ἔσται σώματι.]** Proclus on Plato's *Timaeus* p. 141: [Greek text describing all colors as offspring of light]. *Cf.* [Confer] supra p. 52. F. and p. 166. *sq.*

**p. 830, 12. Εἰ δὲ ἔστιν ἐνέργεια — ἐπεβάλετο.]** A passage to me indeed somewhat obscure, and perhaps not sound. Ficino could be seen to have read: *καὶ εἴχετο εἴσω* [and it was held within] for *ἐχεῖτο* (*profunderetur* [it was poured out]). No help in the *Codd.* [manuscripts]. Accordingly, we left the passage untouched.—Moreover, because Tiedemann in the book: *Spirit of Speculative Philosophy* III. p. 409, calls this the Aristotelian opinion: *that light is an act* (*energeia*), yet he adds it is not confirmed by the examinations of more recent Physicists: he did not yet know those things which have recently been explained by the sharp insight of ingenious explorers of nature and philosophers, about which it is not ours to expound *h. l.* [in this place].
**— 17. Ἐπεὶ καὶ εἰ πολλαπλασία ἡ ἀπόστασις ἦν, ἢ νῦν ἐστι πρὸς ἡμᾶς τοῦ ἡλίου, ἦν ἂν καὶ μέχρι ἐκεῖ φῶς,]** You might suspect: *ἡ τοῦ ἡλίου* [that of the sun]: but in such things one may often desire elegance in Plotinus. Also concerning variety here it should be briefly warned that these [words] of Plato in the *Phaedo* p. 61. e. where mention of the sun is also made: *ἀλλ’ ἐν τῷ μέχρι ἡλίου δυσμῶν χρόνῳ* [but in the time until the setting of the sun], where Heindorf p. 24: [says] *μέχρι* [until] for the common *μέχρις* had already been given by Fischer from the rule of Grammarians along with Aug. and Tub. Codd. (add Paris.).” *Cf.* [Confer] the same at *Gorg.* p. 137. and p. 180. And in the *Symposium* Bast and Bekker by the authority of the books p. 210. gave *μέχρι ἐνταῦθα* [until here]. Similarly Stallbaum in the *Philebus* p. 18. p. 39. from Stobaeus [gave] *μέχρι ἑνὸς* [until one] for *μέχρις*. And the same learned man at the *Phaedo* p. 183. although here and there all the *mss.* [manuscript] books of Plato offer *μέχρις*, nevertheless fights for *μέχρι* and *ἄχρι* in this writer even before a Vowel. Loers at the *Menexenus* p. 155. embraces an entirely different opinion. And Lobeck on the *Eclogues of Phrynichus* p. 14 *sq.* seems to me to have truly pronounced, even in Attic writers “which prerogative is due, must be left in ambiguity”—much less in more recent writers. Accordingly, although in this place and others Cod. Cizensis and Vatican, which give *μέχρις*, perhaps show the hand of Plotinus.

BOOK IV. ENNEAD FOUR. p. 803—806. 235

I have cited, likewise II. 3. 7. and IV. 3. 12. However, the source of all these and similar passages is found in these words of Plato’s *Symposium* p. 202 at the end and p. 203 (p. 48. 430. in Bekker's edition) concerning Love: <note>original: "ἐν μέσῳ δὲ ὂν ἀμφοτέρων συμπληροῖ, ὥστε τὸ πᾶν αὐτὸ αὑτῷ ξυνδεδέσθαι. Διὰ τούτου καὶ ἡ μαντικὴ πᾶσα χωρεῖ καὶ ἡ τῶν ἱερέων τέχνη τῶν τε περὶ τὰς θυσίας καὶ τὰς τελετὰς καὶ τὰς ἐπῳδὰς καὶ τὴν μαντείαν πᾶσαν καὶ γοητείαν."</note> "Being in the middle of both, he fills up the gap, so that the whole is bound together with itself. Through him proceeds the whole of the mantic art <note>The art of prophecy or divination.</note> and the art of priests concerning sacrifices, rituals, incantations, and all prophecy and sorcery." Then, the same Love is called a "terrible sorcerer, a mixer of potions, and a sophist." <note>original: "δεινὸς γόης καὶ φαρμακεὺς καὶ σοφιστής"</note> It would be a long task to recount how many interpreters and imitators these passages have found throughout Greece, and I have touched upon this elsewhere in part in *Symbolica* III. p. 65 and following. Among more recent authors, it suffices to name Cudworth in *Intellectual System* p. 174 and following in Mosheim's edition; Sydenham on the aforementioned passage of the *Symposium*; Moses Mendelssohn in *Philosophical Works* Vol. I. p. 148; Tennemann in *History of Philosophy* VI. p. 155; and Schelling in *Bruno* p. 188 and following; and Heusde in *First Principles of Platonic Philosophy* I. p. 120, who also explained the myth of the birth of Love in the cited passage of Plato.

p. 806, 9. **It is also natural for incantations [to work] by melody]** Villoison wants "and by melody," <note>original: "καὶ τῷ μέλει"</note> and Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino, the famous Renaissance translator of Plotinus.</note> expressed it thus. On the other hand, the next words "but the soul," <note>original: "ἀλλ’ ἡ ψυχὴ"</note> which Ficino likewise expressed, are shown in our remaining books, but the two Marcian manuscripts of Villoison do not have them.

— 13. **And such sorcery is not wondered at, although they love being charmed]** This word "charmed" <note>Greek: "κηλούμενοι" from "kelein"</note> is proper to the power of music, song, speech, and the like. Plato in the *Symposium* p. 215 (p. 482) says of Marsyas the flute-player: "he charmed men through instruments by the power from his mouth." <note>original: "ὁ μέν γε δι’ ὀργάνων ἐκήλει τοὺς ἀνθρώπους τῇ ἀπὸ τοῦ στόματος δυνάμει."</note> In the *Protagoras* p. 315 (p. 160 Bekker): "charming them with his voice like Orpheus, and they follow the voice as if enchanted," <note>original: "κηλῶν τε φωνῇ ὥσπερ Ὀρφεύς, οἱ δὲ κατὰ τὴν φωνὴν ἕπονται κεκηλημένοι"</note> where compare Heindorf p. 482. Compare also *Menexenus* p. 235. a. (p. 378 Bekker) and see Valckenaer on Euripides' *Hippolytus* line 303. Wyttenbach collected other Plutarchan examples on Plutarch p. 844, who likewise teaches that this word is used metaphorically for every method of soothing the mind through pleasure. It is also joined with "to sing" <note>original: "ᾄδειν"</note> and "to chant over" <note>original: "ἐπάδειν"</note> as Jacobsius teaches in *Additions to Observations on Athenaeus* p. 264. Lucian in *Herodotus* p. 833 (Wetstein edition): "singing his histories and charming those present, until even his books were called Muses." <note>original: "ᾄδων τὰς ἱστορίας καὶ κηλῶν τοὺς παρόντας, ἄχρι τοῦ καὶ Μούσας κληθῆναι τὰς βίβλους αὐτοῦ."</note> One might say Himerius imitated this in *Oration* XIV. 27. p. 658: "For the rest, the Hellanicuses and Durises are small to me, as is the poetry of the man from Halicarnassus (meaning Herodotus, of whom he had made mention in Oration VII. 11. p. 530: 'the Carian Muse, I mean that of Herodotus') and as many as had a zeal to write of the inhabited world in prose, compared to those *iunges* <note>Magic "jinxes" or spinning wheels used in love spells.</note> with which [Hermogenes] so thoroughly enchants his listeners." From this, "to charm" <note>original: "κηλεῖν"</note> also means *to transfix someone by a certain power of incantation*. See Lucian's *Images* 14. p. 473: "for you will stand there, I know well, as if enchanted," <note>original: "παρεστήξη γὰρ εὖ οἶδ’ ὅτι κεκηλημένοις"</note> which passage was expressed by imitating the Platonic *Symposium* p. 216 (p. 454 Bekker). Furthermore, compare Jacobs on Achilles Tatius p. 643 and following. Below, Plato's *Republic* II. p. 358 (p. 59 Bekker): "For Thrasymachus seems to me to have been charmed by you like a snake earlier than was necessary" <note>original: "ὥσπερ ὄφις κηληθῆναι"</note> (where see Ast’s *Commentary* p. 389 and following). Plutarch in *Cato the Younger* ch. 56. p. 86 (Coray's edition) concerning the Psylli <note>A North African tribe famous for snake-charming.</note>: "—chanting over the beasts themselves, they dull and charm them." <note>original: "αὐτὰ δὲ τὰ θηρία κατεπάδοντες ἀμβλύττουσι καὶ κηλοῦσιν."</note> Philostratus in *Life of Apollonius* concerning the Indians III. 8. p. 100: "having bewitched them into sleep" <note>original: "ὕπνον ἐγγοητεύσαντες"</note> (the Schellersh. Manuscript has "bewitched" <note>original: "γοητεύσαντες"</note>), namely the dragons. Dio Chrysostom joins these words in *Oration* XVI. p. 244. B. (457 Reiske): "for being charmed and bewitched, they remain with this (pleasure)." <note>original: "κηλούμενοι γὰρ καὶ γοητευόμενοι παρὰ ταύτῃ (τῇ ἡδονῇ) μένουσι"</note> This passage did not escape Baguet's diligence in his work on the same author's *Oration* VIII. p. 88 and following, where he treats learnedly of the word "to bewitch." <note>original: "γοητεύειν"</note> Clement of Alexandria in *The Instructor* II. 4. p. 192 (Potter's edition): "For truly these instruments (the pipe and the flute) must be sent away from a sober banquet, being more suitable for beasts than for men, and for the more irrational of men. For we have received word that deer are charmed by pipes, and are led into traps by hunters being hunted by melody." <note>original: "τὰς μὲν γὰρ ἐλάφους ταῖς σύριγξι κηλεῖσθαι παρειλήφαμεν, καὶ ἐπὶ τὰς ποδάγρας πρὸς τῶν κυνηγῶν θηρευομένας ἄγεσθαι τῷ μέλει."</note> I would believe that stories of this kind were in the minds of the scribes when one wrote in the Plotinian passage "a man [charms] snakes," and others "a snake [charms] a man," which latter, however, was corrected by a second hand in the Medicean manuscript A. We also, along with the good books and with Ficino, have embraced the reading of the Edition, which the following arguments prove to be uniquely true, and other stories confirm: In the work *On Marvelous Things Heard* attributed to Aristotle, ch. 162, a Thessalian sorceress sets out to enchant a snake with various tricks, but the beast "sings back" <note>original: "ἀντάδειν"</note> and the woman, feeling nothing, can scarcely keep from sleep; nor was it far from happening, had not her son standing by awakened his mother, that she would have slipped into a death-like sleep. Pliny in *Natural History* XXVIII. 2. p. 446 (Hardouin's edition): "not a few also (believe) *that snakes themselves sing back*, and this one [remedy]..."

— 13. *And as many things as bring harm to men* <note>original: Καὶ ὅσα λωβᾶται ἀνθρώποις</note>] Two Marcian manuscripts and others read "men" in the accusative case. <note>original: ἀνθρώπους</note> This discrepancy was noted above at p. 54. D.

— 15. *as if someone taking fire from fire—was transferred* <note>original: οἷον εἴ πῦρ τις ἐκ πυρὸς λαβὼν—μετηνέχθη</note>] I have left this passage untouched, as it is undoubtedly corrupted. Ficinus seems to have read "not having contrived" <note>original: οὐ μηχανησάμενος</note> or "not contriving" and then "something transferred." The Medici manuscript gives "to the one transferring." The Marcian manuscripts reject the words "not to come" after the words "that one does." From this, I think these things should be emended thus: "Just as if someone taking fire from fire has harmed another, either the one who contrived it (i.e., who first lit the fire) or that one who took (the second fire from the first) causes it to come, by the fact that he gave something, as if transferred from one to another; and the fire that has arrived also acts (namely, as an agent), if the one into whom the fire is transferred is not able to receive it."

p. 808, 7. *but it must also be granted that something happens with prayer, and without prayer, etc.* <note>original: ἀλλὰ καὶ μετ’ εὐχῆς γίγνεσθαί τι δοτέον, καὶ εὐχῆς ἄνευ κ. τ. λ.</note> Iamblichus, *On the Mysteries* V. 26, p. 141: "I say then, that the first kind of prayer is collective, leading to contact with and knowledge of the divine. The next is a bond of harmonious communion, calling forth the gifts sent down from the gods, which accomplish the whole work even before reason or thought." At this passage, Gale, in his notes (p. 280), added relevant material from other writers, mostly Platonists. I am surprised, however, that these words of Plotinus did not occur to him; they also remind one of the Socratic discussion in the *Second Alcibiades*; in which dialogue Boeckh seems to have found traces of Stoic reasoning (though not in the *First Alcibiades*, as I falsely wrote in the Preface to Proclus’s *Commentary on Plato’s Alcibiades*, p. XIII). In that *Second Alcibiades* (p. 143. A.), these lines of the poet, which are not dissimilar, occur:
*King Zeus, give to us what is good, whether we pray for it or not,*
*but keep from us what is dangerous, even if we pray for it.*
The *Greek Anthology* presents these slightly differently among the anonymous poems, number 466, p. 217 in Jacobs’s edition; consult him in *Observations*, Vol. XII, p. 137. Diodorus Siculus records very similar precepts of Pythagoras in the *Excerpts* from books VIII–X, number 39, in Angelo Mai’s Vatican collection of ancient writers, Vol. II, p. 32. I have placed more on this matter in *Symbolica*, Vol. I, p. 164 and following, second edition. But, what I did not place there, I will certainly touch upon here in a word. Namely, lest anyone doubt that Plato, in his genuine dialogues, teaches as soundly about prayers and vows as those mentioned above, let him read the *Cratylus* p. 400. D., the *Theaetetus* p. 112. C., the *Philebus* p. 12. C., and *Laws* VII, p. 801. A–C; where Plato complains about common poets who compose prayers unworthy of the gods for use in public religion. — 6. **"For what has one suffered that he holds toward another?"** <note>original: Τί γὰρ παθών τις πρὸς ἄλλο ἔχει;</note>] Someone might perhaps wonder why I have left the reading of the Edition untouched, even though five manuscripts of the best quality offer <term>mathon</term> <note>having learned</note>, and Jacobs, a most ingenious man, pronounced thus on this passage in his *Additional Observations on Athenaeus* p. 327: "The man most learned in Greek, Villoison, fell into the same error in *Anecdota* Vol. II p. 235, who in Plotinus's *Diatribe* corrects 'what has one **suffered**...' <note>pathon</note> for 'what has one **learned**...' <note>mathon</note> which is entirely genuine." So he says. But Villoison was ignorant then that these chapters were already read in print; he was ignorant that in the edition from four manuscript books <term>pathon</term> <note>suffered</note> was read; he was ignorant that the Zeitz and Darmstadt books likewise retain <term>pathon</term>; he was ignorant of Ficino, who, although he found "what having learned" in two Medici manuscripts, nevertheless put back: "**what indeed having suffered.**" —And he was right here. For in the whole passage it is discussed what happens from the outside, so that men and spirits are drawn by the charms of prayers, vows, and incantations; and the words **to be moved** and **to suffer** are repeated many times. And immediately after those words "what having suffered—does he have?", these follow: "or being drawn, not by the arts of magi." What more do you want? The argument of the whole passage, where the difference between the suffering soul and the impassive mind is touched upon, requires what Villoison rightly guessed: **what having suffered** <note>ti pathon</note>. On the contrary, the same Jacobs judged most truly in the same place concerning the passage of Philostratus in the *Life of Apollonius* I. 28. p. 36, where even the Schellersheim manuscript shows <term>mathon</term> <note>learned</note>. For which reason my friend Bekker, in *Specimens of Philostratus* p. 90, rightly accommodated himself to Jacobs' authority. This second formula, rare in Plato's writings, was excellently confirmed (as is his custom) from passages of the Comic poets by the most illustrious Heusde in *Critical Specimens on Plato* p. 57.—The nearby **arts of magi** we touched upon above at p. 434. the book might assign; for the word *synapsasēs* <note>original: "συναψάσης" — having joined/connected</note>, which suggested the same thing, differs too much from the common reading.
**page 812, line 7. For as many things as entice men, having become sweet to their desires]** Xenophon, *Memorabilia* II. 1. 4: "For of these (animals) some are enticed by the belly—nevertheless, being led to the bait by the desire to eat, they are captured," where these words are used in their literal sense. The figurative use is very widespread. Plato, *Euthydemus* page 272. D. page 395. following Bekker: "Perhaps we shall lead your sons to them as a bait," where the Bodleian Manuscript and two others inspected by Bekker read: "we shall have for them." And there was a time when I thought this the better reading. For beasts "are led to the bait," as in the passage from Xenophon, or men "lead beasts with a green branch" or "lead them around by a green branch" (see Ruhnken on Timaeus page 136 and Euripides in the fragment of *Erechtheus* I. verse 18. page 442. following Beck: "having a bait for the earth [or the land]"). The same in *Andromache* verse 262. (264. in A. Matthiae’s edition): "Such a bait I have for you." But nevertheless, in the passage from Plato, Socrates is striving to persuade Crito to frequent the Sophists with him: "and you come along too," and to bring his sons with him also, and to bring them to those sophists as if they were a lure. Therefore, that reading holds up well: "perhaps we shall lead your sons to them as a bait," in almost the same way that Xenophon says in the *Hellenica* V. 4. 4: "promising that he would lead the most beautiful women to them," concerning the bringing of prostitutes to men. I return to the verb; concerning its figurative use, the commentators have gathered quite a few things on this passage from the **Epistle of James I. 14: "being drawn away and enticed by his own desire."** (See especially Wetstein on that passage, and compare Hemsterhuis on Lucian’s *Dialogues of the Dead* page 359. Wyttenbach on Plutarch’s *On the Delay of Divine Vengeance* page 52.—Add the passage from Josephus, *The Jewish War* III. 5. 6. page 228. Havercamp: "as if a spontaneous beauty were enticing them into a lack of foresight." Irmisch on Herodian I. 12. 10. Philo the Jew, *Allegorical Interpretation* II. page 220. following Pfeiffer, compares the mind to a man, the senses to a woman, and pleasure to a serpent: "for just as the movement of the serpent is complex and varied, so also is pleasure.—because (pleasure) winds itself around all the irrational parts of the soul." I have set these things forth for the sake of Theodoret, who says in *Epistle 145* page 1257. Schulze: "The Egyptian woman also did this. For having embraced the slavery of shameful desire, and having offered slavish flattery to the temperate man (Joseph), then, having failed to entice him or entangle him in the snares of luxury, she called the lover of temperance a robber of another's bed." Read *peripeirasasa* <note>original: "περιπειράσασα" — having entangled/pierced through</note>. For *peripeiran* is properly said of serpents (Wesseling on Diodorus I. page 291. Heyne on Apollodorus page 140. second edition). Then it is transferred to other things as well (Plutarch, *Agesilaus* XXXI. where see the most learned Coray page 355.) Moreover, *pagais* <note>original: "πάγαις" — snares/traps</note> is properly used by bird-catchers and prostitutes, called "snares of life" figuratively by the Comic poets. The same error in Lucian’s booklet *How to Write History*, chapter 29, page 39, was corrected by critics long ago. The same Theodoret, or his interpolator, in the *Religious History* or *Philotheus* page 1114. Schulze, says of the Arians: "For there were a certain few who thought the opposite, but did not dare to strip bare their own impiety, but covered it with certain baits, not recognizable to all, but very clear to the precise initiates of the truth."

**page 813, line 3. For it seems perhaps reasonable, not to lead oneself out]** <note>A reference to the philosophical debate on suicide (leading oneself out of life).</note> Concerning this opinion and formula, we have explained above at I. 9. 1. page 85.

**— 13. he says that none of these things is good, (so almost all our copies for "is said") of which those things say]** Thus most, except the Medicean A and the Vatican, which read "as those things say," which seems true. But *that other* is the one who was just mentioned, deceived by the appearance of the Good.

**page 814, line 13. in the daemonic place]** Compare above IV. 3. 18. page 385. The source of this doctrine is in Plato’s *Timaeus* page 90, in the *Statesman* page 171, and in the *Republic*. Compare Proclus on the *Alcibiades*, preface, chapter 23, page 74 of our edition: "For so I think Socrates in the *Republic* also called those 'daemons' who had lived well and had moved to a better lot and a holier place." Where I have cited more things concerning the "lots" (seats) of daemons in the notes. Concerning the power of daemons over places, Plato himself disputes in another place, *Laws* V. page 750. page 411. Bekker. Add Damascius on the *Parmenides* page 63. Kopp edition.

**— 21. just as if by certain hauls of nature's cords being moved]** A passage composed in imitation of the words and thoughts of Plato. For he says in *Laws* I. page 644: "Let us consider each of us living beings a divine toy, whether constructed as their plaything or for some serious purpose. For this we do not know. But this we do know, that these passions in us, like tendons or certain cords (so Boeckh on Plato’s *Minos* page 119 and Bekker in his edition for "cords") being within, pull us and against each other—"

— 7. *And in the one* <note>original: "Ἐν δὲ τῷ ἑνὶ"</note> and so forth. p. 817, 7. THE THIRD ON THE DIFFICULTIES OF THE SOUL, OR ON VISION.] <note>original: "ΠΕΡΙ ΨΥΧΗΣ ΑΠΟΡΙΩΝ ΤΡΙΤΟΝ, Η ΠΕΡΙ ΟΨΕΩΣ"</note> This is the twenty-ninth book (See Porphyry, *Life of Plotinus* chapter 25. p. 144. Fabricius) and was therefore written after the preceding one and is thus a kind of continuation of it. After these, Plotinus wrote that short disputation which constitutes the eighth book of the second Ennead, and is inscribed *On Sight*. See what we annotated on the title of that book at p. 189 above. You may also compare what we placed above at p. 312. B. As far as our book is especially concerned, this question of vision was early debated by the Greek philosophers, the Pythagoreans, Empedocles, Democritus, and others. Plato himself touched upon the decrees of Empedocles regarding sight in the *Meno* p. 76. C. indicates both the difficulty and indeed the necessity [of this study] in his book *Against Julian*, Volume V, page 340, Basel edition: <note>original: "ἀλλ’ ὦ γενναιότατε σοφιστῶν..."</note> "But, O most noble of sophists, such an argument will not even allow us to know that we possess a soul, or sensation, or mind, or reasoning, or memory, since the essence of each of these is difficult to know; and what wonder is there in that?" and so forth. Alexander of Aphrodisias in his book *On Sense and Sensibles*, folio 97 and following. The same author in Aristotle’s *On the Soul*, Book II, chapter 12. John Philoponus in Aristotle’s *On the Generation of Animals*, Book V, chapter 1, folio 105. Stobaeus briefly records the decrees of Plato and Aristotle concerning sight in his *Eclogues*, I. 55, pages 1108–1110, Heeren edition. Macrobius, in *Saturnalia* VII. 14, explains the opinion of Democritus, Epicurus, and their followers, judging them primarily according to the rule of Platonic doctrine. Alcinous also touched upon the passage in the *Timaeus* in *On the Doctrine of Plato*, chapter 18, page 497 and following; likewise Nemesius in *On the Nature of Man*, in the chapter "On Sight," page 180, Matthaei edition. Furthermore, *G. A. Heigl* disputes concerning light, sight, and the remaining senses according to the mind of Plotinus in the booklet entitled: *Platonic Physics* (*Die Plotonische Physik*), Landshut 1815, page 128 and following; but in such a way that many points seem to lack the light of interpretation themselves.

**p. 817, 10. of the so-called transparent body]** <note>original: "τοῦ λεγομένου διαφανοῦς σώματος"</note> Aristotle explains what the <term>transparent</term> <note>original: "τὸ διαφανὲς" (diaphanes)</note> is according to the decrees of his own system in *On Sense and Sensibles*, chapter 3, page 7, Sylburg edition. Compare *On the Soul*, chapter 7, page 36, where the Stagirite <note>Aristotle, born in Stagira</note> even speaks against Empedocles, who was of the opinion: <note>original: "εἰ γένοιτο κενὸν τὸ μεταξὺ..."</note> "if the medium between were to become a vacuum, one could see accurately even if an ant were in the heavens." We touched upon these matters above at II. 9. 2.

**p. 818, 19. since not even the reed between the electric ray and the hand [feels] what the hand suffers;]** <note>original: "ἐπεὶ οὐδ’ ὁ κάλαμος ὁ μεταξὺ τῆς νάρκης καὶ τῆς χειρὸς, ὃ πάσχει ἡ χείρ·"</note> He took this example from Plato in the *Meno*, page 80 A: "And you seem to me altogether, if I may make a jest, to be most like in form and other respects to that flat sea-ray <note>The torpedo fish or electric ray, known for numbing its prey</note>. For it makes anyone who approaches and touches it become numb. And you seem to me now to have done something of the sort to me, making me numb." Concerning this fish, see Aristotle, *History of Animals*, IX. 36. (25, and there the annotations of Schneider, Vol. II, p. 170); I. A. Fabricius on Sextus Empiricus, *Outlines of Pyrrhonism*, I. 14. 93, page 26; and Jo. Beckmann on Antigonus of Carystus, chapter 54, page 97, who have praised many testimonies of ancient and more recent writers. I shall add two passages from philosophers. Alexander, *Problems*, Preface, page 249, Sylburg: "No one is ignorant of the sea-ray, how it numbs the body through the fishing line <note>original: "μηρίνθου" (merinthos)</note>, and a red mullet when caught reacts against the numbness." Chalcidius in Plato’s *Timaeus*, page 331, Meursius: "Furthermore, they think the mind perceives just as the spirit has struck it, which transmits that which it suffers from the thickening of visible forms to the depths of the mind. For when extended and, as it were, opened up, it announces that the things seen are white. But when confused and more foul, it signifies black and dark things: and its suffering is similar to those who are numbed by the contact of the sea fish, since that poison creeps through the flaxen thread and the reed and through the hands, and penetrates the innermost sense." And perhaps Chalcidius, who employed this simile similarly to Plotinus in the passage on sight, had our philosopher before his eyes.

**p. 819, 14. even if now—that which lies before the eyes]** <note>original: "εἰ καὶ νῦν—τὸ τῶν ὀμμάτων πρόσθεν κείμενον"</note> I have left this passage untouched as it is perhaps not sound. The version of Ficinus shows how he understood it. I am unwilling, therefore, to decide whether he translated it correctly, or if the end should rather be translated: *that which is placed before the eyes*. The next words: "and those who pour out their sights" <note>original: "καὶ οἱ ἐκχέοντες δὲ τὰς ὄψεις"</note> recall the elegance of Platonic speech. For they are modeled after that in the *Theaetetus*, page 181 A: "the flowing ones" <note>original: "τοὺς ῥέοντας"</note>, those who contend that all things are in flux, as opposed to "the partisans of the whole" <note>original: "οἱ τοῦ ὅλου στασιῶται"</note> "who say the universe is immobile" and "those who move the all" <note>original: "τοὺς τὸ πᾶν κινοῦντας"</note>, "who think the universe is moved." See Heindorf on that passage, page 419, and, to add an example drawn from the same matter, Plutarch, *Table Talk*, I. 8. 2, page 529, Wyttenbach: "others yielded to the opinion of those who join the rays together" <note>original: "ἕτεροι δὲ τοῖς συμβάλλουσι τὰς αὐγὰς προσείχον"</note>, that is, those who adopted the Platonic <term>confluence of light</term> <note>original: "συναύγειαν" (sunaueia)</note>. An example of the same brevity, differing only in that it has a verb with a pronoun instead of a participle, is offered by a passage of Plotinus below, V. 8. 12, page 85 B: "wherefore also they (seem) not rightly who destroy (the sensible world) while the intelligible remains, and thus generate..." and so forth, that is, those who say the sensible world is fleeting <note>original: "caducum"</note>—and thus believe it to have been generated.

**p. 820, 3. But those who blame the resistance]** <note>original: "Οἱ δὲ τὴν ἔνστασιν αἰτιώμενοι"</note> Concerning other meanings of the word <term>resistance</term> <note>original: "ἔνστασις" (enstasis)</note> I have spoken in the preface to Proclus’ *On the Alcibiades*, page 191: in this place, a completely different meaning obtains, to be sought from natural things and from...

BOOK V. ENNEAD FOUR. p. 817—821. 241

<note>The author is discussing the term *enstasis* (resistance/standing-in).</note> ...used by physicists and physicians. Regarding this, consult Foesius’ *Hippocratic Economy* p. 130 under the word *enistemi* <note>original: ἐνίστημι; to set in or resist</note>, Bernard in *Letters to J. J. Reiske* p. 296, the same in *Thomas Magister* p. 313, and Wyttenbach on Plutarch p. 485. Another passage of the same Plutarch—or the one who is cited under Plutarch’s name—is especially relevant here, from *On the Opinions of the Philosophers* IV. 13. p. 633. Wyttenbach: "Others [believe we see] according to the entry of certain rays which, after the **resistance** <note>original: ἔνστασιν; enstasin</note> encountered in the underlying object, return back to the sight." I am surprised that Wyttenbach noted nothing regarding this passage in his *Various Readings*. However, Tib. Hemsterhuis, in *Thomas Magister* p. 314, prefers "secretion" <note>original: ἔκκρισιν; ekkrisin</note> instead of "entry" <note>original: εἴσκρισιν; eiskrisin</note>. Beck, on the other hand, following Galen in *History of Philosophy*, prefers "outpouring" <note>original: ἔκχυσιν; ekchusin</note>. See his *Various Readings and Emendations* p. 240. And this reasoning is supported by our Plotinus’ phrase "those who pour out." The meaning of the Plutarch passage is this: Others indeed (think we see) according to (by means of) a certain effusion of rays, which after the resistance (which they had struck) in the Object, return again to the eye. These words illustrate Plotinus' text excellently. Iamblichus in *Protrepticus* p. 147. Arcerius p. 350. Kiessling: "For the natural organization of hook-clawed animals is fashioned to seize most quickly and easily because of the **resistance** <note>original: ἔνστασιν; enstasin</note> of the claws being curved (on account of *resistance*, since the claws are hooked), in the same way that **shrimps** <note>original: κράγγαι; krangai</note> are naturally disposed to pull in very quickly, but to let go with difficulty, unless one perhaps bends them back by turning them over." (Arcerius edition: *kragai*. The Memm. and Ciz. Manuscripts: *kreagai*. Paris Royal Manuscript: *kreagrai* <note>flesh-hooks</note>, approved by Hemsterhuis in the place cited, whose note Kiessling does not mention. But a learned hand in my copy wrote in the margin: “Read *krangai* <note>shrimps/prawns</note>.” And this is uniquely true.) Regarding *krangai*, which pertain to marine crabs, see Aristotle’s *History of Animals* IV. 2. and Schneider’s *Annotations* on it p. 191 following.

p. 820, 4. **Those who champion the images**] These are Democritus and Epicurus, who "thought we see through the insertions of images (according to the entries of *eidola* <note>original: εἰδώλων εἰσκρίσεις</note>)," as is read in Plutarch in the place cited.

p. 821, 6. **by the counter-resistance—the counter-resistance of the air**] The word <term>antiperistasis<gloss>counter-resistance or compression from all sides</gloss></term> signifies a checking or a compression poured around from every side; in the vernacular it might be called *the surrounding counter-pressure*. See Budé and Estienne in the *Thesaurus of the Greek Language* p. 4610, Valpy edition, and compare Schneider’s *Index to the Works of Theophrastus* p. 315. Plutarch, *On the Opinions of the Philosophers* IV. 1. p. 621. Wyttenbach: "and the **counter-resistance** of the seasons, so that when it is summer for us who live under the warm tropic, it is then winter for those living opposite under the winter tropic." Here it refers to the *opposition* of the seasons of the year, or the *different ratio* of seasons in different Zones, as is rightly explained in the Index. Closer to the similarity of our passage is this from the same Pseudo-Plutarch, ibid. III. 15. p. 611. Wyttenbach, in the passage on earthquakes: "Aristotle [says it is] because of the **counter-resistance** of the cold from all sides, standing around it from below and above. For the heat hastens to move higher, being indeed light; because of this, when the dry vapor is left behind, it is disturbed by the wedging and the counter-rollings." These should now be compared with the fragment of Joannes Laurentius Lydus on earthquakes in the book *On Omens* chapter 53. p. 186—188. Hase. Plutarch in *Platonic Questions* p. 1004. D. p. 88. Wyttenbach: "the **counter-resistance** of motion," where Xylander sought to express the force of the word by translating it: *the circum-resistance of motion*.

— 15. **if the forms are not even present as if in a flow.**] He touches upon Epicurus. Who says thus in the *Letter to Herodotus* in Diogenes Laertius X. 48: "For a **flowing** <note>original: ῥεῦσις; rheusis</note> from the surface of bodies occurs continuously." He offers similar things in the *Herculaneum Papyri* p. 69; from which the editor Rosini not inaptly filled the lacuna <note>gap in the manuscript</note> in another place thus on p. 4: "that the **flow** <note>original: ῥοῦν; rhoun</note> passes through continuously." (Compare our note on Cicero’s *On the Nature of the Gods* I. 39. p. 178, where the typesetters erred in the passage of Diogenes.) Hence in Plotinus someone might perhaps have attempted: "they pass through" <note>original: περῶσιν</note> instead of "they are present" <note>original: πάρεισιν</note>, yet it is not necessary. Gellius V. 16: “Epicurus, however, thinks that certain images of the bodies themselves always flow off from all bodies, and these enter into the eyes, and thus the sense of seeing occurs.” Macrobius, *Saturnalia* VII. 14: “Therefore Epicurus judges that certain images emanate from all bodies in a perpetual flow; nor does even the slightest delay intervene, but that the skins of bodies, clinging together in a hollow figure, are carried forward of their own accord, the receptacles for which are in our eyes: and therefore the senses return specifically to the seat assigned to them by nature.” Ign. Rossi illustrated Epicurus’ opinion from Diogenes in *Commentaries on Laertius* p. 262.—But yet perhaps in this place Plotinus is not so much [discussing] Epicurus’ opinion...

Certainly our author <note>Plotinus</note> used the word "forms" <note>Greek: *eide*</note> at this place.
p. 823, 6. <note>original: "ἐκ τῶν φρυκτωριῶν—καὶ ἐκ τῶν πύργων τῶν ταῖς ναυσὶ σημαινόντων"</note> "from the beacon-fires—and from the towers signaling to ships"] The editions and manuscript books have "beacon-fires." I added the article "the" by the authority of most Codices. Herodian IV. 15. p. 814 and following, edited by Irmisch, concerning the funeral pyres of Roman emperors: "one might liken the shape of the structure to beacon-towers <note>Greek: *phryktoriois*</note> which, situated at harbors, guide ships at night by means of fire toward safe passages. Pseudo-Aristotle, in *On the Universe* VI. 10. p. 224 of Kapp’s edition: "The world was such, and especially with the beacon-fires <note>Greek: *phryktoriōn*</note> signaling to one another in succession from the ends of the empire as far as Susa and Ecbatana, that the King knew on the same day everything happening in Asia." I have cited this passage because it teaches that this kind of night-signal was also customary on the mainland: (Compare Kapp on that passage:) from which it is understood why Plotinus adds: "and from the towers signaling to ships," which refers to lighthouses. Compare also Tzetzes on Lycophron 1096, at the words: "ship-devouring beacons." Add Huschke’s *Critical Analects* p. 240, Boissonade on Philostratus’ *Heroica* p. 553, and Blomfield on Aeschylus’ *Agamemnon* 32: "this beacon-fire having thrown triple-six for me" in the Glossary p. 160.
— 18. <note>original: "ἐπὶ τοῖς νώτοις τοῦ οὐρανοῦ"</note> "upon the backs of heaven"] A poetic expression, which however later prose writers employ. See Jacobs on the *Greek Anthology* IX. p. 248 and on Philostratus’ *Images* p. 326. Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation* 6. p. 59: "somewhere above around the backs of heaven." Synesius, *On Providence* p. 89. C.: "the spring is fastened from the backs of heaven." Compare also Philo the Jew Vol. I. p. 44 Pfeiffer and Ast on Plato’s *Phaedrus* p. 301 and at the end of the *Republic* in the Additions p. 657.
p. 824, 5. <note>original: "τὸ συναφὲς τῇ ὄψει μόριον"</note> "the part joined to the sight."] I did not follow the second Medicean manuscript, which gives "continuous," even though that adjective is rare and in the newest edition of Stephanus’ *Thesaurus* is confirmed by only one example from Josephus. See *The Jewish War* III. 5. 7. p. 228 Havercamp, concerning the Roman battle line: "thus their ranks were joined," where moreover the manuscript books vary wonderfully. But Plotinus’ usage sufficiently protects that reading of both the edition and most codices. See above II. 9. 16, IV. 4. 45, IV. 5. 1, IV. 5. 3. These places should therefore be recorded in the Lexicons.
— 6. <note>original: "ὅσον καὶ ἡ κόρη τὸ καθ’ αὑτὸ μόριον τοῦ ὁρατοῦ δέχοιτο ἄν"</note> "as much as the pupil might receive the part of the visible object corresponding to itself."] Olympiodorus in the preface to *Alcibiades* p. 223: "It must be known that it is called a pupil <note>Greek: *korē*, which also means 'maiden'</note> either because of its proximity to the crystalline part, being pure." The things I cited at that place, I do not repeat here. Isidore, *Etymologies* XI. 1. "Pupil: —It is called *pupula* because it is a pure and unstained girl <note>Latin: *puella*</note>." I have cited these for the sake of Philo, who in *Allegorical Interpretation* II. p. 78 of Mangey (p. 118 Pfeiffer), explaining the passage in Numbers XII. 1 and following, says thus of Moses: "to whom God himself joined the Ethiopian woman, the unchangeable and deep-saturated <note>Greek: *katakorē*</note> mind.—For this is his greatest praise, that he took the Ethiopian woman, the unswerving and fiery and approved nature. For just as in the eye the seeing part is black, so the seeing part of the soul is called an Ethiopian woman." In which place, after Mangey confessed that he did not perceive things clearer than noonday, he nevertheless makes an attempt at a conjecture, wishing to thrust upon us "fiery" <note>Greek: *katapyron*</note> instead of "deep-saturated" <note>Greek: *katakorē*</note>. But truly, he who knows Philo’s license for playing with words will not doubt that he wished to allude with that *katakorē* to the *korē* <note>pupil</note>, which he then describes with these words: "for as in the eye the seeing part is black," in which words there is also the reason why he drags the "Ethiopian woman" here, i.e., a black woman. Furthermore, it is not true that at this place "mind" and "nature" are synonyms. I would rather believe Philo wrote "shining" <note>Greek: *phausin*</note>: concerning which Alexandrian word see what I have placed in the *Antitheses of Nathanael against Plotinus* ch. 6 (p. 441 Heidelberg edition, which place I would entirely wish to be compared with Philo’s). Thus these will correspond best: "the unchangeable and pure <note>Greek: *katakorē*</note> mind." With the word "fiery" Philo again refers to the "Ethiopian woman," i.e., scorched as it were and black in face.—I return to Plotinus. For his opinion compare p. 452 at the end and p. 453 at the beginning, and generally apply Heliodorus (or Damianus, for the name is in doubt; see Schneider on *Physical Eclogues* p. 206 and Boissonade...

### BOOK V. ENNEAD FOUR. pages 823—830. 243

(referring to Lucas Holstenius's *Letters* page 248.) Optics § 5. and following.
page 826, line 6. **Since even seeing in the night—it is difficult to straighten out by this hypothesis.** <note>original: "Ἐπεὶ καὶ τὸ τῆς νυκτὸς ὁρᾷν—χαλεπὸν ταύτῃ τῇ ὑποθέσει ἀπευθῦναι."</note>] To the places collected to illustrate the use of this word <note>the Greek verb *apeuthunein*, meaning to straighten or correct</note> add Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *On Composition* XI. 80. page 134. Schaefer's edition, and Photius's *Library*. Code 165. page 108. b. below Bekker's: and compare P. Wesseling on Sophocles' *Ajax* verse 72. It is used more frequently by Plutarch in his *Moralia*; who says in *On the Education of Children* page 2. D. page 6. Wyttenbach edition: **it is impossible to straighten the curved staffs of actors.** <note>original: "τὰς γε μὴν καμπύλας τῶν ὑποκριτῶν βακτηρίας ἀπευθύνειν ἀμήχανον."</note> If you apply this to our passage, the force of the word should be taken as "to make straight what is crooked," or, to direct and disentangle things that are intertwined and hindered. See the Scholiast <note>ancient commentator</note> on Sophocles' *Oedipus Rex* verse 104. Then the meaning of our passage would be: **Since that—seeing by night—is difficult to explain by this hypothesis (by this reasoning).** But I wonder if that other meaning, which the same Scholiast provides, is more relevant: **I straighten (*apeuthuno*), and I act away from a reckoning (*apo euthunes*), that is, I render blameless.** If you admit this, the end should be translated: *it would be difficult to excuse according to this hypothesis* (or to render it free from blame). This is surely ironic. And there are several traces of mockery in this discussion, as Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino, the Renaissance translator of Plotinus</note> already saw.
— 18. **Concerning hearing, etc.** <note>original: "Περὶ δὲ τοῦ ἀκούειν κ. τ. λ."</note> For the sources of this Plotinian passage, one must look to Plato's *Timaeus* page 67. page 92. and following in Bekker. Aristotle's second book *On the Soul* chapter 8. page 37. and following; compare Theophrastus *On the Senses* page 19. and following; Aristotle's *Problems* II. 6. page 89. and following in Sylburg's edition, and Alexander's *Problems* page 259. 268. Sylburg. Galen in *History of Philosophy* chapter XXVI, Plutarch in *Opinions of the Philosophers* IV. 16. page 901. page 636. and following in Wyttenbach, Stobaeus in *Physical Excerpts* I. 56. and 57. page 1110. 1112, Heeren, and Nemesius *On the Nature of Man* chapter 10. page 199. and following in Matthaei's edition, have reduced the decrees of these and other philosophers concerning Hearing into a compendium. Compare also: *The theory of Aristotle on the nature and origin of sound and the human voice* explained by Kreyssig. Leipzig 1793. and Schneider's *Observations on the Physical Excerpts* edited by him page 168. and following. However, he cared no more for Plotinus's views here than he did in the passage on vision. Nor have the rest of the physicists, as they are properly called today, compared Plotinus's decrees on sight, hearing, and the other senses with the discoveries or opinions of more recent thinkers, as far as I know.
page 829, 2. **but if it is quality only—it is necessary also to seek the light, in which body it will be.** <note>original: "ἀλλ’ εἰ μὲν ποιότης μόνον—ἀνάγκη, καὶ τὸ φῶς ζητεῖν, ἐν ᾧ ἔσται σώματι."</note>] Proclus in his commentary on Plato's *Timaeus* page 141: **for all colors are the offspring of light.** <note>original: "πάντα γὰρ τὰ χρώματα ἔγγονά (read ἔκγονά) ἐστι φωτός."</note> Compare above page 52. F. and page 166. and following.
— 16. **but just as life—is an activity of the soul.** <note>original: "ἀλλ’ ὥσπερ ζωὴ—ψυχῆς ἐστιν ἐνέργεια."</note>] Compare below page 458. B. and the note there.
page 830, 12. **But if it is an activity — he applied himself.** <note>original: "Εἰ δὲ ἔστιν ἐνέργεια — ἐπεβάλετο."</note>] A passage that is to me indeed somewhat obscure, and perhaps not sound <note>corrupted in the manuscript</note>. Ficino might seem to have read: **and it was held within** <note>original: "καὶ εἴχετο εἴσω"</note> instead of **it was poured out** <note>original: "ἐχεῖτο"</note> (*profunderetur*). There is no help in the Codices <note>manuscripts</note>. Therefore, we have left the passage untouched.—Furthermore, as for what Tiedemann says in the book: *Spirit of Speculative Philosophy* III. page 409, calling this an Aristotelian opinion: **that light is an act** (*energeia*), yet adding that it is not confirmed by the examinations of more recent Physicists: he did not yet know those things which have recently been explained by the sharpness of ingenious investigators of nature and philosophers, which it is not our place to explain in this location.
— 17. **Since even if the distance were many times what it is now from us to the sun, there would be light even as far as there,** <note>original: "Ἐπεὶ καὶ εἰ πολλαπλασία ἡ ἀπόστασις ἦν, ἢ νῦν ἐστι πρὸς ἡμᾶς τοῦ ἡλίου, ἦν ἂν καὶ μέχρι ἐκεῖ φῶς,"</note>] You might suspect: **that of the sun** <note>original: "ἡ τοῦ ἡλίου"</note>: but in such matters, one often misses elegance in Plotinus. Also, concerning the variety here, these words of Plato in the *Phaedo* page 61. e. where mention of the sun is also made, remind us to advise briefly: **but in the time until the setting of the sun,** <note>original: "ἀλλ’ ἐν τῷ μέχρι ἡλίου δυσμῶν χρόνῳ"</note> where Heindorf page 24: had already given *mechri* <note>until</note> instead of the common *mechris* according to the rule of the Grammarians with the Augustan and Tubingen (add Parisian) manuscripts, as Fischer had already done. Compare the same on the *Gorgias* page 137. and page 180. And in the *Symposium* Bast and Bekker, on the authority of the books, gave *mechri entautha* <note>until here</note> on page 210. Similarly Stallbaum in the *Philebus* page 18. page 39. from Stobaeus gives *mechri henos* <note>until one</note> instead of *mechris*. And the same learned man on the *Phaedo* page 183. although all the manuscript books of Plato here and there offer *mechris*, nevertheless fights for *mechri* and *achri* in this writer even before a vowel. Loers on the *Menexenus* page 155 embraces a clearly different opinion. And Lobeck on the *Excerpts of Phrynichus* page 14 and following seems to me to have pronounced truly: "which of the two should be given prerogative in Attic writers must be left in doubt"—let alone in more recent writers. Therefore, although in this place and others the Cizensis and Vatican manuscripts, which give *mechris*, perhaps [represent] the hand of Plotinus...

<summary>This page provides a philological commentary on Plotinus's theories of light, vision, and hearing, comparing his terminology with Plato, Aristotle, and later classical commentators. It specifically debates the correct Greek forms of "until" (mechri vs. mechris) and the interpretation of light as an "activity" (energeia).</summary>
