**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

...although they may excel, we were nevertheless unwilling to depart from the reading of the [standard] edition and the majority of manuscripts.

**p. 831, 12. *Ἔστι δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ ὀφθαλμῶν ἰδεῖν ζώων λαμπόντων τοῖς ὄμμασι κ. τ. λ.* [“It is also possible to see in the eyes of animals that shine in the dark, etc.”]** To this point belong what the ancients record here and there, such as Diogenes Apolloniates in Theophrastus, *De Sensibus* p. 29 (Steph. ed.); Aristotle, *De Generatione Animalium* V. 1, on which see Joannes Philoponus fol. 105; and cf. Sturz’s *Empedocles* p. 418–420. Alexander in *Problemata* 20. (78.); Plutarch in *Symposiaka* I. 8. 4. p. 626. D. p. 533 (Wyttenbach ed.). I shall add an illustrative passage from Sextus Empiricus in *Pyrrhonian Hypotyposes* I. 14. 45. p. 13. sq. (Fabricius ed.): “Since, therefore, some animals naturally possess a brilliance in their eyes, and send forth from them a light both refined and mobile, so as even to see at night, we should rightly suppose that external objects do not fall upon them in the same way as they do upon us.” But he records that the same thing has happened even to some men (ibid., Sect. 84), and Fabricius has collected examples of others, such as the Scaligers, etc., at that place, whom you should consult; likewise Schneider in *Animadversiones in Eclogas Physicas* p. 201, and Priestley’s *Optics* I. p. 150 (Klügel ed.) cited there, and the notes of the latter on p. 154.

**— 14. *ταῖς ἀνοιδάνσεσιν* [“by the swellings”]** i.e., where the eyes swell or rise up. The opposite follows: *ἐν ταῖς συστολαῖς* [“in the contractions”], where they wither or subside. The word *ἀνοίδανσις* [swelling] ought to be added to the Lexicons. The verb is frequent enough. Alciphron, *Epistolae* I. 1: “and the sea shuddered as it grew black, and the foam of the water blossomed out, the waves being broken upon one another (*ἐπ’ ἀλλήλων*) everywhere in the sea; for some were dashed against the rocks, while others, swelling within (*ἀνοιδούντα*), were shattered.” Plutarch, *De Placitis Philosophorum* III. 17. p. 615. (Wyttenbach): “the Atlantic sea swells (*ἀνοιδεῖν*).” It is even used of angry persons. Philostratus, *Vita Apollonii* VII. 33. p. 313 (Olear.): “the king, having swelled up (*ἀνοιδήσας*) because of what he heard, said, ‘You have caught a sycophant for me then.’” Concerning this force of the word, see the interpreters on Herodotus p. 261 and p. 529 (Wesseling), and add Jacobs’ notes on Philostratus’ *Imagines* p. 592.

**p. 833, 8. *ἢ εἰ τὸ συμπαθὲς — τοῦδε τοῦ ζώου*** Following that distinction which I have adopted, this meaning comes forth: “Or, if the sympathetic [principle], which belongs to a single animal, consists of sensual things, sensible things, and senses, in this way [this world] would not (perceive that body) unless this body were an external part of this very animal.”

**p. 834, 3. *δέδεικται* [“it has been shown”]** Wyttenbach and others use our passage to illustrate this formula in the notes on Plato’s *Phaedo* p. 160. sq. Cf. below p. 464. A. and the more numerous points we have placed at I. 6. 1. p. 50. B.

**— 9. *μὴ τῶν ἐν αὑτῷ, τῶν δὲ ὁμοίων τοῖς ἐν αὑτῷ, ἡ μὲν ζῶον ἀντιλήψεται*** Thus I have given it from the better manuscripts before the words *ἡ μὲν ζῶον*. After the words *μὴ τῶν ἐν αὑτῷ*, the word *μόνον* [only] must be understood. Regarding this omission, see Davies on Cicero, *De Natura Deorum* II. 64. p. 479–481 in our edition and that of Moser, and what the editors praise in L. Bos, *De Ellipsibus* p. 307–310 (Schaefer ed.). It is quite often omitted when *ἀλλὰ καὶ* [but also] follows, where *δὲ* is in the other member. Lucilius, *Epigram* XII. 4. (p. 319): “you have become not unknown to dogs, but to the city.” See Jacobs’ *Commentary on the Anthology* Vol. IX. p. 319 regarding this passage.

### LIB. VI. [BOOK VI]

**p. 836, 7. *ΠΕΡΙ ΑΙΣΘΗΣΕΩΣ ΚΑΙ ΜΝΗΜΗΣ* [“On Sensation and Memory”]** This little book is among those which Plotinus composed almost in old age, being, if you look to the chronological order, the forty-first. See Porphyry, *De Vita Plotini* c. XXV. p. 144 (Fabricius ed.). It treats the same subject that Plato touched upon in the *Timaeus* p. 45 and p. 65. sqq., as well as in the *Meno, Phaedo, Philebus, Laws*, and other dialogues: (Cf. what we cited above for p. 392. D.) This doctrine was later refined by Aristotle in the treatise *On Sensation and Sensible Objects*, likewise *On Memory and Recollection*, and *On the Soul* book II. chap. 6 sqq.; no less so by Theophrastus in the opuscule *On Sensation and Sensible Objects*. Galen exhibits the opinions of the remaining philosophers on sensation and memory in *Historia Philosophiæ* c. XXIV; Plutarch in *De Placitis Philosophorum* IV. 8–11. p. 626–629 (Wyttenbach ed.) (cf. the same Plutarch in *On the Cleverness of Animals* p. 960. sqq. p. 896. sqq. Wytt.); Diogenes Laertius VII. 51. sqq., X. 31. sqq., and here and there. Among more recent Greek and Latin writers, others have touched upon this place, particularly Nemesius in *De Natura Hominis* chap. 13, “on the faculty of memory,” and in the preceding chapters which I mentioned above...

[[vocabulary: compatiens (sympathetic/suffering with), ἀνοίδανσις (swelling), sensuale (sensual), ἀναμνήσεως (of recollection)]]

### PAGE 252 ###

**...VI–X. as well as Boethius in *De Consolatione Philosophiæ* book V.**

**p. 836, 9. *ΤΑΣ αἰσθήσεις οὐ τυπώσεις οὐδ’ ἐνσφραγίσεις λέγοντες κ. τ. λ.* [“Saying that sensations are neither imprints nor seal-impressions, etc.”]** For the words and the meaning, compare what our philosopher argues above p. 305. B., 391. G., and below p. 461. F. In these and subsequent passages, he refutes Aristotle. The latter, in the treatise *On Memory and Recollection* c. 1. p. 29 (Sylb. ed.), says: “For it is clear that one must conceive the thing produced by sensation in the soul and in that part of the body which possesses it as a sort of painting—an affection (*pathos*) whose habit we call memory; for the motion that occurs leaves an imprint (*ensemainetai*), like a sort of stamp of the sensation, just as those who make impressions with signet-rings. Wherefore memory does not occur in those who are in great motion due to passion or age, as if the motion and the seal were falling into flowing water; while in others, due to the cooling (or 'decaying' in the margin of the Basel ed.), like old buildings, and due to the hardness of the receiving part, the affection does not take hold.” From this, someone might seek support for the Vatican reading in Plotinus: *κατοχὰς παθημάτων* [retentions of affections]. I, with Ficinus, retain the vulgate. Porphyry, in Stobaeus *Eclogae* I. 52. p. 830 (Heer. ed.), in reporting and judging the opinion of Aristo, writes thus: “For sensation is not apprehensive of substance, but of form and shape; that it is a man or a horse is the apprehension of another faculty.” (Heeren thus completed this passage from the books. It is not necessary to add more by conjecture.) “Therefore the movement of apprehension is different; for that of sensation is like an imprint, and is drawn outward toward form, while the other stands apart from the imprint.” Having this opportunity, I wipe away a blemish from a fragment of Hermes in the same Stobaeus p. 1086: “that nature may keep and hold fast—to a type (*typou*) laid down from the beginning.” It had been incorrectly written, as in many places of Plotinus, as *topou* [place]. The Stoics attempted to explain the method of sensing in almost the same way as Aristotle. Plutarch in *De Placitis Philosophorum* IV. 11. p. 630 (Wytt.): “The Stoics say: When a man is born, he has the commanding part of the soul like a sheet of paper (*chartes*) ready for writing (C. D. Beck excellently reads from the Moscow Codex *χαρτίον ἔνεργον* 'as a little chart, active for writing'... see his note in *Variae Lectiones* p. 237), upon which he inscribes each one of his concepts. The first method of inscription is that which occurs through the senses. For those sensing something, like a white object, have a memory of it once it has gone.” Boethius also touches upon this Stoic opinion in *De Consolatione Philosophiæ* book V, in the Meter, p. 304 sq.: “The Porch [Stoics] once brought forth / Sages too obscure. / Who believe that senses and images / Are imprinted on minds from external bodies, / As it is the custom to fix / Pressed letters with a swift stylus / Upon the surface of a page / Which has no marks. / But if the mind, flourishing in its own / Motions, explains nothing, / But merely lies passive, / Subject to the marks of bodies; / And like a mirror returns / The empty images of things, / Whence then does this notion flourish in the soul / Seeing all things?” Proclus in *Alcibiades* pr. p. 281 uses the same simile: “and (souls) are not unwritten tablets receiving imprints from without, but they have always been written upon, and the writer is within them, though not all souls can know what has been written.” Plato in *Protagoras* p. 326. D: “But quite simply, just as writing-masters, for those children not yet clever at writing, trace lines with a stylus and then give them the tablet (*grammateion*) and compel them to write following the guidance of the lines.” Where Heindorf ought not to have retained *grammation* (for *grammateion* is also in the Bodleian Codex and was restored by Bekker) any more than he should doubt the meaning of *grammē* as a letter. Maximus Tyrius VIII. 2. p. 132 (Reiske ed.) expressed Plato’s passage thus: “as writing-masters also devise for children, tracing for them faint signs, upon which they apply their handiwork and are accustomed by memory toward the art.” The interpreters of Maximus were ignorant of this imitation.

**p. 837, 3. *Εἰ δ’ ἐπὶ τῆς ἐναργεστάτης αἰσθήσεως θεωροῖμεν* [“If we should consider the most distinct sense”]** Aristotle *De Anima* III. 3. p. 56 (Sylb. ed.): “Since sight is sensation par excellence, it has even taken its name from light (*phaos*), because without light it is not possible to see.”

**— 9. *οὐδὲ τῷ σφραγῖδα λαμβανούσης — βλεπούσης*** A singular use of the Participle instead of the Infinitive (*τῷ λαμβάνειν*), which can be explained only according to the order of construction by Attraction. Cf. Matthiae *G.G.* §. 555. sqq., where however, among many conveniently placed examples, you will not find a twin passage, as far as I know. On the meaning, Plotinus says similarly below p. 461. F: “or as seals impressed into wax from signet-rings.” Soon, with the Margin of Medicean A., ...

[[vocabulary: tabula rasa, ἐνσφραγίσεις (seal-impressions), αἴσθησις (sensation), χάρτης (paper/chart)]]

### PAGE 253 ###

**...or rather with Ficinus, for *οὕτως* we have placed *οὕτως*.** But perhaps in this place one should also read: *τῷ δὲ δὴ διάστημα προστιθεῖσα τῷ ὁράματι* before *πρὸ τὸ δὲ δὴ κ. τ. λ.*

**p. 837, 18. *οὐκ ἔσται βλέπειν αὐτὰ ἃ ὁρῶμεν, ἰνδάλματα δὲ κ. τ. λ.* [“It will not be the case that we look upon the things we see, but rather images, etc.”]** Cf. the passage of Porphyry from the dispute over the tenets of Aristo, which I placed at the beginning of this chapter p. 452. A. As for what follows in the Plotinian passage, the same Porphyry follows in the footsteps of his master in these words in Stobaeus *Eclogae Physicae* I. 51. p. 780 (Heeren): “And in every way that which uses sensation contemplates by applying itself to things outside, not being unified with those things it contemplates, but merely receiving a type of them from its application to them. When therefore the eye sees the thing seen, it is impossible for it to come into identity with the thing seen; for it would not see unless it were at a distance. Likewise, that which touches, if it came into identity, would be destroyed. From which it is clear that sensation, and that which uses sensation, is always carried toward the outside, if it is to apprehend the sensible object.”

**p. 839, 6. *τὰ δ’, ὅσα αἰσθήσεις αὐτῶν καὶ κρίσεις, τῶν παθῶν εἰσι γνώσεις* [“The others, as many as are sensations and judgments of them, are knowledges of the affections”]** The Stoics designate these with almost the same words. Cicero, *De Natura Deorum* II. 56: “But the senses are the interpreters and messengers of things—for the eyes, like scouts, occupy the highest place—and because a great judgment of food and drink belongs to them (the nostrils), etc.” Cf. also Cicero, *De Legibus* I. 9. init. and see both our notes and those of Davies at that place. Consult also Baguet’s book on Chrysippus §. XXIII. p. 62. I add no more here, since these things have already been explained by us in the preceding annotations to these Enneads.

**p. 840, 4. *ὑπὸ μὲν τῶν εὖ παθοῦσα—ὑπὸ δὲ τῶν (τῇ addidi ex libris nostris plerisque) ὁμοιότητι ἀπατωμένη, καὶ κατιοῦσα ὥσπερ θελγομένη* [“being well-affected by some—but by others (I added 'by' from most of our books) deceived by similarity, and descending as if charmed”]** We have said more about this verb in Proclus on Plato’s *Alcibiades* pr. p. 40, on the verse of the oracle: “charming the souls (*θέλγοντες*), they always lead them away from the rituals,” as well as at p. 257. Cf. also above p. 435. A. and the notes there. Furthermore, Porphyry in *De Gradibus* §. 16. p. 224 comprehends the sum of this chapter within a small compass of words. Cf. also Alcinous’ little book on the doctrine of Plato c. XXV. p. 507. sq.

**— 16. *Διὸ καὶ τὰ παιδία μνημονεύειν λέγεται μᾶλλον* [“Wherefore children are also said to remember more”]** On the contrary, Aristotle in *On Memory* chap. I. p. 326 (Erasmus) p. 29 (Sylb.) says thus: “wherefore both the very young and the old are forgetful. For they are in flux, the former because of growth, the latter because of decay, etc.” S. Maximus in *Sermonum Excerpta* LII. Vol. II. p. 654 (Combefis ed.) attributes this opinion either to Plato or Plotinus himself, saying: “Plato said that the very young and the old are forgetful”; where in the margin it is read *Plotinou* Bal. (i.e., Ballesdens Codex) *Platonos*. In the margin of the Latin version is \*of Plotinus\*. So they say. What is read from Plotinus above p. 392. D. can in some way be compared with the cited Aristotelian opinion, and indeed they agree more with the part read on the following page (455. C.). Tiedemann, in the German book *On the Causes of Contemplative Philosophy* III. p. 354. sq., thinks that many of these decrees are owed to Plotinus as their inventor, and were not brought forward by anyone before him. Compare, however, this chapter with *Ennead* IV. book 3. c. 25 and 26–30, in which places not a few things approach more closely the tenets of Descartes and Leibniz. Soon: *οὐκ ἂν ἐποίησε τὸ πλῆθος ἤτοι μνήμας* [“it would not have made a multitude of memories”]: one might conjecture *μνήμονας* [mindful ones]. But it is not necessary.

**p. 841, 6. *δηλοῦσι δυνάμεσιν ψυχῆς τὸ γινόμενον ὑπάρχον* [“they show that what occurs exists by the powers of the soul”]** Our books indicate a hesitation in this place, and lexicographers offer no example of the word *δυνάμωσις* [strengthening/empowerment]. For we should dismiss Schneider, who held the verb *δυνάμοω* itself in doubt. (See our Note in Proclus, *Institutio Theologica* §. LXX. p. 110.) But Ficinus also translated *δυνάμωσιν*. Therefore, we have left it untouched.

**p. 842, 15. *Γίγνονται δὲ ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ οὐχ οἱ αὐτοὶ μνήμονες καὶ ἀγχίνοι πολλάκις.* [“Usually, those with good memories and those who are quick-witted are not the same.”]** Aristotle, *On Memory and Recollection* c. I. p. 27 (Sylb.): “For the same people are not good at remembering (*mnemonikoi*) and good at recollecting (*anamnestikoi*), but for the most part the slow are better at remembering, while the quick and the quick-learners are better at recollecting.” Whether in what follows: “and yet it did not prevent anyone possessing an excellence of soul from reading the things laid down,” Plotinus designated those whom we today say have “fixed ideas,” I prefer to ask rather than to define. No less, whether he took the next part: “that he who has flowed in this way possesses an inability to be affected” from Aristotle’s words in *On Memory* I. p. 29: “wherefore for those in great motion no memory occurs, just as if into flowing water...”

[[vocabulary: ἰνδάλματα (images/apparitions), δυνάμωσις (strengthening), ἀγχίνοι (quick-witted), ἀναμνηστικοί (reollective)]]

### PAGE 254 ###

**...the motion and the seal [were falling].** These things remind one of the Greek proverb: *καθ’ ὕδατος γράφειν* [“to write upon water”], which was said against those who attempted impossible things, as in Lucian, *Tyrannus* c. 22 and its Scholiast Vol. I. p. 643 (Wetst. ed.). Porphyry in Augustine, *De Civitate Dei* IX. 23. init.: “Perhaps you could more easily write with letters impressed in water.”

**p. 843, 3. *ἢ ὡς πρόχειροι—ἐπιβολαὶ—ἀπατῶσαι.*** Ficinus seems to have embraced the reading of Medicean B: *πρόχειρον*. The meaning of the passage seems to be this: “and otherwise than as sudden (and thus rash, or suddenly and thus rashly) impressions from sensible things arise in them (men), which deceive by similarities.”

### LIB. VII. [BOOK VII]

**p. 844, 7. *ΠΕΡΙ ΑΘΑΝΑΣΙΑΣ ΨΥΧΗΣ.* [“On the Immortality of the Soul”]** Written after the first work by Plotinus, and thus, chronological order considered, this is the second book, according to Porphyry in *De Vita Plotini* chap. IV; cf. c. XXV. And in the former place it is: “concerning the immortality of the soul.” The title of this book is much more divergent in Eusebius, *Praeparatio Evangelica* XV. 22. p. 824 (Cologne): “Against the Stoics, that the soul cannot be corporeal. From Plotinus' *On the Soul*.” But this seems rather to be owed to Eusebius or the scribes of the Eusebian books, although perhaps it may be inferred from this that the title of this book was once simpler: *On the Soul*. The same Eusebius adds at the end of the excerpt p. 835: “these things are from the works of Plotinus against the Stoic opinion on the soul, they claiming that it is corporeal.” But Plotinus refutes in this book not only the opinions of the Stoics, but also those of other philosophers. And Porphyry himself, in the cited book chap. 4, reveals that the twenty-one books which the philosopher of Lycopolis had first composed were variously titled.

As for the sources and the subject matter of this book, there are several passages in Plato which Plotinus might have looked to; such as that brilliant narration in the tenth book of the *Republic* p. 614 sqq. p. 502 sqq. (Bekker) concerning Er the Armenian; from which it is clearly established that there existed in antiquity some doctrine of the Oriental peoples, by which it was handed down allegorically (*allegorice*) regarding the nature of man and the immortality of the human soul, and its fortune after death according to how it conducted itself in life. No less relevant is the primary passage in the *Phaedrus* p. 245. C. sq., to which Hermias’ commentary on that dialogue p. 114. sq. should be applied. Nevertheless, the *Phaedo* p. 78. sq. p. 46. sqq. (Bekker) must be considered the primary source of this book, on which Wyttenbach says on p. 197: “Setting out from this argument of Plato (of the composite body and the simple soul), Plotinus pursued the reasons for immortality more broadly and subtly: as Olympiodorus taught at this place, Cod. I. p. 63 and 185, Cod. III. p. 38 and 40, which would be long to relate. The principal seat of the Plotinian argumentation is *Ennead* IV. book 7, but parts of it occur scattered through other books.” The same author in *Institutiones Metaphysicae* p. 201: “Of the later philosophers,” he says, “*Plotinus* added the most growth, by repeating the reasons from the communion of human souls and the divine nature: then especially by demonstrating more accurately the simplicity of the soul from that argument by which it is effected that the power and action of thinking cannot fall into corporeal nature, *Ennead* IV. book 7: where his argumentation against Aristotle’s *entelecheia* [entelechy], preserved in Eusebius’ *Praeparatio Evangelica* XV. 10, is valid.” (See it above p. 364. b. c.) Cf. also Alcinous on the doctrine of Plato c. XXV. Altogether, the Aristotelian work *On the Soul* should be compared with this Plotinian dispute, especially book III. c. 4. Here too belongs a remarkable passage of Joannes Philoponus in the books against Proclus. He indeed reports thus in VII. 4.: “for the souls, while still in the body, appear, whenever they release themselves from the relation and affection toward it, to be separate and making their intellectual activities independent of every body. For what part, says Aristotle, or how the mind will hold together, is difficult even to imagine. Therefore it is absolutely necessary that the substance of the soul, from which such activity proceeds, be separate and independent of every body, just as it seemed to Plato and all the best of the philosophers; for from this Plotinus also reasoned its immortality, showing from its separate activities that its substance must also be separate and for this reason immortal.” Plutarch enumerates the opinions of Plato and other philosophers on this matter in *De Placitis Philosophorum* IV. 7. Porphyry in *De Gradibus* §. 18. sqq. provides the Plotinian view. The fact that Eusebius in *P.E.* XV. 22...

[[vocabulary: ἀθανασίας (of immortality), ἐντελέχειαν (entelechy), Lycopolites (of Lycopolis), simplicitate (simplicity)]]

### PAGE 255 ###

**...exhibited this argumentation of Plotinus, reminds us of the Fathers of the Church.** Among them the most ancient, who established the trichotomy (*trichotomiam*) of human nature (cf. below p. 467. B. c. 14.), especially the Alexandrians, the supporters of Plato, taught thus: that the body (*τὸ σῶμα*) is by its nature mortal; that the carnal soul (*ψυχὴν σαρκικὴν*) can die and be dissolved (*λύεσθαι*), yet this does not necessarily happen, but it can also become a participant in immortality. However, the spiritual soul, the mind (*ψυχὴν πνευματικὴν*), is by its very nature immortal. (See Tatian, *Against the Greeks* p. 150. sq.; Theophilus, *To Autolycus* II. p. 101; Justin’s *Dialogue with Trypho* p. 222; and cf. Herm. Olshausen, *Commentary on the Opinions of the Most Ancient Greek Church Fathers on the Immortality of Souls*, Königsberg 1827.) Some things pertaining to this were recently extracted from manuscripts by Angelo Mai and exhibited in the *Vatican Collection of Ancient Writers* Vol. I. part. III. p. 76. sqq.; Gregory of Nyssa also in *On the Soul* p. 91 (Paris ed.) says thus: “Commonly, then, against all those who say the soul is a body, what was said by Ammonius, the teacher of Plotinus, and Numenius the Pythagorean, will suffice.” Among more recent authors, not a few have touched upon our book. It suffices to have named Hugo Grotius, *De Veritate Religionis Christianae* I. 23; Cudworth in *Intellectual System* C. V. Sect. III. §. XLII–XLVI. p. 1110–1114; Mosheim; Tiedemann in *Geist der Spekulat. Philos.* III. p. 337. sqq., who, although generally more prone to disparaging Plotinus, nevertheless grants him this: that he says he was the primary asserter of the incorporeal soul, and pronounces that most of the things which were subsequently disputed by philosophers for this cause are already found prepared in these books of Plotinus. Thomas Taylor translated this book into English in *Select Works of Plotinus* p. 221. sqq. Franciscus Vigerus, however, frequently changed the Eusebian text from the edition of Plotinus, sometimes rashly.

**p. 844, 13. *εἴτ’ οὖν ὡς ὄργανον ἡμῖν, εἴθ’ ἕτερον τρόπον προσηρτημένον. Ἀλλ’ οὖν διῃρήσθω γε ταύτῃ, καὶ ἑκατέρου τὴν φύσιν τε καὶ οὐσίαν καταθεατέον*** Thus we have established the place partly from Eusebius, partly from our books: “whether therefore it is joined to us as an instrument or in another way: but nonetheless it must be so distinguished, and the nature and essence of each must be inspected.” Many have said much about the body as an instrument of the soul or a vehicle; see only Plato, *Alcibiades* pr. p. 130. a. p. 360 (Bekker) and Olympiodorus on it p. 4. sq., and cf. Wyttenbach on Plutarch, *De S.N.V.* p. 97. sq. I will add a passage from Athanasius of Alexandria from *Oration Against the Gentiles* Vol. I. p. 35 (Cologne ed.): “what then would this be again, but a rational and immortal soul? For it is not from without but from within the body itself, as a musician sounds the better notes upon the lyre.” Then he explains these things more broadly, so that he seems to have read Plotinus' book on sensation and memory, and continues: “—for these things prove nothing else than a rational soul governing the body. For neither is the body naturally suited to drive itself, but is led and carried by another, just as a horse does not harness itself, but is driven by the one who controls it, etc.” For in what follows he also had before his eyes the classic passage of Plato in the *Phaedrus*. Basil the Great imitated the same in *Constitutiones Vitae Monasticae* c. II. Vol. II. p. 670. sq. (Paris ed. 1618).

**p. 845, 9. *καὶ ταύτῃ φθορὰν ἂν ὑπομένοι*** In some books, the last syllable of the preceding word suppressed the little word *ἂν*. The meaning is: *And thus they also suffer destruction*: *ταύτῃ* i.e., in this way. See Hesychius on the word. Cf. Plato, *Symposium* p. 208. E.; *Lexicon Xenophonteum* III. p. 368. f.; and Blomfield on Aeschylus, *Prometheus* 197 in the Glossary.

**— 11. *Τὸ δὲ κυριώτατον καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ ἄνθρωπος εἴη ἂν, ἢ κατὰ τὸ εἶδος, ὡς πρὸς ὕλην τὸ σῶμα,*** With the help of Eusebius and some of our codices, I have freed Plotinus’ speech from an inept addition. Vigerus also saw this, except that he introduced a less convenient punctuation. — Soon at the words: *ἑκατέρως δὲ ἡ ψυχὴ αὐτὸς* keep in mind these things from Eustathius on the *Iliad* a. v. 4. concerning Homeric usage p. 19. p. 17 (Leipzig ed. inf.): “for it should be known that the word *autos* [self] sometimes refers only to the body, as was said before, sometimes only to the soul, as when he says in the *Odyssey* (X. 601) concerning Hercules: ‘but he himself (*autos*) among the immortal gods delights in fair-ankled Hebe’ (compare Plotinus above p. 7. C.), and sometimes to the combination or composite man.” On this primary tenet of the Platonists, consult Segaar on Clement of Alexandria, *Quis Dives Salvetur* p. 290. sqq. and our note on Olympiodorus in *Alcib. pr.* p. 171, where...

[[vocabulary: trichotomiam (trichotomy), σαρκικὴν (carnal), πνευματικὴν (spiritual), ὄργανον (instrument)]]

### PAGE 256 ###

**...I have placed a twin passage from Basil the Great Vol. II. p. 18. C.**

**p. 845, 14. *ἢ σῶμα μὲν ὃν πάντως ἀναλυτὸν*** Thus I have written with Monacensis B and Medicean A, although many books and Eusebius himself have *ἀναλυτέον* [must be dissolved]. The [printed] edition has *ἀναλύον* corruptly. Seager on Stephanus' *Thesaurus* (London ed.) p. 5867. D. praises *ἀναλύτος* from one passage of Origen against Celsus IV. p. 169. It should be *ἀναλυτὸς*, as it is correctly read there, and as reason requires. (See Athenaeus VIII. p. 338. b. c. p. 246. sq. Schweigh.) Our passage should therefore be added to the Lexicons.

**p. 846, 10. *καὶ οἷς γε δοκεῖ εἶναι καὶ στοιχεῖα—ἐλέχθησαν εἶναι.*** We have adopted the punctuation of Vigerus in Eusebius p. 78. extr., who explains thus: “And if to some, besides these, it is pleasing that there be certain other elements, those they do not call souls, but bodies, nor do they wish them to have life from themselves.” Whether he touches upon Aristotle with these words, who, besides those four beginnings or elements, established a certain fifth essence of the body, more divine and prior to the others (*De Caelo* I. 2. p. 4 Sylb.), I prefer to ask rather than to decide.

**— 12. *Εἰ δὲ ἕκαστον ζωὴν ἔχει κ. τ. λ.* [“But if each one has life, etc.”]** See Cudworth, *Syst. Intell.* p. 1110. Tiedemann in *Geist der spekulativen Philosophie* III. p. 309, calling these disputed points of Plotinus no less new than sharp, contends that they provide the use of a foundation for the whole of what they call *Spiritualism*.

**— 14. *Καὶ δὴ καὶ οὐχ ὁπωσουν κραθέντα—γίγνεσθαι*** Taylor expressed these things, as he usually does, according to the mind of Ficinus, adding a little note: “The words *ἢ νοῦν, ἢ ψυχὴν*, are omitted in the original; but from the version of Ficinus it appears that they ought to be inserted.” But that excellent man, as often happened, was deceived here because he did not know that Ficinus, when he wished to consult clarity, would interpose his own words and even opinions among those of Plotinus. Nor does Eusebius or any Codex of Plotinus acknowledge those words at this place.

**p. 847, 1. *Εἰ δέ τις μὴ οὕτως, ἀλλ’ ἀτόμους κ. τ. λ.* [“But if someone, not in this way, but [asserts] atoms, etc.”]** I suspect *τῇ ὁμοπαθείᾳ* [by sympathy], which a second hand placed in Vindobonensis A. Moreover, I have preferred the reading of the Plotinian edition, confirmed by our books, to the Eusebian one. Soon Vigerus suspects: *ἐκ δὲ ἀμερῶν οὐδὲ σῶμα οὐδὲ μέγεθ’ α. γ.* But neither Eusebius nor our books support this, some of which offer *οὐ μεγ.* Neither is pleasing. [See] supra p. 390: “memory must not be placed around God nor around being and mind,” where this Ellipsis was discussed. — Plotinus touches in this place on the opinions of Democritus and Epicurus concerning the nature of the soul, regarding which see Aristotle, *De Anima* I. 2; Plutarch, *De Placitis Philosophorum* IV. 3; Stobaeus, *Eclogae* I. 52. p. 796. Heer.; Diogenes Laertius IX. 44; Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I. 9. The same ibid. I. 11: “For let us omit Democritus, a great man indeed, but one making the mind out of light and round corpuscles in a certain fortuitous course: for there is nothing among those people which a crowd of atoms does not produce.” Gregory of Nyssa, *On the Soul and Resurrection* p. 184. sq. (Paris ed. 1638): “Where then will the soul be after this? If someone should say it is in the elements, he will necessarily agree with these things [the elements]; for no mixture of the heterogeneous with the alien could occur, and if these things were so, some varied thing mixed toward opposite qualities would altogether appear. But that which is varied is not simple, but is seen altogether in composition; and everything composite is necessarily dissoluble (*διαλυτὸν*) (cf. above on *ἀναλυτὸν* on this very page A.); and dissolution is the destruction of that which has been held together. But that which is destroyed is not immortal.” Then: “and the teacher gently sighing over what was said, says: perhaps these and such things the Stoics and Epicureans brought forward when they once stood against the Apostle in Athens (Acts XVII. 18); for I hear that Epicurus especially is carried by these assumptions, to whom a certain chance and automatic nature of things was imagined, as no providence runs through the matters; and for this reason, as a consequence, he thought human life was like a bubble (*πομφόλυγος δίκην*) (cf. Scholion at this place and apply Wyttenbach on Plutarch, *De S.N.V.* Oxford ed. p. 424); he thought the spirit was placed around our body as long as the spirit is held by that which contains it; but with the collapse of the mass, that which was shut in (*ἐναπειλημένον*) is extinguished along with it.”

**— 7. (*ὕλη γὰρ, ἄποιον*) [“for matter is without quality”]** Plato in *Timaeus* p. 50. p. 61. Bekker. Cf. Wyttenbach on Plutarch VI. 2. p. 661. sq.; Porphyry, *De Gradibus* §. XXI. and see notes on Proclus in *Alcib. pr.* p. 318 and above for p. 315. G. Soon with Eusebius and...

**...nearly all our books, I gave *ἐπιφέρειν τὴν ζωὴν* [to bring life] instead of *ἔχειν τὴν ζωήν* [to have life].**

**p. 847, 10. *Εἰ δὲ πάθημα τῆς ὕλης, ἀλλ’ οὐκ οὐσίαν φήσουσιν εἶναι* [“But if they should say it is an affection of matter, and not a substance”]** He touches upon the opinions of Aristoxenus and Dicaearchus. Regarding the former, we saw above at p. 307. E. At this place, I will in passing correct Gregory of Nyssa in *On the Soul* p. 95 (Paris ed. 1638): “but since even Deinarchus (read Dicaearchus) defined the soul as a harmony.” The same error must be washed away twice at the same place p. 90. Plotinus examines this opinion of the Soul as a harmony accurately in Eusebius *P.E.* XV. 22. p. 834. sq. Regarding both, see Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I. 10. On Dicaearchus in the same place: “that the mind is nothing at all, and this name is entirely empty, and animals and living things are so called in vain; neither does a mind or soul exist in man, nor in a beast; and that all that power by which we either act or feel is equally fused in all living bodies, nor is it separable from the body; since it is nothing: nor is there anything except a single and simple body, so figured that it flourishes and feels by the tempering of nature.” Cf. c. 22 (where also regarding Aristoxenus). Add on Dicaearchus: Sextus Empiricus, *Against the Mathematicians* VII. 349. and *Pyrrhonian Hypotyposes* II. 31. and there Fabricius p. 74.; Plutarch, *De Placitis Philosophorum* IV. 2.; and Atticus in Eusebius, *P.E.* XV. 9. p. 810. A. B. — Soon the words: “there must therefore be something that provides life (*χορηγὸν τῆς ζωῆς*), etc.” remind one of this passage in the *Constitutiones Monasticae* of Basil the Great c. 2. p. 676 (Paris 1618): “For I think the power of the soul is twofold, though being one and the same; one indeed being the vital [power] of the body, and the other, the contemplative of beings, which we indeed call the rational. But the soul provides the vital power naturally through its mixture, and not by choice, since it is mixed with the body. For just as it is not possible for the sun, having shone, not to illuminate that upon which it has brought its rays, so it is impossible for the soul not to make alive the body in which it may come to be.” If you compare these with the earlier words of Plotinus p. 448. D. E., you might suspect that Basil wrote these things fresh from a reading of Plotinus.

**p. 848, 7. *διδοὺς αὐτῷ (τῷ σώματι scil.) ψυχῆς τάξιν μέχρι τῶν ὀνομάτων ἀέρι καὶ πνεύματι* [“giving to it (the body) the rank of soul even in the names ‘air’ and ‘spirit’”]** Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I. 9: “But some call the mind *anima* [soul/air], as our people generally do: the name declares it. (As our people generally declare by the name). For we say both ‘to act the soul’ [breathe] and ‘to breathe out the soul,’ and ‘animated’ [spirited], and ‘well-animated,’ and ‘from the opinion of the mind’: but the word *animus* itself is named from *anima*.” And Plotinus himself could have heard such things while he was living at Rome. — Furthermore, perhaps Julian the Emperor respected this dispute of Plotinus, or certainly a similar one in these Enneads, where making mention of Plotinus he touches upon “life flowed out and torn apart” in *Oration* VII. p. 222 (Spanheim ed.).

**— 17. *ἔννουν τὸ πνεῦμα καὶ πῦρ νοερὸν τιθέμενοι,* [“positing that the spirit is intelligent and a conscious fire”]** It is established that air was called the soul by Anaximenes, fire by Heraclitus, and later by the Stoics. Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I. 9 and there Davies; *De Natura Deorum* III. 14 and there the interpreters, where at p. 544 we touched upon this passage of Plotinus. Diogenes Laertius II. 3. VIII. 51. sq. IX. 1. cf. also Wyttenbach’s *Annotations on Plato’s Phaedo* p. 254. Add Baguet on Chrysippus p. 78. sq. p. 103. 182. 307. sqq.

**p. 849, 5. *τί τὸ πολυθρύλλητον αὐτοῖς πως ἔχον,* [“what is that much-talked-of thing that 'is somehow' for them”]** It was necessarily written thus for *πῶς ἔχον* [how it is]. With these words he seems to touch upon that "nameless" (*ἀκατονόμαστον*) fourth thing which the Epicureans used in describing the Soul (Plutarch, *De Placitis Philosophorum* IV. 3. p. 623. Wytt.) or that *τρόπον τινὰ* [in a certain way] which the Stoic Chrysippus uses in the same matter in Plutarch, *On the Contradictions of the Stoics* p. 1053. C. p. 292. Wytt. — For what follows: “an active nature” (*φύσιν δραστήριον*) apply our Philosopher’s words below p. 592. extr.: “if this, it has neither a whole nor qualities. If this, they are incorporeal and active.”

**— 12. *καὶ ψυχὴν, καὶ θεὸν, καὶ ὄνομα τὰ πάντα,* [“both soul, and God, and a name for all things”]** Thus I have written with Eusebius and his interpreter Vigerus. Concerning these formulas, *ὄνομα* [a name], *ὄνομα μόνον* [a name only], *ὄνομα ἄλλως* [otherwise a name], we have spoken at page 373. E. Soon with most books I placed *πάλιν αὖ* [again]. Concerning which see above for p. 411. extr.

**p. 850, 9. *καὶ δὴ καὶ χρόαν.* [“and indeed even color”]** Namely, insofar as the vehicle of the soul takes on colors. Regarding which matter Wyttenbach explained in Plutarch, *De S.N.V.* p. 111. p. 442 (Oxford ed.).

**p. 851, 11. *τὸ μέν τι ἀποῤῥεύσεται αὐτοῦ—πῶς οὖν ἡμῖν αἱ μνῆμαι;* [“a part of it will flow away—how then do we have memories?”]** The verb *ἀποῤῥεῖν* [to flow away] is frequently used of memory with the addition: “from the memory.” See Wyttenbach on Plutarch, *Apophthegmata Regum* p. 1124. We saw the same verb, but used differently of memory, above p. 455. E. The argument he adds next, drawn from the constancy of memory, is connected with the Platonic doctrine...

**...of recollection (*ἀναμνήσεως*), on which see Wyttenbach’s citations in the Annotations on the *Phaedo* p. 184.** Add Alcinous on the *Doctrine of Plato* c. 25. p. 507: “if indeed learning is recollection, the soul would be immortal,” which he explains more fully in what follows. Soon, for *φύσις δὲ σώματος μεριζομένη εἰς πλείω* (Eusebius has *μεριζομένου*), I gave from most books *μεριζόμενον*: “but the nature of the body is something that is distributed into several parts.” With the same and with Eusebius, I arranged it thus: *ἕκαστον μὴ τὸ αὐτὸ εἶναι τῶν μερῶν τῷ ὅλῳ* [“each of the parts is not the same as the whole”] instead of the Edition's reading. Then for *εἰ οὖν τοσόνδε—ὃ ἐὰν* I placed with Eusebius and most of our books *εἰ τοσόνδε —ὃ ἄν*. — Soon concerning the verb *ἀποσώζειν* [to preserve] see above at II. 9. 8. p. 206. E.

**p. 852, 11. *καὶ προσέτι, εἰ ψυχῆς ἑκάστης τὸ μέγεθος ὡρισμένον ἔσται ἐφ’ ἑκάτερα, ἢ ἐπὶ τὸ ἔλαττόν γε ἢ ἐπὶ τὸ μεῖζον, ψυχὴ οὐκ ἔσται.*** Thus I think it must be read with Eusebius and Vigerus: “Furthermore, if the magnitude of each soul is circumscribed by its own limits on either side, whether toward the lesser or toward the greater, it will not be a soul.” For what follows: “whenever twin offspring are born, or even... very many,” apply those things we have placed below for p. 541. A. or for V. 7. 3.

**— 17. *τοῦτο ἐν τῇ αὑτοῦ οὐσίᾳ τὸ ποσὸν εἶναι ὑπερβέβηκεν.* [“this has transcended being a quantity in its own substance”]** Porphyry in *De Gradibus* XVIII. p. 225 comprehends this dispute, by which Plato’s dispute is integrated, in a few words: “the soul, a substance without magnitude (*ἀμεγέθης*), immaterial, incorruptible. Having its existence in a life that has living from itself.” Cf. also Aristotle, *De Anima* I. 3. p. 11. med. Sylb. I will add a passage from Athanasius, not dissimilar to Plotinus' in both words and meaning, *Against the Gentiles* p. 36 (Cologne ed. 1686): “for the motion of the soul is nothing other than its life; just as, indeed, we say the body then lives when it is moved, and that its death is when it ceases from motion. One might see this most clearly from its activity once for all in the body. For if, even when it has entered the body and is bound to it, it is not contracted and measured according to the smallness of the body, but often when the body is lying on a bed and not moving, sleeping as if in death (*ὡς ἐν θανάτῳ κοιμωμένου*), the soul is awake (*γρηγορεῖ*) according to its own power, and transcends the nature of the body.” — Cudworth used our passage in his disputes in *Syst. Intell.* p. 1023 and especially p. 1110, which you should consult.

**p. 853, 3. *Ὅτι δὲ εἰ σῶμα εἴη ψυχὴ—ἐκ τῶνδε δῆλον. Εἰ τι μέλλει αἰσθάνεσθαί τινος κ. τ. λ.* [“That if the soul were a body—it is clear from these things. If it is to perceive anything, etc.”]** Besides the Platonic passages which we indicated in the next chapters and will indicate in this chapter, the Aristotelian passages from *On Memory* Chap. I. p. 28. sqq. Sylb.; *On Sensation and Sensible Objects* chap. 6. p. 19; *On the Soul* book I. c. 3 must be applied. Moreover, Cudworth, a most intelligent man in these matters, excerpted and explained this chapter of Plotinus in *System. Intellect.* p. 1111. sq. Whose dispute we would wish our readers to handle all the more, since it is not permitted to us in this office of annotating to play the part of a philosopher.

**p. 854, 18. *οὐκ ἂν ἄλλον τρόπον γένοιτο τὸ αἰσθάνεσθαι, ἢ οἷον ἐν κηρῷ ἐνσημανθεῖσαι ἀπὸ δακτυλίων σφραγῖδες—τῶν αἰσθητῶν ἐνσημαινομένων—ἄλλους (τύπους) ἐνσημαίνεσθαι* [“sensation could not happen in any other way, than as seals impressed into wax from signet-rings—the sensibles being imprinted—others (types) being imprinted”]** I thought I should not depart from the authority of our books and, having neglected it here, obey Eusebius. Now I shall touch upon one passage of Dio Chrysostom to be referred there. He, in *Oration* XII. p. 214. p. 409 (Reiske) concerning Homer, says: “partly, simply placing names upon things; partly naming them upon the proper names; as if applying a seal to distinct seals (*σφραγῖδα σφραγῖσιν*) and making it more evident”: where undoubtedly one should read *ἐναργῆ* [distinct/vivid] with Reiske, the error having arisen by Iotacism, even if you do not find it necessary to have *σφραγῖδι* instead of *σφραγῖσι*. Let us look at the verb which Plotinus used three times in this place. Plato in the *Cratylus* p. 395. a. p. 28 (Bekker): “but the sign (*σημεῖον*) of it is the stay in Troy because of the multitude and endurance; that therefore this man, wonderful in his perseverance, is imprinted (*ἐνσημαίνει*) by the name Agamemnon.” Similarly Theodoret Vol. V. p. 94 (Schulz) in a similar meaning uses *ἐνσημαίνειν* for the simple verb: “and he names John clearly, which signifies (*ἐνσημαίνει*) salvation to the peoples and a message of the good things to come.” The same p. 96: “but so as to show the desire and to signify (*ἐνσημᾶναι*) the joys of the day.” But Plotinus here had other passages of Plato before his eyes: *Republic* II. p. 377. B. “for especially then is molded and entered the type which one might wish to imprint (*ἐνσημήνασθαι*)” and particularly these in the *Theaetetus* p. 191. d. p. 281...

[[vocabulary: ἀναμνήσεως (of recollection), ἀμεγέθης (without magnitude), γρηγορεῖ (is awake/vigilant), ἐνσημήνασθαι (to imprint)]]

### PAGE 259 ###

**...Bekker — “that whenever we wish to remember those things we have seen or heard or thought ourselves, holding it [the soul] under the sensations and thoughts, they are imprinted, just as we imprint (*ἐνσημαινομένους*) the signs of signet-rings.”** On the force of the Active and Middle voice, see Pollux in *Onomasticon* V. 149; Sturz, *Lex. Xenoph.* II. p. 192; Valckenaer on Callimachus’ *Elegies Fragments* p. 212; and Boissonade on Philostratus’ *Heroica* p. 286 and p. 294. — As for the imitations of the Platonic passages which learned men have indicated (Ast on the *Republic* l.c. p. 427; Wyttenbach on Plutarch p. 832; and Jacobs in *Lectiones Stobenses* p. 41), the student of Greek elegance will follow them in their own commentaries; I shall add a few things more closely connected with the argument of our passage: Aristotle, *On Memory* c. 1. p. 29 (Sylb.): “—we do not say that the habit is memory; for the motion that occurs is imprinted (*ensemainetai*), like a sort of type of the sensation, just as those who make impressions with signet-rings.” An uncertain writer, hiding under the name of Socrates, in Stobaeus *Florilegium* LIV. p. 369. p. 409 (Gaisford) on the Horn of Amalthea: “but according to the horn of the ox, which is the most hardworking, the worker is imprinted (*ensemainesthai*).” These same words are read in Arsenius’ *Violetum*. Gregory Nazianzen, *Oration* II. *On the Son* p. 216 (Basel ed.): “either when the Father previously worked these things, or it is clear that the Father imprints (*ensemainetai*) the types of the same things, but the Word completes them, not slavishly, nor ignorantly, but scientifically and masterfully, and to speak more properly, paternally.” Pythagoras in Ovid’s *Metamorphoses* XV. 169. sq. in the Planudean version p. 664 (Boissonade ed.): “as the wax, easily persuaded, is always imprinted with new characters, and does not remain as it was before, nor keep the same types, yet it is the same; so I teach that through all things the soul is the same, but migrates into various bodies.”

**p. 856, 3. *τὸ δὲ ἀληθὲς, ἑκάστην ἐκείνων, μὴ (sc. αἰσθέσθαι) τοῦ ἐν τῷ δακτύλῳ ἀλγήματος, ἀλλὰ τὴν μὲν ἐφεξῆς τῷ δακτύλῳ κ. τ. λ.* [“but the truth is that each of those [parts] does not (perceive) the pain in the finger, but rather that which is next to the finger, etc.”]** Vigerus, who filled in the defective context of Eusebius from the Plotinian one, says: “These and following points are quite hindered, and Ficinus seems to make them far more intricate.” I see nothing greatly hindered, nor do I understand what Ficinus has made intricate. Neither does Cudworth, who in *System. Intell.* p. 1112. sq. treated this passage of Plotinus, complain about either the Greek of Plotinus or the Latin of Ficinus. Moreover, concerning transmission (*διαδόσει*), I have explained above for p. 363. E.; that entire passage should be compared with our chapter. Here I will mention in a word that doubt in Gregory of Nyssa, *On the Soul* p. 94: “—for it is doubted whether the body alone is that which feels pain, having taken the sensation from the soul, while the soul remains unaffected; or whether it even feels pain along with the body.” About which many things are disputed there.

**— 12. *δεῖ τοιοῦτον τίθεσθαι τὸ αἰσθανόμενον, οἷον—εἶναι*** Vigerus translates: “For certainly, since different parts of magnitude are present (reading *εἰ* in Eusebius, though it is not in any of our Codices of Plotinus), it is necessary that that which is perceived be of such a kind that it remain one and the same everywhere”—adding in the notes that *τὸ αἰσθανόμενον* [that which perceives] should not be taken actively in this place. Unsuccessfully. For the connection and reason of the entire dispute teaches the contrary. Consult Cudworth, who illustrated this entire argumentation, and whom I also followed in enclosing the words *παντὸς γὰρ μεγ.—τὸ δὲ ἄλλο ἐστί* in parentheses. Taylor also correctly expressed *τὸ αἰσθανόμενον* actively: “the power which perceives.”

**p. 857, 4. *Πῶς οὖν μέγεθος ὂν, τὸ μὴ μέγεθος νοήσει, καὶ τῷ μεριστῷ τὸ μὴ μεριστὸν νοήσει* [“How then, being a magnitude, will it think that which has no magnitude, and with that which is divisible think that which is indivisible?”]** Thus most of our books and Eusebius. In the margin of the Edition *τὸ μεριστόν* is written for *τῷ μεριστῷ*. But the latter is better, and Cudworth also retained it; consult him disputing about this fourth argument of Plotinus on p. 1113. sq.

**— 9. *αὐτὸ ἑκάστου, ἀνάγκη,—γιγνώσκειν.*** Thus also our books. Eusebius on the contrary: *αὐτὸ ἕκαστον*, which reading Vigerus thinks better, and the Latin version of Eusebius has it thus: “that which it understands, so at last, if it be or become free from the body, it is necessary to know.” In Eusebius previously it was read: “that the mind being pure of body, knowing that which comes into it.” Vigerus suspects: *τὸ ἐγγιγνόμενον*: “that which is imprinted in the mind itself.” Wrongly.

**— 17. *Πῶς δ’ ἂν καὶ σώματος ὄντος τῆς ψυχῆς, ἀρεταὶ αὐτῆς, σωφροσύνη καὶ (καὶ not in Euseb.) δικαιοσύνη (Cod. Ciz. lacks this) [σωζομένης καθ’ ὅσον ἂν αὐτοῦ μεταλαμβάνῃ.]]*** Our books have *σωζόμενον*, except that in Medicean A a second hand placed *σωζομένης* above the line; which I indeed think is of Ficinus himself, who when he wished to come to the aid of a struggling sentence, thus tried to change it.

[[vocabulary: ἀποτυποῦσθαι (to be imprinted), διαδόσει (transmission/distribution), μεριστῷ (divisible), σωφροσύνη (temperance)]]

### PAGE 260 ###

**...I have left that untouched for two reasons.** For first, I suspect that these words *σωζόμενον καθ’ ὅσον ἂν αὐτοῦ μεταλαμβάνῃ* [being preserved insofar as it partakes of it] belong to the end of chapter XIV p. 467. B. line 9 and should be placed there after the words: *οὐδὲν γὰρ ἐκ τοῦ ὄντος ἀπολεῖται* [“for nothing of being shall be lost”]. Secondly, because Eusebius continues the sentence, broken after the word *δικαιοσύνη* [justice], most fitly: “and courage, and others; for would being temperate be some spirit, or some blood, etc.?” Indeed, in the judgment of Vigerus on Eusebius page 79, we gain from this writer a distinguished supplement to the Plotinian dispute, which runs through several chapters, and to which all those things should be subjected which are read from the beginning of the following ninth chapter, from the words *Ἡ δὲ ἑτέρα φύσις* [“But the other nature”] down to the end of the fourteenth chapter, i.e., down to the words *οὐδὲν γὰρ ἐκ τοῦ ὄντος ἀπολεῖται*, and (if my conjecture does not deceive me) *σωζόμενον καθ’ ὅσον ἂν αὐτοῦ μεταλαμβάνῃ*. Whence these questions arise for us: First: are these things truly Plotinian? The Scholiast of the Barberini Codex nr. 409 precisely denies it, although another in the same place clearly professes that the speech of the Plotinian passage, if these are removed, is unharmonious. The scholion of the Barberini and Marcian A codices holds thus:

> [Margin note:]
> XXXIV. On the immortality of the soul and its eternity.
> *Temperance and justice, and courage and the others.*
> *For by a spirit...* (C. [in red])
>
> (Note from here... [Marcian A: Note from here that 88 lines are indicated from the red mark Ϙ; because the 88 lines were missing. Down to there: 'Therefore the soul is not a harmony.' But those starting from there are interjected (epieisaktoi) down to: 'that they have not perished.' And they contain nothing of Plotinus, as it seems to me, but of someone else. Wherefore they are not even useful. But neither is the phrasing shown to be that of the wise man Plotinus: especially as 'temperance and justice and courage and the others' follows the argument: but 'temperance and justice being preserved; insofar as it partakes of it' does not fit well.)

Secondly; if these are of Plotinus, to whom is that truncation of the Plotinian book to be imputed? To Porphyry, whom we brought under suspicion of a similar crime above p. 364. D? If you posit this; Eusebius must be thought to have taken these from Eustochius’ recension of Plotinus' works. To the scribes? This is more probable because in several codices of Plotinus’ *Enneads* these are read whole. Be that as it may: we have thought that these very things should be interposed at this place from Eusebius and our books.

**p. 858, 1. *ἀνδρεία τε κ. τ. λ.* [“and courage, etc.”]** From this word, those things which follow here in Eusebius down to the end of the chapter you will not find in Plotinus at that place, nor did Hopper or Ficinus represent them. Nevertheless, they are of Plotinus' genius, they connect most fitly with the preceding parts, and the Royal MSS and Montacutianus acknowledge them. Certainly, those things which follow in Plotinus after *δικαιοσύνη* are neither spoken with any sense, nor do they end. Thus Eusebius will compensate for this so remarkable a fragment with those things which he had thus far borrowed from Plotinus, not without interest. Viger. — Furthermore, in these he seems to touch upon the opinions of Empedocles, or perhaps rather of Critias, and of the rest of the philosophers; about which Cicero in *Tuscull.* I. 9. where see Davies and compare Stobaeus, *Eclogae Physicae* I. 52. p. 796–798. Heeren. and Gregory of Nyssa, *On the Soul* p. 90. Cr.

**— 7. *ἀλλ’ οὖν*** I gave *οὖν* from both MSS, not *οὐ*, as before. Vig.

**— 8. *ψύχεος*** Thus the two Royal and Montacutianus, not *ψύχους*; he seemed to look to that Homeric word *Odyssey* κ. 555: “desiring the cold (*ψύχεος*) he lay down, heavy with wine.” Vig.

**p. 859, 1. *ἀγνοοῦσιν, ὡς καὶ*** These few things, but necessary, we supplied from the Montacutianus codex. *ταῦτα*, which follows, would be better absent. Vig. Or one should read *αὐτά*. Cr.

**— 2. *ἀσωμάτοις, ταῦτα*** We added both these words from the same Montacutianus: likewise the words *περὶ ψυχήν*. Vig.

**— 8. *ἃ δύναται*** From the same Montacutianus. Vig.

**p. 860, 3. *ὡς φασιν οὖσαν*** For *οὖσαν* one should read *εἶναι*. Vig. Perhaps it should be punctuated—*εἶναι, σῶμα, ὡς φασιν, οὖσαν, διάφορα δέ.* Cr.

**— 9. *Ἔτι δὲ κ. τ. λ.*** Again he seems to touch upon the opinions of Dicaearchus and Aristoxenus; about which we saw above in Plotinus' chapter III p. 458. A. Cr.

**— ib. *Ἔτι δὲ κ. τ. λ.*** Previously it was read *ψυχὴ δέ εἰ σῶμα οὖσα*. Montac. *ψυχὴ δὲ ἔτι εἰ σ. οὖσα*. *Ἔτι δὲ* [“furthermore”] was approved by me; *ψυχὴ* seemed redundant; for there follows from the same Montac. *ἢ ψυχὴ διῆλθε*, which words were missing in the prior edition. Viger.

VI—X. and likewise Boethius in *The Consolation of Philosophy*, Book V.

page 836, line 9. **"Saying that perceptions are not impressions or seal-stamps, etc."** <note>original: "ΤΑΣ αἰσθήσεις οὐ τυπώσεις οὐδ’ ἐνσφραγίσεις λέγοντες"</note>] Regarding these words and this sentiment, compare what our philosopher discusses above on page 305 B, 391 G, and below on page 461 F. In these and the following lines, he criticizes Aristotle. The latter, in his short treatise *On Memory and Reminiscence*, chapter 1, page 29 (Sylburg edition), writes: "For it is clear that one must conceive of that which is produced through perception in the soul and in that part of the body which contains it as being like a sort of portrait, the permanent possession of which we call memory; for the motion that occurs leaves an impression, a sort of <term>type</term> <note>Greek: typos; a physical mark or stamp</note> of the sensation, just like those who make a seal with signet rings. For this reason, memory does not occur in those who are in a state of great motion—whether due to passion or age—just as if the motion and the seal were falling into running water; while in others, due to 'chilling' (the Basel edition margin reads 'decaying') like old buildings, and due to the hardness of the receiving surface, the impression does not take hold." From this, someone might even seek support for the Vatican manuscript reading in Plotinus: "retentions of sufferings." I, along with Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino, the 15th-century Platonist translator</note>, retain the common reading. Porphyry, in Stobaeus's *Anthology* I. 52, page 830 (Heeren edition), in reporting and judging the opinion of Aristo, writes: "For perception is not capable of grasping essence, but only form and shape; but whether it is a man or a horse is the grasp of another faculty." (Heeren filled in this passage from the books. It is not necessary to add more by conjecture.) "The movement of the grasp is therefore different; for that of perception resembles an impression and is drawn outward toward the form, while the other stands apart from the impression." Having this opportunity, I am wiping away a stain from a fragment of Hermes in the same Stobaeus, page 1086: "so that nature may preserve and master—the <term>type</term> <note>original: typos</note> established from the beginning." It had been incorrectly written as "place" <note>original: topos</note>, just as in many passages of Plotinus. Furthermore, the Stoics attempted to explain the method of perceiving in a manner almost identical to Aristotle. Plutarch, in *On the Opinions of the Philosophers* IV. 11, page 630 (Wyttenbach edition): "The Stoics say: When a human is born, he has the commanding part of the soul like a sheet of paper ready for writing (Beckius, from the Moscow Manuscript, excellently reads 'like a small tablet ready for writing': 'as a little chart on which one can write most excellently and effectively': See his note in *Various Readings*, page 237.) into this, he writes down each one of his conceptions. The first method of writing is that through the senses. For by perceiving something, such as a white object, they have a memory of it when it has departed." Boethius also touches upon this Stoic opinion in *The Consolation of Philosophy*, Book V, in the Metrical sections, page 304 and following:

"The <insert>Stoic</insert> Porch once brought forth
Old men far too obscure.
Who believe that senses and images
Are imprinted on the minds
From external bodies,
Just as it is the custom with a swift pen
To fix pressed letters
Upon the surface of a page
Which has no marks.
But if the mind, flourishing with its own
Movements, explains nothing,
But merely lies passive,
Subject to the marks of bodies;
And like a mirror reflects
Vain images of things,
From where does this notion flourish in the soul,
Discerning all things?"

Proclus, in his commentary on the *Alcibiades*, page 281, uses the same simile: "and (souls) are not unwritten tablets receiving impressions from without, but they have always been written upon, and the writer is within themselves, though not all souls are able to know what has been written." Plato, in the *Protagoras*, page 326 D: "but simply, just as writing-masters, for those children not yet clever at writing, draw lines with the stylus and then give them the tablet and compel them to write following the guidance of the lines." In this passage, Heindorf should no more have retained "small tablet" <note>original: grammation</note> (the word "tablet" <note>original: grammateion</note> is also in the Bodleian Manuscript and was restored by Bekker) than he should have doubted the meaning of "line" <note>original: grammē</note> as a letter. Maximus of Tyre, VIII. 2, page 132 (Reiske edition), expressed the Platonic passage thus: "as also writing-masters devise for children, tracing for them faint signs, over which they apply their handiwork and become accustomed by memory to the craft." The interpreters of Maximus were unaware of this imitation.

page 837, line 3. **"If we should observe the clearest of the senses"**] Aristotle, *On the Soul* III. 3, page 56 (Sylburg edition): "Since sight is the primary sense, it has even taken its name from light <note>A Greek etymological pun: opsis (sight) and phaos (light)</note>, because without light it is not possible to see."

— line 9. **"neither by receiving a seal — by seeing"**] A singular use of the Participle instead of the Infinitive ("by receiving") <note>original: τῷ λαμβάνειν</note> to be explained solely according to the order of Construction by Attraction. Cf. Matthiae's *Greek Grammar* § 555 and following, where, however, among many conveniently placed examples, you may not find a twin instance, as far as I know. Regarding the sentiment, Plotinus similarly writes below on page 461 F: "or like seals stamped into wax from signet rings."—Presently, with the Median Manuscript A.,

or rather with Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the influential Renaissance translator of Plotinus</note>, we have placed *outōs* <note>original: οὕτως; "in this way"</note> for *outōs*. But perhaps in this passage we should also read: "by adding a distance to the vision before the..." etc.

p. 837, 18. *it will not be possible to see the things themselves which we behold, but images* <note>original: ἰνδάλματα</note> *instead* etc.] Compare the passage of Porphyry from the discussion on the doctrines of Aristo, which I placed at the beginning of this chapter on p. 452. A. Regarding the following parts of the Plotinian passage, the same Porphyry follows in the footsteps of his master in these words found in Stobaeus, *Physical Eclogues* I. 51. p. 780. Heeren: "In every way, that which makes use of sensation contemplates by applying itself to external things, not being united with those things which it contemplates, but only receiving a form <note>or "impression"</note> of them from the contact with them. Whenever, therefore, the eye sees the object of sight, it is impossible for it to become identical with the seen; for it would not see, unless it were at a distance. Likewise, that which touches, if it became identical [with the object], would be destroyed. From which it is clear that sensation, and that which uses sensation, is always carried toward the outside, if it intends to grasp the sensible object."

p. 839, 6. *but those things, as many as are sensations and judgments of them, are knowledges of the passions* <note>In this context, "passions" refers to "affections" or "impressions" received by the soul</note>] The Stoics designate these things with almost similar words. Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II. 56: "The senses, however, are the interpreters and messengers of things—For the eyes, like scouts, occupy the highest place—and because the judgment of food and drink belongs largely to them (the nostrils) etc." See also Cicero, *On the Laws* I. 9. at the beginning, and our notes on both passages. Consult also Baguet’s book on Chrysippus §. XXIII. p. 62. I add no more here, since these matters have already been explained by us in the preceding annotations to these *Enneads*.

p. 840, 4. *on the one hand being well-affected by some—but on the other hand being deceived by a likeness (I added "by the" from most of our manuscripts), and descending as if being charmed*] Regarding this word <note>original: θελγομένη; "charmed" or "enchanted"</note> we have said more in the commentary on Proclus's notes on Plato's *Alcibiades* p. 40. regarding the verse of the oracle:
-> *always charming the souls, they lead them away from the rites,* <-

— 16. *Wherefore also children are said to remember more*] On the contrary, Aristotle in *On Memory* ch. I. p. 326. Erasmus ed. p. 29. Sylburg ed. says: "wherefore both the very young and the old are forgetful. For they are in a state of flux, the former because of growth, the latter because of decay" etc. Saint Maximus, in *Excerpts of Sermons* LII. Vol. II. p. 654. ed. Combefis, attributes this opinion either to Plato or to Plotinus himself, saying: "Plato said that the very young and the old are forgetful": where in the margin is read *Plotinus* in the Ballesdens manuscript, but *Plato* in others. Compare, however, with this chapter *Ennead* IV. book 3. ch. 25. and 26–30. in which places not a few things approach more closely to the doctrines of Descartes and Leibniz. Presently: *it would not have produced the multitude or rather memories*: someone might conjecture *mindful* <note>original: μνήμονας</note>. But there is no need.

p. 841, 6. *they show that what happens exists by the powers of the soul*] Our manuscripts indicate hesitation in this place, and lexicographers offer no example of the word *dynamōsis* <note>original: δυνάμωσις; "strengthening" or "empowerment"</note>. For let us dismiss Schneider, who held the verb *dynamoō* itself in doubt. (See our Annotation on Proclus’s *Elements of Theology* §. LXX. p. 110.) But Ficino also translated it as *dynamōsin*. Therefore, we have left it untouched.

p. 842, 15. *For the most part, those who are mindful and those who are quick-witted are often not the same.*] Aristotle, *On Memory and Reminiscence* ch. I. p. 27. Sylburg: "For the same people are not those with good memories <note>original: μνημονικοί</note> and those good at recollecting <note>original: ἀναμνηστικοί</note>, but for the most part the slow are better at remembering; while the quick and the apt learners are better at recollecting." Whether in the following: "and yet it did not prevent anyone having the advantages of the soul from reading the things lying there," Plotinus designated those whom we today say have "fixed ideas," I prefer to ask rather than to define: Nor less, whether he took the next part: "that he who has flowed in this way possesses the inability to be affected" from Aristotle’s words in *On Memory* I. p. 29: "wherefore also memory does not occur to those who are in great motion, just as if [an impression] were falling into flowing water"

### BOOK VII.

page 844, line 7. ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL.] <note>original: "ΠΕΡΙ ΑΘΑΝΑΣΙΑΣ ΨΥΧΗΣ"</note> Written after the first book by Plotinus, and therefore, considering the chronological order, this is the second book, according to Porphyry in *The Life of Plotinus*, chapter IV; compare chapter XXV. In the former place it is: "concerning the immortality of the soul." <note>original: "περὶ ψυχῆς ἀθανασίας"</note> The title of this book differs much more in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* XV. 22, page 824, Cologne edition: "Against the Stoics, that the soul cannot be corporeal; from Plotinus's work on the soul." <note>original: "Πρὸς τοὺς Στωϊκοὺς, ὅτι οὐ δύναται σωματικὴ εἶναι ἡ ψυχή. ἀπὸ τοῦ περὶ ψυχῆς Πλωτίνου"</note> But this seems rather to be due to Eusebius or the scribes of the Eusebian books, although this might perhaps be gathered from it: that the title of this book was once simpler: "On the Soul." <note>original: "περὶ ψυχῆς"</note> The same Eusebius, at the end of the Excerpt on page 835, adds these words: "these things are from the writings of Plotinus against the opinion of the Stoics concerning the soul, who claim that it is corporeal." <note>original: "ταῦτα μὲν ἀπὸ τῶν Πλωτίνου πρὸς τὴν τῶν Στωϊκῶν περὶ ψυχῆς δόξαν, σωματικὴν αὐτὴν φασκόντων εἶναι"</note> But Plotinus refutes in this book not only the opinions of the Stoics, but also those of other philosophers. And Porphyry himself, in chapter 4 of the aforementioned book, reveals that the first twenty-one books composed by the philosopher from Lycopolis <note>Plotinus was born in Lycopolis, Egypt.</note> were titled in various ways.

Regarding the sources and the argument of this book, there are several passages in Plato which Plotinus may have looked to; such as that brilliant account in the tenth book of the *Republic*, page 614 and following (page 502 ff. in Bekker's edition) concerning Er the Armenian; from which it is clearly established that there existed in antiquity a certain doctrine of the Eastern peoples, by which it was handed down through signs (commonly called allegorically) concerning the nature of man and the immortality of the human soul, and its fortune after death according to how one conducted oneself in life. No less relevant is the primary passage in the *Phaedrus*, page 245 C and following, to which Hermias's commentary on that dialogue (page 114 ff.) should be applied. But nevertheless, the *Phaedo*, page 78 ff. (page 46 ff. Bekker), must be regarded as the chief source of this book, regarding which Wyttenbach says on page 197: "Starting from this argument of Plato (of the composite body and the simple soul), Plotinus pursued the reasons for immortality more broadly and subtly: as Olympiodorus taught regarding this passage in Manuscript I, pages 63 and 185, and Manuscript III, pages 38 and 40, which would be long to recount. The principal seat of the Plotinian argumentation is Ennead IV, book 7, but parts of it occur scattered through other books." The same author says in his *Metaphysical Institutions*, page 201: "Of the later philosophers," he says, "*Plotinus* brought the greatest increase, by seeking reasons from the communion of human souls and the divine nature: then especially by demonstrating more accurately the <term>simplicity</term> <note>In philosophy, "simplicity" means being non-composite or not made of parts, a key argument for the soul's immortality.</note> of the soul, from that argument by which it is effected that the power and action of thinking cannot fall into a corporeal nature, Ennead IV, book 7: where his argumentation against Aristotle's <term>entelechy</term> <note>Aristotle's term for the "actualization" or "form" of the body; Plotinus argued the soul was more than just the body's function.</note> is effective, preserved in Eusebius's *Preparation for the Gospel* XV. 10." (See it above, page 364, b. c.) Compare also Alcinous on the *Doctrines of Plato*, chapter XXV. Generally, the Aristotelian work *On the Soul* should be compared with this Plotinian discussion, especially Book III, chapter 4. To this also belongs a notable passage of John Philoponus in his books against Proclus. He indeed records it thus in VII. 4: "For the souls appear to be still in the body, whenever they are released from their immediate relation and passion toward it, making their intellectual activities separate and unrelated to any body. For what part, says Aristotle, or how the mind will hold together, is difficult even to imagine. Therefore, it is entirely necessary that the essence of the soul, from which such activity proceeds, is separate and unrelated to any body, just as it seemed to Plato and all the best of the philosophers; for from this Plotinus also reasoned its immortality, showing from its separate activities that its essence must also be separate and for this reason immortal." <note>original: "φαίνονται γὰρ ἔτι ἐν τῷ σώματι οὖσαι αἱ ψυχαί... καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἀθάνατον"</note> Plutarch enumerates the opinions of Plato and other philosophers on this matter in *Opinions of the Philosophers* IV. 7; Porphyry gives the Plotinian view in *On the Degrees* § 18 and following. As for what Eusebius says in *Preparation for the Gospel* XV. 22...

# ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS

This argument presented by Plotinus reminds us of the Church Fathers. Among the most ancient of these, who established a <term>trichotomy</term> <note>A three-part division of human nature: body, soul, and spirit.</note> of human nature (see below p. 467. B. c. 14.), especially the Alexandrians and followers of Plato, taught as follows: The body (<note>original: "τὸ σῶμα"</note>) is by its nature mortal; the "fleshly soul" (<note>original: "ψυχὴν σαρκικὴν"</note>) can die and be dissolved (<note>original: "λύεσθαι"</note>), yet this does not happen by necessity, for it can also become a participant in immortality. However, the "spiritual soul" or mind (<note>original: "ψυχὴν πνευματικὴν"</note>) is by its own nature immortal. (See Tatian *Against the Greeks* p. 150 ff.; Theophilus *To Autolycus* II. p. 101; Justin’s *Dialogue with Trypho* p. 222; and cf. Herm. Olshausen’s *Commentary on the opinions of the most ancient Greek Church Fathers regarding the immortality of souls*, Konigsberg 1827.) Some relevant material from ecclesiastical writers was recently recovered from Manuscripts and presented in the *Vatican Collection of Ancient Writers* by Angelo Mai, Vol. I. part III. p. 76 ff. Also, Gregory of Nyssa in *On the Soul* p. 91, Paris edition, says: <note>original Greek translated below</note> "In general, against all those who say the soul is a body, the arguments spoken by Ammonius, the teacher of Plotinus, and Numenius the Pythagorean, will suffice." Among more recent authors, not a few have touched upon our book. Of these it suffices to name Hugo Grotius in *On the Truth of the Christian Religion* I. 23; Cudworth in *Intellectual System* Ch. V. Sect. III. § XLII—XLVI. p. 1110—1114; Mosheim; and Tiedemann in *Spirit of Speculative Philosophy* III. p. 337 ff., who, although otherwise prone to criticizing Plotinus, nevertheless grants him this: that he calls him the primary champion of the incorporeal soul, and pronounces that most of the arguments later debated by philosophers for this cause are already found prepared in these books of Plotinus. Thomas Taylor translated this book into English in *Select Works of Plotinus* p. 221 ff. However, François Viger often changed the text of Eusebius based on the edition of Plotinus, sometimes rashly.

**p. 844, 13.** *“Whether it is as an instrument for us, or attached in some other way. But at any rate, let it be distinguished in this manner, and the nature and essence of each must be observed.”*] We have established the text here partly from Eusebius and partly from our own manuscripts: whether therefore it is joined to us as an instrument or by some other means: but it must be distinguished thus, and the nature and essence of both must be examined. Regarding the body as an "instrument" or "vehicle" of the soul, many have said much. See just now Plato’s *Alcibiades I* p. 130. a. p. 360 Bekker edition, and Olympiodorus’s commentary on it p. 4 ff. and cf. Wyttenbach on Plutarch’s *On the Delay of Divine Vengeance* p. 97 ff. I will add a passage from Athanasius of Alexandria from the *Oration against the Heathen* Vol. I. p. 35, Cologne edition: <note>original Greek translated below</note> "What then would this be again, if not a rational and immortal soul? For it is not from without but from within the body that she, like a musician with a lyre, sounds the higher things." He then explains this more broadly, such that he seems to have read Plotinus’s book *On Sense and Memory*, and continues: —"For these things prove nothing else than a rational soul ruling the body. For the body is not by nature made to drive itself, but is led and carried by another, just as a horse does not yoke itself, but is driven by the one who controls it," etc. For in the following parts he also had before his eyes the classic passage of Plato in the *Phaedrus*. Basil the Great imitated this same passage in *Constitutions of Monastic Life* ch. II. Vol. II. p. 670 ff., Paris edition 1618.

**p. 845, 9.** *“And in this way it would undergo destruction.”*] In several books, the last syllable of the preceding word crowded out the particle <note>original: "ἂν"</note>. The meaning is: *And so also they suffer destruction*: <note>original: "ταύτῃ"</note> that is, *in this way*. See Hesychius under this word. Cf. Plato’s *Symposium* p. 208. E.; *Lexicon to Xenophon* III. p. 368; and Blomfield on Aeschylus’s *Prometheus* 197 in the Glossary.

**— 11.** *“But the most essential part would be the man himself, or according to the form, as the body is to matter,”*] With the help of Eusebius and several of our manuscripts, I have freed Plotinus’s speech from an inept addition. Viger also saw this, except that he introduced a less convenient punctuation.—Presently, regarding the words: *“in either case the soul is the self,”* keep in mind these words of Eustathius on the *Iliad* book 1, verse 4, regarding Homeric usage, p. 19 (p. 17 Leipzig edition): <note>original Greek translated below</note> "For it must be known that the word 'self' (<note>original: "αὐτὸς"</note>) sometimes refers to the body alone, as was said before, and sometimes to the soul alone, as when he says in the *Odyssey* (11. 601) concerning Hercules, that 'he himself (<note>original: "αὐτὸς"</note>) rejoices among the immortal gods and has fair-ankled Hebe' (compare Plotinus above p. 7. C.), and sometimes it refers to the 'both-together,' that is, the composite human being." On this primary doctrine of the Platonists, consult Segaar on Clement of Alexandria’s *Who is the Rich Man that shall be Saved?* p. 290 ff. and our own notes on Olympiodorus’s commentary on *Alcibiades I*, p. 171, where...
