# BOOK VII. ENNEAD FOUR. pages 844—847.

I have placed a parallel passage from Basil the Great, Volume II, page 18, section C.

**page 845, line 14.** *or if it is a body, it is entirely dissolvable* <note>original: "ἢ σῶμα μὲν ὃν πάντως ἀναλυτὸν"</note>] I have written it thus following the Munich B and Medici A manuscripts, although many books and Eusebius himself read *must be dissolved* <note>original: "ἀναλυτέον"</note>. The printed edition has *dissolving* <note>original: "ἀναλύον"</note> corruptly. Seager, in his notes to the London edition of Stephanus's *Thesaurus* (page 5867, D), praises the reading *undissolvable* <note>original: "ἀναλύτος"</note> from a single passage in Origen's *Against Celsus* (IV, page 169). It ought to be *dissolvable* <note>original: "ἀναλυτὸς"</note>, as it is correctly read there, and as logic demands. (See Athenaeus VIII, page 338, b. c. page 246 and following, Schweighäuser edition.) Therefore, our passage should be added to the Lexicons.

**page 846, line 10.** *And to those who think there are also elements—they were said to be.*] We have adopted the punctuation of Viger in his edition of Eusebius (page 78, at the end), who explains it thus: “And if it pleases some that there are certain other elements besides these, they nevertheless do not call them souls, but bodies, nor do they wish them to have life from themselves.” Whether he touches upon Aristotle in these words—who, besides those four beginnings or elements, established a certain fifth essence of the body, more divine and prior to the others (On the Heavens I. 2. page 4, Sylburg edition)—I prefer to inquire rather than to decide.

**— line 12.** *But if each thing has life, etc.*] See Cudworth’s *Intellectual System*, page 1110. Tiedemann, in *The Spirit of Speculative Philosophy* (III, page 309), says these arguments of Plotinus are no less new than they are acute, and contends that they provide the foundation for the whole of what they call *Spiritualism*.

**— line 14.** *And indeed, not having been mixed in just any way—to become*] Taylor, as he usually does, expressed these words according to the mind of Ficino, adding a small note: “The words *either mind, or soul* <note>original: "ἢ νοῦν, ἢ ψυχὴν"</note> are omitted in the original; but from the version of Ficinus it appears that they ought to be inserted.” But this excellent man, as happened quite often, was deceived here because he did not know that Ficino, when he wished to consult clarity, would interpose his own words and even opinions among those of Plotinus. Neither Eusebius nor any Manuscript of Plotinus recognizes those words in this place.

**page 847, line 1.** *But if someone does not think so, but rather atoms, etc.*] I suspect *by sympathy* <note>original: "τῇ ὁμοπαθείᾳ"</note>, which a second hand placed in the Vienna A manuscript. For the rest, I have preferred the reading of the Plotinus edition, confirmed by our books, over the Eusebian one. Presently Viger suspects: *but from indivisible parts neither a body nor a magnitude is produced* <note>original: "ἐκ δὲ ἀμερῶν οὐδὲ σῶμα οὐδὲ μεγεθ’ α. γ."</note>. But neither Eusebius nor our books support this, some of which offer *not a magnitude* <note>original: "οὐ μεγ."</note>. Neither pleases me. See above <note>abbreviation: supra</note> page 390: *memory must not be placed in God nor in Being and Mind*, where this Ellipsis was discussed. — Plotinus touches in this place upon the opinions of Democritus and Epicurus concerning the nature of the soul, regarding which see Aristotle *On the Soul* I. 2; Plutarch *On the Opinions of the Philosophers* IV. 3; Stobaeus *Eclogues* I. 52, page 796, Heeren edition; Diogenes Laertius IX. 44; Cicero *Tusculan Disputations* I. 9. The same author in the same work, I. 11: “For let us omit Democritus, a great man indeed, but one who makes the soul out of smooth and round corpuscles by a certain fortuitous course: for there is nothing among those people which a crowd of atoms does not accomplish.” Gregory of Nyssa, *On the Soul and the Resurrection*, page 184 and following, Paris edition, 1638: *Where then will the soul be after this? If someone should say it is in the elements, he will necessarily conclude it is the same as them* (Read: *If someone should say it is in the elements, he will necessarily conclude it is the same as them*); *for there could be no mixing of one nature with something foreign, and if these things were so, something variegated would certainly appear, mixed with contrary qualities. But that which is variegated is not simple, but is always seen in composition; and everything composed is also dissolvable* (Read: *dissolvable* <note>original: "διαλυτὸν"</note>, cf. above regarding *dissolvable* <note>original: "ἀναλυτὸν"</note> on this very page A.) *by necessity; and dissolution is the destruction of the composite. But that which is destroyed is not immortal.* Then: *And the teacher, gently sighing at what had been said, says: "Perhaps these and such things were brought forward by the Stoics and Epicureans when they once stood against the Apostle in Athens* (Acts XVII. 18.); *for I hear that Epicurus especially is carried away by these assumptions, by whom a certain chance and spontaneous nature of beings was suspected, as if no providence reached through affairs; and because of this, consequently, he thought human life* (perhaps *is kindled* <note>original: "ζωπυρεῖσθαι"</note> has dropped out) *like a bubble* (cf. the Scholion on this place and use Wyttenbach on Plutarch *On the Late Vengeance of the Deity*, Oxford edition, page 424;) *carried by the breath of our body wrapped around us as long as the breath is held in by the container; but with the collapse of the mass, that which was shut in* (Read: *shut in* <note>original: "ἐναπειλημένον"</note>, held within or enclosed) *is extinguished along with it.*"

**— line 7.** (*for matter is without quality* <note>original: "ὕλη γὰρ, ἄποιον"</note>)] Plato in *Timaeus* page 50, page 61, Bekker edition. Cf. Wyttenbach on Plutarch VI. 2. page 661 and following. Porphyry *On the Degrees of Virtues* §. XXI. and see the annotations on Proclus *On the Alcibiades* at the beginning, page 318, and above at page 315. G. Presently with Eusebius and the books...

-> ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINI <-

In almost all of our copies, I have given <note>original: "ἐπιφέρειν τὴν ζωὴν"</note> *to bring life* instead of <note>original: "ἔχειν τὴν ζωήν"</note> *to possess life*.

p. 847, 10. *But if they say it is an affection of matter, but not a substance*] This touches upon the opinions of Aristoxenus and Dicaearchus <note>Aristoxenus and Dicaearchus were 4th-century BCE philosophers who argued the soul was merely a "harmony" or temperament of the body's physical parts.</note>. Regarding the former, we saw above at p. 307. E. In this place, I will briefly correct Gregory of Nyssa *On the Soul* p. 95, Paris edition 1638: *since even Deinarchus* (read: Dicaearchus) *defined the soul as a harmony*. This same error must be erased twice in the same place on p. 90. Plotinus accurately examines this opinion of the Soul as a harmony in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* XV. 22. p. 834. sq. Regarding both, see Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I. 10. Regarding Dicaearchus in that same work: “That the soul is nothing at all, and this name is entirely empty, and it is in vain that animals and living beings are so called; neither is there a mind or soul in man, nor in a beast; and all that power by which we either act or feel is spread equally in all living bodies, and is not separable from the body; for indeed it is nothing: nor is there anything except a single and simple body, so shaped that it flourishes and feels by the temperament of nature.” Cf. chapter 22 (where he also speaks of Aristoxenus). Add regarding Dicaearchus: Sextus Empiricus, *Against the Mathematicians* VII. 349. and *Outlines of Pyrrhonism* II. 31. and there Fabricius p. 74; Plutarch, *On the Opinions of the Philosophers* IV. 2. and Atticus in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* XV. 9. p. 810. A. B.—Presently the words: *there must therefore be something that provides* <note>original: "χορηγὸν"</note> *life etc.* remind one of this passage in the *Monastic Constitutions* of Basil the Great, chapter 2. p. 676: Paris 1618: *For I myself think the power of the soul is twofold, though it remains one and the same; one part is the vital power of the body, and the other is the contemplative power of beings, which we also call the rational power. But the vital power, since it is blended with the body, the soul provides naturally through that blending and not by choice. For just as it is impossible for the sun, having shone forth, not to illuminate that upon which it brings its rays, so it is impossible for the soul not to give life to a body in which it has come to be.* If you compare these with the earlier words of Plotinus p. 448. D. E., you might suspect that Basil wrote these things while fresh from a reading of Plotinus.

p. 848, 7. *giving to it* (namely the body) *the rank of soul even to the names of air and breath*] Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I. 9: “Others call the mind 'breath' <note>Latin: "anima"</note>, as our people generally do: the name declares it. For we speak of 'acting the breath' [living] and 'breathing it out' [dying], and of the 'spirited' <note>Latin: "animosos"</note>, and the 'well-disposed' <note>Latin: "animatos"</note>, and 'from the mind's sentiment': the mind <note>Latin: "animus"</note> itself is named from the breath <note>Latin: "anima"</note>.” And Plotinus himself could have heard such things when he was living in Rome.—Furthermore, perhaps the Emperor Julian had this discussion of Plotinus in mind, or certainly a similar one in these *Enneads*, where, making mention of Plotinus, he touches upon *life having flowed and been torn apart* in Oration VII. p. 222. ed. Spanheim.

— 17. *positing the breath as intelligent and as an intellectual fire,*] It is well known that air was called the soul by Anaximenes, and fire by Heraclitus and later the Stoics. Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I. 9. and there Davis; *On the Nature of the Gods* III. 14. and the interpreters there, where at p. 544 we touched upon this passage of Plotinus. Diogenes Laertius II. 3. VIII. 51. sq. IX. 1. cf. also Wyttenbach’s *Annotations on Plato’s Phaedo* p. 254. Add Baguet *On Chrysippus* p. 78. sq. p. 103. 182. 307. sqq.

p. 849, 5. *what is that much-talked-of "being in a certain state" for them?*] It was necessary to write <note>original: "πως ἔχον"</note> *being in a certain state* instead of <note>original: "πῶς ἔχον"</note> *how is it?* He seems to touch with these words upon that "fourth nameless thing" <note>original: "ἀκατονόμαστον"</note> which the Epicureans used in describing the Soul (Plutarch, *On the Opinions of the Philosophers* IV. 3. p. 623. Wyttenbach) or that "in a certain manner" <note>original: "τρόπον τινὰ"</note> which the Stoic Chrysippus uses in the same matter in Plutarch, *On Stoic Self-Contradictions* p. 1053. C. p. 292. Wyttenbach.—To the next part: *an active nature* <note>original: "φύσιν δραστήριον"</note> apply the words of our Author below p. 592. at the end: *if this is so, it does not even have a whole or qualities. If this is so, they are incorporeal and active.*

— 12. *and soul, and god, and everything is a name,*] So I have written with Eusebius and his translator Viger. Regarding these formulas, *a name*, *a name only*, *a name otherwise*, we spoke at page 373. E. Presently, with many books, I have placed <note>original: "πάλιν αὖ"</note> *back again*. Regarding which see above at p. 411. at the end.

p. 850, 9. *and even indeed color.*] Namely, insofar as the vehicle of the soul takes on colors. On which matter Wyttenbach explained in Plutarch, *On the Delay of Divine Vengeance* p. 111. p. 442. Oxford edition.

p. 851, 11. *a certain part of it will flow away—how then do we have memories?*] The verb *to flow away* <note>original: "ἀποῤῥεῖν"</note> is often used regarding memory with the addition: *of memory*. See Wyttenbach on Plutarch, *Sayings of Kings* p. 1124. We saw the same verb, but used differently regarding memory, above p. 455. E. As for the argument he then adds, drawn from the constancy of memory, this matter is connected with Platonic doctrine.

-> BOOK VII. ENNEAD FOUR. pages 847—854. <-

On **recollection** <note>original: *anamnesis*; the Platonic theory that learning is actually the soul remembering eternal truths</note>, concerning which see the praised remarks of Wyttenbach on the *Phaedo*, Annotations page 184. Add Alcinous on the *Doctrines of Plato*, chapter 25, page 507: "if indeed learnings are recollections, the soul would be immortal," which he explains more fully in the following sections. Shortly after, instead of *the nature of the body being divided into many parts* (Eusebius reads *of the divided*), I have given from many books *being divided* <note>original: *merizomenon*</note>: for the nature of the body is something that is distributed into many. With these same sources and with Eusebius, I have arranged it thus: *each of the parts not being the same as the whole* instead of *each of the parts not being the same as the whole* <note>The translator is noting a subtle change in Greek word order</note>, which is the reading of the Edition. Then, instead of *if therefore so much—whatever*, I placed with Eusebius and many of our manuscripts *if so much—whatever*.—Soon, regarding the word **to preserve** <note>original: *aposōzein*</note>, see above at II. 9. 8. page 206. E.

page 852, 11. **and furthermore, if the magnitude of each soul shall be defined on both sides, either toward the smaller or toward the larger, it will not be a soul.**] I think it should be read thus with Eusebius and Viger: "Furthermore, if the magnitude of any soul will be circumscribed by its own limits on both sides, either to a lesser degree or to a greater, it will not be a soul." Regarding what follows: *whenever twin offspring are born, or even—very many*, apply those things which we have placed below at page 541. A. or at V. 7. 3.

— 17. **this has exceeded being a quantity within its own essence.**] This discussion, by which Plato's argument is completed, Porphyry encompasses in a few words in *On Degrees* XVIII, page 225: "The soul is an **unextended** <note>original: *amegethēs*; without physical size</note>, immaterial, incorruptible essence; possessing being in a life that has living from itself." See also Aristotle, *On the Soul* I. 3. page 11. middle of Sylburg's edition. I will add a passage from Athanasius, similar to Plotinus's in both words and sentiment, *Against the Heathen* page 36, Cologne edition 1686: "For the motion of the soul is nothing other than its life; just as we certainly say the body lives when it moves, and that its death occurs when it ceases from motion. One might see this most clearly from its activity once and for all in the body. For even when it has entered the body and is bound to it, it is not contracted or measured according to the smallness of the body, but often while the body is lying on a bed and not moving, as if sleeping in death, the soul **is awake** <note>original: *grēgorei*</note> according to its own power, and transcends the nature of the body."—Cudworth used our passage in his *Intellectual System*, page 1023 and especially page 1110; consult him.

page 853, 3. **But that if the soul were a body—is clear from these things. If something is to perceive something, etc.**] Besides the Platonic passages which we indicated in the previous chapters, and will indicate below for this chapter, the passages of Aristotle on *Memory* Chapter I, page 28 and following, Sylburg edition, on *Sense and Sensibilia* chapter 6, page 19, and *On the Soul* book I, chapter 3, should be used. Moreover, that most intelligent man in these matters, Cudworth, excerpted and explained this chapter of Plotinus in part in his *Intellectual System*, page 1111 and following. We would wish our readers to study his discussion all the more because we are less permitted to play the part of the philosopher in this duty of annotating.

page 854, 18. **perception could not happen in any other way than as seals from rings impressed in wax—the sensible objects being impressed—to have others (impressions) impressed**] I decided not to depart from the authority of our books, nor to obey Eusebius in this place by neglecting them. Now I will touch upon one passage of Dio Chrysostom to be referred to there. In Oration XII, page 214 (page 409 in Reiske), he says of Homer: "partly, simply assigning names to things; and partly naming them upon the proper ones; as if applying a seal to seals, clearly, and more evidently": where undoubtedly one should read *clear* <note>original: *enargē*</note> with Reiske, the error having arisen through Iotacism <note>a common scribal error where different vowels are pronounced like 'i' and confused</note>, even if you do not find it necessary to have *seal* (singular) for *seals* (plural). Let us look at the verb which Plotinus used three times in this place: **to impress** <note>original: *ensēmainein*</note>. Plato in the *Cratylus* page 395. a. (page 28 Bekker): "the evidence of it is his stay at Troy with the multitude and his endurance; because therefore this man is admirable for his persistence, the name Agamemnon **signifies** <note>original: *ensēmainei*</note> this." Similarly, Theodoret, Volume V, page 94, Schulz edition, uses the same verb for a simple verb in a similar sentiment: "and he names John clearly, which **signifies** salvation to the peoples and a signaling of the good things to come." The same on page 96: "but so as to show the desire and **to signal** the joys of the day." But Plotinus here had before his eyes other passages of Plato: from the *Republic* II, page 377. B.: "for especially then is molded and adopted the stamp which one might wish **to impress**," and especially these in the *Theaetetus* page 191. d. page 281.

-> ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS <-

Bekk.—*that whatever we wish to remember of what we have seen or heard or thought of ourselves, we submit it to the senses and thoughts, to be imprinted, just as we mark the signs of rings.* <note>original: "ὅτι ἂν βουληθῶμεν μνημονεῦσαι... ἐνσημαινομένους." This is a classic metaphor comparing memory to wax receiving a seal.</note> Regarding the force of the Active used for the Middle voice, see Pollux in the *Onomasticon* V. 149. Sturz, *Xenophon Lexicon* II. p. 192. Valckenaer on Callimachus's *Elegies* p. 212. and Boissonade on Philostratus's *Heroica* p. 286 and p. 294. —As for the imitations of Plato in this passage which learned men have pointed out—Ast on the *Republic* p. 427, Wyttenbach on Plutarch p. 832, and Jacobs in *Lectures on Stobaeus* p. 41—the student of Greek elegance may seek those out in their own commentaries: I shall add a few points more closely connected to the argument of our passage: Aristotle, *On Memory* ch. 1. p. 29. Sylburg edition—*we do not say that the habit is memory; for the motion that occurs is imprinted, like a sort of impression of the sensation, just as those who seal with rings.* <note>original: "οὐ φαμεν τὴν ἕξιν εἶναι μνήμην... τοῖς δακτυλίοις."</note> An uncertain author, hiding under the name of Socrates, in Stobaeus's *Florilegium* LIV. p. 369. p. 409. Gaisford edition, regarding the Horn of Amalthea: *according to the horn of the ox, which is most hardworking, the worker is imprinted.* <note>original: "κατὰ δὲ τὸ κέρας... ἐνσημαίνεσθαι."</note> These same words are read in Arsenius’s *Violetum*. Gregory Nazianzen, *Oration II on the Son* p. 216. Basel edition: *either when the Father previously performed these things, or it is clear that the Father imprints the forms of the same things (read: imprints the forms), but the Word fulfills them, not like a slave, nor ignorantly, but scientifically and masterfully, and to speak more properly, fatherly.* <note>original: "ἢ πότε τοῦ πατρὸς... πατρικῶς."</note> Pythagoras in Ovid’s *Metamorphoses* XV. 169. sq. in the version by Planudes p. 664. Boissonade edition: *as pliable wax is always imprinted with new characters, and does not remain as it was, nor keep the same forms, yet is the same; so I teach that the soul is always the same through all things, but migrates into different bodies.* <note>original: "ὡς δὲ κηρὸς εὐπειθὴς... σώματα."</note>

p. 856, 3. *But the truth is, that each of those [parts] does not (sc. feel) the pain in the finger, but the part next to the finger, etc.*] <note>original: "τὸ δὲ ἀληθὲς... κ. τ. λ."</note> Viger, who filled in the defective text of Eusebius from Plotinus, says: “Ficino seems to make these and the following quite hindered passages far more intricate.” I see nothing greatly hindered, nor do I understand what Ficino has made intricate. Neither does Cudworth, who treated this passage of Plotinus in the *Intellectual System* p. 1112. sq., complain about either the Greek of Plotinus or the Latin of Ficino. Furthermore, I have explained <term>transmission</term> <note>original: "διαδόσει" (diadosis) - the process by which a sensation is passed through the body to the soul.</note> above at p. 363. E.; that entire passage should be compared with our chapter. Here I will briefly mention that doubt in Gregory of Nyssa, *On the Soul* p. 94:—*for it is doubted whether the body alone is that which feels pain, having received sensation from the soul, while the soul remains unaffected; or whether it also feels pain with the body.* <note>original: "ἀμφιβάλλεται γὰρ... τῷ σώματι."</note> More is discussed on this there.

— 12. *it is necessary to posit the perceiving subject as being such as—to be*] <note>original: "δεῖ τοιοῦτον τίθεσθαι τὸ αἰσθανόμενον, οἷον—εἶναι"</note> Viger translates: “Since indeed the parts of magnitude are different (the word *if* is in Eusebius but not in any of our Manuscripts of Plotinus), that which is sensed must be of such a kind that it remains one and the same everywhere”—adding in the notes that <term>the perceiving subject</term> <note>original: "τὸ αἰσθανόμενον"</note> in this place should not be taken actively. Unsuccessfully. For the connection and reasoning of the whole dispute teach the opposite. Consult Cudworth, who illustrated this entire argument, and whom I have also followed in enclosing the words *for of every magnitude... the other is* in parentheses. Taylor also correctly expressed <term>the perceiving subject</term> actively: “the power which perceives.”

p. 857, 4. *How then, being a magnitude, will it think that which is not a magnitude, and with the divisible think the indivisible?*] <note>original: "Πῶς οὖν μέγεθος ὂν... νοήσει"</note> Thus most of our books and Eusebius. In the margin of the Edition, *the divisible* (accusative) is written instead of *with the divisible* (dative). But the latter is preferable, and Cudworth also retained it; consult him discussing this fourth argument of Plotinus p. 1113. sq.

— 9. *the "itself" of each thing, it is necessary—to know.*] <note>original: "αὐτὸ ἑκάστου, ἀνάγκη,—γιγνώσκειν."</note> Thus also our books. Eusebius on the contrary: *each thing itself*, which reading Viger thinks is better, and the Latin version of Eusebius has it thus: “that which it understands, it is necessary to know only if it is, or becomes, free from the body.” In Eusebius it was previously read *that the mind, being pure of body, knows what occurs within.* Viger suspects: *that which is imprinted in the mind itself*. Wrongly.

— 17. *And how, if the soul were a body, could its virtues, temperance and (the "and" is not in Eusebius) justice [be preserved insofar as it participates in it?]]* <note>original: "Πῶς δ’ ἂν καὶ σώματος... δικαιοσύνη"</note> Our books have *preserved* (masculine/neuter), except that in the Medici MS A, a second hand placed *preserved* (feminine) above the line; which I personally think is Ficino’s own, who, wishing to come to the aid of a struggling sentence, changed it thus

[[vocabulary: to be imprinted, transmission, with the divisible, temperance]]

# BOOK VII. ENNEAD FOUR. pages 856—860. 253

...has been attempted. I have left that untouched for two reasons. For first, I suspect that these words, *being preserved insofar as it participates in it* <note>original: "σωζόμενον καθ’ ὅσον ἂν αὐτοῦ μεταλαμβάνῃ"</note>, belong to the end of chapter XIV, page 467, section B, line 9, and should be placed there after the words: *for nothing of being shall perish*. Secondly, because Eusebius continues the sentence, which was broken off after the word *justice*, most aptly: *and courage, and others; for would being temperate be a certain spirit, or a certain blood?* etc. Indeed, in the judgment of Viger <note>François Viger (1590–1647), a Jesuit scholar known for his work on Greek idioms and his edition of Eusebius.</note> on Eusebius page 79, we gain from this writer a remarkable supplement to the Plotinian discussion, which runs through several chapters. To this should be added all those things which are read from the beginning of the following ninth chapter, from the words *But the other nature* up to the end of the fourteenth chapter—that is, up to the words *for nothing of being shall perish*, and (if my conjecture does not deceive me) *being preserved insofar as it participates in it*. From this, these questions arise for us: First, are these truly the words of Plotinus? The Scholiast <note>An ancient or medieval commentator who wrote marginal notes (scholia) in manuscripts.</note> of the Barberini Manuscript no. 409 flatly denies it, although another in the same place clearly professes that the speech of the Plotinian passage is awkward if these are removed. The scholion of the Barberini and Marcian A manuscripts reads as follows:

<margin>
34. On the immortality of the soul and eternity.
Temperance and justice, and courage and the others.
For by spirit... [This in red.]

(Note from here: 88 lines are indicated from the red mark Q; that 88 lines were missing up to there: *therefore the soul is not a harmony*. But those starting from that point are interpolated <note>original: "ἐπείσακτοι"</note> until the point: *that they have not perished*. And there is nothing of Plotinus contained in them, as it seems to me, but of someone else. Therefore they are not even useful. Furthermore, the style is not shown to be that of the wise man Plotinus; especially since the phrase *temperance and justice, courage and the others* follows the logic of the argument, whereas the phrase *temperance and justice being preserved insofar as it participates in it* does not fit well.)
</margin>

Secondly: if these are the words of Plotinus, to whom should this truncation of the Plotinian book be imputed? To Porphyry <note>Plotinus's student and editor.</note>, whom we brought under suspicion of a similar crime above on page 364, D? If you assume this, it must be thought that Eusebius took these from Eustochius's edition of Plotinus's works. Or to the copyists? This is more probable because in several manuscripts of Plotinus's Enneads, these are read in their entirety. However it may be: we have decided that these very things ought to be inserted in this place from Eusebius and our own books.

**p. 858, 1. and courage etc.]** From this word, you will not find what follows here in Eusebius at that location in Plotinus; neither Hopper nor Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the famous Renaissance translator of Plotinus into Latin.</note> represents them. They are, however, of the Plotinian character, as they connect most aptly with the preceding parts, and the Royal Manuscripts and the Montacutius manuscript recognize them. Certainly, those things which follow after *justice* in Plotinus are either spoken or end with no sense. Thus Eusebius will compensate for this so remarkable fragment, along with those things which he had borrowed from Plotinus until now, not without interest. —Viger. Furthermore, in these he seems to touch upon the opinions of Empedocles, or perhaps rather Critias and the rest of the philosophers; concerning whom see Cicero in *Tusculan Disputations* I. 9, where see Davis, and compare Stobaeus, *Physical Eclogues* I. 52, pages 796—798, Heeren edition, and Gregory of Nyssa, *On the Soul*, page 90. —Creuzer.

**— 7. but then]** I gave *then* <note>original: "οὖν"</note> from both manuscripts, not *not* <note>original: "οὐ"</note> as before. —Vig.

**— 8. of cold]** Thus the two Royal and the Montacutius manuscripts; not the standard form for "cold," but he seemed to look toward that Homeric usage in *Odyssey* 10. 555: *longing for the cool air he lay down, heavy with wine.* —Vig.

**p. 859, 1. they are ignorant, that even]** These few but necessary words we have supplied from the Montacutius manuscript. *These things* <note>original: "ταῦτα"</note>, which follows, would be better absent. —Vig. Or one should read *them* <note>original: "αὐτά"</note>. —Cr.

**— 2. incorporeal, these things]** And both these words we added from the same Montacutius manuscript: likewise the words *concerning the soul*. —Vig.

**— 8. which it can]** From the same Montacutius. —Vig.

**p. 860, 3. as they say being]** For *being* <note>original: "οὖσαν"</note> one should read *to be* <note>original: "εἶναι"</note>. —Vig. Perhaps it should be punctuated: *—to be, being, as they say, a body, but different.* —Cr.

**— 9. And further etc.]** Again he seems to touch upon the opinions of Dicaearchus and Aristoxenus; concerning whom we saw above in chapter III of Plotinus, page 458, A. —Cr.

**— ibid. And further etc.]** Previously it was read *but if the soul being a body*. Montacutius: *and further if the soul being a body*. The *and further* <note>original: "ἔτι δὲ"</note> is approved by me; *soul* seemed redundant; for there follows from the same Montacutius *or the soul passed through*, which words were missing in the earlier edition. —Viger.

**-> ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS <-**

**p. 860, 10. τοῖς ἄλλοις]** Added from the same [manuscript] of Montague. ***Vig.***
— **11. οὐδὲν ἐνεργείᾳ εἰσεῖναι]** In the prior edition [abbrev: *edit.* → *editione*] these were missing: ἐνεργείᾳ εἰσεῖναι. Montague read οὐδὲ ἐνέργεια εἰσεῖναι. I have corrected it to οὐδὲν ἐνεργείᾳ, in the dative case. The verb εἰσεῖναι can be retained; however, I would prefer ἐνεῖναι, as a little later: ἐνείη τοῖς σωμ. [it might be in the bodies] not εἰσείη. ***Vig.***
**p. 861, 3. οὐ σώματος]** Perhaps τοῦ or ὅλου [of the whole]. ***Cr.***
— **7. φύσει μὲν]** It seems it should be read φύσιν μὲν, as a little later in line 7. ***Viger.*** — He touches upon Chrysippus, who is cited thus in Plutarch, *De Repugnantiis Stoicorum* p. 1052. F. p. 290. Wytt.: (Chrysippus) thinks the fetus in the womb is nourished by nature like a plant; but when it is born, the breath, being cooled by the air and tempered, changes and becomes a living being; hence it is not without reason that the soul [*psyche*] is named after this cooling [*psyxin*]. Cf. also p. 1053. D. and consult Wyttenbach on Plutarch, *De S. N. V.* p. 84. p. 408. Oxford ed. and Baguet in *Chrysippeis* p. 102. — We touched upon the etymology above at p. 379. A. ***Cr.***
— **17. εἰ τὸ δυνάμει,]** I think it should read εἰ γὰρ τὸ δυνάμει, εἰ γένοιτο; I am pleased to retain what follows. But if, as I would prefer, γένοιτο is deleted, there will be no need for the particle γὰρ: nor will anything be lacking for the integrity of this passage. ***Viger.***
**p. 862, 2. ὃ οὐ δυνάμει]** Thus Montague correctly. In the prior edition [abbrev: *edit.* → *editione*] ὃ and οὐ were missing. ***Vig.***
— **9. 'Ἐπεὶ δὲ]** Both Royal MSS: ἐπὶ δὲ ἄλλης φύσεως. correctly. But if ἐπεὶ is retained, it is taken for ἔπειτα [thereafter], as I remember observing above in Plato and Plutarch: and then it must be read ἐπεὶ δὲ ἄλλης φύσεως πέρι, δεῖ κ. τ. λ. [But since concerning another nature, it is necessary...]. Unless, however, one prefers to understand either χάριν or ἕνεκα [for the sake of] in that genitive case. ***Viger.*** — Regarding this opinion on the soul as a harmony [*harmonia*], the dispute in the *Phaedo* is well known; on that passage consult Wyttenbach p. 248 sqq. and the same in *Philomathia* III. 70. Cf. what we placed above at p. 307. E. and p. 458. A. Gregory of Nyssa, *De Anima* p. 95 seq., excerpted the discussion of Plato and Plotinus by which this opinion is refuted (where read Σιμμίας for Σιμίας). ***Cr.***
— **16. Ὅτι δὲ ἀδύνατον]** Plato in *Phaedo* 388, 390, 391 and Aristotle in *De Anima* Book I, cap. 4 refute the same Harmony. Plotinus’ arguments, if you except the last one, are almost the same as the Platonic ones, but gathered more briefly and precisely. ***Viger.***
**p. 863, 2. ὑγεία ἂν εἴη]** Aristotle in the cited place: "it is more fitting to speak of health, and generally of bodily virtues, than of the soul." ***Viger.***
— **5. τὴν ἁρμονίαν]** These words were transposed in the prior edition. For it was read: ταῖς χορδαῖς λόγον ἔχοντα τὴν ἁρμονίαν παρ’ αὐτῇ. Far more suitable is the connection which we have restored from Montague. ***Viger.***
— **7. παρ’ αὐτῶν [Eus. αὐτῶν], οὔτ’ ἐνταῦθα]** Montague also filled these gaps before the lacunae. ***Viger.***
— **10. τὴν τάξιν κ. τ. λ.]** Briefer and better than in the Montague Codex: καὶ τὴν τάξιν οὐκ ἐκ τῆς ψυχῆς ἀλλ’ αὐτὴν ἐκ τῆς αὐτομάτου τάξεως τὴν ὑποστ. εἰληφ. ***Viger.***
— **17. Ἀρχὴ γὰρ κινήσεως ἥδε χορηγοῦσα τοῖς ἄλλοις κίνησιν]** These are drawn from the most noble passage of Plato in the *Phaedrus* p. 245. C: "Every soul is immortal. For that which is always in motion is immortal; but that which moves another and is moved by another, having a cessation of motion, has a cessation of life," etc., which Cicero translated in *Tusc. Disp.* I. 23 and in the *Dream of Scipio* cap. 8. [Cic. *De Rep.* VI. 25. p. 504. sqq. ed. Moser. coll. ibid. p. 537. sqq.] and many have expressed, among them Origen, *De Principiis* III. 1. p. 108. sq. Rue. — Soon the formula: ἣν ἀνώλεθρον καὶ ἀθάνατον εἶναι δεῖ [which must be imperishable and immortal], taken from the *Phaedo*, found many imitators. See *Phaedo* p. 106. B. p. 104. Bekk. Consult Wyttenbach on that passage p. 280—283 and our annotation on Proclus’ *Instit. Theolog.* c. 187. p. 278. sq., where the forms ἀνώλεθρον and ἀνώλεθρον are discussed, and several passages of philosophers, including this Plotinian one, are cited.
**p. 865, 6. Λάβωμεν δὲ ψυχὴν, μὴ τὴν ἐν σώματι (...) ἐπιθυμίας ἀλόγους καὶ θυμοὺς προσλαβοῦσαν]** (Most of our [manuscripts] do not recognize the article). After the word θυμοὺς in Cod. Vindob. A. [Vienna Codex], the following occurs: τε δικαιοσύνη ἀνδρία τε καὶ αἱ ἄλλαι ἀρεταὶ κ. τ. λ., that is, those things which in other Codices are placed at the end of Chapter VIII p. 463. C. and which we interposed there from Eusebius’ *P. E.* and our own books. But the Vienna Codex ends at the words: καὶ ὡς τὰ μὲν ἄρχει τε καὶ ἐπιστατεῖ καὶ μάχεται πολλαχῇ, (omitting τῷ σώματι [the body]) which are read in Eusebius p. 835. A. lin. 7 and 8.

**p. 865, 11. Εἰ οὖν τοιοῦτον ἡ ψυχὴ—φρόνησις γὰρ καὶ ἀρετὴ ἀληθὴς—ἅτε θείων μετὸν αὐτῷ διὰ συγγένειαν καὶ τὸ ὁμοούσιον.]** Thus I have emended the common reading μεστὸν [full] by the authority of several books, one of which has θείων μετὸν [sharing in divine things]. Lucas Holstenius, applying this passage of Plotinus to Sallustius *On the Gods and the World* (at cap. 8. p. 121. Orelli), wrote: ἅτε θείων μεστὸν αὐτῶν. I would not believe this came from any Codex. Even Ficinus expressed our reading. For the rest, as far as the argument is concerned, one should compare, besides Sallustius (loc. cit.), Plotinus himself above p. 54. C—F. and the notes there, and Proclus on Plato’s *Timaeus*, where he treats the difference between the divine and human soul, p. 314.
**p. 866, 15. ὡς πολλάκις αὐτῷ δόξαι τοῦτο δὴ καλῶς εἰρῆσθαι· χαίρετ’, ἐγὼ δ’ ὑμῖν θεὸς ἄμβροτος,]** A verse of Empedocles from the beginning of the *Purifications* [*Katharmoi*], which Diogenes Laertius preserved in full, VIII. 62. Cf. ibid. § 54 and § 66; others report the particle differently. See Davis on Cic. *Tusc.* I. 9; the interpreters on Diog. Laert. (loc. cit.); Fabricius on Sextus Empiricus *Adv. Mathem.* I. § 302. p. 283; Sturz on Empedocles p. 466 sq., who noted various readings. Cf. ibid. p. 530 and p. 646. Jacobs also presented it in the *Paralipomena to the Greek Anthology* I. nr. 75. p. 665 and in the *Palatine Anthology* nr. 569. p. 202, thus:
*O friends, who dwell in the great city by the yellow Akragas,*
*high in the citadel, mindful of good deeds,*
*hail! I am to you an immortal god, no longer mortal,*
*I go among all honored, as it seems,*
*crowned with fillets and blooming wreaths.*
Furthermore, as the entire speech of Empedocles has much Homeric flavor, so does that θεὸς ἄμβροτος [immortal god]. See the Scholia on *Iliad* Ω. 460. Yet, as far as I know, no one who has treated these things has mentioned this Plotinian passage. Similar formulas, however, are found everywhere in Marbles. Thus, to use this example, in that inscription related by the illustrious Münter to the Samothracian mysteries (in *Antiquarr. Abhandll.* p. 183), we read:
*I, a youth, call to you, dear to God, no longer mortal.*
Likewise in Gruter p. DCCLIX. 4.
*Formerly mortal, now a sharer of the gods.*
In the same p. MCXXIII. 7:
*Notable kinsman! Why do you lament me*
*taken away to the stars of heaven? Cease to weep for a god.*
These inscriptions Bened. Bendtsen inserted and explained in the first specimen of *Mystic Marbles* p. 8—11 [p. 3. 8. 11. Copenhagen 1819. 4.]. I wonder, however, that the Empedoclean verses did not occur to him, which were to be applied above all these inscriptions. Others taught that those who lived a just and honest life become **genii** (*daimones*). See Plato, *Cratylus* p. 397. 398; Libanius, *Declamat. pro Socrat.* p. 264 and Jac. Morelli there; and Olympiodorus on *Alcibiades I* p. 15. sq.
**p. 867, 4. ὥσπερ ἀγάλματα ἐν αὐτῇ ἱδρυμένα ὁρῶσα—οἷον εἰ χρυσὸς ἔμψυχος εἴη κ. τ. λ.]** The source of this passage is partly in Alcibiades’ speech in Plato’s *Symposium* p. 216. E., and partly in the *Sophist* p. 228. C. See what we said above on the twin passage of Plotinus p. 54. F. Cf. also below p. 520. F. and the note there.
— **11. Περὶ τοιούτου χρήματος—ὡς οὐκ ἀθάνατον]** See Plato, *Phaedo* p. 105. p. 102. sqq. Bekker, where Wyttenbach in his note p. 279. sq. presents this passage of Plotinus, adding: "Therefore (Plotinus) restrains those who reject the force of this Platonic argument with two other arguments. The first is: ἣ ἀναλύσουσιν ὡς σύνθετον—μοῖραν δέχεσθαι, i.e., *either they will dissolve the soul into parts as being composite, and that until they arrive at one such part which commands itself and the rest, which is immortal, for which it is impious and against nature’s laws to undergo death.* This is that argument we touched upon in *Psychology* V. VIII. p. LV. The second: ἢ πάθος ἐπακτὸν, ἐνέργεια ζῶσα: *or saying that life is an accident of matter, they will be forced to admit that the source from which such an accident comes to matter is immortal and incapable of the contrary of what it brings (i.e., immune from death).* For there is one nature living in act [*actu*]. And thus he recalls the demonstration to that decree: that there is one soul of the entire nature, of which our individual souls are parts. Proclus, *Instit. Theolog.* § CLXXXVII and sq. (p. 278. sqq. ed. Frankfurt), refers to this *Phaedo* passage likewise for interpretation; consult our note there. The later argument ἢ πάθος—ἀδεκτον οὖ τοῦ ἐναντίου ᾧ ἐπιφέρει follows from the axiom which Proclus maintains for another purpose against some Platonists in Plato's *Parmenides* p. 209 ed. Cousin (Vol. V), where he places both other things and these: 'and the cause of life has filled itself with life; and...

### PAGE 263
**[original page: 256]**

**-> ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS <-**

...the cause of perfection makes itself perfect.' Moreover, Tiedemann, in his book on the *Causes of Contemplative Philosophy*, III. p. 365. sqq., admires these ingeniously devised points of Plotinus, yet does not approve them in every respect.
**p. 868, 8. Ἔτι εἰ πᾶσαν ψυχὴν φήσουσι φθαρτὴν,]** Plotinus seems to refer to the Stoics and perhaps the Epicureans. Concerning the Epicureans, see above at p. 457. cap. 3. beginning. Concerning the Stoics, Cicero, *Tusc.* I. 32 and Davis there; Wyttenb. on Plut. *De S. N. V.* p. 400. p. 78. Lugd. ed. Oxford ed.; Van Lynden on Panaetius p. 70; Baguet in *Chrysippeis* p. 101. sq.
— **18. Ψυχὴ δὲ μία καὶ ἁπλῆ ἐνέργεια οὖσα ἐν τῷ ζῆν φύσις, οὐ τοίνυν ταύτῃ φθαρήσεται.]** Marsilius [Ficino] also expressed these, except that before ἐν τῷ ζῆν he thought of καὶ. Taylor, following him, translated: "But soul being one simple energy, and a nature characterised by life, cannot be corrupted as a composite." The Codices persist in the common reading. Wyttenbach suspects: φύσει ἐστί. For on Plato’s *Phaedo* p. 197, after he touched upon Plotinus’ passage p. 557. A., he continues: "now that other thing, διαλυθῆναι ταύτῃ ᾗπερ συνετέθη [to be dissolved in the way it was composed], has this force: that the whole is divided into those parts from which it is composed, and in that manner by which it is composed: like a body into the four elements of which it consists, the bonds holding these parts together having been dissolved. Plotinus looks here (our passage follows—: ἐν τῷ ζῆν φύσις F. φύσει ἐστί :) οὐ τοίνυν ταύτῃ φθαρήσεται. Then he recounts various kinds of composition and dissolution. Aeneas of Gaza p. 66: 'Does not the composite, when dissolved, return again to those things from which it was composed?' For there are various kinds of cohesion of bodies, later celebrated by the Stoics: as in Plutarch, *Precept. Conjug.* p. 142. E: 'Of bodies, some they say are from separate parts, like a fleet or an army; others from joined parts, like a house or a ship; others are united and grown together, as each living being is,' where we have given more on this matter." (See the observations on that passage p. 892. Oxford ed. Add Olympiodorus on *Alcibiades I* p. 25.). Then he continues the explanation: "As to what the Platonists mean by σύνθετον [composite], composed of **parts placed outside parts**, as they are commonly called, filling space, extended, it is understood from the frequency of examples: e.g., Plutarch, *De Animae Procreat.* p. 1022. E; *Adv. Stoicc.* p. 1085. C; Plotinus p. 160. D. E. 161. C. D. 162. D. 163. E. 165. A. 166. E. 310. C. 313. E. 457. A. 466. A. C. 557. A; Albinus, *Doctrin. Platon.* p. 372. D; Aeneas of Gaza p. 59. 66; Zacharias of Mitylene p. 175; Olympiodorus on *Phaedo* Cod. III. p. 40. and elsewhere often: Cod. I. p. 63. 185." Then with Ficino I wrote: ἀλλ’ ἆρα (for ἄρα) μερισθεῖσα, κερματιζομένη ἀπόλοιτο ἄν; with a question mark. — Perhaps before κερματιζομένη [fragmented] the word καὶ [and] fell out besides. Plato, moreover, in *Republic* p. 395. B: "human nature seems to me to have been fragmented [*katakekermatishai*] into even smaller pieces." Plutarch, *De Animae Procreat.* p. 1020. L. p. 153. Wyttenb.; —"whether it be cut, the units being fragmented into parts." Cf. Schleusner’s Lexicon of the N.T. under κερματιστής. Plotinus above in Eusebius *P. E.* p. 833. A: "the body being fragmented, the same quality remains in each part." Cf. Plotinus below V. 8. 9; VI. 2. 2; VI. 2. 12. — Then with Ficino and the Vatican Codex I removed the question mark after ψυχή, and placed it after φθοράν.
**p. 869, 7. Πῶς οὖν—ἥδε (thus I gave from the Vatican for ἡ δὲ) εἰς σῶμα ἔρχεται;]** Taylor, at this place in his version, presents a passage of Proclus on the *Timaeus* p. 343, translated into English, in which this philosopher speaks of the descent of souls. But we spoke of this doctrine above at p. 381. sqq. and will speak of it shortly at the beginning of the following book p. 468. A. Next for ὅσος, "whosoever," Ficinus expressed ὅσον, "how much." The MSS retain the former, and it corresponds in the following to ὃ δ’ ἄν. The same shortly after expressed οἶδεν, "he knows." But most books have εἶδεν, "he saw."
— **12. —ὥσπερ κυοῦν ἀπ’ αὐτῶν, καὶ ὠδῖνον γεννῆσαι]** He imitates Plato, *Symposium* p. 206 near the end, p. 436. Bekk.: "Whence to the one who is pregnant and already swelling, there is much fluttering about the beautiful, because of the release of the possessor from great labor-pains." Cf. *Republic* VI. p. 490. p. 285. Bekk.; *Timaeus* p. 86. p. 139; *Laws* IV. 717. p. 357; *Epistle II* p. 313. A. For the words and sentiments compare Proclus on *Alcibiades I* p. 150; Olympiodorus on the same p. 7: —"as one in labor-pains toward this," as one who was prone to that. See what we cited there in the Notes and confer Plotinus himself above p. 346. D. Add Damascius, *De Principiis* p. 79 ed. Kopp: "so that even the mind, or...

**-> BOOK VII. ENNEAD FOUR. p. 868—870. 257 <-**

...the mind, being a spectator of certain qualities, is in labor with the concept of that nature, but not even he brings it forward, but on the contrary, and gathers toward itself (or toward himself?) the labor-pain—if somehow we might be able—to run back toward that labor-pain."
**p. 870, 7. Περὶ δὲ τῆς τῶν ἄλλων ζώων ψυχῆς, ὅσαι μὲν—εἰ δὲ ἔστιν ἄλλο τι εἶδος ψυχῆς]** Plotinus distinguishes between those souls of brutes which have degenerated into human bodies, and those which, having never been in a human body, serve for the animating of the bodies of brutes. The source of this doctrine is in Plato’s *Timaeus* p. 42. p. 45. Bekk. —"the one who fails in these (virtues) would change into the nature of a woman in the second birth; and if he did not cease from vice even in these, according to the likeness of the manner of his life’s birth, he would change into some such beastly nature," etc. Regarding which I do not know if Ficino did not err when he says Plato (c. 19) established that the souls of brutes are transitory in both soul and body. Be that as it may: Christian philosophers receded furthest from that opinion which would place the souls of brutes as differing only in degree from human ones, and they established that those would utterly perish. Basil the Great, after he placed the souls of beasts as having arisen from blood, flesh, and thus from the earth, continues in *Hexaemeron Homil. VIII* p. 99. B. C: —"do not think that it (the soul of brutes) is older than the substance of their body, nor that it remains after the dissolution of the flesh. Flee the trifles of the arrogant philosophers, who are not ashamed to place their own souls and those of dogs as of the same kind; those who say they themselves once became both women and shrubs and sea-fish," etc. These are cast against Plato no less than against Plotinus. Most teachers of the Church support him. Antiochus of Ptolemais in Ang. Mai’s *Collect. Vatic.* I. p. 81. sq.: "God making the other four-footed animals, produced their souls along with their bodies; but molding man, he first prepares the organ of the body; and then having created the soul, he put it in, so that in this too he might show the superiority of man; since the other animals and beasts, being dissolved by death, also cause the soul to vanish along with the body," etc. Photius pronounces in the same opinion to *Amphilochius* CXLIX. 7. ibid. p. 295. sq. That Plotinus attributes a vital soul certainly to plants as well, in that matter he follows his Aristotle no less than Plato. Aristotle, *De Anima* I. 5. p. 19. Sylb.: "for plants appear to live, not participating in locomotion or sensation, and many of the animals do not have intellect." Cf. also Tiedemann, *Geist der spekulativen Philosophie* III. p. 367.
— **13. Εἰ δὲ τὴν ἀνθρώπου ψυχὴν τριμερῆ οὖσαν τῷ συνθέτῳ λυθήσεσθαι,]** The word δεῖ [it is necessary] must be repeated from the preceding. Since certain scribes did not understand this brevity of Plotinus, they changed it to λυθήσεται. As for the argument, this reasoning, which places the soul as composed of three parts (τριμερῆ/composite): reason, spirit, and desire, should neither be confused with that other reasoning by which philosophers either said or denied the soul to be composite (σύνθετον) **from parts placed outside parts**, as they are commonly called, filling space, extended, as Wyttenbach teaches on the *Phaedo* p. 197. sq.; nor even more so with that Trichotomy of the sacred writers, by which three parts were attributed to human nature: body (τὸ σῶμα), soul (ἡ ψυχή), and mind or spirit (τὸ πνεῦμα), concerning which distribution Herm. Olshausen recently disputed in his Diatribe: *On the trichotomy of human nature received by the writers of the N.T.* Königsberg 1826. — Of that tripartite nature which Plotinus touched upon here, the source is in the same *Timaeus* p. 70. p. 98. sq. Bekk. Cf. the other *Timaeus*, the so-called Locrus, p. 556. Gale; join *Republic* IX. p. 734; Philo Judaeus, *Legis Allegor.* III. p. 310. Pfeiff.; Plutarch, *De Vultu Lunae* p. 943. A; *Placita Philosophorum* IV. 4; Diog. Laert. VIII. 30; Himerius p. 884 and Wernsdorf there; Alcinous, *De Doctr. Platon.* 24. p. 504; Proclus on the *Timaeus* p. 326, on the *Republic* p. 399; Olympiodorus on *Alcibiades I* p. 4. 65. 81. 172. 203; and confer Plotinus himself above p. 398. B. C. D. and p. 420. sqq. — Soon to the words: τὰς μὲν καθαρὰς—τὸ προσπλασθὲν ἐν τῇ γενέσει ἀφήσειν [the pure souls... will let go of what was added in birth]. Cf. the cited passage of *Timaeus* p. 42. A; Porphyry, *De Abstinentia* I. 30. p. 49. Rhoer: "if we are to return to truly proper things, (we must) set aside all things which we have received from the mortal nature along with the attachment to them," etc., where Rhoerius both compares other things and the words of the Apostle II. Corinthians V. 1. Add Libanius’ *Declamation for Socrates* (at the end of Aristides *against Leptines* ed. Jac. Morelli) p. 258.

...*apoleitai*, perhaps those words should be placed which are read above p. 463. C. line 6: σωζόμενον (for σωζομένης) καθ’ ὅσον ἂν αὐτοῦ μεταλαμβάνῃ [being saved in as much as it may participate in it]. See the note on that passage.
**p. 871, 2. ἃ δὲ καὶ πρὸς τοὺς δεομένους πίστεως αἰσθήσει κεκραμένης κ. τ. λ.]** I did not hesitate with the Vatican Codex and Ficino, whom Taylor also follows, to write thus instead of κεκρατημένης [held fast], which is read in the Edition. The opposite is to separate or **withdraw the mind from the senses**, to use that Tullian phrase (*Tusc.* I. 16. 38.). For the rest, because Plotinus subjects to his demonstration (τῇ ἀποδείξει) those things which, taken from history, create faith (πίστιν): in this he follows both the authority of other philosophers and indeed that of Plato himself, to whom Cicero also applied himself in the *Tusculans* I. 12—16: "Thus that one thing was ingrained in those ancients, whom Ennius calls **cascos**, that there is sensation in death, and that a man is not so deleted by the departure of life that he utterly perishes: and this is permitted to be understood not only by many other things, but also by **pontifical law and the ceremonies of tombs**," etc. Cf. on pontifical law and the rest which belong here, Cic. *Topic.* XXIII. 90 and *De Legg.* II. 22. p. 321 ed. Moser, and the notes there. Now let us see specifically concerning the following: ἐκ τε ὧν θεοὶ ἀνεῖλον—ἱλάσκεσθαι. The books of historians and other writers are full of oracles of this kind, especially Pausanias, Porphyry, Stobaeus, and others. The antiquity of this matter is argued by the Homeric **nekyia** (Odyssey λ. 23. sqq.) "And Homer bears witness, showing the son of Laertes, at least according to the instructions of Circe, both having dug the trench and performed the libations." These are the words of Theodoret, *Therapeut.* VIII. p. 910 Schulz. Wyttenbach presents others on Plutarch’s *Consol. Apollonii* p. 752. If you require oracles, go to Porphyry in Eusebius *P. E.* IV. p. 145—147 and V. p. 230; cf. Pausan. VI. 9. 3 and Aelian *V. H.* XI. 3. (where concerning Cleomedes by the command of the oracle heroic honors were imparted by the Astypalaeans—). Soon τιμάς τε νέμειν τεθνηκόσιν—εἰς τοὺς ἀπεληλυθότας [to grant honors to the dead... for those who have departed]. Plato in Diogenes Laertius III. 83: "There are three kinds of justice: the first toward the gods, the second toward men, the third toward the deceased." Concerning this kind he continues: "those who take care of monuments clearly (practice justice) toward those who have gone away." Hence the **justa** among the ancients and the **laws of the Manes**, which it suffices to have named by word at this place (and cf. Odyssey α. 291; Iliad Ω. 38 with Scholia; Wasse on Sallust’s *Jugurtha* cap. XI; and Wyttenbach on Plato’s *Phaedo* p. 293.). Plotinus continues: Πολλαὶ δὲ ψυχαὶ—οὐκ ἀπέστησαν τοῦ εὐεργετεῖν ἀνθρώπους [And many souls... did not cease from benefiting men]. Hesiod, *Works* 122 (124. sq.): "These are genii [*daimones*] of great Zeus by his counsels, Noble, earthly, guardians of mortal men;" concerning the souls of those who lived a good and just life; which verses, slightly changed, Plato turns into his own discussion both in the *Cratylus* p. 397 and in the *Republic* V. p. 469; likewise Olympiodorus on *Alcibiades I* p. 16. Conf. Cic. *Tusc.* I. 12. 28, where concerning the Tyndarid brothers: "Who are said not only to have been helpers in the battles of the Roman people’s victory, but also messengers." The end of the Plotinian passage: αἱ δὲ καὶ μαντεῖα ἀποδείξαμεναι κ. τ. λ. [those who also showed oracles...] as for what concerns this, these pertain to **necromancy**, concerning which consult the same Tully [Cicero] in *Tusculan Questions* I. 16. 37 and *De Divinatione* I. 58. p. 286 ed. Moser, and in both places Davis and the rest of the interpreters. We have treated these somewhat more accurately for this reason: lest we should judge, as is commonly done, that Plotinus drew these arguments for the immortality of souls from the spirit of his own age, but rather that he applied them after the example of Plato and even more ancient ones.

**p. 872, 7. ΠΕΡΙ ΤΗΣ ΕΙΣ ΤΑ ΣΩΜΑΤΑ ΚΑΘΟΔΟΥ ΤΗΣ ΨΥΧΗΣ.]** [On the Descent of the Soul into Bodies]. In some books the article τῆς is absent before ψυχῆς: not badly. This book is sixth in order. See Porphyry, *Life of Plotinus* c. 4 and 25. Plotinus touches on this place often in these Enneads, not rejecting even the delights of fables, being an imitator of Plato in this part as well. Cf. e.g. what is read above p. 381. A. We explained the mythological aspects of this place both in the *Herodotean commentaries* p. 307. sqq. and in the *Symbolica*, especially Vol. III. p. 424. sqq. Add (Th. Taylor) *Dissertation on the Eleusinian and Bacchic mysteries* p. 9—16. 55. 79. and Bened. Bendtsen’s *Marmorr. Mysticc. Specim. I.* p. 7. sq. He had pursued this argument on the Soul in the books *On the Return of the Soul* (περὶ ἀνόδου τῆς ψυχῆς) as is clear from Augustine’s Book X c. 29 of *The City of God*, concerning which consult Luc. Holstenius on the *Life and Writings of Porphyry* cap. 8. p. 46. sqq. Also to be compared are those things which...

### PAGE 266
**[original page: 259]**

**-> BOOK VIII. ENNEAD FOUR. p. 871, 872. 259 <-**

...the same disciple of Plotinus [Porphyry] placed in Book I § 30 *On Abstinence* p. 49 of Rhoerius. But the sources of this Plotinian book are to be sought especially in Plato’s *Phaedrus* p. 246 sq., in *Republic* X. p. 617 sqq. and in the *Timaeus* p. 41 sqq., to omit other dialogues, concerning which see Wyttenbach’s *Disputat. de placito immortalit. animm.* (before the *Phaedo*) p. XVI seq. and as for the descent, to Plutarch *De S. N. V.* p. 113. p. 444 ed. Oxford. From Aristotle there is a memorable testimony of Proclus on the *Timaeus* p. 338. For after he had spoken of Plato’s discussions, he continues thus: — "Now Aristotle also, having emulated him in his treatise on the soul, treating it physically, mentioned neither the descents of the soul nor its allotments, but in his dialogues he treated them separately (perhaps 'concerning them') and laid down the preceding account." That the Stagirite had treated these in his dialogues, therefore, is proof that he wished these discussions to be accommodated only to popular discipline. In the same place Proclus touches upon this doubt debated in the schools of the philosophers: whether the whole soul descends, or not; — "so that what Plotinus says would be a newer account, the one not commanding the whole of it (the soul) to descend." Simplicius, *Proem in Aristotel. De Anima* end: — "wherefore we shall neither establish that any part of it (the soul) remains always in the same way and purely, according to Plotinus, nor that it proceeds entirely in the inclination toward generation. But it proceeds whole and remains sincerely in the inclination toward second things." Hermias touched on the same opinion in *Phaedrus* p. 147. I placed the passage above at Plotinus p. 361. A. Cf. however the last chapter of this Plotinian book p. 476.
Neither Plotinus alone, but also Pythagoras, Plato, and the rest were contested by Christian writers especially because of that decree from which this entire doctrine depends. I mean the **προϋπάρξιν** [pro-yparxin/pre-existence] of souls, which the Scholastics call **praeexistentia**. Since the followers of Plato and Plotinus stubbornly retained it on one side, and the Christian teachers vehemently refuted it on the other, except for Origen and those who acted with him; from there a great crop of books, decrees, and canons arose, even until the times of John of Damascus and later. I will taste only a few. Clement of Alexandria in a fragment of the eighth book of *Stromata* in Ang. Mai’s *Collect. Vaticana* T. I. 3. p. 83: "God made us as not pre-existing; for it was necessary for us to know where we were, if we pre-existed and how and why we came here; but if we did not pre-existed, God alone is the cause of generation. Therefore as he made those not being, so also he saves those who have come to be by his own grace." Antiochus of Ptolemais brings other arguments for this matter in the same place page 81: "God making the other four-footed animals produced the souls along with the bodies; but molding man he first prepares the organ of the body; and then having created the soul he put it in, so that in this too he might show the superiority of man," etc. Then he subjects this other argument: — "and (God) does not make the soul before the body, so that (man) might not become an eyewitness of the things being made (perhaps 'made'); he does not make the soul present at the creation, so that he might not boast as a co-worker of God." The pronouncements of Cyril, Eleutherius, Eustathius of Antioch, and Peter of Alexandria of the same opinion are presented in the same place pag. 76 sqq. Canons of Councils on the same argument exist [e.g.] in the first Canon of the Fifth Council of Constantinople; these are read in Fabricius *B. Gr.* Vol. XII p. 187 Harles: "If anyone prizes the mythical pre-existence of souls, and the monstrous restoration [*apokatastasis*] following it, let him be anathema." Cf. Canon II, VII, XV. And this very doctrine is called by Damascene "the absurdity of Origen’s trifles." Finally, Nicephorus Nathanael rebukes Plotinus himself on this account in a peculiar *Antithetic*, likewise in a *Dialogue* by either the same writer or one holding the same view. We have seen to it that these booklets are appended to these Enneads.
For the rest, Thom. Taylor made this book of Plotinus English in *Five Books of Plotinus* p. 251. sqq.

**p. 873, 1. Ὁ μὲν γὰρ Ἡράκλειτος—ὥσπερ καὶ αὐτὸς ζητήσας εὗρεν.]** The MSS provide no help. Ficino seems to have read: καὶ τὸ μεταβάλλον οὐκ ἀναπαύεται [and that which changes does not rest]. But an ailing limb cannot be cured with such a light remedy. Distinguish and read: "For Heraclitus, who exhorted us to seek this, (positing necessary exchanges from contraries, and speaking of a way up and down, and that changing is to rest, and that it is a weariness to toil and be ruled by the same things) gave material for divining, neglecting to make the account plain to us; as if it were necessary perhaps to seek in him, just as he himself seeking found." Iamblichus in Stobaeus *Eclog.* I. 52. p. 906. Heeren: "For Heraclitus posits necessary exchanges from contraries, he supposed that souls traverse a way up and down, and that to remain in the same things is weariness, but to change brings rest." Ibid. p. 894. sq.—: "according to Heraclitus, of the rest in changing." Where Heeren: "It is certain however from Diog. L. IX. 7 etc. that he (Heraclitus) placed all things as subject to change and arisen from it; nor did he determine otherwise concerning the soul, since he called it 'the always flowing' and 'the always moving,' as Aristotle *De Anima* I. 2 testifies. When therefore he called its conjunction with the body 'rest from change,' or rather contended that the former arose from the latter, he seems to have posited it, not otherwise than Empedocles, as being included in the body to pay penalties." That I placed ἄρχεσθαι [to be ruled] for ἄρχεσθαι [to begin], I am moved by other causes and especially this passage of Hermes in Stobaeus *Eclog.* I. p. 768: — "but (the mind) leaves behind the (soul) attached to the body and strangled by it below." I gave more on this entire Heraclitean passage in *Dionysus* p. 83—86. Cf. also above at p. 97. D. and on the obscurity of Heraclitus cf. Schleiermacher in Wolf and Buttmann’s *Mus. de Alterth. Namely, Empedocles taught that souls are damned to exile because of crimes and are forced to leave celestial things, and thus are bound to these mortal bodies: Plutarch, *De Esu Carnium* I. 7. p. 996. Wherefore I prefer in the *Phaedo*...

Namely, Empedocles taught that to pay the penalties of crimes, souls are thrust down through the elements as if into this world, which he called a cavern [*antron*] and a joyless place and the meadow of Ate, since in this terrestrial and humid place they act as if in a cavern, by whose exhalations the souls lose their wings and fall utterly. — **7. ἐν Τιμαίῳ—ἄνευ δὲ ψυχῆς οὐκ οἷόν τε ἦν τοῦτο γενέσθαι]** [In the Timaeus... but without a soul it was not possible for this to happen]. Plato in the *Timaeus* p. 30. a. p. 26. Bekk.: "Calculating therefore, he found that from the things visible by nature, nothing lacking intellect would ever be a work more beautiful than that which possesses intellect as a whole, and moreover that it is impossible for intellect to be present to anything apart from a soul. Because of this calculation, having composed intellect in soul, and soul in body, he fabricated the whole, so that it might be a work most beautiful and best according to nature. Thus therefore, according to the likely account, one must say that this world became a living being endowed with soul and intellect in truth through the providence of God." (cf. our Plotinus above p. 372. B. C. and p. 397. D.). The same Plato in *Timaeus* p. 34. p. 31. Bekk.: —"for all these reasons he generated it as a happy god." To which words Lindau in the notes: "Plotinus IV. 8. 1 looks to this passage; he says: ἐν Τιμαίῳ, speaking about this whole, he both praises the world and calls it a happy god. These words have such weight that they prevent anyone from thinking that θεός [god] should be rewritten in Plato. For the world is from the number of gods, whom the philosopher mentions below as having been created by the supreme artisan."

**p. 876, 2. Similarly in Plato’s *Symposium* p. 208. c. Bekker p. 439 gave τέλεοι for τέλειοι, as it is likewise varied in the *Cratylus* p. 403. e. where see Heindorf. Moreover, Plotinus looks back here to the same passage of the Platonic *Phaedrus* which he had looked to above p. 376. G. (where cf. our note) and again looks back below p. 548. F. I will repeat the words of Plato p. 246. b. c: "the whole soul takes care of all that is soulless, and it traverses the whole heaven, becoming now in one form, now in another. Being perfect [τελέα] therefore and winged, it flies on high [*meteorporei*] and governs the whole world." This reading of Bekker I also followed above p. 376. G. Others have μετεωροπολεῖ [ranges on high], but very many Codices in Bekker confirm the former, and the best Bodleian also confirms it. What more do you seek? Even Plotinus read it thus in his papyri. For the codices recognize this form in the three places we cited, and that other μετεωροπολεῖ was perhaps born from the preceding περιπολεῖ [ranges around]. But nevertheless, several things argue that the variety is ancient. Himerius, *Orat. XIV* p. 630 Wernsdorf concerning the soul: "what it once saw, when it was turned around the heaven with the gods; and being moved it flies on high [*meteorporei*] and seeks the place there, and investigates the things that are;" Suidas II. p. 543 Kust.: "Μετεωροπολῶν: observing celestial things. And μετεωροπορῶν." Zo... omitted the last two words...

At this place he had before his eyes these words of Plato in the *Phaedrus* p. 249 fin. 250. A. p. 47. Only a few remain, in whom the sufficiency of memory is present." — Eustathius of Antioch, rebuking these Platonic and Pythagorean decrees in Ang. Mai’s *Collect. Platon.* p. 173 and Ast on Plato’s *Laws* V. p. 272. Or perhaps "of the chosen lives," of the lives which individuals chose for themselves? -> BOOK VII. ENNEAD FOUR. pages 860—867. 255 <-

page 865, line 11. **"If the soul is such—for wisdom and true virtue exist—inasmuch as it partakes of divine things through kinship and being of the same substance."** <note>original: "Εἰ οὖν τοιοῦτον ἡ ψυχὴ... ἅτε θείων μετὸν αὐτῷ διὰ συγγένειαν καὶ τὸ ὁμοούσιον."</note> I have thus emended the common reading "full of" <note>original: "μεστὸν"</note> on the authority of several books, one of which reads "partaking of divine things" <note>original: "θείων μετὸν"</note>. Lucas Holstenius, in his work on Sallustius *On the Gods and the World*, used this passage of Plotinus and wrote: "inasmuch as it is full of those divine things." I do not believe this came from any Manuscript. Even Ficinus <note>Marsilio Ficino, the famous Renaissance translator of Plotinus</note> expressed our preferred reading. As for the argument itself, one should compare, besides the aforementioned Sallustius, Plotinus himself above (p. 54. C—F) and the notes there, as well as Proclus in his commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus*, where he discusses the difference between the divine and human soul.

page 866, line 15. **"so that it often seems to him that this was well said: 'Hail, I am an immortal god to you,'"** <note>original: "χαίρετ’, ἐγὼ δ’ ὑμῖν θεὸς ἄμβροτος"</note> These are verses by Empedocles from the beginning of his *Purifications*, which Diogenes Laërtius preserved in full. Others cite fragments of it. See Davies on Cicero’s *Tusculan Disputations*, the interpreters of Diogenes Laërtius, Fabricius, and Sturz on Empedocles, who noted various readings. It was also presented by Jacobs in his supplements to the *Greek Anthology* as follows:

*O friends, who dwell in the great city of yellow Akragas*
*high on the citadel, mindful of good deeds,*
*hail! I am an immortal god to you, no longer mortal,*
*I go about among all honored, as is fitting,*
*crowned with fillets and blooming wreaths.*

Furthermore, just as Empedocles's entire style has much of Homer in it, so does that phrase "immortal god." See the Scholia on the *Iliad*. As far as I know, none of those who treated these verses mentioned this passage in Plotinus. However, similar formulas are found everywhere on Marble inscriptions. For example, in that inscription related to the Samothracian mysteries, we read:
*I, a youth, call to you: a friend to god, no longer mortal.*
Likewise in Gruter:
*formerly mortal, but now a partaker of the gods.*
And in the same:
*O memorable kinsman! Why do you lament that I have been*
*carried off to the stars of heaven? Cease to weep for a god.*

Benedict Bendtsen inserted and explained these inscriptions in his first specimen of *Mystical Marbles*. I am surprised, however, that the verses of Empedocles did not occur to him, as they are more relevant than these other inscriptions. Others taught that those who lived a just and honest life become **spirits** <term>genios/daimones: intermediary divine beings</term>. See Plato’s *Cratylus*, Libanius’s *Defense of Socrates*, and Olympiodorus.

page 867, line 4. **"just as if seeing statues established within itself—as if it were living gold etc."** <note>original: "ὥσπερ ἀγάλματα ἐν αὐτῇ ἱδρυμένα... οἷον εἰ χρυσὸς ἔμψυχος εἴη"</note> The source of this passage is partly in Alcibiades's speech in Plato’s *Symposium* and partly in the *Sophist*. See what we said above regarding the twin passage in Plotinus.

— line 11. **"Concerning such a thing—how it is not immortal"** See Plato’s *Phaedo*, where Wyttenbach in his notes presents this passage of Plotinus, adding: "Therefore (Plotinus) restrains those who reject the force of this Platonic argumentation with two other arguments. One is: *either they will dissolve the soul as a composite... until they reach a part that rules itself and others, which is immortal, and for which it is a crime and against nature to undergo death.* This is the argument we touched upon in Psychology. The other is: *or, calling life an accidental quality of matter, they will be forced to admit that the source from which such an accident comes to matter is immortal and incapable of the opposite of what it brings (i.e., immune to death).* For there is one nature that is living in actuality. And thus he recalls the demonstration to that decree: that there is one soul of the whole of nature, of which our individual souls are parts. Proclus also refers to this passage of the *Phaedo* for interpretation." The latter argument—that the cause of life is incapable of receiving its opposite—is a consequence of the axiom which Proclus defends against certain Platonists in his commentary on the *Parmenides*, where he states: "and the cause of life has filled itself with life; and..."
