-> ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS <-

<note>original: "τὸ τελειότητος, ἑαυτὸ τέλειον ἀπεργάζεται"</note> "that which belongs to perfection, makes itself perfect." Furthermore, Tiedemann, in his book *On the Causes of Contemplative Philosophy* (Vol. III, p. 365 ff.), admires these ingeniously devised ideas of Plotinus, yet does not support them in every respect.

p. 868, 8. **"Furthermore, if they shall say every soul is perishable,"**] Plotinus seems to be addressing the Stoics and perhaps the Epicureans. Regarding the Epicureans, see above at p. 457, chapter 3, beginning. Regarding the Stoics, see Cicero's *Tusculan Disputations* I. 32, and the notes there by Davis; also Wyttenbach on Plutarch’s *On the Delay of Divine Vengeance* (p. 400, p. 78 of the Leiden edition, Oxford edition); Van Lynden on Panaetius (p. 70); and Baguet on the fragments of Chrysippus (p. 101 ff.).

— 18. **"But the soul, being a single and simple <term>activity</term> <note>original: "ἐνέργεια" (energeia) - in Neoplatonism, this refers to the actualized power or "being-at-work" of a thing</note> whose nature is in living, will therefore not perish in this way."**] Marsilio Ficino also expressed this, except that before the phrase "in living" he imagined a "and." Following him, Taylor translates it thus: "But soul being one simple energy, and a nature characterised by life, cannot be corrupted as a composite." The manuscripts persist in the common reading. Wyttenbach suspects it should be: "is by nature." Indeed, in his notes on Plato’s *Phaedo* (p. 197), after touching upon the passage of Plotinus at p. 557 A, he continues: "now that other point, 'to be dissolved in the same way it was put together,' has this meaning: that the whole is divided into those parts from which it was composed, and in the manner it was composed: just as a body is divided into the four elements of which it consists when the bonds holding these parts together are dissolved. Plotinus has this in mind (our passage follows—: 'a nature in living' or 'is by nature'): 'it will therefore not perish in this way.' Then he reviews different types of composition and dissolution." Aeneas of Gaza (p. 66) says: "Does not the composite, when dissolved, return again into those things from which it was put together?" For there are various types of cohesion in bodies, later celebrated by the Stoics, as found in Plutarch’s *Advice to the Married* (p. 142 E): "Of bodies, some are said to be made of separate parts, like a fleet or an army; others of joined parts, like a house or a ship; and others are united and grown together, like every living animal, where we have provided more on this matter." (See the observations on that passage, p. 892 of the Oxford edition. Add Olympiodorus on the *First Alcibiades*, p. 25). Then he continues the explanation: "That the Platonists mean by 'composite' something made of **parts placed outside of parts**, as is commonly said, filling space and extended, is understood from the frequency of examples: for instance, Plutarch’s *On the Procreation of the Soul* (p. 1022 E); *Against the Stoics* (p. 1085 C); Plotinus (p. 160 D, E; 161 C, D; 162 D; 163 E; 165 A; 166 E; 310 C; 313 E; 457 A; 466 A, C; 557 A); Albinus’ *Doctrines of Plato* (p. 372 D); Aeneas of Gaza (p. 59, 66); Zacharias of Mitylene (p. 175); Olympiodorus on the *Phaedo* (Manuscript III, p. 40 and often elsewhere; Manuscript I, p. 63, 185)." Then, following Ficino, I have written: **"but then, having been divided, would it perish by being broken into small pieces?"** <note>original: "ἀλλ’ ἆρα μερισθεῖσα, κερματιζομένη ἀπόλοιτο ἄν;"</note> with a question mark. Perhaps before "broken into small pieces" an "and" has also fallen out. Plato, moreover, says in the *Republic* (p. 395 B): "human nature seems to me to have been **broken into even smaller pieces**." Plutarch, *On the Procreation of the Soul* (p. 1020 L): "whether it be cut by the units being broken into parts." Cf. Schleusner’s *Lexicon of the New Testament* under "money-changer" <note>The Greek root refers to breaking large coins into small change</note>. Plotinus above in Eusebius’ *Preparation for the Gospel* (p. 833 A): "when the body is broken into pieces, the same quality remains in each part." Cf. Plotinus below (V. 8. 9; VI. 2. 2; VI. 2. 12). Then, with Ficino and the Vatican manuscript, I removed the question mark after "soul" and placed it after "destruction."

p. 869, 7. **"How then—does this [soul] come into a body?"**] Taylor, at this point in his translation, presents a passage from Proclus on the *Timaeus* (p. 343) translated into English, in which that philosopher speaks of the descent of souls. But we have spoken of this doctrine above (at p. 381 ff.) and will speak of it shortly at the beginning of the next book (p. 468 A). Next, for "whoever" <note>original: "ὅσος"</note>, Ficino expressed "how much" <note>original: "ὅσον"</note>. The manuscripts retain the former, and it corresponds to the "if" in the following "and whatever." The same [Ficino] soon after expressed "he knew"; but most books have "he saw."

— 12. **"—as if pregnant from them, and in labor to give birth"**] He imitates Plato’s *Symposium* (p. 206 near the end): "hence the great excitement about the beautiful has come to the one who is pregnant and already teeming, because of the release from great labor it provides to the one who has it." Cf. *Republic* VI (p. 490); *Timaeus* (p. 86); *Laws* IV (717); *Epistle* II (p. 313 A). For the words and sentiments, compare Proclus on the *First Alcibiades* (p. 150); Olympiodorus on the same (p. 7): "as one in labor toward this," that is, as one who was prone to it. See what we cited there in the Annotations and compare Plotinus himself above (p. 346 D). Add Damascius, *On First Principles* (p. 79, edited by Kopp): "so that even the Intellect, or..."

<summary>This page provides philological commentary on Plotinus' arguments for the immortality of the soul, contrasting its "simple" nature with "composite" bodies that can be broken into pieces. The author cites various Platonic and Stoic sources to explain the soul's "labor" to give birth to life and its descent into the physical body.</summary>
<keywords>immortality of the soul, simple vs composite, Stoicism, Epicureanism, Marsilio Ficino, Thomas Taylor, Wyttenbach, Plato's Phaedo, fragmentation, activity (energeia)</keywords>

--- Page 264 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on Plotinus's Enneads, specifically Book VII of the Fourth Ennead, focusing on the nature of the soul in animals and the tripartite division of the human soul.</meta>

[[original page: 257]]

-> BOOK VII. ENNEAD FOUR. p. 868—870. 257 <-

The intellect, being a spectator of certain qualities, is in labor with the conception of that nature, yet even the intellect does not bring it forth; on the contrary, it draws that labor back into itself—if we might be able—to return to that original labor. <note>original: "νοῦς, τῶν ποιῶν τινων θεωρὸς ὢν... πρὸς τὴν ὠδῖνα ἐκείνην ἀναδραμεῖν." This passage discusses the intellectual struggle to grasp the essence of the soul.</note>
p. 870, 7. **Concerning the soul of other animals, as many as—but if there is another species of soul]** Plotinus distinguishes between those souls of brutes which have degenerated from human souls out of human bodies, and those which, having never been in a human body, serve to animate the bodies of brutes. The source of this doctrine is found in Plato’s *Timaeus* p. 42, p. 45 (Bekk. edition): —"he who fails in these things shall change into the nature of a woman in his second birth; and if he does not cease from wickedness in these conditions, he shall always change into some such beastly nature according to the similarity of his way of life," etc. <note>original: "σφαλεὶς δὲ τούτων εἰς γυναικὸς φύσιν... εἰς τινα τοιαύτην ἀεὶ μεταβαλοῖ θήρειον φύσιν."</note> Regarding these matters, I do not know if Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino, the famous Renaissance Platonist.</note> did not err when he says (ch. 19) that Plato established the souls of brutes to be perishable in both soul and body. Be that as it may: Christian philosophers have receded furthest from that opinion which would posit that the souls of brutes differ only by degree from human souls, and they established that the former would utterly perish. Basil the Great, after he posited that the souls of beasts arise from blood, flesh, and consequently from the earth, continues thus in his *Hexaëmeron* (Homily VIII, p. 99 B. C.): —"do not think the soul of brutes is older than the substance of their bodies, nor that it remains after the dissolution of the flesh. Flee the trifles of the solemn philosophers, who are not ashamed to claim their own souls and those of dogs are of the same species; those who say they themselves were once women, and bushes, and sea-fish," etc. <note>original: "μὴ νόμιζε πρεσβυτέραν εἶναι... καὶ ἰχθύας θαλασσίους." Basil is critiquing the doctrine of metempsychosis or the "migration of souls."</note> These criticisms are cast against Plato no less than against Plotinus. Many doctors of the Church support him. Antiochus of Ptolemais in Angelo Mai’s *Vatican Collection* I, p. 81 sq.: "God, when making the other four-footed animals, produced their souls along with their bodies; but when fashioning man, he first prepares the instrument of the body, and then, having created the soul, he placed it within, so that in this too he might show the superiority of man; since the other animals and beasts, being dissolved by death, have their soul vanish along with the body," etc. Photius pronounces the same opinion in his letter to Amphilochius (CXLIX. 7, ibid. p. 295 sq.). Because Plotinus certainly attributes a vital soul to plants as well, in this matter he follows Aristotle no less than his own Plato. Aristotle, *On the Soul* I. 5, p. 19 (Sylb. edition): "For plants appear to live, though they do not participate in movement or sensation, and many animals do not possess intellect." <note>original: "φαίνεται γὰρ τά τε φυτὰ ζῇν... διάνοιαν οὐκ ἔχειν."</note> See also Tiedemann, *Spirit of Speculative Philosophy* III, p. 367.

— 13. **But if the soul of man, being tripartite, shall be dissolved with the composite,]** One must supply "it is necessary" <term>dei: it is necessary</term> from the preceding. Since certain scribes did not understand this brevity of Plotinus, they changed the word to "it will be dissolved." <note>original: "λυθήσεται" instead of "λυθήσεσθαι."</note> As for the argument, this reasoning, which posits the soul as composed of three parts (<term>syntheton: composite</term>): **reason**, **spirit**, and **desire**, <note>original: "λόγῳ, θυμῷ, ἐπιθυμίᾳ." This is the classic Platonic division of the soul.</note> ought not to be confused with that other reasoning by which philosophers either said or denied that the soul was composite **from parts placed outside of parts**, as they are commonly called, filling space and extended—as Wyttenbach teaches regarding the *Phaedo* (p. 197 sq.). Nor should it be confused with that **Trichotomy** of the sacred writers, by which three parts were attributed to human nature: **body** (<term>soma</term>), **soul** (<term>psyche</term>), and **mind** or **spirit** (<term>pneuma</term>), a distribution recently discussed by Hermann Olshausen in his dissertation: *On the trichotomy of human nature accepted by the writers of the New Testament* (Königsberg, 1826). —The source of that "tripartite nature" which Plotinus touches upon here is in the same *Timaeus* (p. 70, p. 98 sq. Bekk.); see also the other *Timaeus*, the so-called Locrus (p. 556 Gale); join with this *Republic* IX (p. 734), Philo Judaeus *Allegories of the Law* III (p. 310 Pfeiff.), Plutarch *On the Face in the Moon* (p. 943 A), *Opinions of the Philosophers* IV. 4, Diogenes Laërtius VIII. 30, Himerius (p. 884 and Wernsdorf’s notes there), Alcinous *On Platonic Doctrine* 24 (p. 504), Proclus *On the Timaeus* (p. 326) and *On the Republic* (p. 399), Olympiodorus *On the Alcibiades* (pp. 4, 65, 81, 172, 203), and compare Plotinus himself above (p. 398 B. C. D. and p. 420 sqq.). —Presently, regarding the words: **the pure souls—will cast off that which was fashioned during birth.** See the *Timaeus* in the places cited, namely p. 42 A. Porphyry, *On Abstinence* I. 30 (p. 49 Rhoer.): "if we are to return to our truly own things, we must lay aside all those things we have received from our mortal nature, along with our attachment to them," etc. <note>original: "εἴπερ πρὸς τὰ ὄντως οἰκεῖα μέλλομεν ἐπανιέναι... προσπαθείας."</note> where Rhoerius compares this with other passages and the words of the Apostle in 2 Corinthians 5:1. Add Libanius, *Declamation for Socrates* (at the end of Aristides *Against Leptines*, ed. Jac. Morelli) p. 258.

The words found above on page 463, section C, line 6, should perhaps be placed here: <note>original: "σωζόμενον (pro σωζομένης) καθ’ ὅσον ἂν αὐτοῦ μεταλαμβάνῃ"</note> "preserved (using the masculine *preserved* instead of the feminine) insofar as it may participate in it." See the annotation for that location.

page 871, line 2. <note>original: "ἃ δὲ καὶ πρὸς τοὺς δεομένους πίστεως αἰσθήσει κεκραμένης κ. τ. λ."</note> *And those things which are also for those who require a faith mixed with sensation, etc.*] I did not hesitate, following the Vatican Manuscript and Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the influential Renaissance translator of Plotinus</note>—whom Taylor also follows—to write it this way instead of "governed by sensation," which is read in the printed Edition. The opposite of this is to separate or **call the mind away from the senses**, to use that phrase of Tully’s <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> (Tusculan Disputations I. 16. 38). Furthermore, as for Plotinus subjecting to his own demonstration <note>original: "τῇ ἀποδείξει"</note> those things which, being drawn from history, produce faith <note>original: "πίστιν"</note>: in this he follows the authority of other philosophers and indeed of Plato himself. Cicero also aligned himself with these in the Tusculan Disputations I. 12–16: "Therefore, that one idea was implanted in those ancients, whom Ennius calls **casci** <note>An archaic Latin word for 'ancient' or 'old-fashioned'</note>, that there is sensation in death, and that a human being is not so destroyed by the departure from life that they utterly perish; and this can be understood not only from many other things, but also from **pontifical law and the ceremonies of burials**," etc. Compare, regarding pontifical law and the remaining matters relevant here, Cicero's *Topics* XXIII. 90 and *On the Laws* II. 22, page 321 in Moser’s edition, and the annotations there. Now let us look specifically at the following: <note>original: "ἐκ τε ὧν θεοὶ ἀνεῖλον—ἱλάσκεσθαι"</note> *both from what the gods have commanded... to appease.* The books of historians and other writers are full of oracles of this kind, especially those of Pausanias, Porphyry, Stobaeus, and others. The Homeric **Nekyia** <note>The rite by which ghosts were called up and questioned; original: "νεκυία"</note> (Odyssey, book 11, line 23 and following) proves the antiquity of this matter. "And Homer also bears witness, showing the son of Laertes <note>Odysseus</note>, according to the instructions of Circe, both digging the trench and performing the libations." These are the words of Theodoret, *Cure of Greek Maladies* VIII, page 910, edited by Schulz. Wyttenbach provides other examples in his notes on Plutarch’s *Consolation to Apollonius*, page 752. If you seek oracles, go to Porphyry as cited in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* IV, pages 145–147 and V, page 230; compare Pausanias VI. 9. 3 and Aelian, *Various History* XI. 3 (where he discusses Cleomedes, who was granted heroic honors by the Astypalaeans by order of the oracle). Next: <note>original: "τιμάς τε νέμειν τεθνηκόσιν—εἰς τοὺς ἀπεληλυθότας"</note> *to assign honors to the dead... for those who have departed.* Plato, in Diogenes Laertius III. 83: "There are three kinds of justice: the first concerning the gods, the second concerning men, the third concerning the deceased." Regarding this kind, he continues: "those who take care of monuments clearly [act justly] toward those who have passed away." Hence the **justa** <note>Funeral rites</note> among the ancients and the **laws of the Manes** <note>The spirits of the dead</note>, which it suffices to mention here by name. (And compare Odyssey book 1, line 291; Iliad book 24, line 38, with the Scholia of Wasse on Sallust’s *Jugurtha*, chapter XI, and Wyttenbach on Plato’s *Phaedo*, page 293). Plotinus continues: <note>original: "Πολλαὶ δὲ ψυχαὶ—οὐκ ἀπέστησαν τοῦ εὐεργετεῖν ἀνθρώπους"</note> *And many souls... have not ceased from benefiting mankind.* Hesiod, *Works and Days* 122 (124 and following): "They are spirits <note>original: "δαίμονες"</note> by the will of great Zeus, good, dwelling on earth, guardians of mortal men;" concerning the souls of those who lived life well and justly; Plato converted these verses, slightly changed, into his own discussion in the *Cratylus* page 397 and in the *Republic* V, page 469; likewise Olympiodorus in his commentary on the *First Alcibiades*, page 16. Compare Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I. 12. 28, where he speaks of the brothers Tyndaridae <note>Castor and Pollux</note>: "Who are held to have been not only helpers in the battles of the Roman people's victory, but even messengers." As for the end of the passage in Plotinus: <note>original: "αἱ δὲ καὶ μαντεῖα ἀποδείξαμεναι κ. τ. λ."</note> *and those who have even established oracles, etc.*, these pertain to **necromancy**, concerning which consult the same Tully in *Tusculan Disputations* I. 16. 37 and *On Divination* I. 58, page 286 in Moser’s edition, and in both places Davis and the other interpreters. We have treated these matters somewhat more accurately for this reason: lest we judge—as is commonly done—that Plotinus drew these arguments for the immortality of souls from the spirit of his own age, whereas he employed them after the example of Plato and even older writers.

-> BOOK VIII. ENNEAD FOUR. pages 871, 872. 259 <-

The same disciple of Plotinus <note>Porphyry</note> set this forth in Book I, § 30 of *On Abstinence*, page 49 of Rhoer’s edition. However, the sources of this book by Plotinus are to be sought chiefly in Plato’s *Phaedrus*, page 246 and following; in the *Republic*, Book X, page 617 and following; and in the *Timaeus*, page 41 and following, to omit other dialogues. Regarding these, see Wyttenbach’s *Disputation on the Doctrine of the Immortality of Souls* (before the *Phaedo*), page XVI and following; and regarding the descent, see Plutarch’s *On the Delay of Divine Vengeance*, page 113 and page 444 of the Oxford edition. Concerning Aristotle, there is a memorable testimony by Proclus in his commentary on the *Timaeus*, page 338. For after he had spoken of Plato’s discussions, he proceeds thus: — "Aristotle, having emulated him in his treatise *On the Soul*, treating it from a naturalistic perspective, mentioned neither the descents of the soul nor its allotted portions; but in his dialogues he treated these matters separately <note>original: "περὶ αὐτῶν"</note> and laid down the primary argument." <note>original Greek: Ὁ δὴ καὶ Ἀριστοτέλης... κατεβάλλετο λόγον.</note> The fact that the Stagirite <note>Aristotle</note> had treated these matters in his dialogues is evidence that he intended these discussions to be suited only to popular instruction <term>popularis disciplina: teachings intended for a general audience rather than inner-circle students</term>. In the same place, Proclus touches upon this doubt debated in the schools of the philosophers: whether the whole soul descends, or not; — "so that what Plotinus says would be a more recent doctrine, which dictates that not all of it (the soul) descends." <note>original Greek: ὥστε ὅπερ Πλωτῖνός φησιν... διαταττόμενος.</note> Simplicius, at the end of the Proem to Aristotle’s *On the Soul*: — "wherefore we shall neither suppose that some part of it (the soul) remains always in the same way and pure, according to Plotinus, nor that it proceeds entirely in its inclination toward generation. Rather, it proceeds as a whole and remains purely in its inclination toward secondary things." <note>original Greek: δι’ ὃ οὔτε μένειν τι αὐτῆς... πρὸς τὰ δεύτερα ῥοπῇ.</note> Hermias touched upon the same opinion in his commentary on the *Phaedrus*, page 147. I have placed the passage above at Plotinus page 361. A. See also the final chapter of this book of Plotinus, page 476.

Neither Plotinus alone, but also Pythagoras, Plato, and the rest were eagerly attacked, especially by Christian writers, on account of that decree upon which this entire doctrine depends. I mean the **pre-existence** <note>original Greek: προϋπάρξιν</note> of souls, which the Scholastics call **praeexistentia**. Since the followers of Plato and Plotinus stubbornly retained it on one side, while the Christian doctors—excepting Origen and those who sided with him—vehemently refuted it on the other, there arose from this a great harvest of books, decrees, and canons, lasting until the time of John of Damascus and later. I shall taste only a few. Clement of Alexandria, in a fragment of the eighth book of the *Stromata* in Angelo Mai’s *Vatican Collection*, Vol. I. 3. page 83: "God made us when we did not previously exist; for it would be necessary for us to know where we were, if we pre-existed, and how and why we came here; but if we did not pre-exist, God alone is the cause of our birth. Just as he made us when we were not, so he saves us by his own grace now that we have come to be." <note>original Greek: Ὁ θεὸς ἡμᾶς ἐποίησεν... ἰδίᾳ χάριτι.</note> Antiochus of Ptolemais brings forward other arguments for this matter in the same place, page 81: "While making the other four-footed animals, God produced their souls along with their bodies; but when fashioning man, he first prepares the instrument of the body; and then, having created the soul, he inserted it, so that in this too he might show the superiority of man, etc." <note>original Greek: τὰ μὲν ἄλλα τετράποδα... τὴν ὑπεροχὴν ἀνθρώπου κ. τ. λ.</note> Then he adds this second argument: — "and God does not make the soul before the body, so that (man) might not become an eyewitness of the things being made; he does not make the soul present at the creation, so that it might not boast as a co-worker of God." <note>original Greek: καὶ οὐ ποιεῖ (ὁ θεὸς)... συνεργὸς τοῦ θεοῦ.</note> The pronouncements of Cyril, Eleutherius, Eustathius of Antioch, and Peter of Alexandria on the same opinion are shown there on pages 76 and following. On the same subject, there exist the Canons of the Councils; in the first Canon of the Fifth Council of Constantinople, these words are read in Fabricius, *Greek Library*, Vol. XII, page 187, Harles edition: "If anyone defends the mythical pre-existence of souls, and the monstrous restoration <term>apocatastasis: the doctrine that all beings will eventually be restored to a state of holiness</term> that follows it, let him be anathema." <note>original Greek: εἴ τις τὴν μυθώδη προϋπαρξιν... ἀνάθεμα ἔστω.</note> See Canons II, VII, XV. And this very doctrine is called by Damascus "the absurdity of Origen’s ravings." Finally, Nicephorus Nathanael rebuked Plotinus himself on this account in a specific *Antithetic*, as did the author of a *Dialogue*, whether he be the same man or one of the same opinion. We have seen to it that these booklets be appended to these *Enneads*.

For the rest, Thomas Taylor made an English version of this book of Plotinus in *Five Books of Plotinus*, page 251 and following.

**page 873, line 1. For Heraclitus—just as he himself found by seeking.]** The manuscript books offer no help here. Ficinus <note>Marsilio Ficino, the 15th-century Platonist translator</note> seems to have read: *and that which changes does not rest.* But a limb so ailing cannot be healed by such a slight remedy. Punctuate and read: *For Heraclitus, who urges us to seek this (positing necessary vicissitudes from opposites, speaking of a way up and a way down, and saying that changing is resting and that it is weariness to toil and be ruled by the same things) gave us cause for guessing, having neglected to make the argument clear to us; as if it were perhaps necessary to seek within him, just as he himself found by seeking.* <note>original Greek: ὁ μὲν γὰρ Ἡράκλειτος... ὥσπερ καὶ αὐτὸς ζητήσας εὗρεν</note> Etenim Heraclitus <note>The author provides a Latin translation of the reconstructed Greek text above</note>, who commanded us to investigate that matter (positing necessary changes from contraries, and describing a path both above and below, and that changing is to rest, and that it is exhaustion to labor and be distressed by the same things) provides material for divination, neglecting to make the reasoning plain to us; so that perhaps he must be sought out, just as he himself found by inquiring. Iamblichus in Stobaeus' *Eclogues* I. 52. p. 906. Heeren: ‘For Heraclitus posits necessary changes from opposites, a way up and a way down, and he assumed the souls pass through these, and that to remain in the same things is weariness, but to change brings rest.’ Ibid. p. 894. sq.—: according to Heraclitus, of the rest found in changing. Where Heeren says: "It is well known from Diogenes Laertius IX. 7. etc. that he (Heraclitus) placed all things as subject to change and arising from it; nor did he decide otherwise concerning the soul, since he called it 'that which is always flowing' and 'that which is always moving,' as Aristotle testifies in *On the Soul* I. 2. Since therefore he called its union with the body a 'rest from change,' or rather contended that the former arose from the latter, he seems to have posited—not unlike Empedocles—that it was shut into the body to pay the penalty for sins." The reason I placed *to be distressed* <note>original: ἄγχεσθαι</note> instead of *to begin/be ruled* <note>original: ἄρχεσθαι</note>, I am moved by other causes and especially by this passage of Hermes in Stobaeus' *Eclogues* I. p. 768: — but the mind leaves behind the soul attached to the body and *strangled* <note>original: ἀγχομένην</note> downward by it. I have given more on this entire Heraclitean passage in *Dionysus* pp. 83—86. Cf. also above at p. 97. D. and on the obscurity of Heraclitus cf. Schleiermacher in Wolf and Buttmann’s *Museum of Ancient Science* Vol. I. p. 322. sqq.
**— 6. And Empedocles—trusting in mad strife—and concerning many other things.]** Our author <note>Plotinus</note> below in chapter 5, p. 473. A: they do not disagree with one another—neither the flight and wandering of Empedocles, nor the sin for which justice is dealt, nor the rest of Heraclitus in the flight. Truly Empedocles taught that souls are condemned to exile for crimes and forced to leave the celestial realms, and thus are bound to these mortal bodies: Plutarch *On the Eating of Flesh* I. 7. p. 996. B. 49. Wyttenbach, where however Wyttenbach suspects the words of Empedocles were omitted by the scribe. Iamblichus in Stobaeus' *Eclogues* I. p. 894: these (the Platonists) say that after the disordered and erring movements are already present, there later enter the things that adorn and arrange them, and harmony. From both of these they thus weave together—according to Plotinus, from the first "otherness"; according to Empedocles, from the first flight from God. cf. Proclus on the *Timaeus* p. 175. and Origen *Against Celsus* I. p. 26. who indeed mentions Pythagoras and Plato in this matter similarly to Plotinus in our passage. Add Aeneas of Gaza in *Theophrastus* p. 9. and p. 11. Barth. and consult Sturz’s *Empedocles* p. 452. sqq.
**— 17. to be in a bond, and he says the soul is buried in it,]** Plato in the *Cratylus* p. 400. B. C. p. 39. Bekker: and now some say it (the body) is the *tomb* <note>original: σῆμα</note> of the soul, as if it were buried in the present moment. Cf. *Gorgias* p. 493. Cf. Lambinus on Lucretius III. 556. and Wyttenbach on the *Phaedo* p. 139. sq. Add Libanius' *Declamation for Socrates* (ed. at the end of Aristides by Jac. Morelli) p. 256—whenever we are released from bones and flesh, and from this whole prison, whether one ought to call it a body <note>soma</note> or a tomb <note>sema</note>. Plotinus continues: *and that the great doctrine spoken in the secret mysteries says the soul is as if in a guardhouse.* Plato in the *Phaedo* p. 62. p. 12. Bekker: that we humans are in a kind of guardhouse. Wyttenbach praises Plotinus' words on the *Phaedo* p. 136, by which he demonstrates that the phrase "in the secret mysteries" <note>original: ἐν ἀπορρήτοις</note> both in Plato and other philosophers refers not to religious and anciently handed-down mysteries, but to the more sacred and secret doctrine of the philosopher (Socrates, Plato: cf. *Philomath.* III. p. 86. sq.). For my part, I am not entirely persuaded. For that sentiment regarding the body as a prison or sepulcher is expressly attributed to the Orphics in the cited passage of the *Cratylus*. -> BOOK VIII. ENNEAD FOUR. pages 873—876. 261 <-

I believe we should side with Heindorf (p. 26) on this passage rather than with Wyttenbach, nor do I think Plotinus's words should be understood otherwise, whether you consider them mysteries or oracles, as Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino, the 15th-century Platonist translator</note> understood those words. In Wyttenbach's edition (at the cited place), the word *reason* <note>original: λόγον</note> undoubtedly fell out after *the mentioned* <note>original: λεγόμενον</note> in Plotinus's text due to a printer's error. —Our author adds here: *and the cave for him, just as the cavern for Empedocles, etc.* <note>original: καὶ τὸ σπήλαιον αὐτῷ, ὥσπερ Ἐμπεδοκλεῖ τὸ ἄντρον</note> Porphyry, in *On the Cave of the Nymphs* chapter VIII, p. 9 (Goens edition), says: "Starting from these things, I believe, the Pythagoreans and after them Plato declared the world to be a cavern and a cave. For in Empedocles, the powers that lead the souls say: 'We have come under this roofed-over cavern.'" <note>original: Ἤλυθομεν τόδ’ ὑπ’ ἄντρον ὑπόστεγον</note> There follows the passage of Plato from the seventh book of the *Republic* p. 514 (p. 326 in Bekker). To be sure, Empedocles taught that to pay the penalty for their crimes, souls are thrust down, as it were, through the elements into this world, which he called a *cavern* and a *joyless place* and the *meadow of Doom* <note>original: ἄντρον, ἀτερπέα χῶρον, Ἄτης λειμῶνα</note>, since in this earthly and moist place they live as if in a cave, by whose exhalations the souls lose their wings and fall utterly. See Hierocles on the *Golden Verses of the Pythagoreans* p. 355, and compare Wyttenbach on Plutarch's *On the Late Vengeance of the Deity* p. 115 (p. 446 ff. Oxford edition) and Sturz's *Empedocles* p. 454 ff. Aeneas of Gaza seems to have had this passage of our Plotinus before his eyes in his *Theophrastus* p. 10: "Empedocles made this universe a cavern; but Plato, changing the term in the *Republic*, calls it a cave."

p. 874, 3. *and in the Phaedrus*] <note>original: ἐν δὲ Φαίδρῳ</note> See the *Phaedrus* p. 246 ff. I have provided *for him* <note>original: αὐτῷ</note> instead of *it* <note>original: αὐτὴν</note> following the best manuscripts. Understand it as: "for him," i.e., in his [Plato's] work, just as above: *and the cave for him just as the cavern for Empedocles.*

— 7. *in the Timaeus—without a soul it was not possible for this to happen*] <note>original: ἐν Τιμαίῳ—ἄνευ δὲ ψυχῆς οὐκ οἷόν τε ἦν τοῦτο γενέσθαι</note> Plato in the *Timaeus* p. 30a (p. 26 Bekker): "Having considered, then, he found that among those things which are by nature visible, no work that is without intelligence will ever be fairer than one that possesses intelligence, when each is taken as a whole, and moreover that it is impossible for intelligence to be present in anything apart from soul. Because of this reasoning, then, by composing intelligence in soul and soul in body, he constructed the universe, so that the work he had accomplished might be by nature as fair and as excellent as possible. Thus, then, according to the likely account, one must say that this world became a living being, possessed of soul and intelligence in truth, through the providence of God." (cf. our Plotinus above p. 372 B.C. and p. 397 D.) The same Plato in the *Timaeus* p. 34 (p. 31 Bekker): "—for all these reasons he generated it as a happy god." On which words Lindau notes in his annotations: "Plotinus looks to this passage in IV. 8. 1: 'In the Timaeus,' he says, 'speaking about this universe, he both praises the world and calls it a happy god.' These words have such weight that they prevent anyone from thinking that in Plato's text one should rewrite it as 'God' [as the subject]. For the world is among the number of the gods, whom the philosopher mentions below as having been created by the supreme craftsman."

— 15. *So that it happens to us—to learn from him (having sought)*] <note>original: Ὥστε ἡμῖν συμβαίνειν—παρ’ αὐτοῦ μαθεῖν (ζητήσασιν)</note> This discussion depends mostly on the classic passage of the Platonic *Timaeus* concerning the world, its creator, and his ministers, and concerning both souls—the universal and the individual—or rather, concerning the World Soul and the remaining souls, p. 41 ff.

p. 876, 2. *Wherefore he also says that our soul, if it were to be with that perfect one, having been perfected itself, would travel on high and govern the whole world.*] <note>original: Διὸ καὶ φησι καὶ τὴν ἡμετέραν εἰ μετ’ ἐκείνης γένοιτο τελέας, τελεωθεῖσαν καὶ αὐτὴν, μετεωροπορεῖν, καὶ πάντα τὸν κόσμον διοικεῖν.</note> First, I have given *perfect* <note>original: τελέας</note> and *perfected* <note>original: τελεωθεῖσαν</note> from our best manuscripts in this place, although in other places where the books suggested it, I retained the form *teleias* <note>original: τελείας</note>, etc. Similarly, in Plato's *Symposium* p. 208c, Bekker (p. 439) gave *teleoi* instead of *teleioi*, just as it varies in the *Cratylus* p. 403e, where see Heindorf. However, Plotinus here refers to the same passage of the Platonic *Phaedrus* which he had referred to above on p. 376 G (where see our note) and refers to again below on p. 548 F. I will repeat Plato's words from p. 246b, c: "The soul in its totality takes care of all that is soulless, and it traverses the whole heaven, appearing now in one form and now in another. When it is perfect and winged, it travels on high and governs the whole world." I followed this reading of Bekker's also above on p. 376 G. Others read *meteoro-polei* <note>meaning "to range over the heavens"</note>, but the former is confirmed by very many manuscripts in Bekker, and also by the excellent Bodleian manuscript. What more do you want? Even Plotinus read it this way in his own papyri. For the manuscripts recognize this form in the three places we have cited, and that other form *meteoro-polei* was perhaps born from the preceding *peri-polei* <note>meaning "to range around"</note>. Yet, that the variation is ancient is proved by several things. Himerius, Oration XIV, p. 630 (Wernsdorf edition) concerning the soul: "things which it once saw, when it turned about the heaven with the gods; and having been moved, it travels on high and seeks the place there, and busies itself with the things that are." Suidas II, p. 543 (Kuster edition): "*Meteoropolon*: observing heavenly things. Also *meteoroporon*." These last two words were omitted by Zo—

-> NOTES ON PLOTINUS <-

<note>The author is discussing the Greek term *meteoporountas* (soaring on high).</note> You find this in the Greek Lexicon p. 1354. Philostratus in *Life of Apollonius* III. 15. p. 105. edited by Olearius: <note>original: "μετεωροποροῦντας δὲ ἰδεῖν ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς εἰς πήχεις δύο"</note> "to see them soaring on high about two cubits from the earth." Simplicius in his commentary on *Epictetus's Enchiridion* XXXVIII. p. 243. a. p. 387. edited by Schweighaeuser: <note>original: "εἰ γὰρ ἡ ἀνθρωπίνη ψυχὴ τελεωθεῖσα καὶ εἰς θεὸν ἀναχθεῖσα, μετεωροπολεῖν λέγεται, καὶ πάντα τὸν κόσμον διοικεῖν"</note> "For if the human soul, having been perfected and led up to God, is said to soar on high and administer the whole universe." Schweighaeuser wished to attribute this saying to Stoic grandiloquence, forgetting the Platonic passage; had he remembered it, he would have refrained even from his conjecture of *diekein* (to pervade) instead of *dioikein* (to administer). But I spoke of this reading above at p. 376. G. and Ast spoke of it regarding the *Phaedrus* p. 293; who, although he praised several passages of Plotinus, did not use them to defend the authority of the reading *meteoporein* (to soar on high). Iamblichus, in Olympiodorus's commentary on the *Alcibiades* p. 60, also has the words of Plato before his eyes, though he recites them somewhat freely: "He himself solved it beautifully, saying that in other places Plato says that the more perfect souls <term>co-supervise</term> <note>original: "συνεπιτροπεύουσι" — add this word to the Lexicons</note> the things here with God and co-administer them; but the less perfect are like an instrument, and thus God uses them for things here." Regarding the power of the soul over bodies, see Plato's *Phaedo* p. 80. A. and Wyttenbach's notes on it p. 204.

p. 876, 11. **filling the actor with the nature of the thing acted upon.**] Regarding the sense, Marsilio Ficino translates well: "fills and contaminates": but not so well regarding elegance, since the word *implere* (to fill) sometimes has the meaning of polluting. Livy IV. 30—"by the contact of the disease—the city then is filled." See Ruhnken on Timaeus's *Platonic Lexicon* p. 31. where he explains *anapleos* (full of) and *anapimplasthai* (to be filled/infected). Cf. Heindorf on the *Phaedo* p. 120. Wyttenbach on Plutarch p. 293. Add Apollodorus's *Library* I. 9. 21. p. 89. in Heyne's edition concerning the Harpies and Phineus: <note>original: "—τὰ μὲν πλείονα ἀνήρπαζον, ὀλίγα δὲ ὅσα ὀσμῆς ἀνάπλεα κατέλειπον, ὥστε μὴ δύνασθαι προσενέγκασθαι"</note> "—they snatched away most things, but left a few things full of a stench, so that he was unable to touch them." Add Proclus's *Elements of Theology* XIII. p. 24. in our edition.

— 18. **And the souls of the stars—happiness**] I have helped this passage by inserting a parenthesis, which ought to be done more often in Plotinus's discourse. Our author refers to Plato's *Timaeus* p. 41. at the end and p. 42. a: "having composed the whole, he divided it into souls equal in number to the stars."

p. 877, 9. **For there is no danger that it should ever expect such a body**] Regarding the word *deinos* (terrible/danger), the primary discussion is Plato's in the *Protagoras* p. 341. A. B. cf. also Ast on the *Republic* p. 354. Let us look at the formulas that apply here. First, Herodotus VII. 245: "there is no danger that they will help her while the rest of Greece is being captured by the infantry." <note>original: "οὐδὲν δεινοὶ ἔσονται τοι, μὴ... βοηθέωσι"</note> There is nothing to fear lest they help. (The other passage I. 155. should not have been dragged in here, as was done in the new Stephanus *Thesaurus*.) Ibid. VII. 157: "it now becomes such a danger lest all Greece fall." Plato *Gorgias* 520. D: "there is no danger for him that he might ever be wronged." *Apology* p. 28: "there was no danger that it would stop with me": "nor indeed was it to be feared that that force would fail in me." Wolf. See Engelhardt on that passage p. 183. *Phaedo* p. 84. B: "there is no danger that he should fear" <note>original: "οὐδὲν δεινὸν μὴ φοβηθῇ"</note> "there is no peril, it is not to be feared, lest he fear." Wyttenbach, whom see p. 222. sq. The same author translates these words of Plotinus, which we are treating, thus: *For there is no danger that it should ever expect such a body.* However, the fact that he wrote *toutou* instead of *toioutou* is a printer's error, not a reading from any book.

p. 878, 4. **it was necessary for there to be many souls and one, and from the one, the many different ones.**] Iamblichus refers to this and similar points in these Enneads in Stobaeus's *Physical Eclogues* I. 52. p. 902. Heeren: "Plotinus and Porphyry and Amelius settle all souls equally into bodies from the soul above the heavens. But the *Timaeus* seems to make the first substance of souls very differently, the Demiurge scattering them among all the superior races, throughout the whole heaven, and into all the elements of the universe." See Plato's *Timaeus* p. 42. p. 45. sq. Bekker. The same Iamblichus ibid. p. 924: "—those around Plotinus who lead that faction which separates them (the souls) from the Reason, or even releases them into generation or removes them from the intellect. From which again a distinction of double opinion arises. For either each irrational power is dissolved into the whole life of the universe from which it was partitioned, or it remains mostly unchanged, as Porphyry thinks; or even having been separated from the intellect, the whole irrational life remains and is itself preserved in the world, as the most ancient of the priests declare." Namely the Egyptians. See Heeren in the place cited and the fragment of Hermes cited by him in Stobaeus ibid. nr. 5. p. 806. sqq. As for Porphyry's opinion, see his little book of *Sentences* or *On the Steps* p. 96. There is a third passage of Iamblichus in Stobaeus ibid. p. 886: "and Ploti—"

-> BOOK VIII. FOURTH ENNEAD. pages 876—880. 263 <-

<note>The author is discussing the views of Neoplatonist philosophers on whether the individual soul is distinct from the universal soul.</note>
...and Amelius are of this opinion. "For sometimes they define the divided soul as being different from the whole, and sometimes as being the same as it." As Porphyry would say, the activities of the whole soul are entirely separated from those of the divided soul. See Porphyry’s *Sentences* XI. p. 61. and regarding Plotinus and Amelius, compare Stobaeus in the same place p. 866. and apply the passages of Plotinus below on p. 492. and p. 647. chapter IV. A. B.

**p. 878, 17. if indeed everything that is among beings.]** I did not hesitate to adopt into the text this reading by Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino, the famous Renaissance translator of Plotinus</note>, which a second hand—whether that of Marsilius himself or another learned man—placed in the Medicean Manuscript A. The printed edition has "if indeed everything that is among *intelligible* beings." <note>original: "τῶν νοητῶν"</note> This contradicts the line of argument.

**p. 879, 5. The individual souls, then, making use of a gathering]** Thus I have given it with our better books <note>original: "προ χρωμένοις"</note>, and so did Ficino; you might say he additionally read "it is necessary," <note>original: "χρή"</note> were it not well known that he was accustomed to assist Plotinus’s brevity hundreds of times with such words and additions, as is the case here with the repeated "it is necessary." Furthermore, Iamblichus seems to refer to this place and similar ones in Stobaeus, *Eclogues* I. 52. p. 866. edited by Heeren. where, after he explained Numenius's opinion on the soul, he says: "Plotinus does not entirely agree." Compare Plotinus himself VI. 4. 16. p. 659. Porphyry’s *Starting Points Toward the Intelligibles* §. 32. p. 232. and following. Cudworth’s *Intellectual System* p. 1026. and following, edited by Mosheim, and Brucker’s *Critical History of Philosophy* II. p. 415. who writes thus: "These are the enigmas of a most obscure philosophy concerning the descent of souls, which, unless the obscurity deceives us, tend toward this: that souls, which were in the divine intellect, as if thrusting themselves forward and desiring to exist separately, have fallen into a state of singularity regarding that which is born with them in their descent, and thus have become worse; yet the intellect which resides in them remains in divine realms." These same Plotinian doctrines are treated by Tiedemann in the book *The Spirit of Speculative Philosophy*, III. p. 422. and following.

**p. 880, 14. and to ascend, whenever it takes a starting point from recollection to behold the things that are—to those for whom the opposites occurred either by nature or by chance]** Plotinus deals quite often with the doctrine of <term>reminiscence</term> <note>The Platonic idea that learning is actually "remembering" knowledge the soul had before birth</note>. See for example above p. 391. A. B. and the notes there and elsewhere. In this passage, he had before his eyes these words of Plato in the *Phaedrus* p. 249. end, 250. A. p. 47. Bekker edition: "Every soul of a man has by nature beheld the things that are, or else it would not have entered into this living being; but to be reminded of those things from these present ones is not easy for every soul, neither for those who then saw the things there only briefly, nor for those who, having fallen here, were so unfortunate as to be turned toward injustice by certain associations and thus have a forgetfulness of the sacred things they saw then. Only a few remain who possess the power of memory sufficiently." — Criticizing these decrees of Plato and Pythagoras, Eustathius of Antioch, in Angelo Mai’s *Vatican Collection* I. 3. p. 77, argues thus: "But since they clearly know they are being caught, they change their ground and invent the 'water of forgetfulness' <note>The mythical river Lethe</note>, which they say everyone drinks and thus forgets the births of their previous lives." <note>The editor questions the Greek text here: Did Eustathius write "the births of the lives allotted by lot"? (using the sense Plato uses for "allotted"). Or perhaps "the births of the chosen lives," the lives which individuals chose for themselves? For Eustathius is touching upon the passage in the *Republic* p. 617 near the end: "let him who draws the first lot first choose a life."</note> Certainly he touches upon the following on p. 621. A. in the same work: "that all must travel to the plain of Forgetfulness—that it is necessary for all to drink a certain measure of the water; and he who drinks always forgets everything. That these things are mythical and far from philosophy no right-thinking person seems to be ignorant; for what shall we say, O Pythagoras and Plato, have you yourselves taken and drunk the forgetfulness-inducing water? etc." — Then he concludes thus: "but being <insert>overturned</insert> <note>The editor suggests changing "turned toward" to "overturned"</note> into this barbarian superstition, they were deceived by using Egyptians as their guides." But perhaps "barbarian" <note>original: "βαρβαρώδη"</note> is also due to the scribes, who might have changed it because of the Egyptians, when Eustathius had written "abysmal." <note>original: "βαραθρώδη"</note> Clement of Alexandria, *Miscellanies* IV. p. 568—"the abysses of anger and wrath." Libanius, *On His Own Life* p. 4. Reiske edition: "to fall into the abyss of ignorance." Lucian, *On Astrology* p. 367: "he fell away from the truth and was utterly deceived in his reasoning and was carried down into a sea of bottomless affairs." Philo the Jew, *On Agriculture* III. p. 64. Pfeiffer edition: "in a turbid and abysmal life," unless one should read there "filthy life." You may find more of this kind in Wyttenbach’s observations on Plutarch’s *On the Delay of Divine Vengeance* p. 72. p. 392. and following, Oxford edition. So much for the passage of Eustathius. Let us add others pertaining to Platonic reminiscence. Plato, *Phaedo* p. 72. e: "that for us, learning happens to be nothing other than recollection."

-> ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS <-

Theodorus Metochita §. 88. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 576. Kiessling. *And perhaps this, then, provided a general starting point for Plato and Plotinus, and as many as seemed to follow them, that what appear to be teachings are not actually teachings, but are recollections (anamneseis) for the soul, through the purifications of the rational part that occur from time to time, etc.* **I have thought it necessary to set these things forth first for the sake of Libanius, in his Declamation for Socrates [[abbrev: p. → page]] 256. [[abbrev: ed. → edition]] of Jacob Morell.** thus: *and it is necessary while living to philosophize and to make the memory of death* ([[abbrev: leg. → read]] "practice" [meletēn]: for so Macarius Chrysocephalus reads, and "the practice of death" [meletē thanatou] is well known from the *Phaedo*. Add Porphyry *De Abstinentia* I. 30. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 49—*he practices laying aside everything foreign that he has taken on; and he reminds himself of those things which, though possessing them, he had forgotten.*) *to make the life, recollecting most of the ancient teachings, in which we seem to remain here* (Jacopo Morelli, a most learned man, edits it thus, with this version added: "—revolving in our mind most of the ancient disciplines in which we seem to remain here." What is this? Read confidently: *in which we seem to learn here*, with this meaning: in those things which here, in this life, we seem to learn, we do nothing other than recollect the original doctrines which our soul held in a higher and prior life.) Furthermore, just as Eustathius [[abbrev: l. l. → in the place cited]] and many others record that this doctrine of *reminiscence* reached Pythagoras and Plato from Egypt: so we encounter twin doctrines in that Indian poem inscribed as the *Bhagavad-Gita*. For thus in Canto XVIII. 73. ff. this is posited: that the understanding of *the things that truly are* is in no way achieved by the intellect through the help of dialectical conclusions, which tend toward the goal gradually and as if by steps through argumentation, but rather by the help of that contemplation which, beginning from the purging of the soul, excites recollection (τὴν ἀνάμνησιν). Whence that Indian poet and philosopher seems to have established, equally with Plato and the Platonists, that truth was in the souls of men from the beginning, but was afterwards obscured by the descent into bodies and can be illuminated anew by recollection alone. See Wilhelm von Humboldt disputing most acutely concerning this doctrine in the Commentary *Ueber die Bhagavad-Gita in Comm. Acad. Scientt. Berolinens. ann. 1826. p. 36. sq.*

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 880, 19. *when he divides them from the second crater*] [[abbrev: Vid. → See]] Plato's *Timaeus* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 41. near the end. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 44. Bekker and [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] the annotation above at [[abbrev: p. → page]] 376. G.—

Soon after: *but if he says that God sowed them.* Plato *Tim.* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 42. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 43. Bekk.: *he sowed some into the earth etc.*

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 881, 3. *just as when he makes him both speaking and as it were haranguing*] This refers to a passage of the Platonic *Timaeus* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 41. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 43. where the maker of the world addresses the rest of the gods: *Gods of gods etc.* which the scribes did not grasp, who attributed to Plotinus the reading "demiurging" [δημιουργοῦντα], from which intention even the preceding word "speaking" [λέγοντα] ought to have diverted them.

— 4. *For what things exist in the nature of the wholes, these the hypothesis generates and makes*] There are several similar sentiments in the *Enneads*. [[abbrev: Vid. → See]] [[abbrev: p. → page]] 299. B. C. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 378. G: *one must think that the entrance and the ensoulment occur in the account (logō) for the sake of instruction and clarity.* and especially [[abbrev: p. → page]] 487. B: *let generation in time be far from us when we are making an account concerning things that always are; but we attach generation to them in the account:* From which it is sufficiently understood what "the hypothesis" [ἡ ὑπόθεσις] is in this place. Concerning the expression "the hypothesis generates," for: *Reason posits that the maker generates*, [[abbrev: &c. → etc.]] consult what we said above regarding [[abbrev: p. → page]] 442. B. [[abbrev: inf. → below]] at the words: *those who pour out their visions.* Moreover, the argument pertains to that primary question, debated competitively by philosophers: whether the World was made by God, and whether in time and with a certain beginning, or from all eternity. Proclus on Plato’s *Timaeus*, after he brings forward the opinions of Plutarch, Atticus, Crantor, and others, continues thus on [[abbrev: p. → page]] 85: *Plotinus and the philosophers after Plotinus, Porphyry and Iamblichus, say that the composite is called "generated" in these matters (in Plato's Timaeus), and that this co-exists and is generated from another essence.* Wyttenbach collected more on this matter in *De Placito immortalitatis animorum* (before the Phaedo) [[abbrev: p. → page]] XXII. sqq. *That Plotinus is rightly numbered among those who established that the generation of the Soul and the World is without beginning, the cited passages do not allow us to doubt; as he explicitly pronounces both here and elsewhere that this entire history of the maker and the worldly workmanship was invented solely for the sake of doctrine and clarity.* Therefore he interprets even his own Plato, and does not think the god of the philosophers felt otherwise than that the World and the Soul are eternal, but that the account instituted in the *Timaeus* was employed only for the sake of aiding the understanding. In which matter I profess that Plotinus judges subtly and elegantly.

[[original page: 265]]

-> BOOK VIII. OF THE FOURTH ENNEAD. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 880—883. 265 <-

Indeed, on the contrary, among more recent writers some have fallen so far that, since they could not reconcile that workmanship of the World explained in the *Timaeus* with the rest of Plato's doctrine, they would reject that primary dialogue as not being Plato's.

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 881, 7. *and the descent of the whole into perfection,*] Among the causes of the descent of souls into bodies is also the constitution of the universe, and Plotinus touches upon that cause several times in this very chapter. Moreover, Celsus declares this thus [[abbrev: ap. → in]] Origen [[abbrev: libr. → book]] VIII. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 780. D: *but since humans have become bound to a body, whether for the sake of the economy of the wholes, or paying the penalties for sins, or by certain passions of the soul being weighed down, until it is purified in ordained periods. For it is necessary, according to Empedocles, that for thrice ten thousand hours one wanders far from the blessed ones, becoming all kinds of forms of mortals through time.* [[abbrev: Cf. → Compare]] Wyttenbach on Plutarch *De S. N. V.* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 113. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 444. [[abbrev: ed. → edition]] Oxon. Add the fragments of Empedocles v. 6. where however Sturz [[abbrev: p. → page]] 513. gave *alalesthai*. Moreover, by these words is designated "the wandering" [ἡ πλάνη], which Plotinus soon mentions from Empedocles. Concerning the rest, which pertain to these decrees of Empedocles and Heraclitus, we saw above at [[abbrev: p. → page]] 468. C. Moreover, we touched upon this doctrine of the descent of souls above at [[abbrev: p. → page]] 381. sqq.

— 8. *both necessity, and the voluntary (since necessity has the voluntary)*] Concerning divine necessity, Iamblichus thus disputes in *De Mysteriis Aegyptiorum* I. 14. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 25. *furthermore, the so-called necessities of the gods, this whole thing, are the gods' own (eisin Cod. Gothan. and Monac. here however in the [[abbrev: marg. → margin]] by a [[abbrev: rec. m. → more recent hand]] idian) necessities, and as they occur among gods; therefore not as if from outside nor as if by force... but as it is necessary for the benefit of good things, so they have it by being in every way thus, and in no way otherwise disposed. Therefore this is mixed with a good-form will and such necessity is a friend of love, and possesses so much in its own order of the gods and is immutable, and because it is held together according to the same things and in the same way, it remains in this, and never stands apart.* On which passage [[abbrev: vide → see]] Gale [[abbrev: p. → page]] 198.

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 882, 9. *But the immeasurable form of vice—of punished daimons*] Concerning the punishments of souls, Wyttenbach grants me the leisure of speaking [i.e., has already covered it] in Plutarch *De S. N. V.* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 99. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 426. Oxon. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 122. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 455. sq. Oxon.

[[abbrev: VOL. → VOLUME]] III.

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 883, 2. *never truly being*] You might suspect Marsilio [Ficino] read *ontōs houtō ousan* (truly being thus), but the [[abbrev: MSS. → manuscript]] books differ in no way from the edition. Soon at the end of the chapter—*through the variety of things outside—to do these polished things.* Ficino translated *glaphyra* as *various and most beautiful.* Perhaps *beautiful and pleasing* would be better. Concerning the power of the word *glaphyros, glaphyria, glaphyrotēs*, Tib. Hemsterhuis in *Anecdott.* Vol. I. [[abbrev: ed. → edition]] Jac. Geel and J. C. Th. Ernesti in *Lex. Technol. Graecorr. Rhetor.* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 61. sq. have granted me the leisure of speaking. I shall subjoin certain other examples: Plutarch *De Sanit. tuend.* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 122. E. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 483. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 325. Potter. concerning the Philosophy of the Pagans: *and otherwise the polish of contemplation fits the sketching out of commentaries.* In the preceding things he had called those things *the most beautiful*, and in the following he attributed to them *seasoning* [hēdysma]. To which pertains the instruction of Eustathius in *Odyssey* a. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 1385. concerning this word: *the word is transferred also to thoughts, and they are called polished thoughts, those having something deep, yet with a certain grace and transparency and brightness, so as not to be entirely dark because of the depth.*

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 886, 4. *And if it is necessary to dare to speak the phenomenon more clearly against the opinion of others, not all our soul, even, has sunk*] Hence this opinion is called a "newer account" [neōteros logos] by Proclus in *On Timaeus*. Damascius, on the contrary, pronounces this opinion of Ours [Plotinus] to be true. I have displayed the passages in *Annot. in Procli Instit. Theolog.* CCXI. Consult also Plotinus above II. 9. 2. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 201. A. and the Annotations on that place.

And if they said this was divided indivisibly, like a voice among those hearing, the evil would be moderate; but now they say the essence itself of the soul is divided, and what is hardest of all, that they want it to be essentially in elements, and to be divided with these in the generation of bodies, and again to come together into the same when the bodies are dissolved, like water being divided, and again collected and mixed.* Moreover, Tertullian *Against the Valentinians* [[abbrev: c. → chapter]] 29. From chance they bring in not nature, but indulgence, so that those whom Achamoth rains down from the heights into good souls, that is, inscribed in the psychical census. For the earthly race, that is, bad souls, never receive salvation. For they have pronounced an immutable and irreformable nature." We warned above that Plotinus also speaks against the Valentinians at the beginning of the book *Against the Gnostics*. The same Tertullian in *De Anima* [[abbrev: cap. → chapter]] XXV. sqq. where he relates various opinions of various men, strives to refute Plato pronouncing concerning one soul. -> BOOK IX. ENNEAD FOUR. pages 884—890. 267 <-

...they appear, so that the whole is present in any part of it. <note>original: "φαίνονται, ὡς καὶ ἐν ὁτῳοῦν αὐτῆς μέρει εἶναι τὰ ὅλα"</note> — And of this opinion, Numenius is indisputably a follower, while Plotinus is not entirely in agreement, Amelius wavers unsteadily within it, and Porphyry hesitates about it, at one moment systematically departing from it, and at another following it as a tradition handed down from above. And on page 886: Both Plotinus and Amelius are occasionally of this opinion. For sometimes they define the individual soul as something other than the whole soul, but sometimes as being the same as it. Proclus, in *Elements of Theology* § 184, pages 274 and following, posits three kinds of souls: first, the divine; second, those that always participate in the Mind <term>Mind: the Greek 'Nous', the realm of pure intellect</term>; third, those that sometimes participate in the Mind and sometimes fall away from it. Gregory of Nyssa, in *On the Soul* I, page 90 and following, says it is the opinion of the **Manichaeans** <note>A dualistic religious movement that taught a struggle between light and darkness</note> that there is one and the same soul for all things; he explains it more fully on page 103, sections C and D, thus: — (The Manichaeans say) that there is only one soul for all things, which is carved up and cut into individual bodies, both animate and inanimate; and that some things participate in more of it, and others in less; animate things in more, and inanimate in less, and the heavenly bodies in much more, so that individual souls are parts of the universal soul. And if they said it was divided indivisibly, like a voice heard by many listeners, the error would be moderate; but as it is, they say the very substance of the soul is partitioned, and what is most difficult of all, they wish it to be essentially composed of elements, partitioned among these in the birth of bodies, and again coming together into the same state when the bodies are dissolved, like water being divided and then gathered and mixed together again.

Furthermore, Tertullian, in *Against the Valentinians*, chapter 29, page 26 (Rigaltius edition), reports that the **Valentinians** <note>A prominent Gnostic sect</note> teach thus: "so they also distinguish souls by a double property, the good and the bad: according to the earthly <term>choïcum: from the Greek 'choikos', meaning made of clay or dust</term> state of Cain (or from C.?) and the animal <term>animalem: here meaning 'psychical' or related to the lower soul</term> state from Abel, and the spiritual from Seth. Regarding what happens to them, they do not bring in nature, but indulgence, so that those whom Achamoth <note>A Gnostic figure representing a lower form of Wisdom</note> rains down from the higher realms into good souls—that is, those enrolled in the animal census. For the earthly race, that is, the bad souls, can never receive saving things. For they have pronounced that nature is unchangeable and irreformable." We have already noted above, at the beginning of the book *Against the Gnostics*, that Plotinus also speaks against the Valentinians. The same Tertullian, in *On the Soul*, chapters 25 and following, where he relates various opinions of different thinkers, strives to refute Plato's pronouncements concerning the single soul. Cassiodorus, in chapter 16, page 355, after touching upon the Christian doctrine of souls created by God, proceeds thus: having completed these things, I shall discuss them by their signs and indications. Because, although *their substance seems to be one, it is nevertheless separated by far unequal qualities* (in the <margin>separated</margin>).

Page 889, line 7. **it was necessary** <note>original: "ἐχρῆν γὰρ"</note>] Because the Vatican Manuscript, which is otherwise more accurate in accents than others, has "it was necessary" <note>original: "ἔχρην"</note> in this place. See Fischer on Aristophanes' *Plutus* 406; Matthiae's *Greek Grammar* § 255, page 497, second edition; and there the cited Goettling on Theodosius of Alexandria's *Grammar*, page 218; and Buttmann’s *Detailed Greek Grammar* § 114, page 257.

— 16. **as a man... will be standing**] This passage seems should be read thus: *As a man who is in me while I am moving; for in me, while I am moving, he is moving, but in you he will be standing still.*

Page 890, line 18. **but we call it one** (so I have placed "one" <note>original: "μίαν"</note> instead of "truly" <note>original: "μὴν"</note> by the authority of the better manuscripts) **and a multitude.**] Proclus explains the same sentiment more copiously in *On the Alcibiades*, preface, chapter 82 and following, page 246 and following of our edition, where among other things (page 248) these words are read: Having ascended there and having come among the incorporeal things, you will see that psychic world-order <term>world-order: 'diakosmos', the structured arrangement of the universe</term> above the bodies, which is self-moving and self-energizing, having its existence in itself and by itself, yet nonetheless multiplied (so it should be read) and having received an appearance of the partitioned essences around the bodies; you will behold through the relationships of reasons a vast multitude of proportions and compositions, and wholes and parts, and psychic circles and a variety of powers, and you will see that their perfection is not eternal, nor standing all together at once, but unfolding according to time and existing in transitions. For such is the nature of the soul. But after the multitude in souls, raise yourself up to the Mind and the intellectual kingdoms, so that you may grasp the unity of things, etc. Compare the same author's *Elements of Theology*, chapter 62, page 96 of our edition; and Porphyry’s *Sentences* XV, page 323; XXXIII, page 234; and XXXIX, page 246 and following; and look at Plotinus himself above, page 189 B, and especially below, page 757 D, E; page 761 C; page 766 E. Add Iamblichus in Stobaeus II, page 400; in the *Protrepticus*, page 33; and Proclus *On the Timaeus*, page 329.

IV. 3. 10. IV. 4. 39. (Consult what we have annotated at the last place [[abbrev: p. → page]] 433. B.) and V. 3. 8.

— 12. *But in knowledge [epistēmē], someone might say, the part is not the whole—but it is made potential [endynamoutai], as if having approached the whole.*] Lobeck ordered the word *endynamos* to be added to the Lexicons on Phrynichus [[abbrev: p. → page]] 605. note. Dionysius, who is falsely called the Areopagite, also uses it in *De Divinis Nominibus* [[abbrev: cap. → chapter]] IV. §. 32. Biel in *Thesaur.* I. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 533. and Schleusner in the new *Thesaurus* II. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 359. cite the verb *endynamoō* and *endynamoumai*, to strengthen, to be strengthened and to grow strong from the Septuagint. But in this place it assumes this peculiar power: *to be rendered potential*, i.e. to arrive at the point where you are considered a power (*dynamei*); which Ficino rightly perceived. Therefore this passage, as being unique or especially to be noted for its philosophical argument, must be marked in Lexicons.

Furthermore, I am mistaken or Plotinus in these and following matters up to the end of the book had before his eyes the passages of Plato where the philosopher explains concerning sciences (*epistēmais*); [[abbrev: v. c. → for example]] in *Laws* VIII. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 643. sqq. and especially in *Philebus* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 55. sqq. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 177. Stallbaum. Proclus in turn had Plotinus before his eyes in *On Alcibiades* [[abbrev: pr. → preface]] §. 95. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 307. sqq. where he placed both other things and these ([[abbrev: p. → page]] 308.): *and these things manifest our essence as being separate from the body and standing in itself, seeing that even knowledge being our perfection has obtained such a power. For the body-like powers diminish themselves in transmissions, but knowledge, remaining one and the same, sufficient and undiminished, transmits itself to one and many likewise. Thus then also the soul is present to every body and to all the parts, and some do not participate in it in one way, and others in another. etc.* Then the example of the arithmetician is subjoined ([[abbrev: cf. → compare]] *Philebus* [[abbrev: l. l. → in the place cited]]) Marcus Antoninus [Aurelius] IV. 31. proposed the definition of the man of knowledge and art from the reasoning of the Stoics, on which consult Gataker [[abbrev: p. → page]] 166. The most learned Boissonade recently conveniently applied the same passage of Antoninus to the 23rd letter of Crates, as it is called, in *Notices et Extraits d. Manuscripts d. l. Bibl. du Roi*. Vol. XI. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 45. Proclus relates Plato's opinion on Science, explained in the *Theaetetus* and elsewhere, in *On Euclid's Elements* [[abbrev: Lib. → Book]] I. [[abbrev: c. → chapter]] 4. [[abbrev: cf. → compare]] [[abbrev: lib. → book]] III. [[abbrev: c. → chapter]] 1. The Peripatetics also establish *science as either universal or singular, either in potentiality or in act.* In which discussion John Philoponus on Aristotle *De Generatione Animalium* II. 1. likewise, as Plotinus, uses the example of the Geometer when he says: that the Geometer, when he is awake, *is a geometer in act.*

Finally, at the end of the chapter:—*and through the body it is darkened; but there all things are bright [phana] and each one:* recognize the diligent reader of Plato: *Phaedrus* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 256. [[abbrev: d. → again]]: *for it is no longer the law for those who have already begun the heavenly journey to go into darkness and the journey under the earth, but leading a bright [phanon] life to be happy.*

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 124.) where wisdom is opposed to gold, to which he attributes a *bright [phannan] ray*. Which passage was to be compared with the passage of another poet in Alexander of Aphrodisias in *Problemm.* II. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 300. [[abbrev: ed. → edition]] Sylb. *the sun hid its shining [phaeinēn] ray.*) *Symposium* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 197. a: *that whomsoever this god becomes a teacher, he turns out illustrious and bright [phanos], but of whom Eros does not touch, he is dark.* Iamblichus says for it in *Life of Pythagoras* §. 104. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 224. Kiessl.: *of illustrious and supernatural men.* Philo Judaeus [[abbrev: p. → page]] 651. B: *consecrating more brightly [phanoteron] with the fire-bearing torch of things.* Dorville taught that it is primarily used of gods and divine things on Chariton [[abbrev: p. → page]] 597. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 567. [[abbrev: ed. → edition]] Leipzig. Heliodorus X. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 472. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 394. Matthaei had long ago provided the true reading of the passage on Chrysostom's *Four Homilies* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 117. [[abbrev: not. → note]] 154. at the words *splendid and brighter [phanotera] than the sun.* Philostratus *Imagines* X. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 69. [[abbrev: ed. → edition]] Jacobs: *brighter [phanoteroi] than fire,* where another [[abbrev: cod. → manuscript]] has "phanoteroi", another "phanerōteroi", of which confusion the most learned Jacobs collected several examples in *Annott.* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 460. I shall help Iamblichus on this given occasion, who, treating of the Pythagorean way of teaching in *Life of Pythagoras* §. 104. [[abbrev: sq. → following]] [[abbrev: p. → page]] 88. Kuster. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 226—228. Kiessling.:—*and through symbols they shadowed* (so Kiessling wrote from the *Protreptic*, but since all our books agree in "epeskopoun", I do not know whether Rittershusius' conjecture "epeskotoun", they obscured, might be more probable:) *their discourses or even writings to each other—whenever however it is unfolded according to this way of symbols, and becomes both manifest and clear instead of dark to the many—etc.* Thus Kiessling followed Kuster. But "phana" (bright) which Arcerius has, is confirmed by [[abbrev: Cod. → Codex]] Ciz. and all mine; nor was there any reason why that reading should be departed from. For "euagē" (pure) however one must read "enargē" (evident) or rather "euan-gē" with Schaefer. Moreover "phana" confirms a similar passage of Lucian *On Writing History* [[abbrev: c. → chapter]] 44: *so indeed also the first goal is to show clearly and to manifest the matter most brightly [phanotata] etc.* In which place if our C. Frid. Hermann had remembered the Iamblichean words and others similar, he would not have written, I believe, what he wrote in the annotation to those Lucianic matters [[abbrev: p. → page]] 268. *Phanos* perhaps should also be restored to Theophilus in the *Paraphrase of Justinian's Institutes* I. 6. 117. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 69. [[abbrev: ed. → edition]] G. O. Reitz. He explains what "Consilium" is: *a consilium is an assembly of manifest [phanerōn] men, meeting according to a stated time of the year.* And yet a Consilium, by Ulpian's testimony, was gathered from Senators and Knights; therefore from *illustrious, splendid* men, whence it seems "phanōn" (bright/shining) should be read.

I shall add a brilliant passage pertaining no less to Plato's opinions than to Plotinus': *and indeed especially (I wonder) at Origen, the one who shared in the same education as Plotinus; for indeed he also himself ends in the mind and the first being, but the One, that which is beyond all mind and beyond all being, he lets go. And if as better than all knowledge and all account and all application, we would not say that he erred from the harmony of Plato nor from the nature of things. But if because the One is entirely non-existent and non-subsistent, and that the best thing is the mind, and that the first being and the first one are the same, neither would we agree with him in these things, nor would Plato accept it or count him among his own disciples. For (I think) such a doctrine is far removed from the philosophy of Plato and is filled with Peripatetic innovation. But if you wish also toward this, and toward all the others as many as were leaders of the same opinion, let us go through a few things fighting for the opinion of Plato, and showing that he says the first cause is exalted beyond mind and beyond all beings, just as Plotinus himself and Porphyry and all those who received their philosophy think he says.* Tholuck also touched upon this passage of Proclus in the book inscribed *Ssufismus [[abbrev: p. → page]] 203:* who however seems to pronounce more confidently concerning the causes which moved Origen to omit that "One" (to hen) than this passage allows. D. and annotation there) *and in other places, that even this mind through that which is before itself, the non-mind, is a god; just as the soul, by its own summit above soul, is mind, and the body by the power before the body, is soul:* Duplices enim habet actus (mens), ut ait Plotinus, alteros quidem, ut mens, alteros ut nectare inebriatus, et alibi (in other places [[abbrev: sc. → namely]] Plotinus says) that this mind also through that non-mind, which is before itself, is god, just as the soul by its own summit, which is above soul, is mind, and the body by the power, which is before the body, is soul. Thus these are to be punctuated and translated. Emilio Porto, with the comma omitted before "hoti kai ho nous", had circumscribed the words: "and in others" as: "And in other *Beings it is evident.*" Soon in our passage: *as of fire, the one is the accompanying heat,* from Ficino's version Cyril agrees with us.—Then they maintain the reading "hyphistamenēn", subsisting (i.e. leading its origin from mind) and the following, and these in [[abbrev: l. l. → the place cited]] [[abbrev: p. → page]] 299. C. concerning the soul: *being with mind and subsisting from mind.*

[[abbrev: p. → page]] 902, 1. *mind-form* [nooeidēs]] Thus I corrected from [[abbrev: Cod. → Codex]] Vat., analogy demanding it [[abbrev: v. c. → for example]] in *nooblabēs, nooplanēs, noophalēs* and below [[abbrev: p. → page]] 504. at the end the edition itself and several [[abbrev: MSS. → manuscript]] books exhibit "nooeidē". Furthermore, this word must be added to lexicons.

— 10. *and the life truly under Cronus, of God being satiety (korou) and mind*] Refers to the words of Plato in the *Cratylus* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 396. b. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 30. [[abbrev: p. → page]] 58—68. Moreover, Proclus makes mention of Plotinus himself in this Saturnian doctrine in another place, namely in *On Timaeus* [[abbrev: p. → page]] 93: *Plotinus the philosopher posits a twofold demiurge, the one in the intelligible, the other the ruler of the whole. And he speaks rightly. For somehow even the worldly mind is the demiurge of the whole, and Aristotle at least, for he pronounced this to be, the first, and he called this fate, and addressed it by the name of Zeus; but there is also on the other hand the exalted father and maker, whom he posits to be in the intelligible, calling all that is between the one and the world intelligible. For there he has even the true heaven, and the kingdom of Cronus and the mind of Zeus. As if someone were saying in the heaven both the sphere of Cronus, and that of Zeus and that of Ares. For the whole intelligible is one-many, and one mind comprising many intelligibles. Thus Plotinus indeed philosophizing.* The Platonists used to say the sphere of Saturn was that which is in the eighth, in which are the Elysian fields.

...he might lead back the soul (Macrobius, *On the Dream of Scipio* I. ch. 11. [cf. confer] Zoëga, *On Obelisks* [p. pagina] 297.) Hence, it is called the *seventh operation*: the *Kronia poiesis* [Saturnian creation] according to Proclus himself in *Alcibiades* pr. [p. pagina] 196. [h. e. hoc est] that operation which causes us to separate ourselves in a natural way from the body and corporeal things. To this place the Platonists also used to drag [attribute] the *royal court of Saturn* (Hermias on the *Phaedrus* ch. 29. For the rest, [cf. confer] on Saturn, Plotinus III. 5. 2. and below V. 1. 7. and on the *cosmos* III. 6. 14. III. 8. 10. ([p. pagina] 353. B.) and below V. 9. 8. ([p. pagina] 561. A. B.).
