[p. pagina] 903, 2. *νοεῖ δὲ οὐ ζητῶν, ἀλλ᾽ ἔχων* [he thinks not by seeking, but by possessing]] Aristotle, *Metaphysics* XII. 7. [p. pagina] 203. Sylb. [p. pagina] 249. Brandis.: "And thought in itself is of that which is best in itself, and the highest thought is of the highest object. And the mind thinks itself by participation in the object of thought; for it becomes an object of thought by touching and thinking it. Thus mind and the object of thought are the same; for that which is receptive of the object of thought and of essence is the mind; and it acts by possessing; so that the latter rather than the former is the divine element which the mind seems to have, and contemplation is the most pleasant and best."

— 6. *ποτὲ μὲν Σωκράτης, ποτὲ δὲ ἵππος.* [at one time Socrates, at another a horse.]] I have written *μὲν* instead of *γὰρ* [cum with] Cod. Med. B. Plotinus frequently mentions Socrates. See III. 2. 15. IV. 3. 5. IV. 4. 2. V. 3. 3. V. 7. 1. V. 9. 12. VI. 1. 13. VI. 2. 1. VI. 3. 4. 5. 6. &c. However, those passages in which that specific Socrates is properly commemorated must be distinguished from many others where Plotinus uses the name of Socrates for the name of any man whatsoever, as [h. l. hoc loco; in this place] and V. 7. 1. and many others. In this matter our philosopher follows the common Greek and Latin usage. For writers of both languages are accustomed, as the occasion arises, to use proper names sometimes of famous men or classes universally, and sometimes of obscure people, such as slaves, freedmen, and the like. Thus the Greeks put the names of Callias, Cleon, Dion, Socrates, and Theon for any proper names; the Latins: Caius, Caia, Titius, Mevius, Seius, Sempronius, Numerius, and from the servile names, Dama, Davus, Dionysius, Eros, Stichus. And Aristotle similarly uses the names of Socrates and *Callias* for the sake of example; [v. c. verbi causa] in the beginning of *Metaphysics* I. 1. and likewise XII. 3. [p. pagina] 197. Sylb. [p. pagina] 242. Brandis.: "There are three essences: one is matter, being a 'this' in appearance—another is nature, a 'this' toward which there is also a certain habit; yet a third is that which is composed of these, the individual, such as Socrates or Callias." Sextus Empiricus, *Against the Mathematicians* V. 104: "And in the same way we have observed in medicine that a wound to the heart is the cause of death, not by observing the death of Dion alone, but also of Theon and Socrates and many others." On this, consult Fabricius [p. pagina] 355. [cf. confer] the same at *Outlines of Pyrrhonism* I. 189. [p. pagina] 47. Regarding the designation of *Caius* and *Caia* in marriage formulas [vid. vide] Brisson, *On the Rite of Marriage* [p. pagina] 326. Grupen, *On the Roman Wife* [p. pagina] 205. and [p. pagina] 312. and [cf. confer] Wyttenbach on Plutarch’s *Roman Questions* [p. pagina] 30. [p. pagina] 271. D. (in the notes [p. pagina] 33.)

You have examples of servile names used universally in Horace, *Satires* I. 6. 38. II. 5. 18. where [cf. confer] the interpreters and add these from Persius, *Satires* V. 75. ff.:

"Alas, those barren of truth, for whom a single 
whirl makes a Roman citizen. Here is **Dama**, a groom not worth three farthings, 
a blear-eyed scoundrel, a liar over a little fodder. 
Let his master twirl him round, in the movement of a top [my MS reads *temporis* 'of time' poorly] he comes out 
*Marcus Dama*."

Where in the same MS book the scholion [commentary] reads thus: *Here is Dama; that cheap and worthless slave; for slaves did not have praenomina [first names], but once liberty was attained, praenomina were imposed upon them. Thus here too the slave, who was previously called Dama, is now after liberty called Marcus Dama.* I have said more about the names of slaves in a commentary sent to the Royal Paris Academy of Inscriptions, and translated into French by the most distinguished man Edgar Quinet: *Prolegomena on Slavery among the Romans.*

— 12. *τὸ δὲ ὂν, τῷ νοεῖσθαι τῷ νῷ διδὸν τὸ νοεῖν καὶ τὸ εἶναι·* [But being, by being thought, gives to the mind both thought and existence]] Philostratus, *Life of Apollonius* IV. 28. [p. pagina] 167. Olear.—"O Good Zeus, for you are so good as to share yourself with men." Where Olearius attributes this sentiment to Pythagorean philosophy, comparing both our passage and indeed Proclus on Plato's *Timaeus* [p. pagina] 6. and Hierocles on the *Pythagorean Golden Verses* [v. vide] 1. You should also inspect these Enneads themselves, V. 9. 2. and V. 9. 7.

[p. pagina] 903, 18. *Γίγνεται οὖν τὰ πρῶτα νοῦς, ἑτερότης, ταυτοτης* up to the end of the chapter] To these, apply what our author discusses below V. 9. 8. [p. pagina] 562. A—D. and VI. 2. 8. [sq. sequenti; following]. Moreover, the source of these passages is in Plato's *Sophist* [p. pagina] 255. E. and [p. pagina] 256. Tennemann has touched upon these Plotinian matters and reduced them to the formulas of Kantian reason in *History of Philosophy* Vol. VI. [p. pagina] 96. Near the end of the chapter, I have given from the excellent Cod. Vat. *ταὐτὸν δὲ, ἐπεὶ ἓν* (instead of *ἓν*) *ἑαυτῷ*. Which the adjacent words declare to be uniquely true: *καὶ κοινὸν δέ τι ἓν πᾶσι* [and a certain one common to all]. For which reason the habit of those who, like Tennemann, omit accents in transcribing the words of the Greeks, is to be disapproved.

[p. pagina] 904, 14. *Ὅταν δὲ ὁρισθῇ (ἡ δυάς), ἀριθμὸς ἤδη, ἀριθμὸς δὲ ὡς οὐσία· ἀριθμὸς δὲ καὶ ἡ ψυχή.* [But when (the dyad) is defined, it is already number, and number as essence; and the soul is also number.]] Above [p. pagina] 304. A. our author pronounces thus concerning the Soul: "And indeed, whether its essence be number or logos, how could an affection occur in number or logos?" [Vid. Vide] what we have noted at that passage. In our passage, Plotinus may seem to act in accord with Xenocrates and Pythagoras. Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I. 10: "Xenocrates denied that the soul has a shape or as it were a body, but said it was number, the power of which, as it had already seemed to Pythagoras before, was greatest in nature." [Ubi vid. Ubi vide] Davis. Gregory of Nyssa, *On the Soul* I. [p. pagina] 90. C: "Pythagoras said (the soul was) a self-moving number. Plato said it was an intelligible essence, moving from itself according to a harmonious number." From which it is understood how the followers of Plato were able to attribute number to the soul. (But on these matters, consult Wyttenbach on the *Phaedo* [p. pagina] 228. [sqq. sequentibus] [p. pagina] 248. [sqq. sequentibus]). Regarding the reverence of the Pythagoreans toward numbers and their doctrine, I have praised more at this passage of Proclus in *Alcibiades* pr. [p. pagina] 259: "Pythagoras used to say that of all things that exist, number is the wisest," and at this of Olympiodorus in the same dialogue [p. pagina] 95. concerning the Pythagoreans: "they marveled at those who first discovered numbers, saying that they had known the essence of the mind [κ. τ. λ. καὶ τὰ λοιπά; etc.]." Finally, to Proclus in *Elements of Theology* [§. section] 113. [p. pagina] 164—166: "All divine number is unitary. For if divine number has a preceding cause, the One, just as the intellectual has the Mind, and the psychic has the Soul, and the multitude is everywhere analogous to its cause, it is surely clear that the divine number is also unitary, since the One is God." For the rest, confer our Author himself below [p. pagina] 671. [sqq. sequentibus] where we shall give more.—Plotinus continues in our passage: *οὐ γὰρ ὄγκοι τὰ πρῶτα-ὕστερα* [for the first things are not masses... last]. Proclus touches upon and approves these and similar points of our Author in *On Plato's Republic* [p. pagina] 425: "If every power is colorless and shapeless, for he says one sees neither the shape nor color of power, it is clear that every power is incorporeal according to him. For every body participates in every finite shape; and because of this, what Plotinus says is also true, that in large bodies there are powers not large, and in small ones not small, since masses neither add to nor diminish powers."

[p. pagina] 906, 1. *Ὧδε οὖν λεγέσθω* [Thus let it be said, etc.]] Brucker has touched upon these in *Critical History of Philosophy* II. [p. pagina] 399. adding: "It seems Plotinus accepted this from Ammonius, from the discipline of the Christians, who used to speak reverently and with the greatest devotion about the generation of the *logos* and the mystery of the Trinity itself among their secret doctrines." As if indeed many similar things were not read in the dialogues of Plato himself. Soon, the formula: *θεὸν αὐτὸν ἐπικαλεσαμένοις* [having called upon God himself] is Platonic: *Laws* X. [p. pagina] 893. A. B. "Come then, if ever God is to be called upon by us [κ. τ. λ. καὶ τὰ λοιπά; etc.]" which Platonists and other writers have eagerly imitated.

— 2. *οὐ λόγῳ γεγονότι,* [not with a spoken word,]] Thus from the reading in the margin we have decided to rewrite *γεγονῶτα* instead of *γεγονῶ*, which the edition has. Concerning the etymology and power of this word, there is no need for us to deal with it after the explanations of Valckenaer on Euripides' *Hippolytus* 586. of Coray on Plutarch’s *Flamininus* [p. pagina] 465. (to whom [cf. confer] also our Baehr's note [p. pagina] 186.) and others. Let us touch upon some passages corrupted by copyists: Alciphron, *Epistles* III. 48. [p. pagina] 151. Wagner.: "using a certain piercing and *clear* [gegonotero] sound." Thus *τορὸν* [clear/piercing] and especially *διατόρον* [resonant] and *γεγονὼς* [clear/loud] are often joined, as Wyttenbach teaches on Eunapius [p. pagina] 262. The same is *τρανόν* [distinct]. [Vid. Vide] Our note in Proclus' *Elements of Theology* [§. section] 145. [p. pagina] 216. And Iamblichus used this voice in *Life of Pythagoras* [§. section] 134. [p. pagina] 113. Kust. [p. pagina] 282. Kiessl.: "and the river uttered something clear [*gegonon ti*] and distinct." Thus the edition of Arcerius, and rightly; but my many manuscript books read *γωνόν*, though Cod. Monac. [n. numero] 392. in the margin has *γεγονών*. In Philostratus, *Life of Apollonius* V. 9. [p. pagina] 195. we read today: *ἐπεὶ δὲ ἐξάρας* (write *ἐξάρας*) *τὴν φωνὴν καὶ κεχανὼς ἐφθέγξατο*, doubtless from an unfortunate conjecture of Olearius instead of *γεγονώς*. He ought rather to have kept *γεγονώς* or *γεγονώς* (vid. Heringa's *Observations* [p. pagina] 64. and Boissonade on Philostratus' *Heroica* [p. pagina] 378.) And

For the contrary follows: *ἀλλὰ τῇ ψυχῇ —εὔχεσθαι—δυναμένους* [but being able to pray with the soul]. These, even without my warning, remind readers of the words of the Apostle to the Ephesians VI. 18. *προσευχόμενοι ἐν πνεύματι* [praying in the spirit] and V. 19. *ᾄδοντες καὶ ψάλλοντες ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ ὑμῶν τῷ κυρίῳ* [singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord], and similar ones throughout the books of the New Testament; which it is surprising have not yet been compared individually with Plato and the Platonists and Plotinus himself regarding words and sentiments by theologians, but they have rather labored in comparing Xenophon, Arrian, Polybius [cet. ceteris; etc.] with the sacred writers.—Soon those words *μόνους πρὸς μόνον* [alone to the alone] pertain to the Platonic doctrine of *segregation* and moral *solitude*; about which we spoke above at III. 1. 10. [p. pagina] 234. F.

[p. pagina] 906, 7. *Παντὶ τῷ κινουμένῳ δεῖ τι εἶναι ὃ μὴ κινεῖται·* [For everything moved there must be something that is not moved]] Thus we have given from the MS books and Ficino's version instead of *πάντα*. Taylor also saw this. The next part: *ἐκποδὼν δὲ ἡμῖν ἔστω γένεσις ἡ ἐν χρόνῳ* [let generation in time be far from us] we explained above at [p. pagina] 473. B. Soon: *τῷ δὲ λόγῳ τὴν γένεσιν προσάπτοντας αὐτοῖς, αἰτίας καὶ τάξεως αὐτοῖς ἀποδώσει* [attaching generation to them in speech, he will render to them the cause and order], or it should be read *ἀποδόσει* with Cod. Vat. so that you understand *προσάπτομεν* [we attach]: when indeed we attach generation to them in word (or in the middle of speaking), (we attach it in reality) by the attribution of cause and order (h. e. in reality we want nothing else to be attributed to them by the word generation, except cause and order): or before *ἀποδώσει* one must think of *τὶς* [someone], which perhaps was also swallowed up by the preceding *αὐτοῖς*, and *προσάπτοντας* should be accepted as an anacoluthon for *προσάπτόντων*. As for the fact that in the following Taylor wants *βουλευθέντος* [deliberated] to be read for *βουληθέντος* [willed]: neither do the MS books support this, nor is it necessary that anything be corrected. For the rest, as others have profited from these decrees of Plotinus, so has his disciple Porphyry. This did not escape the most learned Cudworth in *Intellectual System* [p. pagina] 673. ff. treating these matters, whose Latin translator Mosheim in the notes on these very points set out to charge both Plotinus and Porphyry with the crime of Sabellianism.

[p. pagina] 907, 10. *Τί οὖν χρὴ περὶ τοῦ τελειοτάτου λέγειν* [What then must be said about the most perfect]] Cyril praises these in *Against Julian* VIII. [p. pagina] 173. B. C. and Theodoret in *Therapeutics* book II. [p. pagina] 750. Vol. IV. Schulz. And the former prefaces thus: "And indeed Plotinus being a great seeker and having driven through every, so to speak, subtlety of speech, says somewhere thus about the Good:" the latter thus: "And Plotinus, who emulated the philosophy of Plato, wrote a book about the three principal hypostases, in which he also said these things." Hugo Grotius also touched on these in *On the Truth of the Christian Religion* IV. [§. section] 12. [p. pagina] 286. [ed. editio] Koecher. and Cudworth in *Intellectual System* [p. pagina] 687. [Cf. Confer] also our Author below [p. pagina] 512. [sq. sequenti] and [p. pagina] 554.

— 15. *ὅτι τἆλλα μετ᾽ αὐτὸν* [that the other things are after it]] "The things that follow in Plotinus seemed worthy to Cyril to be attached. And rightly so: for they run thus: *οἷον καὶ ἡ ψυχὴ —— — ὡς οὐδὲ ψυχῆς καὶ νοῦ*. By which words, while he was shaping some shadow of the Holy Trinity, but which seemed to favor the Arians too much, Cyril added an antidote, which Eusebius easily omitted. For he says that Mind is our God the Word, says Cyril, since we ourselves call him Wisdom. Except not in lesser or second place, according to some complete superiority and glory of the Father; nor as not having self-sufficiency, do we say he is perfected by the Father as it seems to these men [etc. &c.] and again, those men, holding such opinions and dragging down to a dissimilarity of natures those things admired among them, boast of cold and puerile ideas; but we say the Father is all-perfect, and likewise the Son, as perfect from perfect; and indeed also the Holy Spirit. And Theodoret says, unfolding the thought of Plato, both Plotinus and Nu-

menius say that he spoke of three things beyond time and eternal: the Good, and Mind, and the Soul of the universe; that which we call the Father, naming it the Good, and the Mind, which we call the Son and the Word; and calling the power that animates and gives life to all things the Soul, which the divine words call the Holy Spirit." Viger on Eusebius.

[p. pagina] 908, 1. *Ποθεῖ δὲ πᾶν τὸ γεννῆσαν* [Everything desires that which generated it]] Theodoret has these and the first words of the [seq. sequenti] chapter up to *λέγων* [saying] in *Therapeutics* book II. [p. pagina] 750. Schulz.

— 9. *ἢ ὅτι τῇ ἐπιστροφῇ πρὸς αὐτὸ ἑώρα·* [or that by the conversion toward it, it saw.]] If you write *πρὸς αὑτὸ* [toward itself], this meaning arises: "Doubtless because it (the one or that father) looks back by a conversion toward itself." But without manuscript books I did not wish to depart from the common reading, which Marsilius and Taylor also expressed, the latter of whom fills out the preceding thus: "How therefore did he generate intellect [so as far as it is intellect]?"

— 10. *Τὸ γὰρ καταλαμβάνον ἄλλο, ἢ αἴσθησις ἢ νοῦς· αἴσθησιν γραμμὴν καὶ τὰ ἄλλα· ἀλλ᾽ ὁ κύκλος τοιοῦτος.* [For that which perceives another is either sensation or mind; sensation as a line and the other things; but the circle is such.]] From the traces in the books you might conjecture: *αἴσθησις ὡς γραμμὴ, καὶ τὰ ἄλλα ὡς κύκλος. ἀλλ᾽ ὁ κύκλος.* [sensation as a line, and the others as a circle. But the circle.] The source of this passage is in Plato's demonstration in *Laws* X. [p. pagina] 893. ff. concerning various motions. Likewise at [p. pagina] 898. A. [p. pagina] 204. Bekk.: "Now of these two motions, that which is carried in one and always around a certain center must move as a certain imitation of circles turned on a lathe, being altogether as related and similar as possible to the period of the mind. [κ. τ. λ. καὶ τὰ λοιπά; etc.]" Which Eusebius described in *P. E.* XII. 28. [p. pagina] 601. Both Plato and Plotinus are praised in this matter by Damascius, *On Principles* [p. pagina] 322. [ed. editio] Kopp.: "And the 'likewise' and 'always' and such things (touching on Plato's formulas [l. l. locis laudatis; in the places cited] and [in seqq. in sequentibus; in what follows]) exist and are said according to the immutable; wherefore in this way circular motion imitates the mind, as Plotinus says, or rather as Plato himself in the [book] of the Laws (perhaps in the 10th of the Laws) proposed this image of the motion of the mind, as the apparent immobile imitation of the true immobile." [Cf. Confer] Plotinus himself above III. 7. 3. [p. pagina] 328. B. C. and below V. 5. 1. where the *νοῦς* [mind] is said to be *περιθέων* [running around]. V. 3. 3. where mind (*ὁ νοῦς*) is likewise distinguished from sensation (*τῇ αἰσθήσει*) and V. 6. 5: "thinking is a motion toward the good": finally, on the vision of the mind (*περὶ τῆς τοῦ νοῦ ὁράσεως*) III. 8. 10. V. 3. 8. V. 8. 3. VI. 6. 17. VI. 7. 35. VI. 8. 16. [etc. et cetera] Brucker in *Critical History of Philosophy* II. [p. pagina] 400. and Tennemann in *History of Philosophy* VI. [p. pagina] 95. touched on this our passage and what follows.—Now add the Olympiodorus recently edited by us in *Alcibiades* pr. [p. pagina] 103. who says:—"for it is proper to the mind to turn back; for the mind is analogous to a sphere, making each point both a beginning and an end." To these and what follows apply Proclus' *Elements of Theology* [§. section] 169. f. [p. pagina] 250. ff. [ed. editio] our edition.

[p. pagina] 909, 16. *Ταύτης—ὁ νοῦς οὗτος ἄξιος νοῦ τοῦ καθαρωτάτου, μὴ ἄλλοθεν—φῦναι* [Of this—this mind is worthy of the purest mind, not to have grown from elsewhere]] According to Ficino's mind, *ὀνόματος* [of the name] must be thought of with *νοῦ τοῦ καθ.* [of the purest mind], and therefore this example should be added to L. Bos on *Ellipsis* [p. pagina] 352. [sq. sequenti] Schaef. likewise at *γενόμενον* [having become] again one must supply: *ἀξιόν ἐστι* [it is worthy]. For the other way, that you might arrange it thus:—*ὁ νοῦς οὗτος ἄξιος φῦναι μὴ ἄλλοθεν ἢ ἐκ τῆς πρώτης ἀρχῆς νοῦ τοῦ καθαρωτάτου γενόμενον* (or [f. fortasse] *γενόμενος*, unless [h. l. hoc loco] just as in the preceding and very often elsewhere Plotinus used the Neuter after the Masculine) *δὲ ἤδη γεννῆσαι* [but now to have generated]—both the tenor of this discussion and indeed the universal doctrine of the Platonists seems to reject that arrangement. Soon: *τὸ τῶν ἰδεῶν κάλλος—θεοὺς νοητούς* [the beauty of the ideas—intelligible gods]. [Vid. Vide] Proclus on the *Timaeus* [p. pagina] 357. where among other things this: "every idea is a god." [Cf. Confer] the same author's *Elements of Theology* [p. pagina] 190. and 200. Cudworth in *Intellectual System* IV. 36. [cf. confer] [p. pagina] 687. and Brucker in *Critical History of Philosophy* II. [p. pagina] 402. ff. discuss this tenet.

— 19. *καὶ ὥσπερ καταπιόντα πάλιν τῷ ἐν αὑτῷ ἔχειν, μηδὲ ἐκπεσεῖν εἰς ὕλην—παρὰ τῇ Ῥέᾳ—Κρόνου μὲν θεὸν σοφώτατον—ἢ καὶ μάλιστά καὶ νοῦς ἐν Κόρῳ—Δία γεννᾷν κόρον [κ. τ. λ. καὶ τὰ λοιπά]* [and as if having swallowed them again to have them in himself, nor to fall into matter—near Rhea—of Saturn a most wise god—or even especially mind in Koros—that Zeus generates abundance, etc.]] Also the source of this interpretation is in a passage of the Platonic *Cratylus* [p. pagina] 396. b. part of which words I placed above at a similar passage of our book [p. pagina] 485. A. Now I will attach these things about Saturn and Rhea from the same dialogue [p. pagina] 402. A. [p. pagina] 42. Bekk.: "I think I have long seen Heraclitus saying some wise things, simply those concerning Kronos and Rhea, which Homer also said.—Heraclitus says somewhere that all things move and nothing remains, and comparing existing things to the flow of a river, he says that you could not step twice into the same river." [Cf. Confer] below chapter 9 of this book. [p. pagina] 490. A. and the praises there. In this place it suffices to have perceived from Plato's words the reason why our Plotinus interprets Rhea thus, so that, like fluxing *Matter*, she is contrary to the stable *Mind*.

[p. pagina] 910, 17. *Καὶ διὰ τοῦτο καὶ τὰ Πλάτωνος τριττὰ, τὰ πάντα περὶ τὸν πάντων βασιλέα [κ. τ. λ. καὶ τὰ λοιπά]* [And because of this also the three things of Plato, all things around the king of all, etc.]] Plato's *Epistles* II. [p. pagina] 312. end. [p. pagina] 403. Bekk.: "For thus it is: around the king of all are all things and for his sake are all things, and that is the cause of all beautiful things; second around the second things, and third around the third things." Our author again praises Plato's words below VI. 7. 42. [p. pagina] 733. B. where [cf. confer] the note. Whereas Taylor thinks more has fallen out at the next words *φησὶ γὰρ πρῶτα* [for he says first], the books bring forth nothing more, and these can be explained such that Plotinus says *first things* are designated by Plato by those very words: *περὶ τὸν πάντων βασιλέα πάντ᾽ ἐστὶ*, so that consequently only *τὰ* [the] has fallen out, unless he placed *πρῶτα* [first things] without the article, by which he would mean: *certain first things*.

[p. pagina] 911, 2. *τοῦτον δὲ φησὶ—ἐν τῷ κρατῆρι ἐκείνῳ* [and he says this one... in that mixing-bowl]] [Vid. Vide] Plato's *Timaeus* [p. pagina] 34. and [p. pagina] 43. part of which words I have written above at Plotinus [p. pagina] 376. C. D. E. which passage ought altogether to be compared with ours.

— 3. *Τοῦ αἰτίου δὲ νοῦ ὄντος [κ. τ. λ. καὶ τὰ λοιπά] —ἐξηγητὰς ἐκείνων γεγονέναι* [And the cause being mind, etc. — to have been the interpreters of those things]] Cyril praises these in *Against Julian* IV. [p. pagina] 145. C. introducing them thus: "For Plotinus says thus about it, and interprets not so much his own opinion as that of Plato." For the rest, the more recent authors have eagerly treated these Plotinian matters: Cudworth in *Intellectual System* IV. 36. [p. pagina] 635. Brucker in *Critical History of Philosophy* II. [p. pagina] 409. f. Heyne seems to join himself to this opinion, pronouncing thus in *Academic Opuscula* III. [p. pagina] 309: "In Plato, and the Timaeus itself, as is well enough established, the Demiurge was the *νοῦς* [Mind], a philosophy not unworthy of this philosopher and in which a more holy and vivid mind can dwell with pleasure. But the Platonists soon argued infinitely over this name, making the *λόγος* [Word] sometimes second after the prince god, sometimes third." Then he praises this very passage of Plotinus, as well as Numenius in Eusebius *P. E.* XI. 14. f.—Tennemann also touched on this passage of Plotinus in *History of Philosophy* VI. [p. pagina] 51. For we do not wish to pass over such things as pertain to censuring the more recent Platonists, lest we seem too devoted to these parties, although we profess that elsewhere, and repeat here also, that no one has explained the tenets of these philosophers both more intelligently and more justly than Cudworth. Concerning the word *πιστοῦσθαι* [to be confirmed/assured] it was spoken above at [p. pagina] 229. F.

— 10. *Ἥπτετο—Παρμενίδης—τῆς τοιαύτης δόξης [κ. τ. λ. καὶ τὰ λοιπά]* [Parmenides touched... such an opinion, etc.]] Parmenides' *Fragments* [v. vide] 95. ff.
"The same thing is to think and the reason why there is thought;
for without that which is, in which it is expressed,
you will not find thinking; for there is nothing, nor will there be
anything else besides that which is; since Fate has bound it
to be whole and immobile, for which all things are a name,
as many as mortals have set down, believing them to be true,
both to become and to perish, both to be and not to be,
and to change place, and to alter through bright skin."
[Cf. Confer] of the same author verses 83—89. and see Brandis' *Eleatic Commentaries* [p. pagina] 115. ff. and [p. pagina] 143. ff.

— 14. *σωματικὴν πᾶσαν κίνησιν ἐξαίρων* [removing all corporeal motion]] In a more accurate writer even without books I would have changed it to *ἐξαιρῶν* [taking away]. For [h. l. hoc loco] it is the same as what Plato in *Epistle II* [p. pagina] 310. e. calls *ἐξαίρετον ποιῶν*, *removing, exempting*: in Plotinus I have not dared, mindful of those things which Wyttenbach placed on Plutarch's *On Hearing* [p. pagina] 383: "Let it suffice now to have advised this one thing, that among the Attics indeed and all those who *write carefully, ἐξαίρειν* [exa-irein] is said where the notion of *extolling* prevails, and *ἐξαιρεῖν* [exa-irein] where the notion of *taking away, exempting* prevails:" unless you wish to establish that in such trivialities too Plotinus' notes were corrected by Porphyry. Concerning that confusion after Wyttenbach and Heindorf on Plato's *Theaetetus* [p. pagina] 352. Held recently advised in *Philological Acts of Munich* II. 1. [p. pagina] 30. and Baehr on Plutarch’s *Life of Pyrrhus* [p. pagina] 180.—For the argument [cf. confer] Plato's *Theaetetus* [p. pagina] 180. d. e. and Brandis, the place cited, [p. pagina] 142.

— 18. *Ὁ δὲ παρὰ Πλάτωνι Παρμενίδης [κ. τ. λ. καὶ τὰ λοιπά]* [But the Parmenides in Plato, etc.]] [Vid. Vide] Plato's *Parmenides* [p. pagina] 139. [p. pagina] 28. Bekk. and everywhere. For the rest, it will not be out of place to subjoin to the end of this chapter the words of Cudworth in *Intellectual System* IV. 36. [p. pagina] 689; who explains the *Platonic Triad* thus: "The principal hypostasis is often said of this genus *ἓν πρὸ πάντων*, *the one before all things*, namely the simplest unity, which contains all things efficiently and as Plotinus speaks ([p. pagina] 513), *οὕτως ἔχει πάντα, ὡς μὴ διακεκριμένα, τὰ δὲ ἐν δευτέρῳ διεκεκρίτο τῷ λόγῳ*, *thus it has all things, as not yet distinguished from each other, while in the second reason they are distinguished*; that is, they are actually distinct in their species, even if the first principle is the simple and fecund power of all things. Therefore Parmenides calls the second hypostasis *ἓν πάντα* *the one which is all things*, or which embraces all species of things: which philoso-

--- Page 286 ---
[[original page: 279]]

-> BOOK I. OF THE FIFTH ENNEAD. p. 910—913. 279 <-

pher, that which Plotinus (in our passage) testifies, called the third person *ἓν καὶ πάντα*, *one and all things* (properly *ἓν καὶ πολλὰ*, *one and many*), to signify that it had more change and multitude."

[p. pagina] 912, 3. *Ἀναξαγόρας—τὸ ἓν* [Anaxagoras—the One]] Simplicius on Aristotle's *Physics* [p. pagina] 33. b. praises these Ionic words of Anaxagoras: "But the mind, as much as it is, is both certainly and is now, where also all other things are, in that which contains many, and in those which are added, and in those which are separated." In this passage Carus, Ritter, and Schaubach have eagerly labored. [Vid. Vide] *Anaxagorae Clazomenii Fragmenta* [p. pagina] 137. f. which exhibits those various conjectures. But no one has consulted the words of our philosopher, which bring light to them. They are, however, to be compared with another passage of Plotinus [p. pagina] 162. where he says: Anaxagoras, who posits the mixture to be water, and does not call it (the water) the fitness for all things, but says that the same (water) contains all things in act, removes the mind which he introduced, [etc. &c.] From which it is understood that Anaxagoras spoke in some place as if he established that *the mind embraces all things in act*, but in this doctrine he was not consistent with himself. Whence for that fragment an easy, if I see anything, both emendation and explanation is prepared: *ὁ δὲ νοῦς ὅσα ἐστὶ, ἐστί τε κάρτα—καὶ ἓν τοῖς προσκριθεῖσι καὶ ἓν τοῖς ἀποκεκριμένοις*: *Mind indeed, whatever it is, is (it) strongly and now (even now) it is, where (ἵνα, where, as in the Ionic Herodotus I. 98. and everywhere) also all the rest (are), (doubtless) in that (mind) which embraces many, and it is one (or unity) and one in the joined* (i.e. the rest of the bodies) *and the separated* (elements, i.e. the mind which contains all things in act, performs the function of unity for all things both primordial and secondary and fluxing.)

— 6. *Τῷ δὲ Ἐμπεδοκλεῖ τὸ μὲν νεῖκος διαιρεῖ—ὡς ὕλη* [For Empedocles strife divides—as matter]] I have corrected this passage partly from Cyril *Against Julian* [p. pagina] 67. C. partly from our books. Sturz in *Empedocles* [p. pagina] 227. for *τὸ ἓν* [the one], which is in the common reading, himself conjectures *ἑνοῖ* [unites] or *ποιεῖ ἓν* [makes one] or *διαιρεθὲν ἑνοῖ* [unites the divided]. Cyril confirms that first one. Then the same learned man wants the common *ἀσώματον καὶ αὐτὸς τοῦτο* [incorporeal and itself this] to be integrated so that *τίθεται* [he posits] is understood. Cyril's reading, however, does not need this help. "Incorporeal, however, is even that itself ([sc. scilicet] it is)." These two principles of Empedocles indeed are recalled to the incorporeal by others and Plotinus himself: by others to matter, as the same Sturz teaches there. For the rest [cf. confer] above II. 4. 7. [p. pagina] 162. and the notes there and as pertains to *Heraclitea* [p. pagina] 97. D. with the notes [p. pagina] 468. C. 473. A. ch. 5. and [p. pagina] 497. B.

— 8. *Ἀριστοτέλης δὲ [κ. τ. λ. καὶ τὰ λοιπά]* [But Aristotle, etc.]] [Vid. Vide] Aristotle's *Metaphysics* VI. [p. pagina] 128. [sq. sequenti] [ed. editio] Brandis. and XI. [p. pagina] 257. f. (where also on the principles of Empedocles and Anaxagoras) Taylor added this little note to our passage: "Aristotle in his writings ascended no higher than the intelligible, and this with him is the first principle. And perhaps this was because he knew that the nature, which is beyond the intelligible, is perfectly ineffable and unknown, and therefore accurately speaking, is even beyond principle."

[p. pagina] 913, 8. *καὶ—ὁμονοήσει* [and... will be of the same mind]] From the immediately preceding words *ἕκαστον* [each] is to be thought of and repeated. For what follows: *Πυθαγόρου—Φερεκύδους—ἀφεῖσαν* [of Pythagoras... of Pherecydes... they let go] apply Josephus, *Against Apion* I. [p. pagina] 1034. E: "all agree that those who first philosophized among the Greeks about celestial and divine things, such as Pherecydes the Syrian, and Pythagoras, and Thales, were pupils of the Egyptians and Chaldeans, and wrote little. And these seem to the Greeks to be the oldest of all, and they barely believe they were written by them." [Vid. Vide] Sturz on the *Fragments of Pherecydes* [§. section] 6. [p. pagina] 26. [ed. editio] second ed., and not forgetting the Plotinian passage.—But in the words of Plotinus there seems to remain a blemish, which you will clear up thus, I think: *οἱ μάλιστα συντασσόμενοι αὐτοῖς Πυθαγόρου [κ. τ. λ. καὶ τὰ λοιπά]* [those who especially range themselves with the doctrines of Pythagoras, etc.] At the beginning of the chapter Plotinus enumerates intelligible principles from the writings of Anaxagoras, Heraclitus, and Empedocles. Then he examines Aristotle's principles. Now he returns to those philosophers who before Aristotle had again applied themselves to the tenets of Pythagoras and Pherecydes. *Therefore, those who of the ancients especially compose themselves again to the decrees of Pythagoras* (αὖ τοῖς Πυθαγόρου [sc. scilicet] δόγμασιν) *and of those who were after him, and indeed* (of him who was before him) *Pherecydes, etc.* The same or a similar meaning of the verb is in these words of Xenophon, *Hellenica* III. 3. 7. *οἱ συντεταγμένοι ἡμῶν* (Steph. wanted *ἡμῖν*) "those who *conspired, plotted* with us." I Esdras II. 16. *λοιποὶ οἱ τούτοις συντασσόμενοι*, "the rest, who were making common cause with these." Nor does the force of the verb wander in the construction with *πρός*. Iamblichus, *Life of Pythagoras* [p. pagina] 72. Kust. concerning the Pythagoreans: "and their whole life is composed [συντέτακται] toward following God": [cf. confer] the same author's *Protrepticus* VI. [p. pagina] 98. Kiessl.: "and all other things are to be composed [συντακτέον] toward mind and God." [cf. confer] ibid. [c. capitulo] VII. [p. pagina] 114. [ed. editio] Kiessl.

Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I. 22. and there Davis. *Dream of Scipio* [c. capitulo] 8. with Moser's note. — 15. *Διὰ τοῦτο καὶ [ἔτι] ἔξωθέν φησιν* [Because of this he also says [still] from without]] I have included *ἔτι* [still] in brackets, which is absent from several books and can be seen as retracted here from the following member. For the rest [vid. vide] Plato's *Timaeus* [p. pagina] 36. end. [p. pagina] 34. Bekk. and [cf. confer] Plotinus [p. pagina] 388. C. and [p. pagina] 482. below. To what follows apply the earlier IV. 3. 12. [p. pagina] 381. B. and the note there, and as pertains to the passages from the *Theaetetus* and *Phaedo*, I. 2. 1. I. 2. 2. I. 2. 3. I. 6. 6. and the notes there.

[p. pagina] 915, 10. *δεῖ μὴ τὸν λογιζόμενον—νοῦν ἐν ἡμῖν εἶναι,* [it is necessary that the reasoning mind not be in us,]] I did not hesitate to add *μὴ* [not] from Ficino's version and Cod. Med. A. For the meaning demands it. Moreover, one must think of *ταύτῃ* [in this way] or something similar. Namely *so far as* the mind sometimes does not reason, it must be established that the reasoning mind is not present in it. But those things which Plotinus discusses below VI. 4. 4. [p. pagina] 647. and Porphyry's *Sentences* [§. section] V. XVII. XXX. are to be compared with our passage. Cudworth in *Intellectual System* [p. pagina] 668. [sq. sequenti] explains this passage and similar ones of our philosopher copiously, inquiring what *οἱ νόες* [the minds], or *οἱ νοῖ*, are in Plotinus, which he suspects are nothing else but the heads and summits of the soul.

— 16. *Τῷ γὰρ τοιούτῳ* [For to such a one]] We have decided that the marginal reading of the edition *τὸ γὰρ τοιοῦτο* [for such a thing], although it might be equally suitable if you think of *κατὰ* [according to], should be placed after the reading of the MS books which the text offers.

[p. pagina] 916, 1. *Πῶς οὖν—οὐκ ἀντιλαμβανόμεθα—καὶ οὐ μόριον ψυχῆς ἀλλ᾽ ἡ ἅπασα ψυχὴ ὄντες* [How then—do we not perceive—and being not a part of the soul but the whole soul]] Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I. 22: "Neither are we bodies; nor do I, saying these things to you, speak to your body. When therefore he says *know thyself*, he says this: Know your soul: for the body indeed is as it were a vessel or some receptacle of the soul; whatever is done by your soul, that is done by you." Toward which opinion I have praised more at [cap. capitulo] X. [p. pagina] 491. B. Hence those words: "man, a soul using a body." Proclus in *Alcibiades I* [p. pagina] 296. and: "man is one with the soul." The same [p. pagina] 316. and likewise: "man is reason," Olympiodorus in the same dialogue [p. pagina] 10. and [p. pagina] 198. And our author himself provides things more closely joined with the argument of our passage above [p. pagina] 347. [sq. sequenti] with which passage the next note should be compared.

— 9. *καὶ ἔτι ἕκαστον τῶν ψυχικῶν ζῶν ἀεὶ ἐνεργεῖ ἀεὶ καθ᾽ αὑτὸ τὸ αὑτοῦ.* [and still each of the psychic things living always acts always according to its own.]] Other books have *ζώον* [living thing], Basle [ed. editio] *ζώων* [of animals]. Perhaps that emendation is due to Ficino, who seems quite often to have attached his own conjectures to the Medicean Codices. However, [h. l. hoc loco] I have received it into the order as necessary, unless you prefer to strike out that first *ἀεὶ* [always], which would be bolder. Soon for *ποιεῖ* [he makes] I have restored from the margin of the edition and the MS books *ποιεῖν* [to make]. To our passage, indeed, no one brings more light than Plotinus himself in the book *On Contemplation and the One* (III. 8.) especially in chapter five [p. pagina] 347. [sq. sequenti] which whole chapter should be compared with this one. I will pluck only one little flower for the sake of those words which we are now treating:—"wherefore it is necessary that reason not be from without, but be united to the soul of the learner, until it finds its own."

[p. pagina] 919, 4. *καὶ τὸ ὑπερπλῆρες αὐτοῦ* [and its super-fullness]] Thus I corrected from Cod. Vat. the common *ὑπὲρ πλῆρες*. This compound had not yet been recorded in Schneider’s *Lexicon* [ed. editio] third ed. To the examples collected by Kallis and Wakefield in the London edition of Stephanus’ *Thesaurus*, add this passage and Proclus’ *Elements of Theology* [c. capitulo] CXXXI. [p. pagina] 196. [ed. editio] our ed. where the books twice offer *ὑπέρπληρες*. Soon: *τὸ δὲ γενόμενον εἰς αὐτὸ ἐπεστράφη—ὁμοῦ νοῦς γίγνεται καὶ ὄν* [but that which was generated turned toward it—at once it becomes mind and being]. In this place for the common *προεκεῖνο* I gave *πρὸς ἐκεῖνο* [toward that], then for *θεὰ* I gave *θέα* [vision], and *ἔστη* [stood] for *ἔστι* [is] with the MS books and the margin. Without books I thought nothing should be changed, although Ficino’s version might suggest it; it is likewise clear how he accepted these things. Taylor on the contrary translates thus: "That, however, which is generated from it is converted to it, and is filled, and was generated looking to it. But this is intellect. And the permanency indeed of it about *the one*, produced being; but its vision of *the one*, intellect. When, therefore, it is established about *the one*, in order that it may see it, then it becomes at once intellect and being." For the argument apply below [p. pagina] 511. and [p. pagina] 534. and [vid. vide] Brucker, *Critical History of Philosophy* II. [p. pagina] 400. and Tennemann’s *History of Philosophy* VI. [p. pagina] 93. [sq. sequenti] who bids us compare V. 6. 2. VI. 7. 39. and 40. VI. 8. 16. You should add Proclus’ *Elements* [c. capitulo] IX. [p. pagina] 16. [sqq. sequentibus] [c. capitulo] CIX. [p. pagina] 160. [sqq. sequentibus] [c. capitulo] CXIV. [p. pagina] 166. [sqq. sequentibus] and [c. capitulo] CLX. [p. pagina] 236. [sqq. sequentibus].

[p. pagina] 920, 8. *ᾧ ἂν ἐπίσπηται* [whichever it may follow]] Thus I wrote, the MS books commanding, for the common *ἔπηται* which reading seems born of a neglected abbreviation of writing, just as soon the Basle [Ed. editio] exhibits *ἄνον* for *ἄνθρωπον* without the abbreviation; (at which very place Villoison uses it as an example in *Greek Anecdotes* Vol. II. [p. pagina] 177.) He could seem to have taken the Ionic and thus Attic form from his own Plato, *Theaetetus* [p. pagina] 169. A: *ἀλλ᾽ ἴθι, ὦ ἄριστε, ὀλίγον ἐπίσπου* [but come, best one, follow a little]. [Cf. Confer] also *Lexicon of Xenophon* II. [p. pagina] 315. Below in our Author [p. pagina] 699. C. end. we read: *ἀλλὰ γὰρ ἐπισπόμενοι τῷ ἐφεξῆς εἰς τοῦτο ἥκομεν* [but following what is next we have come to this], where although one Codex exhibits *ἐπισπόμενοι*, I would change nothing, and Ficino also translates *ducti* [led], although I know well that this reading often succeeded in the place of the other. Herodotus III. 14: "for he too happened to be following [*ἐπισπόμενος*] Cambyses to Egypt," where Aldus and other books have *ἐπισπόμενος*. [Tu cf. Tu confer] Poppo on Thucydides IV. 35. [p. pagina] 74.

— 9. *ἄλλο—μέρος τὸ ἐν φυτῷ, τὸ τολμηρότατον καὶ ἀφρονέστατον.* [another—part that in the plant, the most daring and most senseless.]] These are to be explained from the beginning of the previous book [p. pagina] 481. B. below: "the beginning therefore of evil for them is daring and generation and the first otherness," where we gave more. To these Taylor praises Sallust the Philosopher [c. capitulo] XX. beginning: "But transmigrations, if they occur into rational beings, these very things become the souls of the bodies; but if into irrational ones, they follow from without, just as the daemons who have been allotted us." But on these tenets we have said more at II. 9. 6. [cf. confer] III. 4. 2. IV. 3. 9. [Cf. Confer] also below VI. 7. 8. [p. pagina] 700. end and [p. pagina] 701. beginning.

— 16. *ἓν οὖν τῇ ἀρχῇ* [one therefore in the principle]] Cod. Vat. *ἐν* and Taylor: "It is, therefore, in its principle." Which reasoning seems stronger. Soon Ficino seems to have read *ἐλθούσῃ* [to having come], which pleases. For *ἐλθοῦσα* [having come] has nothing to which it may be referred.

[p. pagina] 921, 1. *οὐ γὰρ στενοχωρεῖται.* [for it is not cramped.]] [Cf. Confer] below VI. 5. 10. [p. pagina] 669. A.

-> BOOK III. <-

[p. pagina] 922, 7. *ON THE GNOSTIC HYPOSTASES, AND THAT WHICH IS BEYOND.*] This is the forty-ninth book in order of time, and therefore from those which Plotinus composed in his more mature age. [Vid. Vide] Porphyry, *Life of Plotinus* [cap. capitulo] VI. and [cap. capitulo] XXV. Whereas one book omits *καὶ τοῦ ἐπέκεινα* [and that which is beyond], some others have *καὶ τῶν ἐπ.*, neither is good; since the *one* (τὸ ἓν) must be thought of as that which is superior to those substances. For the rest, Proclus seems to have this book before his eyes in *On the Theology of Plato* [cap. capitulo] XIX. [p. pagina] 52. in these words: "just as Plotinus also rightly says somewhere having spoken about the intelligible hypostases." For it seems it should be corrected: "about the *gnostic* [*νοητικῶν*] hypostases," or, if you prefer to believe that only *hypostases* is faulty, it should be established that Proclus respected the first book of this Ennead, *On the Three Principal Hypostases*. [Sed vide Sed vide] however, what we have noted below at [p. pagina] 501. A. [cap. capitulo] VI. Porphyry reduced this book of Plotinus to a compendium in the *Sentences* [ap. apud] Stobaeus in *Eclogues* I. 51. [p. pagina] 778—784. Heer. and in the Cambridge [Ed. editio] [cap. capitulo] XV. [p. pagina] 222—224. Taylor translated this third book into English in *Select Works of Plotinus* [p. pagina] 402. [sqq. sequentibus]: On the Gnostic (?) Hypostases, and that which is beyond them.

[p. pagina] 923, 12. *Ὁ δὲ νοῦς τούτων γνῶσιν ἔχει—σκέψασθαι προσήκει* [But the mind has knowledge of these... it is fitting to consider]] It seems *εἰ* [if] should be added after *νοῦς* [mind].

[p. pagina] 924, 2. *Τὸ μὲν οὖν αἰσθητικὸν αὐτῆς αὐτόθεν ἂν φαῖμεν τοῦ ἔξω εἶναι μόνον·* [The sensitive part of it we might say right away belongs to the outside only]] Thus I have arranged the words according to the MS books. *Αὐτόθεν* [right away/immediately] Ficino: *from the condition of its very self*; Taylor: *immediately*. Neither is bad. And examples of each usage are found in the Dialogues of Plato. [Vid. Vide] Heindorf on *Gorgias* [p. pagina] 81. and on *Theaetetus* [p. pagina] 348. Stallbaum on *Philebus* [p. pagina] 170. and on *Symposium* [p. pagina] 213. A: where it is *immediately, on the spot*. I omit others whom learned men have praised concerning this word in the London ed. of Stephanus' *Thesaurus* [p. pagina] 2423. f. I add Wyttenbach explaining the causes of various meanings in *Philomathia* II. [p. pagina] 14. and thence at Stobaeus' *Florilegium* Append. Vol. IV. [p. pagina] 57. [ed. editio] Gaisford and our Baehr's note in Plutarch's *Alcibiades* [p. pagina] 135. f.

— 11. *ὃ δὴ καὶ ἀναμνήσεις φαῖμεν ἂν τῆς ψυχῆς εἶναι.* [which indeed we would say are also recollections of the soul.]] [Cf. Confer] III. 7. 1. IV. 3. 26. IV. 8. 4. V. 5. 12. V. 9. 5. As for the fact that Taylor conjectures from Ficino's version that these should be inserted after *δυνάμει* [in power]: *ζητητέον ἄρα, εἰ τὸ λογιζόμενον καὶ εἰς ε. στρεφ.* [it must be sought, therefore, whether the reasoning and turning toward itself...], none of the books exhibit more than the edition, and six hundred times Marsilius [Ficino] studied to consult for Plotinian brevity with additions of that sort. And only *ἢ* [or] [h. l. hoc loco], as very often elsewhere, performs the function of a universal sentiment.—For the rest, concerning the intellect looking at itself (*ὅτι ὁ νοῦς ὁρᾷ ἑαυτὸν*) [vid. vide] soon [cap. capitulo] 4. [coll. collatis; having compared] II. 9. 1. and what things have been noted there [p. pagina] 200. E. and on the difference between *νοῦν* [mind] and *αἴσθησιν* [sensation] note at [p. pagina] 307. G. and on the nature of *αἰσθήσεως* [sensation] [cf. confer] [p. pagina] 452. D. and [p. pagina] 453. and the note there.

[p. pagina] 925, 8. *εἰ πρότερον—λέγει—Σωκράτης* [if previously... Socrates says]] Perhaps it should be read *ἢ, εἰ πρότερον—λέγοι—Σωκρ.* [or, if previously... Socrates should say]. We have converted that *προσχρωμένη* [using] into the Nominative *προσχρωμένη*. For the rest, Aristotle proceeds from a similar discussion on the reason which obtains between sensation (*αἴσθησιν*), memory (*μνήμην*), and calculation (*λογισμὸν*) at the beginning of the *Metaphysics*, which are to be compared with these Plotinian matters by him who wishes to learn accurately the character of Aristotelian philosophy and its difference from the Platonic. Moreover, the Stagirite [Aristotle] uses there (I. [p. pagina] 4. [ed. editio] Brandis.) himself the name of *Socrates* and *Callias* besides, in that way which we explained above at V. 1. 4. [p. pagina] 485. C. Strato the Peripatetic, however, attributed a certain intelligence even to the senses. Plutarch in the book *Whether Land or Sea Animals are Wiser* [p. pagina] 961. A. [p. pagina] 899. Wytt.: "And yet there is a discourse of Strato the physicist, demonstrating that sensing does not exist at all without thinking [κ. τ. λ. καὶ τὰ λοιπά; etc.]" For it is worthwhile to compare the whole discussion with the Aristotelian and Plotinian.—Soon: *εἰ δὲ καὶ ἐξελίττοι τὴν μορφὴν, μερίζει ἃ ἡ φαντασία ἔδωκεν.* [if indeed he should unfold the form, he divides what the imagination gave.]] After Jacobs on Philostratus' *Images* [p. pagina] 728., our Baehr illustrated this force of *unfolding*, which is in the verb *ἐξελίττειν*, with other examples taken from the usage of Plutarch and historians at Plutarch's *Pyrrhus* XXVIII. [p. pagina] 332. Plotinus frequently uses this verb. [Vid. Vide] III. 7. 5. III. 7. 10. III. 8. 7. and [cf. confer] what we placed above at I. 4. 1. [p. pagina] 29. C.

[p. pagina] 926, 10. *ἀλλ᾽ ἔτι δεῖ λέγειν ψυχῆς τοῦτο* [but still it is necessary to say this of the soul]] Taylor conjectures: *α. ε. δ. λέγειν εἴ τι ψ. τ.* [but still it is necessary to say if something of the soul...]. The books do not support this, nor is it necessary. Ficino however correctly expressed the meaning. To the next words the same British man [Taylor] applied a note especially having used Proclus in *Commentary on Plato's Timaeus* [p. pagina] 321.

[p. pagina] 927, 9. *καὶ ὅτι μὴ αὐτῷ ἀεὶ* [and that not to it always]] Thus I restored from the MS books. As for the fact that Taylor besides wants *χρώμεθα* [we use] added, since Ficino expressed this word: I did not wish to add it without books, since I know Plotinus is accustomed to omit such things and [h. l. hoc loco] it can be thought of from the preceding.

— 11. *αἴσθησις δὲ ἡμῖν ἄγγελος, βασιλεὺς δὲ πρὸς ἡμᾶς ἐκεῖνος.* [sensation is for us a messenger, but that one is king toward us.]] [Vid. Vide] above [p. pagina] 49. B. and below [p. pagina] 633. (ch. XVIII.) Plutarch, *On Curiosity* [p. pagina] 521. C. [p. pagina] 97. Wytt.: "But it is necessary, as I think, that sensation not wander about outside like an undisciplined maidservant, but being sent by the soul to things, to meet with them quickly and report back. Then again to be modestly within the reason and attend to it." Philo Judaeus, *Allegories of the Law* [p. pagina] 288. Pfeiff. uses it with another meaning: *νοῦς βασιλεὺς* [mind king] placing the contrary *νοῦν τύραννον* [mind tyrant], in the passage on Melchizedek, *king of peace* (*βασ. τῆς εἰρήνης*). But according to the mind of Plato and Plotinus, Proclus in *Alcibiades I* [c. capitulo] 83. [p. pagina] 249. speaks thus: "But after the multitude in souls, raise (read *ἀνάτεινον* [raise!]) yourself to mind and the intellectual kingdoms." But the same praises our passage in *Commentary on Plato's Timaeus* [p. pagina] 77: "the mind is our king, but sensation is a messenger, says the great Plotinus." From that however I would not have conjectured that he read *ἡμῶν* [our], since the later philosophers are accustomed to cite such things from memory. On the formula *νοῦς ὁ βασιλεὺς* [mind the king] I have collected more at Porphyry, *Life of Plotinus* [c. capitulo] 3. [p. pagina] 98. [ed. editio] Fabricius.

[p. pagina] 928, 2. *ὡς τὸν γινώσκοντα [κ. τ. λ. καὶ τὰ λοιπά]* [as the one knowing, etc.]] I have judged that one should stand by the authority of the MS books: so that consequently he who knows himself is twofold, *that one* indeed, who knows the nature of the thinking soul, but *this one* superior to that, who knows himself, *and who* was made according to that intellect. Ficino undoubtedly read *ὡς τὸ γινῶσκον ἑαυτὸ* [as the thing knowing itself] and so on, of which reading slight traces remain in the books and in the margin of the Basle edition.—As for what Plotinus says in what follows: *ὃ καὶ δύναται μόνου πτεροῦσθαι [κ. τ. λ. καὶ τὰ λοιπά]* [which also is alone able to be winged, etc.] took its color from the Platonic *Phaedrus*, there is no one who does not see.

[p. pagina] 929, 4. *ἔστι δὴ νοῦς—ὡς δὴ οὖν νοῦς ἑαυτὸν ὁρᾷ* [mind is indeed... so indeed therefore mind sees itself]] Jo. Philoponus on Aristotle, *On the Soul* I. B. IV. 2: "For it is proper to the mind to incline toward itself. For it itself is the seer, and itself the seen. For seeing the forms, it sees itself, and seeing itself it has beheld the forms. For it is the fullness of the forms and the form of forms."

[p. pagina] 930, 7. *εἰ μὲν τύποι αὐτῶν, οὐκ αὐτὰ ἔχει—et infra: τύπον γὰρ ἕξει—ὅπερ οὐκ ἔστιν ἀλήθεια.* [if indeed there be traces of them, it does not have the things themselves—and below: for it will have a trace—which is not truth.]] Porphyry in the *Sentences* [ap. apud] Stobaeus *Eclogues* II. 51. [p. pagina] 780. Heer. and [p. pagina] 223. [ed. editio] Cambridge: "But everywhere that which uses sensation, casting itself upon external things, beholds them, not being united to those which it beholds, but only receiving a trace of them from the application to them." [Cf. Confer] our Plotinus above [p. pagina] 452. D. and [p. pagina] 453. and the note there.

[p. pagina] 931, 9. *Εἰ οὖν ἐνέργεια, καὶ ἡ οὐσία αὐτοῦ ἐνέργεια,* [If therefore it is action, its essence is also action,]] If I consider the immediately preceding *δυνάμει* [in power] as well as the following: I think *ἐνεργείᾳ* [in act] should be written twice [h. l. hoc loco]. The same ambiguity recurs below ch. 6: *καὶ ὁρῶν ἐνέργεια ἦν* [and seeing was action], where Cod. Vat. has *ἐνεργείᾳ* [in act], and Ficino preferred *ἐν ἐνεργείᾳ* [in action]. He seems to have wanted the same in the next: *εἰ ἐν δὲ τῇ ἐνεργείᾳ τὸ ὂν καὶ τὸ νοητόν* [if indeed in the action are being and the intelligible].

— 17. *Ἡ μὲν γὰρ ψυχὴ ἐνόει ἑαυτὴν, ὅτι ἄλλον· ὁ δὲ νοῦς, ὅτι αὐτός* [For the soul thought itself as another; but the mind, as itself]] Proclus in Plato’s *Theology* [c. capitulo] XIX. [p. pagina] 52 might seem to touch on these and the earlier things [p. pagina] 499: "the soul unfolds the mind, but the mind has unfolded itself, just as Plotinus also rightly says somewhere having spoken about the intelligible hypostases." [Cf. Confer] above at the title of this book [p. pagina] 496. where I conjectured Proclus wrote: *περὶ τῶν νοητικῶν ὑποστάσεων* [about the gnostic hypostases]. The verb *ἀνελίττειν* [to unfold] however is used elsewhere by Plotinus in discussions of this kind, as [p. pagina] 5. A.—For the rest [cf. confer] [p. pagina] 489. B. C. [v. vide] [p. pagina] 498. A. B. [p. pagina] 507. E.—Soon that Ficino expressed *καὶ ὁρῶν ἐν ἐνεργείᾳ ἦν* [and seeing was in action], was advised at the end of the preceding chapter, and I know not how this reading smiles upon me. The Vatican book recognizes the Dative without a preposition. Nor does the reading of Ficino please less in what follows: *ἢ ἀνάγκην μὲν οὕτως* instead of *ἀνάγκη* [necessity].

[p. pagina] 932, 5. *ἐνέργειαν πιστικήν* [persuasive action]] The books recognize this form, and likewise in Plato's *Gorgias* [p. pagina] 456. a. even the Bodleian Codex; and Bekker recently retained it. Conf. at that place Heindorf [p. pagina] 29. and *Lexicon of Xenophon* III. [p. pagina] 547. In Aristotle’s *Rhetoric* I. 2. the books vary. Gaisford however received *πειστικὴν* [persuasive] into the order [p. pagina] 29. I see they vary not at all in Dio Chrysostom *Oration XVIII* [p. pagina] 481. Reiske: "and the form of the reporting is favorable, and pleasing, and persuasive [*πιστικὸν*], having much probability, and much grace and application." [Cf. Confer] Diog. Laert. IV. 6. 12. and [vid. vide] Ernesti *Lexicon of Technical Greek Rhetoric* [p. pagina] 266. below. In our passage however we ought to accept *ἐνέργειαν πιστικήν* for *πειστικήν*, which the next words declare, and consequently translate *action or efficacy, possessing the faculty of persuading*.—The following remind one of Plato in the *Sophist* [p. pagina] 265. d:—"now by the word we attempt to make one agree with necessary persuasion." *Gorgias* [p. pagina] 527. 6: "persuading and forcing toward this." And Themistocles in Herodotus VIII. 111. says to the Andrians that he brings two goddesses: *Πειθὼ καὶ Ἀναγκαίην* [Persuasion and Necessity], at which passage Wesseling and Valckenaer [p. pagina] 672. have gathered more even from the writings of philosophers: other things, illustrating *πειθανάγκην* [persuasive-necessity] [ap. apud] Synesius, *On the Kingship* [p. pagina] 26. a., the most learned Krabinger in the notes on him [p. pagina] 317.

— 14. *τὴν ψυχὴν ἡμῶν διδάξαι,* [to teach our soul,]] As for the fact that [h. l. hoc loco] the Vatican book has *ἐνδιδάξαι*, it should be added to the places recently recorded by Kallis and Schweighäuser at Stephanus’ London *Thesaurus*. However, in the passage of *Wisdom* VIII. 8. Schleusner in the *New Treasury of the V. T.* teaches that other books offer *ἐκδιδάσκειν*, and the same [h. l. hoc loco] was expressed by Ficino.—Soon *τοῦτο τοίνυν γιγνώσκειν προσήκει, ὡς καὶ αὐτὸ, ὅσα ὁρᾷ γινώσκει* [it is fitting therefore to know this, that it also knows whatever it sees]. Ficino expressed *αὑτὸ* [itself], and repeats *καὶ* before *ὅσα*. But if with several books you read *τούτῳ* [by this] instead of *τοῦτο* [this], perhaps this meaning is born: It is fitting to know by this (ablative [sc. scilicet] by the intellect) just as it also knows whatever it sees, [etc. &c.] For I do not wish to attempt anything in a passage so ambiguous. Taylor thus: "It is fit, therefore, that..."

-> ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS <-

...this part should know, that is, also knows such things as it sees, and such things as it says."
**p. 933, 15.** [οὐδὲ γὰρ ὄρεξις τῷ καθαρῷ νῷ ἀπόντος — *For there is no appetite in the pure intellect for what is absent*] The version shows how Ficino expressed or rather diluted these words. Taylor translates thus: "For appetite is not in pure intellect; but this being absent, &c. [abbreviation: *et cetera*]" I have included this sentence in parentheses, which I think should be understood thus: *for neither is there any seeking in the pure mind for anything, because it is [never] absent.*
**p. 934, 10.** ἡσυχίαν [quiet/stillness],] Pachymeres’ Paraphrase on Dionysius the Areopagite, Vol. I, p. 484, above Corderius: *dianoia* is the scientific habit of the soul; *noesis* is the activity of the mind; *stasis* [rest] is indeed stillness as distinguished from motion, but it is also the same as *idrysis* [establishment/foundation]. These remarks, partly drawn from Plato’s *Cratylus* (see that dialogue p. 426 d.), are also to be applied to another passage of our Plotinus, VI. 3. 27, p. 642, where motion and rest (*kinesis* and *stasis*) are discussed.
**p. 935, 8.** εἴτε πράττοι, εἴτε ποιοῖ [whether one acts or makes]] The difference between these words was already accepted in various ways by the ancients. See Aristotle, *Magna Moralia* I. 35, p. 224 B, and *Nicomachean Ethics* VI. 4, p. 101 Sylburg, p. 263 Zell, and the commentary of Hervetus on that passage. Citing the same Aristotle, Clement of Alexandria brings forward other distinctions (perhaps from the Stagirite’s exoteric books, which the philosopher cites elsewhere), *Stromata* V. 13, p. 697 sq. Potter. That difference pertains also to the formulas *eu* and *kakōs prattein* [to fare well or ill], concerning which you will desire nothing more after Wyttenbach’s annotation on Plutarch, *De Discernendo Adulatore ab Amico*, p. 506. In our passage, it suffices to distinguish *prattein*, to act (*handeln*), as the universal, from *poiein*, to make (*machen, hervorbringen*), as the particular. Let us hold, moreover, these words of Proclus in Olympiodorus’ *In Platonis Alcibiadem*, Preface ch. 14, p. 126: "and here he says that those who do beautiful things fare well (*eu prattousi*), for acting (*prattein*) belongs to souls, as does faring well."
**p. 936, 3.** οὐδὲ γὰρ αὐτὴ ἐγέννησεν [for she did not generate]] Taylor: "for neither did it generate these"—noting in a comment that ταῦτα [these] is omitted in the Greek. But this pronoun is easily understood from the preceding context.
**— 17.** τοῦτο δ' ἔστιν ὡμοίωσεν ἑαυτῷ τῷ ἄνω φωτί [*But this is: it made it similar to itself, the light above*]] I have not hesitated to write thus, following the traces of the codices. Ficino expressed the reading of the edition: ὁμοίως ἐν ἑαυτῷ [*similarly in itself*]. Next, from the books, I have given καὶ μεῖζον [*and greater*] and νομίζων [*thinking*], and in the same place from the margin τοῦτο [*this*] for τούτῳ [*to this*]. Regarding the argument of this passage, compare what is read below in V. 5. 7. Moreover, sentiments of this kind, such as Plotinus brings forward here and in similar places, were not first introduced into philosophy in the age of Plutarch or shortly before in the time of Philo, as Tennemann opines in *History of Philosophy* VI, p. 46—who otherwise correctly compares the "innate knowledge concerning the gods" in Iamblichus, *De Mysteriis* I. 3—but rather the most ancient philosophy already knew them, though the philosophers expressed them in different words. Thus, to use this example, Cicero himself says in *De Natura Deorum* I. 17: "it must be understood that gods exist, *since we have implanted, or rather innate, cognitions of them*." Cf. Gale on Iamblichus, cited above, p. 186, and Gataker on Marcus Aurelius III. 15, p. 88.
**p. 937, 6.** ἀλλὰ τοὐναντίον [but on the contrary]] Taylor: "but the contrary is not true" and says in a note that it must necessarily be read: ἀλλ' οὐ τοὐναντίον: assigning this reason: "The meaning of Plotinus is that intelligible light is not seen more acutely by the perception of visible objects." Without the books, I was unwilling to depart from the vulgate, and the sentiment expressed by Ficino has that which may defend it. Soon after, one might believe Ficino read ἡμεῖς δὲ δι' αὐτοῦ [*but we through it*] for ἡμᾶς δὲ δι' αὐτοῦ [*but us through it*]. However, the Medicean books do not vary from the vulgate.
**p. 938, 2.** ἀπαιτῇ [if one should demand]] Cf. below VI. 3. 7, beginning. It is *to demand, to seek*, and is frequently used in the context of an argument, as Wyttenbach teaches on Plutarch’s *De Discernendo Adulatore*, p. 510. Moreover, in this place it is an attraction for "if someone should demand of what sort the intellect itself is," etc. In the final words of this chapter, Ficino expressed διὰ ζωῆς [*through life*] for διὰ τῆς [*through the...*]. I have entirely kept my hand from such a passage.
**— 10.** εἰ ἀφέλοις πρῶτον τὸ σῶμα—εἶτα καὶ τὴν πλάττουσαν τοῦτο ψυχήν [*if you first take away the body—then also the soul that fashions this*]] Plato, *Phaedo* p. 82 d., p. 55 Bekker: "Therefore, he said, O Cebes, all those who care for their own soul and do not live fashioning bodies, saying farewell to these, do not travel the same path as them." Where Heindorf, p. 116, hesitating, wanted either σώματι λατρεύοντες [*serving the body*] or σῶμα πλάττοντες [*fashioning a body*]. And if he had known our passage, he would undoubtedly have used it to strengthen this conjecture. But Wyttenbach on *Phaedo*, cited above, p. 219: "Regarding the soul forming the body, it is said by Plotinus in a pejorative sense, p. 505 A. That

[[vocabulary: appetition, intelligible, attraction, pleonasms]]

-> BOOK III. ENNEAD V. p. 933—949. 285 <-

however, the Plural Number *bodies* (*sōmata*) is subjoined to the Singular *soul* (*psychēn*) (by Plato, cited above), seems to pertain to the fact that one soul occupies many bodies in succession by migrating. It is said *plattein sōma kai psychēn*, *to form, to fashion, the character and the body*: as we have shown in Plutarch’s *Moralia* p. 3 E." (namely, in the treatise *De Puerorum Educatione*, p. 83). Moreover, he seems besides to have respected another passage of Plato in *Phaedo* p. 66 c., and even more so these words of the *Symposium* p. 211 end, p. 444 Bekker:—"but not full of human flesh and colors and much other mortal vanity." From there certainly Artemidorus in *Oneirocritica* IV. 47, p. 360 Reiff., and Philo Judaeus in *Legum Allegoriae* III, p. 252 Pfeiffer, drew their color. Soon after, the words μετὰ τὴν τοῦ μεγέθους σφαῖραν [*after the sphere of magnitude*], if they are sound, I would take thus: "after the sphere which is reckoned by the magnitude of the body."
**p. 940, 3.** Εἰ δὲ τὰ ποιηθέντα μόνον [But if the things made only]] Ficino, and Taylor following him, expressed οὐ μόνον [*not only*].
**— 15.** καὶ τὸ δρώμενον τὸ ὑπ' αὐτοῦ [and that which is seen by it]] I have given it thus from several books. Ficino, however, read besides: τὸ ὑφ' αὑτοῦ πλῆθος εἶναι οὐχ ἐν παντί. οὐδὲ γὰρ ἔχει τὸ ἐν παντί. Taylor applied himself to this.
**p. 941, 11.** καὶ γὰρ εἰ ἕκαστον λόγος, πολλά ἐστι [For if each is a reason, it is many]] "For if each of the objects of intellectual vision is reason, it is a multitude." And in a note: "i. e. If it is a distributed cause. For this is what reason and reasoning signify when ascribed to intelligible and intellectual, or divine essences." *Taylor*.
**— 17.** Εἴθ' ὅταν λέγῃ, εἰμὶ τόδε κ. τ. λ. [Next, when it says, I am this, etc.]] "In the next place, when it says: I am this thing," and in the bottom margin: "For in this case, it would be at least two things; since in addition to the impartible it would have speech. And the duad is the first multitude. *Taylor*."
**p. 943, 3.** ᭭στε ὥρμησε μὲν ἐπ' αὐτῷ [*So that it hastened towards it*]] Codex Vatican ἐπ' αὐτό. Ficino, whom Taylor follows, seems to have read ἀπ' αὐτοῦ [*from it*]. Immediately after, most books exhibit: ἔχουσα ἐπ' αὐτῇ [*having in itself*] for ἔχουσα ἑαυτῇ. Perhaps: ἐφ' ἑαυτῇ or ἐν ἑαυτῇ.
**— 7.** Καὶ γὰρ αὖ ἔχει τύπον τοῦ ὁράματος κ. τ. λ. [For again it has an impression of the vision, etc.]] "For again, it has an impression of the vision [of that which is beyond itself] or it would never become the recipient of it." And in the margin: "This impression is *the one* of intellect, the summit, and as it were flower of its nature, and a vestige of the ineffable. For by seeing the ineffable, it becomes stamped, as it were, with its super-essential nature." *Taylor*.—Next, Ficino expressed: οὕτω δὲ πολὺς—καὶ οὕτω γνοὺς εἶδεν αὐτόν. Furthermore, a passage of Aristotle in *Metaphysics* XI. 7, p. 203 Sylburg, p. 249 Brandis, is especially relevant here: "but thinking which is in itself is of that which is best in itself, and that which is most so is of that which is most so; and the mind thinks itself by participation in the intelligible; for it becomes intelligible by touching and thinking. So that mind and intelligible are the same. For that which is receptive of the intelligible and of essence is mind. And it acts while possessing [them]."
**— 12.** ἀεὶ δὲ ἐνδιαθέμενος [and always conceiving within]] The reading of Codices Medicean B and Vatican seems born from a neglected abbreviation. Ficino undoubtedly expressed the vulgate. Taylor thus: "But it is always the recipient [of the ineffable] and always becomes intellect, &c. [abbreviation: *et cetera*] It properly means: *Always conceiving in itself and arranging*." Moreover, this word is absent from the Lexicons; which otherwise have much regarding *endiathetos* [internal], to which add Wyttenbach’s *Animadversiones in Plutarchi Moralia* Vol. I, p. 44, p. 378 sq. and p. 835.
**p. 945, 10.** ἄλλο ἄλλοθεν—ἰόν [one thing coming from one place, another from another]] The margin of the edition has ἄλλῳ [*to another*]. Did he want ἄλλου [*of another*], so that it might also be written ἰόντος [*as it comes*]? The books teach nothing.
**— 19.** τὰς ἐνεργείας, ἃς παραχωρῆσαν [the activities which having yielded]] Did Ficino correct it to: τὰς ἐνεργείας παραχωρῆσαι [*to yield the activities*]? For I prefer to inquire into a passage of that sort, where even written books fail us.
**p. 946, 11.** νοήσει, ἡ πρώτη ἐνέργεια [by thinking, the first activity]] Undoubtedly it should be read: νοήσει ἢ ἡ πρώτη ἐ. [*either by thinking or the first activity*] and soon I suspect: ἢ κατὰ λόγον θησόμεθα [*or shall we place according to reason*] for εἰ κ. λ. θ. [*if we shall place...*].
**p. 948, 18.** ἀλλ' εἴρηκε μιᾷ ῥήσει πολλά [but it has said many things in one speech]] Thus several of our books, nor did Ficino read οὐκ [*not*] after ἀλλ' [*but*]. Taylor wanted ἀλλ' οὖν [*but therefore*]. Next, from the books, I have given ἔχον [*having* (neuter)] for ἔχων [*having* (masc.)]. Soon, at λέγοι ἂν [*one might say*], understand τις [*someone*], unless you prefer λέγοιτ' ἄν [*it might be said*].
**p. 949, 6.** εἰ γὰρ ἕξει τὸ ποῦ εἶναι ἕξει [for if it shall have "the where to be," it shall have it]] I have filled this place from Medicean A. But if you read with other codices: τῷ ποῦ εἶναι, you must translate: for if it should have it, *by the fact that it is somewhere*, it will have it. Ficino followed this, as did Taylor, adding in the margin: "But the meaning of Plotinus in this place is, that if the most simple of all things had an intellectual perception of itself, it would be in itself; and consequently would be *somewhere*."

[[vocabulary: ineffable, impartible, essence, abbreviation]]

"For an intellectual essence because self-subsistent, is said to be in itself. For so far as it is the cause of, it comprehends itself; but so far as it is caused, it is comprehended by itself." These are Taylor's words. Furthermore, apply to these discussions of Plotinus Aristotle’s *Metaphysics* VI. 17, p. 132 Sylburg, p. 163 Brandis.
**p. 949, 14.** Ἀλλ' ὥσπερ οἱ ἐνθουσῶντες κ. τ. λ. [But just as those being inspired, etc.]] I have corrected the punctuation and reading of this passage partly from Ficino's version, partly from our books: these things remind us of Cicero's *De Divinatione* I. 2, p. 12 sq. ed. Moser: "And when in two ways the soul, without reason and science, was incited by its own loose and free motion."
**p. 950, 2.** ὡς οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ ἔνδον νοῦς—ὅσα τούτου τοῦ στίχου [that this is the internal mind—as many as belong to this rank/line]] Although it is the same as to sense, I have nevertheless preferred this reading to the other *stichou* before, also prompted by a passage of Plato in *Phaedo* p. 104 b., p. 99 Bekker, where *stichos* is read without any variation. To the argument of this passage—since Ficino in his Argument of this chapter cites Parmenides—compare what I have placed above from his remains at p. 489 end and p. 490 beginning. Add Cudworth, who in *The Intellectual System* IV. 36, p. 691, says: "Thirdly, he says, they thought it was not permitted to them to feel otherwise than that 'the knowledge and intelligence of the supreme and greatest good could by no means hold its place: from which they judged it to follow that there is a certain nature which precedes intelligence and science in dignity and grade. Plato urges and pursues this reason in the sixth book of the *Republic*. Relying on these arguments, therefore, the Platonists confidently and boldly decree ὅτι θεὸς κρείττων λόγου [*that God is superior to reason*], &c. [abbreviation: *et cetera*]" For there follow the very words of Plotinus at the end of this chapter, and likewise of Philo Judaeus in Eusebius, *Praeparatio Evangelica* VII. 13, p. 323.
**p. 951, 1.** Τί γὰρ ἂν τοῦ ἑνὸς βέλτιον—ἢ τὸ μὴ ἕν; [For what could be better than the One—than the not-One?]] I have filled a notable lacuna of this passage by the help of several of our books, especially the first Medicean, whose reading Ficino also expressed. Furthermore, the most excellent Cudworth did not neglect this memorable passage and similar ones in *Intellectual System*, p. 687: "There exists also a general precept in Plotinus, by which he inculcates this very thing (below ch. XVI of this book, p. 513 extr.): ἐν τοῖς γεννωμένοις οὐκ ἔστι πρὸς τὰ ἄνω, ἀλλὰ πρὸς τὸ κάτω χωρεῖν. *Among those things which* (from all eternity) *are begotten (or proceed by a certain natural emanation), the process is not open toward higher things, but toward lower; and that indeed in such a way that one proceeds gradually into a greater multitude. More sayings of this kind could be brought forward from Plotinus; but it will be helpful to subjoin only one, in which he declares his opinion by arguing: (ἢ) οὐ ταὐτὸν (ἔμελλε)—οὐδέ γε βέλτιον [*it was not likely to be the same—nor indeed better*] (these are the words immediately preceding our chapter)—From which precept it follows that it can happen by no reason that that which is subject to the first principle is not inferior to it in grade and order.*" Compare besides above p. 487 E, F.
**— 14.** ὅτι μεγάλην ἀρχή [that a great principle]] Several books offer the accusative μεγάλην ἀρχὴν, which Ficino seems to have wished to express. If this reading be true, it must be judged to hang from the preceding *deixai* [to show]. I thought it best to rest in the Nominative. Soon, however, note the ontological notion of the verb ἐπιβρύθειν [to overflow/burst forth] regarding the inexhaustible and ineffable fecundity of the One as the Principle of all beings; a force of the verb which Lexicographers do not record.
**p. 952, 3.** ἀλλ' ἆρα—ὡς μὴ διακεκριμένα [but then—as not being distinguished]] "They are contained in it, therefore, in such a way as they subsist without distinction and separation" (and in a note): "As all things proceed from *the one*, hence *the one* is all things prior to all." *Taylor*. Next, from many books, I gave ἐν τῷ δευτέρῳ [*in the second*] for ἐν δ.
**p. 953, 2.** ὡς ἐπειδὴ ἐν τοῖς γεννωμένοις οὐκ ἔστι πρὸς τὸ ἄνω ἀλλὰ πρὸς τὸ κάτω χωρεῖν κ. τ. λ. [as since among things generated there is no travel toward the above but toward the below, etc.]] Concerning this passage, it was discussed in the notes to ch. XV of this book, p. 512 B, C. Regarding the words immediately following in this chapter of ours, consult Cudworth's *Intellectual System* ch. IV sect. 36, p. 690 sq. and compare Plotinus himself p. 518 and 535 sq.
**— 13.** πῶς οὖν οὐκ ἐκ λόγου λόγος ; [how then is there not reason from reason?]] We have corrected it thus from good books and as the sense demands. We do not dwell upon the transposition for ἐξ οὐ λόγου [*from non-reason*]. Frequently *ouk* [not] is accustomed to fall out after *oun* [therefore], or vice versa *oun* before *ouk*. Taylor wanted *mē* [not] to be inserted.
**p. 954, 1.** εἰ οὖν ἀγαπητὸν τούτῳ τὸ ζῆν [if therefore living is beloved to this]] The margin of the first Medicean wanted τούτῳ τοῦτο τὸ ζῆν [*to this, this living*], which Ficino also expressed and we were about to receive if some of the other books supported it.
**p. 955, 5.** καὶ ὅτι τούτῳ τὸ αὔταρκες, ἐκ πάντων ἔξω ἐστί [and because self-sufficiency to this is outside of all things]] Without books, I was unwilling to delete even a comma. Taylor translates thus: "and because self-sufficiency to this intellect is the result of all the

[[vocabulary: self-subsistent, emanation, ontological, fecundity]]

--- Page 294 ---
[[original page: 287]]

-> BOOK IV. ENNEAD V. p. 949—958. 287 <-

things of which it consists." For in the bottom margin he placed these words: "Instead of ἐκ πάντων ἔξω ἐστὶν, it is necessary to read ἐκ πάντων ἐξ οὗ ἐστιν. The necessity of this emendation was not seen by Ficino, whose translation of this part is consequently very erroneous. For how can the sufficiency of intellect consist of an accumulation of all things externally? These are Taylor's words. But, with all due respect to that most refined man, I would say first that *toutō* [to this] here does not pertain to the *intellect*, but to the *One* or the *Good* (*to hen, to agathon*); second, if anything has been committed [as an error] in these words, it seems it can be restored solely by deleting *ek* [from], as having been born perhaps from the preceding syllable (αὐταρκΕΣΕΚ), and therefore this is the sense of this passage: *and because for this* (sc. the Good itself) *sufficiency is exempt from* (or immune to) *all things*. In German: "*und weil in Beziehung auf dieses (das Gute an sich) das sich Selbstgenügen als unabhängig von Allem gedacht werden muss*." [And because in relation to this (the Good in itself), self-sufficiency must be thought of as independent of everything.] Which elsewhere among these philosophers is said to be *pantōn exērēmenon einai* [to be set apart from all]. But perhaps it is not even necessary for *ek* to be deleted: which Plotinus could have added for the sake of strengthening the sentiment. Our opinion is confirmed both by what precedes and what follows thereafter, where the Good is called *epekeina autarkeias* [beyond self-sufficiency].
**p. 956, 2.** ἐν δὲ πάντη ἁπλῷ διέξοδος τίς ἐστιν ; [in that which is altogether simple, what path is there?]] By changing only the accent, there arises a question having the force of a negation; so that accordingly there is no need to interpose *ou* [not] with Taylor.
**— 7.** ὅταν ὥσπερ θεὸς ἄλλος, [when as another god] (sc. *parē* [is present] from the preceding *pareinai* [to be present]) ὅταν εἰς οἶκον καλοῦντός τινος ἐλθὼν φωτίσῃ κ. τ. λ. [when having come into a house at the call of someone, he illuminates it, etc.]] I have sought to care for this passage by punctuating it. *Theos allos* [another god], i. e., of the sort that the gods or goddesses of common religion are sometimes said to appear. Taylor at this place does not doubt that Plotinus here respected the help of Minerva carrying a lamp in the house of Ulysses in the Poet, *Odyssey* 19, v. 33 sqq.:
"— — and before them Pallas Athena,
having a golden lamp, made a most beautiful light," etc.
Regarding which passage both Stuart has treated and his recent editor in *Antiquities of Athens*, and I myself have noted in the *Additamenta* to the German edition of Stuart, specifically to Vol. I, Note 11, p. 487 ed. Darmstadt. While I do not wish that conjecture of that excellent man to be entirely rejected, yet, when I consider with myself that Plotinus here mentions a divinity who has been invoked and summoned into a house by someone, I would rather believe our philosopher touched upon the *epiphany* of Ceres in the house of Celeus of Eleusis, since she is said by Homer or a Homerid in the *Hymn to Ceres* to have been summoned and introduced into the house of this petty king. If we assume this: Plotinus must be thought to have considered these verses of that poem (279 sqq.):
"— — and afar the light from the immortal skin
of the goddess shone — — — — — — —
and the sturdy house was filled with a gleam, as of lightning."
Yet I would not precisely contend even for this, since Plotinus could have thought universally of the invocations and appearances of gods that were quite celebrated in his own age.

-> BOOK IV. <-

**p. 957, 7.** ΠΩΣ ΑΠΟ ΤΟΥ ΠΡΩΤΟΥ ΤΟ [How from the first... the... (so also Porphyry *Life of Plotinus* ch. 25, but the same in another place ch. 4 says *ta* [the things], more correctly even in the judgment of Fabricius)] ΜΕΤΑ ΤΟ ΠΡΩΤΟΝ, ΚΑΙ ΠΕΡΙ ΤΟΥ ἙΝΟΣ [the thing after the first, and concerning the One]] The seventh book, if you consider the time in which they were written by Plotinus in succession. Cf. Porphyry cited above.
**p. 958, 3.** Εἰ γὰρ μὴ ἁπλοῦν ἔσται συμβάσεως ἔξω πάσης καὶ συνθέσεως. [For if it be not simple, outside of every coincidence and composition.]] I have deleted the second *pasēs* [every] before *syntheseōs* [composition] on the authority of good books. With our passage should be compared what is read below at p. 590 C, D: "if indeed it is not possible for there to be many things, if the one is not, nor magnitude if the un-magnitudinous is not; if indeed magnitude is not the same as the one, but by participating in the one, and according to coincidence (*symbasin*)": where the same force of the word obtains. But in a third place, p. 749 D, it is: *that which happens rashly, that which occurs by chance*: "that which is truly and first unmixed with chances and the spontaneous and coincidence (*symbasei*), being its own cause, and from itself and through itself he is himself." Where accordingly a similar account of words obtains as elsewhere, where *to kata symbebēkos* [the accidental] and *to kath' hauto* [the essential] are used as contraries to each other, as in Proclus *In Alcibiadem I*, p. 333, 335, 339, and in Olympiodorus *In eundem*, p. 117 and 120. This use of the word *symbasis* by philosophers is to be recorded in Lexicons, which lack many things quite necessary for knowing the speech of philosophers. Soon: τὸ γὰρ τὸ μὴ πρῶτον ἐνδεὲς τοῦ πρὸ αὐτοῦ [For that which is not first is in need of that which is before it]. Cf. above at the beginning of this chapter: τοῦ μὲν ἐπὶ τὸ πρῶτον τοῦ δευτέρου ἀναγομένου [as the second is led back to the first], where the scribe of the Vatican
