-> 288 ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS <-

Codex hesitated at the second *tou*. This repetition of the article is familiar to the best writers and to Plato since Herodotus, although Weiske in *Greek Pleonasms* omitted many of this kind and especially the most signal ones. Plato, *Philebus* p. 41 C, p. 122 C Stallbaum: "Was it not the soul, then, that was desiring the opposite states of those of the body, and the body was that which received the pain or some pleasure through affection" (thus the vulgate, but Bekker, Stallbaum—whose note on this reading is to be remodeled—and likewise the Bodleian Codex: *parechomenon* [providing]: which reading I see neglected by Matthiæ, who in *Greek Grammar* §279. 3, p. 567 second ed., intelligently explained this passage and similar ones). It is another question whether good or at least probable writers allowed themselves to repeat the same article continuously. Boissonade denies it in a learned annotation on the *Epistles of Pseudo-Crates* (in *Notices et Extraits* Vol. XI) p. 22 sq., where he teaches that finally Eumathius, Theodorus Prodromus, and other Byzantine writers wrote thus, so that it does not seem improbable that that Crates also gave: *ton Diogenē ton ton polyn, kai hote exē exelomenon*. See the similar things collected there. Concerning the Article omitted in an infinite sentence, I have recently noted in Proclus, *Institutes of Theology*, p. 281.
**p. 958, 10.** ἡ δὲ ἀρχὴ ἀγέννητος κ. τ. λ. [But the principle is unbegotten, etc.]] The source of this sentiment and discussion is in Plato’s *Parmenides* p. 154 sqq., p. 58 sqq. Bekker. From which also Proclus drew in *Institutes of Theology* §22 sq., p. 40 sqq. To whom Nicolaus of Methone in the *Refutation* 22, p. 41 of the first edition (of our Voemel) thus: "But that which is primarily and originally being, as simply being, both according to him (Proclus) and according to Plato, has no generation, but is always unbegottenly being. And as it is also originally being, it has not even been generated. Perhaps according to neither of these stated things did this philosopher here take *monogenés* [only-begotten], but if at all, as that which is primarily and originally being, being the genus and principle of those things from itself, thus he says this; and thus one might use this gift against the Latins saying two original causes of the Spirit (Holy Spirit), the Father and the Son." I have added these things deliberately, so that from this example it may be understood how much these Platonic decrees were turned to stabilizing the heads of Christian doctrine. Compare with these and following things Cudworth's *Intellectual System* ch. IV (Inequality of the Christian Trinity) §36, p. 708, who in the same place both applied this passage of our Plotinus and compared it with Macrobius, *In Somnium Scipionis* I. ch. 17.
**p. 959, 6.** δεῖ δή τι καὶ ἀπ' αὐτοῦ γενέσθαι, [something must indeed also be generated from it]] In the edition it was faultily written *mē ti* (thus). Taylor wanted: *dei men ti*. We have restored the hand of Plotinus with the help of books.
**— 11.** —νοῦ ἐνδεέστερον [more in need than mind]] That which Ficino adds here: "which is generated from there first," Taylor suspects has fallen out: τὸ ἐκεῖθεν πρώτως γεννώμενον. The books offer nothing, and it can seem that here, as in six hundred other places, Marsilio added these things for the sake of perspicuity.
**p. 960, 1.** Διὸ καὶ εἴρηται ἐκ τῆς ἀορίστου δυάδος καὶ τοῦ ἑνὸς τὰ εἴδη καὶ οἱ ἀριθμοί. [Wherefore it is said that from the indefinite dyad and the One come the forms and numbers.]] One must inspect Plato’s *Parmenides*, *Philebus*, and the primary passages in *Timaeus* p. 35 sq. and p. 51, and likewise in *Sophist* p. 255 sqq., and Aristotle’s *Metaphysics* I. 6 and *Physics* III. 4 and III. 6 should be compared. Moreover, Brucker touched on these Plotinian remarks and what is read at p. 512, p. 514, p. 535 sq. in *Critical History of Philosophy* II, p. 401, and Cudworth in *Intellectual System* IV. 36, p. 690 sq. Add to these the most learned Brandis in *Diatribe on the lost books of Aristotle on Ideas and on the Good or Philosophy*, p. 27, where he placed among other things these: "It must be noted, however, that the term *indefinite dyad* is proper to the later Platonists and Pythagoreans, nor used before them. For Aristotle never attributes it to the Pythagoreans, and quite often records that they placed one infinite, but Plato two, namely *the great and the small*, &c. [abbreviation: *et cetera*]" cf. p. 64. Soon in the margin of the Basel edition is read *eidē dat* [gives forms], others agree with the vulgate. I add a passage of similar argument from Eunapius in the *Historical Excerpts* in Angelo Mai’s *Nova Collectio Vaticana* II, p. 257:—"just as the Pythagoreans say, the monad having moved toward the dyad, the nature of numbers does not rest at all, but is diffused and flows into much." Toward which passage the Editor praises the words of Plutarch on *Isis and Osiris* (p. 365 C, p. 496 Wyttenbach): "but we are accustomed to say 'often' and 'thrice'." Soon: ἔστι μὲν οὖν καὶ αὐτὸς νοητὸν ἀλλὰ καὶ νοῶν. [He is therefore himself both intelligible but also thinking.] The Philosopher expressed the sentiment of Aristotle in *Metaphysics* XI. 7, p. 203 Sylburg, p. 249 Brandis:—"so that mind and intelligible are the same." I have placed more from that passage

above on Plotinus p. 508 B. add Aristotle, *De Anima* III. 4, end, p. 58 Sylburg.
**p. 961, 17.** ἀλλ' αὐτὸς νοῦς τὰ πράγματα [but the mind itself is the things]] Damascius, *De Principiis* ch. 81, p. 227 Kopp: "Perhaps also knowledge wishes to be the generation of being and essence; for that which knows is essentialized by the return into being according to knowledge, not the first, but as it were a becoming essentialization. Wherefore Aristotle also says the mind is the things." See Aristotle, *De Anima* III. 4 and 5, p. 57 sqq. ed. Sylburg, and compare these passages of Plotinus: I. 8. 2, p. 73 A; III. 9. 3; V. 9. 6, p. 560; and VI. 9. 2, p. 759 E. Soon at the end of the chapter, the words: καὶ ἡ ἐπιστολὴ—τὰ πράγματα [and the letter... the things] I have left untouched; for I do not figure out what these might mean. Did Ficino perhaps read *epissēs* [equally] for *hē epistolē*? I do not know; I know this, these things are not sound. Perhaps Taylor saw the truth, who in a letter given to me wrote thus: "Here for *epistolē*, which is obviously erroneous, it is necessary to read *epistrophē* [conversion/return]. Ficino also has *vicissim* [in turn]. For Plotinus having said, 'that intellect subsists together with things, i. e. with the intelligible forms, which it contains, and that it is one and the same with them,' adds, 'and there is a reciprocation.' For the intelligible forms in intellect are one and the same with intellect. The same thing is also asserted by Aristotle."

-> BOOK V. <-

**p. 962, 7.** ΟΤΙ ΟΥΚ ΕΞΩ ΤΟΥ ΝΟΥ ΤΑ ΝΟΗΤΑ, ΚΑΙ ΠΕΡΙ ΤΑΓΑΘΟΥ. [That the intelligibles are not outside of the mind, and concerning the Good.]] More fully Porphyry in the first place in *Life of Plotinus* ch. 5, p. 102 Fabricius: "and concerning the mind and the Good." From there we also learn that in the order of time this book is numbered the thirty-second. Regarding what Fabricius opines at the second passage of Porphyry ch. 25, p. 145, that from this writing of Plotinus Johannes Philoponus brings forward certain things against Proclus on the eternity of the world: in that he is mistaken. For they are taken from the book: *concerning how the multitude of ideas subsisted*, namely Ennead VI, book 7, ch. 1. See our Annotation to that passage p. 693 D, where we have placed the words of Philoponus. Furthermore, Brucker first touched on this first chapter in *Critical History of Philosophy* II, p. 401. Tennemann, however, in *History of Philosophy* Vol. VII, p. 45 and especially p. 58—68, examines what is discussed in these chapters by Plotinus according to the Kantian standard of reason which he professes. Yet in the same place he pronounces that Plotinus looks toward the sublime and that in his decrees lie the beginnings of the greatest things, which the highest philosophers thereafter have refined and confirmed.
**p. 963, 12.** ὁ δὴ νοῦς γινώσκων—εἰ μὲν ἕτερα ὄντα γινώσκει, πῶς μὲν ἂν συντύχοι αὐτοῖς ; [the mind knowing—if indeed it knows things that are other, how then would it meet them?]] I have not hesitated to receive the second *men* into the order with good books. Concerning which iteration, after D'Orville on Chariton p. 560 ed. Amsterdam, our countrymen have recently and accurately explained: Buttmann on Demosthenes' *Against Midias* p. 155, Schaefer in *Meletemata Critica* p. 84 note and p. 111 note, and Stallbaum on Plato’s *Apology of Socrates* ch. 17 (p. 28) p. 52.
**p. 964, 10.** ἤδη γὰρ ἂν καὶ αὐτὰ περὶ ἑτέρων λέγοι [for already they themselves might speak concerning others]] Perhaps you might not ineptly join the Vatican reading with the vulgate: *auta ta peri het.* [the things themselves concerning others].
**— 17.** εἰ μὴ ὥσπερ ἀγάλματα ἐγκείμενα χρυσᾶ ἢ ἄλλης τινὸς ὕλης—πεποιημένα [unless as golden statues lying within or made of some other material]] Thus we have integrated the passage by the help of good books and Ficino, who—whether he also read *enkeimena* [lying in] or only *keimena* [lying]—I would not say. I have retained the former more because Plotinus undoubtedly had before his eyes these words of Plato in the *Symposium* p. 216 E: "but when he (Socrates) had been serious and opened, I do not know if anyone has seen the statues within. But I have seen them already once, and they seemed to me so divine and golden and altogether beautiful and wonderful," etc., which passage others also imitated, as Julian *Oration* VI p. 184 and Hermias: cf. Wyttenbach on Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris* p. 263, and our Philosopher himself respected it. See above p. 54 F and p. 465 B, C and the annotations there. Here I will add two passages where likewise in the mention of beauty a comparison of statues and paintings is instituted. Dius the Pythagorean in Stobaeus' *Florilegium* Title LXV n. 17, Vol. II p. 498 sq. Gaisford: "But beauty provides pleasures to those looking upon it, creeping toward them like a statue or a painting or another hand-wrought endeavor." Severus of Alexandria in *Ethopoeiae* n. 8 (in Leo Allatius' *Excerpta Varia* Rome 1641, p. 227, p. 220 ed. Fischer.) A painter speaks, dying for love of a girl painted by him: "Nothing then is more powerful than beauty, if indeed it knows how to hunt even through colors, and prepares living things to be captured by the soulless. It came together with the variegated wax, and forced the one who had worked to love." Where

I do not know whether it is suitable to suspect a Sophist pursuing ambiguous witticisms: *kērō korē kai t. e. e. k.* [wax girl...]. Certainly if you think of beauty from the preceding things at *synēlthen* [it came together], the following *kai—katēnankasen* [and... forced] resist it. For the painter had not made beauty, but a girl.
**p. 965, 11.** διπλάσιον ἐν αὑτῷ τὸ ψεῦδος γενόμενον [the falsehood being double in itself]] These are drawn from Plato's doctrine concerning "double ignorance" (*diplē agnoia*), which is discussed in several dialogues, especially in the *Alcibiades I*. Consult Proclus' *Commentary* p. 8 sq., p. 102, 189, and likewise Olympiodorus p. 98, 103, 132, 142, 146. Soon at the words: ἀλλὰ δόξα ὅτι παραδεχομένη [but opinion because it is receptive], if Plotinus respected the Etymon *dechesthai* (*dekesthai* [to receive]), he has even the more recent learned Grammarians in agreement. See Lennep, *Etymologicum Linguae Graecae* p. 183.
**— 16.** οὔτε ἀληθείᾳ νοῦς, [nor mind in truth]] By the dictate of the accent, the iota subscript was added by me; which I would not have mentioned, unless it had come into the mind of a man loving Plotinus: *alēthēs* [true] and *alēthōs* [truly].
**p. 966, 9.** καὶ ὁ νοῦς ζήσεται καὶ νοήσει [and the mind will live and will think]] Concerning the relationship between *being, life*, and *mind*, compare with these the discussions of Proclus in *Institutes of Theology* ch. 101 sqq., p. 150 sqq., where we have indicated several sources and streams of this doctrine. Furthermore, Tiedemann in *Geist der spekulat. Philosophie* III, p. 400 sqq., attacks these Plotinian ideas in his usual manner.
**p. 967, 3.** Μία τοίνυν φύσις αὕτη ἡμῖν—καὶ θεὸς δεύτερος κ. τ. λ. [This then is one nature to us—and a second god, etc.]] I have sought to attend to the punctuation. As for the argument, see above p. 148 C and the things praised there. Especially relevant here is the most excellent passage of Proclus *In Platonis Timaeum* II, p. 93, part of which I have placed above at p. 485 A, which passage is to be compared with ours, and no less the things which are read toward the end of these Enneads VI. 9, 10, p. 769. Here it is helpful to add Cudworth's words in *Intellectual System* IV. 36, p. 636 sq.: "Those who studied to philosophize more accurately called those three natures of which we speak three causes, *three beginnings of things*, and finally *three demiurges*. Thus in Proclus (loc. cit.) this dogma is called: ἡ τῶν τριῶν θεῶν παράδοσις (the tradition of the three gods). To which pertains what the same man writes concerning Numenius, that when he wished to celebrate *three gods*, he called them tragically *pappon, eggonon, apogonon*, *grandfather, son, grandson*. For the second of those gods was begotten from the prince god, but the third, whom he therefore called the grandson of the prince, proceeded from both, as much from the first as the second god, from the former as from a grandfather, from the latter as from a parent, Numenius was accustomed to judge. In the same opinion concerning three gods were *Harpocration*, *Atticus*, and *Amelius*, as the same Proclus has handed down to memory. The last of whom indeed called those Divinities *basileas treis*, *three kings*, and *treis dēmiourgous*, *three demiurges* and founders of the world. Nor is Plotinus alien from these, who calls the second of these three principles, namely *noun*, or the *first mind* and intelligence, *deuteron theon*, *a second god*." Thus Cudworth. In the praised words of Numenius, *ekgonon* [offspring] seems rather to be read for *eggonon* [grandson]. As for the fact that Amelius (loc. cit.) and Plotinus himself in this very place use *basileas*, *kings*, this usage of speaking is drawn from the monuments of the Orphics; since these poets in their cosmogonies frequently mentioned *basileiai* [kingdoms]. See what we have collected in *Symbolica et Mythologia* Vol. III, p. 315 sqq. second edition. Nor would this conjecture be improbable, if you should say that even that formula celebrated by the Platonists *ho nous ho basileus* [the mind the king] is of the same origin.
**— 6.** ὁ δὲ ὑπερκάθηται καὶ ὑπερίδρυται ἐπὶ καλῆς οὕτως οἷον κρηπῖδος, ἢ ἐξ αὐτοῦ ἐξήρτηται. [but he sits above and is established above upon such a beautiful foundation as it were, or is hung from him.]] I have given *krēpidos* for *krēpidos*, yielding to the Grammarians, whose passages Boissonade cited at Marinus’ *Life of Proclus* p. 66. cf. Buttmann, *Larger Grammar* §41 note 10. Plato, *Laws* p. 736 end, p. 390 Bekker: "for this becomes the greatest beginning of salvation for a city, and upon this as upon a steady *krēpis* [foundation/pediment] it is possible to build whatever political order one might later build fitting for such a state." If Plotinus is to be thought to have respected this passage, you might gain authority for the Vatican reading *menonta* [remaining] for *bainonta* [walking]; which however the following things also oppose. Moreover, Basil seems to have respected the same in *Homily I in Hexaemeron* p. 8 ed. Paris: "but a beginning is also said to be that from which something of the things inherent in it begins; as the foundation of a house, and the keel of a ship. (cf. another passage of *Laws* p. 803 A: 'the keels being laid down.') according to which it is said, 'The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord'; for piety is like a *krēpis* and a base toward perfection." This passage has a certain redundancy.

[[vocabulary: double ignorance, cosmogonies, foundation, redundancy]]

For the other Basil explains *krēpida* as *hypobathran* [under-base] and *themelion* [foundation] in the *Stelitent.* of Gregory Nazianzen. See Boissonade in *Notices et Extraits* XI. 2, p. 110 and p. 135. Peter the Bishop in Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History* IV. 19, p. 989 Schulz, concerning Lucius the Arian: ἐν κρηπῖδι σκηνῆς ἀτάκτου, in the pulpit. The same Theodoret, *Questions on Genesis* I. 19, p. 24:—"very reasonably he deemed the very *krēpis* of the race worthy of the greatest honor (God);" where *krēpis tou genous* is *humanity, human nature*. For he speaks concerning Christ having obtained human nature. Moreover, many since Victorius (in *Variae Lectiones* XVIII. 9) have illustrated the use of the transferred [metaphorical] meaning starting from Pindar (Fragments 196 (93), p. 658 Boeckh). Wyttenbach on Plutarch, *De Sera Numinis Vindicta* p. 351 ed. Oxford and *De Sententia Profectus in Virtute* p. 60 sq. Ast on Plato’s *Laws* p. 253. Wernsdorf on Himerius’ *Eclogue* X. 10, p. 184, and Krabinger on Synesius, *De Regno* X, p. 200 sqq. Because Plotinus in what follows uses the similarity of the *megalou basileōs* [Great King] in describing that procession of intelligible and superior beings: recent knowledge of Persian affairs had become prevalent in that age, and our philosopher himself had followed the camp of Gordian in the Persian war, as Porphyry witnesses in his life, chapter three. But undoubtedly Plotinus drew his color from the celebrated passage of Plato in the *Phaedrus* p. 246: "but the great leader in heaven Zeus, driving a winged chariot, goes first," and Jupiter at the end of the chapter is said by Plotinus to imitate that supreme god.
**p. 968, 3.** βασιλεὺς βασιλέως καὶ βασιλέων, [king of king and of kings]] Ezekiel Spanheim, *De Usu et Praestantia Numismatum* Vol. I, diss. VIII, p. 461 sq., touched upon the title *basileus basileōn* on coins in explaining these formulas of the Platonic philosophers, and was not unmindful of this Plotinian passage.
**— 4.** ὁ Ζεὺς—τὴν τοῦ ἑαυτοῦ πατρὸς οὐκ ἀνασχόμενος θεωρίαν, ἀλλὰ τὴν τοῦ προπάτορος [Jupiter... not enduring the contemplation of his own father, but that of his grandfather]] Fables applied by philosophers to explain the account of both universal and human nature are observed in this passage. The source of these explanations exists in the Platonic *Cratylus*, where the etymologies of Heaven (*Ouranos*), Saturn (*Kronos*), and Jupiter (*Dios*) are attempted p. 396, p. 30 sq. Bekker. Then the Stoics, Pythagoreans, and Platonists treated these things emulously. See Cicero, *De Natura Deorum* II. 24 sq. and our annotations there p. 303 sq., Cornutus *De Natura Deorum* ch. 1, p. 140 Gale, and the fragments of Chrysippus p. 239 Baguet, and cf. above at p. 485 A. Insisting on these tracks, Plotinus says Jupiter (i. e., the *soul*) does not rest in the contemplation of his father Saturn (*Kronos* i. e., the *intellect*) but tends higher to his *grandfather* (Heaven, *Ouranos* i. e., the *One* or the *supreme principle of all things*) and insinuates himself into his act and thus into the substance of his essence.
**— 13.** ἄξαι [to lead]] We have written thus with the Vatican. Furthermore, this form is rare and, being scarcely used by later writers, can be confirmed by this new example, if there be any authority of Plotinus and his contemporaries in these matters. See Thomas Magister p. 4 with interpreters Lobeck *Ad Phrynichi Eclogas* p. 287 and in *Parerga* p. 735—737.
**p. 969, 13.** καὶ εἰ ταὐτὸ ἐν κ. τ. λ. [and if the same in... etc.]] With these and the following should be compared the discussions of Aristotle in the *Metaphysics* such as book VII ch. 7, IV. 6, IV. 13, X. 1, and passim.
**p. 970, 11.** μένει μὲν πολὺ μᾶλλον τὸ ἓν κ. τ. λ. [the One remains much more, etc.]] We follow the Vatican reading. The edition: *m. p. m. to entautha; menontos de autou, ouk allo.* [the here remains much more; and it remaining, not another]. Then we suspect *ei* [if] after *poiei* [he makes] was born from the second syllable of this word; accordingly we have included it in brackets.
**p. 971, 9.** ὑφίσταται τὸ ἓν—καὶ τὸ ὂν σημαῖνον τὸ φθεγξάμενον, [the One subsists—and that which spoke signifying being]] You might suspect Ficino read: *uphistatai to on—k. t. on sēmainon outō phthegx.* [being subsists... thus signifying being...]. Next, for *outō toi ton men genomenon* [thus indeed the one who has become (masc.)] I have placed from the Vatican *outō toi to m. g.* [thus indeed the thing (neut.)]. Finally, in the last words from the books and the margin of the edition, I have replaced *gennēsin* [generation/begetting] with *genesin* [becoming/origin]. Furthermore, although in this place Plotinus derives *einai, on, ousia* [to be, being, essence] from *hen* [one], yet he undoubtedly had before his eyes these words of Plato in the *Cratylus* p. 401 c., p. 41 Bekker:—"as also in this, which we call *ousia* [essence], there are some who call it *esia* (Codex Darmstadt and Bodleian *essia*), and others again *ōsia*. First then according to the other name of these, the essence of things has a reason to be called *Hestia*; and because we call that which participates in essence *Hestia*, also according to this it would be correctly called *Hestia*. For we also seem anciently to have called essence *esia*." etc. Plotinus could indeed have gained a certain appearance of truth for his etymology if he had reminded his readers that the Aeolians said *els* for the Participle instead of *ōn* [being] [whence the Latin *ens*]. I say appearance, for who would dare to warrant the truth? Nor do we dwell upon these etymologies, e.g., that Lennep in *Etymol. L. Gr.* p. 196 instituted repeating *eis* [one]

from *eō* [to be/to go/to send].
**p. 972, 4.** τί τῶν ἐν τούτῳ ἐκεῖνο ἐρεῖς ; [which of the things in this will you say that is?]] The edition *ti—ereis*. Taylor wanted *outi t. e. t. ereis* [not anything...]. I judged the gentler interrogation preferable, which in Plotinus very often performs the function of a negation.
**— 18.** Τάχα δὲ καὶ τὸ ἓν ὄνομα τοῦτο ἄρσιν ἔχει πρὸς τὰ πολλά. ὅθεν καὶ Ἀπόλλωνα οἱ Πυθαγορικοὶ—ἐσήμαινον, ἀποφάσει τῶν πολλῶν. [And perhaps this name "the One" contains a denial of the many. Whence also the Pythagoreans signaled Apollo—by the negation of the many.]] Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris* p. 381 F, p. 561 Wyttenbach: "but the Pythagoreans also adorned numbers and shapes with the appellations of gods—the one they call Apollo by the pretext and double-most of the monad." Wyttenbach in *Variae Lectiones*: "I correct it to 'by the negation of multitude and the simplicity of the monad' (*plēthous apophasei kai haplotēti tēs monados*)." The same in *Animadversiones* to that place p. 264: "Unity is attributed to Apollo: Nicomachus in Photius Codex 187. Tenullius on Iamblichus' *Arithmetic of Nicomachus* p. 14 note 98. And what confirms our correction, 'by the negation of multitude and the simplicity of the monad,' is Plutarch himself in *De EI Delphico* p. 393 C: 'For Apollo is as it were denying the many, and is the negating of multitude (*to plēthos apophaskōn estin*).'" cf. the same man's *Animadversiones* p. 181. Moreover, we see that Wyttenbach could have strengthened his brilliant emendation by this very passage of Plotinus, and likewise by these words of Joannes Laurentius Lydus, *De Mensibus Romanorum* II. 3, p. 42 ed. Roether: "but the monad is referred to Apollo, that is, to the one Sun, who is called 'Apollo' through his being away from the many (*dia to apōthen einai tōn pollōn*)." Which are undoubtedly drawn from Plutarch, from whom that writer borrowed very many things. To this pertains the etymology of *Solis* [Sun] from the word *solus* [alone/only]. See Cicero, *De Natura Deorum* II. 27, p. 316 of our edition and Moser, and the annotations there and Roether's annotations on J. L. Lydus loc. cit. Moreover, the writer signifies that Pythagorean account in a Doric fragment in Iamblichus, *Life of Pythagoras* §146, p. 123, p. 308 Kiessling: "that the essence of number is an eternal principle, the most foreseeing of the whole heaven and earth, and of the nature between; and besides a root of divine things and of gods and of demons." Cf. Fragment of Archytas in Stobaeus *Eclogae Physicae* I. 43, p. 716 Heeren and those whom Thomas Taylor cited more in *Proclus' Institutes of Theology* ch. 115, p. 376 of the English version and at the end of our edition p. 331.
**p. 973, 4.** ὃ πάντων [ἡ] μάλιστα ἁπλότητός ἐστι σημαντικόν, [which of all things is most significant of simplicity]] I have followed Ficino, and for that reason included in brackets *hē* [the], for which *ē* [or] is offered in the margin of the edition. Plato also makes mention of simplicity (*haplotētos*) in explaining the etymology of Apollo in the *Cratylus* p. 405 C, p. 49 Bekker, but otherwise:—"according to the mantic art—and the true and simple (for they are the same) just as the Thessalians call him, he would be most correctly called. For all Thessalians call this god *Aploun* (vulgate *Aplon*)." But Plotinus with these words no longer touches upon Apollo as much as the *One* itself. Wyttenbach, however, on Plutarch loc. cit., wonders (p. 264) why Plato, when he mentions that Thessalian appellation, was not led into the same meaning of the word *Apollōn* as the Pythagoreans. Perhaps someone might conjecture from this that these Pythagoreans, who followed that etymology of Apollo, existed only after Plato.
**— 10.** τὸ ἐνεργείᾳ βλέπειν, [to see in actuality]] Johannes Philoponus in the little book against Proclus the Successor for the eternity of the world. Greek. Venice 153 fol. editor Victor Trincavellus I. 8: "And one might say the same also according to Plotinus, light is in actuality from that which illuminates proceeding into other things. Wherefore he says also that while that which acts is present, the activity is present; but when it has departed, it departs with it."
**p. 974, 6.** Οὕτω τοίνυν καὶ ἡ τοῦ νοῦ ὄψις ὁρᾷ κ. τ. λ. [Thus then also the sight of the mind sees, etc.]] Cf. Ennead V. book 8, ch. 5, 6, 7. Tennemann touched on our passage in *History of Philosophy* VI, p. 194 sq. and from there seeks to show how much more moderate and modest Plotinus was than his pupils and other philosophers of a later age, as one who says the common mind of all participates in that divine light, while his followers boasted that only very few enjoy the benefit of that light. As for what is read thereafter *mallon stilpnoteron* [more more-shining], we have spoken elsewhere of this pleonasm not infrequent in these Enneads. A little before this, Taylor wanted *ekeino* [that] added to the words καὶ ἐν ἐκείνοις ὄντως ὁρᾷ [*and truly sees in those*]. Ficino expressed it: the written books do not acknowledge it.
**p. 975, 2.** ἔνδον ἄρα ἦν, καὶ οὐκ ἔνδον αὖ [it was inside then, and again not inside]] "Let someone remember here the Aristophanic passage, *Acharnians* 395: 'he is not inside, he is inside, if you have sense. Di.: how then inside and not inside,' etc. See what I have discussed concerning that passage in *Diss. de Poesi Graecorum parodica* in the book entitled *Studien ed. Creuzer and Daub* Vol. VI, p. 285." *Moser*. Next I have filled the lacuna of the edition from our books, and these words *ou gar esti to pothen* [for there is no 'from whence'] Ficino also expressed.

**p. 976, 2.** ἀλλ' ἐν ἐκείνῳ ὢν καὶ οὐ δύο. [but being in that one and not two.]] Margin of the edition: *all' en ekeinō on* [but being (neut.) in that one]. I suspect it should be read: *all' en ekeinō ōn* [but being (masc.) in that one].
**p. 977, 1.** ἔχουσα δὴ καὶ αὐτὴ οὐκ ἐχομένη [possessing indeed itself and not being possessed]] From the following: τῷ μὲν μὴ περιέχεσθαι [*by the fact that it is not contained*] it appears in what sense Plotinus takes *echein* [to possess/have] and *echesthai* [to be possessed/held] in this place, namely in that which Aristotle explains in the *Categories*, and indeed in that Category which is concerning "having" (*peri tou echein*) ch. 12, p. 57 Sylburg, p. 109 Lewald: "or as in a vessel; as the *medimnus* [bushel] has the wheat, or the jar the wine; for the jar is said to have wine and the *medimnus* wheat. All these then are said to have 'as in a vessel'." In which passage of this Category, he who wishes to learn what the Aristotelian interpreters have gathered should consult Joannes Baptista Bernardus, *Seminarium Philosophiae Aristotelicae* p. 589 sq. I myself have exhibited and treated the opinions of the Grammarians concerning the various meanings and constructions of this verb in my *Meletemata* Part I, p. 6 sqq. Others have elegantly discussed this, such as Muretus in *Variae Lectiones* VI. 7, and Isaac Casaubon and Menagius, on those words of Aristippus in Diogenes Laertius II. 75: *echō Laida, all' ouk echomai* [I have Lais, but I am not held by her]. Next, after the word *ho theos* [the god], I suspect a member has fallen out, which Ficino seems to have exhibited: καὶ οὐδὲν ἔτι ἐν αὐτῷ [*and nothing yet in him*]. But six hundred times Marsilio was accustomed to dilate the words of Plotinus.
**— 14.** ὅτι ἐπεὶ εἰ μηδεὶς κόσμος [that since if no world]] It seems *ei* [if] should be deleted, or it must be stated that Plotinus used a singular Pleonasm according to the analogy of the formula *ei tis* [if anyone] for *tis* [someone], concerning which Weiske in *Greek Pleonasms* p. 180 sq.
**p. 978, 2.** σῶμα δὲ ἐν ψυχῇ—ἐν' ἂν—ἐν αὐτῷ [but body in soul—it would be—in it]] These things, which Taylor also had judged lacunose, we have exhibited more fully from good books, from which Ficino had also taken them. Furthermore, I do not know whether in these very words it should be read: τοῦτο δὲ οὐκέτι ἄλλου (for *toutou de ouk eti allo*: This however is no longer *of another* i. e., This however (sc. the One or the Good, in which the mind is) is no longer suspended from another. Marsilio also seems to have divined this sentiment. Furthermore, that this discussion concerning the Good, as the principle and source of all beings, is conjoined with the argument of the Platonic *Philebus*, *Parmenides*, and *Republic*, is not something I need demonstrate laboriously. Cf. also Proclus, *Institutes of Theology* 13, where I have praised more in the annotation p. 24. With the last words of this Plotinian chapter agree especially those which the same Proclus placed in the same book, but in another place, namely ch. 122, p. 178—180.
**— 14.** Ἀλλά προσβαλεῖς μὲν ἀθρόως ὁ προσβάλλων [But you the one approaching will approach all at once]] I have not hesitated to add the Article from our books. Namely, repeat *sy* [you] from the beginning of the chapter. Furthermore, these words remind us of the things above p. 526 B: ἀθρόᾳ εἶδε προσβολῇ [*he saw with a sudden approach/intuition*]. Which force of the words *intueri* [to gaze upon] and *intuitus* [intuition], although frequent in the books of philosophers, Schneider was not able to notice so as to designate it in his Lexicon. But it cannot be said how much is desired today in Lexicons toward the notation of philosophical speech. Furthermore, there seems to have been present to Plotinus’ mind the most noble passage in Diotima's speech in the Platonic *Symposium* p. 210—212, p. 413 sqq. Bekker, celebrated by the imitations of many.
**p. 979, 2.** ὅτι οὐσίας, καὶ τοῦ ὄντος [that of essence, and of being]] Taylor wants *aitios* [cause] added after *ontos*. The books do not support it and Plotinian brevity suggests that we should rather repeat it in the mind from the preceding things. Which same learned man soon wanted filled: ὅτι αὐτὸς μὲν οὐδενὸς ἐδεῖτο [*that he himself indeed needed nothing*]: we have cared for the place by the help of books, which offer *mē* [not] for *men* [indeed].
**— 14.** μὴ τοίνυν ζήτει θνητοῖς ὄμμασι τοῦτο—ὁ λόγος κ. τ. λ. [seek not then this with mortal eyes—the reason, etc.]] I have integrated this whole passage from the books, nor have I hesitated, so that the tenor of the speech might be preserved, to add with Ficino *hos* [which] before *panta aisthēta* [all sensible things], to which words some books also add *einai* [to be], perhaps correctly, yet not necessarily. That *thnētois ommasi zētein* [to seek with mortal eyes] is the same as *tē sarki idein* [to see with the flesh] in the following. Plato, *Symposium* p. 212 A, p. 446 expresses the contrary: ὁρῶντι ᾧ ὁρατὸν τὸ καλὸν [*to one seeing that by which the beautiful is visible*], namely by the light of the soul, as is that saying of Archytas in Cicero’s *De Senectute* ch. 12, or *ommasi psychēs* [with the eyes of the soul], concerning which locution and similar ones you will find more in Valckenaer’s *Scholae in N. T.* I, p. 203, Jacobs in *Anthologia Graeca* XII, p. 191, and myself on Plotinus p. 57 B. (peculiar edition p. 361). In this place I remind of the Platonic words in the *Sophist* p. 254 A, p. 207 sq. Bekker: "But the philosopher, always attached to the idea of being through reasonings, is by no means easy to be seen because of the brightness of the region; for the eyes of the soul of the many are unable to endure looking toward the divine." Which remind of Archytas' words in Stobaeus' *Florilegium* I, p. 17, p. 47 Gaisford: "the bright light brings a dimming of sight to the eyes." Plato—

#### ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS

Proclus cited [Plotinus’] words in *Alcib. pr.* [abbrev: p. → page] 37, where [abbrev: vid. → see] our note [abbrev: p. → page] 980, 8. **Καὶ—ὁ θεὸς οὐκ δρώμενος ἀπιστεῖσθαι ποιεῖ ὡς οὐκ ὢν τοῖς—νομίζουσι.**] The margin of the edition has *οὐκ ὄν*. However, the construction is consistent if you join *οὐκ δρώμενος* with *τοῖς νομίζουσι* and supply *αὐτούς* for *ἀπιστεῖσθαι ποιεῖ*. Regarding the sentiment, Marcus Antoninus [Aurelius] III. 16. [abbrev: p. → page] 88. [abbrev: sqq. → and following] speaks thus: **Σῶμα, ψυχή, νοῦς...** [Body, soul, mind. Sensations of the body, impulses of the soul, doctrines of the mind...] For in this corrupted passage I follow the reasoning of Gataker. Philo [abbrev: Jud. → Judaeus], *Leg. Allegorr.* II. [abbrev: p. → page] 200. Pfeiff.: **καὶ μὴν πολὺ πλέον ἄπρακτος γίνεται (ὁ νοῦς)...** [and indeed the mind becomes much more inactive when taste, rising up greedily, is filled with the pleasures of the stomach.]

— 9. **ὃ τῇ σαρκὶ μόνον ἴδοιεν** [which they might see by the flesh alone]] See above: **μὴ τοίνυν ζήτει θνητοῖς ὄμμασι τοῦτο—ἰδεῖν** [Therefore do not seek to see this with mortal eyes]. Accordingly, [abbrev: h. l. → in this place] **ἡ σὰρξ** [the flesh] is the mortal and perishable body; concerning this usage of speech, the learned men have spared us the labor: [abbrev: Th. → Thomas] Gataker, *de Novi Instrumenti Stylo* [abbrev: c. → chapter] X. [abbrev: p. → page] 66. [abbrev: sq. → following]; *Operr. Critt.*; Valckenaer in his *Scholia to Hebrews* II. 14. vol. II. [abbrev: p. → page] 443; Wyttenbach on Plutarch [abbrev: p. → page] 580 and especially [abbrev: p. → page] 822; and Jacobs on *Anthol. Gr.* vol. X. [abbrev: p. → page] 198.

— 10. **οἷον εἴ τινες διὰ βίου κοιμώμενοι—καταδαρθάνοιεν** [as if some, sleeping through life, should fall into deep slumber]] Sleep and wakefulness are compared in various ways. Thus, to use this example, Heraclitus [abbrev: ap. → in] Clement of Alexandria, *Strom.* III. 3. [abbrev: p. → page] 520: **θάνατός ἐστιν ὁκόσα ἐγερθέντες ὁρέομεν, ὁκόσα δὲ εὕδοντες, ὕπνος.** [Death is what we see when awake; sleep is what we see when dreaming.] To be sure, he wishes it to be signified that "vision is false," as it is [abbrev: ap. → in] Diogenes Laertius IX. 5. Aeschylus in *Eumenid.* 104: **εὕδουσα γὰρ φρὴν ὄμμασιν λαμπρύνεται** [For the sleeping mind is clarified by its eyes], at which passage Stanley touched upon the opinion of the Pythagoreans and Peripatetics, also reminding us of Plato’s *Rep.* IX. [abbrev: p. → page] 571. ([abbrev: p. → page] 426. Bekk.), whose words Cicero rendered into Latin in *de Divinat.* I. 29. 60. [abbrev: p. → page] 145. [abbrev: sqq. → and following] [abbrev: ed. → in the edition] of Moser; from which I transcribe only the end: — "Then it will happen, once the two rash parts of the soul are suppressed, that the third part of reason and mind shines forth, and shows itself vigorous and sharp for dreaming: then tranquil and truthful visions of rest occur to it." Plotinus, moreover, compares the condition of those who, enslaved and obscured by the senses, are blind to the contemplation of intelligible things and the Good itself, with those who are sleeping and dreaming. Philo Judaeus *Leg. Allegorr.* II. [abbrev: p. → page] 200. Pfeiff. on the sleep of Adam: **πῶς οὖν γεννᾶται (αἴσθησις)...** [How then is sensation born? As he himself says again: whenever the mind sleeps...] [abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → etc.] Compare what I have set down above regarding our Plotinus [abbrev: p. → page] 175. C. and especially [abbrev: p. → page] 307. G. where I have also indicated Platonic passages. Finally, the sentiment of our passage agrees with the passages of the Apostle Paul, Rom. XIII. 11: **ἐξ ὕπνου ἐγερθῆναι** [to be awakened from sleep] and Ephes. V. 14: **ἔγειραι ὁ καθεύδων** [Awake, O sleeper], where the perversity of sinners is compared to a heavy sleep. Cf. Glassius, *Philol. Sacr.* [abbrev: p. → page] 1174. Dathii.

[abbrev: p. → page] 981, 5. **ὡς ἄνευ αὐτοῦ οὐ δύναται εἶναι** [as if it cannot exist without it]] I did not hesitate to put this with Ficino instead of **εἰδέναι**, which the [abbrev: edit. → edition] has; presently **οὔποτε** for **οὔ ποτὲ** (which Taylor wishes to be added separately after **ἀνάμνησις**: I did not dare to do so without manuscripts) and **ὀδύνας** [pains] for the faulty **ὠδῖνας** [birth-pangs], unless you prefer **ὠδῖνας**. The argument is certainly joined with these words of Plato in the *Symposium* [abbrev: p. → page] 206. near the end ([abbrev: p. → page] 436. Bekk.): **ὅθεν δὴ τῷ κυοῦντί τε ἤδη καὶ σπαργῶντι πολλὴ ἡ πτόησις γέγονε περὶ τὸ καλὸν...** [Whence to the one who is pregnant and already teeming, there is great excitement concerning the beautiful...]. See the notes above at [abbrev: p. → page] 466. A. B. below. But in this place, **ὀδύνας** is preferable. Nevertheless, Plotinus had especially before his eyes in [abbrev: h. l. → this place] the discussions in the *Philebus* concerning the idea of the Good and the relation that exists between the Good and the Beautiful itself, the True, and Symmetry, which are said to be located in the *vestibules of the Good* (**ἐπὶ τοῖς τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ προθύροις**, near the end of that dialogue [abbrev: p. → page] 64; [abbrev: p. → page] 220. Stallbaum. [abbrev: cf. → compare] his *Prolegg. in Phileb.* [abbrev: p. → page] XXIII. [abbrev: sqq. → and following] and there citing Plato, *de Rep.* VI. [abbrev: p. → page] 508. [abbrev: sqq. → following]). Our philosopher expressed this passage in Book IX of this Ennead, [abbrev: c. → chapter] 2. [abbrev: p. → page] 556. D., at which place we shall cite other references.

— 14. **Καὶ οἴονται δὲ τἀγαθὸν λαβόντες ἀρκεῖν αὐτοῖς—εἰς γὰρ τὸ τέλος ἀφῖχθαι** [And they think that having received the Good, it suffices for them... for they have arrived at the end]] Plato, *Phileb.* [abbrev: p. → page] 20. ([abbrev: p. → page] 46. Stallb.): **τὴν τἀγαθοῦ μοῖραν πότερον ἀνάγκη τέλεον ἢ μὴ τέλεον εἶναι;** [Is it necessary for the portion of the Good to be perfect or not perfect?] [abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → etc.] Aristotle strives to refute these in *Eth. Nicom.* X. 2. [abbrev: p. → page] 435. [abbrev: sqq. → and following] Zell., judging the decrees of Eudoxus and Plato.

### PAGE 302
[[original page: 295]]

#### BOOK V. OF THE FIFTH ENNEAD. p. 980—985. ->295<-

[abbrev: p. → page] 982, 9. **Καὶ ἔστι δὲ τὸ μὲν ἤπιον καὶ προσηνὲς** [And it is indeed the mild and the pleasant]] Wyttenbach illustrated that *ἤπιον* [mild] at Plutarch, *de Sanit. tuend.* [abbrev: p. → page] 847. [abbrev: sq. → following]. Concerning *προσηνὴς* [pleasant] [abbrev: vid. → see] I. 4. 14. [abbrev: p. → page] 38. B.; I. 6. [abbrev: p. → page] 52. E.; IV. 4. 32. [abbrev: p. → page] 426. C. Presently, in the [abbrev: marg. → margin] of the [abbrev: edit. → edition] it was written **παρὼν αὐτῷ** instead of **παρὸν αὐτῷ**.

— 12. **Καὶ γὰρ αὖ καὶ ἕλκει ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ—ὥσπερ ἀπὸ πατρὸς—ὥστε ἐκεῖνος καὶ ταύτης κύριος** [For indeed it also draws from the Good—as from a father—so that he is lord of this as well] [abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → etc.] up to the end of the chapter.] The margin of the [abbrev: Ed. → Edition] has **ψ καὶ τὴν δύν.** instead of **δ.** On the other hand, from the same margin we have admitted into the context in the following parts **ἐμέλησεν** [it was a care] instead of **ἐμέλλησεν** [he was about to], and likewise **ὑπερβεβηκὼς** [having transcended] instead of **ὑπερβεβηκὸς**, and in the penultimate line **οἷός τε** instead of **οἷς τε**. Regarding the argument [abbrev: cf. → compare] below at the beginning of the book on intelligible beauty [abbrev: p. → page] 541. A. **καὶ τούτου (κάλλους) πατέρα** [and the father of this (beauty)] [abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → etc.] and consult Alcinous, *de doctrina Platon.* [abbrev: c. → chapter] X. [abbrev: p. → page] 477. [abbrev: sq. → following]. Moreover, the masked Dionysius the Areopagite watered his gardens from these Platonic fountains in *de Divinis Nominibus* [abbrev: c. → chapter] IV. [abbrev: p. → page] 558. [abbrev: sqq. → following] Corder.: **τοῦτο τἀγαθὸν ὑμνεῖται...** [This Good is praised by the holy theologians both as Beautiful and as Beauty, and as Love...] [abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → etc.] That he likewise says: **διὸ καὶ ταὐτόν ἐστι τἀγαθῷ τὸ καλὸν** [wherefore the Beautiful is the same as the Good], because everything desires the Beautiful and the Good according to every cause, also has Plato as its author, namely in the *Symposium* [abbrev: p. → page] 201. ([abbrev: p. → page] 425. Bekk.): **ἀλλὰ σμικρὸν ἔτι εἰπέ· τἀγαθὰ οὐ καὶ καλὰ δοκεῖ σοι εἶναι;** [But tell me a little more: do not good things seem to you also to be beautiful?] [abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → etc.] These were also borrowed by Proclus and Olympiodorus in *Alcib. pr.*: the former, [abbrev: p. → page] 319. [abbrev: sqq. → following] 327. 335. [abbrev: sqq. → following]; the latter, [abbrev: p. → page] 117. 121. 126. The same decree is examined in the *Timaeus* [abbrev: p. → page] 87, *Philebus* [abbrev: p. → page] 64. [abbrev: sqq. → following], *Hipp. maj.* [abbrev: p. → page] 296, and in the *Meno* [abbrev: p. → page] 77.

[abbrev: p. → page] 983, 10. **εἰ οὐδὲν ἔχει** [if it has nothing]] In this Syllogism, or rather Sorites, the Vatican reading seems not at all absurd, provided you join it with the common reading thus: **εἰ οὖν οὐδὲν ἔχει**. Presently the [abbrev: marg. → margin] of the [abbrev: Ed. → Edition] has **οὐδὲν ἔχον** instead of **οὐδὲν ἔχων**, then we have received **τῷ μηδὲν ἔχειν** instead of **τὸ μ. ε.** For the rest, these words of Eustratius in Aristotle's *Ethic. Nic.* X 2 are most relevant to the meaning of our passage: **ἔθος ἐστὶ τοῖς Πλατωνικοῖς διὰ τῆς προσθήκης τοῦ τ' στοιχείου...** [It is a custom for the Platonists, through the addition of the letter 't' (tau), or the addition of the word 'auto' (itself), to indicate those principles called 'eidetic' by them...] (Cf. ibid. I. 6. 5. with our commentary by Zell [abbrev: p. → page] 27.) ...by the 'tau', **τἀγαθὸν** [the Good], which is nothing else but solely Good and primarily Good. — The Platonists said that the **αὐτοὲν** [the One-itself] and the **αὐτοαγαθὸν** [the Good-itself] were the same thing... for the **αὐτοὲν** is the first of all, then the **αὐτοὸν** [Being-itself], then **αὐτοζωὴν** [Life-itself], then **αὐτοζῶον** [Living-thing-itself]. Hence Proclus, *Instit. Theol.* VIII. [abbrev: p. → page] 14: **πάντων τῶν ὁπωσοῦν τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ μετεχόντων ἡγεῖται τὸ πρώτως ἀγαθὸν...** [The primarily Good leads all things which participate in the Good in any way whatsoever, which is nothing other than the Good.] Then the same author: "For if you add anything else, you diminish the Good by that addition, making it 'a good' instead of the Good simply." Cf. Plotinus himself above [abbrev: p. → page] 352. D. E. which should also be compared with the following.

[abbrev: p. → page] 984, 8. **εἴη γὰρ ἂν ὑπὸ ἓν** [for it would be under one]] We frequently encounter hiatuses in all the books of Plotinus. Examples of this **ὑπὸ ἓν** are available in the books of Plato as in *de Legg.* VII. [abbrev: p. → page] 789. [abbrev: d. → said?]; XI. [abbrev: p. → page] 929. [abbrev: a. → ?]; *Gorg.* [abbrev: p. → page] 464. [abbrev: c. → ?]; *Sympos.* [abbrev: p. → page] 178. [abbrev: d. → ?]; *Rep.* I. [abbrev: p. → page] 342. [abbrev: d. → ?]; V. [abbrev: p. → page] 468. [abbrev: b. → ?]; X. [abbrev: p. → page] 615. [abbrev: c. → ?]. More examples from other writers were gathered by the learned Chriss. Wurm in *Commentar. in Dinarchi Oratt. tres* [abbrev: p. → page] 31.

[abbrev: p. → page] 985, 2. **πολλῷ ἄρα—ἀγαθόν.**] You might think Ficino read: *Πολλαπλάσιον ἄρα τὸ ἀπ' αὐτοῦ μόνον ἀγαθόν* [Many times more, therefore, is the good alone from it]. The manuscripts provide no help. Compare the argument of this chapter with our [passage] above: *on the first good and other goods* [abbrev: p. → page] 61. [abbrev: sq. → following]; likewise Proclus, *Instit. Theol.* CXXI. and others I have cited there [abbrev: p. → page] 178. Below our Philosopher in VI. 9. 6. (which entire passage should be compared with ours) uses **ὑπεράγαθος** [super-good]. Hence the Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite in the exordium of *Theol. Mysticae* [abbrev: p. → page] 707 calls the Trinity **Τριάδα ὑπερούσιον καὶ ὑπέρθεον καὶ ὑπεράγαθον** [Trinity supersubstantial and super-divine and super-good], and in *de Divinn. Nomm.* II. 4. [abbrev: p. → page] 419 uses **τὴν ὑπεράγαθον θεότητα**, just as ibid. I. 5. [abbrev: p. → page] 382 God is called by the same author **ἡ τῆς ὑπεραγαθότητος ὕπαρξις** [the existence of super-goodness].

#### ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS

#### BOOK VI.

[[abbrev: P. → Page]] 986, 7. **ON THAT WHICH IS BEYOND BEING NOT THINKING — SECONDARILY.**] The twenty-fourth book, evidently written at the time when Porphyry was living in Rome with Plotinus, as he himself relates in *Life of Plotinus* [abbrev: c. → chapter] V. (where [abbrev: cf. → compare] Fabric. [abbrev: p. → page] 101. and [abbrev: vid. → see] ibid. [abbrev: c. → chapter] XXV. [abbrev: p. → page] 145.) from which places, as from several of our books, we have twice placed **τί** [what?] instead of **τὶ** [something] in [abbrev: h. l. → this place], since a question is indicated. Alcinous, in *de Doctr. Plat.* [abbrev: cap. → chapter] IX and X, gives a summary of Plato’s decrees which are joined with the argument of this book. No less relevant here are the things Philo touched upon in *Legis Allegorr.* III. [abbrev: p. → page] 260. [abbrev: sqq. → following] concerning the twofold intellect, and likewise Proclus' propositions in *Inst. Theol.* [abbrev: c. → chapter] I—VI and [abbrev: c. → chapter] XXI. Thomas Taylor translated this Plotinian book into English in *Select Works of Plotinus* [abbrev: p. → page] 455. [abbrev: sqq. → following].

[abbrev: p. → page] 987, 9. **Εἰ οὖν τις διπλοῦν φῶς ποιήσειε—εἶτα ποιήσειε καὶ τὸ ὁρῶν ἴσον εἶναι φῶς—ἓν τὰ δύο θήσεται.**] "If anyone therefore *posited* [posuerit] a double light—and then *imagined* [finxerit]—he would *set* [posuerit] those two as one." This agrees with the passage of Demosthenes in *Leptinea* [abbrev: p. → page] 279: **εἰσὶ τῶν ξένων ἀτελεῖς, δέκα θήσω...** [There are foreigners exempt from tax, I will suppose ten...] "Let us suppose them to be twenty." [abbrev: Vid. → See] Valckenaer on Herodotus VII. 184. [abbrev: p. → page] 591, who also praises these words of Cicero, *de N. D.* I. 30.: "Come, let us *make* [faciamus] gods to exist out of these names by which they are called by us;" [abbrev: i. e. → that is] let us *imagine* [fingamus]. [abbrev: Cf. → Compare] our note [abbrev: p. → page] 135 and add Sturz’s *Lexicon Xenoph.* III. [abbrev: p. → page] 581.

— 16. **καὶ ὅτι αὐτὸ ἓν**] Taylor: "And because it is one thing [being intellective]."

[abbrev: p. → page] 988, 10. **Ἔδει δὲ—τέλεον εἶναι παρ' αὑτοῦ τῆς οὐσίας**] Thus I have corrected from the Medicean manuscripts instead of **παρ' αὐτοῦ**: otherwise it would be better to write **τὸ τῆς οὐσίας**. Taylor orders that **κατ' οὐσίαν** [according to essence] be added to the words that follow immediately **ᾧ ἄρα τὸ τέλεον ὑπάρξει**, moved by the Latin version: I did not dare to add it without manuscripts, and it can be understood from the preceding.

— 15. **ἀλλὰ πολλὰ ἤδη**] Thus I have written with our books and Ficino and Taylor instead of **ἀλλὰ καὶ πολλὰ εἴδη**, then [abbrev: e marg. → from the margin] of the [abbrev: Ed. → Edition] I received **ἑαυτὸ** instead of **ἑαυτόν**.

[abbrev: p. → page] 989, 1. **ἓν τούτοις ὑποκείμενον ἔσται** [One will be the substrate to these]] Thus we have given it with Ficino and several [abbrev: MSS. → manuscript] books. The argument of this entire passage is to be compared with Proclus' *Inst. Theolog.* [abbrev: cap. → chapter] I. [abbrev: sqq. → following], whose first proposition ends thus ([abbrev: p. → page] 4. in our [abbrev: ed. → edition]): **πᾶν ἄρα πλῆθος μετέχει πῃ τοῦ ἑνός.** [Every multitude therefore participates in some way in the One.] Cf. also these Enneads [abbrev: p. → page] 168. [abbrev: sqq. → following] 394. 486. and below [abbrev: p. → page] 671. [abbrev: sqq. → following] where we shall touch upon the sources and varieties of this doctrine.

— 7. **Τὸ γὰρ ἐν τοῖς ἄλλοις αὐτὸ—τοῦτο.**] Taylor: "For the imparticipable or exempt *one* is not consubsistent with any thing, but the participable one is consubsistent either with being, or life, or intellect, or soul, or body. See my translation of Proclus' Elements of Theology." [abbrev: i. e. → that is] in the Greek and Latin *Inst. Theol.* [abbrev: c. → chapter] I—VI. [abbrev: p. → page] 2—11. in our [abbrev: ed. → edition].

— 11. **οὐδὲ τὸ συγκείμενον ἐκ πολλῶν ἔσται—ἐκ πολλῶν** [Neither will that which is composed of many be... from many]] The lacuna, which Ficino had filled in the Latin and Medicean books, we have filled in the Greek from those same and other good books. Next you might suspect: **οὐδ' ὑφεστηκότος—ἐφ' ἑαυτοῦ**. This latter is in the Vatican [manuscript].

[abbrev: p. → page] 990, 7. **ἀλλ' ὅλως μὴ ὄντων** [but if they are not at all]] Thus the Medicean and [abbrev: Vat. → Vatican] manuscripts instead of **ὅμως**. In the third to last line of this chapter **μὴ** necessarily had to be added before the word **πλήθει**. Ficino expressed it and Taylor noted it. Accordingly, Cudworth is criticized for not having added this negation in the Greek. For he praises this passage in that chapter titled: *Wisdom and Mind for Plato are not the first principle, but the second*. (*Syst. intell.* IV. §. 36. [abbrev: p. → page] 690. Mosh.) adding: "Hence this philosopher (Plotinus) more often concludes his reasoning thus: **ἐν τῇ δευτέρᾳ φύσει εἶναι τὸ γινώσκειν**, *that cognition* (which is truly and properly so called) *belongs to the second divine nature, but not to the first*." Then he praises two of our Author's passages to the same effect above [abbrev: p. → page] 512 and 514, likewise Philo Judaeus [abbrev: ap. → in] Euseb. *P. E.* VII. 13. [abbrev: p. → page] 323. Thus Cudworth. Let us hear Proclus in *Inst. Theol.* [abbrev: c. → chapter] CXXI. [abbrev: p. → page] 178 of our [edition]: **Διὰ γὰρ τὴν θείαν γνῶσιν...** [For on account of divine knowledge, which is set apart from all things, all other knowledges were established, it being neither intellectual, nor even more any of those things after the mind, but established above the mind according to the divine property.]

— 13. **οὐκ ἄρα πάρεστιν αὐτῷ** [therefore it is not present to him]] These words we have added with Ficino from the [abbrev: MSS. → manuscript] books. Presently, whether the form **δυοῖν** [of two] should be claimed for the Attics or granted to the Macedonians and Alexandrians is still debated today. (Fischer on Weller II. [abbrev: p. → page] 160. Lobeck on Phrynich. [abbrev: p. → page] 211. Buttmann, *Gramm. ampl.*

#### BOOK VI. OF THE FIFTH ENNEAD. p. 986—993. ->297<-

[[abbrev: §. → Section]] 70. and Math. Gr. [[abbrev: §. → Section]] 138.) I am surprised that nothing is recorded in Schweighaeuser's *Lexicon Polyb.*, although Polybian examples are cited. In Diodorus Siculus I. 92, two [abbrev: Codd. → Codices] likewise show **δυοί**. Therefore, nothing should offend anyone in Plotinus, especially where clarity almost requires it.

[abbrev: p. → page] 990, 14. **Ἀγαθοειδὴς γὰρ (ὁ νοῦς) τῷ τὸ ἀγαθὸν νοεῖν.** [For the mind is boniform by thinking the Good.]] Concerning the word **ἀγαθοειδὴς** [boniform/good-like], very frequently used by the Platonists and Plotinus himself, we have seen above at I. 2. 4. It is probable, however, that Plotinus had such passages before his eyes in this whole chapter, such as that of Plato, *Republ.* VI. [abbrev: p. → page] 508, 509. ([abbrev: p. → page] 318. [abbrev: sqq. → and following] Bekk., where both **ἡλιοειδὴς** [sun-like] and **ἀγαθοειδὴς** are used. I shall add the more remarkable parts of that passage in the following [abbrev: cap. → chapter]); likewise of the *Timaeus* [abbrev: p. → page] 29. [abbrev: sq. → following] ([abbrev: p. → page] 25. Bekk.) and of the *Philebus* [abbrev: p. → page] 64. [abbrev: sq. → following] ([abbrev: p. → page] 219. Stallb.). Cf. also these very Enneads above, III. 8, IV. 5. 7. [abbrev: p. → page] 449. (where the verb **ἐπιχρώννυμαι** [to be colored/tinged] also recurs) and below IV. 9. 2. [abbrev: p. → page] 556.

[abbrev: p. → page] 992, 3. **Τὸ γὰρ νοεῖν οὐ πρῶτον οὔτε τῷ εἶναι οὔτε τῷ τίμιον εἶναι.** [For thinking is not first, either in being or in being precious.]] Plato, *Legg.* V. after the beginning, [abbrev: p. → page] 727. a: **θεῖον γὰρ ἀγαθόν που τιμὴ, τῶν δὲ κακῶν οὐδὲν τίμιον.** [For honor is a kind of divine good, but nothing of evil things is precious.] Proclus respects these words in *Alcib.* [abbrev: pr. → primum] L. [abbrev: p. → page] 148. This adjective is frequent enough in Plato. [abbrev: Vid. → See] [abbrev: v. c. → for example] *Sympos.* [abbrev: p. → page] 178. b; *Euthydem.* [abbrev: p. → page] 304. b. Nicolaus Methonensis *adv. Procl.* [abbrev: p. → page] 43: **τὸ ἄγονον οὐδὲν ἔχει τίμιον** [the unproductive has nothing precious]. Below, our author uses the noun **τιμότητος** [of preciousness/honor] in V. 9. 13. [abbrev: p. → page] 564. A. Nevertheless, the source of this whole chapter, as of the previous one, is in Plato's *Republ.* [abbrev: p. → page] 508. near the end and [abbrev: p. → page] 509: from which I transcribe only these: **τοῦτο τοίνυν τὸ τὴν ἀλήθειαν παρέχον...** [Say then that this, which provides truth to the things known and gives power to the knower, is the idea of the Good...] [abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → etc.] ...and as in that case it is right to think of light and sight as sun-like, but not right to think of them as the sun, so here it is right to think of both knowledge and truth as boniform, but not right to think of either as the Good itself, but the state of the Good must be honored even more greatly... and to say that being known is present to the things known by the Good, not as if the Good were essence, but still beyond essence, exceeding it in rank and power. Moreover, Cudworth touched upon this passage of Plotinus also in *Syst. intell.* [abbrev: p. → page] 690. [abbrev: sq. → following].

— 14. **πρὸς γὰρ τὸ ἀγαθὸν βλέπων αὐτὸν νοεῖ.** [For looking toward the Good, he thinks himself.]] Thus I did not hesitate to write instead of **αὐτὸ**, and Ficino seems to have read it so.

[abbrev: p. → page] 993, 1. **ἄλλο γὰρ δεῖ τῷ νοοῦντι τὸ ἀγαθὸν εἶναι.** [For the Good must be something else to the one thinking it.]] [abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → etc.] I have restored this from the books with Ficino instead of the common **τὸ νοοῦν τί**. **Ἀνενέργητον**, *devoid of all action* [omnis actionis expers], as I. A. Fabricius translates following Cicero’s example at Sextus Empiricus [abbrev: p. → page] 210. For it is read several times in this philosopher, as *adv. Math.* X. 165 and *Pyrrhonn. Hypotypp.* I. 23. (likewise **ἀνενεργησία** [inactivity] *adv. Math.* XI. 163.) and no less [abbrev: ap. → in] Theod. Metochit. in *Miscell.* [abbrev: p. → page] 343, 508, 526, 574; Nicolaus Methonensis *adv. Procl. Inst. Theol.* [abbrev: p. → page] 157; Nicephor. Gregor. *Hist. Byz.* lib. XXII. [abbrev: p. → page] 551. [abbrev: ed. → edition] Venet. Whence also below [abbrev: p. → page] 755. near the bottom of the page [abbrev: e marg. → from the margin] of the [abbrev: Ed. → Edition] and from the [abbrev: MSS. → manuscript] books we have restored **ἀνενεργήτου** to Plotinus. Presently after **πρώτην** we have added **ἁπασῶν** [of all] [abbrev: e bonis libris MSS. → from good manuscript books] and from Ficino. In the same place at **ἐπανενεγκεῖν** [to refer back] one must supply **δεῖ** [it is necessary] from [abbrev: e sequentibus → from the following], according to Plotinus' brevity of speech, and at **προστιθέντας** [adding] again we must supply **δεῖ ἡμᾶς εἶναι** [we must be]. But it would be endless to want to inculcate such things too often. He who is accustomed to Plotinian speech understands without being told. Cudworth discusses the following things in *Syst. intell.* [abbrev: p. → page] 592.

— 9. **εἰ λάβοι πῶς ἐν παντὶ τὸ νοοῦν σαφέστερον ὑπάρχει, ἢ διπλῆ φύσις αὐτῃ.**] How Ficino understood this passage his own interpretation does not clearly declare. Taylor thus: "Farther still, the truth of this may be seen in a still greater degree by him who considers how this twofold nature subsists in every thing which is more clearly intellective." What if you read: — **ἐν παντὶ τῷ νοοῦντι [σ. → ?] ὑπάρχει ἡ διπλῆ φύσις**, with the comma after **ὑπάρχει** deleted? For **λέγομεν** [we say] the [abbrev: margo Ed. → margin of the Edition] has **λέγω μέν** [I say, indeed]. — Then before **νεύει** I have deleted **οὐ** [not] with the [abbrev: Vat. → Vatican manuscript]. Taylor wanted **οὐ μένει** [it does not remain]. Finally, **ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον—παρ' αὐτῶν ἔχει** Ficino [abbrev: Fic. → Ficinus] read **παρ' αὑτῶν**. Taylor: "But we assert this of intelligibles, because they possess the perfection of existence." For my part, I would change nothing and would translate: *since they have that perfect [degree] of existence received from those [things which are in the intelligible world]*.

— 12. **τὰ μὲν μένει—τὰ μένοντα—σκιὰν** [Some things remain... things remaining... shadow]] These remind us of those passages where **τὸ μένον** [the remaining] and **τὰ μένοντα** [remaining things] (body, bodies) are opposed **τῇ σκιᾷ** [to the shadow]. Philo Jud. *Legis Allegorr.* III. [abbrev: p. → page] 302. Pfeiff.: **ἔστι δέ τις τελεώτερος...** [There is a more perfect and more purified mind... which knows the cause not from the things that have happened, as if from a shadow...] From which passage Mangey takes the opportunity to examine these passages of the Apostle Paul, Coloss. II. 17: "a shadow of things to come," Hebr. IX. 11: "high priest of things to come," and Hebr. X. 1: "a shadow... of the good things to come."

Scholiast on Aristides' *Orations for Plato* ([abbrev: p. → page] 203. C.; [abbrev: p. → page] 122. Jebb.; [abbrev: p. → page] 167. The feminine noun **ἡ ἱππότης** [horseness] should be added to the Lexicons.

— 14. **ἢν τὸ ἀγαθὸν τῶν ἄλλων**] I have separated this with a parenthesis mark from the rest. Perhaps **αὐτὸ** also dropped out after **αὐτά**. But what? If you write: **ἢ ἦν [τ. α. τ. α. → τὰ αὐτὰ τὰ αὐτά?]** with this meaning: "Or (otherwise) the Good would be of the rest" ([abbrev: i. e. → that is] enslaved to the remaining things). For I prefer to ask rather than to decide in [abbrev: h. l. → this place].

#### BOOK VII.

[[abbrev: P. → Page]] 995, 7. **ON WHETHER THERE ARE FORMS ALSO OF INDIVIDUALS.**] Because the [abbrev: Cod. Ciz. → Cizensis Codex] has **καθ' ἕκαστον**, the late Müller thinks it fits better at the beginning of the first chapter in his *Program on the Cizensis Codex of Plotinus* [abbrev: p. → page] 10. But the remaining books nevertheless agree in the common reading. Because the same Codex and the [abbrev: Vat. → Vatican] show **εἰσὶν ἰδέαι** [there are ideas], it is also the same in Porphyry's *Life of Plotinus* [abbrev: cap. → chapter] IV.; and quite often others, and Plotinus himself, use **εἶδος** [form] and **ἰδέα** [idea] interchangeably. [abbrev: Vid. → See] our note to [abbrev: p. → page] 58. A. This book is, numbered according to chronological order, the eighteenth. [abbrev: Vid. → See] Porphyry in the passage cited and also [abbrev: cap. → chapter] XXV there in Fabricius. Since we have touched upon the doctrine of Ideas as Plato handed it down in the preceding parts (as cited and for the next book, and at III. 2. 5. [abbrev: p. → page] 259. C.), we shall also touch upon it below, [abbrev: v. c. → for example] at [abbrev: p. → page] 547. and [abbrev: p. → page] 559. For the question of this book, it suffices to preface these things: Alcinous, *de Doctrina Plat.* [abbrev: c. → chapter] 9. [abbrev: p. → page] 474. Dan. Heins.: "For it does not please most of those after Plato that there are ideas of technical things, such as of a shield or a lyre, nor of things contrary to nature, such as fever and cholera, nor of particulars, such as of Socrates and Plato, nor even of any trivial thing, such as filth and chaff, nor of relatives, such as of the greater and the transcendent; for the ideas are eternal and self-complete thoughts of God." The discussions of Syrianus on Aristotle's *Metaphyss.* XII. [abbrev: c. → chapter] 2. [abbrev: n. → number] 6. come down to this: those who posit ideas say they are not of all things, because they are not of evils or shameful things, but rather these things are in nature by the privation and absence of ideas (cf. the same in *Metaphyss.* II. 3. and [abbrev: vid. → see] the note on Plotinus [abbrev: p. → page] 52. A. B. [abbrev: i. e. → that is] in the book *on Beauty* [abbrev: p. → page] 175. in the special [abbrev: ed. → edition] and at [abbrev: p. → page] 259. C.). Nor are there ideas of things which behave differently at different times; nor of parts, like the hand and head: nor of composites, like a wise man: nor of those which grow together from different trees, nor of arts which imitate nature and pertain to the utility of nature alone; nor of works which depend on the purpose of the soul. There are only ideas of animals and perfect substances and of those things which contribute to the natural disposition of these substances, such as man, and if anything is altogether perfecting, namely wisdom and virtue. ([abbrev: Vid. → See] the last [abbrev: cap. → chapter] of the preceding book of this Ennead [abbrev: p. → page] 538. A. and the note there.)

[abbrev: p. → page] 996, 4. **ἐπεὶ—ὅσους—λόγους—καὶ ἑκάστην ψυχὴν ἔχειν.**] Brucker [draws] thus from this passage in *Hist. Crit. Philos.* II. [abbrev: p. → page] 401: "As many seminal reasons as the world has, so many does it possess individual souls; there are as many ideas in the divine intellect." Let him see to that himself.

— 7. **ἄπειρον οὖν τὸ τῶν λόγων ἔσται, εἰ μὴ ἀνακάμπτει περιόδοις** [The number of reasons will therefore be infinite, unless it turns back in periods]] Plotinus had used it neutrally above [abbrev: p. → page] 36: **ἀνακάμπτοντος τοῦ νοήματος** [the thought turning back]. Lamb. Bos referred it to ellipses [abbrev: p. → page] 120 and 127. Schaef. Hence not a few locutions, both of literal meaning and metaphorical, concerning which Schleusner in *nov. Thes. Vet. Test.* I. [abbrev: p. → page] 228. and in *Lex. N. T.* under the word. Add Clement of Alexandria, *Stromm.* II. [abbrev: p. → page] 507. Potter.: **repudiata ἀνακάμψει πρὸς τὸν ἄνδρα** [having rejected the return to her husband]. Properly, those are said **ἀνακάμπτειν** who return from the goal to the starting-point, as Jacobs notes on Pallad. *Epigrr.* XLVII. 4. in *Antholog. Gr.* T. X. [abbrev: p. → page] 228. Thence Jo. Laur. Lyd. *de Menss.* in March [abbrev: p. → page] 81. [abbrev: p. → page] 198. Roetheri: **Διόνυσος, δι' ὃν ἡ νύσσα (ὁ καμπτὴρ) καὶ ἡ περικύκλησις τοῦ χρόνου.** [Dionysus, through whom the goal-post (the turning point) and the circling of time...] What I have discussed elsewhere concerning this passage, I now omit. Plato in the *Phaedo* [abbrev: p. → page] 72. b: "For if the one set of things did not always give back to the other in becoming, as if going around in a circle, but generation were a straight line only from the one into the opposite, and did not turn back [**ἀνακάμπτοι**] again to the other, nor make a turn, know that all things ending would have the same form, and suffer the same fate, and cease from becoming." The next note will indicate another passage of Plato which Plotinus respected here. Aristotle, *Metaphyss.* I. 2. [abbrev: p. → page] 30. Sylb.; [abbrev: p. → page] 38. Brandis: — "Wherefore those things do not turn back into one another, nor does a boy become from a man... but the other turns back [**ἀνακάμπτει**]; but in both ways it is impossible to go into infinity... for the destruction of the one is the generation of the other" [abbrev: κ. τ. λ. → etc.]. Philo Judaeus, *de Mund. Incorrupt.* [abbrev: p. → page] 493. Mangey: "For nature has generated the ages as certain steps through which in a certain way man ascends and descends... and as those running the double-course turn back [**ἀνακάμπτουσι**] on the same path." where either we must read with Mangey **ἀποδίδωσιν**, or establish that after **ἀποδιδοὺς**, **ἀνακάμπτει** dropped out. The same in the same place: "Having touched the highest surface it turns back [**ἀνακάμπτει**] again." Pseudo-Aristotle, *de Mundo* IV. 14. [abbrev: p. → page] 116. Kappii: "Of the winds some are straight-blowing, and some are back-blowing [**ἀνακαμψίπνοοι**], like the one called Caecias." Apuleius, *de Mundo* [abbrev: p. → page] 722.; [abbrev: p. → page] 314. [abbrev: ed. → edition] Bosschae: "Those are considered outgoing winds which blow directly; *reflabri* [back-blowing], reciprocating: as *Caecias* is thought to be:" where Salmasius certainly should not have disturbed the word *reflabri*, by which the Latin philosopher had to express that **ἀνακαμψίπνοοι** of the Greek philosopher. I also would not wish that word to have been omitted by the most learned Dutch editor in the Grammatical Index of Latin speech. I judge these to suffice for opening the account of Plotinian reasoning and sentiment in [abbrev: h. l. → this place]. — In the following: **ὅταν ταῦτα ἀποδιδῶται** it is less to be wondered at, since Wyttenbach at Julian, *Or.* I. [abbrev: p. → page] 57.; [abbrev: p. → page] 210. Lips. and at *Phaedon.* [abbrev: p. → page] 179. likewise Heindorf at *Theatre.* [abbrev: p. → page] 398. explained the force of this verb and even more the composite **ἀνταποδιδόναι** [to give back in turn].

[abbrev: p. → page] 997, 1. **ἀλλὰ δεῖ τὴν διάφορον ποίησιν ἐκ διαφόρων λόγων.** [but the differing production must be from differing reasons.]] [abbrev: H. l. → In this place] one must either think of, or interpose between **ποίησιν ἐκ**, the verb **εἶναι** [to be]. **ἡ δὲ πᾶσα περίοδος πάντας ἔχει τοὺς λόγους.** [and the whole period has all the reasons.]] Doubtless Plotinus respects the passage of Plato in *Rep.* VIII. [abbrev: p. → page] 546. ([abbrev: p. → page] 381. Bekk.): in explaining which both ancients and moderns have labored hard, to say nothing of the discord which separates the remaining philosophers in defining the great ambit of the mind; concerning which see Huet at Origen's *Commentar. in Genesin* Vol. II. [abbrev: p. → page] 18. [abbrev: ed. → edition] Ruaei; Davis and Moser on Cic. *de N. D.* II. 20. [abbrev: p. → page] 284. [abbrev: ed. → edition] major; [abbrev: p. → page] 110. — 12. **ἀλλ' ἐκεῖνο ὅτι οὐκ εἰ ἓν τῷ φαίνεσθαι**] Ficinus could seem to have read **ὅτι οὐ μόνον εἴη ἐν τῷ φαίνεσθαι**. I kept my hand off, but presently, persuaded by the books, I interposed **τό** between **τὸ ἄῤῥεν** and **πλεῖστον**. Then for **ἢ θάτερον** the same Marsilio seems to have read **ἢ θατέρου**. In the following it is singular that in **παρά τὴν φύσιν** [contrary to nature] and in **παρὰ τὴν ὕλην** [contrary to matter] this preposition has a clearly different force. As to the words...

...**οἱ δὲ ἐν ἄλλῃ χώρᾳ πῶς διάφοροι;** [how are those in another place different?] cf. Aristot. *de Gen. Animall.* IV. 2. [abbrev: p. → page] 277. — 7. **Πῶς οὖν ἐπὶ πολλῶν διδύμων—τοὺς λόγους;** [How then in many twins... the reasons?]] Aristotle inquires into the natural causes of **τῆς διδυμοτοκίας** [of twin-bearing] in *de Generat. Animall.* IV. 4. [abbrev: p. → page] 289. Sylb.; Ptolemy into the astrological ones, which very many indeed established, in *Tetrabiblo* l. IV. [abbrev: p. → page] 190. [abbrev: ed. → edition] Basil. to which an anonymous interpreter [abbrev: p. → page] 159: **τὴν δὲ ποσότητα (τῶν τέκνων) γνωσόμεθα ἐκ τῆς τῶν ζωδίων φύσεως...** [and we shall know the quantity (of children) from the nature of the zodiacal signs...]. Namely, if the planets which promise offspring (like Venus) are in bicorporeal zodiacal signs (like Pisces) or fertile ones; they bestow twin and more numerous offspring. — Just as in [abbrev: h. l. → this place] certain starry animals are called **πολύσπερμα** [many-seeded], so Aristotle (*de Gener. Animall.* I. 18. [abbrev: p. → page] 183. at the end and more often) calls smaller land animals **πολυγόνα** [prolific]: larger ones, **ὀλιγοτόκα** [bearing few]. For the former he elsewhere (as [abbrev: p. → page] 109. at the beginning) uses **πολυτόκα** [prolific], which Plotinus himself uses, except that in the edition it was erroneously written **πολύτοκα**.

[abbrev: p. → page] 999, 1. **Καὶ εἰ μὲν ἡ ποίησις ἔχει τὸ εἰκῇ τοῦ ὁποσαοῦν**] Thus I wrote with the good books instead of **ὁπωσοῦν**, moved by what Plotinus immediately subjoins.

— 3. **ἐξελίξει καὶ ἀναπλώσει** [by unfolding and expansion]] Concerning the verb **ἀναπλοῦν** [to expand/unfold] it was spoken by us at Proclus in *Alcib. pr.* [abbrev: p. → page] 230: but this passage of Plotinus, which has nouns of similar meaning joined, must be recorded in Lexicons.

— 6. **ἐπὶ τῶν ἄλλων ζώων ἐφ' ὧν πλῆθος ἐκ μιᾶς γενέσεως** [in the case of other animals in which there is a multitude from one birth]] Aristotel. *de Generat.* I. 18: "furthermore from one intercourse of animals some generate many." The same, or whoever is the author of that tenth book, *Histor. Animall.* X. 3. [abbrev: p. → page] 503. Schneid.: — "as many of the animals as bring forth many from one mating...". Hence the account of these words is understood: **ὀχεία** [mating] or **συνουσία** [intercourse] or **σύνοδος** [union] (*the business of parents, procreation*), and sometimes even **γένεσις** [birth]. Cf. also Wyttenb. at Plutarch *de puerorr. educat.* [abbrev: p. → page] 68.) then **γένεσις**, *birth of the one being born*, then **τὰ γεννήματα**, *offspring*; Accordingly, in [abbrev: h. l. → this place] think of a multitude **γεννημάτων** [of offspring].

#### BOOK VIII.

[[abbrev: P. → Page]] 1000, 7. **ON INTELLIGIBLE BEAUTY.**] This is the thirty-first book according to the passage of time in which they were written one after another (Porphyry, *de Vita Plotini* [abbrev: c. → chapter] V. and XXV.). The argument of this Plotinian book is related to not a few passages of the dialogues of Plato: *Phaedrus*, *Symposium* (in the first place to the discussion of Diotima near the end [abbrev: p. → page] 210. [abbrev: sqq. → following]; [abbrev: p. → page] 442. [abbrev: sqq. → following] Bekk.), *Timaeus* [abbrev: p. → page] 28. [abbrev: sq. → following]; [abbrev: p. → page] 23. Bekk., *Philebus*, and others. For the rest, concerning the sources and authors of this doctrine who illustrated it, I have dealt in the *Praeparat. ad Lib. VI. Enn. I.*, which is *on Beauty*. Among these Dius the Pythagorean (two of whose fragments from the book *On Beauty* Stobaeus preserved for us in *Florileg.* Tit. LXV. 16. and 17. Vol. II. [abbrev: p. → page] 497—499. [abbrev: ed. → edition] Gaisford.) agrees in several sentiments with the Plotinian ones; yet not so that Plotinus must necessarily be thought to have read that book. But also concerning the arguments of the dialogues of the Platonists we have cited, we have said more in that *Preparation* for the book of Plotinus *on Beauty* in the special Heidelberg [abbrev: ed. → edition], whence, those things which at [abbrev: p. → page] CXIII pertain to this book, for the sake of those readers for whom that edition is not at hand, it may be permitted to transfer here: "That book ([abbrev: i. e. → that is] this very one on intelligible beauty) you may see referred by Porphyry (*de Vita Plotini* [abbrev: c. → chapter] 25.) to that Ennead which is concerned with the *mind* (**νοῦν**). Namely, that highest [principle], which is called the Good and the One, or God, concerning whom the last book of the last Ennead...

### PAGE 308
[[original page: 301]]

#### LIB. VIII. ENNEAD. QUINTÆ. p. 998—1001. ->301<-

...is, when considered properly in itself, escapes even the intellect itself; and remaining within as if in a hidden dwelling forever, it cannot be known except by degrees. It wished, however, for its essence to be made known through three goods, located at the threshold of its dwelling, as it were. These are the three intelligible monads (**νοηταί**): *truth* (**ἡ ἀλήθεια**), *beauty* (**ἡ καλλονὴ**), and *symmetry* (**ἡ συμμετρία**). See Plato's *Philebus*, from which this doctrine is most derived, [abbrev: p. → page] 64. [abbrev: sq. → following]; [abbrev: p. → page] 219. [abbrev: sqq. → and following] Stallb." No one has more diligently drawn Plato’s doctrine from his own writings, no one has arranged it more elegantly and commended it more eloquently, than my [friend] Heusde, a most distinguished man, in the first part of the book titled: *Initia Philosophiae Platonicae* [abbrev: p. → page] 187. [abbrev: sqq. → and following]. The philosophers who followed thereafter touched upon this doctrine of intelligible beauty with such zeal that it would be infinite to enumerate them individually. Accordingly, I pluck only a few. Thus, to use this [example], Plutarch in his Platonic questions had before his eyes that part of Diotima's speech which I mentioned above [abbrev: p. → page] 1002.; [abbrev: p. → page] 81. Wyttenb. Longinus likewise, and the others who taught about the sublime and the beautiful, borrowed not a few things from Plato’s dialogues. Proclus Lycius had published a singular book on those three monads, as he himself records in his *Commentaries on Plato's Republic* [abbrev: p. → page] 433. Today that writing is missing. Yet what the opinion of that philosopher was concerning beauty can be understood both from other sources and from his books on Plato’s *Theology* (I. 24. [abbrev: p. → page] 59. [abbrev: sqq. → following]; III. 8. [abbrev: p. → page] 150. [abbrev: sqq. → following]) and indeed especially from his *Commentary on Plato's Alcibiades I*. Hermias also touched upon this place concerning intelligible beauty in Plato's *Phaedrus* [abbrev: c. → chapter] XXIII. [abbrev: p. → page] 112. [abbrev: sq. → following] [abbrev: ed. → edition] of Ast. Finally Dionysius, who wishes to be seen as the Areopagite, whatever he declaimed concerning beauty both general and intelligible (*de Divinn. Nominibb.* [abbrev: c. → chapter] IV. [abbrev: p. → page] 558—561. Corderii), those things, like all the rest of that man's [writings], were taken from the books of the Platonists. How much the fathers of the Church celebrated this doctrine is shown by the fuller commentary which we added to the Heidelberg edition of the sixth book of Ennead I, *on Beauty*. Among more recent philosophers who have commented on the beautiful, such as [abbrev: M. → Marcus] Antonius Natta and many others, and in our memory Kant and others, and among these Herder himself in *Calligone*, they respected Plato's writings: as for these books of Plotinus, if you perhaps except Ficino and Schelling, so far as I know, no one has made much of them.

[abbrev: p. → page] 1001, 2. **ἀνθρώπου δὲ μή τινος—ἡ τέχνη** [but art is not of some individual man]] These remind us of the Ciceronian narration in *de Invent.* II. 1. concerning Zeuxis the painter, who, when he was ordered by the Crotoniates to paint Helen, chose the most beautiful parts from the most beautiful virgins, for he did not think, Cicero adds, that he could find all the things he sought for grace in one body; and therefore, because nature has polished nothing that is perfect in all its parts in a single kind. Thus, as if she would not have anything to bestow on the others if she granted everything to one, she rewards one with one advantage, while adding some disadvantage. Pliny reported this was done at Agrigentum [*H. N.* XXXV. 9. 36], Aelian at Heraclea. Yet others agree with Cicero, whom Sillig praises in *Catalogo Artificum* [abbrev: p. → page] 462. [abbrev: sq. → following], who should be consulted on this matter. Also worthy are the things that may be read as subtly argued on this matter by Emeric-David, a man of elegant judgment, in *Biographie Universelle* T. LII. [abbrev: p. → page] 308. [abbrev: sq. → following]. Beware, however, of thinking that Plotinus persuaded himself that the most excellent works of art are produced in this way. Not even Cicero had persuaded himself of this, as is understood from the excellent passage in the *Orator* [abbrev: c. → chapter] 2. which we shall touch upon at the end of this chapter. Consult also the discussions of our Herder in the most excellent work *Calligone* III. [abbrev: p. → page] 194. For the rest, in the choice of the example by which Plotinus joined the Muse to Grace, if you should wish to apply that [line] of Euripides, you would recognize a "most sweet yoke" [**ἥδισταν συζυγίαν**].

— 15. **Καὶ γὰρ δσφ ἰδὼν εἰς τὴν ὕλην ἐκτέταται, τόσῳ ἀσθενέστερον τοῦ ἐν ἑνὶ μένοντος.** [For indeed by as much as it is extended looking into matter, by so much is it weaker than that which remains in the one.]] This entire discussion, in which Plotinus describes the nature of true art so lucidly, is joined with the passage on *matter* and likewise on *ideas* and is therefore to be compared with those passages of the dialogues of Plato in which both are explained. You see the things I have brought together for this matter above at the book on beauty [abbrev: p. → page] 52. A. B. and at the first book on Providence [abbrev: p. → page] 259. [abbrev: sq. → following], which later Plotinian passages must be compared with ours in the first place. — Regarding the following things on *imitation*, Plato must be applied in *Rep.* X. [abbrev: p. → page] 597. [abbrev: sq. → following]; [abbrev: p. → page] 471. [abbrev: sq. → following] Bekk. But especially to be held is the discussion of Aristotle in *Poetic.* II. 1. where three kinds of artists are distinguished: Polygnotus [portrayed them] better, Pauson worse, Diony-
