[[original page: 295]]

->BOOK V. ENNEAD FIVE. pages 980—985.<- ->295<-

"and to possess [the Good] for itself, and it cares for nothing else, except for those things accomplished along with good things." <note>original: καὶ περὶ αὐτὸ κτήσασθαι... This is a quote from Plotinus.</note> Aristotle strives to refute these ideas in the *Nicomachean Ethics* X. 2. page 435 and following, in Zell’s edition, where he judges the decrees of Eudoxus and Plato.
**Page 982, line 9.** "And it is indeed mild and gentle"] Wyttenbach illustrated that word "mild" <note>original: ἤπιον</note> in his notes on Plutarch’s *On Preserving Health*, page 847 and following. Regarding "gentle" <note>original: προσηνὴς</note> see Book I. 4. 14. page 38. B.; I. 6. page 52. E.; IV. 4. 32. page 426. C. Presently, in the **margin** of the **edition**, "being present with him" <note>original: παρὼν αὐτῷ</note> was written instead of "it being possible for him" <note>original: παρὸν αὐτῷ</note>.
— **12.** "For indeed it also draws from the Good—as if from a father—so that he is lord even of this [beauty], etc. until the end of the chapter."] The margin of the **Edition** has "and the power" <note>original: ψ καὶ τὴν δύν.</note> instead of "power." On the other hand, from the same margin, we have restored to the text in the following lines "he cared" <note>original: ἐμέλησεν</note> instead of "he was about to," likewise "having transcended" <note>original: ὑπερβεβηκὼς</note> (masculine) instead of "having transcended" (neuter), and in the second to last line "able" <note>original: οἷός τε</note> instead of "to whom." Regarding the argument, **compare** below at the beginning of the book *On Intelligible Beauty*, page 541. A. "and the father of this (beauty), etc." and consult Alcinous on the *Doctrines of Plato*, **chapter** X. page 477 and following. Moreover, the masked Dionysius the Areopagite watered his little gardens from these Platonic springs in *On the Divine Names*, **chapter** IV. page 558 and following, in Corderius's edition: "This Good is hymned by the holy theologians both as Beautiful and as Beauty, and as Love, and as Beloved, and whatever other fitting divine names there are for the beauty-making and graced loveliness. But the 'Beautiful' and 'Beauty' are not to be divided in the case of the Cause which has gathered the wholes into one.—And the discourse would even dare to say this: that even non-being participates in the Beautiful and the Good, when it is hymned in God beyond-substance <note>original: ὑπερουσίως</note> according to the stripping away of all things. This one Good and Beautiful is uniquely the cause of all the many beautiful and good things." <note>The author is tracing how Neoplatonic ideas about God as the source of beauty influenced early Christian mystical writing.</note> Indeed, where he says the same thing likewise: "Wherefore the Beautiful is the same as the Good, because all things desire the Beautiful and the Good according to every cause," he has Plato as the author of this as well, specifically in the *Symposium*, page 201. page 425 in Bekker's edition: "But say a little more: do not good things seem to you to be beautiful? etc." These things were also borrowed by Proclus and Olympiodorus in their commentaries on the *First Alcibiades*: the former, page 319 and following, 327, 335 and following; the latter, page 117, 121, 126. The same decree is examined in the *Timaeus* page 87, *Philebus* page 64 and following, *Greater Hippias* page 296, and in the *Meno* page 77.
**Page 983, line 10.** "if it has nothing"] In this Syllogism, or rather a "Sorites" <note>A chain of logical arguments</note>, the reading of the Vatican manuscript does not seem absurd, provided you join it with the common reading thus: "if therefore it has nothing." Presently, the **margin** of the **Edition** has "having nothing" <note>original: οὐδὲν ἔχον</note> (neuter) instead of "having nothing" (masculine); then we have accepted "by having nothing" <note>original: τῷ μηδὲν ἔχειν</note> instead of "the having nothing." Furthermore, these words of Eustratius in his commentary on Aristotle’s *Nicomachean Ethics* X. 2. are especially relevant to the meaning of our passage: "It is the custom for the Platonists, through the addition of the letter 't' <note>Turning 'good' into 'the good'</note>, or the addition of the word 'itself' <note>original: αὐτὸ</note>, to clarify the 'ideal principles' as they call them, which are primarily that very thing which is named (Compare the same work I. 6. 5. with our Zell’s Commentary, page 27.) Therefore, through the 't', 'the Good' <note>original: τἀγαθὸν</note> is that which is nothing else but solely good and primarily good.—And the Platonists used to say that 'the One-itself' and 'the Good-itself' are the same thing, and not one thing and another.—For they said the 'One-itself' is the first of all, then 'Being-itself', then 'Life-itself', then 'the Animal-itself'." Hence Proclus in *Elements of Theology* VIII. page 14: "The primarily Good, which is nothing else than the Good, leads all things that participate in the Good in any way." The same author then says: "For if you add anything else, you have diminished the Good by the addition, making it 'a good' instead of 'the Good' simply." Compare Plotinus himself above, page 352. D. E., which should also be compared with what follows.
**Page 984, line 8.** "for it would be under one"] We frequently encounter "hiatus" <note>A gap between vowels in speech</note> in all of Plotinus's books. Examples of this "under one" <note>original: ὑπὸ ἓν</note> are available in the books of Plato, such as *Laws* VII. page 789; XI. page 929; *Gorgias* page 464; *Symposium* page 178; *Republic* I. page 342; V. page 468; X. page 615. More examples from other writers were collected by Christian Wurm, a learned man, in his *Commentary on the Three Orations of Dinarchus*, page 31.
**Page 985, line 2.** "by much then—good."] You might think Ficino <note>The famous Renaissance translator of Plotinus</note> read: "Many times over, then, is the good that comes from him alone." The manuscripts offer no help. Compare the argument of this chapter with our work above: *On the First Good and Other Goods*, page 61 and following; likewise Proclus's *Elements of Theology* 121, and others I praised there on page 178. Below, our philosopher in VI. 9. 6. (which whole passage should be compared with our present one) uses the term "super-good" <note>original: ὑπεράγαθος</note>. Hence the Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, in the opening of *Mystical Theology*, page 707, calls the Trinity a "Trinity beyond-substance, beyond-divine, and super-good," and in *On the Divine Names* II. 4. page 419, he uses the phrase "the super-good deity," just as in the same work I. 5. page 382, God is called by him "the existence of super-goodness."

->BOOK VI.<-

[[page]] 986, 7. <note>original: "ΠΕΡΙ ΤΟΥ, ΤΟ ΕΠΕΚΕΙΝΑ ΤΟΥ ΟΝΤΟΣ ΜΗ ΝΟΕΙΝ—ΔΕΥΤΕΡΩΣ"</note> ON THE FACT THAT THAT WHICH IS BEYOND BEING DOES NOT THINK—SECONDLY.] The twenty-fourth book, evidently written at the time when Porphyrius was living in Rome with Plotinus, as he reveals in the *Life of Plotinus* [[chapter]] V. (compare Fabricius [[page]] 101 and see also [[chapter]] XXV. [[page]] 145.) From these passages, as from several of our own books, we have in this place twice placed <term>tí</term> <note>the interrogative "what?"</note> instead of <term>tì</term> <note>the indefinite "something"</note>, since a question is indicated. Alcinous, in *On the Doctrines of Plato* [[chapters]] IX and X, provides a summary of Plato's decrees which are connected to the argument of this book. No less relevant are the things Philo touched upon in *Allegories of the Laws* III [[page]] 260 and following regarding the dual intellect, and likewise the propositions of Proclus in the *Elements of Theology* [[chapters]] I–VI and [[chapter]] XXI. Thomas Taylor translated this Plotinian book into English in *Select Works of Plotinus* [[page]] 455 and following.

[[page]] 987, 9. <note>original: "Εἰ οὖν τις διπλοῦν φῶς ποιήσειε... ἓν τὰ δύο θήσεται"</note> "If someone, therefore, *should posit* a double light—and then *should imagine*—he will *posit* those two as one."] A passage of Demosthenes in *Against Leptines* [[page]] 279 agrees: "There are some exempt foreigners; I shall posit ten—therefore of both there are sixteen. Let us make them twenty." "Let us assume them to be twenty." See Valckenaer on Herodotus VII. 184 [[page]] 591, who also praises these words of Cicero from *On the Nature of the Gods* I. 30: "Come, let us *make* it so that from these names there are gods, by which they are named by us;" that is, *let us imagine*. Compare our note on [[page]] 135 and add Sturz's *Xenophontic Lexicon* III [[page]] 581.

— 16. <note>original: "καὶ ὅτι αὐτὸ ἓν"</note> and because it is one thing] Taylor: "And because it is one thing [being intellective]."

[[page]] 988, 10. <note>original: "Ἔδει δὲ—τέλεον εἶναι παρ' αὑτοῦ τῆς οὐσίας"</note> "It was necessary—to be perfect from itself in its essence"] Thus I have corrected from the Medicean manuscripts instead of "from him" <note>original: "παρ' αὐτοῦ"</note>: otherwise it would be better to write "that of the essence." Taylor, moved by the Latin version, orders that "according to essence" <note>original: "κατ' οὐσίαν"</note> be added immediately to the words "to which therefore perfection shall belong"; I did not dare to add this without the books <note>manuscripts</note>, and it can be understood from the preceding.

— 15. <note>original: "ἀλλὰ πολλὰ ἤδη"</note> "but many already"] Thus I have written with our books and Ficino and Taylor instead of "but also many forms," then from the margin of the Edition I received "itself" <note>neuter: "ἑαυτὸ"</note> instead of "himself" <note>masculine: "ἑαυτόν"</note>.

[[page]] 989, 1. <note>original: "ἓν τούτοις ὑποκείμενον ἔσται"</note> "one thing will be the substrate for these"] Thus we have given it with Ficino and several manuscript books. The argument of this entire passage should be compared with Proclus's *Elements of Theology* [[chapter]] I and following, of which the first proposition is thus finished ([[page]] 4 of our edition): "Every multitude, therefore, participates in some way in the One." Compare also these *Enneads* [[pages]] 168, 394, 486, and below [[page]] 671 and following, where we shall touch upon the sources and variations of this doctrine.

— 7. <note>original: "Τὸ γὰρ ἐν τοῖς ἄλλοις αὐτὸ—τοῦτο."</note> "For that which is in others—this."] Taylor: "For the imparticipable or exempt *one* is not consubsistent with any thing, but the participable one is consubsistent either with being, or life, or intellect, or soul, or body. See my translation of Proclus' Elements of Theology." That is, in the Greek and Latin *Elements of Theology* [[chapters]] I–VI [[pages]] 2–11 of our edition.

— 11. <note>original: "οὐδὲ τὸ συγκείμενον ἐκ πολλῶν ἔσται—ἐκ πολλῶν"</note> "nor will that which is composed of many be—from many"] The gap, which Ficino had filled in the Latin and Medicean books, we have filled in the Greek from the same and other good books. You might suspect the next part: "nor of that which subsists—by itself." This latter is in the Vatican manuscript.

[[page]] 990, 7. <note>original: "ἀλλ' ὅλως μὴ ὄντων"</note> "but of things not being at all"] Thus the Medicean and Vatican manuscripts instead of "nevertheless." In the third to last line of this chapter, it was necessary to add "not" <note>original: "μὴ"</note> before the word "multitude." Ficino expressed this and Taylor advised it. Cudworth, however, did not add this negation in the Greek. For he praises this passage in that chapter which is titled: *Wisdom and Mind are not the first principle for Plato, but the second*. (*Intellectual System* IV. §. 36. [[page]] 690. Mosheim edition) adding: "Hence this philosopher (Plotinus) quite often concludes his reasoning thus: that knowing is in the secondary nature, *cognition* (which is truly and properly so called) *belongs to the second divine nature, but not to the principal one*." Then he praises two passages of our Author in the same vein above on [[pages]] 512 and 514, likewise Philo the Jew in Eusebius's *Preparation for the Gospel* VII. 13 [[page]] 323. These are Cudworth's words. Let us hear Proclus in *Elements of Theology* [[chapter]] CXXI [[page]] 178 of our edition: "For through the divine knowledge, which is exempt from all things, all other knowledges also subsist, being neither intellectual, nor even more any of those things after the intellect, but established according to the divine peculiarity above the intellect."

— 13. <note>original: "οὐκ ἄρα πάρεστιν αὐτῷ"</note> "therefore it is not present to him"] These words we have added with Ficino from the manuscript books. Presently, it is still debated today whether the form <term>duoin</term> <note>the number "two"</note> is to be claimed for the Attics or granted to the Macedonians and Alexandrians. ->BOOK VI. ENNEAD FIVE. pages 986—993.<- ->297<-

Section 70. and *Mathematical Greeks* Section 138.) I am surprised that nothing is recorded in Schweighaeuser’s *Lexicon to Polybius*, although examples from Polybius are cited. In Diodorus Siculus Book I, chapter 92, two manuscripts likewise show the form *duoi* <note>original: "δυοί" - an archaic or dialectical form of the word "two"</note>. Consequently, no one can take offense at this in Plotinus, especially where clarity almost requires it.

Page 990, line 14. **For it (the intellect) is good-like by thinking the good.**] Regarding the word *agathoeidēs* <note>original: "ἀγαθοειδὴς" - meaning "good-like" or "boniform"</note>, which was quite frequently used by the Platonists and Plotinus himself, we saw above at I. 2. 4. It is probable, moreover, that Plotinus had in mind throughout this entire chapter passages such as that in Plato’s *Republic* Book VI, pages 508, 509, and page 318 following in Bekker’s edition (where both *hēlioeidēs* <note>sun-like</note> and *agathoeidēs* are employed. I will set down the more remarkable parts of that passage in the following chapter.) Likewise *Timaeus* page 29 following, page 25 in Bekker, and *Philebus* page 64 following, page 219 in Stallbaum. Compare also these very *Enneads* above at III. 8. and IV. 5. 7. page 449 (where the verb *epichrōnnumai* <note>to be colored or tinged</note> also recurs) and below at IV. 9. 2. page 556.

Page 992, line 3. **For thinking is not first, neither in being nor in being precious.**] Plato, *Laws* Book V, after the beginning, page 727a: "For honor is surely a divine good, but of things that are evil, nothing is precious." Proclus looks back to these words in *On the First Alcibiades* Book I, page 148. This adjective is frequent enough in Plato. See, for example, *Symposium* page 178b, *Euthydemus* page 304b. Nicolaus of Methone *Against Proclus* page 43: "That which is sterile has nothing precious." Our author <note>Plotinus</note> uses the noun *timiotētos* <note>preciousness/honor</note> below at V. 9. 13. page 564 A. However, the source of this entire chapter, as with the previous one, is in Plato’s *Republic* page 508 near the end and page 509: from which I transcribe only these words: "This, then, which imparts truth to the things known and gives the power to the knower, you must say is the Idea of the Good; and as being the cause of science and of truth as known, so conceive of it; and though both these are beautiful, knowledge and truth, you will be right in esteeming it as something other and still more beautiful than these. Just as in the other case it is right to deem light and vision sun-like, but to think they are the sun is not right, so here it is right to deem these two good-like, but to think that either of them is the Good is not right, but the state of the Good is to be honored even more highly.—And so you must say that for the things known, not only their being known is present from the Good, but also their being and essence are derived from it, though the Good is not essence, but still beyond essence, surpassing it in dignity and power." <note>This is the famous "Sun Analogy" where Plato describes the Good as being "beyond being" (epekeina tēs ousias).</note> Cudworth also touched upon this passage of Plotinus in *Intellectual System* page 690 following.

— 14. **for looking toward the good, it thinks itself.**] Thus I did not hesitate to write "itself" <note>Greek: "αὐτὸν" (masculine, referring to the Intellect)</note> instead of "it" <note>Greek: "αὐτὸ" (neuter)</note>, and Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino, the 15th-century translator of Plotinus</note> seems to have read it this way.

Page 993, line 1. **for the Good must be something other than that which thinks.** etc.] I have restored this from the books, following Ficino, instead of the common reading "that which thinks something." *Anenergēton*, **inactive** or **devoid of all action**, as I. A. Fabricius translates it following Cicero's example in his notes to Sextus Empiricus page 210. For it is read several times in that philosopher, as in *Against the Mathematicians* X. 165 and *Pyrrhonian Outlines* I. 23. (likewise *anenergēsia* <note>inactivity</note> in *Against the Mathematicians* XI. 163.) and no less in Theodorus Metochites in his *Miscellanies* pages 343, 508, 526, 574; Nicolaus of Methone *Against Proclus's Elements of Theology* page 157; Nicephorus Gregoras *Byzantine History* book XXII, page 551 of the Venice edition. From which sources we have also restored *anenergētou* <note>of the inactive</note> to Plotinus below on page 755, near the bottom of the page, from the margin of the Edition and the manuscript books. Soon after "first," we added "of all" from the good manuscript books and Ficino. In the same place, at "to refer back," one must supply "it is necessary" according to Plotinus’s brevity of speech, and at "we adding," again one must supply "it is necessary for us." But it would be infinite to want to insist on such things too often. He who is accustomed to Plotinian speech understands without being told. Cudworth discusses the following points in *Intellectual System* page 592.

— 9. **if one should grasp how in everything that which thinks exists more clearly, or if a twofold nature is in it.**] How Ficino understood this passage, his own translation does not sufficiently declare. Taylor <note>Thomas Taylor, the "Platonist" translator</note> translates it thus: "Farther still, the truth of this may be seen in a still greater degree by him who considers how this twofold nature subsists in every thing which is more clearly intellective." What then if you read:—"in everything that thinks... there exists the twofold nature," deleting the comma after "exists"? Instead of "we say," the margin of the Edition has "I say indeed."—Then before "inclines," I deleted "not" following the Vatican manuscript. Taylor wanted "does not remain." Finally, "but rather—it has from them," Ficino read "from themselves." Taylor: "But we assert this of intelligibles, because they possess the perfection of existence." For my part, I would change nothing and would translate: *since they have that perfection of (their) existence received from those (things which are in the intelligible world)*.

— 12. **some things remain—the things remaining—shadow**] These things remind one of those passages where "that which remains" and "the things..."

->298 ANNOTATIONES IN PLOTINI<-
<note>original: "Annotations on Plotinus"</note>

*Remaining* (referring to bodies or physical substances) are contrasted with the *shadow*. <note>original: μένοντα (corpus, corpora) opponuntur τῇ σκιᾷ (umbrae)</note> Philo the Jew in *Allegorical Interpretation of the Law*, Book III, page 302 (Pfeiffer edition): "There is a certain more perfect and more purified mind, initiated into the great mysteries, which does not know the Cause from the effects, as one might know the substance from the shadow." <note>original: ἔστι δέ τις τελεώτερος... From this passage, the scholar Mangey takes the opportunity to examine these passages in the epistles of Paul: Colossians 2:17 ("a shadow of things to come"), Hebrews 9:11 ("high priest of things to come"), and Hebrews 10:1 ("a shadow of the good things to come").</note> Truly, although a variety of readings appear in these two places, Valckenaer explains the common reading best in his *Scholae* at the final passage, Volume II, page 559 and following. I have traced the origin of the formulas "shadow of being" <note>original: σκιὰ τοῦ εἶναι</note> and similar phrases back to Plato, and I collected similar passages for Book I, Chapter 6, in the special edition, page 203 and following.

Page 994, line 6. **and to those approaching each individual thing** (I have placed this reading from the Manuscripts instead of "upon the things that are") **a human being**] Before "human being," Taylor suggests supplying: "the thought of a human being and": certainly it ought to be thought of, and Ficino expressed it this way. In what follows, instead of "to the being," the margin of the Edition has "a certain being." I have retained the common reading; however, I suspect one should immediately write: "and that which is beyond thinking." Furthermore, the examples of *man* and *horse* are common in the disputes of philosophers. Let it suffice here to cite one passage where the *Ideas* of Plato are discussed. The Scholiast on Aristides in the *Platonic Orations* (page 203 C, page 122 Jebb, page 167 Frommel): — "For Plato says that the patterns of things on earth exist in heaven, as if they were archetypes from which the things on earth come; these are certain incorporeal things, just as **humanity** is to man, and **horseness** <note>original: ἱππότης (hippotes) — a technical term for the abstract essence of a horse</note> is to the horse, and likewise for all other things, which he calls Ideas." The feminine substantive **horseness** <note>original: ἡ ἱππότης</note> should be added to the Dictionaries.

— 14. **if the Good [is] of the others**] I have separated these from the rest with a parenthesis mark. Perhaps also the word "itself" <note>original: αὐτὸ</note> fell out after "them." But what if you were to write: "or were they the same things?" <note>original: ἢ ἦν τὰ αὐτὰ τὰ αὐτά?</note> with this meaning: Or (otherwise) the Good would be of the rest (that is, enslaved to the remaining things). For I prefer to inquire rather than to decide in this place.

->BOOK VII.<-

Page 995, line 7. **ON WHETHER THERE ARE FORMS EVEN OF INDIVIDUALS.**] Because the Cizensis Manuscript has "concerning each individual" (singular), Müller—of blessed memory—thinks this fits the beginning of the first chapter better in his *Program on the Cizensis Manuscript of Plotinus*, page 10. But the remaining books nevertheless agree on the common reading. The fact that this same Manuscript and the Vatican Manuscript show "there are ideas" <note>original: εἰσὶν ἰδέαι</note> is also found in Porphyry’s *Life of Plotinus*, chapter 4; and quite often others, as well as Plotinus himself, use "Form" <note>original: εἶδος</note> and "Idea" <note>original: ἰδέα</note> interchangeably. See our note to page 58 A. This book is, numbered by chronological order, the eighteenth. See Porphyry in the place cited, and also chapter 25, and Fabricius there. We have touched upon the doctrine of Ideas as Plato handed it down both in previous sections (as in the place cited and in the book immediately preceding, and at III. 2. 5. page 259 C) and we shall touch upon it below, for example, at page 547 and page 559. Regarding the question of this book, it suffices to preface these points: Alcinous, in *On the Doctrines of Plato*, chapter 9, page 474 (Heinsius edition): "For it does not please most of the followers of Plato that there are Ideas of artifacts, such as a shield or a lyre; nor of things contrary to nature, such as fever and cholera; nor of individuals, such as Socrates and Plato; nor even of any trivial things, such as filth and chaff; nor of relative things, such as the 'greater' and the 'surpassing'; for Ideas are the eternal and self-perfect thoughts of God." The arguments of Syrianus in *Aristotle's Metaphysics*, Book XII, chapter 2, number 6, come down to this: those who posit Ideas say they are not of all things, because they are not of evil or shameful things, but rather these exist in nature through the privation and absence of Ideas (cf. the same author in *Metaphysics* II. 3. and see the note on Plotinus page 52 A. B., that is, in the book *On Beauty*, page 175 in the special edition, and at page 259 C). Nor are there Ideas of things that behave differently at different times; nor of parts, such as a hand or a head; nor of composites, such as a "wise man"; nor of things produced from different trees growing together; nor of arts that imitate nature and pertain only to the utility of nature; nor of works that depend on the purpose of the soul. There are only Ideas of living beings and perfect substances, and of those things which contribute to the natural disposition of these substances, such as "man," and whatever is entirely perfecting, namely wisdom and virtue. (See the last chapter of the preceding book of this Ennead, page 538 A, and the note there.)

Page 996, line 4. **since—as many—reasons—and each soul to have.**] Brucker, from this passage, writes in his *Critical History of Philosophy*, Vol. II, page 401: "As many seminal reasons as the world has, so many does each individual soul possess; so many Ideas are in the divine intellect." Let him see to that himself.

->BOOK VII. ENNEAD FIVE. pages 994—997.<- ->299<-

— 7. **"The number of formative principles <note>original: *logoi*</note> will therefore be infinite, unless it turns back in circuits"**] Plotinus used a similar neuter construction above on page 36: "of the thought turning back." Lambert Bos included this under ellipses on pages 120 and 127 of Schaefer's edition. From this source come many expressions, both literal and figurative, regarding which see Schleusner in the *New Thesaurus of the Old Testament*, Vol. I, page 228, and in the *Lexicon of the New Testament* under the entry. Add also Clement of Alexandria, *Miscellanies* <note>original: *Stromata*</note>, Book II, page 507, Potter edition: "having rejected the **turning back** <note>original: *anakampsei*</note> toward the husband." Properly speaking, those who return from the finish line to the starting stalls in a race are said to "turn back" <note>original: *anakamptein*</note>, as noted by Jacobs regarding Palladas's *Epigrams*, XLVII. 4, in the *Greek Anthology*, Vol. X, page 228. Hence Johannes Laurentius Lydus, *On the Months*, regarding March, page 81 and page 198 of Roether's edition: "Dionysus, because of whom there is the turning-post <note>original: *nyssa* or *kampter*</note> and the circling of time." I will omit for now what I have argued elsewhere regarding this passage. Plato says in the *Phaedo*, page 72b: **"For if one set of things did not always give back in turn to the others as they come into being, as if moving in a circle, but instead generation were a straight line from one thing only into its opposite, and did not turn back again to the other, nor make a turn, you know that all things in the end would have the same form, and experience the same fate, and cease coming into being."** The next annotation will indicate the other passage of Plato which Plotinus had in mind here. Aristotle, *Metaphysics*, Book I, chapter 2, page 30 Sylburg edition, page 38 Brandis: **"—therefore those things do not turn back into one another, nor does a boy come from a man. For that which is becoming does not come from the process of becoming, but after the process. For in this way day comes from the morning, because it follows it; therefore the morning does not come from the day. But the other kind of things do turn back; and in both cases it is impossible to go on to infinity. For among those things that have intermediates, there must be an end, and those others turn back into one another; for the destruction of one is the generation of the other,"** etc. Philo the Jew, *On the Incorruptibility of the World*, page 493 Mangey edition: **"For nature has produced the ages of life as certain steps"** (where I do not see why Mangey wishes to read "devised") **"through which a human being in a certain way ascends and descends. He ascends while growing, and descends in his decline. The boundary of the highest steps is the prime of life, which once a person reaches, he no longer goes forward, but like those running the double-course race, they turn back along the same path, giving back in weak old age whatever they received from vigorous youth,"** where one must either read "gives back" with Mangey, or conclude that "turns back" fell out of the text after "giving back." The same author in the same work: **"having touched the furthest surface, it turns back again."** Pseudo-Aristotle, *On the Universe*, IV. 14, page 116 Kapp edition: **"Of the winds, some blow straight forward, while others are 'back-blowing' <note>original: *anakampsipnooi*</note>, such as the one called Caecias."** Apuleius, *On the Universe*, page 722, page 314 of Bosscha's edition: **"Those winds are considered 'out-runners' which blow directly; *reflabri* [back-blowing] are reciprocal: as *Caecias* is thought to be:"** where Salmasius certainly ought not to have been troubled by the word *reflabri*, since by it the Latin philosopher had to express that Greek term *anakampsipnooi*. I also wish that the very learned Dutch editor had not omitted that word from the Grammatical Index of Latin speech. I judge these remarks suffice to clarify the logic and meaning of Plotinus's reasoning in this place.—In what follows: **"whenever these things are given back"** <note>original: *apodidōtai*</note> is less remarkable, since the force of this verb, and even more so its compound "to give back in turn" <note>original: *antapodidonai*</note>, has been explained by Wyttenbach on Julian's *Oration I*, page 57 and page 210 of the Leipzig edition, and on the *Phaedo*, page 179; likewise by Heindorf on the *Theaetetus*, page 398.

Page 997, 1. **"But different production must come from different formative principles."**] In this place, one must either supply the verb "to be" <note>original: *einai*</note> in thought, or interpose it between "production" and "from." **"And the whole circuit contains all the formative principles."** Without doubt, Plotinus is referring to the passage in Plato's *Republic*, Book VIII, page 546 (page 381 Bekker), in the explaining of which both ancients and moderns have toiled—to say nothing of the discord that divides the rest of the philosophers in defining the "Great Year" <note>original: *magni animi ambitu* - likely referring to the Great Cycle</note>; regarding which see Huet on Origen's *Commentary on Genesis*, Vol. II, page 18, Rue edition; Davies and Moser on Cicero's *On the Nature of the Gods*, II. 20, page 284 of the larger edition, page 110 of the smaller; Fabricius on Sextus Empiricus, *Against the Mathematicians*, V. 105, page 355; Ast on the previously cited passage of Plato in his *Commentary*, page 580; Synesius, *On Providence*, page 127, below Petavius; and what Thomas Taylor recently argued regarding this passage of Synesius at the end of the book *Select Works of Plotinus*, pages 592—600. It suffices to have cited these, since the enumeration of the years themselves contributes nothing to the understanding of our passage.

— 12. **"But that [it is] not because it is one in appearance"**] Ficinus might seem to have read "that it might not only be one in appearance." I have withheld my hand from changing it, but soon, following the lead of the manuscripts, I interposed the article "the" <note>original: *to*</note> between "the male" and "most." Then, instead of "or the other," the same Marsilio [Ficino] seems to have read "or of the other." In what follows, it is singular that this preposition [para] has a clearly different force in "contrary to nature" <note>original: *para tēn physin*</note> and in "alongside the matter" <note>original: *para tēn hylēn*</note>. pertains to <note>original: "οἱ δὲ ἐν ἄλλῃ χώρᾳ πῶς διάφοροι;"</note> "how do those in another region differ?" cf. Aristotle, *On the Generation of Animals* IV. 2. page 277. Regarding the astrological causes, which many indeed established, see Ptolemy in the *Tetrabiblos* book IV. page 190. Basel edition, to which an anonymous interpreter adds on page 159: "we shall know the quantity (of children) from the nature of the zodiac signs. For being in 'double-bodied' or <term>many-seeded<gloss>original: πολυσπέρμοις</gloss></term> signs, they give either two or even more. But in single signs, they will produce one child." Truly, if the planets which promise offspring (such as Venus) are in "double-bodied" signs of the Zodiac (such as Pisces) or in fertile signs, they bestow twin and more numerous offspring. — Moreover, just as in this place certain celestial animals are called <term>many-seeded<gloss>original: πολύσπερμα</gloss></term>, so Aristotle (*On the Generation of Animals* I. 18. page 183 at the end, and elsewhere) calls smaller land animals <term>prolific<gloss>original: πολυγόνα</gloss></term>: and larger ones, <term>few-bearing<gloss>original: ὀλιγοτόκα</gloss></term>. For the former, he elsewhere uses (as on page 109 at the beginning) <term>prolific<gloss>original: πολυτόκα</gloss></term>, which Plotinus himself uses, except that in the edition it was incorrectly written as <note>original: "πολύτοκα"</note> "much-bearing" <note>The commentator is noting a subtle accentuation error in the Greek text</note>.

Page 999, 1. <note>original: "Καὶ εἰ μὲν ἡ ποίησις ἔχει τὸ εἰκῇ τοῦ ὁποσαοῦν"</note> "And if indeed the making has the randomness of any number whatsoever." Thus I have written with the good manuscripts instead of <note>original: "ὁπωσοῦν"</note> "in any way," moved by those things which Plotinus immediately subjoins.

— 3. <note>original: "ἐξελίξει καὶ ἀναπλώσει"</note> "by unfolding and spreading out." Regarding the verb <note>original: "ἀναπλοῦν"</note> "to spread out," it was discussed by us in the notes to Proclus' *On the Alcibiades* I, page 230: but this passage of Plotinus, which has the nouns of similar meaning joined together, ought to be recorded in the Lexicons.

— 6. <note>original: "ἐπὶ τῶν ἄλλων ζώων ἐφ' ὧν πλῆθος ἐκ μιᾶς γενέσεως"</note> "in the case of other animals in which there is a multitude from a single birth." Aristotle, *On the Generation of Animals* I. 18: "furthermore, from one union some animals beget many." The same author, or whoever the author of that tenth book may be, in *History of Animals* X. 3. page 503. Schneider edition: — "as many of the animals as bring forth many from one mating, and the birth of twins when it happens from one." The same author a little later: "furthermore, if many come from one mating, which (so Schneider with Leonicus and Camotius, approved by Sylburg, instead of 'as if') appears to happen in the case of swine and sometimes twins." (So Schneider from conjecture, page 460. E. F.: "whenever, therefore, from one meeting and one seed, twin offspring are born, or even as in other animals, very many.") From this, the meaning of these words is understood: <term>mating<gloss>original: ὀχεία</gloss></term> or <term>intercourse<gloss>original: συνουσία</gloss></term> or <term>meeting<gloss>original: σύνοδος</gloss></term> (*the business of parents, procreation*, and sometimes even *birth* <note>original: "γένεσις"</note>. Cf. also Wyttenbach on Plutarch's *On the Education of Children*, page 68.) then <term>birth<gloss>original: γένεσις</gloss></term>, *the rising of the one being born*, then <term>the offspring<gloss>original: τὰ γεννήματα</gloss></term>, *progeny*; Therefore, in this place, for "multitude," think of "offspring."

is free; it, viewed properly by itself, escapes even the intellect itself. Remaining within, as if in a forever hidden dwelling, it cannot be known except by degrees. However, it willed its essence to be made manifest through three goods, located as if on the threshold of that dwelling. These are the three intelligible monads <note>original: *νοηταί* (noētai); "monads" here refers to primary units or principles</note>: *truth* <note>original: *ἡ ἀλήθεια* (hē alētheia)</note>, *beauty* <note>original: *ἡ καλλονὴ* (hē kallonē)</note>, and *proportion* <note>original: *ἡ συμμετρία* (hē symmetria); often translated as symmetry or harmony</note>. See Plato’s *Philebus*, from which this doctrine is chiefly drawn, page 64, following page 219, following, Stallbaum edition. No one has extracted Plato's doctrine from his own writings more diligently, arranged it more elegantly, or recommended it more eloquently than my dear Heusde, a most distinguished man, in the first part of the book entitled: *Elements of Platonic Philosophy*, page 187, following. The philosophers who followed thereafter vied with one another in touching upon this doctrine of intelligible beauty, so that it would be an endless task to enumerate them individually. Therefore, I shall taste of only a very few. Thus, to use this example, Plutarch, in his *Platonic Questions*, had before his eyes that part of Diotima’s speech which I mentioned above, page 1002, page 81, Wyttenbach edition. Longinus likewise, and others who have taught concerning the sublime and the beautiful, borrowed not a few things from Plato’s dialogues. Furthermore, Proclus of Lycia had published a specific book concerning those three monads, as he himself records in his *Commentaries on Plato’s Republic*, page 433. Today that writing is lost. Nevertheless, what that philosopher’s opinion on beauty was can be understood both from other sources and from his books on *Plato’s Theology* (I. 24. page 59. following; III. 8. page 150. following) and indeed especially from his *Commentary on Plato’s First Alcibiades*. Hermias also touched upon this passage concerning intelligible beauty in his commentary on *Plato’s Phaedrus*, chapter XXIII, page 112, following, Ast edition. Finally, Dionysius—he who wishes to be seen as the Areopagite—the things he declaimed concerning beauty, both general and intelligible (in *On the Divine Names*, chapter IV, pages 558—561, Corderius edition), those, like all the rest of that man’s work, were taken from the books of the Platonists. How greatly the Church Fathers celebrated this doctrine is shown by the more extensive commentary which we added to the Heidelberg edition of Ennead I, book six, *On Beauty*. Among more recent philosophers who have commented on the beautiful, such as Marcus Antonius Natta and many others, and in our own memory Kant and others—including Herder himself in *Kalligone*—they have looked back to Plato’s writings; but of these books of Plotinus, if you perhaps except Ficino and Schelling, as far as I know, no one has done so to any great extent.

pages 1001, 2. **not of any man—but art**] These words remind one of Cicero’s narrative in *On Invention* II. 1. concerning the painter Zeuxis, who, when he was ordered by the people of Croton to paint a Helen, selected the most beautiful parts from the most beautiful maidens; for, as Tully <note>A common historical nickname for Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> adds, he did not think he could find everything he sought for grace in a single body; and for that reason, nature has polished nothing that is perfect in all its parts within a single kind. Therefore, as if she would not have anything to bestow upon the others if she granted everything to one, she rewards one with one advantage, while attaching some disadvantage. Pliny records that this happened at Agrigentum (*Natural History* XXXV. 9. 36), while Aelian says Heraclea. However, others side with Cicero, whom Sillig praises in the *Catalogue of Artists*, page 462, following, who should be consulted on this matter. Also most worthy of being read are the subtle arguments on this matter by the man of elegant judgment, Emeric-David, in the *Universal Biography* Vol. LII, page 308, following. Beware, however, of thinking that Plotinus persuaded himself that the most excellent works of art are produced in this way. Not even Tully had persuaded himself of this, as is understood from the excellent passage in the *Orator*, chapter 2, which we shall touch upon at the end of this chapter. Consult also the arguments of our Herder in that most excellent work *Kalligone* III, page 194. Furthermore, in the choice of the example by which Plotinus joined the Muse to Grace, if you wish to apply that line of Euripides, you would recognize "the sweetest union" <note>original: *ἥδισταν συζυγίαν* (hēdistan syzygian)</note>.

See what I have brought together on this matter above in the book on beauty, page 52. A. Regarding what follows concerning *imitation*, Plato should be consulted in *Republic* X, page 597, following, page 471, following, Bekker edition. ...and [Dionysius] likened them to similar men. <note>original: σιος δὲ ὁμοίους εἴκαζε</note> Compare what Pliny relates in his *Natural History* (Book 34, chapter 9, page 654, Harduin edition) concerning Clearchus: "he made noble men even nobler." In contrast, that same Dionysius, according to Pliny’s testimony (Book 35, chapter 37, beginning), was called the "Painter of Men" <note>original: Anthropographus; a term implying he painted people exactly as they were, warts and all, rather than idealizing them.</note>. Plutarch addresses a third type in *On the Difference Between a Flatterer and a Friend* (page 53. D., page 203 in Wyttenbach’s edition): "But just as poor painters, being unable through weakness to attain to beauty, bring out a likeness through wrinkles, moles, and scars..." <note>original: ἀλλ' ὥσπερ οἱ φαῦλοι ζωγράφοι... κ. τ. λ.</note> On this argument, one should consult Lessing in *Laocoon* (page 10 and following), Winckelmann in his *History of Ancient Art* (page 589, Vienna edition), and Herder in *Kalligone* (page 196 and following). For the understanding of this entire chapter, these words of Plato in the *Timaeus* (page 28 and following, page 23 and following in Bekker’s edition) are relevant, where the philosopher speaks thus of the Maker of the World: "This then we must consider again concerning him: according to which of the models did the artisan fashion the world? Was it according to that which is always the same and unchanging, or according to that which has come into existence? If this world is indeed beautiful and its demiurge good, it is clear that he looked toward the eternal..." <note>original: τόδε δ' οὖν πάλιν ἐπισκεπτέον... κ. τ. λ.</note> Plotinus disputes this same opinion elsewhere, such as on page 175 and following, page 260 B, and page 406 E.

Page 1002, line 9. "Then Phidias, having created his Zeus according to nothing perceived by the senses, but having grasped what he would be like [if he were to appear to us]..." <note>original: ἔπειτα ὁ Φειδίας τὸν Δία... κ. τ. λ.</note> All our books agree on this reading, which serves as evidence that deep-seated wounds <note>A metaphor for textual corruptions or errors in the manuscript tradition.</note> lie hidden in these *Enneads*, provided that the great Hemsterhuis saw the truth. In his notes on Lucian’s *The Dream* (Section 8, page 11 Amsterdam edition, page 9 Bipontine), he wrote: "The same thought is in Seneca, *Controversies* (Book 5, chapter 34, page 387): *Phidias did not see Jupiter, yet his mind, worthy of that art, both conceived the gods and exhibited them.* <note>original: ἔδειξε</note> Very similar is that passage of Plotinus: 'Then Phidias (read: *fashioned*) Zeus, not by making him according to anything sensible, but by grasping (it seems altogether necessary to add: *in his mind*) what he would be like—if he were to appear.'" These are the words of Hemsterhuis. However, we have not dared to receive either reading into the main text without the authority of the manuscripts, despite them being worthy of such a great man. According to that emendation, it should be translated: *Phidias fashioned Jupiter not so that he produced him according to something sensible, but so that he might conceive in his mind what he was to be,* etc. This last part agrees with Plato’s words in the *Timaeus* (page 29 A): "Thus having been born according to that which is graspable by reason and wisdom, and which stays the same, it has been fashioned." In a similar argument, the same author (in the *Phaedo*, page 75 b.) uses the phrase "to grasp the knowledge of Equality itself." <note>original: λαβεῖν ἐπιστήμην αὐτοῦ τοῦ ἴσου</note> It is truly remarkable how much these Plotinian thoughts agree with these words of Cicero in *The Orator* (Book 2, sections 8 and 9): "But I maintain this: that there is nothing in any genre so beautiful that there is not something even more beautiful from which it is expressed, as an image is from a face; which can be perceived neither by the eyes, nor the ears, nor any sense: we embrace it only by thought and the mind.—Nor did that artist (Phidias), when he was making the form of Jupiter or Minerva, contemplate anyone from whom he might draw a likeness; but there resided in his own mind a certain extraordinary species of beauty, which he gazed upon, and fixed upon it, he directed his art and hand toward its likeness." Hemsterhuis collected other examples in the place cited, in which he doubts the reading of Propertius (Book 3, chapter 7, line 15); Sillig, in the *Catalogue of Artists* (page 342), orders it to be corrected thus:
"With a Phidian statue <note>reading *Phidiaco* for *Phidiacus*</note> of ivory, Jupiter adorns himself."
Because that same author mentions the Homeric verses from which Phidias drew the appearance of his Jupiter (*Iliad* 1. 528), I recently touched upon the same matter in the German version of Stuart’s *Antiquities of Athens* (Vol. I, page 549). Finally, because Hemsterhuis praises these words of Suidas (in *James the Physician*, Vol. II, page 88, Kuster edition): "So also Phidias created while inspired, and so Zeuxis likened his statues [to the ideal]"; that reminds me of Themistius, who in a recently discovered oration *On the Prefecture* also joins Zeuxis to Phidias (page 40, Milan edition): "I have admired Phidias for the Zeus of Pisa; and Polygnotus for the Hall; and Myron for a single heifer. How many more are the works of Pason than those of Zeuxis or Apelles? Who then does not prefer one small tablet of those two men to all the art of Pason together?" To which Angelo Mai notes: "Jupiter of Pisa is also called the Olympian. See Pliny, *Natural History* 34. 19. Themistius in Oration 16 (page 202 B) writes *Pissaeo* but here *Piseos*." You might also use *Pisas* or *Pisatidos*, unless you prefer *Pisaiei* from Stephanus of Byzantium under that entry. See our *Meletemata* (Vol. I, page 19, note 13). Then Mai says: "Aristotle also prefers the paintings of Polygnotus to those of *Pason or Pauson* in *Politics* (Book 8, chapter 5) and *Poetics* (chapter 2)." But in Aristotle’s *Politics*, *Pauson* was long ago restored for *Pason* (see Goettling’s Annotations, page 457) and likewise in the *Metaphysics* (Book 8, chapter 9, page 187, Brandis edition) *Pauson* for *Passon*; so that henceforth...

It seems it should be restored to Themistius, unless you prefer to decide that he sought a play on words between "all" and "the art of Pason" <note>original: πᾶσαν—Πάσωνος τέχνην</note>, and for that reason preferred this writing in the manner of the Sophists, who even delight in such things, like that in Plato’s *Symposium* page 185: "Pausanias having paused" <note>original: Παυσανίου δὲ παυσαμένου</note>. page 1003, line 1. **"or something—the surrounding—like matter?"** <note>original: ἤ τι—τὸ περιέχον—οἷα ὕλη;</note>] I have written it thus with the Vatican manuscript instead of "or what—matter." For after Plotinus had asked what is beautiful in natural bodies: he now poses the opposite question, what is deformed in them. Moreover, this passage is connected with the passages concerning matter <term>hyle: the underlying "stuff" of the universe which Plotinus often views as the source of evil or lack of form</term> and concerning the model or idea <note>original: περὶ παραδείγματος ἢ περὶ εἴδους</note>. F. Xenophon in *Symposium* III. 9: "poverty is least of all much-fought-over." See Sturz’s *Xenophon Lexicon* III. page 523. Jupiter made her nature conspicuous and much-fought-over." Isocrates page 211. C. (in the *Encomium of Helen* 9. page 342. Lange’s edition, page 209. Coray’s). Yet I would not believe that that man, if he had remembered our passage, would have recognized an imitation of the Isocratean passage in this Plotinian one. Furthermore, just as to Venus, so to Helen, whom the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> worshipped with divine honors, they attributed this power: that they made women beautiful. You have examples collected in our *Herodotean Commentaries* (on Herodotus VI. 61.) page 269.

"seeing they would have used" <note>original: ὁρῶντες ἂν ἐχρήσαντο ἂν</note> that is, if they saw. Regarding this use of the particle *an* with a participle see Matthiae’s *Greek Grammar* Section 598 and Section 600, and on the repeated *an* see above page 96. A. and compare what is read below on page 556. A: "fleeing upward to the beauties of the soul, virtues and sciences and occupations;" certainly all drawn from the classic passage of Plato’s *Symposium* page 210. page 443. Bekker edition. Iamblichus, *On the Life of Pythagoras* V. 21. page 52. **ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

*καλῶς ἐστὲ ἄξιοι τυγχάνειν διὰ τὰς αὐτῶν ἀκολασίας, ἐμβαλλόμενοι ῥύπον ἐν ζωὰν ἐλευθέρων παίδων* [“You are rightly worthy to meet with these things on account of your own excesses, casting filth into the life of freeborn children”]. These words agree marvelously with those which Pausanias indignantly laments in Plato’s *Symposium*, p. [pagina: page] 181 at the end and 182 a. Cf. [Confer: Compare] also Fronto, *Greek Epistles*, p. 380, and especially p. 392 of the *editio princeps* [first edition] of Milan.

**p. 1004, 18. Ἔστιν οὖν]** The following words have the same source as that which we just indicated; namely, in Diotima’s speech, *Symposium* p. 210 sq. [sequenti: following].

**p. 1005, 10. ἀλλ' οἷον χρυσοῦ—καὶ εἰ μὴ καθαρός]** Plotinus employed the same simile on p. 54 F. G: *καὶ ἔστι τοῦτο αἶσχος ψυχῇ, μὴ καθαρᾷ μηδὲ εἰλικρινεῖ εἶναι, ὥσπερ χρυσῷ, ἀναπεπλῆσθαι δὲ τοῦ γεώδους, ὃ εἴ τις ἀφέλοι, καταλείπειται χρυσὸς, καὶ ἔστι καλὸς, μονούμενος μὲν τῶν ἄλλων, αὐτῷ δὲ συνὼν μόνῳ* [“And this is a disgrace for a soul, not to be pure or unmixed, just as for gold, but to be filled with earthy matter, which if one were to remove, gold is left behind, and it is beautiful when isolated from other things and existing alone with itself”]; where we have indicated the sources and variations of this comparison. Presently: *καὶ τὸ κάλλος αὐτῶν ἀμήχανον*, Plato *Symposium* p. 218 end; p. 459 Bekk. [Bekker edition]: *ἀμήχανόν τι κάλλος ὁρῴης ἂν ἐν ἐμοὶ καὶ τῆς παρὰ σοὶ εὐμορφίας πάμπολυ διαφέρον* [“You would see an extraordinary beauty in me, far different from the comeliness found in you”]. Conf. [Confer: Compare] our [commentary] above on I. 6. 8, p. 56 E, and the notes there.

**p. 1006, 4. οὐ γὰρ δὴ ποτὲ μὲν φρονοῦσι, ποτὲ δὲ ἀφραίνουσιν]** The Ed. [Editio: Edition] has *ἀφρονοῦσι*, but nearly all the Codices [manuscripts] together with the margin substitute the genuine reading for this interpretation [gloss]. Using the aid of Dion Chrysostom (Vol. II p. 80 Reisk. [Reiske edition]), Jacobs applied the same remedy to Themistius *Orat.* XXIV p. 307 C regarding Phocylides in *Antholog. Gr.* I. 2. p. 196, replacing *Νίνου ἀφρονοῦσης* with *ἀφραινούσης*; and another gnomic poet, Theognis, in Stobaeus XXXVII p. 145, uses that participle. The verb was already used by Homer in *Iliad* II. 258 and VII. 109: *Αφραίνεις, Μενέλαε* [“You are acting foolishly, Menelaus”], which passage—to touch upon this in passing—Nonnus not only imitated in *Dionysiaca* XX. 397: *Αφραίνεις, Λυκόοργε*, but writers also praise it here and there, such as Lucian *Symposium* § 12 p. 426 Wetst. [Wetstein edition] and Plutarch *On Distinguishing a Flatterer* p. 55. For Plotinus, another passage of Plutarch is relevant, *On Stoic Self-Contradictions* p. 1037 D; p. 227 Wytt. [Wyttenbach edition]: *ὁ γὰρ μὴ δυνάμενος σωφρονεῖν ἄνθρωπος, οὐ δύναται μὴ ἀκολασταίνειν· καὶ ὁ μὴ δυνάμενος φρονεῖν οὐ δύναται μὴ ἀφραίνειν* [“For the man who is unable to be temperate is unable not to be licentious; and he who is unable to be wise is unable not to act foolishly”]. The same in the same work, p. 1048 E; p. 274 Wytt.: *τί οὖν περὶ τῶν ἄλλων φρονοῦσιν ἢ ταῦτα ἅπερ λέγουσι; μαίνεσθαι πάντας, ἀφραίνειν, ἀνοσίους εἶναι παρανόμους κ.τ.λ.* [“What then do they think about others except these things which they say? That all are mad, act foolishly, are unholy and lawless, etc.”]. Similarly Clement of Alexandria, *Protrepticus* p. 3 beginning, Potter [Potter edition], calls those celebrating the Bacchanalia *ἀφραίνοντας ἐκτόπως* [acting strangely foolish] with a *θιάσῳ μαινάλῃ* [raving troupe] (or rather *μαινόλῃ*). Theodoret in the *Encomium on the Birth of John the Baptist*, Vol. V p. 93 Schulz [Schulz edition]: *'Αλλὰ γὰρ ἐπεὶ λοιπὸν καὶ ὁ ἀποτεταγμένος καιρὸς τῆς τοῦ τηλικούτου γεννήσεως (l. γενέσεως) ἧκε, καὶ ὁ γλυκὺς οὗτος φόρτος τὰς ὠδῖνας ἔλυε παραδόξως οὐ λυπούσας μᾶλλον ἢ ἀφραίνουσας, καὶ ἡδονὴν ἀῤῥήτου προξενούσας κ. τ. λ.* [“But since at last the appointed time for the birth (read *geneseōs*) of such a one came, and this sweet burden released the pangs, paradoxically not causing pain so much as causing a loss of sense, and procuring an unspeakable pleasure, etc.”], where Garnerius, I know not how, wants to write *ἀφρενούσας*. He ought to have written *εὐφραίνουσας* [gladdening], but to wish to prove that would be tedious. Rather I will give notice of the Lexicographer in Bekker’s *Anecdota Graeca* I. p. 472: *'Αφραίνει· παρανομεῖ, μωραίνει, παραφρονεῖ* [“Acts foolishly: transgresses the law, acts like a fool, is out of his mind”]. You might read: *παροινεῖ* [acts like a drunkard]. For Clement, in the place cited, a little before had called those same people *παροινοῦντας* whom he calls *ἀφραίνοντας*. But it is nevertheless gentler to correct to *παρανοεῖ* from Hesychius, who has: *'Αφραινούντι· παρανοούντι*. Perhaps also nothing should be changed if one considers those Stoics of Plutarch in the place cited, subjoining *παρανόμους εἶναι* to the verb *ἀφραίνειν*. Add these things in Stobaeus *Eclogae* I. 7. p. 192 Heer [Heeren edition]: *ἁμαρτήματα δὲ εἶναι τό, τε ἀφραίνειν, καὶ τὸ ἀκολασταίνειν, καὶ τὸ ἀδικεῖν* [“acts of acting foolishly, being licentious, and acting unjustly are sins”].

**— 7. Τῶν δὲ θεῶν οἱ μὲν ἐν οὐρανῷ ὄντες—to the end of the chapter]** It cannot be doubted that Plotinus has before his eyes that most noble passage of Plato found in the *Phaedrus* p. 246 end: *—τῷ δὲ (Διΐ) ἕπεται στρατιὰ θεῶν κ. τ. λ.* [“and he (Zeus) is followed by an army of gods, etc.”]. The kinds and classes of gods, about which the Platonic philosophers dispute much, you may see arranged in a table which we exhibited from a manuscript Codex for Olympiodorus *On the Alcibiades*, preceding page 20.

**— 16. Καὶ γὰρ τὸ ῥεῖα ζώειν κ. τ. λ.]** The source of this entire passage is in Plato’s *Philebus* p. 61; p. 241 where a twofold knowledge is explained, but especially in the *Phaedrus* p. 247; p. 42 sq. Bekk. (where Stallbaum p. 206 and Ast p. 304 have not forgotten Plotinus. Many things are read concerning the passage in the *Phaedrus* in Hermias’ *Commentary* p. 142—146). Add a third passage from the *Symposium* p. 211; p. 444 Bekk. (with which compare Cicero *Orator* III, and Dionysius the Pseudo-Areopagite who presented those things word for word in *On the Divine Names* IV. 7. p. 559); finally a fourth in the so-called *Epistles* of Plato VII p. 342 sq.

**p. 1007, 9. ἔστι δὲ καὶ κίνησις καθαρὰ—καὶ ἡ στάσις—τῷ μὴ στασίμῳ]** Dionysius the Areopagite, in the place cited p. 560 sq.: *στάσις γάρ ἐστι πᾶσι καὶ κίνησις τὸ* [for there is rest and motion for all things...]

**BOOK VIII. ENNEAD V. p. 1004—1009.**

*ὑπὲρ πᾶσαν στάσιν καὶ πᾶσαν κίνησιν, ἐνιδρύον ἕκαστον ἐν τῷ ἑαυτοῦ λόγῳ, καὶ κινοῦν ἐπὶ τὴν οἰκείαν κίνησιν* [...that which is beyond all rest and all motion, establishing each thing in its own principle, and moving it toward its proper motion]. For thus this passage must be punctuated so that a sound meaning may exist.

**p. 1008, 3. οἷον εἴ τις γένοιτο τὴν ὄψιν τοιοῦτος, οἷος ὁ Λυγγεὺς ἐλέγετο, καὶ τὰ εἴσω τῆς γῆς ὁρᾷν]** I have established this passage from the best books and the margin. Regarding the words *καὶ—ὁρᾷν*, think of either *ὥστε* [so as], or from the preceding: *ὃς (καὶ) ἐλέγετο* [who was (also) said]. For thus it agrees with Plotinian brevity. I did not dare to change *Λυγγεὺς* [Lyngues] without the authority of the books, although I know it is commonly done otherwise. For I think this is a spelling of a later age rather than a negligence of scribes. Moreover, see concerning this diversity of interpretations on Hyginus *fab.* 168 p. 284; Heyne on Apollodorus p. 109; Fischer on Palaephatus p. 58; Jacobs on the *Palatine Anthology* p. 91 and p. 1042 and on Philostratus’ *Imagines* p. 75 (p. 479); Gaisford on Proclus’ *Chrestomathy* p. 473 (where some books have the faulty *Λυγεὺς* and *Λυγέως*). Recently Boissonade, in *Notices et Extraits* XI. 2. p. 190, thought *λύγκουρον* should be restored for Psellus instead of *λιγγούριον*. Yet *λυγγούριον* and indeed *λιγγούριον* could be tolerated if you listen to Schneider and the interpreters of Sextus Empiricus p. 39 and p. 209 Fabricius. It is to be judged differently in words where the etymology rejects the other spelling, as *Σύγγελλος* for *Σύγκελλος*. See Du Cange *Glossarium mediae et infimae Graecitatis* p. 629; cf. [confer: compare] p. 1471. [cf. Meursius’ *Glossarium Graecobarbarum* on this word]. It is unique that in Cleomedes p. 84 of Bak’s Manuscripts, some books offered *γλυκὺς* instead of *Λυγκεύς*. As far as I know, Tib. Hemsterhuys alone made mention of our passage on Lucian’s *Timon* p. 138 Amsterdam; p. 389 Bipont. This fable is frequently used in the writings of philosophers. Thus, to use this [example], Plutarch p. 87 b; p. 335 Wytt.; likewise p. 1083; p. 422 Wytt., with which should be compared Nazarius in the *Panegyric on Constantine* XI. 5. p. 34 Jaeger. Porphyry *On Abstinence* III. 8. p. 234 Rhoer: *τίς μὲν γὰρ ἀνθρώπων τοσοῦτον βλέπει (οὐδὲ γὰρ ὁ μυθευόμενος Λυγκεὺς,* where the Meermann Codex has *Λυγγεὺς*, which Rhoerius curses, who correctly gave the common spelling from other Codices) *ὅσον ὁ δράκων;* [“For what man sees as much—not even the fabled Lynceus—as the serpent?”]. Olympiodorus on Plato’s *Phaedo* in Wyttenbach p. 202: *καθὸ ὁ Λυγγεὺς ἑώρα τὰ πόῤῥω* [“just as Lyngues saw things far off”], which Wyttenbach correctly left untouched. Iamblichus in *Protrepticus* cap. [caput: chapter] VIII p. 52 Arcerius; p. 132 sqq. Kiessling: *ἰσχύς τε γὰρ καὶ μέγεθος καὶ κάλλος γέλως ἐστὶ καὶ οὐδενὸς ἄξια, κάλλος τε παρὰ τὸ μηδὲν ὁρᾷν* (this word Kiessling added from Ciz. [Cizensis Codex]; it is also recognized by the Memm. Codex in my notes) *ἀκριβὲς δοκεῖ εἶναι τοιοῦτον (τὸ τοιοῦτον* one MS book) *εἰ γάρ τις* (missing *τις* in many books) *ἐδύνατο βλέπειν (ὀξὺ* from the Ciz. Kiessling: *πῶς ἂν* by conjecture) *ἔδοξεν εἶναί τινα (this* is absent from the Royal Codex) *ἀνεκτὸν ὁρῶν, ἐξ οἵων συνέστηκε κακῶν;* [“For strength and stature and beauty are a joke and worth nothing, and beauty seems to be such only because of seeing nothing clearly; for if anyone were able to see sharply as they say Lynceus did, who saw through walls and trees, how could he ever have thought anyone tolerable to look at, seeing from what evils he is composed?”]. Apuleius *Metamorphoses* II. 36. p. 146 Oudendorp: “You see a man of iron and sleepless, certainly more perspicacious than Lynceus himself (many books *Lynce*, not badly in the judgment of Oudendorp) or Argus, and all eye.” Themistius *Oratio* VII p. 92: “but they appeared everywhere, or rather scouts were always present with them, eavesdroppers, having more eyes than Argus, sharper-sighted than Lynceus.” Philo Judaeus in Eusebius *P. E.* [Præparatio Evangelica] VIII. 14. p. 387 (in the Armenian version p. 55 Venice ed. Recently a learned young man, J. E. G. **ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

*θείου νόμου τιμωρός* [...divine law]. Interpreters have applied this passage, frequented by Clement in *Stromata* II p. 499 Potter and others, to Sophocles. See Markland and Doederlein on the Sophocles passage cited; Potter on the Clement passage; and as far as mythological matters are concerned, our *Symbolica* II p. 506 sq. of the second edition.

**p. 1009, 4. οἷον ἀγάλματα]** I explained the force and varied use of this Platonic word above on p. 57 D (and on the book *On Beauty* p. 369 Heidelberg ed.). Cf. also p. 465 C and p. 520 F. — Presently, the words *θέαμα—θεατῶν* were no less borrowed from Plato by Plotinus. For he, in the *Phaedo* p. 113; p. 111 Bekk., has it thus: *θέαμα εὐδαιμόνων θεατῶν* [“a spectacle of happy spectators”], regarding which Wyttenbach p. 308 suspects that our Plotinus, in the cited passage of Plato, if he did not read, at least thought *ὑπερευδαιμόνων* [excessively happy], and that this appears from the passage of this book p. 547 B (cap. seq. [caput sequenti: following chapter]); where likewise it is *ὑπερευδαίμονας*. Cf. the same author’s *Philomathia* III p. 106.

**— 10. συμφόρησιν—προτάσεων]** Cf. above I. 3. 4 and 5 and the notes there; likewise IV. 4. 44, V. 5. 1, and VI. 8. 3.

**— 12. ἦν δὴ καὶ ὁ Πλάτων κατιδὼν φησίν, οὐδ' ἥτις ἐστὶν ἄλλη ἐν ἄλλῳ.]** In the *Phaedo* p. 83; p. 56 Bekk.: *ὅ τι δ' ἂν δι' ἄλλων σκοπῇ ἐν ἄλλοις ὂν ἄλλο, μηδὲν ἡγεῖσθαι ἀληθές* [“whatever he considers through other things, being another thing in others, let him consider nothing of it true”]. Regarding these words, Wyttenbach p. 219 says: *“i.e. whatever indeed he considers through other things (i.e. the corporeal through the senses of the body,) since another thing appears in other senses, let him think none of these true.”* Then he compares other passages both of Plato himself and his followers and our philosopher himself below in VI. 7. p. 727 C. To these I add a passage of Damascius, who doubtless had that sentiment of Plato before his eyes when he wrote these things *On First Principles*, Munich Codex fol. [folio] 265 rect. [recto]: “It is better therefore to abide by his distinction, according to the Pythagorean custom and that of Plato himself, who thinks of material things as 'others', and matter itself. For in the *Phaedo* he thus names the 'others', meaning the sensible forms; but also in other places; and Aristotle in the *Archytean* records also that Pythagoras called matter 'other' as being fluid and always becoming 'other and other'; so that it is clear Plato also defines 'the others' in this way.” — The words of Plotinus that follow: *ὅπως δὲ—τὴν ἀρχὴν ποιήσασθαι*, are to be held all the more because the philosopher, prevented by a singular reverence for Plato, very rarely openly confesses (which he nevertheless very often does) that he wishes to strengthen, increase, and polish the discoveries of the god of philosophers.

**p. 1011, 3] Διὸ καὶ τὰς ἰδέας ὄντα ἔλεγον εἶναι οἱ παλαιοὶ καὶ οὐσίας.]** For Plotinus, *οἱ παλαιοὶ* [the ancients] are not only the most ancient philosophers, such as Heraclitus, who had denied that those things which were composite and obvious to the senses were beings (Plato *Cratylus* p. 402 A), but also Plato and his contemporaries. And Plato’s doctrine of ideas is contained especially in the *Parmenides* (which see regarding this question) p. 130 b, 133 b, 1135 b. Cf. *Cratylus* p. 439 D. E. and consult Buttmann’s *Excursus on the Meno* III p. 74: “On abstract notions of things according to the mind of Plato.” Wyttenbach on the *Phaedo* p. 270—272 and Stallbaum’s *Prolegomena to the Philebus* p. XXII with note 5. As for Aristotle, see *Metaphysics* I. 6. coll. [collectio] XIII. 4. p. 265 Brandis, *Nicomachean Ethics* I. 4, *Eudemian Ethics* I. 8, *On Generation and Corruption* II. 3. Cf. Henr. Richter’s pamphlet *On the Ideas of Plato*, Leipzig 1827. This writer wishes to distinguish in Plato between *εἶδος* [form] and *ἰδέα* [idea], and says that the Platonic idea is the universal form of things, in which their eternal essence and nature appear. The same on p. 66 sqq. denies that in any passage of Plato ideas are called substances. For as to Plato attributing *οὐσία* [substance/essence] to ideas, this signifies nothing else according to Plato’s own opinion except that ideas are perennial (perpetual) in the intellect. He says Aristotle understood the notion of *οὐσία* differently and therefore did not everywhere correctly explain Plato’s decrees on ideas; and that the Alexandrian philosophers further propagated the opinion that ideas, which Plato called ideas, are substances. Thus says Richter. — Now first, I do not attribute much to those who think it must be inquired whether Plato placed ideas only in the divine mind, or said they exist by themselves outside the mind. Secondly, I do not offer myself as a defender for Aristotle in this cause, as one who knows that he called Plato’s ideas *τερετίσματα* i.e. musical trills or empty songs (Aristotle *Posterior Analytics* p. 228: *τὰ γὰρ εἴδη χαιρέτω· τερετίσματά γάρ ἐστι* [“Farewell to the forms: for they are trills”]. Cf. Tib. Hemsterhuys on Thomas Magister p. 908 and in *Anecdota* ed. I Geel p. 32 sq.) which the Scholiast of Aristides p. 167 Frommel thus expresses: “that there are no ideas.” Finally, I omit the Alexandrian philosophers for now.

--- Page 314 ---
**BOOK VIII. ENNEAD V. p. 1009—1012.**

Regarding Plotinus, I ask whether the word for substance has such force that the philosopher from Lycopolis must be said to have accepted ideas less incorporeally, or more corporeally (if I may use these terms for brevity’s sake) than Plato; v.c. [verbi causa: for example] as if ideas as substances have various and mutable accidents, etc. If Richter meant this, he has wandered the whole heaven from the mind of Plotinus. Just listen to these words of our author in the next book, p. 560 A: *Νοῦς μὲν δὴ ἔστω τὰ ὄντα καὶ πάντα ἐν αὐτῷ οὐχ ὡς ἐν τόπῳ ἔχων, ἀλλ' ὡς αὑτὸν ἔχων, καὶ ἓν ὢν αὐτοῖς* [“Let Intellect be the beings, and holding all things in itself not as in a place, but as holding itself, and being one with them”]. You see here that for Plotinus, mind or intellect is “the beings”; in our passage, the same is true for ideas. What do you seek? For Plotinus, ideas are neither in the mind nor outside the mind, but are the same as the mind; and this notion is most simple, and can be defined no other way than *that ideas are, and that they are the same as beings and essences.* And I judge that there was no other opinion of Plato himself. This serves as an argument that those are mistaken who think a difference intervenes between Plato’s doctrine of ideas and the Plotinian one. What? Indeed—I do not hesitate to profess that Plato’s decrees will be placed in a clearer light in some other doctrines as well, if his interpreters would wish to study Plotinus more zealously.

**— 5. Δοκοῦσι δέ μοι καὶ οἱ Αἰγυπτίων σοφοὶ κ. τ. λ.]** Plato mentions the writing of the Egyptians in the *Phaedrus* p. 274 sq. and in the *Philebus* p. 18. I have praised many others both in the commentary on Cicero’s *On the Nature of the Gods* III. 22. p. 611, and especially in the *Herodotean Commentaries* I. p. 369 sqq. Moreover, no one who has inspected the writings of the Englishman Young and the Frenchman Champollion and others is unaware that this matter has recently been debated anew by the competing studies of many (cf., to omit others, Silvestre de Sacy in *Journal des Savans* 1827 and Letronne in the Appendix to the *Précis du Système hiéroglyphique* by M. Champollion le jeune, p. 376 sqq. of the second edition). As for Plotinus, an Egyptian man, saying in this passage that the other way of writing of the Egyptians, which we commonly call alphabetical, where the sounds of the voice are represented by the strokes of letters, was not used by the Egyptian priests; this must undoubtedly be understood in such a way that he wants to be understood the books which were properly called sacred, as containing the hidden doctrine of religions. (See the third annotation after this one).

**— 7. μὴ τύποις γραμμάτων διεξοδεύουσι κ. τ. λ.]** Philo uses *διεξόδοις* in the same matter in *On the Life of Moses* I. p. 606. Hermias on Plato’s *Phaedrus* p. 103 Ast: “insofar as (the rational soul) subsists from intellect, it has the intellectual, according to which it seizes the forms by simple intuitions and not discursively (*διεξοδικῶς*)—and in the following: and it acts and reasons discursively.” I have given other examples on Proclus *On the Alcibiades* preceding page 249 and above on Plotinus p. 189 B and p. 478 D.

**— 10. ἐμφῆναι]** I recalled this from very many and the best books instead of *ἐμφῦναι*, and Diodorus Siculus III. 4 uses the expression *ἐξ ἐμφάσεως* in the same matter. — I have taken care of those things which are more hindered in the following parts of this chapter by punctuation. In the fifth line from the end, *καὶ τὸ ἐκ ζητήσεως*, I fear lest more words and perhaps some sentences have fallen out. Ficinus’ version or rather paraphrase helps the understanding of the rest. Iamblichus *On the Life of Pythagoras* V. p. 52 Kiessl. regarding Pythagoras: “he attempted to make the manner of teaching symbolic, and entirely similar to the teachings in Egypt by which (even my many MS books confirm this reading, exhibiting *καθὰ*) he was educated.” The same in *On the Mysteries* VII. 1. p. 150 Gale: “I wish first (several of my books have *δέ*) to interpret for you the manner of the Egyptians’ theology. For they (this one: Cod. Leid. [Leiden Codex]), imitating the nature of the universe and the craftsmanship of the gods, themselves also [modeled] certain images of mystical and hidden and unseen thoughts through symbols, just as nature also modeled in a certain way unseen principles through symbols in visible forms (*ἀπετυπώσατο*—the Munich codex badly has *ἀποτυπ.*).” On Hermes as the author of writing, consult Horapollo in *Hieroglyphica* I. 14.

**— 12. Ὕστερον δὲ—ἐξεύρισκον]** These are those things which were consigned also in the forms of letters called *hieratic* in the sacred commentaries of the Egyptians; whereas the books properly called sacred, i.e. those which contained the hidden doctrine of religions, were written in *hieroglyphic* characters (Plotinus calls them *ἀγάλματα* [images/statues]) (see above). A third kind of writing, pertaining to the use of common life, itself used characters of letters, not images, and was called popular (*δημοτικόν* [demotic]).

**p. 1012, 6. ἆρα οἰώμεθα]** The other reading *οἰόμεθα* could itself be confirmed by passages of Plato, as in *Gorgias*...
