**p. 1014, 2. μετεωροπορεῖ, φησὶ, καὶ πάντα τὸν κόσμον διοικεῖ]** Plato, to be sure, in the *Phaedrus* p. 246 b. c. I have treated this passage above on p. 376 G and p. 470 C; where consult the notes.

**— 5. ἡ γῆ—στρογγύλη]** Very many Socratics are said to have established the round figure of the earth, which Herodotus (IV. 36) and Aristotle (*Meteorology* II. 5. p. 55 Sylburg) had in a certain way mocked (Cleomedes *Meteor.* VIII. p. 40; p. 51 Bak [Bak edition]). That same Claudius Ptolemy defends the same opinion both in the *Μεγαλ. Συνταξ.* [Mathematical Treatise] or *Almagest* I, and in the *Geography* I. 7, VII. 5. Cf. Mannert *Geogr. Græcc. et Romm.* [Greek and Roman Geography] I. p. 144 sqq.; Uckert *Geogr. Græcc. et Romm.* I. p. 299; and Sickler’s *Enchiridion Geograph. Ant.* [Handbook of Ancient Geography] p. XLIV.) Although the authority of this man was already very great in the third century, in which Plotinus flourished, I would nevertheless believe that this philosopher followed the opinions of the old Platonists in this matter as well. — To the following: *καὶ ὁ λοξὸς* cf. the twin passage II. 9. 12. p. 211 B and the note there on the words *λοξώσις τῶν ζῳδίων* [obliquity of the zodiac].

**— 7. τοῦ συλλογισμοῦ—τὸ συμπέρασμα—τῶν προτάσεων.]** Cf. Ocellus Lucanus I. 3, Aristotle *Sophistical Refutations* I. 14. p. 444 Sylb., Quintilian *Inst. Orat.* V. 4, Ernesti *Lex. Technol. Græcorr. Rhetor.* [Lexicon of Greek Rhetorical Technology] p. 325. Add Proclus on the *Alcibiades* preceding page 303 and Olympiodorus on the same p. 99 and cf. our author himself below in VI. 7. 1. p. 693 A.

**p. 1015, 4. Διὸ καὶ Πλάτων κ. τ. λ.—and below C: εἶπε γὰρ ἠγάσθη τε—ἀφομοιοῦσαι.]** Plato in the *Timaeus* p. 37; p. 36 Bekk.: *ὡς δὲ κινηθὲν αὐτὸ καὶ ζῶν ἐνενόησε τῶν ἀϊδίων θεῶν γεγονὸς ἄγαλμα ὁ γεννήσας πατὴρ, ἠγάσθη τε καὶ εὐφρανθεὶς ἔτι δὴ μᾶλλον ὅμοιον πρὸς τὸ παράδειγμα ἐπενόησεν ἀπεργάσασθαι* [“And when the father who begat it perceived it moved and living, having become a statue of the eternal gods, he marveled and, being gladdened, thought to make it still more like the pattern”]. From which it is understood that Plotinus does not report the passage of Plato word for word. Simplicius likewise quotes it from memory in Aristotle *Phys.* IV. 166 and 265. Stobaeus also exhibits it in *Eclogae Phys.* I. 268. Cf. Lindau’s *Annott. in Plat. l. l.* [Notes on Plato in the place cited] who did not neglect our Plotinus. Presently, for *ἐνεργεστέρων* Ficinus seems to have read *ἐναργεστέρων*. The books do not vary.

**— 17. ὅθεν οὐκ ὀρθῶς οἱ μεμφόμενοι τούτῳ]** He touches upon the Gnostic Manichaeans, and others who denied that this World was beautiful and good; concerning whom we have seen above in the Annotations on the books of this argument.

**p. 1016, 6. Ἔστω οὖν ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ φωτεινή τις φαντασία κ. τ. λ.]** Again, that saying of Plato in the *Phaedo* p. 113 is observed by Plotinus in this place: *θέαμα εὐδαιμόνων θεατῶν*. See above p. 546 B. Iamblichus *Myster. Ægypt.* I. 12. p. 23: “It is clear also from the works themselves what we now say to be the savior of the soul. For in contemplating the blessed spectacles, the soul exchanges another life, etc.” to which passage Gale p. 196 [adds]: *“He calls this soul below θεοπτικήν [god-viewing] (Iamblichus).”* Then he calls upon others and this very passage of Plotinus. Clement of Alexandria *Strom.* V. p. 732 Potter: “when with a blessed choir according to Plato, we shall behold a blessed sight and vision, following with Zeus on the one hand, and others with other gods, initiated into a rite which it is right to call most blessed.” Cf. the beginning of our author’s next chapter p. 551 A.

**— 13. μετὰ πάντων τῶν ἐν αὐτῷ θεῶν, εἷς ὢν καὶ πάντες—μᾶλλον δὲ ὁ εἷς πάντες and below E:—μέγα μὲν οὖν καὶ ὅδε ὁ οὐρανὸς, καὶ αἱ ἐν αὐτῷ πᾶσαι δυνάμεις ὁμοῦ.]** A similar color to those in the *Epinomis* among the Platonic dialogues p. 977 a. b.; p. 346 Bekk.: “and which god then do I speak of even in praise, O Megillus and Clinias? Almost the heaven, which it is most just, as all other spirits and gods together, to honor and pray to exceptionally.—For if one lives for the right contemplation of this, whether he calls it the world or Olympus or heaven for the pleasure of speaking, let him speak, but let him follow wherever it presents itself, adorning it and turning the stars in it.” On one god and many at the same time, thus Damascius *On First Principles* cap. 100 p. 314 Kopp [Kopp edition]: “Why say many things? When almost all philosophers before Iamblichus assume the gods thus as many, saying that there is one supra-essential god, and that the others are essential, being deified by illuminations from the One.”

--- Page 316 ---
**BOOK VIII. ENNEAD V. p. 1012—1019.**

**p. 1017, 12. ἀλλὰ ἤδη ἀπειρία δυνάμεως ἀληθινῆς φαντάζονται καλοῦσαι, καὶ φθείρουσαι, καὶ θλίβουσαι.]** From the margin and very many books I have received *ἤδη* [already/now] instead of *εἴδη* [forms]: from two Marcian [codices] *καλοῦσαι* [calling/burning] instead of *καὶ οὖσαι*. This is because *φαντάζεσθαι* [to appear/to imagine] is in other places also contrary to *τοῦ εἶναι* [to be]. (See our note above on I. 6. 3. p. 50 B.) Likewise because the mention of fire seemed to require this, and because *θλίβουσαι* [crushing] agrees well with *καλοῦσαι*. To be sure, *φθείρουσαι* [destroying] pertains to the powers of all bodies, some of which kill by burning, others by thrusting, pressing, breaking. — In defining the force of the substantive *ἀπειρίᾳ* [infinity/inexperience], Ficinus hesitated and, as he is more often accustomed to do, expressed it in two ways. I, who believed the second meaning to be foreign to this place, [included] his words: *they consist in infinity and enclosed within the same hooks:* I did not wish to delete them in this place, any more than similar things elsewhere, lest the power of choosing be snatched away from learned readers.

**— 18. ἀπολειφθῆναι]** That which Ciz. has, *ἀποληφθῆναι*, belongs to that kind of confusion which wanders most widely through the monuments of the ancients, about which after others the most learned Hase recently also gave warning on Leo Diaconus p. 211 D. In Plato’s *Symposium* p. 220 A; p. 461 Bekk. now all the more recent editors after Ast on the *Republic* p. 543 have received *ἀποληφθέντες*; though all MS books exhibit *ἀπολειφθέντες*. One could certainly defend the latter plausibly if one wished to apply Xenophon *Mem.* I. 4. 8, *Ages.* II. 29. Judgment really depends on history, which we do not know.

**p. 1018, 6. μᾶλλον γὰρ οἰκεία ἡ καλή.]** Ficinus moreover expressed what is read in the margin of a single book, *καὶ ἡ καλλονή* [and beauty]. The rest of the books reject this addition. To the argument of this entire passage, apply the book *On Beauty* above, I. 6. 3 and 4, page 52 following, and the notes on it.

**— 7. Διὰ τοῦτο—Ζεὺς—πρῶτος πορεύεται]** It is the same celebrated passage in Plato’s *Phaedrus* p. 246 e and 247; p. 41 sqq. Bekk. so often mentioned by other philosophers and by our author himself. See v.c. [verbi causa: for example] above IV. 4. 9. p. 403 C and the praises there and p. 419 C and p. 544 C. To omit other things, which I both raised above and gathered for the passage in the *Phaedrus*, Heindorf p. 251 sqq. and Ast p. 296 sqq. and at the end of the *Republic* p. 653 sqq. As for Heindorf’s thinking that souls are also included under the name of *δαιμόνων* [demons/spirits]: in this he does not have the support of Plotinus, who expressly adds *ψυχὰς* [souls]. What follows in Plato: *ἄκραν ὑπὸ (ἐπὶ Heindf.) τὴν ὑπουράνιον (οὐράνιον Heindf.) ἀψῖδα πορεύονται πρὸς ἄναντες ἤδη* [“they travel to the summit under (upon) the sub-celestial (celestial) vault already toward the steep”]—these things made room for many disputes of the ancient interpreters, and according to Proclus in Plato’s *Theology* IV. 16. p. 215, Plato had formed for himself: “these three world-orders, the supra-celestial place, the celestial circulation, the sub-celestial vault.” Presently Plotinus himself makes mention of a certain *ἀοράτου τόπου* [invisible place]: and mention of our Plotinus is made in those same disputes about the passage in the *Phaedrus*. For thus Proclus in the place cited: “For the philosopher from Asine (namely Theodorus of Asine), being persuaded by Plotinus, called that which proceeded immediately from the unspeakable the 'sub-celestial vault', as he philosophizes about these things in the book *On Names*.” In our passage, indeed, there is expressly no mention of this *ἀψῖδος* [vault], nor elsewhere, as far as I know, in these *Enneads*; so that perhaps this testimony of Proclus may be an argument that in that other edition (*ekdosei*) of the Plotinian books (of which we have found other traces) these things were more fully explained somewhere. — I will add two passages: Philo Judaeus *On the Cherubim* Vol. II. p. 14 Pfeiffer: “the outermost vault of the entire heaven.” Stobaeus *Eclogae Phys.* I. 27. p. 550 Heer regarding the moon: “having the vault hollow.” Whence the diminutive *ἀψίδιον*; about which see Coray in *Ataktois* II. p. 77. Otherwise cf. Plotin. IV. 1. p. 360 A.

**p. 1019, 17. τοῖς δὲ διὰ παντὸς οἷον οἰνωθεῖσι καὶ πληρωθεῖσι τοῦ νέκταρος]** He borrowed the image from his Plato, both from the *Phaedrus* p. 247 end; p. 43 Bekk. and from the *Symposium* p. 203; p. 429 Bekk. That *οἰνωθεῖσι* [drunk with wine] is joined with the mention of Nectar in this place, brings to mind Apuleius *Metamorphoses* VI. 125. p. 426 sq. Oudendorp: “Then a cup of nectar, which is the wine of the gods, that rustic boy, his cupbearer, served to Jupiter, but Liber to the rest:” where I think Oudendorp should be supported, who thought the words *which... is* should be freed from suspicion of being a glossema [gloss].

--- Page 317 ---
**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

Also Lucian in *Lexiphanes* I. p. 319 Wetstein: “for you seem to be pouring out for us some nectar from it.” Moreover, what Plotinus adds, *καὶ πληρωθεῖσι* [and being filled], is not superfluous, since for the most part the Greeks want *οἰνώμενον* [one having taken wine] distinguished from *μεθύοντι* [one being drunk] (Wesseling on Diodorus I. 57. p. 67; Mangey on Philo I. p. 350). For above (following Plato in the cited passage of the *Symposium*) p. 299 A he employs *μεθύειν τῷ νέκταρι* [to be drunk with nectar], and ibid. D: “and Porus slept there, weighted down by the things with which he was filled.” Philo Judaeus *On the Planting of Noah* p. 234 a; p. 148 Pfeiffer: “Drunkenness is twofold, one equal to taking wine, the other equal to being foolish in wine.” With these passages of Plotinus, these words of Proclus in *Platonic Theology* IV. 15. p. 202 should be compared: “The nourishing cause of the gods is a certain intellectual union containing the whole perfection of the gods in itself, and filling the gods with vigor and power, both for the providence of secondary things and the unchanging intellection of primary things. But above the gods participate in these things in a unified way, but in their own progressions, in a divided way. Where indeed even of nourishment, one part is called ambrosia by Plato, the other nectar. At the manger, he says (Plato in the *Phaedrus* passage) having stood the horses, he served ambrosia, and upon it gave nectar to drink, etc.” Julian *Epistle* XXVII: “for to hear and speak always about them is nectar to me.” Which formula has attained the force of a proverb. See L. H. Heyler on that passage p. 291.

**p. 1020, 3. ἀλλ' ἔχει τὸ ὀξέως ὁρῶν ἐν αὑτῷ τὸ ὁρώμενον]** The Vatican [Codex] does not recognize the *τὸ*, and since Ficinus uses the masculine, I indeed, if a single book had added it, would have restored *ὁ ὀξέως ὁρῶν*, especially since all agree on the following *ἔχων*.

**— 7. ὥσπερ εἴ τις ὑπὸ θεοῦ κατασχεθείς, Φοι-βόληπτος ἢ ὑπό τινος Μούσης]** In Herodotus IV. 13 some MS books offer this very word instead of the Ionic *φοιβόλαμπτος*, less correctly. Longinus *On the Sublime* XVI. 2. p. 68 Weiske: regarding Demosthenes: “but when, as if suddenly inspired by a god and becoming as it were *φοιβόληπτος* [possessed by Phoebus], he uttered the oath by the champions of Greece.” Lycophron in *Cassandra* verse 1460 calls this same virgin “the Phoebus-possessed swallow,” which Tzetzes in the Scholia p. 1046 explain: “the prophetic one,” and they were called *φοιβόληπτοι* or *θεοφόρητοι* who divine by the instinct of a spirit, whether good or evil, or act in any other way not in control of their own mind. Hence it is also transferred to poets and orators, as observed by Meric Casaubon on Antoninus XII. in Gataker’s edition p. 420. As for Plotinus adding: *ἢ ὑπό τινος Μούσης (κατασχεθείς)* [or (possessed) by some Muse], he undoubtedly had before his eyes another passage of the *Phaedrus*. For thus p. 245 a; p. 37 Bekk. Plato: “the third kind is possession and madness from the Muses, which taking a tender and untouched soul, awakening and bacchically inspiring it toward songs and other poetry, etc.” The same in *Laws* VII. 790 d. e.; p. 6 Bekk.: “just as the healings of mindless bacchic revels use this combination of dance and muse in movement.” Philo Judaeus seems to have had this passage before his eyes in *Who is the Heir of Divine Things* p. 482 Mangey’s edition (See our note on Cicero *On Divination* I. 1. p. 5. Moser’s edition). Himerius *Oratio* XIII. 7. p. 596 Wernsdorf: “or as the reveler, for thus the lyre calls him, speaking of Dionysus, when spring has just first shone forth, poets possessed by the Muses conduct him crowned with spring flowers and clusters of ivy, etc.” Philo Judaeus expressed the next parts of the Platonic *Phaedrus* in *On Providence* in the Armenian and Latin version p. 77 Venice ed. (where in the Greek write *ἀφίκτηται*) and likewise Plutarch *On Moral Virtue* p. 452 B; p. 845 Wytt.: “for not only in poems, as Plato says, does the one possessed by the mouses and possessed make the craftsman and the one who is precise look ridiculous, etc.” Olympiodorus on Plato’s *Alcibiades* preceding page 2: “The second enthusiasm is in the *Republic*, where having become *μουσόληπτος* [muse-possessed] Plato acted the Muses, who in the same place in the *Timaeus* is said to be *θεόληπτος* [god-possessed]: in the *Phaedrus*: *νυμφόληπτος* [nymph-possessed].” Iamblichus accurately distinguishes various kinds of obsession (as I might call it) in *On the Mysteries* III. 5. p. 65 Gale, from which passage I will only excerpt the beginning: “There are indeed then many kinds of divine possession and in many ways divine inspiration is stirred up; whence indeed many are its signs being different.” Write *καὶ διαφέροντα*. For thus all codices, whose readings I have, show. But the whole passage should be compared with the Plotinian one.

**— 10. Εἰ δέ τις ἡμῶν ἀδυνατῶν ἑαυτὸν ὁρᾷν]** Dionysius the Areopagite seems to have had what follows before his eyes in *On Divine Names* IV. 9. p. 561: “The motion of the soul is, in a circular way, the entrance into itself away from the outside and the unified winding together of its intellectual powers, as if being turned in a certain circle toward that which is unerring and unmoved, and from the many things from without turning itself back and gathering itself first into itself then as if it were unified (read *ἑνοειδῆ*). You might even read *ἑνοειδῆ ἤδη* [already unified]) having become so, uniting itself to the powers unified in a singular way, and thus leading by the hand toward the beautiful and good, that which is above all beings, and one and the same and without beginning and without end.”

--- Page 318 ---
**BOOK VIII. ENNEAD V. p. 1020—1024.**

**p. 1021, 6. Δεῖ δὲ—γνωματεύειν αὐτὸν]** He has this word from his Plato, *Republic* VII p. 516 end; p. 330 Bekk., which passage, although Ruhnken indicated it with passages of imitators in his *Lexicon of Plato* under *Tim.* p. 72, as almost everywhere else, he here too neglected to mention Plotinus. As for the *Scholion* read in the margin of some of our Codices (see Var. Lect. [Variae Lectiones: Variant Readings]), it is taken from the *Etymologicum Magnum*, or Suidas, or Zonaras under the word. Add *Etymol. Gud.* p. 128 and at the end of Orion p. 622 and the *Scholia on Plato* p. 179 Ruhnken. Philostratus *Life of Apollonius* II. 30. p. 83 Olearius: “and many things lie in the eyebrows and cheeks to judge (*γνωματεύειν*) and observe.” Clement of Alexandria *Strom.* VII p. 869 Potter below: “judging (*γνωματεύουσα*) what is to be done by the just man.” Above others, Themistius wore out this word, as Ruhnken observed in the place cited. In his *Orat.* XXVI p. 312 B, Petavius had found *κνια-ρεύειν* in a Codex instead of *ἀριστεύειν*, he himself conjectures *γνωματεύειν*, which Ruhnken disapproved. Valckenaer wrote in the margin of my copy: *διακρινεῖν* [to distinguish]. Leo Diaconus X. p. 108 regarding the emperor Basil: “daily arranging and training the phalanxes, and exploring (*γνωματεύων*) in what way he might attack the rebel.” See Hase’s philological notes p. 254, quoting many twin passages from Agathias. Presently, after *πίστιν* it might seem that a verb has fallen out, yet it can also be referred to *μαθόντα*. — Next, from Ciz. I gave: *οἷς ἐκεῖθεν ἥκει ἐκλάμποντα τοῖς νοήμασι* i.e. *ἐκλάμποντα τοῖς νοήμασιν ἃ ἐκεῖθεν ἥκει* [shining in the thoughts which come from there]. The edition and the rest of the books have *οἷος*.

**p. 1022, 2. ὡς τῶν κακῶν—Νόσος]** Disease is a vice (*κακία*) in an animal. See Plato’s *Sophist* p. 228 d.; p. 151 Bekk. Which passage Olympiodorus praises on the *Alcibiades* p. 22; p. 191: whence to those things which then follow, let us hold these: “for there are three things that are accustomed to be carried around: I, that which is mine, and the things of that which is mine.”

**p. 1023, 4. τὴν—ἀγλαΐαν ἀσμενίσας]** Cf. Wyttenbach on Plutarch *On Virtue and Vice* (p. 101 D) in the *Animadversions* p. 693, who collected examples of the construction with the Accusative and with the Dative.

**— 6. Ζεὺς παῖς ἐξεφάνη κ. τ. λ.—and p. seq. [pagina sequenti: following page] A. Καὶ γὰρ ζωὴν ἔχει]** Plotinus respects partly the same passage of the *Phaedrus* (p. 246 e. 247) which we praised several times above, partly the *Cratylus* p. 396 a. b. where concerning *Ζηνί* [Zen], as the author of *ζωῆς* [life], and concerning *Διΐ* [Di], as the *παιδὶ* [son] of Kronos, regarding whom Plato says in the same place: “it is reasonable that Zeus is the offspring of some great intellect.”

**— 15. Διὸ οὐκ ὀρθῶς (scil. δοκοῦσιν) οἱ φθείρουσι (sc. τὸν κόσμον τὸν αἰσθητὸν)—καὶ γεννῶσιν οὕτως]** There is in these words the same elegance of brevity which we found above in IV. 5. 2. p. 442 B in these: *καὶ οἱ ἐκχέοντες δὲ τὰς ὄψεις*, where consult the note. But the passage is different from the others we have collected in that it has a Pronoun with a finite Verb instead of a Participle.

**p. 1024, 3. 'Ο οὖν θεὸς, ὁ εἷς τὸ μένειν ὡσαύτως δεδεμένος]** Perhaps it should have been translated: *so that it might remain always in the same state.* To these and following things I do not repeat what I collected in *Meletemata* I. p. 44 sq. and on Cicero’s *On the Nature of the Gods* II. 25. p. 304, these: *“But he was bound by Jupiter, lest he have immoderate courses:”* etc. The source of our passage is in Plato’s *Cratylus* p. 396 b. c. and likewise in the *Timaeus* p. 42; p. 46 Bekk.: “And he indeed, having arranged all these things, remained in his own character according to his custom. And while he remained, the sons, having perceived the arrangement of the father, obeyed it, etc.” On that passage of the *Cratylus*, Proclus disputes much on p. 55 sqq. of Boissonade’s edition; from which I shall excerpt these few things, which especially relate to these Plotinian matters p. 66: “Let no one think because of these things that the activities mentioned among the gods are divided, as if in Zeus alone there were providence, and in Kronos alone the turning toward himself, and in the heaven alone the resurrection toward the intelligible (read *τὴν πρὸς τὸ νοητὸν [μ.] ἀνάστασιν*. I removed a similar fault with the aid of the best Strasbourg Codex from Proclus’ *Inst. Theol.* § 35. where see the note p. 62): for Zeus also provides for the worldly things in no other way than by looking toward the intelligible; 'insofar as intellect sees how many and of what kind the ideas are in that which is living' says the *Timaeus* (Plato *Tim.* § 24.) and Orpheus says with a divinely inspired mouth, and 'swallows' (Orphic Frag. p. 456 Herm.) his ancestor Phanes, and Zeus takes into his bosom all his powers, and all things become intellectually whatever that one was intelligibly, and Kronos gives over (read *ἐκδίδωσι*) to Zeus the principles of the entire craftsmanship and of the providence toward sensible things, and thinking of himself he is united to the primary intelligibles and is filled with the goods from there.” — If therefore the intelligible is food, Kronos is satiated, not only by the intelligibles corresponding to him, but also by the intellection (perhaps *νοήσεως*, unless you want to refer it to *τροφῇ* [food]) of the highest and hidden things. Damascius in the Munich Codex fol. 244: “then they also celebrate him as a craftsman, Kronos, having beheld (read *θεασάμενον*) for himself the management of the craftsmanship (Schæfer added the word *προχειρισμὸς* from our *Meletemata* l. l. to the new Stephanus’ *Thesaurus* p. 10501).” The next words of Plotinus: *μεταξὺ ὢν πατρός τε ἀμείνονος κ. τ. λ.* were treated by Cudworth in *Syst. Intell.* [Intellectual System] IV. 36. p. 687 Mosheim. Cf. Plotinus above p. 487 and p. 512 sq.

**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

**p. 1024, 4. οὐ γὰρ ἦν αὐτῷ πρὸς τρόπου,]** Thus we have written with many books: *“For it was not according to his manner, nor indeed was it fitting for him.”* See Viger *On Idioms* IX. 8. 3 and 4 and Matthiæ *Gr. gr.* § 590 of the second edition.

**— 7. ἔστησε δ' αὖ καὶ τὰ εἰς θάτερα ἀπὸ τοῦ παιδὸς ἀρξάμενα εἶναι μετ' αὐτὸν]** Id est [That is]: he arranged again even the contrary things (i.e. the later things, which incline toward the lower: *πρὸς τὸ κάτω*) making a beginning from his son (that is: from the first things that come after Jupiter) so that they might be after this one (Jupiter). He took the formula *ἀπὸ τοῦ παιδὸς ἀρξάμενα* from Plato; about which see my Heusde *Specim. in Platon.* p. 39; Heindorf on *Gorgias* § 60 p. 83; Buttmann on *Alcibiades* preceding page 116; Sturz *Lex. Xenoph.* I p. 427 and Matthiæ *Gr. gr.* § 557 p. 1100 of the second edition. — Presently perhaps *τῷ πρὸς τὸ κάτω δεσμῷ* should be written. But I fear lest a greater fault lies hidden. Then *ἡ κατὰ κάλλος*, i.e. as beauty can pertain to him. Concerning this expression see Ast on Plato’s *Republic* p. 393 and what I myself placed on Proclus’ *Inst. Theol.* p. 196 following, where it is placed after a comparative Adverb: “and more greatly than according to the similarity of secondary things to primary things in beings.”

**— 15. Εἰ οὖν ἡ ψυχὴ ἡ τοῦ παντὸς—καὶ ἡ 'Αφροδίτη]** See the passage of the Platonic *Timaeus* regarding the generation of the soul p. 34 sqq.; p. 31 sqq. Bekk. and cf. Plotinus III. 5. 2. 3. 4. 5. 7. 8.

**p. 1025, 3. ἐπεὶ καὶ ὅταν καὶ αὐτοὶ καλοὶ κ. τ. λ.]** Cf. above p. 463 A; also p. 54 F; especially p. 55 D and what we noted on this passage both in this edition and in the Heidelberg edition p. 292 following.

**— 7. ἢ κατ' ἄλλην ὁδὸν πάλιν αὖ δεῖ ἐπελθεῖν.]** I added *πάλιν* from many good books. See above IV. 4. 19 at the beginning and the note there. Moreover, these last words of the chapter have I know not what native quality and which does much to move the soul.

**BOOK IX.**

**P. 1026, 7. ΠΕΡΙ ΝΟΥ (some books τοῦ νοῦ, but in Porphyry’s edition the Article is also absent) ΚΑΙ ΤΩΝ ΙΔΕΩΝ ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥ ΟΝΤΟΣ]** The fifth book according to chronological order. See Porphyry *On the Life of Plotinus* cap. IV coll. cap. XXV end. The argument of this book is related to the same dialogues of Plato as we indicated for the preceding book, and no less to Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*. Most of the Platonic philosophers contribute here. It is helpful to set down these words of Alcinous *On the Doctrine of Plato* cap. 10 p. 474: “Furthermore, he (Plato) assumes other principles, both the paradigmatic, that is, that of ideas, and that of the father and god who is the cause of all. An idea is, as toward god, his intellection; as toward us, the primary intelligible; as toward matter, a measure; as toward the sensible world, a pattern; and as examined toward itself, substance.” Cf. also Porphyry’s *Sentences* cap. XXIII—XXVI. Philoponus on Aristotle’s *On the Soul* seems to have had this book before his eyes, as on book III fol. Q. p. 7 of the Venice edition: “Plotinus understood the human intellect as intellect in act, one being always in act, the other sometimes in act. Plotinus was led astray by Plato. For having heard from him that the soul is always in motion, he thought he said it was always in motion by always thinking, and because of this he thinks it is intellect always thinking. Plotinus says then that he calls the human intellect that is always thinking 'intellect in act'.” The same in the same place p. 8: “Plotinus was deceived regarding being always in act, and assumed in us an intellect always acting, and called this intellect in act.” This book is expressly praised by Syrianus on Aristotle’s *Metaphysics* lib. [liber: book] II cap. 4 in the Latin edition of Syrianus, Venice 1580, fol. 29 b: — “But that the form is from separable form, (Aristotle) clearly signifies, subjoining: 'it is necessary that there be some form and species besides the whole at once.' If indeed again someone will place this; it is a doubt, and in what things he will place it, and in what not. For that it is not possible in all things is manifest. For we would certainly not have placed some house besides certain houses, which Parmenides was accustomed to doubt: this he himself asks, in what things there is an idea, and of what not. Accurately therefore in the *Commentaries on the Parmenides* by the divine Iamblichus it was said about these things, and it was placed also among *Plotinus in the consideration of the intellect and of species and of being*.” Cf. ibid. fol. 20 a where likewise Plotinus is praised in the same cause, and no less fol. 6 a. b. The same Syrianus fol. 35 a. b: “He (Aristotle) begins to argue to the opposite, and says it is most doubtful to those assuming the discourse about the substance of beings as being being itself. Which indeed is a profound consideration, in what way from the One, having no duality nor appearance of multitude in itself, nor diversity, all things subsist, as Plotinus, Porphyry, Iamblichus and all who were more considered about this problem declare.” Finally fol. 65 a. after he explained, “of which (beings) there are ideas, of which not,” he thus proceeds: “Those things which indeed happen only to bodies, have determined causes in the principles of nature according to Iamblichus’ opinion. For Plotinus notes that the idea of whiteness is not to be placed in the intellect. Therefore of that which there is one concept in many, of this there is not an idea etc.” You cf. above p. 181 where Plotinus makes mention of whiteness, and cf. also Simplicius in Aristotle’s *Physics* lib. I comment. 25. fol. 27 b of the Latin Paris edition 1544. — T. Taylor translated this book into English in *Select Works of Plotinus* p. 284 sqq.

**BOOK IX. ENNEAD V. p. 1024—1027.**

**p. 1026, 9. Πάντες ἄνθρωποι—αἰσθήσει πρὸ νοῦ χρησάμενοι κ. τ. λ.]** This chapter agrees with Plato in the *Phaedo* p. 81; p. 52 sq. Bekk., to which passage apply Wyttenbach p. 208. Synesius respects the same passage of Plato on p. 144, regarding which Nicephorus in the *Scholia* p. 394 says thus: “(by nature) these things are held from Plato’s opinion, but no less also from that of Plotinus. For Plotinus says that all men, etc.” Indeed, Nicephorus interposed this whole first chapter in his Scholia.

**ib. [ibidem] γενόμενοι]** Nicephorus does not recognize this. The same presently has *πρώτον ὁμιλήσαντες* instead of *προσβαλόντες*. Then he omitted the words: *πρώτοις—διέζησαν*.

**— 13. ἀρκεῖν ἐνόμισαν]** Niceph. *ἀρκ. ψήθησαν εἰ τὸ μὲν διώκειν τὸ δὲ ἀποτρέπειεν καὶ σοφὸν τοῦτο αὐτοῖς ἐνομίσθη κατὰ τοὺς βαρεῖς τῶν ὀρνίθων* [they thought it enough if they pursued one thing and turned away from another, and this was thought wise by them according to the heavy birds] — with the rest omitted. — As for what is read in the margin of some Codices at *ἀποικονομούμενοι*, namely *ἀποσκευαζόμενοι* [getting rid of baggage], we found the same interpretation above in the MS books for I. 4. 6. p. 33 D, where consult our note.

**p. 1027, 1. καίπερ πτερὰ—λαβόντες.]** Nicephorus ignores this. The same [has] *ἥρτησαν*. Presently the same: *κινοῦντες αὐτοὺς ἀπὸ τοῦ ἡδέος πρὸς τὸ βέλτιον τοῦ τῆς ψ. κ.* The same presently: *κατενήχθ. αὖθις ἐπὶ πράξεις σὺν τῷ* [they were brought down again to actions with the same beings...] with the rest omitted.

**— 8. ὀξύτητι ὀμμάτων]** Niceph. *ὀμμ. ὀξ.* omitting the words *ὥσπερ ὑπὸ ὀξυδορκίας*, and presently *καὶ* before *ἐνταῦθα*. The same *ὑπεριδών*. And you would suspect that Nicephorus praised this passage entirely from memory.

**— 11. ὥσπερ ἐκ—πλάνης εἰς πατρίδα εὔνομον ἀφικόμενος ἄνθρωπος]** I will not repeat what I placed on the twin passage I. 6. 8. p. 57 A: *πατρὶς ἡμῖν, ὅθεν παρήλθομεν* [the fatherland for us is whence we came forth], especially in the Heidelberg edition of this book p. 352 sqq. and in the *Preparations* to it p. XCI. Here I will write some things more closely joined with our passage. And just as the author of the *Axiochus* says: “life is a certain sojourn in a foreign land”: so already the Pythagoreans had said. See Fischer’s Note on that passage in Aeschines *Dialogg.* [Dialogues] III. 3. p. 118. Philo Judaeus in *On the Confusion of Tongues* p. 417 Mangey, explaining the sentiment of Jacob in *Genesis* XLIX. 9, says: — “to show that the wise man dwells as an alien as if in a sensible foreign body, but lives as if in a fatherland in intellectual virtues.” Above I gave notice of a twin passage in *Epistle to the Hebrews* XI. 13 sq. To it should be applied John Chrysostom, who has similar things in *Oratio* XXIV p. 1906 of the Commelin edition. I add the very similar words of Theodore Metochites *Miscellanea* CXVI p. 795 of the Müller and Kiessling edition: — “and the truly upward fatherland and commonwealth, standing and without faction.” Perhaps he imitated our Plotinus’ *εὔνομον πατρίδα* [well-governed fatherland]. Certainly these words are to be translated so that you do not only say "legitimate fatherland" with Ficinus, but one established by good laws. A state of this kind is said by the same sentiment *εὐνομεῖσθαι*; which pertains equally to the land, the citizens, and the house. (Thomas Mag. p. 391.) Herodotus regarding the Lacedaemonians I. 66: “having thus changed they became well-governed (*εὐνομήθησαν*).” The same I. 97: “and thus both the land will be well-governed.” Plato *Laws* XII.

**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

...avenger of the divine law. This passage, frequented by Clement of Alexandria (*Stromata* II, p. 499, Potter ed.) and others, has been applied by interpreters to Sophocles. See Markland and Doederlein on Sophocles loc. cit. Potter on Clement loc. cit. and, regarding mythological reasons, our *Symbolica* II, p. 506, sq. second ed.

**Page 1009, 4. ὁ͂ον ἄγαλμα [like a statue/image]** I have explained the force and various use of this Platonic word above, p. 57. D. (and in the book *On Beauty*, p. 369, Heidelberg ed.). Cf. also p. 465. C. and p. 520. F. — Soon after, Plotinus borrowed the words θέαμα — θεατῶν [spectacle — of spectators] no less from Plato. For he, in the *Phaedo* p. 113 [p. 111, Bekker ed.], writes: *θέαμα εὐδαιμόνων θεατῶν* [a spectacle of blessed spectators], regarding which Wyttenbach (p. 308) suspects our Plotinus, if he did not read, certainly thought of *ὑπερευδαιμόνων* [beyond-blessed] in the cited Platonic passage; and that this appears from a passage of this book, p. 547. B. (following chapter), where likewise is found *ὑπερευδαίμονας*. Cf. the same author's *Philomathia* III, p. 106.

**— 10. συμφόρησιν — προτάσεων [a collection of propositions]** Cf. above I. 3. 4. and 5. and the annotations there; likewise IV. 4. 44, V. 5. 1, and VI. 8. 3.

**— 12. ἦν δὴ καὶ ὁ Πλάτων κατιδών φησίν, οὐδ’ ἥτις ἐστὶν ἄλλη ἐν ἄλλῳ. [Which indeed Plato also saw and says: nor is it one thing in another.]** In the *Phaedo* p. 83 [p. 56, Bekker]: "Whatever one considers through other things as being another thing in others, one should consider none of that to be true." To these words Wyttenbach (p. 219) notes: "*i.e., whatever indeed he considers through other things (i.e., the corporeal through the senses of the body), since in different senses a different thing appears, he considers none of these true.*" Then he compares other passages both from Plato himself and his followers, and our philosopher himself below, VI. 7, p. 727. C. To these I add a passage of Damascius, who undoubtedly had that sentiment of Plato before his eyes when he wrote these things *On First Principles* (Cod. Mon. fol. 265 recto): "It is better, therefore, to abide by his definition, according to the Pythagorean custom and that of Plato himself, who thinks of material things and matter itself as 'others' [different]. For in the *Phaedo* he thus names 'the others,' meaning the sensible forms; 'others in others.' Aristotle, however, in the *Archyntela*, records that Pythagoras called matter 'other' as being fluid and always becoming 'another and another'; so it is clear that Plato also defines 'the others' in this way." — The words of Plotinus that follow: "How indeed — to make the beginning," are to be held all the more because the philosopher, restrained by a singular reverence toward Plato, very rarely openly professes (though he does it very often in practice) that he wishes to strengthen, increase, and polish the discoveries of the "god of philosophers."

**Page 1011, 3] Διὰ καὶ τὰς ἰδέας ὄντα ἔλεγον εἶναι οἱ παλαιοὶ καὶ οὐσίας. [Therefore the ancients also said that Ideas were beings and substances.]** To Plotinus, "the ancients" are not only the most ancient philosophers, such as Heraclitus, who had denied that those things which were composite and obvious to the senses were "beings" (*Plato, Cratylus* p. 402. A.), but also Plato and his contemporaries. And Plato's doctrine of Ideas is contained primarily in the *Parmenides* (which see regarding this question, p. 130. b, 133. b, 135. b). Cf. *Cratylus* p. 439. D. E. and consult Buttmann’s *Excursus to the Meno* III, p. 74: "On the abstract notions of things according to the mind of Plato." Wyttenbach on the *Phaedo* pp. 270–272, and Stallbaum's *Prolegomena to the Philebus* p. XXII with note 5. Regarding Aristotle, see *Metaphysics* I. 6. collated with XIII. 4. p. 265 Brandis ed., *Nicomachean Ethics* I. 4, *Eudemian Ethics* I. 8, *On Generation and Corruption* II. 3. Cf. Henr. Richter’s pamphlet *On the Ideas of Plato*, Leipzig 1827. This writer wishes to distinguish in Plato between *eidos* and *idea*, and says that for Plato, *idea* is the universal form of things in which their eternal essence and nature appears. The same author (p. 66 sqq.) denies that in any passage of Plato the Ideas are called *substances* [substantiae]. For although Plato attributes *ousia* [essence/substance] to Ideas, this signifies nothing else, according to Plato’s own view, than that the Ideas are perennial (perpetual) in the intellect. He argues that Aristotle understood the notion of *ousia* differently and therefore did not always correctly explain Plato’s decrees on Ideas; and that the Alexandrian philosophers more widely propagated the opinion that those things which Plato called Ideas are substances. These are the views of Richter. — First, I do not attribute much to those who think it must be investigated whether Plato placed Ideas only in the divine mind, or said they exist by themselves outside the mind. Secondly, I do not offer myself as a defender of Aristotle in this cause, since I know he called Plato's Ideas *τερετίσματα* [teretismata], that is, *tuneful trifles* or *empty songs* (*Aristotle, Posterior Analytics* p. 228: "Farewell to the Forms; for they are mere chirping/teretismata." Cf. Tib. Hemsterhuis on *Thomas Magister* p. 908 and in *Anecdota* ed. I. Geel, p. 32 sq.)...

### PAGE 322 (Original Page 307)
**BOOK VIII OF THE FIFTH ENNEAD, pp. 1009–1012.**

...the rest I omit. I ask regarding Plotinus whether the word *substance* has such force that the philosopher from Lycopolis [Plotinus] should be said to have accepted Ideas less incorporeally or more corporeally (if I may use these terms for brevity's sake) than Plato; for example, as if the Ideas as substances had various and mutable accidents, etc. If Richter meant this, he wandered "by the whole sky" [completely] from the mind of Plotinus. Just listen to these words of our author in the next book, p. 560. A: "Let Intellect be the beings, and all things in it, not as if having them in a place, but as having itself, and being one with them." You see here that to Plotinus, Mind or Intellect is "the beings" [τὰ ὄντα]: in our passage, the same are "Ideas." What more do you seek? To Plotinus, *Ideas* are neither in the mind nor outside the mind, but are the same thing as the mind; and this is a most simple notion, which cannot be defined otherwise than that Ideas *are*, and they are the same as *beings* and *essences*. Nor do I judge Plato's own view to have been otherwise. This serves as an argument that those are mistaken who think a difference intervenes between Plato's doctrine of Ideas and that of Plotinus. What of it? — I indeed do not hesitate to profess that Plato's decrees will be placed in a clearer light in several other doctrines as well, if his interpreters would wish to study Plotinus more zealously.

**— 5. Δοκοῦσι δέ μοι καὶ οἱ Αἰγυπτίων σοφοὶ κ. τ. λ. [And the wise men of the Egyptians seem to me, etc.]** Plato mentions the writing of the Egyptians in the *Phaedrus* p. 274 sq. and in the *Philebus* p. 18. I have cited many others both in the commentary on Cicero's *De Natura Deorum* III. 22. p. 611, and especially in the *Commentaries on Herodotus* I, p. 369 sqq. Moreover, everyone knows that this matter has recently been debated by the studies of many, as seen in the writings of the Englishman Young and the Frenchman Champollion and others (cf. to omit others, Silvestre de Sacy in *Journal des Savans* 1827 and Letronne in the *Appendix to the Précis du Système hiéroglyphique* by M. Champollion le jeune, p. 376 sqq. second ed.). Because Plotinus, an Egyptian man, says in this passage that the other way of writing used by the Egyptians—which we commonly call alphabetic, where the sounds of the voice are represented by the strokes of letters—was not used by the Egyptian priests; this is undoubtedly to be understood as meaning he wants the books to be understood which were properly called *sacred*, as those containing the recondite doctrine of religions. (See the third annotation after this one).

**— 7. μὴ τύποις γραμμάτων διεξοδεύουσι κ. τ. λ. [not proceeding through the types of letters, etc.]** Philo uses *διεξόδοις* [discursive passages/ways] in the same matter, *Life of Moses* I, p. 606. Hermias on Plato’s *Phaedrus* p. 103, Ast ed.: "According to which it [the rational soul] subsists from the mind, it has the intellectual, by which it grasps the forms by simple intuitions and not discursively [*οὐ διεξοδικῶς*] — and in what follows — and it acts discursively [*διεξοδικῶς*] and syllogizes." I gave other examples in the preface to *Proclus on the Alcibiades* p. 249 and above on Plotinus p. 189. B. and p. 478. D.

**— 10. ἐμφῆναι [to manifest]** I have restored this from many and the best books instead of *ἐμφῦναι* [to implant], and Diodorus Siculus III. 4. uses the expression *ἐξ ἐμφάσεως* [from appearance/manifestation] in the same matter. — Regarding the things in the following parts of this chapter that are more difficult, I have tried to assist by punctuation. Five lines from the end, "καὶ τὸ ἐκ ζητήσεως" [and that from inquiry], I fear that several words and perhaps some sentences have fallen out. Ficino’s version, or rather paraphrase, helps the understanding of the rest. Iamblichus, *Life of Pythagoras* V, p. 52, Kiessling ed., on Pythagoras: "He attempted to make the mode of teaching symbolic, and entirely similar to the teachings in Egypt, according to which [*καθ’ ἃ*] (many of my MSS also confirm this reading, showing *καθὰ*) he was educated." The same in *On the Mysteries* VII. 1, p. 150, Gale ed.: "First indeed I wish to interpret for you the mode of the Egyptians' theology. For these, imitating the nature of the universe and the craftsmanship of the gods, themselves created certain images of mystic and hidden and invisible thoughts through symbols, just as nature expressed the invisible reasons through symbols in a certain way in visible forms" (*ἀπετυπώσατο*—the Munich MS wrongly has *ἀποτυπ.*). Regarding Hermes as the author of writing, consult Horapollo in *Hieroglyphics* I. 14.

**— 12. Ὕστερον δὲ — ἐξεύρισκον [But later... they found out]** These are the things which were recorded in the sacred commentaries of the Egyptians even in what are called *hieratic* letterforms; whereas the properly sacred books, that is, those containing recondite religious doctrine, were written in *hieroglyphic* characters (Plotinus calls them *ἀγάλματα* [statues/images], see above). A third kind of writing, pertaining to the use of common life, also used letter characters rather than images, and was called "popular" (*δημοτικόν*).

**Page 1012, 6. ἆρα ὀλώμεθα [shall we perish?]** The other reading *ὀλόμεθα* might also be supported by passages in Plato, as in the *Gorgias*...

**— 5. ἡ γῆ — στρογγύλη [The earth is round]** The round figure of the earth, which Herodotus (IV. 36) and Aristotle (*Meteorology* II. 5, p. 55 Sylburg ed.) had in some way mocked, is said to have been held by many Socratics (Cleomedes, *Meteorology* VIII, p. 40, p. 51 Bak ed.). The same opinion is defended by that famous Claudius Ptolemy both in the *Almagest* I and in the *Geography* I. 7, VII. 5. (Cf. Mannert, *Geography of Greeks and Romans* I, p. 144 sqq.; Uckert, *Geography of Greeks and Romans* I, p. 299; and Sickler, *Handbook of Ancient Geography* p. XLIV). Although the authority of this man [Ptolemy] was already very great in the third century when Plotinus flourished, I would believe that this philosopher followed the views of the old Platonists in this matter as well. — To the next part: *καὶ ὁ λοξὸς* [and the oblique/zodiac], cf. the twin passage II. 9. 12, p. 211. B, and the annotation there on the words *λόξωσις τῶν ζῳδίων* [obliquity of the zodiac].

**— 7. τοῦ συλλογισμοῦ — τὸ συμπέρασμα — τῶν προτάσεων [The conclusion — of the syllogism — from the premises]** Cf. From this, it is understood that Plotinus does not report Plato's passage verbatim. Simplicius likewise quotes it from memory in his commentary on Aristotle’s *Physics* IV, 166 and 265. Stobaeus also shows it in *Physical Eclogues* I, 268. Cf. Lindau's annotations on Plato loc. cit., who did not neglect our Plotinus. ### PAGE 324 (Original Page 309)
**BOOK VIII OF THE FIFTH ENNEAD, pp. 1012–1019.**

"...turning the stars in it—it provides." Regarding the one god and many together, thus Damascius, *On Principles* ch. 100, p. 314, Kopp ed.: "What need to say much? When even almost all philosophers before Iamblichus thus posit the many gods, saying that there is one super-essential god, and that the others are essential, being deified by the illuminations from the One."

**Page 1017, 12. ἀλλὰ ἤδη ἀπειρίᾳ δυνάμεως ἀληθινῆς φαντάζονται καλοῦσαι, καὶ φθείρουσαι, καὶ θλίβουσαι. [but already by an infinity of true power they appear burning, and destroying, and crushing.]** From the margin and many books I received *ἤδη* [already] instead of *εἴδη* [forms]; from two Marcian MSS *καλοῦσαι* [burning] instead of *καὶ οὖσαι* [and being]. This is because *φαντάζεσθαι* [to appear] is in other places also contrary to *εἶναι* [to be]. (See our annotation above on I. 6. 3. p. 50. B.) Also because the mention of fire seemed to require this, and because *θλίβουσαι* [crushing/squeezing] agrees well with *καλοῦσαι*. Specifically, *φθείρουσαι* [destroying] pertains to the forces of all bodies, some of which kill by burning, others by thrusting, pressing, and shattering. — In defining the force of the noun *ἀπειρίᾳ* [infinity/inexperience], Ficino hesitated and, as he often does, expressed it in two ways. I, who believed the other meaning to be alien to this place, did not wish to delete his words: "*they consist in infinity and are enclosed in its hooks*" anymore than similar things elsewhere, lest the power of choosing be snatched from learned readers.

**— 18. ἀπολειφθῆναι [to be left behind]** The fact that the Cizensis MS has *ἀποληφθῆναι* [to be caught/intercepted] pertains to that kind of confusion which spreads most widely through the monuments of the ancients, concerning which, after others, the most learned Hase recently warned in *Leo Diaconus* p. 211. D. In Plato's *Symposium* p. 220. A. [p. 461, Bekker], all recent editors after Ast on the *Republic* p. 543 have received *ἀποληφθέντες*; while all MSS show *ἀπολειφθέντες*. One could certainly defend the latter with plausibility if one wished to apply Xenophon *Memorabilia* I. 4. 8. and *Agesilaus* 11. 29. Judgment actually depends on history, which we do not know.

**Page 1018, 6. μᾶλλον γὰρ οἰκεία ἡ καλή. [for the beautiful is more akin.]** Ficino additionally expressed what is read in the margin of a single book: *καὶ ἡ καλλονή* [and beauty]. The rest of the books reject this addition. For the argument of this whole passage, apply the book *On Beauty* above I. 6. 3 and 4, p. 52 sq. and the notes on it.

**— 7. Διὰ τοῦτο — Ζεὺς — πρῶτος πορεύεται [Therefore — Zeus — goes first]** This is the same celebrated passage in Plato's *Phaedrus* p. 246. e. and 247 [p. 41 sqq. Bekker], mentioned so many times by other philosophers and by our author himself. See for example above IV. 4. 9, p. 403. C. and citations there; also p. 419. C. and p. 544. C. to omit other things which I both cited above and which Heindorf (p. 251 sqq.) and Ast (p. 296 sqq.) and at the end of the *Republic* (p. 653 sqq.) collected for the passage in the *Phaedrus*. As for Heindorf's opinion that souls are also included under the name of *daimons*: in this he does not have Plotinus' support, who explicitly adds *ψυχὰς* [souls]. The words that follow in Plato: "they go under the highest sub-celestial arch [*ὑπουράνιον ἀψῖδα*] to the steep..." — these have given place to many disputes of ancient interpreters, and according to Proclus in Plato's *Theology* IV. 16, p. 215, Plato had formed for himself: "these three world-orders: the super-celestial place, the celestial revolution, and the sub-celestial arch." Soon Plotinus himself makes mention of a certain "invisible place": and our Plotinus is mentioned in those same disputes about the passage in the *Phaedrus*. For thus Proclus loc. cit.: "For the philosopher from Asine (namely Theodorus of Asine), being persuaded by Plotinus, called the thing proceeding immediately from the ineffable 'the sub-celestial arch,' as he philosophizes about names concerning these things." In our passage indeed no mention of this *apsis* [arch] is explicitly made, nor elsewhere that I know in these Enneads; so that perhaps this testimony of Proclus is an argument that in that other edition of Plotinus' books (of which we find other traces) these things were more fully explained somewhere. — I will add two passages: Philo Judaeus, *On the Cherubim*, Vol. II, p. 14 Pfeiffer ed.: "the last arch of the whole heaven." Stobaeus, *Physical Eclogues* I. 27, p. 550 Heeren ed. regarding the moon: "having a hollow arch." Whence the diminutive *ἀψίδιον*; see Coray in *Atakta* II, p. 77. Otherwise cf. Plotinus IV. 1, p. 360. A.

**Page 1019, 17. τοῖς δὲ διὰ παντὸς οἷον οἰνωθεῖσι καὶ πληρωθεῖσι τοῦ νέκταρος [to those who are entirely, as it were, intoxicated and filled with nectar]** He borrowed the image from his own Plato, both from the *Phaedrus* p. 247 fin. [p. 43 Bekker] and from the *Symposium* p. 203 [p. 429 Bekker]. The fact that *οἰνωθεῖσι* [intoxicated/winy] is joined with the mention of Nectar here reminds one of Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* VI. 125 [p. 426 sq. Oudendorp]: "*Then a cup of nectar, which is the wine of the gods, the rustic boy [Ganymede] served to Jove, and Liber [Bacchus] to the others:*" where I think Oudendorp should be supported, who thought the words *which is [wine]* should be freed from the suspicion of being glosses...

---

### PAGE 325 (Original Page 310)
**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

...Also Lucian in *Lexiphanes* I, p. 319 Wetstein ed.: "For you seem as if you will pour some nectar for us from it." Moreover, what Plotinus adds, *καὶ πληρωθεῖσι* [and filled], is not superfluous, since for the most part the Greeks want *οἰνώμενον* [made winy] to be distinct from *μεθύοντι* [drunk] (Wesseling on Diodorus I. 57, p. 67; Mangey on Philo I, p. 350.) For above (following Plato in the cited *Symposium* passage), p. 299. A. he uses *μεθύειν τῷ νέκταρι* [to be drunk with nectar], and ibid. D: "and there Poros [Plenty] sleeps, being weighed down by what he was filled with." Philo Judaeus, *On the Planting of Noah* p. 234. a. [p. 148 Pfeiffer]: "Drunkenness is twofold, one is equal to being 'winy' [*οἰνοῦσθαι*]. The other is equal to raving in wine." With these passages of Plotinus, however, should be compared these words of Proclus in Plato’s *Theology* IV. 15, p. 202: "The nourishing cause of the gods is a certain intelligible union containing the whole perfection of the gods in itself, and filling the gods with vigor and power, both for the providence of secondary things and the immutable intellection of the first things. But above, the gods participate in these in a unitary way, and in their processions in a divided way. Where indeed of the nourishment, one is called ambrosia by Plato, and the other nectar. At the manger, he says (Plato in the *Phaedrus* passage) having stood the horses, he gave them ambrosia, and on top of it he gave them nectar to drink, etc." Julian, *Epistle* XXVII: "For always hearing and speaking about them is nectar to me." This formula has acquired the force of a proverb. See L. H. Heyler on that passage, p. 291.

**Page 1020, 3. ἀλλ’ ἔχει τὸ ὀξέως ὁρῶν ἐν αὐτῷ τὸ ὁρώμενον [but the sharply seeing has in itself the thing seen]** The Vatican MS does not recognize the *τὸ* [the], and since Ficino uses the masculine, I would indeed, if a single book had allowed, have restored *ὁ ὀξέως ὁρῶν* [the sharply seeing man], especially since all agree on the nearby *ἔχων* [having].

**— 7. ὥσπερ εἴ τις ὑπὸ θεοῦ κατασχεθείς, Φοιβόληπτος ἢ ὑπό τινος Μούσης [as if one were seized by a god, Phoeboleptic or by some Muse]** In Herodotus IV. 13. several MSS offer this very thing instead of the Ionic *φοιβόλαμπτος*, less correctly. Longinus, *On the Sublime* XVI. 2, p. 68 Weiske ed.: regarding Demosthenes: "but since, just as if suddenly inspired by a god and becoming as if Phoeboleptic, he uttered the oath against the best of Greece." Lycophron in *Cassandra* v. 1460 calls this very virgin "the Phoeboleptic swallow," which Tzetzes in the Scholia p. 1046 explains: "the prophetic," and those are called *phoeboleptoi* or *theophoretoi* [god-borne] who, by the instinct of a daimon, whether good or evil, divine or do anything else not being masters of their own mind. Hence it is also transferred to poets and orators, as Meric Casaubon observes on Antoninus [Marcus Aurelius] XII in Gataker's edition p. 420. What Plotinus adds: *ἡ ὑπὸ τινος Μούσης (κατασχεθείς)* [seized by some Muse], he undoubtedly had before his eyes another passage of the *Phaedrus*. For thus p. 245. a. [p. 37 Bekker] Plato says: "A third possession and madness from the Muses, taking a tender and untouched soul, awakening and maddening it in songs and other poetry, etc." The same in *Laws* VII. 790. d. e. [p. 6 Bekker]: "just as the healings of insane Bacchic rites use this together with the dance and the muse of motion." Philo Judaeus seems to have had this passage before his eyes in *Who is the Heir of Divine Things* p. 482 Mangey ed. (See our note on Cicero, *On Divination* I. 1. p. 5 Moser ed.) Himerius, *Oration* XIII. 7, p. 596 Wernsdorf ed.: "just as the Bacchic one, for so the lyre calls him, meaning Dionysus, spring having just first shone forth, with spring flowers and ivy clusters, poets possessed by the Muses having crowned him, lead him, etc." Philo Judaeus expressed the words of the Platonic *Phaedrus* in *On Providence* in the Armenian and Latin version p. 77 Venice ed. (where in the Greek write *ἀφίκηται*), as did Plutarch in *On Moral Virtue* p. 452. B. [p. 845 Wyttenbach]: "For not only in poems, as Plato says, the muse-possessed and possessed one makes the technical and precise man appear ridiculous, etc." Olympiodorus in Plato’s *Alcibiades* preface p. 2: "The second enthusiasm is in the *Republic*, where having become muse-possessed, he [Plato] acted as the Muses," namely Plato, who in the same place in the *Timaeus* is said to be *θεόληπτος* [god-possessed]; in the *Phaedrus*: *νυμφόληπτος* [nymph-possessed]. Iamblichus accurately distinguishes the various kinds of obsession (if I may call it that), *Mysteries* III. 5. p. 65 Gale ed., from which passage I will excerpt only the beginning: "There are indeed many kinds of divine possession [*κατακωχῆς*] and in many ways, the divine inspiration is stirred; whence also many of its signs are different." Write *καὶ διαφέροντα* [and different]. For thus all codices whose readings I have. But the whole passage should be compared with that of Plotinus.

**— 10. Εἰ δέ τις ἡμῶν ἀδυνατῶν ἑαυτὸν ὁρᾷν [But if someone of us is unable to see himself]** Dionysius the Areopagite seems to have had the following words before his eyes, *On the Divine Names* IV. 9, p. 561: "The motion of the soul is, in a circular way indeed, the entry into itself from external things and of its intellectual powers the unitary...

### PAGE 326 (Original Page 311)
**BOOK VIII OF THE FIFTH ENNEAD, pp. 1020–1024.**

"...winding together, just as in a certain circle bestowed upon it by the unerring and unmoved, and turning itself back and collecting itself from the many external things first into itself, then as having become unitary [write *ἐνοειδῆ*], uniting with the unitarily united powers, and thus leading by the hand to the beautiful and good that which is above all beings, and one and the same and without beginning and without end."

**Page 1021, 6. Δεῖ δὲ — γνωματόευειν αὐτὸν [It is necessary — to judge/discern it oneself]** He has this word from his Plato, *Republic* VII, p. 516 fin. [p. 330 Bekker], which passage, although Ruhnken indicated it with passages from imitators in *Timaeus' Platonic Lexicon* p. 72, as almost everywhere, here also he neglected to mention Plotinus. What is read in the margin of some of our codices as a Scholion (see Var. Lect.) is taken from the *Etymologicum Magnum*, or Suidas, or Zonaras under the word. Add *Etymol. Gudianum* p. 128 and at the end of Orion p. 622 and *Scholia on Plato* p. 179 Ruhnken ed. Philostratus, *Life of Apollonius* II. 30, p. 83 Olearius ed.: "many things lie in eyebrows and cheeks to judge [*γνωματόευειν*] and behold." Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* VII, p. 869 Potter ed. below: "judging/discerning [*γνωματόευουσα*] for the just man what is to be done." Beyond others, Themistius wore out this word, as Ruhnken observes loc. cit. In his *Oration* XXVI, p. 312. B. instead of *ἀριστεύειν* [to excel] Petavius in a codex had found *κυιαρεύειν*, he himself conjectures *γνωματόευειν*, with Ruhnken disapproving. Valckenaer wrote on the margin of my copy: *διακρινεῖν* [to distinguish]. Leo Draconus X, p. 108 regarding Emperor Basil: "daily arranging and exercising the phalanxes, and judging [*γνωματόευων*] in what way he might attack the rebel": *exploring*. See Hase's philological notes p. 254, citing many twin passages from Agathias. Next, after *πίστιν* [faith] it might seem a word has fallen out, yet it can also be referred to *μαθόντα* [having learned]. — Next from the Cizensis MS I gave: *οἷς ἐκεῖθεν ἥκει ἐκλάμποντα τοῖς νοήμασι* [to whom the thoughts come shining from there], that is, *ἐκλάμποντα τοῖς νοήμασιν ἃ ἐκεῖθεν ἥκει*. The edition and other books have *οἷος*.

**Page 1022, 2. ὡς τῶν κακῶν — Νόσος [as of evils — Disease]** Disease in an animal is a vice/badness (*κακία*). See Plato's *Sophist* p. 228. d. [p. 151 Bekker]. Olympiodorus quotes this passage in *Alcibiades* preface p. 191: whence for the things that follow, let us hold these: "for there are three things that are accustomed to be moved about: I, mine, and the things of mine."

**Page 1023, 4. τὴν — ἀγλαίαν ἀσμενίσας [having welcomed — the splendor]** Cf. Wyttenbach on Plutarch *On Virtue and Vice* (p. 101. D.) in *Animadv.* p. 693, who collected examples of the construction with the Accusative and with the Dative.

**— 6. Ζεὺς παῖς ἐξεφάνη κ. τ. λ. — and p. seq. A. Καὶ γὰρ ζωὴν ἔχει [Zeus appeared as a child, etc. — For he also has life]** Plotinus respects partly that same passage of the *Phaedrus* (p. 246. e. 247) which we cited several times above, partly the *Cratylus* p. 396. a. b. where concerning *Ζηνὶ* [Zēn] as the author of *ζωῆς* [life], and concerning *Διὶ* [Diï] as the son of *Κρόνου* [Kronos/Saturn], concerning whom Plato says in the same place: "it is reasonable that the son of a certain great intellect [dianoia] should be Zeus."

**— 15. Διὰ οὐκ ὀρθῶς (scil. δοκοῦσιν) οἱ φθείρουσι (sc. τὸν κόσμον τὸν αἰσθητὸν) — καὶ γεννῶσιν οὕτως [Wherefore those who destroy (the sensible world) — and thus beget (do not think) correctly]** There is in these words the same elegance of brevity which we found above IV. 5. 2, p. 442. B. in these: "and those who pour out their visions," where consult the annotation. It is a passage different from others we collected in that it has the Pronoun with a finite Verb instead of a Participle.

**Page 1024, 3. Ὁ οὖν θεὸς, ὁ εἰς τὸ μένειν ὡσαύτως δεδεμένος [The god, then, who is bound to remain in the same way]** Perhaps it was to be translated: *so that he might always remain in the same state*. Regarding these and the following, I do not repeat what I collected in *Meletemata* I, p. 44 sq. and on Cicero's *De Natura Deorum* II. 25, p. 304: "*He was bound by Jove, however, lest he have immoderate courses:*" etc. The source of our passage is in Plato’s *Cratylus* p. 396. b. c. likewise in the *Timaeus* p. 42 [p. 46 Bekker]: "And he having arranged all these things remained in his own characteristic habit. And while he remained, the children, having perceived the father's arrangement, obeyed it, etc." On that passage of the *Cratylus*, Proclus disputes much p. 55 sqq. Boissonade ed.; from which I will excerpt these few things which most apply to these Plotinian matters p. 66: "Let no one think that because of these things the activities said to be in the gods are divided, for example in Zeus only providence, and in Saturn only the reversion toward himself, and in the heaven only the tension toward the intelligible (Read *τὴν πρὸς τὸ νοητὸν μ. ἀνάτασιν* [tension]. I removed a similar fault of the best Strasbourg codex by the help of Proclus' *Inst. Theol.* § 35. where see note p. 62): for Zeus does not provide for worldly things otherwise than by looking toward the intelligible; 'whatever ideas then intellect sees being in the animal which is, both how many and of what kind,' says the *Timaeus* (§ 24). Orpheus speaks with a divine mouth, and Zeus 'swallows' (Orph. Frag. p. 456 Herm.) his ancestor Phanes, and embraces all his powers, and Zeus becomes intellectually all things...

**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

"...intellectually as many things as that one was intelligibly, and Saturn [Kronos] gives over to Zeus the principles of all craftsmanship and of providence for sensible things, and in thinking himself he is united to the first intelligibles and filled with the goods from there. — If then the nourishment, the intelligible, is sating, Saturn is sated, not only with the intelligibles coordinate with him, but also with the intellection of the highest and hidden things" (perhaps *νοήσεως* [of intellection], unless you wish to refer it to *τροφὴ* [nourishment]). Damascius in Cod. Schaefer added the word *προχειρισμὸς* from our *Meletemata* loc. cit. to the new Stephanus' *Thesaurus* p. 10501.) The next words of Plotinus: "being between a better father..." **Page 1024, 4. οὐ γὰρ ἦν αὐτῷ πρὸς τρόπου, [for it was not according to his character]** Thus we have written with many books: "Neither indeed was it fit, nor indeed did it become him." See Viger on *Idiotisms* IX. 8. 3. and 4. and Matthiae *Greek Grammar* § 590, second ed.

**— 7. ἔστησε δ’ αὖ καὶ τὰ εἰς θάτερα ἀπὸ τοῦ παιδὸς ἀρξάμενα εἶναι μετ’ αὐτὸν [And he established again also the things on the other side beginning from the son to be after him]** That is: he arranged again also the contraries (that is, the lower things, which tend toward the inferior: *πρὸς τὸ κάτω*) beginning from his son (that is: from the first things which come after Jove) so that they were after him (Jove). He took the formula *ἀπὸ τοῦ παιδὸς ἀρξάμενα* [beginning from the child] from Plato; concerning which see my van Heusde's *Specimen on Plato* p. 39, Heindorf on *Gorgias* § 60, p. 83, Buttmann on *Alcibiades* preface p. 116, Sturz *Lexicon Xenophonteum* I, p. 427 and Matthiae *Greek Grammar* § 557, p. 1100, second ed. — Next perhaps one should write *τῷ πρὸς τὸ κάτω δεσμῷ* [by the bond toward the below]. But I fear lest a greater fault lies hidden. Then *ἡ κατὰ κάλλος* [the one according to beauty], that is, so that beauty might pertain to him. Regarding this expression see Ast on Plato’s *Republic* p. 393, and what I myself placed on Proclus' *Inst. Theol.* p. 196 sq. where it is placed after a comparative Adverb: "and more greatly than according to the similarity of secondary things toward the first in the beings."

**— 15. Εἰ οὖν ἡ ψυχὴ ἡ τοῦ παντὸς — καὶ ἡ Ἀφροδίτη [If then the soul of the universe — and Venus]** See the passage of the Platonic *Timaeus* on the generation of the soul p. 34 sqq. [p. 31 sqq. Bekker] and cf. Plotinus III. 5. 2. 3. 4. 5. 7. 8.

**Page 1025, 3. ἐπεὶ καὶ ὅταν καὶ αὐτοὶ καλοὶ κ. τ. λ. [since even when they themselves are beautiful, etc.]** Cf. above p. 463. A. likewise p. 54. F. especially p. 55. D. and what we annotated on this passage both in this edition and in the Heidelberg ed. p. 292 sq.

**— 7. ἢ κατ’ ἄλλην ὁδὸν πάλιν αὖ δεῖ ἐπελθεῖν. [or it is necessary to go back again by another way.]** I added *πάλιν* [again] from many good books. See above IV. 4. 19. beginning, and the Annotation there. Moreover, these last words of the chapter have something native about them and which does a surprising amount to move the mind.

### BOOK IX.

**Page 1026, 7. ΠΕΡΙ ΝΟΥ (libri aliquot τοῦ νοῦ, sed in Porphyrii edit. Articulus etiam abest) ΚΑΙ ΤΩΝ ΙΔΕΩΝ ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥ ΟΝΤΟΣ [On Intellect (some books 'the intellect', but in Porphyry's edition the article is also absent) and Ideas and Being]** The fifth book in chronological order. See Porphyry, *Life of Plotinus* ch. IV. collated with ch. XXV. fin. The argument of this book is kindred with almost the same dialogues of Plato which we indicated for the preceding book, and no less with Aristotle's *Metaphysics*. Most of the Platonic philosophers contribute here. It is helpful to set down these words of Alcinous, *On the Doctrine of Plato* ch. 10, p. 474: "Furthermore, he [Plato] accepts other principles, both the paradigmatic, that is, that of the Ideas, and that of the god who is father and cause of all. The Idea is, as toward god, his intellection; as toward us, the first intelligible; as toward matter, a measure; as toward the sensible world, a pattern; as considered toward itself, essence." Cf. also Porphyry's *Sentences* ch. XXIII–XXVI. Philoponus seems to have had this book before his eyes in Aristotle's *On the Soul*, as in book III fol. Q, p. 7 Venice ed.: "Plotinus thought of the human intellect as intellect in activity/actuality [*ἐνεργείᾳ*], one always acting, the other acting at some time. Plotinus wandered away from Plato. For having heard from him that the soul is always-moving [*ἀεικίνητός*], he thought he said 'always-moving' by 'always thinking,' and because of this he thinks there is an intellect always thinking. Plotinus says then that he calls the human intellect always thinking 'intellect in activity'." The same ibid. p. 8: "Plotinus was deceived regarding 'always acting,' and hypothesized in us an intellect always acting, and called this 'intellect in activity'." This book is explicitly cited by Syrianus in Aristotle's *Metaphysics* book II, ch. 4 in the Latin edition of Syrianus, Venice 1580, fol. 29. b: — "*Moreover, that there is a form apart from the separable form, he [Aristotle] manifestly signifies adding: it is necessary that there be some form and species besides the whole at once. If indeed again one posits this;*"...

### PAGE 328 (Original Page 313)
**BOOK IX OF THE FIFTH ENNEAD, pp. 1024–1027.**

"...it is a doubt, both in which things he will place it, and in which not. For that it is not possible in all is manifest. For we would not indeed posit that there is some house besides certain houses, which Parmenides was accustomed to doubt: this he also asks, in which there is an idea, and of which there is not. Accurately therefore it was spoken concerning these things in the Commentaries on the Parmenides by the divine Iamblichus, and it is also placed in Plotinus in the consideration 'on intellect and species and being'." Cf. ibid. fol. 20. a. where Plotinus is likewise cited in the same cause, and no less fol. 6. a. b. The same Syrianus fol. 35. a. b: "*Aristotle begins to argue for the opposite, and says it is most doubtful to those proposing a discourse on the substance of beings. This indeed is a profound consideration, in what way from the One, having no duality nor appearance of multitude in itself, nor diversity, all things subsist, as Plotinus, Porphyrius, Iamblichus and all who have been more considerately occupied around this problem declare.*" Finally fol. 65. a. after he explained "*of which (beings) there are ideas, of which not,*" he proceeds thus: "*Those things which happen to bodies alone have determined causes in the reasons of nature from the opinion of Iamblichus. For Plotinus notes that the idea of whiteness is not to be placed in the intellect. I. comm. 25. fol. 27. b. of the Latin Paris edition 1544. — T. Taylor translated this book into English in *Select Works of Plotinus* p. 284 sqq.

**Page 1026, 9. Πάντες ἄνθρωποι — αἰσθήσει πρὸ νοῦ χρησάμενοι κ. τ. λ. [All men — having used sense before intellect, etc.]** This chapter agrees with Plato in the *Phaedo* p. 81 [p. 52 sq. Bekker], to which passage apply Wyttenbach p. 208. Synesius respects the same passage of Plato p. 144, to which Nicephorus in the Scholia p. 394 notes: "(by nature) these things hold to Plato's opinion, but no less also to that of Plotinus. For Plotinus says that all men, etc." Indeed, Nicephorus interposed this whole first chapter in his Scholia.

**ib. γενόμενοι [having become]** Nicephorus does not recognize this. The same soon has *πρῶτον ὁμιλήσαντες* [first having consorted] instead of *προσβαλόντες* [having attacked/applied]. Then he omitted the words: *πρώτοις — διέζησαν* [they lived through — the first things].

**— 13. ἀρκεῖν ἐνόμισαν [they thought it to suffice]** Niceph. *ἀρκ. ᾠήθησαν εἰ τὸ μὲν διώκειν τὸ δὲ ἀποτρέποιεν καὶ σοφὸν τοῦτο αὐτοῖς ἐνομίσθη κατὰ τοὺς βαρεῖς τῶν ὀρνίθων* [they thought it sufficed if they pursued one and turned from another, and this was considered wise by them according to the heavy birds] — with the rest omitted. — As for what is read in some Codd. in the margin for *ἀποικονομόυμενοι* [being managed/arranged away], namely *ἀποσκευαζόμενοι* [getting rid of baggage], we found the same interpretation above in the MSS of I. 4. 6. p. 33. D. where consult our annotation.

**Page 1027, 1. καίπερ πτερὰ — λαβόντες. [although having taken wings]** Nicephorus ignores this. The same has *ἤρτησαν* [they hung]. Soon the same: *moving themselves from the pleasant toward the better of the soul's...* The same soon: *they were brought down again to actions with the...* with the rest omitted.

**— 8. ὀξύτητι ὀμμάτων [by sharpness of the eyes]** Niceph. *ὀμμ. ὀξ.* with the words *ὥσπερ ὑπὸ ὀξυδορκίας* [as if by sharp-sightedness] omitted, and soon *καὶ* [and] before *ἐνταῦθα* [here]. The same has *ὑπεριδών* [having overlooked]. And you would suspect Nicephorus cited this passage entirely from memory.

**— 11. ὥσπερ ἐκ — πλάνης εἰς πατρίδα εὔνομον ἀφικόμενος ἄνθρωπος [as if a man arriving from — wandering into a well-governed fatherland]** I will not repeat what I placed at the twin passage I. 6. 8. p. 57. A: "the fatherland is for us whence we came," especially in the Heidelberg edition of this book p. 352 sqq. and in the *Preparations* for it p. XCI. Here I will add some things more closely joined with our passage. And just as the author of the *Axiochus* says: "life is a certain temporary sojourn [*παρεπιδημία*]": so the Pythagoreans had already said. See Fischer’s note on that passage in Aeschines' *Dialogues* III. 3. p. 118. Philo Judaeus, *On the Confusion of Tongues* p. 417 Mangey ed. explaining the sentiment of Jacob (Genesis XLIX. 9) thus: — "to show that the wise man sojourns as if in a foreign sensible body, but dwells as if in a fatherland in intelligible virtues." Above I warned of a twin passage in the *Epistle to the Hebrews* XI. 13 sq. To it should be applied John Chrysostom, who has similar things in *Oration* XXIV, p. 1906 Commelin ed. I add very similar words of Theodorus Metochites, *Miscellanies* CXVI, p. 795 Müller and Kiessling ed.: — "and the truly upper fatherland and established and non-rebellious state/citizenship." Perhaps he imitated our Plotinus' *εὔνομον πατρίδα* [well-governed fatherland]. Certainly these words are to be translated so that you do not only say "legitimate fatherland" with Ficino, but *constituted with good laws*. A city of this kind is said to be *εὐνομεῖσθαι* [well-governed] by the same sentiment; which pertains equally to the land, the citizens, and the house. (Thomas Magister p. 391.) Herodotus on the Lacedaemonians I. 66: "thus indeed having changed they were well-governed." The same I. 97: "and thus the country will be well-governed." Plato *Laws* XII...

From these passages joined together this is produced: that there are three sources of beauty: the good, the intellect, the soul; but having removed the primary source, which is in the highest Good, no force of the secondary ones exists for the mind and the soul grows sluggish toward intelligible beauty. There follows our passage; with which you may compare what Plotinus placed above IV. 7. 12. p. 466. B.

**Page 1030, 14. Ἐγγὺς μὲν ἀληθείας — ψυχῇ [Near indeed to truth — to the soul]** Taylor did not express these words. Ficino expressed them and all books recognize them. Otherwise, there is no need to show laboriously that the source of this whole passage is in Plato’s *Timaeus*. See especially p. 28 sq. [p. 23 sqq. Bekker]. **— 18. οὐ γὰρ δὴ, ὡς οἴονται, ψυχὴ νοῦν τελειωθεῖσα γεννᾷ [for indeed, as they think, soul does not beget intellect having been perfected]** I would not precisely say that Anaxagoras is touched by Plotinus, who according to Aristotle's testimony (cf. *On the Soul* I. 2. p. 6 Sylburg ed.) had established: "that intellect is the same as the soul," or Democritus, who had contended the same, according to the same witness, ibid. p. 7. He might have touched other philosophers as well. Cf. John Philoponus on Aristotle’s *On the Soul* I. loc. cit. and in book II. number 32. Plotinus' opinion depends on Plato's decree in the *Timaeus* p. 30 [p. 26 Bekker]: "having established intellect in soul, and soul in body (the craftsman)." And indeed Plutarch speaks against that opinion which Plotinus rejects here. For thus *On the Generation of the Soul in the Timaeus* p. 1026. E. sq. Wyttenbach: "for the soul gives forth the passive part from itself, but it participated in intellect from a better principle being engendered in it." Cf. also Proclus' *Inst. Theol.* CXCIII. p. 288: "every soul immediately subsists from intellect, etc." Cf. ch. CXCIV. p. 290.

**Page 1031, 10. -> BOOK VIII. ENNEAD FIVE. pages 1009–1012. <-

I omit the rest. Regarding Plotinus, I ask whether the term *substance* <note>original: "substantiae"</note> has such force that the Lycopolitan Philosopher <note>Plotinus, who was born in Lycopolis, Egypt.</note> should be said to have understood the Ideas less incorporeally, or more corporeally (if I may use these terms for the sake of brevity) than Plato; for example, as if the Ideas, as substances, possessed various and changeable accidents, etc. If Richter intended this meaning, he has wandered entirely away from the mind of Plotinus. Just listen to these words of our Author in the next book, page 560. A: *Let Intellect indeed be the things that are, and let it have all things in itself, not as if in a place, but as having itself, and being one with them.* <note>original Greek: "Νοῦς μὲν δὴ ἔστω τὰ ὄντα..."</note> You see here that for Plotinus, the mind or intellect is "the things that are": in our passage, the same are the *Ideas*. What more do you seek? For Plotinus, *Ideas* are neither in the mind nor outside the mind, but are the same as the mind; and this is a most simple notion, which cannot be defined otherwise than that the Ideas *are*, and that they are the same as *beings* and *essences*. Nor do I judge the opinion of Plato himself to have been any different. This serves as an argument that those are mistaken who believe a difference exists between Plato’s doctrine of Ideas and that of Plotinus. What more? Indeed, I do not hesitate to profess that Plato’s decrees will be placed in a clearer light in several other doctrines as well, if his interpreters would be willing to apply themselves more studiously to Plotinus.

— 5. *And the wise men of the Egyptians seem to me...* <note>original Greek: "Δοκοῦσι δέ μοι καὶ οἱ Αἰγυπτίων σοφοὶ..."</note> Plato mentions the writing of the Egyptians in the *Phaedrus* page 274 and following, and in the *Philebus* page 18. I have praised many others both in my notes on Cicero’s *On the Nature of the Gods* III. 22. page 611, and especially in the *Commentaries on Herodotus* I. page 369 and following. Moreover, everyone knows that this matter has recently been discussed with great zeal by many, if they have looked into the writings of the Englishman Young and the Frenchman Champollion and others (cf. to omit others, Silvestre de Sacy in *Journal des Savans* 1827, and Letronne in the Appendix to the *Summary of the Hieroglyphic System* by Mr. Champollion the younger, page 376 and following, second edition). Because Plotinus, an Egyptian man, says in this place that the other method of writing used by the Egyptians—which we commonly call alphabetic, where the sounds of the voice are represented by the strokes of letters—was not used by the Egyptian priests; this must undoubtedly be understood in such a way that he means the books which were properly called "sacred," as those which contained the hidden doctrine of religions. (See the third annotation after this one).

— 7. *not going through them with the forms of letters...* <note>original Greek: "μὴ τύποις γραμμάτων διεξοδεύουσι..."</note> In the same matter, Philo uses <term>discursive reasoning</term> <note>original: "διεξόδοις" (diexodois), meaning a step-by-step or roundabout way of explaining something.</note> in *The Life of Moses* I. page 606. Hermias in Ast’s edition of Plato’s *Phaedrus* page 103: *insofar as the rational soul subsists from the intellect, it possesses the intellectual, by which it grasps the forms by simple intuitions and not discursively* <note>original: "διεξοδικῶς" (diexodikōs)</note> — and in the following: *and it acts and reasons discursively.* I have given other examples in the preface to Proclus on the *Alcibiades* page 249, and above regarding Plotinus page 189. B. and page 478. D.

— 10. *to manifest* <note>original Greek: "ἐμφῆναι" (emphēnai)</note>] I have restored this from many of the best books instead of "to grow in," and Diodorus Siculus III. 4. uses the expression "from the manifestation" <note>original: "ἐξ ἐμφάσεως"</note> in the same context. — Regarding the things in the following parts of this chapter which are more entangled, I have endeavored to assist by punctuation. In the fifth line from the end, *and that which results from seeking*, I fear that several words and perhaps some sentences have fallen out. The version—or rather paraphrase—of Ficino helps the understanding of the rest. Iamblichus in *The Life of Pythagoras* V. page 52, Kiessling’s edition, says of Pythagoras: *he attempted to make the manner of his teaching symbolic, and entirely similar to the teachings in Egypt according to which he was educated.* The same author in *On the Mysteries* VII. 1. page 150, Gale’s edition: *First indeed I wish to interpret for you the manner of the Egyptians' theology. For these, imitating the nature of the universe and the creation of the gods, themselves expressed certain images of mystic, hidden, and invisible conceptions through symbols, just as nature in a certain way modeled invisible principles through visible forms by means of symbols.* Regarding Hermes as the author of writing, consult Horapollo in *Hieroglyphics* I. 14.

— 12. *But later—they found out* <note>original Greek: "Ὕστερον δὲ—ἐξεύρισκον"</note>] These are the things which were also recorded in the so-called <term>hieratic</term> <note>The priestly cursive script.</note> forms of letters in the sacred commentaries of the Egyptians; whereas the books properly called sacred, that is, those which contained the hidden doctrine of religions, were written in <term>hieroglyphic</term> characters (which Plotinus calls "images" or "statues" <note>original: "ἀγάλματα" (agalmata)</note>) (see above). A third kind of writing, pertaining to the use of common life, also used letter characters rather than images, and was called <term>demotic</term> <note>The popular or common script.</note>.

page 1012, 6. *shall we perish?* <note>original Greek: "ἆρα ὀλώμεθα"</note>] The other reading "we might perish" could also be confirmed by passages in Plato, as in the *Gorgias*.
