Page 480. *how should we say* <note>original: "πῶς λέγωμεν"</note> where others have *we say* <note>original: "λέγομεν"</note>. See Heindorf on that dialogue, page 63 and page 109, and on the *Theaetetus* page 441; but compare Matthiae’s *Greek Grammar* § 516, note 2. Add, regarding the use of the Future tense in such interrogations, the *Philological Acts of Munich* volume I, page 232 and following.

Page 1012, line 15. *by the proximity to another in that which exists* <note>original: "τῇ ἐν τῷ ὄντι ἄλλο γειτονίᾳ"</note>] I have adopted this from several manuscripts. What the margin shows, *neighborhood* <note>original: "γειτονείᾳ" - a different spelling</note>, is worth nothing. (See Stephen’s *Thesaurus* page 2886, London edition. Soon, regarding the word *having communicated* <note>original: "διακοινησαμένης"</note>, consult Thomas Magister page 216, Oudendorp and Bernard’s *Letters of Aristaenetus* II. 7. page 149, Boissonade: *for communicating to both what seems best* and page 150: *if you wish—that I should cooperate and communicate with you again eagerly.* Compare also D'Orville on *Chariton* VIII. 8. page 641, Leipzig edition [p. 720, Amsterdam edition]. Perhaps after the words *of some soul* <note>original: "ἡ ψυχής τινος"</note> something has fallen out. In the following parts, we have adopted the reading of the margin everywhere, as the manuscripts support it and the sense itself commends it.)

Page 1014, line 2. *it traverses the high heavens, he says, and governs the whole universe* <note>original: "μετεωροπορεῖ, φησί, καὶ πάντα τὸν κόσμον διοikεῖ"</note>] Plato, of course, in the *Phaedrus* page 246 b. c. I treated this passage above at page 376 G. and page 470 C; consult the annotations there.

— line 5. *the earth—is round* <note>original: "ἡ γῆ—στρογγύλη"</note>] The round shape of the earth, which Herodotus (IV. 36) and Aristotle (*Meteorology* II. 5. page 55, Sylburg) had in some way mocked, is said to have been established by most of the Socratics (Cleomedes, *Meteors* VIII. page 40, page 51, Bake). The same opinion is defended by the famous Claudius Ptolemy both in the *Great Synthesis* or *Almagest* Book I, and in the *Geography* I. 7 and VII. 5. Compare Mannert’s *Geography of the Greeks and Romans* I. page 144 and following; Uckert’s *Geography of the Greeks and Romans* I. page 299; and Sickler’s *Handbook of Ancient Geography* page XLIV. Although the authority of this man [Ptolemy] was already very great in the third century, when Plotinus flourished, I would nevertheless believe that this philosopher followed the doctrines of the ancient Platonists in this matter as well.—Regarding the next part: *and the oblique* <note>original: "καὶ ὁ λοξὸς"</note> compare the twin passage in II. 9. 12. page 211 B. and the annotation there on the words *the obliquity of the zodiac* <note>original: "λόξωσις τῶν ζῳδίων"</note>.

— line 7. *of the syllogism—the conclusion—of the premises.* <note>original: "τοῦ συλλογισμοῦ—τὸ συμπέρασμα—τῶν προτάσεων"</note>] Compare Ocellus Lucanus I. 3; Aristotle, *Sophistical Refutations* I. 14. page 444, Sylburg; Quintilian, *Institutes of Oratory* V. 4; Ernesti’s *Lexicon of Greek Rhetorical Technology* page 325. Add Proclus on the *Alcibiades*, preface page 303, and Olympiodorus on the same, page 99; and compare our author himself below in VI. 7. 1. page 693 A.

Page 1015, line 4. *Wherefore also Plato etc.*—and below at C: *for he said he was struck with admiration—to make it like.* <note>original: "εἶπε γὰρ ἠγάσθη τε—ἀφομοιῶσαι"</note>] Plato in the *Timaeus* page 37 [page 36, Bekker]: *But when the father who begat it perceived that it moved and lived, having become an image of the eternal gods, he was struck with admiration and, being gladdened, he thought even more to work it so as to be similar to the paradigm.* From this it is understood that Plotinus does not report the passage of Plato entirely word-for-word. Simplicius likewise quotes it from memory in his commentary on Aristotle’s *Physics* IV. 166 and 265. Stobaeus also presents it in the *Physical Selections* I. 268. Compare Lindau’s *Annotations on Plato* at the cited place, who did not neglect our Plotinus. Soon, instead of *more active* <note>original: "ἐνεργεστέρων"</note> Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino, the Renaissance translator of Plotinus</note> seems to have read *clearer* <note>original: "ἐναργεστέρων"</note>. The manuscripts do not vary.

— line 17. *whence those who find fault with this do not do so rightly*] He is touching upon the Gnostic Manichaeans, and others who denied that this World was beautiful and good; about whom we have seen above in the Annotations to the books on this argument.

Page 1016, line 6. *Let there be then in the soul a certain luminous mental image etc.* <note>original: "Ἔστω οὖν ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ φωτεινή τις φαντασία"</note>] Again, that passage of Plato in the *Phaedo* page 113 is observed in this place by Plotinus: *a vision of blessed spectators*. See above page 546 B. Iamblichus, *On the Egyptian Mysteries* I. 12. page 23: *It is clear from the works themselves what we now say is the salvation of the soul. For in contemplating the blessed visions, the soul exchanges its life for another, etc.* on which passage Gale (page 196) says: "He [Iamblichus] calls this soul *divine-seeing* <note>original: "θεοπτικὴν"</note>." Then he calls upon others and this very passage of Plotinus. Clement of Alexandria, *Miscellanies* V. page 732, Potter edition: *when with the blessed chorus, according to Plato, we shall behold the blessed sight and vision, following with Zeus on our part, and others with other gods, being initiated into the rite which it is lawful to call most blessed.* Compare the beginning of the next chapter of our author, page 551 A.

— line 13. *with all the gods in it, being one and all—or rather the one is all* and below at E:—*great then is this heaven, and all the powers in it together.*] The tone is similar to those in the *Epinomis* among the Platonic dialogues, page 977 a. b. [page 346, Bekker]:—*what god then shall I ever speak of with reverence, O Megillus and Clinias? Nearly the heaven itself, which it is most just for all other spirits and gods together to honor and to pray to especially.—For if anyone goes toward a right contemplation of this, whether he calls it the universe or Olympus or heaven, let him be glad in the saying, but let him follow where it adorns itself and...*

*turning the stars within himself—he provides.* <note>original: "τὰ ἐν αὐτῷ ἄστρα στρέφων—παρέχεται"</note> Concerning the one god and the many existing simultaneously, Damascius writes in *On First Principles*, chapter 100, page 314 of Kopp’s edition: "Why say more? Since even regarding the gods, almost all philosophers before Iamblichus assumed the many in this way, saying that while the <term>super-essential</term> <note>original: "ὑπερούσιον" (hyperousios) - existing beyond the category of Being or substance</note> god is one, the others are <term>essential</term> <note>original: "οὐσιώδεις" (ousiōdeis) - possessing substance or being</note>, being made divine by the illuminations from the One."

page 1017, 12. *but now, through an ignorance of true power, they imagine themselves calling, and destroying, and crushing.* <note>original: "ἀλλὰ ἤδη ἀπειρίᾳ δυνάμεως ἀληθινῆς φαντάζονται καλοῦσαι, καὶ φθείρουσαι, καὶ θλίβουσαι"</note>] From the margin and several manuscripts, I have adopted *now* <note>original: "ἤδη" (ēdē)</note> instead of *forms* <note>original: "εἴδη" (eidē)</note>: and from two Marcian manuscripts, *calling* <note>original: "καλοῦσαι" (kalousai)</note> instead of *and being* <note>original: "καὶ οὖσαι" (kai ousai)</note>. This is because "to imagine" <note>original: "φαντάζεσθαι"</note> is in other places also the opposite of "to be" <note>original: "τοῦ εἶναι"</note>. (See our previous note on I. 6. 3. page 50. B.) Likewise, because the mention of fire seemed to require this, and because *crushing* <note>original: "θλίβουσαι"</note> agrees well with *calling*. Clearly, *destroying* <note>original: "φθείρουσαι"</note> pertains to the forces of all bodies, some of which kill by burning: others by thrusting, pressing, and shattering.—In defining the force of the noun *ignorance* <note>original: "ἀπειρίᾳ" (apeiria)</note>, Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino, the 15th-century Renaissance translator of Plotinus</note> hesitated and, as he often does, expressed it in two ways. I, believing the second meaning to be foreign to this passage, have included his words: *they consist in infinity and by the same hooks* <note>original: "infinitate constant ejusdemque uncinis inclusi"</note> within brackets: I did not wish to delete them here any more than similar instances elsewhere, lest the power of choice be taken away from learned readers.

— 18. *to be left behind* <note>original: "ἀπολειφθῆναι"</note>] The fact that the Cizensis manuscript has *to be intercepted* <note>original: "ἀποληφθῆναι"</note> belongs to that kind of confusion which spreads widely through ancient monuments, about which the most learned Haas recently warned, following others, in his notes on Leo Diaconus, page 211. D. In Plato’s *Symposium* page 220. A. (page 461 of Bekker’s edition), all recent editors following Ast on the *Republic* page 543 have adopted *intercepted* <note>original: "ἀποληφθέντες"</note>, though all the manuscripts show *left behind* <note>original: "ἀπολειφθέντες"</note>. One could certainly defend the latter plausibly if one wished to cite Xenophon’s *Memorabilia* I. 4. 8. or *Agesilaus* 11. 29. The judgment actually depends on history, of which we are ignorant.

page 1018, 6. *for the beautiful is more akin.* <note>original: "μᾶλλον γὰρ οἰκεία ἡ καλή"</note>] Ficino additionally expressed what is read in the margin of a single book: *and beauty* <note>original: "καὶ ἡ καλλονή"</note>. The remaining books reject this addition. For the argument of this entire passage, consult the book *On Beauty* above, I. 6. 3. and 4. page 52 and following, and the notes on it.

— 7. *Because of this—Zeus—proceeds first*] This is the same celebrated passage in Plato’s *Phaedrus* page 246. e. and 247 (page 41 and following in Bekker), so often mentioned by other philosophers and by our author himself. See, for example, above IV. 4. 9. page 403. C. and the citations there, and page 419. C. and page 544. C., to omit other instances which I have both cited above and which Heindorf (page 251 and following) and Ast (page 296 and following, and at the end of the *Republic* page 653 and following) collected for the *Phaedrus* passage. As for Heindorf’s belief that the name of "daemons" <note>divine spirits or lesser deities</note> also includes souls: in this he does not have the support of Plotinus, who explicitly adds "souls." The words that follow in Plato: *they travel toward the steep [path] already under (upon, according to Heindorf) the sub-celestial (celestial, according to Heindorf) arch* <note>original: "ἄκραν ὑπὸ τὴν ὑπουράνιον ἀψῖδα πορεύονται πρὸς ἄναντες ἤδη"</note>—these have given rise to many disputes among ancient interpreters, and according to Proclus in *On the Theology of Plato* IV. 16. page 215, Plato had formed for himself: *these three world-orders: the supra-celestial place, the celestial revolution, and the sub-celestial arch.* Shortly after, Plotinus himself mentions *a certain invisible place*: and mention of our Plotinus is made in those same disputes concerning the passage in the *Phaedrus*. For Proclus says in the place cited: "For the philosopher from Asine (namely Theodorus of Asine), following Plotinus, called that which proceeds immediately from the ineffable the 'sub-celestial arch,' as he philosophizes about these things in his work *On Names*." In our passage, there is no explicit mention of this <term>arch</term> <note>original: "ἀψίς" (apsis) - the vault of heaven</note>, nor elsewhere, as far as I know, in these *Enneads*; so that perhaps this testimony of Proclus is evidence that in that other edition of Plotinus’s books (of which we have found other traces) these matters were explained more fully somewhere.—I will add two passages: Philo the Jew, *On the Cherubim*, Vol. II. page 14 of Pfeiffer’s edition: *the furthest arch of the whole heaven.* Stobaeus, *Physical Eclogues* I. 27. page 550 of Heeren’s edition, concerning the moon: *having a hollow arch.* From which comes the diminutive *apsidion*; concerning which see Coray in *Atakta* II. page 77. Otherwise, compare Plotinus IV. 1. page 360. A.

page 1019, 17. *but for those who are, as it were, perpetually intoxicated and filled with nectar*] He borrowed this image from his beloved Plato, both from the *Phaedrus* page 247. end (page 43 Bekker) and from the *Symposium* page 203 (page 429 Bekker). The fact that *intoxicated* <note>original: "οἰνωθεῖσι"</note> is joined with the mention of <term>Nectar</term> in this place brings to mind Apuleius’s *Metamorphoses* VI. 125 (page 426 and following in Oudendorp): "*Then a cup of nectar, which is the wine of the gods, was served to Jove by that rustic boy of his, the cupbearer; but to the others, Liber [Bacchus] served it:*" where I think Oudendorp should be supported, who suspects the words *which is [the wine of the gods]* are glosses—

decided he should be freed from the [physical] condition. Also Lucian in *Lexiphanes* I. page 319, Wetsten. edition: <note>original: "νέκταρος γάρ τινος ἔοικας οἰνοχοήσειν ἡμῖν ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ"</note> "For you seem likely to pour out for us some nectar from it." Furthermore, what Plotinus adds, "and having been filled," is not superfluous, since the Greeks generally wish to distinguish "being affected by wine" <note>original: "οἰνώμενον"</note> from "being drunk" <note>original: "μεθύοντι"</note> (Wesseling on Diodorus I. 57. page 67; Mangey on Philo I. page 350). For above (following Plato in the passage from the *Symposium*) on page 299 A, he uses the term "to be drunk with nectar," <note>original: "μεθύειν τῷ νέκταρι"</note> and in the same place at D: "and there Porus <note>The personification of Plenty or Resource</note> sleeps, being weighed down by those things with which he was filled." Philo the Jew in *On the Planting of Noah*, page 234 a. page 148, Pfeiffer edition: <note>original: "Ἔστι τοίνυν τὸ μεθύειν διττόν..."</note> "Drunkenness is therefore twofold: one is equivalent to being affected by wine; the other is equivalent to talking nonsense while in wine." With these passages of Plotinus, however, these words of Proclus in *Platonic Theology* IV. 15. page 202 ought to be compared: <note>original: "ἡ δὲ τρόφιμος τῶν θεῶν αἰτία..."</note> "The nourishing cause of the gods is a certain intelligible union, containing within itself the whole perfection of the gods, and filling the gods with vigor and power, both for the providence of secondary beings and the unchanging intellection of primary ones. But above, the gods participate in these things in a unified way, while in their progressions they do so dividedly. Wherefore, of the nourishment, one part is called ambrosia in Plato’s work, and the other nectar. Toward the manger, he says (Plato in the passage from the *Phaedrus*), having stood the horses, he threw before them ambrosia, and gave them nectar to drink, etc." Julian, *Epistle* XXVII: "For to always hear and speak about them is nectar to me." This formula has attained the force of a proverb. See L. H. Heyler on that passage, page 291.

Page 1020, 3. <note>original: "ἀλλ’ ἔχει τὸ ὀξέως ὁρῶν ἐν αὐτῷ τὸ ὁρώμενον"</note> **"But the one seeing keenly has within himself the thing seen"**] The Vatican manuscript does not recognize the word "the" <note>original: "τὸ"</note>, and since Ficinus <note>Marsilio Ficino, the famous Renaissance translator of Plotinus</note> uses the masculine, I would indeed have restored "he who sees keenly" <note>original: "ὁ ὀξέως ὁρῶν"</note> if even one book had supported it, especially since all agree on the following word "having."

— 7. <note>original: "ὥσπερ εἴ τις ὑπὸ θεοῦ κατασχεθείς, Φοιβόληπτος ἢ ὑπό τινος Μούσης"</note> **"Just as if someone were possessed by a god, seized by Phoebus or by some Muse"**] In Herodotus IV. 13, several manuscript books offer this very word instead of the Ionic "shining Phoebus," <note>original: "φοιβόλαμπτος"</note> though less correctly. Longinus, *On the Sublime* XVI. 2. page 68, Weiske edition, regarding Demosthenes: "But since, just as if suddenly inspired by a god and becoming as it were **seized by Phoebus**, he uttered the oath concerning the best of the Greeks." Lycophron in *Cassandra* v. 1460 calls this very maiden "the **Phoebus-seized** swallow," which Tzetzes in the *Scholia* page 1046 explains as: "the prophetic one." And those are called **seized by Phoebus** <note>original: "φοιβόληπτοι"</note> or **god-borne** <note>original: "θεοφόρητοι"</note> who divine by the instinct of a spirit <note>original: "daemonis"</note>, whether good or evil, or who do anything else while not in control of their own minds. From here it is also transferred to poets and orators, as observed by Meric Casaubon on Antoninus XII in Gataker’s edition, page 420. Regarding what Plotinus adds: "or by some Muse (possessed)," he undoubtedly had before his eyes another passage of the *Phaedrus*. For thus on page 245 a. page 37, Bekker edition, Plato says: "The third is the **possession** <note>original: "κατακωχή"</note> and madness from the Muses, which, taking hold of a tender and untouched soul, awakening and throwing it into Bacchic frenzy in songs and other poetry, etc." The same in *Laws* VII. 790 d. e. page 6, Bekker: "Just as the cures for frantic Bacchic revelries use this movement together with dance and music." Philo the Jew seems to have had this passage before his eyes in *Who is the Heir of Divine Things*, page 482, Mangey edition (See our note on Cicero, *On Divination* I. 1. page 5, Moser edition). Himerius, *Oration* XIII. 7. page 596, Wernsdorf: "Just as the Bacchic one—for thus the lyre calls him, speaking of Dionysus—when spring has just first shone forth, poets **possessed by the Muses**, having crowned him with spring flowers and clusters of ivy, lead him, etc." Philo the Jew expressed the nearby words of the Platonic *Phaedrus* in *On Providence* in the Armenian and Latin version, page 77, Venice edition (where in the Greek write "arrives" <note>original: "ἀφίκηται"</note>), and likewise Plutarch in *On Moral Virtue* page 452 B. page 845, Wyttenbach: "For not only in poems, as Plato says, does the one **seized by the Muses** and possessed make the technical and precise poet appear ridiculous, etc." Olympiodorus in Plato’s *Alcibiades*, preface page 2: "The second **enthusiasm** is in the *Republic*, where having become **seized by the Muses**, Plato acted the part of the Muses, who in the same place in the *Timaeus* is said to be **seized by a god**; in the *Phaedrus*: **seized by nymphs**." Iamblichus accurately distinguishes the various types of "obsession" (so to speak) in *On the Mysteries* III. 5. page 65, Gale edition, from which passage I shall extract only the beginning: "There are indeed many kinds of divine **possession**, and in many ways the divine inspiration is stirred up; whence also its signs are many and different." Write "and different" <note>original: "καὶ διαφέροντα"</note>. For so say all the codices whose readings I possess. But the whole passage should be compared with that of Plotinus.

— 10. <note>original: "Εἰ δέ τις ἡμῶν ἀδυνατῶν ἑαυτὸν ὁρᾶν"</note> **"But if any of us, being unable to see himself..."**] Dionysius the Areopagite seems to have had the following words before his eyes in *On Divine Names* IV. 9. page 561: "The movement of the soul is: circular indeed, the entry into itself from external things, and the unified [entry] of its intellectual powers..."

It explores the distinction between mere intoxication and divine frenzy (enthusiasm) as metaphors for the soul's mystical experience.</summary>

...a winding-inward, as if bestowed upon her in a circle that is itself fixed and motionless, turning her away from the many things outside and gathering her first into herself, then—having become <note>original: "ἐνοειδῆ" (enoeidē)</note> like a single form—uniting her with the powers that are singularly unified, and thus leading her by the hand toward the Beautiful and the Good, which is above all beings, and is one and the same, without beginning and without end.

**Page 1021, line 6. He must—judge it himself]** Plotinus takes this word <note>original: "γνωματεύειν" (gnōmateuein) - to judge or discern</note> from his beloved Plato, *Republic* VII, page 516 at the end. Although Ruhnken, in his notes on Timaeus's *Platonic Lexicon*, pointed out this passage along with those of other imitators, he (as is often the case elsewhere) neglected to mention Plotinus here. As for the Scholion <note>A marginal explanatory note in a manuscript</note> found in the margin of some of our manuscripts, it is taken from the *Etymologicum Magnum*, or from Suidas, or Zonaras under that entry. See also the *Etymologicum Gudianum* and the end of Orion, as well as the Scholia on Plato. Philostratus, in the *Life of Apollonius* II. 30: "much lies in the eyebrows and cheeks to judge <note>gnōmateuein</note> and to observe." Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* VII: "judging what must be done by the standard of justice." Among others, Themistius wore this word out, as Ruhnken observed. In his 26th Oration, where the text had "to excel," Petavius found "to be a lord" in a manuscript, while he himself conjectured "to judge," though Ruhnken disapproved. Valckenaer wrote in the margin of my copy: "to distinguish." Leo Diaconus, speaking of Emperor Basil: "daily drawing up and training the phalanxes, and *judging* <note>exploring/discerning</note> in what manner he might attack the rebel." Shortly after the word "faith," it might seem a verb has fallen out, yet it can still refer back to "having learned." — Recently, from the Cizensis manuscript, I provided: "to those thoughts which come shining forth from there," that is, shining in the thoughts which come from that place. The printed edition and other books have "of such a kind."

**Page 1022, line 2. as of evils—Disease]** Disease in a living creature is a vice <note>original: "κακία" (kakia)</note>. See Plato’s *Sophist* 228d. Olympiodorus praises this passage in his commentary on the *Alcibiades*: from which, regarding what follows, let us hold onto these: "for there are three things usually spoken of: I, that which is mine, and the things belonging to what is mine."

**Page 1023, line 4. having welcomed—the splendor]** <note>original: "ἀγλαίαν ἀσμενίσας" (aglaian asmenisas)</note> Compare Wyttenbach on Plutarch’s *On Virtue and Vice*, who collected examples of this construction with both the Accusative and Dative cases.

**— line 6. Zeus appeared as a child etc.—and the following page A. For he also has life]** Plotinus refers partly to the same passage in the *Phaedrus* (246e) which we praised several times above, and partly to the *Cratylus* (396a) where he speaks of *Zēn* <note>Zeus</note> as the author of life <note>original: "ζωῆς" (zōēs)</note>, and of *Diì* <note>Zeus</note> as the son of Cronus, about whom Plato says in the same place: "it is reasonable that Zeus is the offspring of some great intellect."

**— line 15. Because they do not (seem to) rightly—those who destroy (the sensible world)—and thus give birth]** There is in these words the same elegance of brevity which we encountered above in IV. 5. 2. regarding "those who pour out their sights." This passage differs from the others we collected because it uses a Pronoun with a finite Verb instead of a Participle.

**Page 1024, line 3. God, therefore, who is bound so as to remain in the same state]** Perhaps it should be translated: *so that he might always remain in the same state*. Regarding this and what follows, I will not repeat what I gathered in *Meletemata* I and on Cicero’s *On the Nature of the Gods*: "He was bound by Jove, lest he should have immoderate courses," etc. The source of our passage is in Plato’s *Cratylus* 396b, and likewise in the *Timaeus* 42: "And he, having arranged all these things, remained in his own accustomed nature. And while he remained, the children, having understood the father’s arrangement, obeyed it," etc. Proclus disputes much regarding that passage in the *Cratylus*; from which I will excerpt these few points which most apply to these Plotinian matters: "Let no one think because of these things that the activities described among the gods are divided, such as providence being in Zeus alone, or the turning toward oneself being in Cronus alone, or the ascent <note>corrected to "extension"</note> toward the intelligible being in Uranus alone: for Zeus does not provide for worldly things in any other way than by looking toward the intelligible; 'whatever and of what kind the ideas are that the Mind sees existing in the Living Being,' says the *Timaeus*. And Orpheus says with a divinely inspired mouth that Zeus 'swallows' his ancestor Phanes, and takes all his powers into his own bosom, and becomes all things intellectually—"

<note>The following Greek passage discusses the Neoplatonic interpretation of the god Cronus as "Intellect" (Nous).</note> ...clearly all those things that he was intellectually, and Cronus gives over <note>original: ἐνδίδωσι; Manuscript V reads ἐκδίδωσι, "surrenders"</note> to Zeus the principles of all creation and of providence toward sensible things; and by thinking upon himself, he is united to the very first intelligible beings and is filled with the goods from that source.—If, therefore, the "intelligible" is food, then Cronus is sated <note>original: διακορής, "fully satisfied"</note>, not only with the intelligible things corresponding to him, but also with the highest and most hidden thoughts <note>The editor notes: perhaps read "thought" in the singular, unless you wish to refer it back to "food."</note>. Damascius in the Munich Manuscript, folio 244: "Then they also hymn Cronus himself as the Creator, having beheld for himself the first undertaking <term>procheirismos: the initial preparation or taking in hand</term> of creation." (Schaefer added the word *procheirismos* from our *Meletemata* to the New Stephanus Thesaurus, page 10501.) The next passage of Plotinus: "being between a better father etc." was treated by Cudworth in *The True Intellectual System of the Universe*, Book IV, chapter 36, page 687, edited by Mosheim. Compare Plotinus above, page 487 and page 512 following.

**Page 1024, line 4. For it was not according to his character,]** We have written it thus following most manuscripts: "For it was neither fitting, nor was it becoming for him." See Viger on *Greek Idioms*, IX. 8. 3 and 4, and Matthiae’s *Greek Grammar*, section 590, second edition.

**— 7. and he established again the things on the other side, beginning from his son to exist after him]** That is: he arranged again even the contrary things (that is, the inferior things which tend toward the lower: <note>original: πρὸς τὸ κάτω</note>) making a beginning from his son (that is: from the first things that come after Zeus) so that they might exist after him (Zeus). He took the formula "beginning from the son" from Plato; regarding which see my friend Heusde’s *Specimen on Plato*, page 39; Heindorf on the *Gorgias*, section 60, page 83; Buttmann on the *Alcibiades*, preface page 116; Sturz’s *Xenophon Lexicon*, volume I, page 427; and Matthiae’s *Greek Grammar*, section 557, page 1100, second edition.—Presently, perhaps one should write "by the bond toward the lower." But I fear a greater error lies hidden. Then "that according to beauty," that is, so that beauty can pertain to him. Regarding this locution, see Ast on Plato’s *Republic*, page 393, and what I myself placed in the notes to Proclus’s *Elements of Theology*, page 196 following, where it is placed after a comparative adverb: "and more greatly than according to the similarity of secondary things to the first among beings."

**— 15. If therefore the soul of the universe—and Aphrodite]** See the passage of the Platonic Timaeus concerning the generation of the soul, page 34 following, page 31 following in Bekker’s edition; and compare Plotinus III. 5. 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8.

**Page 1025, line 3. since even when they themselves are beautiful etc.]** Compare above, page 463 A; also page 54 F; especially page 55 D; and what we have annotated on this passage both in this edition and in the Heidelberg edition, page 292 following.

**— 7. or again one must approach by another way.]** I added "again" <note>original: πάλιν</note> from several good manuscripts. See above IV. 4. 19 at the beginning, and the annotation there. For the rest, these final words of the chapter have a certain natural quality which is wonderfully effective at moving the soul.

-> ### BOOK IX. <-

**Page 1026, line 7. ON INTELLECT (some books say "the" intellect, but in Porphyry’s edition the article is also absent) AND THE IDEAS AND BEING]** The fifth book according to chronological order. See Porphyry’s *Life of Plotinus*, chapter IV, compared with chapter XXV at the end. The argument of this book is related to those same dialogues of Plato which we indicated for the preceding book, and no less to Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*. Most of the Platonic philosophers contribute to this. It is helpful to set down these words of Alcinous from *The Doctrines of Plato*, chapter 10, page 474: "Furthermore, he (Plato) accepts other principles: the exemplary, that is, the Ideas; and that of the Father and God, the cause of all. The Idea is, in relation to God, his thinking; in relation to us, the primary intelligible; in relation to matter, a measure; in relation to the sensible world, a model; and examined in itself, it is essence." Compare also Porphyry’s *Sentences*, chapters XXIII–XXVI. Philoponus, in his commentary on Aristotle’s *On the Soul*, seems to have had this book before his eyes, as in Book III, folio Q, page 7 of the Venice edition: "Plotinus understood the human intellect as intellect in activity <term>energeia: actualized function</term>, one part always acting, the other acting only sometimes. Plotinus was led astray by Plato; for hearing from him that the soul is 'always-moving' <term>aeikinētos</term>, he thought he meant it was always-moving by always thinking, and because of this he thinks there is an intellect always thinking. Plotinus says, therefore, that he calls the human intellect 'intellect in activity' as that which is always thinking." The same author, ibid. page 8: "But Plotinus was deceived by the 'always acting,' and he hypothesized in us an intellect always acting, and this he called 'intellect in activity'." This book is expressly praised by Syrianus in his commentary on Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*, Book II, chapter 4, in the Latin edition of Syrianus, Venice 1580, folio 29 b:—"*But that there is a form of the separable form, he (Aristotle) clearly signifies by adding: it is necessary that there be some form and species beyond the whole together. If, however, someone posits this again;*"

<meta>This page continues the scholarly commentary on Plotinus's Enneads, specifically Book 9 of the Fifth Ennead. The text focuses on the origin of Ideas (Forms) and the soul's journey back to its true "fatherland."</meta>

there is a doubt as to which things he will place [Ideas] in, and which he will not. For it is manifest that it is not possible in all things. For we would certainly not posit that there is some "house" beyond certain houses, a point which Parmenides <note>The Greek philosopher featured in Plato's dialogue of the same name</note> was accustomed to doubt: he himself asks this, in which things there is an Idea, and of which there is not. "This has been discussed accurately, therefore, in the *Commentaries on the Parmenides* by the divine Iamblichus, and it is also set down in Plotinus in the consideration *On Intellect, Ideas, and Being*." Compare the same work, folio 20. a. where Plotinus is likewise praised in the same cause, and no less so on folio 6. a. b. The same Syrianus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and teacher of Proclus</note> says on folio 35. a. b: "*Aristotle begins to argue for the opposite, and says it is a matter of the greatest doubt for those who suppose a discourse on the substance of beings. Indeed, it is a profound consideration how all things subsist from the One—which has no duality nor appearance of multitude in itself, nor diversity—as Plotinus, Porphyry, Iamblichus, and all who have been more carefully occupied with this problem declare.*" Finally, on folio 65. a. after he explained "*of which beings there are Ideas, and of which there are not,*" he proceeds thus: "*Those things which happen only to bodies have determined causes in the 'reasons' of nature, according to the opinion of Iamblichus. For Plotinus notes that the Idea of whiteness <note>original: "albedinis"</note> is not to be placed in the Intellect. Therefore, that of which there is one concept in many things is not necessarily an Idea, etc.*" You should compare the above, page 181, where Plotinus mentions whiteness, and also compare Simplicius in his commentary on Aristotle’s *Physics*, Book I, commentary 25, folio 27. b. of the Latin Paris edition, 1544. — T. Taylor translated this book into English in *Select Works of Plotinus*, page 284 and following.

page 1026, 9. **All men—using sense-perception before intellect etc.** <note>original Greek: Πάντες ἄνθρωποι—αἰσθήσει πρὸ νοῦ χρησάμενοι</note>] This chapter agrees with Plato in the *Phaedo*, page 81, page 52 and following in Bekker's edition, for which passage you should consult Wyttenbach, page 208. Synesius refers to the same passage of Plato on page 144, to which Nicephorus <note>Nicephorus Gregoras, a Byzantine scholar</note> in his *Scholia* (page 394) says: "(By nature) these things hold to the opinion of Plato, but no less to that of Plotinus. For Plotinus says that all men, etc." Indeed, Nicephorus inserted this entire first chapter into his *Scholia*.

In the same place, **having become** <note>original: γενόμενοι</note>] Nicephorus does not recognize this word. Shortly after, instead of **having applied themselves** <note>original: προσβαλόντες</note> he has: **having first associated with** <note>original: πρῶτον ὁμιλήσαντες</note>. Then he omitted the words: **with the first things—they lived through.**

— 13. **they thought it sufficient** <note>original: ἀρκεῖν ἐνόμισαν</note>] Nicephorus: *they thought it sufficient if they pursued some things and averted others, and this was considered wisdom by them, after the manner of heavy birds*—omitting the rest.—As for the word **getting rid of** <note>original: ἀποσκευαζόμενοι</note> which is found written in the margin of some Manuscripts for **managing to get away** <note>original: ἀποικονομόυμενοι</note>, we encountered the same interpretation above in the manuscript books I. 4. 6. page 33. D. where you may consult our note.

page 1027, 1. **although having taken wings.** <note>original: καίπερ πτερὰ—λαβόντες</note>] Nicephorus ignores this. The same has **they hung.** Soon the same: **moving themselves from the pleasant toward the better of the soul.** The same soon: **they were carried down again to actions with the name of the [active life]**, omitting the rest.

— 8. **by sharpness of eyes** <note>original: ὀξύτητι ὀμμάτων</note>] Nicephorus: *by sharpness of eyes*, omitting the words *as if by clear-sightedness*, and soon *and* before *here*. The same has *looking down upon*. And you might suspect that Nicephorus cited this passage entirely from memory.

— 11. **just as a man arriving from wandering into a well-governed fatherland** <note>original: ὥσπερ ἐκ—πλάνης εἰς πατρίδα εὔνομον ἀφικόμενος ἄνθρωπος</note>] I will not repeat what I placed at the twin passage I. 6. 8. page 57. A: *the fatherland is for us whence we came*, especially in the Heidelberg edition of this book, page 352 and following, and in the *Preparation* for it, page XCI. Here I will add some things more closely connected with our passage. And just as the author of the *Axiochus* says: *life is a kind of temporary sojourn* <note>original: παρεπιδημία</note>: so the Pythagoreans had already said. See Fischer’s Note to that passage in Aeschines' *Dialogues* III. 3. page 118. Philo the Jew in *On the Confusion of Tongues*, page 417 (Mangey edition), explaining the sentiment of Jacob in Genesis 49:9, says: —*to show that the wise man dwells as a stranger as if in a foreign sensible body, but lives as if in a fatherland in the intelligible virtues.* Above I gave a reminder of a twin passage in the *Epistle to the Hebrews* 11:13 and following. To that should be added John Chrysostom, who has similar things in Oration 24, page 1906 of the Commelin edition. I add the very similar words of Theodorus Metochites in *Miscellanies* 116, page 795 (Müller and Kiessling edition):—*and the truly upward fatherland and the established and peaceful citizenship.* Perhaps he imitated the **well-governed fatherland** <note>original: εὔνομον πατρίδα</note> of our Plotinus. Certainly these words are to be translated so that you do not merely say "legitimate fatherland" with Ficino, but **constituted by good laws**. A city of this kind is said to be **well-governed** <note>original: εὐνομεῖσθαι</note> in the same sense; which pertains equally to the land, the citizens, and the home. (Thomas Magister, page 391.) Herodotus says of the Lacedaemonians (I. 66): *having changed in this way, they became well-governed.* The same (I. 97): *and thus the country will be well-governed.* Plato, *Laws* XII.

**Page 950 and following:** He says three times: *a well-governed city* <note>original: "πόλις εὐνομουμένη"</note>. Aristotle, *Politics* IV. 8. page 109. below Sylburg, where it is *a well-governed and aristocratic city*. The same in II. 1. page 23: *which (constitutions) some of the cities said to be well-governed employ*. Libanius in *Odysseus* Vol. IV. page 17. Reiske: *since even among the Greeks themselves in the well-governed cities*: where I do not know from where Reiske added *especially* <note>original: "μάλιστα"</note> in a note; no one who has weighed the force of this word will miss that little particle.

**Page 1027, 15. as one inclined to love** <note>original: "ἅτε ἐρωτικὼς"</note>] Compare *Enneads* I. Book III. chapters 2 and 3. page 20. and following, and the *Preparation for Plotinus on Beauty* page 104 of the Heidelberg edition. For the following: *towards the beauties of the soul* <note>original: "ἐπὶ τὰ τῆς ψυχῆς καλὰ"</note> apply what we placed in the preceding book on *Intelligible Beauty* page 543. E.

**Page 1028, 1. if there should be anything again before this** <note>original: "εἴ τι ἂν πάλιν αὖ πρὸ τούτου"</note>] Namely, *it would be* <note>original: "εἴη"</note>, if you leave *should* <note>original: "ἂν"</note> untouched, which is absent from several books. For if that which the Condition contains is posed as being probable, or likely to happen, *if* <note>original: "εἰ"</note> is most especially joined with *should* <note>original: "ἂν"</note>. See Reisig, *Critical Commentary on Sophocles' Oedipus at Colonus* page 399. and compare Matthiae, *Greek Grammar* § 525. 7. note 10. add Stallbaum on Plato’s *Symposium* in the Greek Library Vol. I. part 3. page 150. and our own Voemel’s *Annotations on Demosthenes' First Philippic* § 18. page 174. and following.

— **5. this beauty which is upon bodies—what then is it that made the body beautiful?**] Compare to these and the following passages above page 50. C. D. and page 55. E. For what Plotinus encompasses there in a small circuit of words, he explains more richly and plainly in this place. He also deals copiously with these very things in the book: *How the multitude of ideas exists and concerning the Good itself* page 714. and following and page 724. and following. From these places joined together, this is established: there are three sources of beauty: *the Good, the Intellect, and the Soul*; but if the primary source, which is in the highest Good, is removed, no power of the secondary sources exists for the mind, and the soul is numb toward intelligible beauty. Indeed, even in the beauty of bodies, a certain flash of the highest good shines forth. Compare *Annotations on the book On Beauty* page 293. and following, Heidelberg edition.

— **15. but Intellect—as if in the vestibule of the Good** <note>original: "νοῦς δὲ—ὥσπερ ἐν προθύροις τἀγαθοῦ"</note>] Plato, *Philebus* page 64. page 246 Bekker (220 Stallbaum): *Socrates: Would we not then perhaps speak correctly in a certain way by saying that we now stand at the vestibule of the Good and of the dwelling of such a thing?* Compare ibid. page 62. page 242 Bekker (208—210 Stallbaum) where compare Olympiodorus' *Scholia* page 283. and following, edited by Stallbaum. Proclus also touches upon the Platonic passage in *Platonic Theology* V. 28. page 309. and likewise in the *Preface to Alcibiades* page 111 of our edition, where he says: *beauty in the very first ranks of the good things*. Damascius, *On Principles* chapter XXXIII. page 89. Kopp: —*which Socrates also showed through the three monads appearing in his vestibule in whatever way: truth, beauty, and symmetry; the latter providing order in all things, beauty providing the sympathetic blending with one another, and truth providing existence, as that which truly belongs to that One, all things together ineffably.*

**Page 1029, 1. It must be inspected** <note>original: "Ἐπισκεπτέον"</note>] What the Vatican manuscript offers, *It must yet be inspected* <note>original: "Ἔτι σκεπτέον"</note>, pertains to a confusion very widely spread through the monuments of Greek writers; concerning which Valckenaer collected many observations of critics in his *Lectures on the Epistle to the Hebrews* XI. 14. Vol. II. page 579. As for what the two Marcian manuscripts have next, *and—to go the way* <note>original: "καὶ—ὁδὸν ἰέναι"</note>, it might perhaps please one who considers that it is common to use *to go, to journey, to send a way*. Xenophon, *Cyropaedia* II. 4. 13. Plato, *Republic* VI. 506. C. page 315 Bekker, and more which Matthiae collected in *Greek Grammar* § 409. 4. The common reading confirms Bos’s opinion on *Ellipses* page 441. page 718 Schaefer.

— **8. all composite things—by art—by nature**] Wyttenbach applied our passage to the words of Plato in the *Phaedo* chapter 26. page 36, which are punctuated by him thus: *to that which has been put together and is composite by nature, it is fitting to suffer this, to be divided in the same way it was put together* <note>original: "τῷ μὲν συντεθέντι καὶ συνθέτῳ ὄντι φύσει..."</note> i.e. "*to that which was made by composing, and that which is composite by its own nature; so that two kinds of composites are signified; one 'put together,' made by art, and not having arisen so from the beginning: the other so born, and existing by its own nature, 'being composite by nature.'*" And Plotinus seems to refer to this in what he says. Our passage follows; with which you may compare what Plotinus placed above in IV. 7. 12. page 466. B.

— **13. and mixtures** <note>original: "καὶ συγκρίματα"</note>] See above page 103. G.

— **16. for matter by itself—is formless** <note>original: "ὕλη γὰρ παρ’ αὐτῆς—ἄμορφος"</note>] Thus I have written with one Marcian and Munich manuscript, and from Ficino I added *you will seek the form* <note>original: "τὸ εἶδος—ζητήσεις"</note>, which sentiment Taylor thought should be omitted in his version since he had not found it in the Greek editions. In the third place, I received a fuller reading with Ficino and two Codices: *that which is as form before that which is form* <note>original: "τὸ δὲ ὡς εἶδος προ τὸ δὲ εἶδος"</note>: finally, with several books supporting it, *as that upon the—shape* <note>original: "ὡς ἡ ἐπὶ τῷ—μορφᾷ"</note>, instead of *as upon the—shape*.

# BOOK IX. ENNEAD FIVE. Pages 1027–1034. 315

**Page 1030, 14. *Close to the truth—the soul***] <note>original: "Ἐγγὺς μὲν ἀληθείας—ψυχῇ"</note> Thomas Taylor did not translate these words. Ficino did, and all the manuscripts recognize them. Furthermore, there is no need to laboriously demonstrate that the source of this entire passage is Plato’s *Timaeus*. See especially page 28 and following, and page 23 and following in Bekker’s edition. Regarding the **Craftsman Mind** <term>demiurgos nous: the divine intellect that fashions the universe</term>, see Proclus on the *Alcibiades*, preface, page 311.

— **18. *For it is certainly not the case, as they think, that the soul, having been perfected, generates the mind***] <note>original: "οὐ γὰρ δὴ, ὡς οἴονται, ψυχὴ νοῦν τελειωθεῖσα γεννᾷ"</note> I would not say precisely that Plotinus is targeting Anaxagoras, who, according to Aristotle (see *On the Soul* I. 2), established that "the mind is the same as the soul," or Democritus, who contended the same thing in the same source. He may have touched upon other philosophers as well. See John Philoponus’s commentary on Aristotle’s *On the Soul* and in Book II, number 32. Plotinus’s opinion depends on Plato’s decree in the *Timaeus*: "setting mind within soul, and soul within body" (the Craftsman). Indeed, Plutarch speaks against that opinion which Plotinus rejects in this passage. For he says in *On the Generation of the Soul in the Timaeus*: "For the soul gives off the passive element from itself, but it participates in the mind which comes into it from a higher principle." See also Proclus, *Elements of Theology*, CXCIII: "Every soul subsists immediately from Mind," etc. See also chapter CXCIV.

**Page 1031, 10. *For if that which is in the world is in body and matter, nothing remains the same***] Archytas of Tarentum, in the book *On Mind and Sense Perception* (found in Stobaeus): "Similarly, both sense and mind behave; for sense [uses] the sensible object [perhaps we should write 'the sensible'], and the sensible object both moves and changes and never rests in the same state; therefore, seeing becomes more or less, better and worse. But mind [uses] the intelligible, and the intelligible is by its essence unchanging; therefore, to think the intelligible is neither more nor less, nor better nor worse." <note>The editor notes a dialect correction from "cheiron" to "cherēon" typical of Pythagorean fragments.</note>

— **14. *One must grasp the Mind, etc.***] John Philoponus and Syrianus had these and the following words before their eyes in their respective commentaries on Aristotle. I have placed the passages from both above at the Title of this book on page 555. Tennemann also touched on these in his *History of Philosophy*, Vol. VI.

**Page 1032, 12. *For the form in them—an image—is a likeness of that one.***] Archytas in Stobaeus: "And bodies, in which there is a certain resistance, are sensible; but those things participating in the forms are objects of opinion, like images—for instance, a particular man compared to 'Man' itself, or a particular triangle compared to 'Triangle' itself." See also Plato’s *Timaeus*, 28 A.

— **14. *And if indeed a maker—of this universe***] Plato in the *Timaeus*: "Now to find the maker and father of this universe, etc." See our own author [Plotinus] above, pages 175, 260, and 406.

**Page 1033, 6. *But like a lawgiver—the law itself of being***] Similar things are found in Plato’s *Laws* and *Minos*, as well as in the *Philebus* where Stallbaum cited other passages. Add Archytas in the fragments of the book *On Law*. The Ancients reciprocated this sentiment, in that they frequently called law the "mind of nature." See Cicero, *On Laws* I. 6. 8.

— **15. *from the art of statue-making***] <note>original: "παρὰ ἀνδριαντοποιϊκῆς"</note> I did not hesitate to adopt this form, even though two of our books offer "andriantopoiētikēs" [a more common form of the word]. A similar variation occurs in Plato’s *Gorgias* regarding the word for "cookery." This form for "statue-making" should be added to the Lexicons. — Soon after in section D, line 4, perhaps we should read: "both a statue and a couch."

**Page 1034, 2. *For the nature of bodies desires to be saved by another***] <note>original: "σωμάτων γὰρ φύσις σώζεσθαι παρ’ ἄλλου θέλει"</note> He alludes to the Etymology of the word **body** <term>soma</term>. Plato in the *Cratylus*: "It seems to me most likely that those around Orpheus established this name (body/soma) as the soul paying a penalty..."

**p. 1034, 5. *Now let Mind indeed be the beings* etc.]** **Brucker** touched upon this passage in ***Hist. Crit. Philosoph.* II. p. 401.** Compare above p. 518 G. and the things I have discussed at V. 8. 5. near the end p. 547 B.

— **13. *and the powers of seeds—but another account of hands—having been known*.**] Aristotle, *On the Generation of Animals* I. 18. p. 186 Sylb.: "so that the seed is that of the hand, or of the face, or of the whole animal—an undefined hand, or face, or whole animal; and just as each of those is in actuality, so the seed is in potentiality, either according to its own bulk, or because it has a certain power in itself. For this is not yet clear to us from what has been defined, whether the body of the seed is the cause of generation, or whether it has a certain habit and principle of generative motion; for neither the hand, nor any other of the parts, is a hand without soul or some other power, nor is it any part at all, but only homonymous [called so by name only]." Plotinus perhaps had these very words before his eyes in this place. — **Next: *The powers therefore—to each of them before each* [m. oun tōn—dunameōn]** holds nothing of wonder in other writers, let alone in Plotinus. Regarding what follows (B. line 4), Taylor orders it to be read: "but the whole mind contains all things just as a genus contains species": no Manuscript supports this, nor is there a need for "all things" (*panta*) to be added.

**p. 1035, 4. *not pushing nor using the much-talked-of leverings* etc.]** i.e., as it is commonly said, not by a mechanical ratio, but by a dynamic one. Concerning the Plotinian formula, consult what we annotated above at p. 344 A. and 380 B. I have received *ton logon* [the account] from the good books instead of the vulgar *tōn logōn*.

— **6. *Knowledge—of sensibles—but the name of opinion fits them.—but of intelligibles—knowledge***] Archytas in Stobaeus, *Eclogues* I. 51. p. 788. (after those things we placed above at page 558 C. below, which are to be compared) continues thus: "knowable things are those that follow upon forms by necessity, as in geometry the things following upon shapes. But the intelligibles are the forms themselves, and the principles of the knowables; such as the circle itself, and the triangle, and the sphere." Iamblichus, *Life of Pythagoras* XXIX. 159. p. 336 Kiessl.: "Pythagoras called wisdom the knowledge of the truth in beings (compare, however, many Manuscripts do not recognize the small words *tēs en*, which escaped Kiessling); he knew and called beings those things which are immaterial and eternal and alone active, which is to say the incorporeal; the rest are beings homonymously and called so according to participation, namely bodily and material forms, both generated and perishable, and truly never being; but wisdom is the knowledge of the primary beings, but not of the homonymous ones, since indeed bodily things are not even knowable nor do they admit certain knowledge, being infinite and incomprehensible to science and as it were non-beings by distinction from the universals, nor are they able to fall under the eye in a well-defined way; but of those things which are not by nature knowable, it is not even possible to conceive of a knowledge. Therefore it is not likely that there is a desire for a non-existent knowledge, but rather for that which concerns the primary beings, which always remain according to the same things and in the same way, and which always coexist with the true appellation." This passage of Plotinus is especially connected with Plato's discussion in the *Theaetetus* p. 152 sqq. and p. 208. p. 317 Bekk.: "knowledge—to be right opinion with an account." Maximus Tyrius XVI. 6. p. 298 Reisk.: "for the discovery of the soul, being a certain self-generated, natural, and innate thing, what else is it but true opinions being awakened, by whose awakening and arrangement the name is knowledge." Cf. regarding the *epistemonikos* [scientific] and *doxastikos* [opinative] Proclus on the *Alcibiades* pr. p. 100. The same in the same place, accommodating himself to the nearest things of Plotinus p. 311, calls knowledge a "offspring of mind." Especially compare Plotinus himself IV. 9. 5., VI. 1. 6., VI. 5. 10. end, VI. 6. 16. and VI. 9. 4.

— **11. *and from within they have both the intelligible and the intellection* etc.]** To this point belong these words of Simplicius on the *Categories* of Aristotle, Fol. 48 b: "But since it is necessary to examine even opposing accounts, even if they are not true, lest those who are more superficial be deceived when argued against by the knowledgeable, he proposes a refutation of the aforementioned well-regarded account. For he says it does not seem true in all cases that relatives are simultaneous by nature. For the sensible and the knowable seem prior, the former to sensation, the latter to knowledge."

### PAGE 332
**[Original page: 317]**

**— BOOK IX. OF THE FIFTH ENNEAD. p. 1034—1038 —**

"And he shows this, first from evidence; for he says that for the most part, since things pre-exist, we receive the sciences. For we approach them as they exist, and when we were altogether infants, the knowable things which later came to us were even then present, but the knowledge of them was not yet present. And the knowledge of the eclipse came later to the Greeks through Thales, but the eclipse itself and the knowable pre-existed. But this is more evident; yet there are some few things in which knowledge is simultaneous with the knowable. The intelligibles without matter (cf. also Plotinus VI. 9. 4.) are together with the knowledge that always stands according to activity, whether there is some such thing in us always remaining above, as it seems to Plotinus and Iamblichus, or in the mind according to activity, if someone should choose to call that intellection 'knowledge.' It can also be said through the subsistence of common things by abstraction. For simultaneously with the subsistence of these is knowledge. It is true also in the case of fabrications, both those in the imagination and those of art. For a chimera and the knowledge of a chimera are simultaneous. Why then did he add 'or in none'? Either because some people were doing away with universals and intelligibles, and things conceived in any way whatever; or because even if these things are in nature, we received the conceptions of them later? And because of this, it happens even in these cases that the knowable pre-exists the knowledge. Thus, therefore, according to the former argument, he seems to show that the knowable is prior to knowledge, and not simultaneous by nature. But according to the second assault, since 'prior' is said in many ways, as he himself will later teach, he uses it in one way now, insofar as the prior by nature does away with the other, but is not done away with by it." etc.

**p. 1035, 14. *but it stands in itself* etc.]** Plato in the *Cratylus* p. 437 A. p. 114 Bekk.: "Let us then consider, taking up from them first this name, 'knowledge' (*epistēmē*), how it is ambiguous and rather seems to signify that it *stays* (*histēsin*) our soul upon things rather than that it is carried around with them (cf. the same dialogue p. 412 A.)—then 'certainty' (*bebaion*), that it is an imitation of a certain base (*basis*) and status (*stasis*), but not of motion." Cf. also Plato's *Definitions* p. 414. p. 570 below Bekk. Maximus Tyrius *Dissert.* XII. 4. p. 216 following Reisk.: "Perhaps then sensation and experience are not a human thing, but reason is proper to man; and knowledge would be nothing else (Rightly Markland orders *an* to be interposed after *ouden*. See Matth. Gr. § 514 p. 976 sq.) except the certainty of reason journeying according to the same things" etc. What Markland wishes to be written for "human thing" (*anthrōpinon*), "proper to man" (*anthrōpou idion*), is indeed plausible, but not necessary: certainly I would change nothing without manuscripts, and things are called "human" which are proper to men, both with respect to animals, as in this place, and to gods, as in Iamblichus *On the Pythagorean Symbols* V. p. 330 Kiessling.

**p. 1036, 6. *If therefore intellection is truly one.***] Edition: *enontos*, which Ficinus expressed. I have received the reading of the margin, a trace of which appears in Cod. Marc. A. Taylor agrees with me, who translates thus: "If, therefore, intelligence is truly one, that from which is the object of its perception and idea itself are one." Soon from the Marcian Manuscripts, I wrote *holos* for *holōs men ho nous*.

**p. 1037, 5. *so that being in [en onta] they might have the mind upon themselves***] Thus I wrote with most books instead of *echein*. Ficinus, moreover, expressed *enonta* for *en onta*, and that seems true. However, I was unwilling to receive it without the manuscripts. Soon from all the books and from Ficinus's version, I restored the words which had fallen out of the Edition: "therefore there is one activity of both" (*mia oun amphoin energeia*). Moreover, this end of the chapter ought to be compared with those things read above at p. 485 E.F. and annotated there, and likewise those read below in VI. 2. 8. p. 602 following.

— **12. *it is necessary—to bring forward, such as—to look upon***] Ficinus and Taylor expressed "and such as" (*kai oion*); which conjunction I would have added if one book had supported it.

**p. 1038, 2. *which Plato says***] Plato in the *Timaeus* p. 39 towards the end p. 40 Bekk.: "Insofar therefore as the Mind sees ideas existing in the 'Living Being that is,' of what sort and how many they are, it thought it necessary that this [world] also should have such and so many." Plotinus looks back at this passage several times. See p. 203 end, 204 beginning, and p. 356 A.

— **13. *but the casual ruin of the form.***] Taylor follows Ficinus, translating: "But the injury which the form sustains, is a casual circumstance." I prefer to inquire rather than to decide whether these words can be punctuated and explained thus: "but that which is from chance (scilicet is lameness) is a ruin of the form" (*hē de ek tychēs [sc. chōleia estin] lymē eidous*). Next from almost all manuscripts, I received "magnitudes" (*megethē*) instead of "generations" (*geneseis*) with the support even of Ficinus, namely in the Basel edition. For in the first Florentine edition, "generations" is read instead of "magnitudes." In both, however, after "habits" (*habitus*), "progress" (*profectus*) is added, as if one were to say he had read *kai prokopai* [and advancements] besides. Yet no trace of that word exists in the manuscripts.

**p. 1038, 17. *eternity instead of time***] See Plato’s...

**[Original page: 318]**

**— ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS —**

*Timaeus* p. 37. 38. p. 36 following Bekk. which passage Plotinus also looks back to above at p. 326. 329. and 330. D. Next, those words: "the one in another" (*to allo en allō*) lest you confuse them with those in the *Phaedo* p. 83: "nor which is another in another," by which bodily nature is signified, which is perceived through the senses. See our annotation to V. 8. 4. p. 546 D. These are rather to be compared with those things which our philosopher discusses in V. 8. 9., especially p. 550 C. D.

**p. 1039, 5. *for of no evil***] How Ficinus took these things, his version shows. Taylor: "For there is no paradigm of evil there." Perhaps after "of no" (*oudenos*) the word "form" (*eidos*) [scilicet *estin ekei*] has fallen out. Moreover, to these final parts of the tenth chapter are to be applied those things which we brought forward regarding the title of this book from the commentaries of Syrianus on Aristotle's *Metaphysics*. See above p. 555.

— **8. *Of the arts, as many as are imitative—would not reasonably be referred thither***] This entire passage is connected with the discussion at the beginning of the tenth book of the Platonic *Republic* p. 595 following p. 466 following Bekk. where painters and tragic poets, as imitators, are said to be distant from nature by the third degree, and various arts which are handled by men are subjected to examination. For the whole passage is to be compared with ours. But if anyone should say that Plotinus is inconsistent with himself, as one who in this place judges the art of statuary (*tēn andriantopoiian*) as an imitator of bodily forms not to look sublimely, although the same man taught all other things above concerning Phidias the statuary; (V. 8. 1. p. 542. E: "Phidias fashioned Zeus by making him according to no sensible thing" etc.) Plotinus does not contradict himself more than Plato, who in the same books of the *Republic* (as V. p. 472. p. 259. Bekk. and especially VI. beginning p. 484. p. 275. and in the *Timaeus* p. 28. A. B. p. 23.) is not ignorant of the divine geniuses of the most excellent craftsmen looking up at divine examples. See also what we placed above in the Annotations to p. 541 B. and at l. l. p. 542 E.

— **16. *the one concerning rhythm and harmony having the thoughts***] I do not delay over the fact that in some books *arithmon* [number] was written twice in this place instead of *rythmon* [rhythm]. For this confusion is common, and some little Greeks, who had not attained the power of the word *numerus* in Latin writers, could easily be turned aside to "correct" it. We have refashioned Ficinus's version of this passage, which Taylor had also done.

**p. 1040, 1. *As many as are productive of sensibles—medicine—and that which is about strength—and good health (In these last words everyone sees that gymnastics is designated)*** etc.] This part of this chapter reminds one of the discussions and comparisons which are instituted in Plato's *Gorgias* p. 464 following concerning various arts. Arts are also reviewed for another purpose by Olympiodorus on the *Alcibiades* pr. XX. p. 178 following.

— **9. *if any of them share in the beautiful***] Perhaps someone might suspect *koinousi* [they make common/divulge] (i.e. they explain into the admiration and love of many). But yet since two books exhibit "to the beautiful" (*tō kalō*), I would have thought that Plotinus wrote: "they share in the beautiful things" (*tōn kalōn koinōnousi*). — Because our philosopher, near the end of the chapter, reckons Geometry among those disciplines which are concerned with eternal things, he follows his Plato in that judgment. See *Republic* VII. p. 526 following p. 348 following Bekk., who indeed himself follows the method of the Pythagoreans in this matter. See, to use this one, the passage of Archytas of Tarentum, which we placed above at the seventh chapter of this book (p. 560 below).

— **17. *but the particular, because it is not the same, one to another***] [Scilicet *estin*]. How Ficinus took these things, the Latin version declares. Taylor thus: "Though it must be considered with respect to man, whether the form of a particular man is there, *not because he is the same with another man*." These last words I do not understand. I interpret the passage thus: "But that singular thing (I say) because not the same (for example, a limb) is one thing to one, another to another." Because after the mention of Socrates, Plotinus immediately subjoins the example of *simotētos* [snub-nosedness]: passages of Plato and other Socratics were occurring to him which report that Socrates was **snub-nosed**; whence Alcibiades compares him to Sileni, though not for this reason alone, in Plato's *Symposium* p. 215. p. 452. Bekk. where use the Scholia and compare the annotations in Cicero *On the Nature of the Gods* I. 34. p. 154. Moser's edition. On the other hand, the Persians recounted that Cyrus had been eagle-nosed, as witnessed by Olympiodorus on the *Alcibiades* pr. p. 154. where compare the annotations; and since the beauty of Alcibiades is mentioned there, see Proclus on the *Alcibiades* pr. and the annotations on him p. 114 our edition. But yet these examples were also used elsewhere in dialectical discussions. See only Aristotle *Sophistical Refutations* II. 6. p. 462. Sylb.: "for the hollow, in common, indicates the same thing in the case of the snub and the bow-legged" etc. Porphyry in the *Isagoge* to the *Categories*...

### PAGE 334
**[Original page: 319]**

**— BOOK IX. OF THE FIFTH ENNEAD. p. 1039—1044 —**

III. p. 387. Buhle: "but to be hook-nosed, or snub-nosed, or rational, or irrational, are inseparable." Add from Aristotle himself *Metaphysics* book V. 1. p. 99. Sylb. VI. 5. p. 109. p. 135. Brandis: "there is nose and hollowness and snub-nosedness," and more often.

**p. 1041, 7. *so also of soul, Soul-itself—and of mind, Mind-itself***] I thought the vulgar reading should be retained, which is not lacking in the authority of manuscripts, although most recede from it. (See Var. Lect.) Concerning these appellations and reasons, consult the annotations above to III. 2. 16. p. 267. D. Next, let the rare Substantive *timotēs* [value/honor] be added to the Lexicons. See Schaefer in Stephanus’s *Thesaurus* London p. 9515. A.

**p. 1042, 9. *Concerning those from putrefaction and the difficult things [chalepōn]*** etc.] Taylor translates these thus: "With respect, however, to things generated from putrefaction, and to things *artificial*," and etc. adding in a note: "Instead of *chalepōn* [difficult/burdensome] here it is evidently necessary from what afterwards follows to read *technikōn* [artificial] or *technōn* [arts]. Ficinus, from not seeing the necessity of this emendation, has made nonsense of the passage." I would not want this excellent man to have let these things slip from him. For first, to say nothing of our Manuscripts, which to a man all maintain the vulgar reading (for we find inveterate ulcers in these Enneads, and those which have corrupted all books alike); it is so far from being the case that those things which follow (B.) "but concerning the arts" (*peri de tōn technōn*) etc. favor the conjecture, that they rather seem to detract from it, since this transition shows that Plotinus only now and separately wishes to inquire concerning the arts and things made by art. Then that *arista* [best things], which are said to come from the mind, confirms the contrary, i.e., "the difficult things" (*ta chalepa*). But what are those "difficult things"? — Plotinus asks whether there are also ideas or species of them in the intelligible world, namely those which are born from rot (for example, worms), likewise those which are harmful (for example, moths), or troublesome (for example, flies, gnats, fleas etc.) — Consequently, Ficinus is also to be excused from this part for adding the word *difficilis*, provided you take it for *noxious*, *lethal*, and similar things. Moreover, in these things Plotinus follows the opinions of the ancient physicists. Theophrastus *Eclog. de Animall.* p. 326. Sylb.: "for of these (the flies) both dung is the cause, and the putrefaction of other things." Tzetzes on Hesiod *Op.* v. 412. p. 220. Gaisford: "for excessive moisture produces rot and worms (in wood)." Compare Gaisford's note to vs. 418. p. 225. and *Geoponica* III. 1. 2. p. 218. Niclas. The physicists attributed the power of rotting and begetting worms to the moon: Athenaeus VII. p. 276. d. p. 7. Schweigh.: "for the star of the moon—being septic" etc. More things are discussed on that matter in Plutarch in the *Symposiacs* III. 10. p. 657 following p. 682 following Wyttenbach's edition, where Moschion the physician defines it thus: "rot is the melting and flowing of flesh changing into the fluid of destruction, and in general things that rot become moist." Cf. also Plutarch *on water and fire* p. 957. Olympiodorus on the *Alcibiades* pr. p. 19: — "wherefore it is well said:"

> "You increase when increasing, but when waning you trouble all things,"

[addressing] the moon. Hence it was the opinion of the ancients that "difficult things" (*ta chalepa*), i.e., flies, worms, and other things of that kind, are generated by the moon.

— **14. *how from one, a multitude.***] He signifies the 7th book of Ennead VI., which is inscribed: *how the multitude of ideas subsisted, and concerning the good*.

**# BOOK I. OF THE SIXTH ENNEAD.**

**p. 1044, 7. ON THE GENERA OF BEING.**] Porphyry in the *Life of Plotinus* chapter V. "concerning the genera of being first," and chapter XXVI. in the same order as the edition in this place, but with the addition: "first," which word some manuscripts also add in this place. Moreover, these three books are placed at the front of Ennead VI., to be marked with numbers XLI, XLII, and XLIII, if you consider the order of time in which each was written. They pertain to the doctrine of the **Categories**. The beginnings of this are all the more to be sketched by us here because Plotinus in this matter, having departed from the authority of Aristotle, gathered himself more to the reasoning of the ancients. It was discovered by the Pythagoreans, which is probable in itself...

**— ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINI —**

...if you look at their manner of philosophizing (cf. Buhle in *Hist. Philosoph.* I. p. 227.) and it is confirmed by the testimonies of Simplicius and Boethius; the former of whom in the *preface* to the *Categories*: "Archytas the Pythagorean even before Aristotle made the division into ten of the first genera in the book which he inscribed *On the All*." Which book seems to be the same as that which others call the *Universal Accounts* (*katholou logous*), according to the great Gerhard Vossius *On Logic* IV. 7. 2. (*Opp.* Vol. III. p. 213.) Themistius, indeed, striving to claim that discovery for his Aristotle, produces a younger Archytas the Peripatetic as the author of that booklet, yet he does not persuade. Another question is whether that booklet, which survives today, and which after others J. Conr. Orellius recently edited in *Opuscula Graecorum veterum sententiosis et moralibus* Vol. II. p. 273 following, Leipzig 1821, inscribed with this title: *The Ten Universal Accounts of Archytas*, whether, I say, that is by that Pythagorean Archytas, or by another man who wished to deceive us. That we should suspect the latter is caused mostly by the fact that the things which Simplicius brings forward from the Archytean *Categories* (we shall exhibit more passages from this interpreter of Aristotle and others in their respective places in this book of Plotinus), those are not found in that booklet. See Fabricius *Biblioth. Graec.* Vol. I. p. 834 Harles edition. Joseph Navarro did not distinguish the two questions in *Tentamine de Archytae Tarentini Vita et Scriptis*, Copenhagen 1820, p. 40 following. And just as Archytas of Tarentum first wrote about *predicaments* (*peri Katēgoriōn*), so Clinomachus of Thurii is said to have first written about *predicates* (Diog. Laert. II. 112: "And Clinomachus of Thurii, who first wrote about axioms and predicates..." Since he borrowed these word for word from Ger. Vossius l. l. Navarro p. 37, he ought also to have added from the same: that these were falsely translated by Diogenes' interpreter as *on the predicaments*. For *katēgoriai* are, certainly called by Boethius, *predicaments*: *katēgorēmata*, *predicates*. These are also called *katēgoroumena* [predicables] and *symbamata* [accidents]. See Voss l. l. and compare Wyttenbach's *Praecepta Philosophiae Logicae* I. 3. 2. p. 39 following. Moreover, this Clinomachus, who is said to have proceeded from the school of Euclid of Megara, is incorrectly written as *Clitomachus* in the same Voss *On the Greek Historians* II. 16. or in the newest edition. Suidas also knows the same Clinomachus in *Pyrrhon* Vol. III. p. 246 Kust. Plato then placed five genera of being (*ta genē tou ontos*) (see *Sophist* p. 255 e. sqq.) which Plotinus in these books set out to explain and confirm (See below at p. 602 A.) An Anonymous author in our Heidelberg-Palatine Manuscript No. 132 illustrates Aristotle's ten Categories with examples thus added (See our *Meletemm.* I. p. 8.):

> Substance. Quantity. Quality. Relation. Where.
> **Andronicus. Great. Faithful. Son of Palaeologus. In Constantinople.**

> When. Position. Habit [to have]. Action. Passion.
> **Now. Standing. Armed. He reigns. Being reigned over.**

Cf. Aristotle *Categg.* chapter 2. p. 24 Sylb. and Suid. II. p. 278 Kust. who, however, perhaps following Alexander in Aristotle's *Topics*, orders the last ones thus: *Action, Passion, Position, Habit*. And likewise Wyttenbach in *Praeceptt. Philos. Log.* l. l.: "*Substance, Quantity, Quality, Relation, Action, Passion, Where, When, Position, Habit*:" to which he subjoins five Predicables: "*Genus, Species, Difference, Property, Accident.*" After Aristotle, Theophrastus, Eudemus, and Phanias wrote books on the Categories (see Buhle's *Argumentum Categoriarum Aristotelis* p. 434 following). Andronicus of Rhodes, Porphyry, Ammonius son of Hermias, Simplicius, and Boethius made Commentaries or Introductions (*Isagogas*) into the same. Regarding Porphyry, although Parius found this title in the Palatine manuscripts: *Introduction of Porphyry the Phoenician, disciple of Plotinus of Lycopolis*: nevertheless no mention of Plotinus is injected in this *Isagoge*, unlike what happens in the remaining commentaries, especially that of Simplicius. A commentary by Photius exists on this *Isagoge* of Porphyry, from which I plucked a little flower (from Cod. Monac. nr. 222.) in *Meletemm.* l. l. There I exhibited a passage of Dexippus transcribed from the Laurentian-Medicean Manuscript nr. 33. We shall exhibit more things also from other Manuscripts for the sake of explaining...

...these books in this our edition of the *Enneads*. Concerning that **Dexippus**, Gerhard Vossius teaches us these things *On Logic* l. l. p. 213: "Dexippus mentions the *Categories* of Archytas in book I. ch. 6. also book III. ch. 1. where he says that in that Aristotle receded from Archytas, because he assigned to *quantity* the place nearest from *substance*, not to *quality*, as *Archytas* did, whose opinion *Plotinus* more approved. This Dexippus is Herennius the Athenian, who lived under the Emperors Aurelian and Probus, a distinguished leader in war, a disciple of Iamblichus who, besides the *book on the Categories against Plotinus* (John Tzetzes says he read only this one, *Chiliad* IX. Histor. 274. verses 497—499:

> Wrote many other books indeed,
> In the one I encountered, the one on the Categories.")

also recorded Macedonian and Scythian matters in letters. Concerning which matter I have said more in the 3rd Book *On the Greek Historians* ch. 16." And consequently, from the Platonic and thus Plotinian family itself, a defender had stood up for Aristotle against Plotinus. For which reason we have judged it advisable to place in the annotation on these Plotinian books also the passages of the others who make mention of Plotinus—of the ancient interpreters of Aristotle, and indeed of Dexippus himself—so that Plotinus's reasoning in this doctrine of the Categories might be compared with the reasoning of Archytas, Plato, and Aristotle, and it might be understood how later Greek philosophers again pleaded the cause for Aristotle against Plotinus. We have said more about Dexippus in the Prolegomena to § VII. note 3. Simplicius (in Aristotle's *Categorr.* Ed. Basil 1551 fol.) Fol. 1. a. after having enumerated the others who wrote on Aristotle, says this concerning Plotinus: "And Plotinus the Great brought to the book of the Categories the more business-like examinations in three whole books inscribed *On the Genera of Being*... And Dexippus the disciple of Iamblichus also himself briefly explained Aristotle's book; and primarily he proposes to dissolve the doubts of Plotinus proposed to him as if in a dialogue." (Note of the transcriber: Plotinus, in the book whose title was *On the Genera of Being*, had collected doubts about the *Categories* of Aristotle. Therefore if mention is made of the *aporiai* [doubts] of Plotinus in our book, it is very likely they are taken from the cited book which is sometimes also named by Simplicius (see fol. 32. b.) Moreover, the Categories themselves are called *genē tou ontos* [genera of being] by Plotinus. (See fol. 4. b.) Where Simplicius deals with various ways in which this book of Aristotle is inscribed, he says, "But those who inscribe it *On the Genera of Being* or *On the Ten Genera*, as also seems good to Plotinus in his contradiction against them, look only to the things, but not to the logical purpose; for the genera of being are the things themselves." For the sake of aiding understanding, I will subjoin a passage from Porphyry's *Isagoge* to the *Categories* ch. II. p. 384. Buhle: "For the most general is said of all the genera and species and individuals under itself; and the genus which is before the most specific is said of all the most specific and individuals; but the species alone is said of all the individuals; but the individual is said of one only of the particulars. — Therefore the individual is contained under the species, the species under the genus. For the genus is a certain whole; but the individual is a part; and the species is both whole and part." We exhibited more from this passage to Olympiodorus on the *Alcibiades* pr. ch. 34. p. 204. whom consult. From the more recent authors, to touch on this also, concerning the Dialectic of Plotinus, and what this philosopher found fault with in attacking the established views of the Aristotelian doctrine of Categories, Brucker dealt with in few words in *Hist. Crit. Philos.* T. II. p. 393. Tennemann pursued the same with more words in *Hist. Philos.* VI. p. 175 following, who set out to show both other things and these especially: first, that among philosophers Plotinus correctly found fault with some things in the Stagirite's ten Categories, and that he especially acts so as to teach that those Categories are not primary ontological notions; consequently that Plotinus himself in the second place applied effort to dig out the original notions of things, and thereby lay the foundations of objective science, as it is called. Moreover, that Plotinus wishes the genera (*ta genē tou ontos*) to be taken so that they are simple notions and not to be derived from elsewhere, of predicates which ought to be attributed to all things (i.e. objects), and which are the principles...
