And the form of the simple is one thing compared to the composite, and the composite another; for it is one thing to be a man, and another to be a soul, another to be in a body, and another to be a man."

**p. 1044, 13. *But as many as having examined—themselves in defined genera—neither infinite because it would neither be possible nor would there be science.***] Thus with the better books and Ficinus, we have corrected and filled out the passage. Soon "and certain genera—ten" etc. That Plotinus refers by these words to the *Categories* of Aristotle is not something we need strive to prove after those things placed at the title of this book, where it was also spoken concerning Archytas and other philosophers who had established the highest genera of being. Concerning Aristotle's *Categories*, Simplicius says thus in his [commentary] on them fol. 7. b. Basel edition 1551: "For some indeed inscribed the book before the *Topics*; others *On the Genera of Being*; others *On the Ten Genera*; others *Ten Categories*; others *Categories*, just as it is now carried." — Mention of the Categories is also made by **Marius Victorinus** in *Exposition on Cicero's Rhetoric* I. p. 130 Capperonner's edition: "Aristotle," he says, "says that all things which are done in words and deeds and in the whole world, are ten; the names of which things we shall place. The first is *substance*: then *quantity, quality, relation [ad aliquid], where, when, position, to have, to do, to suffer*." Then he subjoins the Greek.

**p. 1045, 8. *For because being is not synonymous—or homonymously***] See Aristotle *Categg.* chapter 1 which is inscribed *On Homonyms, Synonyms, Paronyms*; whence I will subjoin these excerpts: "Equivocal things (*homōnyma*) are called those whose name alone is common, with the notions of the things being different among themselves which pertain to explaining it; such as is the word *animal*, signifying both a *man* and a *painted image of an animal*." — "Univocal things (*synōnyma*) however are called these, whose name is common, and the explanation corresponding to that name is the same, just as *animal* signifies both a *cow*," &c. Cf. Simplicius's *Commentary* on Aristotle's *Categories* fol. 7. and there also the praises of Iamblichus and Syrianus. — *Steinhart*, however, in *Quæstionib. De dialectica Plotini ratione* p. 24 note 80, thinks that Plotinus also calls those things homonyms which are transferred metaphorically or through *metalepsis* [transumption] from the mind to bodies.

**— BOOK I. OF THE SIXTH ENNEAD. p. 1044—1048 —**

*...descend from Romulus*. But who, having known the license of the ancient interpreters, would not see that the interpreter using the Latin language wished to substitute a Roman example for a Greek one?) "but after these [and] the multitude from one principle such as [that of] Hercules, which defining and separating from others we said was the whole collection, the genus of the Heraclidae." Cf. Ammonius, Dexippus, and Boethius on Porphyry. I wonder that none of the more recent interpreters has made mention of the Plotinian passage; whence nevertheless Porphyry could seem to have snatched the handle of this example. Or should we say that these examples of the Heraclidae, Cecropidae, etc. in this doctrine of the Categories belonged to commonplaces? Certainly this was a common place in the orations of the Greek Orators and Rhetoricians, especially funeral ones. See Himerius *Orat.* II. § 3. 10. 11. and the annotations on it by Wernsdorf p. 374. 385 following. Regarding the affairs of the Heraclidae, we have gained something new from the Excerpts of Polybius in *Scriptiorr. Vett. Collect. Vatic.* New edition by Ang. Mai Vol. II. p. 386. The Adjective *Hērakleios* [Herculean] is to be taken out of Proclus on Plato's *Cratylus* § 79. p. 42 Boissonade. The Philosopher expounds on the names of those who bring forth and celebrate by their actions and whole life the virtue of those divinities from whom they were named, such as those who are joined to the Minervian series (*tēs Athēnaïkēs seiras*). Then, after some intervening things, he continues: "At least Hercules, they say, being addressed as Alcides from his mortal fathers, was called Hercules by the Pythia, because of the kinship toward the Herculean order and divinity; for a god bestowing a name on a man, looking to his own whole series and the life which he has put forward, places the fitting surname." Read: "because of the kinship toward the Junonian [Heraian] order" etc. For Hercules had composed himself toward the Junonian order, and that goddess had stood forth as the author of his contests and of the glory won through contests: see Proclus ibid. § 123. p. 78. Astyages the Grammarian contradicts the etymologies of the name, with the ancient Lexicographers assenting. See *Etymol. Gud.* p. 248. Orion of Thebes in *Etymol.* and there Larcher p. 69. Cf. Koes's *Excerpta* from Cod. Reg. Paris. at the end of Orion p. 186 Sturz edition. Mention of *seirōn* [series/chains] is frequent in similar places. Proclus p. 159 on the *Alcibiades* pr.: "and you have again here the series of the good-formed causes being revealed. For Socrates indeed looks toward a daemon, but the daemon looks toward the god whose follower he is, and Socrates is joined to the divine through the daemonic." Eunapius in *Excerptt. Historr.* XVI. p. 264. (in A. Mai's *Nova Collect. Vatic.* II.) concerning the emperor Julian: "just as his (Plato's) Socrates says, 'we are with Zeus, but not with another of the gods.' By this he also himself refers and is joined to the solar kingdom and the golden chain." — On this matter Simplicius also discusses in the *Categories* Fol. 43. a: "Since more relatives are spoken of by Aristotle, and here as the greater and the double, and habit, and reclining, and the rest, and others handed down by him, of which we made mention earlier, both those according to excess and defect, and those according to power and weakness [adynamian] and other such things, Plotinus asks what the commonality is in all these. Whether it is a certain generic one, or in another way, according to the reference to one, just as we say the Heraclidae are referred to one common one, Hercules. For if on the one hand they touch the subjects and those having the relation, of which some are in substance, some in quantity, and some in others, the relatives will be changed along with the others; but if they have no commonality toward those things having the relation, but the category of relatives is unrelated, those things will not have a relation, nor will that commonality of these exist: Perhaps then it is not even necessary to change along with the things, nor to abstain from them altogether, but simultaneously since the different things are suspended, it holds together the commonality toward each other according to the very property of the relation. For even if to the different and distinguished things one thing being the same is everywhere present, it will be separate and better than the opposites, so that it would not, even if it were held by one of them, be hindered even from being present to the other. If we say these things are true, however many and of what sort the differences of relatives are, they will all be arranged under one separate category, that category being in no way displaced from itself by the difference of those participating in it." etc.

**p. 1048, 1. *Number indeed they say is the first quantity***] Concerning numbers there is a peculiar book of our philosopher, the sixth of this Ennead, where see the annotations on the title and the chapters themselves. In this place Plotinus examines and strives to refute the fourth chapter of Aristotle's *Categories*, which is inscribed *On Quantity*, and begins thus (p. 30 sq. Sylb.): "Of quantity, one part is discrete, the other continuous; and one part consists of parts having position..."

**— ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS —**

"...relative to each other, but the other part from those not having position. Moreover, discrete is [for example] number and speech; but continuous is [for example] a line, a surface, a body. Further, besides these, place and time." Cf. *Metaphysics* IV. 13. p. 86 following Sylb. and Simplicius on the *Categories* l. l. fol. 31.

**p. 1049, 11. *And they themselves, why quantity?***] Simplicius on the *Categories* Fol. 32. b: "further Plotinus seeks in the first [book] *On Being* whether if the continuous is quantity, the discrete is not quantity; but if both are quantities, it must be shown what is the common thing in both; and he solves the inquiry in the third [book] saying (cf. of this Ennead lib. III. ch. 13. p. 628.) that the common thing to them is 'so much,' clearly that which is considered as measure and as limit, insofar as each quantity is known; for this was not given to magnitude from number as it seems to some, but is a property of measure and of the united and of the interconnected, and even furthermore of the discrete. For there is a particular nature for each, as it is also considered in the whole world. Of the continuous, the nature which is called magnitude, according to unity and interconnection; but of the discrete, that which is called multitude, according to heap and juxtaposition. For according to the substance of magnitude, the world is one and is conceived as spherical and grown together with itself, extended and interconnected. But according to multitude, both the arrangement and the decoration which is from so many elements, say for example, and animals or plants, is considered, and of so many and so many contrarieties or similarities; if therefore in images these things are thus separated, much more so in the conceived genera; and before these, they stand apart in the immaterial forms in themselves, having a common thing, as has been said, measure and limit. But those around Lucius and Nicostratus find fault with the division" etc.

**p. 1050, 11. *they would not have anything common toward these, but only a name.***] Thus with two more excellent books we have written. Concerning the locution "only a name" (*onoma monon*) we spoke at IV. 3. 2. p. 373. E.

— **14. *for (speech) is indeed measured; but being speech it is 'so much.' But insofar as it is speech, it is not quantity; for it is significative, just as the name and the verb—but speech is rather the stroke [plēgē]* etc.**] Thus by the authority of good books we have established this passage. Aristotle *Categories* IV. p. 31. Sylb.: "likewise also speech [is of discrete things.] For that speech is quantity is manifest; for it is measured by a short and long syllable; and I mean speech produced with voice" etc. Philosophers, and others of the Stoics, early attempted the definition of *logos* (speech/oration). Plato in the *Theaetetus* p. 206. c. d. p. 313. Bekk. places this one: "Soc. Come then, what [some others and Heindf. *tina*, but Cod. Bodleian. and Darmst. confirm Bekker's reading *ti*] does 'speech' ever wish to signify to us? For it seems to me to say one of three things. Theai. What are they? Soc. The first would be making one's own thought manifest through voice with verbs and names just as into a mirror or water [making manifest] the opinion into the stream through the mouth. Or does such a thing not seem to you to be speech?" Nevertheless, Plotinus also looks back at this definition of the Stagirite in *On Interpretation* ch. IV. p. 59. Sylb.: "Speech is a significative voice, of which some part is significative when separated; as an utterance, but not as an affirmation [or negation; I say] for example, 'man' signifies something, but not that he is or is not; but it will be an affirmation or negation, if something is added." And Gerhard Jo. Vossius in *Aristarchus* C. I. p. 366. (*Opp.* Tom. II.) pronounces this to be the true definition, putting forward other definitions simultaneously from Charisius, Diomedes, and Priscian. You, compare besides Porphyry and Simplicius on the *Categories* l. l. and Ammonius on *Interpretation* l. l. Olympiodorus on Plato *Alcibiades* pr. p. 66: "that speech is the face of the echo." The same Chapter VI. p. 53. concerning the Delphic Apollo prophesying: "that it was not a stroke of air alone that said these things and with voice, but vitally and directly," which things are to be composed with the Plotinian B. line 5 following: "but if voice is not according to the stroke, but according to the air."

**p. 1051, 7. *from the significative into the co-significative of that category***] Thus for "into the significative" (*eis sēmantikon*) we wrote with Ficinus from the traces of good Manuscripts. A single example of this Adjective [co-significative] is cited from *Etymol. M.* p. 649. 20 Heidelb. p. 588 Lips. Therefore let this Plotinian one be added, and let this word be added to Schneider's Lexicon. Soon with most of our books we gave *eniausios* [yearly] for the edition's *eniausiaios*, and *ephaptomenē* [touching] for *eph' haptomenē*, finally after "the participants" we added "all" (*panta*) from our books. Moreover, in this place concerning *Time*, he looks back to these things of Aristotle in *Categg.* IV. 6: "Time and place are also of such things; for the 'now' time joins both to the past and to the future." The examples also, for example *the three-cubit* at the end of the fifth Chapter of Plotinus, are taken from...

**— BOOK I. OF THE SIXTH ENNEAD. p. 1049—1058 —**

...Aristotle's *Categg.* See IV. 12. Let it suffice to have warned of this once, lest we be forced to transfer a large part of the booklet of Categories into our Annotations.

**p. 1052, 1. *But relation [to pros ti]* etc.]** Aristotle *Categg.* V. 1: "Relatively things are called such as, whatever they are, are said to be of others, or in any way whatever toward another."

**p. 1053, 10. *and likewise upon disposition; what then would there be besides these things relative to each other, other than us conceiving the juxtaposition? but the exceeding is indeed a magnitude of so much—but the right—we conceived the right and the left.***] Thus with the help of our Manuscripts we have completed and corrected this passage with Ficinus. The last things of this chapter: "but the prior and the later we likewise [conceive]" seem to come very close to those things which the philosopher of Konigsberg, Kant, in that place of his Critique which he called the Transcendental Aesthetic, set forth concerning Time and Space as forms of our contemplation (*Formen unserer Anschauung*).

**p. 1055, 15. *a father having departed—this one similar to the dead one***] Above I. 4. 7. page 34 F. Plotinus placed "to depart" (*apelthein*) concerning voluntary death. In this place it is simply "to die," as in Diogenes Laertius II. 6: "Socrates having departed" (cf. our Annotation above in I. 4. 7. p. 34. D.), for which writers also use "to depart" or "to go away to the necessity" (See Wyttenbach on Plutarch *Consolat. Apollon.* p. 753 following) and "to depart from men" Diog. Laert. VII. 184. cf. Baguet on the *Relics of Chrysippus* p. 39 following note 69.

**p. 1056, 4. *Should one then divide relations in this way, in which way***] Thus from the books we have restored with Ficinus instead of *ar'—ē*. The same interpreter soon did not express *theōrein* [to contemplate] after *keimenēn* [placed], therefore in the version we added "if you contemplate." Then with the same Ficinus from the Manuscripts we gave: "but these—either in some way always held the relation even before the readiness."

— **5. *idle relation***] Cf. my annotation in Proclus *Inst. Theol.* p. 180. and cf. below p. 582.

**p. 1057, 7. *for the double itself is the cause of being double; but to that, the half***] Two books [read] *to de to hēmisy*. It seems it should be written "but of that [scilicet being the half] the half [is the cause]" (*tou de [sc. hēmisy einai] to hēmisy*).

**p. 1058, 17. *But quality from which the so-called* etc.]** Simplicius on the *Categories*, after he explained the opinions of others concerning the common [notion] of quality (Fol. 57. b. 20.) reports concerning Plotinus: "But Plotinus placed the common [notion] of quality to be power, from which the thing having it is able or is able [dynamis... dynatai ē dynatai]. For this fits all four qualities. And it is manifest that he uses 'power' and 'to be able' in a unique way, even though they are accustomed to be predicated in many ways. For each of the categories fits this. But it is necessary to attend to that, lest the doubt has run back into the same place for us. For the thing sought was whether, if it is said in many ways, there is nothing common; but having taken 'power' in exchange for 'quality,' we seem to have done nothing more. For if it itself is also said homonymously, and again just as it is difficult to find the common of quality, so it is not easy to collect what the genus of power ever is. And perhaps the account of Plotinus is true. For because quality is in the middle of both acquired accidents and natural substances, because of this it is like a power being itself in the middle in nature. And because it shares in the substance of the form in some way, because of this it is characterized according to one common account. But since it has also participated in the offspring-like category, just as the category of position and habit, because of this it also receives being said in many ways. Just as power does. For even in this, its being said in many ways has the common co-existing from it, either by being arranged from one or toward one, or by the remission of the power being made about the same thing." In the following, Simplicius transitions to the division of powers, nor is there further talk about Plotinus up to fol. 58. a. 23. where it is read: "But if power is such, says Plotinus, weaknesses will no longer be qualities; but if they are qualities themselves, the definition of quality will not fit against all of them. Toward this it is necessary to distinguish how 'power' and 'weakness' are said. For if they are rendered as the Stoics do, power is that which is productive of more symptoms, as prudence is of walking prudently and of discussing prudently, there will be, according to such a definition, even those things now called weaknesses, powers; for even lacks of art bring on more slips; if however according to another arrangement of the Stoics it should be called power, that which is productive of more symptoms and overmastering the subordinate activities, even so Plotinus's term fits. For even vice, being a weakness, according to the Stoics' term overmasters its own activities and the middle arts, as falling away..."

<meta>This page continues the philological commentary on Plotinus's Enneads, specifically focusing on the relationship between knowledge and the object of knowledge, and the nature of the Intellect.</meta>

[[original page: 317]]

->BOOK IX. ENNEAD V. pages 1034—1038.<-

And this he demonstrates, first from self-evidence; for he says that for the most part we acquire sciences <note>original: "ἐπιστήμας"</note> when the things themselves already pre-exist. For we approach them as they already exist, and when we were mere infants, the objects of knowledge <note>original: "ἐπιστητὰ"</note> which later became known to us were already there, though the knowledge of them did not yet exist. For instance, the knowledge of the eclipse came later to the Greeks through Thales, but the eclipse itself and the object of knowledge pre-existed. But this is the more obvious case; there are, however, a few cases where knowledge exists simultaneously with the object of knowledge. These are the immaterial, intelligible things <note>original: "τὰ νοητὰ"; cf. also Plotinus VI. 9. 4.</note>, which exist together with the knowledge that is always established in activity <note>original: "κατ᾽ ἐνέργειαν"</note>, whether there is some such part in us that always remains "above" (as Plotinus and Iamblichus believe), or whether it is in the Intellect-in-activity, if one should choose to call that intellection "knowledge." This could also be said regarding the subsistence <note>original: "ὑπόστασιν"</note> of universals derived from abstraction. For the knowledge of these exists simultaneously with their subsistence. This is also true of the fabrications of the imagination and of the arts. For the Chimera and the knowledge of the Chimera exist together. Why then did he add the phrase, "or in no case"? Either because some people denied the existence of universals, intelligibles, and things conceived in any way whatsoever; or because even if these things exist in nature, we acquired the conceptions of them later? And for this reason, it happens even in these cases that the object of knowledge pre-exists the knowledge. Thus, according to the first argument, he seems to show that the object of knowledge is prior to the knowledge, and not simultaneous by nature. According to the second approach—since "prior" is said in many ways, as he himself will teach later—he now uses it in one specific way: insofar as that which is prior by nature entails the destruction of the other if it is destroyed, but is not itself destroyed if the other is destroyed. etc.

**p. 1035, 14. but it stands in itself etc.**] Plato in the *Cratylus* p. 437. A. p. 114. Bekker: "Let us consider, taking up from these things, first this name, 'knowledge' <note>original: "ἐπιστήμην"</note>, how it is ambiguous and seems rather to signify that it *stays* <note>original: "ἵστησιν"</note> our soul upon things rather than that it moves with them" (<note>original: "cf."</note> compare the same dialogue p. 412. A.)—"then 'steadfastness,' because it is an imitation of a certain base <note>original: "βάσεώς"</note> and standing <note>original: "στάσεως"</note>, but not of motion." See also Plato’s *Definitions* p. 414. p. 570. <note>original: "infr."</note> below in Bekker. Maximus Tyrius, *Dissertation* XII. 4. p. 216. <note>original: "sq."</note> following, Reiske: "Perhaps then sensation and experience are not uniquely human, but reason is the property of man; and knowledge would be nothing else" (Markland rightly orders "would be" <note>original: "ἂν"</note> to be interposed after "nothing." See just now Matthiae's *Greek Grammar* § 514. p. 976. ff.) "except the certainty of reason proceeding according to the same things, etc." What Markland wishes to be written as "the property of man" instead of "human" is indeed plausible, yet not necessary: certainly I would change nothing without the manuscripts, and things are called "human" which are characteristic of men, both with respect to animals, as in this passage, and to gods, as in Iamblichus, *On the Pythagorean Symbols* V. p. 330. Kiessling.

**p. 1036, 6. If therefore intellection is truly one.**] The <note>original: "Edit."</note> Edition has "being in," which Ficino expressed. I have adopted the reading from the margin, a trace of which appears in the Codex Marcianus A. Taylor agrees with me, translating it thus: “If, therefore, intelligence is truly one, that from which is the object of its perception and idea itself are one.” Shortly after, from the Marcian Codices, I wrote "whole" <note>original: "ὅλος"</note> instead of "generally" <note>original: "ὅλως"</note> regarding the Intellect.

**p. 1037, 5. so that it may have the Intellect, being one, over themselves**] I wrote this with most manuscripts instead of "to have." Ficino, moreover, expressed "being in" <note>original: "ἐνόντα"</note> instead of "being one" <note>original: "ἐν ὄντα"</note>, and that seems true. However, I was unwilling to accept it without the manuscripts. Shortly after, from all the manuscripts and from Ficino’s version, I restored the words which had fallen out of the Edition: "therefore there is one activity <note>original: "ἐνέργεια"</note> of both." For the rest, this conclusion of the chapter should be compared with those things read above on p. 485. E.F. and noted there, and likewise what is read <note>original: "infra"</note> below in VI. 2. 8. p. 602. ff.

— **12. it is necessary—to bring forward, such as—to observe**] Ficino and Taylor expressed "and such as"; I would have added this conjunction if even one manuscript supported it.

**p. 1038, 2. which Plato says**] Plato in the *Timaeus* p. 39. <note>original: "sub fin."</note> near the end, p. 40. Bekker: "Insofar as the Intellect sees the ideas existing in the 'Living Being that truly is,' of what kind and how many they are, it decided that this [the universe] should also have such and so many." Plotinus refers to this passage several times. <note>original: "Vid."</note> See p. 203. <note>original: "extr."</note> at the end, 204. <note>original: "init."</note> at the beginning, and p. 356. A.

— **13. but the injury of the form is by chance.**] Taylor follows Ficino, translating: “But the injury which the form sustains, is a casual circumstance.” I prefer to inquire rather than to decide whether these words can be punctuated and explained thus: "But that which is by chance (namely lameness) is an injury of the form." Next, from almost all the manuscripts, I restored "magnitudes" <note>original: "μεγέθη"</note> instead of "generations" <note>original: "γενέσεις"</note>, with Ficino also supporting this, specifically in the Basel edition. For in the first Florentine edition, "generations" is read instead of "magnitudes." In both, however, after "states," "progress" is added, so that you might say he additionally read "and advancements" <note>original: "καὶ προκοπαί"</note>. However, no trace of that word exists in the manuscripts.

->ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS<-

*Timaeus* p. 37. 38. p. 36. and following, Bekker edition; a passage which Plotinus also refers to above on p. 326. 329. and 330. D. Soon after, those words: <note>original: "τὸ ἄλλο ἐν ἄλλῳ"</note> "the one thing in the other" beware lest you confuse them with those in the *Phaedo* p. 83: <note>original: "οὐδ᾽ ἥτις ἐστὶν ἄλλη ἐν ἄλλῳ"</note> "nor that which is one thing in another," by which the corporeal nature is signified, which is perceived through the senses. See our note to V. 8. 4. p. 546. D. These should rather be compared with those things which our philosopher discusses in V. 8. 9., especially p. 550. C. D.

**p. 1039, 5. For of no evil**] <note>original: "κακοῦ γὰρ οὐδενὸς"</note> How Ficinus <note>Marsilio Ficino, the 15th-century Renaissance translator of Plotinus</note> understood these words is shown by his version. Taylor <note>Thomas Taylor, the "Platonist," who produced the first complete English translation</note> says: “For there is no paradigm of evil there.” Perhaps after "of no [evil]" the word "Form" <note>original: "εἶδος"</note> has fallen out, namely: "there is no Form of evil there." For the rest, to these final parts of the tenth chapter should be applied those things which we brought forward regarding the title of this book from Syrianus’s commentaries on Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*. See above p. 555.

— **8. Of the arts, as many as are imitative—would not reasonably be referred to that place [the intelligible world]**] <note>original: "Τῶν δὴ τεχνῶν ὅσαι μιμητικαὶ—οὐκ ἂν εἰκότως ἐκεῖ ἀνάγοιντο"</note> This entire passage is connected with the discussion at the beginning of the tenth book of Plato’s *Republic* p. 595. and following, p. 466. and following, Bekker edition, where painters and tragic poets, as imitators, are said to be at a third remove from nature, and various arts practiced by men are subjected to examination. For the whole passage is to be compared with ours. But if indeed anyone should say that Plotinus is inconsistent with himself—insofar as he judges the art of statuary <note>original: "τὴν ἀνδριαντοποιΐαν"</note> in this place to be an imitator of corporeal forms and thus not looking toward the sublime, yet the same man taught quite differently above regarding the sculptor Phidias (V. 8. 1. p. 542. E: "Phidias fashioned his Zeus without looking to any sensible model," etc.)—Plotinus contradicts himself no more than Plato does. Plato, in those same books of the *Republic* (as in V. p. 472. p. 259. Bekker and especially VI. at the beginning p. 484. p. 275. and in the *Timaeus* p. 28. A. B. p. 23.), is not ignorant of the divine genius of the most excellent craftsmen who look upon divine models. See also what we have placed above in the Annotations to p. 541. B. and to the same place p. 542. E.

— **16. that [art] which, being concerned with rhythm and harmony, possesses the thoughts**] <note>original: "ἡ μὲν περὶ ῥυθμὸν καὶ ἁρμονίαν ἔχουσα τὰ νοήματα"</note> I do not dwell on the fact that in several books "number" <note>original: "ἀριθμὸν"</note> was written twice in this place instead of "rhythm" <note>original: "ῥυθμόν"</note>. For this confusion is common, and certain "Greeklets" <note>A derogatory term for minor Byzantine or late-antique scribes</note> who had not mastered the power of the word *numerus* in Latin writers could easily be led astray into "correcting" it. However, we have reshaped Ficinus's version of this passage, as Taylor had also done.

**p. 1040, 1. But as many as are productive of sensible things—medicine—and that which concerns strength—and good condition (in these last words everyone sees that gymnastics is designated) etc.**] <note>original: "Ὅσαι δὲ ποιητικαὶ αἰσθητῶν—ἰατρική—ἥτε περὶ ἰσχὺν—καὶ εὐεξίαν"</note> This part of the chapter calls to mind the discussions and comparisons instituted regarding various arts in Plato’s *Gorgias* p. 464. and following. The arts are also enumerated for a different purpose by Olympiodorus in his commentary on the *First Alcibiades* XX. p. 178. and following.

— **9. if any of them share in the beautiful**] <note>original: "εἴ τινες αὐτῶν τὸ καλὸν κοινωνοῦσι"</note> Someone might perhaps suspect the word should be "make common" <note>original: "κοινοῦσι"</note>, that is, they explain it for the admiration and love of many. But nevertheless, since two books show "with the beautiful" <note>original: "τῷ καλῷ"</note>, I would rather think Plotinus wrote: "they share in beautiful things" <note>original: "τῶν καλῶν κοινωνοῦσι"</note>.—As for the fact that our philosopher, toward the end of the chapter, reckons Geometry among those disciplines concerned with eternal things, he follows his own Plato in that judgment. See *Republic* VII. p. 526. and following, p. 348. and following, Bekker, who indeed himself follows the reasoning of the Pythagoreans in this matter. See, to use this one example, the passage of Archytas of Tarentum which we placed above at the seventh chapter of this book (p. 560. below).

— **17. but the individual, because the same thing is not one for one and another for another**] <note>original: "τὸ δὲ καθ᾽ ἕκαστον, ὅτι μὴ τὸ αὐτὸ ἄλλο ἄλλῳ"</note> Namely, "it is." How Ficinus understood these things is declared by his Latin version. Taylor thus: “Though it must be considered with respect to man, whether the form of a particular man is there, *not because he is the same with another man*.” These last words I do not understand. I interpret the passage thus: But that singular thing (I say) because the same (for example, a limb) is not one thing for one person and another for another. Because Plotinus immediately adds the example of **snub-nosedness** <note>original: "σιμότητος"</note> after the mention of Socrates, there were occurring to him passages of Plato and other Socratics who record that Socrates was **snub-nosed**; whence Alcibiades compares him to Sileni <note>Forest spirits often depicted as snub-nosed and ugly but containing divine images within</note> in Plato’s *Symposium* p. 215. p. 452. Bekker, where you should consult the Scholia and compare the note in Cicero’s *On the Nature of the Gods* I. 34. p. 154. Moser edition. On the other hand, the Persians used to relate that Cyrus was hook-nosed, as witnessed by Olympiodorus in *First Alcibiades* p. 154. where compare the note; and since the beauty of Alcibiades is mentioned in the same place, see Proclus on the *First Alcibiades* and the note on him p. 114 of our edition. But nevertheless, these examples were also commonly used elsewhere in dialectical discussions. See just now Aristotle, *Sophistical Refutations* II. 6. p. 462. Sylburg edition: "For 'hollow' in a general sense signifies the same thing in the case of the snub-nosed and the bow-legged," etc. Porphyry in the *Introduction to the Categories*...

Brandis edition: <note>original: "ἔστι ῥὶς καὶ κοιλότης καὶ σιμότης"</note> "there is the nose, and hollowness, and snub-nosedness," and frequently elsewhere.

**page 1041, 7. "so also of the soul, the Soul-itself—and of the mind, the Mind-itself"** <note>original: "οὕτω καὶ ψυχῆς αὐτοψυχὴ—καὶ νοῦ αὐτονοῦς"</note>] I have decided that the common reading should be retained, as it does not lack the authority of the manuscripts, even if many depart from it. (See the Various Readings.) Concerning these titles and principles, consult the notes provided above for III. 2. 16. page 267. D. Closely related in the Lexicons is the rare noun <term>timotes</term> <note>meaning "preciousness" or "honor"</note>. See Schaefer in Stephanus’s *London Thesaurus* page 9515. A.

**page 1042, 9. "Concerning things arising from putrefaction and troublesome things etc."** <note>original: "Περὶ δὲ τῶν ἐκ σήψεως καὶ τῶν χαλεπῶν κ. τ. λ."</note>] Taylor translates these words as follows: “With respect, however, to things generated from putrefaction, and to things *artificial*,” etc. adding in a note: “Instead of <term>chalepon</term> <note>troublesome/difficult</note> here it is evidently necessary from what afterwards follows to read <term>technikon</term> <note>artificial</note> or <term>technon</term> <note>arts</note>. Ficinus, from not seeing the necessity of this emendation, has made nonsense of the passage.” I would not wish that excellent man <note>referring to Taylor</note> to have allowed these words to escape him. For first, though I do not dwell on our Manuscripts, which all to a man support the common reading (for we encounter ancient sores in these Enneads which have corrupted all books alike); it is so far from the case that what follows—(B.) "concerning the arts etc."—favors his conjecture, that they rather seem to detract from it, since this transition shows that only now and separately does Plotinus wish to inquire about the arts and things made by art. Furthermore, the word "best" <note>original: "ἄριστα"</note>, which refers to things said to come from the mind, confirms the opposite, i.e., "the troublesome things" <note>original: "τὰ χαλεπά"</note>. But what are these "troublesome things"?—Plotinus asks whether there are also <term>Ideas</term> <note>the perfect spiritual archetypes in Plato's philosophy</note> or species of them in the intelligible world, such as those born from rot (for example, worms), likewise of those which are harmful (for example, moths), or annoying (for example, flies, gnats, fleas etc.)—Therefore, Ficinus is to be excused on this part as well for adding the word *difficult*, provided you understand it as *harmful*, *deadly*, and the like. In these matters, Plotinus follows the opinions of the ancient natural philosophers. Theophrastus in *Selections on Animals* page 326. Sylburg edition: "for of these (flies) dung is the cause, as is the rot of other things." Tzetzes on Hesiod’s *Works and Days* verse 412. page 220. Gaisford edition: "for excessive moisture produces rot and worms (in wood)." Compare Gaisford’s note to verse 418. page 225. and the *Geoponica* III. 1. 2. page 218. Niclas edition. The natural philosophers attributed the power of rotting and begetting worms to the moon: Athenaeus VII. page 276. d. page 7. Schweighäuser edition: "for the star of the moon—being of a rotting nature etc." More is discussed on that matter in Plutarch’s *Table Talk* III. 10. page 657. following, page 682. following, Wyttenbach edition, where the physician Moschion defines it thus: "rot is the melting and flowing of flesh as it changes into the moisture of decay, and in general, rotting things become moist." Compare also Plutarch *On Water and Fire* page 957. Olympiodorus in *On the Alcibiades* at the beginning, page 19:—wherefore it is well said:

->“Increasing you increase, but waning you trouble all things,”<-

referring to the moon. Hence it was the opinion of the men of old that even "troublesome things" <note>original: "τὰ χαλεπά"</note> were generated by the moon, that is, flies, worms, and other things of that kind.

— **14. "how from the One comes the many."** <note>original: "πῶς ἐξ ἑνὸς πλῆθος"</note>] This refers to Ennead VI. book 7. which is titled: "How the multitude of Ideas subsisted, and concerning the Good."

->ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINI<-
<note>original: "ANNOTATIONES IN PLOTINI"</note>

It is so, if you consider their manner of philosophizing (compare Buhle in *History of Philosophy* Vol. I. p. 227) and it is confirmed by the testimonies of Simplicius and Boethius; of whom the former, in his *Preface to the Categories*, says: *Archytas the Pythagorean, even before Aristotle, made a division into ten primary genera in the book which he inscribed "On the Universe."* <note>original Greek: Ἀρχύτου τοῦ Πυθαγορικοῦ... περὶ τοῦ παντὸς ἐπέγραψε.</note> This book seems to be the same as that which others call the *Universal Discourses* <note>original Greek: καθόλου λόγους</note>, according to the great Gerard Vossius in *On Logic* IV. 7. 2. (Works Vol. III. p. 213.) Themistius, indeed, striving to claim that discovery for his own Aristotle, declares a younger Archytas, a Peripatetic <note>A follower of Aristotle's school.</note>, to be the author of that little book, yet he does not persuade. It is another question whether that little book, which exists even today, and which Jo. Conrad Orellius recently published among others in *Sententious and Moral Opuscules of the Ancient Greeks* Vol. II. p. 273 and following (Leipzig, 1821) inscribed with this title: *The Ten Universal Discourses of Archytas* <note>original Greek: Ἀρχύτου καθολικοὶ λόγοι δέκα</note>—whether, then, that is the work of the famous Archytas the Pythagorean, or of another man who wished to deceive us. What leads us especially to suspect the latter is that the passages which Simplicius brings forward from the *Archytean Categories* (we shall, however, present several passages from this interpreter of Aristotle and others for this book of Plotinus in their respective places) are not found in that little book. See Fabricius' *Greek Library* Vol. I. p. 834, Harles edition. Joseph Navarro did not distinguish between these two questions in his *Attempt on the Life and Writings of Archytas of Tarentum* (Copenhagen 1820, p. 40 and following). And just as Archytas of Tarentum first wrote about *predicaments* <term>predicaments: another term for categories or classifications of being</term> (concerning the Categories), so Clinomachus of Thurii is said to have first written about *predicates* (Diogenes Laërtius II. 112: *And Clinomachus of Thurii, who first wrote... concerning axioms and predicates.* <note>original Greek: Κλεινόμαχός τε ὁ Θούριος... περὶ ἀξιωμάτων καὶ κατηγορημάτων</note> Since Navarro (p. 37) borrowed these words word-for-word from Gerard Vossius in the place cited, he ought also to have added this from the same source: that these were falsely translated by the interpreter of Diogenes as *concerning predicaments*. For *categories* <note>original Greek: κατηγορίαι</note> are certainly called *predicaments* by Boethius; but *predicates* <note>original Greek: κατηγορήματα</note> are *predicata*. These are also called *things predicated* <note>original Greek: κατηγορούμενα</note>, *predicables*, and *accidents* <note>original Greek: συμβάματα</note>. See Vossius in the place cited and compare Wyttenbach’s *Precepts of Logical Philosophy* I. 3. 2. p. 39 and following. Furthermore, this Clinomachus, who is said to have come from the school of Euclid of Megara, is wrongly written as *Clitomachus* in the same Vossius' *On Greek Historians* II. 16, even in the newest edition. Suidas also knows the same Clinomachus in the entry *Pyrrho* Vol. III. p. 246, Kuster edition. Plato then established five genera of being (the kinds of being) <note>original Greek: τὰ γένη τοῦ ὄντος</note> (see *Sophist* p. 255 e. and following) which Plotinus undertook to explain and confirm in these books (See below at p. 602. A.) An anonymous author in our Heidelberg-Palatine Manuscript No. 132 illustrates Aristotle's ten Categories with examples added as follows (See our *Meletemata* I. p. 8):

->**Substance. Quantity. Quality. Relation. Where.**<-
->**Andronicus. Great. Faithful. Son of Palaiologos. In Constantinople.**<-

->**When. Position. Possession. Action. Passion.**<-
->**Now. Standing. Armed. He rules. He is ruled.**<-

Compare Aristotle's *Categories* chapter 2, p. 24, Sylburg edition, and Suidas II. p. 278, Kuster edition, who however, perhaps following Alexander, arranges the ends in the *Topics* of Aristotle thus: *action, passion, position, possession*. And likewise Wyttenbach in *Precepts of Logical Philosophy* in the place cited: “*Substance, Quantity, Quality, Relation, Action, Passion, Where, When, Position, Habit* :” to which he subjects five Predicables: “*Genus, Species <insert>Space</insert>, Difference, Property, Accident.*” After Aristotle, Theophrastus, Eudemus, and Phanias wrote books on the Categories (see Buhle’s *Argument of Aristotle's Categories* p. 434 and following); Andronicus of Rhodes, Porphyry, Ammonius son of Hermias, Simplicius, and Boethius made commentaries or *Introductions* <term>Isagogas: introductory manuals</term> to the same. As far as Porphyry is concerned, although Parius found this title in the Palatine manuscripts: *Introduction of Porphyry the Phoenician, disciple of Plotinus the Lycopolitan* <note>original Greek: Πορφυρίου Φοινίκος εἰσαγωγὴ... Πλωτίνου τοῦ Λυκοπολίτου</note>: nevertheless, no mention of Plotinus is cast into this *Introduction*, unlike what happens in the remaining commentaries, especially that of Simplicius. A commentary by Photius exists on this *Introduction* of Porphyry, from which I plucked a small flower (from the Munich Manuscript no. 222) in *Meletemata* in the place cited. In the same place, I presented a passage of Dexippus transcribed from the Laurentian-Medicean Manuscript no. 33. We shall present more from other Manuscripts also, for the explanation of these books—

->BOOK I. ENNEAD SIX. p. 1044.<-

...for the sake of clarity, in this our edition of the Enneads. Concerning that **Dexippus**, Gerard Vossius teaches us the following in his *On Logic*, book 1, page 213: “Dexippus mentions the Categories of Archytas <note>Archytas of Tarentum, a Pythagorean philosopher</note> in book I, chapter 6; likewise in book III, chapter 1, where he says that Aristotle departed from Archytas in this: that he assigned to *quantity* the place closest to *substance*, and not to *quality*, as *Archytas* did, whose opinion *Plotinus* more greatly approved. This Dexippus is Herennius of Athens, who lived under the Emperors Aurelian and Probus, an outstanding leader in war and a disciple of Iamblichus, who, besides his *book on the Categories against Plotinus* (John Tzetzes says in his *Chiliads* IX, History 274, verses 497–499, that he had read only this one:

->Dexippus the philosopher, an initiate of Iamblichus,<-
->Composed many other books as well,<-
->But I encountered the one on the Categories. <note>original Greek: Δέξιππος ὁ φιλόσοφος... Ἐν τῷ ἑνὶ ἐνέτυχον τῷ εἰς κατηγορίας.</note> [Perhaps read: *among those*?])<-

also recorded Macedonian and Scythian history. I have spoken of this matter at greater length in Book III of *On Greek Historians*, chapter 16.” And therefore, from the very family of the Platonists and even the Plotinians, a defender of Aristotle had stood forth against Plotinus. For this reason, we have deemed it advisable to include in the annotation to these Plotinian books, and in other passages, the mentions of Plotinus made by the ancient interpreters of Aristotle, and indeed by Dexippus himself. By this means, Plotinus’s reasoning in this doctrine of the Categories may be compared with the reasoning of Archytas, Plato, and Aristotle, and it may be understood how later Greek philosophers again pleaded the cause for Aristotle against Plotinus. We have said more about Dexippus in the Prolegomena to § VII, note 3. Simplicius (in *Aristotle’s Categories*, Basel Edition, 1551, folio), on Folio 1. a., having enumerated the others who wrote on Aristotle, says this of Plotinus: <note>original: Πλωτῖνος δὲ ὁ μέγας...</note> “But the great Plotinus, in addition to these, brought more practical examinations in three whole books entitled *On the Genera of Being* <term>Genera of Being: the highest classes or categories of reality</term> to the book of the Categories... And Dexippus, the student of Iamblichus, himself briefly explained Aristotle’s book; but primarily he sets out to resolve the difficulties of Plotinus, which are proposed to him as if in a dialogue.” (Note of the transcriber: Plotinus, in the book titled *On the Genera of Being*, had collected doubts <note>original: ἀποριῶν / aporion</note> concerning Aristotle’s Categories. Therefore, if mention is made of Plotinus’s "doubts" in our book, it is likely they were taken from the cited book, which is also sometimes named by Simplicius (see folio 32. b.). Moreover, the Categories themselves are called *genera of being* by Plotinus (see folio 4. b.). Where Simplicius treats the various ways in which this book of Aristotle is inscribed, he says: “Others, entitling it *On the Genera of Being* or *On the Ten Genera*, just as Plotinus also thinks in his contradiction <note>original: ἀντιλογίᾳ / antilogia</note> against them, look only to the things themselves, but not to the logical purpose; for the genera of being are the things themselves.”) For the sake of aiding understanding, I will add a passage from Porphyry’s *Introduction to the Categories*, chapter II, page 384 of Buhle’s edition: <note>original: Λέγεται γὰρ τὸ μὲν γενικώτατον...</note> “For the most general <term>genus</term> is said of all the genera, species, and individuals under it; but the genus which is before the most specific is said of all the most specific and the individuals; the species alone is said of all the individuals; and the individual is said of only one particular thing.—Therefore, the individual is contained under the species, and the species under the genus. For the genus is a certain whole; but the individual is a part; and the species is both a whole and a part.” We have presented more from this passage in the notes to Olympiodorus on the *Alcibiades*, at the beginning of chapter 34, page 204, which you may consult. Among more recent authors, to touch upon this as well, Brucker dealt briefly with the Dialectic of Plotinus and what this philosopher criticized in attacking the tenets of the Aristotelian doctrine of Categories, in *Critical History of Philosophy*, Vol. II, p. 393. Tennemann pursued the same at greater length in *History of Philosophy*, VI, p. 175 and following, who undertook to show, among other things, first that Plotinus was the first among philosophers to rightly criticize several points in the Stagirite’s <note>Aristotle, born in Stagira</note> ten Categories, and that he primarily aims to teach that those Categories are not the primary ontological notions; and secondly, that Plotinus himself labored to unearth the original notions of things, and thereby laid the foundations of so-called objective science. Moreover, Plotinus wishes the *genera* (the genera of being) to be understood as simple notions, not derived from elsewhere, of predicates which must be attributed to all things (or objects), and which are the principles of constitution—

<note>original: "ANNOTATIONES IN PLOTINI"</note> history not of science or knowledge, but of the things themselves (Objects).—And these very points Tennemann next proceeds to pierce and finish off with Kantian weapons.—This war will by no means be fought by us, who have accepted the duty of editor. Let this be the warfare rather of philosophers, who either build up or tear down systems. David the Armenian, a philosopher, in a Manuscript on Aristotle’s *Categories* in Vatican Code <note>original: "Cod. Vat."</note> number 1023 and others:—"There are six titles circulated for the present book. For some entitled it (as the Paris manuscript 1900 notes) *Categories*, as Aristotle himself did; others *On the Categories*; of whom some were associates <note>original: "ἑταῖροι"; the editor notes a common error in Paris manuscripts where "others" (ἕτεροι) is written instead</note> of Aristotle; others *On the Ten Genera of Being*, as Plotinus does when speaking against the categories; others *On the Topics* (or *Before the Topics* in Paris manuscripts 1900, 1937, 1938; corrected in 1939), as Archytas of Tarentum; others *On Universal Words*, as Adrastus of Aphrodisias (Paris 1937 and 1938 write 'Aphrodissus,' but it should read 'the Aphrodisian.' L. M. E. Sahune.) the Peripatetic; but the title of Aristotle wins out over all." The same author on the same work, chapter II, section 6 and following—"Others (namely those who accuse the categories of being too numerous, according to Krabinger) ask why there are not four categories, as Plotinus says: *substance, quantity, quality, relation*. For the rest were created from the combination of these. And the same author solves this by saying that even if they are composite, nevertheless the conception <note>original: "νόησις"; some manuscripts read "composition" (σύνθεσις)</note> of them is simple. For the form of the simple is one thing compared to the composite, and the composite is another; for it is one thing to be a man (these words are omitted in Paris 1939), and another to be a soul, another to be a body, and another to be a man."

**p. 1044, 13. But as many as they examined—themselves in defined generations—neither infinite because it is neither possible nor would there be knowledge.**] Thus, with the better books and Ficino, we have corrected and filled out the passage. Presently, the words *certain genera—ten etc.* refer to Aristotle’s *Categories*; there is no need for us to strive to prove that Plotinus is looking at these after what was placed at the title of this book, where it was also spoken concerning Archytas and other philosophers who had established the highest genera of being. Concerning Aristotle’s *Categories*, Simplicius says in his work on them, folio 7. b. ->BOOK I. ENNEAD SIX. pages 1044—1048.<-

*descend from Romulus*. <note>original: "descendunt Romuli"</note> But who, knowing the liberty taken by ancient interpreters, would not see that an interpreter using the Roman language wished to substitute a Roman example for a Greek one? <note>The author is discussing how Latin translators often swapped Greek mythological figures for Roman ones like Romulus to make the text more relatable.</note>) *after these things [and] the multitude of those from one origin, such as [that of] Hercules, which defining and separating from the others, we called the whole collection the race of Heraclidae.* <note>original: "μετὰ δὲ ταῦτα [καὶ] τὸ πλῆθος τῶν ἀπὸ μιᾶς ἀρχῆς οἷον [τοῦ] Ἡρακλέους..."</note> Compare Ammonius, Dexippus, and Boethius on Porphyry. I marvel that none of the more recent interpreters have made mention of this passage in Plotinus; from which, however, Porphyry might seem to have seized the opportunity for this example. Or shall we say that these examples of the Heraclidae, the Cecropidae, etc., belonged to the "commonplaces" <term>commonplaces: standard rhetorical or philosophical examples used by many authors</term> in this doctrine of the Categories? Certainly, this was a common theme in the speeches of Greek orators and rhetoricians, especially in funeral orations. See Himerius, Oration II, sections 3, 10, 11, and the notes on it by Wernsdorf, pages 374, 385, and following. Regarding the affairs of the Heraclidae, we have gained something new from the *Excerpts of Polybius* in the *Vatican Collection of Ancient Writers*, New Edition by Angelo Mai, Volume II, page 386. The adjective *Heraclean* <note>original: "Ἡράκλειος"</note> is to be removed from Proclus' commentary on Plato’s *Cratylus*, section 79, page 42, edited by Boissonade. The Philosopher explains concerning the names of those who, by their actions and entire life, reveal and celebrate the virtue of those deities after whom they are named, such as those who are joined to the *Minervian series* (the Athenian series). <note>original: "τῆς Ἀθηναϊκῆς σειρᾶς"</note> Then, after some intervening remarks, he proceeds: *Hercules, at least, they say, though called Alcides after his mortal fathers, was named Hercules by the Pythia because of his kinship with the Heraclean order and divinity; for a god, imparting a name to a man, looks toward his entire series and the life which he has put forward, and bestows the fitting surname.* <note>original: "Τὸν γοῦν Ἡρακλέα... πρέπουσαν τίθησιν ἐπωνυμίαν."</note> Read: *because of his kinship with the Junonian order* <note>original: "Ἥραιαν τάξιν"</note> etc. For Hercules had composed himself according to the Junonian order <note>The order of Hera/Juno</note>, and that goddess had stood as the author of his labors and the glory won through those labors: see Proclus, ibid., section 123, page 78. Astyages the Grammarian speaks against the etymologies of the name, with the ancient lexicographers in agreement. See *Etymologicum Gudianum*, page 248; Orion of Thebes in the *Etymologicum*, and Larcher there, page 69. Compare Koes' *Excerpts from the Royal Paris Codex* at the end of Orion, page 186, edited by Sturz. Mention of *Series* <note>original: "Σειρῶν"</note> is frequent in similar passages. Proclus, page 159, on the *Alcibiades*, at the beginning: *and you have here again the series of good-form causes appearing. For Socrates looks toward a divine spirit, and the spirit toward the god of whom he is a follower, and Socrates is joined (read: is joined) to the divine through the spiritual.* <note>original: "καὶ ἔχεις πάλιν ἐνταῦθα τὴν σειρὰν..."</note> Eunapius in *Historical Excerpts* XVI, page 264 (in A. Mai’s *New Vatican Collection* II) concerning the Emperor Julian: *just as his (Plato’s) Socrates says, "we are with Zeus, but not with any other of the gods." In this way he himself, referring back and joining himself to the solar kingdom and the golden series—* <note>original: "ὥσπερ ὁ ἐκείνου (Πλάτωνος) Σωκράτης φησὶ..."</note> On this matter Simplicius also argues in his commentary on the *Categories*, Folio 43. a: *Since many things are called "relative" by Aristotle, and here as the "greater" and "double," and "habit," and "reclining," and the rest, and others handed down by him which we mentioned before—those according to excess and defect, and those according to power and weakness, and other such things—Plotinus asks what the commonality is in all these. Is it a generic one, or in another way, according to the reference to one, as we say the Heraclidae are referred back to one common Hercules? For if they are attached to the subjects and have the relation—of which some are in substance, some in quantity, and some in others—the relatives will be changed along with the others; but if they have no communion with those things having the relation, but the category of relatives is unrelated, those things will not have a relation, nor will they be relative, nor will there be that commonality of these. Perhaps, then, they should neither be changed along with the things, nor entirely abstain from them, but while the different things are suspended together, the communion toward one another holds them together according to the very property of the relation. For even if the same one thing is present everywhere to things that differ and are distinguished, it will be separate and superior to the opposites, so that even if it were held by one of them, it would not be hindered from being present to the other also. If we say these things are true, however many and of what kind the differences of relatives may be, they will all be arranged under one separate category, that category being in no way displaced from itself by the difference of those participating in it. But they ask another question, etc.* <note>original: "Πλειόνων δὲ τῶν πρός τι λεγομένων..."</note>

**p. 1048, l. 1. They say that number is the first quantity** <note>original: "Ἀριθμὸν δὴ πρῶτον ποσὸν λέγουσιν"</note>] There is a specific book by our philosopher concerning numbers, the sixth of this Ennead, where see the notes on the title and the chapters themselves. In this place, Plotinus examines and strives to refute the fourth chapter of Aristotle’s *Categories*, which is inscribed *On Quantity*, and begins thus (p. 30 and following, Sylburg edition): *Of quantity, one kind is discrete and another continuous; and one consists of parts having position—*

consists of parts having a position in relation to one another, while the other consists of parts not having a position. Examples of discrete quantity are number and speech <note>original: *logos*</note>; examples of continuous quantity are the line, surface, and body. Furthermore, besides these, there are place and time. Compare Aristotle’s *Metaphysics* IV. 13. p. 86. following, edited by Sylburg, and Simplicius in his commentary on the *Categories* at the same place, folio 31.

**p. 1049, 11. And why are these themselves quantities?**] Simplicius in his commentary on the *Categories*, Folio 32. b: "Furthermore, Plotinus seeks in the first book *On Being* whether, if the continuous is quantity, the discrete is not quantity; but if both are quantities, it must be shown what is common to both. And he resolves the inquiry in the third book, saying (compare this Ennead, book III, chapter 13, p. 628) that what is common to them is 'being so much' <note>original: *to tosónde*</note>, clearly that which is viewed as a measure and a limit, according to which each thing is known as a quantity. For this was not bestowed upon magnitude by number, as it seems to some, but is a property of measure—both of the united and the interconnected, and even further of the discrete. For there is a private nature to each, as is also observed in the whole cosmos. The nature of the continuous, which is called magnitude <note>original: *megethos*</note>, is according to union and interconnection; that of the discrete, which is called multitude <note>original: *plēthos*</note>, is according to a heap and juxtaposition. For according to the essence of magnitude, the cosmos is one and is conceived as spherical and grown together with itself, extended and interconnected. But according to multitude, there is observed the arrangement and the decoration arising from so many elements, so to speak, and of animals or plants, and of so many oppositions or similarities. If, therefore, these are thus separated in the images <note>i.e., the physical world</note>, much more so are they distinct in the intelligible genera; and before these, in the immaterial forms existing in themselves, they stand apart while having a common element, as has been said: measure and limit." But Lucius and Nicostratus and their followers find fault with this division, etc.

**p. 1050, 11. they would have nothing in common with these, but only the name.**] Thus we have written, following two of the more excellent manuscripts. Regarding the expression "only the name" <note>original: *onoma monon*</note>, we spoke at IV. 3. 2. p. 373. E.

— **14. for it (speech) is measured; but being speech, it is 'so much.' Yet as speech, it is not a quantity; for it is significative, just like the noun and the verb—but speech is rather the impact [of air], etc.**] Thus, by the authority of the good manuscripts, we have established this passage. Aristotle, *Categories* IV. p. 31. Sylburg: "In the same way, speech <note>original: *logos*</note> [is among the discrete quantities]. For that speech is a quantity is evident; for it is measured by the short and long syllable—I mean speech produced with the voice, etc." The philosophers, and other Stoics, attempted a definition of *logos* (speech/discourse) early on. Plato in the *Theaetetus* p. 206. c. d. (p. 313. Bekker) posits this one: "Socrates: Come then, what <note>others and Heindorf read 'whom,' but the Bodleian and Darmstadt manuscripts confirm Bekker's reading</note> does he wish 'speech' to signify to us? For it seems to me to mean one of three things. Theaetetus: Which ones? Socrates: The first would be making one's own thought manifest through the voice with verbs and nouns, as if reflecting the opinion in the stream through the mouth as in a mirror or water. Or does such a thing not seem to you to be speech?" Nevertheless, Plotinus also has in mind this definition by the Stagirite <note>Aristotle</note> in *On Interpretation* chapter IV. p. 59. Sylburg: "Speech is a significant sound, of which some part is significant when separated; as a phrase, but not as an affirmation [or negation; I mean] for example, 'man' signifies something, but not that he is or is not; but it will be an affirmation or negation if something is added." And G. Jo. Vossius pronounces this to be the true definition in *Aristarchus* Book I, p. 366 (Works, Vol. II), setting down other definitions from Charisius, Diomedes, and Priscian at the same time. You should furthermore compare Porphyry and Simplicius on the *Categories* in the places cited, and Ammonius on *On Interpretation*. Olympiodorus in Plato’s *Alcibiades*, at the beginning, p. 66: "that speech is the face of the resonance." The same author, Chapter VI, p. 53, concerning the Delphic Apollo prophesying: "that he did not say these things merely by an impact of air and with a voice, but vitally and directly," which should be compared with the words of Plotinus in Book B, line 5 following: "but if the voice is not according to the impact, but according to the air."

**p. 1051, 7. from the significative into the co-significative of that category**] Thus, instead of "into the significative," we have written with Ficino based on the traces in the good manuscripts. A single example of this adjective <note>original: *syssēmantikon*</note> is cited from the *Etymologicum Magnum* p. 649. 20. Heidelberg (p. 588 Leipzig). Therefore, let this Plotinian instance be added to it, and let this word be added to Schneider’s Lexicon. Presently, with most of our manuscripts, we have given "yearly" <note>original: *eniausios*</note> instead of the "lasting a year" <note>original: *eniausiaios*</note> of the edition, and "touching" <note>original: *ephaptomenē*</note> instead of "upon touching," and finally after "the participants" we have added "all" from our manuscripts. Moreover, in this place concerning *Time*, he has in mind these words of Aristotle in *Categories* IV. 6: "Time and place are also of such a kind; for the 'now' of time joins both the past and the future." Examples also, for instance "three cubits long" at the end of the fifth chapter of Plotinus, are from Ari—

taken from Aristotle’s *Categories*. <note>original: "Aristotelis Categg."</note> See <note>original: "Cf."</note> IV. 12. Let it suffice to mention this once, so that we are not forced to transfer a large part of the book of *Categories* into our Annotations.

**p. 1052, 1. But the relative etc.**] <note>original: "Τὸ δὲ πρός τι κ. τ. λ."</note> Aristotle’s *Categories* V. 1: "Those things are called relative which, being either what they are, are said to be of other things, or in some other way in relation to something else." <note>original: "Πρός τι δὲ τὰ τοιαῦτα λέγεται, ὅσα αὐτὰ, ἅπερ ἐστὶν, ἑτέρων εἶναι λέγεται, ἢ ὁπωσοῦν ἄλλως πρὸς ἕτερον."</note>

The end of this chapter: *but the before and after we likewise* <note>original: "τὸ δὲ πρότερον καὶ ὕστερον ἡμεῖς ὡσαύτως"</note> seem to come very close to those things which the philosopher of Königsberg, Kant, set forth in recent memory in that part of the *Critique* which he called the *Transcendental Aesthetic*, concerning Time and Space as *forms of our intuition*. <note>original: "Formen unserer Anschauung"</note>

**p. 1055, 15. the father having departed—this one is like the deceased**] <note>original: "πατρὸς ἀπελθόντος—ὅμοιος οὗτος τῷ τεθνηκότι"</note> Above <note>original: "Supra"</note> I. 4. 7. page 34. F. Plotinus used "to depart" <note>original: "ἀπελθεῖν"</note> for voluntary death. In this place it simply means *to die*, as in Diogenes Laërtius II. 6: "Socrates having departed" <note>original: "Σωκράτους δ᾽ ἀπελθόντος"</note> (see our Annotation above on I. 4. 7. p. 34. D.), for which writers also use "to depart" or "to go to what is necessary" <note>original: "ἀπελθεῖν vel ἀπιέναι εἰς τὸ χρεὼν"</note> (See Wyttenbach on Plutarch’s *Consolation to Apollonius* p. 753. following) and "to depart from among men" <note>original: "ἀπελθεῖν ἐξ ἀνθρώπων"</note> Diogenes Laërtius VII. 184. See Baguet on the *Remains of Chrysippus* p. 39. following, note 69.

**p. 1056, 4. The same interpreter shortly thereafter did not express "to contemplate" <note>original: "θεωρεῖν"</note> after "lying," therefore in the version we added *if contempleris*. It seems it should be written "but of the" (namely, *half being*) "the half." <note>original: "τοῦ δὲ (sc. ἥμισυ εἶναι) τὸ ἥμισυ."</note>

**p. 1058, 17. But the quality from which the so-called etc.**] <note>original: "Τὴν δὲ ποιότητα ἀφ᾽ ἧς ὁ λεγόμενος κ. τ. λ."</note> Simplicius, in his commentary on the *Categories*, after he explained the opinions of others concerning the common element of quality (Fol. 57. b. 20.), reports concerning Plotinus: "But Plotinus established the common element of quality to be a <term>power</term> <note>original: "δύναμιν"</note>, from which the possessor is able or is not able. For this fits all four qualities. And it is clear that he uses 'power' and 'being able' in a single sense, even though they are usually predicated in many ways. For each of the categories fits this. But one must consider whether our difficulty has not run back into the same place. For the question was, if it is spoken of in many ways, is there nothing common? But by taking 'power' instead of 'quality,' we seem to have done nothing more. For if 'power' itself is also said equivocally, and again just as it is difficult to find the common element of quality, so it is not easy to conclude what the genus of power is. And perhaps Plotinus’s account is true. For because quality is in the middle of both acquired accidents and natural essences, for this reason it resembles power, which itself has a middle nature. And because it shares in the essence of the <term>form</term> <note>original: "εἴδους"</note> in some way, for this reason it is characterized according to one common account. But since it also participates in the derivative category, just as the category of 'position' and 'having,' for this reason it also takes on being spoken of in many ways. Just as power does. For even in the case of power, that which is spoken of in many ways has the common element co-existing with it, either by being ordered from one thing or toward one thing, or by the abatement of power being made around the same thing." In the following, Simplicius passes to the division of powers, and there is no further talk of Plotinus until fol. 58. a. 23. where it reads: "But if power is such, says Plotinus, <term>weaknesses</term> <note>original: "ἀδυναμίαι"</note> will no longer be qualities; but if they themselves are also qualities, the definition of quality will not fit all of them. Regarding this, it is necessary to distinguish how 'power' and 'weakness' are said. For if, as the Stoics render it, power is that which brings about several symptoms, as wisdom brings about both walking wisely and conversing wisely, then according to such a definition, even the things now called weaknesses will be powers; for even lack of skills brings about several failures; if however power were said according to another Stoic arrangement, as that which brings about several symptoms and masters the subordinate <term>activities</term> <note>original: "ἐνεργειῶν"</note>, then Plotinus’s definition fits. For even vice, being a weakness according to the Stoic definition, masters its own activities, and the middle arts, as if falling away..."

**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

**[Original Page 326]**

...of acting firmly, nevertheless they are of such a kind that the possessor is able to do what he is able to do from them; thus, such "impotencies" (*adynamiai*) are encompassed within the power (*dynamis*) according to quality. And if, according to Aristotle, we distinguish the many senses of power, even so the account of Plotinus will agree both in the case of power and in the case of impotence. Power being spoken of by him in six ways: one is that which proceeds from the potential (*tou dynamei*), according to which it is possible to be in a state of fitness (*epitēdeiotēs*), as a child is "able" to read because he possesses the fitness. Another is the perfection of that fitness, being a principle of motion, as he who knows his letters is "able" to read; and this power is also called actuality (*entelecheia*), and compared to this, the first power is incomplete, and impotence will be encompassed by the incomplete power. 

In another way, powers are spoken of by him as either active (*poiētikē*) or passive (*pathētikē*): the one because it proceeds from itself into another, the other because it proceeds from another into itself. And again, the power in "suffering" (being acted upon) will be an impotence of "acting," being in another power, namely that according to suffering. Again, in another sense he speaks of power according to which one acts alone or better than others, as one who walks as no other can, or one who has swum across a sea as no other; and again, the opposite of this: for we say that that which is able to suffer something worse possesses a "power" for this, as in the case of a human being’s capacity to be destroyed. And it is clear that this power is a privation (*sterēsis*), and thus the impotence of better things will be a power toward worse things; and universally, the impotence of some things will be the power of others, and impotence does not fall entirely outside the account of power but is mastered by it. For incomplete things are gathered up in the complete; for they have the cause of their being from them. And therefore, impotencies are encompassed in the account of power, as if from the primary and most perfect power reaching down even to the weaker things. Because of this, even virtue knows vice. And if this is so, quality will also encompass impotencies, because these too are powers of whatever sort. Or indeed, both impotencies and privations are called powers in this respect: that they perform their own works, being qualities themselves, and providing those who possess them with certain characters, and bringing on forms, even if they are shapeless; and because they provide those participating in them with certain characters, they are called qualities. Insofar as they also complete their own proper works, they shall also be called powers. Generally, in each category, privations were said to be reduced under the same genus as the habits (*hexeis*). Clearly, Aristotle likewise says that that which is according to impotence, just like that which is according to power, produces being, saying: "or simply as many things as are spoken of according to natural power or impotence."

**[p. 1058, 17]** "But quality, from which the so-called 'qualified' (*poios*) comes, one must first grasp what it is that provides the so-called 'qualified' things [etc.]." Thus we have given from the **Codd.** [Codices] instead of *prōta tis ousa*. Aristotle in *Categories* **cap. VI. 1—3**: "I call quality that according to which certain things are said to be 'qualified.' Quality is among those things spoken of in many ways. Let one species of quality be called habit (*hexis*) and disposition (*diathesis*) [etc.]." Presently, in the words *kai lepton* [and thin], if you compare **Ficino's** version, you might say either *pimelēs* [fat] or *liparon* [oily] has fallen out. Nevertheless, none of our books offers anything more, and **Ficino** is often accustomed to consult Plotinian brevity in such a way that he adds something of his own. Presently, with almost all the **Codd.**, I have written *aph’ hēs to echon dynatai ha dynatai* [from which the possessor is able to do what he is able to do] instead of the corrupt *to eschaton* [the last].

**[p. 1059, 12]** "But is it according to the powers [adventitious to] the essences themselves, such as the power of boxing?" **Ficino** corrected [etc.] "after the essences themselves" and thus he also translated, undoubtedly moved by the following: "power adding to the essences after themselves (certain books 'after them') the state of being qualified." **Cod. Vatic.** and **Cic.** have *epaktas* [adventitious]. If you substitute *epaktous*, a convenient sense arises: "according to powers adventitious to the essence—as the faculty of a pugilist." I, however, did not wish to tempt the passage. Plotinus here regards these words of Aristotle, *Categg.* **VI. 7**: "Another genus of quality is that according to which we call people 'boxers' or 'runners' or 'healthy' or 'sickly'; and simply as many things as are spoken of according to natural power or impotence."

**[p. 1060, 5]** "But ugliness and disease and weakness, and impotence altogether." You might conjecture that **Ficino** read [etc. "and virtue"] somehow. Yet in the **Codd.** there is no variation. Therefore, *pōs* [how/somehow] must be repeated in the mind from the preceding and translated: *and impotence in universum* [and impotence in general].

**[— 18]** "both impotence and disease—and disease and vice." Aristot. *Categg.* **VI. 7**: "Those are called healthy by having a natural power of not suffering easily from chance occurrences; sickly by having a natural impotence of not suffering easily from chance occurrences." The same in *Topp.* **VIII. 2. p. 404. Sylb.**: "For they bring forward that to health, being a lesser good than vigor, a greater evil is opposed; for disease is a greater evil than cachexia." Regarding disease, see also Plato in the *Timaeus* **p. 89. p. 135. Bekk.** However, the discussion in the *Sophist* **p. 228. p. 150. sqq. Bekk.** is more relevant here, where...

**BOOK I. ENNEAD SIX. p. 1058—1066.**

**[Original Page 327]**

...Plato disputes concerning the diseases of both soul and body; the summary of which passage **Olympiodorus** encompasses in a small space in *Alcibiad. pr. XXII. p. 197.*

**[p. 1061, 12]** "But if according to the shaping [etc.]" **Simplicius** in the place cited, **fol. 60. verso (Ed. Basil. 1551.)**: "Plotinus, being in doubt regarding the opposite of these, says: 'If it is common to every quality to be a character (*charaktēra*) from outside the essence, and that which supervenes after the essence into the "how" the subject is disposed, why are there more species? Are habit and disposition counted as qualities?' For the permanence is a difference of something else, and not of quality; rather, the disposition, being in whatever state, suffices for providing the 'qualified.' And the remaining permanent is an addition and from outside. But if the permanent and hard to move, and the being maintained in the same species, belongs to essences, or to the account of essence—by Zeus!—how does the difference according to these things not also make a species of quality in qualities, having some difference toward itself in one species, and not being some superfluous addition? For habit has not become more permanent than disposition by differing by some chance thing, but by the participation in some immutable and indissoluble power. This is not an addition of some formal variation, but a proper difference of the perfection of the same species—not that dispositions are incomplete, but that they themselves have a certain proper perfection of this sort, participating in the perfection of the same species. For some things are according to disposition, others according to habit. And indeed, habit does not remain entirely the same as disposition (for it would not be other than it), nor does it stand entirely apart; for habit would not be a disposition with an addition, but how is it the same as disposition, and how is it not, seeing that they remain distinct by differences in the same species?"

**[p. 1062, 2]** "For the permanent and non-permanent is not a difference of quality." He contradicts Aristotle in *Categg.* **VI. 4**: "Habit differs from disposition by being more long-lasting and more permanent [etc.]." Presently, with almost all books, after *paraschesthai* [to provide], I have deleted *to*, and I have written *oupō* [not yet] with the same instead of *houtō* [thus] after *ateleis* [incomplete]; likewise at **B. line 7**, *dynamis* after *hexesi* instead of *dynameis*, and finally at **C. line 4**, *pro* instead of *to pothen*.

**[— 6]** "But how are natural powers another species?" **Simplicius** in the cited place, **folio 62. verso**: "Plotinus doubts how natural powers are another species. For if qualities are according to powers, the [nature] of power does not apply to all, which is contained in one species of quality. To which it must be said, that the appropriate power is demonstrated for all species of quality, extending along with the whole genus. Power being spoken of in many ways, he, assigning at least two, makes one species of it according to actuality; reasonably he distinguishes the other as that viewed according to incomplete fitness, which is understood according to the potential, being itself viewed as twofold: the one according to chance fitness, viewed in all things, so to speak; the other according to that which has already received some advancement from nature, which belongs to the few."

**[p. 1063, 3]** "and the dense, and roughness." Thus with **Ficino** from the good **Codd.** I gave for *trachy tis*.

The edition defectively reads "and before other categories." For the rest, there is no need to explain in many words that in these chapters Plotinus, as the logic of the dispute required, touched upon several chapters of Aristotle's *Categories*, especially from the beginning of the fifth to the end of the ninth.

XII** concerning "prior" and **cap. XIII** concerning "simultaneous."
