...entirely cast out from beings. But that he does not want it to be quantity, he showed in his remarks on quantity: 'If time is taken according to the measurer, what must the measurer be taken to be? For it is either the soul or the mind' [**margin: (marg. the "now")**]. 'But if according to the measured, if indeed it is according to being "so much," such as a year, let it be quantity; but according to being "time," it is some other nature; for being "so much" is being "so much" while being something else, for time is certainly not quantitativeness. For quantitativeness, not touching another thing, would be strictly quantity for that very reason. But if one were to place all things participating in quantity as quantities, essence will be the same thing as quantity. In the third [book] concerning the genera of this, he says place and time are not understood according to quantity, but time, as it is the measure of motion, must be given to relation. And place, as it contains body, is also placed in relation and in "towards something," since motion is also continuous, and was not placed in quantity.' For Plotinus marked off for them a private category of motion. In the [treatise] concerning time, however, he declares it not a measure, but rather a measured thing. Whether he declares it a measure or measured, being other than measuring and being measured, it would have the measuring or being measured accidentally; just as that which is measured by a cubit is not said to be that thing itself, and if someone assigns motion [to it], he does not say what this motion is by which it is measured; so also he who says measure or measured does not say 'time,' but an accident, if anything, to time. But if he calls it a moving image of eternity, as Plato says, he removes its being a relation. For even if measuring and being measured belong to it, it is according to a relationship, but not being a relationship; rather, it belongs to something else established before the relationship. Thus it is neither according to itself, nor toward something. Such are the things against Plato [**margin: (marg. Plotinus)**]. But it is possible to say on his behalf, that time is viewed in essences, being neither quantity nor toward something, and thus it will be brought under one of the five categories established by him. For if it is a moving image of eternity, it also analogously encompasses the things here, just as eternity encompasses beings; and if that [eternity] is a Mind encompassing all intellections and all species, this [time] also has encompassed in itself all the reasons (*logous*) of things that come to be. And if that [eternity] is defined in station and remaining in one, this [time] is defined in moving according to some essential life and motion, and has its being in passing from one reason to another reason, whether time is established in the reasons of the soul and in their transitive activity, in the same genus in which the reason of the soul is. For if Plotinus denied that the motion of reasons was essential, as some others do, he would have to say that time must be placed not under essence, but under motion, according to the transitive motion of the soul. But if the activities of reasons are essential, time will also be under essence according to them—that essence, namely, which is middle between the intelligible and the sensible; and thus he would say that "when" is not properly added to the categories. For it belongs to time, and time is arranged under essence. He says these things clearly, as if "when" and time are not distinct, or if they are distinct, that "when" is not worthy of the placement of a private category, but these things shall be examined shortly." The same, **p. 88. a**: "When, therefore, those around Plotinus and Andronicus say that 'yesterday' and 'tomorrow' and 'last year' are parts of time, and for this reason claim they are arranged with time, we shall say they are not parts of time, but contain a relation of the things that exist in time, and each of these is something else. But if they say 'yesterday' is time past, or a measure of time, it will be something composite: either the 'past' is one thing and 'time' another, and there will be two categories, and 'when' will not be one simple thing. Or by the same reasoning, we shall say if 'animal' is one thing, and 'rational' another, and 'mortal' another, it will not be simple, but three categories. But if in this case we gather the three into one species, then both time and the past contribute to one thing, and do not make two categories. Perhaps 'yesterday' is not simply past time, nor do more concepts run into the same thing in this case. For according to that relation alone of the thing toward time, 'yesterday' is informed. But if they say 'when' is said of 'that which is in time,' this 'in time,' if you mean some thing, such as Socrates—that Socrates was 'last year'—belongs to another category; if you mean time, that too is of another; if you mean the composite, it will not be one category; or neither the things in time, nor time itself, nor the composite of both informs the category of 'when'; but it is the bare relation of the thing toward time. Therefore, we shall neither take parts of time in 'when,' nor things; but this too shall be simple, just like the other genera. It has been shown, then, from what has been said, how Aristotle places 'when' in another category, attending to the differences of...

...significations; and how Archytas arranged 'when' with time, looking toward the kinship according to things; and how Plotinus removed the category of 'when,' because of gathering the first genera into the smallest number, and not giving much at all to the variations of concepts and significations; but one must go to the remaining difficulties brought against 'when' and bring the solutions to them [etc.]."

**[p. 1067, 14]** "'Where' (*pou*), in the Lyceum and in the Academy." These pertain to Aristotle's *Categories* **IV. 6 and 7**, where time (*chronos*) and place (*topos*) are treated. Plotinus [takes] the examples of the Lyceum and the Academy from the writings of the Socratics and Plato himself (cf. the beginning of the *Euthyphro* and Fischer there; *Symposium* at the end) rather than from Socrates himself, whom we see used elsewhere and in the next chapter in examples.

**[Ibid.]** "'Where,' in the Lyceum [etc.]" Plotinus also doubts in his remarks concerning "where," saying this: "if 'in time' is one thing and 'in place' another, distinct from time and place, why will 'in a vessel' not also make another category, and 'in matter' another, and 'in a subject' another, and 'part in a whole,' and 'whole in a part,' and 'genus in species,' and 'species in genus'? And thus we shall have more categories." Iamblichus, solving this difficulty, says: "the 'as in a vessel,' and 'as in matter,' and 'as in a subject,' reveal local relations. But 'the whole toward the parts,' and 'the parts toward the whole,' have the relationship of 'towards something' (*pros ti*). Likewise, the 'genus toward the species,' and the 'species toward the genus,' have nothing similar in the relationship of 'towards something' to that toward place and toward time [etc.]." This is from **Simplicius, p. 88. b.** But on **p. 90. b.** the same, where he discusses the category of "where" having set out the opinions of other philosophers, passes to the opinion of Plotinus thus: "Just as it is absurd to say that the 'double' and the 'equal' are quantity because they are something of quantity, so also he who says 'place' when speaking of 'according to place' or 'something of place,' would be absurd. Plotinus, however, entirely removed the category of 'where,' assigning 'where' to place, just like Archytas and Andronicus; but assigning place, like time, either to quantity or to 'towards something.' 'Where' signifies two things: place, and that which is in place, just as 'when' was said to signify two things: past time, and that which is in time; but the category of 'where' is defined according to the second signification. For that which is spoken of as a 'form' (*typos*), would be quantity according to Aristotle, but that which is 'in place' belongs to the category of 'where.' Even if someone is in place in a composite way; and in time 'voice,' something simple must be understood from the composite expression as from 'good spirit' (*agathos daimōn*) and 'holy city,' we understand one simple thing." The same, **p. 91. a**: "Plotinus, bringing forward 'in the Academy,' 'in the Lyceum,' 'above,' 'below,' seeks whether these signify different places, or other things in other things. For if places, why seek something else for 'where' besides place? If another in another, such a thing is neither one nor simple. To which it must also now be said, that neither place simply is signified by these, nor some composite; for things in place and place itself are not entwined; but this relation alone is co-revealed in a single form. Nor does the 'in' part produce a composition in saying 'in the Lyceum,' but presents the relation alone toward the place. But if we say this, he says, we generate some relation of 'this in this,' of the receiver toward what it received; why then are these not 'towards something,' having their being from the relationship of each toward each? To which it must be said, that one relation is equalizing and reciprocal, and of those things which are said to be of others just what they are, or in any other way toward another, which is viewed peculiarly in the case of relations. But another is that which is not reciprocal, but inclines toward other things alone, and peculiarly makes the relation toward time or place, which was not of those things peculiarly called 'towards something,' which is why it did not reciprocate, like the 'towards something' things; for in 'where' and 'when,' the relation of place and time is not taken toward the 'in place' and 'in time,' but that of the 'in place' toward the place. There is nothing strange if this sometimes also takes on the relationship of 'towards something,' as in 'on this side,' and 'beyond,' and 'above,' and 'below.' So also in the case of things according to time: 'elder,' and 'young,' and 'recent,' and 'ancient,' are outside the category of 'towards something,' although they have a relation toward time, or of those things peculiarly concerned with times; but 'older' and 'younger' and 'more recent' and 'older,' and such things, peculiarly reveal the relationship of 'towards something.' And the additions of conjunctions do not make a composition in the categories, because they are not reduced by themselves into a category as conjunctions, nor do they signify anything by themselves. But if they signify [etc.]."

For if it were said to be incomplete in this way, as diminished in the same nature, nothing prevents putting forward activity as a genus, and subordinating motion as a species; but if it departs into another genus, activity cannot be its genus. If, then, motion hastens toward the end, as coming to be beyond it, and not yet having it in itself, and activity stands according to the end, being full of itself and its own perfection, that which is most perfect would not have some communion of nature with that which is urged toward perfection. And if activity has the species perfect in itself, but motion journeys toward the species, having it only in power and according to a material and formless fitness, that which was said will be clear also in this way; again, if indeed activity is viewed in transit and continuity, being always continuous and divisible to infinity, but activity stands at one limit, having its being from itself, and at once gathering the whole one...

**[Original Page 331]**

...within itself, not even thus would activity be the genus of motion. And if motion has its substance mixed with the contrary, and always passes from the contrary to the contrary, as when black comes to be from white—for the motion from one to the other is neither of the extremes, but is mixed from both—but activity being entirely unmixed, stands according to one of the contraries, being in no way filled with the contrary nature, how can activity be the genus of motion? And if one should say that motion extends against time, as being extended, but activity against eternity as being unextended, and being present as a whole at once in the "now," not even thus would there be some homogeneous nature of eternal things and those in time. Even more, activity pre-exists unmoved, holding together the beginning and the end of motion in one rest. But motion is in a transit proceeding according to number, or it would be distinguished; but it seems, says Plotinus, that it does not agree with the purer opinions concerning activity; but it is carried off to that concept according to which some define acting according to moving. And they suppose that motion according to moving and activity are the same; which is far from being true. Furthermore, one must be persuaded by **Theophrastus**: for to him it seems that motion is not separated from activity; and that motion is also activity, as being contained in it, but activity is no longer motion; for that the essence of each thing and its proper species is the activity of each, this not being motion. For perfection is not prevented from being even in the intelligibles and those naturally unmoved. And there are many such even in the sensibles, such as that according to the shape of a statue. The shape stands according to the same perfection; but if activity exceeds motion to such an extent, one ought not to join them, nor make one the genus of the other. But if someone says that activity puts forward 'moving,' according to being arranged toward the same, but the 'in activity' (*energeia*), according to the shape of the statue, and the actuality (*entelecheia*) of each standing, to be spoken of in relation to 'in power' (*dynamei*), it having been removed from it, but activity not being removed from motion, he is ignorant that 'in activity' is opposed to 'in power,' and is the perfection of the incomplete, and has taken on a relation toward the contrary; however activity is absolutely by itself, spoken of in relation to no contrary, which also provides perfection to the thing being in activity. It is far, then, from the shape being activity, but not existing in activity. For altogether those saying this do not know the pure genus of activity, nor its separation from motion, nor its priority to being 'in activity'; nor do they remember this: how we say intellections are activities, presenting the impartibility of their knowledge, at once, and in the 'now' and in the 'already' as a whole, and such things. For what is in the time of the 'now,' this is understood to be the activity in motion. And pure activity must be outside motion. And from it other activities proceed, which are viewed not without motion, just as we call imagination and sensation, according to the passion, to be of motion, but according to the species, activity. And thus some are inseparable from motions, and others separable. Inseparable are those which are perfecting of motions, leading them and bringing them forward into activity. Separable are those which were of a single form and entirely unmoved. Up to these points, then, one might endure those dragging down activities in this way. Because there were also certain material species, with which material activities are revealed to coexist. But those proceeding further and dragging them down to motions, one would in no way endure, nor those placing under the so-called common activity that some are impartible and at once, and others in the state of becoming, and generations which are also called motions. For neither could there be a genus of impartible and partible things, nor of those in being and those in becoming, nor could the same activity be both impartible and extend over partible things, and exist both at once and in becoming. For all these things destroy the nature of beings, and do not preserve the essence of activity. It is clear that the 'doing' (*poiein*) as a common genus of doings and sufferances, namely motion, is contrary to the opinion of Aristotle, both elsewhere and now in the division of the categories currently arranged. For there will no longer be two genera, doing and suffering, but one before them: motion. But how do they extend 'being moved' commonly to both those things viewed in suffering and those in doing according to motion, such as walking, and according to relation, such as having been clothed, or sitting? For these are mixed from passion and activity—not the strictly so called, but that mixed with passion."

Plotinus in **Simplicius on Aristotle's *Categories* p. 78. b.**

**[p. 1069, 14]** "But if someone should say that motion is an incomplete activity, nothing prevented activity [etc.]" Plotinus does not even concede that motion is incomplete, nor does he say that it is perfected, but the thing which it aimed at; for instance, walking is walking from the beginning. If it were necessary to walk a stadium, but he had not yet finished this, it is not of the walking, nor of the motion that there is a deficiency, but of the *so much* walking. For it was already walking and motion, even if of whatever amount. Iamblichus, meeting him, says: "you do not take the work of motion insofar as it is movable, nor do you join it to the power, since insofar as it is movable it is not yet a whole. Therefore, you do not take the actuality as of a movable thing." And he says, I think, rightly: "for it seems to me to suffer some such thing, as if someone were to call the incomplete itself perfect, whenever it is incomplete, being viewed according to its incompleteness; thus also motion is incomplete, because its nature is mixed, from the potential and the actual, having come from the indefinite and the defined, and the formless and the species, and the non-being at once and being." From which it becomes clear, that no movable thing [moves] by motion toward pure activity. For this is pure of every infinite and indefinite mixture, and exceeds such things. Since he seemed to those from the Peripatus to reduce motion to quantity, Plotinus wants to reduce it to activity itself, so that just as activity is not quantity, so also motion may be demonstrated not to be quantity. And that motion is quantity is clear, not from being in time. For this belongs to it accidentally, but from its extension and insofar as it was otherness, as Plato says, and unlikeness. For as long as it is one and the same, it entirely rests. But insofar as it takes on difference, it has moved; since, then, it is necessary for rest to be one, and motion to be many, motion is quantity. That not every activity is motion is manifest. For indeed the activity of the mind is unmoved. But concerning some things a search has arisen, whether they ought to be called motions, such as sensation and the intellection of the soul, which seem to some to be not without motion, yet not to be motions, if indeed they are impartible, as has been shown in the [books] *On the Soul*, and every motion is partible; if they are completed even in the "now," both sensation and intellection, not even thus would they be motions, but they would more correctly be called activities. Melissus having said that every generated thing has a beginning, Aristotle says that not in all generated things is there a beginning of the thing, but there is a beginning of the time, yet no longer of the thing. For it is able to change at once (*athroōs*), as in the case of the air being illuminated. For the whole is illuminated at once. Not, however, without time (*achronōs*). For it was illuminated at the sunrise; however, the sunrise is not without time; for it is not according to the "now," nor is the illumination according to the "now," even if the air is illuminated at once, and not this part after that part. Aristotle having thus spoken of change at once, Plotinus says, if change is at once, motion is also at once and without time; Aristotle would then say, that one change is according to the "changing"; another, according to the "having changed," is rest. If, then, the [change] according to the "having changed" is entirely composed from the change according to the "changing"; and the "changing" pre-exists, the sun being about to rise; and to us only the "having changed" occurs imperceptibly, the instance of illumination would be not without motion, yet not a motion; but if it is possible for the "having changed" to occur without the "changing," it would not be motion, nor would such a change be with motion, or in the "having changed," but such changes are activities, and not motions. Many of the things said by Plotinus concerning motion do not fit motions. For the being called a "timeless" motion fights against its completion and its transit, and its beginning at some time in a timeless way destroys the continuity of its nature; again, to think that the same motion is concluded is impossible in the case of a continuous thing. For in the case of those things defined according to number alone, it is possible to conceive a unit and another unit, and thus to arrange into the same thing the defined multitude. But in those things where there is an unlimited continuity, it is not possible to summarize into the same thing, as if it were some defined multitude. It is not rightly said, even if change happens at once and timelessly, that such a motion also happens. For if they happen according to species, being unmoved presences of species, there will be timeless changes, but not motions. But they do not even suppose this rightly, as if the account of motions and activities were one. And if activity is timeless, motion is likewise timeless. For activity stands the same according to the unmoved presence and perfection of the species; but motion always proceeds, until it...

**Simplicius on the *Categories* fol. 81. b.**

Therefore Plotinus [says] that it seemed to some not to characterize "doing" and "suffering" from that which is from itself or from another, but from that which is according to nature or contrary to nature. For those things attaining their proper end are in "doing"; but the contraries of these are in "suffering"; at least he says that the one dying for his country does not suffer, but acts, both saving according to reason and according to his own perfection; but the one acting unjustly, even if he kills all men, he says, destroying that which is according to reason and the natural starting points, suffers, but does not do; wherefore it happens that the same motion is of doing and of suffering. For the same thing, as artificial, does according to nature; but as natural, contrary to nature, as the fire in animals moving downward, and the earth upward; according to the art of the demiurge, they are moved according to nature, wherefore such motion is not passive, but active. But toward the essence from the beginning, it is passive. Against these things, they say that the productive cause is one thing, and the final cause another; even if the final cause has an exceeding dignity among the causes, yet in "doing" the productive is more sovereign, and needing nothing else in this; whenever, then, in doing he misses the end, according to the productive cause in himself, he would be said to "do" justly; but according to the error of the end, to "suffer," if he were disposed contrary to nature; perhaps according to the attainment of the end, when he is disposed according to nature, he would be said to "suffer" even thus. For not every passion signifies the contrary to nature, but there is also something according to nature; and if he has both the end and the good in himself, as they say, the so-called "doing," then this account rendered concerning "doing" will be fixed: that to do is to have the cause in oneself. Perhaps in the case of simple things, the productive and the end are not divided, but have run together into the same; but if they are divided, it is nothing strange to "do" according to the productive, and to "suffer" according to the end. But whenever the end does, it is said to do according to that; at least the one dying for his country, the "doing" according to the end, by which he saves that which is according to nature and according to reason, this he activates, and has in himself the cause of such an activity, which provides the proper end. But the participation in the end is a "having-suffered," but by himself. However, he no longer has the saving and seeking activity of himself when he dies, but another is the cause of the dying. Wherefore insofar as he does not have the cause in himself, but in another, in this respect he suffers, but does not do; unless perhaps giving himself for his country, he is again both the doer or even the sufferer, according to one thing and another; everything, therefore, insofar as it does, has the cause of doing in itself; but everything suffering insofar as it suffers, [has it] in another. And the one acting unjustly **[82. a.]** whenever someone says he suffers, the [principle] according to reason being destroyed in him, even if he kills all men, he views many things in him. For he himself does in himself the destruction of the [principle] according to reason, if indeed he should destroy himself. And he suffers as if by another [to himself] being destroyed. And indeed he also does the killing of others. If, however, he should become unjust by another, that person does toward him. This man suffers by the one doing toward him, but does toward those being killed. And fire in animals, if it moves downward, and earth upward, Iamblichus says toward the art of the demiurge, being itself a beginning of doing, it does this. But toward the cause of nature, if indeed it moves contrary to nature, it suffers this. I wonder if now what Plotinus wants, we also say, that things according to nature are in "doing," but things contrary to nature in "suffering." Perhaps then it is clearer to say, that the downward motion of fire, and the upward of earth, are passions generated from the demiurgic doing, but are final and form-giving of the composite. But a passive "doing" of the elements themselves, if anyone seeks it, let it be defined as that activating according to the species and the cause in them; wherefore according to the activities, it both is strong and increases according to the passions, even if generated from demiurgic [reasons] or words (*logōn*). For the composites, it contributes to the constitution of the species, toward which even the demiurge looks; but they being forced, both wane and are obscured. And in animals, the impulses and motions happening unsuitably to the species, departing from their productive principle, both have [existence] contrary to nature, and are changed into the contrary cause of doing; wherefore they must be said to be in "suffering," for other reasons and because the principle of doing holds them together into being, but these decline into destruction. But if this is so, even the principles of these will be not in...

**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

**[Original Page 334]**

...themselves, but outside, if indeed they are in "suffering." If, however, the principles were given, these too must be called "doings," even if they depart from that which is according to nature; for there are also destructive doings, just as there are perfecting sufferings. And not all doing leads into being, but also into non-being, whether it activates something into itself, or into another; for that which is contrary to nature activates certain activities from this disposition contrary to nature, even if not pure, because they are mixed with passion, and brought forward from a suffered disposition. And in the case of those things moving from outside, whenever they move toward nature, just as farmers and teachers, since the productive principle of nature and that of art fall into the same, and two activities are held together, those of art, having the principle from outside as art, become passions in that which is according to nature; but those saving nature having the principle from within, remain in the species of activity. And whenever the hearing of the teacher enters into the learner, the activity from the voice has the passion through hearing as its yoke-mate, and thus in these "doing" is yoked with "suffering," the activity according to the voice being one thing, and the passion according to the hearing another; but whenever that which has suffered by the voice no longer stands in the passion, but puts forward from itself another activity of apprehension, then another beginning of the activity from itself comes to be: the recognition by the one who learned. But if the one who received the prior activity according to passion makes another activity out of the passion, one must not for this reason join it toward the activity which preceded the passion, leaving out the passion in the middle; nor must the beginning of the second activity be placed in the teacher, so that the cause of the doing may appear in another; but just as it is a yoke-mate—of the passion in the hearing through the voice in the learner, the cause is in another, the teacher—the apprehension, however, must be supposed as being raised from the reasons (*logois*) in the soul, so that he may both truly recognize what was said, and receive it properly, and not remain in the blow and the hearing alone; and thus the beginning of the activity will be in himself, and not in another; from the same concept Plotinus also brings these things forward: "Is it then where there is not activity, but suffering alone, these things will be in 'suffering'? What then if the sufferer becomes better, but the activity has the worse? Or if one should activate according to vice and should rule another licentiously, shall we place these only in 'suffering'?" And these things are said from the concept of suffering and doing. Saying doing is saving, but suffering is destructive. And the one better, the other worse. But it fights against usage, which calls wicked things activities and doings, and contrary to nature; and conversely considers perfecting passions according to nature. For simply "doing" is not one genus of activities, but as many differences of doings as are defined according to species, all are contained under the one "doing." Likewise under "suffering," there are perfecting passions, and there are incomplete ones; and some are beautiful, others ugly. And some, according to nature in each, and others, contrary to nature; but if someone takes only one of the opposites in them, he contracts these genera into a short space, just as if someone were to say only the quality according to nature is outside, or only that contrary to nature. But he says not all doing is from itself, but also from another. From itself, the absolute, like walking; and the straight, like hitting; but from another, like desiring; for whenever the object of desire forces the appetite, what does it differ from having been struck, or having been carried down after being pushed? But in **p. 82. b.** these he says desires being activities are not from themselves, but from the object of desire they have been urged. And yet they are urged from themselves. But the object of desire leads the way in another way, not leveraging, nor pushing the desire, but calling it forth by fitness; for it is absurd for desire to be such in the self-moving soul, or the unmoved according to Aristotle; if however desire is a passion, as he himself says, it is nothing strange if it has that which moves from outside. And yet it is absurd to introduce an unchosen desire, and one not having the principle from itself. It is much more absurd to subordinate such a thing to "doing"; concerning "doing," so many things have been said in reply to Plotinus; concerning "suffering," it must be said in order. Since Plotinus himself, taking it privately, examines it. "For maybe it is not," he says, "the characterization of suffering by 'from another.' For there is something even from itself, and not everything is from another. [From itself the rotting, but from another the being struck; and thus it differs nothing from doing, if indeed that too was from itself and from another.]" But it was said before, that neither in the case of "doing" must "from another" be added, nor in the case of "suffering" "from itself"; and concerning rotting, how it happens from outside, was said before. "But whenever," he says, "it undergoes an alteration which does not lead to essence, while contributing nothing itself, or which removes it toward the worse, or not toward the better, such an alteration..."

"...I shall say is a suffering (*peisō*)"; but this neither teaches the cause of the passion, and the contrary; or it wants to gather: for if it itself contributes nothing to the suffering, either the passion will be contrary, or of some other thing from outside. Even if of those things being in it, some do, and others suffer. And thus the passion will be as from another. "But how is it necessary," says Iamblichus, "not to lead passions into essence, if indeed some of the passions also lead into essence, as many as are generative. Maybe this is proper to passion? For if the essence which will receive the passion must pre-exist, the passion is not essence-making, just as alteration is nothing proper; and he said the sufferer undergoes an alteration, that which does not lead to essence; but how do we judge passions to contribute toward the worse, or not toward the better, when some of them work the more beautiful in us? Or since Plotinus himself doubted this, let us see what he opposes to himself." "But if the bronze is better from being heated, the [passion] according to the heating prevents nothing of the suffering; for suffering is twofold: one, in becoming worse, the other in becoming better, or neither." And it is clear that before, suffering was placed in becoming worse; here, however, that there are certain indulgent passions leading even toward the better. "The inclination toward both having been placed in suffering," says Iamblichus, "the 'or neither' was not rightly brought in. For it is said in conflict with the hypothesis of doing and suffering, if indeed the one was placed in that according to nature and better; the other, in that contrary to nature and worse; although if the sufferer becomes similar, clearly it will become neither worse nor better, so that it is 'neither'; but it is also possible to become different, not having the comparison according to the worse or better, as when red comes from grey." But even toward the not leading into essence of passions, Plotinus doubts. "For if the being heated," he says, "is to have heat, and the heating of the bronze were to contribute to the essence of the statue, but no longer to the bronze, it would be the same thing to suffer and not to suffer, if indeed to suffer was not to contribute to the essence." To this Iamblichus says, that the definition of suffering was badly taken, according to the not contributing to essence. For whether it contributes to essence, or to alteration, or to anything else, the being heated is in "suffering"; maybe the 'not contributing to essence' of the passion was well said, for the cause which I said before; here, however, the bronze is heated, and suffers being heated, but the statue is heated accidentally, because it is bronze. Iamblichus does not accept this either, that "suffering" happens by having motion in itself, the alteration, that according to the being altered in whatever way. "For one must not," he says, "place the motion according to alteration alone in 'suffering,' but also many others. For even that which is increasing would be said to suffer, and that which is moving according to place. And as Iamblichus says, also that which is being led into essence." Furthermore, Plotinus says, "both risk being 'towards something,' as many as belong to 'doing' in relation to 'suffering.' For some same thing is 'doing' according to this, but 'suffering' according to this. And each is viewed not according to itself, but with the doer and the sufferer, where this one moves, and this one is moved, even if each is two categories, both the 'towards something' and the 'doing' or the 'suffering'; and thus he gives motion to this, so that this one receives, so that there is giving and taking, and 'towards something.' Or if the taker has it, as it is said to 'have' color, why does he not have motion?" And maybe even under "having" (*echein*) a category is subordinated, not only the things toward each other, but also the absolute; for even the absolute motion of walking has a "walking." To these things it is easy to say, that thus everything will be of "having," since it is viewed in being participated; for the white has whiteness; and the two-cubit has so much magnitude. And likewise in the case of others; but each thing must be reduced to the genus according to that which it is said to be; and 'towards something,' it has been said many times, that viewed according to the relation alone according to itself, it has its being in the other categories [etc.].

### PAGE 351

[[original page: 336]]

**-> ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS <-**

...is reduced to a relation, by the fact that activity belongs to that which is potentially active, and motion to that which is potentially movable; Plotinus, rightly arguing against this, says that this relation constitutes a "relative," but not that it is merely spoken of in respect to another. Whenever there is a certain subsistence [hypostasis], even if it belongs to another or is directed toward another, it possesses its own nature prior to the relation. Therefore, this activity, motion, and habit [hexis], even if they belong to another, are considered according to the relation itself only because they are something prior to the relative, just as right-handedness or similarity are. But those things which belong to others in such a way as to exist by participation—as motion is in the thing moved, and activity in the thing acting—do not represent the relative relation, but rather a participation in the motion, etc.

**p. 1072, 9. It must be considered, whether in the etc.]** Simplicius, in the place cited [abbrev: *loco citato*], page 79. b: Again Plotinus says, "It must be considered whether they will say that in 'acting' some things are activities and others are motions; and that activities occur all at once, while motions, such as 'cutting,' do not; for cutting takes place in time. Either every acting is also a motion, or it is accompanied by motion. And [it must be considered] whether they refer all actings to 'suffering' [passion], or some as absolute, such as walking or speaking; and whether all those directed toward suffering are motions, while the absolute ones are activities, or whether each exists in both." Certainly, everyone would call walking, which is absolute, a motion; but thinking [intellection], although it has the thing thought as its object [passive], must, I believe, be called an activity. To the first of these, it must not be admitted that every acting is a motion or accompanied by motion; on the contrary, that which acts either acts and possesses pure activity without being moved at all, so that in acting one ought not to say some are activities and others motions. For motions are not in acting at all, for the reasons mentioned. But we shall not simply say that instantaneous things are activities insofar as they are instantaneous, because being "all at once" was also a characteristic of changes, and activity is never distinguished from motion in this way (one being instantaneous and the other in time), but rather by certain other differences. To the second point—whether all actings are directed toward suffering or some are absolute—it is possible to say that "acting" is not that which is opposed to "suffering" as Aristotle established the genus, but rather the more general sense equivalent to "energizing" and acting from oneself, so that walking and sitting and all absolute things fall under it; but that which is opposed to suffering also falls under it, insofar as one has the principle and cause of motion in itself, and the other in another. It may also be said that the distinction opposed to suffering, as stated correctly by the Stoics, has not been grasped as clearly as it might. Likewise with "suffering," it is not the "passive" spoken of in relation to the actor, but the common sense. It is better to establish the first and most proper genus of acting as pure, having no entanglement with suffering; for thus the activity from itself is understood as pure. If one wished to take the opposition of acting and suffering, this too must be accepted, not according to relation, but according to the individual subsistence of each, which, being in each, takes on the character of opposition secondarily. The third point is not easily distinguished, because of the mixture of the two principles in many things. Walking, therefore, is a mixture of motion and activity. Perhaps thinking also is a mixture of suffering and activity, and for this reason it is not easy to declare in which genus the proposed things lie. But one must divide generally, calling the first actings "pure and unmixed," and the second those derived from them in mixed genera; and of these there are many differences. Some of them are entangled with suffering, others with different things. Some prevail according to their internal activity, others are prevailed upon by the things mixed with them, and others are woven together variously. Iamblichus, having set himself against Plotinus in such matters, says more technically: "It is necessary first to distinguish the specific nature of these genera, of acting and suffering, and to demonstrate their difference from one another. From this it will appear both what things ought to be subordinated to them and what kind of mixed things lie between them."

**p. 1073, 3. And perception is either toward another etc.]** Simplicius on the *Categories*, folio [abbrev: *fol.*] 81. B: For concerning perception Plotinus himself says, "perception, prior to relation, is an activity or a passion." Likewise with intellection. But even if someone considers intellection among the relatives, nonetheless the act of thinking will be in "acting," since it is the principle of the relatives; but the principle of acting is "acting." Since Plotinus, assuming the same motion and activity, declared motion to be one genus, let us see how he divides this genus. He says that some motions are bodily, others psychic. And of the psychic, some are rational, others irrational. And it is clear that such a difference follows accidentally according to the participants in which they arise, but does not arise according to the proper difference of the genus. Bodily motions are in acting,

whether using the body as an instrument, as in striking, or whatever forms belong to the body, such as being heavy. In the soul, motion in "acting" includes "doing geometry" through the soul. The proper activity of the soul is life. It is also possible to place some things in the soul and others in the body, according to those who hold that passions [affections] also occur around the soul. Again, he says some motions go from themselves into other things, while others go from other things into themselves; and it is clear that these distinguish the active and passive motion from each other, insofar as the one from themselves has "acting upon others," for this is acting; while the one from others or out of others into themselves is passive. But the sincere and pure character of acting is in that which is from itself; while for suffering, it is having the cause in another. But he does not preserve their purity, adding "acting from itself" to "acting into another." For through the mixture and the leaning toward another, he does not preserve pure activity. By making "from another" into "into themselves" a kind of composition, it makes a great difference whether one has the cause of suffering in another separately, or is joined to the cause of the suffering; for in a way, in these cases the two principles are confused into this. The cause of this has been the preference for motion as a common genus, through which it is no longer possible to distinguish clearly between suffering and acting. Hence, even regarding "cutting," the argument confuses these, placing motions into others as identical to motions from others; for let "cutting" [the event] be one, yet "to cut" and "to be cut" are different. This must by no means be conceded. For as it is with the cutting, so it is with the act of cutting and the being cut; just as the activity from the cutter is separated from the nature [or passion] in the thing being cut, so also the section according to the "cutting" stands apart from the section according to the "being cut." For the one is the pre-existing cause from activity and active motion; the other is the successor of this, being a passive change in the thing cut. Just as in the case of hair, the separation of the hands extending the hair is one thing, and the smoothing out of the hair is another. Thus, even in "cutting," the section according to the acting and cutting will be one thing, and the section according to the being cut will be another. But because they lie near or close to each other, their duality is hidden, and sometimes it might give the impression to some that the composite is in the acting, and at other times in the suffering. However, the truth is not so; there are two movements, distinct from each other by nature, but confused into the same thing in composites. This is hidden both because of the mixture and because they reduce acting and suffering to one genus. Next, Plotinus seeks this also according to the stated forms of motion, whether acting is everywhere linked with suffering. These forms of motion were generation and corruption, increase and decrease, alteration, and also change of place. Iamblichus says, "We immediately resist the start of this approach, not thinking it right that actings should be characterized by motion." For the genus of the movers is one thing, and that of the moved is another. Then we argue against it, not thinking it necessary to characterize actors and sufferers by the same thing, as if by "being moved." But perhaps it should be said to Iamblichus that the same forms of motion belong to both movers and moved. For that which is generated is generated by an actor, and that which is destroyed is destroyed by a destroyer. The same logic applies to alteration and change of place. To these difficulties of Plotinus, his successors brought such solutions. Since Plotinus approved another definition instead of the one given for acting and suffering by the Pythagoreans, let us try to understand this too, recording briefly what was said against him by Iamblichus and the others, etc.

**p. 1073, 9. It must be considered, whether even some etc.]** After Simplicius refuted the opinions of others, he returns to the opinion of Plotinus, which I transcribed above under note 93. b: (**p. 94. a.**) "But if Plotinus says that bodily things pertain to the body and are not incorporeal, he makes another category; why then, in acting, where there is much difference, is there not one category for cutting, and another for burning, or burying, or casting away? Or is the activity of acting one, having one logic, and needing nothing of the different reception of those receiving the act? For the cutter and the burner and the others do not differ in the respect of 'acting.' However, the category of 'having' has its material character in this: in being a body that surrounds a body, rather than something incorporeal. Or is it characterized not by a chance relation, but is properly viewed from the relation toward another within itself? But if he says the surrounding garment makes another category, why would the one lying on a bed not make another? Or is 'lying on a bed' part of the category of 'position' [lying] or 'place'? For the bed provides no activity...

...toward "having"; for the category of "having" suggests a certain habit [hexis] and possession, but of acquired bodies. If this is true, "having" is verified only in the case of animate beings, so that if an ornament surrounds a statue, as an inanimate thing, the statue would not be said to "have" the ornament, but the ornament would be said to "lie" on the statue; but if it were viewed as an animate thing, it would be said to "have" the ornament according to the reference to the animate. But if "having" is characterized according to habit, it will be reduced to habit, he says. But habit is in quality. Or is this "habit" homonymous? For one was the cohesion of bodies; the other is the possession of acquired bodies. And the "having" comes about through the activity of those having; but that of qualities does not come about through the activity of either the participated or the participants. They also differ in the things held: there, they are incorporeal; here, they are bodies. And in the things having: there, in the substance [essence]; here, around the substance from without. But if he says one should not say "having a quality" because quality has already been mentioned, nor "having quantity" since quantity was mentioned, nor "having parts" since substance was mentioned, why should "having weapons" be called another category, even though the substance in which the weapons are has been mentioned? Is it because the weapons or sandals are not said to be of the category of "having" in themselves, nor is the ownership of them if one who owns them does not use them, but the possession of them and the "habit" spoken of from having them makes the category of "having"? It is one thing to "have quality and quantity," and another to "have weapons and sandals." For there, the habit is of incorporeals; here, of corporeal things. And there, the things participated in are alterative of the participants; here, they only surround. But he says: "How is it a genus if it is in few things?" Is it because this genus is in the extremes and around bodies, and exists in bodies, and for this reason it has been contracted into a very small space—and on that account would it not be a genus? For even the phoenix, being one, has the whole species in itself. But why did he not join the discussion of "having" with the other categories, but as if by an afterthought, mentioned "having" after the discussion of opposites, and of "simultaneously," and of motion? Or, having completed the discussion of categories, since he remembered some things in passing, he works them out as well. Since the category of "having" is the last, and he was concerned with order, he reasonably mentioned the homonymy of "having" last; not only giving the proper order to the categories themselves, but also giving the same to the external things chosen and worked out. But he says it is "absurd," rejecting the common usage of saying a man "has" a wife. But if he had not mentioned it, he would have been absurd for omitting what is in custom. He who mentioned and judged it performed the work of a dialectician, to whom the judgment of truth is most important. Let these things be said in response to the difficulties.

...whatever unique characteristics of acting and suffering he recorded there. For Iamblichus also explains those; Archytas writes thus: "It is characteristic of the actor to have the cause of motion in himself. Of the thing being made and the sufferer, to have it in another. For the sculptor has the cause of making the statue in himself; but the bronze has the cause of being made both in itself and in the sculptor." And the same logic applies to the passions [affections] of the soul. For anger is naturally aroused toward something else and is irritated by something else from without, such as neglect, dishonor, or insult. But he who does these things has the cause of doing them in himself. Explaining these things, Iamblichus says that acting has the cause of activity in itself. Suffering, however, has the cause of motion in another and in itself, as the bronze-worker is in himself and in the sculptor, because suffering has a certain stability of its own essence, and is not entirely dependent on the actor. And finally, he brings objections against the argument. For he says some people argue that even some "acting" has its cause in another, such as thinking [intellection]. Or, if one does not place intellection in acting, but being thought [the object of thought] as the act of thinking being in suffering, not even thus does being thought provide the entire cause of motion to the thinker. Or the mode of communion is not such as those who are at a loss suppose concerning the mind and the object of thought; but perhaps that belongs to the contemplation of the mind. The difficulty must be solved in a manner measured to the present subjects, saying, I think, that Archytas accounted for pure actings and passions; and intellection, even if it is a kind of suffering, nevertheless has a certain activity aroused from within, just like seeing and knowing in general. And one ought not to bring an objection to the argument from these mixed things. Others bring the same difficulty from desiring and impulse, as if these have the cause of motion in themselves, but are not entirely free from the cause pre-existing from another and from without. Solving this difficulty, Iamblichus says that things which have impulse and desire are not simple. Being composite, they neither have the cause of acting universally, nor properly from themselves. But from some part of the things and powers in them, they are impelled into actings. Hence they also need cooperation from without, whether a pre-existing or contributing motion, and they participate in passive motion arising around something else. I mean the composite living being, with the cause of the activities' power being given from another. Therefore, this is neither pure acting nor suffering alone. Nor should one resist the given definition of acting from this, which says the cause of acting is present from itself. One only needs, says Iamblichus, to add "properly and primarily from itself and from its whole self providing the cause, and having this solely in itself and perfect [self-sufficient], sending it forth into the whole." It is clear that the argument will be clearer thus through the addition. And Archytas indicated all these things in a brief word. For "in itself" is taken properly and primarily as "in the whole." Again, he says it is characteristic of suffering to have the cause of motion in another. For if not, the passion is without cause, which is absurd for any event to happen by no cause or to have no cause. And if there is one, it is either in the sufferer itself (and thus it is not suffering alone but also acting) or from without and in another. For in whatever way the actor acts, and whatever things it does, those things the sufferer suffers. Plotinus also wonders about this, how there are some absolute things even in suffering, not arising from others, such as decaying and rusting; and many things having the cause of motion in another do not suffer, as a swan, brought to its proper perfection by becoming white from the reason [logos] within it, does not undergo such a thing through passion from another. And growth from the inherent reason is surely not brought into increase according to passion. But to such a thing it must be said that neither does the swan have the cause of being white in another, but in itself, nor does any other thing brought into its own innate form have the participation of its proper form from without. We call it passion to participate in this way, not because such a passion does not happen by another, but since the participation in form was an acquisition of essence according to activity, happening by air or water or some other moist vapor. Perhaps because of the composition of things decaying and rusting, there are some things in them in the "acting" and others in the "suffering," which those who are unable to distinguish suppose to be absolute passions; but many, they say, having the cause of acting in themselves, were affected, insofar as we say all the wicked are passionate from the vice in them. Or it seems to Plotinus himself that the passions of the soul are not passions but activities; either in the soul they are activities, but in the body passions. Just as, therefore, the wicked have the cause of vice in...

[[vocabulary: ἀνδριαντοποιός (andriantopoios) - sculptor/statue-maker; ὀλιγωρία (oligōria) - contempt/neglect; αὐτοτελής (autotelēs) - self-complete/perfect; σήπεσθαι (sēpesthai) - to rot/decay; ἐντελέχεια (entelecheia) - entelechy/perfection]]

[[original page: 340]]

**-> 340 ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS <-**

...themselves, so also they have the activity of it in the acting, since passion is not spoken of regarding the soul. But if the suffering occurs around the body, the passion will be in another, and from another, and thus the definition of suffering becomes true. But perhaps even in the soul, there being many parts, or many judgments, and many differing imaginations or powers or opinions, the wicked become passionate according to their disagreement, with some oppositions acting and others suffering, and the logic of suffering remains sound, as they have the suffering in "another" [another part of the soul]. But the fitness [aptitude] of matter being a passion of matter, how is it not from the matter itself, but from without? Or can one say that the fitness, being a reflection of the form, is given to the matter from the form; some say that matter itself is this very passion. But if it is not a passion, but suffers regarding the fitness, it must be asked: if it suffers the fitness, there is certainly something that makes it; if it does not suffer, but is itself fitness, it is the essence of the matter; but the discussion is about passion, whether internal or external. But it seemed, he says, that neither "from itself and not from another" was sufficient to characterize acting, nor "from another and not from itself" for suffering, since in acting upon another thing, the actor appeared to be the sufferer, but in that which it acted upon, not a sufferer but an actor. For instance, tin acting upon silver is itself suffered by being consumed and destroyed; but it purifies the silver, casting off what destroys it, so as to rather hold the silver together in the same quality. But since in composite things, actings and passions are mixed, neither does the tin act alone, but also suffers; it acts by purifying the silver, but suffers by being consumed by it. And the silver suffers by being purified, but acts by consuming, in different respects. But since it has been defined universally what acting is and what suffering is, and what the characteristics of each are, one must finally return to distinguishing the forms of acting and suffering. Once these are defined, it will be clear which are not rightly referred to the most proper genera, and which are, and which are mixed in both, and which are simply referred to one. From these, Plotinus' views will also be clear, whether he rightly subordinates certain things under acting or not. Here too one must set forth the division of acting by Archytas, who says: "In acting, the highest is activity; and of activity there are three differences: for one is in contemplating, such as doing geometry or astronomy; another is in making, such as healing or carpentry; another is in doing [practice], such as military command or politics." Activity occurs even without thought, such as in irrational animals, and these are most generic. Among these, the highest and common part of acting is defined according to simple activity, which in itself has grasped all activities distinguished by species, being free from all motion, and having the moving power pure, and the cause from itself and not from some other pre-existing or cooperating thing. From this, multiple species of acting proceed partially, of which the first is the theoretical; using activities that are instantaneous and unchangeable, and this itself is divided into more species; of which the first would be homonymous with the proximate genus in itself, this too being theoretical, and properly called theoretical; this is that which considers intelligible and indivisible essences with simple thoughts, such as the intellectual; this Archytas omitted, although he was of the Pythagorean division, perhaps because such contemplation was disproportionate for an introduction; the second is that which performs thought [dianoia] concerning unmoved and mathematical essences, such as doing geometry, using applications that are defined but no longer simple, but already composite and discursive, such as are the activities of pure thought; the third in these is that which performs contemplation concerning eternal and ever-moving sensible essences, using perception with reasoning, such as doing astronomy, demonstrating reasons in harmony with appearances. And thus the whole activity of contemplation proceeds from above from pure thoughts to calculations according to perception. After this species, Archytas places the poetic [making], homonymous with the genus, which properly subsists in bringing into essence things not yet participating in being. Of this, much is divine, which is contained in the craftsmanship [demiurgia] of the gods; and much is in the nature of the universe, especially that descending from heaven concerning everything that becomes. Much is also in the arts imitating nature and filling in what is left behind by it; for as nature instills the form of health in bodies, so also the physician in healing restores the perfection of nature in bodies; and as nature provided caves and natural coverings for animals,

[[vocabulary: ἐπιτηδειότης (epitēdeiotēs) - aptitude/fitness/suitability; κασσίτερος (kassiteros) - tin; θεωρητικόν (theōrētikon) - theoretical/contemplative; ἀΐδιος (aidios) - eternal; δημιουργία (dēmiourgia) - craftsmanship/creation]]

...so also architecture, carpentry, weaving, and the other arts fill the deficiencies for humans, constructing useful things for the self-sufficiency of life. The third genus of acting is that detached in "doing" [practice], which oversees actings concerning sensible and composite things, providing choice [proairesis], counsel, opinion, inquiry, and such actings; of this, one part manages the affairs of cities universally—commanding in war, and correcting cities in peace—the more partial part arranges private households, which is called "economic" [domestic management]. This whole genus belongs to the soul's opining reasons, acting upon sensibles, and admitting virtue and vice, because it is completed according to choice and vital impulse; thus Archytas divides "doing" [practice] from "making." Some call those things "making" [poietic] whose results remain even after the making, such as carpentry and architecture; and "practical" those whose results have their being in the process of becoming, such as flute-playing and dancing, and the like. Another genus of activity exists after these, which Archytas collectively calls "without thought," found in irrational animals; and it is clear that however many and of what kind the species of irrational animals are, so many and such are the differences of species in acting according to such activity, which we are accustomed to enumerate in histories about animals. Let a final genus of activities be understood, says Iamblichus, which no longer demonstrates the acting of soul, nature, reasons, or life; but of bodies, or things that are inanimate bodies, it makes manifest the body-like activity, according to all the apparent properties around the body; and according to all their powers, not only insofar as they are solid and resistant, but insofar as they have many active powers around them. For the innate activities of the elements, and the motions of weight, either toward the depth [bottom] or toward the height, as well as striking and cooling, are the last and are viewed in composites, and are mixed with other natures. These are no longer activities, nor do they have the active power in the same way, but are mixed with passions, being both in themselves and receiving a certain entanglement into themselves from others; thus, whatever things fall under "acting" are naturally through these. It is worth noting why Archytas completely omitted this last species viewed in inanimate things. It seems to me that, having intended to distinguish actings properly so-called, which properly have the principle of motion in themselves, he declined these bodily ones, as being mixed with passion and occurring with motion and alteration. Once these are divided, it would be time finally to consider the things said by Plotinus; therefore, to call motions leaning toward suffering "actings" confuses the two genera with each other. For motions entangled with suffering are not simply in acting. But if someone says that motions are also contained in acting, he will clearly take the causes of being moved according to the act of moving, which as in the sense of a cause contain the entire principles of the motions. But one should not characterize activities in the absolute way. For the absolute belongs to motions, such as walking; and does not belong to activities, as in thinking, since being thought is either acting or suffering. But to say that perhaps thinking and walking do not even belong to acting because they are absolute, rather establishes the opposite, etc.

**p. 1079, 1. therefore suffering occurs by having motion in itself—and acting or having]** I established this place thus from good Codices. In the Edition *tō echein* is missing, *autō* is written, and *oun* is inserted after *poiein*. Then B. lin. 9. I received from the margin of the edition *outōs diatithetai* instead of *outos*. Ficino, however, expressed this. Our reading should be expressed thus: *since these things are so effected*.

**p. 1080, 7. but from his being something else than acting]** It seems *aliud quid* [something else] should be read in the Ficinian version, and so I corrected it, instead of *aliquid* [something].

**--- 11. Concerning having, if having is said in many ways etc.]** Plotinus comes to the last Category: "Concerning having," Aristotle's *Categories* chapter [abbrev: *c.*] XII, which chapter begins thus: "To have is spoken of in several ways—" and ends thus: "Perhaps some other ways of having might appear; but nearly all those commonly spoken of have been enumerated." Simplicius on the *Categories*, page 93. b: Difficulties have arisen for many concerning this genus too; for Plotinus also wonders, saying: "Concerning having, if having is spoken of in many ways, why will not all the ways be reduced to this category? So that even quantity, because it 'has' magnitude; and quality because it 'has' color; and the father because he 'has' a son; and the son because he 'has' a father, and that he has possessions." To which it must be said, that it is not possible for things homonymous and different by genus to be one category and one genus.

Neither is quantity in this "having" because it has magnitude, nor quality because it has color. For quality and quantity are incorporeal; but this category was for acquired bodies around us. The father, if considered as a body, was not something put around [like a garment]. If considered by the relation he has to a son, the relation is of a body [erratum: of an incorporeal]. Thus far concerning Plotinus: thence he passes to Nicostratus and others.

**p. 1080, 13. and the father—because he has a son and the son a father]** Thus I seemed to integrate the place with Ficino, whose authority I would not have joined had there not been the authority of the Darmstadt Codex, which exhibits the added words in order. Then B. lin. 5: I showed *kan himation kenētai* from many books instead of *keitai*. Plato recognizes that form of the subjunctive in the *Philebus* p. 41. B. p. 122. Stallb. and *Phaedo* p. 92. fin. p. 76. Bekk. where it is *xyngkeētai*.

**p. 1081, 7. How is "this man has weapons" simply of one category? For this means "being armed."]** That this example was used in the place concerning "having" is proved by the excerpt of the *Categories*, which our Palatine Heidelberg Codex No. 132. fol. 180. rect. has (cf. our Annotation on the title of this Plotinian book) where, after Andronicus is placed in the position of "substance," *hōplismenos* [armed] is placed under *echein* [to have] (for so it must be written instead of *echei*).

**--- 9. or even if it be a statue, to whom do these belong?]** Thus from good books I amended the faulty Edition reading and punctuation: *ē k' andrias. ē otō tauta.*

**--- 12. Regarding "lying" [position]—reclining, sitting]** Aristotle treats these in two categories: both in *On Quantity* ch. IV. 8. and *On Relatives* ch. V. 3. Simplicius on the *Categories* p. 85. b: But finally one must go to the difficulties mentioned by Plotinus against "position" [lying]. He says therefore that "position" is in few things, and for this reason is not worthy of being categorized in its own genus. But if it belongs to all bodies, both the eternal ones and those under the moon, how is it not worthy to obtain its own genus? Archytas also says it extends to many things. But he says "reclining" and "sitting" are not simple. It means "lying in such a shape," that is, to be in a place; therefore shape is one thing, and place another. Both have been discussed, and there was no need further to join two categories into one. To which it must be said, that these shapes, such as sitting and reclining, do not signify shapes simply, but the differences of shapes according to position. Even if they indicate quality, since shape is a quality, they will not speak of quality simply, but of that of "position." He himself also thought it right to reduce the supplementary qualities of something to that genus under which the thing being supplemented is reduced; for example, around a line there is straightness; but the line will be of quantity; therefore straightness will also be of quantity, and this whole thing is a quality of quantity. Just as "carrying" [bearing] does not exit its proper category when we say "carrying up," so neither does reclining or lying down. Furthermore, those after him, resisting the difficulty more strongly, argue that "position" touches neither shape nor place. But these follow otherwise, just as in other categories many things are viewed together. However, the peculiar category of "position" is understood purely by the position itself, with us not thinking simultaneously in what it lies, or how it itself lies. But it is not even necessarily in a place: Iamblichus says "position" [exists], since even place "lies" somewhere, while not being in a place. Therefore it is not sound that place is included in "position." If it is possible to think of a certain position even without shape for unshaped or incorporeal things like a line or a point, "position" will exist even without shape. But if he says "position" signifies activity, it must be placed in the activities. If passion, in the suffering. Again, therefore, it must be said here that "position" purely understood is not filled with any actings or passions. Apart from both, it has its own category by itself. If then someone says that acting and suffering are co-indicated by "position," as different genera coexist with another because of the mixed gathering of sensibles. It is better to define "position" with accuracy, as Boethus also thinks. For in those things where neither acting nor suffering is present according to the position in which it lies and the order in which it is arranged, these alone he says belong to the category, such as standing or sitting when said of a statue, or a picture reclining. In our case such things co-indicate activity; but in the case of inanimate things, these indicate neither acting nor suffering, but only purely "position." Since the place "above" and "below" is co-thought, and a relation appears toward certain places in reclining and lying down, one must understand that since "position" exists in itself first, the relation toward the above and below comes in after,

...just as "relative" was always growing alongside the other categories. However, "position," having taken its nature before the relative, is in itself, just as each of the other genera which preceded the relative. If we place everything into which relatives enter among the relatives, we would not stop, as Plotinus himself said, placing all the genera among the relatives. Let these things be said in response to Plotinus' difficulties.

**p. 1081, 14. of position signifying something else etc.]** No one fails to understand that this place is mutilated, and the Darmstadt Codex proves it. How Marsilius tried to integrate it is understood from the version. I preferred to leave everything intact, the more so as the MS books do not provide enough protection. Next, at A. lin. 7, with all Codices, I transposed the words *ei men to to men* [to] *ei to men*. Furthermore, at B. lin. 4, I wrote with the best books: *Dia ti de anakliseōs ousēs en tō pros ti.* The participle is absent from the edition.

**p. 1082, 8. Toward those establishing four etc.]** Simplic. on Aristot. *Categories* p. 72. a: There are four sects concerning the "tension" [intensification] and "remission" of qualities and of the qualified. For some declare that both all qualities and all qualified things admit of the "more" and "less," as Plotinus and other Platonists believe, because everything material admits of the more and less, with matter having the more and less due to its innate infinity. Another opinion is contrary to this, which says that in the qualities themselves, such as in justice and whiteness, there is by no means the more and less. For each is a whole, and stands according to one reason [logos], and for this reason does not admit the more and less. But in those participating, there is intensification and remission. For participations have breadth. And some participate more, others less; and for this reason even the habits [hexeis] themselves are thought to admit the more and less, although they are of the qualified things that admit it. Aristotle seems to mention this opinion when he says: "For if justice were said to be more than justice, someone might wonder." and following: "justice is not very much said to be more or less than justice; but he says the qualified things spoken of according to them unquestionably admit the more." For one is said to be more grammatical than another, and more just, and healthier. But when he says: "likewise also grammar and the other dispositions," he called the habits "dispositions" more generally, just as in the things before these, he called qualities "qualified things." The third sect is that of the Stoics, who, having separated the virtues from the middle arts, say these are neither intensified nor remitted; but they say the middle arts admit both intensification and remission. Therefore, according to these, some of the habits and qualified things are neither intensified nor remitted, while others admit both. The fourth is the opinion which said that immaterial and self-existent qualities do not admit the more and less, but material ones and the qualified things according to them do. This opinion differs from the former, because that one made no distinction between immaterial and material ones. Porphyry resists this opinion, saying it does not place immaterial qualities well, for those are essences [substances] and for this reason admit neither remission nor intensification, just as other essences do not.

**p. 1086, 16. but it can become all things by being shaped, just as the dancer makes himself all things—thus they do not say matter was—if in some way matter having the other things, as the dancer having the shapes.]** In this member I know not why Ficino turned the words: *energeia gar autou ta alla* [for the other things are its activity] as: "For the gestures of him (the dancer) are the figures," since Cod. Marcianus offers nothing of variant reading. He ought rather: *For his acts are the rest, scilicet [namely], all which the mime represents by dancing*. Nor will the meaning differ if someone perhaps thinks *energeia* [in activity] should be read. I will add another conjecture, which pertains to the argument of the whole place. The poet in *Odyssey* δ. 417 sq. concerning Proteus:
> "Becoming all things, he will try, as many as on earth
> are creepers, and water and divinely-kindled fire."

Lucian *On the Dance* XIX. p. 278 sq. ed. Wetst.: "For the old myth seems to me to say Egyptian Proteus was nothing other than a certain dancer, a mimetic man, and able to shape himself toward all things.—but the myth taking it up toward the more paradoxical, described his nature as becoming these things which he mimicked. Which also is present to those dancing now. You might see them therefore at the same time swiftly changing, and mimicking Proteus himself." Plato similarly uses "becoming all kinds" regarding poets in *Rep.* II. p. 381. p. 102. Bekk. and III. 389. p. 129. The same elegantly applied the Proteus fable to philosophers who turn themselves in all directions, and do not wish to openly declare their opinion, in the *Euthydemus* p. 288. b. c. p. 426. Bekker, (who, against Heindorf's judgment, left *hyphēgēsasthai* untouched there, which reading even the most excellent Bodleian Codex confirms). Now on the testimony of Eustathius on the *Odyssey* in the place cited p. 177. Basil. p. 174. ed. Lips. there were philosophers who took Proteus for Matter, which in act is none of the forms: but in power all: saying, "Proteus is the first-born matter, the receiver of forms, being in activity none of the forms, but in power, all things." When these are gathered into one, it becomes probable that Plotinus, who would undoubtedly know that allegorical interpretation of the Homeric passage, and perhaps himself approved it, and had seen mimes in Rome or other places expressing the person of Proteus by dancing, snatched the opportunity from there to use the likeness of dancers. Cf. our annotation above in III. 6. 16. p. 319. B.
