<meta>This page continues the philosophical commentary on Plotinus's Enneads, specifically focusing on the categories of "Acting" and "Being Acted Upon" (Action and Passion) as discussed by Simplicius and Iamblichus.</meta>

[[original page: 337]]

-> BOOK I. ENNEAD SIX. p. 1072, 1073. <-

...whether using the body as an instrument, as in the act of striking, and all those forms that belong to the body, such as being heavy; but in the case of the soul, motion consists in doing, such as the act of practicing geometry through the soul. The proper activity of the soul is life. One can also place some things in the soul and others in the body, according to those who posit that passions <note>Greek: *pathe*, referring to emotions or passive states</note> also occur around the soul. Again, he says some motions proceed from themselves toward other things, while others proceed from other things toward themselves. It is clear that these distinguish "active" and "passive" motion from one another, insofar as the motion from oneself has the quality of acting upon other things—for this is "Action" <term>poiesis: the act of making or doing</term>. That which is from others or out of others toward oneself is "Passive" <term>pathetike: the state of being acted upon</term. 

However, the sincere and pure characteristic of *Acting* lies in proceeding out of oneself; while the characteristic of *Being Acted Upon* lies in having the cause in another. But he <note>Plotinus</note> does not maintain their purity, adding to the "out of oneself" the "acting into another." For because of this mixture and the leaning toward another, he does not preserve the pure activity. Regarding the "out of another," he creates a certain composition by directedness toward themselves. For it differs greatly whether one has the cause of the passion separately in another, or is joined to the cause of the passion; for in a certain way, in these cases, the two principles are confused into this one. The cause of this has been the preference for "Motion" as a common genus, because of which it is no longer possible to distinguish "Being Acted Upon" and "Acting" purely. 

Hence, in the case of "cutting" <note>original: *tmēsis*</note>, the argument confuses these things, positing the motions toward others as the same as the motions from others. For let the "cut" be one thing; however, "to cut" and "to be cut" are different. This must by no means be conceded. For as the "cut" is, so also are "to cut" and "to be cut." Just as the activity from the cutter is separated from the nature <insert>affection</insert> in the thing being cut, so also the incision according to the "cutting" stands apart from that according to the "being cut." For one is the preceding cause from the activity and the active motion; the other is the successor to this, being a passive change <note>original: *tropē*</note> produced in the thing being cut. Even in the case of a hair, the separation of the hands stretching the hair is one thing, and the spreading out of the hair is another. Thus, in the case of the cut, the "cutting" according to acting and cutting will be one thing, and that according to being cut will be another. 

But because they lie close together, or one is near the other, their duality is overlooked; and sometimes it might give the impression to some that the combination exists in the "Acting," and sometimes in the "Being Acted Upon." Yet the truth is not so; rather, there are two movements, distinct from one another by nature, but in composite things they are confused into the same. This is overlooked both because of the mixture and because they bring "Acting" and "Being Acted Upon" into a single genus. Next in order, Plotinus seeks this according to the so-called species of motion: whether "Acting" is everywhere linked to "Being Acted Upon." According to the species of motion, these were: generation and corruption, increase and decrease, alteration, and furthermore, change according to place <note>locomotion</note>. 

But Iamblichus says: "We immediately object to the beginning of the approach, not thinking it right that 'Actions' be characterized by 'Motion.' For the genus of things that move is one thing, and the genus of things being moved is another." Then we argue against it, not thinking that the "Acting" and "Passive" things should be characterized by the same thing, as if by "being moved." But perhaps one should say to Iamblichus that the species of motion are the same for both the movers and the moved. For that which is generated is generated by the generator, and that which is destroyed is destroyed by the destroyer. The same logic applies to alteration and change of place. Regarding such difficulties of Plotinus, those after him brought forward these solutions. Since Plotinus approved another definition of "Acting" and "Being Acted Upon" instead of the one given by the Pythagoreans, let us try to understand this one too, writing also the things said against it by Iamblichus and the others briefly, etc.

**p. 1073, 9. It must be examined whether some, etc.**] After Simplicius refuted the opinions of others, he returns to the opinion of Plotinus, which I transcribed above under note 93. b.: (**p. 94. a.**) "But if Plotinus says that 'having' bodily things concerns the body and is not incorporeal, he makes another category; why then, in the case of 'Acting,' where there is much difference, does one category not arise for 'cutting' and another for 'burning,' or 'burying,' or 'casting away'? Or is the activity of 'Acting' one and possessing one principle, needing nothing from the different reception of those receiving the action? For the one cutting and the one burning and the others do not differ at all in respect to 'Acting.' However, the category of 'Having' <note>Greek: *echein*</note> has its material identity in this: that the thing surrounding is a body and not incorporeal—or is it characterized not by a chance relationship, but is viewed properly from its relation to another thing within itself? But if he says the 'garment' being worn creates another category, why will the 'lying' on a bed not create another? Or is the 'garment lying on a bed' part of the category of 'Position' <note>Greek: *keisthai*</note>, or that of 'Place'? For the bed provides no activity..."

<meta>This page continues the philosophical commentary on Plotinus, specifically focusing on the Aristotelian categories of "Having" (Habit) and "Acting/Being Acted Upon" (Action and Passion). It references the works of Simplicius and Iamblichus.</meta>

-> ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS <-

Regarding *having*: for the category of *having* indicates a certain state <note>original: ἕξιν (hexis)</note> and a mastery, but of acquired bodies. If this is true, *having* is verified only in the case of animate beings; thus, even if an ornament is placed around a statue, because the statue is inanimate, it would not be said to *have* the ornament, but rather the ornament *lies* upon the statue. But if it were viewed as something animate, according to that reference to the animate, it would be said to *have* the ornament. But if *having* is characterized according to a state, he says it will be reduced to the category of State. Now, State <note>original: ἕξις (hexis)</note> falls under Quality; or rather, this term "state" is used equivocally <note>original: ὁμώνυμος (homōnymos)</note>. For one kind of state was the cohesion of bodies, while this other kind is the mastery of acquired <insert>qualities</insert> of bodies. Furthermore, the state of *having* comes about through the activity of those who have; but the state of qualities comes about neither through the activity of the things participated in, nor of those participating. They also differ according to the things held: in the former case they are incorporeal <note>original: ἀσώματά (asōmata)</note>, while here they are bodies. They also differ according to the possessors: in the former case the state is within the essence, while here it is around the essence from the outside. 

But if he says one should not speak of "having quality" because "quality" has already been discussed, nor "having quantity" since "quantity" has been discussed, nor "having parts" since "essence" has been discussed, why must we say that "having weapons" belongs to another category, even though "essence" (in which the weapons exist) has been discussed? Is it because the weapons or the sandals are not said to belong to the category of *having* in themselves, nor is the possession of them—if someone possessing them does not use them—but rather the mastery of them and the state <note>original: ἕξις (hexis)</note> resulting from having them? This itself creates the category of *having*. It is one thing to have quality and quantity, and another to have weapons and sandals. For in the former, the state is of incorporeal things; in the latter, of corporeal things. <note>The text repeats this distinction for emphasis.</note> In the former, the things participated in are transformative of the participants; in the latter, they are merely placed around them. 

But he asks, how can that which exists in only a few instances be a "genus"? Is it because this genus exists in the lowest things and concerns bodies, and exists within bodies, and for this reason it is contracted into a very small scope—and because of this, would it not be a genus? For even the phoenix, being a single individual, contains the whole species within itself. But why did he not join the discussion of *having* to the other categories, but mentioned it as if by an afterthought after the discussion of opposites, and of "simultaneous things," and of motion? Perhaps having completed the account of the categories, since he remembered certain things in passing, he works those out as well. Since the category of *having* is the last, and being mindful of order, he reasonably mentioned the ambiguity of *having* last; not only giving the categories themselves their proper order, but also giving the same to the things added and worked out from the outside. But he says it is "absurd," rejecting the common usage of saying a man "has" a wife. Yet if he had not mentioned it, he would have been absurd for omitting common custom. By mentioning and judging it, he performed the work of a dialectician, for whom the judgment of truth is most important. Let these things be said in response to the difficulties.

**p. 1075, 11. that which is not opposite to acting.**] Thus from our books, along with Ficino and many other volumes, we have corrected the faulty reading "to act" <note>original: τὸ ποιῆσαι</note>.

**--- 14. if motion is both]** Ficino expressed this, and so does <term>Codex Marcianus A</term> and traces in the <term>Vatican Codex</term>. The <term>Printed Edition</term> has "or the." Soon after, at line 6, I filled in from several books "he being unaffected," which Marsilius [Ficino] also expressed. Next, partly from the margin of the <term>Edition</term> and partly from the <term>Codices</term>, I corrected: "but if acting upon another, such as striking, it should also be acted upon." <term>Codex B</term>, line 6: "and how the same thing is both action and passion," from the books. The first "and" is missing from the <term>Edition</term>. Line 7: "and thus it is action by being from one, but passion by being into another, being the same thing" (deleting "and" before "the").

**p. 1076, 1. But if acting upon another etc.]** Simplicius in the <term>place cited</term>, page 78. a: "But to speak of 'activity' only in the case of 'actions' is said without due examination. For not every activity is an action—for instance, thought is not—nor is every action an activity. For there are some 'passive actions.' From these things it must be concluded that Plotinus and the others, who transfer the common element of acting and being acted upon to be 'motions' (following the Stoic habit into the sect of Aristotle), these people confuse motion and activity into the same thing, and they do not keep 'action' pure and free from 'passion,' if indeed they see it accompanied by motion. And furthermore, they do not keep the principle of motion unmoved, as seems right to Aristotle."

**--- 9. For how could that which acts in another be acted upon?]** Simplicius in the *Categories*, page 80. a: "Iamblichus, having set himself against Plotinus in such matters, says: 'It is possible first to distinguish more technically the unique character of these genera, both of acting and of being acted upon, and to show their difference from one another. For from this it will appear both what things must be subordinated to them, and what kind of mixed things lie between them.' But if it is necessary to set forth the views of Archytas before those of Iamblichus..."

<meta>This page continues the philosophical commentary on Plotinus's Enneads, specifically discussing the nature of action (doing) and passion (being acted upon) as defined by Archytas and interpreted by Iamblichus.</meta>

[[original page: 339]]

-> BOOK I. ENNEAD SIX. pages 1075, 1076. 339 <-

...all those characteristics which he <note>Archytas</note> assigned specifically to "acting" and "being acted upon." For indeed, Iamblichus also explains those points; Archytas, then, writes as follows: "It is characteristic of the **actor** to have the cause of the motion within himself. But for that which is **acted upon** and the **passive**, the cause is in another." For the sculptor has the cause of making the statue within himself; but the bronze has the cause of being made into a statue both within itself and in the sculptor. And the same logic applies to the passions of the soul. For anger is naturally awakened toward someone else, and is provoked by something else from the outside—such as neglect, dishonor, or insult. But the one doing these things has the cause of doing them within himself.

Now, explaining these things, Iamblichus says that **acting** has the cause of its activity within itself. But **being acted upon** has the cause of its motion in another and in itself—just as the bronze-worker <note>The text likely means the bronze material here, as clarified by the context of the statue</note> is in himself and in the sculptor—because "being acted upon" also possesses a certain stability of its own essence, and is not entirely dependent on the actor.

Next, he introduces objections to this reasoning. For he says some people argue that even some forms of "acting" have their cause in another, such as the act of thinking <term>noein: the intellectual act of the mind</term>. Or, if one does not place thinking in the category of "acting," but rather "being thought of" <note>original: *noeisthai*</note>—as if the act of thinking were in the category of "being acted upon"—even so, "being thought of" does not provide the entire cause of motion to the thinker. Or perhaps the manner of this communion is not such as those who are perplexed suppose regarding the mind and the object of thought; but that discussion belongs properly to the theory of the Mind.

We must resolve the difficulty in a way consistent with the present subject, saying, I think, that Archytas accounted for "pure" actions and passions. Even if thinking is a kind of "being acted upon," it has an activity awakened from within, just like seeing and knowing in general. One should not bring an objection against the argument based on these "mixed" states.

Others bring the same difficulty regarding **desire** and **impulse**, arguing that these have the cause of motion within themselves, yet are not entirely free from a cause that originates from another on the outside. Solving this difficulty, Iamblichus says that things which feel impulse and desire are not simple entities. Being composite, they do not have the cause of their activity universally or sovereignly from themselves. Rather, they are moved toward actions by some part or power within them. Hence, they require cooperation from outside—either as a primary cause or a contributing one—and they participate in a "passive motion" occurring in something else. I mean the "composite living being," where the power that causes the activities is granted by another. Therefore, this is neither pure action nor mere passion. One should not object to the given definition of "acting"—which says its cause is present in the activity itself—based on this.

One only needs to add, says Iamblichus, the phrase: "that which provides the cause **principally and primarily** from itself and from its whole self, and possesses this cause solely in itself and sends it forth as self-complete <term>autotelēs: perfect or complete in itself</term> into the whole." It is clear that the definition will be more distinct with this addition. And Archytas indicated all these things in a brief word. For "in itself" was taken to mean "as in a whole," principally and primarily.

Again, he says it is characteristic of **being acted upon** to have the cause of motion in another. For if not, the passion is uncaused, which is absurd—that anything which happens should occur by no cause or have no cause. And if it has a cause, it is either in the passive thing itself (in which case it is not only passive but also active) or it is outside and in another. For in whatever way the actor acts, and whatever things he may do, these the passive thing suffers.

Plotinus also raises a difficulty regarding this: how can some things be "absolute" even in the state of being acted upon? For instance, things that are not produced by others, such as **rotting** or **rusting**. Many things that have the cause of motion in another do not "suffer" in the passive sense; for example, a swan becoming white according to its internal principle <term>logos: here, the formative biological blueprint</term> is led to its own perfection <term>entelecheia: the realized state of a thing</term>, yet this is not due to a passion caused by another. And growth from an internal principle is surely not led toward enlargement according to a "passion."

But to such a point it must be said: neither does the swan have the cause of being white in another, but in itself; nor does anything else led toward its own innate form have the participation in its own form from the outside. We call it "passion" to participate in this way, not because such a passion does not happen by another, but because the participation in form was a sharing of essence according to activity, occurring through air, or water, or the vapor of some other liquid. Perhaps also, due to the composition of things that rot or rust, there are some elements in them that are acting and others being acted upon; those who cannot distinguish these assume such passions are "absolute" <note>i.e., independent of an external actor</note>. But they say many things having the cause of acting in themselves were "suffered," just as we say all wicked men are "passive" <note>enslaved to passions</note> because of the vice within them. Or it seems to Plotinus himself that the passions of the soul are not passions at all, but activities; or in the soul they are activities, but in the body they are passions. Just as the cause of vice is in...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical commentary on Plotinus, specifically examining the definitions of "acting" (doing) and "being acted upon" (suffering/passion) within the soul and material world.</meta>

-> 340 ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS <-

Just as the wicked possess [evil] within themselves, so too do they possess its activity in their doing, if indeed "passion" <note>original: *pathos*, meaning a passive undergoing or suffering</note> is not predicated of the soul. But if "suffering" occurs in relation to the body, the passion will be in one thing and derived from another, and thus the definition of suffering becomes true. Yet perhaps, since there are many parts in the soul—or many judgments, and many imaginations, or powers, or differing opinions—the wicked become "impassioned" <note>subject to passions</note> according to the discord between these parts; some parts act while others suffer from the oppositions, and the logic of "suffering" remains sound, as they experience the suffering in "another" [part of themselves].

But as for the *suitability* <term>epitēdeiotēs: the natural fitness or capacity of matter to receive a form</term> of matter, if it is a passion of matter, how is it not from matter itself, but from without? Or one might say that suitability, being a reflection of the Form, is bestowed upon matter by the Form. Some say that matter is this very thing: a passion. But if it is not a passion, yet it "suffers" in regard to its suitability, we must ask: if it suffers suitability, there is certainly something that produces it; but if it does not suffer it, but is suitability itself, then this is the very substance of matter. The argument concerns passion, whether it comes from within or from without.

But it seemed, he says, that neither "that which is from itself and not from another" is sufficient to characterize *acting*, nor is "that which is from another and not from itself" sufficient for *suffering*. For in acting upon something else, a thing might appear to be suffering itself, while that upon which it acts is not suffering but acting. For instance, **tin** <note>original: *kassiteros*</note> acting upon **silver**, is itself "suffering" by being consumed and wasted away; yet it purifies the silver by casting out what corrupts it, so that it rather preserves the silver in the same quality. But since in composite things, actions and passions are taken as mixed, the tin does not only act, but also suffers: it acts by purifying the silver, but suffers by being consumed by it. And the silver suffers by being purified, but acts by consuming [the tin], in different respects.

But since it has been defined in general what *acting* is and what *suffering* is, and what the unique characteristics of each are, we must return to distinguishing the species of acting and suffering. Once these are defined, it will be clear which are incorrectly referred to the primary genera, which are correctly referred, which are mixed between both, and which are simply referred to one or the other. From this, Plotinus’s views will also become clear, as to whether he correctly subordinates certain things under "acting" or not.

Here we must also set forth the division of *acting* by **Archytas** <note>A Pythagorean philosopher</note>, who speaks as follows:

> In *acting*, the highest is **activity** <note>original: *energeia*</note>. There are three differences of activity: one part consists in **contemplating** (such as practicing geometry or astronomy); another in **making** (such as healing or carpentry); and another in **doing/practicing** (such as commanding an army or engaging in politics). Activity occurs even without deliberation, as in irrational animals, but these are the most general types.

Among these, the highest and common element of *acting* is defined according to "simple activity," which has gathered within itself all the distinct species of activities. It is released from all motion, possessing the "motive power" in a pure state, and having its cause from itself and not from some other prior or cooperating source. From this, several species of "doing" proceed in a divided way, the first of which is the **theoretical** <note>contemplative</note>. This employs activities that are unified and unchangeable, and is itself divided into further species. The first of these would be synonymous with the genus immediately above it—this too is "theoretical," and is called theoretical in the primary sense. This is the activity that inspects **intelligible and indivisible substances** with simple intellections, such as the **Intellectual** <note>the realm of pure Mind</note>. Archytas passed over this, though it belongs to the Pythagorean division, perhaps because such contemplation was disproportionate for an introductory work.

The second type of contemplation performs its thinking upon **immovable and mathematical substances**, such as the practice of **geometry**; it uses defined but no longer simple applications [of the mind], being already composite and discursive, such as are the activities of pure reason. The third among these is that which performs contemplation upon **eternal and ever-moving sensible substances**, using sensation along with reasoning, such as the practice of **astronomy**, demonstrating that the underlying principles are in harmony with the appearances. Thus, the whole activity of contemplation proceeds from above, from pure intellections down to the reasonings based on sensation.

After this, Archytas places the **productive** <note>poetic/making</note> species, synonymous with the genus, which primarily consists in bringing into substance those things which do not yet participate in being. Much of this is **Divine**, which is contained in the "craftsmanship of the gods" <note>original: *dēmiourgia*</note>; much is also in the **Nature** of the universe, especially that which descends from the heavens regarding everything that comes into being. Much is also in the **Arts** which imitate Nature and fulfill what is left behind by her. For just as Nature implants the form of health in bodies, so the physician, in healing, restores the perfection of Nature in bodies; and as Nature provided caves and natural coverings for...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical commentary on Plotinus's Enneads, specifically focusing on the classification of "Action" (Doing) and "Passion" (Being Acted Upon), drawing heavily from the Neo-Platonic interpretations of Archytas and Iamblichus.</meta>

-> BOOK I. ENNEAD SIX. p. 1079, 1080. 341 <-

In animals, just as architecture, carpentry, weaving, and other arts fulfill what is lacking for human beings, they provide the useful things for the **self-sufficiency** <term>autarkeia: the state of needing nothing external</term> of life. The third genus of "doing" is that which is detached within "acting" <note>distinguishing *poiein* (making/producing) from *prattein* (acting/conducting)</note>, which oversees the rational productions concerning sensible and composite things, providing choice, deliberation, opinion, investigation, and such productions. Of this, one part manages the affairs of cities as a whole—commanding in war and correcting the cities in peace—while the more specific part arranges private households, which is called **domestic management** <term>oikonomikos: the root of "economics," referring here to the administration of a home</term>. This entire genus belongs to the "opinion-forming" reasons of the soul, operating around sensible things and admitting both virtue and vice, because it is carried out according to choice and vital impulse. Thus Archytas divides "acting" from "doing." But some say those things are "productive" whose results remain even after the doing, such as carpentry and architecture; while those are "active" whose results have their being only in the process of becoming, such as flute-playing and dancing, and the like.

After these, there is another genus of activity which Archytas calls "common without intellect," found in irrational animals. It is clear that however many and of whatever kind the species of irrational animals are, there are just as many and such differences in the species of "doing" according to this activity, which we are accustomed to enumerate in histories concerning animals. Finally, let a genus of activities be understood, says Iamblichus, which no longer displays the "doing" of soul, nature, reason, or life, but makes manifest the body-like activity of bodies (or of things that are soulless bodies). This occurs according to all the apparent properties of the body and all their powers—not only insofar as they are solid and **resistant** <term>antitypos: the quality of matter that pushes back or occupies space</term>, but insofar as they possess many active powers. For the innate activities of the elements, and the movements of weight (either toward the depth or toward the height), and those involving striking or cooling, are the lowest forms; they are observed in composite things and are mixed with other natures. These are no longer "activities" in the pure sense, nor do they possess the "active" quality in the same way, but are mixed with "passions" <note>passive states or being acted upon</note>, being both independent in themselves and receiving a certain **interweaving** <term>epiplokē: a complex entanglement or connection</term> from others. Whatever falls under the category of "doing" is by nature through these things.

It is worth considering why Archytas completely omitted this last species observed in soulless things. It seems to me that, having proposed to divide the "doings" in the primary sense—those which possess the principle of motion primarily within themselves—he declined these bodily ones, as they are mixed with passion and occur alongside motion and alteration.

Having divided these, it would be the proper time to examine what is said by Plotinus. To say that motions leaning toward "passion" are "doings" confuses the two genera with one another. For motions **interwoven** with passion are not simply within the category of "doing." If someone were to say that motions are contained within "doing," they will clearly take the causes of being moved according to the act of moving, which contain the entire principles of motions as a causal reason. But one must not characterize activities in an absolute way. For "absoluteness" belongs to motions, such as walking; yet it does not belong to activities, such as in thinking, since "being thought" is either a doing or a passion. To say that perhaps thinking and walking do not even belong to "doing" because they are absolute, rather establishes the opposite, etc.

**p. 1079, 1. Therefore passion occurs by having motion in itself—and doing or having]** I have established this passage thus from the good Manuscripts. In the **Edition**, "by having" is missing, "itself" is written, and "therefore" was inserted after "doing." Then at Book B, line 9, I accepted "is thus disposed" from the margin of the edition instead of "this." However, Ficino expressed this. Our reading should be expressed thus: *since these things are so effected*.

**p. 1080, 7. but from his being something else than doing]** It seems "something else" <note>Latin: aliud quid</note> should be read in the Ficinian version, and so I have corrected it, instead of "something" <note>Latin: aliquid</note>.

**--- 11. Concerning "Having," if "to have" is said in many ways etc.]** Plotinus comes to the final Category: *Concerning Having*, Aristotle's Categories, **chapter** XII, which begins thus: "To have is said in several ways—" and ends thus: "Perhaps other ways of having might appear; but those usually mentioned have nearly all been enumerated." Simplicius, in his commentary on the Categories, **page** 93. b: "Difficulties have arisen for many regarding this genus; for Plotinus also raises a difficulty, saying: 'Concerning having, if to have is said in many ways, why will not all the ways be reduced to this category? So that even quantity, because it *has* magnitude; and quality, because it *has* color; and the father, because he *has* a son; and the son, because he *has* a father, and that one has possessions.' To which it must be said, that it is not possible for things that are homonymous and changed according to genus to be one category and one genus—"

It also begins a critique of the Aristotelian category of "Having" as analyzed by Plotinus and Simplicius.</summary>

<note>original: "νος"</note> <note>This is the end of a word from the previous page, likely "man" or "human."</note>. However, neither is quantity found in the "having" of these things <insert>in this</insert>, because it possesses magnitude; nor is quality found there, because it possesses color. For quality and quantity are incorporeal; but this category <note>The category of "Having" or "Possession"</note> pertained to the acquired bodies around us. But the father, if considered as a body, was not something "put on" <note>original: "perithetos" - referring to external accidents or clothing</note>. If, however, he is considered according to the relation he has toward a son, that relation is of a body <insert>but rather of the incorporeal</insert>. Thus far on Plotinus: from here he passes to Nicostratus and others.

**p. 1080, 13. and the father—because he has a son and the son a father]** I have seen fit to complete the passage in this way following Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino, the famous Renaissance translator of Plotinus</note>, whose authority I would not have joined had it not been supported by the authority of the Darmstadt Manuscript, which presents the added words in order. Then, in Book B, line 5: I have provided "lest a garment be worn" <note>original: "κἂν ἱμάτιον κένηται"</note> from many books instead of "lies." Plato recognizes that form of the subjunctive in the *Philebus* p. 41. B. p. 122. Stallbaum and in the *Phaedo* p. 92. at the end, p. 76. Bekker, where it is "be composed."

**p. 1081, 7. How is it at all simple and of a single category, that "this man has weapons"? For this is what "to be armed" signifies.]** That this example was used in the section "On Having" is proved by the excerpt of the *Categories* which our Palatine Heidelberg Manuscript No. 132, folio 180, recto, contains (<gloss>compare our Annotation on the title of this book of Plotinus</gloss>) where, after Andronicus is placed in the location of "Substance," "armed" is placed under "to have" (for it should be written thus instead of "has").

**--- 9. or even if it be a statue, to whom do these belong?]** I have thus corrected the faulty reading and punctuation of the Edition from good books: "or even a statue. Or to whom these."

**--- 12. Regarding "Position"—to be reclined, to be seated]** Aristotle treats these in two categories, both in "On Quantity" chapter IV. 8. and "On Relatives" chapter V. 3. Simplicius <note>A 6th-century commentator on Aristotle</note> in his *Commentary on the Categories* p. 85. b says: "But we must finally turn to the difficulties raised by Plotinus regarding 'Position' <note>original: "keisthai"</note>. He says, in short, that 'Position' exists in only a few things, and for this reason is not worthy of being classified in its own genus. But if it belongs to all bodies, both the eternal ones and those beneath the moon, how is it not worthy of obtaining its own genus? Even Archytas says it extends to many things. But he says that 'to be reclined' and 'to be seated' are not simple terms. They signify being in a certain posture, that is, being in a place; therefore, the posture is one thing, and the place is another. Both have been discussed, and there was no further need to join two categories into one. To which it must be said, that these postures, such as sitting and reclining, do not signify postures simply, but the differences of postures according to 'Position' <note>original: "thesis"</note>. Even if they indicate quality, since posture is a quality, they will not speak of quality simply, but the quality of 'Position.' He himself <note>Plotinus</note> thought that the qualities which complete a thing should be reduced to that genus under which the completed thing is also brought; for example, there is 'straightness' regarding a line; but the line belongs to 'Quantity,' therefore straightness will also belong to 'Quantity,' and this whole thing is a quality of quantity. Just as 'carrying' does not depart from its own category when we say 'carrying up,' so neither do 'reclining' or 'lying down.' Furthermore, those after him, standing more firmly against the difficulty, argue that 'Position' touches upon neither posture nor place. Rather, these things follow in another way, just as in the other categories several things are observed together. However, the specific category of 'Position' is conceived purely according to the placement itself, without us thinking simultaneously of what it lies in, or how it is situated. Indeed, it is not even entirely in a place; Iamblichus says that 'Position' exists because even place 'is positioned' somewhere, without being in a place. Therefore, it is not sound to include 'place' within 'Position.' If it is possible to conceive of a certain position even without posture for things without shape or the incorporeal, such as a line or a point, then 'Position' will exist even without posture. But if he says 'Position' signifies an 'Activity,' it must be placed among activities. If an 'Affection' <note>a passive state</note>, then among 'Affections.' Again, it must be said here that 'Position' understood purely is not filled with any actions or affections. Outside of both, it has its own category by itself. If, then, someone says that 'Acting' and 'Being Acted Upon' are implied by 'Position,' it is as different genera coexist with another due to the mixed gathering of sensible things. It is better to define 'Position' with precision, as Boethius also thinks. For in those cases where neither acting nor being acted upon is present according to the position in which it is placed and the order in which it is arranged, he says these alone belong to the category—such as 'standing' or 'sitting' when said of a statue, or the 'reclining' of an image. For in our case, such things imply an activity; but in inanimate things, these indicate neither acting nor being acted upon, but only 'Position' purely. Since 'above' and 'below' are conceived simultaneously, and a relation appears toward certain places in 'reclining' and 'lying down,' one must understand that 'Position' exists first by itself, and then the relation to 'above' and 'below' is introduced."

-> BOOK I. ENNEAD SIX. pages 1080—1086. 343 <-

just as the category of "Relation" <note>original: *to pros ti*</note> was always growing alongside the other categories. However, "Position" <note>original: *to keisthai*</note>, having taken its nature before "Relation," exists in its own right, just as each of the other genera did which preceded "Relation." But if we place everything into which "Relation" enters into the category of "Relation," we would not be long—as Plotinus himself said—in placing all the genera into "Relation." Let these things, then, be said in response to Plotinus’s difficulties.

**p. 1081, 14. "But since 'Position' signifies something else," etc.]** No one fails to understand that this passage is mutilated, as the Darmstadt Manuscript <note>Cod. Darmst.</note> proves. How Marsilio <note>Marsilio Ficino, the famous Renaissance translator of Plotinus</note> sought to complete it can be understood from his version. I have preferred to leave everything untouched, all the more so since the manuscript books do not offer enough protection <note>i.e., they don't provide a reliable alternative reading</note>. Soon after at A. line 7, I transposed the words with all the manuscripts from "if indeed the one if the one" to "if the one indeed." Furthermore, at B. line 4, I wrote according to the best books: "But why, since reclining is in the category of Relation." The participle is missing from the printed edition.

**p. 1082, 8. "Against those who posit the four," etc.]** Simplicius, in his commentary on Aristotle’s *Categories*, page 72. a: "There are four schools of thought concerning 'intensification' <term>epitasis: the stretching or increasing of a quality</term> and 'relaxation' <term>anesis: the loosening or decreasing of a quality</term>, both of qualities and of things possessing quality. For some declare that both all qualities and all things with quality admit of the 'more' and the 'less,' as it seems to Plotinus and other Platonists, because everything material <note>original: *enylon*</note> admits of the more and the less, since matter possesses the more and the less through its innate infinity. There is another opinion contrary to this one, which says that in the qualities themselves—such as in justice or whiteness—there is in no way the 'more' and the 'less.' For each is a certain whole and stands according to a single definition, and for this reason does not admit of the more and the less. But in those things that participate <note>original: *metechousin*</note> in them, there is intensification and relaxation. For participations have a breadth; some participate more, others less. And because of this, even the habits <note>dispositions or states of being</note> themselves are thought to admit of the more and the less, even though it is the things with quality that admit of it. Aristotle seems to mention this opinion when he says: 'For if justice were said to be more than justice, one might be puzzled.' And following that: 'Justice is not quite said to be more or less than justice; but the things called "qualified" according to them, he says, indisputably admit of the "more."' For one person is said to be more 'grammatical' than another, or more 'just,' or 'healthier.' But when he says: 'likewise also grammar and the other dispositions,' he called the habits 'dispositions' in a more general sense, just as in the passages before these, he called the qualities 'qualified things.' The third school is that of the Stoics, who, having separated the virtues from the intermediate arts, say that the former are neither intensified nor relaxed; but they say the intermediate arts admit of both intensification and relaxation. According to them, then, some habits and qualified things are neither intensified nor relaxed, while others admit of both. The fourth opinion is that which said that immaterial <note>original: *aylous*</note> and self-existent qualities did not admit of the more and the less, but material ones, and the things qualified according to them, did admit of it. This opinion differs from the former because that one made no distinction between immaterial and material qualities. Porphyry <note>Plotinus's student and editor</note> stands against this opinion, as it does not correctly posit immaterial qualities; for those, he says, are 'essences' <note>substances</note>, and for this reason, they admit of neither relaxation nor intensification, just as other essences do not."

**--- 13. "and they have not left behind differences"]** I have given "of difference" <note>original: *diaphoras*</note> from the Munich, Venice A and B, and Vatican manuscripts. The printed edition has "of difference."

**p. 1083, 8. "from matter, I think, to the others," etc.]** Regarding the word "I think" <note>original: *oimai*</note> being inserted in various ways, it is enough to cite Tiberius Hemsterhuis on Lucian’s *Marine Dialogues*, Vol. 2, p. 303; Sturz’s *Xenophon Lexicon*, Vol. III, p. 244 ff.; Heindorf on Plato’s *Gorgias*, § 86, p. 123; and Stallbaum on the same dialogue, Vol. II. 1, p. 135. Next, at B. line 3, we have written more fully "counting the substrate as one." So say most books and Ficino. Finally, at C. lines 3–4, we have given with the good books: "but rather by being divided" instead of "but rather the being divided," and at line 5, "continuous" <note>nominative</note> instead of "continuous" <note>dative</note>.

**p. 1084, 7. "And why is this more 'being'—namely matter—but not that?"]** So say most books. The printed edition has "those things." Then, instead of "or without quality," I gave "or matter without quality generates the quality" from the Venice Manuscript A: *the matter, being void of form or shapeless, generates that which partakes of form*: "or without quality," namely matter. For matter is very often designated in this way. See Book I. 8. 10. with the note; II. 4. 1; II. 4. 7. Soon at B. line 6, I wrote: "for the 'in actuality' was present within" with the good books instead of "to the actuality." And at line 8: "for even a body being out of matter and form" from the Vatican manuscript, which Ficino also expressed, instead of "and matter."

**--- 12. "God would be incorporeal"]** See Ezechiel Spanheim, *On the Caesars of the Emperor Julian*, p. 256, note 874.

**p. 1086, 6. "then if a substrate"]** The word "if" <note>original: *ei*</note> is absent from the printed edition. Otherwise, this passage of Plotinus must be maintained.

to understand his judgment on the Theology of the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle</note>, whom he here quite eloquently accuses of **atheism** <note>original: "ἀθεότητος" (atheotēs)</note>. Regarding matter, one should compare Aristotle in *Metaphysics* I. 6, a passage which Cudworth and Mosheim discuss in *The Intellectual System* IV. 2. 27. p. 943. and following.

**p. 1086, 16. But it can become all things by taking on forms, just as the dancer makes himself into everything—thus they do not say it was matter—if indeed matter possesses other things in some way, just as the dancer possesses the poses in some way.]** In this section, I do not know why Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino, the 15th-century translator of Plotinus</note> translated the words: *for its activity is the other things* as: "For his (the dancer's) gestures are indeed the figures," since the **Marcian Manuscript** offers no variation in the reading. He ought rather to have translated: *For the rest are his own acts, namely, all the things which the mime represents by dancing*. Nor will the meaning differ if someone should perhaps think it should be read as "in activity" <note>original: "ἐνεργείᾳ" (energeia)</note>. I will add another conjecture which pertains to the argument of the whole passage. The poet in *Odyssey* IV. 417 and following says of Proteus:
> He will try to become all things, as many as 
> crawl upon the earth, and water, and divinely-kindled fire.

Lucian in *On the Dance* XIX. p. 278 and following in the Wetstein edition: "For it seems to me that the ancient myth says Proteus the Egyptian was nothing other than a certain **dancer** <note>original: "ὀρχηστήν" (orchēstēn)</note>, an imitative man, capable of **shaping himself** <note>original: "σχηματίζεσθαι" (schēmatizesthai)</note> into everything.—But the myth, taking it toward the more miraculous, described his nature as becoming those very things which he imitated. This is also present in those who dance today. You might see them changing swiftly at the same moment, and imitating Proteus himself." Plato similarly uses the phrase "to become all sorts of things" regarding poets in *Republic* II. p. 381. p. 102 Bekker and III. 389. p. 129. He elegantly applied the same fable of Proteus to philosophers who turn themselves in every direction and do not wish to declare their opinion openly, in *Euthydemus* p. 288. b. c. p. 426 Bekker (who, contrary to Heindorf's judgment, left "to suggest" untouched there, a reading which the excellent Bodleian Manuscript also confirms). Now, according to Eustathius on the *Odyssey* at the cited place, p. 177 Basel, p. 174 Leipzig edition, there were philosophers who took Proteus to represent Matter, which in act is none of the forms, but in potentiality is all things: "saying that Proteus is the first-born matter, the receiver of forms, being in activity none of the forms, but in potentiality, all things." When these points are gathered together, it becomes probable that Plotinus—who undoubtedly knew that allegorical interpretation of the Homeric passage and perhaps approved of it himself, and had seen mimes in Rome or other places expressing the character of Proteus through dancing—seized the opportunity from that very source to use the simile of the dancers. **Compare** our **annotation** above on III. 6. 16. p. 319. B.

**p. 1090, 2. just as if someone dividing knowledge should speak of grammar]** He seems to refer to Aristotle's *Categories* VI. 26. where the same examples are used.

**p. 1109, 5. says each is a certain nature]** <note>original: "ἑκάτερόν τινα φύσιν λέγει"</note> So I have written partly with Ficino, partly with the Manuscripts, instead of "each might say what nature."

**p. 1110, 5. so that in there, like an army or a choir.]** <note>original: "ὥστε ἐν ἐνταῦθα, ὡς στρατὸς ἢ χορός."</note> Plotinus uses this simile elsewhere as well. Dexippus uses the simile of the army in the passage on the *Categories*, in the "Problems and Solutions on Aristotle's Categories" at the beginning of the second book (Laurentian Medici Manuscript, Codex XXXIII): "Does the division then resemble those on a military expedition? For example, those arranged by companies, etc."

**--- 8. of which—the one will be told truly]** <note>original: "καθ’ οὗ—ἀληθεύσεται τὸ ἓν"</note> Thus I have placed with Ficino and four Manuscripts, and "it will be" follows. The Edition has "it is told truly" also in this place.

**p. 1111, 18. the common and in many]** <note>original: "τὸ κοινὸν καὶ ἐν πολλοῖς"</note> Ficino expressed "the common in many," which seems to be the true reading.

**p. 1112, 14. Is it then in each?]** <note>original: "Ἀρ’ οὖν ἐν ἑκάστῳ"</note> I added "in" <note>original: "ἐν"</note> from several books with Ficino, and in the Latin version from the first edition I corrected: "in *each*" instead of "into *each*."

**p. 1114, 2. and in itself as beginning and end]** <note>original: "καὶ ἐν αὐτῷ ὡς ἀρχὴ καὶ τέλος"</note> Thus with the Edition and all Manuscripts: "*and one to it* (namely, to being)"

**p. 1114, 16. πῶς ἀγαθοῦ μετέχει (*how it participates in the good*)**] Thus I have given it from three books instead of μετέχοι [*might participate*]: unless perhaps you prefer to conjecture: πῶς ἂν ἀγαθοῦ μετέχοι [*how it might indeed participate in the good*]. Then at **B. 1. 6.** I have written more fully: καὶ πῶς ἔτι ἕν; ἢ τὸ γένει ἕν, ὡς ἐν πολλοῖς ὅλον [*and how is it still one? or is it one in genus, as a whole in many things*] following **Marc. A.** and others, who nevertheless have τῷ γένει. These are absent from the [Ed. → Edition]. Nevertheless, **Fic.** also expressed it.

**p. 1115, 10. καὶ τὸ ὕστερον παρὰ τοῦ προτέρου (*and the posterior from the prior*)**] Thus I have placed it with many books: “and that very thing, because it is posterior.” **Fic.** however expressed καὶ τὸ ὕστερον, which the [Ed. → Edition] has, and in line 2 **B.** with almost the same: καὶ ἐνυπάρχει τὰ ὕστερα ἐν τοῖς προτέροις, *prioribus* [*and the posterior things are inherent in the prior things*]. **Fic.** however expressed: ἐν τοῖς πρώτοις [*in the first things*], which is in the [Ed. → Edition].

**p. 1116, 8. ’Αλλὰ περὶ γενέσεως κ. τ. λ. (*But concerning generation etc.*)**] This passage seems disturbed. **Fic.** in his version ordered the last part thus: μᾶλλον δὲ ὑποστάσεως καὶ ἐπινοίας ὕστερον θεωρητέον [*rather, it must be considered posterior in hypostasis and conception*]. I would have received this into the text if even a single [Cod. → Codex] agreed.

**p. 1117, 3. καὶ συνθέτων δεῖ ποιεῖσθαι (*and of composites it is necessary to make*)**] **Fic.** added a negation in his version, which seems necessary. However, no book [manuscript] acknowledges it.
— **13. ἀλλ’ ἔστιν οὐσία ἄνωθεν (*but it is essence from above*)**] In the Latin: “sed est essentia desuper.” Thus from the [edit. princ. → editio princeps] we have corrected the faulty *essentiæ*.

**p. 1118, 3. ἐνεργείᾳ ὄντως (*truly in actuality*)**] Two [Codd. → Codices] have ὄντος [*of being*]. **Fic.** in his version expressed ὄντως ὄντος [*of truly being*], which seems convenient; and more often readings which are found disjoined in books ought to be joined.
— **13. Τὸ δὲ πρός τι παραφυάδι ἐοικὸς (*But the 'relative' is like an offshoot*)**] What properly a παραφυὰς [*offshoot*] is, and how it is distinguished from a παρασπὰς [*side-shoot*], Schneider teaches in his annotations on Theophrastus's *History of Plants* **II. 2. 4. p. 100.** It is also read in Nicander’s *Georgics* in Athenaeus **II. 71. d. p. 275.** Schweigh. concerning palms. Julian, *Epistle to Oribasius* **XVII. p. 384.** Spanhem. **p. 23. ed. Heyler.**: οἷον δένδρου· κίνδυνός ἐστι μηδὲ τὴν παραφυάδα σωθῆναι [*as of a tree; there is danger that not even the offshoot be saved*]. Plotinus, however, borrowed the tropical [metaphorical] use from Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics* **I. 6. 2:** "But the good is spoken of both in 'what it is,' and in 'quality,' and in 'relation'; but that which is in itself and essence is prior by nature to the relative. For this is like an offshoot (παραφυάδι), and an accident of being; so that there would not be any common idea over these," to which place consult Giphanis and Zellius **p. 26:** whom, however, the passage of Plotinus escaped. The same philosopher in *Rhetoric* **I. 2. 7. p. 31. Gaisford.:** "so that it happens that Rhetoric is as it were a certain offshoot (παραφυές τι) of Dialectic." There is therefore a certain force in Plotinus's passage. For he strives to refute Aristotle with Aristotle's own words.

**p. 1119, 3. καὶ τὸ ποιεῖν δὲ δύο (*and 'to act' is two*)**] **Ficinus** before δὲ δύο repeated τὸ ποιεῖν, which ought to have been received by us if any book had supported it. It is indeed in the [Cod. Med. → Medicean Codex] in the [marg. → margin] καὶ τὸ ποιεῖν, τὸ ποιεῖν δὲ δύο. But this seems to be a correction of **Ficinus**. That the text is disturbed in [h. l. → this place] is argued by the reading of codex **Marc. B.**
— **14. ’Αλλὰ καὶ τὰ ἄλλα (*But also the others*)**] **Fic.** expressed *ἄλλα* [*others*], although most books offer τὰ ἄλλα [*the others*]; we have added *reliqua* [*the rest*] in the Latin: which we wish to be noted once. For Marsilius [Ficino] does so everywhere.

**p. 1120, 2. τὸ ὕστερον παρὰ τοῦ προτέρου (*the posterior from the prior*)**] Thus I have given it with the books and **Ficino** instead of ὑστέρου: but what **Fic.** adds: *rursumque inde posterius eorum verborum* [*and again from there the posterior of those words*] traces are lacking in our books.
— **11. τοῦτο εἶναι τὸ ἀγαθὸν αὐτοῦ (*this to be its good*)**] Thus I have written, for the common: τὸ ἀγαθὸν τοῦ εἶναι τὸ αὑτοῦ, with **Fic.** and the approved [Codd. → Codices].
— **15. ἡ πρώτη καλλονὴ (*the first beauty*)**] **Jacobs** in *Ephemeridd. Scholasticc. Darmst.* **1829. p. 827** judges that this word should be restored to Aelian *V. H.* XIII. 1., where he has set down examples of it from Themistius and Manasses. He could have cited many more from the more recent Platonists. For now, it suffices to praise Our Author [Plotinus] **I. 6. 6. and VI. 7. 32.**

**p. 1121, 10. Δικαιοσύνη δὲ καὶ σωφροσύνη—ἐνέργειαί τινες νοῦ πᾶσαι. (*Justice and temperance—all are certain activities of Intellect.*)**] [Vid. → See] **I. 2. 6:** "To be temperate is the inward turning toward Intellect." [Cf. → Compare] **I. 6. 6.** and the annotations there, and compare Plato’s *Phaedrus* **p. 237. extr. p. 23. Bekk.** and Ast’s *Commentary* on that place **p. 257.** Plato in *Phaedo* **p. 69. c:** "But the truth is in reality a certain purification from all such things, and temperance, and justice, and courage." Which our philosopher received at **p. 54. A.**, where consult the Annotations. Add **Ben. Bendtsen’s** *Marmora Mystica*. Copenhagen **1819. Specim. I. p. 9. sq.**
— **11. καὶ ὕστερα γένος καὶ εἴδη. (*and later genus and species.*)**] **Ficinus** expressed *γένους* [*of genus*], which seems true, yet does not appear in the books.
— **19. συνδυαζομένων (*being paired/joined*)**] **Fic.** expressed the reading of the [Codicis Med. A. → Medicean Codex A] συνδιασωζομένων [*being preserved together*]. The third reading συνδιαζομένων is worth nothing. We, in the vulgate [common reading], have

Bekk.:** "they were much worse educated in their souls, but much more vigorous (σφριγῶντες) in their bodies," which place Timaeus respected in his *Lexicon* **p. 244.** where Ruhnken has excellently set forth the use of this word. To which join now the most elegant Jacobs on Philostratus's *Images* **p. 587. and especially p. 665. sq.** Let it suffice to add some things especially from the best writers of the Church: Diogenes [ap. → in] Stobaeus *Florilegium* **T. XXIX. p. 207. p. 23. Gaisford.:** "and those whose bodies were corrupted by luxury to work hard in the gymnasia and pirate-ships and make them strong and vigorous (σφριγῶντας)." Herodian **III. 13. 14. p. 747:** "they were becoming unbridled and were giving themselves over to the worse; inasmuch as they were young men, vigorous (σφριγῶντας), and under royal authority rushing insatiably into all desires for pleasures." Philo Judaeus *On the Creation of the World* **p. 14. Marg. p. 40. Pfeiff.** concerning fish: "and some are vigorous (σφριγᾷ) in calm weather, others in surge and swell." Where what the [Codd. → Codices] of Augsburg add, ἀφρῷ [*with foam*], seems a gloss intruded from the [marg. → margin]. σφριγᾷ indeed ought not to have been translated *delectantur* [*they are delighted*] but *roborantur* [*they are strengthened*]. For it corresponds most closely to κραταιότερα τέ ἐστι [*it is stronger*] (in the [edit. → edition] of Pfeiffer it is falsely written κρατερότερά). Used absolutely of an old man leaping over a stone wall, Theodoretus *Hist. Relig.* **XVIII. p. 1230. extr.:** "he leaps over the coping-stone, it not being easy to mount even for those who are quite vigorous (σφριγῶσι)." Basil the Great in *Hexaemeron* Homily **I. p. 15. A:** "otherwise someone of the vigorous (σφριγώντων) rising up again against these according to plausible speech." The same in *Psalm* **LXI. p. 38. C:** "those who are vigorous (σφριγῶντες) at the peak of their age." The same Homily **XIII. on Baptism p. 481. A.B:** "how he who grows old and is corrupted according to the desires of deceit becomes vigorous (σφριγᾷ) again and grows young, and returns to the true flower of youth." Which place most agrees with the one of Diogenes above. The same Basil Homily **XII. on Proverbs p. 465:** "he who is vigorous (σφριγῶν) toward the actions of piety, and at his peak toward every intensity of good works." John Chrysostom Homily **X. p. 387. D. p. 2. ed. Matthaei:** "You saw the old man and the youth. Old indeed in body, but young in mind. You saw gray hair at its peak and old age vigorous (σφριγῶντα) in tone." Where Matthaei conjectures either γῆρας τὸν νοῦν σφριγῶν [*old age vigorous in mind*] (which conjecture he could have in a way confirmed by this passage of Plotinus, where the powers of the mind are said to be σφριγῶσαι [*vigorous*]) or: γήρως τόνον σφριγῶντα [*the tone of old age being vigorous*]. You might also suspect: καὶ γῆρας εὐτόνως σφριγῶν [*and old age vigorously being vigorous*] (cf. Plotinus **p. 691.**) or εὔτονον [*well-toned*]. But I do not wish to play at divination.

**p. 1127, 5. F:** μᾶλλον τοῦτο εἶναι ἠνιγμένος [*rather having hinted that this is so*], where [Ciz. → the Cizensis MS] has likewise ἠνιγμένως, and **p. 364. D:** τοῦτο ἄρα ἐστὶ τὸ θείως ἠνιγμένον [*this then is what is divinely hinted at*], where it is likewise used passively. In our place the edition has ἠνιγμένος and some books ἠνιγμένως and ᾗπερ, the margin of the [Ed. → Edition] has ᾗπερ. The words of Plato which our Philosopher praises are read in the *Timaeus* **p. 39. extr. p. 40. Bekk.** quite often praised by Plotinus **p. 203. infr. and 204. supr. p. 356. A. p. 362. B. and p. 690. B.** from which Lindavius cited only one at his [page] **58.** Our author praised Plato more freely in [h. l. → this place], as he often does elsewhere, putting: ἐν τῷ παντελεῖ ζῴῳ προ τῷ ὅ ἐστι ζῶον [*in the all-perfect living being before that which is a living being*]. That, however, is itself read in the *Timaeus* in another place **p. 31. p. 27. Bekk.**

**p. 1128, 1. κατακερματίζεσθαι (*to be parcelled out*)**] Thus I have written it as one word instead of κατα κερματίζεσθαι. Plato *Meno* **p. 79. A. p. 47. sq. Stallb.:** "not to break nor to parcel out virtue." *Republic* **279.** where there is a compound verb, which our author uses several times, as **III. 9. 5. V. 1. 2.**
— **4. εἰς τὸ ἄπειρον μεθέντα—εἰς ἀριθμὸν ἔρχεται ἤδη. (*having let go into the infinite—it now comes into number.*)**] A remarkable variety of the Vatican reading in [h. l. → this place] ought to turn our attention. I, the more I am blind in these matters, the less have I attempted to disturb the vulgate. For the rest, the argument of this passage is joined with the discussion of the infinite, the limit, and number in the *Philebus* **p. 23. extr. sqq. p. 59. sqq. ed. — **17. ἀλλ’ ὡς τὰ ἐν τοῖς κατόπτροις (*but as things in mirrors*)**] Another passage concerning mirrors **III. 6. 9.** we treated above at **p. 312. B. cf. also p. 316. C:** οἷον καὶ εἰς τὸ κάτο-

**πτρου ἐνορῷτο τὰ εἴδωλα. (*as if images were seen in a mirror.*)**] which passages Porphyry reduced into a compendium in *Sententiae* **XXII:** "just as that which is established elsewhere appears as a phantom in a mirror elsewhere." Plato *Alcibiades* **p. 132. fin. p. 367. Bekk.:** "just as in a mirror." Olympiodorus in his commentary on that Dialogue **p. 9.** relates that before the temples of the Egyptians mirrors were placed, by which the priests wished the same thing signified as the Greeks did with that Delphic inscription "Know Thyself" (γνῶθι σεαυτόν). [Cf. → Compare] the same author **p. 217. sq. 223.** and the annotation there. Plato, *Laws* **X. p. 905. p. 219. Pallad.* **21. p. 623.** who rightly warns in the same place that this passage recedes from the common meaning among the Platonists of ἐκμαγεῖον as an *expressed image* or likeness. [Cf. → Compare] our annotation above on Enn. **III. book 6. chapter 2. p. 305. A.** Aristides *Panathenaic* **I. p. 342. p. 196:** students of wisdom look again and again in their minds at Athens—"gazing into the words as if into a mirror." Themistius *Oration* **16. p. 410:** "I, O King, say that that speech ought to be set forth as if a mirror every day, into which looking and gazing, one will not arrange his hair more decently, but rather the Roman Empire." (Which passage ought to be applied to the epigram of Phanias in *Anthol. Gr.* **II. 53.** at the *Animadversions* of Jacobs **VIII. p. 169.** For mirrors are among the instruments of the barber-shop.) Just as Aristides and Themistius in the [l. l. → cited places] compare the decrees of wisdom to a mirror into which everyone ought to look, so also the Apostle compares the doctrine of the Gospel. [Cf. → Compare] Lambert Bos, *Exercitations on the Epistle of Paul II. Corinthians III. 18.* who orders the word *κατοπτρίζεσθαι* to be taken there as meaning *to look accurately and diligently, to consider well*; others on the contrary ordering these to be compared with the same Apostle’s *I. Corinthians XIII. 12:* "for now we see through a glass in enigmas." (where because Bos wishes *specularia* [windowpanes] or *windows* to be understood, Valckenaer expresses doubt in *Scholae in N. T.* Vol. **II. p. 311. sq.**) Furthermore, no one will fail to understand that the sentiment of this Plotinian passage and the Pauline one are in some way similar. Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogus* **III. p. 258. Potter.** mentions the use of mirrors in censuring the luxury of women: "and the highly-prized preparations of mirrors, by which they fashion themselves, hunting those who, like foolish children, are fluttered by forms." Tertullian uses the comparison of the window-pane in *On the Soul* **chapter 53. p. 305. Rigalt.:** “For if that body is a prison by the Platonic sentiment, but the temple of God by the Apostolic when it is in Christ; yet in the meantime it obstructs and stops up the soul with its enclosure, and fouls it with the concretion of the flesh; whence to her, as if through a *corneous window* [specular], the *light of things is* more dim,” etc.

### BOOK III.

**P. 1130, 7. ON THE GENERA OF BEING, THIRD.**] The last little word is absent from one [Cod. → Codex]. One Marcian manuscript plainly neglected the inscription. From the order of time in which the individual books were committed to writing, this is the forty-fourth (Porphyry, *Life of Plotinus* **chapters V. and XXVI.**) The rest, which it is necessary to know, I set forth above at the title of the first book of this Ennead **p. 566.**

**p. 1131, 9. ἐν τῷδε τῷ παντὶ (*in this universe*)**] Thus I have corrected from the good books, whereas ἐν was absent and it was written τῷ δε: “and *in this universe* [to seek] other things and diverse from those.”

**p. 1132, 6. τὸ δὲ εἶδος ἐπ’ αὐτῇ (*but the species upon it [matter]*)**] In the Latin I have corrected from the [Ed. prc. → editio princeps]: “that however as species *in matter*” for *into matter*, and in the Greek γένεσιν [*generation*] for

### PAGE 364

**BOOK III. OF THE SIXTH ENNEAD. p. 1129—1142.**

γένεσιν. For the rest, concerning the notion of γένεσις [*becoming/generation*] among the Platonic philosophers, this is a classic passage, and especially those things in the preceding parts are to be held: "nature concerning bodies—not at all as essence because of applying the notion of flowing things, but appropriately to be called generation." And this force of "generation" (γενέσεως) extends most widely through all the Enneads. [Cf. → Compare] also Proclus on the *Alcibiades* [pr. → prooemium] **I. 108:** "generation and mortal nature." [cf. → compare] **p. 187. ibid. and p. 257. sq.** and the same author's *Theological Elements* **p. 74. p. 158. and p. 308. sqq.**

**p. 1133, 11. Πῶς δὲ λέγωμεν (*How then should we speak*)**] Thus we have given it with the good books for λέγομεν [*we speak*].

**p. 1135, 5. καὶ ἕδρα δοκεῖ τῷ εἴδει εἶναι—καὶ ἕδρα ὥστε (*and a seat seems to be for the species—and a seat so that*)**] Thus we have restored this passage from [Codd. plurr. → most manuscripts] and **Ficino**, which is lacunose [gapped] in the [Ed. → Edition]. The word ὑποβάθρα [*pedestal/base*] occurred also at **VI. 1. 28. p. 593. C.** Porphyry joins it with the word θεμέλιος [*foundation*] in *Sententiae* **§. 34. p. 239.** [Cf. → Compare] also Proclus, *Theological Elements* **LXXI. p. 112. of our edition**, where I summoned Hesychius **II. 1467, Suidas III. 551, and Zonaras p. 1772,** and in addition Dionysius the Areopagite, *On the Celestial Hierarchy* **c. 5.**

**p. 1136, 14. καὶ ἀφ’ ἧς δὲ τὰ ἄλλα (*and from which indeed the others*)**] Perhaps δὴ should be read instead of δὲ.

**p. 1141, 9. ἡ δ’ ἐναργεστέρα (*the clearer one*)**] I received this reading from the margin of the edition alone instead of ἡ δὲ ἐνεργεστέρα [*the more active one*]. For first, ἐνεργέστερον and ἐναργέστερον are found confused with each other six hundred times; ([Vid. → See] Upton and Schweighaeuser on Arrian's *Discourses of Epictetus* **III. 3. 4. p. 620. sq.** and the latter on Polybius **I. 1. 2. p. 117. sq.**): then because of the opposite ἀμυδρά [*dim/faint*]. I can cite many passages: one will suffice. Proclus on Plato's *Alcibiades* [pr. → prooemium] **I. p. 2. of our edition:** "each thing participates in being more dimly or more clearly (ἐναργέστερον)." Plotinus proceeds: "and of images one is a certain sketch (ὑποτύπωσις), the other more of a finished execution (ἐξεργασία)." This meaning of the word ἐξεργασία must be held as referring to *images accurately expressed* and absolute, the contrary of which is ὑποτύπωσις, *sketching, beginning*. Above at **p. 57. D.** Our Author says: "and do not cease carving your own statue," imitating Plato in the *Phaedrus* **p. 252. d.** which passage Cicero also had before his eyes in *On the Laws* **I. 22. 59. p. 142. ed. Moser.** And concerning the care of oneself and the cultivation of character and the refining of the soul, Arrian in *Diss. Epict.* **III. 13. 8. p. 411. Schweigh.:** "what things are against the oppressive; how even these may be healed, how they may be removed. If any requires finished execution (ἐξεργασίας), to execute it according to its own reason." Where I would believe ἐξεργασία, if I consider the passages of Plato and Plotinus, to be transferred from an artist finishing and polishing an image.

**p. 1142, 16. ποιαὶ γὰρ οὐσίαι αὗται. κ. τ. λ. (*for what kind of essences are these etc.*)**] Simplicius on Aristotle's *Categories* **Fol. 55. a:** "But Plotinus asks, what then being 'Quality' does it provide for those called 'qualified'? For that qualified things are spoken of according to quality, has been said. But what this quality is according to its own definition has not been determined; to which Porphyry says, that the discourse concerning quality is conceptual (ἐννοηματικός), but not essential (οὐσιώδης). But it is conceptual, being taken from things known to everyone and commonly agreed upon among all, as for example, that 'good' is that from which it happens that one is benefited. 'Soul' is that from which life exists. 'Voice' is the proper sensible of hearing. Essential definitions, however, are those teaching the essence of the things defined themselves, as for example 'good' is virtue, or that which participates in virtue. 'Soul' is a self-moving essence, 'voice' is struck air. And conceptual definitions, as being commonly agreed upon among all, are the same; but essential ones, proceeding according to particular sects, are contradicted by those of other opinions. At least the ancients do not agree with those saying that voice is air and a body, defining it as an incorporeal activity and a stroke. And those placing the good in virtue and the beautiful alone are disputed by those extending it through all things. It has seemed best, then, in the first introductions, to use definitions agreed upon by all. For they are more known, and more suitable for a first hearing. But the others require 'first philosophy,' which considers beings as beings. Wherefore Aristotle gave back the essential definition of quality in the *Metaphysics*, but the conceptual one here. And these things are well said. But better is the account which says, that if quality existed by itself, it would be necessary to seek what it is that is participated; but if it is in us and does not stand outside of the qualified, it is clear that its being is not one thing and its being participated another, nor is it by itself in one way and in another way providing being and speech to the qualified, but in the same thing, both aspects of quality are considered. For quality is the form of the possessor. He, therefore, who renders quality through the qualified, characterizes its most sovereign property, and at once presents in beings what it is and what sort of finished execution (ἀπεργασίαν) it provides."

**p. 1143, 15. ζωγραφία (*painting*)**] [Conf. → Compare] Plato, *Statesman* **p. 277. p. 289. sq. Bekker.**

**p. 1144, 1. Καὶ περὶ μὲν τῆς λεγομένης οὐσίας κ. τ. λ. (*And concerning the so-called essence etc.*)**] These words of Simplicius on Aristotle's *Categories* **69. a** seem to pertain here: "whatever of these is not arranged with quantity, but with character and quality, whether it is arranged in another species besides the mentioned ones of quality, as both Andronicus and Plotinus suppose, or whether it is possible to bring them under one of the four; this will be clear if it is known what sort of things heaviness and lightness themselves are. For if heat, by thinning bodies, makes that which is light identical to itself, and cold by contracting makes that which is heavy identical to itself, these will be brought back into passive qualities. But if lightness follows the hot, and heaviness follows the cold, and both heat and cold are productive; but the heavy and the light are not naturally disposed to act or suffer anything, those will seem to be brought back into passive qualities. But these into another proper genus; and if they belong to elements according to essence, they will seem not even to be qualities. But if the thing having received them is also qualified, and is called qualified, and from the essential difference there arises in the participating bodies a certain formative character, these also would be qualified things."
— **13. στοιχεῖα—τὸ δὲ τὸ πῦρ κ. τ. λ. (*elements—but the fire etc.*)**] John Philoponus *against Proclus*: "and as it were fire insulting because of satiety, and not the elemental and vital fire. But the fire there, he says, is smooth and quiet, fitting the nature of the stars, and pleasantly warm—for the most pure and most unmixed portion of the elements was separated for the composition of the celestial body. So that neither is the nature of the celestial body outlandishly foreign to the elements among us, nor is the fire or the earth or any other there unvaryingly such as here. But among us the dreg-like and as it were the sediment of the elements flows off. But there the most subtle and better part of them was separated. Since also in other animals Plotinus says, in the most sovereign of them especially, nature chooses the better parts. Many other testimonies could indeed be put forward to confirm the present opinion of Plato. For his own student Aristotle, as is agreed among us, both bears witness to these things and blames Plato for this very thing. For Aristotle seems first of all to have introduced the opinion concerning the fifth body. But I think for well-disposed men even what has been said is sufficient for perfect persuasion; and lest we extend the discourse about this beyond what is needed."

**p. 1146, 19. ὑλικάτερα εἴπομεν καὶ ὀργανικὰ (*we called [them] more material and organic/instrumental*)**] [Cf. → Compare] [chapter IX. A:] "more material indeed: fire, earth, water, air; but organic/instrumental: the bodies of plants and of animals." Concerning the Platonic and Stoic reason by which the soul (anima) of God is an *organon*, an instrument: the body is called the instrument of the soul, [Vid. → See] Gataker on *M. Antoninus* **X. 38. p. 316.** and Wyttenbach [ad → in] Plutarch's *Banquet of the Seven Sages* **p. 988.** Add Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogus* **II. 4.** Isidore of Pelusium, *Epistles* **I. 364. p. 95:** "and by 'strings' he indicates the senses in us, by which the plectrum of the tongue is struck. Aristotle uses the adjective in *Nicomachean Ethics* **III. 1. 6. p. 110. Zellius:** "to move the organic parts." Especially relevant here is another passage of the Stagirite, *On the Soul* **II. 1. p. 22. sq. Sylb.:** "wherefore soul is the first entelechy of a natural body having life in potentiality; and such a body is that which is organic. But organs are also the parts of plants, although entirely simple; as the leaf is the covering of the pericarp, and the pericarp of the fruit. The roots are analogous to the mouth; for both draw in nourishment." No one will fail to understand that Plotinus had this and similar passages before his eyes.

**p. 1147, 6. Περὶ δὲ ποσοῦ καὶ ποιότητος κ. τ. λ. (*But concerning quantity and quality etc.*)**] Regarding the words of Aristotle "quantity does not admit of the 'more' and the 'less'" (quanta, nec magis quanta, nec minus quanta dici possunt) after Simplicius (in *Categories* **Fol. 38. a.**) approved this sentiment, he proceeds thus: "and I think the cause of quantity not admitting of the more and the less is that other things are defined and measured according to quantity; if therefore quantity becomes the limit of other things, how could it participate in the indefiniteness of the more and the less? If however we call a magnitude greater than a magnitude, and a number more than a number, in this we observe much of the more and the less. For the Caucasus is more greater than Hymettus than Athos is, and seven are more many than three than five are; we shall say that the more and the less exist for them according to 'relation.' But if the Caucasus is more greater, and Athos less, and Hymettus still less, according to the indefinite, one might concede that quantity also admits of the

### PAGE 366

**BOOK III. OF THE SIXTH ENNEAD. p. 1143—1150.**

more and the less, just as it admits of contrariety. For that which is not spoken of as 'great' in relation to something, but 'in itself,' is opposed to that which is spoken of as 'small' in itself; and so Andronicus arranges it. But Plotinus says that the 'great' is not at all a relative, but that we often say 'great' improperly instead of 'greater.'" The same author, ibid. **Fol. 36. b:** "But perhaps, says Iamblichus following Andronicus, the great and small, and the many and few, are not only relative, but also indefinite quantity. For when we say 'great,' we indicate an indefinite quantity; for it is not indicated by how much or by what magnitude it is great, or by what multitude it is many. But when we say 'greater' and 'smaller,' it is considered according to the relation toward each other. But Aristotle considered the great and the small only according to 'relation,' just as Plotinus considered it only according to 'simply' [* (quantity)]. For he says that the 'great' in relation is said instead of 'greater'." And a little lower, when he explains the opinion of Iamblichus:—"and the divine Iamblichus wishes that 'great' and 'small' and 'many' and 'few' in themselves be observed in the 'in themselves' and immaterial species, some according to the excellence of power, others according to the multitude of pure reasons. But relatives, which are spoken of by comparison, he sees in the enmattered, in which also are the more and the less, and contraries at once according to the reference to one thing or another. For when species approaches matter, a certain mingled power arises from both. Insofar as it participates in species, it is assimilated to it, and the immaterial becomes many and great. But according to its own infinity, it participates more and less both in the 'relation' and in the change toward contraries. This being the case, then, he (**Iamblichus**, speaking against Plotinus regarding the definition of the 'great') says that they do not suppose rightly who think all these things are spoken of simply, as Plotinus does. For even common usage often uses them for relatives, and those calling a grain of millet 'great' according to comparison with its own kind, as indicating the 'greater,' speak according to 'relation'; but magnitude, says Plotinus, is not among relatives, but 'greater' is, just as 'double' is. Or is it not so? For the notion of magnitude extends both over magnitudes in themselves and those in relation to each other. For 'greater' would not be spoken of without participating in magnitude, and indicating the excellence according to magnitude. But many say, etc." Simplicius proceeds from there to the opinion of others, and does not return to Plotinus.
