**p. 1156, 2. Καὶ γὰρ εἰ ἐν ὕλῃ λόγοι κ. τ. λ. (*For even if reasons are in matter etc.*)**] Simplicius on Aristotle's *Categories* **p. 73. b: ([cf. → compare] the other passage of Simplicius applied at p. 588 above:)** "For toward those from the Porch [the Stoics], saying that the virtuous kind is stable, but the middle admits of intensification (ἐπίτασιν) and remission (ἄνεσιν), it is worth asking whether he who has virtue, but is lacking in training or nature, would be less virtuous; but perhaps they will say that virtue, being knowledge, has stability from itself. For being theoretical of its own reasons, and always aiming to do everything according to itself, it acts firmly established in the unchangeable species of knowledge. But how is this possible over a mutable and passive essence of quality, and especially according to them having 'flowing' and 'contraction' into infinity in itself and in virtue? Because they say even qualities are bodies. Perhaps then they transfer things said about other principles among the ancients even to other principles, unless indeed they, placing the virtuous habit according to the most, and not observing it in motion, reasonably thought it worthy to observe neither intensification nor remission in it. But if this is also of each of the arts a certain 'most,' which also itself stands firm. For of every 'more' and 'less,' there is certainly also a 'most.' And perhaps according to this notion is the opinion which Aristotle mentions, taking perfect habits not only in virtue but also in health and grammar, and other dispositions, saying they are without intensification and remission, observing intensification and remission in those participating in the habits rather or less. And yet it is possible to see this in them, not only in arts, but also in virtues. For of virtues some are perfect, others imperfect. Imperfect indeed, those only by nature, or habit, or reason; perfect, however, those completed by these three; unless indeed virtue itself is perfect and whole, but is participated in also by part, just as grammar and each of the other arts, and through the imperfect, the 'more' and 'less' is observed in the participation. But what sort of dispositions does Aristotle see as perfect besides those possessed? Is it the separate species, and 'self-justice,' or is this neither customary to him, nor suitable to the present matters, nor would those be called 'dispositions'? But having beheld the participating perfect ones, according to the reference to those, he wishes those falling short of them to have the 'more' and the 'less.' And this account is more accurate in all dispositions, both observing the perfect according to their peak, and the 'more' and 'less' according to participation in breadth. Of the others, that of the Stoics seems imperfect, beholding neither the imperfect of virtues, nor the perfect of other arts. For if virtue were observed in reason alone, he having the reason and the knowledge would not be intensified. For true reason is one. And true reason is not more than true reason. But if he having the knowledge should fall short in training or nature, he would be less just, so that if perfect habit is not composed of theorems alone, but also of nature and habit, one would be more just than another. And in this case the reason is one and the same, being completed by the theorems; but the training, according to which the imperfect grammarian

### PAGE 368

**BOOK III. OF THE SIXTH ENNEAD. p. 1152—1156.**

is observed, produces the 'more' and the 'less' in the different manner of participation in the same reason. Likewise also, the reason of whiteness is one. But snow is said to be whiter than milk because of the non-mixing of the white [with something else]; for where there is a mixture of matter, it is necessary to participate in the 'not-such,' and intensification and remission to occur. But how does he say something becomes whiter, not being white before, or more grammatical, if it is not yet grammatical? But surely he who does not have it is not called grammatical, though progressing and still approaching toward grammar, nor likewise white. And whenever we say this is greater than that, neither is simply great. For that which is simply great is one, and is greatest, and simply grammar is one, and peak virtue is one. But the difficulty must be solved by saying that comparisons are spoken of according to reference to the perfect. But these being said so, it is wondrous if it is possible for this perfect quality to be enmattered. For the perfect and that which stands in the same way would be of another nature and not of the enmattered. Moreover, concerning this Iamblichus says it is more absurd, if quality is indeed enmattered, but does not suffer the same things as the enmattered subjects receiving it. For so it becomes almost separate if it has certain proper works separate from the common. And he says that is absurd, if quality is indeed always joined with the qualified as having its nature twin to it and unvarying, but is separated again in everything, the quality indeed not being intensified, but the qualified being intensified; perhaps then he says in all these things, they were referring to immaterial reasons. For also in virtues, those giving the progresses, but denying the perfect among men, were unaware that they were supposing [the perfect as immaterial], and for this reason they were denying these to the enmattered; but if this is so, the opinion falls away into another nature differing entirely. For the nature of quality was not of the immaterial. These things Iamblichus wrote in these very words. But perhaps by this reason it is necessary to place the 'more' and 'less' even upon essence. For it too is enmattered. But the perfect and stable would be of another nature, and quantity likewise, and the limited itself, and all qualities. But I think it is necessary to take the 'more' and 'less' not according to the enmattered, but according to the adventitious and less essential. For essence indeed, considered according to being itself, which is spoken of, does not have the 'more' and 'less.' But quality, existing according to participation in essence, reasonably admits of this. For it is more in the less essential things, but less in the more essential, as in shapes. And quantity, being nearer to essence, does not admit of the 'more' and the 'less.' But neither do qualities, considered according to their own peak perfection, just as perfect virtue and perfect grammar admit of the 'more' and 'less.' For these are considered according to the 'most.' And these perfections are not immaterial and separate reasons, but enmattered indeed, yet considered according to the species itself. According to which also we define each of the enmattered, looking not toward the matter, but toward the species. And if none of the enmattered ever attains its own perfection, it is well to say that the 'more' and 'less' exist in all; but if this is absurd, there is also a 'most,' and thus for us even Plotinus's opinion will be corrected, being taken only according to the enmattered and generated, but not according to the property of quality, by which it differs from essence and quantity; but Iamblichus, meeting Plotinus's opinion which similarly changes qualities and similarly the qualified in intensifications and remissions, says it is absurd that the same turns should alter the reason, just as the composite. For what will the participated differ from the participating? And at the same time his common axiom concerning the incorporeals, that they are both impassive and immutable, will be overturned thus; and having said these things against Plotinus, he brings in the truest theory of the doctrine: for being, he says, a certain incorporeal essence of reasons, it gives itself to those receiving, and producing the 'qualified' in the body, it nevertheless remains incorporeal by itself in the body, having being by itself and imparting of its hypostasis to it along with not losing its own nature. Whence indeed there is the form impressed from it, as it were admitting of intensification; but there is also the incorporeal essence of the quality able to stand in the same species, and it does not become immaterial because of this, but enmattered, yet not of the whole matter, because they are the species of themselves, and are limited primarily according to the one and the same. And for this reason, even in becoming in matter, it does not depart entirely from its whole nature; but remaining in it, in a certain way it is filled with the opposite extension and indefiniteness toward it. But the remaining last sect Iamblichus corrects, which thinks the intelligible qualities are non-intensifiable, but the enmattered participate in intensification and remission; he says that of Porphyry, that all intelligibles, even which are beings, are essences, and

VOL. III. Z Z

### PAGE 369

**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

therefore do not admit of the 'more' and the 'less.' But he says it is possible to say against this, that even in the intelligibles the order of the reason of quality is preserved, even if all things exist there according to essence. For according to his reason, station and motion are observed around essence, preserving as in intelligibles the reason of activity existing in another and about another. But entirely, the present discourse is not about intelligibles. These things then have been sufficiently said."

**p. 1156, 10. Καὶ δὴ καὶ μουσικήν φησιν ὁ Πλάτων κ. τ. λ. (*And indeed Plato says music etc.*)**] [Vide → See] Eryximachus's speech in the *Symposium* **p. 186. extr. and p. 187. a. and p. 188. b. p. 397. and 399. of Bekker.**

**p. 1157, 13. διαιρετέον τὰς μὲν ψυχικὰς, τὰς δὲ σωματικὰς (*one must divide those of the soul, and those of the body*)**] Simplicius [l. c. → in the place cited] **p. 69. b:** "Plotinus indeed divides, saying some are qualities of body, others of soul, not making a division of quality thus according to truth, but only showing a distance of those things in which quality is, but this does not show a difference of quality. Wherefore also Aristotle, in passive qualities, having spoken of some as of soul, others of body, did not go out into another genus of quality, but remained in the same, knowing well that the reception of species being changed, makes a difference of the lying space, but makes no difference of the inherent species or character. But again he divides those of the body according to the senses, falling into the same absurdity; and yet one thing, says Iamblichus, parcelling out into other things according to number, and not into those differing in species. For the sensible as sensible is one species, even if he takes what is joined to each sense as a proper sensible, he distinguishes them according to number. Aristotle also shows this. For arranging passive qualities as sensibles toward sense, he brought them back commonly toward all senses; but those joined toward each, he did not add, as not making the difference according to species, but differing in number only; it is worth attending whether senses also do not differ from each other in species, and the proper sensibles of the senses, whose difference in species Plotinus attempted to show from the senses; for such a difference is not according to number, being divided into individuals even itself, this visible thing and that; but if Aristotle did not divide until this point, it is not wondrous, bringing the discourse as far as the first division of the highest genera into species, which it was necessary even for Plotinus to guard, making the division of the highest genera; but the qualities of the soul Plotinus set apart according to the parts of the soul. And yet it is possible even in more parts for there to be the same quality, as the 'tractable' [easy-to-guide?] and 'hard.' And in one many, whenever it is multi-potent, as in the rational many sciences and differing in species. But after this he divides those of the rational, they being more, according to sciences and according to arts falling away into the extremes, and not remaining in Aristotle's enclosure of these, according to whom the genus becomes that of habit; nor considering that it is not now proposed to bring the division of genera through everything, but the most generic of all and those close to these, of which those are predicated, these alone it is now proposed to hand down, so that even when he adds the powers in the desiderative, the progress of the division up to that point is not to be accepted. For this is a counting-up of the extremes, not a division of the first genera. Entirely, every division ought to happen according to the proper nature of each. For in quantity division according to parts is fitting. For this is partible even among composites, or of incorporeal things having a certain remission of essence in themselves, for this is not foreign. But when someone divides quality not as quality, this is as being whole present everywhere insofar as it is qualified, and as being the same, both in the small and great, and in whatever parts, as the sweetness of honey in however many bulks of honey, he does not make the division rightly; for not where it is natural, does he attempt to cut it. But perhaps not even this is true, that every quality has gone through the whole of the qualified, if the fourth species of quality was observed according to the surface, and if the triangle, and each of other such shapes having lines, and having angles, is not whole present everywhere. For not in the same place are all lines, nor are angles with lines. Then not the same quality, such as temperance or blackness, is present to soul and body. Nothing then is absurd in this to divide psychic and somatic qualities. But to infer from different activities different qualities, when they happen according to them, to transfer things concerning powers into qualities—for powers being hidden are distinguished from the activities they bring in. But qualities show forth manifest 'qualifieds' through the things done, other 'qualifieds' being present. And these will be distinguished according to the most sovereign

### PAGE 370

**BOOK III. OF THE SIXTH ENNEAD. p. 1156—1162.**

genera. But here also it must be noted, that qualities also have powers, and nothing is absurd, from activities to distinguish powers, and from powers to distinguish existences. But when Plotinus divides psychic and somatic qualities by the beneficial and harmful, and again divides benefits and harms as thinking these proper differences of quality, because from quality all benefit and harm arises, he does not make the division appropriately even here, and because he changes from the 'qualified' to the 'relative.' For the same honey being according to quality is beneficial toward this person; but toward that, harmful. And perfume is sweet and beneficial to others; but to beetles harmful and deadly, so that the beneficial and harmful is not a quality, but a relative. Then why do benefits and harms provide differences of quality rather than of essence, or of acting? For also in these benefits and harms are observed. And that quantity also, well-fitted into power, and again not well-fitted, becomes a cause of much benefit and harm, the art of the Asclepiads shows, and things announced by them concerning the symmetry of quantity. In addition to these, if qualities were active and provided 'qualifieds' according to activity, it would be possible to say that they themselves benefit or harm. But if they do [so] by being possessed, they bring in no harm or benefit from themselves insofar as they are qualities. In general all such divisions are inappropriate, as being according to the relative rather, but not divided according as they are qualities. After the great Plotinus we must consider, even what division Aristotle sets forth in other places etc."

**p. 1157, 14. ὡς σώματος οὖσας (*as being of the body*)**] “*Utpote quae corporis sunt.*” These Ficino did not express: they appear however in all our books.

**p. 1159, 13. ἀλλὰ γὰρ ὅτι ἕτερα ἡ αἴσθησις κ. τ. λ. (*but for because sense is other things etc.*)**] [Cf. → Compare] above **p. 491. B. and p. 499. A.B. chapter 3.** John Philoponus had these passages before his eyes in Aristotle's *Prior Analytics* fol. **III.:** "but intellect and sense do not syllogize [reason]. Intellect as being better than syllogizing. Wherefore also the divine Plotinus says about it: that it either touches, or not. And it is in every way unerring. For either it touches, knowing things by simple applications. Or it does not even touch the principle and similarly is unerring according to both. But sense as being worse than syllogizing, does not syllogize. But neither does imagination syllogize etc."

**p. 1161, 19. Τὰς δὲ στερήσεις πῶς; [τὰς δὲ στερήσεις] εἰ ὦν αἱ στερήσεις ποιότητες, καὶ αὐταὶ ποιότητες (*But what of privations? [But what of privations] if those things of which they are privations are qualities, then they too are qualities*)**] I have included these in brackets nor did **Fic.** express them, then with [plurr. → several] books I gave *αὐταὶ* [*they*] for *αὐτὰ* [*them*] of the edition: in the Latin however *tametsi forte* [*although perhaps*] from the [ed. pr. → editio princeps] for *tametsi si forte* [*although if perhaps*]. The examples which follow, "as toothless or blind," like many others, had been applied by Aristotle himself. Thus, to use this, the Stagirite in *Categories* **VIII. 9:** "for we call toothless not that which does not have teeth, and blind not that which does not have sight; but that which does not have them when it is natural to have them; for some things from birth have neither sight nor teeth." [cf. → compare] ibid. **§. 17.** and Ammonius **p. 131. b.** Archytas in [ap. → in] Simplicius on this passage of the *Categories* used it in another sense, and νωδὸς [*toothless*], from α [*not*] and αὐδὴ [*voice/sound*], is often the same as ἄφωνος [*voiceless*], and likewise stunned. But in both meanings writers quite often join both the toothless and the astonished or mute with the blind (τυφλὸς), whose passages Sallier and Tib. Hemsterhuis collected at Thomas Magister **p. 635—637.** and Ruhnken at Timaeus, *Platonic Lexicon* **p. 102.**

**p. 1162, 11. ἐρυθαίνεσθαι (*to redden*)**] Thus all our books, and only two a little lower ἐρυθραίνεται: the rest ἐρυθαινεται. On which account I did not wish to change this form, which they call poetic, with the form ἐρυθραίνεσθαι; and a softer pronunciation could have brought in this writing usage later. Kiessling in Iamblichus's *Protrepticus* **XXI. p. 316.** from conjecture placed Ἐρυθρίνον for Ἐρυθίνον: but the [Cod. Reg. → Royal Codex] and Memmian [MS] persist in this reading. Compare concerning other forms of this kind Lobeck, *Parerga V. on Phrynichus p. 727. sq.* In Plato's *Lysis* we read **p. 204. b. p. 110. Bekk.:** καὶ ὃς ἐρυτηθεὶς ἠρυθρίασε [*and he, being reddened, blushed*]. Ficinus translated: *obticuit, nihil respondit* [*he was silent, he answered nothing*]. Furthermore, this itself pertains to the Aristotelian examples in *Categories* **VI. 12:** "for neither is he who blushes through being ashamed called a 'blusher' [by habit]; nor he who turns pale through being afraid a 'pale-one'." But that whole passage is to be compared with ours.
— **16. Ὁρᾷν δὲ δεῖ, εἰ μὴ πάση ποιότητί ἐστί τις ἄλλη ἐναντία. (*But one must see, if to every quality there is not some other contrary.*)**] Simplicius on Aristotle's *Categories* **p. 71. b:** "but why are the intermediates neither contrary to each other, nor to the extremes, because it will be toward more opposites, and no longer will one be contrary to one, if the intermediates are also contrary. But Plotinus asks, whether there is not some contrariety to every quality. For also the middle is contrary to the extremes; for virtue being a middle according to Aristotle, is contrary to the excesses—"

Philo the Jew, *On the Creation of the World* **p. 14. Margin p. 40. Pfeiffer** concerning fish: "and some **thrive** <note>original: "σφριγᾷ"</note> in calm weather, others in the surge and waves." Indeed, <term>sphriga</term> <note>original: "σφριγᾷ"</note> ought not to have been translated as *they are delighted* but *they are strengthened*. Used absolutely of an old man leaping over a wall, Theodoret in *Religious History* **XVIII. p. 1230. at the end:** "he climbs over the coping-stone, which is not easy to mount even for those who are very **vigorous** <note>original: "σφριγῶσι"</note>." Basil the Great in *Hexaemeron* Homily **I. p. 15. This passage agrees most with the one from Diogenes above. The same Basil in Homily **XII on Proverbs p. 465:** "he who is **vigorous** <note>original: "ὁ σφριγῶν"</note> toward the deeds of piety, and peaking toward every strength of good works." Where Matthaei conjectures either "old age **vigorous** in the mind" (which conjecture he could have confirmed in some way by this passage of Plotinus, where the powers of the mind are said to be **vigorous**) or: "the **vigorous** tension of old age." # ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS

...the images might be seen as if in a mirror <note>original: "πτρου ἐνορῷτο τὰ εἴδωλα"</note>. Porphyry reduced these passages into a compendium in *Sentences* **XXII:** "Just as in a mirror, that which is established in one place appears in another." <note>original: "ὥσπερ ἐν κατόπτρῳ τὸ ἀλλαχοῦ ἱδρυμένον ἀλλαχοῦ φανταζόμενον"</note> Plato in *Alcibiades* **p. 132. end p. 367. Bekker edition:** "Just as in a mirror." <note>original: "ὥσπερ ἐν κατόπτρῳ"</note> Olympiodorus, in his commentary on that Dialogue **p. 9**, relates that mirrors were placed before the temples of the Egyptians, by which the priests intended to signify the same thing as the Greeks did with that Delphic inscription: *Know thyself*. <note>original: "γνῶθι σεαυτόν"</note> Compare the same author **p. 217. ff. 223.** and the annotations there. Plato in *Laws* **X. p. 905. p. 219. Bekker:** "And then, as if in mirrors, you thought you had observed in their actions the neglect of all the gods." <note>original: "κᾴτα ὡς ἐν κατόπτροις αὐτῶν ταῖς πράξεσιν ἡγήσω καθεωρακέναι τὴν πάντων ἀμέλειαν θεῶν"</note> Valckenaer applied this passage of Plato to Euripides' *Hippolytus* **428** with an excellent annotation; no less conveniently did Wyttenbach in his *Observations* **p. 152** apply it to his edition of Plutarch (*On the Education of Children* **p. 14. A.**). Lucian in *On the Dance* **81. p. 212. Wetstein edition:** "Rather, as if in a mirror, he sees himself in the dancer, and sees both what he is accustomed to suffer and what he is accustomed to do." <note>original: "μᾶλλον δὲ ὥσπερ ἐν κατόπτρῳ, τῷ ὀρχηστῇ ἑαυτὸν βλέπῃ, καὶ ἃ πάσχειν αὐτὸς καὶ ἃ ποιεῖν εἴωθε"</note> There follows a mention of the Delphic epigram which we just mentioned. A third passage is from Plato in the *Timaeus* **p. 72. p. 102. Bekker** where the divine philosopher says this regarding the spleen: "Furthermore, the composition and seat of the neighboring organ [the spleen] was placed on the left for its sake, to keep it bright and pure, like a <term>mirror</term> <note>original: "κατόπτρῳ"</note> prepared and always lying ready as a <term>mold</term> <note>original: "ἐκμαγεῖον" - literally a substance for taking impressions, like wax or a sponge</note> etc." i.e. "just as a sponge prepared and ready for wiping the mirror to which it is applied," as Isaac Vossius correctly explains in his notes on Catullus, approved by Ezechiel Spanheim in his notes on Callimachus' *The Bath of Pallas* **21. p. 623.** who in the same place rightly warns that this passage departs from the common meaning of *mold* <note>original: "ἐκμαγείου"</note> among the Platonists, which usually refers to an *expressed image* or likeness. Compare our annotation above on Ennead **III. book 6. chapter 2. p. 305. A.** Aristides in the *Panathenaic Oration* **I. p. 342. p. 196:** "Students of wisdom look again and again into the soul of Athens—looking into her words as if into a mirror." <note>original: "ὥσπερ ἐν κατόπτρῳ τοῖς λόγοις ἐμβλέποντες"</note> Themistius in *Oration* **16. p. 410:** "I, for my part, O King, say that one ought to set forth that reason like a mirror every day, looking and gazing into it, not to arrange one's hair more becomingly, but rather the Roman Empire." (Which passage ought to be applied to the epigram of Phanias in the *Greek Anthology* **II. 53.** in the *Observations* of Jacobs **VIII. p. 169.** For mirrors are among the tools of the barber shop.) Just as Aristides and Themistius in the cited passages compare the decrees of wisdom to a mirror into which everyone ought to look, so the Apostles compare the teaching of the Gospel. Compare Lambert Bos in his *Exercises on Paul's Second Epistle to the Corinthians* III. **18.** who directs that the word *to reflect as in a mirror* <note>original: "κατοπτρίζεσθαι"</note> be understood there as *to look accurately and diligently, to consider uprightly*; while others, on the contrary, direct that this be compared with the same Apostle in I. Corinthians XIII. **12:** "For now we see through a mirror in riddles." <note>original: "βλέπομεν γὰρ ἄρτι δι’ ἐσόπτρου ἐν αἰνίγμασι"</note> (where the same Bos wishes *windowpanes* or *windows* to be understood, though Valckenaer doubts this in his *Lectures on the New Testament* Vol. **II. p. 311. ff.**) Furthermore, everyone will understand that the sentiment of this passage in Plotinus and the Pauline passage are in some way similar. Clement of Alexandria mentions the use of mirrors in the luxury of women, censuring it in *The Instructor* **III. p. 258. Potter edition:** "And the costly preparations of mirrors, by which they adorn themselves to hunt those who, like foolish children, are fluttered by outward forms." <note>original: "κατόπτρων τε πολυτίμητοι κατασκευαὶ..."</note> Moreover, Tertullian uses the comparison of a windowpane in *On the Soul* **chapter 53. p. 305. Rigalt edition:** "For if this body, in the Platonic view, is a prison, but in the Apostolic view is the temple of God when it is in Christ; yet in the meantime, it obstructs and stops up the soul with its enclosure, and stains it with the thickness of the flesh; whence to the soul, as if through a *window of horn*, the *light of things* is more dim," etc.

**p. 1129, 4.** **as it is written**] <note>original: "ὡς τὸ γεγραμμένον"</note> Thus I have written from the good manuscripts instead of "so that it is written." <note>original: "ὥστε γεγρ."</note> Furthermore, this discussion concerning the relationship between the mind and the soul etc. should be compared with the classic passage of our author on the fall and vicissitudes of souls, which appears above in **IV. 3. 12.**

-> BOOK III. ENNEAD SIX. pages 1129—1142. <-

**Becoming** <note>original: γένεσις</note>. Moreover, regarding the notion of *becoming* among the Platonic Philosophers, this is a classic passage, and those points in the preceding text must be especially kept in mind: "the nature concerning bodies—is not at all a true being because the concept of flowing things fits it, but is properly called *becoming*." And this force of *becoming* extends most widely through all the Enneads. **Compare** also Proclus in *On the Alcibiades* <note>a commentary on Plato's dialogue</note> **Preface I. 108:** "becoming and mortal nature." **Compare page 187 in the same work and page 257 following** and the same author's *Elements of Theology* **page 74, page 158, and page 308 following.**

**page 1133, 11.** **How should we speak** <note>original: Πῶς δὲ λέγωμεν</note>] Thus we have given this reading from the good manuscripts instead of "we speak" <note>original: λέγομεν</note>.

**page 1135, 5.** **and there seems to be a seat for the form—and a seat so that** <note>original: καὶ ἕδρα δοκεῖ τῷ εἴδει εἶναι—καὶ ἕδρα ὥστε</note>] Thus we have restored this passage from **most Manuscripts** and **Ficino** <note>Marsilio Ficino, the 15th-century translator of Plotinus</note>, which is full of gaps in the **Edition**. The word *base* or *pedestal* <note>original: ὑποβάθρα</note> also occurred in **VI. 1. 28. page 593. C.** Porphyry joins it with the word *foundation* <note>original: θεμέλιος</note> in his *Sentences* **Section 34. page 239.** **Compare** also Proclus's *Elements of Theology* **LXXI. page 112 of our edition**, where I have called upon Hesychius **II. 1467**, Suidas **III. 551**, and Zonaras **page 1772**, and additionally Dionysius the Areopagite in *On the Celestial Hierarchy* **chapter 5.**

**page 1136, 14.** **and from which indeed the others** <note>original: καὶ ἀφ’ ἧς δὲ τὰ ἄλλα</note>] Perhaps one should read "surely" <note>original: δὴ</note> instead of "and/but" <note>original: δὲ</note>.

**page 1141, 9.** **the clearer one** <note>original: ἡ δ’ ἐναργεστέρα</note>] I have adopted this reading from the margin of the edition alone instead of "the more active one" <note>original: ἡ δὲ ἐνεργεστέρα</note>. For first, "more active" and "clearer" are found confused with one another six hundred times; (**See** Upton and Schweighäuser on Arrian’s *Discourses of Epictetus* **III. 3. 4. page 620 following** and the latter on Polybius **I. 1. 2. page 117 following**): secondly, because of the opposite "dim" <note>original: ἀμυδρά</note>. I can cite many passages: let one suffice. Proclus in Plato’s *Alcibiades* **Preface I. page 2 of our edition:** "each thing participates in being more dimly or *more clearly*." Plotinus continues: "and of images, one is a sketch, the other a more finished execution." This meaning of the word **execution** <note>original: ἐξεργασίας</note> must be maintained regarding *images accurately expressed* and finished, the contrary of which is **sketch** <note>original: ὑποτύπωσις</note>, *an outlining, a beginning*. Above on **page 57. D.** our author says: "and do not cease carving your own statue," imitating Plato in the *Phaedrus* **page 252. d.**, a passage which Cicero also had before his eyes in *On the Laws* **I. 22. 59. page 142 of Moser’s edition.** And regarding the care of oneself and the cultivation of character and the refining of the soul, Arrian says in the *Discourses of Epictetus* **III. 13. 8. page 411 of Schweighäuser's edition:** "what things are for those who are oppressed; how these might be healed, how they might be removed. If anything requires *execution* <note>refining/finishing</note>, to execute it according to its own reason." Where *execution*, if I consider the passages of Plato and Plotinus, I would believe to be a term transferred from a craftsman finishing and polishing an image.

**page 1142, 16.** **for what kind of substances are these, etc.** <note>original: ποιαὶ γὰρ οὐσίαι αὗται. κ. τ. λ.</note>] Simplicius in Aristotle’s *Categories* **Folio 55. a:** "Plotinus asks, what then is **Quality** <note>original: ποιότης</note> that it provides the so-called 'qualified things'? For it has been said that qualified things are so named according to quality. But what this quality is according to its own definition has not been determined. To which Porphyry says, that the definition concerning quality is **conceptual** <note>original: ἐννοηματικός</note>, but not **essential** <note>original: οὐσιώδης</note>. A conceptual definition is one taken from things known to all and commonly agreed upon by all, such as: 'the good is that from which it happens that one is benefited.' 'The soul is that from which living exists.' 'Voice is the specific object of hearing.' But essential definitions are those which also teach the very essence of the things being defined, such as: 'the good is virtue, or that which participates in virtue.' 'The soul is a self-moving substance.' 'Voice is struck air.' And while conceptual definitions, being commonly agreed upon by all, are the same; essential definitions, proceeding according to specific schools of thought, are disputed by those of different opinions. For instance, the ancients do not agree with those who say voice is air and a body, defining it instead as an incorporeal activity and a striking. And those who place the good in virtue and the beautiful alone are disputed by those who extend it through all things. It has been decided, therefore, in the first introductions, to use definitions agreed upon by all. For these are better known and more suitable for a first hearing. But the other kind requires 'first philosophy' <note>metaphysics</note>, which contemplates beings as beings. Therefore, Aristotle gave the essential definition of quality in the *Metaphysics*, but the conceptual one here. And these things are well said. But there is a better explanation which says: if quality existed by itself, one would have to seek what it is that is participated in; but if it is in us and does not stand outside of qualified things, it is clear that its being is not one thing and its being participated in another... for quality is the **form** <note>original: εἶδος</note> of the thing that possesses it. He, therefore, who defines quality through the qualified thing, characterizes its most authoritative property, and presents at once what it is and what kind of **finished product** <note>original: ἀπεργασίαν</note> it provides among beings."

# ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS

**p. 1143, 15.** **painting** <note>original: ζωγραφία</note>] Compare Plato's *Statesman* **p. 277, p. 289 and following, Bekker edition.**

**p. 1144, 1.** **And concerning what is called substance, etc.** <note>original: Καὶ περὶ μὲν τῆς λεγομένης οὐσίας κ. τ. λ.</note>] These remarks by Simplicius in his commentary on Aristotle’s *Categories* (**69. a**) seem relevant here: "As many of these things as are not classified by quantity, but by character and quality—whether they are classified in another species besides the aforementioned types of quality, as both Andronicus and Plotinus suppose, or whether it is possible to bring them under one of the four [categories]; this will be clear if it is understood what gravity and levity themselves are. For if heat, by expanding bodies, makes them light like itself, and cold, by contracting them, makes them heavy like itself, then these will be reduced to 'passive qualities' <note>A technical term in Aristotelian physics for qualities that cause a sensation or result from a physical change.</note>. But if levity follows heat, and gravity follows cold, and heat and cold are 'active,' while the heavy and light are by nature neither acting nor being acted upon, then the former will seem to be reduced to passive qualities, but the latter to some other distinct genus. And if they belong to the elements by their very substance, they will not even seem to be qualities. But if that which has received them is 'qualified,' and is called 'qualified,' and if from the substantial difference there arises in the participating bodies a certain formative character, then these too would be qualities."

— **13.** **elements—but as for fire, etc.** <note>original: στοιχεῖα—τὸ δὲ τὸ πῦρ κ. τ. λ.</note>] John Philoponus in *Against Proclus*: "And as it were, a fire behaving insolently through excess, and not the elemental and vital fire. But he says the fire there [in the heavens] is even and calm, fitting the nature of the stars, and pleasantly warm—for the most pure and unmixed portion of the elements was set apart for the composition of the heavenly body. Thus, the nature of the heavenly body is neither alien nor foreign to the elements found among us, nor is the fire or earth or any other thing there exactly the same as here. Rather, among us, the dregs and, as it were, the sediment of the elements flow down; but there, the most refined and better part of them is separated out. Since even in other living beings, says Plotinus, and especially in the most sovereign of them, nature selects the better parts. One could cite many other testimonies confirming this present opinion of Plato. For Aristotle, Plato's own student, is acknowledged among us as testifying to these things, even while he finds fault with Plato for this very reason. For Aristotle seems to be the first of all to have introduced the doctrine of the 'fifth body' <note>The aether, or quintessence, which Aristotle argued made up the heavens, distinct from the four earthly elements.</note>. But I think that for those of good will, even what has been said is sufficient for full persuasion; and let us not extend the discourse on this matter further than is necessary."

**p. 1146, 19.** **we called more material and organic** <note>original: ὑλικάτερα εἴπομεν καὶ ὀργανικὰ</note>] Compare **chapter IX. A:** "more material things are fire, earth, water, air; while organic things are the bodies of plants and animals." Regarding the Platonic and Stoic reasoning by which the soul <note>Latin: anima</note> of God is an instrument <note>Latin: organon</note>: the body is called the instrument of the soul. And the whole human being is found to be an instrument." Compare Olympiodorus on the *Alcibiades*, **preface XXIV. p. 202 and following**, and the annotations there. Aristotle uses the adjective in the *Nicomachean Ethics* **III. 1. 6. p. 110, Zell edition:** "to move the organic parts." Especially relevant is another passage of the Stagirite <note>Aristotle, who was from Stagira.</note>, *On the Soul* **II. 1. p. 22 and following, Sylburg edition:** "Therefore the soul is the first entelechy <note>The realization or complete expression of a potential.</note> of a natural body having life in potentiality; and such a body is one that is organic. Even the parts of plants are instruments <note>Greek: organa</note>, but entirely simple ones; for example, the leaf is a covering for the pericarp, and the pericarp for the fruit. The roots are analogous to the mouth; for both draw in nourishment." No one fails to understand that Plotinus had this and similar passages before his eyes.

**p. 1147, 6.** **Concerning quantity and quality, etc.** <note>original: Περὶ δὲ ποσοῦ καὶ ποιότητος κ. τ. λ.</note>] Regarding the words of Aristotle, "quantity does not admit of the 'more' and the 'less'" (things that are quantities cannot be said to be 'more' quantities or 'less' quantities), after Simplicius (in *Categories* **Fol. 38. a.**) approved this opinion, he proceeds as follows: "I think the reason quantity does not admit of the more and the less is that other things are defined and measured according to quantity; if, therefore, quantity becomes the definition of other things, how could it itself partake of the indefiniteness of the more and the less? But if we speak of a magnitude greater than another magnitude, and a number more than another number, we observe much of the 'more' and 'less' in this. For Caucasus is more 'greater' than Hymettus than Athos is, and seven is more 'more' than three than five is; we shall say the 'more' and 'less' belongs to them in respect to relation. But if Caucasus is more 'greater,' and Athos 'less,' and Hymettus still 'less,' according to the indefinite, one might concede that quantity also admits of the..."

# BOOK III. ENNEAD SIX. pages 1143—1150.

-> <note>original: "μᾶλλον καὶ τὸ ἧττον..."</note> <-

...the more and the less, just as there is also contrariety. For that which is called "great" not in relation to something else, but in itself, is the opposite of that which is called "small" in itself; and this is how **Andronicus** <note>Andronicus of Rhodes, a 1st-century BCE philosopher who organized Aristotle's works</note> arranges it. But **Plotinus** says that the "great" is not a relative term at all, but that we often loosely use the word "great" instead of "greater." The same author in the same place, **Leaf 36. b:** Perhaps, says **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who often critiqued Plotinus</note> following Andronicus, the great and small, and the many and few, are not only relative, but also an indefinite quantity. For when we say "great," we indicate an indefinite quantity; for it is not indicated by how much or by what magnitude it is great, or by what multitude it is many. But when we say "greater" and "smaller," it is viewed according to their relation to one another. **Aristotle**, however, viewed the great and the small only according to the relative, just as Plotinus viewed them only according to the simple \* quantity (\* <gloss>quantity</gloss>). For he says that the relative "great" is spoken of instead of "greater." And a little lower, when he explains the opinion of Iamblichus:—The divine Iamblichus wishes that the "great" and "small," and "many" and "few" in themselves, be viewed in the self-existent and immaterial forms, some according to the excellence of power, and others according to the multitude of pure reasons <note>Logoi: formative principles</note>. But the relatives, which are spoken of by comparison, he sees in material things, in which there is also the more and less, and opposites existing together according to the reference to one thing and then another. For when the Form approaches Matter, a certain power is produced from both combined. Insofar as it participates in the Form, it is made like it, and the immaterial becomes "many" and "great." But according to its own infinity, it participates in the more and less, and in the relative disposition, and in the change toward opposites. Therefore, he says (**Iamblichus**, speaking against Plotinus regarding the definition of the great) that since this is the case, those who think all these things are spoken of simply, like Plotinus, do not understand correctly. For even common usage often employs them as relatives, and those who call a millet seed "great" do so by comparison to those of the same kind, as indicating the "greater," and they speak according to the relative; but magnitude, says Plotinus, is not among the relatives, but the "greater" is, just as is the "double." Or is it not so? For the concept of magnitude extends both to magnitudes in themselves and to those in relation to one another. For it would not be called "greater" if it did not participate in magnitude, and thus indicate the excellence according to magnitude. But many say, etc. Simplicius then proceeds to the opinions of others and does not return to Plotinus.

So Bekker edited it from the conjecture of Sydenham and the judgment of Heindorf, who calls it indubitable: "I do not know if *of humans* is better," Bekker adds in his critical commentaries. But all the Manuscripts of Plato agree on *to another race*: and indeed, that Plotinus read it thus in his copy of Plato is proved by his own words, since he cites these from memory: *to a different race*. Similarly, the same confirms the reading of most manuscripts of Plato, *to compare* <note>original: "συμβάλλειν"</note> instead of *to have compared*.—This serves as an argument that Plotinus may be compared with Plato not without use for facilitating criticism, to say nothing now of interpretation. Perhaps they will say that virtue, being a science, has stability from itself. For being a contemplation of its own internal principles, and always aiming to do everything according to itself, it acts firmly standing in the unchanging form of science. But how is this possible in the case of quality, which is a changeable and passive substance, and especially according to them, having expansion and contraction to infinity within itself and within virtue? This is because they say that even qualities are bodies. Perhaps, then, they transfer what was said by the ancients about other principles to different principles—unless, by placing the virtuous state at the highest point and not viewing it in motion, they reasonably thought it right to see neither intensity nor remission in it. But if this is true of each of the arts, there is a certain 'highest point' which itself stands still. For in everything that has 'more' and 'less,' there is certainly also a 'most.' And perhaps according to this notion, the opinion which Aristotle mentions—taking perfect states not only in virtue but also in health and grammar and other dispositions—says that they are without intensity or remission, viewing intensity and remission in those who participate in the states 'more' or 'less' rather than in the states themselves. And yet one can see this in the states themselves, not only in the arts but also in the virtues. For of the virtues, some are perfect and others imperfect. Imperfect are those by nature alone, or by habit, or by reason; perfect are those completed by these three together—unless virtue itself is perfect and whole, but is participated in partially, just as grammar and each of the other arts is viewed as 'more' or 'less' in its participation due to incompleteness. But what kind of dispositions does Aristotle see as perfect beyond those possessed? Does he mean the separate Forms, and Justice-itself? Neither is this usual for him, nor suitable to the present subject, nor would those be called 'dispositions.' Rather, having seen the perfected states that are participated in, he wishes those falling short of them to have the 'more' and the 'less' by reference to those perfect ones. And this account is more accurate in all dispositions, viewing the perfect according to their peak, and the 'more' and 'less' according to the breadth of participation. Of the others, the Stoic view seems incomplete, seeing neither the incompleteness of the virtues nor the perfection of the other arts. For if virtue were viewed in reason alone, the one who possesses reason and science would not be 'intensified.' For true reason is one. And one true reason is not 'more' than another true reason. But if the one possessing the science falls short in practice or nature, he would be less just; so that if the perfect state is not composed of theorems alone, but also of nature and habit, one man would be more just than another. And in this case, the reason is one and the same, being filled by the theorems; but the practice, according to which the imperfect grammarian..."

# BOOK III. ENNEAD SIX. p. 1152—1156.

-> Centered: On the nature of participation and quality <-

It is observed that the "more" and the "less" <note>The degrees of intensity in a quality</note> are produced by the different ways in which the same rational principle <term>logos: the formative principle or "reason-rule" that gives shape to matter</term> is participated in. In the same way, the rational principle of whiteness is one. Yet snow is said to be whiter than milk because of the lack of admixture in the white; for wherever there is a mixture of matter, it is necessary to participate in that which is not of such a kind, and thus "tension" <note>original: *epitasis*, meaning intensification</note> and "relaxation" <note>original: *anesis*, meaning weakening</note> occur. 

But how, he asks, can something become whiter if it was not previously white, or more grammatical if it is not yet a grammarian? Indeed, one who does not possess the skill is not called a grammarian, though he may be progressing and drawing closer to grammar; likewise with the white object. And when we say this thing is greater than that, neither is "great" in an absolute sense. For the "absolutely great" is one, and it is the greatest; and absolute grammar is one, and supreme virtue is one. 

But the difficulty must be resolved by saying that **comparisons** are made by reference to the **perfect** <note>The ideal or complete form of a quality</note>. If things are spoken of in this way, it is a wonder if this perfect quality can be "enmattered" <term>ennylos: existing within physical matter</term>. For that which is perfect and stands fixed in the same way would belong to another nature, not the enmattered one. 

Furthermore, Iamblichus <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher who often critiqued Plotinus</note> says it is even more absurd if quality is enmattered, yet does not suffer the same effects as the enmattered subjects that receive it. For in this way, it becomes almost "separate" if it has certain activities of its own that are distinct from the whole. He also calls it absurd if quality is always joined with the "qualified" object—as if having a nature twin and indistinguishable from it—yet is separated from the whole again, such that the quality itself does not intensify, but the qualified objects do. 

Perhaps then, he says, in all these cases they were referring to **immaterial principles** <term>auloi logoi: formative rules that exist without physical matter</term>. For even regarding the virtues, those who allow for "progress" but deny "perfection" among men were unknowingly assuming that the perfect states are immaterial <insert>the perfect ones</insert>, and for this reason, they denied these to enmattered things. If this is so, the opinion falls away into an entirely different nature. For the nature of "quality" did not belong to immaterial things. 

Iamblichus wrote these things in these very words. But perhaps by this reasoning, it is necessary to place the "more" and "less" even upon **Substance** <note>original: *ousia*, the fundamental being of a thing</note>. For substance itself is also enmattered. But the perfect and fixed would belong to another nature, and quantity likewise, and the definite itself, and all qualities. 

However, I think one <insert>must</insert> take the "more" and "less" not according to the enmattered state, but according to what is adventitious <note>added from the outside</note> and less essential. For substance, when viewed according to its very being, does not admit the "more" and "less." But quality, subsisting according to its participation in substance, reasonably admits this. For it is "more" in those things that are less essential, and "less" in those that are more essential, as in the case of geometric shapes. And quantity, being closer to substance, does not admit the "more" and "less." 

But neither do qualities, when viewed according to their own peak perfection—such as perfect virtue and perfect grammar—admit the "more" and "less." For these are viewed according to the "most." And these perfections are not immaterial and separate principles, but are enmattered, yet viewed according to the **Form** itself. It is by looking at this that we define each enmattered thing, looking not at the matter, but at the Form. 

And if no enmattered thing ever happens to reach its own perfection, it is well to say that the "more" and "less" exist in all things. But if this is absurd, then there is also a "most," and thus our opinion of Plotinus will be corrected—taking it as referring only to the enmattered and generated, but not to the specific characteristic of quality, by which it differs from substance. 

But Iamblichus, meeting the opinion of Plotinus—which holds that qualities and qualified things change equally in their intensifications and relaxations—says it is absurd for the rational principle <note>the *logos*</note> to be altered by the same turnings as the composite object. For how will the "participated" differ from the "participants"? At the same time, his general axiom concerning incorporeal things—that they are impassive and unchangeable—would be overturned. 

Having said these things against Plotinus, he introduces the truest contemplation of the doctrine: for he says that an **incorporeal essence** of the rational principles exists, giving itself to those that receive it. While producing the "qualified" state in the body, it nonetheless remains incorporeal by itself within the body, having its being by itself and imparting existence to the body without losing its own nature. 

Hence, the "shape" <note>original: *morphoma*</note> imprinted from it is capable of receiving intensification; but the incorporeal essence of the quality stands fixed in the same Form. It does not become immaterial because of this, but remains enmattered—yet it does not belong to the matter as a whole, because Forms belong to themselves and are strictly defined according to the "one and the same." Therefore, even in becoming part of matter, they do not depart entirely from their own whole nature; but remaining in it, they are in a certain way filled with the contrary extension and indefiniteness of the matter. 

Finally, Iamblichus, correcting the last sect—which thinks that intelligible qualities are incapable of intensification, while enmattered ones participate in intensification and relaxation—cites that saying of Porphyry: that all intelligible things, and those which truly are, are substances, and...

<meta>This page continues the critical commentary on Plotinus, specifically focusing on the categorization of qualities (qualitas) and how they differ from substances or activities. It engages heavily with the Neoplatonic commentator Simplicius.</meta>

# ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS

For this reason, they do not admit of "the more and the less" <note>A technical logical phrase: essential properties either exist or they don't; they don't have degrees of intensity like "whiteness" might.</note>. But he says it is possible to argue against this, that even in the realm of the intelligible <note>The higher reality of forms/ideas</note>, the order of the definition of quality is preserved, even if everything there exists according to substance. For according to this reasoning, rest and motion are observed around substance, preserving—as is the case in the intelligibles—the definition of an activity that exists in another and around another. But generally, the present discussion is not about the intelligibles. These things, then, have been sufficiently stated.

**p. 1156, 10. And indeed Plato says that music etc.**] See the speech of Eryximachus in the *Symposium* **p. 186. end and p. 187. a. and p. 188. b. p. 397. and 399. in Bekker’s edition.**

**p. 1157, 13. a division must be made between those of the soul and those of the body**] Simplicius in the **place cited, p. 69. b:** Plotinus, then, makes a division by calling some qualities those of the body and others those of the soul, not actually making a division of "quality" itself according to its truth, but merely showing a distinction between the things in which the quality exists; but this does not show a difference in the quality itself. Therefore, Aristotle also, in speaking of "affective qualities," <note>Qualities that produce a sensation or arise from an affection, like heat or sweetness.</note> some of the soul and some of the body, did not go outside the genus of quality, but remained within the same one. He knew well that while the reception of forms varies and creates a difference in the "place" where they reside, it creates no difference in the inherent form or character itself. 

Again, Plotinus divides the qualities of the body according to the senses, falling into the same absurdity; and furthermore, Iamblichus says he "minces" the unity into things that are numerically different rather than different in kind. For the "sensible" as a sensible thing is one kind, even if one takes it as a specific sensible object linked to each sense; he distinguishes them only by number. Aristotle also shows this. For by arranging the affective qualities as sensibles in relation to perception, he referred them generally to all the senses; he did not add those linked to each specific sense, as they do not create a difference in kind, but differ only in number. 

It is worth considering, however, whether the senses themselves do not differ from one another in kind, as well as the specific objects of those senses, which Plotinus attempted to show as a difference in kind derived from the senses. For such a difference is not merely numerical, being divided into individuals like "this visible thing" and "that visible thing." If Aristotle did not divide it down to this point, it is no wonder, as he was leading the argument only as far as the first division of the highest genera into species—which is what Plotinus should have observed while making a division of the highest genera. 

Plotinus also separated the qualities of the soul according to the parts of the soul. And yet, it is possible for the same quality to be in several parts, such as "tractability" <note>original: εὐήνιον</note> and "hardness." And many qualities can be in one part when it is multi-functional, just as in the rational part there are many sciences, differing in kind. After this, he divides the many qualities of the reasoning faculty according to the sciences and arts, falling away into the most extreme details and not remaining within Aristotle’s grouping of these things, according to whom they become a genus of "habit" <note>term: habit (hexis) — a stable disposition or learned quality like knowledge.</note>. Nor does he realize that the current goal is not to carry the division of genera to the very end, but to provide only the most general types and those closely related to them. Thus, even when he adds the powers in the desiring part of the soul, we should not accept a progression of division to such an extent. For this is an enumeration of the extremes, not a division of the primary genera. 

In general, every division ought to happen according to the unique nature of each thing. Division by parts is appropriate for quantity. For this is divisible even in composite things, or in incorporeal things that have a certain decline in their substance—for this is not foreign to them. But when someone divides a quality not as a quality—that is, as a whole present everywhere insofar as it is a "quality," being the same in both small and large things and in whatever parts, like the sweetness of honey in any volume of honey—he does not make the division correctly; for he does not attempt to cut it where its nature allows. 

But perhaps even this is not true: that every quality has pervaded the whole of the qualified object, since the fourth species of quality was observed in respect to the surface; and if a triangle and each of the other such figures has lines and angles, the whole is not present everywhere. For all the lines are not in the same place, nor are the angles together with the lines. Furthermore, the same quality, such as temperance or blackness, is not present in both soul and body. There is, therefore, nothing absurd in dividing qualities into mental and bodily according to this. But to judge different qualities from different activities when they occur according to them, is to transfer matters concerning "powers" into "qualities." For powers, being invisible, are recognized from the activities they bring about. But qualities display visible "sorts" through the resulting "qualified things" which are different. And these according to the most sovereign...

# BOOK III. ENNEAD SIX. pages 1156—1162.

-> <note>The following is a Greek commentary on Plotinus's theories of quality and relation.</note> <-

...the genera will be distinguished. But here too we must observe that qualities also possess powers, and it is not at all strange that powers are discerned from activities, and existences from powers. However, when Plotinus divides psychic and bodily qualities by the "beneficial" and the "harmful," and again divides benefits and harms as if they were proper differences of quality—believing that all benefit and harm proceed from quality—he does not make the division appropriately here either, because he shifts from the "qualified" <term>poion; a thing with a certain quality</term> to "relatives" <term>pros ti; things defined by their relation to something else</term>. For honey, being the same in its quality, is beneficial to one person but harmful to another. And perfume is pleasant and beneficial to most, but to beetles it is harmful and deadly; thus, the beneficial and the harmful are not qualities, but relatives. Furthermore, why do benefits and harms provide differences of quality any more than they do of substance or of acting? For benefits and harms are observed in these as well. That quantity also, when aptly fitted to a power—and again when not fitted—becomes the cause of much benefit or harm, is shown by the art of the Asclepiads <note>The descendants of Asclepius; i.e., physicians</note> and the instructions they give regarding the symmetry of quantity. In addition to this, if qualities acted and provided "qualified things" through their activity, one could say they themselves benefit or harm. But if they produce results merely by being possessed, they impart no harm or benefit from themselves insofar as they are qualities. In general, all such divisions are inappropriate, as they are divided according to relation rather than according to what they are as qualities. After the great Plotinus, we must also consider the division Aristotle sets forth elsewhere, etc.

**p. 1157, 14.** **as being of the body**] <note>original: "ὡς σώματος οὖσας"</note> "*As if they belong to the body.*" Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino, the famous Renaissance translator of Plotinus</note> did not express these words; however, they appear in all our manuscripts.

**p. 1159, 13.** **but because sensation is different, etc.**] <note>original: "ἀλλὰ γὰρ ὅτι ἕτερα ἡ αἴσθησις"</note> Compare above **p. 491. B. and p. 499. A.B. ch. 3.** John Philoponus <note>A 6th-century Christian philosopher and commentator</note> had these passages before his eyes in his commentary on Aristotle’s *Prior Analytics*, leaf **III:** "But the intellect and sensation do not reason. The intellect does not, as it is superior to reasoning. Wherefore the divine Plotinus says of it: that it either touches [the truth] or it does not. And it is entirely infallible. For it either touches it, knowing things by simple intuitions, or it does not touch the principle at all, and is likewise infallible in both cases. Sensation, however, being inferior to reasoning, does not reason. Nor does the imagination reason, etc."

**p. 1161, 19.** **And what of privations? [And what of privations] if those things of which they are privations are qualities, then they themselves are qualities**] I have included these words in brackets; **Ficino** did not express them. Furthermore, following several manuscripts, I have given *autai* <note>feminine "they"</note> instead of the *auta* <note>neuter "they"</note> of the printed edition. In the Latin, however, I used *forte* <note>perhaps</note> from the first edition instead of *si forte* <note>if perhaps</note>. The examples that follow, such as "toothless" <note>original: "νωδὸς"</note> or "blind" <note>original: "τυφλὸς"</note>, like many others, were employed by Aristotle himself. Thus, to use this example, the Stagirite <note>Aristotle</note> says in the *Categories* **VIII. 9:** "For we call 'toothless' not that which simply lacks teeth, and 'blind' not that which lacks sight, but that which does not have them at a time when it is natural to have them; for some things from birth have neither sight nor teeth." Compare ibid. **§. 17.** and Ammonius **p. 131. b.** Archytas used these terms in another sense according to Simplicius in his commentary on these passages of the *Categories*; and "toothless" <note>nōdos</note>, from *ne* and *audē* <note>voice</note>, is often the same as "voiceless," and likewise "stupefied." In both meanings, writers not infrequently join the toothless and the astonished or mute with the blind (*typhlos*); their passages were collected by Sallier and Tib. Hemsterhuis in their notes on Thomas Magister **p. 635—637.** and Ruhnken on Timaeus's *Platonic Lexicon* **p. 102.**

**p. 1162, 11.** **to grow red**] <note>original: "ἐρυθαίνεσθαι"</note> So all our manuscripts, and only two a little further down have "he turns red" <note>erythrainetai</note>; the rest have "he grows red" <note>erythainetai</note>. For this reason, I did not wish to change this form, which they call poetic, for the form *erythrainesthai*; it is possible that a softer pronunciation later introduced this writing habit. Kiessling, in Iamblichus's *Protrepticus* **XXI. p. 316.** by conjecture placed *Erythrinon* for *Erythinon*; but the Royal Codex and the Memmian manuscript persist in this reading. Compare other forms of this kind in Lobeck’s *Parerga* **V. on Phrynichus p. 727 sq.** In Plato’s *Lysis* we read **p. 204. b. p. 110. Bekk.:** "and he, having grown red, blushed." Ficino translates: *he fell silent, he answered nothing*. Moreover, this itself pertains to the Aristotelian examples in the *Categories* **VI. 12:** "For neither is he who blushes because of shame called 'red-faced,' nor he who turns pale because of fear called 'pale-faced.'" But that entire passage should be compared with ours.
— **16.** **One must see if there is not some other contrary to every quality.**] Simplicius on Aristotle’s *Categories* **p. 71. b:** "But why are intermediate things neither contraries to each other, nor to the extremes? Because then there would be contraries to many things, and it would no longer be one thing contrary to one, if the intermediates were also contraries. But Plotinus wonders whether there is not a contrariety to every quality. For even the mean is contrary to the extremes; for virtue, being a mean according to Aristotle, is contrary to the ex—"

-> ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS <-

[Greek text begins:] ...by excesses and deficiencies, which are vices. It must be said in response to this that quality is conceived in one way as a mean, and in another as a virtue. According to the mean, it no longer possesses opposition; but according to virtue, it does. Furthermore, we consider the mean as equality, and excess and deficiency as inequality. Whenever, therefore, we say that equality is opposite to excess and deficiency, we mean nothing else than that equality is opposed to inequality, and so it happens in other cases, but the opposition does not occur in the mean itself. But regarding colors, one might say, the opposition of the extremes to the middle does not occur in this way; for gray is opposed to white either according to the mixture of white inherent in it, or according to the mixture of black inherent in it. But if it is according to the mixture of white, white would be opposed to white, which is impossible; if according to black, black is opposed to white, not some third different mixture. While the conclusion is true—that gray is not opposed to white or black as a contrary—the method of approach admits many objections. For it makes the middle a composite of the extremes, as consisting of both, but not as something unique apart from the extremes. It preserves the simple elements in the mixture in actuality (*energeia*) but not in potentiality (*dynamis*), if indeed even this is possible. For perhaps the intermediate colors do not subsist from the extremes being mixed at all; rather, there are certain prior principles (*logoi*) of these, just as there are of the extremes, not subsisting according to mixture, but possessing a simple and self-originated otherness and variety, engendering it in sensible things, and ordered with the other principles according to the same equal arrangement. And if one says the middle has its subsistence from the extremes, it might not even be a mixture that produces the intermediates, but a juxtaposition of the extremes, or an overlapping, or a distance from afar. For according to all these, as in the treatise *On Sense and Sensible Objects*, the intermediate colors seem to subsist. Plotinus, however, says that if the intermediates were produced according to the composition of the extremes, one ought not to distinguish them by saying "either white, or black, or gray, or yellow," or any such thing, but only divide them into white and black, and call the others compositions. But as it is, we distinguish and oppose them, because even if there is a mixture of extremes, it is not a juxtaposition, but a tempering (*krasis*) which produces another quality from the temperament. Therefore, by the fact that some other quality has arisen among the intermediates, even if it is viewed as a composition, we oppose it thus. Saying these things, those after him concede that the intermediate quality of color has become something else; but they no longer agree that it is viewed as "another" arising from temperament or composition. For he says this is not the manner of the essence of incorporeal qualities; rather, incorporeal things being mixed, or tempered, or composed, are able to produce different bodies. For the composite and mixed genus, in which the nature is contained, becomes different from itself by being altered according to this. But that which has its being neither in temperament nor in composition, having pre-received a certain simple incorporeal essence according to a single quality, this being utterly different, would not be affected by temperament or composition, just as the indivisible is not affected by the divisible. But since he said white is contrary to black, but nothing is contrary to red and yellow, it would be worthwhile, having proceeded a little, to examine the definition of contraries and what correctness it possesses. For from this we shall learn both the theorems concerning contraries and those now mentioned concerning colors, if they have been stated correctly. Contraries are said to be those things which are most distant from each other under the same genus, such as black and white. For these are unmixed with each other; but gray and yellow and red and such things are not most distant, because they are mixed with each other. Plotinus asks: from whence are contraries so defined? For if from the intermediates and the distance toward them, you do not make the opposition toward the extremes, nor the distance, but toward the intermediates; and how will you call the *immediate* [Note: *amesa* in margin] things contraries, such as health and disease? But if you take the distance according to the form itself, when they have nothing identical in species, being in one genus, say, "Quality," why shall yellow not be contrary to white, having no proximity to white, as gray seems to have? Opposing these things, they will say that the extremes do not admit of the "greatest distance" derived from the intermediates. For contraries do not make their distance from each other through some journey, nor do they thus establish themselves in the contrary region by overstepping the middle, but the distance is according to their principles (*logoi*) and species (*eide*). One must attend, therefore, to the properties, whether some are such as to annihilate each other, while others show some proximity of nature toward one of the contraries, or some appearance of the extremes, or a remission of the one and an intensity of the other, or some other such mediation. For those that are so are separated individually, the extremes in one way, and the intermediates in another. And the intermediates do not lead the way, so that the extremes take their distance around them. But on the contrary...

[[Vocabulary: μεσότης (mesotes - mean), ἐναντίωσις (enantiosis - opposition), κρᾶσις (krasis - mixture), ἀσώματος (asomatos - incorporeal).]]

[Greek text continues:] ...the extremes are more authoritative than the intermediates regarding distance, and the intermediates receive their definition from the extremes, and the things between from the contraries, either by comparison, or by appearance and similarity, or by juxtaposition, or by another way. And if the generation proceeds according to change, it would be possible to say that the contraries, advancing through the middle, distance themselves from one another. But if neither change nor generation is considered, but the extremes are primary in themselves, and not produced through a movement through the intermediates, they would not take their distance from the intermediates, so that they would not even take their being from them; rather, much more so according to the form itself and its otherness, they have received their distance, whenever the wholes appear differing from the wholes. But will yellow be contrary to white according to this definition, or is it not so? For yellow has a certain proximity to white, as Plato also confesses in the *Timaeus*, and Aristotle in *On Sense and Sensible Objects*; for both produce the subsistence of yellow around the white as something kindred, using different ways of derivation, but agreeing in this one point: that yellow possesses a certain adjacent appearance toward white. One might be easily persuaded of this also from sensation. For we are not similarly disposed when placing white and yellow side by side as we are with white and black. For viewing yellow alongside white, we do not fall entirely into a contrary sensation, as if being separated and combined regarding the others. In this way, also, immediate things will be contraries, having nothing identical in species, even if there are no intermediates between them that fluctuate between both. For it will have its opposition not from the intermediates, but from the property of the wholes. But the intermediates will not be contraries, because they possess something common, and they manifest both contraries to themselves equally. But to say that if yellow is not contrary to white and black, it will be contrary to something else, is entirely absurd; for that which consists in a mixture or appearance of contraries, and has not stood apart by the greatest distance from anything, how could it be contrary to anything? But these things would have been more appropriately stated in what follows, where the teaching on contraries is primary. Yet even now it has some relevance for those struggling against the arguments stated by Aristotle.

...expressed, which he thinks should be added in the margin of Medic. A.: **καὶ ἡ διάκρισις αὖ** ("and the separation again"). The books [manuscripts], however, do not support it; and in partitions of this kind, Plotinus sometimes omits even those things which seem to belong necessarily to the equality of the members.

**p. 1172, 13. κατὰ τὸ ποσὸν]** Thus I have corrected from the Ciz. MS. Ficino conjectured and expressed **τὸ ποιὸν**, "of quality": now put **quantitatis** (of quantity). The edition has **κατὰ τόπον** (according to place).

**p. 1173, 4. μανὸν δὲ αὖ ἠλλοίωται]** Simplicius in Aristot. *Categg.* p. 68. b: "But those around Nicostratus strive to show that both porosity and density are qualities, citing fire as being porous, and air; but earth as dense, not according to position, but according to quality. It must be said to them, as also in these matters according to the divine Iamblichus, each of these signifies two things: both position of parts and quality. Position, as in the case of weavings; quality, as in the case of air. It was not necessary to distinguish these in an introduction; for one thing is 'porous,' whose parts are distant from one another, not because there is a vacuum between, but because there is a different, thinner body. Air, however, is not porous by its parts being distant from one another, but by being light and easily divided. Therefore, it would be among such things according to quality, but not those according to position. Iamblichus says that against such a 'porous' thing we shall oppose not the 'dense,' but the 'solid,' to which belongs being difficult to divide and heavy. And such a thing will be according to quality; but that which is according to position will be reduced to 'relation.' It is worthwhile to consider which meaning of 'solid' is opposed to the 'porous.' For if it is the three-dimensionally extended, the surface and the line are opposed to this; if it is the 'strong,' the 'decayed' would be opposed to it; if the 'hard to divide,' if it possesses this through hardness, the 'soft' is opposed to it. If through density, the 'rare'; and the 'dense' would properly be opposed to the 'porous,' not the 'solid.' Plotinus, however, does not think one should hear two meanings of porosity and density—one reduced to 'relation,' the other to 'quality'—but sees only quality. For the porous and the dense are not in intervals. And if someone should concede this, he says even the interval is a quality. To which it must be said that one ought not to confuse this duality of nature. For it is the part of a philosopher to account for the differences even in those things that share commonalities. But they say one must not, by blaming the interval, reduce it to another category. For the essence is united and one. But it was said earlier that Aristotle does not blame the first and elementary positions of the parts, but those already circumscribed in composites, which, being excluded by thinner bodies, escape sensation as to how they possess that which is united in interval."

**— 11. οὕτω γὰρ ἄν τις καὶ κενὸν παραδέχοιτο κ. τ. λ.]** Simplicius *l. c.* Fol. 109. b: "They seek also in generation and corruption what rests (*eremias*) should be opposed to them, and they say for generation, that of *not being*. Thus also for growth, the rest according to the imperfect is opposed; for decrease, the rest according to the perfect. But Plotinus remarks that rest (*eremia*) is the negation of being moved. Because rest is not in another genus. Then having asked, 'Why is motion not also a negation of standing still?' he says because it is motion that carries there, and because motion is an act, and there is something else acting and as it were pushing the substrate, and working a myriad of things upon it and destroying it; but the rest of each thing is nothing other than itself. It signifies only that it does not have motion. But in the case of the intelligibles, he says, the manner is not the same for the one not to annihilate the other, but for both to be together, both motion and standing still." Thus far concerning Plotinus. Thence he passes to the opinions of other philosophers, nor does he return to refute the opinion of Plotinus, as is otherwise Simplicius's custom.

...first, is also in two of our MSS books. As for the fact that a scribe or some other learned reader added a warning in Cod. Marc. **p. 1185, 10. ἢ ὅλου πανταχοῦ]** Ficino expressed the Medicean reading **εἰ ὅλου πανταχοῦ**. But the same meaning arises if you mentally repeat **ἐφ’** for **ὅλου** from the nearest words.

**— 16. ἐὰν γὰρ ἐόντι πελάζει]** These are read in the *Fragments of Parmenides* v. 86: "all is full of being; wherefore all is continuous, for being draws near to being." To which words Brandis in *Commentt. Eleatt.* p. 115. cited other places, and this very one of ours. For the argument of our place, employ these Plotinian passages: p. 364. D. p. 385. sq. and p. 475. ...these words: *as Parmenides says,* Taylor in his version placed these in brackets: *as Parmenides says:* adding: “The words, **ὡς ὁ Παρμενίδης φησὶ**, are omitted in the original, but ought to be inserted, as is evident from the verses of Parmenides cited by Simplicius in his Commentary on the first book of Aristotle’s Physics.
