**p. 1187, 11. πρὸς ὄγκον]** Thus I corrected from the good books (for **ὄγκου**): *to non-bulk, or to that which is not bulk.*

**p. 1188, 4. τί γὰρ διαφέρει; ἢ καὶ ταῖς προσθήκαις.]** Cf. Cudworth. *System. intell.* p. 1015.

**p. 1189, 6. οὐκ ἄμοιρον τοῦ αὐτοῦ πολλαχῇ κείμενον.]** “For **κείμενον** (lying) here, it is necessary to read **κειμένου**, conformably to the version of Plotinus.” *Taylor.* Ficino expressed **κειμένων**, but the books nevertheless agree with the edition.

**p. 1190, 10. οὐκ οὔσης ἄλλοθεν αὐγῆς]** Ficino expressed the reading of Medic. A. **γῆς**, *earth.* In its place we have put *lux* (light). Taylor on this place thus: “It is singular, that Ficinus should have translated **αὐγῆς** in this passage, as if it was **αὖ γῆς**. For his version is: *where there may not be from elsewhere* EARTH *to an external mass.*”

**— 13. τοῦ μικροῦ ἐκείνου]** The Ed. wrongly has **μικροῦ** (small). Taylor: “For **μικροῦ** in this place, which is evidently erroneous, it is requisite to read, conformably to the version of Ficinus, **κέντρου** (center).”

**— 17. ἢ ἐπ’ ἴσης ἂν εἴη]** “Here immediately after **ἢ ἐπ’ ἴσης ἂν εἴη** in the original, it is necessary to add **ἔνδον καί**. Ficinus also has: *and within.*” Taylor.

**p. 1191, 7. δηλοῦσι δὲ αἱ ἀποτομαὶ κ. τ. λ.]** Plutarch. *de Placitt. Philosophorr.* II. 24. p. 587. Wyttenb.: "Xenophanes says there are many Suns and Moons (Wyttenb. would prefer many eclipses of the Sun and Moon) according to climates (Stobaeus I. 26. p. 534. Heer.: according to the climates, and Beck vindicated this to Plutarch p. 56. cf. p. 200.) of the earth and sections (*apotomas*) and zones. And according to a certain time ("More harmoniously Stobaeus: but according to a certain") the disk falls (Stob. falls out) into some section of the earth not inhabited by us, and thus as if treading on a void it undergoes an eclipse (Stob. shows an eclipse. Otherwise cf. Brandis's *Commentt. Eleaticc.* I. p. 54.)" From this it is understood what Plotinus wished to declare in this place, where he treats of the light of the Sun, through those *sections*. Indeed, this meaning of the word is to be added to the Lexicons. The astronomers also argue that the verb **ἀποτέμνεσθαι** (to be cut off) is used in a passage of Aratus in *Phaenomm.* v. 541: "as much light as is cut off from the dart of the eye," where in the Scholia p. 125. Buhlii: "as much light of the ether as is cut off and taken away from the dart and ray of the eye."

**— 18. οὔτε ἔκ τινος τόπου]** Ficino expressed **οὔτε ἐντός τινος τόπου** (nor within any place): but the books do not offer this reading.

**p. 1192, 15. Τὸ δὲ ἓν ἐν αὐτοῖς κ. τ. λ.]** Matter touched upon these in *Histoire crit. du Gnosticisme.* Vol. II. p. 467.

**p. 1195, 6. φανότερου]** The Ed. erroneously has **φανερώτερου**. That which is in the Vatican, **φανωτέρου**, is a common fault of scribes ignorant of the lengthening of the penultimate syllable. Regarding which matter others have recently advised, like Stallbaum on Plato’s *Phileb.* p. 31. and our C. Hermann on Lucian *de conscrib. histor.* 49. and 268. Concerning this word frequented by imitators of Plato, it was said above p. 481. B. Add Jo. Chrysostom's *Homil.* II. p. 371. A: "and the prologues are bright and clearer than the sun," where Matthaei collected more p. 117.

**— 13. αὐτὴ ὅλη]** If you embrace the reading of the Marcian books **αὐτὴ ὅλη**, and reject **καὶ** before **οὐκέτι**, this sense emerges: *no longer to the whole itself, but to the partition, impotence (thus certainly to be written for: in potentiality) will happen.*

**p. 1196, 1. τὸ εἴδωλον τοῦ συνηρτῆσθαι]** I suspect: **του**, i.e. **τινὸς**, the image *of anyone.*

**— 13. τὰ γενόμενα]** Thus I wrote from the good books with Ficino instead of **γεγενημένα**. See Wyttenb. in *Selectis Historr.* on Herodot. I. 1. p. 341—344.

**— 17. χωρὶς πυρὸς ποιήσει]** I have included *not* in brackets in the Latin, as it is visible in no book, nor in the Medicean MSS which Ficino used.

**p. 1197, 5. ῥέοντα τὰ ἐξ αὐτῆς]** If that **τὰ** were absent from one or two Codices, I for one would not miss it.

**— 7. ’Αλλ’ ὅτι μὲν μὴ κ. τ. λ.]** In the Ed. in the Latin the words were missing: *they become intelligible, are not subject to death, and are of the soul and of every intellect*—which I have filled in from the first edition.

...in Ficino’s version it is: *but as a transparent body,* desires **ἀλλ’** (but) to be prefixed, and thinks it ought to be added.

**p. 1200, 11. οὐδὲ γὰρ οὕτω προητοίμαστο ὥστε μέρος αὐτῆς ὧδι κείμενον εἰς τοῦτο ἐλθεῖν κ. τ. λ.]** “Ficinus has in this passage evidently mistaken the meaning of Plotinus... For his version is: *For the thing was not so prepared, that a part of the soul placed here would approach this.* For Plotinus is here speaking of soul, and not of the thing which is prepared to receive it.” *Taylor.*

**p. 1201, 3. οὐ μέρους, ὅλου]** Since in the Ed. it is wrongly **μέρος**, Taylor without the books conjectured from Ficino’s version **οὐ μέρος, ἀλλ’ ὅλον**. But I believe he meant to write **μέρους** (of a part).

**— 9. ᾗ προσέχοντες ἀπιστοῦμεν κ. τ. λ.]** See Cudworth. *Syst. Intellect.* p. 1020.

**p. 1202, 4. πανταχοῦ ἀμερὲς ὂν, παρεῖναι κ. τ. λ.]** Cf. Cudworth. *Syst. Intellect.* p. 1018.

**p. 1203, 5. ἀλλ’ οὕτως εἶχεν ἀεί·]** Ficino expressed **εἶχον**, which seems true, yet it appears in no book.

**— 9. ‘Ημεῖς δὲ, τίνες δὲ ἡμεῖς;]** These remind one of Pindar's *Pyth.* VIII. 135. sq.: "Creatures of a day. What is anyone? What is he not? A dream of a shadow, are men."

**— 11. καὶ τινες καὶ θεοὶ]** Ficino did not express the words: **καὶ θεοί** (and gods). Nor do the words appear in the first edition after: *and certain others*: *even gods (they were),* which Marsilius undoubtedly omitted, restrained by religion. This sentiment, however, is connected with the tenets of some Alexandrian philosophers, and its traces exist elsewhere as well as in Porphyry's *Life of Plotinus* chapter II. p. 94. Ed. Fabric. and chapter X. p. 111, where see our annotation. On this place Taylor says: “The version of Ficinus has erroneously nothing more than *alii quidam.* For Plotinus is here speaking of human souls, when (according to Plato in the *Phaedrus*) they ascend in conjunction with the mundane Gods to the survey of the supercelestial place. For such souls as ranking among the divine choir, are denominated in that dialogue Gods.”

**p. 1205, 5. οἷον ἐκκλησία δημογερόντων καθημένων κ. τ. λ.]** I wrote in this place **συννοίᾳ** (with shared intent) for **συννοίᾳ**: but so that the logic of the construction might be consistent, it should also have been written **ἐκκλησίαν** (assembly). But since no book offers this reading, and Anacolutha of this kind are very frequent in these *Enneads*, I stayed my hand. As for the Vatican book having **δημηγόρων** (of orators), that indeed has Platonic authority, but yet it is foreign to this place, which opposes a calm *Senate* to the assembly of a disturbed populace. The source of the comparison is in *Iliad* γ. 149: "the elders of the people sat at the Scaean gates—" and what the same elders then pronounce concerning the dismissal of Helen: "but even so, being such as she is, let her go in the ships," etc. In applying this simile, Aristotle preceded Plotinus in *Ethicc. Nicomach.* II. 9. 6: "what the elders felt toward Helen, we too must feel toward pleasure; and in all things repeat their voice; for thus dismissing it we shall err less." Writers thereafter frequented the same passage of Homer in different ways. See Sext. Empir. *adv. Gramm.* II. 3. p. 288. Fabric. Chariton. V. 5. p. 116. ed. Lips. Aristaenet. I. 1. p. 9. Boissonade, which passage Casp. Barth had already treated in *Adversarr.* XLV. 6. at the end, warning at the same time about the word **δημογερόντες** (elders of the people).

**— 6. δῆμος ἄτακτος τροφῆς δεόμενος]** These too remind one of Homer's *Odyss.* μ. 341, where Eurylochus in the assembly of his hungry companions says: "To die by hunger is the most piteous fate to meet." Which passage Plato reproves with others in the *Republic* III. p. 240. p. 114. Bekk. And it has passed into a proverb, as it were: *The belly has no ears;* and **οἱ ἐν ἀρχαῖς καὶ πλήρεις τραπέζης καὶ πλούτου** (those in power and full of table and wealth), who are called by Libanius in *Thersites* Vol. IV. p. 945. Reisk. are exposed in public necessity to the execrations of the people, unless they follow the counsel of Basil the Great in the *Homily on Avarice* p. 386. D. Paris.: "do not be heavy-priced in imposing upon needs; do not wait for a grain shortage in order to open your granaries; for he who holds grain for a high price is cursed by the people," etc.—Furthermore, this whole comparison of the *multitude* or *vulgar* and *reason* was repeated by Platonic philosophers from the Pythagorean symbol: "avoiding the high-roads, walk by the foot-paths." See Iambl. *Protrept. Symb.* V. p. 330, who thus begins to explain:

"for this also commands to leave behind the vulgar and human life, and deems it worthy to pursue the separate and divine life." Maximus Tyrius *Diss.* XVII. 7. p. 323. Reisk.: "but the intelligible, being freed from the touch and pressure of these, is naturally seen by itself by the mind; but the mind implanted in the whole soul is torn apart by the senses, and is disturbed, and is occupied with business, so that it does not see clearly its own spectacles; and already, being led as by a demagogue, it is persuaded to voice together with the voices of the senses, and to think nothing else exists besides the visible, and audible, and smellable, and tastable, and touchable." (Where no one who has weighed this passage of Plotinus and especially read those words: "first it voiced itself into the common part of the animal and gave its own disturbance to the whole," no one, I think, would agree with Markland that **σπαράττεται** (is torn) should be read instead of **ταράττεται** (is disturbed). Nor is Reiske's conjecture more pleasing: **μὴ ἀεὶ ὁρᾶν** (not always to see) for **μὴ διορᾶν** (not to see clearly).) Proclus in *Alcib. pr.* §. 80. p. 244. of our edition: "the present discourse therefore exhorts to stand apart from infinite desire, and to cast off the multitude of life and the mob within us," etc.

**p. 1206, 11. ἀλλ’ ὅς τις τρόπος τῆς κ. τ. λ.]** Because the Vatican MS has **ὥς τις**, it might lead us to the conjecture that Plotinus wrote: **ἀλλ’ ἄλλως ὅς τις τρόπος**. And this Ficino expressed.

**p. 1207, 10. οἷον ἐξέθορεν ἐκ τοῦ παντὸς]** These remind one of Hesiod's *Theog.* 281: "there leaped forth (*ekthore*) great Chrysaor and the horse Pegasus," where previously it was **ἐξέθορε**. See Gaisford on this place in *Poëtt. Grr. Minorr.* I. p. 88. and that form is in the Oracle in Proclus *Alcib. pr.* p. 65: concerning Love: "—— who first leaped forth from the mind;" where some books have **ἔθορε**. The other form accommodated to prose is found in the same place p. 51: "where then did it first subsist, and how does it go forth into all things, and with what units did it leap forth." From which words the use of this word among philosophers is also understood, who use this verb concerning gods and powers and forces, insofar as they either flash out from superior gods or powers as if from their own source, leap forward and exist, or even glide away and depart from their origin. In this sense Plotinus here also says the **ψυχὴν** (soul) **ἐκθορεῖν** (to leap forth). Another construction is in the passage of Marcus Aurelius VIII. 51. init. p. 257: "neither to trail along in actions, nor to be confused in conversations, nor to wander in imaginations, nor for the soul as it were to be pulled together and to leap out."

**— 13. οὐ τόπῳ, ἀλλ’ ἐνεργείᾳ γένηται κ. τ. λ.]** “Here after **ἐνεργείᾳ** it is requisite to read **καὶ γένηται τὸ καθ’ ἕκαστον** κ. τ. λ. And this reading is confirmed by the version of Ficinus.” *Taylor.*

**— 16. Τὸ δὲ εἰς Ἅιδου γίνεσθαι κ. τ. λ.]** The source is in Plato’s *Cratylus* p. 403. a: p. 44. Bekk.: "but as for **Ἅιδης** (Hades), the many seem to me (omitted in Cod. Darmst.) to suppose that the 'unseen' (*aeides*) has been addressed by this name—" where the Darmstadt codex alone offers the reading **ἀϊδὲς** not found by Bekker and yet confirmed both by most books of Plotinus in this place and indeed by Proclus on that passage of the *Cratylus* §. 152. p. 92. Boisson.: "and Socrates now stitches Hades to the unseen (*aides*) and dark and fearful." But in those words of Plato, by which the opinion and fear of the vulgar are declared, **ἀειδὲς** seems nevertheless to excel, i. e. **δυσσιδὲς**, or "foul to look upon" and "horrid," see Valckenaer on Euripides *Phoeniss.* 373. The universal discussion of Socrates on the underworld in the passage of Plato is to be compared with this passage of Plotinus. No less to be employed are two other passages, where the divine philosopher treats of the word and notion of Pluto (**Ἅιδου**): in *Gorgias* p. 493. b. and in *Phaedo* p. 80. d. where consult Wyttenbach p. 206.

**p. 1208, 1. ’Αλλ’ οὐκ ὄντος ἐστὶ τοῦ σώματος;]** Ficino expressed **ἐστί**, which I ought to have received if even one book supported it. Now, however, all agree with the edition and have **ἔστι**. Otherwise, on these things cf. Cudworth. *Syst. intell.* p. 1024. sq. and Moshem. p. 955. sq. and cf. above p. 374. E.

**— 5. οἷον ἐλλάμψη πρὸς αὐτὴν]** For **αὐτὴν**, which is in the Ed., Taylor wants **αὐτὸν** to be read, adding: “For Plotinus is here speaking of the soul with reference to the **εἴδωλον**, or image of it. Ficinus therefore was mistaken in translating this passage as if Plotinus was speaking of the soul illuminating *herself*, and not her image. For his version is: *But when she herself as if in herself reflects.*”

**p. 1218, 2. Ἔξω μὲν οὖν ὁρῶντες ἢ ὅθεν ἐξημμέθα κ. τ. λ.]** “Thus in the original. But for **ἢ ὅθεν** both the sense and the version of Ficinus require that we should read **καὶ μὴ ὅθεν**.” *Taylor.*

**— 4. Εἰ δέ τις ἐπιστραφῆναι δύναιτο]** “Or if it happened to him to be so happy as to be pulled back by Minerva herself.” These are drawn from *Iliad* A. 194. in the passage on the anger of Achilles: "Athena came from heaven—and stood behind, and took the son of Peleus by his golden hair, appearing to him alone—and he turned back, and immediately knew Pallas Athena." Which passage was so accepted by many philosophers that they called Minerva **φρόνησιν** (practical wisdom). See Clarke and Heyne on those verses of the poet, and cf. Jo. Laur. Lydus *de Menss.* IV. 6. 39. and those whom our Roether praised at that place p. 204. sq.

**— 6. θεόν τε καὶ αὑτὸν]** Ficino with Cod. Marc. A does not acknowledge **καί** (and). From our reading these are to be translated: *and god and himself and the universe he would behold.*

**p. 1219, 4. ὡς ἐπὶ τῶν αἰσθητῶν λέγομεν εἰς αἰσθητὸν]** I have integrated this passage from many books: *as* IN SENSIBLE THINGS WE SAY ILLUMINATIONS OCCUR IN THE SENSIBLE.

**— 15. αὐτὸ δὴ πῦρ τὴν ὕλην]** Thus I wrote for **δέ**. Ficino besides expressed **κρατῆσαν** (mastering); which however appears in no book.

**p. 1220, 3. ἐν ἀτόπῳ]** What is in the margin of the Ed. is **ἐν οὐ τόπῳ** (in no place), written by the "side-correction" of a scribe who wished to be careful lest we think of "absurdity" (*in-eptus*).

**— 11. ὑφ’ ἑκάστης]** Ficino expressed **ὑφ’ ἑαυτῆς ἄλλης**, which is read in Med. B. From our reading, which is of the remaining books and the edition, it is to be translated: “so that each fire is formed by *one other idea*—but that one by another.”

**p. 1221, 14. εἰ πλείων ὁ κόσμος ἦν]** To these and the following employ Cudworth. *Syst. Intell.* p. 1014. with Mosheim’s notes.

**p. 1222, 12. τούτῳ ἐν ὄντως εἶναι]** Perhaps **τοῦτο** should be written. Taylor thinks **τῷ** should be written.

**— 14. καὶ τὸν περιέχοντα αὑτὸν εἶναι]** “The sense requires that we should read **καὶ τὸν περιεχόμενον** κ. τ. λ. And this emendation is also supported by the version of Ficinus.” *Taylor.*

**p. 1223, 9. ἐφιέμενος τοῦ καλοῦ]** Plotinus here regards Diotima’s words in Plato’s *Symposium* p. 203. p. 430. init. Bekk. concerning Love: "sleeping at doors and in the paths in the open air:" which passage our author also touched on at p. 295. e. Wherefore in this place Plotinus's words should be written and translated thus: **καὶ οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ θυραυλῶν Ἔρως**: and this is Love sleeping before the doors.

**p. 1224, 1. διὸ καὶ ξυνὸν τὸ φρονεῖν]** Because two books have **συνὸν**, it pertains to the same thing as that **κοινὸν** (common), which scribes elsewhere thrust in for that word...

...as observed by Dorville on Chariton p. 424. ed. Lips. Most of our books, however, correctly persist in **ξυνόν** (common). For this sentiment has the color of an ancient proverb, and Pindar also added **ξυνὸν εὐ καλόν** (*Isthm.* I. 64). Otherwise, regarding Plotinus's opinion, compare Socrates’ discussion in Xenophon’s *Memorabilia* concerning the common mind or mind of the world, which no one alone could snatch for himself as a whole. I. 4. 6—8. and Cic. *de N. D.* II. 6. III. 11. and Sext. Empir. *adv. Mathem.* p. 573. Fabric. From which passage of Xenophon Philostratus also seems to have drawn color in *Life of Apollonius* I. 28. p. 36. cf. G. Joseph Bekker’s *Specim. Philostr.* p. 91.

**— 4. ἓν δεῖ—συνόν]** I left the corrupted passage untouched, even though it was attempted by conjectures, as the margin of Cod. Medic. A. argues. For the books offer no great help.

**— 8. ἐν τῇ συνόδῳ καὶ τῇ ὡς ἀληθῶς συνέσει τὸ φρονεῖν ἐγέννησε]** Plotinus slightly touched upon the double force of the word **σύνεσις** (understanding/union), which also declares a conjunction, as in *Odyss.* κ. 515. Consult Apollonius's *Lex. Hom.* p. 484. Tollii. Cf. also above III. 6. 11. and our annotation there p. 313. In particular, however, Aristotle's discussion on the distinction between **σύνεσιν** (understanding) and **φρόνησιν** (practical wisdom) in *Ethicc. Nicomm.* VI. 11. must be held, from which I transfer only these here: "for understanding is neither about things that are always and immovable, nor about any things that come to be, but about those things which one might doubt and deliberate upon. Wherefore it is about the same things as practical wisdom. But understanding and practical wisdom are not the same," etc. On which passage consult Eustratius, Victorius, and Giphanius in our Zell’s *Commentar.* p. 235. sqq.

**— 17. τὰ δὲ παρ’ αὐτοῦ ἐνταῦθα, καὶ τὸ διδὸν]** Ficino filled in the lacunose passage with conjecture and translated more fully: in the books there is no protection.

**— 19. οὐ πόμπιος ἡ νοερὰ δόσις]** Concerning the form see Wesseling on Diodor. XII. 40. p. 504. The meaning, however, in which the word is accepted in this place, must be noted in Lexicons [as "intellectual gift"].

**p. 1225, 3. εἰ δὴ ἐπὶ σώματος οὐδὲν κ. τ. λ.]** “This is asserted by Plato, in the *Timaeus*, of the body of the universe.” *Taylor.* The same wants **ἑαυτὸ** to be distinguished in the following, but not after **ἀδιαστάτου** (unextended).

**— 12. ὥσπερ οὐχ ὁρῶντες πᾶν μάθημα—στενοχωρυμένας κ. τ. λ.]** Cf. above V. 9. 6. and 7. p. 560. Add Aeneas of Gaza’s *Theophrast.* p. 51. Barth.: "in the immaterial logical essences, multitude is not a crowded narrowness, for all things are one." Cf. also above p. 495. A: "for it is not crowded."

**p. 1226, 3. ἀποδέδεικται μὲν οὖν ἤδη πολλαχῇ κ. τ. λ.]** Cf. below to VI. 7. 40. p. 731. A.

**— 10. ταύτῃ γὰρ ἑτέρα]** I am mistaken, or Ficino read **γὰρ αὖ ἑτέρα**. This is in some books: and it is not unpleasing.

**ib. πᾶσά ἐστι δύναμις οὐδαμοῦ τοσήδε]** See Cudworth. *Syst. Intellect.* p. 1021. sq.

**p. 1227, 3. [ἀνταιωρουμένην]** The verb **ἀνταιωρεῖσθαι** (to be suspended over against) should be added to the lexicons. The rest of this passage I have left untouched. For the MSS books do not sufficiently clear up these more difficult points. Taylor on these things says: “Plotinus is here speaking of a corporeal nature which is suspended from eternity, and runs together with time to the permanently abiding power of true being.” The same contends that **πρὸς μένουσαν** must necessarily be written instead of **προσμένουσαν**.

**— 14. παρῆν μέν τοι παντί]** At the end of this chapter Taylor says: “There is obviously in the original a defect in the latter part of the passage within the words **πρὸς πᾶν** and the last words of the chapter. For the original is: **ἀλλὰ πρὸς τὰ πρῶτα τῶν γενῶν, εἶτ’ ἐπὶ τούτοις ἄλλα. παρῆν μέν τι παντί.** But it appears to me to be necessary instead of this to read: **ἀλλὰ πρὸς τὰ πρῶτα τῶν γενῶν· εἶτ’ ἐπὶ τούτοις πρὸς τἄλλα. ἡ δὲ ὑπερτέρα φύσις παρῆν μέντοι παντί.** Ficinus also has: ‘*but in the first place to the primary genera, then through these to the rest: nevertheless the superior nature was equally present to the universe.*’ ”

**p. 1228, 2. οὐ γὰρ ἐν ζωῇ τὴν ὕλην]** In this variety of reading, the conjecture is not absurd which Ficino added in the margin of Med. A. and expressed in the version.

**p. 1229, 6. ἀλλ’ οὗτοι μὲν οἱ θεοὶ—ἐπιστρωφῶσι τὰς πόλεις]** Taylor thinks **εἰς τὸ ὄντως ὄν** (into true being) must necessarily be added before **ἐπιστρωφῶσι**. But Plotinus regards those verses of *Odyss.* ρ. 485. sqq.: "and the gods, like foreign guests, taking all sorts of shapes, visit the cities, overseeing the insolence and the law-abiding of men." Where it is: they wander through cities in varied figure and appearance. Cf. Eustath. p. 644. Plato provided the handle for praising this passage to Plotinus both in the *Sophist* p. 216. p. 126. Bekk. (where see Scholia and Heindf.)...

### LIB. VI.

P. 1230, 7. ΠΕΡΙ ΑΡΙΘΜΩΝ (ON NUMBERS).] According to the chronological order, this book is the thirty-fourth (Porphyry, *Life of Plotinus*, c. V and XXVII). The sources are found both in the writings of the Pythagoreans and in the books of Plato and the ancient Platonists. I do not wish to inquire now whether Pythagoras drew this doctrine from the discipline of Zaratas (whom they think to be Zoroaster [cf. Ursinus, *De Zoroastre*, Sect. 4. p. 22. sqq.]), as is found in Plutarch, *De Animarum Procreatione in Timaeo*, p. 1012. E. (p. 124, Wyttenb.), or from the Orphics (Iamblichus, *Life of Pythagoras*, XXVIII. 146, p. 308, Kiessl.): this must be held above all else, that the most ancient Pythagorean philosophers call the doctrine of Numbers primary and preach its power for wisdom and a more holy life. Just read the words of Philolaus in Stobaeus, *Eclogues* I. 3, p. 8, Heeren, which Boeckh treated in the book entitled *Philolaus*, p. 139 ff. Perictyone in Stobaeus, *Florilegium*, Tit. I. p. 7 (p. 25, Gaisford): *"Whoever is able to resolve all genera (all the genera, Iamblichus in Protrepticus IV. p. 20. Arcer. p. 58. Kiessling) under one and the same principle, and again from this (both words are absent from Iamblichus) to synthesize and enumerate them,"* (Learned men, who did not know that Iamblichus had these same things, attacked this word with unhappy conjectures. Iamblichus has *συναριθμήσασθαι* [to number together]. Kiessling: “I would prefer *συναριθμήσασθαι*—to arrange matters according to the Pythagorean doctrine and method of numbers:” Excellent) *"this man seems (to me, adds Iamblichus) to be both the wisest (to be, Iamblichus rightly) and the truest (all-true, Iamblichus), and moreover to have discovered a beautiful vantage point from which he will be able to behold God and all things (the 'te' is not in Iamblichus) in their coordinate series and order (Iamblichus, coordinate series, etc. Jacobs noted this diversity in Lectt. Stobenss. p. 37) distinguished from his own things."* (Cod. Ciz. *τῷ ἐκ.* Kiessl. *τᾷ ἐκείνῳ*). From which it is understood that Gaisford rightly left that *ἀριθμήσασθαι* (to enumerate) untouched. Nor did Rudelbach attempt it, who presented these words of Perictyone (or Archytas, for they are ascribed to him by Iamblichus) in Latin in *Comment. De Ethices Principiis*, p. 109. Concerning Pythagoras himself, Stobaeus records in *Eclogues* I. 11. 12. p. 299: *"Pythagoras son of Mnesarchus, the Samian, first addressing philosophy by this term, calls the principles numbers and the symmetries in them, which he calls harmonies,"* etc. But if you truly ask in what sense Pythagoras and his disciples, and the subsequent Pythagoreans, called Numbers principles (and Ficinus himself touched upon this below, p. 681), besides the genuine fragments of these philosophers, the authority of Aristotle must be considered greatest of all. And with this philosopher as witness (*Metaphysics* I. 5, p. 15, compared with I. 6, p. 20, ed. Brandis), the Pythagoreans partly posited numbers not only as principles of things, but even as the substances and matter (*ὕλην*) of things (which seems to have been the most ancient method); partly (probably by the authority of Hippasus; Simplicius in *Aristot. Phys.* fol. 104. b.) they posited them as the archetypes of beings, or taught that all beings existed according to the image of numbers; partly they established that all beings existed by the imitation (*μιμήσει*) of numbers. (Ritter gives more on these in *Hist. Phil. Pythag.* p. 92 ff; Rudelbach in the place cited, and especially Brandis in *Comment. De numerorum doctrina et Pythagoreorum philosophorum et Platonicorum*; in *Rheinischen Museum für Philol. Philosophie* II. 2. p. 209—241.) I add the words which are read in Iamblichus, *Life of Pythagoras*, in the place cited, p. 308, Kiessl.:—*"he said (most of my manuscripts have 'they said') that the essence (ousia) in number"* (I am surprised that no manuscript gives *ὡσίαν* [the Doric form]. But several things in these depart from Doricism:) *"is eternal, being the most provident principle of the whole heaven and earth and the nature between them; and moreover the root of the permanence of divine things and gods and daemons (most manuscripts: 'of divine gods and...' incorrectly)."* All other things are read in the Fragment of Theano in Stobaeus.

[[language: Latin]]

LIB. VI. OF THE SIXTH ENNEAD. p. 1230—1233. 367

[[original page: 367]]

*Eclogues* I. 11. 13. p. 302. Heeren. from which I shall pluck only this: *"But he (Pythagoras) said that all things happen not out of number, but according to number"*: “He indeed said that all things arise *not from numbers, but according to numbers*.” But Brandis rightly considers that fragment spurious in the place cited, p. 214. I come to Plato. He indeed, while in other books, such as *Republic* VII and VIII, p. 522 ff. and 546, and likewise *Laws* V. p. 747, celebrates the excellence of numbers, also descends deeper into their doctrine, as in *Timaeus* p. 35—37, 41 (in which passages apply Chalcidius XXXII ff., p. 288 ff., ed. Fabric.). To this, the author of the *Epinomis* applies himself, p. 977 ff., or rather this writer feels almost nothing that is not Pythagorean. The Emperor Julian reflects on this passage in *Orat.* IV. p. 152, calling Plato the author (in *Parmenides* p. 144 ff. and in *Theaetetus* p. 146 ff.). Now if you ask how Plato shaped the numbers for himself: the following writings argue that this cause has recently been pleaded with zeal: *Platonis de ideis et numeris doctrina ex Aristotele illustrata* by Fr. A. Trendelenburg, Leipzig 1826; Ernest Reinhold’s *Symbola ad illustrandam Pythagoream Metaphysicam*, Jena 1827; and Chr. Aug. Brandis’s *Diatribe de perditis Aristotelis libris de Ideis et de Bono sive Philosophia*, Bonn 1823. And indeed, this learned man at p. 33 posited this: “If numbers therefore are the highest principles of things, insofar as they remain of a simple nature even if all other things are removed (for so Plato's reasoning proceeds), *the ideas too must be referred to them*. Aristotle testifies more often than it is worth the effort to heap up proving passages that Plato taught that the ideas *are numbers*: and his Greek interpreters rightly affirm by his words (*Metaphysics* XIII. 9. p. 234. 5.) *'he who first posited that the forms are numbers'* that that prince of philosophers is signified (Pseudo-Alexander and Syrianus in *Arist. Metaph.* in the place cited).” After Plato, the philosophers of the Old Academy, Speusippus and Xenocrates, labored in the doctrine of numbers (Theophrastus, *Metaphysics* p. 255; Alexander in *Aristotel. Metaph.* XIII. 6; cf. Brandis’s book recently cited, p. 45 ff., p. 60 ff.). Nor did the followers of later families neglect this inquiry; which various Excerpts shown by Stobaeus in *Eclogues* I. 2. 8. p. 18—24, Heeren, teach. Sextus Empiricus strives to utterly overthrow the Pythagorean and Platonic doctrine of numbers both elsewhere and especially in two disputations entitled *Concerning Number*, in *Pyrrhonian Hypotyposes* III. 18. p. 164—168, Fabric., and *Against the Mathematicians* X. 4. §. 248 ff., p. 674—684. Conversely, Philo Judaeus, both in other books and in *On the Creation of the World*, p. 21 ff. Mangey, applied the doctrine of numbers to explain the beginnings of the world brought forth in Genesis. Some more recent Platonists seem to have accepted the Pythagorean doctrine of numbers in the same sense as Theano, who indeed wishes to seem so, accepts it in the fragment cited above. (Cf. Brandis, *De Pythagorr. et Platonicorr. numeris* p. 214.) I have presented excerpted passages of Proclus and Olympiodorus on Pythagorean numbers above at V. 1. 5. p. 486. A. I will cite other passages of Proclus, in which mention of this Plotinian book is made, below at p. 678. Here I will add this one thing: that which Proclus in *Inst. Theol.* c. 113 had called "divine number" (*ὁ θεῖος ἀριθμὸς*), is heavily criticized by this name by Nicolaus of Methone in *Ἀναπτύξει τῆς Θεολογικῆς Στοιχειώσεως* (p. 140 ff. Voemel), who leaves no stone unturned in order to defend the Christian doctrine of the One God and the Trinity against the pagan philosophers.

p. 1230, 9. *Ἀρ' ἔστι τὸ πλῆθος ἀπόστασις τοῦ ἑνὸς, καὶ ἡ ἀπειρία ἀπόστασις παντελὴς—καὶ ἡμεῖς κακοὶ ὅταν πλῆθος* ("Is then multitude a departure from the one, and is infinity a total departure... and we are evil when we are multitude?")] These are joined with the doctrine of the Pythagoreans, and especially of Philolaus, *concerning the limiting and the infinite*, and with Plato’s doctrine *concerning the limit*, which he says in the *Philebus*, p. 91, is the same as *the One* (see Boeckh’s *Philolaus*, p. 45 ff. and Brandis, *De Numeror. doctr.*, p. 221 ff., where Aristotle's opinions on this principle are also touched upon). Of more recent Platonists, Proclus in *Alcib. pr.*, p. 50 and especially p. 245—250, should be called upon. Also the same in *Inst. Theol.* c. XIII, p. 22—24, which concludes thus: *“therefore goodness is also unification, and unification is goodness, and the good is one, and the one is primarily good”*: where I have cited Porphyry's *Sententt.* XXXVIII, *On Abstinence* I. 28, Iamblichus *On the Common Mathematical Science* in Villoison, *Anecdott.* II. p. 195 ff., and Plotinus himself, p. 199. A., p. 524 ff., p. 667 ff., and p. 763.

the passage of the Platonic *Timaeus* concerning matter, p. 49 ff., from which the color of several opinions is also drawn; especially p. 52 ff., p. 64 ff. Bekk. This argument was subsequently treated by philosophers both in Physics and Metaphysics (Ontology), and in the doctrine of the Categories; such as the so-called Hermes, in *Poimandres* chapter 2, c. 11 and 12, and in *Asclepius* c. 7. Consult especially Aristotle’s *Physics* IV. 1, also IV. 5 and IV. 10, and what Simplicius and John Philoponus [Grammaticus] commented on those passages.

p. 1234, 9. *μὴ ἐπιβάλλων τι πέρας ὥσπερ δίκτυον ὑπεκφεύγουσαν ἕξεις* ("unless casting some limit like a net, you will have it fleeing away")] Plotinus might seem to have added that *"like a net"* (*ὥσπερ δίκτυον*) remembering that Homeric fable (*Odyssey* θ. 266 ff.) where Vulcan casts a net over Mars and Venus, or subtle and invisible bonds; which fable some philosophers themselves reduced to cosmogonical reasons (see Eustathius in the place cited; cf. our *Symbolica* II, p. 325). Our author himself touched upon the fable, but according to the opinion of his Plato (see above II. 3. 6. p. 140. C. and cf. Plato, *Republic* III. p. 390, p. 115, Bekker). Yet the nearest simile is drawn from fishing and thence variously transferred to the snares of enemies who, wishing to secretly escape, are intercepted. See just the oracle in Herodotus I. 62; on which passage I have collected more. Moreover, the verb *ὑπεκφεύγειν* (to slip away), and what is used thereafter toward the end of the chapter, *ἀποδράναι* (to run away), correspond to each other. Phavorinus: *"ἀποδράναι: for someone who has withdrawn to be unclear where he is"* etc. (cf. Ammonius on the word and Xenophon, *Anabasis* I. 4. 8, and likewise *Lexicon Xenophont.* I. p. 332.)

p. 1235, 9. *ὁ μὲν οὖν Πλάτων εἰς ἔννοιαν ἀριθμοῦ τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ἐληλυθέναι εἰπὼν* κ. τ. λ. ("Plato indeed saying that men have come to the notion of number...")] In *Timaeus* p. 37 ff. We learn Plato's true opinion concerning numbers and their relation to ideas from Aristotle’s *Metaphysics* I. 6. p. 16, Sylburg, and his interpreters, especially Alexander; from which it is understood that he, equally with the ancient Pythagoreans, called numbers the principles of things. See Brandis’s *Diatrib. de perditis Aristotelis libris de Ideis et de Bono*, p. 30—33.

— 16. *ἀλλὰ μὴν ὅταν λέγῃ ἐν τῷ ἀληθινῷ ἀριθμῷ* ("But indeed when he speaks of true number")] He refers to the disputation instituted in Plato's *Parmenides* p. 144 ff. (p. 44 ff. Bekker). For this, apply Ficinus’s *Commentary* c. 95. Cf. our author below, p. 686. C., where *"most true numbers"* are mentioned.

p. 1236, 10. *οἷους ἔλεγον οἱ Πυθαγόρειοι—οἷον δικαιοσύνην τετράδα* ("such as the Pythagoreans said—as for instance justice as a tetrad")] One manuscript: *ἐκ τοῦ ἀναλόγου*. But see what was said above at p. 416. B. and p. 440. D. about this form, usually used for *ἀνὰ λόγον* (proportionally). Instead of *δικαιοσύνην* (justice, acc.), the margin of the Edition has *δικαιοσύνη* (nom.), one book has *δικαιοσύνην*. Aristotle refers to this naming in *Metaphysics* I. 5. p. 15, Brandis: *"that such an affection of numbers is justice, and such is soul and intellect."* The classic passage is Iamblichus in *Nicomachus, Arithmethic Introduction*, p. 20, for which apply Joachim Camerarius p. 48 ff. and Sam. Tenulius p. 103. Add Wyttenbach on Plutarch, *De Iside et Osiride*, p. 264. To this point also belong these things in *Theologumena Arithmeticae* p. 24 (p. 23, Ast): *"the Pythagoreans honored it (the tetrad), as being generative of the decad. And it is called, as Anatolius says, justice, since the square from it, that is, the area, is equal to the perimeter"* etc. cf. ibid. p. 28. I have placed other things concerning the quaternary number in *Commentatt. Herodott.* p. 134. Add Jo. Laur. Lydus, *De Mensibus Romanorum*, and Roether’s and my notes there, p. 61 and p. 233 ff., ed. Roether. *Soon ὅμως καὶ τὸν ἀριθμὸν συζυγή* (nevertheless also the conjugate number). Some Manuscripts have *συζυγεῖ*. Plato, *Republic* VIII, p. 546. B. (p. 381, Bekker; a most obscure passage on the perfect number, which passage Aristotle notes in *Politics* V. 12; consult Goettling's notes, p. 411—413 on this)—*"of which the sesquitertian root joined with the pentad (two manuscripts in Bekker: συζυγὴς [nom.]) produces two harmonies when increased thrice."* Iamblichus, *Life of Pythagoras*, c. 27. p. 110. Kuster (p. 278): *"Plato saying clearly in the Republic, that sesquitertian root, that which is joined to the pentad"*; for which Kuster cites the same passage of Plato from Aristides Quintilianus, *On Music* III. p. 152, referring to it as: *συζυγέντα* (having been joined). Plato himself uses the substantive *συζυγία* (conjugation/yoke) in the passage on the one and numbers in *Parmenides* p. 143 near the end (p. 37, Bekker). The Pythagoreans knew of *συζυγίας* (conjugations) of numbers in sounds. See Iamblichus, *Life of Pythagoras*, c. XXVI. p. 248, Kiessling. Ibid. p. 250, concerning Pythagoras: *"then striking two strings together alternately (my Memmian manuscript and others have 'successively') he found the aforementioned consonances, one in one conjugation, another in another"* (So also Memm. and several Manuscripts in my notes for the corrupt *συντυχίᾳ*): “one consonance in another conjunction.” And given this opportunity, let me add these few things: No one is ignorant that the Pythagoreans

[[original page: 369]]

preached that *tetractys* of theirs by this name, because it held the *ῥίζωμα* (root) of perennial nature (Iamblichus, *Life of Pythagoras* §. 150. p. 316.). Now hear what Theodoret relates concerning Simon Magus in *Haereticarum Fabularum Compendium* I. p. 217. Schulz: *"he hypothesized a certain infinite power; and this he called the root of all things. And he said that it was fire—and that the world—was generated from the apparent activity of the fire. And first from it were projected three conjugations (συζυγίας)"* etc. You see that this man imitated not only the principles of Heraclitean philosophy, but also Pythagorean formulas. Lexicons exhibit *συζύγως* (conjugately) from Apollonius Dyscolus. Nor do Grammarians alone, but also Arithmeticians use this Adverb. See, for example, Iamblichus in *Nicomachus* p. 20 and p. 22, Tenulius. Add from Proclus in *Alcib. pr.* p. 21 of our edition: *"to contemplate all intelligible things conjugately (συζύγως) by a simple, uniform, and intellectual knowledge"* (copulate or conjointly to contemplate.)

p. 1238, 1. *καὶ δεκὰς—ἔσται αὐτοδεκάς* ("and a decad... will be the Decad-itself")] Theo Smyrnaeus, *On Mathematics in Plato*, c. IV. p. 26. Bullialdus (p. 28 ff., ed. Gelder): *"Simply, on the principles of numbers, some later people say they are the monad and the dyad. But those from Pythagoras say all the successive expositions of terms, through which even and odd are conceived, for instance the triad as the principle of three things in sensibles, and the tetrad as the principle of four things in sensibles, and in the same way for other numbers."* Stobaeus gives these same things more briefly in *Eclogues* I. 1. 9. p. 20. Heeren. On those points, Bullialdus p. 229: “The form of number is treated here; for example, it is asked what is the form of the ternary or the quaternary. The Pythagoreans say that individual numbers have their own forms, which Theo calls *principles* (*ἀρχὰς*), for example that all ternary numbers have as their principle *the Triad*, all quaternary numbers *the Tetrad*, and so forth. Therefore *monad, dyad, triad, tetrad* etc. are before the things numbered, since they are the forms of numbers. Plotinus departs into the same opinion.” This Plotinian passage itself follows. With which, moreover, Plato's disputation in *Philebus* p. 23 (p. 53 ff. Stallbaum) is to be compared, and, regarding the Pythagoreans, Boeckh’s *Philolaus* p. 53 ff., compared with p. 147 ff. Furthermore, see also below p. 686. C.

p. 1240, 1. *οὐ γὰρ ἡ ἐπιστήμη πρὸς αὐτὴν* κ. τ. λ. ("For knowledge is not toward itself...")] Ficinus in this place expressed the reading of the second hand in Medicean A: *αὐτό*. Next, he did not express *οὐ μένουσαν*. What if you correct *αὐτὴν* in this place, and translate the whole passage thus: “For neither is knowledge (there) turned toward itself: but the things there make the knowledge not remaining (not stable), such as is the knowledge of a thing, to be another (diverse from itself), that is, (to be) true knowledge—?”

— 10. *δικαιοσύνης—ἧς ὡς ἀληθῶς καλὸν τὸ πρόσωπον, καὶ οὔτε ἕσπερος* κ. τ. λ. ("of justice—of which the face is truly beautiful, and neither evening [star]...")] A passage very similar to the previous I. 6. 4. p. 53. D: *"how beautiful is the face of justice and temperance, and neither the evening star nor the morning star are so beautiful."* On which passage both my Wyttenbach and I myself have given more.

— 15. *πάντα ἔχουσαν* ("having all things")] Two Medicean manuscripts have *πανταχοῦ ἔχουσαν* (having everywhere). Ficinus expressed: *πάντα πανταχοῦ ἔχουσαν* (having all things everywhere). Not badly.

p. 1241, 5. *πιστούμεθα δὲ—ἢ κατά τι ὡμοίωται* ("we trust... or it has been likened in some respect")] I fear lest deeper ulcers lie hidden here. I certainly, in passages of this sort which I do not fully grasp, prefer to seem too timid than too bold. Therefore, except for two typographical errors, I have attempted nothing. Ficinus expressed: *τῶν εἰς ψυχὴν ἔρωτι* (of those with love for the soul), and in the following line: *ᾗ κατά τι*.

— 9. *αὐτοζώου μὴ θαυμαστοῦ τὸ κάλλος καὶ ἀφράστου ὄντος.* ("unless the beauty of the Living-Being-itself be wonderful and ineffable.")] Because six manuscripts show *ἀψαύστου* (untouched/intangible), it is not absurd if you explain it as "intact" or *"unblemished"* (Stephanus in *Thesaurus* p. 2435, ed. London). You could also suspect: *ἀφάτου* (unutterable). Hesychius I. p. 637. Alb.: *"ἄφατον: impossible"* (and *impossible beauty* Plotinus himself uses rather often, as above p. 549, at the end; cf. Index) *"much; unspeakable; immeasurable; terrible."* (as, for example, *ἀφάτων κακῶν* [unspeakable evils] in Plutarch’s *Marius* c. XLV. p. 540.) But the same force is in the word *ἄφραστον* (ineffable) (Hesychius I. p. 649; *Etymol. Gud.* p. 97. 1; and the learned men cited in Steph. *Thes.* IV. p. 69, p. 9969, ed. London; where, however, delete two passages: Philo Judaeus II. p. 262. Pfeiffer, p. 230. Mangey, for there no manuscript has *ἀφραστοτάτοις*: all have *ἀφραστάτοις*, and Jacobs on *Anthol. Gr.* XI. p. 100, for there *ἄφαστος* is explained, and add Reiske on Eunapius’s *Aedes.* p. 276.) Wherefore I acquiesce in the common reading: “unless the animal itself be of a wonderful and *ineffable* beauty.”

p. 1242, 6. *καὶ δύναμιν—ἐφ' ἑαυτῆς βεβῶσαν* ("and power... standing upon itself")] This decree, that true essence is force, is nothing other than what Leibniz posited, as Tiedemann records in *Geist der specul. Philosophie* III. p. 307.

p. 1242, 8. *οὐ τὸ ἐφαψάμενον—ἐπαφῆς* ("it is not the having touched... of touch")] Simplicius in *Aristotel. de Anima* III. fol. 73. a. mid.: *"And generally falsehood consists in not touching the thing, so as even to say something about it, yet in some respect not, so as even to lie about this very thing; but the indivisible does not approach touch in some respect, because of its being indivisible, but the whole, if it is necessary to speak of 'the whole' regarding indivisibles, is known, or not at all."* And this was what Plotinus said, as I have already mentioned (See ibid. p. 70. a. mid.) *"that the intellect either touched or did not touch; so that it is unerring."* Above at p. 6. E. we read: *"But if the soul is unerring"* etc. This adjective has a double force: first, to designate him who does not wander from the mark, and thus who does not wander from the law, who does not sin; then, he who cannot wander and sin (Gellius calls it *impeccable* in XVII. 19.); then, he who is immune to the lust of carnal things, as shown by passages collected by Sturz in *Lex. Xenoph.*, Upton and Schweighaeuser in *Indic. Graecitat. Epicteteae*, Biel in *Thes. LXX. Interprr.*, Schleusner in *Lex. N. T.*, and Suicer in *Thes. Eccles.* under the word. For Plotinus's sake, I will set down some passages whence an understanding of these opinions may arise. The primary passage is in Plato's *Republic* I. p. 339 ff. (p. 27 ff. Bekker), which begins thus: *"But are the rulers in the various cities unerring (ἀναμάρτητοι), or are they such as might also err? By all means, he said, such as might also err."* Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Judic. de Thucyd.* III. p. 816 (p. 66, Krüger): *"for no human nature is sufficient, either in words or in deeds, to be unerring."* Longinus XXXII. 8: *"for he presents the orator (Lysias) as unerring and pure, while Plato failed in many places."* cf. XXXIII. 2. XXXVI. 1. Dio Cassius LVIII. 16. p. 889. Reimar: *"but on equal ground both the wrongdoing and the unerring, both the suspecting and the fearless, were subjected to the inquiry of Sejanus’s crimes."* Synesius, *Epist.* LXVII. p. 42: *"being unerring is directly of divine portion and nature."* Theodoret, *Dialog.* I, *Concerning the Holy Trinity*, Vol. V. p. 948. Schulz: *"A. But even if some of the angels once sinned, yet there are unerring angels. B. We do not ask if there are unerring angels, but if they were able to sin"* etc. Similarly Diogenes Laertius VII. 122: *"furthermore they are unerring, by being incidentless in sin"* (because they cannot fall into sin). Plutarch, *De aud. poett.* p. 25. D. (p. 95, Wyttenbach) joins *"impassive and unerring,"* and rather often. The word *ἀναμάρτητος*, unearthed from a sepulchral inscription, was recently used to explain the New Testament by the most learned man *Frid. Münter* in *Symbolis ad interpretationem Evangelii Johannis ex marmoribus et numis*, Copenhagen 1824. VIII. 7.

— 12. *τὸ δὲ πρῶτον, εἶτα νοῦν, εἶτα τὸ ζῶον* ("first the First, then Intellect, then the Living Being")] Proclus in *Platon. Timaeum* p. 130: *"Plotinus posits the Autozoon (Living-Being-itself) in two ways, sometimes as superior to Intellect, as in the inquiry into differences (i.e., above III. 9. 1. p. 356. B.), sometimes as inferior, as in the book on numbers, when he says that first is Being, then Intellect, then the Autozoon."* Plato had already used this naming in the passage on Numbers and ideas. Brandis in *Diatrib. de perditis Aristot. libris de Ideis et de Bono* p. 56: “Since, however, he says, that first *tetrad* contained within itself whatever could be reached by mind and senses, and was like a prototype of the universe of things, Plato called it *Autozoon*, which is confirmed by Aristotle's own words.” Then he cites Aristotle, *De Anima* I. 2: *"likewise it was also defined in the things said 'Concerning Philosophy', that the living being itself is from the idea of the One and the first length and breadth and depth."* cf. the same Diatribe p. 57.

p. 1243, 5. *εἰ γὰρ ἐφ' ἑαυτοῦ ἄνευ τῶν ἀριθμητῶν δύναιτο εἶναι* ("for if it could exist by itself without the numbered things")] Sextus Empiricus, *Pyrrhon. Hypotypp.* III. 18. 156. p. 165. Fabric. concerning the Pythagoreans: *"Therefore they dream these things, and they establish that number is something else beyond the things numbered"* etc. Soon, regarding the words of Plotinus at the end of this page: *"and it must be granted that number arises from being,"* Proclus seems to refer in *Plato’s Theology* c. XI. p. 27: *"For Plotinus in the book on numbers, having asked whether beings subsist before numbers, or numbers before beings, says expressly that the first being subsisted before numbers, and thus generates the divine number."* Cf. Proclus in the same work IV. 32. p. 231.

— 15. *καὶ μὴ κατὰ τὸ ἐπελθὸν* ("and not according to what occurred [by chance]")] The reason appears why Plotinus added *κατὰ* (according to) to the formula *τὸ ἐπελθὸν* (what occurred), otherwise usually used concerning speech, where we bring forth whatever just comes into the mind. Concerning this, see Tib. Hemsterhuis on Lucian, *Diall. Deorr.* XX. 4. p. 255. where *ἄλλως* (otherwise) is added. For *ἄλλως ἐπελθὸν* is that which is spoken not on purpose, with no fixed plan or industry. Cf. the same on

— 13. *βάσιν δὲ ἔχει τὰ ὄντα ἐν αὐτῷ, καὶ πηγὴν, καὶ ῥίζαν καὶ ἀρχήν* ("beings have in it a base, and a source, and a root and a principle")] Cicero, *Academica* II. 37. 118. p. 213. Goerenz: “The Pythagoreans wish all things to proceed from numbers and the beginnings of mathematicians:” where see Davies. Moreover, these words of Theo on Mathematics in Plato agree word for word with the Plotinian ones at the end of lib. c. II. p. 23 (p. 25, ed. Gelder): *"according to the Pythagorean ambassadors, the things of numbers are as the principle and source and root of all things."* Both, however, respected the *technical* names of the Pythagoreans. Let us look at each: *Basis* (base/foundation) is believed to have been used in the rhythmic books of the Pythagoreans; Plato, *Republic* III. 399: *"for following the harmonies would be for us the matter concerning rhythms, not to pursue them in their variety, nor all sorts of bases (βάσεις), but to see what are the rhythms of a orderly and brave life."* Which Longinus reflects upon in *On the Sublime* XXXIV. 2 (where see Ruhnken and the other interpreters cited by Ast in *Comment. ad Republ.* p. 457). Compare Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *De Compositione* XXII. p. 298 and p. 334, ed. Schaefer. Ernesti, *Lex. Technol. Graecc. Rhetor.* p. 56. Add Olympiodorus in *Alcib. pr.* p. 79: *"for 'basis' is a common name for 'arsis' and 'thesis', which are of the rhythm."* And Franc. Goeller on Dionysius, *De Compositione* p. 187 and p. 300, and there cited Hermann, *De metrorum quorundam mensura rhythmica* p. V, where it is taught what *basis* is to musicians: namely, now *thesis*, now *the place and seat of a full foot*, now even *the whole movement of a number*. Ficinus, however, accepted *basis* simply for *firmament*. But if you believe Plotinus respected the passage of Plato in *Timaeus* p. 81. a. (p. 119, Bekker), you could interpret *basis* here as *vessel, receptacle*; concerning which meaning of the word see Lindau on *Timaeus* in the place cited, p. 123. I decide nothing.—The next, *πηγὴν καὶ ῥίζαν* (source and root), remind one of the Pythagorean oath (in Sextus Empiricus, *Adv. Mathemm.* IV. 2. VII. 94; Plutarch, *De Iside* p. 381. E.; *De Placitt. Philoss.* I. 3. p. 527. Wyttenbach; Iamblichus, *Life of Pythagoras* XXVIII. 150. p. 316. and XXIX. 162. p. 344. Kiessling; and among many others):
*"By him who gave to our soul the tetractys"*
*"Holding the source and the root of ever-flowing nature."*
where our manuscripts partly confirm the reading *ἀενάου* (ever-flowing), but all have either *ῥίζωμάτ' ἔχ.* or *ῥίζωμέτ' ἔχ.* I do not tarry here over the remaining variation, intending to give these Iamblichean matters to the public at another time, if God permits. I come to the word *ἀρχήν* (principle). Philolaus in Iamblichus, *In Nicomachus* p. 109, Tenulius: *"for he says, One, is the principle of all things"* (cf. Boeckh’s *Philolaus* p. 150.) Alexander in Diogenes Laertius VIII. 25: *"The Monad is the principle of all things."* Anonymous in Stobaeus, *Eclogues Phys.* I. 2. 9. p. 20. Heeren, and in Theo c. IV: *"that they introduced the principles of numbers"* (cf. de Gelder on Theo p. 136 and p. 140 ff.) Stobaeus, *Eclogues* I. 11. 12. p. 298 ff.: *"Pythagoras—calls numbers principles."* I have reserved these things pertaining to this entire chapter for the end on purpose. Proclus in *Theol. Plat.* IV. 22. p. 231: *"Since Plotinus places number before the Autozoon, and says that the First Being produces number from itself, and that this is established in the middle, between the One Being and the Autozoon, being the base and the place of beings, it is worth saying briefly concerning this also."* A longer disputation follows, which must be read in his own work. That Proclus added *καὶ τόπον* (and place) after *βάσιν* (base) shows that in this place it should not be accepted in that musical sense which we touched upon above, but for *foundation*, as Ficinus also rightly translates in our passage. At the end of the same page, the same Proclus in the place cited posited this:—*"for this tetrad subsisted before as the source of every formation."*

p. 1245, 4. *βούλομαι—πλῆθος χρυσοῦ ἢ οἰκείων* ("I want... a multitude of gold or of household [servants]")] So I have written with Ficinus instead of *οἰκιῶν* (houses). A trace of that reading was preserved by the Vatican book showing *οἰκειῶν*.

— 14. *ἕκαστόν τε ἓν, εἰ ὁμοῦ πολλὰ ἦν τὸ ἓν τὸ ἐπ' αὐτοῖς* ("and each thing is one, if the one upon them was many together")] So I have written with most manuscripts instead of *πολλὰ ὁμοῦ*. Moreover, Ficinus translated this sentence, which according to the Greek stands thus: "But if indeed each is one, if the one which is in them were many at once." Soon in the Latin, I added *decies* (ten times) to the word *millenarius*, and at *mille* I placed *decies millies* (ten thousand times). Soon I gave *προσφωνεῖσθαι* (to be addressed) instead of *προφανεῖσθαι* (to appear), not without the support of manuscripts and Ficinus’s version. Then the same expressed: *δεικνύντων ὥσπερ τὰ χρώματα τοὺς ἀριθμοὺς αὐτῶν*. p. 1246, 13. *ἢ αὐτοαγαθὸν* ("or the Good-itself")] Elsewhere *αὐταγαθόν*. Concerning both, see the note on I. 8. 13. above, p. 80. D. Sceptics on the other hand departed into all other views concerning number. See the disputes of Sextus Empiricus, *Pyrrhon. Hypotypp.* III. 18, of which I only add the beginning of §. 157. p. 166. Fabric.: *"The difficulty concerning number has entered in. For it is said that if there is number, either the numbered things themselves are the number, or it is something else beyond these from outside. p. 1248, 16. *ἓν ψιλὸν ἀπηρημωμένον τῇ οὐσίᾳ αὐτοῦ* ("one bare thing, stripped of its essence")] Concerning the verb *ἀπερημοῦσθαι* (to be stripped/desolated) we spoke above at II. 6. 1. p. 179. A. Iamblichus enumerates various definitions of Unity in *Nicomachus* p. 11 ff. Cf. also Theo Smyrnaeus in *Platon. Mathemat.* c. We have corrected individual words from the manuscripts.

p. 1250, 5. *πρὸς οὓς περὶ αὐτῶν καιρίως ἂν λέγοιτο* ("to whom it would be said opportunely concerning them")] I did not hesitate to adopt the Medicean reading with Ficinus instead of the common *κυρίως* (properly). And *κύριος* is often confused with *καίριος* (opportune). Concerning which matter Jacobs recently noted on Philostratus’s *Images* (p. 92) p. 531. Pollux treats this family of words in *Onomasticon* VI. 204. p. 688. Hemsterhuis. Hence *καιριολεκτεῖν* (to speak opportunely). The opposite is *ἄνευ καιροῦ λέγειν* (to speak without opportunity). Cf. Matthaei on John Chrysostom, *Oratt. Selectt.* III. note 189. p. 52. Poets instead of that also say *καίρια*, as Callimachus, *Epigram* XXXVII. 2. *καιριωτέρως* (more opportunely) is found in Xenophon, *Cyrop.* IV. 5. 15.

— 9. *οὐδ' ἡ ἑορτὴ παρὰ τοὺς συναχθέντας καὶ εὐθυμουμένους ἐπὶ ἱεροῖς* ("neither is the festival besides those gathered and rejoicing at the rites")] So I have written on the authority of good books instead of *εὐθυμουμένους*. This itself is added according to the custom of the Greek peoples especially, who used to perform almost all festivals joyfully, nor did they judge what was sad to be pleasing to the gods. Concerning which matter, there is nothing much to add after Spanheim’s note on Callimachus’s *Delos* v. 324, with which compare Plutarch, *De Iside et Osiride* p. 360 at the end and p. 361. A. and Wyttenbach’s *Animadvv.* on it, p. 207 ff. Moreover, this passage of Plotinus should be recorded in Lexicons, because here *ἑορτὴ* (festival) has a very rare meaning. Cf. the immediately preceding: *"both a crowd and a festival and an army and a multitude"*. Therefore in this place *ἑορτὴ* is the same as *πανήγυρις* (general assembly), or *"a multitude of festival-goers"*. Proclus in *Alcib. pr.* XVIII. p. 56 introduces *χορδὺν* (string/cord) disputing on the force of the word *ὄχλος* (crowd), which he distinguishes from *πλῆθος* (multitude) simply, also from *δῆμος* (people), and finally from *χορός* (chorus). I cite a passage of Nilus on the eight vices c. II. p. 420 (in *Opuscull. Graecorr. sententiosis* ed. Jo. Conr. Orelli): *"The sight of a woman is a poisoned arrow; it wounds the soul, and deposits the venom; and as long as it lingers, it produces more rot. He who guards against these arrows does not frequent public assemblies, nor go about gapping in festivals"* (Cod. Palatin. Heidelberg. N. 356. fol. recto with a notable variation: *"produces; the one struck [?] with paler letters. perhaps πτοούμενος [terrified]? he does not throw these arrows at assemblies; he does not linger in peoples nor in festivals...*

*...go about gapping."*) for it is better to be at leisure for prayer remaining at home (Cod. at constant leisure for prayer) than thinking that honoring the festivals (Cod. or through honoring the festivals) they become a side-task for enemies (Cod. become a side-task for the enemies).

— 13. *ἢ ὅτι μὲν ὡδὶ, ὁ δ' ὡδὶ* ("or that indeed thus, and he thus")] We received the Vatican reading *ἢ ὅτι ὁ μὲν ὡδὶ*, unless I had seen from not a few other places that this is characteristic of Plotinian brevity, so that in the second member such things are left to be supplied by thought, not by writing, from the first member.

p. 1251, 3. *ἄλλου μὲν ὄντος τοῦ φανέντος τοῦ ἀνθρώπου—τοῦ ἕν* ("the man who appeared being one thing... [and another] of the One")] Plotinus seems to respect Aristotle’s disputation in *Metaphysics* III. 2. p. 49 ff. Sylburg (p. 62—70, Brandis). Moreover, cf. below VI. 8. 2. p. 758.

p. 1252, 2. *ἡ διάνοια δηλόν που ἐνταῦθα ποιεῖ ἢ διδοῦσα τὸ ἓν—ἡ ὀξέως—ἰδοῦσα* ("the thought clearly makes it there, either giving the one... or sharply seeing")] Ficinus in Medicean I read what was written by the second hand, or he corrected it himself as *οὐ διδοῦσα* (not giving). But since in the other member the Vatican manuscript offers *ἢ*, I suspect both should be read as *ἢ διδοῦσα—ἢ ὀξέως ἰδοῦσα*, “either giving (imparting) the one,—or sharply perceiving.”—Moreover, for these and the following, Aristotle should be applied in *Metaphysics* VI. p. 134 at the bottom, Brandis, and IX. 1. p. 192; from which I pluck these last words: *"the one is therefore said in so many ways, namely the continuous by nature and the whole, and the singular and the universal"*: “In so many ways then is 'one' said, namely the continuous by nature and the whole and the singular and the universal.” He expounds on the notion of multitude (*πλήθους*) in the same place III. p. 63 and IV. p. 106. Regarding the same notions compare also Porphyry's *Sententt.* XV. p. 223 and Proclus's *Institut. Theolog.* LXII. p. 96 and our author himself above V. 3. p. 496 ff.

— 7. *δῆλον ὅτι—ὑφεστώσης* ("it is clear that... subsisting")] Edition: *δ. ὅτι τοῦ ὄντος ἑνός τινος φύσεως καὶ ὑφεστώσης*. Margin of the Edition: *δ. ὅτι ὄντος ἑνός τινος φ. κ. ὑφ.* We have received the reading which all the best books show and Marsilius expressed. Soon at B. line 5, we did not wish to depart from the common reading, which everyone maintains. One Marc. B. with the margin of the Edition omits *αὐτοῖς* after the words *ἐν τε τοῖς αἰσθητοῖς* (both in sensibles).

p. 1253, 8. *'Ἀλλ' οὗ χρεία—καὶ νοήσεως* ("But of which there is need... and of thought")] I have emended these partly from the margin of the Edition and partly from our books. *πρὸς παντὸς γένεσιν* (toward the generation of everything), which Ficinus expressed, is also confirmed by the Darmstadt manuscript and indeed by those things which immediately follow: *πρὸς τὴν τούτων γένεσιν* (toward the generation of these).

p. 1254, 7. *τῆς αἱρέσεως αὐτὸ φθειράσης* ("the choice having destroyed it")] Ficinus expressed *τ. διαιρέσεως* (the division), and thus he himself seems to have corrected it in Medicean I. For no other book shows this reading, which however you may hold as genuine, if you consider how easily through Iotacism that *δι* especially after *τῆς* could have been absorbed in pronunciation. Soon with Ficinus and Cod. Marc. B. I gave *τὸ αὐτὸ* instead of *τῷ αὐτῷ*.

p. 1255, 8. *Τί οὖν τὸ κύριον αἴτιον; κ. τ. λ.* ("What then is the principal cause? etc.")] This example is also found elsewhere (namely *that it is one by the presence of the One, but two of the Dyad, just as also white of white* etc.). See above IV. 3. 2. VI. 3. 4. (p. 619. A.B.C.). Moreover, it is Aristotelian. See, for example, *Metaphysics* VI. 4 and 5. p. 107 ff. Sylburg (p. 132 ff. Brandis); XII. 8. p. 230 (p. 281). And in this entire disputation Plotinus institutes a refutation especially of Aristotle. Namely in *Metaphysics* XII (or XIII) 8. p. 228 Sylburg (p. 279, Brandis), after he touches on the decrees of Plato and the Pythagoreans concerning numbers, the Stagirite philosopher thus proceeds: *"if therefore it is necessary, if indeed number is one of the beings in itself, that it be one of these aforementioned ways, but none of these is possible, it is manifest that there is no such nature of number as those who make it separate establish."* Then after a more abundant disputation on numbers (*monad, dyad, triad—decad*) p. 233 (p. 285), he thus concludes the reasoning: *"all these and other such things make it manifest that it is impossible for number and magnitudes to be separate; and furthermore that the first ones disagree concerning numbers is a sign that these things, not existing, provide the confusion for them."* These last things agree exactly with those which we brought forth above at p. 680. F. from Sextus Empiricus, *Pyrrh. Hypp.* p. 166. Plotinus, on the contrary, as in almost this entire sixth Ennead, so in this book stands as the defender of that ancient doctrine of the primordial and perennial substance of numbers.—Concerning the *Dyad*, see the Pythagorean decrees expounded in Proclus, *In Plato’s Tim.* p. 54 ff.; cf. Theo in *Platon. Math.* c. V. p. 30, Bullialdus; Plutarch, *De Placitt. philoss.* I. 7. p. 545; *Theolog. Arithm.* 9. p. 7. Ast, and the *Annotations* on Jo. Laurentius Lydus, *De Mensibus* II. 6. p. 48 ff. Roether. I touched upon Plato's passages concerning the *dyad* above in the note on V. 4. 2. p. 518. A.

p. 1257, 7. *'Εν δὲ τῷ νῷ—νοῦ ἐνέργειαι* ("But in the intellect... activities of intellect")] First I wrote *οἱ νοῖ* for *ὡς νοῖ* with Ficinus and from the traces of the Vatican manuscript; then with the same and several manuscripts: *πρώτως* (primarily) for *πρῶτος* (first); then from the margin of the Edition and all manuscripts I recalled: *ὡς δὲ ἐν νῷ* (but as in intellect). The Edition has: *ὡς οὐδ' ἐν νῷ* (as not even in intellect). Moreover, this Plotinian disputation depends on Plato's *Timaeus* p. 41 ff. (p. 43 ff. If these do not come into being, the heaven will be incomplete; for it will not have all the genera of living beings in it, but it must, if it is to be sufficiently perfect."* and those things which follow concerning the generation of the particular soul and the rest; which are to be compared with those things which are handed down in the same place concerning the soul of the universe p. 34—38, and Plutarch’s *Concerning the Procreation of the Soul in the Timaeus* p. 1016 ff. (p. 136 ff. Wyttenbach) should be applied. Plotinus has these Platonic passages before his eyes in other books too. See, for example, p. 326. 329. 330. 376. 470. 473. 489. 562. 674. In our passage apply Proclus in *Theol. Platon.* IV. 32. p. 231. Furthermore, concerning the *perfect number* and the virtues, of which Plotinus makes mention immediately, consult Ficinus on Plato’s *Republic*, Dialogue VIII. c. 17, that is, the Platonic passage p. 576 ff. which we touched upon above at p. 675. B.

p. 1258, 10. *Ἀρχὴ οὖν καὶ πηγὴ—ὁ ἀριθμὸς—ἀληθής* ("Therefore the principle and source... number... true")] See above p. 679. E. and the note on that passage. Cf. also the preceding chapter p. 686. C. Moreover, this entire Plotinian passage includes things no less hidden and obscure than that Platonic one in the *Parmenides*, where it is disputed concerning the One and concerning being, and which, regarding the argument, is to be compared with this Plotinian one p. 144 ff. p. 1259, 10. *Λεκτέον οὖν—ὡς ὅταν μὲν—ὅταν τοίνυν—εἴπῃς—μερίζων καθ' ἕνα—ποσού* ("It must be said then... as when indeed... whenever therefore... you say... dividing according to one... of quantity")] First I consulted this passage by punctuating; then, for the common readings *ἐνταῦθα—εἴποις—μερίζον*, I restored the proper ones from our manuscripts; then by exterminating these words interposed in the Edition and a few manuscripts between *αἰσθητοῖς* (sensibles) and *ἀλλὰ καθαρῶς ἓν* (but purely one): *"πῶς ὁ ἀριθμὸς ὁ μὲν οὐσιώδης ὁ δὲ ποσώδης: How one number is essential, the other quantitative"*; which also show a manifest character of a Lemma, nor were they rendered in Latin by Ficinus.

p. 1260, 8. *Τί γὰρ ἂν γένοιτο—ἄλλῳ ἀνθρώπῳ—ἀριθμουμένῳ.* ("For what would happen... to another man... being numbered.")] In the Edition is written *αὐτῷ* (to him) for *ἀνθρώπῳ* (to man), by a vice arising from a shorthand mark: as in our Palatine Heidelberg manuscript of Lysias N. 88, you may see this sort of shorthand compendium used rather frequently. Soon *καὶ ποσῶν τοῦτο δέκα*. In the margin of the Edition is *καὶ ποσῶν τοῦτο δέκα*, in the context of the Edition: *καὶ ποσὸν τοῦτο τὸ δέκα.* I have joined both. Nor did Ficinus do otherwise. Nicolaus of Methone against Proclus’s *Inst. Theolog.* c. 70. p. 97: *"bodies made quantitative"* (*σώματα πεποσωμένα*). Soon after the words *καὶ σοί* (and to you), which a learned hand, probably that of Marsilius himself, added in the margin of Medicean manuscript A; and certainly you would say these have fallen out, if you consider what immediately follows. I however, without the authority of the manuscripts, did not wish to insert them into the text. Recently for: *ἢ μὲν πρὸ τοῦ ἀριθμεῖν*, the margin of the Edition has *ὁ πρὸ μὲν τὸ δέκα.* Concerning the examples of *"army, chorus"* etc. we have seen above at p. 682. C. D.

*χουσαν φύσιν* (partaking nature): in its margin *μετέχων (sic) φησίν*, which seems to be a correction by someone who judged it necessary for this Participle to be referred to the preceding *ἀριθμός*. Separately, however, this sentence is to be accepted: *It is a partaker, he says, of number and harmony*. Soon *ἀριθμὸς ἄρα ἡ ψυχή* κ. τ. λ. (therefore the soul is a number...). The source of these opinions is in the celebrated passage of the Platonic *Timaeus* concerning the generation of souls p. 35 ff. (p. 32 ff. Bekker), which Gellius III. 10, or rather Varro in his *Hebdomades* cited by him, has before his eyes, and Macrobius in *Dream of Scipio* I. 6. Who indeed: “Hence also the Timaeus of Plato remembered that God the maker of the mundane soul interwove its parts from the even and the odd, that is, from the double and triple number.—The preceding treatise, however, found that numbers were even before the soul of the world, with which that was most augustly woven together, the reason of nature itself in the Timaeus being conscious and a witness. Hence it is that the wise have not hesitated to pronounce that the soul is a self-moving number.” (A disputation follows on the septenary number; on which it suffices now to have cited Valckenaer’s disputation on Aristobulus the Jew p. 97 ff.) Cf. the same Macrobius II. 2. Porphyry in *Sententt.* XIX. p. 225 Cambridge: *"for whenever the living being perceives, the soul is like a separate harmony, moving the strings from itself having been tuned; but to the inseparable harmony in the strings, the body."* Cf. Plotinus himself above p. 307. E. F. But because Plato in the *Phaedo* refutes the opinion of those who established that the human soul was a harmony, this by no means fights with his own doctrine in the *Timaeus* in the place cited, where he teaches that the soul was made by God from diverse matters according to a certain ratio and proportion, and Proclus in *Timaeum* III. p. 178 vindicated him from the charge of inconsistency in this cause. Wyttenbach treats this more fully in *Phaedonem* p. 248. Moreover, those decrees of the *Timaeus* are respected by the so-called Hermes in *Poimandres* I. 24. p. 11, ed. Geneva 1630, in the passage concerning the return of the human soul, whose faculties of the senses he says are resolved and restored each to its own sphere: *"and both anger and desire go into the irrational nature. Thus it rushes for the rest (leg. τὸ λοιπὸν) upward through the harmony, and to the first zone it gives the augmenting activity and the diminishing. and to the second the device of evils"* etc.—*"and to the seventh zone the ensnaring lie, and then stripped of the activities of the harmony he reaches the eighth nature having his own power, and hymns the father with the beings."* Where we will either note the rarer construction *γυμνωθεὶς ἀπὸ τῶν ἐνεργημάτων* (stripped of the activities), which writers of a later age frequent (Dorville on *Chariton* p. 534, ed. Leipzig; Borger on *Epist. ad Galat.* I. 1. p. 78), or we shall substitute *ὑπὸ* (by), or if perhaps, which however is hardly probable, he wrote: *γυμνωθεὶς ἀπὸ τῶν ἐνεργημάτων* instead of *γυμνωθεὶς τῶν ἐνεργ.* and wished not so much the liberating harmony of the spheres to be understood, as the sensible harmony of the human soul, from which the mind is liberated, in the preceding for *διὰ τῆς ἁρμονίας* (through the harmony), we shall necessarily write *δίχα τῆς ἁρμονίας* (without the harmony).

**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

The manuscripts [MSS] of the books read *ἐν τῇ μεγίστῃ* [in the greatest]. I have adopted, along with three Marcian manuscripts, a more refined reading, which the scribes, failing to grasp, replaced with *ἐν*. However, it is to be understood as *τῆς μεγίστης* [of the greatest] or *ἢ τὴν μεγίστην* [or the greatest]. Cf. Matthiæ, *Greek Grammar*, § 455, note 3. a. Regarding the argument, it can only be understood by one who has compared Plato’s discussion in the *Philebus*, where he treats the "limit" [*πέρας*] and the "unlimited" [*ἄπειρον*] especially from Pythagorean principles, p. 16 ff. [sqq.], p. 32 ff. [sqq.]. See Stallbaum with his *Prolegomena*, p. L ff. [sqq.]. On Plotinus’ view that "the unlimited is at odds with number" [*τὸ γὰρ ἄπειρον μάχεται τῷ ἀριθμῷ*], compare these passages in the *Philebus*, p. 25, p. 65 f. [sq.]. Stallbaum: "that which, by introducing the nature of the equal and the double... brings to an end the state of opposites being at variance with one another, and by establishing symmetry and harmony, produces number." Here Baumgarten-Crusius teaches that "number" signifies *anything defined and ordered*; which itself constitutes the character of the "limit" [*τοῦ πέρατος*]. Cf. the passages cited by him in the *Epinomis*, p. 979. a.; Diogenes Laertius III. 10.—Nevertheless, regarding infinite number, consult Proclus, *On Euclid’s Elements*, Book I, c. 2, and Plotinus above, VI. 6. 2. at the beginning, where we find "the number of infinity" [*ὁ ἀριθμὸς τῆς ἀπειρίας*].

[[margin: p. 1262, 9.]] *Τί οὖν ἐκεῖ γραμμὴ καὶ ποῦ; ὕστερον μὲν [γὰρ] ἀριθμοῦ.* [What then is the line there, and where? For it is later than number.] I have enclosed *γὰρ* in brackets, as two manuscripts omit it and it recurs immediately. In these and the following lines, Plotinus had before his eyes the passage on "soul-generation" [*ψυχογονίᾳ*] in Plato’s *Timaeus*, p. 35 f. [sq.], p. 32 f. [sq.] Bekker, on which Chalcidius, p. 105, p. 288 Fabricius, writes: “For that which has no parts, and therefore does not come under the senses, yet exists and is perceived by the mind; geometers call it a mark [point]; a line, however, they call a length without breadth, which ends at its marks: furthermore, that in which there is some breadth, they call a surface, so that a surface is a length that has acquired breadth. But that which consists of three dimensions—namely length, breadth, and depth—they name a solid body.” Macrobius, in *The Dream of Scipio* I. 5, likewise discusses many things regarding this Platonic argument, from which I shall excerpt only these: “From these things it appears that number is prior to surfaces and lines, of which we mentioned the former consists, and to all forms. For from lines one ascends to number as to something prior, so that it may be understood that from different numbers of lines, geometric forms are described.” Cf. Proclus, *On Euclid’s Elements* II. 11. Cf. also Plotinus himself, IV. 4. 23 and VI. 5. 11.

[[margin: p. 1263, 3.]] *οἷον πυρὶ—ἡ ἐκεῖ πυραμίς* [As with fire—the pyramid there.] Plato in the *Timaeus*, p. 56, p. 71 f. [sq.] Bekker: “Let the solid form of the pyramid be the element and seed of fire.” Cf. Plutarch, *Platonic Questions*, p. 609 f. [sq.]; Chalcidius, *On the Timaeus*, p. 90 f. [sq.], p. 283 Fabricius; Theon, *On the Mathematics of Plato*, XXXVIII, p. 152 Bulialdus.

[[margin: —9.]] *’Αλλὰ νοῦς, φησὶν, ὅσα ὁρᾷ ἐν τῷ παντελεῖ ζῴῳ* [But Intellect, he says, sees as many things as are in the complete living being.] Plato, *Timaeus* p. 30, p. 27 Bekker: “in the complete living being.” Ibid. p. 39 at the end, p. 40: “In the same way, therefore, as Intellect perceives the Ideas existing in the 'Living Being that is,' of what sort they are and how many, so he thought this [world] also ought to have such and so many.” Plotinus referred to these words in three places above: p. 203 at the end and following, p. 356. A, p. 362. B.

[[margin: p. 1264, 1.]] *οὐδ’ ἐλείφθη τις οὐδè λειφθήσεται, ἵνα καὶ προστεθῇ αὐτῷ.* [Nor was any left behind, nor shall be, so that something might be added to it.] Thus I did not hesitate to write, partly with the Codex, partly with Ficinus [Fic.], instead of *ἐλήφθη—ληφθήσεται—προτεθῇ*.

[[margin: —11.]] *ἀλλ’ ἡ πρώτη καὶ ἐναργεστάτη (ζωὴ) καὶ τὸ τρανὸν ἔχουσα τοῦ [ζῇν]* [But the first and most manifest (life), having the clarity of [living].] Our philosopher, above I. 4. 2: "a clearer [*τρανωτέρα*] life." IV. 4. 20: "the clear [*τρανὴν*] desire." Proclus, *Elements of Theology* 145, p. 214 ff. [sqq.] our edition: “And the stone participates in the purifying power only bodily; but the plant, even more clearly [*τρανώτερον*], according to its life; and the animal has this form also according to impulse”; i.e., *more clearly, more distinctly, more effectively*. Cf. those whom I cited at that passage, p. 216; add the annotations of Coraïs on Theodoros Prodromos, verse [vs.] 124, in *Ataktis* I, p. 112.

[[margin: —15.]] *ἀγαθώτερον αὐτὸ—παρέχεται* [renders it more good.] Thus I wrote with the best Codices. However, after *ἐπιχρώσας* [having colored], a *τε* [and] is missing, unless you prefer to insert *καὶ* before that participle. On the Alexandrian form *ἀγαθώτερον*, see [vid.] Fischer on Weller II. 95 f. [sq.] and Sturz, *On the Alexandrian Dialect*, p. 143. On the meaning of this passage, compare above p. 556 f. [sq.] and below p. 714 f. [sq.].

[[margin: p. 1265, 4.]] *καὶ μᾶλλον εὐτόνως ζῶντα ὁρᾷν* [and to see them living more vigorously.] Ficinus translates this not badly. Cf. on this adverb, Sturz, *Lexicon of Xenophon* II, p. 420; Schleusner, *Lexicon of the New Testament* under the word; and Valckenaer, *Scholia on the New Testament* I, p. 558 f. [sq.]. In Pollux’s *Onomasticon* IX. 105: “it was necessary to send the ball back after striking it vigorously [*εὐτόνως*] against the ground,” learned men conjecture *ἐντόνως* [intensely] or *εὐπόνως* [with ease]. I see no suitable reason for either. Lucian, *Nigrinus* 36, p. 77 f. [sq.] Hemsterhuis, concerning archers: “but some of them, stretching the strings too much, shoot more vigorously [*εὐτονώτερον*] than is necessary.” Josephus,
