**BOOK VI. ENNEAD SIX. p. 1262—1267.**

*On the Jewish War* IV. 8. 4. p. 295 Havercamp: “and the cavalry cut off their fugitives, and the infantry vigorously [*εὐτόνως*] destroyed the skirmishes,” where the verb immediately follows: “nor were they able to break the phalanx.” In Aristophanes, *Plutus* 1096: *εὐτόνως προσίσχεσθαι* is *to cling firmly, tenaciously*. See [Vid.] Fischer, p. 286. Cf. also Matthiæ on John Chrysostom, *Homilies* IV, p. 125 and III, p. 4. Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogus* III, p. 297 Potter, in the description of a virgin by Zeno the Stoic: “the neck not supine, nor the limbs of the body relaxed, but the upper parts like things that are intense [*ἐντόνοις*].” I shall see if I can elicit a better emendation by the conjecture of another critic. For the time being, I suspect: “nor other members of the body relaxed [*ἀνειμένα*], but the upper parts like things that are vigorously firm [*εὐτόνοις*]” (Sylburg noted this reading instead of *ἐντόνοις* from the Palatine Codex); i.e., “no supine neck, nor the remaining members of the body relaxed, but the upper parts (which are most usually seen) like those that are nobly firm (nobly intense).” For *εὔτονος* is also *γενναῖος* [noble] (Zonaras, *Greek Lexicon*, p. 903).

[[margin: —18.]] *ὥστε ταύτῃ Παρμενίδης ὀρθῶς ἓν εἰπὼν τὸ ὂν καὶ οὐ δι’ ἐρημίαν ἄλλου ἀπαθές* [So that in this respect Parmenides was right in calling Being one and impassive, not through the lack of anything else.] Fragments of Parmenides, verses [v.] 97 ff. [sqq.]:
— — — for there is nothing else, nor will there be
other than Being; since Fate bound it
to be whole and immovable; wherefore all things are a name,
which mortals have established, believing them to be true:
both to come into being and to perish, to be and not to be,
and to change place, and to alter bright color.
Cf. Brandis, *Commentaries on the Eleatics* I, p. 118, and the passages cited by him: Plato, *Parmenides* p. 132. b. c., 134. a.; *Sophist* p. 252. e., etc.; *Theaetetus* p. 180. d. e., and other places. Compare also Plotinus above, p. 648. A. Moreover, I have written *ἐρημίαν* [solitude/lack] at the bidding of the best books, and therefrom I corrected the version of Marsilius [Ficino].

**BOOK VII.**

[[margin: p. 1267, 7.]] **ON HOW THE MULTITUDE OF IDEAS SUBSISTED, AND CONCERNING THE GOOD.** As some Codices offer *καὶ περὶ τ’ ἀγαθοῦ*, the same variation appears in two places in Porphyry’s *Life of Plotinus*, chapters V and XXVI. From the same source, we learn that this book is to be placed thirty-ninth in order, if one calculates the time when each was composed. However, there is no reason to say much in advance about its argument after those things which I indicated both at the beginning of the book on the first Good and the other Goods (*Ennead* I, p. 61) and at p. 169. A. How close a bond this book has with the preceding one on Numbers, the argument of both teaches. Yet no one will regret reading what Brandis has discussed concerning the ratios of numbers, ideas, and the Good from the doctrine of Plato, Speusippus, and other Academics in his *Diatribe on the lost books of Aristotle on Ideas and on the Good or Philosophy*, 10, pp. 61–68. From which it has pleased me to apply these few points (p. 65 f. [sq.]): “But some things the Platonists derived from the 'defined dyad' using numbers, others directly from the principles, namely from the 'supreme unity' and that 'dyad'; (Aristotle, *Metaphysics* XIII. 8. p. 230. 10. Sylburg)—That he (Plato) referred the Good [*τὸ ἀγαθόν*] to the supreme unity is excellently demonstrated both by what he discusses in Book VII of the *Republic*, and by those Aristotelian words, and finally by the indices of the commentaries which Aristotle and others left written concerning Plato’s philosophy. Therefore, there is no doubt that Plato was among those of whom Aristotle says: 'Of those who say that there are immovable substances, some say that the One itself is the Good itself; they thought, however, that its substance was most of all the One.' (*Metaph.* XIV. 4. p. 246 f. [sq.] Sylburg, p. 301 Brandis.)—Furthermore, as to the reason by which all things depend on the Idea of the Good, Plato does not seem to have pursued it with enough accuracy in the Schools. Aristotle certainly affirms that the notion of the 'final cause' [*τοῦ οὗ ἕνεκα*] was neglected in the Platonic philosophy, and Alexander in the *Commentary on the Good* warns that it was not treated. (There follows a passage of Aristotle in *Metaph.* I. 6. p. 18. 3. Sylburg, p. 23 Brandis, and Alexander upon it.)” These things can teach anyone that after Plato and the Academics, there remained a most ample material in these questions concerning ideas and the Supreme Good in which philosophers might labor, and in which Plotinus himself also labored in these very books.

[[margin: —10.]] *φωσφόρα περὶ τὸ πρόσωπον ἔθηκεν ὄμματα* [he placed luminous eyes about the face] Plato in the *Timaeus* p. 45. a. b., p. 50 Bekker: “And of the organs, they first fashioned luminous eyes, binding them in for such a reason.” Plutarch, *On the Face in the Orb of the Moon* p. 928. B.: “just as luminous eyes fixed in the face of the universe, they wander about.” The same, *On Fortune* p. 98. B.: “Plato says not sight nor luminous eyes”; to which

--- Page 393 ---
**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

passage Wyttenbach, in his *Animadversions* p. 670, cites *ἐτεκτήναντο* [fashioned] from Plato, doubtless by a slip of memory or pen. The error of previous editions of Plato showing *συνεκτήναντο* also appears in the marginal correction [*παραδιορθώσει*] which someone made in the margin of Codex Med. B. in the discourse of Plotinus, ordering *ἐκτήνατο* [sic] to be written instead of *ἔθηκε*. But that error had already been removed by Jungermann for Pollux in the *Onomasticon*, citing Plato’s words, II. 63. p. 183, Hemsterhuis edition. Whether it should be conjectured from the cited passage of Plutarch and Plotinus that Plato’s words were anciently fuller, certainly that the word *πρόσωπον* [face] was read there, I would not say. For in Stobaeus' *Eclogues* I. 55. p. 1110, Heeren edition, Plato’s words are not shown in full, and Proclus’ Commentary does not reach as far as that place. The written books in Immanuel Bekker's critical apparatus offer nothing more. Lindau, at this place in the *Timaeus*, noted nothing about the reading; nor indeed did he know the passages of Plutarch and Plotinus.

[[margin: p. 1268, 3.]] *ταῦτα δὲ εἰδὼς* [but knowing these things etc.] The *δὲ* was wrongly neglected in the Vatican Codex; for it serves the apodosis. See [Vid.] Wolf on Demosthenes, *Against Leptines* p. 297, and Buttmann on *Against Meidias* p. 126 f. [sq.], Spalding edition. Soon, partly with Ficinus, partly with the Codices, I wrote *καὶ δι’ ὧν ἐνεργήσουσιν ὀργάνων* [and through what organs they shall act].

[[margin: —10.]] *ἵνα ἄλλου ὦσι, καὶ ἵνα ἐν κακῷ εἶεν,—ἵνα σώζοιτο ἐν τῷ κακῷ* [so that they might belong to another, and so that they might be in evil,—so that it might be preserved in evil.] Thus we have written by the example of many books and Ficinus and the margin. In the first member, the sudden change of construction from the Subjunctive to the Optative is to be observed; in the second member, *ἵνα* with the Optative has the meaning of a thing we wish to happen, or hope for, and which we think can happen (cf. Matth. *Gr. Gr.* § 514. and § 518. 4.). But reflecting on this association of the Subjunctive with the Optative, it now pleases me less that above at II. 2. 1. p. 108. C: *Θεῖ οὖν ἐν ᾧ ἔχει—οὐχ ἵνα μένοι* (the best books have *μένῃ*), *ἀλλ’ ἵνα φέροιτο*, I placed *φέρηται*. Otherwise, I judge the second member here is to be understood thus: that the souls, although established in evil (i.e., in this life), if indeed it be possible, are nevertheless preserved.—For the rest, regarding the argument of this place from the beginning of the chapter, I prefer to inquire rather than to decide whether Plotinus reflects on the tenets of Anaxagoras, Democritus, and other ancient philosophers, and perhaps Socrates himself, concerning the plans of the Fashioner of the world in generating and forming animals, likewise on the use of body parts and senses, etc. He who wishes to know these tenets should read Xenophon, *Memorabilia* I. 4. and Aristotle, *On the Parts of Animals* I. 1.—This is certain, that the Platonic *Timaeus* was before Plotinus' mind when he wrote these things.

[[margin: —14.]] *ἀλλὰ αἴσθησις μέν οὔπω—πῶς ἔνι ταύτην τὴν ἕξιν πρὸς αἰσθητοῦ διανόησιν ἀφικέσθαι;* [But sensation is not yet—how is it possible for this habit to arrive at the thought of the sensible?] We have endeavored to attend to this place with the help of the codices and better punctuation. In the final parts, Ficinus expressed the reading of the first Medicean Codex. The reading of the edition and other books is to be translated thus: “How can it be that such a habit arrives at the thought of that which is sensible?” Regarding the word *συμπέρασμα* [conclusion], see what we cited above at page 579. A.—What follows immediately concerning reasoning [*λογισμῷ*] pertains to the cited passage of Plato in the *Timaeus*. For since that philosopher frequently uses the word *λογισμοῦ*, Plotinus warns his readers not to twist it into a false meaning. Indeed, this entire chapter is especially to be held by those who desire to understand Plato’s *Timaeus* correctly.

[[margin: p. 1269, 15.]] *ἀλλ’ εἰ δεῖ ἑκάστην ἐνέργειαν μὴ ἀτελῆ εἶναι* [But if every activity must not be incomplete etc.] Cf. my note on page 519, namely on *Ennead* V. 5. 1. at the beginning.

**John Philoponus, *Against Proclus on the Eternity of the World***

II. 5. And the philosopher Plotinus, in the [book] *On the Intelligibles* or *On the Good*, declared similar things concerning the demiurgic and providential power of God, saying: “Nevertheless, if every activity must not be incomplete, nor is it lawful to think anything else of God than that He is whole and all, all things must be present in whatever is His. There must, therefore, be also eternal being. There must, therefore, be even the future as already present. For there is no 'later' in that. But what is already present there becomes later in another. If therefore the future is already present, it must be present in such a way as having been fore-thought into the later. And this means needing nothing then. And this is, lacking nothing. All things therefore already were and always were. And they were in such a way that one might say 'later this because of that.' For being extended and as it were unfolding, it has the showing of this after that. But being all together, it is this one thing. And this is having in itself also the cause.” And Plotinus, therefore, says that not only existing things but also

--- Page 394 ---
**BOOK VII. ENNEAD SIX. p. 1268—1270.**

future things are already present to God by foreknowledge [*προγνώσει*]. For that which subsists later among things that come to be, he says this is present always in that [God]. Then he added the manner how the future is present to God, namely by thinking even the things not yet existing. For it is necessary, he says, for them to be present in such a way as having been fore-thought into the later. If therefore all things are present to God by foreknowledge, even those not yet existing as if existing, He surely knows in what manner each of the things to come will be and according to what reasons [logoi] they will come to be. And as they come to be, by what reasons following each choice of life they will have the consequences from unerring providence. For Plotinus says all things already were and always were; for "already" shows that before they come to be, the things that will be later are present to God. And lest anyone should think the "already" signifies some beginning, he added "and always were." And they were in such a way, he says, as to say "later this because of that." That is, those things whose causes of generation we think of after their existence—as perhaps only through the activity of reason among the animals here does man use hands, the Fashioner having made hands as organs for the reason. This, therefore, we knew after existence. This "this because of that" always pre-subsisted in the knowledge of God. And this same reason applies not only to whole species, but also to things happening individually to each. Explaining himself, he added: "for being extended," he says, "and as it were unfolding, it has the showing of this after that." That is, being brought into generation. As perhaps after the mixing of the elements, the cohesion and alteration occurs; then the shaping; then the animation. And likewise in all things. "But being all together," he says, "it is this whole thing. And this is having in itself its cause." By "together," he means in the foreknowledge of God. For the reasons [*λόγοι*] of all things are present impartibly in that.

**John Philoponus, *Against Proclus*:**

IV. 16. If therefore, according to pious conceptions of God, God is His own fullness, needing nothing of what has been produced by Him for perfection [*τελείωσιν*], it is clear that He does not receive anything for perfection from the existence of things. Nor from their not being will He be more incomplete than Himself, just as according to Plotinus even the things not yet existing are present to God as existing. We have previously cited for him a passage from the discourse *On the Intelligibles* or *On the Good*, which is worth remembering now. For discussing the demiurgic power of God, he says the same things in those words: “But indeed if every activity must not be incomplete, nor is it lawful to think anything else of God than that He is whole and all, all things must be present in whatever is His. There must, therefore, be also eternal being. There must, therefore, be even the future as already present. For there is no 'later' in that. But what is already present there becomes later in another. If therefore the future is already present, it must be present in such a way as having been fore-thought into the later. And this means needing nothing then. And this is, lacking nothing. All things therefore already were and always were. And they were in such a way that one might say 'later this because of that.' For being extended and as it were unfolding, it has the showing of this after that. But being all together, it is this whole thing. And this is having in itself also the cause.”

**John Philoponus, *Against Proclus* XVI. 3.**

If therefore the knowledge of God is not divided along with the things known, but remaining unchangeably [*ἀμεταβάτως*] in the One it knows all things indivisibly, not only the universal but also the individual and most atomic. God knows each thing in the same way as He established each. Impartibly and unchangeably; not only the universal but even the most atomic. And those having their being in time. And at one time existing, at another not existing. Without Him being moved along with the motion of things that come to be, even if the things coming to be sometimes exist and sometimes do not. If the will of God by its very being produces what it wills, as Proclus says, the will of God therefore impartibly and unchangeably establishes all things according to the One. Not being divided among the things produced. Nor moved about them. But He makes the manifold things in a unified manner. And the divisible impartibly. And those having their being by the transition of time, unchangeably. If the will of God makes even the most atomic things impartibly and unchangeably, without being moved about them—and the particular and most atomic things at one time exist and at another do not—it is possible therefore that even the will of God concerning the world that at some time exists, at one time is and at another is not, without having the "before" and "after," as not being moved about the things produced by it. And with these very things Plotinus also [concurs] etc.

[[margin: p. 1270, 11.]] *ἢ, εἰ δοίημεν, χωρίς.* [or, if we grant, without.] Ficinus expressed *οὐ χωρίς* [not without], which is also read from a correction in Med. A., and Taylor wishes it to be restored in a letter given to me. Other books do not support it. If, however, a negation is required, perhaps *οὐ* could be thought of as repeated from the preceding *οὐκέτι*, which is not unheard of in Plotinian brevity.

[[margin: p. 1271, 12.]] *ταῦτα μηδενὶ ἐλλείποντα, μηδè τῷ διὰ τί ἐλλείπειν.* [these things lacking in nothing, not even lacking in the 'wherefore'.] Thus we have written on the authority of good books. The edition has *τό*. Above I. 5. 9. p. 45. [[margin: p. 1272, 9.]] *ἡ συνυπόστασις* [the co-subsistence] This noun, which is read again below at VI. 7. 40. p. 732. B., must be added to the Lexicons.—Soon: —*καὶ δεῖ μὴ ἀπηρτῆσθαι ἐν αὐτοῖς ἂν ἔχοι τὰ αἰτιατὰ τὰς αἰτίας* [and it is necessary not to be detached, that the effects may have their causes in them]. The Epistle of Phalaris (as it is called) L. p. 168 Lennep: “for when each of you names many causes, you show them to be detached [*ἀπηρτημένας*] outside”; i.e., "alien." Lennepius himself, after others cited by him, accurately treats this force of the verb as meaning "to separate." Regarding its other power, Wyttenbach has no less accurately explained it in his *Animadversions on Plutarch's Consolation to Apollonius* p. 717, beginning thus: “For *ἀπαρτᾶθαί τινος* [to be detached from something] has a double and different notion.”—Therefore *ἀπαρτᾶσθαι* is *to be remote from someone*: —it is also *to be suspended from some thing*, as *ἐξαρτᾶσθαί τινος*. To this latter force pertains the noun *ἀπάρτησις* [dependence/attachment], which is read above V. 1. 2. p. 483. D.—Iamblichus, *On the Mysteries of the Egyptians* I. 8. p. 16 Gale: “But since it is necessary (some books have *μει δή* [sic], wrongly) to aim at reason rather and divine knowledge, but not to discourse against a man, we also for this reason will fit the suspended [*ἐπηρτημένην*] dispute to a reasonable and theological perception.” (Codex Fesch. has *ἀπηρτημένην* [detached] doubt, separate (remote, alien) just as *τὸ ἀπηρτημένον* is read ibid. III. p. 93 and as Lennepius had suggested. And this conjecture is plainly confirmed by the Vienna Codex n. CCLXIV, whose excerpts I owe to my friend Schubart.)

[[margin: p. 1273, 4.]] *οἷον καὶ ἀνθρώπου* [as also of man] Ficinus expressed: *οἷον κατὰ ἄνθρωπον* [as according to man], as it is corrected in Med. A. and written by the first hand in Darmstadt. Nor indeed is it necessary to be so corrected, provided you take the Genitive objectively, as they say, *concerning man*.

[[margin: — 10.]] *ἀλλὰ τὸ βουλεύσασθαι καὶ τὸ λελογίσθαι διὰ τὴν ὑπόθεσιν* [but deliberating and reasoning because of the hypothesis etc.] These things also pertain to those passages of the Platonic *Timaeus* where plans and reasons seem to be attributed to the artisan god in the fashioning of the world. Cf. what I noted above at page 693. A.—Soon the reading of the Vatican book: *τὸ δ’ ἀεὶ γινόμενα ἐνδείξασθαι* pleases me somehow. For the rest, many of Plotinus' views, both elsewhere and stated in this book, magnificently agree with the book which, often translated from Arabic into Latin, falsely bears the name of Aristotle and is titled *On the Theology of the Egyptians* (concerning which book see [vid.] Fabricius, *Bibl. [[margin: p. 1274, 3.]] *καὶ διὰ τί ὀφρύες;* [and why eyebrows?] Ficinus: “Again why nostrils.” I have corrected it since all the MSS books agree on *ὀφρύες* [eyebrows]. What follows immediately: “for even if for the sake of safety etc.” seems said concerning Socrates and those who after him pursued "teleological" reasons, as they call them today. Cf. above p. 692. [[margin: p. 1275, 8.]] *ἀλλ’ εἰ μὲν ζῶον λογικὸν ὁ ἄνθρωπος* [but if man is a rational animal etc.] Plotinus instituted this question *concerning man* again near the end of his life in the little book which Porphyry placed at the threshold of these *Enneads*, namely so that it is now the first book of the first Ennead. It is titled: *What is the Living Being and What is Man?* and is to be compared with this discussion.

[[margin: p. 1276, 9.]] *ἆρ’ οὖν αὐτὸς ὁ λόγος ζῶόν ἐστι λογικὸν, ἢ τὸ συναμφότερον—ἢ ἡ ψυχὴ ὁ ἄνθρωπος* [is then the Logos itself a rational animal, or the composite—or is the soul man? etc.] Plotinus has before his eyes the discussions of Socrates in the *First Alcibiades* p. 123. To which Olympiodorus c. XXIV. p. 202 writes:—"what is our essence; man is not the body, nor the [composite] [*συναμφότερον*]—The categorical argument is such: man uses the body as an organ. For he also masters it, since when he wills, and as far as he wills, and where he wills, he moves it. That which uses the body as an organ is the soul; man therefore is soul" etc. For that entire passage is to be compared with the Plotinian one in chapters XXIV and XXV up to p. 209, where in the notes we have summoned both Plotinus and Julian and others to the discussion.

[[margin: p. 1277, 8.]] *ἐν σώματι δὲ μορφώσασα κατ’ αὐτὴν καὶ ἄλλο εἴδωλον ἀνθρώπου.* [but having formed in the body according to itself also another image of man.] Ficinus expressed: *καθ’ αὑτὴν*, which I would have adopted, if only the books

[[margin: p. 1282, 10.]] *τὸ γὰρ πλῆθος ἐν ἐλλείψει. τί οὖν κωλύει δυάδα εἶναι* [for multitude is in lack. what then prevents it from being a dyad etc.] See [Vid.] what we noted above regarding the "dyad" [*δυάδι*] and the "first otherness" [*πρώτη ἑτερότητι*], which was also called "daring" [*τόλμα*] by the Pythagoreans, at p. 494. A. below. With the end of this chapter, moreover, are to be compared what Plotinus discussed in the book: *If all souls are one?* IV. 9. For the rest, if you read these things in the books of Aristotle, if it please the Gods, *On the Theology of the Egyptians* (concerning which offspring mention was made by us in the note at the beginning of chapter III of this book, p. 695 below), Book XIV. chapter 7: “The multitude of irrational animals, of brutes, is in the intellectual world, because the author is one, and created one world, and first created, *since his unity is not equal to the unity of the creator, he creates many:*” if you read these things, you will confidently pronounce with me: either Plotinus was read by that writer, or both drew this opinion from one and the same source of oriental philosophy, no doubt.

[[margin: p. 1283, 13.]] *ἔνι γάρ πως καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις ζώοις πολλὰ διανοίας ἔργα.* [for there are somehow also in other animals many works of thought.] Anaxagoras had attributed acting reason [*λόγον ἐνεργητικόν*] to all animals, according to Plutarch (as he is called) in *On the Opinions of the Philosophers* V. 20. p. 668 Wyttenbach. But nevertheless Plotinus seems to follow Pythagoras and Plato most in these matters. The same writer in the same place: “Pythagoras and Plato [say] that the souls even of the so-called irrational animals are rational, yet not acting rationally because of the bad mixture of their bodies and their not having the power of speech, just as in the case of apes and dogs; for these speak, but do not articulate.” Concerning rational and irrational animals, Plato discusses briefly in the *Statesman* p. 263, p. 259 Bekker, and accurately Simplicius in Aristotle’s *On the Soul* III, Section 2, number 57; Porphyry, *On Abstinence* III. 16 and passim. Consult those explaining this argument, even among more recent ones such as Descartes, taking Cudworth and Mosheim into account in *The Intellectual System* I. 37. p. 54 ff. [sqq.].

[[margin: p. 1285, 5.]] *οἷον—ἀνεφάνη ὄνυξ καὶ τὸ γαμψώνυχον ἢ τὸ καρχαρόδουν ἢ κέρατος φύσις* [as—there appeared the nail and the crooked-clawed or the jagged-toothed or the nature of the horn.] Thus word for word this place is to be translated, which Ficinus treated rather freely, who also interposed "beak" [*rostrum*], of which no trace exists in the MSS books. Doubtless Marsilio is accustomed rather to look at the universal meaning in such cases. For the rest, lest you think *ὀδοὺς* [tooth] had fallen out, no trace of that word appears in the books, and Plotinus is not accustomed to care for the equality of the members of speech. For *τὸ γαμψώνυχον* [the crooked-clawed] consult Eustathius and Apollonius, *Homeric Lexicon*, and Villoison there, p. 68 Tollius, on these lines of the poet, *Odyssey* II. 217: “appearing or vultures with crooked claws.” Aristotle acknowledges the other form in *On the Parts of Animals* II. 13. p. 42 Sylburg; both in IV. 12. p. 119. Iamblichus, *Protrepticus on the Pythagorean Symbols* XX. p. 348 Kiessling: “do not nourish anything with crooked claws advises more Pythagoreanly”; what follows we treated above at IV. 5. 2. p. 442. B.—*Καρχαρόδουν* [jagged-toothed] is not for us to explain after the notes of Schneider on Aristotle’s *History of Animals* II. 3. 8. p. 84. On the metaphorical use of the words *κάρχαρος* and *καρχαρόδους* our friend Karl Friedrich Hermann has treated learnedly on Lucian’s *How to Write History*, chapter 43, p. 261 f. [sq.]. Add the Lexicographer on *καρχαρό-

*δους* in Bachmann’s *Greek Anecdotes* I. p. 268. *ἀνακύπτειν* [to emerge] is a Platonic word. See [Vid.] Wyttenbach on the *Phaedo* p. 302 f. [[margin: — 10.]] *τί γὰρ κέρατα ἐκεῖ πρὸς ἄμυναν;* [for why are there horns there for defense?] He has before his eyes Plato, *Tim.* p. 76 end, p. 111 Bekker. Regarding the words, cf. [[margin: p. 1287, 2.]] *ἐπεὶ καὶ τὸ τῇδε φυτὸν λόγος ἐστὶν ἐν ζωῇ κείμενος* [since also the plant here is a reason [*logos*] situated in life.] Plotinus is considering the most noble passage of Plato on plants in the *Timaeus* p. 77. A. B., p. 111 f. [sq.] Bekker:—“for everything, whatever participates in living, would most rightly be called a living being etc.” To which Galen refers V. f. 144, and Stobaeus excerpted in *Physical Eclogues* p. 752 Heeren. Ammonius, son of Hermias, tries to refute it in the *Tim.* p. 45. A. Lindau used these writers in his Notes on the *Tim.* p. 118 f. [sq.]; he did not use Plotinus nor Proclus in *Platonic Theology* III. 1. p. 128 end and f. [sq.]: “but all living things no longer participate in the intellectual power; since also plants are living beings, as Timaeus says, but they do not participate in sensation or imagination, unless one calls 'co-sensation' [*συναίσθησιν*] (perhaps [f.] *λέγοι* [should call]) their awareness of pleasures and pains. And in general the appetitive powers everywhere are lives and images [*ἰνδάλματα*] of the whole life, and the last productions. But they are without share in intellect by themselves, and without part in the cognitive power; wherefore indeed they are without part by themselves and are indefinite, deprived of all knowledge.” These are to be joined with these Plotinian passages on the differences, or [s.] grades, of life, II. 16. 1 above p. 267; likewise on contemplation (*θεωρίᾳ*) which even plants are said to desire, III. 8. 1. p. 343, and what more is discussed in that matter in that book, pp. 345–350. For the rest, even Cudworth, most intelligent of Platonic philosophy, descends into these questions in the *Intellectual System*, and indeed in the *Dissertation on Plastic Nature*, especially § 16 and 17, p. 171 f. [sq.] Mosheim. Gotthold Heinrich Schubert sides with Plato and Plotinus in his excellent book: *Ansichten von der Nachtseite der Naturwissenschaft* [Views from the Nightside of Natural Science], Dresden 1818, who on p. 305 writes thus: “*Almost the entire plant kingdom shows in the highest moment of its existence a foreboding of animal life.*” etc. [&c.] But it is a long task, though not at all foreign to the office of interpretation, to compare everywhere the acute and ingenious thoughts of this man and others, especially throughout Germany, with Plotinus' tenets. Therefore, I restrain myself and desire these writings to be commended to our Readers.

[[margin: — 9.]] *γῇ δὲ πῶς* [and how to earth etc.] See [Vid.] Plato, *Tim.* p. 40, p. 41 f. [sq.] Bekker, likewise p. 55 f. [sq.], p. 71 Bekker, and cf. [cf.] Plotinus II. 1. 6, III. 6. 6, IV. 3. 15 ff. [sqq.], IV. 4. 22, IV. 5. 1.

[[margin: p. 1288, 7.]] *εἰ δè καὶ τὸ πῦρ λόγος τις ἐν ὕλῃ ἐστὶ* [if also fire is a certain reason in matter etc.] Concerning fire, Plato in the *Tim.* p. 56, p. 71 ff. [sqq.] Bekker. Cf. [Cf.] Plotinus I. 6. 3, II. 2. 1, IV. 4. 23, IV. 5. 2, IV. 7. 2 ff. [sqq.], V. 3. 7, VI. 6. 17.

[[margin: — 9.]] *ἤδη γὰρ ὄντος ἐν τῷ παντὶ πυρὸς ἡ παράτριψις* [for fire already existing in the universe, the friction [*παράτριψις*].] This discovery is attributed to Mercury by Homer, in the *Hymn to Him* verses [v.] 108–110:
Taking a bright branch of laurel, he peeled it with iron
fitted in his palm; and the warm breath panted.
What is *παράτριψις* [friction] to Plotinus, is simply *τρίψις* [rubbing] to Theophrastus in *History of Plants* V. 10. Lucretius describes it clearly, V. 1095 ff. [sqq.]:
And yet when a branchy tree, buffeted by the winds,
wavers and seethes, leaning branch against branch,
fire is squeezed out by the strong force of heat;
and sometimes the glowing heat of flame flashes,
while branches and stems are rubbed together mutually;
either of which might have given fire to mortals.
Seneca calls it *attritum* [rubbing] in *Natural Questions* II. 22, whom see, and compare the *Animadversions* of Schneider on the *Physical Eclogues* XIII. 47. 48. p. 136 f. [sq.].

[[margin: — 13.]] *διὸ καὶ Πλάτων—ψυχήν φησιν εἶναι—τὸ αἰσθητὸν πῦρ* [wherefore also Plato says—sensible fire—is soul.] Tennemann denies in his *History of Philosophy* VI. p. 132 that Plato ever said this, and thus, if he wished to be consistent, could not have said it. Yet some things could have been taken in this sense which Diogenes Laertius reports from Plato’s doctrine on the elements, book III, § 74; and the more recent Platonists could have had many decrees of Plato, which he had not included in his dialogues but had produced in the schools and explained more accurately,

**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

having them preserved as if passed through hands. Certainly, it is not of Plotinus' character to fabricate anything against any of the ancient philosophers.

[[margin: p. 1289, 10.]] *καὶ ὅτι ἂν σὰρξ γένηται ἐκ τοῦ αἵματος.* [and that flesh comes to be from blood.] He follows Plato in the *Timaeus* p. 80 end, p. 119 Bekker: “what we call blood, the pasture (food) of the flesh and of the whole body.” Longinus, in *On the Sublime* § XXXII. p. 108 Weiske, placed these words among examples showing that the fabric of the human body was depicted with a divine style of speaking.

[[margin: — 16.]] *τοῦτον τὸν τρόπον πάρεστι καὶ τὴν ψυχὴν—καὶ οὐ πάρεισι* [in this way the soul also is present—and they are not present.] Ficinus expressed: “the soul is also present—and is not present,” and thus a convenient meaning arises. But without the books we did not wish to introduce this reading into the context.

[[margin: p. 1290, 9.]] *ἐν ῥοῇ καὶ ζωῇ μενούσῃ* [in flow [*rhoe*] and remaining life [*zoe*].] Thus we have corrected from the books. For the rest, this similarity of sound in the two words is not to be thought of as studiously sought by Plotinus, who is most foreign to the blandishments of words. Not the same judgment should be made of that "Calliclean" floweret in Plato’s *Gorgias* p. 494, p. 98 Bekker: *νόμον τε καὶ λόγον καὶ ψόγον* [law and reason and blame], nor of those "Agathonian" ones in the *Symposium* p. 137. D: *ἐν πόνῳ, ἐν φόβῳ, ἐν πόθῳ, ἐν λόγῳ* [in toil, in fear, in desire, in speech]. But nevertheless, that quite a few such things (as for example [v. c.] that in the *Republic* VI. p. 495. E: *ἐκ δεσμῶν λελυμένου, ἐν βαλανείῳ δὲ λελουμένου* [released from chains, but washed in a bath]) fell from Plato himself was proved by examples by the most learned Groen van Prinsterer in *Prosopographia Platonica* 104 f. [sq.]; cf. [cf.] Geel’s *History of the Sophists* p. 54 and p. 254 f. [sq.] and C. Fr. Hermann on Lucian, *How to Write History* p. 268, and J. F. Boissonade, who recently collected similar things from church writers in *Notices et Extraits* Vol. XI. 2. p. 141 f. [sq.]. I shall add one from the speech of a Roman prince: Cicero, *Against Verres* II. 2... “—yet in a new manner, that the envoys harm: the embassy praises.” I touched on this matter very briefly above at p. 542. E. end. On the word *ῥοὴ* [flow] we saw likewise above at page 443. E.

[[margin: p. 1291, 4.]] *καὶ ὁμοῦ οἰνώδους ποιότητος* [and together with wine-like quality.] I have retained the common reading, which some codices protect and Ficinus expressed. But what if you read: *καὶ ὁμοῦ οἰνώδους πυρότητος* [and together with wine-like fieriness], to signify the fiery power of wine? For wine is called "fire-struck," and the rare word not recorded in the Lexicons, yet appearing above on p. 180. A: *πυρότης* [fiery nature], could easily have been obscured by scribes with the most common one frequent in the preceding parts.

[[margin: — 16.]] *ὁμοιομερές τι καὶ ἀποίκιλον* [something like a homeomer and unvariegated.] This passage is to be added to those three which learned men recently collected under the word *ἀποίκιλον* [unvariegated] in Stephanus' *Thesaurus* p. 7797 London edition. The passage of Iamblichus in *Life of Pythagoras* XXIII. § 103, p. 222 Kiessling, has it thus: “if someone should clearly articulate the indications and secret thoughts of the Pythagorean symbols, how much correctness and truth they participate in when revealed and freed from their enigmatic type, (and the Munich Codex B. adds *καὶ*) having been made familiar according to a simple and unvariegated [*ἀποίκιλον*] tradition to the great natures of these philosophers, and having been contemplated as divine beyond human thought” (Arier. *θεωθεῖσι* [contemplated (Dat.)], in which error all our Codices persevere. On this confusion, the most learned man Krabinger, in the excerpts of the Munich Codices, cites Bast’s *Palaeographical Commentary* p. 752).

[[margin: p. 1293, 2.]] *ἡ δè πλάνη αὐτῷ ἐν τῷ τῆς ἀληθείας πεδίῳ.* [but for him the wandering is in the plain of truth.] Plato, *Phaedrus* p. 248. b., p. 43 f. [sq.] Bekker: “but for the sake of which there is great haste, to see the plain of truth where it is etc.” Proclus, in *Platonic Theology* IV. 15. p. 201: “in these things let us contemplate another triad pre-existing in this place, which Socrates himself also praised, the plain of truth, the meadow, the nourishment of the gods” (regarding this nourishment [nutrimento] see above at p. 552. C.). The same, ibid. p. 204: “the plain of truth is the expansion of the light of the intelligible, and the manifestation, and the unfolding of the inner reasons, and the perfection proceeding everywhere etc.” Plotinus above p. 21. B. on Dialectic:—“but having ceased from wandering about the sensible, it establishes [the soul] in the intelligible, and there has its business [*πραγματείαν*], having dismissed falsehood, nourishing the soul in the so-called plain of truth etc.” Whence it is also understood that in this name the Article is sometimes placed before the word *ἀληθείας*, and sometimes omitted.

[[margin: p. 1294, 3.]] *οὐδέν ἐστιν αὐτοῦ* [nothing is of it.] Perhaps *οὐδè ἕν* [not even one] should be written. Thus certainly, or reading *καὶ οὐδèν ἐστὶ*, Ficinus seems to have understood.

[[margin: — 8.]] *ὡς οὐκ ἀνέχεται—μὴ ἄλλος εἶναι.* [how it does not tolerate—not to be another.] Our philosopher I. 6. 2. p. 52. A: “matter not tolerating being shaped entirely according to the form,” and, as in this place [*h. l.*], without the article, Olympiodorus in *Alcib. I* XI. p. 101: “not tolerating to confess.” Ibid. XXVIII.

**BOOK VII. ENNEAD SIX. p. 1289—1297.**

p. 226: “for virtue is by nature free, not tolerating to be subjected to worse things.” To which passages we have said more concerning this rather unusual construction.

[[margin: — 13.]] *ἀλλὰ καὶ ῥῖνες* [but also nostrils.] The edition and many books read *ῥῖνες*. The same error had occupied Pollux's *Onomasticon* II. 76. p. 191 before the correction of Jungermann, whom see. And the two Marcian books among ours present a better writing. For the rest, *αἱ ῥῖνες* are nostrils, which in common speaking usage are called *τὰ ῥινία* (Aristotle, *Physiognomy* III. 57.). For the rest, the reading of Mediceus A is plausible: *οὐχ ἡ οὖσα ἓν* [not that which is one], yet the common one is not bad.

[[margin: p. 1295, 6.]] *ἀλλ’ ἔστιν ἡ λεγομένη ἐν τῷ παντὶ φιλία τοῦτο* [but the friendship spoken of in the universe is this etc.] Our philosopher V. 1. 9. p. 490. [[margin: — 12.]] *ἀτιμάσας* [having dishonored.] On the three forms *ἀτιμάζω*, *ἀτιμάω*, and *ἀτιμόω* see [vid.] Suidas I. p. 371 Kuster; Zonaras, *Greek Lexicon* p. 337 (where in a fragment of Aelian *οὐκ ἠτίμασαν οἱ φαν.* should be corrected). [[margin: p. 1296, 10.]] *συνέθραυσε* [shattered.] Thus we have written with many Codices instead of *συνέθραυε*, and that the margin of the edition no doubt also wanted, but the workers did not obey. Hesychius II. p. 1308: *συνθραύεσθαι· συντρίβεσθαι* [to be shattered: to be crushed], where Alberti cites in a note two passages of Dio Cassius p. 392 and p. 628 Reimar. But see [vid.] Sturz, *Lexicon of Xenophon* IV. p. 187, and there Xenophon, *Agesilaus* II. 14. and Euripides, *Orestes* 1569. 1571.

[[margin: — 12.]] *Διὸ καὶ εἴ τις αὐτὸν ἀπεικάζοι* [Wherefore even if someone should liken him.] Thus I wrote instead of *ἀπεικάζει*, by which the system of Modes might be consistent with itself, on account of the following *φαντάζοιτο—ὁρῴη* [should imagine—should see].—Then I retained with all MSS books *ὡς φέγγει* [as with light]. The margin of the edition has *ὡς φωτί* [as with light], which is to be held as an interpretation. However, this passage of Plato in the *Phaedo* p. 110. B., p. 111 f. [sq.] Bekker seems to have been before Plotinus: “It is said then, he said, O friend, that first of all the earth itself is such to see, if someone should see it from above, as the twelve-stitched leather balls, variegated, distinguished by colors, of which the colors here are as if samples, which indeed painters use.” Which Wyttenbachius, not forgetful of Plotinus, learnedly illustrated in the note pp. 304–307 and touched upon again in the *Animadversions on Plutarch's On the E at Delphi* p. 285 Oxford edition.

[[margin: p. 1297, 1.]] *Χρὴ δè—μεταβαίνειν—πρὸς τὰ ἄνω ἀΐξαντα* [But it is necessary—to pass over—having darted toward the things above.] Plato, *Theaetetus* p. 144. b: “toward angers they are quick-tilting and are borne darting like unballasted ships”: (which passage I treated on account of the last words above at I. 8. 8.). *Alcib. I* p. 118. b: “wherefore you also dart [*ᾄττεις*] toward political things.” Which Olympiodorus renders: “you rush toward political affairs,” plainly as Hesychius on *διάττειν* [to dart through], and the Scholiast of Philostratus, *Heroics* p. 600 Boissonade. Cf. our note on Olympiodorus p. 134. Add Lexicographer in Bekker's *Greek Anecdotes* I. p. 460. *Republic* X. p. 621. 6., p. 515 Bekker, concerning souls rushing into corporeal life: “and thence suddenly one here, another there, were borne upward into generation, darting [*ᾄττοντες*] like stars.” Concerning stars and meteors, Clement of Alexandria, *Protrepticus* p. 81 Potter: “how then also the shooting stars and the comets, having come into being through a condition of the air?” Similarly Plutarch in *Agis* XI. p. 304: “if—a star should dart through [*διάξῃ*].” And Nonnus, *Dionysiaca* book 2 verse 192: “darting stars” and soon “a darting thunderbolt.” Plutarch, *On the Soul* in *Fragments* vol. V. p. 724 Wyttenbach and in Stobaeus' *Florilegium* CXIX. p. 604 (Vol. III. p. 465 Gaisford edition): “which indeed has reason, just as if some caterpillar [*κάμπης*] being released, so as to kindle and run up the soul when the body expires, itself breathing out and reviving” (where before Koen, Valckenaer, and Gesner, it was read: *ἐξάπτειν καὶ ἀναθεῖναι* [to kindle and to set up]). I touched upon this place and similar Plutarchs in *Symbolica* III. p. 569 f. [sq.] second edition, where I said that these words are to be compared with Plato's *Cratylus* p. 399. D., and that *κάμπην* [caterpillar] in this place also is the *eruca* [caterpillar], from which the butterfly is excluded, an image often used for the vicissitudes of the human soul. Philostratus, *Life of Apollonius* IV. 42. p. 226 f. [sq.] Olearius, on a tamed lion: “for the blood of the sacrifices was not licked up, nor upon the divided and slaughtered [parts]...”

**386 NOTES ON PLOTINUS**

...it led the [blood] poured from the victims. *Cod. Florent.—Schellershem.:* *ἥττεν* [hetted]. Read *ἥττεν*, as Jacobs plainly emended it (see *Additamm. in Athen.* p. 161; on the Greek Epistles of Fronto in F. A. Wolf’s *Analectt.* I. p. 116; and in *Philostrati Imagg.* p. 472); to which conjecture, since the support of the *Codex Vratislaviensis* had recently been added, another now comes from the *Schellershemianus*. (From this same book, a little before, *λέοντα ἥμερον* [tame lion] should be restored to Philostratus instead of *λ. ἥμερον*.) Theodoretes, *De Providentia* II. p. 505. Schulz.: "For lest you think that the nature of waters rushes [ᾄττειν] upward of its own accord, the poet teaches you," etc.

**p. 1297, 10. ἐνόει αὐτὸν πολλὰ μερίζων αὑτὸν παρ' αὑτῷ [he was perceiving himself by dividing himself much within himself]** Ficinus expressed *αὐτὸ* [it] twice, which seems true, but without the support of the books [manuscripts], which partly offer *αὑτὸν* [himself], I was unwilling to change it. However, following the books, I wrote *τῷ νοεῖν μὴ—δύνασθαι* [by not being able to think] instead of *τὸ νοεῖν* [thinking].

**p. 1298, 5. Ὥσπερ δὲ ὁ ἥλιος τοῦ ὁρᾶσθαι—αἴτιος ὤν—οὕτω καὶ ἡ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ φύσις αἰτία οὐσίας κ. τ. λ. [Just as the sun is the cause of being seen—so also the nature of the Good is the cause of being/essence, etc.]** Recall again to your mind that passage of Plato in *Republic* VI. p. 509. a., to which we referred you in the notes on the preceding chapter, p. 708. B.

**p. 1300, 2. διὰ μὲν τὸ πολὺ τῆς ζωῆς πολλὰ ὁρισθεῖσα [having been many things defined through the abundance of life]** Ficinus expressed *ὁρισθέντα* [things defined]. But the books do not support this. Therefore, I have retained the *vulgata* [standard reading], which, if it is true, this participle again depends upon the preceding *ζωή* [life].

**p. 1301, 1. Αλλ' ἀγαθοειδῆ—καὶ ζωὴ καὶ νοῦς καὶ ἰδέα [But of the form of the Good—both life and intellect and idea]** We have provided for this passage partly by the help of good books and partly by more suitable punctuation. Regarding the argument, one should compare what our philosopher discussed in II. 1. 7. p. 102. A.

**— 10. ἐπεὶ καὶ ἄλλο τὸ εἰς πρώτην ἐνέργειαν—δοθέν [since also another thing given toward the first activity]** Margin of the Edition: *ἐπεὶ καὶ εἰς ἄλλο*, and so several manuscript books. Ficinus expressed *ἐπεὶ καὶ ἄλλο, εἰς ὃ ἡ πρώτη ἐνέργεια*, yet of this reading there is no trace in the Codices. Wherefore, in such places I prefer to retain the *vulgata* than to err by innovation.

**p. 1302, 1. 'Αλλ' εἰ ἐν τῇ ζωῇ ἐκείνῃ ἐνίοιτο ἐξ ἐκείνου [But if in that life there were something from that]** *Vat.* [Vatican Codex] *ἐνίοιτο*. Ficinus expressed *ἔνι τὸ* [it is in] or *ἐνείη τὸ*, [which seems to have been obliterated by Iotacism:] which I would have restored to the text if even one book agreed. Next, with the good books, I gave *ὄντως* [really] instead of *ὄντος* [being].

**p. 1303, 1. καὶ τὸ συνάμφω [and the 'together']** The Edition incorrectly has *καὶ τὸ συναμφότερον*, for which the margin of *Marciani B.* rightly has *συναμφότερον*. But we have nevertheless given the reading of the best codices. For the sake of the philosopher's speech, it is helpful to cite these passages: Lucian, *Dialogg. Mort.* III. p. 340. ed. Amst.: "something composed of man and god.—which is neither man—nor god. and it is 'both together' [*συναμφότερον*]." The same in *Prometh.* V. p. 31: "Why then could not conversely a beautiful thing be composed of two best things, just as from wine and honey the 'both together' [*συναμφότερον*] is sweetest." The Scholiast on *Odyssey* θ. 1. explaining *ἠῶ* [dawn], while narrating other meanings, says it is "both together" [*τὸ συναμφότερον*], day and night; or as in Eustathius on the *Odyssey* p. 140 and 1430, it is the whole twenty-four hour period [*τὸ ὅλον νυχθήμερον*]. Plato speaks more distinctly and in his own more explanatory manner in *Philebus* p. 21. fin. p. 52. Stallb.: "Pr.: Neither life—would appear to me—choiceworthy. Soc.: What of the 'both together' [*ὁ συναμφότερος*]—mixed from both, becoming common? Pr.: You speak of pleasure and intellect and wisdom." This passage ought to be compared with the same philosopher's *Symposium* p. 198. p. 402. Bekk.: "For first there were three kinds of men, not, as now, two, male and female, but also a third was present, being common to both—for there was then a single 'androgynous' one." Yet it is also almost both at once and therefore almost the same as *συνάμφω*. Schweigh[aeuser] gives examples of both words in *Lex. Polyb.* p. 585. We, however, distinguish well in German: *συναμφότερον*: *von beyden Zusammen* [from both together], *συνάμφω*: *Beyde Zusammen* [both together]. Aristotle [speaks] brilliantly in *Metaph.* XI. 5. p. 221. Brandis.: "For just as when they are divided, the affirmation is no more true than the negation, in the same way regarding the 'both together' and the 'intertwined,' as if there were one affirmation, the negation will be no more true than the whole set forth as in an affirmation." The same, ibid. p. 168: "—and likewise also the definitions which Archytas used to accept; for they are of the 'together' [*τοῦ συνάμφω*]. For instance, what is a calm? Stillness in a mass of air," etc. The same, *περὶ ἑρμην.* [On Interpretation] XV. p. 69. extr. Sylb.: "For if because each is true, the 'together' [*τὸ συνάμφω*] must also be true, many absurdities will follow." Our Philosopher p. 165. A: "Whenever—he perceives things that have been magnified, he perceives them as composites; for as separated and entirely qualified. He perceives therefore the whole and the 'together' [*τὸ συνάμφω*]." Cf. also p. 600. B. and Olympiod[orus] in *Alc. pr.* c. I. p. 3. extr.

**— 10. 'Αρ' οὖν τῇ ἐφέσει καὶ τῇ ψυχῇ ἐπιτρέψομεν; κ. τ. λ. [Shall we then entrust it to desire and the soul? etc.]** See what we placed above at the end of p. 530 from *Philebus* p. 20. p. 46. sq. Stallb. likewise—

**p. 1304, 8. κἂν ἄλλο φῶμεν αἴτιον, τὸν θεὸν [even if we call the cause another thing, God]** Philo Jud[aeus], *Leg. Allegorr.* III. p. 101. Mang. p. 284. Pfeiff.: "Do you see that it is not the Lord who kills Er (Genes. XXXVIII. 7. where it is *Ηρ*, and so Suid. and Zonar. in voc.), but God? For he does not slay the body according to that by which he rules and leads, using the power of sovereign might, but according to that by which he uses goodness and kindness. For 'God' is the name of the cause’s goodness, so that you may know that even inanimate things he made not by power, but by goodness, by which he also made animate things. For it was necessary for the manifestation of better things that the generation of worse things also stand, by the power of the same goodness of the cause, which is God." Wherein it is preferable, what Pfeiffer brings forward from the editions and Cod. A. instead of *αὐτεξουσίῳ* [by his own power]. In passing, I note from Eustath. in *Iliad* Δ. p. 335. *ἡ αὐτεξουσία* is praised, but there on p. 354. ed. Lips. it is read *αὐτὸ ἐξουσία*. Likewise in the *Indic. Initt. Philosoph. Platon.* [Index of the Beginnings of Platonic Philosophy] our *αὐτεξουσία* is praised. But the passage is Proclus in *Alcib. pr.* p. 143. where it is correctly read *τὸ αὐτεξούσιον* [free will], which is also often met with in Plotinus. Furthermore, Philo in the place cited, as elsewhere occasionally, seems in this opinion also—concerning God as the cause of the Good—to follow the Stoic philosophers, whose doctrine you may learn this to have been from Gataker's notes on Marc. Antonin. II. 11. p. 47.

**— 9. οὐ μὴν ἀποστατέον [one must certainly not desist]** Marg. Ed. and three manuscript books have *καὶ μὴν*, which Ficinus expressed: *Sed denique* [But finally]. To me it seems a *παραδιόρθωσις* [a corruption in correction], both because of what follows and because Plotinus, in such questions, is accustomed to cry out to his readers that *one must not desist*.

**p. 1305, 1. καὶ τοῦτο τὸ ἀγαθὸν θησόμεθα; [and shall we posit this as the Good?]** Lest perhaps you believe Ficinus read *κ. τοῦτον*: the Medicean books themselves do not vary, and nothing is more frequent in these Enneads than a sudden change of gender. With the same Ficinus, I have retained *θησόμεθα* [we shall posit]. The margin and not a few books here also have *στησόμεθα* [we shall establish].

**— 2. κρίνουσα μὲν δικαιοσύνῃ κ. τ. λ. [judging indeed with justice, etc.]** The color of this passage seems drawn from that most noble passage of Plato concerning the lot-casting of souls in *Republic* book X. p. 617. p. 509. Bekk.

**p. 1306, 5. Τὸ γὰρ οἰκεῖον, εἰ μὴ ἀγαθὸν εἴη, οἰκεῖον μέν ἐστι, φεύγει δέ τις αὐτό. [For one's own, if it be not good, is indeed one's own, but one flees from it.]** Diotima in Plato's *Conviv.* [Symposium] p. 205. E. p. 434. Bekk.: "But my argument says that love is neither of the half, nor of the whole, unless it happens to be, my friend, good, since men are willing to have their own feet and hands cut off if their own things seem to them to be wicked. For each person does not embrace their own things, I think, unless one calls the good 'one's own' and belonging to oneself, and the evil 'alien'; as there is nothing else men love but the good." For the end, apply *Charmid.* p. 163. C. Porphyry seems to have had the former part before his eyes in the *Epistle to Marcella* c. XXXIV. p. 36, to which the most elegant Jacobs recently applied a healing hand in *Lectionibus Stobenss.* p. 63. note.

**— 14. καὶ τοῦ φωτὸς—γλιχόμενος [and striving after the light]** Which I do not find recorded in the new *Thesaurus* of Stephanus Londin. p. 3004. sq. [sequenti → following], the *Etymolog. Gud.* p. 126. 49. 50 notes: "Γλιχόμενος [striving], persisting or desiring, from 'clinging greatly' [λίαν ἔχεσθαι] to something. It is construed with the genitive and dative"; that caught my attention. Is the passage sound, or should we read *καὶ αἰτιατικῆς* [and accusative]? This I believe. See the Scholiast of Lucian on *Aëtion* p. 833. ed. Amst. (on the words "thinking the time had come, which [οὗ, so this οὐ must be corrected] he especially strove after"): "*γλίχομαι* [I strive], I cling greatly. With genitive and accusative." Cf. Suid. I. p. 484. Kust. from which Zonaras p. 442 is to be filled. You may learn the reason for the construction even from Demosthenes. See Reiske's *Indic. Græcit. Demosth.* p. 179. Concerning the construction with *περὶ* [around/about], it is debated. See Cattier's *Gazophyl.* p. 96 and Steph. *Thes.* l. l. [loco laudato]. Antiphanes in Stob. *Floril.* p. 608. Vol. III. p. 473. **p. 1310, 10. ὃ τάχ' ἄν τις δυσχεραντικὸς ἀνὴρ εἴποι, ὡς ὑμεῖς, ὦ οὗτοι, τί δὴ ἀποσεμνύνετε τοῖς ὀνόμασιν, ἄνω καὶ κάτω ζωὴν ἀγαθὴν λέγοντες [which perhaps some annoyed man might say, that you, O men, why do you speak so solemnly with names, calling life good up and down/back and forth]** Thus we have written on the authority of good books, which show both *ὑμεῖς* [you] and *ἀποσεμνύνετε* [you speak solemnly of], but *ὄμμασιν* [eyes] instead of *σώμασιν* [bodies] of the edition. This indeed Ficinus also expressed by that *spectando* [by looking] of his. But I might seem too religious if I left this itself untouched. Nevertheless, I do not easily dare to receive conjectures into the text without the support of the books. But since Plotinus undoubtedly wrote *ἀποσεμνύνετε τοῖς ὀνόμασιν* [you speak solemnly with names], I have received this. Others have dealt with this confusion, among them the great Porson on Euripid. *Orest.* 1081. and I myself recently on Olympiodor. in *Alcib. pr.* p. 281. I add one passage from Plato himself, *Phædon.* p. 83. A. p. 56. Bekk.: "showing that the investigation through the eyes [*διὰ τῶν ὀμμάτων*] is full of deceit." Iamblichus, *Protrept.* XIII. p. 79. Arc. p. 198. Kiessl. who presents Plato's words: "that the investigation through the eyes [*διὰ τῶν ὀμμάτων*] (one of my books and one of Bekker’s in *Var. Lect. Platon.* has *ὀνομάτων* [names]) is full of deceit." Let us look at the use of the word: Plato *Apolog.* 17. p. 89. sq. Bekk.: "Not however, by Zeus, O men of Athens, speeches beautified, as those of these men, with phrases and names [*ὀνόμασιν*], nor decorated, but you shall hear things said at random with the names that happen along." *Sympos.* p. 198. p. 419. Bekk.: "But who would not be astounded hearing at the end the beauty of the names [*ὀνομάτων*] and phrases?" *Phædr.* p. 234. a. p. 16. Bekk.: "The speech; is it not extraordinarily spoken both in other respects and in its names [*ὀνόμασιν*]?" *Menex.* p. 235. a. p. 378. Bekk.: "beautifying in some most excellent way with names [*τοῖς ὀνόμασι*] they bewitch our souls." — *Ὀνομάτων καινοτομία* [Innovation of names] is also Platonic. Libanius uses it; on which occasion, given this opportunity, I can wash away a foul stain. He praises in Epistle MDC p. 727. Wolf the eloquent speech of Basil: "For my tongue was not accustomed to these things, but as if struck by the innovation of names [*τῇ τῶν ὀνομάτων καινοτομίᾳ*] of one traversing some precipice, it said to me the father: Father, you did not teach me. This man is Homer, but Plato, but Aristotle, but Susarion who knows all things." And these things the tongue [said]. To be sure, Libanius imagines the tongue reproached him as father (i.e., Basil’s teacher). I omit lighter matters. Instead of *Σουσαρίων*, other books have *Σουδαρίων*. Wolf praises Bentley regarding Susarion. But he could have learned from Bentley that Susarion, a most ancient comic poet, was not of such authority that he could hold a place next to Homer, Plato, and Aristotle, and thus be called *ὁ πάντα ἐπιστάμενος* [he who knows all things]. What do you seek? Our Palatine Codex Heidelberg. nr. 356 provides the true reading: *ἀλλ' 'Αριστοτέλης—ἀλλὰ σοῦ γὰρ μείζων* [but Aristotle—but for he is greater than you]. Surely, to the names of Homer, Plato, and Aristotle, the tongue adds: *but indeed greater than you, and he who knows all things*, has bestowed that eloquence upon Basil. Unless you prefer to conclude that Libanius, using a poetic form: *σοῦ γὰρ ἀρείων* [for better than you], made the scribes more prone to that error. I return thither. Plotinus could have taken the verb *ἀποσεμνύνειν* from Plato. See *Theæt.* p. 168. d: "solemnly speaking of the measure of all things." Iamblich. *De Mysterr.* I. 21. p. 38: "and indeed to speak solemnly of some as divine, and to consider others that happened as human to be despicable," where Cod. Gothan. and Vindob. reject *γενέσθαι*. Rightly. I will add passages coming closer to the similarity of the Plotinian passage. Plato *Phædr.* p. 244. d. p. 36. Bekk.: "they named it *oionistike* [augury]. Which now the young call *oionistike*, solemnizing it [*σεμνύνοντες*] with the *omega*." Dio Cass. LX. 5. p. 943: "thus indeed having solemnly spoken of his fathers, he himself received nothing outside the names of those bearing onto the rule." Basil the Great in *Hexaëm.* 2: "those solemnly speaking of him (the man) by this name." Max. Tyr. *Diss.* XXIX. 1. p. 69. Reisk.: "Can you say whom Homer names—born of Zeus—and shepherds of people, and other such things as a poet is likely to say when solemnly speaking with names [*ἀποσεμνύννοντα τοῖς ὀνόμασιν*] of the virtue of a man." The formula *ἄνω καὶ κάτω* [up and down/back and forth] no less proves a reader of Plato. *Gorg.* p. 493. a: "of the soul this—happens to be such as to be persuaded and to change back and forth [*ἄνω καὶ κάτω*]," where see Heindf. p. 157. cf. 115. and on *Theæt.* p. 320. add Stallbaum on *Phileb.* p. 127. Jo. Chrysost. Tom. III. p. 445. VI. p. 275. C. T. X. p. 669. B. Theodoreti *Epistol.* 86. p. 1157. Schulz. which passage I shall write out, because it comes closer to the similarity of the Plotinian passage: "Why ever, blustering at my justifications and talking back and forth [*ἄνω καὶ κάτω*] about the law, did you not receive the benefit from there?" Wherefore, the passage of Plotinus is to be translated thus: "You, O men, why then do you magnificently celebrate in words, calling life back and forth the Good?" *ὡς* after verbs of speaking is not as frequent as *ὅτι*, but...

...nevertheless, it is used by good writers, as shown by the collections in Viger p. 564 and Matthia in *Gramm. gr.* §. 539. 1. second edition.

**p. 1311, 1. ἢ τί ἂν διαφέροι ἐν τῷ εἶναι ἢ ὅλως μὴ εἶναι—καὶ τὸν φόβον τῆς φθορᾶς κ. τ. λ. [or what would it differ in being or not being at all—and the fear of destruction, etc.]** These things bring to mind Cicero in *Tuscull.* I. 6: "M. Where then are these, whom you call wretched? or what place do they inhabit? For if they are, they cannot be nowhere. A. I indeed think they are nowhere. M. Therefore they are not even. A. Exactly in that way; and yet wretched for that very reason, because they are none." He whom Plotinus introduces objecting these things in this place seems to argue from the opinion of the Epicureans, who both placed happiness in pleasure and were accustomed to boast that: "Death is nothing to us." Wyttenb. on Plato's *Phædon.* p. 142—144. Yet it closely refers to the dogmas of Callicles and his like, which Socrates refutes in the *Gorgias*. To which also pertain those things read here concerning *φιλία* [friendship]. See *Gorgias* p. 507. e. p. 133. Bekk. Did Plotinus refer to the passage of the Platonic *Timaeus*, where the friendship [*φιλία*] of the Universe is discussed p. 32. e. p. 29. Bekk. (which passage Eubulus cites against Aristotle in Aug. Mai's *Collect. Vatican.* II. 674, which also has *συνδήσαντος* [binding together], and therefore does not favor the conjecture of Lindavius *συμφύσαντος* [growing together]).

**— 5. Πλάτων—ἐν τῷ Φιλήβῳ [Plato—in the Philebus]** That noble discussion in that dialogue is observed by Plotinus on p. 22. sq. p. 154. Bekk.: "—for not even your intellect, Socrates, is the good, but it will have somewhere the same accusations, etc." At which passage I wonder Plotinus was not applied by Stallbaum p. 54. sq. since our philosopher explains the intention of Plato and his opinions. Moreover, it should be compared with that other discussion in Plato's *Gorgias* p. 506 sq. p. 130 sqq. Bekk.: "Soc. Hear then from me taking up the argument from the beginning. Are the pleasant and the good the same? etc."

**p. 1313, 6. παρὰ τῶν ζώντων ἡ ἐπιμέλεια καὶ ἡ κήδευσις [care and burial-rite from the living]** Thus the margin and the best manuscript books for *ζώων* [animals/living things] and *ἐπιμένεια*. The substantive *κήδευσις* [burial care/kinship duty] should be added to the examples which learned men recently collected for Stephanus’s *Thesaurus* and recorded in Schneider’s *Lexicon*. This kind of word is used properly of the care usually bestowed upon the dead, Zonar. *Lex.* 1204: *κήδεια* [care/funeral]. burial; and kinship. More have been collected by Heyne from the Grammarians on *Iliad* ψ. 160, in which even the word *κήδευσις* itself occurs. *ἐπιμέλεια* [care] is joined with words of this family. Dio Cassius XLIII. 17. near the end p. 353. Reimar.: "reaping the providence and the guardianship [*κηδεμονίαν*] from me.—and I care for you as for my children." Dio Chrysost. *Orat.* LIII. p. 556. C. p. 279. Reisk. concerning Jove as father of men: "—as it is necessary that the care of kings be fatherly and protective." Theodoretes in *Ezech.* XXXVI. Vol. II. p. 993: "for since I set them apart like sheep under my protection [*κηδεμονίαν*], I shall share with them pastoral care [*ἐπιμελείας*]." Soon also *ἀμετανόητον* [unrepentant/unchangeable] as a third example of this usage should be recorded in the Lexicons.

**— 15. οἷον ἐπὶ τῷ παιδὶ ὅτι πάρεστιν ἥδεσθαι [as for example being pleased that the boy is present]** Lest perhaps someone think this passage was less correctly understood by Ficinus, and boys should be thought of, whom those who hold them in delight always wish to be with them, and as it is in Plato's *Symposium* p. 192. p. 408. Bekk.: "to be in the same place as much as possible with one another, so as not to be separated from each other day and night." and in *Charmides* p. 155. e: "and I thought Critias most wise in erotic matters, who said speaking of the beautiful boy, etc."—first such an interpretation would be more suited to an Attic writer and an equal of the free republic—secondly, Plotinus only then transitions to the mention of venereal matters in the following. Furthermore, the indefinite use of the Article from the cited passage of *Charmides* is to be held even for our passage; on which usage Heindorf discussed ibid. Cf. Matth. *Gr. gr.* §. 267. In the final words I have included that *re* [the thing] in brackets, in the Latin, and added *omnino* [altogether]: I did the former so that a *woman* might be thought of, which the little word *ᾗ* [by which/whom] requires; the latter, so that no one refer that *δρῶντα* [acting] to *concubitus* [sexual intercourse]. — Above p. 321. F. 322. A: Plotinus himself used *ἐργασίαν* [work/business] of performing a venereal act, which elsewhere is meretricious gain. (See Valcken. on Herodot. I. 93.) *Concubitus* itself is *ἔργον πορνείας* [work of fornication] for Gregory Nazianzen: *περὶ βλέψεως ἐμπαθοῦς* [On Passionate Looking] in Cod. Heidelb. nr. 356. where the Theologian says thus: "I saw the beauty of a woman tormenting my mind and my temperance. and indeed I fled the 'work of fornication,' but I defiled my own virginity in the mind of the heart." — Furthermore, Plotinus may seem in this place to refer to Plato's words in *Republic* VI. p. 505. p. 313: "—but as for good things...

**LIB. VII. ENNEAD. SIXTH. p. 1311—1321. 391**

"...no one is satisfied with possessing those things which seem so, but they seek the things that are, and here everyone now dishonors opinion. — Quite so."

**p. 1314, 6. κἂν ἐθέλῃ αὐτὸ, καὶ χαίρῃ τῷ ὁμοίῳ [even if he wants it, and rejoices in the like]** Marg. ed. and several written books: *κἂν ἔχῃ* [even if he has]. Ficinus joined both readings in his version. Not badly, I think. Furthermore, that proverb pertains here: "as like always approaches like," as it is expressed in Plato's *Conviv.* p. 195. b. or as it is brought out differently in other places. See *Lysid.* p. 214. Ast. on *Phædr.* p. 336. Zell. on Aristot. *Ethic. Nicomach.* VIII. 1. 4. p. 333. Ciceron. *De Senect.* III. init. and there Gernhard p. 15. sq.

**p. 1315, 1. Διὸ καὶ μᾶλλον οἰκείωσις πρὸς αὑτοὺς—τοῖς μᾶλλον ἀγαθοῖς [Therefore also more kinship/affiliation toward themselves—for those who are more good]** Plato explains this sentiment more fully in *Gorgias* p. 507. sq. p. 132. sq. Bekk.

Ficinus studied to provide for this place otherwise, namely by interposing *καὶ* [and] before *ἀγαθόν ἐστιν αὑτῷ*.

**— 10. ἀλλὰ τὸ μὲν εἰ μὴ ἐποιεῖτο ἡδονῇ [but if on the one hand it were not done with pleasure]** With *τὸ μὲν* understand *κτᾶσθαι τὸ ἀγαθόν* [possessing the good]. "But even if the acquisition of the Good were not performed with pleasure."

**p. 1316, 4. 'Αλλὰ τοῦ εἴδους ἐπελθόντος ὥσπερ ὀνείρατος ἀγαθοῦ [But with the form coming upon it like a good dream]** The philosopher of Lycopolis [Plotinus] has before his eyes that description of matter which Plato wonderfully executed in the *Timaeus* p. 49. sqq. where many other things are said about matter, and indeed these: (p. 51. p. 62. Bekk.) "partaking in some most difficult way of the intelligible." The comparison of a dream is also common to Plato, as in the same dialogue p. 52. p. 64. **— 14. τὸ δ' ἐπὶ μᾶλλον—καὶ νοῦς ψυχῆς) τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἂν προσχωροῖ τῷ τῆς ψυχῆς ἐναντίῳ, καὶ οἷον καθαιρομένῳ. [but the more—and the intellect of the soul) the Good would approach the opposite of the soul, and as if being purified.]** Ficinus expressed *δ' ἔτι* [and still], and so it is corrected in Med. A. (Perhaps Plotinus gave *δ' ἔπι* i. e., *ἔπεστι* [is upon]); then *τῷ τῆς ὕλης ἐναντίῳ* [to the opposite of matter] (and next Darmst. shows: *δ,τι ψυχῆς ἀποτυπ.* for *ὕλης*); I changed nothing, except *προχωροῖ* into *προσχωροῖ* [approach], which the good books offered. And *τῷ τῆς ψυχῆς ἐναντίῳ* [to the opposite of the soul] may seem sound to one thinking that the soul is inclined toward lower things and desires the delights of sensible things, which the Good itself would scorn and flee. I have provided for the punctuation of this entire passage.

**p. 1317, 8. καὶ μὴ κινεῖσθαι, ἀλλ' ὡς μετὰ τὸ αὐτὸ ἔχειν· δ—ἐνδεεῖ [and not to be moved, but as after having the same thing; which—lacks]** Ficinus expressed *κ. μ. κινεῖσθαι ἄλλως* [and not to be moved otherwise], which seems true, yet does not have the support of the books.

**392 NOTES ON PLOTINUS**

"...Socrates p. 220. A: 'and not wishing [*ἐθέλων*] to drink—he overcame everyone.' As far as the argument and color are concerned, Plotinus seems to have imitated Plato. For he in *Legg.* [Laws] VIII. p. 836. d: p. 91. Bekk.: 'for we always seek whether some of the things posited lead toward virtue and what does not. Come then, if we grant this to be beautiful or in no way shameful, to be legislated now, what part would it contribute to us toward virtue? Would the character of courage be implanted in the soul of the one persuaded, or in that of the persuader the genus of the temperate idea? Or would no one ever be persuaded of these things, but rather the entire opposite, that everyone will blame the softness of the one yielding to pleasures and unable to endure, but will he not blame the one going into imitation of the female for the likeness of the image?' In the *Symposium* likewise Pausanias discusses the laws regarding love p. 184 sq. From which I shall transcribe only this p. 392. Bekk.: 'for whenever the lover and the beloved come to the same thing, each having a law, the one serving the beloved who has granted favors, that he would justly serve in anything, and the other to the one making him wise and good, that he would justly perform any service, and the one being able to contribute toward wisdom and other virtue, and the other needing to acquire education and other wisdom.' Cf. *Euthydem.* p. 282. b. p. 414. Bekk. except that in the passage of Plotinus the 'beloved' appears as a partaker of temperance and the rest of virtue."

**p. 1321, 14. ὑπεροψίαν τῶν τῇδε ἔχει—ὑποψίαν ἔχει πρὸς αὐτά. [it has a disdain for the things here—it has a suspicion toward them.]** You might say Ficinus also read *ὑπεροψίαν* [disdain] in the latter place in his books. Yet there is no trace of this variety in the Medicean books more than in others. In the second place it is: "the soul has a suspicion about beautiful things" which are in this world. — Soon *ὅτι ἐν σαρξὶ καὶ σώμασιν ὁρᾷ αὐτὰ ὄντα* [because it sees them being in flesh and bodies]. Plato *Conviv.* p. 211. p. 444. Bekk.: "nor again will beauty be imagined by him as some face nor hands nor anything else of which the body partakes;" and p. 445: "what then, she said, do we think, if it should happen to someone to see beauty itself sincere, pure, unmixed, but not full of human flesh, etc." Cf. Plotinus above p. 505. A. (c. 9.) — Soon *μὴ γὰρ ἂν τολμήσαι ἐκεῖνα—ἐμβῆναι* [for it would not dare to immerse itself into those things]: for *τολμᾶν* [to dare], like the Latin *tolerare*, is more often "to dare" even in Plato. Cf. J. A. Ernesti on Tacitus’s *Ann.* III. 3. In this doctrine of the fall of the higher things to these lowest, there is additionally that *τόλμα* [audacity] or *audentia* of the Pythagoreans and indeed the Platonists; regarding which see what I placed above p. 481. extr. — In the following, on the authority of many Codices, I substituted: *ἐπιθέον* [running over/supervening] for the faulty *ἐπιθετέον*. See just the next chapter p. 721. C: *οἷον τὸ ἐπιθέον* [such as the supervening]. I said more on this word at I. 6. 5. p. 54. A.

**p. 1322, 4. καὶ ἐπεῤῥώσθη—πληρωθεῖσα [and it was strengthened—having been filled]** Sophocl. *Œdip. **— 16. ὃ δὲ μηδεὶς ἐποίησε τίς ἂν ποιήσειε; [that which no one made, who could make?]** From the version of Ficinus you might conjecture: "what could anyone make?" Yet the written books do not support it.

**p. 1323, 13. ἐράσμιον δὲ ὂν—τὸ κάλλος. [and beauty being lovely/beloved.]** Cf. Plato's *Phaedrus* p. 250. p. 47. sq. Bekk.: where both other things and this are found toward the end of the page: "but now beauty alone has had this lot, so as to be most manifest and most lovely [*ἐρασμιώτατον*]."

**p. 1324, 5. Διὸ—φευκτέον—ἵνα μὴ ἐκπέσῃς—εἰς τὸ—καλὸν λεγόμενον [Therefore—one must flee—lest you fall—into the—so-called beautiful]** Our philosopher I. 6. 8. p. 56. E. **— 9. ὡς δικαιοσύνη καὶ σωφροσύνη—καίτοι καλὰ ὄντα [as justice and temperance—though they be beautiful things]** I have restored the final words in the Latin, which Ficinus had separated from the rest, in their own place. — Plato *Conviv.* p. 209. p. 440. **p. 1325, 7. Μαρτυρεῖ δὲ καὶ τὸ τῶν ἐραστῶν (ed. male ἀρετῶν) πάθος, ὡς ἕως—ἐν ἐκείνῳ τῷ τὸν (ed. τὸ, sed pertinet ad sequens τύπον, quæ ratio constructionis non rara in his libris) αἰσθητὸν ἔχοντι, οὔπω ἐρᾷ. [And the passion of lovers (ed. poorly: of virtues) testifies, that as long as—in that one having the sensible [type] (ed. *to*, but it pertains to the following *typon*, which kind of construction is not rare in these books), he does not yet love.]** These things seem to conflict with Plutarch’s *Symposiacon* V. 7. p. 681. A. B. p. 790. Wyttenb.: "and of erotic matters, which are indeed the greatest and most vehement passions of the soul, sight gives the beginning; so that the lover flows and melts, whenever he looks at beautiful things as if they were coming into themselves." Yet they do not actually conflict.

**— 10. βλέπειν δὲ ζητεῖ τὸ ἐρώμενον, ἵνα ἐκεῖνο ἐπάρδῃ μαραινόμενον [but he seeks to look at the beloved, so that he may water [*ἐπάρδῃ*] that which is withering]** Above II. 9. 3. p. 201. D. at the words *καὶ ἄρδεται τούτῳ τῷ φωτί* [and it is watered by this light] we touched upon the origin of this formula and some imitations. Let us add a few things pertaining to the composite verb. Lucian, *De Gymnass.* XXVI. p. 909. Wetst.: "much heat flowing from within—immediately fills up, watering [*ἐπάρδον*] with its prime, and provides tireless things for the longest time." The same in *Amoribus* XLV. p. 448: "watering [*ἐπάρδων*] a still tender soul with such virtues." Heraclides *Allegorr. Homerr.* p. 2. ed. Schow.: "we water [*ἐπάρδομεν*] the souls with his (Homer’s) verses as if with drinkable milk;" the reason for which passage Boissonade finally dispatched in *Philostrati Heroica* p. 311. Himerius *Orat.* XIV. 35. p. 668: "the Muses indeed grew your wings in the gardens of Mnemosyne, and the Seasons and Graces nourished them, watering [*ἐπάρδουσαι*] from the springs of Truth." Wernsdorf did not remind us of Plato, and yet perhaps by these things the reading in *Phaedrus* p. 246. e. p. 41. Bekk. can be strengthened: "by these things the plumage of the soul is especially nourished and increased." Thus all books of Plato in this place: on the other hand, all have *ᾄδεται* [is sung] in the second place p. 251. b. But very many Codices of Proclus in *Alcib. pr.* p. 29. our ed., from the first place also cite *ἄρδεται* [is watered]. Himerius *Eclogg.* XXXII. 2. p. 300: "And he himself plants his own soul in this plant, watering [*ἐπάρδων*] it with Attic streams." Theodoretes *Hist. Religios.* p. 1202: "—indeed he enjoyed the streams of Basil the Great who was neighboring and watering [*ἀρδεύοντος*] the Cappadocians, and he returned fruits worthy of the watering [*ἀρδείας*];" Clem. Alex. *Strom.* I. p. 321. Potter.: "Plato orders farmers not to water [*ἐπαρδεύσαι*]." Nonn. *Dionys.* XI. 166: "they water [*ἐπαρδεύουσιν*] the vine-filled harvest with waters." — Concerning the sentiment cf. Platon. *Sympos.* p. 211. p. 445. Bekk.: "—whom (the boys) seeing now you are astounded, and you and many others are ready, seeing the beloveds and always being with them—but only to behold and be together." Concerning the power of the lovers' gaze at each other add Plutarch. *Symposs.* l. l. p. 791. Wytt. Because Ficinus added in the following: "so to speak," he wished to caution the readers, lest in this Plotinian passage they should perhaps take *ἄμορφον* [formless] and *ἀμορφότερον* [more formless] in such a way that it meant "deformed" etc.; as for example *ἀμορφότερος* is in the *Symposium* of Xenophon VIII. 17.

**p. 1327, 1. μίμησις δὲ τοῦτο καὶ οἱ ἐνταῦθα ἐρασταὶ καὶ ἐρώμενοι συγκρῖναι θέλοντες [but this is an imitation and the lovers and beloveds here wishing to unite [*συγκρῖναι*]]** Ficinus expressed *τούτου* [of this], and perhaps he corrected it himself in Med. A. Without the books I was unwilling to change, although the change is attractive. If *συγκρῖναι* [to unite/compare] is true, *ἑαυτούς* [themselves] ought to be thought: or does another thing lie hidden, either *συγκραθῆναι* [to be mixed together] or *συντακῆναι* [to be melted together]? Aristophanes in Plato’s *Symposium* p. 192. e. p. 408. Bekk. regarding the lover: "coming together and being melted together with the beloved to become one from two." Below C. penultimate line I would prefer: *ἀνθ' αὑτῆς* [instead of itself].

**p. 1327, 15. οὐδὲ γαργαλιζομένου λέγει τοῦ σώματος. [nor does he speak of the body being tickled.]** Thus I wrote with the best books instead of *γαργαλιζομένου* of the edition, and *γὰρ γαλιζομένου* of the margin. Plato *Conviv.* p. 189. A. p. 400. Bekk.: "if the orderly part of the body desires such sounds and ticklings [*γαργαλισμῶν*], etc." Plutarch. *De Esu Carn.* p. 997. B.: "and from which that which is broken and made effeminate by touch (Jacobs. *Lectt. Stobb.* p. 156: *τὸ ἐπαφῆς*) produces handlings and womanly ticklings [*γαργαλισμούς*]." Plato *Philebus* p. 46. p. 209. Bekk.: "Soc. Say then, when more pains than pleasures arise, those called of the itch, now these very ones, and those of the ticklings [*γαργαλισμῶν*], whenever the boiling and the inflammation is within, but one does not reach it by rubbing and scratching." Thus long ago Wyttenbach on Plut. p. 1013 and Heusde had corrected the *vulgata* *κινήσει* [movement] to *κνήσει* [scratching]. Similarly in Plato’s *Symposium* p. 185. e. p. 394. Bekk. it is now edited *κνήσαιο* [scratch yourself] instead of *κινήσαις*. Plato *Phaedrus* regarding the feathering of souls p. 251. c: "scratching [*κνῆσις*] and irritation—it boils and is irritated and is tickled [*γαργαλίζεται*] growing the wings." Ibid. p. 253. E. regarding the charioteer: "whenever he is filled with the stings of tickling [*γαργαλισμοῦ*] and longing." Plutarch. *De Sanit. tuenda* p. 126. B: "just as those with the itch always need scratchings and ticklings [*γαργαλισμῶν*]." The same *De Discrim. Amici et Adul.* p. 61. D. p. 233. Wytt.: "scratches and tickles [*γαργαλίζει*]." And, unless my mind deceives me, from here a medicine must be prepared for Philo Judaeus, *Legis Allegorr.* III. 118. p. 336. Pfeiff.: "Wherefore he also does not agree with those who say that pleasure is stable; for stillness is suitable for stone and wood and every inanimate thing, but alien to pleasure (pleasure ed. Pfeiff. faulty). For it desires tickling [*γαργαλισμοῦ*] and the spasmodic, and for some it is not stillness, but the need of intense and vehement torment (torment Pfeiff. poorly)." Others [read] *ἀσκήσεως* [exercise]. Ruhnken on Timaeus’s *Lex. Platon.* p. 19 says thus: "But *ἄκκισις* [affectation], which Mangey [gave] to Philo. T. I. p. 118, is unheard of among the Greeks." I read: "for it desires tickling [*γαργαλισμοῦ*] and the spasmodic, and for some it is not stillness, but there is always need of intense and vehement scratching [*κνήσεως*]": a vehement and intense continuous titillation is needed. For thus Cicero translates the Epicurean word *γαργαλισμὸν*. See *De Nat. Deorr.* I. 40. p. 183. ib. Davis. and our note cf. Moser on Cic. *De Legg.* I. 17. extr. p. 116. Add Bak on Cleomedes *Meteora* II. 1. p. 431. sq. on the Epicurean words *γαργαλισμὸς σώματος* [tickling of the body], which Tib. Hemsterhuis noted from that place in the excellent discussion on Thom. Magistr. p. 179—181; to which Lobeck on Phrynichus’s *Eclogg.* p. 97 is now to be joined. I add a passage of Basil the Great to be compared both in words and sentiments with Philo in the place cited and Plotinus in this place. For he in *Homil. Attende Tibi Isr.* p. 351. B. C. utters these things: "if therefore you attend to yourself, and are initiated that this indeed reaping the providence and the guardianship from me.—and a calm and quiet will arise around the soul, as if the uproar of wanton servant-girls were silenced by the presence of some temperate mistress."

**p. 1328, 14. οὐ κατὰ τὴν τῶν ἀγαλμάτων φύσιν ὄντα [being not according to the nature of statues]** For the sense Ficinus translates correctly. Properly: so that statues can be compared with it. Plato *Sympos.* p. 211. p. 445. Bekk.: "which (beauty itself) if you ever see, it will not seem to you to be according to gold and clothing and beautiful boys and youths, etc." (Which passage should also be compared with ours for the sake of the argument generally:) cf. *Republic* VIII. p. 555. a. and consult Viger on *Idiotismm.* p. 637. and Matth. *Gr. gr.* §. 581. second ed. and those cited there.

**p. 1329, 3. καὶ τάχ' ἂν σώζοι τὸ ἀνάλογον ἢ εἰκών [and perhaps it would preserve/save the analogy or image]** i. e., And perhaps this comparison will maintain the consistency (or: this comparison applied by me of the house and the master will retain and protect the congruence with the thing compared, if etc.) See Wyttenbach on Plut. *De Profectt. in Virtute* (p. 75. A.) p. 552, who teaches thus: "*λόγος σώζει τι* [the argument saves something], the sentiment preserves something, that is, it retains and protects, does not take away or deny," citing Aristid. *Orat. Plat.* I. p. 32. Plato himself *Republic* X. p. 621. p. 515. Bekk.: "and thus—the myth was saved [*ἐσώθη*] and did not perish." Cf. Ast on Plato’s *Sympos.* p. 255.

**— 10. μεθυσθεὶς τοῦ νέκταρος [drunk on nectar]** Plato *Convivio* p. 203. p. 429. Bekk. I have placed the words themselves above at page 721. D. Next *ἢ σεμνοτέρῳ εἶναι τοιαύτης μέθης* [than to be too solemn/grave for such drunkenness] is properly: than to be more serious than to indulge in such drunkenness for himself; or, to be too reverend etc.

**p. 1330, 6 μήτε ἐν τῷ ἄλλῳ—ἄλλο ἐν ἄλλῳ εἶναι· [neither in the other—another to be in another]** See Plato’s *Phædon.* p. 83. p. 56. Bekk. and Wyttenbach on that Dialogue p. 219, whom...
