**LIB. VII. ENNEAD. SIXTH. p. 1327—1333. 395**

...we applied above at V. 8. p. 546. C. which passage I wish to be inspected.

**— 15. καὶ μέγιστόν φησι τοῦτο εἶναι μάθημα [and he says this is the greatest study/learning]** Plato *Republic* VI. p. 505. a. p. 312. Bekk.: "—since that indeed the idea of the good is the greatest study [*μέγιστον μάθημα*] you have often heard, by using which also other things become useful and beneficial." — Soon: *διδάσκουσι μὲν οὖν ἀναλογίαι* [analogies indeed teach]. One should inspect what our writer discusses above concerning analogy [*ἀναλογίᾳ*] in the universal order of things: III. 3. 6. p. 276. D. E. and the note for those things.

**p. 1331, 3. καὶ ἀναβασμοί τινες [and certain steps]** Plato *Sympos.* p. 211. p. 444 sq. Bekk.: "—beginning from these beautiful things for the sake of that beauty always to go up, as if using steps [*ἐπαναβαθμοῖς*], etc." Regarding the forms *ἀναβασμὸς* [step] and *ἀναβαθμὸς* [stair/step] Lobeck has explained copiously on Phrynichus’s *Epitome* p. 324. Furthermore, for the matter, compare Plotinus above p. 50 and p. 292. F. Next, from the readings of the edition, the margin, and the codices *ἀρεταὶ* [virtues], *ἀραιαὶ* [thin/rare], I have made *ἀραί τε* [and prayers], and Ficinus also has *precibus* [with prayers]. These words, however, are drawn from sacred rites, especially of the initiations; and Plato himself preceded Plotinus with the words in the *Symposium* p. 210. A. I do not wish to add more now. Let my Heusde be consulted in *Initiis Philosophiæ Platonicæ*, I. p. 57. and compare Plotinus VI. 9. 11. p. 770.

**— 16. αὐτὸς δὲ αὐγὴ μόνον γεννῶσα νοῦν [but itself only a radiance generating intellect]** These things are joined with the doctrine of Plato, which posits God as both generating mind and ideas. See *De Republic* X. p. 596. b. c. d. cf. ib. VI. p. 508. e. p. 509. a.

**p. 1332, 11. δεῖ νοεῖν, εἰ μὲν οὐσία ἐστὶν ἀεὶ νοοῦσα [one must perceive, if it is a substance always perceiving]** Here Ficinus may seem to have read more in his books to him who does not hold—what must be held everywhere by one comparing these Latin things with the Greek—that he [Ficinus] added these members for the sake of aiding the understanding. For Marsilio everywhere studies to provide for readers hindered by that dense brevity of Plotinian speech.

**— 13. καὶ οὐχ' ἁπλοῦν λέγουσιν—τὸ ὁρᾷν κατ' ἐνέργειαν [and they do not call—seeing in activity simple]** Nicephorus Gregoras, who in *Hist. Byzant.* Book XXII. p. 688 sq. Paris. p. 549 sqq. Venet. in the mention of the discussion with Cabasila, and indeed in the question whether the nature of God suffers a distinction of substance and operation, has separately presented testimonies of Plotinus from several places, also cites this passage p. 551 sq.: "And again he says, that simple is the substance of the intellect and not one thing the thinking [*νόησις*] and another thing the intellect [*νοῦς*]. For those who speak otherwise add to him seeing [*τὸ ὁρᾷν*] just like to eyes. One must therefore leave other things upon the simple nature as needing no assistance, for whatever you add has diminished by the addition that which needs nothing." The rest are read below p. 733. A.

**p. 1333, 7. Διόπερ νοῦν φησιν ὁ Πλάτων εἶναι ὀρθῶς [Wherefore Plato rightly says it is intellect]** I am mistaken, or Ficinus read *Διὸ ὑπέρ*. But in the written books there is no diversity from the edition: yet the tenor of the discussion demands that, and if you read what Plato teaches in *Republic* VI. p. 508. p. 348 sq. Bekk. concerning the sun as the author of sight and the good as the cause of intellect, you would say that passage occurred here to our philosopher. Nicephorus Gregoras could have provided us the use of *δᾳδούχου* [torch-bearer] if he had rendered these Plotinian things to us more accurately. Now however he writes in the place cited p. 552: "and having gone through many things in many ways about this, he (Plotinus) also brings in Plato, confirming his argument. For intellect, he says, not thinking would be unthinking. And Aristotle likewise. Perfect intellect, he says, is self-existent activity, and the same is in it, the same even activity; or it does not change its substance being something else, and its activity another." Cf. also Schol. on Proclus’s *Theol. Platon.* II. 1. p. 90. where it is taught: "from Plato's opinion the first cause is above mind."

**— 12. μηδὲν δὲ ἔργον εἶναι αὐτῷ, ὅτι μηδὲν ἐπιβάλλει αὐτῷ ποιεῖν [and no work to be for him, because nothing pertains [*ἐπιβάλλει*] to him to do]** Ficinus ought: "because nothing *pertains* to him to do." Dio Cass. XXXVI. 15. p. 95: "—to all those of it (of honor) to whom it pertains [*ἐπιβάλλει*], it is fitting to happen." Marcus Antonin. V. 15. p. 156. Gatak.: "what things to a man, insofar as he is a man, do not pertain [*ἐπιβάλλει*]," where see Gatak. Ibid. VII. 7. p. 209: (this passage exists under this title: *Epictetus’s Handbook second*, in the manuscript Cod. Monacensis 529. from which I have these excerpts in my papers: "Do not be ashamed (Schol. in marg. cod. cover yourself) being helped, for it is set before you to act that which pertains [*τὸ ἐπιβάλλον*] (Cod. *τοὐπιβάλλον* and in marg. schol. *τὸ ἁρμόζον σοι* [what is fitting for you]))" where likewise consult Gataker and Upton in the Index of the Greek of Epictetus p. 328. Schweigh. Add Valckenaer’s *Scholas in N. T.* I. p. 225 who applied Antoninus’s later passage to these words of the Gospel of Luke XV. 12: "Give me the portion of the substance that pertains [*τὸ ἐπιβάλλον μέρος*] to me," where there may be someone who judges *μέρος* [portion] a Scholiastic addition. Evidently one who would look at passages of this kind: Archytas in Stob. *Florileg.*

which we have applied to this argument from Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics* X. 2. Compare Stallbaum’s *Prolegomena to Philebus* XXIII. LXVII. XC. Add the so-called *Definitions* of Plato, page 413. a. page 568. Bekker: <note>original: "’Αγαθὸν τὸ αὑτοῦ ἕνεκεν (scilicet ἐφετόν)"</note> "The Good is that which is desired for its own sake." Entirely contrary views are found in Cicero’s *On the Ends of Good and Evil*, Book III. 8. 27: "But it is quite absurd that something should be good, yet not be worth seeking," etc. Compare the same work, IV. 6. 15, where he discusses virtue in conjunction with the notion of the Supreme Good. From these sources, one may conjecture which philosophers Plotinus was attempting to refute while writing this chapter.

p. 1304, 8. **and if we call another the cause, namely God**] Philo the Jew, *Allegorical Interpretation* III. page 101. Mangey, page 284. Pfeiffer: "Do you see that it is not the Lord, but God, who kills Er? <note>Genesis 38:7. The commentator notes the spelling variation between 'Eir' and 'Er' found in ancient lexicons.</note> For he does not destroy the body in his capacity as ruler and leader by using the absolute power of his might, but rather in his capacity as one who employs goodness and kindness. For 'God' is the name of the causal goodness, so that you may know that he created even inanimate things not by power, but by the same goodness with which he created living things. For it was necessary for the manifestation of better things that the generation of worse things should also subsist, by the power of the same causal goodness, which is God." In this passage, the reading <term>autexousio</term> <note>meaning "by his own absolute power"</note> which Pfeiffer brings forward from the editions and Manuscript A, is preferable. I mention in passing that <term>autexousia</term> <note>free will or self-determination</note> is praised in Eustathius’s commentary on the *Iliad* Δ. page 335, but there on page 354 of the Leipzig edition it is read as <note>original: "αὐτὸ ἐξουσία"</note> "power itself." Likewise, in the *Index of the Beginnings of Platonic Philosophy*, our authors praise <term>autexousia</term>. However, the true passage is in Proclus’s commentary on the *First Alcibiades*, page 143, where <term>to autexousion</term> <note>the principle of free will</note> is correctly read, a term which is also frequently met in Plotinus. Furthermore, Philo in the cited passage—as he does elsewhere—seems to follow the Stoic philosophers in this opinion regarding God as the cause of the Good; you may learn that this was their tenet from Gataker’s notes on Marcus Aurelius II. 11. page 47.

— 9. **yet one must not desist**] The margin of the Edition and three manuscript books read "and yet," which Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino, the famous Renaissance translator of Plotinus</note> expressed as: *But finally*. To me, this seems a <term>paradiorthosis</term> <note>a "false correction" by a later scribe</note>, both because of what follows and because Plotinus is accustomed to cry out to his readers in such inquiries that *one must not give up*.

p. 1305, 1. **and shall we establish this as the good?**] Lest you believe by chance that Ficino read "this person" <note>masculine vs. neuter</note>: the Medicean manuscripts themselves show no variation, and nothing is more frequent in these *Enneads* than a sudden change of gender. Along with Ficino, I have retained "we shall establish" <note>original: "θησόμεθα"</note>. The margin and several books here also have "we shall stand/stop."

— 2. **judging with justice, etc.**] The color of this passage seems drawn from the most noble passage of Plato concerning the casting of lots for souls in the *Republic*, Book X. page 617. page 509. Bekker.

p. 1306, 5. **For that which is one's own, if it be not good, is indeed one's own, but one flees from it.**] Diotima in Plato’s *Symposium* page 205. E. page 434. Bekker: "My argument says that love is neither for the half nor for the whole, unless, my friend, it happens to be good; since men are willing to have their own feet and hands cut off if their own members seem to them to be evil. For I think people do not embrace what is their own, unless one calls the good 'one's own' <note>original: "oikeion"</note> and belonging to oneself, and the evil 'alien'; since there is nothing else that men love but the good." For the latter part, apply the *Charmides* page 163. C. Porphyry seems to have had the former part before his eyes in his *Letter to Marcella*, chapter XXXIV. page 36, to which the most elegant Jacobs recently applied a healing hand in his *Readings on Stobaeus*.

— 14. **and striving after the light**] Regarding the word <term>glichomenos</term> <note>striving or longing for</note>, which I find is not recorded in the new London edition of Stephanus’s *Thesaurus*, the *Etymologicum Gudianum* says: "Striving: enduring or desiring, from the sense of clinging tightly to something." It is used with the genitive and dative cases; this caught my attention. Is the passage sound, or should we read "and the accusative"? I believe so. See the Scholiast on Lucian’s *Aetion*: "striving: I cling tightly to. Used with genitive and accusative." Compare Suidas, and Zonaras. You may learn the reason for this construction even from Demosthenes. Regarding the construction with the preposition "about," it is disputed. Antiphanes in Stobaeus’s *Florilegium*:

-> — — — — — No one ever, <-
-> O Master, died while being eager to die; <-
-> But those who **strive** to live, Charon drags <-
-> by the leg against their will, and leads to the ferry— <-

as Valckenaer excellently restored this passage. Iamblichus, on the contrary, in the *Exhortation to Philosophy*, chapter VII: "nor is it necessary for the sake of money to sail to the Pillars of Hercules and frequently risk—"

[[original page: 388]]

...to incline, but through wisdom to suffer no pain <note>original: "νεύειν, διὰ δὲ φρόνησιν μηδὲν πονεῖν"</note> (so the Memmian Manuscript in the text: in the margin "to do" <note>original: "ποιεῖν"</note>, which the later edition by Arcerius had in the text) nor to spend. Truly it is a slavish thing to merely cling to living, but not (this is absent from one book) to cling to **living well** <note>original: "τοῦ ζῇν εὖ γλίχεσθαι"</note> (so also our copies; the Ciz. and Arcerius editions wrongly have "the" <note>original: "τὸ"</note>). Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *On the Composition of Words*, XXII: "In names, then, he tries to pursue these things, and to **strive** <note>original: "γλίχεσθαι"</note> for them" (so the Aldine in the Greek Rhetoricians, but the margin says: "read: he strives" <note>original: "γλίχεται"</note>; in Goeller p. 61, more recent editors have accepted "he strives").

p. 1307, 1. **And therefore the soul, receiving from that place an outflow into itself—and truly it takes wing—is lightened by memory**] The primary sentiment of this passage is drawn from the most celebrated passage of Plato’s *Phaedrus* p. 251. B. cf. our notes above on p. 54. D. 294. B. 297. A. and p. 691. A. However, I shall not leave this passage entirely "without a contribution" <note>original: "ἀσύμβολος" - meaning without adding his own insight</note>. Regarding what Plotinus says, that it **is filled with stings** <note>original: "οἴστρων πίμπλαται"</note>: similarly the verb "to be driven by a gadfly/frenzy" <note>original: "διοιστρεῖσθαι"</note> is used of Centaurs excited by the smell of wine in Diodorus IV. 12: "it happened that these were driven into a frenzy." Eunapius in *Excerpts of History* regarding Constantius meditating on war against Julian: "and being driven by the gadfly of envy and grief, he was swollen toward civil war." Philostratus, *Life of Apollonius* I. 34, regarding eunuchs: "for since the cutting away deprives them of the ability to perform the sexual act, they are allowed into the women's quarters; and if they wish to sleep with the women (the Schellershem Manuscript correctly has "wish" <note>original: "βούλωνται"</note>), do you think," he said, "that the capacity for love or for being with women has been cut out of them? Both, he said; for if the organ by which the body **is driven into frenzy** <note>original: "διοιστρεῖται"</note> were extinguished, love would not come upon anyone." For the following, an elegant passage of Nilus the Ascetic *On Purity and Temperance* should be applied. From this, perhaps, a remedy can be prepared for a passage of Tacitus attempted by many conjectures of learned men, *Annals* XIII. 44: "Then, as is customary in love and anger, there were quarrels, prayers, reproaches, satisfaction: and a part of the darkness was set aside for lust. **Incensed by which heat** <note>original: "Ex qua æstu"</note>, he ran through the unsuspecting man with a sword." Nemesianus, *Cynegetica* 3: "my heart seethes from the sting <note>original: "œstro"</note>." What if Tacitus wrote: "**And as if incensed by a gadfly/sting**" <note>original: "Et quasi œstro incensus"</note>—?

— 15. **in which a grace running over the beauty does not shine forth** <note>original: "ᾧ μὴ ἐμπρέπει χάρις ἐπιθέουσα τῷ κάλλει"</note>] On the construction and use of the verb "to be conspicuous/shine forth" <note>original: "ἐμπρέπειν"</note> see Pierson’s preface to *Moeris* and Valckenaer on Herodotus VII. 67. Jacobs recently restored it to Euripides. Himerius, *Oration* XV. 6: "so that having been depicted (or 'nourished' according to Wernsdorf) under these Attic customs, they might **shine forth** in the meadows, and taking the beauties of their training from here, they might thus practice them upon their own." Theodoret, *On Providence* IV: "I shall proceed in my discourse to the grammatical art, which is more rational than the others, and **befitting** <note>original: "ἐμπρέπουσα"</note> the rational animal." Regarding the verb "to run over" <note>original: "ἐπιθέειν"</note> I have spoken above. Regarding **symmetry** <note>original: "συμμετρία"</note> as the producer of beauty, our philosopher himself disputes on p. 50: "how symmetry of parts... creates beauty," on which passage we have collected much in our special edition of the book *On Beauty* <note>Plotinus, Ennead I.6</note>. This passage, however, which we are now treating, is especially to be held for understanding the inner nature of beauty, grace, and the arts.

p. 1309, 5. **but this is impossible**] Compare Lucas Holstenius and Conrad Orelli on Sallustius *On the Gods and the World* p. 99.

On which passage Lucas Holstenius called upon these Plotinian passages, as well as Proclus, *Elements of Theology* XII, and Dionysius the Areopagite, *On Divine Names* ch. 4. -> BOOK VII. ENNEAD SIX. pages 1307—1310. 389 <-

[[original page: 389]]

I have restored to this location the material that was cut off from this chapter and placed at the threshold of the following one.

page 1310, 10. <note>original: "ὃ τάχ' ἄν τις δυσχεραντικὸς ἀνὴρ εἴποι, ὡς ὑμεῖς, ὦ οὗτοι, τί δὴ ἀποσεμνύνετε τοῖς ὀνόμασιν, ἄνω καὶ κάτω ζωὴν ἀγαθὴν λέγοντες"</note> [Which a certain irritable man might quickly say: "You there, why do you speak so solemnly with these names, speaking back and forth of the 'Good Life'?"] We have written this on the authority of the good manuscripts, which show both "you" <note>original: "ὑμεῖς"</note> and "speak solemnly" <note>original: "ἀποσεμνύνετε"</note>, though they show "eyes" <note>original: "ὄμμασιν"</note> instead of the edition's "bodies" <note>original: "σώμασιν"</note>. Ficino indeed expressed this with his word *spectando* <note>Latin: "by looking/observing"</note>. But I would seem too scrupulous if I left this very point untouched. However, I do not otherwise easily dare to admit conjectures into the text without the support of the books. But since Plotinus undoubtedly wrote "speak solemnly with names" <note>original: "ἀποσεμνύνετε τοῖς ὀνόμασιν"</note>, I have adopted this. Others have dealt with this confusion [between "eyes" and "names"], among them the eminent Porson in his notes on Euripides' *Orestes* 1081, and I myself recently in the notes to Olympiodorus's *On the Alcibiades*, page 281. I add one passage from Plato himself, *Phaedo* page 83 A: <note>original: "ἐνδεικνυμένη ὅτι ἀπάτης μὲν μεστὴ ἡ διὰ τῶν ὀμμάτων σκέψις"</note> [pointing out that the investigation through the eyes is full of deceit]. Iamblichus in the *Exhortation to Philosophy* XIII, page 79, who presents Plato's words: "that the investigation through the eyes <note>original: "ὀμμάτων"</note> is full of deceit" (the word "indeed" <note>original: "μὲν"</note> is omitted in my two books, but rightly inserted from Plato by Kiessling; one of my books and one of Bekker's in the *Various Readings of Plato* has "names" <note>original: "ὀνομάτων"</note>). Let us look at the usage of the word: Plato, *Apology* 17: "not indeed, by Zeus, O men of Athens, speeches composed of fine phrases, like theirs, with terms and names <note>original: "ῥήμασί τε καὶ ὀνόμασιν"</note>, nor even adorned, but you shall hear things spoken at random with the names that happen to occur." *Symposium* page 198: "who would not be struck hearing the beauty of the names and terms at the end?" *Phaedrus* page 234: "the speech; is it not extraordinary in other respects and spoken with [fine] names?" *Menexenus* page 235: "somehow most beautifully embellishing with names, they bewitch our souls." — "Innovation of names" <note>original: "Ὀνομάτων καινοτομία"</note> is also Platonic. Libanius uses it; on which occasion I can wipe away a foul stain. In Epistle 1600, page 727 of Wolf's edition, he praises the eloquent speech of Basil: "For my tongue was not accustomed to these things, but as if struck by the innovation of names <note>original: "ὀνομάτων καινοτομίᾳ"</note> while traversing a cliff, it said to me, its father: 'Father, you did not teach me this. This man is Homer, no, he is Plato, no, Aristotle, no, Susarion who knows everything.'" And these things the tongue said. To be sure, Libanius imagines his tongue reproaching him as its father (that is, as Basil's teacher). I omit minor points. For "Susarion," other books have "Sudarion." Wolf praises Bentley regarding Susarion. But he could have learned from Bentley that Susarion, the most ancient comic poet, was not of such authority that he could hold a place alongside Homer, Plato, and Aristotle, and thus be called "the one who knows everything." What then? Our Palatine Codex from Heidelberg, number 356, provides the true reading: "but Aristotle—but [he is] greater than you" <note>original: "ἀλλὰ σοῦ γὰρ μείζων"</note>. Truly, to the names of Homer, Plato, and Aristotle, the tongue adds: *but indeed greater than you, and he who knows all things*, has bestowed that eloquence upon Basil. Unless you prefer to conclude that Libanius, using a poetic form: "better than you" <note>original: "σοῦ γὰρ ἀρείων"</note>, made the scribes more prone to that error. I return to the point. Plotinus could have taken the verb "to speak solemnly" <note>original: "ἀποσεμνύνειν"</note> from Plato. See *Theaetetus* page 168 d: "speaking solemnly of the 'measure of all things'." Iamblichus, *On the Mysteries* I. 21, page 38: "and to venerate some things as divine, but to consider others as having become human and thus contemptible." where the Gotha and Vienna manuscripts reject "to have become." Correctly. I will add passages coming closer to the similarity of the Plotinian passage. Plato, *Phaedrus* page 244 d: "they named it the art of augury <note>original: "οἰωνιστικήν"</note>, which the moderns now call 'augury' <note>original: "οἰωνιστικήν"</note>, solemnizing it with the letter omega." Dio Cassius LX. 5: "Thus having solemnly honored his fathers, he himself accepted nothing beyond the names that lead to power." Basil the Great in *Hexaemeron* 2: "those who solemnize him (man) with this name." Maximus Tyrius, *Dissertation* XXIX. 1: "Can you say whom Homer names—'born of Zeus'—and 'shepherds of the people,' and other such things as a poet would likely use to solemnize the virtue of a man with names?" The formula "up and down" or "back and forth" <note>original: "ἄνω καὶ κάτω"</note> no less reveals a reader of Plato. *Gorgias* page 493 a: "and this part of the soul—happens to be such as to be persuaded and to shift back and forth," where see Heindorf page 157. cf. 115. and on *Theaetetus* page 320 add Stallbaum on *Philebus* page 127. John Chrysostom Volume III page 445. VI page 275 C. Volume X page 669 B. Theodoret, Epistle 86, page 1157 Schulz, which passage I shall transcribe because it comes closer to the similarity of the Plotinian passage: "Why then, swaggering over my rights and talking back and forth <note>original: "ἄνω καὶ κάτω"</note> about the law, did you not accept the benefit therefrom?" Wherefore the passage of Plotinus is to be translated thus: "You, O men, why then do you magnificently celebrate with words, back and forth, calling life 'the Good'?" [[original page: 390]]

Nevertheless, that this [usage] was employed by good writers is shown by the collections of Viger (p. 564) and Matthiae in *Greek Grammar* § 539. 1. second edition.

p. 1311, 1. <note>original: "ἢ τί ἂν διαφέροι ἐν τῷ εἶναι ἢ ὅλως μὴ εἶναι—καὶ τὸν φόβον τῆς φθορᾶς κ. τ. λ."</note> **"Or what difference would it make to be or not to be at all—and the fear of destruction etc."**] These words bring to mind Cicero in *Tusculan Disputations* I. 6: "M. Where then are these people whom you call miserable? Or what place do they inhabit? For if they exist, they cannot be nowhere. A. I truly think they are nowhere. M. Therefore they do not even exist. A. Exactly so; and yet they are miserable for that very reason, because they are nothing." However, the person whom Plotinus introduces as raising these objections in this passage seems to be arguing from the opinion of the **Epicureans** <note>Followers of Epicurus who believed pleasure was the highest good and death was the end of sensation</note>, who both placed happiness in pleasure and were accustomed to boast: *Death is nothing to us.* See Wyttenbach on Plato’s *Phaedo* p. 142—144. Yet, he most closely regards the decrees of **Callicles** and similar men, which Socrates refutes in the *Gorgias*. To this also belong the things read here concerning **friendship** <note>original: "φιλίᾳ"</note>. See *Gorgias* p. 507. e. p. 133. Bekker edition. Or did Plotinus regard the passage in Plato’s *Timaeus* where the **friendship** of the Universe is discussed p. 32. e. p. 29. Bekker (which passage Eubulus praises against Aristotle in Angelo Mai’s *Vatican Collection* II. 674, who also has "having bound together," and therefore does not support the conjecture of Lindau, "having breathed together").

— 5. **Plato—in the Philebus**] That noble dispute in that dialogue is observed by Plotinus p. 22. ff. p. 154. Bekker:—"For neither is your mind, O Socrates, the Good, but it will likely have the same complaints, etc." I am surprised that Stallbaum (p. 54 ff.) did not apply Plotinus to this passage, since our philosopher explains Plato’s purpose and his opinions. Moreover, it should be compared with that other dispute in Plato’s *Gorgias* p. 506 ff. p. 130 ff. Bekker: "Socrates: Listen then to me taking up the argument from the beginning. Is the pleasant and the good the same thing? etc."

p. 1313, 6. <note>original: "παρὰ τῶν ζώντων ἡ ἐπιμέλεια καὶ ἡ κήδευσις"</note> **"the care and the funeral rites from the living"**] Thus the margin and the best manuscript books read instead of "animals" and "permanence." The noun **funeral care** <term>κήδευσις: specifically refers to the care given to the dead or the duties of kinship</term> should be added to the examples which learned men have recently collected for Stephanus’s *Thesaurus* and should be recorded in Schneider’s *Lexicon*. This class of words is properly used for the care usually bestowed upon the dead; see Zonaras’s *Lexicon* 1204: "kedeia: burial; and also relationship by marriage." Heyne collected more from the Grammarians on the *Iliad* book 23, line 160, among which the word **funeral care** itself occurs. Furthermore, **care** <note>original: "ἐπιμέλεια"</note> is joined with words of this family. Dio Cassius XLIII. 17. near the end p. 353. Reimar: "enjoying the foresight and the **guardianship** <note>original: "κηδεμονίαν"</note> from me.—and I care for you as my children." Dio Chrysostom *Oration* LIII. p. 556. C. p. 279. Reiske, concerning Jupiter as the father of men:—"as it is necessary that the **care** of kings be fatherly and **protective**." Theodoret on *Ezekiel* XXXVI. Vol. II. p. 993: "for since I set them apart like sheep under my **guardianship**, I will grant them shepherd-like **care**." Soon also **unrepentant** <note>original: "ἀμετανόητον"</note> must be recorded in the Lexicons as a third example of this usage.

— 15. <note>original: "οἷον ἐπὶ τῷ παιδὶ ὅτι πάρεστιν ἥδεσθαι"</note> **"as if to be pleased that the boy is present"**] Lest anyone think this passage was incorrectly understood by Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino, the 15th-century translator of Plotinus</note>, and that one should think of boys whom those who hold them in affection wish to be with them always, as in Plato’s *Symposium* p. 192. p. 408. Bekker: "to be in the same place as much as possible with one another, so as not to be separated from one another day or night." and in the *Charmides* p. 155. e: "and I thought Critias was most wise in matters of love, who said, speaking of the beautiful boy, etc."—firstly, an interpretation of that kind would be more suited to an author contemporary with the Attic and free republic—secondly, Plotinus only transitions to the mention of venereal matters in the following parts. For the rest, the indefinite use of the Article from the cited passage of the *Charmides* must be maintained for our passage; Heindorf discussed this usage in the same place. Cf. Matthiae *Greek Grammar* § 267. In the final words, I have included "re" in brackets in the Latin and added *altogether*: I did the former so that a *woman* might be thought of, which the small word "to whom" <note>original: "ᾗ"</note> requires; the latter, so that no one refers that "doing" <note>original: "δρῶντα"</note> to *intercourse*.—Above p. 321. F. 322. A: Plotinus himself used **work** <note>original: "ἐργασίαν"</note> for performing a venereal act, which elsewhere refers to the trade of a prostitute. (See Valckenaer on Herodotus I. 93.) Intercourse itself is a **work of fornication** for Gregory Nazianzen: *concerning a passionate gaze* in the Heidelberg Codex no. 356, where the Theologian says: "I saw the beauty of a woman torturing my mind and my sobriety. And I escaped the **work of fornication**, but I defiled my own virginity in the thought of my heart."—Furthermore, Plotinus may seem in this place to look back to the words of Plato’s *Republic* VI. p. 505. p. 313:—"but good things..."

-> BOOK VII. ENNEAD SIX. p. 1311—1321. 391 <-

[[original page: 391]]

"No one is any longer satisfied with possessing what merely seems to be, but they seek what truly is, and here everyone already holds mere opinion in contempt." <note>original: οὐδενὶ ἔτι ἀρκεῖ τὰ δοκοῦντα κτᾶσθαι... This quote emphasizes the philosophical transition from appearance to reality.</note> —Quite so.

p. 1314, 6. **even if it desires it, and rejoices in its like**] The margin of the edition and several manuscripts read: *even if it possesses it*. Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the influential Renaissance translator of Plato and Plotinus.</note> joined both readings in his version. Not a bad idea, in my opinion. Moreover, that proverb applies here: "as like always approaches like," as expressed in Plato's *Symposium* p. 195. b. or as it is uttered differently in other places. See *Lysis* p. 214. Ast on *Phaedrus* p. 336. Zell on Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics* VIII. 1. 4. p. 333. Cicero's *On Old Age* III. beginning, and there Gernhard p. 15. sq.

p. 1315, 1. **Wherefore there is also a greater kinship toward themselves—for those who are more good**] Plato explains this sentiment more fully in the *Gorgias* p. 507. sq. p. 132. sq. Bekker. <note>The term <term>kinship (οἰκείωσις)</term> refers to the natural affinity or "belonging" between the soul and the Good.</note>

— 5. **if where there is in no way "other," but the "other"—is good to itself**] We have written it thus with Ficino and the best Codices instead of *is in*, from which corruption I think it happened that later *is* was added before *the kinship*, which we have therefore included in brackets. Ficino sought to remedy this passage differently, namely by interposing *and* before *is good to itself*.

— 10. **but if it were not done with pleasure**] Regarding "it," understand "the acquisition of the Good." "But even if the attaining of the Good (the achievement of the Good) were not carried out with pleasure."

p. 1316, 4. **But the form having come upon it like a beautiful dream**] The philosopher of Lycopolis <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD), born in Lycopolis, Egypt.</note> has before his eyes that description of matter which Plato wonderfully executed in the *Timaeus* p. 49. sqq. where many things are said about matter, and indeed these: (p. 51. p. 62. Bekker) "participating in some most difficult way in the intelligible." The simile of the <term>dream (ἐνύπνιον)</term> is itself common to Plato, as in the same dialogue p. 52. p. 64. Bekker, although there indeed in a slightly different way. Cf. also Plotinus above p. 164. E. p. 175. C. p. 367. G.

— 14. **but the more—and the intellect of the soul) the good would approach the opposite of the soul, and as if being purified.**] Ficino expressed *but still*, and it is so corrected in Medicean MS A. (Perhaps Plotinus gave *is upon* i.e., *is present*); then *to the opposite of matter* (and most recently the Darmstadt MS shows: *whatever of the soul is imprinted* instead of *matter*); I have changed nothing, except *would proceed* into *would approach*, which the good books provided. And it may seem sound to one considering "the opposite of the soul," that the soul inclines toward lower things and desires the delights of sensible things, which the Good itself would despise and flee from. I have provided for the punctuation of this entire passage.

p. 1317, 8. **and not to be moved, but as if possessing the same thing; which—is lacking**] Ficino expressed *and not to be moved otherwise*, which seems true, yet does not have the support of the manuscripts.

— 13. **having pushed away the opposing argument. And this is it.**] See the places cited above from Plato in the *Philebus* p. 22. sq. p. 154. sqq. Bekker and in the *Gorgias* p. 506. sq. p. 130 sqq. Bekker and what Plotinus himself makes those dissenting philosophers say toward the end of chapter XXIV. p. 716. C. D. E. and the notes there.

p. 1319, 2. **Therefore, to think that the Good is from both the intellect—positing**] See the cited passage of Plato, namely in the *Philebus* p. 22. sqq. p. 154 sqq. Bekker.

p. 1320, 3. **the being drunk on nectar, and at the feast—the banquet**] Plato in the *Symposium* p. 203. p. 429. Bekker: "For when Aphrodite was born, the gods held a feast, the others and also Poros (Plenty), the son of Metis (Wisdom). When they had dined etc.—Poros then, being drunk on <term>nectar (νέκταρ)</term> etc." which passage Plotinus treated extensively above in III. 5. 5. 7. 8. 9. III. 6. 14. As for how often a "feast" is mentioned regarding the gods in the *Iliad* and *Odyssey*, it would be tedious to demonstrate with examples. Cf. also Plato's *Phaedrus*: "whenever they go to a feast and a banquet (the gods)" [p. 247.] —and "the father was drunk" is in *Iliad* 5. 426. 15. 47.

— 8. **Wherefore he will also add truth to the mixture**] Plato in the *Philebus* p. 60. sqq. p. 200. sqq. Stallbaum, from which I add only this: *Socrates: Therefore, if we should see the truest parts of each having mixed them, would these, having been blended, be sufficient to provide us with the most desirable life, or do we still need something more, even of those things that are not such?*

p. 1321, 7. **so as not to be left behind according to one's power, wishing (so the best books. The edition has "to wish" with others) for the temperance of the beloved**] Regarding the construction, see Thomas Magister with the interpreters p. 160. ed. Bernard. However, <term>to wish (θέλειν)</term> has in this place a greater force of zeal and desire. We: *so as by no means to remain behind*, or: *earnestly desiring not to remain behind*. Regarding this force of the word, see Wesseling on Herodotus IX. 14. Markland on Lysias I. p. 152. p. 616. Reiske. Plato in the *Symposium* concerning So-

p. 220. A: *and not wishing to drink—he overcame everyone.* <note>original: καὶ πίνειν οὐκ ἐθέλων—πάντας ἐκράτει</note> Regarding the subject matter and tone, Plotinus seems to have imitated Plato. For the latter says in *Laws* VIII. p. 836. d: "for we are always seeking which of the proposed things leads to virtue and which does not. Come then, if we allow this to be beautiful or in no way shameful, being now legislated, what part would it contribute to virtue for us? Whether in the soul of the persuaded one will the character of courage be implanted, or in the soul of the persuader the genus of the temperate idea? Or would no one ever be persuaded of these things, but rather everyone will blame the weakness of the one yielding to pleasures and unable to endure, and will he not reproach the one going into imitation of the female for the likeness of the image?" In the *Symposium* likewise, Pausanias disputes concerning the laws looking toward love p. 184 sq. From which I shall add only this p. 392. Bekk.: "for when the lover and the beloved come to the same point, each having a law, the one serving the beloved who grants favors, that he might justly serve in anything, and the other justly serving the one making him wise and good in anything he might provide, and the one being able to contribute to wisdom and the rest of virtue, and the other needing to acquire education and the rest of wisdom." Cf. *Euthydemus* p. 282. b. p. 414. Bekk. except that in the passage of Plotinus the *beloved* appears as a participant in temperance and the rest of virtue. Cf. also Xenophon’s *Symposium* c. VIII. §. 15 sqq.

p. 1321, 14. *he has a disdain for the things here—he has a suspicion toward them.* <note>original: ὑπεροψίαν τῶν τῇδε ἔχει—ὑποψίαν ἔχει πρὸς αὐτά</note>] You might say Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino, the 15th-century Renaissance translator of Plotinus</note> also read *disdain* <term>hyperopsian: looking down upon</term> in the latter place in his books. Yet there is no trace of this variation in the Medicean manuscripts any more than in others. In the second place, however, it is: the soul *has a suspicion about the beautiful things* which are in this world.—Soon after: *because he sees them being in flesh and bodies.* <note>original: ὅτι ἐν σαρξὶ καὶ σώμασιν ὁρᾷ αὐτὰ ὄντα</note> Plato *Symposium* p. 211. p. 444. Bekk.: "nor again will the beautiful appear to him as some face or hands or anything else of which the body partakes;" and p. 445: "what then, she said, do we think, if it should happen to someone to see the beautiful itself, sincere, pure, unmixed, but not full of human flesh etc." Cf. Plotinus above p. 505. A. (c. 9.)—Soon after: *for they would not dare—to enter into.* <note>original: μὴ γὰρ ἂν τολμήσαι ἐκεῖνα—ἐμβῆναι</note> For *to dare* <note>original: τολμᾶν</note> to immerse themselves; for *to dare*, like the Latin *tolerare*, is more often *to venture* even in Plato. Cf. J. A. Ernesti on Tacitus *Annals* III. 3. In this doctrine of the fall of higher things to these lowest, one must additionally consider that <term>tolma: audacity or daring</term> of the Pythagoreans and indeed the Platonists; concerning which see what I placed above p. 481. at the end.—In the following, by the authority of many Codices, I have substituted: *running over* <note>original: ἐπιθέον</note> for the faulty *to be placed upon*. See just in the next chapter p. 721. C: "as that which runs over." Concerning this word I have said more at I. 6. 5. p. 54. A.

p. 1322, 4. *and she was strengthened—having been filled* <note>original: καὶ ἐπεῤῥώσθη—πληρωθεῖσα</note>] Sophocles *Oedipus at Colonus* 661: "and perhaps it was strengthened in them to say terrible things;" where it is *she received strength*. See Elmsley p. 171. below. Plotinus again imitates Plato: *Symposium* p. 210. d. e. p. 443. Bekk.: "—until there, having been strengthened and increased, he may look upon a certain single knowledge of such a kind, which is of such beauty;" which passage Proclus also had before his eyes in *Alcibiades* pr. p. 246.

— 9. *is it good to remain here?* <note>original: καλὸν μὲν ὧδε μένειν;</note>] These words remind one of the words of Peter to Christ when he appeared in divine form, saying: *it is good for us to be here.* Gospel of Matthew XVII. 4. Mark IX. 5. Luke IX. 33.

— 16. *that which no one has made, who could make?* <note>original: ὃ δὲ μηδεὶς ἐποίησε τίς ἂν ποιήσειε;</note>] From the version of Ficino you might conjecture: *what could anyone make?* Yet the written books do not support this.

p. 1323, 13. *and being lovely—beauty.* <note>original: ἐράσμιον δὲ ὂν—τὸ κάλλος</note>] Cf. Plato’s *Phaedrus* p. 250. p. 47. sq. Bekk.: where among other things this is at the end of the page: "but now beauty alone has obtained this lot, so as to be most manifest and most lovely."

— 15. *so that it is the beginning of beauty and the end of beauty etc.* <note>original: ὥστε ἀρχὴ κάλλους καὶ πέρας κάλλους</note>] Cf. above I. 6. 9. p. 58. A: "both the fountain and the beginning of the beautiful" cf. Plato *Greater Hippias* p. 289. d. Moreover, the sources for this entire dispute are to be considered the passages of Plato in *Philebus* p. 64. C. and in the *Symposium* p. 210. a. b. c. in *Republic* VI. p. 509. From which also flowed what is read in Iamblichus *On General Mathematical Science* in Villoison’s *Anecdota* II. p. 191. in Proclus in *Platonic Theology* III. 18. p. 151. cf. II. 4. p. 90. in Damascius *On First Principles* p. 233. Cf. Plotinus both in the places cited p. 58. A. B. and p. 555. sq. from which again Dionysius the Areopagite profited in *On Divine Names* c. IV. p. 558. sq. This very passage of our writer which we are treating, Brucker touched upon in *Critical History of Philosophy* II. p. 397.—That which immediately precedes, *it is the flower of beauty that makes beautiful*, is itself a word of Plato (See *Symposium* p. 183. E. Cf. Heusde’s *Critical Specimens on Plato* p. 114. sq.) by the imitation of many thereafter.

celebrated. It suffices to add these two: Proclus in *On the Timaeus* page 330: <note>original: "ἄνθος νοερόν"</note> *an intellectual flower*. Olympiodorus in *On the Alcibiades* preface II. page 109: <note>original: "κάλλος τὸ ἄνθος τοῦ εἴδους"</note> *beauty is the flower of form*.

— 9. **as justice and temperance—even though they are beautiful**] I have restored the final words in the Latin, which Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino, the 15th-century Platonist translator.</note> had separated from the rest, to their proper place.—Plato in the *Symposium* page 209. page 440. Schow edition: *with his (Homer's) verses we water our souls as if with drinkable milk;* the sense of which passage Boissonade finally cleared up in his notes to Philostratus's *Heroica* page 311. Himerius, *Oration* XIV. 35. page 668: *The Muses produced your wings in the gardens of Memory, and the Hours and Graces nourished them, watering them from the springs of Truth.* Wernsdorf did not remind us of Plato, and yet perhaps by these the reading in the *Phaedrus* page 246. e. page 41. Bekker edition can be confirmed: *by these things the plumage of the soul is especially nourished and increased.* So all the books of Plato have it in this place: though all have <note>original: "ᾄδεται" (is sung)</note> *is sung* in the second place on page 251. b. But many manuscripts of Proclus in *On the Alcibiades* page 29 of our edition also praise <note>original: "ἄρδεται" (is watered)</note> *is watered* from the first place. Himerius, *Eclogues* XXXII. 2. page 300: *He himself plants his own soul in this plant, watering it with Attic streams.* Theodoret, *Religious History* page 1202: *—he enjoyed the streams of Basil the Great who was a neighbor and watered the Cappadocians, and he returned fruits worthy of the watering.* Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* I. page 321. Potter edition: *Plato commands the farmers not to irrigate.* Nonnus, *Dionysiaca* XI. 166: *they irrigate the vine-clad harvest with waters.*—Regarding the sentiment, cf. Plato's *Symposium* page 211. page 445. Bekker: *—whom (the youths) you are now struck by seeing, and you and many others are ready, seeing your darlings and being always with them—but only to behold and be with them.* On the power of the gaze of lovers between themselves, add Plutarch's *Table Talk* in the place cited, page 791. Wyttenbach. Because Ficino added in the next part: *so to speak*, he wished to warn readers lest in this Plotinian passage they take <term>amorphon (formless)</term> and *more formless* to mean *deformed* etc.; as for example *more formless* appears in Xenophon's *Symposium* VIII. 17.

page 1327, 1. **and this is an imitation, and the lovers and beloved here wishing to join together**] Ficino expressed *of this*, and perhaps he himself corrected it thus in the Medicean manuscript A. Without the books I did not wish to change it, although the change is attractive. If *to join together* <note>original: "συγκρῖναι"</note> is the true reading, *themselves* must be understood: or does another word lie hidden, either *to be mixed together* or *to be melted together*? Aristophanes in Plato's *Symposium* page 192. e. page 408. Bekker, concerning the lover: *coming together and being melted with the beloved to become one out of two.* Below in section C, second to last line, I would prefer: *instead of herself.*

— 7. **where indeed he would exchange nothing of all things for this etc.**] Both the preceding parts in this chapter and indeed even more the following parts have again flowed from the speech of Socrates in Plato's *Symposium*, especially near the end, pages 210—212. A. pages 443—446. Bekker.

-> 394 NOTES ON PLOTINUS <-

[[original page: 394]]

**p. 1327, 15. nor of the body being tickled.]** I have written it thus following the best manuscripts instead of the "being tickled" <note>original: γαργαλιζομένου</note> of the printed edition, and the "for of the [sea] being calmed" <note>original: γὰρ γαλιζομένου</note> of the margin. Plato, *Symposium* p. 189. A.: "if the orderly part of the body desires such noises and ticklings <note>original: γαργαλισμῶν</note> etc." Plutarch, *On the Eating of Flesh* p. 997. B.: "and from which the part softened and made effeminate by touch <note>Jacobs, *Lectures on Stobaeus* p. 156: 'by touch'</note> produces <note>the same author: 'begets'</note> strokings and womanish ticklings." Plato, *Philebus* p. 46.: "Socrates: Speak then; when the pains are greater than the pleasures—those called the 'itchings' <note>original: ψώρας</note> just now—these are the ones, and those of the ticklings, whenever the boiling and inflammation is within, and one cannot reach it by rubbing and scratching <note>original: κνήσει</note>." Wyttenbach on Plutarch p. 1013 and Heusde had long ago corrected the common reading "movement" <note>original: κινήσει</note> to this. Similarly in Plato’s *Symposium* p. 185. e. it is now edited as "you might scratch" <note>original: κνήσαιο</note> instead of "you might move." Plato, *Phaedrus*, on the growing of the soul's wings, p. 251. c: "there is scratching and irritation—it boils and is irritated and is tickled <note>original: γαργαλίζεται</note> as it grows wings." Ibid. p. 253. E. concerning the charioteer: "whenever he is filled with the stings of tickling and longing." Plutarch, *On Preserving Health* p. 126. B: "just as those with the itch always need scratchings and ticklings." The same author, *How to Tell a Flatterer from a Friend* p. 61. D.: "it scratches and tickles." And, unless my mind deceives me, a remedy must be prepared from this for Philo Judaeus, *Allegorical Interpretation of the Law* III. 118: "Therefore he does not agree with those who say that pleasure is a 'stable state'; for stillness is appropriate to stone and wood and every inanimate thing, but foreign to pleasure. For it aims at tickling <note>original: γαργαλισμοῦ</note> and convulsive movement, and in some cases there is need not of stillness, but of intense and violent scratching <note>original: κνήσεως</note>." <note>Pfeiffer's edition incorrectly reads 'pleasure' and 'need'. Others read 'exercise'.</note> Ruhnken on Timaeus' *Platonic Lexicon* p. 19 says: "But *akkisis* [affectation], which Mangey thrusts upon Philo, is unheard of in Greek." I read: "for it aims at tickling and convulsive movement, and in some cases there is need not of stillness, but of intense and violent *scratching* <note>original: κνήσεως</note> continually": *there is need of a vehement and intense continuous titillation.* For this is how Cicero translates the Epicurean word *gargalismos* [tickling]. See *On the Nature of the Gods* I. 40. and our own notes; cf. Moser on Cicero's *On the Laws* I. 17. Add Bak on Cleomedes' *Meteora* II. 1. regarding the Epicurean words "tickling of the body," which Tib. Hemsterhuis noted from that passage in his excellent discussion on Thomas Magister; to which should now be joined Lobeck on Phrynichus' *Eclogae* p. 97. I add a passage from Basil the Great, which in both words and sentiments should be compared with Philo and Plotinus here. For he, in the *Homily: Give Heed to Thyself*, p. 351, speaks thus: "If therefore you attend to yourself... there will be a calm and silence around the soul, as if the noise of wanton maidservants were silenced by the presence of a certain temperate mistress."

**p. 1328, 14. not being according to the nature of statues]** Ficino translates the sense correctly. Literally: *so that statues can be compared with it.* Plato, *Symposium* p. 211.: "which (Beauty itself) if you ever see, it will not seem to you to be according to [in the same category as] gold and clothing and beautiful boys and youths etc." (Which passage should also be compared generally with our passage for the sake of the argument.) Cf. *Republic* VIII. p. 555. a. and consult Viger on *Idioms* p. 637.

**p. 1329, 3. and perhaps the analogy or image might be preserved]** i.e., And perhaps this comparison will maintain the consistency (or: this comparison I have used of the house and the master will retain and protect the congruence with the thing compared, if etc.) See Wyttenbach on Plutarch's *On Progress in Virtue*: "a 'reason preserves something' <note>original: λόγος σώζει τι</note>, a statement preserves something, that is, it retains and protects it, it does not remove or deny it," citing Aristides. Plato himself in *Republic* X. p. 621.: "and thus the myth was preserved <note>original: ἐσώθη</note> and did not perish." Cf. Ast on Plato’s *Symposium* p. 255.

**— 10. drunk with nectar]** Plato, *Symposium* p. 203. I have placed the words themselves above at page 721. D. Presently, "or to be too dignified for such drunkenness" <note>original: ἢ σεμνοτέρῳ εἶναι τοιαύτης μέθης</note> is literally: *than to be [too] serious to indulge in such intoxication*; or, *to be too venerable etc.*

**p. 1330, 6. nor in the other—that one thing is in another;]** See Plato’s *Phaedo* p. 83. and Wyttenbach on that Dialogue p. 219.

<summary>This page provides a philological analysis of Plotinus's text, specifically debating the correct Greek terms for physical sensations like "tickling" and "scratching" by comparing them to usage in Plato, Plutarch, and Philo. It also clarifies the soul's relationship to the body using the metaphor of a master in a house.</summary>

-> BOOK VII. ENNEAD SIX. pages 1327—1333. 395 <-

[[original page: 395]]

we applied above to V. 8. p. 546. C. <note>A reference to a previous section of the commentary</note> which passage I would wish to be inspected.

— 15. **and he says this is the greatest study**] <note>original: "καὶ μέγιστόν φησι τοῦτο εἶναι μάθημα"</note> Plato *Republic* VI. p. 505. a. p. 312. Bekker edition: — "Since you have often heard that the idea of the Good is the greatest study, by which also other things, using it as a supplement, become useful and profitable." — Soon after: **analogies, then, do teach.** <note>original: "διδάσκουσι μὲν οὖν ἀναλογίαι"</note> One should inspect what our author discusses above regarding **analogy** <term>analogy: the proportional relationship between different levels of reality</term> in the universal order of things: III. 3. 6. p. 276. D. E. and what the annotation to those lines contains.

p. 1331, 3. **and certain steps**] <note>original: "καὶ ἀναβασμοί τινες"</note> Plato *Symposium* p. 211. p. 444 sq. Bekker: — "beginning from these beautiful things, for the sake of that Beauty, to always ascend, as if using **steps**..." <note>original: "ἐπαναβαθμοῖς"</note> etc. Regarding the forms *anabasmos* and *anabathmos* <note>two Greek variations of the word for "step" or "stair"</note> Lobeck has explained extensively in his *Epitome of Phrynichus* p. 324. For the rest, on this matter compare Plotinus above p. 50. and p. 292. F. Soon after, from the readings of the edition, the margin, and the manuscripts, where they had *aretai* (virtues) or *araiai* (thin/rare), I have restored **and prayers**; <note>original: "ἀραί τε"</note> and Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino, the 15th-century translator of Plotinus</note> also has *precibus* (by prayers). These words are drawn from sacred rites, especially those of the initiations; and Plato himself preceded Plotinus in these words in the *Symposium* p. 210. A. I do not wish to add more now. Let my friend Heusde be consulted in *The Beginnings of Platonic Philosophy*, I. p. 57. and compare Plotinus VI. 9. 11. p. 770.

— 16. **but he himself is only a radiance generating mind**] <note>original: "αὐτὸς δὲ αὐγὴ μόνον γεννῶσα νοῦν"</note> These things are connected with the doctrine of Plato, which positions God as generating both the mind and the ideas. See *Republic* X. p. 596. b. c. d. cf. ibid. VI. p. 508. e. p. 509. a.

p. 1332, 11. **one must understand, if it is a substance always thinking**] <note>original: "δεῖ νοεῖν, εἰ μὲν οὐσία ἐστὶν ἀεὶ νοοῦσα"</note> Here Ficino might seem to some to have read more in his manuscripts, but one who compares these Latin passages with the Greek must hold that he added these members for the sake of aiding the understanding. For everywhere Marsilio <note>Ficino</note> strives to look out for readers hindered by that dense brevity of Plotinian speech.

— 13. **and they do not say it is simple—seeing in actuality**] <note>original: "καὶ οὐχ' ἁπλοῦν λέγουσιν—τὸ ὁρᾷν κατ' ἐνέργειαν"</note> Nicephorus Gregoras, who in his *Byzantine History* Book XXII p. 688 sq. Paris edition, p. 549 sqq. Venice edition, in the mention of the dispute with Cabasilas—specifically on the question of whether the nature of God admits a distinction between substance and operation—exhibited testimonies of Plotinus from several places separately; he also praises this passage on p. 551 sq.: "And again he says, that the substance of the mind is simple and that thought is not one thing and mind another. For those who say otherwise attribute **seeing** to it just as one does to **eyes**. One must therefore leave other things aside in the case of a simple nature that needs no assistance; for whatever you add diminishes by that addition that which needs nothing." The rest are read below on p. 733. A.

p. 1333, 7. **Wherefore Plato says rightly that it is mind**] <note>original: "Διόπερ νοῦν φησιν ὁ Πλάτων εἶναι ὀρθῶς"</note> I am mistaken, or Ficino read "Wherefore above." <note>original: "Διὸ ὑπέρ"</note> But in the written books there is no difference from the edition: nevertheless, the tenor of the argument demands it, and if you read what Plato teaches in *Republic* VI p. 508 regarding the sun as the author of sight and the Good as the cause of intellect, you would say that passage was before our philosopher's eyes here. Nicephorus Gregoras could have provided us with the use of "torch-bearer" <note>original: "δᾳδούχου"</note> if he had rendered these Plotinian words more accurately for us. But now he writes in the place cited p. 552: "And having discussed many things in many places concerning this, Plotinus also brings in Plato, confirming his argument. For Mind, he says, if not thinking, would be mindless. And Aristotle likewise. Perfect mind, he says, is a self-sprung activity, and in its case, the thing and the activity are the same; or it does not change, being one thing in substance and another in activity." Cf. also the Scholiast on Proclus's *Platonic Theology* II. 1. p. 90. where it is taught: **from the opinion of Plato the first cause is above the mind.**

— 12. **and that there is no work for him, because nothing falls to him to do**] <note>original: "μηδὲν δὲ ἔργον εἶναι αὐτῷ, ὅτι μηδὲν ἐπιβάλλει αὐτῷ ποιεῖν"</note> Ficino ought to have said: "because nothing *pertains* to him to do." Dio Cassius XXXVI. 15. p. 95: — "it is fitting for all those to obtain it (the honor) to whom it **falls**." <note>original: "ἐπιβάλλει"</note> Marcus Antoninus <note>Marcus Aurelius</note> V. 15. p. 156. Gataker edition: "things which do not **pertain** to a man, insofar as he is a man," where see Gataker. Ibid. VII. 7. p. 209: (this passage exists under this title: *Second Manual of Epictetus*, in the Munich manuscript 529, from which I have these excerpts in my notes: "Be not ashamed [Scholiast in the margin: *covered*] when being helped, for it is set before you to act on what **pertains** to you [Manuscript: *what pertains* and in the marginal scholia: *what is fitting for you*]") where likewise consult Gataker and Upton in the *Index of Epictetus's Greek* p. 328. Schweighäuser edition. Add Valckenaer’s *Lectures on the New Testament* I. p. 225. who applied the later passage of Antoninus to these words of the Gospel of Luke XV. 12: "Give me the **portion** of the property that **falls** to me," where there might perhaps be someone who judges "portion" <note>original: "μέρος"</note> to be a Scholiast's addition. Clearly, one should look at passages of this kind: Archytas in Stobaeus's *Florilegium*.

**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

**XLIII. Page 170, Gaisford:** *ὁ νόμος—διανεμεῖ τὸ κατ’ ἀξίαν ἑκάστῳ καὶ τὸ ἐπιβάλλον* [the law... distributes to each what is according to merit and what is appropriate]. And he who sees the word *μέρος* [part] included in brackets after the words *τὸ ἐπιβάλλον* in Demosthenes’ *De Corona*, page 312, Reiske—will be deterred from that attempt by the restoration of the passage by Immanuel Bekker, page 219 (where compare the Scholia, page 324)—and indeed by the annotations of H. Grotius on the Gospel of Luke, Book I, and Wesseling’s note on Diodorus, Book I, chapter 1, page 4. Furthermore, the Scholiast on Aristides, page 107, Frommel, explains *ἐπιβάλλειν* as *μερίζεσθαι* [to be divided/distributed], from which you may learn another meaning of this word. Concerning *ἐπιβάλλειν*, it was discussed above at I. 8. 11, page 79, G. Moreover, there is no need for us to demonstrate how greatly this Plotinian sentiment differs from the sentiment of Epicurus: *τὸ μακάριον καὶ ἄφθαρτον οὔτε αὐτὸ πράγματα ἔχει, οὔτε ἄλλῳ παρέχει* [the blessed and incorruptible neither has troubles itself, nor provides them to another]. See Cicero, *De Natura Deorum*, I. 30, and Plotinus himself, II. 9. 15, page 213, F., and compare our author [Plotinus] very closely in chapter XXXIX, page 730, D.

**Page 1333, 15. Ἔστι δὲ οὐδὲ τὸ ἔστιν·]** "But neither is there the 'is'." [Marsilio] Ficinus had initially tried *ἔτι* [still/further] instead of *ἔστι* [is] at the beginning, and expressed this as "even." We have followed the best books, and the reading of these possesses more sharpness and elegance. The seat of this dispute, however, lies in the words of Plato in *Republic*, VI, page 509 (page 320, Bekker): —*καὶ τοῖς γιγνωσκομένοις τοίνυν μὴ μόνον τὸ γιγνώσκεσθαι φάναι ὑπὸ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ παρεῖναι οὐκ οὐσίας ὄντος τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ, ἀλλ’ ἔτι ἐπέκεινα τῆς οὐσίας πρεσβείᾳ καὶ δυνάμει ὑπερέχοντος* [Therefore, say that for the things known, not only is their being known present from the Good, but the Good is not being, but even beyond being, exceeding it in dignity and power]. (In explaining this passage, I can in no way agree with that most excellent man Stallbaum. See his Prolegomena to the *Philebus*, page LXXXIX.) From the same source is drawn another passage of our author [Plotinus] above, III. 8. 9, page 352, B: —*ἣ ἔστι μὲν μηδὲν τούτων, ὧν ἔστιν ἀρχὴ...* [which is none of these things of which it is the principle... that which is above all these things]. If, having removed "being," you should grasp it, you will possess a wonder. To that passage of the *Republic* must be added another in the *Timaeus*, page 29, E (page 25, Bekker): *λέγωμεν δὴ δι’ ἥντινα αἰτίαν γένεσιν καὶ τὸ πᾶν τόδε ὁ ξυνιστὰς ξυνέστησεν. ἀγαθὸς ἦν.* [Let us say for what cause the composer composed becoming and this all. He was good.] (Plotinus refers to this passage on page 330, D, and page 474, B.) Indeed, lest Plato should perhaps seem inconsistent to anyone, it must be held that the method of teaching instituted in the *Timaeus* demanded this. I shall speak in the words of our author, page 727, B: *ὁ λόγος διδάσκων γινόμενα ποιεῖ* [The discourse, in teaching, makes things as if they were coming-to-be]. Clearly, in the *Timaeus*, all things *become*. There exists God as the primary maker of the world; there exist the secondary gods as his ministers. Both the former and the latter work. Now, if you seek the cause why that God turned himself to working, the answer is: *because he is good*, and for that reason, he begrudged nothing to anything. Yet no one is ignorant that Plato’s true opinion was this: that he posited *the world as eternal*. If our own distinguished countrymen had reflected on these things and had devoted more labor to understanding Plotinus, they would not have been led into the error of denying the *Timaeus* to Plato. —Compare, on the previous points, our author VI. 8. 8, page 742, and Sallustius, who is accustomed to imitate Plotinus, *On the Gods and the World*, chapter V, page 20, Orelli: *ὑπερούσιον μὲν ἀγαθὸν δὲ εἶναι τὸ πρῶτον ἀνάγκη* [It is necessary that the First be supra-essential and good].

**Page 1334, 8. Ἐγὼ εἰμί.]** ["I am."] These things bring to mind the *Commentaries of Theodoret on Exodus*, XV, page 133, Schulz: *ὁ γὰρ τοῖς πατριάρχαις οὐκ ἐδήλωσεν ὄνομα τοῦτο αὐτῷ δῆλον ἐποίησεν...* [For the name which he did not reveal to the patriarchs, he made manifest to him...]. This is called the "unutterable" among the Hebrews. The Samaritans call it *Iabe*, but the Jews *Aia* (others *Ia* or rather *Iao*). See Thomas Gataker, *Dissertation on the Tetragrammaton Name*, page 40 ff.; Potter on Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, V, page 666; Wesseling on Diodorus, I. 94, page 105; and what the most learned Gesenius collected in his *Hebrew Lexicon* under the word יהוה [YHWH]. And indeed, that *Iao* is very frequently met with in phylacteries (amulets), as on a leaden plate which I have in my possession, on which the inscribed title begins: ΑΒΡΑΣΑΣ [ABRASAX] and ends ΙΑΩ [IAO]. As for the rest, there is no reason to add it, since two men curious in these matters recently exhibited this title in its entirety.

**— 17. ἔστιν ἤδη τὸ ἀγαθὸν πρὸ τῆς νοήσεως αὐτοῦ]** ["The Good is already before the intellection of it."] Where the marginal edition gives *ἀναστάσεως* [resurrection/rising] for *νοήσεως* [intellection], and several manuscripts give *ἀναστάσεως*, they might seem to have intended *ἀνατάσεως* [stretching up/tension], concerning which we spoke above at V. 8. 13, page 554, A. Nevertheless, this does not seem sufficiently suited to this place, and the continuation of the argument confirms the common reading.

**Page 1336, 5. καὶ ἐπίκτητος αὐτῶν ἡ νόησις]** ["and their intellection is acquired."] This adjective is of Platonic usage, as in *Phaedrus*, page 341, regarding which Hermias, page 131, posits as contraries: *ζωὴν ἐπίκτητον καὶ σύμφυτον* [life acquired and innate]. Galen in the *Protrepticus*, page 4, δ. (chapter γ., page 6, Willet): *οὐκ ἐπίκτητον οὐδὲ κομμωτικὸν κάλλος* [not an acquired nor an artificial beauty], to which is then added *ἐμφυές* [innate]. Iamblichus, *On the Pythagorean Life*, XXXI, § 205, page 416 f., Kiessl.: *εἶναι δὴ τὰς πολλὰς τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων ἐπιθυμιῶν ἐπικτήτους* [indeed, many human desires are acquired] (Kiessling added *τε* from the Cizensis MS, and it is clearly thus in the Memmianus MS in my excerpts) *καὶ κατεσκευασμένας ὑπ’ αὐτῶν τῶν ἀνθρώπων...* [and constructed by men themselves]. —*τὸ δὲ ἐπιθυμεῖν περιέργου... ἐπίκτητον εἶναι* [and the desiring of a meddlesome/lavish... dwelling is acquired]. (The Arcerian edition has *οἰκίσεως*, but the Memmianus MS has *οἰκήσεως*.) Proclus in *Alcibiades*, preface, page 103: the third point shows that existing great things are adorned with acquired magnitude (*ἐπικτήτῳ μεγέθει*), but not by that which is proper to souls nor by the natural. Compare also Wyttenbach on Plutarch, *On How to Tell a Flatterer from a Friend*, page 502, and our author himself, II. 9. 17, V. 1. 4, and what I have placed in the annotation on page 54, C, D, especially in the Heidelberg edition, page 242.

--- Page 412 ---
**BOOK VII. OF THE SIXTH ENNEAD. PAGES 1333–1341.**

**— 11. ἔλεγε μὲν οὖν ὁ Πλάτων περὶ τῆς οὐσίας λέγων ὅτι νοήσει]** ["Plato therefore said, when speaking of essence, that by intellection..."] The Vatican Codex has *Πλάτων* without the article, and we have deleted the article elsewhere in these *Enneads* on the authority of several manuscripts before this name. For the sentiment, consult Plato, *Republic*, page 509, A (page 319 f., Bekker); *Phaedrus*, page 247, B, C (page 42, Bekker).

**— 17. Δεῖ γε μὴν παραμύθια ἄττα πρὸς τοῖς εἰρημένοις κομίζειν]** ["One must indeed bring some consolations/persuasions in addition to what has been said."] Our author above, VI. 5. 11, after the beginning, page 669, A: *δεῖ δέ τινων καὶ παραμυθιῶν...* [there is need of some consolations, though it is not the least but the greatest factor for Persuasion, which that nature is]. He took this from his Plato, who says thus in the *Phaedo*, page 70, b: *ἀλλὰ τοῦτο δὴ ἴσως οὐκ ὀλίγης παραμυθίας δεῖται καὶ πίστεως* [but this perhaps requires no small consolation and faith], on which see Heindorf, page 64, and especially Wyttenbach, page 175. The other form is also recommended by Plato’s example. *Laws*, IX, 880, A (page 171, Bekker): *καὶ ἐὰν μέν τις τοιούτοις παραμυθίοις εὐπειθὴς γίγνηται...* [and if anyone becomes obedient to such consolations/exhortations...]. Compare ibid. X, page 885, A (page 177, Bekker) and on both passages Stephanus and Ast in the latter's *Animadversions*, pages 466 and 470; likewise in the *Critias*, page 115, b (page 161, Bekker): *παραμύθια πλησμονῆς μεταδόρπια* [dessert-consolations for satiety]. Consult also Wasse on Thucydides, V, page 371, and on these forms, Lobeck on Phrynichus, *Parerga*, page 517. Alciphron, *Epistles*, I. 9, page 49, Wagner: *τὸ μὲν γὰρ ἐπὶ λεπτῶν κερμάτων... τὴν παραμυθίαν* [for to buy and sell necessities for small coins is a starving consolation]. (The Palatine Heidelberg MS A has *λυμηράν*; he perhaps wanted *λυπηρὰν* [painful], but this is not to be approved.) The same author, I. 35, page 204: *μικρὰ δὲ ἔπεστί μοι παραψυχὴ καὶ μαραινόμενον ἤδη παραμύθιον* [there is a small comfort for me and a now-fading consolation]. For which he had used *παρηγόρημα* [comfort/solace] a little before. With a similar sense, *παραμυθία* is used by Theodoret on *Ezekiel*, page 1038, Schulz: —*ἄλλης πάλιν τοῖς ἱερεῦσιν ἀφοριζομένης εἰς παραμυθίαν γῆς* [...of another land again being set apart for the priests as a consolation].

**Page 1339, 1. ἣ συνυπόστασις οὖσα]** ["which, being a joint-hypostasis."] See above VI. 7. 2, page 695, B, and the annotation there.

**— 8. ἡ δύναμις αὐτοῦ ἣν ἐμάνθανεν, ἄλλη δὲ ἣ ἐμάνθανεν]** ["its power was that which was learning, and another that which had learned."] In passages of this kind, the Platonic use of the verb *μανθάνειν* [to learn] for "to understand" must be maintained. See Stallbaum on the *Philebus*, page 157, and on the *Euthyphro*, page 14.

**— 10. κινδυνεύει γὰρ βοήθεια τὸ νοεῖν δεδόσθαι κ.τ.λ.]** ["For it is likely that intellection was given as a help, etc."] To these and the following points, the discussion in Plato’s *Republic*, page 507 f. (page 316 ff., Bekker) must again be applied.

**Page 1340, 5. Ἐκείνου οὖν—οὐδενὸς δεομένην]** ["Therefore of That... needing nothing."] Nicephorus Gregoras excerpted these in *History of Byzantium*, XXII, page 551, where it reads: *ἐπὶ τῆς ἁπλῆς φύσεως, τἆλλα* [upon the simple nature, the other things], omitting *πάντη* [entirely]. We have exhibited the full words above at page 729, A.

**— 7. ὅτι ψυχὴ δεῖται νοῦν ἔχειν]** ["that the soul needs to have intellect."] See Plato, *Republic*, VI, page 507 f.; compare 511 and 486; *Phaedo*, page 65, A.; and on the intellectual essence of the human soul, Wyttenbach on the *Phaedo*, page 245.

**— 11. καὶ τὸ γνῶθι σεαυτὸν]** ["and 'Know Thyself'."] Compare above IV. 3. 1, page 371, B, and see Plato, *Phaedrus*, page 229, e (page 8, Bekker); *Protagoras*, page 343, B (page 213, Bekker). Cicero, *De Legibus*, I. 22. 58, and more which Wyttenbach collected on Plutarch, *On the E at Delphi* (page 385, D), *Animadversions*, page 275. Add Proclus on *Alcibiades*, preface I, page 5 and page 19, our edition; and Olympiodorus on the same dialogue, pages 8, 172, and 201 f. Porphyry, who reduced Plotinian doctrines to a compendium in his *Sentences*, XXXIV, page 239, Cambridge edition: *πρῶτον μὲν οἷον θεμέλιος καὶ ὑποβάθρα... τὸ γνῶναι ἑαυτὸν ψυχὴν ὄντα...* [first, as it were a foundation and base for purification, is to know oneself as being a soul bound in an alien and other-essential thing].

**Page 1341, 8. οὔτε ἐπιστήμη, ὅτι μηδέν ἐστι—αὐτοῦ κατηγορεῖν ὡς παρόν.]** ["neither is it knowledge, because there is nothing... to predicate of it as present."] See Plato’s *Timaeus*, page 28, d, e (page 23, Bekker). Plato, *Republic*, page 508, e (page 319, Bekker) and 511, b (page 324, Bekker).

From the same sources Dionysius the Areopagite also drew...

**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

...in *On the Divine Names*, XII. 3, page 866, where he celebrates that lordship (*κυριότητα*) of the first cause "and the kingdom which lies above, etc." To the words: *κἀκείνου ἕνεκα πάντα* [and for the sake of that all things], Proclus in the place cited and Cudworth and Mosheim in the *Intellectual System*, V. 5. 20 ff., page 1184 ff., and for the whole passage IV. 23, page 488, should be consulted. **BOOK VIII.**

**Page 1343, 7. ΠΕΡΙ ΤΟΥ ἙΚΟΥΣΙΟΥ ΚΑΙ ΘΕΛΗΜΑΤΟΣ ΤΟΥ ἙΝΟΣ.]** ["On the Voluntary and the Will of the One."] The same title is found in Porphyry’s *Life of Plotinus*, chapter XXVI, but in another place (chapter V) it is much shorter: *περὶ τοῦ ἑκουσίου* [On the Voluntary]. The fact that *καὶ* [and] was omitted after this word in the Cizensis Codex happened because a less learned scribe took it as an adjective modifying *θελήματος* [will]. This book is the thirty-ninth in number, if you respect the chronological sequence. Aristotle had written a specific work *On the Voluntary*, cited by Diogenes Laertius in his Life, V. 24. Now the primary opinions of this philosopher on this argument must be sought from the *Nicomachean Ethics*, III. 1, the *Magna Moralia*, I. 9, and the *Eudemian Ethics*, II. 6, 7, 8, and 9. And let us hold this definition of the Stagirite: *Λέγω δὲ ἑκούσιον, ὃ ἄν τις τῶν ἐφ’ αὑτῷ ὄντων εἰδὼς καὶ μὴ ἀγνοῶν πράττῃ* [I call voluntary that which someone does, knowing and not being ignorant, of the things that are in his power]. Nemesius, *On the Nature of Man*, should also be compared, both in the chapter titled "On the Voluntary and Involuntary" (*περὶ ἑκουσίου καὶ ἀκουσίου*): "Concerning that which happens spontaneously and by constraint": XXIX, page 260 ff., Matthäi edition, and in the rest which follow until chapter XLII, page 331. To Lucretius, Cicero, etc., it is "done of one's own accord" (*sponte factum*); to others it is sometimes "spontaneous" (*spontaneum*), "voluntary" (*voluntarium*), and sometimes "free choice" (*liberum arbitrium*). However, this is rather *τὸ ἐφ’ ἡμῖν* [what is up to us]. See Joachim Camerarius at the beginning of the cited Aristotelian book, *Nicomachean Ethics*, and compare Zell’s *Commentary*, page 81, and the definitions of the formulas used in this doctrine produced in Plutarch’s book *On Fate*. As for the argument of this Plotinian book, everyone understands that it is connected with those questions treated in the book *On Fate* (III. 1). At its title (page 228) and here and there at several passages of the book itself, we have touched upon the opinions of the ancient philosophers regarding that which happens spontaneously and by constraint. Here, therefore, it suffices to indicate the source of that opinion which Plotinus defends in this book, and to add one or two passages of those philosophers who agree with our author’s primary tenet. Plotinus, however, took the material for his discussion both from other dialogues of Plato—such as from the *Phaedrus*, page 248 (with which passage compare Plotinus’ book *On Providence*, preface, page 264, E, F, and the annotations there), the *Timaeus*, page 41, e, page 42 (compare Plotinus page 376, C, D, 470, 473, A, 489, A, chapter 8)—and especially from this passage of the *Republic*, X, page 596 (page 468, Bekker), where these words are read concerning the supreme Deity: *ὁ αὐτὸς γὰρ οὗτος χειροτέχνης...* [for this same craftsman is able not only to make all vessels, but he makes all things that grow from the earth, and works all animals... and himself, and in addition to these, earth and heaven and gods...]. From this, the philosophers following Plato concluded that the supreme god is *self-natural* (*αὐτοφυῆ*), *self-begotten* (*αὐτογενῆ*), not dependent on another source, and entirely of his own and free will. Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, II. 7, page 4, Bünemann: "But because it cannot be but that that which is (other MSS: *that which was made*) at some time began to be; it follows that when nothing was before him, he was procreated from himself before all things: and therefore he is called *αὐτοφυὴς* by Apollo, *αὐτογενὴς* and *ἀγένητος* and *ἀποίητος* [unbegotten and unmade] by the Sibyl; which Seneca, a sharp man, saw in his *Exhortations*: *We,* he says, *depend elsewhere. Therefore we look back to someone to whom we owe what is best in us. Another brought us forth, another instructed us: God made himself.*" The same author, II. 8, page 227: "He is from himself, as we said in the first book, and therefore *he is such as he willed himself to be*, impassible, immutable, incorruptible, blessed, eternal." Apuleius, *On the Doctrine of Plato*, I, page 584 (page 205, Bosscha edition): "Wherefore he thinks that not all things are to be referred to the lot of fate. For he thus defines: Providence is a divine judgment, preserver of the prosperity of that for whose sake it undertook such an office: *Fate is a divine law through which the inevitable thoughts and undertakings of God are fulfilled.* Whence if anything is done by providence, it is also done by fate: and what is terminated by fate must be seen to have been undertaken by providence." where compare Elmenhorst’s annotation. Add Apuleius, *On the World*, page 749 (page 365) and Plutarch, *On Fate*, IX, page 573, B (page 308, Wyttenbach): *καὶ ἡ μὲν Εἱμαρμένη πάντως κατὰ Πρόνοιαν, ἡ δὲ Πρόνοια...* [and indeed Fate is entirely according to Providence, but Providence...].

--- Page 414 ---
**BOOK VIII. OF THE SIXTH ENNEAD. PAGES 1343–1347.**

...[Providence] is in no way according to Fate. Several passages in Plato’s *Timaeus* are then explained. Proclus in *Platonic Theology*, IV. 16, page 205, bottom: *τῶν μὲν γὰρ εἱμαρμένων νόμων...* [For not only are the gods superior to the laws of fate, but also partial souls living according to intellect, and giving themselves over to the light of providence]. Compare also Alcinous, *On the Doctrines of Plato*, chapter XXVI, and especially chapter 30: *πῶς ἑκούσιον ἡ ἀρετὴ, ἀκούσιον δὲ ἡ κακία* [how virtue is voluntary, but vice involuntary]. Cudworth, in the *Intellectual System*, IV. 23, page 487, says that Plotinus’ purpose in writing this book is chiefly this: "partly that he might inculcate the supreme Deity’s existing by himself with a certain more efficacious and express reason, partly that he might refute the insane opinion which some might foster concerning God, as if he had become what he is by chance and fortune, or indeed had been compelled by a certain law of nature and necessity to be that which he is. This indeed was the kind of thing the philosopher desired to teach: that God *is always that which he wills to be*, nor does he hold himself otherwise than if he had made and established himself by his own accord and freely."

**Page 1344, 18. Ἑκούσιον μὲν γὰρ πᾶν—ἐφ’ ἡμῖν δὲ—πρᾶξαι]** ["For all that is voluntary... but what is up to us... to do."] See our annotation on the title of this book and the passages of Aristotle etc. cited there. Add Epictetus, *Enchiridion*, I. 1, and the notes, and the passages cited under the word *ἐφ’ ἡμῖν* in the Index of Greek terms in Epictetus. Hierocles, *On Providence and Fate*, page 2 ff., London edition 1673; *On Providence*, page 62 ff. (compare Photius, *Bibliotheca*, Codex 251, page 463, Bekker edition) and Nemesius, *On the Nature of Man*, chapter 39: *περὶ τοῦ αὐτεξουσίου, ὅ ἐστι τοῦ ἐφ’ ἡμῖν* [On the self-power, which is the 'up to us'], page 311 ff., Matthäi. —Those things which depend on us, or are in our power, are also said to be *παρ’ ἡμᾶς εἶναι* [within our power to be] or to happen. Regarding which formula Baguet has commented at the fragments of Chrysippus, page 222, note 89.

**Page 1345, 15. καὶ μαινομένοις—καὶ πεπλανημένῳ τῷ λογισμῷ]** ["both to those who are mad... and with a wandering reasoning."] Hierocles, *On the Golden Verses of Pythagoras*, page 269 f.: *καὶ τὰ ἑπόμενα τῇ ἀβουλίᾳ παραδείκνυσι...* [and he points out the things that follow from ill-counsel, and teaches how errors are both involuntary and voluntary at once, saying that the life of the foolish is like the movement of a cylinder on a plane, which moves in a circle and in a straight line at once...]. Chrysippus had used the simile of a stone cylinder in his doctrine on fate and free choice. See Cicero, *De Fato*, chapter 18. 42 (page 641, Moser edition). Gellius, *Attic Nights*, VI. 2, and Chrysippus’ fragments, page 219, Baguet. I add Olympiodorus on *Alcibiades*, preface, page 45: *οὕτω δὲ καὶ ἐν Τιμαίῳ· αἰτία ἑλομένου, θεὸς ἀναίτιος.* [Thus also in the Timaeus: the cause is in the chooser, God is blameless]. (Plato, *Timaeus*, page 47, c.) and further in the *Republic*: (X, page 617, c.; compare Plotinus above, page 141 ff.) *ὑμεῖς (thus to be read instead of ὑμᾶς) δαίμονα αἱρήσεσθε...* [you shall choose a divinity, a divinity shall not be allotted to you; for it is in us to choose such a life... but having chosen, to do the things following that life is not in us, but by necessity; just as it is in us to throw a stone. So that one must say...]. How the lacunose passage may be filled is sufficiently understood from the cited passages of Gellius and Hierocles.

**Page 1346, 6. Εἶτα—τῶν παθημάτων—φαντασία—πῶς ἐν τούτοις κυρίους ποιεῖ;]** ["Then... of the passions... imagination... how does it make [us] masters in these?"] I have thus written *κυρίους* with the marginal edition and the better books instead of *κυρίως* [properly]. To this point belong the words of Alcinous, *On the Doctrine of Plato*, XXX, page 524, Heinsius: *αὗται γὰρ βλάβαι διάφοροι...* [for these are different harms, and the involuntary lies in some ignorance or passion]. Plutarch, Fragments, XX. 2, page 837, Wyttenbach: *θηρίον ἐστὶ δουλαγωγὸν ἡδονὴ...* [pleasure is a slave-leading beast, but not a wild one; if only it were; for then, openly warring, it would be quickly caught. But it is even more hateful for this: that it steals enmity by putting on the appearance of goodwill...]. Compare his fragment *On Love*, XXV. 3, where the same simile is found, drawn indeed from Plato in *Republic*, IX, 588, C.; compare IV, 439, b, and not unknown to our Plotinus. See above I. 1, page 4, G. To these imitations is now added a passage of Eunapius in the *Historical Excerpts*, page 258 (New Collection of Vatican Writers, II): *ὁ μὲν γὰρ Ῥωμαῖος Μάριος...* [for the Roman Marius, calling his rival Sulla a double beast, a fox and a lion, etc.] where Angelo Mai rightly praises Julian’s *Epistle* XXIII. For there (page 31, Heyler) he calls the courtiers of Constantius "beasts" (*θηρία*) eyeing all things. Plotinus himself, I. 1. 10, page 6, A, calls the body a "beast" (*θηρίον*).

**Page 1347, 16. Καὶ γὰρ κενώσεις σίτων καὶ ποτῶν—καὶ πληρώσεις κ.τ.λ.]** ["For indeed emptyings of food and drink... and fillings, etc."] Compare Xenophon, *Cyropaedia*, I. 6. 17; *Memorabilia*, I. 3. 6; and on the force of excess in drink, food, and venereal matters upon the human mind, morals, and character, Galen’s *Protrepticus*, chapter...
