...XI, and the more examples which Willet collected there, page 116 ff.

**Page 1349, 8. καὶ δουλεύει τοῦτο, ὃ μὴ κύριόν ἐστιν ἐπὶ τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἐλθεῖν—διὰ τοῦτο—δουλεία ψέγεται κ.τ.λ.]** ["and that is enslaved which is not master of reaching the good... for this reason... slavery is blamed, etc."] It will not be out of place here to recall the passages of Plato, as in *Republic*, X, page 617, e (page 509, Bekker): *ἀρετὴ δὲ ἀδέσποτον...* [Virtue is without a master; honoring or dishonoring it, each shall have more or less of it] (compare Ast’s *Commentary*, page 632). *Symposium*, page 184 (page 392, Bekker): —*οὕτω δὴ καὶ ἄλλη μία μόνη δουλεία ἑκούσιος λείπεται...* [thus indeed only one other voluntary slavery remains that is not shameful; and this is that concerning virtue, etc.], which is then called *ἐθελοδουλεία* [willing slavery]. Plato, *Alcibiades*, preface, page 135, b: *πρὶν δέ γε ἀρετὴν ἔχειν τὸ ἄρχεσθαι ἄμεινον ὑπὸ τοῦ βελτίονος...* [before having virtue, it is better to be ruled by the better than to rule, for a man, not only a child... And virtue is worthy of a free man]. To which Olympiodorus, page 231: [he establishes that virtue is not only free, but also ruling. For virtue joins itself to God and to the ruler of all, but vice to matter which is ruled by all and is the lowest part. What then? Does the good man not serve God? Rather, this service is better than all rule, and by such he rules others. "For such a thing moved by another is better than the self-moved."] Similar things are found in Epictetus, *Fragment* VIII, and in Paul’s *Epistle to the Romans*, VI. 6, VII. 25.

**— 14. καὶ οὐδὲ τὸ δυνάμει ἔχουσα ἄλλο, ἄλλο δὲ τὸ ἐνεργείᾳ]** ["and not having one thing in potentiality, and another in actuality."] The understanding of this passage, and no less of those discussed in the following chapter, is aided by these words of Alcinous, *On the Doctrine of Plato*, XXV, page 511, Heinsius: *τὸ μὲν γὰρ δυνάμει ἐπιτηδειότητά τινα ἀποσημαίνει...* [for 'in potentiality' indicates a certain suitability toward something for one not yet having the habit/state, as a child will be said to be in potentiality a grammarian and a flute-player and a builder. But he will then be in the habit of one or two of these, whenever he acts from that habit which he has acquired]. Plutarch, *On Fate*, page 566, C (page 290, Wyttenbach), distinguishes in fate both action and essence: *πρῶτον τοίνυν ἴσθι, ὅτι Εἱμαρμένη διχῶς... ἡ μὲν γάρ ἐστιν Ἐνέργεια, ἡ δὲ Οὐσία.* [first therefore know that Fate is both said and thought in two ways. For one is Actuality, the other Essence.] (But if you consider that in what follows one is called *κατ’ ἐνέργειαν*, the other *κατ’ οὐσίαν*—page 291; in that former place you might think it should be written: *ἐνεργείᾳ* and *οὐσίᾳ*.) Plutarch then explains both copiously. Compare his discussions in the following, page 570 f. (page 299 ff., Wyttenbach).

**Page 1351, 5. καὶ πενίαν, ἵνα τὸ ἐλευθέριον ἐνδείκνυοιτο]** ["and poverty, so that it might show the quality of a free man."] We have preferred this reading to the other, *τὸ ἐλεύθερον* [the free]. Confusion is frequent. Concerning this and the distinction, see Sturz, *Xenophon Lexicon*, III, page 132 f., and Wyttenbach on Plutarch, *On the Education of Children*, page 65. And I wonder that Heindorf and Bekker did not restore *ἐλευθερίως* [liberally] to Plato from Athenaeus instead of *ἐλευθέρως* [freely] in *Theaetetus*, page 175, e (page 246, Bekker). Teles in Stobaeus, *Florilegium*, Title XCVII, page 523 (page 271, Gaisford): *Διὸ καὶ εἰ βούλει τὸν υἱόν σου...* [Therefore also if you wish to stop your son from need and lack, do not send him to Ptolemy that he may acquire money; otherwise, he will go away having taken on arrogance, and will accomplish nothing; but send him to the Academy to Crates. He was able to make the insatiable and lavish into liberal (*ἐλευθερίους*) and simple men]. Ibid., page 268: *οὐχ ὁρᾷς ἐνίους κεκτημένους μὲν πολλὰ...* [do you not see some possessing many things, as it seems, but not using them because of illiberality (*ἀνελευθερίαν*)]. And thus quite often in the same fragment. In this whole Title as well, many things are present that belong here; and no less in Plutarch’s fragments from the book *Against Riches*, XXI, page 840 f., Wyttenbach. To which are now added the sentiments excerpted from the *Oration of Fabricius to Pyrrhus* in Dio and Dionysius of Halicarnassus in Angelo Mai’s *New Vatican Collection*, II, page 175 f. and page 512 f.

**— 8. ὥσπερ ἂν εἴ τις ἰατρὸς οἷον Ἱπποκράτης—τέχνης]** ["just as if some physician like Hippocrates... of the art."] Not only is the simile of medicine and physicians frequent in the writings of the Socratics, but even the name of Hippocrates is celebrated by the authority of Plato and likewise Aristotle. For the former makes mention of him with praise in two places, both in the *Phaedrus*, page 270, c, and in the *Protagoras*, page 311, b; which latter passage I wonder escaped the diligence of the most excellent van Prinsterer in *Prosopographia Platonica*, page 193. The Stagirite’s passage is in the *Politics*, VII. 4, page 224, Goettling edition: *οἷον Ἱπποκράτην οὐκ ἄνθρωπον ἀλλ’ ἰατρὸν εἶναι μείζω φήσειεν ἄν τις...* [as if someone should say that Hippocrates is a greater physician than he is a man, etc.]. See also Suidas under *Ἱπποκράτης*. Whence it is no wonder that his sentiments are also used by the later Platonists without his name (for example, Porphyry, *On Abstinence*, III, page 233, Rhoer) or his authority is expressly applied. See, for example, Olympiodorus on *Alcibiades*, preface I, page 6; XIV, page 124. Moreover, entirely contrary to the Plotinian sentiment is this one of the comic poet Philemon, most abusive toward physicians, in Stobaeus, *Florilegium*, Title II, page 332, Gaisford (compare fragments of Menander and Philemon, XLVI. a, page 413, Meineke):
> [For not a single physician, if you look closely,
> wishes his own friends to be healthy,
> nor a soldier to see a city without evil.]

**Page 1352, 3. οἷον νωθῆναι τὴν ψυχὴν ποιοῦσα]** ["as if making the soul sluggish."] Compare below, chapter 6. C. Brucker touches on this in *Critical History of Philosophy*, II, page 417, pronouncing in this manner: "Thus indeed Plotinus confuses the notions of intellect and will, by recalling all things to contemplation."

**Page 1353, 1. καὶ τὸ ζῆν κελεύουσαν προτέσθαι—ἀλλ’ οὐ τὸ εἶναι τῶν ὑπ’ αὐτὴν]** ["and commanding life to be set before... but not the being of the things under it."] Perhaps Sallustius had these before his eyes in *On the Gods and the World*, Chapter Five (Orelli, page 20): *τοῦ γὰρ εἶναι διὰ τὸ ἀγαθὸν οἱ σπουδαῖοι καταφρονοῦσι ψυχαὶ...* [for the sake of the good, good souls despise being, whenever they wish to risk danger for country or friends or virtue]. where Lucas Holstenius also praises other things, page 100.

**— 8. Ταῦτα γὰρ ἔοικε φησὶν ἐγγύς τι τείνειν τοῦ σώματος]** ["For these things seem, he says, to stretch near to the body."] I have written this on the authority of four manuscript books. Plato in the *Phaedo*, page 65, a (page 18, Bekker), in that passage where he discusses the duty of philosophy in freeing the soul from the slavery of the body: *Καὶ δοκεῖ γέ που, ὦ Σιμμία, τοῖς πολλοῖς ἀνθρώποις...* [And it seems surely, O Simmias, to most men, that for him to whom nothing of such things is pleasant nor does he participate in them, it is not worth living, but he stretches near to being dead]. Heindorf explained *similem esse alicujus* [to be like someone/something], page 39; Wyttenbach discussed the sentiment, page 149 f. It seems, therefore, that Plotinus cited these words of Plato from memory.

**Page 1354, 15. εἴ μή τις τολμηρὸς λόγος ἑτέρωθεν σταλεὶς λέγοι, ὡς τυχοῦσα οὕτως ἔχειν ὡς ἔχει κ.τ.λ.]** ["unless some bold discourse sent from elsewhere should say that it happens thus to be as it is, etc."] Plotinus might seem in this place to be reproving Democritus, the Epicureans, and Strato the Peripatetic, and the others who had made all things depend on chance and fortune. See Aristotle, *On the Parts of Animals*, I. 1; Cicero, *De Fato*, chapters X and XI; Plutarch, *Against Colotes*, page 1115, B (page 557, Wyttenbach), who reports these things concerning Strato: *τελευταῖον τὸν κόσμον αὐτὸν οὐ ζῶον εἶναί φησι...* [finally he says the world itself is not an animal, but that the natural follows the accidental. For spontaneity gives the beginning, and then each of the natural affections is thus completed]. Consult nevertheless also Cudworth’s *Intellectual System*, page 100 ff. and page 152 ff.

**Page 1356, 1. οὔτε οὐ κύριον τῆς αὐτοῦ γενέσεως, ὅτι μηδὲ γέγονε]** ["neither is he not master of his own genesis, because he did not even become."] These last three words are especially to be held, because they give faith to everyone as to how Plotinus thought the words of Plato in *Republic* X, page 596, should be taken: *ὁ αὐτὸς—καὶ ζῶα πάντα ἐργάζεται τά τε ἄλλα καὶ ἑαυτόν* [the same one... works all animals and the others and himself]. See what more we have praised at the title of this book, page 734, middle. Those words of Plato are observed by Plotinus both in this passage and in others of this same book. Compare also what our author proposes more explicitly concerning this argument below in chapter 20, page 754.

**Page 1357, 5. καίτοι οὐδὲν ἂν εὕροιμεν εἰπεῖν—περὶ αὐτοῦ—ὕστερα]** ["and yet we would find nothing to say... about him... things that are posterior."] Plato, *Philebus*, page 65, a (page 222, Stallbaum): *Οὐκοῦν εἰ μὴ μιᾷ δυνάμεθα ἰδέᾳ τὸ ἀγαθὸν θηρεῦσαι...* [Therefore if we cannot hunt the good with one idea, taking it with three—beauty and symmetry and truth—let us say, etc.]. Sallustius, chapter V, calls this the *τὴν οὕτως ἀῤῥητον δύναμιν* [the thus unutterable power] concerning the *first cause*. To which passage Orelli, page 102, applied both these words of Plotinus and these of Arnobius, I. 31: "For you are the first cause, infinite, unbegotten, immortal, perpetual, alone—concerning whom nothing can be said or expressed by the significance of mortal words."

**— 16. τό,τε γὰρ εἶναι ἀφῃροῦμεν]** ["for we were taking away 'being'."] See our author, VI. 7. 38, page 729, A, and what we annotated there.

**Page 1358, 4. συμβῇ—συνέβη—πῶς οὖν ἦλθε; τύχη τις]** ["it happens... it happened... how then did it come? some chance."] To this passage must be applied Plutarch’s discussion in the booklet *On Fortune*, where he treats of chance (*τύχῃ*) and accident (*συμβεβηκότι*), chapter VII, page 571 f. (page 304 ff., Wyttenbach), which learned man also applied that passage to Plato in the *Phaedo*. See his annotation, page 113 f.

**Page 1359, 3. ἀλλ’ ὅπερ ἐχρῆν εἶναι· οὐ τοίνυν οὕτω συνέβη, ἀλλ’ ἔδει οὕτω]** ["but what it was necessary to be; therefore it did not happen thus, but it was necessary thus."] Cudworth used this passage in his discussion against the Atheists in the *Intellectual System*, V. 5. 1, page 1167, where Mosheim placed these in Annotation 4: "To this therefore returns the sentiment of the words (of Plotinus) which are here brought forward: that God is such as he is by the very necessity of his nature, nor is it lawful even in thought to imagine that God can have himself in another way." —The following: *ὁ βασιλεὺς,—ὄντως βασιλέα* [the king... truly king] drew their color from the passage in the *Epistles of Plato*, II, page 312, e (page 403, Bekker): *περὶ τὸν πάντων βασιλέα πάντ’ ἐστὶ καὶ ἐκείνου ἕνεκα πάντα...* [around the King of all are all things and for his sake all things...], which we touched upon above at page 733, B, bottom.

**Page 1361, 8. ἐν δὲ τοῖς μὴ προηγουμένως—ἀλλὰ συμπτώμασι]** ["but in those things not primarily... but by accidents/symptoms."] This adverb is read also in III. 8. 3, IV. 4. 39, and compare the Annotation in I. 8. 2 at the word *προηγούμενα*. Concerning *συμπτώμασι* [accidents], add to those which have recently been collected for Stephanus’ *Thesaurus*, Menander’s fragments LXIII, page 218, Meineke, and CCLXXXI, page 269, where *Τύχη* [Fortune] and *τύχαι* [fortunes] are joined with this word. Compare Wyttenbach on Plutarch’s *Consolation to Apollonius*, page 700 and page 781 f. Eunapius, *Historical Excerpts*, page 258, Angelo Mai edition: *ἔοικε μὲν οὖν καὶ ἄλλως ὁ χρόνος...* [Indeed it seems also otherwise that time in long periods and movements often falls upon such accidents].

**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

**Page 1361, 11. πολλῶν μὲν ἡ τύχη κυρία, νοῦ δὲ—οὐ κυρία]** ["of many things fortune is mistress, but of intellect... she is not mistress."] There are similar sentiments in the monuments of ancient writers, even in those which so proclaim the power of fortune that they are turned even into the contrary opinion. See Herodotus, I. 32. Plato, *Laws*, IV, 709 (page 340, Bekker): [that no mortal legislates anything, but that chances are almost all things that pilot human affairs]. Chaeremon or another poet in Plutarch, *On Fortune*, page 97, C: [Fortune, not good counsel, rules the affairs of mortals]. Theophrastus in Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, V. 9, from a poet:
> Fortune, not wisdom, rules life.
More on that matter was collected by Davis on Cicero in the place cited, Lennep on the *Epistles of Phalaris*, LV, page 182, and Wyttenbach on Plutarch *On Fortune*, page 665. Presently the words of Plotinus: *εἰ οὖν μηδὲν πρὸ ἐκείνου κ.τ.λ.* [if therefore nothing is before that, etc.] were exhibited in the collection of Plotinian decrees by Brucker in *Critical History of Philosophy*, II, page 398.

**Page 1363, 4. ζήτησιν ἅπασαν χρὴ νομίζειν κ.τ.λ.]** ["one must think all inquiry, etc."] Aristotle says it somewhat differently in *Posterior Analytics*, I, page 244, Sylburg: [the things sought are equal in number to all the things we know. We seek four: the fact, the reason why, if it is, what it is]. To which passage apply Joannes Grammaticus’ *Commentary*, fol. 75, verso; compare Alexander of Aphrodisias on *Prior Analytics*, I, chapter 27, and Themistius on *Posterior Analytics*, II. 1.

**Page 1365, 6. αὐτουσία]** ["Self-essence."] It is recorded in Stephanus’ *Thesaurus* (London edition) from Epiphanius. To which add this passage, and entirely add it to the Lexicon of Schneider and others.

**— 13. Τὸ δὲ πεποιηκὸς ἐλεύθερον—ἐλευθεροποιὸν—εἴπερ—θεμιτὸν φθέγγεσθαι;]** ["But that which made [one] free... making-free... if indeed it is lawful to speak?"] This formula of deprecation has a double cause: first, because he is speaking of the first principle or supreme Deity; second, because the word for slavery was unpleasant to hear from the customs of the Ancients, not to say ignominious; which philosophers translate into Ethics. Epictetus, II. 1. 23: [freedom and slavery, the one the name of virtue, the other of vice]. The same author, IV. 1. 176: [to acquire a making-free doctrine]. And *ἐλευθεροῦσθαι* and *ἐλευθερώτης*, "to be manumitted," "manumitter," are found among the Jurisconsults (Theophilus, *Paraphrase of the Institutes*, I. 4. 77, where is added: "from slavery"—and I. 19. 294). Similar locutions were used by the writers of the New Testament and the Fathers of the Church to signify Christian liberty. See Valckenaer’s *Scholia on the New Testament*, I, page 520; Borger’s *Commentary on Galatians*, V. 1, page 326 f., and Suicer, *Ecclesiastical Thesaurus*, I, page 1088. —Concerning God, Plato similarly deprecates in the *Timaeus*, page 29, a (page 24, Bekker): [But if, which it is not even lawful for anyone to say, he looked toward that which has become... (the demiurge)]. Compare our author in the following chapter, page 748, B: [But one must allow the names... which we do not permit to be said with precision].

**Page 1367, 17. οὔτε ἔξω τῆς βουλήσεως αὐτοῦ ἡ οὐσία κ.τ.λ.]** ["neither is his essence outside of his will, etc."] Cudworth treats these and more from what follows in the *Intellectual System*, pages 485, 486, 487, Mosheim edition; with which compare Brucker’s discussions in *Critical History of Philosophy*, II, page 398, and Tiedemann’s in the book: *Spirit of Speculative Philosophy*, III, page 384 f.

**Page 1368, 13. Ἔστι γὰρ—θέλησις αὐτοῦ οὐ δεδεκασμένου—ἐπισπωμένου—ἑλομένου]** ["For his will is... not bribed... not attracted... but having chosen."] "*For in truth the nature of the Good is its very own will, of one neither corrupted nor attracted by its own nature, but of that which chose itself.*" Thus I think the Ficinian version should be corrected, *Οὐ δεκασμένου* [not bribed]. See Timaeus, *Platonic Lexicon*, page 75 (page 64, Koch edition): [He bribes (*Δεκάζει*), he who buys a judgment from a judge. He is bribed (*Δεκάζεται*), he who sells a judgment]. Where Ruhnken, if he had known the passage of Plotinus, would have suspected even more that this word had been obliterated in Plato. Add the *Rhetorical Lexicon* edited by Bekker, *Anecdota*, I. 236, and Bast’s *Critical Epistle*, page 56, correcting in Timaeus’ cited passage: *ἔνθεν ἀδέκαστος* [unbribed/impartial]. (See Koch’s additions to the cited passage.) Lysias, *Against Philocrates*, page 182 (page 834, Reiske): [that five hundred of them had been bribed]. More on the verb *δεκάζειν* and its derivatives was collected by Wyttenbach on Plutarch, *On Profit from Enemies*, page 636, and Karl Friedrich Hermann on Lucian, *On Writing History*, page 247 f. —The last words: *ἀλλ’ ἑαυτὸν ἑλομένου* [but having chosen himself], are drawn from Plato’s *Republic*, X. 617 (page 509, Bekker): *οὐχ ὑμᾶς δαίμων λήξεται, ἀλλ’ ὑμεῖς δαίμονα αἱρήσεσθε* [a divinity shall not be allotted to you, but you shall choose a divinity]. Plotinus therefore wishes it to be signified that the Good and the supreme Deity was compelled neither by blandishments as it were and corruption, nor by some force as it were of his nature, but is that which he is by his own free election.

**Page 1369, 11. ὥστε αὐτὸν πεποιηκέναι αὐτὸν, ὁ λόγος ἀνεῦρεν]** ["so that he has made himself, the discourse found out."] See Plato, *Republic*, X, page 596 (page 468, Bekker). We have cited the words themselves at the title of this book above, page 734. Consult besides concerning this passage and similar ones Cudworth and Mosheim in the *Intellectual System*, IV. 23, page 486.

**Page 1371, 15. αἴτιον ἑαυτοῦ—αὐτός.]** ["Cause of himself... himself."] Plato, *Republic*, X. 596 (page 468, Bekker). Cudworth treated these in the *Intellectual System*, IV. 23, page 486. Brucker, however...

...in *Critical History of Philosophy*, II. 400, pronounces concerning this passage of Plotinus: "This observation pertains also to the bolder locutions of Plotinus, when he says that *God makes himself*." You, see what our philosopher placed above at page 741, C, and compare besides the annotation on page 734, middle, and page 748, D. The adverb *ὑπερόντως* [supra-essentially] is to be added to the Lexicons from here. Concerning *ὑπερὼν*, compare Corderius’ *Onomasticon* on Dionysius the Areopagite under the word. Nicolaus of Methone also has it in the book against Proclus’ *Theological Institutes*, chapter VIII, page 17, first edition, Frankfurt. No less does the same Nicolaus have the adverb ibid., chapter XXII, page 41, and chapter XXXV.

**— 18. Καὶ ἐράσμιον, καὶ ἔρως ὁ αὐτὸς]** ["And lovely, and Love himself."] Plato, *Timaeus*, page 87, e (page 132, Bekker): [of all spectacles for the one able to see, it is the most beautiful and most lovely], and Plato uses it quite often. Compare also our author, VI. 7. 22, VI. 7. 33. This passage, however, has an Orphic color. *Orphic Hymns*, LVIII (57). 1:
> I call upon the great, holy, lovely, sweet Love.
Gassendi praises this discussion of Plotinus in *On the Life, Morals, and Doctrines of Epicurus*, Vol. II, page 55.

**Page 1372, 6. πάλιν αὖ αὐτός ἐστιν οὗτος ὁ ποιῶν ἑαυτὸν κ.τ.λ.]** ["again he himself is this one making himself, etc."] Our author so embraces the redundancy *πάλιν αὖ* [back again] that he uses it even before a similar syllable, as in this place. Concerning this sentiment of Plato, see the annotations on page 734, middle, page 748, D, 749, D. Nor did Cudworth neglect this passage of ours in the *Intellectual System*, IV. 23, page 485, Mosheim edition.

**— 13. Πάντα γὰρ τὰ ἄλλα—δουλα καὶ κείμενα τύχαις]** ["For all other things... are slave and lie [exposed] to fortunes."] You might believe Ficinus read *καὶ ἐκκείμενα τύχαις* [and exposed to fortunes], which is also constructed with the dative. Alciphron, III. 29, "I lie exposed (*ἔκκειμαι*) to those who wish, etc." Concerning the other construction with *πρὸς*, see Proclus, *Theological Institutes*, LXXX, page 124: [exposed (*ἐκκείμενον*) to being divided and suffering], liable; see the annotation on that passage. Truly, no Codex departs from the common reading. Nor is there any which exhibits *κείμενα ἐν τύχαις* [lying in fortunes], as is found in Aelian, *Historical Miscellany*, IX. 37: [hopes lie (*κεῖνται*) in a bowl of soup], *are placed*. Therefore, if one must acquiesce in the common reading, it ought to be explained as "are established and fixed by fortunes, just as a law is said to *κεῖσθαι* [be laid down/enacted]." (See Lysias, *Oration* VI, page 107: [the law laid down concerning it]. Compare Schleusner, *Lexicon of the New Testament*, under *κεῖσθαι*) unless you prefer to take it thus: all our slave-like things are [enslaved] and buried by fortunes. For Hesychius teaches that *Κεῖσθαι* is said of the dead and buried: [it lies (*κεῖται*); this is always placed for the bad, either of death or of inaction] (see the praises by Ast on Plato, *Laws*, VI. 20, page 327); and presently our author says: "to attach to fortunes."

**Page 1374, 10. αὐτὸς ὢν τοῦτο ὅπερ ἠγάπησε]** ["being himself that which he loved."] Cudworth also applied this sentiment and others included in this chapter to his disquisition in the *Intellectual System*, IV. 23, page 485 f.

**Page 1375, 9. ἣ δὲ ἐγρήγορσίς ἐστιν—καὶ νοῦ καὶ ζωῆς ἔμφρονος]** ["and it is a wakefulness... of both intellect and prudent life."] Compare above III. 6. 5, III. 6. 6. Basil the younger in the dedicatory epistle to Constantine Porphyrogenitus, as it seems, in *Notices and Extracts*, Paris 1827, Vol. XI, part 2, page 61: [for what of all things is lovelier to you or what is more precious than to mirror and shoot the [words] of Gregory and the things of Gregory? Whose words is it sweeter to track, or whose intellect, than that of this wakeful intellect (*τοῦ γρηγόρου νοῦ τούτου*)—for it is more proper to call him thus] where Fr. Boissonade in an Annotation has placed two other examples of that appellation with which they commonly addressed Gregory Nazianzen. The word *ὑπερνόησις* [supra-intellection], however, is to be added to the Lexicons from here. Concerning the adjective *ὑπέρνους* [supra-intellectual], it was discussed in Proclus’ *Theological Institutes*, chapter CXV, page 168, Frankfurt edition. Whose adversary Nicolaus of Methone, chapter XXIII, page 43, first edition, Frankfurt, used the same word.

**— 18. οὕτω τοι... καὶ ἀεὶ ἐν τοῖς συνοῦσι κεῖσθαι τοὺς λόγους ἐν μείζονι εὐθημοσύνῃ]** ["thus indeed... and always the reasons/words lie in those things that are together in greater good-order."] I thought this passage should be read thus above at IV. 4. 6, page 401, C, where the edition and good books have: [for there is another way of the good-order toward the all from them]. But in our place all Codices and Ficinus with the Edition agree in *εὐθυμοσύνῃ* [tranquility/cheerfulness]. I shall not repeat what I collected there to confirm this change; I shall add certain other things, whence it may be understood how widely this confusion ranges, and by which the necessity of emendation is shown. Plato, *Laws*, VI, page 758 (page 426, Bekker): [remaining at their own private affairs, to be well-ordered (*εὐθημονεῖσθαι*) in the things according to their own dwellings]. where Codex V in Bekker gives: *εὐθυμονεῖσθαι*. But see Ast’s *Commentary*, page 291, who explains "to set in order, to arrange, to manage." I would add "rightly" or "neatly," as Blomfield did in the *Glossary to Aeschylus’ Choephori* at verse 78: [female servants, good-orderers of the house]; see him at page 119. Add Orion’s *Etymologicon*, page 59, Sturz: good-order (*εὐθημοσύνη*)...

**ANNOTATIONS ON PLOTINUS**

...[from the future *θήσω* comes *θῆμος*, a derivative, and *θημόσυνος*, and *εὐθημοσύνη*; as *ἵππος* [horse] gives *ἱπποσύνη* [horsemanship]; and *δίκαιος* [just] gives *δικαιοσύνη* [justice]. *θήσω* [I shall place], *θῆμος*, *θημοσύνη*. Philoxenus.] From here others took it, including Zonaras, page 907, who adds *τάξις* [order] to *εὐθημοσύνη*. In Theophrastus’ *History of Plants*, III. 18. 7, page 115, Schneider, there were those who, instead of *γωνοειδῆ καὶ εὐθυμότερα* [angle-shaped and more cheerful(?)], would wish to read from Pliny, who translates "angled and more neatly arranged": *γωνιοειδῆ καὶ εὐθημονέστερα* (which I see was passed over by Schneider in the annotations, page 263); but in the same place it is now more correctly read: *καὶ τῷ γωνιοειδεῖ καὶ εὐρυθμότερα* [and by the angle-shape and better-proportioned], toward which Dioscorides and Oribasius also lead, who wrongly have *ἐρυθρά* [red]. Synesius, *On Providence*, I, page 98, A, concerning demons: [a nature erratic and bold and, by the multitude of the departure from there, not perceiving the good-order (*εὐθημοσύνης*) of the divine things], where the old translator, who translated: "they perceive nothing of the divine *tranquility* of mind," seems to have found *εὐθυμοσύνης* in his codex. He ought to have [translated]: "Not sensing (understanding) the fitting disposition of divine things." Maximus’ *Prologue to the Works of Dionysius the Areopagite*, page XXXV, Corderius: [that they measure the learning-loving good-orders (*εὐθυμοσύνας*) of the men following with the ignorance of the wise]. The British editors placed an asterisk before this passage in Stephanus’ *Thesaurus*, page 4343, and I suspect: *εὐθημοσύνας* [good-orders], "learning-loving and well-ordered habits." Dionysius himself, *On the Divine Names*, VIII. 5, page 776: [and he empowers the united toward the friendship and communion of one another, and the distinguished toward being unconfused and unmixed according to each proper reason and limit; and he preserves the orders and good-orders (*εὐθημοσύνας*) of the all unto its proper good]. From here also Corderius in the *Dionysian Onomasticon*: "*εὐθυμοσύνη, Right order.*" Read: *εὐθημοσύνας*, and thus Maximus has it in the *Scholia*: [he calls good-orders the well-placed positions and orders of well-arranged and well-fashioned creation]. What more do you seek? I believe Dionysius took this word from Plotinus, nor did I hesitate to receive into the text *εὐθημοσύνη*, which word, as the passages cited both above and here show, is accustomed to be used especially concerning the divine workmanship and order of the world.

**Page 1377, 4. Τὸ γὰρ ἔξω αὐτός ἐστι, περίληψις πάντων καὶ μέτρον]** ["For the 'outside' is he himself, the enclosure of all things and the measure."] The source is in Plato’s *Laws*, IV, page 716, e (page 355, Bekker): *ὁ δὴ θεὸς ἡμῖν πάντων χρημάτων μέτρον ἂν εἴη μάλιστα...* [God then would be to us the measure of all things in the highest degree, and much more so than, as they say, any man]. Plato touches upon that [saying] of Protagoras: "man is the measure of all things." See *Theaetetus*, page 152, a, with Heindorf’s note, page 313; compare *Cratylus*, page 385, e; to which passage apply Proclus’ *Scholia* 39, page 14 f., Boissonade. Aristotle, *Metaphysics*, III. 5, page 61, Sylburg (page 76, Brandis). Proclus should especially be compared with Plotinus in the *Theological Institutes*, chapter CXVII, which begins thus on page 172: *πᾶς θεὸς μέτρον ἐστὶ τῶν ὄντων...* [every god is a measure of beings; for if every god is unitary, he defines and measures all the multitudes of beings]. Compare above I. 8. 2, page 72, D, with our Annotation.

**Page 1379, 7. Ὅθεν καὶ δέον καὶ καιρὸν ὁ Πλάτων ὡς οἷόν τε ἦν σημῆναι ἐφιέμενος, ὅτι πόῤῥω τοῦ ὡς ἔτυχε]** ["Whence Plato, desiring to signify 'the fitting' and 'the opportune' as much as was possible, [showed] that it is far from 'as it happened'."] Plotinus seems to refer to the passage of the Platonic *Cratylus*, page 419, a (page 76, Bekker): [but the fitting (*δέον*) and the beneficial and the profitable and the gainful and the good and the advantageous and the easy-of-passage appear to others to be the same, signifying by different names that which orders and goes everywhere]. In the preceding, mention is made of "the Good." *Phaedo*, page 99, C (page 89, Bekker): [and they think that truly the good and the fitting (*δέον*) bind and hold together nothing], where Ficinus likewise translates "good and *decens* [fitting/decent]"; to which passage Wyttenbach, page 262: "*δέον* [the fitting] denotes both necessary, duty, debt, just, but also binding, tying. Which Etymology the Stoics frequented in the topic *On the Good*, for example in Diogenes Laertius, VII. 98, 99." Compare Heindorf on that passage, page 189. For which reason I have left Ficinus’ version intact. Eubulus praises the passage of Plato *Against Aristotle*, page 674, Angelo Mai edition; which passage I shall place below at page 764, B. The notion of *Καιροῦ* [Opportunity] is not to be repeated here from the *Definitions* (*Ὅροις*), page 114, a (page 570, Bekker). Aristotle in *Prior Analytics*, I. 35, page 142, Sylburg: [again, that opportunity is not a fitting time. For to God there is opportunity, but there is not fitting time, because nothing is beneficial to God; for one must posit the limits: opportunity, and fitting time, and God]. Which passage Olympiodorus cited in *Alcibiades*, preface, page 39. Moreover, Ion of Chios had called *Καιρὸν* [Opportunity] a god in a Hymn (Pausanias, V. 14. 7.), and Menander also according to Palladas, *Epistle* 118. See Jacobs’ *Annotation on Callistratus’ Statues*, VI (at the end of Philostratus), page 698.

**Page 1380, 2. καὶ οὐδ’ ἂν ἔχοι ἀξίας που εἰπεῖν περὶ αὐτοῦ]** ["and he would not even have [words] of worth anywhere to say about him."] To this reading I have refashioned Ficinus’ version. For the sentiment compare the earlier VI. 7. 16, beginning, page 708: [to pass over still toward the things above the worth...], and what I annotated there.

**— 5. χρὴ δὲ ἴσως καὶ τὸ ἐπέκεινα οὐσίας καὶ ταύτῃ νοεῖσθαι τοῖς παλαιοῖς λεγόμενον δι’ αἰνίξεως]** ["and perhaps it is necessary also that 'beyond essence' be understood in this way by the ancients as having been said through riddles."] First compare our author VI. 7. 38, beginning, page 729, middle, and what we commented there; then apply what I placed on these words from Olympiodorus in *Alcibiades*, preface, page 133: [but if also the first cause is unutterable, yet as being above form...] from Damascius, *On First Principles*, page 238, page 258, and page 60, Wolf, where the Babylonians are said "to pass over the one principle of all in silence," and it is said by the Egyptians "the one principle of all is hymned as unknown darkness." Whence it is understood, what Plotinus says, that to the ancients that supreme thing, which is above essence, was signified only obscurely and through tokens. It is probable indeed that he thought of the Orphic songs and the utterances of the oracles and the sacred Initiations. Proclus in the *Theological Institutes*, CXXXIII, page 182, begins thus: [Every divine thing itself, because of the supra-essential union, is unutterable and unknown to all secondary things, etc.]. The color of this passage and similar ones is drawn from Plato’s *Sophist*, page 239, a, b, likewise from the *Timaeus*, page 28, e: [the maker and father of this all is both a task to find, and having found him, it is impossible to speak of him to all]. Compare our author below, VI. 9. 3, page 759, A, and Proclus in *Platonic Theology*, page 106, above.

**Page 1381, 15. Νῦν δὲ εἰ καὶ πρὶν αἰῶνα εἶναι ὅπερ ἐστὶν ἦν—καὶ οἷον γεννήσει ἀϊδίῳ]** ["But now if also before eternity he was what he is... and as if by an eternal generation."] These are to be compared with Plato’s *Timaeus*, page 37, d, e (page 36, Bekker) and page 42, e (page 46, Bekker), likewise with the *Parmenides*, page 136, b, and page 154 f., and the discussions of Plotinus himself, page 329, D, and page 554, A. Add Proclus, *Theological Institutes*, LV, page 86, and CIV, page 154. Concerning the "eternal generation" (*γεννήσει ἀϊδίῳ*) of the Son of God from the Father, you may find passages collected in Suicer’s *Ecclesiastical Thesaurus*, page 756 f., to which add Nicolaus of Methone’s *Disputation against Proclus*, page 41, Voemel edition. Whether those doctrines of the Christian doctors may lawfully be compared with the doctrines of the Platonic philosophers or not, there is disagreement between Cudworth and Mosheim. See, for example, *Intellectual System*, IV. 15, page 315 ff. Moreover, no one fails to see that this "eternal generation" is only a mode of speaking invented for the sake of doctrine. For "that which is primarily and originally, being as it were simply being... according to Plato has no generation, but is always unbegottenly being," according to Nicolaus of Methone in the place cited. And Alcinous, *On the Doctrines of Plato*, X, page 481, says it is absurd to think God "begotten" (*γεννητόν*). He is rather to be called "unbegotten principle" (*ἀγέννητος ἀρχὴ*). Compare our author himself, V. 4. 1.

**Page 1383, 5. ἀπὸ οὐσίας ἀνενεργήτου]** ["from an un-actuating essence."] This reading exhibited in the marginal edition, instead of the faulty *ἀνεργήτου* [unworking] which defiles the context, is confirmed both by very many manuscripts and truly also by Nicephorus Gregoras in the Plotinian excerpts in the *History of Byzantium*, book XXII, page 683, Paris (page 551, Venice). There has quite often been an error in this word. Thus, to use this example, in the passage of Iamblichus in Stobaeus, *Physical Eclogues*, I. 52. 32, Canter’s edition gives: *ἐνέργειτον*, where it is now correctly read *ἀνενέργητον*. Compare Heeren’s note a, page 882. Add what we ourselves annotated above in our author, V. 6. 6, page 537, A.

**Page 1384, 1. ἀφελὼν πάντα—μήτι προστιθείς]** ["taking away all things... adding nothing."] Compare our author, page 332, C, and page 352, D, E. Proclus had these passages before his eyes when he wrote these words in the *Theological Institutes*, VIII, page 14 ff.: [that which is primarily good is therefore nothing other than good, for if you add anything else, you have diminished the good by the addition, having made it "the good" instead of the Good simply, etc.].

**BOOK IX.**

**Page 1385, 7. ΠΕΡΙ ΤΑΓΑΘΟΥ Η ΤΟΥ ΕΝΟΣ.]** ["On the Good or the One."] I have written thus with very many books of Plotinus and Porphyry. The edition is faulty: "On which Good." This book is the last, the ninth in number if you respect the order of time. See Porphyry, *On the Life of Plotinus*, chapter IV; compare chapter XXVI. If you seek the sources of this book, they are in several dialogues of Plato, especially in the *Parmenides* (where consult Ficinus, chapter 36), in the *Sophist*, page 238 f. (where compare Ficinus, chapter 31), in the *Philebus*, page 20 (which passage Aristotle reproves in *Nicomachean Ethics*, X. 2, to which apply the passage of Eustratius in our Zell’s *Commentary*, page 426 f. and compare Plotinus, page 530, end), in the *Republic*, VI, page 505 (compare Plotinus, page 718, B, C, and page 727, end), finally in the *Timaeus*, page 29, e, and page 30 (to which must be applied Proclus on the *Timaeus*, page 112 ff.; compare also Plotinus, page 216, B, 330, D, 474, B, below, 721, A, below, and the whole book III. 8, "On Nature and Contemplation and the One"). Alcinous reduced these doctrines of Plato on the Supreme Good or the One into the form of a compendium in *On the Doctrine of Plato*, chapter X, pages 476–481, Dan. Heinsius. **[that this is understood by the ancients as being spoken through riddles]** <note>original: "ταύτῃ νοεῖσθαι τοῖς παλαιοῖς λεγόμενον δι’ αἰνίξεως"</note> First, compare our author Plotinus VI. 7. 38. at the beginning, page 729, in the middle, and the things we have commented upon there; then apply what I have placed here from Olympiodorus's preface to the *Alcibiades*, page 133: **"Even if the First Cause is unspeakable, it is so because it exists in a manner beyond all form"** <note>original: "εἰ δὲ καὶ τὸ πρῶτον αἴτιον ἀῤῥητόν ἐστιν, ἀλλ’ ὡς ὑπερειδῶς ὂν (read: ἀλλ’ ὡς ὑπὲρ εἶδος ὂν, as that which is above the idea)"</note> from Damascius's *On First Principles*, page 238, page 258, and page 60 of Wolf’s edition, where the Babylonians are said **"to pass over the one principle of all things in silence,"** and it is said by the Egyptians that **"the one principle of all things is celebrated as unknown darkness."** From this it is understood, as Plotinus says, that to the ancients that highest thing, which is above essence, was signified only obscurely and through tokens <term>tesseras: passwords or symbols used in mystery religions</term>. It is probable indeed that he was thinking of the songs of the Orphics and the utterances of the oracles and the sacred Initiations. Proclus, in *Elements of Theology* CXXXIII, page 182, begins thus: **"Everything divine is itself unspeakable and unknown to all secondary beings because of its supra-essential unity..."** <note>original: "Πᾶν τὸ θεῖον αὐτὸ διὰ τὴν ὑπερούσιον ἕνωσιν ἀῤῥητόν ἐστι καὶ ἄγνωστον πᾶσι τοῖς δευτέροις κ. τ. λ."</note> The color of this passage and similar ones is drawn from Plato’s *Sophist*, page 239. a. b. and likewise from the *Timaeus*, page 28. e: **"To find the maker and father of this universe is a task, and having found him, it is impossible to speak of him to all."** Compare below our author VI. 9. 3. page 759. A. and Proclus on Plato’s *Theology*, page 106, above.

page 1381, 15. **[But now, even if before eternity existed, he was what he is—and as if by an eternal generation]** <note>original: "Νῦν δὲ εἰ καὶ πρὶν αἰῶνα εἶναι ὅπερ ἐστὶν ἦν—καὶ οἷον γεννήσει ἀϊδίῳ"</note> These are to be compared with Plato’s *Timaeus*, page 37. d. e. (page 36 Bekker) and page 42. e. (page 46 Bekker), likewise the *Parmenides*, page 136. b. and page 154 and following, and the discussions of Plotinus himself, page 329. D. and page 554. A. Add Proclus's *Elements of Theology* LV, page 86, and CIV, page 154. Concerning the **eternal generation** <note>original: "γεννήσει ἀϊδίῳ"</note> of the Son of God from the Father, you may find collected passages in Suicer’s *Ecclesiastical Thesaurus*, page 756 and following, to which add Nicholas of Methone’s *Disputation against Proclus*, page 41, Voemel’s edition. Whether it is right to compare these decrees of the Christian doctors with the decrees of the Platonic philosophers or not, there is a disagreement between Cudworth and Mosheim. See, for example, *Intellectual System* IV. 15. page 315 and following. Furthermore, anyone can see that this "eternal generation" is merely a mode of speaking invented for the sake of teaching. For **"that which is primarily and originally Being, insofar as it is simply Being—according to Plato, has no generation, but is always unbegottenly being"** <note>original: "τὸ πρώτως καὶ ἀρχικῶς ὂν, ὡς μὲν ἁπλῶς ὂν—κατὰ Πλάτωνα γένεσιν οὐκ ἔχει, ἀλλ’ ἔστιν ἀεὶ ἀγεννήτως ὢν"</note> according to Nicholas of Methone in the place cited. And Alcinous, in *On the Doctrines of Plato* X, page 481, says it is absurd to think God is **begotten**. He should rather be called the **unbegotten principle**. Compare our author himself, V. 4. 1.

page 1383, 5. **[from an inactive essence]** <note>original: "ἀπὸ οὐσίας ἀνενεργήτου"</note> This reading, shown in the margin of the edition in place of the faulty "inactive" <note>original: "ἀνεργήτου"</note> which defiles the context, is confirmed by very many manuscripts and indeed also by Nicephorus Gregoras in the *Plotinian Excerpts* of the *Byzantine History*, book XXII, page 683 Paris edition, page 551 Venice edition. Errors have often been made regarding this word. For instance, in a passage of Iamblichus in Stobaeus's *Eclogues* I. 52. 32, Canter’s edition gives: "active" <note>original: "ἐνέργειτον"</note>, where now it is correctly read as "inactive" <note>original: "ἀνενέργητον"</note>. Compare Heeren’s note a, page 882. Add what we ourselves annotated above regarding our author, V. 6. 6. page 537. A.

page 1384, 1. **[taking away all things—adding nothing]** <note>original: "ἀφελὼν πάντα—μήτι προστιθείς"</note> Compare our author, page 332. C. and page 352. D. E. Proclus had these passages before his eyes when he wrote these things in *Elements of Theology* VIII, page 14 and following: **"The primarily Good, therefore, is nothing other than Good; for if you add anything else, you diminish the Good by the addition, making it 'the good' instead of 'the Good' simply, etc."** <note>original: "τὸ ἄρα πρώτως ἀγαθὸν οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἐστὶν ἢ ἀγαθὸν, ἂν γάρ τι ἄλλο προσθῇς, ἠλάττωσας τῇ προσθήσει τὸ ἀγαθὸν, τὸ ἀγαθὸν ποιήσας ἀντὶ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ τοῦ ἁπλῶς κ. τ. λ."</note>

<summary>This page provides a scholarly apparatus for Plotinus's writings on the "One" and the "Good," tracing the philosophical lineage of these concepts from Plato through later Neoplatonists and comparing them to Christian theological doctrines like "eternal generation." It emphasizes the "unspeakable" nature of the divine principle as found in ancient Egyptian, Babylonian, and Orphic traditions.</summary>

Likewise chapter IX: *On Self-Sufficiency*. The same author [Proclus], in the same place, chapter XIII, page 24: "Therefore, goodness is also union, and union is goodness, and the good is one, and the one is primarily good." The same author, chapter CXXXIII, page 198: "But the very first (is God) simply One." For in the place where—according to the arrangement of Porphyrius—these *Enneads* end, namely in the inquiry *On the Supreme Good and the same as the One*, he [Proclus] took the beginning of his discussion in those *Elements* of his. For he proceeds from the *One* and *Multiplicity*. The same author in *Platonic Theology* II. 4, page 95, touches upon a twofold reason by which Plato indicated that One: "The manner of the indication of the One is twofold: for Plato hands down to us twofold names for the ineffable cause. For in the *Republic* he calls it the Good itself, and shows it to be the fountain of truth which illuminates both the mind and intelligible things. But in the *Parmenides* he names such a principle the One, and declares it the sustainer of the divine unities." Proclus touches upon the reasoning of the Platonic *Timaeus* in the same work, V. 17, page 280, from which it is established that the One, the Good, and God are the same. Syrianus pronounces similarly in [his commentary on] Aristotle's *Metaphysics* (XII) XIII. 7, in the Latin version: "The One and the Good are the same in Plato, and it is abstracted from all substance and intellect and life." In the same vein, Bessario, the restorer of Platonic philosophy, in the book *Against the Calumniator of Plato*, book II, chapter 3, says: "Plato calls the very One the supersubstantial divinity of God." Let these suffice for understanding both the title and the matter of this Plotinian book. Thomas Taylor translated it into English in *Select Works of Plotinus*, pages 468–506. Tennemann reduced the more notable parts of this book into a series of pronouncements in German in *History of Philosophy* VI, pages 69–89.

Page 1385, 12. "For neither is there an army, if it is not one, nor a chorus, etc." Compare above VI. 6. 12, page 682. C. D. where the same similes are employed. But the argument of that passage should also be compared with ours.

Page 1386, 2. "The bodies of plants and animals, each being one, if they flee the one, being broken into multiplicity, [lose] their essence—he has lost it."] The word *thryptein* [to break/crumble] obtains its proper meaning of "breaking" in this place, yet with a certain added note of corruption and baseness. Maximus' *Scholia* on Dionysius the Areopagite, *Letter* VIII. 1, page 123, Corderius edition: "*Thryptesthai* properly means to be broken down. But the word is also used regarding lovers, who, putting off an encounter with those they love, use such a bodily (Stephanus wants *tethrymmenō* [broken/effeminate]. I do not attempt it on account of examples, part of which I shall bring forward:) that is, a broken-down [affected] character." Regarding the proper force of the Verb and the simple form *thryō*, from which it is derived, see the excellent note of Coray on Heliodorus’ *Aethiopica* II, page 63. Add Hemsterhuys and Ruhnken on Timaeus' *Platonic Lexicon*, page 46 sq. Plato uses it several times, for example in the *Phaedrus* page 228, chapter on *Laws* VI, page 778. For instance, the Comedians also (see Eupolis in the *Rhetorical Lexicon* in Bekker's *Anecdota* I. 43. where it is joined with *hōraizisthai* [to give oneself airs/beautify oneself].) Baguet recently cited other examples in [his notes on] Dion Chrysostom, *Oration* VIII, page 127. It is joined with *paizein* [to play]. Himerius, *Oration* XXVI. 4, page 308, concerning a painter: "He made the breeze (*habran* [delicate] Wernsdorf conjectures) both breaking/fluttering [*thryptomenēn*] and playing." With *kataklasthai* [to be broken down]: Philo the Jew, Vol. I, page 360, middle, Mangey edition: "Because of a delicate lifestyle (hence a foundation is prepared for Wernsdorf's conjecture), they break down and crush [*thryptousi*] the powers of their bodies." Cyril in Suidas under *spathōn*: "to walk in a broken manner, to speak in a broken/effeminate manner [*tethrymmenōs*]." John Chrysostom, *Homily IV* in *Selects*, page 108, Matthæi edition: "Seeing a harlot, with head bare, entering with much shamelessness, clothed in golden garments, being softened, being broken [*thryptomenēn*], singing harlot's songs, broken melodies [*katakeklasmena melē*]." It is also joined with *akkizesthai* [to affect indifference/coquet]. Alciphron, *Letters* III. 8: "For having perceived that the youth's love was inflamed, she acts broken/coquettish [*thryptetai*] and constantly affects indifference." Ruhnken collected other examples in his notes on Timaeus, page 19. To which I shall add a passage of Psellus from *Letter* XXV from the Palatine Codex, recently published by me in Friedemann and Seebode’s *Miscellanea Critica*, page 618: "And you perhaps, so to speak, act broken and affect indifference, showing one part of what is desired, but keeping the other part unseen." What prevents me from adding the most elegant passage of Nilus the Ascetic, *On Incontinence*, page 420 sqq., edition of Jo. Conr. Orellius, especially since by the aid of our same Codex I can wash away several faults from it? "Flee the company of women, if you wish to be temperate, and do not give them the liberty ever to be bold. For in the beginning they either have or feign flattery (rather read *eulabeian* [piety/caution] with the Palatine Codex), but later they dare all things shamelessly. In the first meeting (rather: "In the first meeting, they...") they have their gaze downcast, they speak mildly, and they weep sympathetically; they compose themselves solemnly (more elegantly *semna* [solemn things] in the Codex), and

— 13. "just as a woman conceiving a man toward a man"] In place of the last word, the margin and several Codices have *blepousan* [looking]. The next part: "For of those things called one—that which is" Taylor explains thus: that is, "The nature of its being depends on the nature of the unity which it participates; so that its being is more or less excellent according as this unity partakes in a greater or less degree of *the one itself*."

Page 1390, 12. "Therefore, the one will not even be all things"] Taylor, a man most studious of the monuments of the Platonists, illustrates these things thus: "It is well observed by Damascius *On Principles*, that neither *the one* nor *all things* accords in reality with the nature of *the one*. For these are opposed to each other, and distribute our conceptions. For if we look to the simple and *the one*, we destroy its immensely great perfection: and if we conceive all things subsisting together, we abolish *the one* and the simple. But this is because we are divided, and look to divided particularities. In short, so far as it is *the one*, it is exempt from all things, and is without any multitude; but so far as it is the principle of all things, it is all things prior to all." To the next part: "of the mind being all things" you may compare I. 8. 2. page 73. A.

Page 1397, 8. "and wishing to unite the soul"] The Edition has the corrupt *en ou*, Ficino and Taylor had conjectured *en einai* [to be one]. But I say this not as defining these things, but as he benefits into power according to all things, being the cause of all good." He reduced to a compendium those things which are read in Plato's *Timaeus* page 29, page 25 Bekker; likewise in *Republic* VI, page 509, page 320 Bekker.

— 15. "or as a monad and point it is unified—the soul having taken away—multiplicity, etc."] Alcinous page 479: "But the first thought of it (the One) will be that according to the abstraction of these, just as we have thought of a point by abstraction from the sensible, having thought of a surface, then a line, and finally the point."

Page 1398, 7. "not by the impassable—but by the incomprehensible"] Thus we have restored *aperilēptō* [incomprehensible] from our books instead of *perilēptō*. Taylor also saw this: his fellow countryman had seen and restored it before him, whom he honorably imitates in the study of Plato and the Platonists, Cudworth in *Intellectual System* V. 3. 11. page 1018, who employed this and similar passages of Plotinus. Regarding the word *adiexitētos* [impassable/unsearchable], it was discussed at II. 4. 7. Cf. VI. 6. 17.

— 13. "for it must be the most sufficient of all and the most self-sufficient and most in-need-of-nothing"] Plato in the *Timaeus* page 33, for example page 30 Bekker, concerning the World: "For he who composed it thought it would be better being self-sufficient rather than needing others." Clement of Alexandria, *The Pedagogue* II. 12, page 247 Potter: "sufficiency is a habit reaching toward its proper end without deficiency and without excess. But their mother is justice, and the nurse is self-sufficiency. This, then, is a habit being content with what is necessary, and through itself providing those things contributing to the blessed life." Add Proclus in *Elements of Theology* IX, *On Self-Sufficiency*, where he declares the nature of the Good itself and of the Self-Sufficient thus, page 18 of our edition: "If therefore the self-sufficient has filled itself with the good, that from which it has filled itself would be better than the self-sufficient, and beyond self-sufficiency; and the simply good is in need of nothing." Cf. Plotinus himself page 352 following, and Simplicius on Aristotle's *Physics* page 7. b. Add the passage of Eubulus upon Aristotle's *Politics* II. (in the *New Vatican Collection of Writings*, edition of Angelo Mai II, page 674.): "And yet it was necessary to hear Socrates in the *Phaedo* shouting that he knows nothing that thus binds beings and holds them together as the good, being stronger than any Atlas for this power (Plato *Phaedo* page 99, chapter page 89 Bekker, where cf. Wyttenbach's annotation page 262; cf. our annotation above in VI. 8. 18, page 753. E.) and being itself the very thing which is necessary; for he would be persuaded following these, that everything more self-sufficient is more united to anything whatsoever, and is one in a greater degree, just as it is more self-sufficient in a greater degree. For that which partakes more of the binding principle is more one. But that which has participated more of the good, is able to partake of the binding principle on account of the discourse in the *Phaedo*; but the more self-sufficient partakes more of the good (perhaps

Page 1400, 1. "But he is the super-good"] See above V. 5. 13, where in the Annotations page 532. F. we ordered both passages to be compared. Cf. also Nicephorus in the cited place.

Page 1402, 1. "such as perhaps also Minos made, being called the confidant of Zeus—for the establishment of laws."] Plato, *Laws* I. page 624. after: "You speak of Minos according to Homer, as Minos went to the society of his father every ninth year and according to the reports from him established the laws for your cities" (cf. the Dialogue which is inscribed *Minos* page 319. Plutarch, *Dissertation on whether the Philosopher ought to converse with Princes* page 776, for example page 115 following Wyttenbach: "we hear indeed from Homer calling Minos the confidant [oaristēn] of God. And this is, as Plato says, a companion and student." Add Julian in Cyril, book VI, page 190 Spanheim.) The passage of Homer, *Odyssey* τ. 179 following, has it thus:
->Among them is Cnossos, a great city; there Minos<-
->ruled as king for nine years, the confidant [oaristēs] of great Zeus.<-
Which passage has given handle to so many discussions of ancients and moderns, there is no one who does not know. See only the *Homeric Lexicon* of Apollonius page 263 sq. with the annotations of Villoison and Tollius. Our *Symbolics and Mythology* IV, page 99, and the things cited and discussed there, and Hoeck’s book, which is titled *Kreta* I, page 234 sqq. What Plotinus subjoins, "was called" [*ephēmisthē*], signifies an old report handed down from ancestors. Regarding this force of the word *phēmē*, Wyttenbach treated at Julian page 59, page 152 Leipzig edition, and at Plutarch's *On the Multitude of Friends* page 643. The explanation of the word *oaristēs*, which is read in the margin of the Codex Marcianus A. as *homilētēs* [companion], is held besides Plutarch by the Grammarians in Eustathius on the cited passage of Homer, and Apollonius in the *Homeric Lexicon* page 264, Tollius edition.

Page 1403, 1. "but the (souls) of the gods are always carried, etc."] There occurs to Plotinus the most noble passage of the *Phaedrus*, where Plato page 246, for example page 41 Bekker: "good and everything that is such. By these indeed the plumage of the soul is most nourished and grows, but by the foul and the evil and the opposites it wastes away and perishes; the great leader in heaven, Zeus indeed, driving a winged chariot, proceeds first, arranging all things and caring for them; whom a host of gods and demons follows arranged in eleven parts." Cf. Plotinus page 201. D. with Annotation, likewise page 403. C. page 551. A. middle and page 725. A. What Plotinus subjoins to ours: "but that which stands far off is the common man and the beast," and these things prove him a constant reader of Plato: *Republic* IX. page 588, chapter page 458 Bekker: "Fashion then one idea of a variegated and many-headed beast, etc." Cf. our Author himself I. 1. 7. page 4. G: "the true man almost; but those things are the lion-like and the entirely variegated beast." Proclus in *Alcibiades* preface 78: "thirdly, that even in each of us there is a certain many-headed beast, which is analogous to multiplicity." cf. ibid. page 143.

Page 1404, 10. "but as a chorus singing out of tune, etc."] Plato, *Phaedo* page 85. a. concerning swans: "laments their death, singing out [*exaidein*] from grief." Cf. Wyttenbach on that Dialogue page 193. In our passage also "to sing": Plotinus loves the simile of the Chorus. Here I. 8. 2 is to be compared: "a soul dancing around the mind."

Page 1406, 2. "both flight and the shedding of wings"] Plato, *Phaedrus* page 246, chapter page 40 Bekker. Cf. our Author II. 9. 4. IV. 3. 7. IV. 8. 1. and 4. Soon "according to which also Love [Eros] is yoked to souls both in writings and in myths." Ficino translated that "in scriptis" [in writings]. For he could have thought of pictures or painted tables and similar things. —in myths. Most celebrated is the fable of Cupid and Psyche produced by Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* IV. 83, page 300 Oudendorp and VI. 125, page 429; regarding which we explained in *Symbolics and Mythology* III, page 566 sqq.

— 7. "but here she becomes common—the birthday of Aphrodite"] Plato, *Symposium* page 180. D. page 385 Bekker and page 203, page 429 Bekker. Cf. our Author page 293 sq.

Page 1407, 9. "so that we may embrace him with the whole of ourselves"] See Annotation on IV. 4. 16. at the end at page 409. D. where I conjectured that *auton* [him] should be read in this place, but nevertheless, since all books agree in the common reading [*autōn* - of themselves], I left it intact.

— 12. "becoming a god"] Taylor, after he employed the passage of Aristotle's *Politics*, thus proceeds: "Observe, too, that when Plotinus calls the man who is able in this life to see divinity a God, he means, that he is a God only according to *similitude*; for in this way, men transcendently wise and good are called by Plato, Gods and divine." Some Platonic philosophers distinguished thus: he who is endowed with civil virtue (political virtue), him they call *spoudaios* [excellent], he who has purgative power (the *kathartikē* power), *daimonios* [daemonic], he who has *theōria* [contemplation], him they must call *theios* [divine]. But in that question, whether a man in this life can be *theousthai* or *become a God*, these same philosophers disagreed among themselves. See Porphyry's *Sentences* XXXIV, page 235 sqq. Iamblichus *On the Mysteries* II. 2. and Olympiodorus on Plato's *Phaedo*. I add a passage of Eunapius in the *Excerpts of Histories* page 261, edition of Angelo Mai: which writer thus says of the Emperor Julian: "who indeed through the authority of nature and being equal in magnitude to the divine, ceased from the necessity of education pulling him toward the worse, and having risen from so many waves, he both saw heaven and recognized the beautiful things in himself, having conversed with incorporeal things while still having a body."

Page 1408, 3. "knowledge [science] which is in demonstrations, etc."] Wyttenbach on Plutarch's *Conjugal Precepts* page 900: "Demonstration [*apodeixis*], the effectress of science, the proper instrument of philosophy, is held above childish instruction." The learned man cites not a few passages of Plutarch. Proclus in *Alcibiades* preface page 298: "for as demonstrations from the more universal lead us in a greater degree to science, so indeed even refutations from common applications become effective toward purification." Cf. Olympiodorus in *Alcibiades* preface page 55 and page 121. Add Diogenes Laertius VII. 45, where the Stoics thus define demonstration: "a discourse presenting through things more apprehended that which is less apprehended"; as Davis emended that passage at Cicero's *Academics* II. 8. 26: where Ernesti translates "conclusion of an argument." Cf. Goerenz at Cicero, Book I, page 54 and Rosini on Epicurus' book *On Nature* in *Volumina Herculanensia* Vol. II, at Column IV, page 11. Furthermore, Cudworth and Mosheim in *Intellectual System* page 637 touched upon these Plotinian points. Compare our Author himself above page 148. C. and page 522. A.

— 10. "but not in both"] Taylor from the reasoning of the conclusion judges it necessary that *alla mēn* [but indeed] be written. Ficino and all our Codices persist in the common reading. To the next parts cf. above VI. 8. 7. page 740. B: "unless some bold discourse sent from elsewhere should say."

— 18. "the command of the mysteries"] With the argument of this chapter agree several things which Iamblichus placed in the *Protrepticus* chapter 13. Tholuck, however, compares those things which Plotinus hands down at the end of this chapter regarding *henōsis* [unification] or *haplōsis* [simplification] with the mystical doctrine of the Persians regarding the conjunction and union of man with God, in the book: *Sufism or the Pantheistic Theosophy of the Persians*, chapter III, page 79 sq. which passage we also cited at Porphyry’s *Life of Plotinus*, chapter XXIII, page 137 below Fabricius. Furthermore, as for the mention of mysteries, consult Wyttenbach's Annotation on Plato's *Phaedo* page 134–139; whom also the same Tholuck employed for explaining these things in another book, which is titled: *Collection of Flowers from Eastern Mysticism*. Berlin 1825, page 2–6, where he likewise touched upon our passage. Bened. Bendtsen also employed our passage in *Specimen of Mystical Marbles* I, page 11. Primary is the passage regarding the order of sacred Initiations of Theon of Smyrna, *Mathematics of Plato* page 18, page 21 Gelder edition (where see his annotation page 123 sq.) I do not wish to add more on this subject after those things said partly by Plotinus, partly elsewhere by me.

Page 1409, 13. "having already passed beyond also the chorus of the virtues."] This expression seems to have pleased the Stoics. For since they placed the virtues as connected among themselves (Diogenes Laertius VII. 125. Cf. J. Lipsius’ *Commentary on Seneca* page 605. D.) they added to each of them a certain kind of retinue, as it were. For thus he makes Justice, as it seems, speaking in Nonius [citing] Cicero in the *Hortensius*: "Or when she sees me *and my companions*, fortitude, greatness of soul, patience, constancy, gravity, faith, would she herself withdraw?" To which passage M. A. Muretus adds these things, *Various Readings* III. 20. page 78, Ruhnken edition: "But they (the Stoics) used to illustrate that opinion

**Translator’s Notes:**
1. **Proper Nouns:** Names such as *Marsilius Ficinus* (Marsilio Ficino), *Empedocles*, *Dionysius Areopagita*, *Epicurus*, *Averroes*, and *Egidius Romanus* (Giles of Rome) have been kept as in the original Latin or provided in common English scholarly forms.
2. **"Fic. p."**: This indicates a reference to the specific page in the 15th-century Latin translation/commentary of Plotinus by Marsilio Ficino.
3. **Abbreviations**: *ib.* (*ibidem*) means "in the same place"; *v.* (*vide*) means "see."
4. **Scholarly Terminology**: 
    - *Ens*: Translated as "Being" (that which exists).
    - *Esse*: Translated as "to be" or "Being" (the act of existing).
    - *Essentia*: Translated as "Essence."
    - *Intelligibile*: Translated as "Intelligible" (objects of the intellect).
    - *Hypostasis*: A core Neoplatonic/theological term for a distinct substance or reality.
5. **OCR Unclear Readings**:
    - Page 444: *agnat* is likely a typo for *agit* (acts) or *gignit* (begets/generates) in the context of substantial form.
    - Page 449: *ine (einai)* and *en (hen)* are transliterations of the Greek words for "to be" and "one," used by the author to show etymological links.

This text is an **Index of Subjects and Words** (Index Rerum et Verborum) from a scholarly edition of the works of **Plotinus**, translated and commented upon by the Renaissance humanist **Marsilio Ficino**.

The index provides references to two different paginations: the page numbers of the specific volume (often the Ficino commentary or a specific edition) and the page numbers within the main text of Plotinus’s *Enneads*.

### Translator’s Notes:
*   **Fic. p. / F. p.**: Abbreviation for *Ficini pagina* (Ficino’s page). This refers to Marsilio Ficino's commentary or his specific translation pages.
*   **ib.**: Abbreviation for *ibidem* (in the same place/page as the preceding entry).
*   **Proper Nouns**: Names such as **Plotinus**, **Plato**, **Mercurius** (Mercury), **Jove**, and **Porphyrius** have been retained as requested.
*   **Terminology**: 
    *   *Materia*: Matter.
    *   *Mens*: Mind or Intellect (the Neoplatonic *Nous*).
    *   *Mundus*: World or Universe.
    *   *Ens / Entia*: Being / Beings.

*(Note: Pages 454-460 follow a similar structural index format, continuing the entries for **Mundus** (World), **Natura** (Nature), **Numerus** (Number), **Oratio** (Prayer), **Ordo** (Order), **Passio** (Passion), **Planeta** (Planet), **Principium** (Principle), **Providentia** (Providence), **Pulcritudo** (Beauty), **Qualitas** (Quality), and **Quantitas** (Quantity).)*

### Summary of Key Themes in the remaining pages:
*   **Mundus (454-455):** The world is an image of the intelligible; it is eternal; it is an animal; it is a "statue of God." Plotinus's critiques of the Gnostics are noted.
*   **Musica (455):** Comparison between celestial harmony and earthly music; how music leads to the intellect.
*   **Natura (455-456):** Nature acts without deliberation; it is a "sleeping" intelligence; it follows seminal reasons.
*   **Numerus (456):** Number is the basis of divinity and being; the difference between mathematical number and substantial (essential) number.
*   **Oratio (456):** The nature of prayer; how it acts as a ladder to the divine.
*   **Plotinus (458):** Biographical notes (he was a "vates" or seer; he imitated St. Paul; he was an antagonist to heretics).
*   **Principium (458-459):** The first principle (The One) is beyond essence and intellect; it is the cause of all but contains nothing; it is reached by a "seven-step scale."
*   **Pulcritudo (459-460):** Beauty is not merely proportion (symmetry) but the splendor of form; how beauty leads the soul from the sensible to the intelligible.
*   **Qualitas/Quantitas (460):** Aristotelian vs. Platonic definitions of quality and quantity; how they relate to matter and form.

<keywords>The One, Universe, Unity, Will, Pleasure, Marsilio Ficino, Zoroaster, Neoplatonism, Metaphysics</keywords>

--- Page 471 ---
This text is a comprehensive **Index of Subjects and Words** (Index Rerum et Verborum) typically found in a scholarly edition of Plotinus's *Enneads* and Porphyry’s *Life of Plotinus*. As is common in such indices, the headwords are in Latin or Greek, and the explanations are in Latin, referencing specific books, chapters, and sections of the *Enneads* (e.g., VI. 1. 14) or chapters of Porphyry's biography (e.g., Porph. 22).

***

**Leading upward** (*anagōgē*). I. 3. 1. VI. 8. 6. VI. 8. 21. end.
**The uncaused** is not to be accepted. III. 1. 1. (<note>original: "i. e." — that is</note> that something happens without a cause).
**Without cause.** VI. 7. 2.
**To purify.** VI. 7. 29. (but <note>original: "vid." — see</note> "to purify further").
**The thought turns back.** I. 4. 10.
**To return in cycles.** V. 7. 1.
**To be dedicated** (*anakeitai*), what else is it than "to lie above"? VI. 1. 24.
**To mix together.** III. 5. 7.
**To stir up.** IV. 4. 5.
**To be stirred up.** I. 6. 5. VI. 6. 4.
**Reclining.** VI. 1. 6.
**To lighten** and **to be lightened.** VI. 7. 22.

**ADDENDA AND CORRIGENDA.**

**Regarding the Prolegomena from Fabricius's Greek Library and the annotations subjoined to them. § III. end:**

THE BOOK which falsely claims the name of Aristotle, *On the Mystic Philosophy of the Egyptians*, published twice, at Rome in 1519 and at Paris in 1571, is nothing but a patchwork of excerpts from the *Enneads* of Plotinus. See the **Classical Journal** vol. XV. page 279 and cf. Schoell, **Histoire de la Littérature Grecque** T. III. page 298. Cf. what I have placed at the end of § VIII of Fabricius’s Library.

*Regarding the same § III. end.* **J. Fichte** also disputed concerning the philosophy of the Alexandrians in the commentary entitled: *On the Origin of the New Platonic Philosophy* [De philosophiæ novæ Platonicæ origine]. Berlin 1818. 4to. likewise **Ern. Reinhold** both in a specific dissertation and in the *Handbuch der allgemeinen Geschichte der Philosophie*, Part. I. page 514 ff.; finally, **Porretus** recently treated it in a few words. See *Cours d'histoire de la philosophie ancienne: Ecole d'Alexandrie* delivered by **M. H. Porret. Paris. 1832.**

*Regarding § IV. end.* **Frid. Muenter**, in *Primordiis ecclesiæ Africanæ* page 21, asserts that Neoplatonic philosophy cleared the way for the Christian religion, especially among the Africans learned in the cultivation of letters. "*On the Gnosis of Clement of Alexandria and on the vestiges of Neoplatonic philosophy occurring therein*" is the title of the historical and theological Commentary written by **A. F. Dachne. Leipzig 1831.** Conversely, **Ullmannus** disputed the influence of the doctrine deposited in the New Testament upon that philosophy in the short commentary: "*Parallels from the writings of Porphyrius to New Testament passages, as proof of the influence of Christianity upon an opponent of the same*" in Ullmann and Umbreit's *Theologischen Studien und Kritiken*. 1832. fasc. II. page 376—394. In the same **Studies** 1834. fasc. II. page 349 ff. I myself disputed regarding the relationship that existed between Ammonius Saccas, Plotinus, and their associates and the Christians, namely in a review of the booklet entitled: "*The book of Plotinus against the Gnostics. In Greek.* Edited more correctly, with notes and variant readings from the Munich codex no. 449 collated with the Basel edition, added by **Georg. Antonius Heigl. Regensburg 1832.**" about which book I shall speak below in the Addenda to this book of Plotinus (II. 9.) page 358 ff. Oxford edition.

*Regarding § IX. lit. y.* Regarding the codices of Plotinus preserved in the Escorial library in Spain, see also: "*Catalogues of manuscript books—now published for the first time by Gustav Haenel.*" Leipzig 1832. page 933.

**ADDENDA AND CORRIGENDA.**

*Chapter 5. (page 101. line 13 ff.) ἓν τὸ μὲν, περὶ τοῦ ἐπέκεινα τοῦ ὄντος μὴ νοεῖν, καὶ τί τὸ πρώτως νοοῦν καὶ τί τὸ δευτέρως* [one indeed, concerning that which is beyond being not thinking, and what is the primarily thinking and what is the secondarily]. Ficino's version, which could deceive less intelligent readers into taking this inscription for the title of two books, Leopardi refashions thus: "**one indeed: that which is superior to being does not think, and what it thinks first, or what second. But another etc.**"

*Chapter 7. (page 104. line 11.) ᾧ (Ἀμελίου) τὸ ὄνομα ἦν Γεντιλιανὸς τὸ κύριον* [whose (Amelius's) name was Gentilianus as his proper one]. Leopardi rightly notes the error of Cyril *Against Julian* VIII, who from this passage of Porphyrius fashioned two men, one Amelius and the other Gentilianus. Regarding the city of Ameria, consult also C. O. Muller's *Etrusker*. I. page 103 ff.

*Chapter 9. (line 6 ff. from the end) Ἀμφικλείαν τε τὴν Ἀριστῶνος τοῦ Ἰαμβλίχου υἱοῦ γεγονυῖαν γυναῖκα* [and Amphicleia, who had become the wife of Ariston, the son of Iamblichus]. Rightly at this place Leopardi notes the inconsistency of Fabricius, who in another place (see *Bibl. Græc.* III. page 194. Harles edition) wrote: "**Amphiclia, daughter of Ariston, wife of the son of Iamblichus,**" nor did Harles correct this matter. Leopardi adds: "**and in the fourth book (Fabricius), reviewing various Iamblichi, does not mention that one whom Porphyrius names here, and who in his opinion differs from the famous philosopher of this name, the disciple of Porphyrius.**" See Fabricius *B. Gr.* vol. V. page 773. Harles ed. cf. Ernesti *Cl. Ciceron.* under Iamblichus and add Frid. Munter’s Program on the affairs of the Ituraeans regarding the Gospel of Luke III. 1. Copenhagen 1824. page 9 and 43 where from a Mainz stone a soldier of the cohort of the Ituraeans is mentioned by the name Iamlicus, i.e., **יַמְלִיךְ**, Iamblichus. [Creuzer]

*Chapter 11. (page 113. line 14.) Πρόβον* [Probus]. "**That Probus whom Porphyrius names here, Constantinus Lascaris also mentions in the booklet: *On Greek writers from the Sicilian homeland*, inscribed to Ferdinand Acuna, Viceroy of Sicily: 'Probus, a most learned man from Lilybaeum, whom that Porphyrius had come to see and hear.' I do not know, however, why Lascaris counts him among the Sicilian writers, since Porphyrius neither says that he wrote nor calls him a Sicilian, but only calls him the man *ἐλλόγιμον* 'learned' and relates that he was active in Lilybaeum at the time when he himself set out for Sicily.**" *Leopardi.*

*Chapter 14. (page 116. line 20.) καὶ τοῦ Φιλαρχαίου* [and of the Philarchaeus]. Leopardi also set forth various opinions concerning this place, applying himself to the Toupian one, and to examples of similar titles adds these: "**To these can be added Celsus's *Philalethes* [Lover of Truth]; Damophilus's *Philobiblos* [Lover of Books],—Hierocles's *Philostores logoi* [Stories of Love?]; Telephus's *Poikile philomathia* [Variegated Learning] and Longinus’s own *Philelegoi*. Finally, I do not wish to omit that the opinion in question pleased the most celebrated Tillemont (*Hist. des Empereurs Romains* in Emperor Aurelian article 16) and Giovanni Lami (on Meursius's *Bibl. Attic.* book VI.)**"

*Chapter 17. (page 119. extreme end and page 120. beginning) βασιλεὺς δὲ τὸ ὄνομα τῷ Πορφυρίῳ ἐμοὶ προσῆν κατὰ μὲν πάτριον διάλεκτον Μάλχῳ κεκλημένῳ* [and 'King' was the name for me, Porphyrius, being called 'Malchus' according to my native dialect]. To the examples of similar names collected in the annotation on this place, add that of **Malichus** in an inscription showing Idumaean names, in Pacho's book: *Voyage de Marmarique et Cyrenaïque* page 396 where Letronne says this is the Syriac **Malchi.**—To the following (line 10 ff.) Leopardi adds these: "**It was observed by the most learned Edward Bernard (on Josephus, *Antiq. Jud.* book V. chap. 15 [rather book I. chap. 15. see p. 44 ed. Havercamp. Cr.]) that 'Cleodemus' means the same in Greek as 'Malca' in Syriac. In Josephus (loc. cit.) Alexander Polyhistor cites a certain Cleodemus also called Malchus: 'Cleodemus the prophet says, who is also called Malchus.' In Eusebius (*Præp. Evang.* book IX. chap. 20) quoting this passage, it is read 'who is also Malchas.' Hieronymus (*Quæst. Hebraic.*) also cites that Cleodemus: 'Witness to this matter is Alexander who is surnamed Polyhistor, and Cleodemus surnamed Malchus.' In Porphyrius, however, in this very chapter, where it is read: 'O Cleodemus and Malchus,' these names designate different men.**"

*Chapter 18. (page 123. middle.) Regarding the last words of this chapter Leopardi wrote:* "**Πρόθυμον ἐποίησεν** [He made (him) eager]. Better perhaps Dobler: *πρόθυμον ἐποίησα* I made (him) inclined/eager."

<meta>This page begins the "Addenda and Corrigenda" (Additions and Corrections) section of the volume, providing updated bibliographic references and scholarly notes to supplement the introductory material (Prolegomena) and the biography of Plotinus by Porphyry.</meta>

->ADDITIONS AND CORRECTIONS.<-

->*To the Prolegomena from Fabricius's Greek Library and the annotations added to them. Section III. end:*<-

**THE BOOK** which falsely claims the name of Aristotle, concerning the mystical philosophy of the Egyptians <note>original: "de mystica philosophia Ægyptiorum"</note>, published twice, at Rome in 1519 and at Paris in 1571, is nothing but a patchwork <term>cento: a literary work made up of quotations from other authors</term> of excerpts from Plotinus's *Enneads*. See the **Classical Journal** vol. XV. page 279 and compare <note>original: "cf." for "confer"</note> Schoell's **History of Greek Literature** <note>original: "Histoire de la Littérature Grecque"</note> Vol. III. page 298. Compare what I have placed at the end of Section VIII of Fabricius's Library.

*To the same Section III. end.* **J. Fichte** also discussed the philosophy of the Alexandrians in the commentary entitled: **On the origin of the New Platonic philosophy. Berlin 1818.** <note>original: "De philosophiæ novæ Platonicæ origine"</note> in quarto; likewise **Ernst Reinhold**, both in a specific dissertation and in the *Handbook of the General History of Philosophy*, Part I. page 514 and following; finally, **Porret** recently dealt with it briefly. See: *Course on the history of ancient philosophy:* **The School of Alexandria** <note>original: "Ecole d'Alexandrie"</note> *delivered by* **Mr. H. Porret. Paris. 1832.**

*To Section IV. end.* **Friedrich Münter** asserts in *The Origins of the African Church* <note>original: "Primordiis ecclesiæ Africanæ"</note> page 21, that Neoplatonic philosophy paved the way for the Christian religion, especially among the Africans who were educated in literary culture. "**On the knowledge <term>gnosis: spiritual or mystical knowledge</term> of Clement of Alexandria and the traces of Neoplatonic philosophy found within it**" is the title of the historical and theological commentary written by **A. F. Daehne. Leipzig 1831.** Conversely, **Ullmann** disputed the influence of the doctrine preserved in the New Testament upon that philosophy in a short commentary: "**Parallels from the writings of Porphyry to New Testament passages, as proof of the influence of Christianity upon an opponent of the same**" in Ullmann and Umbreit's *Theological Studies and Critiques*. 1832. part II. pages 376—394. In the same **Studies** 1834. part II. page 349 and following, I myself discussed the relationship that existed between Ammonius Saccas, Plotinus, and their associates and the Christians, specifically in a review of the booklet entitled: "**Plotinus's book against the Gnostics. In Greek.** Edited with corrections, including notes and variant readings from the Munich manuscript number 449 compared with the Basel edition, by **Georg Anton Heigl. Regensburg 1832.**" concerning which book I will speak below in the Addenda to this book of Plotinus (II. 9.) page 358 and following of the Oxford edition.

*To Section IX. letter y.* Concerning the manuscripts of Plotinus which are preserved in the Escorial library in Spain, see also: "**Catalogs of manuscript books—now published for the first time by Gustav Haenel.**" Leipzig 1832. page 933.

*To Section IX. regarding the words of Harles:* "**But later (Villoison) recognized his own error and Fr. Chr. Grimm—illustrated it:**" Jacopo Morelli, in a letter sent to me (**Friedrich Creuzer**) from Venice on the Kalends of December <note>December 1st</note> 1812, declares as follows: "**Villoison wrongly presented those (two dissertations of Plotinus) as unpublished, but he discovered his own error and stated it publicly before Grimm had pointed out those same works among the published writings of Plotinus, as I noted in the *Library of Manuscripts* Vol. I. p. 136.**" To be sure, Villoison had corrected that error in the year 1784. Grimm's booklet, however, saw the light of day in the year 1788. And the former [Villoison] placed these remarks in his *Commentary on Triple Theology* (at the end of Sainte-Croix's book *Research on the mysteries of paganism* vol. II. page 102. Silvestre de Sacy edition): "**In the *Greek Anecdotes*, where two Dissertations of Plotinus are read—which I, along with Lambeck, Fabricius, etc., called unpublished and brought forward—because various fragments of them do not occur in the works of Plotinus except scattered here and there, and are not to be collected without great labor.**"
