<meta>This page contains supplementary notes and corrections (Addenda et Corrigenda) to a scholarly edition of Porphyry’s *Life of Plotinus*. The translator/editor is discussing various manuscript readings and historical interpretations of the text.</meta>

500 ->ADDITIONS AND CORRECTIONS.<-

In subsequent years, he earned the praise of learned men through both poems and other writings; likewise, this same fact <note>original: "eadem"</note> ought to have this influence on me: that I do not pour out **the whole sack** <note>original: "ὅλῳ τῷ θυλάκῳ" — a Greek proverb meaning to exhaust everything at once</note> into these Addenda, which he—let it be said with his kind peace and pardon—had cast onto paper almost as a boy, but rather that I select only the more notable points and send them forth into the public on this given occasion.

*Regarding Chapter 1. Plotinus—he seemed like one who was ashamed that he was in a body.* The words of Theodulus placed by me at this location were not transcribed from the letter to John the philosopher, as I had said following Du Cange, Fabricius (and Leopardi, as I saw later), but to Joseph the philosopher; for my brother Boissonade presented it in its entirety in the *Greek Anecdotes* vol. II. Paris 1830. page 212—228. where these words of Theodulus, or Thomas Magister (see Boissonade at page 188.) are read on page 224 and following.—*Regarding the words at the end of the chapter: the natural talent of Carterius provided a most similar image of him to be made.* From this tablet of Carterius, the face of Plotinus might seem to be expressed, which appeared quite recently engraved on an oriental carnelian <term>carnelian: a reddish gemstone often used for signet rings</term> among the remaining gems of the collection of the most illustrious man. (See *Catalogue of engraved stones of His Highness Prince Stanislas-Poniatowsky*. Rome 1831.) Do not believe it. It is a deceptive work <note>original: "mangonium opus"</note> of a sculptor of our own century. I have said more on this matter in a small book in the vernacular <note>German</note>, which is titled: "**On Gemology; ancient cut stones from the tomb of Saint Elizabeth in Marburg. Leipzig and Darmstadt 1834.**" page 16 and following, and page 144 and following.

*Chapter 2. saying that he did not even admit the nourishment of the body from living animals.* Count Leopardi added these notes: "**Ficino translates 'since he said he did not take food even from the bodies of tame animals.' But, unless I am mistaken, one should further read 'nothing' [meden] for 'not even' [mede], and render it: 'Saying that none of the tame animals take nourishment from a body,' so that here Plotinus hints at the dogma concerning abstinence from living things, about which there exist books by Plutarch and Porphyry hardly unworthy of reading. However, I have changed nothing.**" And he did rightly in not receiving that conjecture into the text.
—— page 94. line 5 from the end of the Fabricius edition. *And saying that he tried to lead the divine within us back to the divine in the universe.* Leopardi also prefers this reading to that other one: **the god within us.**

*Chapter 3. (page 97. line 3 from the end of the Fabricius edition.) Origen wrote nothing except the treatise on demons, and under Gallienus, that the king is the only poet.* G. A. Heigl, in his notes on Plotinus *Against the Gnostics* page 80, placed these words in brackets regarding the former phrase: "**Perhaps 'under Gallus' from the year of Christ 252 until the year 254.**" He leaves the rest untouched, nor does he mention Ruhnken’s conjecture upon this most difficult passage; however, he adds not a few passages from writers from which it is understood that he himself saw that these words include a philosophical sentiment, so that the maker of the world is called its king. Indeed, if you put Gallus for Gallienus, this passage cannot be understood otherwise, since no one could recognize and celebrate poetic faculty in the Emperor Gallus. There is no reason for this change, nor does any manuscript support that conjecture, and Leopardi clearly agrees with me, who himself thinks a philosophical sentiment is in those words, yet thinks nothing should be changed in the reading. But just as flatterers compared Gallienus with Catullus and could compare them without blushing—at least in the judgment of Eckhel in *Doctrine of Ancient Coins* VII. page 407—so an author of a Scholium <term>Scholium: an ancient or medieval marginal note</term> added to Catullus’s *Epithalamium* no. 62 in the Heidelberg manuscript displays a foul ignorance of Catullus's era: "**Valerius Catullus, a lyric writer, is born in Verona in the 163rd Olympiad, the year before the birth of Sallust Crispus, in the times of the leaders Marius and Sulla, on which day Plotinus first taught Latin Rhetoric at Rome.**" And lest you doubt that the man from Lycopolis <note>Plotinus</note> is meant, the Scholiast continues in the following: "**Plotinus, according to Macrobius, is a prince among the professors of philosophy along with Plato, concerning whom Augustine says in book nine, chapter ten [of the City of God]: Plotinus, in times near to our memory, is praised for having understood Plato more excellently than the others.**" What more do you want? The mention of the Olympiad seems drawn from some chronology of a Greek writer; the rest was wonderfully muddled by the stupor of a little Latin schoolmaster <note>original: "magistelli"</note> who, since he thought the name of Plotinus was that of a Latin man, makes him teach Latin Rhetoric at Rome. Likewise, since he had heard that Plotinus was a contemporary of Gallienus—whom the courtiers perhaps repeatedly called a second Catullus—he persuaded himself that this philosopher opened a school at Rome on the very birthday of Catullus, and did not hesitate to attach these absurdities to Catullus's poem.

*Chapter IV. (page 99. line 14 from the end) he is found to have written twenty-one books.* Suidas in the entry *Plotinus* (page 3015. Gaisford edition), after he made mention of the fifty-four books of Plotinus distributed into Enneads, adds: "**He also wrote others.**" Where the Lexicographer received this is not clear; nor does Porphyry seem to recognize other writings of Plotinus besides the Enneads. But nevertheless, since he reveals immediately in this place that different people titled these books differently, later writers could have taken one and the same book for different ones. Nor indeed should it be overlooked—as I have noted elsewhere regarding these Enneads—that here and there sentiments and doctrines attributed to Plotinus occur which are not read in these Enneads.

->ADDITIONS AND CORRECTIONS. 501<-

*Chapter 5. (page 101, line 13 and following)* <note>original Greek: "ἓν τὸ μὲν, περὶ τοῦ ἐπέκεινα τοῦ ὄντος μὴ νοεῖν, καὶ τί τὸ πρώτως νοοῦν καὶ τί τὸ δευτέρως"</note> **"One point indeed: concerning the fact that what is beyond being does not think, and what it is that thinks primarily, and what thinks secondarily."** Ficino's version <note>Marsilio Ficino, the 15th-century Renaissance humanist who first translated these works into Latin</note> could mislead less-informed readers into taking this inscription as the title of two separate books; Leopardi corrects it as follows: "**One indeed: that which is above being does not think; and what it understands first, and what second. The other, however, etc.**"

*Chapter 7. (page 104, line 11)* <note>original Greek: "ᾧ (Ἀμελίου) τὸ ὄνομα ἦν Γεντιλιανὸς τὸ κύριον"</note> **"to whom (Amelius) the name was Gentilianus as his proper name."** Leopardi notes an error by Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria</note> in his work *Against Julian* (Book VIII), where he mistakenly turned Amelius and Gentilianus into two different people based on this passage from Porphyry. For more on the city of Ameria, consult also C. O. Müller's *The Etruscans*, vol. I, page 103 and following.

*Chapter 9. (page 106, line 6 and following from the bottom)* <note>original Greek: "Ἀμφικλείαν τε τὴν Ἀριστῶνος τοῦ Ἰαμβλίχου υἱοῦ γεγονυῖαν γυναῖκα"</note> **"And Amphiclea, who had become the wife of Aristo, the son of Iamblichus."** At this passage, Leopardi rightly points out the inconsistency of Fabricius, who in another place (see *Greek Library*, vol. III, page 194 in Harles's edition) wrote: "**Amphiclea, daughter of Aristo, wife of the son of Iamblichus,**" a mistake that Harles did not correct. Leopardi adds: "**and in the fourth book, Fabricius, while listing various men named Iamblichus, fails to mention the one Porphyry names here, who in his opinion is different from the famous philosopher of the same name who was Porphyry's student.**" See Fabricius, *Greek Library*, vol. V, page 773, Harles edition. Compare also Ernesti's *Ciceronian Lexicon* under 'Iamblichus,' and add Friedrich Münter's *Program on the Affairs of the Ituraeans regarding the Gospel of Luke 3:1* (Copenhagen, 1824, pages 9 and 43), where a soldier of the Ituraean cohort named Iamlicus is mentioned from a Mainz stone—that is, **Yamlikh** <note>original Hebrew: "יַמְלִיךְ" — meaning "He will rule"</note>, or Iamblichus. <margin>Creuzer</margin>

*Chapter 11. (page 113, line 14)* **Probus.** "**The Probus whom Porphyry names here is also mentioned by Constantine Lascaris in his pamphlet *On Greek Writers of Sicilian Origin*, dedicated to Ferdinand Acuna, Viceroy of Sicily: 'Probus, a most learned man from Lilybaeum, whom the famous Porphyry had come to see and hear.' I do not know, however, why Lascaris counts him among the Sicilian writers, since Porphyry neither says that he wrote anything himself, nor calls him a Sicilian, but only calls him a** <note>original Greek: "ἐλλόγιμον"</note> **'learned' man and relates that he was living in Lilybaeum <note>modern Marsala, Sicily</note> at the time when Porphyry himself set out for Sicily.**" *Leopardi.*

*Chapter 14. (page 116, line 20)* <note>original Greek: "καὶ τοῦ Φιλαρχαίου"</note> **"and of the Lover of Antiquity."** Leopardi has also set forth various opinions on this passage; he aligns himself with Toup's view and, using examples of similar titles, adds these: "**To these can be added Celsus's *The Lover of Truth*; Damophilus's *The Lover of Books*; Hierocles's *Loving Speeches*; Telephus's *Varied Love of Learning*; and Longinus's own *Lover of Words*. Finally, I do not wish to omit that this interpretation was favored by the most illustrious Tillemont (*History of the Roman Emperors*, under 'Emperor Aurelian,' article 16) and Giovanni Lami (in his notes to Meursius’s *Attic Library*, Book VI).**"

*Chapter 17. (page 119, end and page 120, beginning)* <note>original Greek: "βασιλεὺς δὲ τὸ ὄνομα τῷ Πορφυρίῳ ἐμοὶ προσῆν κατὰ μὲν πάτριον διάλεκτον Μάλχῳ κεκλημένῳ"</note> **"the name 'King' belonged to me, Porphyry, being called Malchus in my native tongue."** To the examples of similar names gathered in the notes on this passage, add the name **Malichus** from an inscription showing Idumaean names, found in Pacho’s book *Travel in Marmarica and Cyrenaica* (page 396), where Letronne says this is the Syriac **Malchi.**—Regarding the following lines (line 10 and next), Leopardi adds this: "**The most learned Edward Bernard observed (on Josephus’s *Jewish Antiquities*, Book V, ch. 15 [rather Book I, ch. 15; see p. 44, Havercamp edition — Creuzer]) that the Greek name Cleodemus means the same as the Syriac Malca. In Josephus (at the cited location), Alexander Polyhistor quotes a certain Cleodemus also called Malchus: 'Cleodemus the prophet says, who is also called Malchus.' In Eusebius (*Preparation for the Gospel*, Book IX, ch. 20), quoting this same passage, one reads 'who is also called Malchas.' That same Cleodemus is also cited by Jerome (*Hebrew Questions*): 'A witness to this matter is Alexander, surnamed Polyhistor, and Cleodemus, by the surname Malchus.' In Porphyry, however, in this very chapter where it reads: 'Cleodemus and Malchus,' these names designate different men.**"

*Chapter 18. (page 123, middle)* To the final words of this chapter, Leopardi added this note: "**'He made [him] eager'** <note>original Greek: "Πρόθυμον ἐποίησεν"</note>. Perhaps better, as Dobler suggests: **'I made [him] eager'** <note>original Greek: "πρόθυμον ἐποίησα"</note>."

*Chapter 20. (page 126, end and 127, beginning)* "**'The book is inscribed: Longinus to Plotinus and Gentilianus Amelius **on the goal** <note>original Greek: "περὶ τέλους" — also meaning 'on the ultimate purpose'</note>,' Ficino translates it: 'The book is indeed inscribed "On the Goal," addressed to Plotinus and Gentilianus surnamed Amelius.' More correctly, however, Meursius says: 'The book is inscribed, however, "Longinus **Against** Plotinus and Gentilianus Amelius, on the Goal."' Where the word** <note>original Greek: "πρὸς"</note> **'pros' which Ficino translates as 'to' (addressed to), is rendered 'against.' In fact, in the preface to the work *On the Goal* quoted here by Porphyry, Longinus addresses Marcellus, not Plotinus and Amelius; he speaks about Plotinus and Amelius without addressing his words to them at all.**" *Leopardi.* Toup also understood it this way in his notes on Longinus (Fragment V. 1): "**It is the preface to the book *On the Goal*, which Longinus wrote *against* Plotinus and Gentilianus Amelius.**" I shall say more about inscriptions of this kind regarding the title of the ninth book of the second *Ennead*, "**Against the Gnostics**" <note>original Greek: "πρὸς τοὺς Γνωστικούς"</note> (page 358, Oxford edition). <margin>Creuzer</margin> At the beginning of the preface: <note>original Greek: "Πολλῶν κ. τ. λ."</note> **"Of many, etc."** Leopardi also prefers Toup's reasoning. For he translates: "**Of the many philosophers, O Marcellus, who existed in our times... some indeed set out to treat their own favorite doctrines... while others thought it sufficient for themselves to teach their dogmas to their close associates.**"

**Page 1. C. Basle edition, in Var. Lect. [Variant Readings] note 9, end.** read *prætulerim* [I should have preferred] instead of *prætuli* [I preferred]. For I did not admit the Nominative into the text.
**Ibidem [In the same place] in the Latin version, second column, line 3.** read *suscipere ipsam* [to receive itself] for *s. ipsum*. Ficinus, reading *εἴδη* [forms], translated: "receive itself species and others now."
**Page 4. D. Which reading I had approved in note 15.** *οὐχ αὐτὴν δοίης—ἀλλὰ ποιήσης* [you should not give it itself—but make it], I ought to have admitted it into the text, as it was also expressed by Ficinus; but quite often—for why should I not confess it?—I was excessively scrupulous in reshaping the text.
**Page 12. D. line 4 from the end.** read *τὸ ἀφ' οὗ* instead of *τ. α. οὗ*.
**Page 14. B. line 4 from the end.** read in the text *ἢ οὐχ ἱκανὴν* for *η. ο. ἱκανὴν.* and in note 14, line 1, *οὐχ ἱκανὴν* for *ο. ἱκανὴν.* and line 2, *οὐχὶ κακὴν* for *οὐχὶ κακήν.*
**Page 22. D. penultimate line.** delete the comma between *ἀρετὴ* and *καὶ ὄμμα*. But in six hundred places, where modern writing usage in Greek speech also omits commas or semicolons, I have left these untouched, following the account of the manuscripts and the edition, for fear that, if I removed these barriers, I might corrupt the abrupt and concise style of Plotinian discourse.
**Page 34. D. line 10 sqq. On the words of Plotinus:** *αὐτὸς δὲ, εἰ τυθείη, κακὸν οἰήσεται αὐτῷ τὸν θάνατον—τῆς μικρολογίας* [But he himself, if he were sacrificed, will think death an evil to him—out of small-mindedness]. Victor Cousin was not mindful of this passage when he placed these things in his review of Olympiodorus’s Commentary on Plato’s *Gorgias* (in *Journal des Savans*, 1832, page 746): "Here is an anecdote about Plotinus, which is found neither in Porphyry nor in Eunapius, and which is very consistent with what we know of this philosopher's contempt for life. *πραξ.* XVIII. The philosopher Plotinus, when someone told him that a certain person had died a violent death and not a natural death, cried out: 'O weakness of man who imagines that such a death is evil!' *Ὁ φιλόσοφος Πλωτῖνος, εἰρηκότος τινὸς...*" These things the Most Distinguished Vir [man] Cousin [wrote]. Moreover, Olympiodorus took these, like many other things, from the Commentaries of Proclus, and these indeed from the commentaries on Plotinus, who seems to have added these very things for the explanation of this Plotinian passage. David the Armenian, in *Five Voices of Porphyry* (in Paris Royal manuscript, folio 32)—"The fourth argument of Proclus, who wrote a commentary on Plotinus."—"For indeed Plotinus the philosopher, being asked whether the man who lives virtuously is happy, even if he falls into Priamic fortunes (see above I. 4. 5. page 32. F. and our note there) and is surrounded by Trojan evils, and after death is cast unburied upon the earth, answered nothing else except: 'Away with such small-mindedness' (perhaps *τῆς μικρολογίας*), that is, that all these things, both the body and those things concerning the body, being superfluous, do not even contribute to the virtue of the soul."
**Page 36. C. (page 71, line 5 from the end of this Oxford edition.)** Read in the Latin *fit* [becomes] a likeness instead of *sit* [may be] a likeness.
**Page 37. E. (page 74, line 6 from the end of the Oxford edition.)** Read in the Latin *pronuntiat* [it proclaims], as it is in the *editio princeps*, instead of *pronum nuntiat*.
**Page 43. C. (page 85, line 3, Oxford edition.)** Read in the Latin, *voto potitus* [having obtained his wish] for *v. potius*.
**Ibidem D. (line 5 from the end.)** Read in the Latin, *voluptatem* [pleasure, acc.] for *voluptate* [pleasure, abl.].
**Page 57. A. (page 113, line 2, Oxford edition.)** *οὐ τοσί* [not thus]. What I added from the Scholia on Plato’s *Gorgias* in the Notes, Olympiodorus drew from this same passage of Plotinus in his commentary on the same dialogue: "That the soul is led back, not by foot, but by life," as Cousin reports in *Journal des Savans* 1832, page 747.

**Page 199. A. (page 358, Oxon.)** I noted above that this book of Plotinus was recently published separately under this title: *The book of Plotinus against the Gnostics. In Greek.* Georg Anton Heigl published it more correctly and added variant readings from a collation of Munich Manuscript 449 with the Basle edition.—**Ratisbon [Regensburg] 1832.** 8vo. minor, 114 pages. Regarding this little book, commendable neither for its paper nor its typeface, yet useful for the purposes of academic schools if any Professor wishes to explain it to students of Theology and Philosophy, I spoke more fully in a review I made in the collection: *Theologische Studien und Kritiken...* Hamburg 1834. Issue II. pages 337-380; from which I will give only the more notable excerpts in this place: And first, because the editor made the Greek title of this book *πρὸς τοὺς Γνωστικοὺς* into the Latin: "to the Gnostics," he lapsed in that just as Ficino did in translating the words of Porphyry on the *Life of Plotinus* chap. 20, page 126 sq. Fabricius: "The book is inscribed 'Longinus to Plotinus' etc." See what is added to that passage in these *Addenda et Corrigenda*; because Heigl in note page 44 instituted a confirmation of his own change with these words of Lactantius (*Div. Instit.* V. 2.): "A certain person composed two books not *against* the Christians, lest he seem to persecute, but *to* the Christians, that he might seem to consult them humanely and kindly." But the intent of that man, Hierocles, as it seems, was plainly different from that of Plotinus, who did not hesitate to inveigh against the Gnostics gravely and candidly. Nor did the Distinguished Man Matter accurately cite this book of Plotinus from memory (in *Histoire critique du Gnosticisme* Vol. II, page 462): *κατὰ τῶν Γνωστικῶν*, which title no manuscript recognizes. But it ought to have been held entirely what the difference is between *κατὰ* with the Genitive and *πρὸς* with the Accusative in the titles of forensic Orations, such as *κατὰ Μειδίου* "Against Meidias," just as *Against Verres*, and *πρὸς Λεπτίνην*, "against" Leptines, and likewise in Aristotle (*Topics* I) *πρὸς τοὺς ὁρισμοὺς*, "against" definitions. Regarding which difference, after Robortellus and Muretus, Taylor noted on Demosthenes *adv. Eubulid.* page 965 and F. A. Wolf in...

### PAGE 533 ###

**Original page: 504**

-> ADDENDA ET CORRIGENDA. <-

*Prolegomena to the Leptinean*, page CLI sq. Nor does any force of a mild and friendly mind reside in that title, as is shown by the inscription of the book in which Nicephorus Chumnus attacks Plotinus's own doctrine on the Soul: *Antitheticus against Plotinus* and even more explicitly the books of Cyril against Julian, *Speeches against the [writings] of Julian among the atheists*. Therefore Ficino ought to have translated the title of this Plotinian book as: *against* the Gnostics, just as Morus most excellently translated the title of that book of Longinus (in *Notes on the fragments of Longinus* Vol. page 519, Weiske edition) *against* Plotinus.
Next, however, Heigl is to be praised because he used that Munich manuscript for his edition, which I myself once examined and whose quality I learned by experience; yet he is not to be praised so far as he neglected the second and third manuscripts preserved in the same library. Nor will it be approved by anyone that the same editor omitted the prolegomena, in which the question was to be explained whether Plotinus in his writing attacked all Christians or only certain heretics, and which ones in particular. Then, in the note added at the end, the same learned man gathered a great hodgepodge of passages from various ecclesiastical writers, yet he neither digested them nor arranged them by reason and order, so that many things seem poorly adapted to the needs of a student of literature destitute of the discipline of a prudent teacher; nor are a few things lacking which are required for the explanation of obstructed passages. Although Heigl corrected the punctuation in many places, the exclamation marks repeatedly interposed in Plotinian sentences are contrary to the character of that philosopher. For his speech is more placid than fervent, for the most part, and although Longinus praises in Plotinus "the density of thoughts," a frequency of sentiments enclosed in few words, he is not a declaimer here, but an investigator, and he possesses what the same critic calls "the philosophical [nature] of the arrangement of inquiries." Finally, how he practiced criticism, that is, what Heigl achieved in emending the text, the learned will best judge from these examples:
**Page 199. line 10. 11. *ἀλλ' ἔν τι*, Heigl.: *ἀλλὰ ἔν τι* from four books:** the others hold our reading.
**--- line 13. *ταύτην δεῖ νομίζειν τὴν φύσιν καὶ μίαν λέγειν*. Heigl.: *τὴν αὐτὴν δ. ν. τ. φ. κ. μ. λ.* from the version of Ficino alone,** who nevertheless did not read it thus, but wished to express *καὶ μίαν* at the same time.
**--- (page 359. Oxon.) line 5. *καὶ τὸ νοῦν πρώτως*, Heigl.: *καὶ τὸν νοῦν πρότερον*, which departs too much from the common reading *καὶ τὸ νοῦν πρώτως**, nor does it rest on the authority of any book.
**--- line 7. *εἴτε γὰρ ἐλάττω—ταὐτὸ φήσουσιν*. Heigl.: *εἰ γὰρ ἐλάττω—ταὐτὸν φ.* But *εἴτε*** all books recognize with the Basle edition, and that *τὸ* is to be referred to the following *λοιπὸν δὲ*, (compare Hermann on Viger page 836 and Schaefer on Dionysius of Halicarnassus *On Composition* page 192.)
**--- line 8. *φήσουσιν*. More correctly Heigl *φήσουσιν,*** for a major punctuation should be changed into a minor one. On the other hand:
**--- line 10. Between *τούτων* and *τίνες* Heigl ought to have replaced the period with a comma.**
**--- line 18. "*ἔστι γὰρ ὡς ἔστι, νοῦς ἀεὶ ὡσαύτως ἐνεργείᾳ κείμενος ἑστώςῃ*. Heigl.: *Ε. γ. ὡς ἔστι νοῦς, ἀεὶ ὡσαύτως ἐν ἐνεργείᾳ κ. ἑστ.***" plainly as I had conjectured in the Var. Lect.
**Page 200. C. (page 360. line 4.) Place a comma between *ποιεῖν* and *εἰ*, as Heigl did.**
**--- line 5. *καὶ γὰρ εἰ ἄλλο τὸ ἐν τούτοις νοεῖν*, Heigl.: *κ. γ. εἴ ἄλλο τὸ ἐν τῷ νοεῖν* without manuscripts and rashly. For Ficino correctly interpreted these: "For if in these it is another thing simply to understand."**
**--- line 8. *ἀλλὰ πάντως γε ὁ αὐτὸς ἔσται ὥσπερ ἐνόει*, Heigl.: *α. π. γ. ο. α. ἔσται τῷ ὥσπερ ἐνόει*. Badly.**
**--- line 9. *ἄλλου ὄντος, ἀλλ' οὐκ αὐτοῦ τοῦ νενοηκότος* Heigl.: *α. ὄντος ἀπ' αὐτοῦ τ. ν.* Compare Var. Lect.**
**--- E. line 14. 15. *εἰ καὶ μετρίως σπουδαῖοι εἶεν, αἰτίαν ἂν ἀφροσύνης ἔχοιεν*. Heigl.: *εἶμεν—αἰτίαν ἀφροσύνης ἔχοι ἄν,*** from Ficino, by conjecture and without manuscripts.

-> **On the passage of Plotinus translated from Eusebius into this edition after page 364 of the Basle edition:** <-

These same things are read in a fragment of a paper manuscript, which *J. Th. Voemelius* acquired at Frankfurt am Main, and very kindly communicated with me. Therefore, whatever variant reading is in that book, I will note it here:
**Frankfurt Fragment page 1. line 1. *δδ' ἄν τις ἐπισκέψαιτο ὅπως*.**
**--- page 1. line 6. *ἀλλὰ ψυχικοῦ ὀργανικοῦ*.**
**--- lines 7-9. *εἰ μὲν οὖν ᾗ παραβέβληται σώματος συμμερίζεσθαι τὴν ψυχὴν ἀποκοπτομένου τινὸς μέρους*, middle parts omitted.**
**--- line 12. *εἴπερ δὴ προσφυᾶ*.**
**--- line 17. *αἰσθήσεις δὲ μόνον δυνατὸν τίθενται· τὰς δὲ νοήσεις ἀδύνατον*.**
**--- page 2. line 6. *τοὺς τόπους ἔχει* and next *ἐν ἔσονται*. Both badly.**
**--- line 10. *ὡς ἀχώριστα ἐντελέχεια*, however immediately following correctly: *ἀχώριστος ἐ.***
**--- line 14. *ὃ ἀμφισβήτησιν δόξειεν ἂν ἔχειν*, more mildly; immediately, *μὴ τοῦτον τὸν τρόπον*.**
**--- line 19. *τὰ κάτω ἐν πολλοῖς*. Compare Viger’s note in this place.**
**--- page 3. lines 1, 5, 6. *μεριστοῦ σώματος ἐντελέχεια γένοιτο*, omitting *τοῦ* and *μεριστή*. Next *τοῦ* also omitted before *ἐφεξῆς*.**
**--- lines 10, 11. *οὐκ ἄρα τοῦ εἶναι εἶδος τινὸς τὸ εἶναι ἔχει*, the same next: *οὐ περὶ τὸ ἐν σώματι ἱδρύσθαι λαμβάνουσα*.**
**--- line 16. *πράξεις δὲ καὶ ποιήσεις*, which the Latin interpreter expressed.**

To the *Annotation* on the passage page 403. A. Basle edition (IV. 4. 9.), I touched upon the sources from which Plato seems to have drawn in the most noble passage of the *Phaedrus* (page 246. b-e. "The soul... traverses the heavens. Zeus the great leader in heaven" etc.): now let it be permitted to add that Heusdius (in *Beginnings of Platonic Philosophy* I, page 138 sq.) calls these and similar things, which migrate beyond the bounds of prose speech, "the vices of a youthful and luxuriant genius;" Astius (in *New Notes on the Phaedrus* page 398 sqq.) says that these same things, as far as the sentiment is concerned, flowed from the reasoning of the most ancient peoples and sages...

### PAGE 537 ###

**Original page: 508**

-> ADDENDA ET CORRIGENDA. <-

but as for the words, that the Homeric passages were mostly expressed by Plato; finally, Gottfried Hermann very recently (in the *Dissertation on the duty of the interpreter* page 10 sqq.), who says that quite manifest traces of Empedocles’ doctrines are present in those passages, judges that a great part of these Platonic words (up to Plato *Phaedrus* page 247. b.) were taken from the verses of the same Empedocles and other epic poets and perhaps even Aeschylus, and were changed here and there by Plato; and led by that judgment, he has recalled these Platonic [words] even to the laws of meters.
To the *Note* on page 520. F. Basle. As to the fact that I attempted the passage of Severus of Alexandria *Ethop.*, I wish it had not been done; and later I saw these same things read in the same words in Libanius Vol. IV, page 1097, Reiske, nor does the reading differ more in the newest edition of Severus by Chr. Walzius (*Rhetorr. Græcc.* Vol. I, page 546.)
At the end of the *Annotation* to the title of the book *on Intellectual Beauty* (page 541 Basle) to Herder and Schelling, who are mentioned in the same place, let Goethe now be added. For he translated the first chapter of this book (V. 8. 1.) into German, following mostly the Latin of Ficino (in letters to Zelter Part I, pages 190-192), and both judge that in these doctrines of Plotinus the summit of the teaching on beauty is contained, (compare Zelter’s words page 185 sq.)
To the *Note* on the passage page 726. B. Basle edition, at the words of Plotinus: *οὐδὲ γαργαλιζομένου λέγει τοῦ σώματος* [neither does he speak of the body being titillated], in the passage of Philo Judaeus *Leg. Allegorr.* III, page 118, first the words: *ἀλλὰ συντόνου καὶ σφοδρᾶς ἀεὶ κνήσεως* were to be translated: by a vehement and intense continue *pruritus* [itching/stimulation], for Cicero uses *titillation* rather for *γαργαλισμῷ*. Then a second emendation was to be attempted: *ἀεὶ κινήσεως* [always of motion], since Philo in the same place compares the opinion of the Cyrenaics, who place pleasure in motion (*ἐν κινήσει*), with the opinion of the Epicureans, who say that pleasure is stable (*ἡδονὴν καταστηματικὴν*).

To the *Index of Plotinian Greek* add these before the letter B: **ἄψυχα ἢ ἔμψυχα τὰ ἄστρα.** II. 3. 2. [whether the stars are inanimate or animate]. Before **κυριεύομαι** the word **κύκλος.** II. 6. 1.

**Page 96. A. (Page 178 of the Oxford edition, line 1 of the text.)** Delete the comma between *body* <note>original Greek: σῶμα</note> and *having* <note>original Greek: ἔχοντα</note>.
**Page 97. D. C. E. C. Schneider praises these passages of Plotinus in his edition of Plato's *Republic* [Civitas], Book VII, page 456. B. (Page 308 of Schneider's edition).** However, regarding the words: *it will hold unchangeably and likewise* <note>original Greek: ἀπαραλλάκτως ἕξει καὶ τὸ ὡσαύτως</note>, he inserted after the word *the* <note>original Greek: τὸ</note> in parentheses: "perhaps *always*? <note>original Greek: ἀεὶ</note>"; but neither our manuscripts nor Philoponus <note>John Philoponus, a 6th-century Christian philosopher and commentator</note> support this; that which he wrote next, *as* (read *that*) *he said* <note>original Greek: ὡς (l. ὅτι) ἔφη</note>, I have given thus from the manuscripts and from Philoponus.
**Page 98. A. In the Latin, place the number (III) before the words:** "In what way therefore."
**Page 100. A. Line 8. Read, as stated in the Variant Readings, *for the one having made* <note>original Greek: πεποιηκότι</note> instead of *of the one having made* <note>original Greek: πεποιηκότος</note>.**
**Page 101. F. Line 6 from the end in the Latin, read *God kindles the light* <note>original Latin: Accendit Deus lumen</note> instead of *God approaches the light* <note>original Latin: Accedit D. l.</note>.**
**Page 108. A. (Page 200, line 12 of the Oxford edition.)** *or it proceeds straight until it comes to that where it is stationed* <note>original Greek: ἢ εὐθυπορεῖ ἕως ἂν ἥκοι εἰς τὸ οὗ τέτακται</note>. I ought to have corrected *it comes* <note>original Greek: ἥκοι</note> to the subjunctive form *it may come* <note>original Greek: ἥκῃ</note> on the authority of three manuscripts, as I did on page 21. C. of the Basle edition and in the same place at E. Compare also page 31. G. and page 43. C., where the same variation is found in the manuscript books and the Basle edition. See my note at page 57. D. (Page 114, lines 2 and 3 of the Oxford edition) where it says: *until it might shine forth—until you might see, etc.* <note>original Greek: ἕως ἂν ἐκλάμψειεν—ἕως ἂν ἴδῃς κ. τ. λ.</note>.
**Page 121. Basle edition. (Page 220, in the note on Ficino's commentary placed by me at the second to last line of the Oxford edition)** read *The Christian woman* <note>original German: Die Christin</note> instead of *The Christians* <note>original German: Die Christen</note>.
**Page 138. A. (Page 244 of the Oxford edition.)** Olympiodorus <note>a Neoplatonist philosopher and commentator on Plato</note> touched upon this dispute in his work on Plato’s *Gorgias*. See Victor Cousin in the *Journal des Savans* 1832, page 747; who writes: "Section [praxis] XLVIII contains the opinion of Plotinus on astrology. Plotinus crushes astrology with this dilemma: 'The stars are either animate or inanimate. If they are inanimate, which is not the case, how can they produce any effect acting without a soul <note>original Greek: ἀψύχως ἐνεργοῦντα</note>? If they are animate, and their action is divine <note>original Greek: θειοτέρως ἢ καθ' ἡμᾶς ἐνεργεῖ</note>, how do they give wealth and all advantages of this kind to one, and to another poverty and all other sorts of misfortune?'" "This dilemma is the basis of the eleventh paragraph of the third book of the eleventh Ennead." The illustrious man <note>Victor Cousin</note> meant the second chapter of the third book of the second Ennead.
**Page 145. D. (Page 260, lines 4 and 5 of the Oxford edition.)** *But Plato—choices* <note>original Greek: 'O δὲ Πλάτων—προαιρέσεις</note>. C. E. C. Schneider also corrected this in Plato's *Republic*, Volume III, page 300. Likewise, shortly after (line 11), *entwined* <note>original Greek: συγκλωσθέντα</note>, just as I restored from the manuscript books.
**Page 147. F. (Page 265, line 1 of the Oxford edition.) Read *forming* <note>original Greek: τυποῦσα</note> instead of *to form* <note>original Greek: τυπῶσα</note>.**
**Page 165. G. (Page 296, line 3.) Read *of mass* <note>original Greek: ὄγκου</note> instead of *of masses* <note>original Greek: ὄγκων</note>, as indicated in the Variant Readings.**
**Page 166. (Page 297, line 7 from the end in the Latin.) Either it must be read: *it—matter* <note>feminine: eam—materiam</note> instead of *him—matter* <note>masculine: eum—m.</note>, or it must be said that Ficino read *itself* <note>feminine: αὐτὴν</note> instead of *itself* <note>the same word, likely a breathing mark distinction in the original Greek</note>, though no trace of this reading exists in the manuscripts.**
**Page 173. C. (Page 311, line 8 of the Oxford edition.) Write *after itself* <note>original Greek: μεθ' αὑτὸ</note>, and likewise in the Variant Readings, instead of *after itself* <note>original Greek: μετ' αὑτό</note>.**

Punctuate: *according to which it is a certain kind of substance, not a difference of the quality—making* instead of *according to which it is a certain kind of substance of the quality, not a d.—m.* <note>The note clarifies the grammatical grouping of the Greek words *ποιὰ οὐσία* (qualified substance) and *τοῦ ποιοῦ* (of the quality)</note>.**
**Page 181. C. (Page 327, line 13.) Delete the colon between *quality* <note>original Greek: ποιότητα</note> and *disposition* <note>original Greek: διάθεσιν</note>.**
**Page 199. A. (Page 358 of the Oxford edition.)** I mentioned above that this book of Plotinus was recently published separately under this title: *Plotinus's Book to the Gnostics. In Greek.* It was edited more correctly, with variant readings added from a collation of the Munich Manuscript 449 and the Basle edition, by Georg Anton Heigl.—**Regensburg, 1832.** small octavo, 114 pages. Regarding this booklet—which is commendable neither for its paper nor its typeface, yet useful for academic study should any Professor wish to explain it to students of Theology and Philosophy—I have spoken at length in my review of it, which I published in the collection: *Theological Studies and Critiques—edited by Dr. Cs. Ullmann and Dr. F. W. C. Umbreit.* Hamburg 1834, part II, pages 337–380; from which I will give only the more notable excerpts here: And first, because the editor rendered the Greek title of this book *Toward the Gnostics* <note>original Greek: πρὸς τοὺς Γνωστικοὺς</note> into Latin as "To the Gnostics" <note>original Latin: ad Gnosticos</note>, he slipped in the same way as Ficino did when translating the words of Porphyry in the *Life of Plotinus*, chapter 20, page 126 sq. in Fabricius: *The book is entitled "Of Longinus to Plotinus," etc.* <note>original Greek: ἐπιγράφεται δὲ τὸ βιβλίον Λογγίνου πρὸς Πλωτῖνον κ. τ. λ.</note>. See what was written on that passage in these *Additions and Corrections*; because Heigl, in a note on page 44, attempted to justify his change with these words of Lactantius <note>early Christian author, c. 250 – c. 325 AD</note> (*Divine Institutes* V. 2.): "A certain man composed two books not *against* <note>Latin: contra</note> the Christians, lest he seem to be attacking them, but *to* <note>Latin: ad</note> the Christians, that he might seem to counsel them humanely and kindly." This man’s intention—Hierocles, it seems—was clearly different from that of Plotinus, who did not hesitate to inveigh against the Gnostics heavily and candidly. Nor did the illustrious Matter <note>Jacques Matter, author of *Histoire critique du Gnosticisme*</note> (in *Critical History of Gnosticism* Vol. II, page 462) record this book of Plotinus more accurately from memory as: *Against the Gnostics* <note>original Greek: κατὰ τῶν Γνωστικῶν</note>, a title which no manuscript recognizes. In general, however, one ought to keep in mind the difference between *against* <note>Greek: κατὰ</note> with the Genitive case and *toward/against* <note>Greek: πρὸς</note> with the Accusative case in the titles of forensic Orations, such as *Against Meidias* <note>Greek: κατὰ Μειδίου</note>, just as in Cicero's *Against Verres*, and *In response to Leptines* <note>Greek: πρὸς Λεπτίνην</note>, and likewise in Aristotle (*Topics* I) *against definitions* <note>Greek: πρὸς τοὺς ὁρισμοὺς</note>. Regarding this difference, after Robortello and Muretus, Taylor noted it in his work on Demosthenes' *Against Eubulides* page 965 and F. A. Wolf in...

[[original page: 504]]

-> ADDITIONS AND CORRECTIONS. <-

**Introduction to the *Leptinean Oration* <note>An oration by the Greek statesman Demosthenes</note>, page 151 and following.** That there is no force of a "gentle and friendly spirit" in that title is proven by the inscription of the book in which Nicephorus Chumnus <note>A 13th-century Byzantine scholar and statesman</note> attacks the doctrine of Plotinus himself regarding the Soul: *Opposition to Plotinus* <note>original Greek: 'Αντιθετικὸς πρὸς Πλωτῖνον</note> and even more clearly the titles of Cyril's books against Julian <note>Cyril of Alexandria’s work against Emperor Julian "the Apostate"</note>: *Arguments against the writings of Julian the godless* <note>original Greek: πρὸς τὰ τοῦ ἐν ἀθέοις 'Ἰουλιανοῦ λόγοι</note>. Accordingly, Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino, the 15th-century Renaissance philosopher who first translated Plotinus into Latin</note> ought to have translated the title of this Plotinian book as: *against* the Gnostics, just as Morus <note>referring to Thomas More or a similar scholar in Weiske's edition of Longinus</note> most excellently translated the title of that book by Longinus as *against* Plotinus.

Next, Heigl <note>Karl Heigl, a 19th-century editor of Plotinus</note> is to be praised because he employed the Munich manuscripts for his edition, which I myself once examined and whose quality I recognized through experience (see my *Preparation for Plotinus on Beauty*, page 130 and following); yet he is not to be praised for the fact that he neglected a second and third manuscript which are preserved in the same library. Nor will anyone approve of the fact that the same editor omitted the introduction, in which he should have explained the question of whether Plotinus attacked all Christians in his writing, or only certain heretics, and which ones specifically. 

Furthermore, in the annotation placed at the end, the same learned man gathered a great jumble <note>original Latin: farraginem</note> of passages even from various ecclesiastical writers, yet he did not arrange them nor set them in any logical order. Thus, to a student of literature who lacks the guidance of a wise teacher, many of these notes seem poorly suited to his needs; and not a few things are missing which are required for the explanation of difficult passages. Moreover, although Heigl improved the punctuation in many places, the exclamation marks he repeatedly inserted into Plotinus's sentences are contrary to the character of that philosopher. For his speech is more placid than fiery, for the most part; and although Longinus praises in Plotinus "the density of thoughts" <note>original Greek: τῶν ἐννοιῶν τὴν πυκνότητα</note>, a frequency of ideas enclosed in few words, he is not a declaimer <note>a flashy orator</note> but an investigator, and he possesses what the same critic calls "the philosophical arrangement of inquiries" <note>original Greek: τὸ φιλόσοφον τῆς τῶν ζητημάτων διαθέσεως</note>. Finally, scholars will best judge how he practiced the art of criticism—that is, what he achieved in emending the text—from these examples:

**Page 199. line 10. 11. *but some one thing* <note>original Greek: ἀλλ' ἔν τι</note>, Heigl: *but one certain thing* <note>original Greek: ἀλλὰ ἔν τι</note> from four books:** the rest of us hold to our reading.
**--- line 13. *it is necessary to consider this nature and to call it one* <note>original Greek: ταύτην δεῖ νομίζειν τὴν φύσιν καὶ μίαν λέγειν</note>. Heigl: *it is necessary to consider the same nature and to call it one* <note>original Greek: τὴν αὐτὴν δ. ν. τ. φ. κ. μ. λ.</note> from the version of Ficino alone,** who nevertheless did not read it this way, but wished to express the idea of "and one" at the same time.
**--- (Page 359 Oxford edition) line 5. *and that which is intellect primarily* <note>original Greek: καὶ τὸ νοῦν πρώτως</note>, Heigl: *and the prior intellect* <note>original Greek: καὶ τὸν νοῦν πρότερον</note>, which departs too much from the common reading *and that which is intellect primarily*, and rests on the authority of no manuscript.**
**--- line 7. *for whether less—they will say the same* <note>original Greek: εἴτε γὰρ ἐλάττω—ταὐτὸ φήσουσιν</note>. Heigl: *for if less—they will say the same* <note>original Greek: εἰ γὰρ ἐλάττω—ταὐτὸν φ.</note>. But all the manuscripts, along with the Basle edition, recognize "whether" <note>original Greek: εἴτε</note>, and that article "the" <note>original Greek: τὸ</note> should be referred to the following "it remains,"** (compare Hermann on Viger <note>Standard works on Greek idioms</note>, page 836, and Schaefer on Dionysius of Halicarnassus *On Composition*, page 192.)
**--- line 8. *they will say* <note>original Greek: φήσουσιν</note>. Heigl more correctly has *they will say* <note>original Greek: φήσουσιν</note>, for the major punctuation mark should be changed to a minor one.** On the contrary:
**--- line 10. Between *of these* <note>original Greek: τούτων</note> and *who* <note>original Greek: τίνες</note>, Heigl ought to have replaced the period with a comma.**
**--- line 18. "for it is as it is, intellect always situated in the same way in activity, standing firm." <note>original Greek: ἔστι γὰρ ὡς ἔστι, νοῦς ἀεὶ ὡσαύτως ἐνεργείᾳ κείμενος ἑστώςῃ.</note> Heigl: "For it is as there is intellect, always in the same way in activity..."** exactly as I had conjectured in the Variant Readings.
**Page 200. C. (Page 360, line 4.) Place a comma between *to make* <note>original Greek: ποιεῖν</note> and *if* <note>original Greek: εἰ</note>, as Heigl did.**
**--- line 5. *for even if thinking in these is something else* <note>original Greek: καὶ γὰρ εἰ ἄλλο τὸ ἐν τούτοις νοεῖν</note>, Heigl: *for even if something else in the act of thinking* <note>original Greek: κ. γ. εἴ ἄλλο τὸ ἐν τῷ νοεῖν</note> without manuscripts and recklessly. For Ficino correctly interpreted these words: "For if in these it is one thing simply to understand."**
**--- line 8. *but entirely the same will be as he was thinking* <note>original Greek: ἀλλὰ πάντως γε ὁ αὐδὸς ἔσται ὥσπερ ἐνόει</note>, Heigl: *but entirely the same will be to that as he was thinking* <note>original Greek: α. π. γ. ο. α. ἔσται τῷ ὥσπερ ἐνόει</note>. Poorly done.**
**--- line 9. *another being, but not he himself who has thought* <note>original Greek: ἄλλου ὄντος, ἀλλ' οὐκ αὐτοῦ τοῦ νενοηκότος</note>. Heigl: *being another from himself who has thought* <note>original Greek: α. ὄντος ἀπ' αὐτοῦ τ. ν.</note>. Compare the Variant Readings.**
**--- E. line 14. 15. *if they were even moderately serious, they would have a cause for folly* <note>original Greek: εἰ καὶ μετρίως σπουδαῖοι εἶεν, αἰτίαν ἂν ἀφροσύνης ἔχοιεν</note>. Heigl: *if we were—there would be a cause of folly* <note>original Greek: εἶμεν—αἰτίαν ἀφροσύνης ἔχοι ἄν</note>, following Ficino, by conjecture and without manuscripts.**
**--- F. (Page 361 Oxford edition) line 3. *as in a dream* <note>original Greek: ὡς ἐν ὄν.</note>. Heigl: *as being in* <note>original Greek: ὡς ἐνόν</note> from mere conjecture. Poorly done.** Soon after, the same man gave "it has double" <note>original Greek: ἔχει δ.</note> instead of "there it is double" <note>original Greek: ἐκεῖ διπλοῦν</note>. The manuscripts do not vary at all. However, the same man:
**--- line 5. after *that he thinks* <note>original Greek: ὅτι νοεῖ</note> aided the understanding by placing a question mark, and likewise in line 8 after *thus* <note>original Greek: οὕτω</note>.**
**--- G. line 9. *then from this there arises in the soul another, from the word itself* <note>original Greek: εἶτα ἀπὸ τούτου γίγνεσθαι ἐν ψυχῇ ἄλλον, ἀπ' αὐτοῦ τοῦ λόγου</note>, Heigl: *then there arises in the soul (another from the word itself)*. See Variant Readings.**
**Page 201. A. line 13. *and entirely he will not know intellect* <note>original Greek: καὶ ὅλως οὐκ εἰδήσει νοῦν</note>, Heigl: *and entirely and he will not know intellect*. But these selections from the first chapter of this book will be sufficient to designate the type of criticism which the editor practiced; from the following pages we shall note down only a few things here and there.**
**--- E. (Page 363 Oxford edition, line 3. 4.) correct to: *unless after that which primarily lives it should live also secondarily* <note>original Greek: εἰ μή τι μετὰ τὸ πρώτως ζῆν ζῴη καὶ δευτέρως</note> (this latter part Heigl also accepted). Compare our Variant Readings and Ficino's version, in which from the first edition one should likewise correct: "unless after that which lives first, another also lives (instead of *from elsewhere*)" and shortly: "and certain things are engaged in generation" (instead of *by a certain*).**

Soon, however, at line 15, the same [Heigl] correctly gave: "not masters" <note>original Greek: οὐ κύριοι; see our Variant Readings</note>. Then indeed:**
**--- D. (Page 371. line 3.) the same [Heigl] ought to have corrected *engkrithethen* to *engkrithesthen* <note>original Greek: ἐγκριτησθέν; a technical grammatical correction of the passive participle</note> (see our Variant Readings); and at line 9, retain *epithei* <note>original Greek: ἐπιθεῖ; meaning "attacks" or "rushes upon"</note>, and not substitute *epidei* <note>original Greek: ἐπιδεῖ; meaning "needs" or "is lacking"</note>. In the same place in Ficino’s version (column 2, line 2 of the Oxford edition), it seems it should be corrected to: *religantur* <note>Latin: "they are bound back"</note>, although even the first edition has *redigantur* <note>Latin: "they are reduced"</note>.**
**Page 206. D. (Page 373. line 5.) Because Heigl placed "from there" <note>original Greek: ἐκεῖθεν</note> instead of "runs there" <note>original Greek: ἐκεῖ θεῖ</note>, the manuscripts do not support it, and Plotinus by this word looked back to "the gods," as the following lines (9–11) argue: "the stars—gods, carried in order and going around the world."**
**Page 209. A. B. (Page 378. line 9, 10.) Even Heigl accepted from the Munich manuscript the reading "formerly" <note>original Greek: πρότερον</note> instead of "primarily" <note>original Greek: πρώτως</note> (see our Variant Readings), and the same [Heigl] compiled much in his Notes on this place, including among other things what I myself had added to Porphyry's *Life of Plotinus* and his *Enneads*. The following:**
**--- line 13–16. They seem to be punctuated thus: "speaking (for more—but of those becoming arrogant) we have said these things" <note>original Greek: λέγοντες (πλέον γὰρ—ἀλλ' ἀπαυθαδιζομένων) ταῦτα εἰρήκαμεν</note>.**
**--- E. (Page 379. line 12.) correct "or whatever they wish to name" <note>original Greek: ἢ ὅ, τι ὀνομάζειν θέλουσι</note>.**
**Page 210. D. (Page 381. line 5.) "but why first fire?" <note>original Greek: διὰ τί δὲ πρῶτον πῦρ;</note> Heigl changed this place thus:—"how or having made the what? 'the what indeed first,—but why first the what?'" <note>original Greek: πῶς ἡ ποιήσας τοῦ τί; τὸ τί μὲν πρῶτον,—διὰ τί δὲ πρῶτον τὸ τί;</note>—but neither the manuscripts nor Ficino support that change, just as [they do not] in the following Chapter 12.**
**Page 211. B. (Page 382. line 13.) "the motion" <note>original Greek: τὴν φοράν</note>. Heigl: "the difference" <note>original Greek: τὴν διαφορὰν</note> as in the text of the Basel edition; poorly. (See our Variant Readings.)**
**--- E. (Page 383. line 9.) "it was not clear, that, wherever he might have nodded," <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἦν δῆλον, ὅτι, ὅπου ἂν ἔνευσεν</note> Heigl: "it was not clearly that he did not nod back" <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἦν δηλονότι ὅτι οὐκ ἀνένευσεν</note> (but see our Variant Readings and Annotations). The same [Heigl] however soon correctly gave: "of the nodding" <note>original Greek: τῆς νεύσεως</note>, which I myself gave, for the faulty "of the non-nodding" <note>original Greek: τῆς ἀνεύσεως</note>.**
**Page 212. E. (Page 385. line 10.) "to say these and such songs," <note>original Greek: εἰπεῖν ταδὶ καὶ οὑτωσὶ μέλη</note> Heigl: "to sing thus and so the songs," <note>original Greek: ᾄδειν ὡδὶ καὶ ὡδὶ μέλη</note> with the books resisting; yet the same [Heigl] soon correctly [gave] "breathings upon" <note>original Greek: προσπνεύσεις</note>, as I myself had corrected. The same soon changed a place, which I suspect to be lacunose <note>term: lacunose — a text containing a "lacuna" or physical gap where words are missing</note>, thus: "but if not this, but with voices the most solemn things as far as possible, by which they make the arguments appear more solemn than them, and so forth."**
**Page 213. B. (Page 386. line 13.) Even Heigl gave: "that he was nourished by the disease" <note>original Greek: ὅτι ἐτρέφετο ὑπὸ τῆς νόσου</note> (see our Variant Readings).**
**--- D. (Page 387. line 6.) Distinguish: "it indicates, the solemnity not the arrogance alone" <note>original Greek: ἐνδείκνυται, τὸ σεμνὸν οὐ τὸ αὐθαδες μόνως</note> as Heigl did, though why I do not agree with him in the rest, my annotation in this place will show.**
**Page 214. B. (Page 388. line 15.) Even Heigl gave "beautiful" <note>adjective: καλὸν</note> for "of the beautiful" <note>noun: καλοῦ</note> (see our Variant Readings note 15, in which at line 4 "than" <note>Latin: *quam*</note> should be written for "when" <note>Latin: *quum*</note>).**
**--- C. (Page 389. line 9.) "of the God" <note>original: τοῦ θεός</note>. Heigl, with the Basel edition, "of the God" <note>using the standard genitive: τοῦ θεοῦ</note>, but see our Variant Readings.**
**--- D. line 14. 15. Heigl: "For even every bad man might despise the gods, and even before despising [them] be utterly wicked, and even if he were not bad in all other things, by this very thing he would have become so." Not bad. (Compare Variant Readings.)**
**Page 215. E. (Page 391. line 15. and following) "will he not be pleased? who, seeing the same things not similarly (neither in voices nor through eyes) of the art—and the loves moving." <note>original Greek: οὐχ' ἡσθήσεται; οἴπερ, οὐχ ὁμοίως τὰ αὐτὰ (οὐδὲ ἐν ταῖς φωναῖς οὐδὲ δι' ὀμμάτων) τῆς τέχνης βλέποντες—καὶ κινοῦντες οἱ ἔρωτες</note> Heigl. You see our Variant Readings. Soon the same (page 395. line 5): "will be moved" <note>original Greek: κινηθήσεται</note> for "will move" <note>original Greek: κινήσεται</note>, like Ficino.**
**--- F. (Page 392. line 9.) "what kind from what kinds," <note>original Greek: οἷα ἀφ' οἵων</note> Heigl: "what kind of gods" <note>original Greek: οἷα θεῶν</note> (but see our Variant Readings).**
**Page 216. A. (Page 392. line 16.) Heigl: "leading into a separation (as the magnitude of what has become by the indivisible magnitude of the pattern—in mass)." <note>original Greek: εἰς διάστασιν προαγαγοῦσαν (ὡς τὸ μέγεθος τοῦ γενομένου τῷ μεγέθει ἀμερεῖ τῷ τοῦ παραδείγματος—ἐν ὄγκῳ)</note>**
**--- B. (Page 393. line 7.) "giving so much power to the soul of the world" <note>original Greek: τοσοῦτον διδόντες τῇ τοῦ κόσμου ψυχῇ δυνάμεως</note>.**
**Page 217. C. (Page 395. line 11.) Heigl "until he might come" <note>original Greek: ἕως ἂν ἥκοι</note>, and see the next [word] "it might be necessary" <note>original Greek: δεήσοιτο</note>.**

**Page 284. C. (Page 514. line 13.) C. E. C. Schneider, who praises these words of Plotinus in his [commentary on] Plato's Republic Book 10, page 620 A (Volume III, page 297), writes it thus: "always being raised up into heaven (perhaps *seen*) into birds" etc. <note>original Greek: εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν ἀεὶ αἰρομένους (f. ὁρωμένους) εἰς ὄρνεις κ. τ. λ.</note>. Clearly he seems to have fashioned that conjecture from Ficino's [Latin translation] *looking up* <note>original Latin: suspicientes</note>. -> **Regarding the passage of Plotinus from Eusebius translated into this edition after page 364 of the Basel edition:** <-

These same things are read in a fragment of a paper manuscript which *J. Th. Voemelius* <note>Johann Theodor Vömel, a 19th-century German philologist</note> acquired at Frankfurt am Main and very kindly shared with me. Therefore, I will note here whatever variant readings exist in that book:
**Frankfurt Fragment, page 1, line 1. "how one might examine" <note>original Greek: δδ' ἄν τις ἐπισκέψαιτο ὅπως</note>.**
**--- page 1, line 6. "but of the psychic organic [part]" <note>original Greek: ἀλλὰ ψυχικοῦ ὀργανικοῦ</note>.**
**--- lines 7—9. "if indeed in the way it has been applied to the body, the soul is divided when some part is cut off" <note>original Greek: εἰ μὲν οὖν ᾗ παραβέβληται σώματος συμμερίζεσθαι τὴν ψυχὴν ἀποκοπτομένου τινὸς μέρους</note>, with the middle parts omitted.**
**--- line 12. "if indeed [they are] naturally joined" <note>original Greek: εἴπερ δὴ προσφυᾶ</note>.**
**--- line 17. "they posit only sensations to be possible; but thoughts to be impossible" <note>original Greek: αἰσθήσεις δὲ μόνον δυνατὸν τίθενται· τὰς δὲ νοήσεις ἀδύνατον</note>.**
**--- page 2, line 6. "has the places" <note>original Greek: τοὺς τόπους ἔχει</note> and next "they will be in" <note>original Greek: ἐν ἔσονται</note>. Both [readings] are poor.**
**--- line 10. "as inseparable actuality" <note>original Greek: ὡς ἀχώριστα ἐντελέχεια</note>, though the next bit is correctly: "inseparable actuality" <note>original Greek: ἀχώριστος ἐ.</note>.**
**--- line 14. "which would seem to have a dispute" <note>original Greek: ὃ ἀμφισβήτησιν δόξειεν ἂν ἔχειν</note>, more mildly; immediately, "not in this way" <note>original Greek: μὴ τοῦτον τὸν τρόπον</note>.**
**--- line 19. "the things below in many" <note>original Greek: τὰ κάτω ἐν πολλοῖς</note>. Compare Viger's note <note>François Viger, a Jesuit scholar of Greek idioms</note> on this passage.**
**--- page 3, line 1, 5, 6. "it might become the actuality of a divisible body" <note>original Greek: μεριστοῦ σώματος ἐντελέχεια γένοιτο</note>, omitting "the" <note>original Greek: τοῦ</note> and "divisible" <note>original Greek: μεριστή</note>. Next, "the" <note>original Greek: τοῦ</note> is also omitted before "successively" <note>original Greek: ἐφεξῆς</note>.**
**--- lines 10, 11. -> ADDITIONS AND CORRECTIONS. <-

...the words, however, demonstrate that Homeric passages were most especially expressed by Plato. Finally, Gottfried Hermann <note>original: Godofredum Hermannum</note> has very recently (in his *Dissertation on the Office of the Interpreter*, pages 10 and following) argued that quite manifest traces of the doctrines of Empedocles <note>Empedocles was a Pre-Socratic philosopher known for the theory of the four elements</note> are present in those passages. He judges that a large part of these words of Plato (up to Plato’s *Phaedrus*, page 247. b.) were taken from the verses of the same Empedocles and other epic poets, and perhaps even Aeschylus, and were changed here and there by Plato; led by this judgment, he has even restored these Platonic passages to the laws of poetic meter.

To the *Annotation* on page 520, Section F of the Basel edition. I wish I had not attempted to emend the passage of Severus of Alexandria’s *Ethopoeiae* <note>Ethopoeia is a rhetorical exercise where a student writes from the perspective of a historical or mythological character</note>; I later saw these same words recorded with the exact same phrasing in Libanius <note>a 4th-century Greek sophist and rhetorician</note>, Volume IV, page 1097 in Reiske’s edition, nor does the reading differ in the newest edition of Severus by Christian Walz (*Greek Rhetoricians*, Volume I, page 546).

To the end of the *Annotation* on the title of the book *On Intelligible Beauty* (page 541 of the Basel edition). To Herder and Schelling, who are mentioned there, Goethe <note>the famous German polymath Johann Wolfgang von Goethe</note> should now be added. For he translated the first chapter of this book (Ennead V. 8. 1) into German, following Marsilio Ficino’s Latin translation for the most part (in his letters to Zelter, Part I, pages 190–192), and both judge that the summit of the doctrine of beauty is contained in these teachings of Plotinus (compare Zelter’s words, page 185 and following).

To the *Annotation* on the passage at page 726, Section B of the Basel edition, regarding Plotinus' words: "nor does he say the body is being tickled" <note>original Greek: οὐδὲ γαργαλιζομένου λέγει τοῦ σώματος</note>. In the passage of Philo Judaeus <note>a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher</note> from *Allegorical Interpretation of the Laws*, Book III, page 118, first the words: "but of an intense and violent itching continually" <note>original Greek: ἀλλὰ συντόνου καὶ σφοδρᾶς ἀεὶ κνήσεως</note> were to be translated as: with a vehement and intense *pruritus* <note>a Latin term for "itching"</note> continuously, for Cicero uses "titillation" <note>original Latin: titillationem</note> rather for *gargalismos* <note>original Greek: γαργαλισμῷ, meaning tickling</note>. Next, a second emendation was to be attempted: "continual motion" <note>original Greek: ἀεὶ κινήσεως</note>, since Philo in the same place compares the opinion of the Cyrenaics <note>philosophers who believed pleasure was the highest good and consisted of "smooth motion"</note>, who place pleasure in motion, with the opinion of the Epicureans, who say pleasure is stable <note>original Greek: ἡδονὴν καταστηματικὴν; the Epicurean ideal of "katastematic" pleasure, which is the absence of pain rather than active stimulation</note>.

In the *Index of Plotinian Greek*, add before the letter B these: **the stars, whether lifeless or ensouled.** <note>original Greek: ἄψυχα ἢ ἔμψυχα τὰ ἄστρα</note> II. 3. 2. Before **I am ruled** <note>original Greek: κυριεύομαι</note>, the word **circle.** <note>original Greek: κύκλος</note> II. 6. 1.

**315. 6. a. infr. l.** it ought to be χέρηον, without iota subscript. **Page 1033. line 9.** "And I sought myself as one of the things that are." And although I had long ago collected many Heraclitean fragments for myself, and had written this very saying at the margin of Schleiermacher's commentary: "Cf. Valkenaer, on Euripides' *Phoenissae* verse 1168," nevertheless I know not how, in composing the Annotation, I had passed over these things in silence, until recently *Albertus Jahn Bernas*, a learned young man and a member of our Seminar, conveniently turned my attention here. Moreover, not a few writers have celebrated this saying; see Casaubon and Ménage on Diogenes Laërtius IX. 5, the commentators on Hesychius, Volume I, page 1084, Alberti edition, and on Suidas [Volume] II, 3058, Gaisford edition; however, not all have grasped its meaning. How Plutarch understood it is shown by these [words] *Against Colotes*, page 1118. C. page 569, Wyttenbach edition, which words, because they reflect the Ionic form, I shall append: "But Heraclitus, as if having accomplished something great and solemn, says, 'I searched for myself' (*Ἐδιζησάμην ἐμεωυτόν*); and of the inscriptions at Delphi, the most divine seemed to be: 'Know Thyself.'" Yet no learned man, as far as I know, has applied this Plotinian passage to this fragment of Heraclitus, although this seems especially conducive to the understanding of that saying. But the question is asked whether those [words]: "as one of the things that are" (*ὡς ἓν τῶν ὄντων*) are of Heraclitus himself, or of Plotinus, who may have added them for the sake of interpretation. If you accept the latter, then that "ἐδιζησάμην" and "ὡς" must be separated by an interposed comma; and this is what Jahn urged. Nevertheless, Dio Chrysostom almost leads me to the other reasoning, who in *Oration LV*, page 558 (page 282 ff. Reiske), placed these things: "But Heraclitus (says) that he himself found out the nature of the universe, of what sort it happens to be, with no one having taught him, and that he became wise by his own means."— But, however it may be, for I do not wish to decide, the late Schleiermacher—although he seems to have known neither the passage of Plotinus nor of Dio—by that sagacity which he possessed, excellently (if I see anything) interpreted this Heraclitean saying thus (in Wolf and Buttmann's *Museum der Alterthums-Wissenschaft*, I, page 531): *"Namely, Heraclitus may well have actually said that he sought himself in this eternal flux, and also did not find himself as something being [or] abiding, but from that very fact all knowledge first dawned upon him,"* etc.; for I would wish the whole passage to be read. Moreover, the same Ionic word recurs in another Heraclitean fragment in Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* IV. 2, page 565, and in Theodoret, Volume IV, page 716: "For those who seek (*διζήμενοι*) gold," etc.
